stories.title: Before She Paints the Ending
stories.prompt: Every story ever imagined exists somewhere, separated by the boundaries of time. But when those boundaries suddenly collapse, dragons, starships, pirates, robots, dinosaurs, and armies from a thousand different realities find themselves fighting on the same impossible battlefield. At its center stands a princess whose magic flows like living paint, protected by three ancient knights forged from red, green, and blue light. Nobody knows who started the war, but every invading army is here for the same reason: Capture the Princess before she paints the ending.
stories.body:
# Before She Paints the Ending

Blue caught the pirate's hook a finger's width from her wrist.

His fingers held the iron fast against the rim of his round shield. The Princess kept painting. Cyan ran from her forefinger across the broken terrace, rose in a shining curve, and hardened into a wave of glass. The pirate struck it boots first. Behind him, six companions came swinging down from a galleon that had sailed halfway into the starship above them.

“Mine,” announced the starship, in a voice that moved the stones.

The galleon's captain fired a cannon into its loudspeaker.

Red laughed. His spear lengthened through the smoke, a straight line of red light that severed the seven grappling ropes. Green spread his shield beneath the falling pirates, caught them on a broad green slope, and tipped them into the arms of an astonished cavalry regiment.

Blue let the hook fall. The Princess tapped the inside of her wrist twice, their old signal, and he resumed his place at her left shoulder.

They had defended her together for three hundred and eighty-six years. Before that, the three knights had been ancient already. There were fortresses whose names she had forgotten but whose stairways she could still descend without looking, because Red would take the high side, Green would close the gap, and Blue would catch whatever reached for her painting hand.

Nothing in those centuries had prepared them for a tyrannosaur in siege armor landing on a submarine.

The impact threw her off her feet. Her broad black hat stayed on by its pins; cyan, magenta, yellow, and black streamed from beneath its brim, mingling with her hair. She swept one hand down. Yellow paint burst across the stones as a flight of steps, and she landed running.

“Princess!” Green called.

“I see it.”

A dragon had gripped the submarine in its claws. It was lifting the dinosaur, submarine, and three crews of would-be captors together, making a platform broad enough to land beside her. On its back, soldiers in silver masks were assembling a cage.

Beyond it, the battlefield climbed into the sky. A castle hung upside down over a prehistoric forest. Trains ran between its towers. Airships fought with saucers among the branches, while armies marched out of doors standing alone on the plain. An ocean ended in a straight line across a desert, and ships came over that line with their sails still full of the wrong world's wind.

There had been walls between all those places yesterday.

She had not seen the first wall fall. No one she had questioned had seen the first blow. Everyone had a different account of who had attacked first, but the orders carried across the field were remarkably alike.

“Capture the Princess before she paints the ending!”

The words came from a brass horn, then a radio, then the throat of something with three heads. They were stitched on banners and burned in the air behind missiles. Every army had arrived with a place for her: a cage, a carriage, a throne with straps beneath the arms.

“Our king will protect you,” a herald shouted from the dragon's back. “Paint him victorious and every surviving kingdom will be yours!”

“How generous,” said Red.

The starship opened a hatch below its wounded loudspeaker. A column of pale force gripped the Princess's skirts and began lifting her toward it. She pressed both palms down. Magenta poured from her cuffs, wrapped her ankles in roots, and took hold of the terrace. The ship strained. Stones tore loose around her.

“White,” she said.

Red lowered his spear. Green turned his shield inward. Blue opened his hand.

Their three lights crossed between them. Red and green met in yellow; green and blue opened cyan; blue and red made a trembling magenta edge. Where all three filled the same space, the colors vanished into a white so clean that it made daylight look stained.

The Princess raised her hands into it.

Cyan spread beneath her right palm. Yellow flowed under her left. She touched them together, and a green plain opened in the white, filled with the small, exact shapes of the cavalry charging toward them. She drew their distant door behind them and curled two fingers back.

The whole regiment slid backward. Horses screamed as the ground carried them away from her. Their general clung to his saddle, still waving his command to advance.

“She's sending us back!” the cavalry general cried. “Take her hands!”

For an instant, she had room.

She reached for black. One closed line around their painted door would finish that retreat and shut their way back to her. Then she would turn to the fleet.

A shadow crossed the painting. Above her, the dragon dropped its cage. Behind her, the pirate captain came through the shattered glass wave with a weighted net. The white ground demanded all three knights; her two hands could not turn the cavalry, hold down the terrace, and stop two new captures at once.

“Break,” said Green.

His shield rose beneath the cage. Red's spear threw the dragon sideways. Blue's hand closed around the pirate captain's wrist before the net touched hers.

The white tore apart.

Her unfinished plain went with it. Out on the field, the regiment lurched forward again, several hundred soldiers suddenly discovering that they had been shouting their war cries while traveling in the wrong direction.

The Princess's black touched empty air.

She closed her fist around it before a drop could fall.

***

The first horseman came out of a sentence on page nine.

I had been carrying *The Upward Rain* back to its shelf when I heard hooves on paper. An open book lay on the long reading table. A cavalryman was climbing over the word *advanced*, drawing his horse after him by its reins. He crossed the white margin and stepped through a slit standing above the page. Beyond it, a castle hung upside down.

The sentence he had left read: *The       .*

He was followed by another man, then twenty, then enough horses that I could feel their passage through the table's legs. They went straight from the print into that impossible country. The pages flapped in the wind of their leaving.

All along our library, books were opening.

Some had proper titles, worn into familiar places on the shelves. Some still had questions for names. I saw *Four Crowns in Hiding* lying open beneath a book with no lettering on its cover at all. In that one, stars moved between the lines. Something enormous turned behind the paper, and a ship's bow nosed through a paragraph.

I dropped what I was carrying and shut the cavalry book.

The slit pinched closed. Out in the field, the last horseman to clear it wheeled around, furious. He remained where he was. All the men already out remained. Only the next rider, whose head had not yet crossed the margin, dwindled back into type.

I shut the star book before its ship could get through. Then I began closing everything I could reach.

I heard the same order from a dozen pages. Sometimes it was translated in small print beneath the shouting. Sometimes I understood it without a translation.

*Capture the Princess before she paints the ending.*

I had never heard of her. There was no portrait of her in any of the books I first opened. But in every visible piece of battlefield, among the smoke and running armies, four colors streamed toward the same distant point, and three lights stood around them.

***

The door behind the cavalry vanished.

So did a ladder of stars that had been delivering armored infantry into the air. The infantry already falling continued to fall. Green caught them before they struck the terrace, and Red chopped the chains from their empty capture harnesses.

“Someone is shutting the doors,” Green said.

“Let them,” said the Princess.

She pulled a cyan road across the wreck of the submarine. Green brought his shield beneath the tyrannosaur's jaw and lifted, turning its enormous head away from her as she passed. Green's sword swept a rider's lance aside. The dinosaur's other riders hauled the reins. One lifted a pair of golden manacles.

“Alive!” the man with the manacles shouted. “She's no use dead!”

The Princess slapped yellow across his saddle. It became a bright wooden box with him inside. The manacles rattled against its lid.

A starship's beam found her road and lifted the entire thing.

Red ran up it toward the ship, shots sparking against his round shield. His armor shone through the smoke in long, crimson seams; at the crest he drove his spear into the beam's mouth. A red crack crossed the vessel's underside. The beam winked out. Her road fell apart, and she stepped off its falling end onto Green's shield.

“You could have left me the stairs,” Red said as he landed beside her.

“You keep breaking the things they're attached to.”

Blue lifted a hand.

A hundred small metal spheres were rising out of the dust.

They did not fire. They watched. Each turned as a knight moved, keeping its single dark lens trained upon him. When Red raised his spear, the spheres watching him shifted to preserve their view of the Princess behind his shoulder.

She flicked magenta at the nearest. It became a flowerpot, dropped, and shattered.

The others retreated beyond her reach.

Across the battlefield, pirates were cutting down the soldiers who had come to put her on a throne. A dragon closed its jaws on a cage dangling beneath a saucer. None of them was trying to protect her. They were trying to prevent the others from taking her first.

In the places where worlds overlapped, that rivalry was becoming something worse. The forest beneath the inverted castle was disappearing under its masonry. A city at the edge of the desert had lost half its sky to an ocean. Every retreating army met another advancing one, and there was less world left behind them each time.

“Princess,” said a new voice. It came from every watching sphere at once. “Our transport offers sanctuary.”

Above the battle, a low black vessel turned to show its armored belly. Other ships fired upon it immediately. Their shots broke against overlapping plates. A dragon struck it claws first and skidded off, leaving four bright wounds in its hull.

The Princess saw those wounds close beneath shutters.

“Does sanctuary come with a lock?” she asked.

“Your survival is required.”

“And afterward?”

“Victory.”

Three spheres descended together. Each unfolded a great sack of translucent dyed mesh gathered around a metal throat. Cyan spread above Red, magenta above Green, yellow above Blue.

Red lunged to cut the nearest suspension cable. Cyan fell over him.

His spear vanished inside it. So did the brilliant planes of his armor. There was only a dark, struggling shape beneath the blue-green sheet. Red light struck the net from within and was swallowed.

Green drove his shield up under the magenta bag. Its rim caught. The sheet slipped around him, gathered beneath his feet, and closed with a metallic snap. His green went out of the world.

The Princess flung out her right hand. Yellow and cyan raced toward the two nets in a twisting green branch.

A piece of paper fluttered over her wrist.

She almost brushed it aside. Then iron fingers came out of its print and closed around her arm.

The branch went crooked. It struck a wreck behind Red and blossomed uselessly into leaves.

The paper opened wider. More iron hands emerged, finding her elbow, the shoulder of her gown, her other wrist. A robot pulled itself across the margin, its body still flattening and filling as the letters became metal.

The black transport overhead rang under a dragon's blow. Through the paper's widening fold, she saw a metal deck and a shutter jolting in its frame with the same impact.

Blue moved to interpose.

The yellow net waited above him. He could catch the hand that held her, as he always caught it. The bag would close over his shoulders. Then there would be no white anywhere she could reach.

The Princess looked up at the transport, at its thick plates enduring the other armies' fire. A galleon struck its side and broke. While it held her, the machine would fight to keep its prize alive.

It might give her a little time.

Below the cyan sheet she could just make out Red's fist striking the net's metal throat. On the inside. Blue could reach it. His light would pass through cyan where Red's could not.

She opened the hand with which she always gave Blue his signal.

“Away,” she said.

He checked. Even through his closed helm, she felt the question.

She had called him nearer in fire, in darkness, under falling towers. She had never ordered him to let a hand take hers.

“Blue. Away.”

He sprang backward as the yellow net fell. Its mouth snapped shut on nothing.

The robots hauled her through the page.

***

An iron hand had reached out of the robot book and torn off a leaf before I could close it.

The figure in the illustration pulled the paper through its own opening. I caught one corner. For a moment we had a tug-of-war across the margin. Then the corner tore in my fingers, and the robot carried the rest away.

I slammed the covers together.

It made no difference to the loose page. I could see it through the cavalry book when I opened that one a crack: a white fleck crossing the field, almost lost beneath the running feet. The robots inside its lines remained there, waiting to come out.

Two of the three lights had disappeared. The blue one moved away from the woman they had been guarding, and the page opened around her like a mouth.

I shut the cavalry book again.

All through the library, empty sentences waited for their people to return.

***

She landed upright, held between two robots in a chamber that rocked beneath her feet.

The paper lay open on the floor behind them. Through it she could see the broken terrace. Blue was kneeling at the mouth of Red's net. Half his arm had passed through the cyan weave; his fingers closed on its inner fastening and tore it apart. Red blazed free. He went straight to Green, thrusting a crimson hand through the magenta sheet to find its metal throat.

Then a guard turned her toward the press.

The transport climbed. Its engines strained against grappling lines, against dragons, against a second ship trying to tow it sideways. Something immense struck the roof and began walking there.

“Sanctuary,” the Princess said.

One robot turned its head toward her. It wore the same armor as the others, with a small white square upon its chest. Within that square, the word *COMMAND* changed to *SECURE*.

“Present your hands.”

The guards did it for her. They brought her to a standing press: two narrow cuffs beneath a pane of glass, a fresh sheet of paper stretched beyond it. Her hat scraped the top bar. A robot removed it and dropped it beside the page on the floor.

She crooked a finger.

A thread of black slipped down the cuff. Before it reached the metal, the press straightened her finger and held it still.

“You will have use of your hands when we permit it,” said the command robot.

Fine channels opened against her palms. Paint entered them. Cyan first, then magenta, then yellow: the living colors pulled from her skin and gown, made to travel beneath the glass. On the waiting sheet, the shape of a woman began to appear.

The portrait wore her gown. Its arms were raised into drawn chains.

She pulled against the cuffs. The portrait pulled too.

“A book?” she said.

“A secure binding.”

There was no white light here. This was no ending, only a place to keep her. The soldiers had come out of print; the machine was pressing her into it.

The command robot brought a heavy cover from a rack. Its hinges had teeth.

“Your lights will follow,” it said. “They will provide the ground. You will paint our victory. Until then, you remain closed.”

It laid the cover beside the portrait.

Through a narrow observation slit, she saw a thousand rival banners turning toward the rising vessel. A dragon's head filled the view, one gold eye fixed upon her. Its rider leaned out, reaching for the slit with a hooked pole. The shutter slammed before the hook entered.

The ship gave her time, and took her colors in exchange. Yellow faded from the folds of her skirt. A lock of hair slid over her shoulder, white from root to tip. She tried to curl it toward the cuffs, but her fingers could not make the smallest directing stroke. Beneath the glass, black began moving into the portrait's outlines.

She watched it go. The machine was being thorough. It even found the little black line at the edge of each fingernail.

Her left thumb was turned inward against its cuff. Under that nail, a thin crescent remained.

The robot lifted the cover.

Above them, something tore through the first layer of armor. Daylight flashed across the chamber. The guards looked up.

A blue hand came through the gap and caught the descending cover.

Blue wrenched it sideways. Red followed him through the roof and drove his spear beneath the press's glass. Green landed last, his shield raised against the claws reaching through after them.

Cyan fluttered from Blue's gauntlet. A torn strip of magenta hung from Red's shoulder. They had freed each other. Of course they had. The Princess had known how they could, but knowing had been a colder thing than seeing them arrive.

Red broke the pane. Blue drew his sword and cut the cuffs from her wrists.

The portrait's chained hands dissolved. Its face blurred and ran into four pools of color. The Princess folded her fingers at last, and the paint still upon her answered, gathering in thin ribbons in her palms. Most of it lay beneath the shattered glass. She reached toward those pools.

The command robot seized the sheet and thrust it into a slot. Metal closed over it.

Green's shield rang. The dragon above them had found the hole.

“Princess,” he said.

She looked from the sealed slot to the colors she still held. There was enough cyan. Enough magenta and yellow, if she spread them thin. Black shone beneath her left thumbnail, scarcely more than a stain.

Through the observation slit, the battlefield had become one vast converging movement. Every ship was turning, every wing beating toward the transport. The forest and the castle were grinding together below.

She left the stolen colors where they were.

“White.”

***

The robot book was opening again. Metal fingers had pried the covers apart from inside.

I found the transport in an illustration near its end.

It was our Princess in the press. Her three knights were breaking through the roof. The next sentence was filling itself in as I watched, and the men named in it were rising from its letters.

*The reserve guard entered the prize chamber.*

Six metal figures were already halfway across the margin.

The words farther down the page had not appeared. I could not read ahead to discover whether she escaped.

I put both hands on the cover and pushed. An iron arm caught between the pages. I leaned on the book with all my weight. The table slid. My spectacles fell off, and I heard a lens break beneath my shoe.

The arm became a line of print.

The covers met. I dragged *The Credit Book* from the nearest shelf and laid it on top, then *A Crown for the Endless Fire*. Under their weight, the robot book thumped once.

“Stay in,” I told it.

***

A guard coming through the chamber's side hatch flattened abruptly into a dark stroke. The stroke folded back into a white margin, and the margin vanished.

The command robot turned toward the hatch. Its chest changed from *SECURE* to *RESERVE*. No one answered it.

Red laid his spear down. Green drove a buckled roof plate across the gap above them, trapping the dragon's claw, then lowered his shield. Blue laid his shield beside the press, sheathed his sword, and opened both hands.

The dragon beat upon the wedged plate. A pirate's harpoon tore through a seam beside it. The transport's armor shuddered under them. Yet for this moment the walls still kept out most of the armies, and the guards inside could come at her from only one side.

Three colors flooded together.

White filled the broken press. Its frame stood between the Princess and the guards, holding a new surface where the glass had been. It was broad enough for her two open hands.

She began with the nearest robot.

Cyan and magenta made the dark blue of its armor. Yellow found the little scratches along its hands. She gave it a white margin beneath its feet and drew its outline backward into a sentence.

The guard slid away from her.

It caught a stanchion. Its fingers shrank around the metal, losing depth. They became five dark marks, then part of a word. The loose leaf on the floor filled with new type.

The command robot lunged for her wrist.

She painted the lunge. It carried the machine headfirst past her, toward the same white margin.

Behind her, Blue made a small sound. It had cost him something to stand still.

“Hold,” she told him.

He held the white.

She swept the guards into their page. It buckled on the floor under the weight of its new sentences. They were still moving in the print, pushing against its edge. Without black to close the picture, they could come out again.

She could not spend her last black on the guards. The Princess pressed her palms wide.

The white ground widened beyond the press. She began the ocean at the desert's edge, laying in the hulls of the pirate fleet. A little blue prow formed beneath her fingers. Its ship swung away from the transport, drawn toward the homeward margin she had given it.

Her cyan stopped halfway down its sail.

She pressed her palm harder. A thin, clear thread came out. Beyond the slit, the ship turned back toward her. Another fleet rose behind it on a sea that had no place in that sky.

Behind her, metal scraped paper. The command robot had reached the loose leaf's edge again.

She could not finish a picture of every ship, every soldier. She swept her hands across the white, wiping away the small, unfinished fleet. Only its long strokes remained: the sea's edge, the margin home. She drew those together.

The ocean lifted away from the desert.

She caught the next join with magenta: forest against inverted castle. Yellow carried it around the prehistoric plain. She left out the crowded ranks and the towers' fine windows, following the rents where the worlds had met. Each stroke opened another stretch of pale margin. Beneath them lay the places the armies had left.

The transport tilted. Green planted himself behind her; she braced her back against his breastplate and her heels against the press's footbar. His hands kept giving white. Cannon fire tore through the roof's seams, and a chain caught Red's discarded spear and drew it out into the battle.

He watched it go. “That was old.”

“So are you,” she said, and brought the last yellow stroke around.

Across the field, armies stumbled as their ground divided into paths. The dinosaur riders hauled on their reins, but their beasts ran for the warm plain opening before them. A starship fought the pull of its own black sky. At the white margins, captains were still turning their soldiers around to come for her.

The command robot's hand gripped the leaf's edge. Its head rose from the print.

Her picture was bare in wide places. The joins lay open; the loose leaf still led to her. She could not hold the armies back while she filled in what was missing.

She had kept her left thumb curled against her palm. Now she lifted it.

Black gathered at the nail: her key-color, clear and exact. Mixed cyan, magenta, and yellow could make a muddy darkness, but this black would decide precisely where one thing ended and another began.

She drew it along the painting's edge. The robot's shoulders broadened out of the print. It reached her as she brought the line down the final side.

Blue's white flickered.

“Stay,” she said.

The wedged roof plate tore free. Sunlight and a dragon's claw came through together.

The robot closed its hand around her left wrist.

For three hundred and eighty-six years, that had been Blue's hand to stop. This time he did not move.

The Princess turned her thumb into the machine's pull and let it drag her arm sideways. Her nail stayed against the white. Its pull carried the last black stroke to the corner, leaving a small thumbprint where the boundary joined.

She closed her hand.

The ending held.

The robot's grip became a row of letters against her skin. Its body folded down into the page. The loose leaf rose after it, suddenly no heavier than paper, and flew through the closed observation shutter without disturbing the metal.

All around the transport, the battlefield opened.

Dragons went wing first through bright margins, their shadows sweeping back across the mountains of their own worlds. Galleons rolled into lines of moving ink and broke out again upon their own seas. The starship that had called her *mine* diminished through a paragraph, its engines still burning. The word passed out of hearing before the ship did.

A thousand armies followed their roads. Some ran. Some resisted until the ground beneath them became the ground they had left. Their banners crossed the closing borders; their cannons, cages, and thrones went with them.

The transport flattened around the Princess. Its engines lost their roar. The sealed slot unfolded into the illustration around her feet, releasing four long threads of paint. They ran back into her open hands, leaving a blank sheet to vanish with the broken press. The monster walking on the roof was gone, and the roof itself was gone, and she stood on the white stones of her terrace with all her weight suddenly her own.

Above her, the castle was upright. On the far side of the last closing door, a row of pines still lay broken where the inverted towers had crushed them. The door narrowed to the width of a brushstroke and closed.

Red, Green, and Blue stood around her.

Their white separated slowly. Each color returned to its own hands, its own armor, its own weary stance. A white lock hung against her cheek. Blue looked at the place where the robot had held her wrist.

She held it out to him.

“I was there,” he said.

“I know.”

He laid his hand beneath hers without closing it.

Red went to retrieve her hat. It had come home with her, lying upside down on the terrace. He shook a few black letters from its brim before he brought it back.

***

The books grew heavy beneath my hands.

Their covers stayed shut. Ink traveled between the edges of the pages: dark rows of soldiers, the long strokes of ships, a dragon's wing narrowing into a line. The loose leaf slipped between the robot book's closed covers and drew the torn corner out of my fingers.

When I lifted the books weighing it down and opened it, the page was whole. The empty sentences had filled without my turning a cover. The army in its illustration stood beneath a different sky, looking toward a door that was no longer there.

There was no first account of the war. I searched the opening pages and found the same thing I had seen at the end: someone else's forces arriving, someone else's attack already under way.

But on the reading table, beside my broken spectacles, lay a book I had never seen before.

*Before She Paints the Ending.*

Its final page showed four figures on a white terrace. Three stood in their own colors around a woman lifting one tired hand. Beneath the picture was a small black thumbprint.

I touched it before I thought to be careful.

The paint was still wet.

stories.title: The World Before Us
stories.prompt: The first humans awoke together on a small island surrounded by a perfectly still lake. Beyond its shores stretched an untouched paradise of green valleys, towering mountains, and magnificent sunsets. Yet something about the world was wrong. Paths already wound through the hills, ancient stone monuments stood along the ridges, and the remains of enormous structures could be seen beneath the lake's clear waters. The first people had no memories of their creation, but the world around them bore unmistakable evidence of a civilization that had existed long before humanity's first breath.
stories.body:
# The World Before Us

She knew the word for tree. It stood over her, with one branch reaching across the water and another broken short against the sky. She knew that the small hard things among its leaves were fruit. She had never seen either before.

All around her, people drew breath.

Some sat up. One rolled onto his side and coughed. A woman with silver in her hair began to laugh, stopped to listen to herself, and laughed again.

The young woman beneath the tree lay still a little longer. Her body was full of instructions. Her chest rose, her eyelids closed when the light hurt them, her fingers caught the branch she reached for. But when she tried to remember reaching before, there was nothing. No darkness, no journey, no place from which she had come. The attempt stopped at a smooth edge.

She was lying in a shallow hollow lined with grey cloth. Beyond its rim grew grass, flattened in an oval around her body. Similar hollows lay scattered beneath the tree and down the island's gentle slope. People were climbing out of them, pulling on the loose grey garments which had been folded against their sides.

She put hers on. Her hands knew how to find the armholes.

A man nearby stood too quickly and went over backwards into the grass. He lay looking at the sky, then raised one hand with its fingers spread.

“That,” he said, “was farther than I expected.”

She went to help him. His palm was warm.

“Where were you?” she asked.

“Just there.” He pointed at the hollow.

“Before.”

His smile went away. He sat up carefully this time.

By the time they had all asked one another, the sun stood clear of the eastern ridge. Twenty-nine people occupied the island. They counted twice, because nobody had done it before. There were tall people and short people, pale faces and dark faces, tightly curled hair, hair straight and black, a broad-shouldered man whose beard came in white at the chin. All wore grey. All knew how to speak. None could remember hearing a voice before that morning.

Their names came when they were asked for them. Nothing followed the names.

She was Neral. The man who had fallen was Orr. The silver-haired woman was Sivven, and she had counted them.

The island was small enough that they could hear one another from opposite shores. A narrow fringe of reeds grew on its southern side. Everywhere else, grass and bare stone met water so still that the tree appeared to stand upon its own branches.

Beyond the lake rose green slopes, long valleys opening between them, and mountains with pale snow caught beneath their summits. Neral could see a bird going from one end of the world to the other. It took a long time to reach the nearest ridge.

“Someone else will be here,” Orr said.

“Where?”

He turned slowly, searching the hills. “I don't know.”

Neral walked to the water. She crouched to look at her face. A dark crescent marked the skin beneath her left eye. She leaned closer to see its edge and found something below her reflection.

At first she thought the lake had another shore below its surface. A long pale line ran out from the island, crossed by darker lines at regular intervals. Farther down stood two upright forms, with an opening between them large enough to swallow the tree. Behind those, blue with depth, rose a succession of enormous terraces.

She put a finger in the water. Her face broke into widening rings. The terraces remained.

Orr knelt beside her. He dropped a pebble and watched it fall past the pale line, smaller and smaller, until it settled somewhere they could not see.

“Who did that?” he asked.

He meant the structures. Neral understood him perfectly, although his question had come out in a frightened whisper.

They followed the pale line around the island. On the northern side it rose beneath the water until Neral could touch it with her foot. It was the top of a wall, broad enough to walk along, running towards the nearest shore. Below its outer edge, steps descended into the clear blue. Each step was higher than her waist.

They crossed in single file, the lake first at their knees, then their ankles. Some carried the loose linings of their hollows folded over their arms. The last person took Sivven's hand to climb onto dry land. Behind them, ripples travelled out across the drowned avenue.

No one on the island had made it. No one could remember making anything.

***

The path began on the shore.

Grass had grown over much of it, but here and there the same pale stone showed through. It curved between low bushes, climbed a hill, vanished behind a spur of rock, and appeared again far above them. Neral looked for footprints in a patch of soft earth. Their own were the only ones.

They found fruit in the bushes. They found cold shade under an overhang, and a shell with a hole through it. Orr held the shell to his eye until Sivven asked whether he could see more that way.

“Less,” he admitted.

Their voices travelled strangely in the open country. Sometimes they all spoke at once. Sometimes a silence fell, and every one of them turned at the scrape of a foot.

By midday they had reached the first difficult stretch. The path ended against a steep face of rock. Above it, six hollows surrounded a shallow depression, then another six, then another. They climbed diagonally towards a ledge.

Orr put his feet in the lowest two and stretched for the next.

“Too far.”

Neral stood back. Some of the hollows faced sideways. Others opened downwards, where a foot would have fallen out of them.

“They aren't steps.”

“Then what are they?”

She could not answer. They went around, pushing through bushes and helping one another up a short, muddy slope. From the ledge they could see that the hollows continued all the way to the ridge. They had been cut to a pattern. Whatever had used them must have been able to hold on in several places at once.

The first monument stood against the sky.

It had looked like a crooked pillar from the lake. Up close it was a figure, worn so deeply that only one side remained legible. A broad body hung among six jointed limbs. The ends of the limbs opened into clusters of digits. Its small head was tucked between two high plates which swept backwards over its body.

One of its hands rested on a square block. Rain had collected in the hand's central hollow. Neral set her own hand beside it. Hers would have fitted between two of its fingers.

There were others along the ridge. One had fallen and broken, its stone face turned up among the roots of a bush. Another held something round against its body. A small version of the same many-limbed form clung to the round thing's edge.

Orr walked around that one twice.

“Could people have made these?”

“We could make a shape that wasn't us,” said Sivven.

“Then they could have been like us.”

Neral looked down the cliff. Six hollows, six more, six again, fitted the reach of the stone creature's limbs.

“They used the path.”

Orr followed her gaze. He was quiet after that.

The route over the mountain was worse. It rose beyond the last monument in a great sweep of sheer stone, with the familiar six-part clusters set widely apart. A low shelf ran beneath an overhang at its base, disappearing under a curtain of trailing stems. Neral crouched on it. There were little dents beneath the growth, filled with soil; above her, the deep six-part holds climbed out of reach. Even Orr did not try them. He threw a stone upwards. It struck far short of the first useful handhold and came rattling down.

They made their resting place in a hollow below the ridge. A few people explored towards the next valley. Others went back for more fruit. Someone discovered that the grey cloth from the island could be pulled apart into long, strong strips. Neral sat beside the fallen figure and picked soil from a crease in its hand.

The roots around it were thicker than her arms. A dead root passed through a split in the wrist; a younger one had grown through that root's rotted centre. Under both, the stone had weathered smooth.

She had no memory of yesterday, but there had been enough yesterdays for this.

Towards evening the mountains darkened. Light gathered along the undersides of the clouds until the whole western sky seemed to be opening over a fire. People stopped what they were doing. Orr came to sit beside her.

“Look,” he said, too late. Everyone was looking.

The sun reached a notch in the distant ridge. A bright line flashed across the hand Neral was cleaning.

It came from the standing monument above them. There was an opening through its square block. Along the opening's upper edge, a narrow polished facet shone clear of the dirt. A chain of pale reflections ran down the cliff towards a dark cleft close to the lake.

Neral stood. The bright marks were showing a second path.

She could see three turns before the cliff hid the rest.

“Tomorrow,” Sivven said.

Orr had already taken a step towards it. He looked at the descending sun, then at the distance below them, and stepped back.

That night, Neral woke at every unfamiliar sound. They were all unfamiliar. Once she heard someone whispering the twenty-nine names, trying to keep them.

***

In the morning, six of them helped Neral and Orr down the first part of the cliff. Where the holds stretched beyond a human reach, they used the cloth strips. Where the old route passed around an overhang, they found a narrow shelf below it and shuffled along with their backs against the rock.

They had agreed that two would go into the passage. The others would wait above until afternoon, then return to the ridge. Sivven made Orr repeat that part.

“I heard you.”

“You were looking over the edge.”

“I can do both.”

“Repeat it.”

He did.

The entrance lay well above the lake. Inside, the passage descended in a long curve. Daylight followed them through a series of slanting shafts, changing from white to green as they went lower. Water trembled somewhere overhead. Eventually Neral looked up through a broad, cloudy pane and saw fish passing across the sky.

She stopped so abruptly that Orr bumped into her.

They were under the lake.

Beyond the pane lay the avenue they had seen from the island. Its enormous steps went down between buildings with open arches high in their walls. Roofs had fallen in. Long plants drifted through the empty rooms. A tree trunk, silver and stripped of branches, lay against a tower.

The passage continued into a building whose lower chambers remained dry. Here the holds ran across walls and around doorways. Broad resting surfaces projected at different heights. Some had been polished into shallow curves by bodies settling on them again and again.

Nothing was at the right height. Nothing offered a place for two feet and two hands.

Orr climbed onto a low shelf. He had to haul the rest of himself up after his shoulders. Above him a smaller shelf projected from the wall, with six shallow depressions surrounding its centre. A little object lay in one of them.

He brought it down.

It was a ring of dark metal, with six flexible spokes joined to a bright bead. When he turned it, the bead ran around the ring. Neral took one spoke, Orr another. The bead darted between them and made a clear, ridiculous chirping sound.

Both of them startled. Orr let go.

The bead stopped.

He looked at the shelf again. There were more little objects on it, within easy reach of something much smaller than the figures outside.

Neral turned the ring once more, gently.

They left it where they had found it.

Farther in, the walls changed. The great climbing holds continued overhead, but below them stood rows of narrow platforms. Twenty-nine, arranged around a central shaft.

Each platform had a shallow hollow, rounded at one end, widening below it, then narrowing to two long channels.

Orr lay down in one before Neral could stop him.

His head fitted the round end. His shoulders settled into the wider space. His legs filled the channels.

He sat up at once.

The grey lining had come away from the platform with him. It was the same cloth as his garment.

For a while neither spoke.

Near the foot of each hollow stood a cluster of delicate tubes. Most had broken. One remained attached to a soft cap, with branching threads inside it, and Neral found herself touching the back of her head. There was a little ridge beneath her hair, no longer than the tip of her finger.

Orr had one too.

“Beds,” he said.

“Perhaps.”

“What else would fit like that?”

Neral looked at the tubes.

Orr got off the platform.

At the room's centre they found a model of the lake. Buildings rose around an open basin. Where their island should have been stood a low, round roof. Twenty-nine shapes lay beneath it in a circle. A narrow shaft joined the roof to the room in which they stood.

The real shaft above them was closed. Roots had found their way through its upper seams; several had been pulled apart, showing wet white ends.

Neral imagined the hollow she had woken in travelling upwards through the dark. She could not make that imagined journey turn into a memory.

“They put us here,” Orr said.

She looked at the great climbing holds above the beds. “Or they found us.”

“What would they want with us?”

She had no answer for that either.

Beside the model lay several short cylinders in a fitted rack. Some had cracked. One remained whole, translucent, wound through with lines finer than hair. Neral lifted it carefully. Six grooves circled its base.

In the weak green light, something seemed to move inside it. She held it up to a shaft of daylight. Fragments crossed her palm: part of a limb, a black curve, a scatter of white. She turned the cylinder. They slid across one another, all their separate pieces superimposed.

“Broken?” Orr asked.

On the model, at the edge of the basin, stood a little version of the ridge monument. Its square block held a socket surrounded by six channels.

Neral set the cylinder beside it. The shapes matched.

“I think it needs the thing above.”

They wrapped it in a strip of grey cloth. Orr carried it against his chest on the way out. At the difficult places he passed it up to Neral, and she passed it back when his feet were secure.

Their companions were still on the ledge when they emerged.

Sivven had come down to wait with them. Her face changed at the sight of the bundle.

“What is it?”

“Something we can't see yet,” Neral said.

***

They told the others about the rooms, the ring that chirped, the narrow hollows beneath the island. People asked them to describe the hollows again. Several touched the small ridges beneath their hair.

The man with the white beard wanted to know whether anyone had been in the city.

“No one we saw.”

“Could they still be there?”

Neral looked at the figures along the ridge. For the first time she wished she had looked behind more doors.

They brought the cylinder to the standing monument. Orr climbed onto its square block and cleared the earth from the socket. Beneath the dirt was a ring of dark metal. The cylinder fitted it.

Nothing happened.

“It fits,” Orr said, defending it.

Sivven looked through the opening towards the western mountains. “It isn't evening.”

Waiting was harder than the climb. Neral went back to the mountain route, then returned. She ate without tasting much. Clouds gathered beyond the peaks and she watched their edges, afraid that the light would fail them.

At last the sun came beneath the clouds.

Gold spread over the slopes. The aperture in the stone brightened, and the cylinder inside it began to turn. Neral heard a series of small, dry clicks.

A red limb reached across the valley.

People cried out and stumbled backwards. Orr dropped from the block. The limb passed through a standing figure and disappeared. Another appeared beside it, then a broad body, then the small head sheltered beneath a fan of golden plates.

The creature stood upon the opposite slope, taller than the trees.

It moved one of its lower hands, shifting its weight. Two other hands held a smooth slab on which a smaller creature lay kicking all six limbs. Another small one clambered onto the adult's back, caught a plate, slipped, and was caught without the adult turning its head.

Sivven gave a short, startled laugh.

The little creature on the slab was holding a ring. A bright bead ran around its edge.

Neral felt the sound of it again in her fingers.

The scene changed. Light ran over the grass in broad, broken sheets. The great avenue appeared dry beneath a sky streaked with unfamiliar pale bands. Hundreds of the six-limbed people climbed its terraces. They moved easily along walls which had seemed sheer to Neral. They carried folded materials, bowls, young ones. One stopped above a doorway and bent down to touch another's face.

For a few moments, the lake and the drowned city occupied the same place. The water shone through bodies going about their day.

Then there were fewer of them.

The pictures came in fragments. A hall full of empty resting places. People wearing rigid shells over their small heads. One reached for a climbing hold, but its fingers slid open again. Another came down the wall to brace its body from below. A tree with bare black branches. Rows of plants beneath glass, tended by figures whose movements grew slower as the images changed.

Something had happened to their world. Neral could see its effects without understanding its cause. She wanted the cylinder to stop, to return to the crowded avenue. It kept turning.

Now a room appeared which she knew.

The platforms around the central shaft were new. Their surfaces gleamed. A six-handed figure lowered a vessel towards one hollow. Inside the vessel floated a small curved body, pale against its red hands.

The body had two arms. Two legs.

Orr made a sound beside her.

Another image: the body larger, still curled, its closed face turning slowly in clear fluid. Fine threads branched around its head. On a surface above it, pictures succeeded one another. A tree. A stone. A hand. Marks beneath each, which Neral found she could read.

Then a fully grown woman lay in the hollow, eyes shut. Tubes joined her to the platform. The figure above her drew one enormous finger along her palm, opening the little fingers one by one, examining them with care.

The woman had a dark crescent beneath her left eye.

Neral touched her own face.

She had seen that mark in the lake.

Around her, people began to move closer to the monument. The white-bearded man came until his shoulder touched hers. Nobody tried to speak over the images.

The figures in the room changed. One had a cracked plate, another a white band around its middle. Their great hands fitted tubes, adjusted the narrow platforms, held the sleeping heads. One carried a second towards the door. Later the one with the cracked plate worked alone.

It stopped beside Neral's hollow. Four hands held the platform. A fifth rested over her chest, broad enough to cover her from shoulder to shoulder.

The sixth reached towards something outside the image.

For an instant the creature's small face turned towards them. Neral saw two dark eyes beneath the plates. Then the room was empty.

Only the sleeping humans remained.

The picture held long enough for her to count the hollows.

Twenty-nine.

Above the real lake the clouds burned orange and rose. Wind passed over the ridge, lifting the loose edges of their clothes. Neral looked down at the water. A whole city lay there, under the rippled gold. Its doorways had led into homes. Its high shelves had held toys.

Orr's hand found hers. He gripped it hard, watching the empty room.

The sun went into the ridge. The image of the room thinned, its platforms filled with distant grass, and it was gone.

The cylinder clicked once and stopped.

They stood together in the afterlight. Far below, a bird skimmed the lake, cutting a line across the last bright water.

Neral let go of Orr's hand and put her own against the stone hand beside her. Her fingers fitted between two of its fingers.

She looked towards the mountain. The dirt-filled marks beneath the low overhang had seemed like little scars in the stone. She had been looking upwards, measuring the enormous reach they could never make. The little dents had been much closer together than the old holds.

“They made the beds to fit us,” she said. She pointed to the low overhang. “What if there's a path for us under there?”

“We can look,” Sivven said.

They stayed until the first stars appeared. Before they went down to their resting place, Orr lifted the cylinder from its socket and wrapped it again in the grey cloth. When Neral woke in the night, he was asleep with the bundle held in the crook of one arm.

***

In the morning they went to the mountain.

Orr carried the cylinder back to the monument before they left. He put it in its socket and stayed there a moment, his hand resting on the stone. The rest waited for him.

At the cliff, Neral knelt beneath the overhang. Sivven held her by the waist while she leaned out and pushed aside a curtain of trailing stems.

Her fingers found a hollow.

She cleared the soil from it. It was worn by weather, a little rough along one edge, and just large enough for her hand. No ring of six surrounded it.

The next lay within easy reach.

She set her foot, lifted herself onto the low shelf, and turned beneath the great climbing holds. Her heart began to beat harder. The lake opened below her. For a moment she could see the island, its single tree, the small pale hollows among the grass.

Around the turn, the shelf widened. An opening broke the rock behind a tangle of leaves. Light showed through at the far end. She stepped inside and pushed her way forward until the leaves parted against her face.

On the other side, the mountain fell away into green country.

A valley opened, then another beyond it, vast slopes blue with distance. Snow shone above the clouds. Down on a far ridge stood a line of crooked stone figures, so small from here that she would once have mistaken them for broken rock.

Sivven came through behind her, then Orr. One by one, the others emerged into the morning. The man with the white beard stood with both hands on his head, looking out.

After a while he turned to look back through the passage.

“We'll be able to go back?”

“Yes,” Neral said.

“I keep thinking of the doors.”

“So do I.”

The path descended from the passage. Grass grew across its centre. Where it met a steep patch of rock, the great six-part clusters continued upwards, and beneath them, close together, ran the smaller holds.

Neral waited until all twenty-nine had crossed. Behind them the lake lay hidden by the mountain, but she could still feel its shape: the island above the sleeping chambers, the empty homes, the little ring left on its shelf.

Orr went ahead a few paces. He turned to see whether she was coming.

She followed him. Before them the ancient path curved out of sight, keeping, wherever the rock rose steeply, the measure of a human hand.

stories.title: The Unread
stories.prompt: For twenty years, the most gifted fortune-teller in the kingdom has predicted the future with perfect accuracy. Wars, marriages, betrayals, even the deaths of kings—her cards have never been wrong. Until one afternoon, a young stranger asks for a reading, and every card in her enchanted deck turns completely blank. For the first time in her life, she encounters someone who has no destiny. And judging by the terrified whispers coming from the cards themselves, fate is can't even look upon them.
stories.body:
# The Unread

On the afternoon her cards went blank, Meret found a girl inside a wall.

She did it sitting on her terrace, with a cold pear on a plate beside her. The girl's father had brought a hammer. After three days of searching, he wanted something he could hit.

“The old bakehouse,” Meret said. “Behind the drying oven. There are flowers painted on the plaster. Break the blue one.”

“We've been in there.”

“You will hurt your thumb. Your daughter will tell you off for swearing.”

He stared at the cards. The little painted mason on the third one was lowering his hammer.

“She's alive?”

“Go.”

He went. His wife stayed, turning a copper coin over and over between her fingers. Meret left the pear alone. She had seen the woman put both hands over her mouth when the child came up the terrace steps, and she found she wanted to watch it happen.

While they waited, a royal servant arrived with the evening summons. Meret put it beneath the pear plate. The king wanted the full audience before he sealed the war orders. He had been very particular about that, although she had already given him his victory, his day of return, and the number of his dead.

Forty minutes later, the girl's father climbed the steps carrying her against his chest. His thumb was wrapped in his neckcloth. The child had lost a shoe.

“He said a wicked word,” she announced.

Her mother made the sound Meret had heard in the cards, and covered her mouth with both hands.

Meret had been doing this for twenty years. She had foretold three wars, a hundred marriages, the knife beneath a bishop's pillow, and the exact evening on which the king's father would die. The present king had threatened to hang her for that last reading. Later he had ordered his mourning clothes in good time.

She never accepted payment for a lost child. The mother set the copper down anyway, beside the untouched pear.

The terrace wind had loosened Meret's headscarf. She tucked a length of brown hair beneath the purple silk and reached for the deck.

Meret was putting away the cards when the stranger came up the steps.

They were young, perhaps twenty, with brown skin, black hair roughly cut at the jaw, and a green coat shiny at the elbows. There was white road dust in the stitching of their boots. They had waited at the bottom until the family left.

“Are you closing?”

“For the afternoon.”

“I've come a long way.”

Meret looked at the coat. It had been mended with three different colors of thread. She took the royal summons from beneath the plate and folded it.

“One question.”

The stranger sat. Meret smoothed the purple shawl over her knees and laid the deck between them. The gold sun on its back shone briefly as she turned it in her hands.

“Your name?”

“Oreth.”

“And your question?”

“When the king's army is finished, will I have a home to go back to?”

Meret dealt the first card.

There was nothing on it.

She had seen the moon on that card a moment before. She turned it over. The gold sun was gone too.

Oreth leaned forward. Meret put a hand over the card, an old habit from readings she did not want a client to see too soon. Under her palm, something gave a tiny, dreadful gasp.

She lifted her hand.

The next card was white. So was the next. She spread the rest across the table. The violet backs emptied as they slid over one another, the last gold stars vanishing at their edges. There was no face or border left anywhere.

“Close us,” said a thin voice.

Meret stopped breathing.

The cards had spoken to her before, once a year, in the royal audience. The painted king had a bass voice; the lovers spoke a word each; the child on the Hearth card could make a room of courtiers weep. All were mouths of the same living being. But she had never heard them without asking, and never heard them afraid.

“Close us. Turn us down.”

“They are down,” she said.

One of the white cards curled at a corner.

“Not that way.”

Oreth had gone very still. “What does it mean?”

Meret gathered up the deck. It was warm and damp as a small animal held too tightly.

“I don't know.”

She had told kings that they would lose their sons. She had told a condemned woman the hour of her pardon, and the woman had struck her for making a joke. She had never said those three words at this table.

From inside the closed deck, in the voice of the painted child, something whispered, “It has nowhere to look.”

“What hasn't?” Oreth asked.

“Fate,” said Meret.

The little voice became almost too faint to hear.

“Everywhere but that chair. Everywhere but that chair.”

Oreth looked down at themself, then back at Meret.

“I'm sitting in it.”

“Yes.”

“I know how that sounded. I mean, I'm here.”

Meret looked into their face. A pulse beat at the base of their throat. There was a healing split in their lower lip. They smelled of dust and orange peel.

She could not find the least sense of what they would do next.

Usually the future was quiet around her, unless she went looking for it. It waited like the next room of a familiar house. Now she felt the edge of something that had no other side.

“Has anyone read for you before?”

“Three people. One said I'd spilled something on his cards. One wanted money to lift a curse.”

“And the third?”

“Gave my money back and locked her door.”

Meret laid one card on the table. White.

“For me,” she said.

The violet border returned. The face filled with a painted stair, and beneath it a little silver cup. Meret let her sight settle on an ordinary future: herself entering the palace, a servant offering her wine. She caught the shape of the cup's chipped foot.

Oreth was still sitting opposite her.

“For the man on the scaffold,” she said.

Across the square, a mason in a yellow cap stood on a narrow plank beneath the eaves of a house. A new card showed him falling. Meret felt the sick weight of the fall, the broken wrist, the weeks of work lost. She looked for who would help him afterward.

“What's happening?” Oreth asked.

“That plank will go. The man will catch himself badly.”

Oreth was out of the chair.

“Wait.”

They did not wait. They went down the terrace steps three at a time and ran across the square. Meret rose, the card in her hand.

The mason turned at their shout. One end of the plank slipped.

The picture whitened.

Oreth caught the ladder and drove its top hard against the man's hip. He fell against the rungs instead of into the street. Two tiles smashed beside Oreth's feet. For a moment all three of them, man, ladder, and stranger, leaned at an impossible angle. Then the mason got his hands around the ladder, and Oreth dragged its feet outward until it stood firm.

Meret was halfway down her own steps. She had no memory of starting.

The mason was swearing. Oreth was laughing, a breathless, angry laugh.

“You might have shouted sooner,” they called to Meret.

She looked at the white card in her hand.

In twenty years she had learned to recognize a broken wrist in any deck, at any distance, through grief or drink or a king shouting in her ear.

The mason climbed down with both hands.

Back on the terrace, Oreth took off their coat and drank two cups of water. Their hands shook when they set the second one down.

“It was going to happen,” Meret said.

“The plank did fall.”

“He didn't.”

“Nearly.”

Meret watched them rub a scrape on their palm. The danger had not been an illusion. The tiles lay broken in the square. But the fall she had seen had acquired a cause she could not see, and become something else.

She read the mason again. She saw him that evening, eating with the yellow cap on the table beside him. He lifted a bowl. Both wrists were sound.

The cards had not hidden Oreth's destiny from her. There was none to show.

Oreth touched the edge of the royal summons.

“You're going to the palace?”

“Tonight.”

“Take me.”

“You haven't heard what happens there.”

“Tell me.”

Meret looked toward the royal hill. Above the roofs, the king's red standard moved in the late sun.

At the full audience, she told them, Fate stood above the deck, entire and breathing, its life in the room with her own. She held every card in mind while its pulse pressed against hers; even now the memory made her jaw ache.

“Could you hold it while I spoke?” Oreth asked.

“If it agrees to come. I decide when to let go.”

“Then make it look at me in front of the king,” Oreth said.

“Why?”

“Because you told him he would win.”

“I saw it.”

“And now?”

Meret had no answer ready.

“My town is on the road his army will take,” Oreth said. “We're getting out the good plates for them. Burying the grain. Both. Nobody knows which will help.” They rubbed their palm again. “If he hasn't counted me, what else hasn't he counted?”

“He has counted what I gave him.”

“Then take me to him.”

The deck began to murmur.

“Meret.”

She knew that voice. It was the gentle contralto in which Fate had answered her at her first royal audience. She had asked whether her father would recognize her when she went home. It had said yes. For one afternoon, before his fever took him, he had.

“Meret. In autumn there will be a boy in the north wood. His name is Iven. He will have a green glass marble in his mouth because he is afraid of losing it.”

Meret sat down.

“There will be snow before his family finds him. Unless I show the next reader where to look.”

Oreth's hand withdrew from the summons.

“I found the child today,” said Fate. “You have never asked me for a child I did not find.”

That was true. Some had already been dead. But every one had come home.

The next reader, Meret thought. It knew she understood.

She had read her own death eleven years ago, by accident, while teaching herself how to hold the full audience. Tonight, at the fifth stroke of the sunset bell, she would lie beside the royal table with the standard's spear-point at her throat. Her shawl would be caught beneath its gold head. Her eyes would be open. She had seen it as plainly as she had seen the girl coming up the steps without a shoe.

She had checked the standard's fastenings each year. She had considered burning the Hall. People who tried to avoid a reading generally supplied it with a more elaborate road. Eventually she had stopped spending every evening trying to imagine tonight.

It had comforted her to know that the gift would outlive her.

“I could still leave,” she said.

“Yes,” said Fate at once.

Meret took up the card with the stair and cup and let Oreth's request become her own intention.

The stair vanished. The silver cup went after it. Nothing took their place.

Her heart struck once, painfully.

She did not know whether she would die tonight.

Oreth watched her face. “What did you see?”

Meret put the white card in her pocket.

“Get your coat.”

They climbed toward the palace through streets already dressed for victory. Red ribbons hung between the houses. Outside an armorer's shop, two boys were trying on helmets, shouting through the visors at each other.

Oreth stopped to watch them.

“How many?”

“Three thousand and eighty-six,” Meret said.

“Is that us, or the people we're fighting?”

“Our soldiers.”

Oreth walked on.

Meret had been asked how many of the king's soldiers would die. She had answered the question. The other dead had not appeared in that reading. She had known there would be others.

At the first palace gate, she slid out a card for the guard. She saw his cap come off as he stepped back from the wicket. Then Oreth reached for the iron before he opened it.

The picture vanished. The guard kept his cap on and put his hand on his sword.

“Hands away.”

Oreth let go.

Meret showed the summons. It took five minutes of argument to secure what, a moment before, had seemed assured.

“Tell me before you do things,” she said as they crossed the court.

“I was opening a gate.”

“I know.”

At the inner stair, she saw a page coming down with the silver cup. She guided Oreth aside and caught the page before he turned toward the kitchen. The foot was chipped exactly where she remembered.

“Tell the king I'm here.”

“He knows, madam.” The boy looked at Oreth. “Who shall I say?”

“Oreth.”

“Oreth what?”

“He can ask me himself.”

The page went up the stairs instead of down. Meret lost the next piece of the way.

They waited beneath a painted king who had been dead for two centuries. Oreth examined a tear in their coat.

“You could send me away,” they said.

“I could.”

“You don't look well.”

“I expected to die tonight.”

They looked up sharply.

Meret took the white card from her pocket and told them what she had seen. Oreth listened without interrupting. When she finished, they took the card from her hand, looked at it on both sides, and gave it back. She slid it into the deck.

“And now you don't know.”

“No.”

“Good.”

She laughed. She could not help it. It was an ugly, startled laugh, and it left her trembling.

Oreth stayed beside her until the doors opened.

The Hall of Lots was narrow and very high. The king sat at its far end, with the war orders laid before him and the great seal beside his hand. A guard held the sword of state flat across his palms at the foot of the chair. Captains and ministers stood along the walls. Several had come in their armor.

The audience table occupied the raised floor below the king. It was low enough that Meret could kneel beside it, long enough for her four rows of nine cards. Above it hung the royal standard. The butt of its ash pole rested in a bronze cup on the left pillar; a heavy cord from the right pillar held its gilded iron spear-head up over the place where the reader stood. The red cloth fell behind the table like a second wall.

Meret looked at the cord. She had had it replaced last spring. New white silk, thicker than her thumb.

“You brought someone,” the king said.

“Someone I cannot read.”

“Then you should have brought another reader.”

“No reader could do it.”

A minister smiled. Meret had told him once that his secret marriage would become public. He still behaved as if she had betrayed him.

“We are rather occupied,” the king said.

Oreth stepped forward. “I'm from the border. The east road, below the watch hill.”

The king glanced at a captain, who nodded as if confirming the existence of a place were an answer.

“I want you to hear my reading,” Oreth said.

“You cannot demand the royal audience.”

“I can,” Meret said.

She knelt and laid out the cards.

The first row was white. So was the second. By the time she reached the fourth, nobody was smiling.

“For this person,” Meret said. “Their home, their life, their ending.”

The cards lay empty beneath the windows.

“You have damaged them,” said the minister.

“Remove it,” said the deck.

The king straightened. The minister's mouth closed.

The familiar contralto came from every card at once.

“Remove it from the Hall.”

“My name is Oreth.”

“Captain,” said the king.

Meret looked toward the man at the right-hand door and put a thumb on the Sword card. At the change of subject, a little hand rose on its face; she saw the captain's left arm lift, his right foot turn inward. Beyond that the sight failed. Whatever would happen when he reached Oreth was as blank as the card had become again. She opened her mouth to warn them.

Oreth stepped toward the table instead.

The captain's hand closed on air. Trying to catch them, he struck his shin against the low table and fell. His shoulder hit the edge of the spread.

“Mind the cards,” Meret said, and almost laughed again.

Two guards lowered their spears. Oreth backed against the right pillar, beneath the standard's supporting cord. They had turned pale.

“Enough,” the king said. “All of you.”

The guards stopped. The captain got up with blood on his lip.

“It cannot see what they will do,” Meret said. “Your Majesty, it can't promise you anything about them.”

The king looked from her to the fallen captain, then to the white deck.

“Can you still promise my victory?”

“Ask the source.”

He put both hands on the arms of his chair.

“I ordered the full audience.”

Meret laid her palms beside the spread. She found the small, separate attentions she had trained for twenty years: each card held in mind, each way open, all the ways meeting in one place. Even empty, they made a shape she knew. She offered it.

Nothing entered.

“Come before us,” she said.

The blank Hearth card whispered in its child's voice. “You know what will happen to you.”

“I know what you showed me.”

“Let it go.”

“Will the king win?” Oreth asked.

No answer.

“If he sends his army past my house. Will he win?”

The king rose.

“Answer.”

Meret felt the presence hesitate beyond the spread. She could feel its attention going outward, down all the ways that still opened for it: the captains, the army, the granaries, a boy not yet lost in a northern wood. Here in the Hall, a young person in a mended coat had become a place none of those ways could cross.

Then its attention returned to the sword of state. The captain had failed it. In a body, it would have a hand of its own.

“I will answer in my own person,” said Fate.

It accepted the offered shape.

Meret bore down on the deal as a weight entered the world.

A tall figure stood a hand's breadth above the cards. Its skin was silver, its hair black and fine as smoke, its robe the pale color of the sky before sunrise. Three narrow gold eyes lay along each temple. It turned its head toward the king. All six eyes were strained to the left.

Oreth stood on its right.

The king bent his head. Around the Hall people bowed, slowly or at once. Meret remained on her knees. Holding the whole living presence was already making her jaw ache.

“The sword,” said Fate.

A guard carried forward the sword of state and laid its hilt in the silver hand. This happened at every full audience. Fate touched the blade to the king's shoulder; the king undertook to govern according to what had been shown. Tonight the silver hand closed around the hilt, but did not lift the blade toward the king.

“Look at me,” Oreth said.

Fate's head turned a little farther away.

“Please. I want to know what's wrong.”

For an instant, its eyes opened wide. Meret saw terror without any human effort to hide it. Then the lids narrowed almost shut.

“There is no place for you,” it said.

Oreth pressed a scraped palm to the pillar.

“There wasn't room at the inn either. I slept outside.”

Nobody laughed. Meret thought the words had cost Oreth more courage than the run across the square.

“Meret,” said Fate. “Dismiss me.”

“Tell him what you cannot see.”

The sword moved.

Oreth hit her hard in the shoulder. Meret fell sideways, one hand skidding through the spread. The blade passed where her neck had been and cut the loose end of her shawl.

Two of the cards lifted. The silver body thinned.

Meret caught the shape in her mind. The two cards fell flat. Fate became solid again above the table, its arm still extended toward her.

The king shouted something. A guard started forward and stopped when the silver face turned toward him. He had spent his life in the service of a being that saw every weapon before it was drawn.

“You tried to kill her,” Oreth said.

Fate held the sword level. Its eyes did not move toward the voice.

Meret could let go. A little less attention to the Hearth, a failure to hold the Sword beside it, and the body would withdraw. She knew exactly how little effort it would take. The being would live. It would speak through the cards again. It would ask this king, another king, a frightened reader with a locked door, to remove the person it could not bear to look at.

It would also find the boy in the wood.

Meret rose to her feet.

“You missed,” she said.

Her teeth were chattering. She moved around the table to her appointed place, under the gold spear-head. The red banner touched her shoulder.

The silver eyes followed her. One by one, they opened.

Above the Hall, the sunset bell began to toll.

Meret saw recognition settle over the face she had known for twenty years. Here was something already seen. Here was an ending that had once been sure: the woman beside the table, the gold head at her throat, the deal broken by her death. It could still be done.

She was offering it that road.

She could not know that it would take it.

The second stroke sounded.

Oreth was against the right pillar, behind the source's turned face. Meret did not look at them. She held every blank card in her attention and waited beneath the point that had been waiting for her for eleven years.

“This much,” said Fate, “I know.”

It lifted the sword toward the white silk cord.

“Oreth,” Meret said. “The pole.”

The cord parted under the blade.

The standard fell. The gold head came down toward Meret's face; the long ash shaft swept the space above the cards.

Oreth jumped onto the low table. They caught the shaft in both hands below the spear-head, knees folding with its weight. The red cloth came over their head. For one dreadful moment Meret could see neither their face nor their hands.

Fate's head turned toward the falling weapon and stopped as if its neck had met a wall. Its sword came across blind and struck the table behind Oreth.

Under the cloth, Oreth heaved sideways. The pole's butt tore free of its bronze cup. The whole weight came down onto their shoulder.

Meret stood close enough to the source to touch its robe. She could still dismiss it. She held the shape.

Oreth shoved the bunched banner away from their face and turned the spear-point toward Fate's right side. The pale robe brushed their cheek. Bracing a foot against the table's edge, they drove the point upward with both hands.

Fate made the small gasp Meret had heard beneath her hand on the terrace.

The spear shuddered in Oreth's grip. Six gold eyes opened, searching the empty air beside their face. The source had moved out of the way of poisoned cups, falling stones, and hidden blades for centuries before Meret was born. This time there had been no next moment in which to see the weapon coming.

“Hold it,” Oreth said.

Meret held it.

The fifth stroke of the bell sounded.

The silver body grew heavy. It dropped onto the table, scattering the white cards. One table leg broke. Oreth went down with it, still holding the pole.

Meret felt every path through her cards close at once.

There was no voice behind the deck. No attention going outward through it. The tall body lay across the broken table with its six eyes shut. Its foot rested on the Hearth card.

Nobody moved until Oreth began trying to pull their coat free of the wreckage.

Meret helped them. Their left hand would not close properly. They tried once, then stopped. Their other hand was still clamped around the pole.

For a while they looked at the silver face. Then, very carefully, they let go.

“Stay there,” she said.

“I am.”

She put her fingers against the silver throat. No breath stirred the robe. Nothing answered her touch.

The king came down from his chair.

“Is it gone?”

“It's dead.”

He looked at the body for a long time. Behind him the captains waited, and beyond them the army waited in its new boots, with sharpened swords and wagons already loaded.

“Read the war again,” he said.

Meret picked up a card. She did not know which one. Its front and back were equally white.

“I can't.”

“Use another deck.”

“Every reader in your kingdom drew their sight from this.”

“You told me I would win.”

“I did.”

“Will I?”

“I don't know.”

The words seemed to anger him more than the sight of the body. His hand rose, then fell against his side.

“How many, then?”

“I don't know.”

Oreth sat on the edge of the broken table, holding their injured hand against their coat. The king looked at them. Meret could not tell what he was thinking, or what he would do with that thought.

She had changed what would come. She and Oreth, together. She had also left the next mother who climbed her terrace steps with nobody who could tell her where to look. Somewhere in a future she could no longer find, a boy might put a glass marble in his mouth and walk between the trees.

She kept the white card in her hand. She did not try to make it mean anything else.

“The orders, Your Majesty,” said a captain.

On the king's desk, a candle burned beside the seal. The wax had been warmed for him.

He went back to his chair. Meret watched him take up the seal, then set it down beside the waiting orders.

“No messengers leave tonight,” he said.

One of the captains began to object. The king turned toward him, and the man stopped.

Oreth put their sound hand against Meret's sleeve. She looked down. There was a piece of white silk caught in their hair.

“You're here,” they said.

Meret touched her throat. The bell had finished.

“Yes.”

stories.title: The Contracts of Saint Nocturne
stories.prompt: After humanity abandoned religion, the Vatican Archives became the most heavily guarded library on Earth. The eight sisters of Saint Nocturne have spent generations preventing anyone from opening its deepest vault. When an international expedition finally breaches the complex, the world discovers the sisters aren't protecting evidence of God's existence. They're protecting the original contracts humanity made with the things it once called gods.
stories.body:
# The Contracts of Saint Nocturne

The sisters lost the courtyard at eleven in the morning. Until then, Sister Ione had only ever seen its palms from below.

Now a machine was carrying her above them. Its padded arms held her elbows against her ribs, and her boots hung clear of the battered fronds. The radio in her black veil crackled against her ear. Down on the paving, Sister Peret struck another machine with her empty rifle. It caught the rifle, considered her for a moment, and took her under both arms.

The expedition had promised to capture them alive. This was turning out to be worse than Ione had expected.

Across the court, Neri was still firing from the bell tower. Olwen, whose hands shook until she held a weapon, had made a barricade of the western gate. Maud sat beside a wounded expedition soldier and pressed both their hands against his bandage. Tavia's last small aircraft rose from the roof, struck a much larger one, and came down burning in a stone planter.

Sister Agnet emerged from the smoke. She was the oldest of them, and she had promised Ione they would never see the trees from above.

She looked up, saw Ione dangling there, and made an obscene gesture at the machine.

Then Mother Damaris came out of the library carrying a white cloth.

They had spent eleven days dismantling the most heavily guarded library on Earth. Six countries had supplied the expedition's machines; nineteen had supplied people; every government had signed its authority. Three centuries of secular custodians had added fortifications to the Vatican Archives without being permitted to ask what the fortifications protected. The eight women of Saint Nocturne had inherited all of it. Each generation had improved it.

None had improved the white cloth. It was an old towel from the infirmary, with a darn in one corner.

Damaris lifted it above her white coif. At her gesture, Neri stopped shooting.

The machine lowered Ione into a line of soldiers. A woman in a dusty blue jacket was waiting beside them. On her breast was the commission's eight-pointed seal, gold against blue. She looked at Ione's bound wrists, then at the palms, and seemed to decide against whatever she had meant to say.

“Dr. Ada Nasse,” she said instead.

“I know.” Ione had watched her announce the expedition. Everyone in the archives had watched.

“Is anyone left inside?”

“No.”

“Children? Trainees?”
