“There are eight of us.”

Ada glanced at the library. Its reading rooms could have housed a town.

“There have always been eight of us,” Ione said.

Damaris arrived between two soldiers. Her white gloves were blackened. A thin line of blood had dried on her dark forehead, above one eyebrow.

“You may have the upper collections,” she told Ada. “No resistance. All the catalogues. Everything down to the red stair.”

“That was the offer before we came.”

“It is still an offer.”

“And what would you like me to tell the people whose money built those walls?” Ada pointed at the ruined tower. “Or him?” She indicated the wounded soldier beside Maud.

Damaris looked at him. “That I am sorry.”

“They've been told that before. By your predecessor, and hers. We're going down.”

“Then go as readers. Resign your mandate. Leave the commission's seal here.”

Ada touched the badge. “Why?”

“If you open an original before an accredited human assembly, you acknowledge receipt of a claim.”

For the first time, Ada seemed angry.

“You understand what you just said? That something down there makes a claim on the people who sent us?”

“Yes.”

“Then they have a right to see it.”

Damaris caught Ione looking at her. Ione had never heard this part.

“Let me show you an unopened instrument,” Damaris said. “Photograph it. Record its existence. Take that back to them.”

“And let you decide when we can read it?”

“There will be consequences.”

Ada took her hand from the seal.

“There have been consequences for centuries. We just haven't been allowed to know what they were.”

The camera above her shoulder turned toward the library.

***

Ione had stood guard at the red stair for six years. She had not been below it.

Agnet knew the way. She walked in front of Damaris, moving her right knee carefully after the fight. Tavia followed the camera with her eyes, working out what it could see. Neri and Peret were still furious; Olwen was silent; Maud kept trying to get a soldier to look at the burn on Peret's neck.

The expedition let all eight come. Ada said this was partly a matter of safety and partly a matter of witnesses.

“Also,” she added, “I think you should see it with us.”

“Mother has seen it,” Ione said.

“Yes,” Damaris answered.

Ione waited. Damaris walked on.

There were no crosses below the stair. The cross had been taken off the archives' public entrance when the last church closed, generations before Ione was born, but she had expected one here. Something left over. Instead there were calculations cut into the walls, lists of supplies in obsolete languages, and a succession of marks at shoulder height.

“Those are fingerprints,” Ada said.

“The early custodians,” Agnet told her. “Every one of them.”

Ada slowed to look. A soldier urged her on. Above them, behind several metres of stone, the breaching crew was finishing its work on the last door.

When the charge went off, grit fell from the fingerprints.

The door had no image on it. Eight women had spent their lives defending a grey slab. It lay inward on the floor, its broken edges showing layers of steel and something dark that smelled of crushed leaves.

One of the soldiers crossed himself, then looked embarrassed. The gesture survived in people who had never prayed.

“Are you expecting a body?” Damaris asked Ada.

“I don't know what I'm expecting.”

Inside were eight stone benches. On each lay a wrapped object. Some were flat, one was cylindrical, and the smallest would have fitted in Ione's palm. Clay seals marked the wrappings. The air smelled of dust and cedar.

Ada stood very still.

Above the benches, cut into the wall in a language Ione had been taught to read but never needed, were the words:

*Here lie the undertakings, in their first and binding forms.*

“Undertakings,” Ada murmured. “Not testaments.”

Her camera light moved along the benches. The labels gave dates by kings, eclipses, migrations. There were names of human peoples that had not survived into any language spoken upstairs.

Damaris turned toward the door.

“You have your pictures. We can leave.”

Ada went to the first bench.

Its label was repeated in several hands. The newest was only a few centuries old.

**Concerning the safety of sleepers.**

The seal beneath it showed a closed eye.

“Wait,” Ione said.

Ada looked round.

“Let me stand where I can see.”

Damaris shut her eyes. A soldier brought Ione forward.

The wrapper opened around a great folded sheet, supple and grey. Its writing was crowded, practical, amended in the margins. Different hands had made the lines. At the bottom were eleven human thumbprints and one deep impression like the track of a many-jointed foot.

Ada's breath caught.

“These names. We have fragments of these names.” She bent closer. “They aren't invocations. They're parties.”

The last line of the outer sheet lay beneath the camera:

*We, who are not made by you, and who owe you nothing before this agreement.*

Ione read it twice.

Ada took the commission's seal from her jacket. It was also the instrument with which she authenticated accessions. She set it beside the sheet so the camera could record the mandated commission receiving the original.

“Don't,” Damaris said.

Ada looked at her. Her hand stopped, but she did not remove the seal.

“If it concerns us, we have to receive it.”

Something beyond the broken door said, “Received.”

***

The soldiers turned their lights toward it.

At first Ione thought a strip of the doorframe had come loose. The thing was that narrow. It unfolded into the doorway, taller than a person, with long white hands and a head whose many folds moved independently around six shut eyes. Dust stirred where it breathed.

It had been outside. It had come in through the corridor they had just used.

“How comfortable you have all been,” it said.

The soldier nearest the door raised his weapon. Damaris shouted, “Wait.”

The thing reached past him toward the bench.

He fired. The shot struck its hand and drove it against the stone. Its mouth opened vertically between the folds of its face. The sound it made hurt Ione's teeth.

Three more weapons came up.

“Keep it there,” Damaris said. “It is alive.”

Ada looked at her, then at the captain beside the door.

“Their hands,” she said.

“Weapons too,” Damaris told her.

For a moment Ada did nothing. Then she nodded. The captain ordered the bindings cut and the confiscated rifles brought forward. He helped Olwen load hers, watching the doorway over her shoulder.

The creature drew its damaged hand against its chest. Dark fluid soaked into a fold of skin.

“Is that necessary?” it asked.

No one answered.

Ada was staring at the thumbprint beside her seal.

“The Guest Beneath the Eyes,” she said.

The thing inclined its head.

“Is it a god?” someone asked from behind the camera.

“Not any longer,” Damaris said. “That doesn't mean it died.”

The Guest smiled with its eyes still shut.

“We have business.”

Ada reached for the seal. The Guest's head turned precisely toward her hand.

“You may put that away. You have acknowledged receipt.”

On the little screen attached to the camera, the broadcast's heading changed. For a moment it read **FIRST CONTACT: VATICAN ENTITY**. Then someone somewhere replaced *entity* with *DEITY*.

Ione wanted to tell them to stop doing that.

The Guest extended its uninjured hand, palm upward.

“Services outstanding.”

“We haven't agreed to anything,” Ada said.

“You have received the agreement. Your ancestors agreed.”

“Our ancestors had no right to promise us.”

“An objection frequently made by heirs.”

Ada looked down. Ione read over her shoulder.

There were lists of beings: the Guest, its household, the things that followed its household, the things it could restrain. Against them stood an undertaking that no human sleeper would be entered, hunted, or carried away, so long as the promised services were rendered.

Beside one name was a restraint: *It shall not call the sleeper in any loved voice, nor draw the sleeping body after the mind.* The next line forbade carrying anyone into a place from which there was no waking road back.

Below it, the human obligation ran for two lines.

One night in every seven. From sunset to first light, kneeling and speaking the names of the Guest and its household. Their descendants were to do likewise.

“You sold them protection from yourselves,” Ada said.

“Among others.”

“And if they didn't want it?”

“They very much wanted it.”

The eleven thumbprints were small. One had been pressed twice, as though its owner had been frightened of doing it wrong.

Pinned behind the first sheet was another, much newer. Ione recognized the order's hand.

*Collection being suspended in the sealed custody of the eight mortal watchers, and resuming only on presentation of this original before an accredited human assembly.*

Beneath were successive renewals. Eight names. Eight more. Eight more.

The last list named all eight of them. Ione remembered signing its copy six years earlier. The form she had seen had said only that she would keep watch over the entrusted originals.

“You are the reason it stopped,” she said.

“The reason it stayed stopped,” Damaris answered.

The Guest looked toward the ceiling.

“But now it resumes.”

***

Dr. Kem Hazi's phone began to ring.

He was the expedition physician. He had a strip of black adhesive across his forehead where a fragment had cut him in the courtyard. Until then, he had been watching Peret's burn.

He silenced the call. It rang again. Then Ada's headset filled with voices, and the camera operator said, “They want you to look at this.”

The image on the camera screen divided.

In a hospital ward, four adults were kneeling on their beds. Their eyes were shut. They were speaking together. A nurse tried to lift one man's face; it turned back toward the wall.

“Sedation?” Kem asked at once.

The nurse shook her head.

“They were asleep. They won't wake up.”

Ione knew the words they were saying. She had just read the first of those names.

“Stop,” Ada told the Guest.

“They are still under my shelter. This is collection.”

“Stop collecting.”

“We may discuss terms.”

Kem answered his phone.

A boy's voice came out of it, thin and angry with fright. “Dad, he keeps singing. He's doing it again.”

Kem turned the screen. A younger boy sat upright in a bunk, eyes closed, swaying a little. Someone was calling his name out of view.

“Don't hold him down,” Kem said. “Let me see his face. Yes. Like that.”

“They remain safe,” the Guest said. “The services are overdue, but I do not hunt my own clients.”

“He's nine,” Kem said.

“He is an heir.”

“And the ones who can't speak? Babies?” Ada demanded.

“Sheltered. Owing what they cannot yet render. They are not forgotten.”

Kem made a noise and went toward it. A soldier caught his jacket.

The Guest did not move. “Your household can clear its arrears. Resume the observance, in waking life. One night in seven. You know how to arrange a rota, surely.”

“Everyone has to do it?”

“Everyone who wishes to continue receiving shelter. Each for themselves.”

Ada said, “There is a choice?”

The Guest's folded face turned away from her.

Ione looked at Damaris. Damaris was watching the small singing boy.

Ione bent over the original.

At the foot of the sheet was another line, partly covered by a fold. She drew it flat.

“Any heir,” she read.

Damaris put a hand on the sheet.

“Ione.”

“Any heir to whom the entire terms have been made known—”

“May refuse this agreement in their own person,” Damaris said, “owing neither service thereafter nor service outstanding, and receiving thereafter neither shelter nor ward.”

She said it without looking down.

Ione stared at her.

“A complete and faithful copy,” Ada read from the next line, “may stand for the original in the making known of these terms.”

“Do not,” the Guest said, “confuse information with safety.”

The camera was still showing the hospital. Ione looked up at its dark lens.

Her hands were on the page. Damaris's hand was on hers.

“You knew,” Ione said.

“Yes.”

“All of it.”

“Yes.”

“You let me promise my life without ever telling me.”

“So you could sleep. So they could.” Damaris indicated Kem's phone. Her voice had lost its command. “When I first read it, I refused. I thought I should know what we were guarding.”

“You went without?”

“One of them called in my father's voice. My predecessor woke me, but its hand was still in my hair. She had to pull me free.”

Ione looked at the list.

“I begged her to get me back under the shelter,” Damaris said. “The Guest agreed to readmit me under the suspended agreement. I wasn't owed that.”

“You got to choose. Why didn't I?”

Damaris did not answer.

The Guest bent toward the bench. The soldiers raised their weapons again. It paused, hands displayed.

It angled its folded face toward the camera.

“This can still be postponed,” it said.

***

A pale membrane unfolded from beneath its wrist and lay on the bench, marked in the same crowded hand as the old settlement.

“Eight living custodians,” it said. “Their remaining lives. The original resealed, the complete terms uncirculated. Collection suspended again. You have recorded our existence. Your achievement is secure.”

“Our achievement,” Ada repeated.

“You may leave with it.”

Agnet came forward. She held her bad knee straight and looked at Damaris.

“Give me a pen.”

“Agnet,” Ione said.

“I heard.”

“You don't have to.”

“I heard that too.”

Ada found a pen. Agnet took it with the hand that had made the gesture in the courtyard. She put her name beneath the offer.

The Guest's eyes tightened in their folds.

“Eight,” it said. “No bond until the eighth assent.”

Damaris read the membrane. “No replacement after signing.”

“For these lives, no. They end; another settlement may be offered.”

Olwen signed beside Agnet. Then Maud.

Neri, Peret and Tavia had come round the bench. They waited for the pen.

Ione could see the old life returning. The kitchen window she had looked through every morning. The drill hall. The red stair. The palms from below. A new girl brought in before one of them died, taught the languages and the weapons, told what she would preserve, never what she could refuse.

“I won't,” she said.

Agnet kept her place at the bench. She did not look hurt or surprised. “All right.”

“I will,” Kem said.

The boy on his phone was still singing. The older child had stopped trying to wake him and was sitting on the floor beside the bunk.

Kem looked at Damaris. “It doesn't have to be one of you?”

“No.”

“Then I'll replace her.”

Ione opened her mouth.

“Don't tell me I don't understand,” he said. “I understand enough. I can spend one night in seven on my knees, or I can stay here and they don't have to. I would rather stay here.”

“You'd never go home,” Maud said.

“Yes.”

He took the pen from Maud. His hand was steady. He signed beneath her name.

Ione stepped back from the bench.

It was possible. Someone could take her place. She could go out of the gates and sleep safely because Kem Hazi had stayed inside them. If he changed his mind, perhaps someone else would come forward.

She could not call that her imprisonment.

Ada looked from the membrane to the original. The camera above her shoulder still carried the divided picture: the hospital, the singing boy, the vault.

“If we accept this,” she said, “what may we publish?”

“What you have already shown. Our existence. The general nature of our undertakings.”

“The service. The shelter.”

“Yes.”

“But not the complete terms.”

The Guest inclined its head.

Kem said, “Then don't. Give us time.”

Ione looked at the boy beside the bunk. He was old enough to read the words on the sheet. He had not asked to be an heir.

She turned to the camera operator. “Put the page on.”

Damaris caught her wrist.

“You can leave,” she said. “You can leave now.”

“I know.”

“If we can pay, they need never make this choice.”

“We can keep it from them.”

“Yes,” Damaris said. “That is what I mean.”

There was nothing careless in her face. Ione saw how long she had been afraid for people she would never meet.

Kem held out the pen. “Mother.”

Damaris did not take it.

Ione drew the old sheet out from beneath her hand.

“I won't decide what they should do,” she said. “But I'm putting it where they can read.”

“That decides something too,” Kem said.

“Yes.”

She lifted it toward the lens.

The Guest moved.

It struck Ada aside without looking at her and caught the edge of the original. The grey sheet pulled tight between its white fingers and Ione's hands. A soldier shouted. Damaris seized Ione's jacket and hauled her sideways. Ione stumbled clear of the creature's face, both hands still locked on her edge of the sheet.

The first bullet struck stone. The second hit the Guest beneath the shoulder. It folded around the impact, made that terrible open-mouthed sound, and kept its grip.

“That is ours,” Damaris said.

“Then keep it,” the Guest answered. “Seal it.”

Its grip loosened. It held its corner out to Damaris, above the waiting wrapper.

The weapons stopped. For a moment Ione could hear Kem's son singing through the phone.

Damaris closed her hand over the corner in its grip. Only then did the Guest let go.

She looked down at the eleven thumbprints. She put a finger beside the doubled one.

“They made you put that in,” she said.

The Guest said nothing.

Ione was still holding the other edge. For six years she had obeyed Damaris at the red stair. She did not let go.

“I am frightened,” Damaris told her.

“So am I.”

Damaris looked at Kem. “You can still keep your shelter.”

“I was offering to keep theirs.”

“I know.”

She lifted her corner of the sheet and turned it toward the camera.

“Ada,” she said. “Can they read it?”

***

The Guest screamed. Olwen drove it back from the bench with a burst of fire. Neri hauled Ada to her feet, Peret caught the falling camera, and Tavia picked up a fallen light and aimed it at the wall.

“Both sides,” Ada said. “Every margin. Hold it still.”

Ione climbed onto the bench and spread the original against the wall. Damaris held its lower corners. The camera's little screen showed the sheet, whole and legible, then its reverse. A line of text appeared beneath it: **DOWNLOAD ORIGINAL**.

“Copies?” Damaris asked.

The operator was crouched behind the bench, holding a cable against its socket.

“Everywhere.”

The Guest came forward again. Maud fired once. It fell against the broken door, caught itself with a long hand, and began to drag itself upright.

“You will dream of me,” it said.

“Some of us,” Damaris answered.

Ada turned the camera toward the bench with the new settlement. Only four names stood on the membrane.

“Incomplete,” Damaris said.

“Incomplete,” the Guest agreed.

She drew a line through the four names, then tore the membrane across the blank places. Agnet let out a long breath. Kem put down the pen.

The thing in the doorway had opened one eye. Ione could not bear to look into it.

“Where may they send their refusals?” Ada asked.

“I will hear them.”

“They must understand all of it?”

“They must have received all of it. Tell them to be sure. Tell them what I keep out.”

“We will.”

“And tell them they may return.”

Damaris looked up sharply.

The Guest's face folded around its eye. “A new agreement. New terms. I am not obliged to offer the old price.”

It slipped backward into the corridor. Its wounded hand left a dark print on the stone.

No one followed it.

For a while there was only breathing. Then Tavia began checking the seven unopened seals. One by one she called them intact, and Ada photographed each against its bench number. No one suggested opening another.

Kem picked up his phone.

“I'm here,” he said. “I'm still here.”

***

They brought the original up to the courtyard in its wrapper, with the broken clay eye kept beside it. All eight sisters walked out. Agnet leaned on a soldier's arm and complained whenever he slowed down for her.

Above the palms, the sky was pale with the approach of evening.

Maud refused to let anyone talk to Peret until the burn had been dressed. Olwen sat under a tree and began to shake. Neri went to sit beside her. Tavia asked to use a terminal, and when the operator hesitated she held up both her empty hands.

The copies had spread beyond anything the expedition could recover. There were translations already, competing transcriptions, arguments over the marks made by people who had not expected a world like this one to inherit them. Lawyers were calling the commission. Parents were calling anyone who would answer. Some of the messages simply demanded that the vault be shut again.

Ada read one, put the screen facedown, and went to give another interview.

Kem was sitting on a folded blanket with the terms open on his phone. The physician who had relieved him offered a sedative. He shook his head.

His partner had sent a picture of their youngest eating breakfast. Dawn where they lived had ended the night's service. Kem enlarged the boy's face, then passed Ione the phone.

“I'm going to learn the observance,” he told Ione. “For me. My partner is reading it to the boys. We haven't decided what to tell them to do.”

“They stay sheltered unless they refuse.”

“Yes. And they owe.” He rubbed his face. “I know you didn't write it.”

She sat beside him for a minute.

“I hope you were right,” he said.

She handed the phone back. She could find nothing to say to that.

Agnet came out of the medical tent with a fresh bandage around her knee. She stopped by the phone and asked Kem to enlarge the line that began the spoken service. Together they worked out the first name.

Ione left them there.

The expedition had set up cots in the old infirmary. Its windows stood open to the palms. Ione had been awake for most of two days, but she waited until Damaris came in.

“You could wait,” Damaris said.

Ione had read the copy three times. She had gone back to the line about the sleeping body following the mind, and the places from which waking would not bring her home.

“I know.”

She pressed her fingers against her lips. “I need to sleep tonight. I don't want it singing with my mouth.”

Damaris stood beside the cot. There was no coif on her head now. Without it, Ione could see the white scar that ran back into her close-cropped hair.

“That's where it held you?”

Damaris touched the scar.

“Yes. Mother got hold of my collar. I wouldn't have come back by myself.”

Ione looked at it for a long time.

Then she spoke her own name, the name of the agreement, and her refusal. She did it without a camera or a seal.

Nothing in the room changed.

Damaris pulled a chair beside the cot and sat down, her rifle across her knees.

“That won't help,” Ione said.

“I know.”

From the courtyard came Agnet's voice, stumbling over an old word, and Kem gently correcting her. Ione could hear the palms moving above the roof.

She lay down and closed her eyes, leaving her rifle where it could not follow.

stories.title: Caelorum
stories.prompt: Humanity has lived within the colossal mountain city of Caelorum for as long as its histories remember. Generation after generation, its inhabitants have constructed increasingly magnificent buildings, bridges, and monuments, following architectural instructions engraved into the cavern walls. Nobody knows who wrote them, only that disobeying the designs brings disaster. When an apprentice architect notices that the city's structures form an enormous mechanism, she realizes the builders have spent thousands of years unknowingly assembling something. And now with it almost complete, she must discover whether their ancestors intended to build it or not.
stories.body:
# Caelorum

At dawn, Isera stood inside her bridge and touched the place where her name would go.

The cartouche was six fingers long. Hadran's name had already been cut above it, his thirty-first bridge and his last, he said, although he had said that about the previous four. Below his broad letters the stone was smooth. She had practiced hers on offcuts until she could carve the whole name without letting the chisel slip in the narrow space between the R and the A.

From the scaffolding she could see half of Caelorum. Its terraces climbed into blue shadow, crowded with houses and pillared halls. Bridges crossed above bridges until distance made them look as delicate as threads. At the highest opening, where snow blew through the cleft in the mountain, the Watchful Sisters stood beneath their matching domes. The lower city still burned with lamps. A baker was carrying a tray across a bridge built nine hundred years before her great-grandmother was born.

By tomorrow he might be carrying one across hers.

For thousands of years, each new building had come from a drawing on the cavern walls. The oldest histories described the engravings already there. None named a person who had cut them.

She took out her dividers and crouched beside the eastern springing, where the arch rose from its pier. The arch's long iron binding ended here in a great shoe. Oak wedges held it high in its socket, its upper flange caught behind an overhanging lip. When permanent stone pads replaced the oak, it would be locked there. At sunrise the carpenters had eased the first row of centering wedges; part of the arch's weight rested on its piers already. One final bed to check, then Hadran would give the order to lower the rest.

Her plumb line would not agree with yesterday's mark.

She waited for it to stop swinging. Far below, someone called for a basket to be lowered. A hammer rang twice. She set her thumb against the stone and felt a faint, steady tremor, too slight to trouble a mason.

Yesterday's mark stood a finger's width to the left.

She checked the western bed. There the arch had risen a hair's breadth without shifting sideways.

Back at the eastern bed, at the very bottom of the iron shoe, a polished strip had appeared. It curved down into the pier. Isera brushed the white dust away. The strip continued beyond the bed where, according to the section she had drawn, solid masonry should have begun.

She lay flat and put her cheek against cold iron.

It was not a foundation plate. It was part of a circle.

Above her, Hadran's boots crossed the planks.

“You will wear the bridge out before anyone walks on it.”

She pointed. He knelt with a grunt, the knees of his dark coat going white.

“That was covered yesterday,” she said.

Hadran touched the bright iron. He was a thickset man with a short grey beard, and ordinarily he looked at stone as though waiting for it to admit a fault. Now he put down his measuring rod and stretched full length beside her.

Below her, across a cleft between the lower terraces, a line of washing moved.

The air was still. Isera watched a red shirt travel behind the corner of a tower rooted in the cavern's rear wall, taking its line and the little balcony with it.

She was on her feet before she understood what she had seen.

“Keep the centering!”

The shout came out so fiercely that the nearest carpenter dropped his mallet.

Hadran looked down. At the far end of the washing line, the balcony continued its slow passage behind the tower. He seized the scaffold bell and struck the order to hold.

All along the bridge, work stopped.

For a moment Isera could hear the city she had interrupted: hooves on a distant stair, a woman laughing, the deep morning bell from the Hall of Measures. Then the timbers beneath her began to creak.

***

By the time the sun reached the Watchful Sisters, they had doubled the shoring beneath the eastern end.

Not every timber was doing the work it had been cut for. The bridge wanted to move sideways as well as settle. Carpenters drove braces across the scaffold and watched their ends bite into the stone. Below, the red shirt hung motionless again. Its balcony had moved the width of a man's hand.

Hadran sent a runner to close the crossings around the bridge. He wrote the order on the back of Isera's section drawing, signed it, and gave the boy his seal.

“The whole terrace?” Isera asked.

“Until we know which part.” He looked down at her drawing. “Where does that circle go?”

She had no answer. The engraved design showed the great shoe, every bolt and flange beautifully particular, but nothing of what lay beneath it. A little sun had been cut where the drawing met the limit of its stone panel. In the apprentices' school they had been taught that this was a blessing on the foundation.

“The gallery,” she said.

They went up by the long stair behind the masons' lodges. In its lower flight stood the memorial to the Broken Span. Seven tall names, forty-three small ones. Someone had tucked winter flowers into a crack at its foot.

Isera had copied it during her first month of training. Everyone did. The architects of that bridge had widened the deck beyond the engraved measure to accommodate a procession. On the night the last stones were laid, the east quarter had dropped. Three streets had been lost.

Under the memorial's lower molding, a piece of the old bearing remained exposed. A fractured iron curve, exactly like the one beneath her bridge.

She stopped so abruptly that Hadran nearly walked into her.

“They added the width on one side,” she said.

“You know what they did.”

“I know what we were told they did.” She put her palm against the iron. The break ran diagonally through it. “They put the extra weight here. Whatever this is, they pulled it crooked.”

Hadran glanced toward the names. “Do not ask me to find that reassuring.”

“I'm not.”

They climbed on.

The survey gallery was cut into the living rock above the Hall of Measures. From there, buildings Isera had known all her life ceased to conceal one another. She could see the stepped pediments of the lower city, the pale crowns of the theaters, the immense stair towers that had taken whole lifetimes to finish. Snow lay along their upper edges. Smoke rose between them in thin, separate columns.

She opened her folio.

Architects were taught to draw what the eye could not see: a stair passing behind a wall, the thickness of an arch, the empty chambers inside a pier. Isera had always liked sections best. A façade could be made to promise anything. Cut through a building and it had to tell you how it stood.

She began with her bridge. Then the fractured bearing at the memorial. Then a line through the stair tower below it, curving under the roof of the theater.

“There is a chamber there,” she said.

Hadran frowned. “There is a bakery.”

“Under it.”

She drew the next curve. A ceremonial stair followed its rising edge. Across the city another stair answered it, built in another century from another quarry's stone. Her hand moved faster.

Behind the shining fronts, behind shops and rooms where people were getting dressed, the same shapes repeated. Some were vertical. Some lay on their sides. Once she saw them, she could not make the city return to what it had been.

The lowest tiers stood together on a single immense cradle.

Its curved iron runners rested in the mountain. Towers rose from it like weights placed along the arm of a balance. Across the gulf, the upper monuments concealed the other parts of that balance, and the lines continued upward, toward the Sisters.

She drew the mountain around them. Its sloping face covered almost half the cavern, running from the high cleft down toward the city's outer edge. Snow entered through cracks in it. In summer, little stones fell from its underside.

The Sisters' domes stood at opposite ends of the same straight line.

Two ends of a hinge.

Isera lowered the pencil. She could feel the drop beyond the gallery rail in the soles of her feet.

“Show me,” Hadran said.

She put his measuring rod across the drawing. One end under the lower city. The other under the sloping face. Her bridge ran west from the cradle's inner edge: its eastern pier stood on the inhabited cradle, its western foot was held by the iron arm rising toward the mountain face. The arch's binding joined them into one rigid piece.

The first weight taken off its timber that morning had set the whole thing moving.

“When that goes down,” she said, touching the inhabited terraces, “this comes up.”

He did not answer immediately.

The long granite sides of the mountain lay above them, blue with distance, veined with ice. A thousand small buildings clung to their foot. Hadran looked from the drawing to the Sisters and back again.

“All of it?”

“That face. The rest is the frame.”

“And we are the weight.”

From below came a report like a door slammed in an empty hall. They both turned. One of the new braces under the bridge had split along its length.

Hadran rolled up the drawing.

“We could leave it on the centering,” Isera said, although she had seen the brace break.

“It was made to hold an arch while we built it.” He looked toward the houses below. “Not to hold back those.”

***

The movement had opened a seam behind the eastern pier. At its widest, Isera could fit her shoulders through.

Hadran wanted to come with her. Then a carpenter arrived to say that the lowest cross-brace was slipping at its socket, and he turned back toward the scaffold.

“A bell if you need us,” he said.

She showed him the little survey bell on her belt. He took it off her and tied it to a cord leading back through the gap.

“You will not be where we can hear that.”

He held the lamp while she squeezed between the stones. Her coat caught. For an instant she was wedged with her arms in darkness and her cheek against the moving city. Then she pulled free, leaving a scrap of green wool on the rough edge.

Beyond the seam was a stair.

Its treads were too deep for the quick rhythm of Caelorum's stairs. She descended sideways, keeping one hand against the wall. Above her, the gap narrowed to a blade of light.

The chamber below was larger than the Hall of Measures.

She could not see its far end. Her lamp found portions of an iron curve taller than a house, a row of stone teeth, the foot of a column she had thought began nine storeys overhead. Everything was dry and furred with dust. The floor shivered against her boots.

Along one wall, low structures huddled between the great foundations. A blackened cooking niche. A doorway too short for her. A row of sleeping hollows screened by slabs of thin stone. Over one hollow, someone had scratched a bird with an extravagant tail.

Isera lifted the lamp.

The homes had been built against the iron. Their little walls closed around bolts already old enough to be pitted when the mortar was laid. A child's palm print survived beside a door, five short fingers pressed into plaster.

She had come looking for the people who built the engine. Here were people who had found room beside it.

What they had understood, she could not tell. They had made a place to cook. Someone had wanted a bird above their bed.

Beyond the dwellings the wall had been smoothed for a drawing.

She knew its conventions at once. Sections, elevations, a little sun where an arm turned on its support. The engraved lines were dark with age. A cut through the mountain showed the great face folded inward, the spaces beneath it, the low cradle on which her city now stood.

In the last part of the drawing that cradle descended into a narrow pit.

There was nothing to stop it.

Isera followed the line with her lamp until the rim of the pit disappeared beneath a later cut. This second line was less elegant, deeper and broader. It left the old descent and curved outward into a broad, shallow hollow. Beyond the hollow it rose to a low lip, where the way ended above the pit.

She turned.

On the far side of the chamber, above the empty dark of the original pit, a wide bearing way had been cut into the mountain. It curved toward a ledge. A workman's stair ran along its edge, broken in places, but passable.

The city had not reached it yet. Its nearest runner hung a little above the new way, held where her bridge and the remaining timbers restrained it.

Isera walked beneath the runner with the lamp held high. Rows of houses stood somewhere above her head. The red shirt. The baker. The public steps where she had sat on examination mornings, mouthing the nine prescribed ratios until the words lost their meaning.

In the original design they would all have gone into the pit.

She went back to the wall.

The later cuts crossed an old dwelling's plaster and carried on into bare stone. Whoever had made them had worked after people began to live here. At the foot of the amended drawing, a group of little rectangles stood on the cradle. Roofs, doorways, the hatching for an occupied floor. The old drawing had shown a mass of stone.

Someone had drawn the houses in.

She put the lamp down and made a rubbing with the side of her charcoal. Her hands were shaking now, and she had to stop twice to keep the paper flat.

Above the altered ways the older design continued. The high monuments had their weight marks. At the top was her bridge, still recognizable through the dust: the long central arch, the two great shoes, the connection held rigid from end to end.

The deeper, later cuts climbed toward it. They stopped below its western pier.

She searched the stone beyond. Some lines had been begun and rubbed down. There were trial holes, and a place leveled for a new section that had never been cut. The upper design remained untouched.

Nothing told her what had happened to the people working there. They might have lost the argument or the knowledge. They might have meant to return. In the centuries since, everyone had copied what survived as if one hand had drawn it all.

The floor gave a long, low groan.

A little fall of dust passed through her lamplight. From above came three urgent pulls on the bell cord.

Isera took her rubbing and began to climb.

Halfway up, she stopped.

Through a gap in the stair wall she could see the underside of a bridge. A very small bridge, smoke-blackened and old, buried inside the piers of the vast one above. It should have formed a complete arch. Instead, its crown had been opened. The two halves stopped short of one another.

The gap was deliberate. Chisel scars crossed the broken ends, and packing stones had been inserted beneath both sides so that each stood without its lost middle. The old bridge's cradle-side foot rested a handspan below its first bed, on an added shoulder. A scrape along the iron behind it marked the short descent.

She pushed her lamp through the gap.

Behind the old bridge, the larger one also had a seam. A gilded lion's head concealed it from the street.

How many times had she crossed that bridge? She had bought the little brass dividers in her pocket from a stall beside its eastern lion. Under the stall, under the lion, someone had arranged for the two ends to move apart.

The old experiment had carried a load, let it go, and stood after the separation.

It did not tell her how to release her own bridge. It did tell her that a bridge need not remain what it had been built to be.

She squeezed back into daylight with black dust across her face and her rubbing held inside her coat.

Hadran took her elbow. A broad white crack ran down the pier behind him.

“What did you find?”

“A way for the lower city to land.” She drew breath. “And a reason we cannot leave the bridge whole.”

***

They spread the rubbing on a stone block beside the unfinished parapet.

Hadran kept one hand on it against a wind that had not been there that morning. Somewhere above the Sisters, a narrow seam had opened in the mountain face. Snow blew through it in a white, continuous streamer.

Isera showed him the original pit. The later landing. The houses drawn into the amended section.

“Those are the instructions we follow below,” he said.

“And these are the ones we followed here.”

She put her finger on the untouched upper bridge.

Hadran looked at the white crack in the pier. “Can that shelf carry the city we have now?”

“I don't know.”

He nodded once, as though that had been the answer he was waiting for.

They sent men down with lamps to expose the beginning of the added way. Others cleared the lowest open crossings. Already people were gathering at the barriers with bundles, demanding to know where they should go. From an upper stair Isera could see a man trying to lead a balking donkey through a door too narrow for its panniers. The moving quarter held the lower markets, the theaters, the whole deep tangle of streets around the morning baker. Its people could not all climb out in the time the shoring had left.

Hadran sent the runner again. Stay inside the lower terraces. Clear the crossings. Keep away from the outer parapets. His seal traveled with orders that sounded like madness.

Isera went back into the bearing chamber.

They had tied a cord from the added way to the scaffold bell. She stood beyond the city's nearest runner, where she could see both the old descent and the first part of the new curve. The men had scraped centuries of dust from a patch of black stone. It looked too small to accept the weight above it.

She made herself look at its depth instead. The way ran back into the mountain, broadening as it went. It was not a ledge hung over the pit. It was the mountain, cut to receive them.

She rang twice.

Above, Hadran's crew eased one set of wedges. The answering movement came through Isera's feet before she saw it.

The iron runner lowered.

Its outer edge touched the added way. A thin grey crust burst off the stone and rattled into the pit. Isera flinched. The man beside her gripped her sleeve.

Then the broad bearing behind the crust took the load.

The sound changed. Instead of the high, strained ticking she had heard since morning, a low note passed through the chamber. The runner settled the breadth of her thumb. On its worn inner edge, old scratches met the new ones their descent had made.

She watched the stone. No crack opened.

At the scaffold above, something broke with a noise like a tree splitting. Their bell rang hold.

Isera gave the answer with both hands on the cord.

They had placed a fraction of the present city's weight on the old way. It had held. They had also used up a timber that could not be put back under that load.

She climbed until the air grew cold again.

Hadran was standing over a broken brace. It had crushed its own iron socket through the scaffold floor. He looked at her before she spoke and saw the answer.

“It takes the weight,” she said. “Here. At the beginning.”

“Can we send it on?”

She shook her head and laid the rubbing on the stone again.

“The bridge is still tying us to the face.” She traced the hollow at the end of the new way. “Our weight can settle here. The pull will drag us up the far side, over the lip. There's nothing beyond it.”

He studied the line. “Then take the connection out.”

“Not yet.”

The high face had lifted far enough for daylight to shine behind its lower edge. Isera could see the thickness of it now: whole avenues of stone. She took Hadran's rod and laid it across the engraved hinge. With her other hand she raised the edge of the rubbing, making the paper face turn.

“Until this has gone past upright, it can fall back. The bridge has to carry the pull that gets it there.”

He held the far corner while she let the paper turn beyond the rod. Its free edge fell away from the drawing.

“After that,” he said, “it keeps going.”

“With us if we stay tied to it.”

Together they looked along her bridge.

Even unfinished, it was beautiful. Its pale arch crossed the highest open space in Caelorum. Three hundred carved rosettes filled the underside, each a little different where a carver had taken liberties with a leaf. In the morning she had been angry about the fifth rosette from the west, which sat a fraction out of line.

Hadran followed her gaze to the cartouche.

“Where?” he asked.

She had been thinking of the crown. Take the keystone and let the arch come apart. But the lower roofs jutted from the cradle beneath the eastern half of the span. Breaking the crown would drop that half straight onto them. West of the last roof, the shaft fell sheer and empty.

She went to the eastern springing.

The oak packing beneath its iron shoe was already crushed, but it still held the flange high behind the socket's lip. The permanent stone pads had not been fitted. The temporary iron dogs across the joint were keeping the shoe square while the scaffold carried part of its load.

She knelt in the white dust and put her hand on the joint she had measured that morning.

“Here. Take out the oak and the shoe drops below the lip. Then the western arm can draw the arch off the cradle. Its binding will hold through the first turn.” She traced that turn on the stone with her finger, westward, away from the houses. “Over the clear part of the shaft.”

Hadran looked down through the scaffolding at the empty shaft beyond the lower roofs. Then he looked up at the lifting mountain.

“You will have very little time.”

“Yes.”

“The lower way held at the first contact. That is all we know.”

“Yes.”

For the first time since the washing had moved, she wanted him to take the drawing away from her. Let him find another line. He had thirty-one bridges. She had not yet made one stand without timber beneath it.

Hadran took his seal back from the returning boy. Then he went to the masons and began telling them which tools to bring.

***

They worked under the engraved design.

Its lines stood clear above the scaffold, each stone of the bridge fitted forever to the next. Isera had spent two years enlarging those lines into patterns, choosing blocks, working out the joins the engraver had compressed into a groove no wider than her little finger. She could have drawn the bridge blind.

Now she marked what must come out.

The first carpenter hesitated over the oak beneath the shoe. She saw his glance go from her chalk to the wall.

“The Broken Span,” he said.

“They added weight without knowing where it went.” Her mouth was dry. “We know where ours is going. You've seen it move.”

He kept looking at her.

“I saw the way take it,” she said. “I was underneath.”

Hadran came down beside them. He put his own chalk mark through hers.

The carpenter bent to his work.

They withdrew the iron dogs. The shoe remained caught behind the lip, held high by the oak beneath it. The wedges could not be pulled under the load, so they left a final pair to be driven clear with a long beam from the narrow scaffold beside the pier. Once those were out, they would have to reach the stone before the timber went.

Isera set the beam herself. Then she checked the route back, lifting a coil of rope out of it and breaking off a splinter that could catch a coat.

Below them, the last people were leaving the crossing. A woman with a small boy stopped in the middle and looked up. The boy pulled her hand. She picked him up and ran.

Farther down, the red shirt had vanished from its line. All the washing was gone. Someone had thought to bring it in.

The city began to descend.

At first Isera saw it only at the edges. A doorway slipped behind the fixed tower beside it. Steps that had joined at a landing drew apart. Along the old bridges the gilded lions divided down their centers, revealing clean black seams.

Then a bell tower went down against the line of the opposite roofs, and the whole scale of it reached her.

Caelorum was moving with its people inside.

The deep note she had heard under the city rose until it filled the cavern. Snow shook loose from cornices. On the lower terraces, people clung to doorposts and one another. A market awning bellied in the new wind. The great cradle passed onto the added way, its iron runners grinding through the grey surface into black stone. The pier carrying Isera sank with the houses; across the span, the western arm rose and drew away.

Above the city, the mountain face lifted.

Blue daylight spread behind it, wider than any opening Isera had ever seen. Its light reached the undersides of bridges that had never been touched by the sun. Bronze fittings shone in the façades. The Watchful Sisters lost their domes as thin stone shells broke away, and beneath them two enormous black ends turned in their housings.

Hadran stood at the pier rail with a plumb line hanging from the crane. Isera had marked the hinge line on the parapet. From here they could sight the thick edge of the face against it, watching the rising mass approach the upright.

Not yet.

The bridge gave a hard shudder. One of the centering ribs below broke free, struck another, and vanished into the shaft. Dust roared up through the gaps in the planking.

Isera crouched, her hands locked around the release beam. Hadran braced behind her. Two carpenters held the rear end.

The face rose. Along its outer edge she could see snow blowing backward into a sky too bright to look at.

A second rib broke.

“Isera,” Hadran said.

She could not see his plumb line through the dust.

She let go of the beam and scrambled to the parapet. The stone under her palm was warm with friction. She leaned past the pier, coughing, until the two black ends of the hinge were visible again.

For a moment the face seemed still. It stood above the city like another city raised on end, enormously thick, its ancient cracks shining.

Then its edge moved beyond the line.

She watched long enough to see the movement increase.

“Now.”

They drove the beam forward. The first wedge shot out and struck a scaffold post. The second moved a little and stopped.

The arch had begun to pull on its shoe.

Isera threw her shoulder against the beam beside Hadran's. Behind them the carpenters shouted to one another and heaved. The crushed oak shrieked.

Beyond the end of the beam, the iron shoe shifted sideways.

She wanted to say stop. Her whole body knew what it meant when the foot of an arch left its bed. There was no drawing, no calculation, that could make it feel like anything but the beginning of a terrible mistake.

They struck again.

The second wedge broke across its grain and fell out in pieces. The shoe dropped, its flange clearing the lip.

Hadran caught Isera around the middle and hauled her backward. The others were already running. They reached the stone of the pier as the scaffold tore loose behind them.

For a breath, the bridge remained.

She saw the rosettes. The fifth one, wrong by half a finger. The smooth blank underneath Hadran's name.

The western arm drew the bound arch with it. Its freed eastern foot swept off the cradle, carrying the crown beyond the line of roofs. Then the iron binding broke and the great stones opened at their joints. Pale blocks fell against the darkness of the shaft. The crown went last, spinning once, and the sound of its fall disappeared beneath the voice of the mountain.

Beneath their pier, the cradle continued down.

Isera could see its bearing from where she lay. The great iron runner had cleared the old pit. It was moving along the added curve toward the broad landing, far below the place she had tested.

The mountain face fell outward into the light.

Without the bridge, it could no longer pull the cradle after it.

The lowest houses shuddered. A chimney fell from one of them. Windows burst white with dust. The runner struck the bottom of the hollow with a blow that drove Isera's teeth together. It climbed a little way up the far side.

Then it settled back and stopped.

For a long time there was only falling stone.

***

When Isera stood, the city had a horizon.

Beyond the opened face, ridges fell away through immense blue distances. Snow lay on their upper slopes. Far below, something dark spread over the land in branching masses; she could not tell whether she was seeing forest or the shadows of clouds. The daylight had no frame she could take in at once.

The great face lay beyond its hinge, supported now by the outer slope of the mountain. Its weight was still settling. From time to time another crack sounded across it, and fragments slid glittering into the distance.

The lower city stood farther down and outward than before. Gaps had opened between its districts and the fixed heights, but the old double bridges had separated onto their waiting supports. Some stairs ended in air. Others had become shallow ramps. There were broken roofs, a fallen colonnade, white dust everywhere. People were coming out of doors and calling across the changed spaces.

Below Isera, a red shirt waved from a balcony. The woman holding it had come out to call across the gap beside her building. Now she stood silent, cloth in hand, staring beyond the city.

Hadran came to the end of the broken bridge. He had lost his cap. There was blood along one cheek where a splinter had caught him, and his beard was grey with stone dust.

He looked at the gap, then down toward the bearing.

“I shall need your section,” he said.

Isera tried to answer and could not. She took the rubbing from inside her coat. It was torn at one edge and black where she had gripped it.

He spread it on the parapet. Together they looked at the houses someone had drawn onto the old mass of stone. Whoever had cut them had not lived to see the whole city land. Perhaps they had been frightened, too, working beneath the instructions they were changing.

Hadran held the paper flat with a broken piece of the bridge.

A call rose from the lower terraces. It traveled up, taken by other voices, until Isera could make out the words. One of the broad stairs at the city's outer edge now ended on the mountain's exposed shoulder. People were gathering there, keeping back from the settling stone. Beyond them a slope ran down into daylight.

She turned to look for the rosette blocks, absurdly hoping to pick out the fifth one among the pale wreckage. The shaft was too deep. Her name had never been cut.

Below, someone stepped off the lowest stair. Another person followed, and another, their shadows stretching away from Caelorum across the snow.

stories.title: What the Sun Is Owed
stories.prompt: The sun doesn't kill vampires. It recognizes them. Long ago, the first vampire stole something from the sun, and every sunrise since has been an attempt to reclaim it. After centuries of hiding, a young vampire discovers she can hear the sun speaking her name. When she finally answers, daylight turns crimson, shadows begin moving independently, and the sun offers her a bargain: return what was stolen, or become the next star in the sky.
stories.body:
# What the Sun Is Owed

Ordan fastened the clasp in Neris's hair while she drank.

The blood was still warm. Neris held the white cup in both hands and felt its warmth pass through the walls of her stomach, into her wrists, along the roots of her teeth. The ache beneath her canines eased. A little blood remained on her lower lip. She caught it with her tongue.

“Keep still,” he said.

“You caught a hair.”

“I am attempting to release it.”

He had given her the brass clasp two hundred years ago, when she cut her black hair with a ship's knife and complained for a month about the pieces falling in her eyes. Now he held a caught strand between finger and thumb, working it free with a care she could feel all the way down her back.

He had been her father for two hundred and eighty-seven years. Before that he had been a stranger on a beach, kneeling beside the woman of twenty-four the sea had almost finished with. She remembered his mouth beside her ear, asking whether she wanted to live. She had managed to answer him.

The clasp clicked shut.

“There, daughter. You may shake your head at me again.”

She did. He smiled and went to inspect the shutters.

Beyond them the sailmakers' square was beginning its last hour of darkness. Someone was harnessing a horse below. Through the soles of her feet Neris felt the familiar shudder of the first cart taking the cobbles. She had rented these rooms because the square woke early. For a little while she could listen to a whole town beginning a day she would have to sleep through.

“It said my name again,” she told him.

Ordan's hand stopped on the shutter bar.

She had heard it at six dawns. At first she thought someone had come looking for her. The voice was quiet and close, although she could never place it beneath the window or outside her door. Yesterday she had heard it through the warm stone behind her bed.

“You know what to do.”

“I know what you told me.”

“That is a useful beginning.” He tried the bar a second time. “It calls to our kind. You close your mouth and let it pass.”

“Why?”

He turned toward her. Age had left him at the broad-shouldered, silver-templed man he had been when he took his first blood. Beside him, even after nearly three centuries, she was young.

“Because answering is how it kills you.”

“You always said the light did that.”

“Must I distinguish the teeth from the mouth?”

She set the cup down. He came back and put his palm against her cheek. It was warm; he had eaten before coming. She knew the small rough place beside his thumbnail, the weight of his hand, the ordinary pleasure of being touched by someone who expected her to be here tomorrow.

“We have a good life,” he said.

They had crossed seas and watched cities change their names. Sovel was planning a voyage with her beneath a comet that would return in a hundred and thirteen years. Last week Neris had heard a boy singing a song she had taught his great-grandmother. She loved being alive with an appetite still large enough for another century.

She wanted the other half of the world as well.

Ordan kissed her forehead and left for his cliff house by the covered walk. She heard his steps diminish beneath the cart wheels. When the square's lamps went out, she took the cup to the window.

“Neris.”

The voice was on the other side of the shutters.

She put her fingers on the bar. The wood had begun to warm.

“Neris.”

She had opened shutters thousands of times at dusk. She knew the weight of this one, the place where its hinge scraped, the splinter beside the handle. Her hand performed the familiar movements before she had finished imagining how much they might hurt.

The first blade of light lay across her pale wrist.

Nothing happened to her skin.

She pushed the shutter wide. Above the roofs the sun had risen clear of the eastern ridge. It was the pale, intolerable brightness she had spent her long life turning away from. Tears filled her eyes. She stood with her fangs pressing into her lower lip and waited for the pain.

“Neris.”

“Yes,” she said. “I hear you.”

The daylight turned crimson.

The colour passed over the square in a single movement. The white horse below became red, the cart wheels black. A woman cried out at the bread stall. Far beyond the roofs the sea darkened until it looked like a field of iron under the red sky.

Neris's cup fell from her hand.

Her shadow, cast long across the floor, turned its head to watch it roll.

She did not turn hers. She stood rigid while the dark outline stretched an arm across the boards. Its fingers hooked the cup's handle and pulled. The cup struck a table leg and broke. Blood spread between the white pieces.

The shadow kept reaching toward the window.

Outside, the shadow of the bread stall climbed the house behind it. The horse's shadow flowed under the cart while the horse remained where it was, trembling in its harness. Every dark shape in the square had begun moving against the things that made it.

Neris backed away. Her shadow did not come with her at once. Its hands spread on the floorboards as if it had found something to hold.

“I recognize you,” said the voice.

It came from the black shape at her feet. There was no volume to it, nothing she could have covered her ears against.

“You said my name.”

“I have said it at every sunrise since you took my fire into your mouth.”

She looked at the broken cup. Without thinking she crouched to retrieve the largest piece. Its edge cut her palm.

“Ordan said you would kill me.”

“I do not burn away what I am trying to recover.”

The blood in her hand shone. For a moment she could see a point of white inside each drop.

“Long ago, the first of you stole a star before it was born. He has it under his tongue. He drank of it and made others drink of him. I recognize what it has become.”

She had seen the dark thing beneath Ordan's tongue and thought it a broken tooth.

Her shadow reached for the blood in her palm. She lifted her hand. Its fingers slid up the table leg and stopped at the tabletop; they could not lift themselves from the wood.

“Bring it back before I leave this sky.”

“What happens if I do?”

“My fire leaves you. All of you.”

She thought of Ordan's hand against her face.

“We've been alive too long. There would be nothing left.”

“Your bodies are as they are. What has healed will stay healed. But nothing more will be renewed. You will live until your bodies end.”

“And if I don't bring it?”

“You will become the next star in the sky.”

Neris looked up. Beyond the red glare, somewhere she could no longer see, were the small lights she had used to find her way across dark seas.

“Will I be dead?”

“You will be alive without these hands. You will burn with what you have borrowed. The original theft will remain below.”

She closed her bleeding fingers.

The sun waited while the people in the square ran from their shadows.

***

At the bottom of the stairs Neris stopped beneath the unlit arch of the sailmakers' shop. No red beam reached the floor. Her shadow disappeared.

Under her ribs, something turned over in its sleep.

She pressed her fist against it. Her blood was warming without food.

“You are not hiding from something outside you,” the sun said.

She went on.

The square had emptied. Its abandoned stalls cast shadows that wandered along the walls without moving so much as a loose apple. Only hers had weight. When she crossed a thin strip of light between two awnings, a dark hand caught the hem of her black coat and pulled it toward the sun.

She stepped backward into the shade. The hand lost its grasp at the beam's edge. She put one boot into the light again; the fingers appeared on the cobbles beside it, reaching. She moved her foot an inch. The fingers moved an inch. They could choose what they did within her shadow, but they could not go farther than the light cast them.

“You gave me weight when you answered,” said the sun.

She tucked her coat clear and ran.

Sovel called from a doorway beside the navigation hall.

Her short grey hair was flattened on one side, as though she had risen too quickly from bed. She was wearing the green seacoat Neris had first seen on her eighty years ago. Her shadow had climbed the lintel and was examining the empty street.

“Get under here,” Sovel said.

Neris held out her bare hand in the light.

Sovel stared. “How long?”

“Since sunrise.”

“Does it hurt?”

“The light doesn't.”

Very slowly Sovel put one hand out of the doorway. Crimson brightened the old seams of her knuckles. She turned it over, then let a little of the light fall on her face.

She laughed once. The sound broke in the middle.

“All that time,” she said.

Neris had no answer. Sovel was looking down the bright street with a hunger Neris understood better than the one beneath her teeth.

“I brought the chart,” she said after a moment. “I thought I'd leave it with the night porter. Before all this.”

She had it rolled inside her coat. She unrolled it on the navigation hall's doorstep and knelt to hold down one corner. A comet's path had been added in blue ink above the coastlines. Neris recognized the small crosses they had made together, arguing over where the thing would look largest and which coast would give them the longest night.

“The new tables agree with the old ones,” Sovel said. Her voice was settling into familiar work. “A hundred and thirteen years. We can see it rise from here, make the southern crossing, and see it again from the islands. Unless you'd rather spend the whole voyage telling me I'm holding the chart upside down.”

Neris knelt beside her. The cut in her palm had begun to close. She put her uninjured hand flat on the paper and felt a century of future spread beneath it.

“Sovel. I answered it.”

Her friend stopped smiling.

Neris told her what the sun had said. While she spoke, Sovel's shadow came down from the lintel and lay across the blue comet. Sovel tried to push it away. Her hand passed through it and struck the paper.

When Neris had finished, Sovel folded the far edge of the chart over the blue line.

“And you've come to ask me.”

“I don't know.”

“Ask.”

“Would you give it up?”

“No.”

It was spoken at once, without anger. Neris found that worse.

“For me?” she asked, and hated herself while she was saying it.

Sovel took her hand off the chart.

“Don't.”

Down the street a man emerged to retrieve the white horse. Its shadow ran along the wall beside him. Neris watched him take hold of the bridle as carefully as if he were approaching a strange animal.

“I'm not asking you to go up there,” Sovel said. “I couldn't. But I want my life. The rest of it. Don't tell yourself I wanted this.”

Neris looked at the century they had folded away.

“I won't.”

The sun slipped over the navigation hall's roof. Light fell across Sovel's face. Neris lifted her hand between it and her friend's eyes before remembering there was nothing to protect her from.

“Why are you still covering her?” the sun asked.

Sovel could not hear it. She looked at Neris's raised hand.

“Habit,” Neris said.

“You could watch her for a thousand years. You would never do that again.”

She lowered her hand. Her fingers were shaking.

“Give me time,” she said to the red light. “There are people I have to ask.”

“You have had two hundred and eighty-seven years.”

“They haven't had today.”

The shadow beside her turned toward the cliff.

“The stolen star has had no days at all.”

Sovel rolled the chart, slowly, matching one edge to the other.

“I'll walk with you,” she said.

They went up the cliff road together. It wound away from the town and returned above it, climbing through the long morning until the roofs lay small beneath them. On the other side the red sea moved under a wind they could not feel from the road. Sovel kept the chart inside her coat, held against her ribs.

At Ordan's gate she stopped.

“I can't help you take it.”

Neris nodded.

“I'll be here,” Sovel said. She sat on the low wall where, for centuries, Ordan's visitors had waited for sunset.

Neris went into his house.

***

His shadow came down the stairs to meet her.

Ordan remained at the top. A narrow window behind him admitted a line of red light. His shadow stretched along the treads, touching each with its long hands. As she closed the front door, hers reached up the wall toward his.

“You came through the square,” he said.

“Yes.”

“In the light.”

“Look at me.”

He did. She watched him take in her face, her bare hands, the blood dried at the edge of her mouth. His relief was so plain that she had to hold the banister to keep from going to him.

“Let me see under your tongue.”

His mouth closed.

“Neris.”

“I know what it is.”

He looked past her at the door, then up toward the roof. Every part of this house could be closed against daylight. He had taught her how to check a room: door, window, chimney, the seam around a loose tile. She had learned the order before she learned to feed herself without shaking.

She climbed the stairs.

The high room opened onto a narrow roof terrace through a tall shuttered window. They had sat out there on summer nights with their feet against the parapet, listening to the sea beneath the cliff. Now the shutters were barred and a strip of cloth had been stuffed beneath the sill. Her shadow's fingers came over the top stair and stopped at the edge of the light from the stairwell window.

Ordan saw her injured hand.

“Let me have that.”

She held it behind her.

“Show me.”

He stood silent for a moment. Then he opened his mouth and lifted his tongue.

The supposed tooth was smooth and black, no larger than a plum stone. A tiny brightness moved far inside it. Looking at it made her remember the sea over her face: the weight, the depth, the smallness of the air she had once been able to hold.

He took it between finger and thumb.

“Give me your hand, daughter.”

She obeyed before she could stop herself.

He placed the seed against her cut.

Warmth ran up her arm. Her skin closed, leaving a clean line in the dried blood. The fire reached her mouth and she tasted the rich, sharp pleasure of being made whole. For a moment her fear receded beneath it. Her fingers wanted to close around the thing and keep it.

Ordan watched her.

“You remember.”

On the beach she had said yes to living. After the first swallow of his blood she had tried to take his wrist and drink again. He had let her. She remembered that too.

“Does it know?” she asked. “What you've done with it?”

“It has never woken.”

“It has waited,” said the sun.

Neris looked down. Her shadow had found the thin line beneath the terrace shutters. One black fingertip lay against the floor there, rubbing the wood.

Ordan followed her gaze.

“What did it say?”

“That it's waited.”

He took the seed off her palm and held it tightly.

“It has no use for the years as we do.”

“You don't know that.”

“No.” He put his closed hand against his chest. “I know I was afraid. I know I wanted another morning. That was all I wanted at first.”

“And then?”

He looked at her.

She sat down on the edge of the old cedar chest. There was still a notch in its lid where she had dropped a knife, learning to hold one with her new strength. Ordan had turned the chest around so she would not have to look at the damage. A hundred years later she had turned it back.

“Why didn't you tell me what the light was?”

“Would you have kept the shutters closed if I had told you it could speak?”

“I might have.”

“You opened them this morning.”

Her palm was whole. He had healed it as easily as he had once lifted her out of a dying body. She rubbed away the dried blood with her thumb.

“There are things outside the shutters,” she said.

“Yes. There is one outside them now.”

He went to the window and pressed the cloth more firmly beneath the sill. The fingertip disappeared. Somewhere below, a shutter banged although the wind had not changed.

“It wants you to think everything we have belongs to it,” he said. “When you see Sovel, will you tell her those were borrowed years? That the seas she crossed were someone else's?”

“I've seen her.”

“Then you know.”

Neris looked at her restored palm. “It says we stay as we are. We grow old from here.”

“How long do you think I have?”

“I don't know.”

“Neither do I. I had stopped counting.”

His voice had changed. She knew the tone he used when he wanted to make a hard thing gentle enough for her to accept. This was smaller and less certain.

He sat beside her, leaving room between them.

“I made you because I could not bear to let you die. It wasn't the only time. I've been selfish. I've been afraid. But you were alive, Neris. Every one of you has been alive. What does it think it can take back?”

She remembered Sovel turning her hand over in the light. The laugh that had almost become weeping.

“My fire,” said the sun.

The words came through the boards beneath the cloth. Ordan could not hear them. He sat waiting for her answer as though there were only two people in the room.

She asked where the others were. He gave her a winter port six weeks away, an island neither had visited in a century. She made him try to remember someone she could reach before dark. The afternoon light travelled along the floor while his answers took her farther from anyone she could ask. At last he told her of a woman who had stayed in this room after the sun called her name. Years earlier, when he made her a vampire, she had asked him to wait until her children were asleep.

Neris stood.

“I want to know what happens to a star.”

“You know what happens. Something calls your name, you answer, and there is no one left to bury.”

“Did you look for her?”

His fingers tightened around the seed.

“I searched this room. There was light where she had been standing.”

“And the stars that weren't there before?”

“Light is all that's left. Don't let it tell you that makes a person.”

She went to the terrace window. Ordan rose with her.

“Leave that closed.”

“I can't choose it without knowing.”

“You can choose to stay here.”

“Until sunset.”

He put his free hand over hers on the bar. She could have let it remain there. The room was familiar, the chest beneath the window, his warm hand over hers. Beyond the walls the world was red and strange, and she had been offered no way back to the morning before it.

She pulled her hand free and lifted the bar.

He caught the left shutter. She pushed the right one open.

Red light flooded the room. Their shadows sprang across the floor. Hers reached up the wall toward the seed in his hand. His flowed down the stair, leaving his feet behind.

Ordan shielded his face.

Neris put herself in front of him.

She realized what she had done when the sun spoke.

“Again.”

She held her place.

“What would I be?” she asked.

“You have seen stars.”

“I've seen lights. Is someone still inside?”

The red sky hung beyond the window. The sun had passed the height of the roof and was beginning its long descent toward the sea.

“I won't help you bring it back until you show me.”

“Neris,” Ordan said behind her. “There are things you cannot ask to be shown.”

The living sun narrowed its light upon her. Her own shadow turned its face up the wall and opened its mouth.

“Then hear.”

The sky parted.

The red glare drew away along a black seam, exposing a depth of night that should have been invisible at that hour. Within it stood a single star. Neris had sailed by it thirty years before. It had first appeared when she was young enough to believe that anything new in the sky was an omen meant for her.

Its light entered the room.

Her hands lost all sensation.

She looked down. They were still her hands, fingers bent, a clean line across one palm. Ordan took her wrist. She saw the pressure of his thumb against her skin and felt nothing.

“You still close the shutters,” someone said.

The voice came through Neris's teeth.

Ordan went still.

The star moved within its own light. At its centre Neris saw a face too large to grasp at once, a mouth she could have mistaken for a bright fold until it spoke again. The features changed as the immense fire moved. They returned to themselves. Someone was making them return.

“I thought you might open them before long.”

Neris tried to move her wrist in Ordan's hand. It moved. She could see that it moved. She had no way of feeling whether he was still holding her.

“Can you hear me?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Are you alone?”

The fire folded inward. Far behind the face, in the deep night that had opened around it, small dark bodies shifted in paths Neris could almost comprehend. The star brightened; they turned. She felt the weight of them pass through the numb places where her hands should have been. For one instant she understood holding something too large to have an edge.

“No,” the star said. Then, after a pause: “Sometimes.”

Ordan spoke a name Neris did not know.

The face turned toward him. A white line crossed its mouth. It was the brief, unmistakable shape of fangs.

“After I answered, you said it would stop calling if I shut myself in,” the star said. “I waited behind the shutters until sunset.”

“I thought—”

“I know.”

He let go of Neris's wrist. She knew because she saw his hand drop.

“Can you come down?” she asked.

The face held its shape. Around it the burning surface lifted into peaks taller than the world below them. The little dark bodies kept turning.

“Where would I put myself?”

Neris tried to touch the clasp at the back of her head. She saw her fingers find it. She could not feel its teeth or the caught strands beneath them.

“You would remember,” the sun said to her. “You would remember how that felt.”

“Stop.”

The sky closed.

Sensation returned to her hands in a rush so sharp that she pressed them against her ribs. The brass clasp tugged her scalp. The room smelled of cedar and sea wind and the blood she had spilled into her sleeve.

She turned toward Ordan. His hand was out as if he had forgotten what he had meant to do with it.

Below the window, out on the cliff road, people were speaking all at once. They had seen the sky open too. A child called to someone to look again.

Neris had forced the room open. The strip of cloth lay in the middle of the red floor. There would be no returning to an uncertainty she could bear by keeping still.

“You didn't know,” she said.

Ordan shook his head.

She believed him. He had been wrong about how to save that person. He had still tried.

“I can't live up there,” she said.

The shadow on the wall turned toward her.

“You can.”

She looked directly into the sun.

“I won't.”

***

For a while Ordan said nothing.

Neris heard Sovel's voice below the window, answering one of the people on the road. The words were indistinct. Her friend was alive beneath this light, carrying a chart for a century Neris meant to take from her.

“What do you intend?” Ordan asked.

Neris turned back to him.

“To give it back.”

“Sovel doesn't want you to.”

“I know.”

“She could have another thousand years.”

“I know.”

He made a small, impatient movement. “Then say something else.”

Neris's shadow had come down the wall. It was reaching across the floor toward his closed hand. She stepped in front of it and put her foot on its wrist. The dark fingers flattened against the boards. She could feel their pull through her boot.

“I want to keep my hands,” she said. “I want to go somewhere without lighting it. I want to be able to leave. I want you to touch me and have it be more than something I remember.”

“So you will take our lives instead.”

“You'd still be alive.”

“Do you hear yourself?”

She did. She heard the sun saying that their bodies were as they were, as if that settled what the people inside those bodies might want.

“You can all keep living if I go,” she said. “That's what I know. I could do that for you.”

He watched her.

“I won't.”

The word hung between them. Ordan looked down at the hand he had put over hers on the shutter bar.

Outside, the sun had dropped low enough to send a long red band across the floor, from the terrace window to the head of the stairs.

Ordan opened his fist.

The seed lay against his palm. Its small inner brightness had quickened. Neris saw how tightly he had been holding it: it had left a smooth oval in his skin.

“Hold it,” he said.

She did not move.

“Before you decide for us. Hold it once without being hurt.”

He held out his other hand to her. It was the gesture he had used on the beach, offering something to take when she could no longer feel the ground beneath her.

She took the seed.

Its warmth gathered in her palm. Her hunger stirred and opened. She wanted to drink blood and sail beyond the charts, learn a new language, come home to a hand on her cheek. She wanted Sovel's blue comet. She wanted this afternoon to have happened to somebody else.

“You can keep it,” Ordan said. “It needn't stay with me. You can be the one who carries it. I'll show you where we went before there were houses to close. We can still go.”

She looked past him at the top of the stairs. His shadow was there, lying halfway down, its fingers spread toward the little star in her palm.

“Neris.”

This time both voices said it.

She turned her open hand toward the window.

Ordan caught her wrist.
