His other hand closed her fingers over the seed. He had the strength she had learned to trust when he lifted her from a deck or caught her after a foolish jump. She could not loosen a single finger.

“I am not letting you do this.”

She pulled away. He held her easily. With one boot on the top tread he leaned over her, pressing her closed fist down against her chest.

The seed burned warmly through her fingers. In the blood beneath it something answered, glad to be alive.

He was forcing her sideways out of the sunlight. Her shadow narrowed across the top tread; the fingers beside his boot began to vanish.

Neris planted her free hand against the side wall and twisted her shoulder back into the red band.

The shadow spread across the tread. Its fingers caught his heel.

It was no more than the pull that had broken her cup. His weight was already forward, his heel half off the tread. His foot slipped the width of a finger.

He caught himself on one knee.

For that instant his grip loosened.

Neris tore her hand free and opened it to the light.

“Here.”

The sun took its star.

There was no warmth in her palm afterward.

***

The seed rose past the window, making a black point against the red sky.

Ordan got to his feet. He reached for it with the empty hand that had held it for so long. Neris caught his wrist, then let it go. She had no way to help him that he had asked for.

Above the town the point opened.

Crimson lines sprang from Neris's fingers, her mouth, the healed place in her palm. She felt them draw through her without taking any part she could name. The fierce renewal in her blood uncoiled. The cold beneath it did not vanish. It entered the room with the evening wind.

Lines shone from Ordan too. One passed out through his open mouth. He shut it and tried to catch the light against his lips.

Below, on the cliff road, Sovel cried out.

Neris went to the window.

A thin red thread climbed from her friend's hands. Sovel had dropped the chart. She was standing very still with her fingers held apart, watching the light leave them.

Across the town there were more threads. They rose from shuttered attics and covered passages, from a cart at the edge of the square, from the dark beneath a boat's upturned hull. Farther off, beyond the land she could see, lines curved over the world toward the opening star. Each had come out of someone who had expected a different tomorrow.

The sun gathered them.

For a moment Neris could see the whole sweep of its claim: the cliff, the town, the unseen coasts, the distant people standing up in rooms where night had just begun. The light had found every one of them. She felt how far her opened hand had reached.

The seed broke into white fire.

The sky gave way around it. Something large was being born at a distance she could not measure. The new light flooded the sea, filling every moving wave with a brightness of its own. On the road Sovel put an arm across her eyes. Ordan stepped past Neris onto the terrace and looked up without covering his face.

The newborn star grew smaller. The depth behind it lengthened until it stood among the others. It was still visible through the daylight, a clear white point in the western sky.

Across the roofs the red began to fade. The chimneys' shadows returned to their feet. The moving darkness beneath the horse settled into its proper shape. Neris's own shadow lay along the boards, one hand lifted because her hand was lifted.

She lowered it. The dark hand lowered too.

Ordan stood at the parapet. The sea below had become blue again.

Neris stepped out beside him. His face was the same face. The silver at his temples had not spread. The cut on her palm had not opened, and when she touched a fang with her tongue it was still there. But her pulse was beating faster than she had ever felt it beat at rest. She could hear Ordan's heart as well, hurried and small beneath the waves.

“Does it hurt?” she asked.

“No.”

He looked down at his hands.

After a while she felt a cramp beneath her ribs. She braced herself for the old hunger, the cold search for blood. It did not come. Instead she remembered the bread stall in the square, the smell that had risen from it every morning while she lay listening behind the shutters.

She would have to eat. Tomorrow she would have to learn what else her body needed.

On the cliff road, Sovel picked up the chart. She stood looking at it. Then she rolled it and put it inside her coat.

Ordan watched the new star. Neris could not tell whether he was seeing what he had stolen or what he had lost.

Then he lifted his gaze to the place the other star had appeared and spoke that person's name again. Neris looked for the face. She could not find it through the daylight. Somewhere beyond it the little dark bodies were still turning.

She reached for his hand, the hand that had worked the caught hair loose from her clasp that morning.

He did not take hers.

She let it rest on the stone between them. There was warmth in the parapet, the last of a day's sunlight. Below it the sea moved against the cliff. Sovel remained by the gate.

“Neris,” said the sun.

Her name came through the cooling stone. Nothing followed it.

The sun went down.

stories.title: The Final Familiar
stories.prompt: After centuries of guiding witches through wars, curses, and the occasional apocalypse, a powerful familiar is assigned his final witch: an ordinary schoolgirl who doesn't believe in magic. His only instruction is to keep her happy. For the first time in nine lifetimes, he discovers that might be the hardest assignment of all.
stories.body:
# The Final Familiar

I had held a city against an army for eleven days. I had bitten a curse out of a queen's throat, which required better manners than you might imagine. In my seventh life I helped put an end to an apocalypse that had already advertised itself as permanent.

I mention these things because the woman at the order's office appeared to have forgotten them.

“Keep her happy,” she said.

I waited for the rest.

She turned the card over. There was nothing on the back.

“Is she under a curse?”

“No.”

“Being hunted?”

“She goes to school.”

“That is not an answer.”

The woman put down her pen. She was the fourth registrar I had known, and still young enough to regard a talking cat as an excellent reason to continue eating a biscuit.

“Your ninth life. Your last witch. When she releases you, you retire. Nobody sends you anywhere again.”

Through her window I could see rain beginning to collect on the tram wires. The name on the card was Miri. Thirteen years old. A school, an address, no accomplishments listed.

“Does she practise?”

“She doesn't believe in magic.”

I put one claw through the card.

“Keep her happy,” the registrar repeated, and went back to her biscuit.

I had given considerable thought to retirement. There would be a south-facing wall, an orchard, perhaps a low population of easily discouraged birds. There would be no human shoes by the door. No one to leave an empty pair behind.

One more witch, then. I took the card in my teeth.

By the time Miri came home, a bramble had caught my tail, an ordinary dog had challenged me, and someone had offered me a sausage roll in a manner I found difficult to refuse. I was wet through, my long black fur plastered to my sides. For reasons concerning the disposal of a siege engine in my fourth life, I dislike drying myself by magic.

Miri found me under her building's front steps. She had dark hair twisted into a loose bun, a grey hoodie over her uniform, and two black paper ears sticking out of her bag. One ear was crushed.

“Oh,” she said. “You're awful.”

I looked behind me. There was no other cat.

She crouched and held out two fingers. I permitted an inspection. She had a small scar on her thumb and smelled of poster paint, apples, and somebody else's dog.

“Have you got anyone?”

I had had eight.

Before I could answer, she took off her hoodie, wrapped it around me, and carried me upstairs.

Her flat was on the fourth floor. The sitting room had a tall window, a small sofa, and a radiator with one hot end and one cold end. Miri tested them with her hand, laid a towel beside the hot end, and unwrapped me.

“Stay there. I'm asking Mum.”

She fetched her phone. There was a brief exchange about fleas, followed by a longer exchange about whose job it would be to buy food.

“Until we find out where he's from,” she said at last. “Yes. I know.”

She put the phone down.

“Temporary. Don't get ideas.”

On the towel, without being asked, she had folded one corner into a pillow.

I sat beside it. A sensible familiar does not become attached before establishing the terms of an assignment.

“I am here,” I told her, “to keep you happy.”

Miri stared. Then she looked at the television, which was off, and out through the sitting-room door.

“Dulcie?”

“No.”

She got down on her knees and examined the radiator.

“Where's the speaker?”

“Inside the cat.”

She checked beneath the sofa.

It was not an auspicious beginning.

***

The following morning I brought her sunshine.

It was precise sunshine, a circle three paces across, centred on Miri as she walked to school. Rain fell all around it. Her shoes remained dry. For four hundred yards I considered myself successful.

Then a boy across the road pointed. Miri shut her umbrella, opened it again, and stopped beneath a shop awning until I withdrew the circle.

“It's a gap in the clouds,” she said.

“A particularly attentive gap.”

“Don't do that at school.”

Sunshine was only the first of my provisions.

I had noticed her unhappiness over a page of arithmetic the previous evening. After she went to bed, I moved the ink into its proper arrangements. At lunchtime she returned to the flat carrying a sheet marked twenty out of twenty.

“You changed my homework.”

She was not smiling.

“The calculations were incorrect.”

“Yes. They're supposed to be my wrong answers.”

This seemed an unusual educational policy, but I was willing to learn.

“Mr Senn asked me to do the last one on the board. Because apparently I'd found a really interesting way.” She dropped the sheet in front of me. “I couldn't even read it.”

The interesting way had been devised by a woman who counted enemy soldiers from the intervals between their footsteps. I had perhaps been ambitious.

“Were you punished?”

“He thought somebody had done it for me.”

I examined the paper. There was room beneath the score for a correction.

“I can explain.”

“To my teacher? A cat?”

“My previous witches found me persuasive.”

“Your previous witches.” Miri rubbed both hands over her face. “Right. We're doing this properly.”

She took her last two biscuits out of a tin and put them on the table. I made my way towards them.

“No. On the towel.”

“You are offering an unclear incentive.”

She set a clear glass bowl over one biscuit, put her phone on a shelf, and asked me to move the biscuit without touching anything. I lifted it through the unbroken glass, brought it down, and lifted it again. She checked the glass, the table, the biscuit, and my paws.

“Again.”

I obliged.

“Now the other one.”

I obliged. Both biscuits revolved above the bowl. It was a tedious little orbit, but she watched it for some time.

“So,” she said.

I waited.

“Magic.”

“Yes.”

She sat down. A bus went by outside. The biscuits continued on their stately course.

“Does that mean I'm supposed to be able to do it?”

“Not unless you have omitted something from your description of yourself.”

She tried making one finger look commanding. Nothing happened.

“Good,” she said. “I've got enough homework.”

She made me put her arithmetic back as it had been. Then she ate one biscuit and gave me the other.

“You help when I ask. All right? No doing things to my stuff. Or to people.”

I agreed. Negotiating terms was familiar ground.

“And you're not a wizard called something ridiculous, are you?”

I considered telling her three of my titles.

“Bramble will do,” she said. “You've still got a bit in your tail.”

***

Dulcie arrived after school with a small keyboard and a bag of costume fur. She had two tight plaits, broad hands, and a laugh that began with a snort she tried to conceal by coughing.

“Mum says there isn't room for this in the car,” she said, setting down the keyboard. “So I'm leaving it with you.”

Miri plugged it in without answering.

They were performing at the school fête the next evening. They had performed the same song for three years, although Dulcie said it was now embarrassing and Miri said that was the point. I gathered the song concerned two cats who stole increasingly improbable objects.

“We ate the moon,” they sang.

“We ate the mayor.”

“We ate his most expensive chair.”

An indictment of municipal greed. I approved.

Dulcie played the wrong chord and they laughed so hard that Miri had to sit on the floor. I watched from the window. Her happiness, when it appeared, was easy to recognise. Getting it to appear was the difficulty.

“Last verse,” Dulcie said.

Miri picked up an ear. “This needs more tape.”

“We can do it without the ears.”

“It keeps falling over.”

They did the second verse again. Then Dulcie looked at her phone and began winding the cable around the keyboard.

“We haven't finished,” Miri said.

“I've still got to pack my bedroom.”

“You've been packing for weeks.”

“Yes, and somehow my bedroom's still in it.”

Miri put another piece of tape on the ear.

When the door had closed, she remained on the floor with the tape stuck to one finger.

“Where is she being sent?” I asked.

“Moving. She isn't being sent anywhere.”

“Ah.”

“Her mum got a different job. It's a good job.” She peeled the tape away. “Everyone keeps telling me that.”

“How far?”

“Four hours on the train.”

I had once crossed a winter kingdom in twenty-three minutes. I knew a way through distance, several ways around it, and a way to fold it which had unfortunately left my fourth witch's kitchen facing the wrong mountain.

“I could bring her back.”

“She's not a library book, Bramble.”

“I was contemplating a visit.”

“Then she'll go again.”

She began collecting the little pieces of tape. I went to the window, where the dying light lay warm on the sill. In my second life a witch had worn yellow shoes so I could pick her out among the wounded. I could still remember them standing side by side beneath her empty bed.

Miri stopped beside me and rubbed the place behind my ear where the bramble had caught.

“At least you don't have to move away,” she said.

I did not tell her about the orchard.

***

The fête was held in the school hall. There were stalls along the walls, a stage at one end, and high windows looking towards the city. Children ran between the chairs with prizes that appeared to consist chiefly of smaller objects inside larger objects. Someone had made a cake in the shape of a dragon and then cut off its head.

Miri brought me in a basket. Since I had agreed to help only when asked, I refrained from correcting the sign that said NO ANIMALS EXCEPT ASSISTANCE ANIMALS.

“You are assisting,” she whispered.

That was satisfactory.

There was already a spare costume ear in the basket. I sat on it.

Dulcie's mother had arranged a hired car to collect her from the school at five to eight. Her mother and their two large suitcases would be waiting in it. The train left at sixteen minutes past eight. These details were written on a scrap of paper tucked into Dulcie's keyboard case, as if writing them made them less likely to happen.

At half past seven, the girls put on their ears and drew whiskers on one another with a soft black pencil. Miri had changed out of her uniform blouse, but kept her skirt and the grey hoodie. Dulcie wore a red cardigan with one sleeve stretched over her palm.

“Do we want to run the ending?” Dulcie asked.

“We know it.”

“We haven't done it once.”

“We know it, Duls.”

Dulcie shut the keyboard case. For a moment her face was unlike the face she used with Miri. Then she looked down and tugged her sleeve straight.

Beyond the windows, the rain was thinning. Orange light lay between the towers across the city, catching the wet roofs. Miri stood beside my basket and watched it.

“Can you do big things?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“How big?”

“This building would present no particular difficulty.”

She glanced at me, trying to see whether I was joking.

“Could you make tonight not end?”

There were several things I ought to have asked her then. She was thirteen, wearing paper ears, with a piece of tape caught in her hair. I had led witches into rooms from which I knew they would never return. Surely I could give this one an evening.

“I have held places through worse than a sunset,” I said.

Her hand rested on the edge of the basket. She gave a little laugh.

“That would be something.”

At five to eight, their names were finally called. Dulcie glanced at her phone, then picked up the keyboard.

I stepped out of the basket, set my paws squarely on the floor, and opened my shadow.

It travelled beneath the chairs. It climbed the walls, slipping between stone and plaster, and reached out around the school. The working was old and strong. I had held a city inside it while my sixth witch broke the army at its gates. Nothing had entered. Nothing had been taken from us until I let the walls fall.

The hall warmed. The last orange light spread across the windows, and the ceiling shone as though the sun were just above it. Outside, raindrops brightened and hung. They did not stop falling; I kept lifting them as they reached the school, a shining curtain raised again and again. I could feel each of them through the tips of my whiskers.

Onstage, Miri looked towards me. Her eyes were enormous. Then she grinned.

The first verse went badly. Dulcie came in too early; Miri came in too late; they arrived at the mayor's expensive chair together, and the hall laughed. By the second verse they had recovered. Dulcie's fingers bounced on the keys. Miri forgot to be careful with her voice.

I watched her and held the light.

At eight o'clock a man carrying three jars of marmalade walked out of the hall and came back in through the same doorway.

He stopped. Looked behind him. Tried again.

The school clock ticked. Beyond my walls, the city was going dark.

Dulcie's phone, propped beside the keyboard, lit up. She glanced down and missed a note.

“Mum's outside,” she whispered.

“One more verse,” Miri whispered back.

At the rear of the hall a teacher was trying the other door. Each time she crossed the threshold she stepped back into the room. A few children laughed. Then the teacher called for quiet, and they stopped.

Dulcie took her hands off the keys.

“What is it?” Miri said.

The teacher stood at the door with one hand flat against the frame. Through the high window above her, a great black ear rose against the orange light. The shadow of my head sheltered the roof; my tail lay around the far wall.

“Oh,” Miri said.

I went to the stage. Dulcie was looking from the windows to the doors.

“It's all right,” I said. “Nothing can get in.”

Miri crouched in front of me.

“Can we get out?”

The question had never sounded like that during a siege.

There had been a witch, my fifth, who asked me to leave a door open. She was going out to speak to an enemy. I had obeyed, and she had come home. Another had asked the same thing, and hadn't. For a long time I had found it easier to remember the second.

My claws gripped the boards.

“I am holding the school.”

Dulcie had come to the edge of the stage. “Is that your cat?”

“Yes.”

“Is he talking?”

“Yes.”

“Has he shut us in?”

Miri's eyes flicked from the clock to the song sheet. There was time for the last verse now. There was time for an encore. Dulcie's mother could wait outside, and for a little while longer nothing would have to be packed away.

She stood up.

“We can finish it,” she said, very quietly.

Dulcie stared at her.

“I've got to go.”

“I know.”

“Now, Miri.”

“You don't have to sound so pleased.”

Dulcie's face changed. She caught the end of her sleeve, twisted it, and let go.

“I'm not pleased about this.” She pointed at the doors. “I'm scared.”

Miri glanced at me. I had not thought to look at Dulcie's hands. They were shaking.

“You sounded pleased before. You keep checking the time.”

“Because I don't want to miss the train.”

“You can't wait to go.”

“What am I meant to do? Not go? Have Mum give back her job?”

“I didn't say that.”

“You don't say anything. You just go all funny if I talk about it.”

The teacher was asking who had a key. A woman in the front row pulled her small son onto her lap.

Miri looked down at the song sheet. It had a drawing of the two cats in one corner, done when the girls were ten. They had signed their names across the top so their teacher would know it was their own work.

“You're going to have all new friends,” she said.

Dulcie rubbed her nose with the stretched sleeve.

“I hope so.”

Miri held the paper very still.

“I don't know anyone there,” Dulcie said. “I'm allowed to want friends.”

Miri looked towards the microphone. Dulcie had gone back to the keyboard and was lifting her fingers to the keys.

Miri put the song sheet face down.

“Don't play it,” she said.

Dulcie took her hands away.

Miri went to the microphone. It was too high, and she pulled it down with a small, horrible squeal.

“Sorry,” she said. She tried to swallow. “We aren't doing the last bit. Dulcie has to go.”

The hall was quiet now, although a child near the back was crying.

“And this is our last one,” Miri added. Her mouth trembled. “So thank you.”

She did not bow. She folded the song sheet into her pocket, then began pulling the keyboard cable out of its socket. Dulcie knelt beside her, and together they wound it up.

I had meant to hold an evening in which Miri was happy. Instead I had held Dulcie's frightened hands, a mother waiting in a car, a little boy pressed against his mother's coat. And Miri, who could have had her final verse, was giving it up.

My paws had begun to ache. It would have been easier to keep holding. I knew every part of the working. I knew how to make the walls thicker.

“The doors,” I said, in the voice I had used to cross battlefields. Everyone looked at me. “That is my doing. I'm opening them.”

I drew my shadow back through the stone.

The immense head lifted from the roof. The tail uncurled. Light ran down the windows like spilled paint, and the ordinary night came in behind it. Hundreds of raindrops struck the glass at once.

The man with the marmalade tried the door. This time he stayed on the other side. He leaned back into the hall.

“It's open.”

Miri did not look at me. She took the keyboard case from Dulcie and led the way out.

I followed with my tail low.

***

Dulcie's mother was standing beside the hired car. She grabbed Dulcie so hard that the paper ears fell off.

“I could see you through the glass. I couldn't get in. What happened?”

“It was the cat,” Dulcie said into her coat.

The driver looked at me.

“I held the school closed,” I said. “I shouldn't have.”

He got back into the car.

Dulcie's mother loosened her grip enough to look at her watch.

“We can't make it now. We can't.”

It was nine minutes past eight. The station lay beyond a tangle of wet streets, two rows of traffic lights, and the railway's long goods yard. The next train would not leave until morning.

Miri stood with the keyboard case bumping her shin.

“Bramble.”

I looked up. She was still not offering me her hand.

“Could you take us?”

“Yes.”

“All of us. And the cases.” She looked at Dulcie. “If you want.”

Dulcie's mother looked from her watch to the black shape of my shadow, which was already lengthening across the pavement.

“Wait,” she said.

I drew it back under me. She watched until the shadow lay small and still beneath my paws. Her hand remained closed around Dulcie's wrist.

“Can you do that safely?”

“Yes.”

“And if I tell you to put us down?”

“At once.”

She looked along the line of red brake lights in the road, then checked her watch again.

“Dulcie?”

Dulcie reached for Miri's free hand.

“Yes.”

Her mother paid the driver and helped him lift the cases from the boot. I let my body grow to meet my shadow. My back rose higher than the car; rain pattered on the broad bridge of my nose. The driver stood quite still, holding the receipt.

“How do we get on?” Dulcie's mother asked.

I lay down.

She climbed up first, hauling the cases into the hollow between my shoulders. The girls clambered after her. When they were settled, I rose.

“Please keep your claws to yourself,” I said, and leapt.

We crossed the school roof in one bound. For the next, there was only air, so I made it sufficient.

The city dropped beneath us. Rain streaked past my face. Behind my ears, Dulcie made a breathless noise that turned into a shout; Miri answered her, and their hands tightened in my coat. We passed a tower full of lit windows, close enough to see a man stop with a spoon halfway to his mouth.

“That's our bus stop!” Dulcie shouted.

“That's the shop where you dropped all the eggs!”

“You dropped them!”

“You were holding the bag!”

I gave them the length of that street, then turned towards the station. They called places to one another until the platforms came into view. Dulcie's mother, with her arms around both suitcases, was laughing and saying, “Oh, goodness. Oh, goodness,” as if she had misplaced the rest of her vocabulary.

I came down beside the station entrance with three minutes to spare.

There was a brief difficulty over the luggage. I wanted to carry it inside. Dulcie's mother said that she could manage it and that I would not fit through the door. It was a kind lie, and I accepted it.

Miri set down the keyboard case, and Dulcie hugged her. Miri put her face against the red cardigan and held on.

“I'm still cross with you,” Dulcie said.

“I know.”

“Not about the cat. Well. Also about the cat.”

“I'm sorry.”

“I know.”

A departure announcement sounded inside. Dulcie's mother touched her shoulder.

The girls pulled apart. Miri handed over the little paper ears she had picked up outside the school.

“You forgot these.”

“I'll send you a picture of my room.”

“Before you unpack it. So I can see it once.”

Dulcie snorted. Then they were laughing with their faces wet, and then her mother said they really did have to run.

Miri stood beside me until the doors of the station had closed behind them.

“Do you want to see the train leave?” I asked.

She shook her head. After a moment she sat down on the wet step.

I made myself small and sat beside her.

***

We walked home. She had asked to walk.

For much of the way she cried. I could have made the streets warmer, the distance shorter. I kept pace with her ordinary shoes.

At the flat she phoned her mother, who had heard a version of events from the school and required another. It was a long conversation. Miri did not conceal my part in it. Afterwards she sat on the floor and took off her wet socks.

“She says she's talking to you when she gets in.”

“Very well.”

“She sounds worse when she's being polite.”

“I have encountered that.”

The keyboard case stood by the sofa. Miri opened it and put the song sheet inside, with its last verse unsung.

“I liked the bit over the roofs,” she said.

“So did I.”

“You can't shut people in places, Bramble.”

“I know.”

“Even if you think it's good.”

“Yes.”

She closed the case.

“Can you go?” she asked.

I had prepared myself for this on the walk. I had several suitable phrases. The order had not always placed me with gracious people, and a familiar ought to know how to leave.

“Yes.”

“When you're finished with me. Where do you go?”

I told her about the orchard. It had a real location; I had visited it twice, and a gardener there knew exactly where to scratch a cat's chin.

“Is that what you want?”

I looked at the keyboard case. She would outgrow the grey hoodie. There would be other cases, other departures. One day I might be the one watching her hurry through a station door.

“I thought so.”

Miri pulled her knees up beneath her chin.

“I was horrible to Dulcie. She was scared and I still wanted her to finish the song.”

“You let her go.”

“After I was horrible.”

I had no useful correction to offer. We sat without one.

Then Miri said, “If keeping me happy is your job, you can stop. I don't want to be a job.”

There it was. The end of nine lifetimes of service, spoken by a girl with pencil whiskers smudged across her cheek.

“I understand.”

“But you could stay here. As a cat. If Mum says.”

She looked at me properly then. It was an invitation, and she was waiting for an answer.

“I would like that,” I said.

Her phone buzzed. The picture showed Dulcie and her mother in two train seats, their hair blown in every direction. Dulcie had put the paper ears back on. Behind them, the station lights made long bright lines in the window.

Miri made a small, uneven noise. She typed for a while, erased something, and typed again.

Then she got up and went to our tall window. The rain had softened. Lights shone in the flats across the street, and the low clouds caught an amber glow from the city. She stood with her hands in the pockets of her hoodie.

I jumped onto the sill beside her.

“Bramble?”

“Yes?”

“Next time we fly, can we go a bit slower?”

“That will depend on the train.”

She laughed, and put one hand on my back.

I settled my tail over the cold end of the sill. For the rest of that evening we watched the windows come on.

stories.title: The Greatest Conquest
stories.prompt: When the kingdom's most notorious orc chieftain dies, his estranged daughter inherits his greatest conquest: a rundown tavern in the middle of human territory. She's prepared for angry villagers, racist knights, and the occasional assassination attempt. What she isn't prepared for is discovering that her father secretly spent thirty years turning the tavern into neutral ground for the kingdom's most dangerous enemies—and that every one of them considers her their new boss.
stories.body:
# The Greatest Conquest

At the toll post, the knight read Harka's deed twice, then turned it over to look for the trick.

“Your father owned a tavern?”

“Apparently.”

“Here?”

She waited. He glanced from the seal to her green hands.

“You'll find we're particular about who serves decent people.”

“I'm selling it.”

“Sensible.” He held the parchment just beyond her reach. “Keep to the main road. No wandering through the farms.”

Harka took it from him. He had expected her to stretch up; he hadn't expected her to step forward.

She had allowed a week for finding a buyer. Perhaps she could manage it in three days.

Beyond the post, the road forked around an orchard. Fresh wheels had cut deep into both branches. Heavy wagons going uphill, though the barley harvest was over. She looked at the ruts, at a strip of white cloth snagged on a thorn, and then at the knight pretending not to watch her go.

She loosened the knife at her hip.

The tavern stood alone where the branches met again: a sprawling timber building with a sagging stable, a crooked chimney, and a red banner hanging limply from the upper window. On it, a horned skull grinned above two crossed axes.

Her father's banner. Of course he had put it on a public house.

The smaller sign said GOOD ALE. GOOD TALES. Someone had painted over GOOD BEDS.

Harka tied her mare beside an old black carriage. A sword hilt protruded from its luggage. So did a shovel.

Inside smelled of woodsmoke, onions, and wet wool. Candles leaned in their sockets. A stair climbed along the wall behind the bar, its middle steps worn pale. Twenty or thirty people had gathered around the tables, some dressed for a funeral, some for quite different emergencies.

They all stood up.

Harka stopped with the deed in her hand.

“Chief,” said a thin man by the hearth.

She knew him. Not personally. There had been a woodcut nailed to the gate of every town she had entered for the last six years. The artist had given him a villainous beard, but the right little finger missing at the second joint was correct.

Veyr. Two thousand crowns alive. Considerably less with proof.

“You've mistaken me for someone,” she said.

“No.” He inclined his head. “My condolences.”

At the next table, a broad woman in a scarlet scarf put down a cup. Harka recognized the silver staff laid beside it, its head an elaborate knot of finger bones.

“You,” the woman said to Veyr.

He turned. “Dame Cadrel.”

“You were told to use the west door.”

“I did. You were told to face the east wall.”

“I have been facing the east wall for eleven years.”

The candles bent towards Cadrel. Under the table, something scraped along the floor.

“Sit down,” Harka said.

It came out in the voice she used when recruits spotted their first enemy and all tried to stand on the same hill.

Cadrel sat. Veyr sat. The scraping stopped.

Every face turned back to her.

An elderly woman near the bar closed a black book. She wore copper combs in her iron-grey hair and a travelling coat too warm for the room. Something about her yellow eyes made Harka wish she had brought a longer knife.

“You must be tired,” the woman said. “Sit where you please. Your father had the big chair, but it does squeak.”

“Where's the keeper?”

“You've just arrived.”

Harka looked around the room again. A woman with the brand of the king's disbanded Black Company on her cheek. A hooded man whose shadow had antlers although his head did not. At the back, the supposed dead duke of a province Harka had been paid not to enter.

There were enough rewards in this room to purchase a small fort.

“Igrith,” the elderly woman said.

Harka's hand closed on the back of a chair.

Igrith had burned the royal summer palace while the king's grandfather was still in it. People used the foundations as a quarry now.

“You're a dragon.”

“Yes.”

“You're all—”

“Hungry,” said the dead duke. “But we thought we ought to wait.”

Harka put the deed on the bar very carefully.

“I need someone to explain what my father has left me.”

“We hoped you could tell us what to do about the soldiers,” said Igrith.

* * *

Borzug had bought the tavern thirty years ago, after his famous defeat of the king's western army. Harka knew the battle. Every orc child knew it: the broken royal standard, the surrendered swords, the chieftain who had ridden through a burning gate with his beard on fire.

She had not known he subsequently spent four days arguing over the price of the inn.

“He wouldn't pay for the stable,” said Igrith. “He'd burned half of it down.”

“And this?” Harka gestured at the company.

“Came later.”

Some came to buy back captives. Some came to sell information. A defeated general could meet the woman who had defeated him, hire a different army, and leave by another door. No one touched another guest under the roof. Anyone who tried was put outside, where Borzug waited.

Eventually people began coming without any business beyond a meal somewhere their enemies could find them and do nothing about it.

“The Crown?” Harka asked.

“Your father and the old marshal understood one another,” said Cadrel. “The Crown pretended not to know who drank here. Borzug pretended not to know where the Crown's informers sat.”

“Third table by the window,” Veyr said. “One of them had a lovely tenor.”

Harka looked at him.

“He retired.”

“And now?”

Igrith opened the black book. The pages were crowded with names, some scarcely more than scratches, some accompanied by elaborate seals.

“We agreed to keep the peace here and follow Borzug's direction in defending it. Including the direction of the successor he named. Otherwise the first person who outlived him could take the place from everyone else.”

“He named me.”

“Last winter. At that table.”

Harka looked at the empty chair. For a moment she could hear his voice filling the room, his certainty making dissent seem something that would happen later, elsewhere, when he wasn't busy.

He had used that voice with the mountain envoys fourteen years ago. The pass would open in spring. Harka would marry their chief's son at midsummer.

She had told him no. In front of everyone.

Borzug had put a hand on her shoulder and told the envoys not to mind her. She would come round.

By morning she was four miles beyond the clan boundary, carrying a blanket and a knife. She had earned the mare later, and the boots, and the right to tell a captain when he was wrong about a road.

She pushed the black book away.

“I didn't agree to any of this.”

“We know,” said Igrith.

“You could have sent a letter.”

“We told him.”

That answer was worse than an excuse.

Harka picked up the deed. “Then I can leave.”

“Certainly,” said Veyr.

“And you won't stop me?”

He looked faintly offended. “You are not a prisoner.”

The dead duke began putting on his gloves. Someone near the hearth drew a cloak around a sleeping companion. Cadrel folded her scarlet scarf and tucked it inside her coat.

“What happens to you?” Harka asked.

“I go north,” said Cadrel. “He follows.” She nodded at Veyr.

“Not immediately,” he said. “I have other work.”

“I burn this place,” said Igrith. “After everyone leaves. There ought not to be a royal garrison here.”

She said it without looking away from Harka, in the same mild voice she had used about the chair.

A knock sounded at the open door.

The knight from the toll post stood outside, carrying a white cloth on the end of his spear.

“Lord Othred, western marshal of His Majesty's forces, wishes to speak to the daughter of Borzug.”

“Here she is,” said Harka.

He saw past her. His spear dipped.

Veyr raised his cup in greeting.

* * *

The marshal waited on horseback at the orchard's edge. Harka went out alone.

There were sixty men drawn up across the road and two stone-throwers behind them. Men carried bundles of pitch-soaked brushwood towards the machines. A royal standard stirred above the marshal's white plume.

He had come prepared for a wooden building full of people.

Harka stopped where a low fence gave her a view along both branches of the road. On the western one, the tracks she had noticed disappeared through an opening in the orchard wall. The visible stone-throwers had come by the eastern branch.

A tarpaulin lifted among the trees. Under it she glimpsed two enormous paired bows, each mounted on a wheeled frame. Bolt-throwers. Their crews pulled the covering down again.

“My condolences,” said Othred.

“Popular words today.”

He was a lean man with a weathered face and a voice trained to carry without sounding loud. He passed down a document.

It offered eight hundred crowns for the estate. Below that, under his own seal, was a guarantee of safe passage south for Harka, her horse, and her possessions. All other occupants would remain for arrest.

“You have no part in their crimes,” he said. “Your father's quarrel with the Crown need not become yours.”

“And if I refuse?”

“The property will be seized. Today.”

His men could hear. He wanted them to.

“The old marshal left it alone.”

“The old marshal left many things unfinished. I have a new appointment and a royal warrant.” He drew a second paper halfway from his saddle case. “Every outlaw in the kingdom seems to have come to the funeral. An opportunity like this will not recur.”

Harka looked at the stone-throwers. “There are rooms upstairs.”

“They will be invited to surrender.”

“And the brushwood?”

“An encouragement.”

She folded the offer.

Othred studied her for a moment. “Take the south road. My men will let you through. You have until the bell.”

At the tavern she untied her mare. The south road lay clear, descending between the harvested fields. She could pass the toll post before they finished loading those machines.

Through the open door she saw Cadrel rolling up a map. Veyr was checking the latch of the west window. Neither looked towards her.

If she stopped the seizure, she could still sell tomorrow.

She had been given a horse once before, for a journey someone else had arranged. A good horse. A wedding gift. She had left it in the stable.

This mare turned her head and blew impatiently against Harka's wrist. Harka had bought her with three seasons' pay. She could ride her anywhere.

She retied the reins.

Inside, Igrith was putting away the book.

“I'd like to know what each of you can do,” Harka said.

The dragon's yellow eyes brightened.

“Be specific,” Harka added. “I already know you can make this much worse.”

* * *

“There are two more engines in the orchard,” she told them. “And another body of men. Those on the road are meant to draw you out. The ones under cover will shoot into your flank.”

Igrith had unbuttoned her coat. Under it she wore a dress the colour of old copper.

“It has been some time since an arrow troubled me.”

“These are engines, not bows. They brought something they believe will trouble you. Can you get behind them?”

“Yes.”

“Without flying straight over the road?”

Igrith smiled, and Harka saw how little of the woman belonged to the smile.

Cadrel leaned on her staff. “The orchard was a battlefield before it grew apples. I can reach it from the fence.”

“How many?”

“Enough.”

“Keep the soldiers off their feet. Let them breathe.”

Cadrel's fingers stopped moving on the silver shaft.

“Othred commanded at the burning of my tower,” she said. “I know how he encourages surrender.”

“We need his men alive to walk home and tell people what happened.”

“We don't need him.”

“I do. Veyr will bring him.”

The assassin looked up from tying back his sleeves.

“Alive,” Harka said.

“He will be loud.”

“Then bring him loudly.”

Around them, the others listened. Harka put the Black Company woman in charge of keeping the yard clear. The dead duke had four loyal men who, remarkably, had not even pretended to die with him. They took the kitchen door and the stable. The antler-shadowed man listened to something no one else could hear, then told Harka there were indeed men among the trees.

“Tell me when they load,” she said.

He nodded.

Cadrel had not moved.

Harka faced her. She had commanded frightened people before. She had commanded exhausted people, and once a man whose brother had just died. She had never commanded someone who could reach into a battlefield and lift its dead.

“Can you do it?” she asked.

“You ask for the difficult thing.”

“Yes.”

Cadrel's staff tapped once against the floor.

“Then you had better give your signal clearly.”

Outside, a soldier on the road began ringing a bell.

Igrith went out through the kitchen, shedding her coat as she walked. The duke caught it. A moment later the chickens in the yard began making a terrible noise.

Harka took her place at the fence. From here she could see the marshal and the gap in the orchard wall; Cadrel, standing in the doorway, could see her.

The toll knight called the invitation to surrender. Harka let him finish. She wanted the men on the road looking towards the tavern.

Behind the trees, branches broke.

“They are loading,” said the antler-shadowed man.

Harka raised her arm.

Cadrel's free hand opened. The orchard soil heaved.

A soldier shouted. Beyond the wall, ranks broke apart as pale hands closed around ankles and dragged men gently, horribly down into the fallen leaves. Old helmets emerged beneath the apple trees. Bones unfolded, streaming earth. Cadrel's fingers flexed, and a hundred long-buried soldiers lifted their shields between the living and the engines.

Othred wheeled his horse. “Loose!”

Veyr shifted beside the fence, ready to move. Harka caught his sleeve.

“Wait. Let them see Igrith first.”

The first bolt struck the tavern's corner post. Chips stung her cheek. The Black Company woman swore and pulled the antler-shadowed man down.

Harka stayed where she could see.

The hidden engine crews were turning their weapons towards Cadrel. Men on the road looked into the orchard, searching for the threat.

Then Igrith rose behind them.

She came up above the trees in a shower of leaves, black wings spreading wider than the tavern's roof. Copper plates shone along her throat. One enormous claw closed around an engine's bowstave; wood cracked like a dropped basket. She lowered her head and breathed a narrow line of white fire along the second machine.

Its crew ran. She let them.

Every horse on the road tried to leave at once.

“Now.” Harka dropped her arm.

Veyr slipped through the fence and was gone.

Othred's horse reared. The marshal fought it down, still calling orders, while his men tried to decide which direction offered the least dragon.

Cadrel turned her wrist. The dead came over the wall.

They caught reins. They pressed shields against breastplates. They lowered the living carefully to the road, and held them there. A swordsman hacked through a bony arm; another hand caught his wrist. The bell fell from its ringer's hand.

Igrith struck the stone-throwers on the road from above. One collapsed beneath her weight. She picked up the other in her jaws and flung it into the empty field.

Harka saw Veyr on the far side of the marshal's horse.

Then the white plume vanished.

There was still shouting, still the scrape of iron on stone. But no one was looking at the tavern now.

“Hold,” Harka called to Cadrel.

“I am holding.”

Sweat stood on the woman's upper lip. Her hand trembled, and along the road the dead tightened their grip.

A pinned soldier's calls broke off. His free hand beat against the shield above his chest.

“Looser, Cadrel. He needs air.”

Cadrel eased her fingers apart. The shield lifted a little, and the soldier got an elbow beneath it before the dead caught his wrist. He dragged in a breath and began loudly thanking every god he could remember.

Veyr arrived with the marshal's arm twisted behind his back and a knife under his jaw.

He was loud.

Harka left the fence and backed towards the tavern, watching the knife.

“Put that away,” Harka said.

“We have not reached the door.”

“We have now.”

At the threshold, Veyr stopped. Harka held his eyes until he took the blade away and released the arm.

Othred stumbled. She caught his elbow. He jerked free, knocking her hand aside.

Behind them, Cadrel stood very still.

“You can lower your hand,” Harka told her. “Have them hold the road. No chasing.”

Slowly, Cadrel set both palms against her staff. In the field beyond the open door, the dead stood motionless over the fallen men.

“A hostage,” Othred said, looking around the room. “Your father's daughter after all.”

Harka felt the words where he had intended them.

Veyr's knife had not quite disappeared into its sheath. Cadrel was watching the marshal's throat. From the kitchen came a crash, then Igrith's human voice asking who had put a lintel there.

Harka moved away from the doorway.

“You were captured in a battle. Under this roof no one will hurt you. You're free to leave.”

“Harka,” said Cadrel.

She had not used her name before.

“He goes safely,” Harka said. “Whether he gives me anything or not.”

Veyr sheathed the knife.

Othred looked from her to the open door. “My men.”

“They put their weapons down, Cadrel lets them stand up, and they walk home. We won't follow them.”

“And their horses?”

“Those too.”

Igrith appeared in the kitchen doorway, barefoot, fastening her coat. There was a blackened apple twig in her hair. The royal standard lay furled around its pole under her arm.

“Must we give back the standard?”

“Yes.”

“I hadn't asked to keep it.”

“You were about to.”

The marshal took one step towards the door. No one moved to stop him. He could reach his men. Send messengers. Fetch more men, if he could find any willing to march down this road before morning.

Harka wanted him to sit down so badly her hands ached.

“I'd like to discuss your warrant,” she said.

He turned back. “You think this makes you safe?”

“No. I think you thought we weren't.”

Outside, a man called for help with his horse. The horse was quite unharmed. It simply refused to come within twenty paces of the tavern.

Othred looked at his seal on the offer Harka had laid on the bar. Then he took off his gloves.

“I will need a chair.”

* * *

They did not make peace. There were too many people in the room with good reasons to dislike it, including the marshal.

They made terms for a withdrawal. Othred wrote an order suspending the seizure, and safe passage for everyone leaving the tavern, valid throughout his command. He would carry an offer to renew the old understanding to the king. Until the king answered, there would be no second attempt on the property.

“His Majesty may refuse,” he said.

“Then send someone to tell me before he sends another army,” said Harka.

She brought the paper outside and had the marshal read it to his men. They watched her, and the dead standing over their discarded weapons, and the elderly woman picking splinters from her sleeve. None of them would go home unsure who had given the orders.

Cadrel lifted her hand. The dead withdrew into the orchard. The living got up.

By dusk the royal standard was a small white mark on the south road. Veyr had given it back. Harka had watched him do it.

She washed the wood dust from her face at the kitchen basin. Her hands shook now. There was a shallow cut on one cheek she hadn't felt until the water touched it.

In the next room, someone began arguing about who had ordered the onions.

Harka sat on the worn stair and pulled off her boots.

For a while she listened. The dead duke had resumed being dead in the eyes of a guest who insisted he had attended the burial. Igrith wanted her book. Veyr was asking Cadrel whether eleven years facing a wall had improved her opinion of it.

Her father's chair stood empty.

When she was small, he had let her stand on the toes of his boots while they waited for the first snow. He would take enormous slow steps across the yard, and she would give the orders. Left. Right. Faster.

Later, he had stopped listening when she told him where she wanted to go.

She had thought leaving meant she would never miss the earlier man again.

Cadrel turned her cup between her hands.

“Othred burned my tower with my brother inside,” she said.

The room quieted. Harka had no answer that would make releasing him kind to her.

“I didn't know about your brother,” she said.

“Now you do. Don't forget it next time you ask something difficult.”

“I won't.”

Cadrel drank. She did not look satisfied. She did not leave.

Veyr came over carrying a small stack of sealed letters.

“These arrived for your father. We thought we should wait.”

Harka took the top one. Under a black wax seal, someone had written REQUEST FOR A PRIVATE ROOM. At the bottom, in a different hand: HE MUST NOT WEAR THAT RIDICULOUS CROWN THIS TIME.

“Who is this from?” she asked.

“The king's two exiled brothers. They want the room a week from Thursday. Each has asked us to bar the other.”

Harka set her bare feet on the step below. There was an empty chair at the head of the table, but from here she could see both doors.

“Write back,” she said. “I'll see them then. One at a time.”

stories.title: The Queen They Knew
stories.prompt: When the Dark Queen finally dies, the world celebrates. Her armies collapse, her cursed forests begin to thaw, and the surviving kingdoms prepare for an age of peace. Then her estranged daughter arrives to claim the throne. Unlike her mother, she has no interest in conquest, cruelty, or forbidden magic. Unfortunately, the monsters bound to the royal bloodline don't recognize the difference.
stories.body:
# The Queen They Knew

For six days, Orsane heard how happy everyone was that her mother was dead.

At the southern ports they gave away wine. Inland, a woman stood outside a posting house with the names of her missing sons pinned to her coat, laughing so hard she could scarcely breathe. Soldiers came down the north road without their badges. Some had deserted; some said there was no army left to desert. Their generals had fled with the pay chests when the Dark Queen fell.

Orsane bought a horse. She joined in one toast. She found that she could be glad and still wake at night with something unfinished to say.

Snow had begun on the warm southern evening the messenger found her. By morning, it lay thick on the inn's courtyard. It fell at the next town too. From a hill beyond that town she had looked back and seen sunlight on the roofs, while the white cloud moved with her along the road. Her mother's winter had passed to her without asking what she wanted.

On the seventh day she entered her mother's forest.

Snow still loaded the firs, but it had begun slipping from the branches in heavy, wet falls. A brown run of earth showed through the road. Beside it, the stump of a cursed tree put out a single green shoot.

Fresh snow filled the hoofprints behind her. Beyond the falling white curtain, the farther hillside ran dark with thaw.

She dismounted to look.

The horse screamed.

Vask came between the trees, folding his wings to pass. Black fur brushed the trunks at either side of him. His horns swept back over his shoulders, and his yellow eyes were level with Orsane's head even before he straightened his forelegs.

He had carried her on his back when she was small enough to sleep between those horns.

She put a hand over her horse's eyes. With the other she caught Vask's lowering muzzle.

“You still smell of snow,” she said.

“You smell of foreign soap.” His breath stirred her white hair. “We have waited a long time.”

“I didn't come back for her.”

“No, Majesty.”

Far away, a bell began to ring. Vask's ears turned toward it.

“They've been doing that for days,” Orsane said.

“My sister will stop them.”

“I like bells.”

He considered this. “Then we shall make them continue.”

She looked up at him. Twelve years away, and he still made it possible for a person to be cruel simply by enjoying a sound.

“Nobody is to be made to do anything about bells.”

Vask lowered himself. She could have stepped from the road onto the broad place between his wings. As a child, she would already have been climbing.

“I have a horse,” she said.

He walked beside her instead.

There had been creatures near her lodgings on the journey north. Once, at dusk, every dog in a village had crawled under something and stayed there. At an inn, she had found a huge print in the kitchen garden, close enough to the back door that the cook must have stepped inside it on her way to gather herbs. Orsane had left before breakfast. The next night the print appeared outside a different inn.

“You found me at the coast?”

“At the second posting house. I went ahead to the crags and told Leth. The others are waking.”

“I thought they might follow me.”

“Always.”

He said it with such love that she had to look at the road.

The old blood-binding required them to keep her alive. It gave her no power to make them obey. She had come north to put a throne and castle walls between that devotion and the people she had lived among. She was beginning to doubt that walls would be enough.

By the time they reached the castle, the road was white again. Old drifts banked the northern walls; fresh snow blew across the courtyard and gathered on the unshovelled steps. Leth lay along the gatehouse roof. She was pale where Vask was black, with the same great wings and backward horns. She lifted her head when Orsane passed beneath her.

“Little thorn.”

Orsane stopped. Her mother had called her that; Leth had made it affectionate by saying it with a whole apple balanced on her nose.

“Leth.”

“Your crown is waiting.”

“I don't want her wars.”

The pale creature's lip lifted from her teeth. “Of course. You shall have your own.”

Inside, the servants had taken down the banners and had not known what to put in their place. Bare rectangles marked the walls. Someone had washed the throne room, but a scorch reached from the foot of the dais to the broken western windows. Snow drifted through them onto the blackened stone. Servants stood with their hands tucked beneath their arms, watching it settle.

Her mother's crown rested on a cushion, black thorns set with red stones. Orsane put it on. One of the points caught in her hair.

Marshal Harnet watched from beside the doors. He had come that morning to meet the reported heir.

He had surrendered his weapons to the castle steward. His right hand was bandaged, two fingers stiffly splinted. He looked less like the man who had ended a reign of terror than a tired guest who had arrived before his room was ready.

“Your face,” he said, then stopped.

“Yes.” Orsane freed the caught hair. “I'm told the resemblance is considerable.”

“I had hoped the reports about a daughter were wrong.”

“I hoped a great many reports about my mother were wrong. Come in.”

He came as far as the scorch.

Orsane sat on the throne. She had imagined that doing so would feel like an answer to something. The stone was cold through her black skirts.

“I am Orsane, her daughter. I claim the throne.”

Harnet's jaw tightened.

“And I want a ceasefire while we discuss what that means.”

“The kingdoms are meeting in my capital in three days. If you send an envoy—”

Vask moved.

Harnet struck the floor before Orsane could rise. One enormous forepaw covered his chest. Vask bent to smell him.

“You held her.”

Harnet tried to draw breath.

“Vask.”

“You held her while the swords went in.”

For a moment Orsane could think only of his hands on her mother's wrists.

Orsane ran down the steps and put herself between his muzzle and the marshal. Vask drew back so quickly that his horns scraped the wall.

“Lift your foot.”

He did, though he kept it over Harnet.

“He came under truce.”

“I understand.” Vask's voice softened. “You wish to keep him.”

She knelt. Harnet pushed her hand away and got to his elbows himself.

“I wish him to go home alive.”

Vask glanced toward the western windows. “That may distress you.”

Outside, the gatehouse roof was empty.

Orsane stood slowly.

“Where is Leth?”

“West.”

Harnet looked up.

“I told her your blood was home,” Vask said. “She asked whether the kingkillers still had their city. I said they did.”

“Call her back.”

“She is beyond hearing.”

“Then call the others.”

“They went with her.”

Orsane stared at him. “You knew I wanted peace.”

“Yes, Majesty.”

“What do you think peace is?”

His ears sank a little. He seemed hurt to be asked something so elementary.

“No one left who can hurt you.”

Harnet made a short sound. He was trying to stand.

“How many?” he asked.

Vask did not look at him. “Enough.”

Orsane reached for one of the straps of the old riding harness still hanging beneath Vask's folded wing.

“Take me there.”

He recoiled. “They will finish before evening. There is no need for you to see—”

“I am going. You can carry me, or you can watch me take the horse.”

For a moment she thought he would put a paw over her too.

Harnet caught the second strap.

“I'm coming.”

“You can barely stand,” she said.

“They won't lower a bow because you ask them.”

Vask looked from one to the other. Then he lay down.

They flew west over the thawing forest, beneath a low white cloud that kept pace with them. When Vask banked, the snowfall banked with Orsane. It whitened his back and streamed behind his wings, laying a fresh swathe across the brown breaks in the woods. Beyond that moving winter, the thaw continued.

Orsane's skirts snapped against Vask's flanks, black lace over dark red. Cold pinched her bare shoulders. Harnet clung behind her, his breath white beside her cheek. Below, people moved along roads that had been closed for a generation, carrying bundles and pulling handcarts toward the western valley.

She had met one of those families the previous day. A man had shown her an iron key and said he was going to find out whether his front door still existed. He had asked if she was going home too.

She had said yes.

Vask turned his head far enough for one yellow eye to find her.

“You needn't be afraid.”

“I am afraid for them.”

He looked down at the moving dots.

“I know,” he said gently.

That gentleness frightened her more than his teeth.

“You don't know. You think I'm saying it because he's listening.”

Harnet's grip tightened on her belt.

Vask flew on.

“Do you remember the fox?” she asked.

His wings changed their beat. “In the south courtyard.”

“I asked you to let it go.”

“Your mother let it reach the gate before she loosed the hounds.”

“I was eight.”

“You hid beneath my wing.”

“I was crying.”

He was silent so long that she thought the wind had taken the words.

“She said you were laughing,” he said at last.

Orsane remembered his fur against her mouth. She had been trying to be quiet. Her mother had grown so angry when she cried in front of guests.

“You could feel me shaking.”

Vask's head turned forward again.

“I could feel you,” he said.

The western valley opened beneath them.

Smoke rose from an orchard outside the capital. The eastern gate stood open for the people hurrying in from the road. On the towers, little figures wound the great bows.

Above the city wheeled the creatures her mother had kept for difficult sieges.

Orsane had never seen so many in daylight. Some had shapes she could name. Others made her eyes search for missing pieces of familiar animals. They circled the roofs, keeping the city under their shadows.

Leth had landed on the eastern gatehouse. Men ran from beneath her feet.

“The wall,” Orsane said.

Vask banked away.

She hauled on the harness. It was like trying to steer a hill.

“The wall, Vask.”

“There are weapons.”

“And people. Put me beside them.”

An arrow struck his shoulder and vanished into the fur. Harnet rose against the straps, shouting his own name.

The snowfall reached the eastern wall with them, sweeping over stones that had been bare a moment before. Vask landed hard on the wall walk beside the gatehouse. Stone broke beneath his claws. A young soldier stared at the crown through the falling white, then aimed a crossbow at Orsane's face.

“Stand down,” Harnet said.

“Marshal—”

“Look at me. Stand down.”

Orsane slid from Vask's back. Her knees nearly failed. She gripped the parapet until she could trust them.

Across the gap in the wall walk, Leth lifted her head.

“Little thorn?”

“Stop the attack.”

Leth's gaze moved to Harnet, then to the crossbow still shaking in the soldier's hands.

Her wings opened.

“They have you.”

“I came here.”

Leth screamed. Across the city, the creatures turned from the roofs and towers toward Orsane at the gate.

“Back!” Harnet pushed Orsane against the parapet and raised a discarded shield over her. Something struck it hard enough to drive him to one knee. Above the rim, she saw a hooked foot withdraw into the sky.

The soldier with the crossbow began to sob. He lowered the loaded bow, unable to hold it steady.

“I've made it worse,” Orsane said.

Vask thrust his head between her and the sky. “Get on.”

Beyond his shoulder, Leth crossed the broken walk in one jump. Her pale forepaw closed on Harnet's shield. She ripped it away.

“No,” Orsane said.

Leth reached for him.

A short sword lay against the parapet. Orsane snatched it with both hands and drove it into the crease above the reaching claws.

The shock went up her arms. Leth shrieked. The blade twisted out of Orsane's grip, opening her palm, and clattered down the steps.

Leth stared at her.

Orsane put her bleeding hand on Harnet's shoulder.

“You leave him alone.”

“What have they done to you?”

The pale creature's voice was almost tender.

Vask caught Orsane by the back of her dress. She felt the cloth tighten beneath her arms, felt her heels leave the stone.

“Put me down!”

“I can get you clear.”

She caught his lower jaw with both hands, just as she had on the forest road.

“You can get me clear,” she said, breathless. “Then what?”

He held her above the walk. Snow gathered on the black lace stretched between his teeth.

She could see it in his face: the flight home, the closed doors, his wing over her while the city screamed. He would keep every sharp thing away from her. He would be so gentle.

“I won't go with you.”

His grip loosened. Her feet touched stone.

“They held your mother,” he said.

“I know.”

“They killed her.”

“I know.” Her injured hand slipped on his jaw. She held on with the other. “Help me keep them alive.”

His eye was close enough for her to see herself in it, small beneath the crooked crown.

Leth struck at Harnet over Orsane's shoulder.

Vask's wing came down between the marshal and her claws. They pierced the membrane. He made a sound Orsane had never heard from him, then shoved Harnet and the young soldier back beneath the wing's great ribs.

Leth climbed onto the gatehouse roof to reach around him.

“Move, brother.”

Below the arch, a cart overturned. People were pressed shoulder to shoulder there. Orsane saw an iron key swinging from a man's neck as he tried to lift a child above the crush.

A roof beam split beneath Leth's forefoot.

Vask braced his shoulder under the sagging eave before it could fall into the packed arch. The movement opened his throat to her.

“Let me take her,” Leth said. “You can keep those two when we've finished here.”

Orsane looked up at the pale muzzle. Leth had once held an apple there until an impatient little girl stopped crying long enough to laugh.

“Leth. I am staying.”

“You do not know what you want.”

Orsane stepped beneath the reaching paw. It stopped above her hair. Leth lifted it over her and hooked the eave farther along, beyond Orsane's reach. Tiles slid into the gateway. The man with the key bent over the child.

“Vask,” Orsane said. “Kill her.”

He did not move at once.

Leth looked at him. Their horns almost touched.

Then he heaved the broken eave outward and lunged. His jaws closed on Leth's throat.

Orsane dragged Harnet back. The roof tipped away from the gateway and spilled down the outer face of the wall. Vask and Leth went over with it. A white wing beat once above the parapet.

When Vask rose, he rose alone.

Leth lay in the road beyond the carts. Her head was at an angle it had never taken in sleep.

Vask looked down at her. Orsane waited for him to turn on her. It seemed impossible that he should carry that face back to her and do anything else.

He landed on the broken gatehouse, facing outward.

The sky came down on him.

“Under his wing!” Orsane shouted.

Harnet caught the young soldier by the collar and pulled him into shelter. Orsane snatched up the fallen shield. A narrow head darted between two of his wing's great ribs and she struck at it with the shield's edge until it withdrew.

Vask could not spring without exposing the people below him. He fought where he stood, tearing one attacker out of the air, hurling another toward the empty slope. A third landed beside Orsane. It looked from her shield to the dead white shape below the wall.

“They hold you?” it whispered.

She shook her head.

It stretched its neck toward her, offering its back. She did not climb on. After a moment it edged away, then launched itself from the wall and did not return.

The others kept coming.

Orsane found a gap beneath Vask's torn wing and pointed through it.

“Vask, throw the creatures east, over the orchard. The carts are clear. Harnet, the stairs—”

“I see them.”

He sent the soldier down to bring up the spears. Orsane held the shield over Vask's exposed foreleg while he turned. She could not tell how much time passed. Her arms shook; each blow knocked the iron rim against her crown. Snow crusted the handle between her stiffening fingers. Once Vask stumbled, and hands she did not know reached out beside hers to hold the shield in place.

The spears came up. Men who had been trying to kill him less than an hour before stood beneath his wings and stabbed at anything that came through.

A blunt-headed creature settled on the parapet and opened its jaws wide enough to take the sheltering wing. Orsane raised herself behind the shield. The jaws checked. It could not bite through to the men without taking her too.

It thrust its snout into the narrow gap beneath the wing instead. A spear caught in its jaw. It recoiled, wrenching the shaft from the soldier's hands, and climbed into the air with the wood still hanging from its mouth. Once it circled back. Vask waited, his wing braced against the stone, spear points beneath it. The creature turned toward the forest.

Another followed. The next tried the same gap and was driven back. Those still circling began making single, wary approaches, testing for a way past Vask's teeth and the spears.

At last there was room between the shapes in the sky. Then there were only a few, circling beyond the bow range. One by one, they went toward the forest.

Vask stayed facing outward until the last had vanished.

Orsane set the shield down. She could not make her fingers let go of its handle.

Harnet prised them loose.

“Not your sword hand?” he asked.

She laughed once, painfully. “I don't have one.”

He took a strip of cloth from his coat and bound her palm. Neither of them looked over the wall.

Below, people were being carried away from the gate. Others knelt in the trampled snow calling names. The man with the key stood holding the child, staring at the ruin that had missed them.

“This doesn't buy you a kingdom,” Harnet said.

“I have one.”

“It doesn't buy you peace.”

“Will you give me a day?”

He looked at Vask's ruined wing. “A day.”

She went to Vask.

He stood with his head hanging beyond the parapet. She rested her forehead against his cheek. He did not lean into her as he once would have done.

“You asked me to kill her,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I heard you.”

Orsane shut her eyes. Beneath her hand his fur was warm, and the muscles in his jaw would not stop trembling.

They stayed on the wall through the night. Vask would not leave it, and Orsane would not leave him. Snow banked against the broken parapet and lay deep on the gatehouse ruins. The people still sheltering beneath his wing pressed closer to his warm fur; Orsane made room for the young soldier beside her. She slept briefly against Vask's foreleg, waking whenever someone was brought up the stairs to ask whether the monsters would return.

At dawn, snow was still falling around them. A bell rang inside the city.

Vask's head came up. His good wing opened. Orsane felt the people sheltering beside them go still.

Then he turned and looked at her face.

stories.title: The Wrong Sort
stories.prompt: Fairy wings reveal their owner's magical bloodline, and the elaborate patterns determine everything from social standing to whom they're permitted to marry. Hers were supposed to mark her as the next royal heir. Instead, she tattooed over the sacred markings, pierced her ears with cold iron, and joined a band of magical outcasts. Nobody realized that changing the patterns on her wings would also change the ancient laws they represented
stories.body:
# The Wrong Sort

Nim had asked Veska for one love song.

She knew three songs, and two concerned the deaths of kings. They compromised on the third, which concerned a landlord being carried away by crows. There was a verse about fidelity, if you listened generously.

Hox kept time on his father's copper-bellied drum. Nim played the fiddle against his shoulder, his six narrow wings trembling to the tune: three green as young leaves, three smoky brown. No herald had ever found an approved name for that combination. On the palace family trees, people like Nim were left out.

Here, he had his name scratched into the fiddle.

Veska sang on the plank stage between them, violet-streaked hair escaping its knot. Her boots were too heavy, her blue shirt had an orange pumpkin grinning across it, and cold iron throbbed in the ear piercings she had acquired on the day she left the palace. When she spread her great moth wings, people cheered. Black briars climbed through the cream and violet bands, curling over the golden crescent eyespots that had occupied twenty-four years of other people's attention.

This afternoon, Nim had finished the briar, driving a thorn through one sacred crescent.

He had asked what she wanted.

“Something they'll hate.”

“That leaves a lot of room. What do you like?”

She had thought of the palace gardener stripping every thorn from the roses before allowing her to walk among them.

“Briars.”

Nim had drawn her something wicked and alive. She had fallen in love with it before he finished the first leaf.

Now she turned, letting the field see the thorns. A little girl sitting on a pumpkin raised both hands to imitate her wings. Veska nearly missed the verse in which the landlord's wife ran away with the crow.

Eight days with the Wrong Sort. Already they trusted her with the chorus.

Beyond the stage, pumpkins glowed along the furrows. Fairies with unlicensed wings perched on fence rails beside furred people, horned people, people who had left their houses because the houses could not bear what they loved. Someone was passing hot chestnuts through the crowd in an overturned helmet.

The song ended. Hox struck his drum once more.

“Before she learns another,” he said, “we're getting married.”

The applause faltered, then gathered itself into something louder.

Nim laid his fiddle on its case. His smile had gone peculiar. Veska knew it: the smile people wore when they had decided to let a thing hurt them again.

He held out his hand to Hox.

They had tried twice before. They had no reason to expect the law to be kinder in a pumpkin field. But Hox had spent the afternoon polishing his drum, and Nim had borrowed a white ribbon, and neither wanted another year of pretending the refusal did not matter.

An old woman climbed the stage with a willow switch.

“Same terms?” she asked them.

“Same people,” Hox said.

“That wasn't what I asked.”

Nim laughed. Hox's copper wings made a small nervous clatter against the drumstrap.

“Same terms.”

The old woman looped the ribbon around their joined hands. She breathed into the loop, drawing on the ancient pattern as every marriage-maker did. Gold light gathered beneath the white cloth.

On Veska's upper left wing, something warmed.

She glanced back. A black thorn lay across the double crescent that confined each wing-line to its approved partners. For Veska, that had meant seven families. The gold beneath the thorn seemed to be slipping sideways.

“Hand to hand,” said the old woman. “Line to line.”

Nim and Hox braced themselves.

Veska had seen a rejected joining. The ribbon tightened, the old law separated the hands, and everyone found somewhere else to look. She reached for Nim's shoulder.

The ribbon opened.

For a moment it hung in the air like a little gate. Then the ends drew gently around their wrists and settled into two loose white bracelets.

The old woman stared at her switch.

Hox looked at Nim.

“Did you do something?”

“No.”

“Neither did I.”

“Good,” said the old woman, recovering. “Keep it that way.”

Hox kissed his husband so hard the drum banged against Nim's knees.

The field erupted.

Veska laughed with it. Then Nim, still holding Hox, looked over his shoulder at her wing.

The double crescent had opened around the briar thorn. Where a finger's breadth of gold had been, the membrane was plain cream.

For the first time in her life, a herald's lesson failed to tell her what she was looking at.

***

The first royal officer arrived before anyone had finished the wedding chestnuts.

He came with four guards, a lantern, and a sealed silver tube. His eyes passed over the husbands, stopped at Veska, and widened at her wings.

“Don't,” she told him.

He broke the seal.

She heard the beginning of the call, thin and sweet as a remembered lullaby, and then the iron in her ears took it apart. Words remained. The hook beneath them did not.

“By the royal pattern and the regency vested in Orset, Veska of the Crown Eye and Hox of the Copper Circle shall attend the accession at the twelfth bell tomorrow.”

Hox took a step toward the city.

Nim caught his arm.

“I wasn't doing that,” Hox said.

Veska stepped in front of the officer.

“Leave him out of it. Orset's business is with me.”

“The regent requires your musicians beside you, my lady. He would prefer you all to arrive willingly.”

He looked at Nim's mismatched wings and then carefully away. The call had found Hox by his Copper Circle. The regency had never troubled to find a category from which it could call Nim.

Hox took another involuntary step.

“Not yet,” the officer said hastily. “At noon. The summons requires his presence then.”

Hox planted his feet. This time they stayed.

Veska pulled a hoop from her ear, ignoring the sting, and pushed it into the empty piercing above Hox's copper stud. He hissed.

“Try,” she said.

He faced the dark road leading away from the city. His wings lifted. His body leaned forward, then stopped so abruptly that Nim had to catch him.

The old marriage-maker came down from the stage.

“Iron keeps a call out,” she said. “It doesn't take one back.”

Veska stared at the officer. He looked desperately unhappy to have become the nearest part of the government.

“Can you release him?”

“No, my lady.”

“Can Orset?”

“At the appointed place.”

Of course. They could always be kind once they had you where they wanted you.

Veska gave Nim her other hoop. He put it through his ear.

The officer watched this with open distress.

“Those are cold iron.”

“We'd noticed,” said Nim.

The guards had not drawn their swords. One was staring at the wedding ribbons. Another kept glancing from Veska's wing to the silver summons tube as though waiting for it to explain matters.

“I will attend,” Veska said. “Tell Orset the band comes with me.”

“You may bring your household—”

“They aren't my household.”

The officer bowed and withdrew before she could make another distinction.

For a while they listened to his boots retreat through the furrows.

Then Hox said, “I think we're married.”

Nim touched the ribbon on his wrist.

“I think we'd better find out what else you've done,” he told Veska.

***

At dawn, they went to the Sky Court.

Hox had to be there by noon, but he could choose the way and the pace. The summons pulled only when he tried to turn toward a road that would take him too far away. He tested it three times, swore at it three times, and eventually made Nim stop asking.

Veska walked between them with her wings folded inside an old cloak. She had found a bent iron pin in the drum case and threaded it through one sore piercing. Nim had offered his hoop back. She had refused.

At the foot of the court's high stairs, Hox stopped for a reason that had nothing to do with the summons.

The Sky Court rose above the city on three white terraces. Its upper stage had a gold canopy, good acoustics, and a view of every tiled roof down to the southern wall. Veska had endured three hours of approved music there every midsummer. From below, the place looked almost attractive.

Hox set his father's drum down on the lowest step.

“They made him play down here,” he said.

“Your father?”

“Forty years. Every midsummer. They liked the copper sound from underneath the harps.”

He looked up at the empty stage.

“When he died they sent a wreath down the stairs. Wouldn't let us carry the drum up to thank them.”

A golden band shone across the first landing. Hox stretched a boot toward it. The air resisted him, gently and absolutely.

Veska remembered a tutor tapping that same band in a drawing of her wings.

The Copper Circle stood below the Seventh Stair. It was among the first distinctions she had learned. Before the order of the seasons. Before her mother's private name.

She took off the cloak.
