Nim crouched beside her lower wing with his ink and bone points. They had spent the last hour comparing his sketches of yesterday's tattoo with what remained beneath it. The marriage crescent had not merely vanished under black pigment. It was gone.

“You're sure which one?” he asked.

She pointed out the copper-coloured oval at the bottom of a long golden stem.

“Not across it this time. Turn the stem back into the oval.”

He studied it, then looked up at Hox.

Hox put his drumstrap over his head.

“I'm going to play up there,” he said.

Nim worked.

A milk-seller paused. Two women in court silk stopped on the opposite pavement, holding hands. Both wore wedding ribbons. Yesterday their wing-lines would have forbidden them to stand together beneath a marriage-maker's switch.

One of them saw Veska's briars and gripped the other's hand more tightly.

The inked line reached the oval.

Gold ran along it in a bright bead, circling once, twice. Then the stem shrank into the oval, and the oval collapsed to a pale freckle.

The band across the landing went out.

Hox climbed the stairs.

At the top, he set his father's drum beneath the canopy and played a roll that flung pigeons off every roof around the court.

A guard with pale blue wings and one copper notch near the root started toward him. She stopped short of the canopy, lowered her spear, and let him finish before going to fetch Orset.

Veska sat down hard.

Nim cleaned the little tattoo.

“Can you put it back?” she asked him.

He drew a tiny copy of the vanished oval on an unused patch of membrane. Black ink. Nothing more.

“No gold.”

Veska touched the edge of the pale freckle. It felt like the rest of her wing.

In the court portraits, all the laws had been displayed as circles and crescents. Her tutors had made her follow their paths until she could read rank, inheritance, permitted marriages, summonses, punishments. She had been a child tracing the shape of her own cage.

Every path led eventually to the open gold crescent on her upper left wing.

The Crown Eye.

When her mother died, its last closed arc had opened. Across the realm, the old queen's authority had passed into Veska's living wings. Orset could exercise powers already granted to the regency. He could command guards. He could not grow a Crown Eye.

There was only one.

From its upper horn, a fine golden spiral carried the right of inheritance. Someday that spiral was meant to open in her child's wings, and hers would fade.

Nim followed her gaze.

“That one?”

“Yes.”

Above them, Hox began a second roll. This time he let it run into a tune.

Veska looked at the dark rank-line, then the source from which all the others grew.

“They told me the eye never grows twice.”

Nim sat beside her on the step.

Neither spoke until Hox finished.

***

Regent Orset found them on the upper stage.

He wore a grey coat cut around his narrow, silver-banded wings. His own patterns permitted him a great many things. None of them included changing what the patterns permitted.

He listened to Hox's final beat before he spoke.

“Your father had a finer touch.”

Hox's hand flattened on the drumskin.

“Did you ever hear him from this close?”

“No,” Orset said.

It disarmed Hox for an instant. Veska disliked the regent more for noticing.

Behind him stood six guards and a court restorer carrying a white case.

Orset looked at the pale freckle on her lower wing. He had already been told about the stairs.

“Walk with me, Veska.”

“They come too.”

“If you wish.”

“No. They decide.”

Nim closed his ink bottle with his teeth. Hox lifted his drum.

They walked along the back of the stage while workers hung accession banners over the terraces. Every banner showed the Crown Eye as it had appeared in Veska's childhood: gold, immaculate, and empty of her.

“We have received reports from seventeen marriage houses,” Orset said. “Some delighted. Some less so.”

“Have the others fallen down?”

“No.”

“Then that's encouraging.”

“The goldsmiths have also walked out of their assigned quarter. Apparently your latest alteration affects everyone whose line lies beneath the Seventh Stair.”

She had known it would. Hearing it was different.

Across the lower terrace, a copper-winged woman in a servant's apron stood on a step that had never admitted her before. She held the railing with both hands. She did not look delighted yet.

The restorer watched Veska's wings as she walked.

At the parapet he opened his white case. Beside ivory points lay a fine brush and a vial of clear unbinding fluid.

“Can you repair it?” Orset asked him.

“We have her pre-molt tracings. While the source remains, a fresh path can be drawn from it to carry the original rule.”

He did not sound as certain as he wanted to.

“Without taking off the wing?” Veska asked.

He recoiled.

“Yes, my lady.”

Orset dismissed him a few paces.

“The guards can hold you,” he told her quietly. “I would rather they did not. We know very little about what your friend has done, and less about what might happen if a living charter is damaged during a struggle.”

“Then let us go.”

“Into a realm where the next mark you acquire may abolish an army's oath in the middle of a battle?”

Veska folded her wings.

He had found the fear she had been keeping behind the excitement. She had not known she was writing law when she asked for briars. Another leaf could have done something else.

“I am offering you a way to choose,” he said. “Attend the accession. Permit restoration. Your companions enter the royal household under your personal protection, whatever their lines. Their marriage will be recognized by a specific royal exception. No officer will touch them.”

Hox looked at Nim.

There it was: a room with a door that would stay shut against the world. Their names spoken properly. No running at a stranger's boots. Veska wanted it for them so sharply that she nearly answered.

Nim got there first.

“And if we leave?”

“Members of the sovereign's permanent household serve for life.”

“Do we get to keep playing?”

“At her pleasure.”

Nim looked at Veska. He was not smiling.

Orset waited.

“I can make a place for you,” she said.

“I have a place,” Nim answered. “You joined it last week.”

She looked at his fiddle case, rubbed pale where he carried it. He had made room for her name beside his and Hox's on the side. She had been absurdly pleased when she saw it.

“You don't have to answer now,” Orset said.

“What happens if the answer is no?”

His gaze moved to the guards.

Hox settled the drum more firmly against his belly.

“Give us until the eleventh bell,” Veska said.

***

They were given a windowless musicians' room behind the stage. A servant brought bread, cheese, and hot wine. A guard remained outside the door, and Veska heard a key turn after the servant left.

Veska unrolled a tracing on the floor.

Here was the girl she had been at seventeen: four immaculate wings, every crescent drawn in gold. Beside it Nim laid his sketch of the briars.

Veska put her finger on the Crown Eye.

“If we bring this path around the outer edge, everyone could be admitted. Every line. No more lowest stair.”

“And where do the paths end?” Nim asked.

She followed one inward.

At the eye.

“I wouldn't order people about.”

“What would your child do?”

“I haven't got a child.”

“They'll find you a husband. They'll grow another eye.”

She took her hand away.

Hox sat on the narrow bed with his drum between his knees. Now that he was near the appointed place, the summons had stopped troubling his legs. He rubbed them as though the motion belonged to him again.

“We could take the exception,” he said.

Nim looked at him.

“I'm saying it because we could. Not because I'm asking.”

They could play on the high stage. They could be married. Nim would have a recognized place, written specially for him. If something frightened them, they could come to her.

Veska looked at the last small spiral of inheritance on the tracing.

She had hated the prospect of her life continuing along that line. It was much harder to surrender the possibility of helping someone from its far end.

“I could break the other rules first,” she said. “Keep the eye in case we need it.”

“Yes,” said Nim.

“I could help people.”

“Yes.”

“If we turn it back into itself…”

“There won't be more gold to borrow.” He picked up his pen. “The source goes. The branch to the next bearer goes with it. You won't have a small crown left somewhere.”

Veska traced the route without touching the paper. The stair barrier had gone out with its gold. This would end every barrier, every call already lodged in someone. Orset's army could feel its oath let go in front of an enemy. She could not know who would stay.

“What about your marriage?”

Hox lifted his ribboned wrist.

“You changing your mind?” he asked Nim.

“No.”

“Me neither.”

Nim drew the loop.

It was smaller than she expected.

For a long time Veska listened to the workers outside calling for more white cloth. At noon they would spread her wings under the canopy. Everybody would kneel to the bright shapes she had been born with. Orset would thank her for choosing properly.

She turned her left wing toward Nim.

“Finish the briar,” she said.

He did not reach for his tools.

“I need you to mean that.”

“I do.”

“I can close it here,” Nim said.

“Out on the stage.”

“People will feel it wherever we do it.”

“So will Orset. That door stays locked. He can tell them I'm ill while he decides what to do with us. Let him take us out while he still thinks I'll agree.”

“With guards,” Hox said. “The restorer beside you. They'll take the iron off us.”

“I know. He wants them to watch him put me right. Let them watch him fail.”

Hox rested his hand on the worn drumrim, then stood up.

“Then we'll need a longer second verse.”

***

They spent the last hour before noon preparing for a performance.

Nim worked on Veska's wing while Hox played the proposed phrase softly on the bedframe. The new loop travelled through plain membrane beneath the curling briar, approaching the Crown Eye without touching it. At the meeting point Nim left a gap no wider than the tip of his bone needle.

Nothing gold moved.

“Until that closes,” he said, “it's just a leaf.”

He bound the little point to the heel of his fiddle bow and turned the bow in his right hand, holding the projecting tip just below the gap. Hox practised the extra bars, then stopped and looked at the drum his father had worn smooth around the rim.

“If I knock the restorer's brush away, will you have time?” he asked.

“For one dot,” said Nim.

Hox nodded once.

Veska sent their answer to Orset: the band would perform before the restoration, and remain with her through the crowning. Afterward would come the permanent household oaths.

He came to inspect her himself.

“You've added to it.”

“I wanted it finished.”

The restorer examined the ink without touching her. He found the surviving gold connections intact.

“We can begin after the song,” he told Orset.

“And the iron,” the regent said.

Veska took the bent pin from her ear. Hox met her eyes, then put down his borrowed hoop. Nim set his beside it. The guard collected all three on a silver tray.

Veska watched the pin leave.

Orset opened the door for her.

***

They had covered the throne in white silk so it would not be seen empty.

The terraces were full. Fine wings glimmered on the upper seats. Below them, families stood in their prescribed places with their children held in front so the heralds could see their patterns. The copper-winged woman in the servant's apron had climbed to the second landing. Her hands still gripped the rail.

Under the canopy, guards stood on either side of Veska. The restorer opened his white case. Nim set his fiddle against his shoulder.

Near the stairs the pale-blue guard had made a space beside the railing for a little girl, holding the impatient adults back with her spearshaft.

Hox put his father's drum where the harps had stood.

The herald called for the Crown Eye to be shown.

Veska spread her wings.

A murmur swept the terraces. She felt it more distinctly than the wind: disgust, delight, shock. The black briars climbed her royal crescents. The violet bands glowed where sunlight passed through them.

Then the herald spoke the old instruction, and the terraces knelt.

It happened in a little wave. First the heads bowed, then the wings lowered, then the knees. The woman on the landing tried to catch the rail. Her fingers slid down it as the law took her weight.

The musicians had leave to stand. Hox watched the woman for a moment before he lifted his hands.

He began.

Veska sang about the landlord, the crows, and the wife who had taken a ladder to rescue his best hat. On the third line she nearly laughed. The acoustics were excellent.

Orset's face tightened.

In the second verse, Nim's fiddle wandered from the melody. Hox went with it.

They had played the piece often enough that a few people on the lowest terrace knew what was coming. One man began to grin. A woman beside him put a hand over his mouth.

Veska looked out across the kneeling city.

She had never stood up here and seen how long the stairs were.

The verse ended.

The restorer breathed on his fine brush. Its bristles stirred, wet with clear unbinding fluid that would draw the pigment out of the wing-membrane. He approached her left wing. Behind him Orset held the crowning oath.

Nim's bow drew out the last note.

Veska turned her wing toward him.

“No,” she said.

Orset lowered the oath.

The restorer stopped.

For one suspended instant she could still give them the wing, keep the old oaths holding and her friends safe. Tomorrow, if someone brought her another cruel rule, she would still have the means to break it.

Then Nim turned the fiddle bow in his right hand, bringing its bone point toward the gap.

“Hold her,” Orset said.

A guard seized Veska's right arm. Another caught the hard leading edge of her left wing, carefully, firmly, exactly as someone had practised.

The guard pulled her wing out of the needle's reach.

The restorer lunged for the little black loop.

Hox swung his drum between the brush and Veska.

Solvent splashed across the copper belly. The restorer grabbed the rim to wrench it away. Hox held on with both hands.

A guard brought the butt of a spear down on the drumhead.

The skin split. A wooden rib cracked underneath it.

Hox made a sound Veska had never heard from him.

Then he shoved the broken drum forward, carrying the restorer back against the silk-covered throne.

Veska pulled against the guard on her arm. He was stronger. The one holding her wing had locked his elbow; she could not turn far enough to bring the little gap to Nim.

Orset reached for the bow. Nim drew it back in his right hand and let the fiddle fall. With his left he caught the wing's free, scalloped edge and drew the membrane inward above the upturned bone point.

“Steady,” he said, holding the bow motionless.

Veska stopped pulling at the guard and pressed the prepared gap down onto the bone needle at the bow's heel.

It was a tiny prick.

The Crown Eye closed.

Gold rushed into the black leaf. The crescent drew its horns together, tightened to a ring, then shrank. The fine spiral of inheritance unwound into it.

For a moment the whole design shone through the black tattoo, brighter than the noon sky.

Then the eye was gone.

The hand on Veska's arm loosened. Its owner had felt something give way inside his own wing and glanced back.

Down the terraces, knees rose.

Some people stood quickly. Some remained where they were, bewildered by the choice. The copper-winged woman hauled herself up by the rail.

Hox released the drum.

He took a step away from the appointed place. Another. He laughed once, fiercely, and caught Nim's hand.

The white wedding ribbons loosened.

Nim snatched his before it could fall.

“The ink,” Orset said. “Take the ink off.”

The restorer was staring at Veska's wing.

Where the Crown Eye had been, there was cream membrane and a black briar leaf. No gold. No little spiral waiting to grow into someone else's life.

“Now,” Orset said.

The restorer dipped his sleeve into the unbinding fluid and rubbed at the leaf. Black pigment came out of the membrane and smeared across the cloth.

He looked through the clean patch at the sky.

Nothing returned.

The copper-winged woman on the landing gripped the rail and stared at the clean patch.

***

Orset still had guards.

“Take them,” he said.

The one at Veska's right tightened his grip again. The command had reached him as an ordinary sentence, but he knew his work.

Nim bent for his fiddle. Hox caught the spearshaft coming toward his head.

And the guard nearest the stairs stepped sideways.

She had pale blue wings with one copper notch near the root. Veska knew that notch. It had forbidden its bearer every house on the upper terrace.

The guard set her spear across the way.

“There's a child underfoot,” she said.

There was. The girl had slipped from her place at the rail while her parents were still rising. She stood behind the guard, gazing at the black briars.

The guard looked at Veska.

“Go.”

For a moment the other guards hesitated between her spear and the regent's voice.

Hox caught up his broken drum by its strap. Nim snatched his fiddle case from the floor.

Veska stamped on the foot of the man holding her.

The little girl jumped out of their way.

They ran.

Behind them, Orset shouted for someone to close the terrace gates. Farther down, two silk-winged women passed through a marriage-maker's abandoned circle hand in hand. A man in court brocade stood in their path; they turned and went around him.

At the second landing, the copper-winged servant took off her apron.

The city kept appearing between beating wings and grasping hands. People moved aside. People tried to stop them. Someone laughed at her bleeding ear. Someone else threw a basket at a pursuing guard.

The three of them reached the street.

Hox was still carrying the drum.

“You can leave it,” Nim said.

“No.”

They went on.

***

They stopped in the pumpkin field because that was where the wagon was.

In daylight the magnificent stage was six borrowed planks. Burnt-out candles leaned in the pumpkins. The old marriage-maker was asleep beneath it with a bottle tucked into her elbow.

Veska stood in the furrow, looking at the pale place on her wing.

She tried to remember the weight of the eye. It had been there every moment of her life. She ought to have felt lighter.

Instead her shoulders shook.

Nim came up beside her. He had tied his fallen ribbon back around his wrist, in an ordinary knot.

Hox set the ruined drum on the stage. For a while he rested a hand on the split skin.

Then he turned it sideways and tapped the copper belly.

The note was ugly and deep.

He hit it again.

Nim climbed up after him, shook the dirt from his fiddle, and tried the note on a string.

Veska waited below.

Hox looked at her.

“You're late.”

She stared at him.

“We're starting,” he said.

Nim shifted his case to make room.

Veska climbed onto the planks. Her boot caught on a pumpkin vine, and both of them reached to steady her.

This time, when she spread her wings, they watched her face.

Hox gave them four beats on the broken drum.

Veska came in on the fifth.

stories.title: The Last Thing Heaven Saw
stories.prompt: For a thousand years, the most beautiful woman in the kingdom has worn a crimson blindfold. She is neither prisoner nor queen, yet emperors kneel before her, and gods avoid her path. The blindfold is not there to protect her from the world, but to protect the world from what happens when she opens her eyes.
stories.body:
# The Last Thing Heaven Saw

The emperor took off his crown before he crossed her threshold. He had kept it on while his brothers died.

Ilessa heard the hinges of its case, the small disturbance among the men behind him, and then his bare footsteps on her tiles. He had removed his boots as well. That was excessive, but she let him decide how frightened he wished to be.

“Your men can wait outside the garden.”

Darovan dismissed them. When the last harness stopped ringing, he knelt.

She sat beside an open window. The afternoon had warmed the stone beneath her hands. In the garden, fruit was splitting in the heat; she could smell the sweetness through the bitter leaves. This was an hour she liked. For most of her life there had been someone who believed his need more urgent than her pleasure in it.

He laid something at her feet. Gold struck gold, four times.

“My crown,” he said. “And those of the west.”

“I asked you to leave your men. Have you brought their kings instead?”

“Their kings are dead.”

She waited.

“I need your help.”

“Then you should have begun with what you need.”

He drew a breath through his nose. He had a soldier's care for his breathing, using it to hold still what wished to shake. She had heard men breathe like that before a charge. Beyond the window, a wasp worried at the open flesh of a peach.

“Namar has taken the high throne.”

“I heard the bells.”

“He defeated the Nine at their own gates. He broke the Spear-Bearer. The others have sworn to him.”

“And you?”

“My armies closed their temples in the west. My people fill his.”

There was pride under the fear. She was glad he had not tried to hide it.

“What does your god want?”

Darovan's next breath was less orderly.

“Your eyes, to be set into his coronation crown. Two places have been cut in the gold.”

Ilessa lifted her hands from the warm stone.

“He put it in those words?”

“He said the last power that would not kneel would be made an ornament.”

“What were yours?”

“I said I could carry a demand. I could not give him what was yours.”

“Yet you carried the crowns of the west.”

The wasp left the peach. She listened to it go.

“I have thirty thousand men within a day's march,” Darovan said. “The northern passes can be held. If you will come behind my walls—”

“When is he coming?”

“He will send his war hand at noon tomorrow. He stays on the throne when he uses it.”

“Then you have until noon to clear the imperial avenue. Clear the pilgrimage stair as well, from its first step to Heaven's gates. No soldiers. No priests.”

“You mean to go to him?”

“He has announced that he means to come to me.”

The emperor shifted on his knees. One of the crowns scraped across the tile. She reached toward the sound, and he put it into her hand.

The fourth point had been bent inward. She knew it under her thumb.

“This one should be in a grave.”

“It was my ancestor's.”

“He had a loud laugh. He thought that made his jokes good.”

Darovan was silent for a while.

“There is a portrait,” he said at last. “In the old palace. He stands beside you. When I was a boy I thought the painter must have loved you.”

“He disliked me. I would not let him use white for my hair. It was silver even then.”

“Your face has not changed.”

She heard him look. They always grew quiet when they did, even those who had rehearsed what they would say. She was still the most beautiful woman in his kingdom. A thousand years of portraits had failed to prepare a single emperor for the woman at the window, with the crimson cloth over her eyes and the old crown loose in her hand.

She returned it.

“Your ancestor asked me to look at his enemies.”

“What did you tell him?”

“He was standing in front of them.”

Darovan took the crown very carefully.

“Will Namar listen?”

“I don't know him.”

“He has beaten gods.”

“Yes,” she said. “You told me.”

She rose. Dark cloth slipped over the edge of her chair. Darovan drew back to give her room, still kneeling, and she went past him to the door.

“Ilessa.” He had to force her name out. “If there is a war—”

“There is already a war. You brought four crowns into my house.”

He said nothing more.

“Take them with you,” she said.

She heard him gather them by their bands. He had difficulty carrying so many without letting them strike one another.

Outside, the sun lay warm upon her covered eyes.

She had tied the first crimson strip a thousand years before Darovan's visit. Everyone who had watched her tie it was dead. The woman who had held her hair away from the knot; the man who had been unable to stop thanking her; all the people who had promised she would never be asked for anything again.

The peach trees still ripened. Men still mistook the gift for a debt.

She went into the garden and sat beneath the leaves until the stone lost its heat.

***

At noon the imperial avenue was empty.

No carpet had been laid for her. She had sent it back. Her shoes sounded plainly on the pale paving, beneath the balconies and the shut doors of the goldsmiths. People waited in upper rooms. She heard a shutter open, a hurried whisper, the shutter held before it could slam.

The city had grown toward her house over the centuries. There had been a field here once. Later, a wall, and a gate at which a man had asked her business. She remembered being pleased with him. He had been very young and had taken his duty seriously.

Now there were victories carved along the avenue, high enough for a conqueror on horseback to admire. Darovan had ordered the newest figures gilded. When the wind came from them it smelled of worked metal and the last bitter drying of size.

At the Temple of Spears, something heavy moved backward.

Ilessa stopped.

The bronze feet moved again. A long shaft rattled against a lintel.

“I thought he broke you,” she said.

“He broke my spear.”

The voice came from well inside the temple. Once it had spoken over battles. Men had heard it with blood running from their ears. Now it was having trouble getting past the doorway.

“And you swore to him.”

“He had the high throne. What would you have had me do?”

“I have not asked you to do anything.”

A quick breath, too large for a human chest.

“I did not advise this.”

“Keep out of the avenue.”

The god retreated until its feet no longer sounded on the temple floor.

She resumed walking.

Farther on, incense ceased to burn. A small god who lived in the heat above a jeweler's altar fled through the roof with a noise like tearing silk. Three priests called after it by three different names. None brought it back.

The silver bells at the palace began the noon measure. Before they reached the seventh note, a voice rolled down from the mountain.

“At last.”

Its force pressed the air against Ilessa's face. Every shutter in the avenue shook.

She stopped where the street widened before the palace. The paving here was bare for a hundred paces. Behind her, an iron bolt was drawn very softly.

“Where are you?” she asked.

“Where this kingdom kneels.”

The heat arrived before the hand. She felt the hairs at her temples stir in it. Above her a vast palm turned, and the avenue darkened. Rings rang against one another, each larger than a wheel. Something brushed the top of the victory arch; stone burst into dust and fell well behind her.

“Give me the cloth,” Namar said.

She tilted her face up. A broad, hot finger lowered toward the back of her head, seeking the knot.

Ilessa raised the lower edge of the blindfold over one eye.

She saw gold.

After so long, its brightness startled her. For a heartbeat she wanted only to look: the intricate creases of a hand too large to be born, the white fire in its joints, a narrow piece of blue between its fingers.

The nearest finger vanished. The absence widened through the palm. Its rings disappeared with it, and the heat broke away from her face.

She closed her eye and lowered the cloth before moving her head.

Sunlight returned to the avenue. Nothing fell from the place where the hand had been.

Namar did not speak.

There was a murmur behind the upper shutters. Someone began to pray and was silenced by someone else.

“That was your hand,” Ilessa said. “Will you come yourself?”

From the mountain came the hard crash of gates closing. Its echoes moved down the slopes, striking the lesser temples one by one.

She waited until they were finished.

“Come down without your crown. Tell the kingdom you had no right to demand my eyes. Renounce your claim upon me. Then I will leave you alive.”

Her voice was not loud. In the emptied avenue it carried.

The mountain gave no answer.

She turned toward the pilgrimage stair.

***

Namar had chosen his seat well. From the low city, the mountain's rim hid his living body. An emperor could see the banners of Heaven and the light it cast into the clouds, but never the god who received his petitions.

Ilessa could have looked at the mountain. The houses climbing its slopes would have gone first.

She took the stair.

At the first turn she put a hand to the wall. There was a deep groove in the stone where pilgrims had touched it for luck. Higher up, the groove became intermittent. Most people who began the climb never reached Heaven. There were lower altars at which to surrender their gifts.

She went past the altars. The sun moved to her left. Her breath shortened on the steep sections, and the muscles above her knees began to ache.

She had not promised to preserve Namar's peace. He had reached into a city to take her eyes, then shut a door when he failed. If she let the closed door settle the matter, he would come back with a better hand. Or the next emperor would.

She stopped to tighten the knot behind her head. It was hard to do with her hair lifting in the wind. Once secure, she smoothed the silver strands out from beneath the cloth and continued.

The first god fled above her at the eightieth turn. Six wingbeats struck the air in rapid succession. Ilessa leaned against the wall until the gust had passed.

From far above came Namar's summons.

It was an immense note, shaped by a living throat. She had heard it before, from the city, on the day he took the high throne. Then the Nine had answered, one after another, until the windows rattled in her house.

This time something scraped along an upper ledge. A heavy body launched itself into the air and departed southward, keeping far to the west of the stair.

Namar called again.

A voice answered him from a considerable distance.

“You knew what she was.”

“Come here.”

The wind carried a thin, undignified cry. The speaker was going farther away.

Namar's summons followed her up the mountain. He called upon oaths, upon debts, upon the seats he had allowed the Nine to keep. She heard him promise victory to anyone who would stand beside him.

Ilessa climbed into cold air.

Above the last inhabited terrace, the stair crossed a stretch of bare rock. She stopped there to rest. The wind had the clean mineral smell of the summit. No cook smoke, no grain, none of the warm scents of people pressed together. A loose offering bowl rolled somewhere nearby, struck a step, and went ringing down the mountain.

She remembered this slope before the stair was cut, when there had been only a narrow track. There had been flowers in the cracks. She had seen them: small yellow things with five petals, before anyone called her dangerous.

The memory still had its yellow. She was grateful for that.

She could have gone back. The thought came without shame. Darovan would call the broken hand a victory; priests would find a way to leave Namar's retreat out of their songs. There would be fruit in the garden for another week.

She rose.

Above her, the great gates were being barred.

At the final turn her hand ran out of wall. Wind came from ahead now, cold and unobstructed. She had reached the little shelf beneath the gatehouse. Six broad steps led up from it into the court. Before there were gates here, she had stood on this shelf and watched clouds pass beneath the summit's far lip. Behind her were the warm smells of the terraces.

The first king who built a hall on this summit had asked whether he could put a throne in it for her. She had refused it.

Now she set her palm upon the old threshold stone. The notch he had cut for the first gate remained beneath the later metalwork.

“I am here,” she said.

An enormous breath moved on the other side.

She waited.

Footsteps hurried across the court to her right, into the white-pillared gallery. A chain began to run through a winch there.

He was lowering the high drawbridge. It led from Namar's court to the old gods' refuge on a separate pinnacle. She had crossed it once with a god who spent most of the journey describing the terrible distance below. He had thought he was amusing her.

“Will they receive you?” she asked.

The chain stopped.

For a moment there was only the wind.

“Go back,” Namar said. “You have had your answer.”

Ilessa faced the high gold doors and lifted a corner of the blindfold.

Gold filled the narrow slit, with a strip of pale sky above it.

The gold parted without bending. A lane of absence opened straight across the court to the sky beyond. She shut her eye.

Wind rushed through the opening. The winch rattled violently.

She turned her covered face toward the bridge.

She lifted the cloth again.

The white bridge swung down from the gallery's outer end, bright against the sky.

She looked at the middle of the span.

A gap opened in the bridge and widened to either end. Ilessa closed her eye before turning back toward the gallery.

The chain rattled to a stop against its wheel.

“You knew that road,” Namar said.

“I crossed it before you had an altar.”

Namar called the Nine by their oldest names.

He called the Spear-Bearer, whose western temples Darovan had closed. He called the god of the western air and the twins who carried evening between them. His voice grew rough. He offered the high seats back. He offered the conquered kingdoms.

At last, from the direction of the refuge, a god answered.

“We will not cross in front of her.”

“Come behind her, then.”

“You come behind her.”

No one laughed. Ilessa felt the cold wind moving over her hands.

“The stair is open,” she said. “You can walk down it.”

Namar came back along the gallery, his steps heavy now.

“You would have me crawl past you.”

“Walk. There are steps. Take them carefully.”

She heard the sound he made at that. Anger suited him better than fear. He found his great voice again.

“I have waited three hundred years for this crown. They used to ring for me when their banquet lamps went out. Little Flame, they called me. They will ring again if I go down past you.”

“Let them ring. You may have three hundred more years without that crown.”

He was quiet.

“What would you leave me?”

“Your life. Your own altar. Those who choose to kneel before it. Give back the high throne and renounce your claim upon me. No one will take my eyes for you. Say it where the kingdom can hear, and I will go down the stair.”

She meant it. She had no desire for his temples, and three hundred years was long enough to acquire something worth keeping. Let him remember it. Let him live beside it.

“And the other gods?”

“You can ask them what they will forgive.”

His breath came out slowly. Far below them, an eagle cried.

She could feel how badly he wished her to be someone else: an old god to whom he could offer a kingdom, a woman to whom he could offer a god's bed, a rival whose followers could be starved into submission. There was nothing in her hands for him to take. Even the cloth was tied with an ordinary knot.

“You will swear to leave?” he asked.

“I have given you my word.”

The pause lasted long enough for her to hope.

Then metal struck stone in the gallery. He had set his crown down, but she heard the scrape of its rim being driven into a groove. A ringing note rose from the gold. She had heard that note from the mountain when he took the high throne, followed by a blaze she had felt in the city below.

She took her hand from the threshold.

“Namar.”

He drew a vast breath.

“I will not go back.”

The court filled with heat.

It struck her face hard enough to hurt. Her sleeves snapped against her arms. In the pillared gallery, the living god gathered his force into the crown beneath his hands. He had broken the Nine with one sudden stroke, catching them still in their seats. He sent the whole of that strength at her now, without another word. Stone cracked, and the wind bent away from him.

Ilessa turned her covered face toward the sound. She raised her chin a little. The gallery stood above her; beyond it there was only sky. The stair ran down behind her heels.

Fire rushed toward the threshold.

She lifted the crimson cloth and opened both eyes.

***

Namar stood among the gallery's white pillars, taller than any of them, with the crown blazing between his hands. He had made himself beautiful. His skin shone like the inside of a shell. Six arms spread from his shoulders, each scarred by an old victory. There was fury in his face, and the effort of holding something enormous. Above the crown's rim, two empty settings waited for her eyes.

The fire came to an end in front of her.

For an instant he could see her plainly: the silver hair blown back, the dark dress drawn tight in the wind, the cloth held against her brow. She was looking up at him. Her mouth was closed.

He drove the crown forward.

The gold disappeared between his hands.

His lower arms went with it. Blue opened in his body. He tried to bring the remaining hands together, holding his fire in the narrowing places where he still existed.

Ilessa kept looking.

She saw the lines cut into his throne, the crowded figures of kneeling gods along its base. The throne ceased to be. Pillars opened from their bright capitals downward. The roof went, and with it the banners she had heard so often from the city, beating above a place she could not see.

Namar made one last attempt to strike her. His surviving hand reached out through the vanishing gallery, immense and empty.

She watched until it was gone.

Beyond him the sky was the same blue she remembered. She had expected, after a thousand years, to find it altered.

She closed her eyes before her gaze could lower, and brought the cloth down over them.

The heat left her. Wind came across the ruined summit from the far side. Nothing crashed into the valleys. There was no great weight left to fall.

She stood a while on the lower shelf, with her feet on the stone where the first king had cut his gate notch.

Then she retied the blindfold.

“Come here,” she said.

No one answered.

She waited with the patience that had outlasted their temples.

At last wings moved beyond the court. A large body settled at the far end of the shelf, careful to keep away from the space directly before her face.

“We did not help him.”

It was the god who had answered from the refuge. Its voice was quite small now.

“Bring the others.”

“What do you want?”

“You will carry me down through the city.”

A pause.

“The stair remains.”

“Yes.”

The god said nothing more.

Soon she heard the weight of the Spear-Bearer upon the shelf, and the arrival of things whose passage changed the pressure in her ears. They spoke quietly to one another. Six gods lowered themselves until their joined hands lay level with the shelf. She stepped onto their palms. They lifted her standing.

They carried her over the intact stair, past the abandoned altars, out above the inhabited slopes. Below, doors opened. People came into streets from which they had been forbidden, looking up at the gods who bore the blindfolded woman down from Heaven.

She felt the warmth of the city rise to meet her.

***

Darovan waited in the imperial avenue with his crown in his hands.

Behind him stood the court, the commanders, the priests whose gods were descending without their high king. The emperor knelt before the bearers had set Ilessa on the paving. This time the sound traveled backward through the people behind him: cloth, buckles, knees upon stone.

The gods stepped out of her path.

“Namar?” Darovan asked.

“He chose to keep his crown.”

Darovan drew a breath. The same soldier's breath, taken carefully, to make something bearable.

“What would you have of me?”

“Stand aside.”

He moved on his knees. She passed him, and the gathered court opened before her without a word.

In an upper window, someone began to weep. Elsewhere a voice called a god's name. No one answered it. The Spear-Bearer's great feet withdrew toward its temple, then stopped until she had gone by.

Ilessa walked toward the quieter streets. The paving was warm. Beyond the walls there would be grass, and then the path to her unbarred house. She could smell smoke from the little kitchens the city had lit again.

She paused where the wind from the mountain reached the avenue. For a moment, in the warmth behind the cloth, she could still see the blue.

Above her road, the gods began their long way round.

stories.title: The Uninherited
stories.prompt: In a kingdom where magic is inherited through bloodlines, a young woman discovers a way to steal it by tattooing the spells directly onto her skin. Every new marking grants her another impossible ability, but the oldest tattoos have begun moving when she sleeps.
stories.body:
# The Uninherited

On the night she meant to become an ancestor, Desra stole the talent of hearing through stone.

The last stroke lay just below her thumb. She watched it darken, waiting for the familiar little theft inside her: a sense of something finding a room it had not known was there. Then the castle spoke.

Behind six inches of plaster, a mouse was eating a moth. Below her, someone set a tray on a table and swore at it. Farther down, through floors and joists and a very expensive carpet, Lord Ossel said, “Speak up, will you?”

Desra smiled. He had never needed to say that before.

His family had listened through walls for eleven generations. He had paid Desra to copy the branching shape of their gift into a wedding book, and left a bloody thumbprint on the account when he cut himself on its clasp. She had kept both the tracing and the stained scrap. An account, he had told her, was no place for expensive red pigment.

Now he would have to put his ear to a keyhole like anyone else.

She cleaned the needle and set it beside the other instruments. The room had once been a portrait studio; empty frames leaned against the wall, and a queen without a mouth stared from a canvas on an easel. Desra had slept here for seven nights, among old commissions nobody wanted and old work nobody remembered paying for. Her dark dress hung from the easel. In the small mirror above her pallet, the gold ring in her nose was a point of warmth among the black branches climbing her throat.

She had cut her hair short to watch them.

On the table lay seven sheets of thin paper, each carrying a tracing of the same part of her arm. On the first, the door-gift curled tidily around her wrist. On the second it had crossed the boundary she had drawn in red before going to bed. By the fifth night a hook of it had reached her shoulder. Last night, after she woke with her face in a cushion, it had joined the long feather of the gift that let her arrest a fall.

The changes had come while she slept. Staying awake had seemed a satisfactory answer until she caught herself dreaming with a needle in her hand.

She touched the first tracing. Of all her thefts, the door had been the easiest. An injured nobleman, a family book she was repairing, an idle little design pricked into her wrist with the pigment on her pen. When every locked cupboard in her lodging sprang open, she had thought the noise would bring the whole street running.

Afterward she had been more deliberate.

Blood from the living bearer. The whole branching spell, written into living skin. There was nothing like it in any book she had been allowed to read. She had taken seven gifts before Ossel's hearing, and she had gone to sleep each night feeling richer than when she woke.

Until the first one moved.

The king kept the remedy in his inheritance chamber. Desra had painted copies of the ceremony often enough: the kneeling heir, the royal hand, the gold knot beneath them both. The Knot of Descent could settle a loose gift into new blood and make it heritable. Every house had a first ancestor. Desra intended to be hers.

Let the genealogists do the uncomfortable part afterward.

She put on her dress, buckled her instruments under its skirt, and climbed out of the studio window.

The gap to the gallery parapet was six yards wide. She could have crossed where the roofs nearly touched, but the moon was out and she had been awake too long, and she wanted something easy.

She stepped.

Distance tightened once around her ribs and let go. Her foot came down on the far parapet. The courtyard remained below, all that cold air she had declined to travel through. She had once taken a paying passenger by the hand and carried him in a step to his sweetheart's balcony. He had wept. Desra had charged him extra for making her wait while he finished.

She loved this gift best.

The gallery ran open to the courtyard behind its parapet. Along the panelled inner wall, a little service door had been painted to disappear; at the far end, a guard nodded in a chair beside a great oak door. Desra lifted her hand toward the little door. The old hinge-shape stirred at her shoulder.

The little door stayed shut. Across the gallery, the great oak door banged open.

The guard jerked upright. For a moment they regarded one another across the length of the gallery. Then he shouted, and Desra went backward over the parapet.

She caught her fall halfway down.

The sudden stillness hurt her teeth. Above, the guard's lantern leaned into view. She hung with her cheek beside a stone saint, unable to go up, unwilling to let go. A bolt struck the saint's hand and took two fingers off it.

Desra released the fall and stepped in the same breath. The two gifts dragged against each other. She hit the studio's window frame with her hip, scrambled inside, and lay on the floor listening to boots begin to move through the walls.

“You could have used the stairs,” said Ildenne.

She was sitting on Desra's pallet. Her pale wool gown was torn below one knee, and her fair braid had come half unpinned. A length of knotted curtain cord lay beside her, and she held Desra's newest tracing flat with both hands.

Desra sat up slowly.

“My room had good locks,” Ildenne said. “It also had a window. They seem to have forgotten I have arms.”

“How did you find me?”

“I saw you climbing out. You still keep your elbows in when you work. As if the whole world were a piece of vellum.” She looked at Desra's side. “Is it there?”

The distance-gift lay below Desra's ribs, a black fork beneath the edge of her dress. Once she had painted that fork with powdered silver in Ildenne's family book. Ildenne had leaned over her shoulder to watch.

“Yes.”

“Give it back.”

Below them, a door slammed. The guard captain was sending men to the roofs. Desra could hear a buckle being done up, each impatient scrape of its tongue.

“You should go,” she said.

“My father signed the succession to my cousin yesterday. In the morning he means to send me to my aunt. She is very good at finding husbands for inconvenient women.”

Desra picked up the fallen tracing and set it on the table. The corner had crumpled.

“You asked me what happened to heirs who lost their gifts,” Ildenne said. “Do you remember?”

“I remember.”

“I thought you were interested in the book.”

“I was.”

Ildenne stood. Desra put a hand out, and Ildenne recoiled from it with such plain disgust that she let it drop.

“I can give it back,” Desra said.

She had worked out how three nights ago, when the door first reached her shoulder. She could go back to every bearer, offer her own blood for the return, empty herself of every marvel. It had seemed a grotesque solution. Like burning a house because the windows rattled.

“Then do it.”

“The inheritance chamber. Is it still behind the west nursery?”

“So that's what you're after.”

“I need the knot.”

“And you think I'm going to help you keep all the rest?”

Desra looked toward the window. Beyond it lay the convenient gap, the gallery parapet, the royal tower. She could still cross it. She could leave Ildenne here, take another route, and trust the gifts for one more night.

The fork beneath her ribs gave a small, hungry pull.

“You don't have to,” she said. “But if you know another way, I'll pay for it.”

Ildenne looked at the instruments, then at the blackwork climbing Desra's face.

“My step first.”

Through the stone, Desra heard the captain send the search toward the occupied guest rooms, away from the abandoned studio wing.

The return took most of an hour.

Ildenne kept her forearm on the table and watched the window. Desra worked beneath the lamp, using her own blood this time. The shape was familiar enough that she could have made it blind. She had, after all, been paid very well to copy it the first time.

Partway through, the old door-mark shifted.

She had been awake. She was certain of it. But there had been a little blankness between one stroke and the next, and now a narrow black tip extended toward her thumb.

“Don't stop,” said Ildenne.

Desra pressed a clean pin across the narrow black tip, holding it still.

The door-gift vanished from her reach. She tried the locked instrument case beside her; nothing answered. Under the pin, the black tip curled against the pressure, withdrew, then tried to get around it.

She lifted the pin. The tip darted beneath the edge of the new hearing-mark and stayed there.

Desra picked up yesterday's tracing. Then the one before it.

“What?” Ildenne demanded.

There were lines that had not existed before. Not displaced lines, not stretched ones. New joints. She had spent years learning to distinguish a flourish from the smallest necessary turn in a spell. She had copied these particular turns into her own skin. The hook from the door was bending against the fall-feather.

It was a hinge, certainly. But it was also a jaw.

“They're growing,” Desra said.

Ildenne looked at her own unfinished mark.

“Not that one. That one has somewhere to go.” Desra swallowed. “The others are growing together.”

She put her arm near the lamp. A fine offshoot lifted within her skin and turned toward the warmth. When she moved away, it followed as far as it could. At her shoulder, the long feather folded. She felt it trying to continue beyond the edge of her body, and failing.

She had imagined ownership as a kind of silence. A thing was hers when it did what she wanted and nothing she did not.

Ildenne drew her arm back.

“Finish.”

Desra did.

At the last stroke, the fork beneath her ribs loosened. For a moment she felt the gap she had crossed outside, felt its entire ordinary width. Then the gift was gone.

Ildenne rose, took one step, and stood beside the far wall.

Her hand flew to her mouth. She tried it again, across the room and back. On the third crossing she shut her eyes. Desra watched the pleasure move through her, sharp enough to look like pain.

Then Ildenne opened her eyes and saw her watching.

“The nursery door is watched,” she said. “Go through the old dressing room beside it. The back of the linen press opens onto the ceremonial passage. We used it when my sister's son was presented. You can open the door at the other end.”

“And after?”

“There is one high casement. Below it is the kitchen roof. Don't look at it and decide you can jump. It's farther than it looks.”

Desra nearly said that she knew.

Ildenne gathered her curtain cord. “That's my part.”

She left through the door. Desra did not ask her to stay.

The way to the royal tower was very long without the distance-gift. Desra had to go downstairs to get upstairs. She waited behind a statue while two guards searched the gallery, holding herself still until her calf cramped. At the linen press, the old door-shape answered only on her third attempt.

In the ceremonial passage she brushed past the painted founders of seven noble houses. Each portrait showed the family's gift in gold, branching behind the founder's head. Her own marks pulled toward one another under her dress.

She wanted them still. She wanted to sleep. She wanted to step across a courtyard because she happened to dislike walking round it. These were separate wants, and she counted them separately as she opened the inheritance chamber.

The room was smaller than the paintings made it. There was a stone table, a padded kneeling stool, and a high casement whose leaded panes had gone grey with approaching morning. The book rested beneath a glass cover. No royal hand guarded it. No ancestral voice asked her name.

She opened the cover and found the knot.

For a while she forgot the guards.

The knot was not one design but a way of closing other designs. The old illuminators had drawn each crossing clearly. A temporary catch first, to hold the loose gift; then the gathering turns; then the final line, which would carry the closure inward, beyond the skin and the reach of any needle. The gift would be hers, and her children's after her. There would be no opening it again.

She knew the work was good. Whoever had first drawn it had been very clever.

Desra began the catch on the unmarked skin inside her elbow.

The door-gift shuddered. Its long wandering line drew back down her arm. At her wrist, the familiar hinge lay still.

She turned toward the cabinet beside the table and lifted her hand.

Its little doors opened.

Just those doors. Exactly those doors.

Desra laughed once, shakily. She opened and closed them again. Four short turns and the closing stroke remained; she could make them in a dozen heartbeats. They would gather the other gifts, hold every part in its own proper shape. She could close it, catch her fall from the window, and leave the castle with everything except Ildenne's step.

That loss was bearable. She could bear it.

She looked down at the book to find the next turn.

Having seen how the knot caught, she could see how it might open instead. The little temporary catch would have to be released. The divided shapes could be joined without the final gathering line. What was trying to grow through her would have a way out.

The hinge strained against its catch.

She set down the needle.

Boots sounded in the passage. Even without Ossel's hearing she could have heard them now. A man tried the outer door of the linen press. Someone said to fetch the captain.

Desra looked at the window. A thief caught stealing a royal gift was hanged from the tower's eastern beam. She had passed beneath it on her way in, empty and waiting for the day's flags.

She could still keep the gifts. She could sleep safely with them closed inside her. In time there might be a portrait, a gold branching shape behind her head.

At her shoulder something tried to spread a wing.

She wanted to see it.

The desire was so strong that she resented it. She had spent three years assembling this wealth. The woman whose fall-feather she wore had written twice to ask if the old books said anything about gifts fading. *I still go up to the roof before I remember*, the second letter said. Desra had answered neither. Once she joined these gifts, there would be no separate gifts to give back. Now, at the last turn, there was another impossible thing beyond her reach.

It would not belong to her.

Desra picked up the needle and opened the catch.

The hinge ran up her arm. She followed it with one short joining line, through the blank space between the old door and the fall-feather, leaving the shape open where the royal knot would have closed. Her hand shook. She stopped to steady it, furious at the wasted seconds, then finished.

Black lifted from her shoulder.

It rose as slowly as a wet page being peeled from another. A narrow head emerged first, its jaw opening soundlessly. Then a jointed neck, a breast of tangled dark strokes, a foot that gripped her arm with the light, definite pressure of a living thing.

Desra held still.

The wings came last. They had been folded into so many places that she could not follow their leaving: her throat, her temple, the long black fields of her arm. The little hearing-mark below her thumb opened like an eye and disappeared into the creature's head.

It spread across the chamber. For a moment it was larger than anything the room could hold, black pinions passing through one another without tangling. The air under them stood perfectly still.

Desra reached up.

The creature stepped off her arm and onto the table. It did not look at her. Its head turned toward the window.

Outside the door, a guard struck the panel with the butt of his spear.

The creature put its beak to a lead seam. The pane opened the width of a penstroke. It drew itself through, wing after immense wing, and spread on the other side of the glass.

For a moment it hung over the courtyard, motionless, holding its own fall.

Then its wings took up the weight.

Desra watched until she could no longer distinguish it from the last darkness above the roofs.

The guards struck again. The door-gift was gone. The fall-gift was gone. When she put her hand against the wall, she heard nothing beyond the ordinary knocking.

She dragged the kneeling stool under the door latch, its back legs braced against the stone table.

The casement catch had rusted shut. Desra hit it with the brass candlestick from the table, missed, hit it again. Her skin looked bare and unfamiliar in the grey light. Pale brown paths remained where the gifts had been, but nothing answered when she reached inward.

The catch bent. She threw her weight against the casement and forced it open.

Below lay the kitchen roof. Ildenne had been right about the distance.

Desra climbed onto the sill anyway. An iron flag bracket projected to her left, well beyond her reach, and farther down was a projecting course of stone. She could not see a way between them. Behind her the stool scraped, then caught hard against the table. The next blow only rattled the door.

She gripped the outer frame and moved one foot out. The cold went through the sole of her shoe. She had never noticed how much the castle leaned away beneath this window.

“Give me your hand.”

Ildenne stood on the roof below, her torn skirt caught in one fist.

Desra nearly let go of the frame.

“Don't,” Ildenne said. “Stay there.”

She crossed to the sill in a step. There was scarcely room for their feet. Desra flattened herself against the stone while Ildenne reached round her and took her hand.

The courtyard tightened and released.

They landed badly behind the broad kitchen chimney, its brickwork blocking the high casement from view. Ildenne sat down hard, and Desra caught her by the shoulder before she could slide. For a little while both of them breathed.

Wood cracked above them. Then a man shouted from the casement for the kitchen court to be searched. Both women stayed low.

“They were going up the passage,” Ildenne whispered. “I heard them say they'd found you.”

Desra looked at her own hands. She could feel every place where the stone had scraped them.

“You came back.”

“I wanted my step. I didn't ask for your head.” Ildenne pulled the torn wool over her knees. “Where are the others?”

Desra pointed toward the sky.

Ildenne followed her hand.

“Can you give them back now?”

“No.”

Her face closed. “You could have.”

“Yes.”

Ildenne looked as though she might say something more. Instead she shook out her torn skirt.

“I'm going to my father. If they ask whether I've seen you, I shall answer.”

Desra nodded.

Ildenne stayed low as she went to the roof's little stair door. There she hesitated. “I'll need a moment to make myself presentable.”

Then she was gone.

The morning had reached the ivy on the outer wall. Beyond it, close enough to be infuriating, the roofs of the city sloped into sunlight. The easy way down was through the kitchen court. The watch would be there already.

From behind the chimney, Desra studied the wall instead.

A cracked lion projected from its far corner, around from the tower window. Above the lion, ivy hid a line of old putlog holes. The crossing from the roof to the lion was too wide for a step. She measured it with her eye, then measured it again, feeling the absence beneath her ribs.

In the city somebody would have breakfast for sale. Somebody would have a purse carelessly tied. She was so tired she could have slept standing up, and so hungry that the thought of hot bread made her jaw ache.

She took off her shoes and tied them to her belt. There were three finger-widths of stone beneath the lion's paw. She could get both hands there, if she turned sideways, if she trusted the second foothold rather than the first.

Desra put her empty wrist against the cold wall and began to climb.

stories.title: The First Year
stories.prompt: The Wheel of Ages oversees the months. It rules and is ruled by the Cat, the Serpent, the Fox, the Boar, the Frog, the Wren, the Bear, the Salmon, the Spider, the Wolf, the Hawk and the Stag.
stories.body:
# The First Year

Before there were months, the Cat could walk from winter into summer in an evening, provided she did not let the Bear see her.

The Bear hated the Cat's footsteps in her strawberries. The Cat hated the Bear's noon. Between their countries the Serpent kept a slope of warm stone, and anyone crossing it paid her in secrets. The Fox usually paid with somebody else's.

Elsewhere the Boar broke the earth and the Frog filled the hollows. The Wren made flowers grow wherever she sang. The Salmon's rivers ran toward the sea and, beneath the sea, found their way home. The Spider caught dew, the Wolf hunted beneath a frost that never melted, the Hawk owned the height from which everything could be seen, and the Stag stood among bare trees with the cold caught in his antlers.

They were living spirits. Their shadows went deeper than the shadows of other creatures. The black shape beneath the Wren's feet reached through every flowering branch in her country; the Salmon's shadow lay along the beds of his rivers. A spirit could withdraw into that darkness and come out a hundred hills away. It was how each knew its own land, and how the land knew its sovereign.

Their borders were bitter places. Rain trespassed on ripe fruit. Frost stopped a river. The Hawk stripped the Wren's blossoms from their stems, then said she should have grown them lower. Each wanted the others' countries. None would yield its own.

At the meeting of their twelve borders grew a stone table.

Its round top stood level on a single massive central leg. It had no tool marks. A pale vein crept across its surface as the twelve watched, dividing and joining again beneath the polish. The stone was alive, and warm even on the side that lay in shadow.

“Who owns this place?” it asked.

All twelve answered.

The table listened. Each sovereign saw a different country reflected in its black surface. The Bear saw her berries growing beneath every mountain. The Wolf saw frost on the sea. The Wren saw a forest flowering from horizon to horizon, with no Hawk above it.

The Fox saw himself running through all eleven kingdoms without once being caught.

“I can settle this,” the table said.

“And afterward?” asked the Wren.

“Each shall have what it sees.”

“With what?” asked the Boar.

“I have no country. I have no quarrel. Lay your shadows on me, and let each show the others how far its kingdom ought to reach.”

The Stag stood at the northern edge. The Salmon came up through a spring. The Spider lowered herself from a thorn. Each let its shadow reach across the stone toward the country it had been shown.

The Fox watched the pale vein.

It was growing over the shadows.

He sprang, but the stone caught him by the dark shape of his hind feet. The table widened beneath the twelve, lifting them from the ground. Its central leg thickened and drove deep into the meeting of the borders.

The Stag thrust his antlers beneath the rising edge. For a moment it could not move. Then the stone bore down. The sound carried into every country, and the Stag fell without his crown.

The others struck, sang, spat, leaped. Their shadows sank through the polish.

The table drew the Wren out of her blossoms and the Salmon out of his rivers. Each found itself bound at a place around the edge. The part of its shadow held inside the stone became a black root, running inward toward the center. It could stretch, but it could not be pulled free.

The table had grown broad enough for all twelve. The border thorn scraped along its new edge. Its surface held the reflection of the whole country.

“Everything,” it said. “As promised.”

A ridge of stone grew across the Cat's root.

***

The Cat had never been made to do anything.

She clawed the ridge until splinters of black stone fell between her feet. It thickened. Pain ran out through her shadow into every roof and branch she had once crossed, and she put her darkness over them to stop it.

Night went across the country.

The Bear's strawberries disappeared beneath stars. In the Frog's country, people carrying baskets home stopped on paths they had walked in daylight a thousand times. The Wren's flowers closed. The Cat could feel all of it, but she could not set one paw upon the ground.

“There,” said the table. “Your kingdom.”

She called her darkness back. The ridge pressed harder. It held her until she put the night out again.

At dawn the pressure eased. At dusk it returned. The moon grew round above the hills and dwindled to a horn. People burned the wood they had saved for crossing the Wolf's country. Children who had never seen frost began to dream of it.

The Cat made her nights as short as she could. The table made them longer.

When the moon vanished, it let her root lie slack and pressed upon the Serpent's.

Warmth entered the ground. Ice slid from roofs in great sheets. People came out to find the whole country smelling of stone in sunlight, and they said that the season had changed.

The Serpent looked at her hills in the polished surface. She could have reached them in a breath if the shadow rooted in her belly had stretched one inch farther.

She went still. She loosened her scales. Slowly, with the patience that had made the stones warm before anything else awakened, she slipped out of her skin.

The empty skin lay on the table.

The Serpent rose new and bright. Her root rose with her, still fixed in the stone.

The table laughed until pebbles fell from distant hills.

It let the empty skin blow from its edge, spreading it wider and wider over the fields. The people found it stretched across three of them and built their first shrine beneath its glittering scales.

The moon waxed and waned over the warm country. Seeds woke in the earth. The shed skin whitened where people touched it for good fortune.

“They think you gave it to them,” the Fox said.

The Serpent turned her new head toward him.

“I know.”

***

The Fox walked backward to his place when his root began to tighten.

“You could have asked,” he told the table.

“You could have refused.”

“I still can.”

Stone closed across his shadow.

Outside, dusk spread through the country. The Fox drew one last brightness along the western hills, made the path beside a village seem to fork where it did not, sent warm weather over a frozen field and a sharp shower across the Bear's former country. The people learned to hesitate before believing an evening sky.

While the table watched his work in its surface, the Fox left an afterimage beside his root and slipped behind it.

He tried the edge first. He got his head and forelegs over it. Grass brushed his nose. A woman on the path saw a red creature straining down from the stone and dropped her firewood.

The Fox stretched toward the earth. His root drew tight. The table pulled him backward, through his own afterimage, and struck him against the ridge.

For three dawns he could not stand. On the fourth he crawled beneath the overhanging edge.

There he found a crack in the underside, cold and dry. A seam in the old stone curved beneath the rim toward the Cat's place; here it widened enough for him to curl up inside. The table had grown around that stone without bringing it to life. Its dark surface could reflect what happened above, but no warmth entered that blind place beneath it.

The Fox pushed himself inside. He tucked his tail over his injured legs.

The table called him.

He said nothing.

Stone rose around his abandoned place and crushed the afterimage flat.

For the first time since his shadow had been taken, the Fox slept.

He could still be dragged out by his root when the table wanted dusk. Between those hours, he had somewhere to go.

When the next moon began, the Boar's root was pressed. The ground of the country split beneath his power. Hard fields turned over. Shoots thrust up beside roads, through floors, between the white scales of the Serpent's shrine.

The Boar saw them and charged.

He drove his tusks beneath the ridge that held his shadow. Stone split from his feet toward the center of the table. In the fissure lay his root, a black curve embedded in the pale grain.

“At last,” he said, and bit it.

His right foreleg thinned. Through it the Fox could see the sky. Outside, shoots blackened from their tips downward. A woman knelt in a field with both hands full of dead leaves.

The Boar let go.

His leg grew solid again. The dead shoots did not rise.

New stone crept into the fissure, then stopped short of the root. The table had felt the thinning too. It had almost lost something it meant to keep.

The Boar lay with his snout against the crack.

“That was me,” he said.

No one answered him.

The rain began when the Frog's turn came. It struck dust from the leaves and filled the Boar's furrows. For days people stood in doorways, listening to water that no longer stopped at a border. Wells rose. The spring on the north side of the pedestal ran again, though the Salmon did not come out of it.

Rain gathered in the Boar's crack. The Frog put her head into it and listened.

She leaped toward the dripping sound beneath the slab. The table pulled her root, and she landed hard at her place.

She leaped again. Again she came down where she had begun.

But the rain went on through the stone. A drop touched the Fox's nose inside his refuge.

“Do that again,” he called.

“I have done it twice.”

“The rain.”

She sent a little more along the crack. The Fox followed it beneath the edge, where a narrow seam ran around the underside of the table. He could hear the Serpent breathing above him and the Boar worrying the stone with his tusks.

There was a path between their places. It led nowhere off the table, but it was a path their captor had not given them.

The Fox said nothing about the cold crack in which he slept.

***

The Wren's moon began with flowers.

They came out on bare wood, over the Boar's dead field, in the wet straw of roofs. People woke to petals on their blankets. Orchards blossomed before anyone had known the trees were orchards. The Wren had never sung to so much country.

“Again,” said the table, whenever her song faltered.

The Boar had kept his snout against the fissure all through the rain. He was trying to work his root free without biting it, and sometimes he forgot and put his teeth down.

“Stop that,” the Wren told him.

“Sing something else.”

She put her feet beside his exposed root and sang the hard little song she had once used to split the shells of seeds.

The stone hummed.

The ridge over her own root lifted a hair's breadth. For one beat she was silent and no pain followed. Outside, flowers stood half open, waiting.

Then the ridge came down.

The Wren fell against the stone. The table kept pressing until she sang, and the flowers opened too far, tearing themselves from their stems. Petals covered the paths so deeply that people could not find their way home.

Later the Fox came up from beneath the edge.

“Do it again,” he whispered.

The Wren's breast moved fast.

“Not while it is listening.”

At the end of her moon, the Stag's new antlers scraped the stone beside his place.

The Bear followed the flowers with fruit.

Heat thickened over the country. Berries bent branches to the ground. Plums split their skins. Children came home with purple hands and no hunger. The Bear smelled all of it on the wind, and the table let her smell it.

It would not let her eat.

“You have fat enough,” it said.

She watched a boy reflected in the stone climb a tree that had once grown in her country. He filled his shirt with little yellow pears.

That night, instead of sending another wave of heat across the hills, the Bear put her head upon her paws. She remembered her deepest cave. She remembered the weight of snow above it and the sound of her own breathing beneath the earth.

Sleep went down her root.

The pale veins in the stone slowed. Its warmth ebbed. The pressure on the Bear's root slackened, and she slept more heavily.

“Wake,” said the table.

She let a long breath out through her nose.

The table seized the Wolf's shadow beside hers. His frost tore across the Bear's hot country. Pears froze in the boy's shirt. Branches broke under fruit suddenly hard as stones. The boy got down from the tree and could not feel his hands.

The Bear woke.

“Lie down again,” said the table.

She stood until her moon was done.

From her place the Cat said, “One at a time.”

The black surface cleared around her reflection.

“You will take one of us at a time,” she said. “And when the moon is gone, you will let the next one begin.”

“Will I?” said the table.

It let the Bear look at the frozen pears.

The Salmon came to rivers filmed with frost that should never have been there. Beneath it, the fish of the country were gathering to return. Their bodies shone red and silver in the dark water. They struck the ice from below.

Water filled the hollow that had formed about his place. The table pressed his root, making the current run out through the country. He faced it, as he had always faced the current, and drove upstream.

Outside, fish broke through the ice. They climbed falls that had never before known their return. Along the banks, people ran beside them shouting.

Inside the stone, the black flow in the Salmon's root began to run backward.

The Boar's fissure opened again. The roots rose in it, twelve living shadows sunk into a single bed of stone. The ridge above the Salmon shivered. Water rose between it and his root.

The table pulled him out of his pool and held him above his own water until he could no longer struggle.

It put him back before he died.

The ridge settled. A little black water remained in the fissure.

That night the Spider came down into it.

***

The Spider's moon left dew on everything.

At dawn every field carried a thousand small reflections of the sky. Mist lay between houses. Travelers stopped at familiar turnings and saw white roads where there had been no roads before. Webs stretched between the tines of the Stag's growing antlers.

On the table, beads of water settled along the roots the Salmon had exposed. The Spider followed them into the fissure.

“There are twelve,” she told the Fox.

“I had counted.”

“You counted prisoners.”

She laid a foot against his root.

The Fox felt the foot inside his own chest.

He drew back.

“Be still.”

She fastened a thread. Then she went to the next root, letting the mist conceal the silver line behind her.

The Fox waited until she had gone and crept back to his refuge. Through the thread he felt the Spider pause at the Serpent. He felt the Wren's quick heart. When the Boar shifted in his sleep, the Fox's foreleg ached.

He lay very still in the only place where the stone was cold.

When the Wolf's proper moon came, frost silvered the fields each morning and hardened the paths beneath people's feet. The fruit the table had frozen in the Bear's reign still hung on the boughs. Deer came down from the high country to find what they could beneath it.

The Wolf smelled them.

The table pressed his root and made him call. Packs answered from every part of the country. Their howls went through doors and into the sleep of children.

Then it stopped him and let him listen to the hunt.

The Spider was halfway around the roots when the fissure began to close. The Wolf came to it along the underside seam and thrust his jaws beneath the descending stone.

The table stopped calling for him. It pressed.

The thread trembled in the Fox's chest. He felt the pressure on the Wolf's teeth, felt the animal hold, and then the Spider went on.

For the rest of that moon the Wolf could not howl. Frost came in silence. Outside, the packs hunted without him.

By the Hawk's moon the Spider had passed every root but the Cat's. Here the fissure ended. Between the last two roots stood a thickness of stone she could not enter.

The Hawk spread her wings.

Wind stripped the trees. It tore the last fruit down and drove it against walls. People bound their doors shut. Up on the hills, the shrines built under the Serpent's skin came apart and went flapping across the country in pale pieces.

The Hawk flew over the rim and down beneath the slab. Her root stretched behind her, and the table pulled. She flew farther along the underside, while the whole country bent beneath her wind.

She saw the seam in the dead stone, and where it ran up toward the Cat's root.

The Fox looked out from his refuge.

The Hawk looked in at him.

“There,” she said.

Above them, the Spider waited with the loose end between her feet.

The Fox shook his head once.

The Hawk's root jerked her inward. She struck the pedestal, caught herself, and flew back beneath the edge. Roofs lifted outside. Somewhere above, the Wolf's teeth scraped against the stone.

The Fox came out.

He took the thread in his mouth. It tasted of dew and the other prisoners. He carried it through the cold crack where his body had fitted, and up through a narrow break beside the Cat's root.

Warmth followed him.

The living thread had crossed the dead place. A pale vein reached into it, following the warmth of the twelve. The table found the little hollow in which the Fox had slept and filled it with new stone.

The Fox kept going. He laid the thread against the Cat's root.

For the first time all twelve felt the slow pulse beneath the surface on which they stood.

***

The Stag's moon came with bare boughs and deep cold.

Across the country, people cut branches to burn. They had learned that a season would end, but they did not know what would follow this one. They stacked wood against the houses and took the old and the small into the warmest rooms.

The table pressed the Stag's root and watched winter spread through its reflection.

His antlers had regrown during confinement. He had turned his head a little each day to keep them from the stone. Now their branches lay back along his shoulders, pale and crowded, ending in points his captor had not yet felt.

The moon grew round and thinned. Each dawn the Stag gave the country his cold. Each night he brought his crown a little farther into the fissure the Wolf was holding open. Through the thread they could all feel where the table's weight lay, and the thin place beneath the ridge that pressed his root.

Beyond the edge, people counted the wood left in their houses. Above the stone, the Wren counted the days.

The next dawn came without a moon. The Cat waited for her root to tighten. Instead the pressure on the Stag grew heavier, driving cold deeper into the country. Frost stopped the smoke in chimneys. People brought their last wood in from the stacks.

“My moon is done,” the Stag said.

“This one pleases me,” said the table.

He lowered his head.

The Wren gave one small note. The stone hummed. The Bear sent sleep along her root, and the pale veins slowed.
