As the ridge loosened, the Salmon drove against the pull. For a moment the pressure that had forced winter into the country ran backward into the stone.

The Stag sent his cold after it.

The Serpent put her warmth into the same grain from the other side. A sharp report rang through the table. The Boar's old fissure ran to the center, beneath the Stag's ridge.

A shard bit into the Boar's root. He cried out; his foreleg began to thin.

With his own root stretched tight, the Fox crossed from the Cat's place to the fissure. He eased his shoulder beneath the exposed black curve and lifted it clear of the shard. The Boar's foreleg grew solid again; through the thread the Fox felt the foot meet stone.

The Boar drove his tusks beneath the breaking edge. The Stag thrust his crown beside them. Together they caught it before it crushed the exposed shadows.

The table bore down.

The Stag's hind feet slid. The Frog wedged herself behind them, her wet feet spread against the stone. The Serpent held the other roots clear of the broken edge while the others pushed their power inward. Through the taut thread the Fox felt their weight settle across the Stag's neck.

The ridge lifted from his root.

Outside, winter stopped deepening. Frost ceased its climb over a child's blanket. The smoke caught in a chimney broke loose and rose.

The Stag's root still lay embedded in the table. He could feel his cold country through it. He could not go there.

The table tried to press him again. The Wren's note sharpened; heat and cold met inside the stone. It stopped before the new crack cut through what it had taken such care to own.

“Let go,” it said.

No one did.

From her bound place the Cat sent night across the country.

Stars came out above the bare trees. In a thousand houses people saw the frost loosen at their windows and carried their lamps to the doors.

The table gave one great shudder. The stone above the Stag's root shifted aside. He drew his head back from beneath the broken edge and left a tine behind.

For a while there was no sound among the prisoners but the Wolf's breathing.

***

The Cat's nights had returned.

People recognized them. In the country that had once been twelve countries, they counted back through the changing moons. They named each for the creature whose work they had seen, and called the completed round a year.

The table had not moved from the meeting of the borders. Yet twelve reigns had passed around it and come back to the first.

People marked twelve places around the rims of their bowls. They called the twelve reigns months, and the thing that held them the Wheel of Ages.

New stone crept across the Cat's root.

She watched the pale vein reach the new crack. It divided, skirted the break, and rose on the other side. Her shadow tightened beneath it.

Night deepened. Frost took the edges of the lamps. At the hour when dawn ought to have come, a child went to a door and found the stars still there.

“A little longer,” the Wheel told the Cat.

She felt its pulse through the thread. She felt the Wren begin to count the beat, and the Bear stir at her place. The Salmon faced the current. The Fox, with nowhere left to hide, stood beside her.

The Cat took the darkness from the sky and laid it across the polished stone.

The ridge pressed harder, trying to drive the night out again. Beneath the cover of her darkness, the Wren's note made the pale vein falter. Sleep entered the stone; the current pulled backward. The pressure slackened, and the Cat kept her darkness on the table.

Dawn reached the hills.

The Wheel clamped her root. The Fox felt her bones bend. It held her while, outside, people opened their doors and saw the light. Then it eased its grip just enough to keep her alive.

The lamps went out, one by one. Children were lifted to windows. In the orchards, the fruit killed in the Bear's moon lay frozen beneath the trees, and beyond them smoke rose straight from a thousand roofs.

The Cat did not cry out. She could feel all eleven bearing the pressure with her through the stone.

At dusk her root tightened.

Her darkness still covered the table, but its voice came through it.

“Again,” it said.

stories.title: The Weight of Everyone
stories.prompt: In a kingdom where everything has a measurable value, a young traveling merchant possesses a set of miniature brass scales capable of weighing things that should have no weight: love, loyalty, courage, and even human souls. She's made a comfortable living exposing counterfeit blessings and dishonest bargains, until a stranger offers her a beautiful blue gemstone that weighs exactly as much as the entire kingdom's population.
stories.body:
# The Weight of Everyone

The blessing was genuine. Merryn had to disappoint the woman about that first.

“Seven grains of love,” she said. “A very good weight.”

The woman shifted the baby against her shoulder. He wore a yellow cap, much too large, with the front rolled back three times.

“Then why hasn't it worked?”

“What did you want it to do?”

“Let him sleep.”

Merryn glanced at the child. He was asleep now, his mouth open against his mother's collar.

“When I sleep,” the woman added.

Behind them, the seller of blessings made a sympathetic noise. He had been making sympathetic noises since Merryn unfolded her scales.

They stood at the corner of his stall, between strings of painted saints and a little shrine whose candles were priced according to the sincerity of the prayer. Merryn's own pitch was across the lane: two trays of rings, knives with soundness certificates, a box of winter courage bought cheaply in a very brave village. All of it was already paid for. So were the mule, the cart, and her room above the best pastry shop in town. At twenty-three she had discovered that people would pay generously to be told a bargain was dishonest, provided she could tell them before they signed it.

She lifted the charm from the left pan. It was a silver bell with no clapper, suspended from a blue thread.

“May I undo this?”

“You break it, you buy it,” said the seller.

“We can certainly weigh your loss afterward.”

He subsided. Merryn worried the tight knot with a fingernail, then caught the end between her teeth and pulled. The bell came free. She set it in one brass pan and the thread in the other, breathed along the beam, and asked for the love in each.

The bell rose. The thread sank.

“He tied this on while you were holding the baby?”

The woman nodded.

“It's yours,” Merryn said. “He caught a little of what was already coming from you. A proper blessing adds something. This one sold you a window and charged for the view.”

“There was workmanship,” the seller said.

“Three coppers' worth. Shall we measure?”

He reached beneath the counter for his cashbox.

The woman caught Merryn's sleeve. “Wait. I paid for the whole thing. His receipt says the whole thing.”

Merryn liked her better at once.

She flattened the receipt. Beneath the seller's crooked signature was the ordinary title warranty, printed on almost every market bill: the lot entire, the goods my own. A buyer could reject a whole lot when one part belonged to somebody else. Even a king's horse came home if it proved to be a stolen horse.

“Quite right,” she said. “And did you ever give him your love?”

“Certainly not.”

Merryn set the thread in one pan and brought the seller's signature against the other.

“His title to it,” she asked the beam.

The love weighed seven grains. His ownership weighed nothing.

“Twenty-six coppers back, then.”

The seller counted them out.

The woman took off the bell herself and returned it. She kept the thread.

“Lenet,” she said to Merryn. “I work at the royal weigh-house. Come to the side door if anyone gives you trouble over your traveling weights.”

“I usually am the trouble.”

“Then you'll know the way.”

She bought a paper bag of hot chestnuts from the next stall and put half into Merryn's hand before she could refuse.

The baby opened his eyes as they left. His mother sighed at him without conviction.

Merryn ate a chestnut, burned her tongue, and went back to selling things she actually owned.

By noon she had sold three rings, weighed a cook's loyalty to the tavern that had just cut his wages, and recovered a handsome fee from a dealer whose six bottles of bravery contained five bottles of drunkenness. She was choosing between a custard tart and a plum tart when a man in a dark green coat laid a blue gemstone on her counter.

It was the size of a walnut. Light seemed to enter it by several different doors and meet in a blue so deep that Merryn leaned forward before she remembered herself.

“For those,” he said.

His finger pointed past her merchandise to the little brass scales at her hip.

She touched their leather case.

“You haven't asked their price.”

“You haven't weighed my offer.”

He had silver hair, neatly cut, and a green stone in one cuff. The other cuff was plain. His gloves were very soft and worn through at the right thumb.

“Merryn, isn't it? Halden.”

“Do we know one another?”

“I know your work.”

She looked again at the gem. No flaws, no milky patches, no anxious little imitation glimmer where the color ought to be. Her hand wanted it with an uncomplicated greed she usually reserved for ripe peaches.

“I won't buy anything I haven't tested.”

“I should be disappointed if you did.”

She set up the scales on their folding stand. Each pan would have held half a plum. At her request the gemstone settled comfortably into one of them.

Its ordinary weight was two ounces.

Its workmanship was excellent. Its color was natural. Its age made the beam tremble, as old things often did, but age alone commanded no particular price. Merryn had sold a very old turnip the week before at a considerable discount.

Then she asked what claim the gemstone carried.

The blue pan fell to the stop.

Halden smiled.

She turned the counting screw. A hundred. A thousand. Ten thousand. The empty pan stayed high.

There was no strain in the brass. Weight of this kind lived between the thing and the questioner; the stand did not have to bear it. But her breath shortened as she fed the question through the beam. Usually a merchant could discover the upper limit of an offer without undoing the counting screw completely.

This time she had to use the extension.

Four hundred and eighteen thousand, six hundred and seventy-three soulweights.

She took her hands away. The magic ceased. The gem was two ounces again.

The ordinary market went on around them. A man was arguing over the tenderness of a goose. The plum-tart boy had begun packing his tray.

“What is it?” she asked.

Halden laid a copper disk beside the stone. The royal census seal was impressed on it, and beneath the seal a small dial showed the number of living people within the kingdom's borders. Clerks kept the great count alive in the weigh-house; their daily impressions served for tax estimates, army provisions, the sale of grain.

The disk showed 418,673.

Merryn put it into the empty pan.

“The living souls of this kingdom,” she said, and gave the balance her breath.

The beam stood level.

She waited. Halden waited with her. A breeze lifted a curl from her cheek and blew the scent of lavender across the counter.

The copper dial clicked.

418,674.

The beam quivered, then leveled again. The blue stone had gained precisely one soulweight.

Somewhere beyond the roofs and fields, a child had arrived.

Merryn felt her own mouth opening in the foolish smile she had worn when she first discovered the scales could weigh a kiss left on a letter.

Then she looked at Halden.

“What claim?”

“The Crown's pledge to me.”

“Of what?”

“It's there on your scales.”

She brought out her traveling token. It bore her name, the mark of her birth town, and the royal stamp certifying that her road dues were paid. She laid it beside the census disk.

“The people of this kingdom, except Merryn.”

The blue pan sank.

By exactly one soulweight.

Her own.

She put a hand flat on the counter. Beneath it were the fine scratches left by years of weighing, counting, wrapping. A little crust of old sealing wax caught her palm.

Merryn looked toward the street where Lenet had disappeared with the baby. When she turned back, Halden was holding the blue stone up to the sun.

She kept her hand flat until she could trust it to move.

“And the whole claim would be mine?” she asked.

“An indivisible claim, transferable before collection. The most valuable object you will ever hold.”

“In exchange for my scales.”

“There are other kingdoms. With those, I can test what the next king offers before I lend to him. I would rather travel with a tool than an estate.”

She could see it then: herself accepting the stone, him walking out through the city gate with her scales in his pocket. Wherever he went next, he would be able to test every lie he told and every lie he bought. Behind him would remain a king's seal and a beautiful blue claim no ordinary assayer could look inside.

“When is collection?”

“I've booked the evening bell. Until delivery, the original pledge may be challenged. Afterward, disputes go to court.”

“Delivered where?”

“The stone can contain what it measures.”

“Me included?”

“You'd take my place as creditor. You decide when to collect, and you hold the receiver's anchor while it happens. Your own soul stays outside.”

She had been resting her fingers against it. She withdrew them.

Halden watched the movement.

“You could hold it for income,” he said. “Think what they'd pay to be released.”

The attraction had not gone out of the jewel. That was unpleasant. It remained the loveliest thing on her counter.

She picked it up again, turning it toward the light.

“At whatever price I chose?”

His shoulders eased.

“Of course.”

“I'll see the deed,” she said.

He took a folded bill from his coat.

“The original. I buy no title from a copy.”

His eyes moved from her face to the scales. She made herself pick a chestnut skin out of a seam in the counter and flick it away.

“You'll be taking them to another kingdom,” she added. “You ought to see them used properly first.”

He tucked the bill back into his coat.

“Very well.”

Merryn paid a neighbor to watch her trays. She took her scales, her purse, and the chestnuts she had not finished.

At the palace end of the market stood the royal weigh-house, a square building with white steps and two carved lions supporting an enormous balance over the door. The left lion held a sword. The right held a purse. Somebody had stuck a feather into the purse lion's nose.

Halden went in through the front.

Merryn followed him.

Inside, people waited on benches with sacks, documents, a caged red bird, a wedding veil. Bells rang at different counters. Everything had a value; nothing obliged two people to agree what ought to be paid for it. Most of the kingdom's arguments eventually came through these doors.

Halden led her past the public hall to a chamber where a wide copper frame hung over a stone table. Thin metal links spread from it across a map of the kingdom, joining cities, villages, and the little brass circles that stood for lonely farms. Beneath the map, a larger census dial turned in the hands of a clerk seated with his fingertips against its rim.

Lenet stood at the table with her baby asleep in a quilted box beside her. She had put on a plain dark gown and a chain of office. A yellow cap lay on the floor.

“Trouble already?” she said.

Halden glanced at Merryn.

“We met this morning,” Merryn said.

Lenet's smile diminished when she saw what Halden carried.

“You're early.”

“My business has gone well.”

He set the blue stone into an empty socket beneath the copper frame.

For an instant all the little links stood out from the map. Merryn felt a pinch behind her breastbone, as if she had swallowed a hook no larger than an eyelash.

Lenet took one hand off the frame. The links relaxed.

“Don't do that again until we're ready,” she told him. She bent to the baby, who had begun to stir.

“What was that?” Merryn asked.

“The pledge finding its goods.” Lenet lifted the boy against her.

“It found me,” Merryn said.

Lenet stared at her.

“It shouldn't have found you. My docket says mines and Crown revenues.”

Halden said, “The royal security extends very widely.”

“Let me see the deed,” Merryn said.

Lenet laid it out on the stone table. It was three sheets long, held together by a broad red ribbon. The king had signed each sheet. At the bottom hung his heavy seal, enclosed in a brass cage attached to the frame.

Halden unbuttoned his cuffs. With his gloves off, the fingertips of his right hand were dark blue.

“A quarter of a million gold crowns,” he said. “To settle the army's arrears. You'll find the acknowledgment on the second sheet.”

Merryn read the first sheet, then the second. The king had pledged the gold mines, hunting lands, palaces, and all else that he owned within the boundaries of the kingdom. Halden's appended schedule named the goods to be delivered: all living human souls within those same boundaries.

She looked up.

“I haven't sold you my soul.”

“No,” Halden said. “His Majesty has.”

“These people aren't an estate.”

“You'd be surprised what appears in an estate.”

Merryn looked down at the last sheet.

The title warranty was at the end, above the king's seal. The lot entire, the goods my own. While settlement remained pending, a proven owner could reclaim any falsely included part and void the whole levy. Merryn had read that language on bills for sheep.

“How does a challenge stop delivery?” she asked.

Lenet pointed to the cage. “Withdraw the original seal. That releases every link made under it. After delivery, my key won't open it.”

Halden rested a hand on the empty creditor's grip projecting from the frame.

The receiver's anchor. He had made provision for himself.

“His Majesty's assayers examined this.”

Merryn was still reading. “Did they?”

“For six days.”

“I should have charged more.”

She had seen a Crown beam. It could measure the extent of an obligation to a hair; it could not tell whether the obligation had ever been given. The royal seal was supposed to settle that.

She moved her folding stand onto the table, close to the caged seal. Halden followed her hands.

“What are you testing now?”

“One part of your lot.”

He looked at the blue stone.

She put her traveling token into the left pan.

“My soul.”

Lenet set the baby down in his box. Carefully, she drew the edges of his quilt away from his face.

“You belong to the king?” Merryn asked her.

Lenet looked at Halden's schedule again.

“I serve him.”

“So do I. Mine's a yearly license. His are the road dues. I never transferred the rest.”

“You were born here,” Halden said.

“Yes. That's why I know whose taxes to pay.”

She could feel the hook in her chest again, a faint coldness from the dormant stone. Four hundred and eighteen thousand people. Almost certainly more, now. Whatever Halden expected her scales to find, he had put that number in her hands because he thought it would be more than she could refuse.

She took the scales off their stand.

To weigh another person's soul, the person could touch the pan. To weigh her own, Merryn had to keep the balance suspended from one hand and touch her token with the other. There must be a living bridge from question to weight. She had done it often enough to calibrate the scales and disliked it every time: the peculiar double feeling of being herself and being something she could drop.

She let the weight settle. The left pan sank.

The cold hook behind her breastbone slackened, as though it could no longer find her.

“One soulweight,” she said.

“We can see that,” said Halden.

“Now the Crown's ownership of that soul.”

Lenet guided the right pan against an edge of the gold seal exposed between the cage's bars.

The pan remained high.

Merryn held her breath, released it, and made the question again. Exact subject. Exact claimant. The transfer that would make this soul the Crown's to pledge.

Nothing.

Halden did not look at the empty pan. He watched Lenet's face. He had never needed Merryn to believe the title, only to want its power.

On one side of the beam, her whole soul. On the other, a seal whose gold content alone would keep her in tarts for a year. Between them, no transfer at all.

“I am claiming this part,” she said. “It is mine. You can have the whole pledge weighed if you disagree.”

Halden reached across the table.

Lenet caught his wrist before his fingers reached the beam.

“There's an ownership challenge.”

“The Crown has sold its subjects before.”

“Then it can show how it acquired this one.”

He pulled his hand away. “Ask the king.”

“He's had six days,” Merryn said. “I'm here now.”

Lenet took a key from her chain. She put it into the lock on the brass cage.

“Put them down first,” she told Merryn. “You're shaking.”

Merryn tried to smile. “This one's expensive.”

The lock clicked.

Halden drove his blue-stained hand into the creditor's grip.

The stone flashed.

Every link rose from the map.

Merryn's soul pulled sharply toward the blue socket. Her left arm jerked; the empty pan struck the seal with a tiny ringing noise. She kept her right fingertip pressed against her token, but the skin beneath it seemed very far away.

Across the room, the census clerk cried out. His chair hit the wall. He had taken his hands from the dial, but Halden was supplying the working now, his bare wrist buried in the grip.

Lenet shoved at his arm.

“Let go!”

“After delivery,” he said through his teeth. “Challenge it after delivery.”

The blue was climbing his fingers. He had been inside this working before. He knew what it cost him to hold it open; he had decided it was affordable.

Merryn backed a step away from the socket. For now her scales were doing what Halden's grip did: anchoring her soul outside the collection. Her left hand held the suspension ring steady. Her right fingertip kept her soul's weight in the pan. Both contacts had to hold; let either go and her soul would fall back into her body, where the stone could take it. The open cage was beyond her reach.

The baby began to cry.

Lenet looked toward the box. The copper circle nearest the capital was filling with blue, spreading outward through the map. Beyond the chamber, a bell rang once and stopped halfway through its next note.

“The seal,” Merryn said.

Halden lunged at the scales with his free hand.

Lenet threw herself between them. She caught his sleeve against the table edge and twisted the cloth around her forearm. He struck her shoulder with his elbow. She held on.

“I have him,” she said, though she plainly had only half of him. “Do it.”

Merryn moved toward the cage.

The nearer she came to the socket, the more her soul pulled. It was no longer merely weight. There was a thin clear gleam above the left pan, and within it she could feel the unchosen continuance of her own life: tomorrow's appetite, the shape of a road she hadn't taken, all the years in which she might become someone she could not yet imagine. None of it had been promised to a king.

She could let go of the suspension ring with one hand. The scales would fall and the gleam would go with them.

She could lift the other fingertip. She felt the stone waiting for it.

The caged seal swung six inches beyond her knuckles. The red ribbon lay over the cage's open door.

Merryn bent her head and caught the ribbon between her teeth.

Halden saw. He pulled against Lenet so hard the table scraped the floor.

“That's the king's seal!”

The ribbon tasted of dust and bitter wax.

Merryn pulled.

For a moment nothing moved. Her arms shook hard enough to set the chains ringing. The gleam in her pan thinned to a thread.

Lenet braced one foot against the table leg.

Merryn pulled again.

The seal struck the brass door and cleared the cage.

All the raised links fell flat.

Halden's hand came out of the grip. He staggered into Lenet, who let go of his coat and pushed him away from the table with both hands.

Merryn lifted her fingertip from the token.

Her soul's weight returned so abruptly that she sat down on the floor.

For several breaths she could only be pleased by the floor. It was cool. It was solid. She was a woman sitting on it, and likely to remain so.

Above her, Lenet was saying, “Stay where you are.”

Halden said something Merryn did not hear. Lenet repeated herself, with less courtesy. Two door guards came in. The census clerk pointed a shaking finger at Halden's blue hand.

Merryn still had the scales. She checked. A chain had twisted round the beam, but nothing was broken.

Then she heard the baby.

Lenet had him against her, capless and furious. She was crying too, with her mouth pressed into the fine hair on his head. A warm spark showed beneath his breastbone, then sank out of sight.

On the map, little flashes traveled along the fallen links. A spark at a farm in the north. A scatter of them at the coastal towns. A whole shining handful where the capital lay beneath their feet. They were traveling out from the broken pledge, returning what had begun to be drawn in.

The census clerk put his hands back on the dial.

418,679.

He made a sound between a laugh and a sob, and checked it again.

The number held.

Merryn let her head rest against the table leg.

One of the guards had taken Halden's wrist. He was watching the fallen links.

Lenet knelt beside her, holding out the baby with an uncertainty Merryn had never seen in a person offering something to her.

Merryn set the scales down and took him.

He was heavier than any love she had weighed that morning. His cheek was damp and hot. He seized one of her loose curls, wound it into his fist, and ceased crying.

“Oh,” said Lenet. “So that's the blessing we needed.”

Merryn laughed, and it hurt, and she laughed again.

They kept her at the weigh-house until after the evening bell. There were statements to take and a messenger to send to the palace. The king's six assayers were summoned. Halden demanded to know who would repay his quarter of a million crowns.

Lenet turned the first sheet of the deed toward him.

“It has the king's name on it,” she said.

Merryn refused three requests to make the same demonstration again. Her hands were still trembling. She ate the remaining chestnuts, cold, and let Lenet bring her a cup of wine whose honesty nobody tested.

When she was finally allowed to stand, she found the blue gemstone lying in a shallow evidence tray beside the withdrawn royal seal.

“What does it weigh now?” Lenet asked.

It seemed possible that she would dislike the stone now. She did not.

She unfolded the stand. Two ounces of stone. No souls, no claim on anybody, and a blue that had lost none of its depth.

“Two ounces,” she said. “A very good color.”

“They'll sell his property if the fraud is upheld. You could bid.”

Merryn touched her sore jaw. She looked at the jewel for a long time, then tucked the scales into their leather case.

“I will.”

Outside, the market was closing. Her neighbor had packed her trays and bought the last plum tart on her behalf. It had survived the afternoon under an upturned bowl.

Merryn sat on the edge of her cart to eat it. All down the street people were holding each other, or arguing, or peering into one another's faces. A man stood beneath the lion with the feather in its nose, taking his hat off and putting it on again. He kept saying that he had felt himself go, and that he was here.

Lenet came down the steps with her son asleep against her shoulder. When she saw Merryn, she crossed the cobbles and sat beside her without asking.

Merryn broke the tart in half.

The baby's yellow cap slipped. Lenet caught it, then took the pastry.

Above the rooftops, the palace bell struck another hour. The boy slept through it.

stories.title: A Perfectly Normal Hobby
stories.prompt: A goth teenager begins studying witchcraft and has to hide it from his parents, who are completely oblivious.
stories.body:
# A Perfectly Normal Hobby

The first thing Orson Dacre learned about witchcraft was that he needed a better lamp.

The little print kept disappearing into the crease of the book. He had spent eleven months making his bedroom suitably gloomy, and now, when the gloom might finally be of some use, he had to turn the desk lamp up and put his glasses on. He angled the light across the carpet toward the old cupboard. His bed and the freestanding clothes rail beside it could stay in the dark.

*Elementary Witchcraft* lay inside his chemistry revision guide. The covers were approximately the same size. To make room, he had removed the section on acids, which he understood, and kept the section on chemical bonding, which he did not.

Downstairs, his parents were arguing pleasantly about whether a film they'd seen contained a second dog. There had been one dog. Orson had counted. He had been waiting six days for them to find something else to discuss.

He bent over the page.

*Keep an ordinary light at your back. Make a seam in your own shadow. Invite one witchlight. Close the seam before attending to your guest.*

Below this was a small illustration of a moth, and below that a pronunciation guide considerably longer than the invitation.

Orson had bought the book from a box marked HOME AND GARDEN. Its previous owner had underlined things in brown pencil. One sentence in the introduction had been underlined twice: *Admiration is not instruction.*

He had admired the book for a week. At sixteen, he already knew how long he could admire something before his mother offered to laminate it.

He'd met his closest friends at an all-ages goth night, under a speaker that made his boots hum with bass. They sent one another songs long after midnight and never asked who he was dressed as.

His parents liked the goth thing. They liked it so much that his father had made a family-chat album called Our Little Prince of Darkness. It contained Orson in his secondhand velvet coat, Orson learning eyeliner, and Orson standing beside a cake whose black icing had turned everybody's teeth green. His mother had once asked whether he wanted to bring a friend to the cemetery, then suggested making it a picnic.

They meant well. That was the difficulty.

If they found the book, there would be themed bookmarks. There would be a photograph. His father would use the word *warlock* in front of a cashier.

Orson wanted time to be terrible at this in private.

He stood with the lamp behind him, facing the old cupboard he'd turned into a clothes alcove. His shadow fell across a row of black shirts, the velvet coat, and a pair of boots still being paid for in birthday money. He pressed his thumb into the shadow's middle and pulled sideways.

Nothing happened.

He tried the invitation. The last sound caught somewhere behind his teeth. He started again, followed the pronunciation guide, and kept pulling.

A white line opened between the shirts.

Orson stopped breathing. The line widened. Behind it stood pale tree trunks, wet black leaves, and stars that were not on his ceiling.

Something small came fluttering through.

The moth settled on his raised hand. It had a white furry body and broad blue wings marked with silver crescents. Light sifted from it onto his black nail varnish. He could feel its six tiny feet.

He had wanted something strange enough to deserve the room he'd made for it. Now that it was here, he couldn't think of anything suitably solemn to say.

“Hello,” he whispered.

The moth cleaned one antenna.

Orson held out his other hand. The book had said to offer a direction with one finger and a slow breath. He did, and the moth floated across to it. His shadow swelled and swept along the shirts.

He tried again. The moth followed. There was no wire, no battery, no sensible place for the light to come from. He was grinning so hard that his eyeliner felt tight.

“Orson?” Dad called from the stairs. “Found you something.”

He clapped the book shut.

The moth startled upward. Orson pointed frantically behind the velvet curtain beside the alcove, and it went there. Blue light showed through the gap. He pulled the curtain across it, shoved the chemistry guide onto his desk, and turned to the door.

A hanger clicked behind him.

The thing emerging from the seam in the alcove was too large to have been concealed by the curtain.

Its head came first: a narrow hound's head, carried low, with branching black antlers above the ears. Then a long back, then forelegs so thin they seemed drawn in ink. One paw touched the carpet. The room smelled suddenly of leaves left in a closed bag.

Orson snatched a shirt from the bed and threw it at the animal's head.

The hound ducked. Orson made a small, entirely unsolemn sound. The shirt caught on the corner of the desk. In the lamplight its falling sleeve swung an enormous arm over the bright carpet and up the wall.

The hound sprang sideways.

Its whole body flattened against the moving shadow, black muzzle snapping at the sleeve's outline. Cloth slithered off the desk. The shadow vanished. The animal spilled back down the wall and gathered itself in the darkness beneath the clothes rail.

There was a knock.

Orson stood between the door and the rest of the room, opened it a hand's width, and said, “Thanks, you can leave it there.”

Dad, in his mustard jumper, held up a folded phone tripod.

“For your outfit pictures. Found it at the back of the cupboard. You'll get the whole boots in.”

“Great. Thanks.”

“Here, I'll just—”

Dad nudged the door wider with his elbow. Orson moved with it. Beyond his father's shoulder the landing was bright and empty.

The hound waited beneath the clothes. Only the tips of its antlers showed, among buckles and hangers. Behind the curtain, the moth's light was hidden in thick black folds.

“No room on this desk,” Dad said affectionately.

He reached past Orson, turned the lamp aside, and put the tripod down.

The bright strip of carpet between the clothes rail and the desk disappeared. Their shadows joined, a dark road running to the open door.

The hound poured onto it.

Orson caught the lamp by its hot metal shade and swung it back.

Light struck the carpet. The animal recoiled into the rail's shadow. A cold black nose had been less than a foot from Dad's slipper.

“Careful,” Dad said. “That's hot.”

“Yes. Thanks. Please don't come in. I've got something balanced.”

“What sort of something?”

“Something I really need you not to knock over.”

Dad withdrew his hand.

“Fair enough. Dinner in five.”

Orson shut the door and pressed his back against it. On the other side, his father began whistling as he went downstairs.

The hound lifted its head.

Orson held still. It lowered its head again, staring at the thin, bright strip it hadn't crossed.

He couldn't leave it here. He couldn't let Mum come in. If it got onto the landing, he would have to shout for them to get out of the house, and hope they did that before asking what he meant.

He edged along the lit side of the room and retrieved the primer.

The sentence about closing the seam had a small brown arrow beside it. He followed the arrow down to a footnote.

*The light attracts other inhabitants. Shadehounds move wherever shadows meet. Keep your own shadow small, and do not run.*

“That,” Orson whispered, “should be at the top.”

The book explained closing on the next page. Hold both edges of the seam and smooth them together, from top to bottom, without stopping. He could do that. The hound, however, was on this side of it. He would be shutting a large hungry animal in his bedroom.

Across the room the sleeve of his fallen shirt stirred in the breeze from the alcove.

The hound's ears turned toward it.

Orson looked from the sleeve to the lamp. Then he looked at his velvet coat.

“Dinner!” Mum called.

“One minute!”

“You said that yesterday, and we found you asleep.”

“I'm awake!”

“Then come and eat while it's hot.”

He put the book open on the bed. He read the closing instructions again, slowly, while the coat hangers ticked together in the wind.

“I'm in the middle of something.”

“Bring it down.”

Orson looked at the hound.

“Can't.”

There was a pause.

“All right,” Mum said. “I'll bring yours up in a minute. You needn't stop, but you do need to eat.”

He had perhaps sixty seconds.

He eased the curtain aside and offered the moth his finger. It came down, brushing his cheek with light. The hound pressed itself lower beneath the rail.

The coat was the first thing he'd owned that made him look exactly as he meant to look. Orson took it off the hanger anyway. His throat felt small and dry. He stood close to the alcove so his shadow fell into it, rather than toward the door, and made himself look past the shirts.

The seam had spread to the width of the cupboard. One edge ran down its wooden side. Beyond the threshold, a short stretch of open ground led between the trees. A broad pale stone stood upright at the far side, with black branches tossing above it.

He held his coat up by the shoulders. It cast a long, empty-headed figure onto the leaves beyond the opening.

The hound rose.

Orson pointed above his shoulder, his breath trembling. The moth hovered behind him. Its blue light caught the coat's spread sleeves and made the figure on the leaves darker still.

The hound watched it.

The bright strip barred the hound from the alcove as well as the bedroom door. He would have to let it across.

He backed toward the desk and switched off the lamp. The barrier vanished. Before the hound could turn toward the bedroom door, Orson jerked the coat up. Its blue-lit shadow slid ahead into the wood. He sidestepped back to the alcove and across the threshold.

Cold struck through his socks. His bedroom carpet ended in a sharp line against damp earth. He could still see the corner of his bed, the chemistry guide, the stupid helpful tripod.

The hound came after him.

It flowed through the opening, a long dark body passing without a sound over the wooden sill. Orson retreated sideways, keeping the moth behind his shoulder and the coat's shadow sliding ahead of him over the leaves.

The hound followed the moving outline.

Seven steps took him to the stone. It was taller than Dad, smooth and white on one face. He hung the coat from two low twigs in front of it and brought the moth down until its light cast the coat's outline onto the stone. Wind flapped the empty sleeves. On the white surface, a huge stooping figure beckoned.

The hound crouched.

The wind dropped.

So did the coat's empty sleeves.

For a moment everything was still except Orson's breath. The animal turned its head. It looked at him.

From the square of his bedroom, he heard a plate clink.

“Orson?”

He didn't answer. He crouched close beside the stone, keeping his shadow small against its base.

Mum knocked.

Any moment she'd shift the plate to one hand and try the handle.

The hound's hindquarters bunched.

Orson caught an empty cuff and whipped it upward.

A giant arm lashed across the stone.

The hound sprang. Orson let go and ducked. An antler ripped through the coat as the animal leapt past him. It struck the coat's moving shadow on the stone and spread flat across it.

“Just a second!” he shouted.

He ran for his bedroom.

The moth streaked after his pointing hand. Behind him the coat fell from the twigs. Its shadow shrank and folded. He heard leaves shift as the hound peeled itself away from the stone.

Orson crossed the sill, caught both edges of the opening, and pulled them together.

They dragged at his palms like heavy curtains. He smoothed down from above his head, stumbling onto his knees as the seam narrowed. Through the remaining gap he saw the hound racing toward him along the shadow of a tree.

He pressed his hands to the floor. A dark muzzle struck at the last inch of opening with a dull thump.

The wood disappeared.

He was kneeling among his boots. A hanger rocked against his ear.

“What was that?” Mum asked.

“Coat fell.”

He looked up. The moth hovered over his shoulder.

He clicked the desk lamp on, slid the primer back into its chemistry cover, and offered the moth his wrist. He held very still until it settled. Then he folded the loose black cuff of his shirt over it. The blue light vanished beneath two layers. Tiny feet tickled his skin.

He opened the door.

Mum stood on the landing with a covered plate. She had her green cardigan buttoned wrong, and a tea towel over one shoulder. Beyond her, the ordinary house smelled of roast potatoes.

“You all right?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the tripod, the fallen shirt, the hangers on the carpet, and his socks, which were muddy.

“Are you doing one of those little films?”

Orson swallowed. “Trying something.”

“Well, don't rush on our account. It's nice to see you getting interested in the technical side.”

He took the plate in his free hand.

“Please don't put it in the chat.”

Mum glanced at the folded tripod. “You haven't even made your film yet, have you?”

“No. Not yet.”

She reached up and straightened his glasses.

“Eat first. And open the window if you're getting that hot.”

He waited until she had gone downstairs before letting his breath out. Then he shut the door, set the plate on the desk, and unfolded his cuff.

The moth emerged, shook out its wings, and settled on the edge of the chemistry guide.

“Sorry,” Orson whispered.

It cleaned its antenna again.

He ate three potatoes with his fingers before he remembered the fork.

Later, after carrying his plate down and answering several questions about frame rates with noncommittal noises, Orson returned to the alcove. A ragged piece of velvet lay caught on the sill. The rest of his coat was still in the wood. He drew the scrap free and rubbed his thumb over it before laying it beside the book.

He moved the desk lamp until its bright strip lay across the carpet. He checked the page on closing. Then he checked it again.

This time he made the seam no wider than his thumb.

Stars shone between the shirts. Beyond the pale trunks, high above the clearing, something vast and blue moved slowly across the sky. It had too many wings to be a bird.

The moth left the book and settled on his shoulder.

Orson watched until the blue shape passed behind a cloud. Then he pinched the top of the seam and smoothed it shut, all the way to the bottom.

Dad's voice came through the door.

“Your mum says you're making films. We've got that little microphone somewhere, if you want it.”

Orson looked at the moth. Silver crescents opened and closed against his black sleeve.

“I've got everything I need, thanks.”

“All right. Don't stay up all night.”

Dad went away. Orson took *Elementary Witchcraft* out of the chemistry guide and opened the next chapter.

It was called *Finding Your Way Back*.

stories.title: Late Onset
stories.prompt: Everyone knows that, if you’re born with the right genetic mutation, you may develop superpowers during puberty. You thought that meant you were in the clear—until you started menopause.
stories.body:
# Late Onset

The first thing I levitated was a Number Six bus. This was inconsiderate of me. It was already running late.

I had just come from the doctor's, where we had discussed my sleep, my periods, and the sudden conviction, several times a day, that someone had installed a furnace behind my breastbone. Menopause, she said. We made a plan. I put the leaflet in my handbag beside the train tickets for my walking holiday and went out into the afternoon.

At the bus stop the heat came again. I pulled off my green raincoat and put one hand against the bus while I untangled the sleeve from my watch.

Its tyres left the road.

For a moment I thought I was fainting. The whole bus seemed to move strangely against the stationary shelter. A man inside rose out of his seat, still holding his newspaper open. The driver's cap hovered above his head.

My hand slid up the warm metal. I snatched it away. The bus bobbed a little higher, then came down hard enough to make the shelter rattle.

The driver opened his window.

I said, "I'm terribly sorry."

He looked at me. He looked at the tyres.

"Was that you?"

I was fifty-three. I had owned a bookshop for twenty-seven years. I had brought up a daughter, learned to dance reasonably well, and finally sold my share of the shop to a partner who enjoyed ordering calendars. I had never, before that afternoon, been a plausible answer to this question.

"I don't think so," I said.

Then my watch rose away from my wrist, taking my hand with it.

*

I had tested positive for the mutation at thirteen. My parents had bought fire blankets and taken the glass out of my bedroom door. At school I wore a yellow wristband for three years, so a teacher would know to press the red button if I became unusual during a lesson.

Nothing happened. The glass went back. By twenty, when even the slow starters had started, I was delighted to be ordinary. The girl who sat behind me in chemistry had spent her sixteenth birthday giving an interview about the ethics of lightning. I had spent mine failing to kiss a boy behind the bowling alley. Nobody had asked me to defend this publicly.

Thirty-three years later, the agency physician turned my old screening record toward me on her desk.

"Same marker," she said. "It's active now."

"Bit late."

"Yes."

"The other doctor said menopause."

"Another major transition. It may be relevant. We don't know enough yet."

She did not sound pleased to be handed an interesting case. She sounded annoyed that the screening system had no box for it, which I appreciated.

My daughter rang while I was waiting for the induction officer.

"Are you hurt?" she asked.

"No. Neither is anybody on the bus. They've checked."

"Good. I've watched it eleven times."

There was a pause.

"You're not cancelling your trip, are you?"

I looked down at my handbag. Six weeks until the sleeper train, then eleven days crossing the ridge country on foot. I had chosen the route myself. I had paid extra for a room with a bath at the far end. Nobody was coming with me.

"I don't know," I said.

That was the first part of the afternoon I truly resented.

*

Joss Bell came into the waiting room with a tablet and a pencil behind his ear. He had short black curls, a yellow flight jacket, and the narrow, unfinished look of someone who might yet grow into his own elbows.

"Delia Moss? I'm your instructor."

"How old are you?"

"Nineteen."

I managed to stop before asking whether his mother knew where he was.

"How long have you been flying?"

"Four years. Professionally, two."

He handed me the tablet. The first field asked for my parent or guardian.

"Sorry," he said, reaching for it. "Wrong form."

"I think it may be the right form with the wrong question."

He considered that, then sat beside me and opened a blank page.

The agency used an old airship hangar at the exhibition grounds. Beyond its great doors lay an oval arena, empty for the season. Along the north side, a grandstand climbed the steep bank in tiers, topped by glass-fronted rooms. The public cable cars crossed high above the arena's western end on their way from the lower town to the ridge station. I had sold postcards of the view for years.

Inside, the hangar smelled of rubber mats and cold metal. Joss brought out a trolley, put a padded training dummy and a crate on it, and asked me to hold the handle.

"What did you do to the bus?"

"I wanted some air."

"Did you imagine it moving?"

"I wasn't thinking about it at all."

He tapped his pencil against his teeth.

"Try wanting it to go up. A little."

The hangar was cool. I had no furnace in my chest, no particular emotion beyond doubt. I put my hand on the trolley and thought about its wheels leaving the floor.

It rose. The dummy and the crate rose with it. A loose strap floated above the crate, neither falling away nor dangling down.

"Keep touching it," Joss said quickly.

I did. He drew the whole assembly toward him with two fingers.

"And stop it."

I stopped wanting it to rise. It kept coming. Joss caught the handle before the frame struck his shins.

We spent most of that first lesson establishing that removing gravity did not remove the motion something already had. By the end I had driven the trolley into a crash mat twice and learned to pull it the opposite way before it reached what I wanted to avoid. The dummy looked reproachful. Joss kept moving the mat back into position.

The power took the whole trolley and everything on it. It did the same with a closed equipment box and the things inside. It could also take just me, although we discovered that rather abruptly when I made the wrong choice while sitting on the trolley.

Joss caught my ankle before my head reached a light fitting.

For a few seconds I floated above him. My cardigan had migrated over my face.

"Take your time," he said. "Normal down when you're ready. I'll lower you."

I had to trust that he could. I pulled the cardigan away from my eyes and looked at him, his hand secure around my ankle, his boots clear of the floor.

"Ready," I said.

He brought me down without a jolt.

Afterward, sitting on a mat, I had a thoroughly ordinary hot flush. Joss offered me water. The trolley stayed where we had left it.

"I can get you an interview slot," he said. "They're very interested."

"I don't want an interview slot."

"Okay."

"Just like that?"

"It's optional. They don't make that clear."

I fanned my face with my appointment card. He lay back on his elbows, considering the lights I had nearly hit.

"They asked me to do an advert for trainers last month," he said. "I don't run."

I laughed. He looked pleased.

Before I left, I asked whether I could safely walk alone in the mountains in six weeks.

He sat up again.

"I don't know yet," he said. "You need to be able to choose nothing even when you're frightened. And choose normal without dropping yourself."

I wanted a reassuring answer. That one was more useful.

*

On the third afternoon I managed to float myself from one end of a low practice lane to the other. I spent most of the journey facing backward. Joss flew beside me and called corrections while I discovered how little my ears cared for a floor that had become a wall.

Rain swept across the hangar doors. The ridge had vanished into a low bank of cloud. We were putting the trolley away when a sound came from outside, a great metallic crack that brought every conversation in the hangar to a stop.

Joss was in the air before his radio spoke.

Through the open doors I saw one of the red cable cars hanging at an angle above the arena. The others had stopped along the line. This one dangled below it, suspended from a thin emergency sling, its broken hanger swinging against the cabin roof.

Joss went straight up. I heard his breathing on the hangar radio.

"Eight inside. Ninety metres above the field. No injuries I can see. Sling's separating."

The duty officer asked how many he could take.

"One a trip. I don't think I've got that long."

A strand flashed loose above the car.

I went to the duty officer's desk.

"Tell him I can take the weight off it."

She looked from me to the open doors. She had seen my lessons.

"You'd have to get inside."

"Yes."

She pressed her transmitter.

Joss came down so fast he bent his knees on landing, though his boots never touched the concrete.

"If I get you there, can you keep a hand on it?"

"I can. Can you carry me?"

"Yes."

He put a harness over my shoulders and drew the straps snug. His fingers moved quickly; mine kept trying to help with the wrong buckle.

"You've lifted a bus," he said. "This is lighter."

We went out into the rain.

He carried me facing outward, one arm through my harness. The arena opened beneath my shoes. My body wanted to clutch him and climb over his head. I kept my hands where he had put them.

Above us, faces filled the cable car's windows.

Joss brought me up beside the open service hatch in its roof. The torn hanger struck the metal a few feet from his head. He caught the edge, lowered my legs through, and put me inside.

I dropped onto a bench beside a woman holding a little boy. Across from us, a man in a grey suit was gripping his briefcase with both hands.

"She's with me," Joss said through the hatch.

I got my palm flat against the vertical rail beside the door. He passed down a rescue strop, looped it around my wrist and the rail, and pulled it tight enough to keep my hand in place.

Then the last sling broke.

The car fell out from under my feet.

I had been going to take its weight away. That thought vanished. There was only the field below, sickeningly far away, and the sudden certainty that it was coming to meet us.

Up.

The loose end of the strop rose beside my face. The woman's boy came off her lap, still in her arms. My own legs drifted away from the bench.

I had selected all of us, car and contents. For an instant the stillness inside was so complete that I almost let it go.

"Keep up," Joss said. He had caught a rail inside the hatch. "We're still falling."

"I can't feel it—"

"Look at the station. Red roof."

Beyond the window, the roof of the lower station was climbing toward us.

I kept wanting up. The roof rose more slowly. The duty officer's voice came over the radio, a string of numbers I could not make into anything useful.

The red roof stopped.

"None," Joss said.

I took the pull away.

We were hanging above the western end of the arena. We had lost much of our height. The grandstand roof was no longer something to look down on.

Rain hissed against the glass. A blue scarf drifted from one end of the cabin to the other. The man in the suit let go of his briefcase, then tried to retrieve it by swimming.

"There's a restraint under each seat," Joss told the passengers. "Pull the red tab. Pair up. Keep hold of each other."

He moved down the cabin, giving people something solid to catch and guiding them toward the seats. Nobody cheered. The woman had both arms around her boy and was whispering into his hair. A teenager near the far door kept saying, very quietly, "Oh, no. Oh, no."

I wanted to tell them I knew what I was doing. Instead I checked that my palm was still against the rail.

The wind pushed us toward the grandstand.

At first I noticed only that the grandstand's windows were growing larger. Then the roof began to fill the view.

"The field," I said. "We need to get over the field."

"White flagpole," Joss said. "Pull toward that."

I found it at the far edge of the grass, leaning in the wind. I chose that way, and the grandstand slowed its approach.

A gust caught the side of the cabin. The whole view swung, and my mouth filled with the sour taste of the practice lane. I kept the flagpole in sight and pulled until Joss said, "Now none."

The car drifted away from the grandstand. Below us, people in orange jackets were shutting the arena gates. There was room to land. There was an enormous amount of room, if I could stop thinking about the places we must not go.

"Back toward the stand now," Joss said.

"We're not over the middle."

"We will be by the time you stop."

I remembered the trolley and its reproachful passenger embedded in the mat.

I pulled back. The far side of the field kept coming, but more slowly, until Joss told me to stop.

Another gust sent the painted centre circle sliding sideways beneath us. I pulled against it while the circle was still under the car. It slid a little farther, then stopped.

The wind did not pause to let us be clever. I kept correcting against the circle while he watched our height. My forearms ached from clenching the rail. The strap would have held my right hand in place if I relaxed. I could not persuade either hand of this.

Heat ran up my chest and into my face. Of all the possible times. Sweat slipped down behind my glasses. I could not make myself let go to wipe it.

"My glasses," I said.

Joss took them off, dried them on the inside of his jacket, and put them back on my nose.

The field was still beneath us.

"I'm bringing us down," I said. "Tell me how far to the grass."

Joss leaned through the open door. "Twenty metres."

I wanted earth to be down again, wanted it with an intensity that frightened me. I let it pull for a moment, then sent us up to brake. We sank in a series of ugly little stages, down, up, then no pull while I listened for his next distance.

"Five metres. Two."

The man in the suit had recovered his briefcase. He hugged it against his chest. The boy's mother had her eyes shut.

The car's lower skirt brushed the grass. We slid a foot to the side, caught, and settled.

I restored ordinary gravity.

Everyone came down into their seats. The scarf dropped onto the boy's head.

Outside, someone knocked on the glass. Two responders had hold of the door. One was laughing, though she seemed to be trying to stop.

I undid the strop. My fingers stayed curled for a moment after I took them off the rail.

Joss sat on the floor.

"You all right?" I asked.

He nodded, then shook his head, then put his forehead against his knees.

I sat beside him while the passengers got out.

*

There were interviews afterward, most of which I declined. There were examinations and questions I could not answer. Somebody asked if the car had been difficult because it was heavy. I said it had been difficult because it was moving, which seemed to disappoint him.

My daughter sent me a photograph of the red car sitting in the middle of the arena. Under it she wrote: Still going?

I sent back a photograph of my train tickets.

Joss and I kept our lessons. He stopped telling me where I was going before asking where I wanted to go. I stopped pretending I could judge a landing by how brave I felt.

Four weeks after the bus, we met on the practice field before sunrise. My walking boots were broken in, the bags were nearly packed, and I had been awake since three. The early waking was still a nuisance. That morning, at least, I had somewhere to take it.

Joss wore his yellow jacket. I had my green coat buttoned and my hair tucked into a wool hat. He checked my radio and stood back.

"A lap of the field?" he asked.

Beyond the grandstand, the ridge lay black against a pale strip of sky. There was a notch near its eastern end that I knew from the walking map. My train would pass beneath it in a fortnight, through a long tunnel. I had been looking forward to coming out the other side.

"That gap," I said. "Can we get high enough to see through it?"

He looked up at the clouds, then toward the ridge.

"Yes. We'll want to stay south of the cable line."

I put my handbag on the bench. The hat itched against my forehead. My heart was going much too fast for a woman standing perfectly still on grass.

I chose myself, and up.

The ground loosened its hold. At the height of Joss's shoulder I let the pull go, then corrected while there was still time, and came gently to a stop.

Joss lifted his own feet off the grass. I chose up again, and we rose side by side. Neither of us spoke until the grandstand lay below our feet.

Through the notch in the ridge, the first sunlight reached the far slopes. There were whole folds of country beyond them that my map had flattened into a page.

I turned toward the gap and began to fall that way.

stories.title: The Briar’s Terms
stories.prompt: You wake up in your fairytale world. Now you have to explain to your intense elven lover why he can't just use magic to fix your disability.
stories.body:
# The Briar’s Terms

The first thing I did was look for my crutches.

The second was recognize the bed.

White branches held up its canopy, still alive, with tiny leaves furled along the wood. Beyond the open windows, the towers of the Briar Court stood among trees that had been old when the moon was young. I knew the window on the left would stick if you tried to close it. I remembered the crack in the green glass pitcher beside the bed.

I had never felt the weight of its blankets before.

“Dulcie.”

Rhaedren stood in the doorway. His black hair was loose over his dark green coat, and one of his pointed ears showed through it. He had a cup in each hand. Neither cup moved, though the tea spilled over his fingers.

He looked at me as though I had done something appalling and wonderful.

“I appear to be here,” I said.

He put down the cups. Then he was beside the bed, holding my face between his hands.

“Stay.”

For seven years, every morning had taken me from him. Sometimes we had parted gently. Sometimes I had vanished halfway through a quarrel, which was an excellent way to spend the following day unable to think about anything else.

“I’m trying.”

He kissed me once, hard, then drew back to look at me again. His thumb moved over my cheek. I could feel its small callus.

I had been dreaming my way into this country since I was twenty-seven. At thirty-four, I knew his face better than I knew the view from my office window. But dreams had never given me the cold air on my teeth, or the smell of his wet coat, or the uncomfortable way I had slept on my right shoulder.

My left leg jerked beneath the blankets.

His gaze dropped.

“It’s all right,” I said. “That happens.”

I pushed the blankets away. My faded blue sleep shirt had come with me, and my soft grey trousers. So had my crutches: they lay across the foot of the bed, black cuffs neatly nested together.

Rhaedren reached for them before I could.

“Those are mine.”

“I know. You told me.” He gave them to me, watching my face. “Did the crossing hurt you?”

“No. I don’t think so.”

I sat on the edge of the mattress and waited for my legs to settle. Rhaedren crouched in front of me. He had once made a visiting ambassador finish his threats from that position. Seeing him there now did something peculiar to my stomach.

“Then who has done this?”

“Do you remember the car accident?”

“Nine years ago.”

“Yes.”

He went very still.

I had told him about the accident. I had told him about the hospital, the wheelchair I used for distances, the crutches. But here I had crossed streams on stepping stones and run down corridors to meet him. Here, my dreaming body did whatever I expected of it.

He looked at my legs, then back at my face.

“They never healed you.”

There it was. I had heard that tone before, just before he declared war on the winter.

“They did what they could.”

“Bring me one of these healers.”

“You’d have to make an appointment.”

“Dulcie.”

“I’m serious. They’re busy.”

He took a breath. Outside the window, something long and thorned scraped the stone, then withdrew.

“Let me see.”

He held out his hand. Silver light gathered along his fingers: the mending I had seen close a split lip, a knife wound, the torn wing of a furious little bird.

“No,” I said.

The light went out.

His hand stayed where it was for a moment, empty. Then he rested it on his knee.

“Explain it to me.”

I rubbed at the mark my crutch cuff had left on my arm the night before. It was absurdly comforting to find it there.

“The nerves in my back were damaged. Some messages get through. Some don’t. I spent a long time learning what I could do afterward.”

“But the wound—”

“Is closed.”

He looked at me.

“Years ago,” I said. “You’re looking for something fresh to mend.”

His thumb moved across his own palm. A pale line ran through it, crooked at the base of his smallest finger.

I took his hand and turned it upward.

“You can still feel this when it’s cold.”

“It was old before I learned.”

“And your mending can’t reach it now.”

“No.”

For a while neither of us spoke. His palm was warm. He had that same hand in the first story I had written about him, though I hadn’t known about the scar then.

I had drawn his country at sixteen and written him into it at twenty-two. When I began to dream my way here, I had assumed that made me an authority. Rhaedren, who disliked half his dialogue and all the honey I had tried to feed him, had corrected that impression very quickly.

He believed I had glimpsed his world before I knew how to visit it. I still had a notebook full of crossed-out place names to offer in evidence. Neither of us had won the argument.

“There must be another working,” he said at last.

“There might be. If someone knows how to do it, I’d like to hear about it. Properly. What it does, what could go wrong.”

“I could seek—”

“Yes. We can ask.” I squeezed his hand. “But the spell you were about to use can’t do this.”

He looked at his extinguished fingers.

“No,” he said.

I leaned forward until my forehead touched his.

“And I would like some breakfast.”

His eyes closed. He made a sound that might, in a less alarming man, have been a laugh.

“Anything else?”

“The starflowers. They open tonight, don’t they?”

He opened his eyes.

“At moonrise.”

“I want to see them.”

“You have described them to me a hundred times.”

“I’ve imagined them a hundred times. That’s different.”

The starflowers bloomed once in a century, and were gone by dawn. I had filled three pages with them at sixteen: blossoms that opened with cold light, whole constellations growing on the branches. In the margin I had drawn a girl kissing an elf beneath them. I had given her flowing hair and a dress that would have been an absolute nuisance to get around in.

Rhaedren looked toward the window. Beyond the towers, the Briarwood rose in a dark ring against the afternoon sky.

“My parents took the lovers’ path on a flowering night,” he said. “My mother kept the shoes she left at the gate. I have them still.”

I remembered the shoes: green silk, embroidered with little gold birds, preserved in a glass case. He had shown them to me with a tenderness I had wanted for myself.

“Then let’s go,” I said.

He looked down at my crutches.

“You don’t expect me to walk there.”

“No.” He said it at once. “Certainly not.”

***

The moon-hind was broad-backed and taller than a horse. She bent her knees until the saddle was level with the mounting bench.

I had written that she was as white as snow. In person she was white with a brown patch above one hoof and a strong conviction that the last apple belonged to her.

“You missed a spot,” Rhaedren said.

“Artistic license.”

“On her part?”

I gave her the apple.

He had shaped a saddle from living willow, with deep cushions and a broad strap. He listened while I told him where I needed the support, then changed it twice. When I was settled, he fastened my crutches beside my knee, where I could reach them, and swung up behind me.

“Too close?”

“No.”

His arm rested around my waist.

“Now?”

“You know perfectly well what you’re doing.”

“I should hope so.”

I took the reins from his hand.

We rode through the orchard, where the apples turned their red cheeks after us, and out beneath the first great trees. His breath touched my hair. The hind’s gait was smoother than a horse’s; even so, by the time the towers disappeared, I was glad of the cushions.

At the heart of the Briarwood, the thorns grew so thickly that they shut out the sky. Roots crossed and recrossed the ground. The hind stopped before a narrow arch woven from branches, each thorn as long as my hand.

Beyond it lay a path barely wide enough for two people to walk abreast. Its stones shone pale in the dark.

The arch stirred. A branch reached toward the hind’s bridle, then curled back on itself. White flowers closed all along its length.

“It won’t admit the hind,” Rhaedren said.

I looked up at the living arch.

“Barefoot and unaided, let those who love come through,” I said.

The words were mine. I could see them on the page, in purple ink, beneath a drawing of two clasped hands.

At sixteen, I had thought they were beautiful.

“Is there another way?” I asked.

“The ring brings every road to this gate. Fly over the trees, and you find yourself here again.”

Of course it did. I had been very thorough about keeping unworthy lovers out of my grove.

Rhaedren dismounted and walked to the arch. The branches inclined toward him. For a moment I thought they would open at once; he was their lord, after all. Then a thorn settled against the silver clasp of his coat, and he stopped.

He had dressed for this. I saw it suddenly. There was no sword at his hip, no ring of office on his hand.

He had expected to leave his shoes here with me.

“We can go back,” he said.

“And miss the flowering.”

“The grove will still be here.”

“The flowers won’t.”

He turned. He did not smile.

“I won’t have you hurt yourself for this.”

“Neither will I.”

The hind shifted beneath me. I steadied myself against the saddle and waited for the little tightening in my left leg to pass.

Rhaedren watched, his hands empty at his sides.

“Then we cannot cross tonight.”

The arch creaked softly. It sounded pleased.

I looked beyond him, at the pale path, and tried to remember the girl who had written it. She had wanted love to matter more than crowns or swords or money. She had stripped everything else away and called what remained enough.

There were things she had not thought to include.

“Can you open it?” I asked.

Rhaedren looked back at the gate.

“I swore to keep this path as it was.”

“To whom?”

“My mother. When I took the wood.”

That stopped me.

The little green shoes were older than the stories in my notebook. She had been a real woman, with a son who remembered her. I had never written her a single line.

“I’m sorry,” I said.

He rested his hand against the arch. A twig curled around his wrist.

“She walked it with my father on the night they made their vows. She said that here, at least, the wood knew true love when it saw it.”

I could have let him take me back. He would have been gentle. We could have sat at the window and watched whatever light escaped the trees.

I wanted the grove.

I wanted to smell the flowers I had given no scent to. I wanted to kiss him beneath something neither of us had seen before. I wanted to get there in this body, with the crutches knocking against the saddle and his arm warm behind my back.

“It’s looking at us now,” I said.

He turned his head.

“I love you. You love me. What is it waiting to see?”

The twig tightened around his wrist.

He looked at it for a long time. Then his gaze travelled up through the thorned arch, toward the black roof of the wood.

“I have kept her shoes,” he said quietly. “I needn’t keep this.”

He closed his hand around the branch.

“Hold the hind.”

“Rhaedren. I want the trees left alive.”

He looked back at me, and there was the man I had fallen in love with: furious, certain, much too beautiful when he had decided on something.

“You do make demands.”

“Several. I’ve been very patient about the kiss.”

The corner of his mouth lifted.

Then he pulled.

The arch struck at him. Thorns caught his sleeve and tore it from shoulder to wrist. The roots under the hind’s hooves heaved. She tossed her head, and I shortened the reins, speaking to her over the growing noise.

Rhaedren did not let go.

Silver light ran beneath the bark. It passed from his hand into the arch and down through every root crossing the path. The branches bent toward him, then away, then toward him again, fighting an order he had never given them before.

His boots slid in the earth.

“You kept what I asked you to keep,” he said to the wood. “Now release it.”

Something snapped high above us. A great thorned limb swung down, and he caught it with his free hand. For an instant he stood holding the whole arch apart. A closed blossom slid down his torn sleeve and dropped between his boots.

The hind backed a step. I kept my voice low and my hands steady. Beyond Rhaedren, the narrow path was coming apart: roots unthreaded themselves from the stones, lifting in long, straining curves. Trunks leaned away from one another. The dark roof split.

Moonlight fell through.

“No one,” Rhaedren said, “will have to satisfy this gate again.”

The root beneath his feet broke loose from its knot. It rose, carrying the arch with it, and the branches swept overhead in a single enormous motion.

I ducked. Leaves brushed my hair.

When I looked up, the path was wide enough for a carriage. Living boughs held themselves high on either side, still bristling, still covered in flowers. Far away, through the parted trees, a pale light was gathering.

Rhaedren stood in the middle of the ride with his ruined sleeve hanging from his arm.

I let the hind walk forward.

He watched us pass beneath the arch. Then he looked back once at the place where he would have left his shoes. I let the hind stand until he turned back to me.

“Come on,” I said, reaching down for him. “You’re the one who knows the way.”

***

We reached the grove just as the first flower opened.

It was small enough to sit in my palm. At first I could see only a narrow blue seam in its white petals. Then they drew apart, and light spilled across the branch.

Another opened. Then twenty. Then the trees all around us were flowering, their branches lifting into constellations. Pale sparks came loose and drifted through the grove, turning slowly as they fell.

They smelled of pears.

I began to laugh.

I drew the hind to a halt beneath the largest tree, and Rhaedren slid down. I had planned to sit with him on the grass. Now my back ached and my left calf was stubbornly tight, and the saddle was a very good saddle.

“I think I’m staying here,” I said.

“Then I shall have to come up.”

He climbed onto the hind behind me again. I leaned back against him, with my crutches beside me and a thousand impossible flowers overhead.

“What do you need?” he asked.

“Some warmth. On this leg, if you can.”

He laid his palm over the tight muscle. Heat spread slowly through the cloth.

“Like that?”

“A little more. There.”

He kept his hand still. After a while the spasm began to ease. I loosened my grip on the reins.

“Did it hurt,” he asked, “when you went back? All those mornings?”

I watched a flower turn above his wrist.

“Some of them.”

His other arm tightened around me.

“I should have understood.”

“I liked leaving it behind.” I rubbed my thumb along his torn cuff. “The appointments. All the explaining. Here I could just turn up and be late for something.”

“You are remarkably good at that.”

“Seven years of practice.”

He lowered his face into my hair.

“Tell me about one of the mornings.”

I thought about it.

“Last Thursday I had coffee with my sister. We argued about whether she should marry her boyfriend.”

“Should she?”

“Absolutely not. He calls every woman he meets ‘young lady.’ He’s twenty-six.”

Rhaedren made a sound of disgust.

“You see? You understand the important things.”

“And afterward?”

“I went home. Did some work. Had a bad afternoon with my back. Ate the cherries I’d bought for a cake.” I tilted my head against his. “Thought about you.”

He was quiet for a little while.

“I sealed the green pitcher with resin yesterday morning,” he said.

I looked up at him.

“It will no longer spill on you. Then I waited for night.”

“Will you still be here at dawn?” he asked.

“I don’t know.”

I took his free hand and kissed the crooked scar in his palm.

Above us, a cluster of blossoms opened at once. Light moved across his cheek, the sharp line of his ear, the mouth I had spent an unreasonable portion of my adult life thinking about.

“Come here,” I said.

He did.

When I finally let him go, a little fallen star was caught in his black hair. I reached up and took it out.

It opened in my hand.

stories.title: The Other Majority
stories.prompt: Humans discover how to grant individuals immortality. However, you can only acquire it by winning a national-wide popular vote.
stories.body:
# The Other Majority

When Isabet Orris won immortality, she was using both hands to lift a glass.

The left had begun to fail in February. By June she could no longer strike a clean octave; by election night she needed the right to keep champagne off her jacket. She had refused a straw. On television a straw would have become the whole campaign.

Around her, people were shouting the returns from the southern districts. Her campaign had sent observers to every station, and the observers had photographed every signed count. There were still photographs coming in, grainy paper squares held against coats and car doors. The sum on the wall passed the number they needed.

“Don't jump,” she told her campaign manager. “You'll break something I have to pay for.”

He embraced her anyway. Someone caught the glass.

Outside the election hall the crowd took up her name. It was the same chant she had heard after concerts, except that now they were asking her to come out and live forever.

She wanted to. She had been remarkably plain about that. Other candidates promised centuries of service, wisdom ripening in an inexhaustible body. Isabet had said she wanted to play the second movement of the Kessel concerto without wondering whether it would be the last time. She wanted a hundred more summers. She wanted to eat cherries after her doctor had stopped worrying about what she swallowed.

The speech had been called selfish. Millions had sent her cherries.

She had promised to spend the award's civic endowment on free concerts. Ordel had pledged it to hospital equipment. The treatment itself carried no obligation to be useful; she had said that too, and lost the endorsement of three newspapers.

The electoral commissioner arrived before she could go onto the balcony. He wore his ceremonial white coat over a rumpled shirt and carried no glass.

“May we speak privately?”

“If it's about my tax return, I intend to pay it over the next thousand years.”

He did not smile.

In the little room behind the stage he said, “You have not won.”

Through the door she heard somebody singing the opening of the concerto, with entirely wrong words.

“We have the returns.”

“You have some of them.”

“Every station. There are pictures.”

“Yes,” he said. “That has made this difficult.”

She set her hands flat on the table so he would not see them shake.

The commissioner placed a folded printout between them. At the bottom were two columns: BIOLOGICAL and CONTINUED. In the first, Isabet had her narrow majority. In the second, the physician Renn Ordel had beaten her by nearly forty million votes.

“Continued what?”

He turned the next page. A sample of the electoral roll. She read six names before she stopped.

MARET TAL.

The name was uncommon. The date of birth was right.

“My wife,” Isabet said, very softly, “has been dead for twenty-three years.”

“I know.”

She reached across the table and caught his immaculate sleeve. Getting hold of it took two attempts.

“Then you have twenty-three seconds to explain why you're using her name.”

*

There was a lift beneath the election stage. Isabet had performed in the hall six times and never known it existed.

As they descended, the commissioner pointed to the faint square behind his ear. She had one too. Most people did. The neural mesh watched for damage, kept a recovery profile in a hospital vault, and let surgeons restore what a stroke or an accident had taken. At certified death the profile was deleted. Her consent forms had said so.

“There was a period,” he said, “before regenerative medicine, when we could preserve a person but could not repair the body.”

“Preserve.”

“Continue. On other equipment.”

“I know what you're saying.” She let go of his sleeve. “I don't know why you're saying it in that voice.”

The lift opened onto a broad gallery. Behind glass, ranks of dark cabinets extended into the distance. Small amber lights burned on them. A screen above a desk showed a street where no such street could fit: red buildings, people in a square, a woman closing a striped awning. The movement stopped. A number in the corner changed. The movement resumed.
