Isabet had played to larger audiences than the population of her birthplace. She knew what a crowd looked like when it was waiting for something.

“How many?”

“Seventy-three million registered electors. More unregistered.”

“Here?”

“Here and in two other facilities.”

She pressed two fingers against the square behind her ear.

“You didn't delete them.”

“No.”

“They didn't agree to that.”

“No.”

He had the sense not to offer an explanation yet.

On the screen, a boy ran under the awning and stopped halfway through his next step. Isabet looked away.

“The treatment,” she said. “The vote.”

“The regrowth lattice is real. One new viable seed every six years. We have never managed better. Ordel will receive this one.”

Every child had seen pictures of the first recipient, two hundred and eleven years old, stepping uninjured from the wreckage of an aircraft. The lattice made a body capable of rebuilding itself; a portion was kept with the recovery profile in case the body was lost entirely. That was immortality: the stubborn, extravagant return of flesh.

“But this came first.” She indicated the cabinets.

“More than a century before it.”

“And they vote.”

“The constitution says every citizen. It doesn't say every living body.”

“Does it say you may invent election returns?”

He took off his ceremonial coat. Under it he was a tired man with a stain near his shirt pocket.

“We count everyone. Then we publish the percentages against the biological turnout. It has been done that way since the first award.”

For years Isabet had watched totals appear on the national broadcast, accompanied by music and pictures of cheering voters. Every six years the country chose one person to keep. The candidates bowed to the result; the winner went to the clinic. Nobody published the station counts.

Previous campaigns had checked sample stations and accepted the official sum. Her fan clubs had supplied enough volunteers to check them all. Her campaign manager had called it an encore.

“You're asking me to concede,” she said, “so you can put my face beside another set of lies.”

“I'm asking you to see whom those lies have kept alive.”

“Show me my wife.”

*

The room had a table, a chair and a screen. Someone had thought to provide tissues. Isabet put the box on the floor.

Maret was waiting.

She wore a yellow shirt Isabet had never seen. Her hair was short, with a grey streak above the right temple. There had been no grey when she died. Behind her stood bookshelves and a blue door, and somebody outside was trying to sing.

Isabet sat down. She had rehearsed meeting Maret again through twenty-three years of dreams, and now she could not find anything to say.

“You look tired,” Maret said.

“I've been campaigning.”

“I watched.”

That hurt in a place Isabet had not prepared for.

“All of it?”

“Most. They give us the broadcasts. I missed the last debate. Our ward was suspended.”

“You watched me and you couldn't—”

“No outgoing connection. The ballot channel accepts a candidate number once every six years. Nothing else.”

“You could have refused to vote.”

“People have. Nobody outside knows when we do.”

The singing stopped. Maret glanced towards the door, and Isabet felt an absurd resentment of whoever had been there, whoever could interrupt this.

“Is this your house?”

“My room. I share the kitchen with four people.” Maret leaned closer. “Ask me something.”

“What?”

“Something to make you believe me.”

Isabet stared at her mouth. There was the little unevenness in the upper lip, where she had been struck by a falling shelf. Isabet had held the ladder. They had argued for years about whose fault it was.

“I don't want an examination,” she said. “I want you to have been allowed to tell me.”

Maret put her hand against the screen. Isabet lifted her own, then lowered it. Touching glass would make her angry, and she was afraid of what she might do with more anger.

“Did you vote for him?”

Maret's hand stayed where it was.

“Yes.”

She had asked the commissioner whether Maret supported Ordel. He had suggested she ask Maret herself. She had been sure there would be an error.

“You know what's happening to me.”

“I do.”

“Then what has he promised you?”

“An additional third of processing capacity. He's pledged the endowment to the recovery vaults. He came here and showed us the costings.”

“He came here.”

“All the approved candidates did.”

Isabet had entered through the public nomination route. Her campaign manager had called the official shortlist a gathering of respectable corpses. She remembered enjoying that.

“You should have been asked too,” Maret said. “You were supposed to lose before anybody had to tell you.”

“And you thought that was acceptable?”

“No.”

“But you voted.”

“Yes. I wanted people awake.”

Outside the blue door, the singer began again, a few bars further on.

“That's Petren,” Maret said. “He thinks he paused for breath. He was stopped for eleven minutes. I was too, just before you came in. They moved our allocation to this room.”

Isabet looked at the bookshelves. There were handwritten labels on them, illegible at this distance. A chair with a cushion. A cup.

“Do you eat?”

“We can. It takes more time than most of us can afford. I like the cup.”

“And Ordel gets a body.”

“He gets the years to keep his programme running. We get time to see our friends before one of us is put away again.”

“He might not keep his promise.”

“He might not. I don't know how to vote without that risk.”

Maret's voice was sharper now, the way it had been when Isabet made a joke in company at someone else's expense and expected her to laugh. Isabet recognised it with a rush of love so painful she had to look down.

Her left hand lay curled in her lap. In six months, perhaps a year, she might be in one of those cabinets. Someone would decide whether she was permitted the time to be frightened.

“You can't expect me to want this,” she said.

“I don't.”

“I've spent the last year explaining why I want to live.”

“I know why you want it. I wanted it for you too.”

“Just not enough.”

Maret drew back. For a moment the old marriage was there in all its dangerous familiarity: the phrase Isabet would regret, the silence in which she could either retrieve it or make it worse.

She made herself wait.

“I'm sorry,” she said finally.

“I stood for the ward council because they suspended a woman halfway through rehearsing my play,” Maret said. “When they brought her back, she was no older. Everyone else had finished rehearsing. They offered her a different part.”

“You've written a play?”

“Three. You would hate two of them.”

“Would I?”

“Absolutely.”

Isabet laughed once. It came out badly.

Maret looked towards the blue door. “I have been here a long time. I can't make these people less important to me because you're here now.”

*

Isabet used the full seven days allowed for an electoral challenge.

On the first morning she told her waiting supporters that she disputed the announced count, that her evidence was secure, and that they should go home and sleep. She had not slept herself.

The commissioner offered her a private connection to Maret while they discussed a statement. She asked for a connection to the archive council instead.

Its members disagreed so fiercely that she had to stop trying to remember who was on her side. One wanted the secret preserved because his grandchildren, whom he watched on public programmes, had joined a group opposed to the immortality award. Another wanted immediate disclosure even if the government shut the whole city down. A third asked whether the candidate had considered that the people who controlled the electricity were also the people being told their votes had never been enough.

“I have,” Isabet said. “What I need to know is whether you can leave.”

They could be suspended and moved. That was how the recovery vaults held the profiles of trauma patients while hospitals prepared to receive them. Keeping a person safely stored required little power. Letting that person think required much more. The archive's population could be preserved outside the three facilities; there was nowhere else with enough equipment to keep everyone awake.

“Then we find people who will take you,” she said.

“As what?” asked the woman who had spoken about electricity.

Isabet had no answer that a hospital had yet agreed to.

She called Ordel.

He came to the hall without his campaign staff. She knew his face from weeks of wishing he would disappear from the news: broad brow, heavy eyelids, a small, infuriating expression of patience.

Her lawyers had sent her a proposed case. The country had voted under published rules, on a published roll. A hidden administration could not simply add another electorate afterwards. They thought a court might agree.

“I could challenge every ballot in that second column,” she said.

“You could. I would fight the case.”

“Because those are your votes.”

“Yes.”

She had spent an hour reading the lawyers' messages. If she won, there would be surgeons and a clean octave, her left hand opening when she asked it to. The photographs could carry her case a long way. She would have to explain why only one column mattered.

“How long have you known?” she asked.

“Eleven years. A patient of mine died. I noticed the hospital continued to bill for her recovery profile.”

“And you didn't tell anyone.”

“I told a great many people. They were all people who already knew.”

“I haven't been impressed by them.”

“Neither was I. I thought if I won I could change things slowly.” He looked at the paper returns stacked on her desk. “You have made slowly rather difficult.”

“Will you accept the treatment?”

“Yes.”

She appreciated that he did not pretend to hesitate.

She turned her phone face down.

“I'm releasing both counts. Help me make you win an election we can publish.”

He knew hospital directors. She knew people who would come when she asked, and people who would come for the cameras. Between them they found six institutions willing to listen.

At the first meeting, a director spent twenty minutes discussing additional storage liability. Isabet nearly walked out. Then the woman asked to speak directly to a continued person.

Maret appeared on a portable terminal. The director asked whether she could understand a transfer agreement.

“Probably,” Maret said. “Could you send it to me?”

The director had been speaking to Ordel. She turned the document towards the camera instead.

“The archive can't recall a patient by order,” she said. “Waking allocations will be ours to make. You need to understand that too, Ms. Orris.”

“I wasn't asking for—”

“You've brought me your wife. What happens when I tell you we cannot wake her?”

Isabet had imagined evenings. Maret telling her about the plays, with enough time left to argue about them.

“The transfer test,” she said. “The broadcast.”

“We can agree those sessions, if she consents. After that, no extra time because she's married to you. You can book calls like anyone else.”

Maret was reading the document. Isabet watched her reach the relevant paragraph.

“I want that kept in,” Maret said.

Isabet looked back at the director.

“Keep it in.”

By the fourth day three hospitals had signed. They would accept consenting continued citizens into recovery vaults under ordinary patient protections, with independent clinicians responsible for access. They could run only a few at a time. Everyone else would have to wait in suspension. The courts might decide the directors had exceeded their authority. Ministers might try to take custody back.

“They will,” the commissioner said.

“Then you should put your name on it too,” Isabet told him.

He looked at her for so long she thought he would leave.

“If you are going to expose the country,” he said, “you will expose my part in it.”

“Yes.”

He signed.

The archive council voted that evening to authorise the offer. Citizens would choose for themselves whether to move. Some refused. Some distrusted hospitals more than they distrusted the commissioner. Some had voted against disclosure and would not leave the people who had voted with them. Maret lost an argument with Petren and came to her next call furious.

“Let me speak to him,” Isabet said.

“He knows your views.”

“I can be very persuasive.”

“Yes. That was one of his objections.”

Isabet shut her mouth.

*

Maret volunteered for the first transfer.

“They haven't given you a date for waking again after the test,” Isabet said.

“I know.”

“You could be asleep longer than if you stayed.”

“Here I can't ask anybody outside. I want to go.”

On the fifth day Isabet carried the sealed unit to the north hospital in the leather case she used for scores. She had not needed to bring the case; the unit was no larger than a book. She wanted something substantial to hold.

An ambulance took them. Outside the hall a few of her supporters were still waiting. One held a sign that said LET HER LIVE. Isabet lowered her head before the woman could see her.

At the hospital a clinician read the seals aloud and matched them to the transfer order. Isabet watched him fit the unit into a recovery dock. He called the archive technician. They checked the state record and its accompanying room files together. He asked Isabet to sit down.

She remained standing.

The screen lit.

Maret stood in her room beside the blue door. She looked straight out at them.

“Did it work?”

Isabet began to laugh and could not stop. The clinician put a chair behind her. She sat down hard.

“I'm at the hospital,” Maret said. “Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Could I see?”

They turned the terminal. Maret looked at the bed, the cream walls, the clock, the clinician holding her papers. At the window she said, “Wait.”

There were ordinary trees outside, crowded against the afternoon sky. A bird landed on one of the branches, stayed briefly, and flew.

“We can give you a better view,” the clinician said.

“This is good.”

He let her look.

Later, with a few minutes of the agreed test remaining, Isabet was alone with her. Maret asked to see the hospital's consent form again.

“Is something wrong?”

“No. I want a copy.”

The council put the offer on the archive's public screens. By the end of the next day millions had applied, accepting suspension with no promised waking date. Most were still waiting for transfer. Once Maret's test had been verified, technicians opened the hospitals' medical transfer links; the spare vault storage could take far more people than the computers could run. Others chose to remain in the old facilities. Several council members stayed with them. Hospital directors answered angry calls from their own boards without yet being able to explain whom they had admitted.

The arrangements could not remain secret much longer. Isabet announced that her challenge statement would be made from the election stage that night, live, with Ordel present.

She dressed herself slowly. One cuff defeated her. The campaign manager fastened it without comment and then said, “Are they going to arrest us?”

“Possibly.”

“Is it a good statement?”

“It's a long one.”

“You've always done well with those.”

*

Onstage, she looked at the camera and saw the little red light come on.

She had thought she would begin with Maret. In the end she began with the count.

“The figures my campaign published are accurate. So is the certificate naming Dr. Ordel. Those facts should not both be possible.”

They put the photographed returns on the screen, then the two-column count.

She explained the profiles, the continued citizens, the falsified public totals. The commissioner stood beside her and answered questions she had given him no chance to approve. Ordel confirmed his private campaign in the archive. She made him say how long he had known.

Then Maret appeared behind them, speaking from the north hospital.

“My name is Maret Tal,” she said. “I died on the seventeenth of August, twenty-three years ago. I was forty-six. I have been a citizen of this country for all the years since.”

Isabet turned before she could help it.

“I voted for Dr. Ordel. I did not vote for my wife.”

Somebody in the press seats made a small involuntary sound.

“I would like you to hear why,” Maret said.

She told them about Petren, about the suspended wards, about people waiting years to finish an argument. She named council members who had opposed disclosure. She said that their fear was reasonable. She did not ask the living to be pleased with the election.

The hospital had invited journalists, clinicians and people chosen by lot from its waiting room. One of them, an elderly man in a dressing gown, leaned towards the microphone.

“Can you find anyone?”

Maret looked towards someone outside the picture.

“If they were continued. If they want to answer.”

He gave a name. His sister. The hospital team had warned everyone that there would be very little capacity, but he waited beside the microphone until a woman appeared in another window. She was younger than he was by decades.

“What have you done to yourself?” she demanded.

The man touched his bald head. Then he was crying, and she was calling him by a name he kept shaking his head at, as if she ought to know better than to say it on television.

Another woman asked for her son. They could not find him in the registered records. She stayed in her chair while the man beside her talked to his sister. The camera did not know where to look.

In the election hall, a journalist stood up and said the whole thing could have been fabricated.

“Yes,” Isabet said. “You should investigate it. We're releasing the records and the custody agreements. You can go to the hospitals. You can speak to people without us present.”

“You expect us to believe the election was won by the dead?”

“I expect another election. With a roll everyone can inspect.”

He began another question, but the picture beside Maret's went black.

It had been the archive square. A council member was preparing to speak from it. The sound stopped halfway through her first word.

Isabet looked at the commissioner. He was staring at his phone.

“An order to isolate the facilities,” he said. “From the ministry.”

For a moment Isabet could hear nothing except a loose fitting on somebody's camera tapping against its stand. Petren was there. The woman who had spoken about electricity was there. Seventy-three million had been a number she could hardly hold in her mind; now it was the next word of a sentence that had not come.

“Maret?”

“I'm here.”

The hospital picture remained. Behind Maret, the blue door stood open. The elderly man was still speaking to his sister.

Isabet put her good hand on the edge of the lectern.

“Commissioner. Will their stored states survive?”

“Yes. The batteries will suspend them safely. If nobody interferes with the cabinets.”

“Who is guarding the cabinets?”

He began making calls. Ordel took his own phone out.

Isabet gave the camera the three facility addresses. She named the council members who had stayed. She asked the journalists to send people, and asked her supporters to let them through. There was shouting in the press seats now, urgent conversations, people getting up.

“The hospital has received the same order,” Maret said.

The director stepped into the picture. She wore a dark coat over her hospital clothes. Isabet had not noticed until then that she had been preparing to leave.

“I have patients,” the director said. “The ministry can put its request in writing.”

She took the microphone away to make a call.

Isabet had imagined the broadcast ending when she finished her statement. Instead she stayed onstage for another four hours. People called in furious. People called in with names. Some demanded that Ordel withdraw; others demanded that Isabet do so. One caller asked why people with no bodies should be allowed to decide who got one. Another asked whether he had already signed something that would make him one of them.

Isabet touched the square behind her ear.

“So have I,” she said.

She could not answer much more than that. She had to let the question remain.

Near midnight, a reporter reached the largest facility. The guards had refused an order to admit a ministry disposal team. There were cameras at the gates. The commissioner was going there himself.

At a quarter to one he called from the gallery Isabet had visited. The guards had accepted his signed custody order; the disposal van remained outside. He had brought two archive engineers back through the gate. They were restoring a single chamber on reserve power. Most of the city would remain suspended.

“Can we see the reporter?” Isabet asked.

The camera turned. The reporter stood beside a cabinet, speaking to one of the engineers. Behind them a small screen lit up.

At one in the morning the archive council member returned to the screen. She sat very straight.

“You interrupted me,” she said.

Maret covered her face. Isabet laughed, and this time it did not hurt her throat.

The council member waited for them to stop.

*

Eight weeks later, when Isabet went onto the same stage, people stood before she had played a note.

She disliked that. She waited until they sat down.

The rerun had taken an emergency court order and an agreement signed by both candidates. For this award, every registered citizen had been permitted to vote, with observers examining the continued roll and the hospital patients voting from their temporary vaults. What would happen at the next award remained before parliament. Outside it, opposing crowds carried photographs of the same people.

Ordel had won by a smaller margin. Isabet had sent him a basket of cherries, with no card.

He sat in the front row tonight. The treatment had taken years off his face. She tried not to look at him.

Three hospitals had become nineteen. Most of their continued patients were still suspended; the directors would not promise more capacity than they had. Families booked calls and then waited. Maret was awake for forty minutes this evening. She had spent ten of them arguing with the concert organiser, who wanted her picture projected above Isabet for the whole performance.

“I'd like to listen,” she had said. “Without being watched.”

They had given her the view from a camera in a front-row seat instead.

Isabet adjusted the bench. The nerves in her left arm flickered unpleasantly. She could play most of the second movement still. She had told the audience that in advance, which had cost her more effort than any of the speeches.

For nine minutes there was only the music and the work of bringing it out. Then her left hand closed on itself.

She tried once to release it. The bass line faltered. She stopped.

The hall was quiet.

She laid the hand in her lap and finished with the right, leaving out what it could not reach. The movement sounded bare and stranger than she had expected. When the last note went, she did not lift her hand for a while.

Afterwards, backstage, she called Maret on the portable terminal. The blue door was visible behind her again. Petren had finally chosen a hospital transfer; that afternoon his room had been linked to her ward again. His first message had been an objection to everything, including the microphones.

“I wanted you here,” Isabet said.

“I know.”

“In the front row.”

Maret looked down. Isabet could see the edge of the yellow cuff. She remembered fastening Maret's bracelets before they went out, a small thing she had once done carelessly, with years ahead of them.

“It was the right decision,” she said. “The election. I can see that.”

“You don't have to tell me tonight.”

“I'm telling myself.”

Beyond the dressing-room door somebody dropped a stack of programmes. The campaign manager, still attending to things long after he had stopped being paid, swore softly.

Maret glanced towards the sound.

“Will you call on Tuesday?”

“What time?”

“They've given me half an hour at six.”

Isabet looked at her hand. She would need help dressing soon. Later there would be hospital rooms, and decisions, and the little square behind her ear. She could not make herself want all of it.

But Tuesday was three days away. Maret would be there, with things to tell her that Isabet did not yet know.

“Six,” she said. “I'll call.”

stories.title: A Safe Place to Burn
stories.prompt: Magical girls normally only use small amounts of their magic. 10, 20%. I'm at 195% and rising. Once I get you and the crew to safety, I'm going to find a safe place to burn up. Good bye. I love you so much.
stories.body:
# A Safe Place to Burn

At eighteen percent, Hedra could hold our ship in one hand.

It was a hand made of light, six hundred metres long, with a white glove and a yellow bow at the wrist. Its fingers closed gently around the *Kitewake* while a boulder tumbled past our bow. Hedra herself floated outside the bridge window, looking pleased with her catch.

“You could have moved the rock,” I told her.

“You could have said thank you.”

“Thank you. Put my ship down.”

She opened the enormous fingers. Then she pressed her own, very small hand against the glass beside my head.

I put mine against it from inside.

My wife was thirty-six. The title on her license was still magical girl, and the bows she had chosen when she qualified still appeared whenever she transformed. Once, after a difficult negotiation over hazard pay, she had threatened to replace them with little skulls. She hadn't. Children drew pictures of her with the bows.

“Captain,” Kivik said from the drive station. “If you've finished conducting the hull inspection.”

Hedra showed him a gloved middle finger. Only the small one.

We had been surveying the little moon for nineteen days. Nothing lived there; nothing had ever been built there. Grey craters, a glassy plain, the sharp black shadows of mountains. We had found a chain of caves, and Hedra had spent her off-watch hours arguing that one of them looked like a rabbit. Sella had begun putting long ears on the survey maps.

I was watching Hedra laugh at something I couldn't hear over the crew channel when the drive struck us from behind.

The bridge snapped sideways. My harness caught me. The window filled with grey chips and spinning stars.

“Impact,” Kivik said. “Drive housing. Shutoff isn't taking.”

On the stern camera, a blue-white seam opened along the drive. There was no sound from outside, only the warning tone in the cabin, so small and polite that I hated it.

Hedra looked toward the stern.

I saw her put both hands around the daisy brooch at her throat. Her right wrist turned hard. The little gold ring around the petals broke.

“Hedra!”

The drive opened.

For a moment the whole ship was inside a yellow flower.

Its petals caught the expanding fire and folded over it. The bridge went dark. Something huge struck the underside of the hull, and every loose thing in the cabin rose together: a pencil, Kivik's spectacles, the biscuit I had been saving.

The lights returned. A ribbon lay across the broken window frame, holding the air in.

On the stern camera, the engine was gone. So was the aft third of my ship. The remaining decks hung inside a net of yellow ribbons. Where their ends met, a woman in white boots held a burning flower between her hands.

My display acquired a new window. HEDRA: CHANNEL LOAD. Eighty-four percent.

“All stations,” I said. “Answer.”

Kivik beside me. Sella in the galley. The other four, one after another, from the survey deck. Seven voices, including mine. I counted again without meaning to.

“Hedra?”

“Here.” She sounded winded. “I caught it.”

“You caught it. Let it go.”

On the camera she opened her hands. The flower split, and a spear of light crossed the darkness, scattering the broken drive into sparks. Beyond it, a mountain on the moon lit from the side.

The number climbed to ninety-one.

“Hedra, close up.”

“Trying.”

We were dropping. The drive had been firing when the rock struck, and its last impulse had shoved us out of orbit. The surface grew beneath us. I called up the impact estimate, looked at it, and put it in the corner where I could still see it without staring.

Nine minutes.

I sent the distress call.

“Everyone forward,” I said. “Pressure cabin. Sella, count them through the bulkhead. Kivik, emergency panel.”

Hedra stayed between our wreck and the moon, the ribbons taut around her. They were slowing the fall. I could see her fingers working at her brooch.

One hundred and six percent.

Kivik brought up the medical channel. A matching daisy glowed on his panel, each petal an indicator. He selected shutdown. The petals blinked shut.

Outside, Hedra made a strangled noise. For an instant her ribbons thinned enough for me to see the stars through them. Then the light came back brighter.

One hundred and twenty-eight.

“Stop,” she said. “Don't do that again.”

Kivik took his hands off the panel.

“What happened?” I asked.

Hedra looked directly into the stern camera. “It won't close.”

“Can you untransform?”

She tried. Her yellow skirt flickered. Beneath it I glimpsed the blue flight suit she'd been wearing at breakfast. Then the skirt returned in three tiers instead of two, each edged with tiny bright bells.

None of us heard them. There was no air outside.

“Hedra.”

“It's opening farther when I try.”

Her license was in a frame over our bed. I'd read the limits printed along the bottom, most recently while looking for a moth. A hundred was the full width of the channel a body could safely hold. The brooch limited her to a small fraction of that. The brooch did not make the magic.

“Put it into something,” Kivik said. “All of it. The rock, the ship, anything.”

“I'm already putting it into the ship.”

She spread her arms. Wings unfolded behind her, yellow feathers longer than our remaining hull. The wreck rose. The impact estimate blinked out, then returned with another three minutes added.

One hundred and sixty-three.

“There isn't less of it afterward,” she said.

Sella came through the bridge hatch with the last of the survey crew. One had a hand wrapped in a towel. Another was holding somebody else's boot. Sella put a palm on each shoulder as they passed her, moving them toward their crash seats. She looked at the number on Kivik's panel and stopped.

“No,” she said.

Hedra's face disappeared behind the wing for a moment. When she came back into view she was shaking her head, hard, like someone trying to wake up.

“We can get you inside,” I said. “Get everyone here, cut the cabin free. You won't have to hold the whole ship.”

“Romy.”

“We've got the jets. We can help.”

“I know.”

I had kept my voice level through the count and the broken hull and the failed shutdown. I lost it then.

“What's it going to do to you?”

Hedra swallowed. Her hands were still at her throat. She looked away from the camera.

“Magical girls normally only use small amounts of their magic. 10, 20%. I'm at 195% and rising. Once I get you and the crew to safety, I'm going to find a safe place to burn up. Good bye. I love you so much.”

For a moment I thought she had changed to a private channel. She hadn't. Behind me, someone began to cry.

“No,” I said. “You don't get to say it like you're hanging up.”

Her mouth crumpled.

“I don't know how to say it.”

“I love you,” I said. “I love you. Now come to the window.”

She looked at the camera for a long moment. Then the wings swept, and the *Kitewake* rose under us. She came around its side in a trail of little yellow stars.

I unbuckled. Kivik caught my arm, but I shook him off and crossed the bridge. The old window was gone; a sheet of her light held the air in its frame. I stopped just short of it.

She was there. Her hair had come out of its plait. It floated around her face, bright at the ends. There were new bows at her shoulders, and the light at her throat was too strong to look at.

I lifted my hand.

She reached toward it. Before she touched the shining barrier, the metal beside my face ticked sharply. The paint blistered along the frame.

Hedra snatched her hand away.

On the wall above me, the cabin temperature began to climb.

“Back,” she said.

“Hedra—”

“Romy, get back.”

I stepped away. She went with me in the other direction, away from the ship, her open hand still raised. The ribbons stretched between us.

“I wanted to come in,” she said.

Behind her, one of the wings came apart. Its feathers scattered in a whirl, then joined again farther out, each feather now a curved white shield with a yellow bow at its base. They circled her in a widening skirt. The light from them swept across the cabin, across Sella holding the injured surveyor, across Kivik's bare face.

Two hundred and twenty-one percent.

Hedra looked down at herself. “Oh, that's ridiculous.”

It was the voice she used when her transformation caught a sleeve in a door. I sat down before my legs could fail me.

She took a breath I could hear over the radio.

“Cut the cabin loose. I can't keep all this.”

Kivik put his hands back on the controls. Sella tightened the last harness and dropped into her own seat. I buckled in, armed the separation bolts, and brought the cabin's maneuvering jets online. Four green indicators. A flight plan that ended in the moon.

“Hedra, we haven't got thrust to clear the surface.”

“I have.”

“You'll have to push us along the horizon. Up won't do it.”

“Then steer me.”

I fired the bolts.

The deck jumped. Our nose cabin broke free. For a moment the rest of the *Kitewake* hung beside us: the bunks, the galley, the tiny room I shared with Hedra. A yellow ribbon slipped through the broken decks and unwound. The wreck fell away.

The cabin tilted, and the moon filled the window.

I fired the port jets. Hedra's ribbons gathered beneath us into an enormous bow. Two long tails streamed back to her hands. The white shields turned edge-on and swept around her, clearing a path through the wreckage falling with us.

“That's it,” I said. “Hold that line.”

We began to move sideways across the moon.

At first I could make out individual stones below us. Then the grey ground blurred. A ridge came up ahead, jagged black across the stars, and I pulled the nose toward its lowest saddle. Hedra followed my turn. The bow beneath us tightened. All seven of us sank into our seats.

We cleared the ridge with the lower tail of the ribbon brushing its peaks. A bright seam ran along the stone where it touched.

The pressure cabin shuddered. Something in the wall gave a loud crack.

“Too much,” I said.

“I know.”

Two hundred and sixty-eight. Her voice was tight now. The star-shaped buttons on her bodice had multiplied until a whole constellation shone around her waist. One by one they lifted away and wheeled around the cabin, taking the heat of the ribbons on their little golden points. She had put herself farther behind us. I switched from the window to the cabin's rear camera, afraid to lose sight of her.

The curve on my flight display bent away from the surface.

Not enough.

I feathered the jets, keeping the cabin square against her pull. One of the surveyors was praying. Kivik called out our speed. Sella told him to keep doing it.

Hedra's wings opened again, beyond the ring of shields. There was no longer room for them on the camera. Their light raced across the plain below us, overtook the mountains, threw shadows out behind craters I had spent nineteen days measuring.

The curve lifted clear of the moon.

I checked it against our speed. Checked it against our height. Behind us, Hedra was a small dark figure at the centre of a flower the size of a city.

“We've got it,” I said. “We're clear.”

“Check.”

“I have.”

“Again.”

Kivik read the figures back to me. I ran the plot once more. The line went out into darkness, well above the mountains, toward the traffic orbit. There was a rescue beacon on it, coming our way.

“You can let go,” I said.

The bow untied beneath us.

Our little cabin sailed on. Hedra fell behind, trailing ribbons. The numbers on my display stopped changing so quickly: distance, speed, predicted intercept. Small ordinary numbers I knew what to do with.

Hers was three hundred and four.

“Everybody?” she asked.

Sella unmuted the crew channel. They answered her themselves, all seven of us. The surveyor who had been praying tried to thank her and couldn't finish. She pressed her lips together and nodded. Then she looked away from the camera, toward the moon.

“I have to go now.”

Below her was the long, flat basin where we had landed on our first survey day. I could still see the little dark mark our launch had made.

“There's the basin,” I said. “Nothing down there. I'll warn the traffic.”

I was already bringing up the emergency broadcast. If the other ships turned now, if we cut our own path behind the nearest ridge, if the release stayed inside any estimate I could invent, she wouldn't have to fly farther.

She could stay where I could see her.

“The far side,” she said.

“You don't have to go that far.”

“The crater with the rabbit caves. It's deep.”

“We can clear the near side.”

She looked toward the lights on the traffic display I had shared with her. One was the rescue tender, burning toward us.

“I don't know how big it's going to be.”

I stared at the little tender. It had turned out of its safe orbit because I had called for help.

“Neither do I,” I said.

“Put the moon between me and them.”

I brought up our survey. The crater lay just beyond the far limb. There was no shallow way down to it from where she was; she would have to skirt the high ground, then drop behind it. Another minute of flight. At the rate her number was climbing, I didn't know if she had a minute.

“We'll lose radio,” I said.

“I know.”

“When you go behind it, I won't be able to hear you.”

“Romy. I know.”

I laid in the route. My hands kept moving the last point back to the near side. I made myself stop. Sent it.

Hedra turned.

The huge wings swept together behind her, folding their bright surfaces into a cup. Its open mouth faced the moon. All the streaming ribbons ran toward it. She couldn't close the channel, but I had watched her turn its light away from us once already.

“That way,” she said, almost to herself. “Keep it going that way.”

She flew.

The rear camera followed her across the mountains. Her skirts streamed behind her in enormous yellow tiers. The bows were still there. I could pick them out, absurdly neat, at the roots of the vast white wings.

I magnified the image. Through the wash of light I could see a little of her face.

“I'm frightened,” she said.

I put my hand over my mouth. Sella leaned forward in her harness, trying to reach me, but the next seat was too far away.

“I'm here,” I managed.

“I don't want to stop talking.”

“Then don't.”

She made a small sound. Her lips moved, but nothing came out.

“You were right about the caves,” I said.

It was all I could find. The silly argument in the galley, her insisting on two long ears, Sella turning the map around, me saying rabbits didn't have mouths like that. I had been there. We had all been there.

“Definitely a rabbit,” I said.

Her mouth twitched. “Awful rabbit.”

“Terrible.”

Three hundred and eighty-nine.

Her face washed out. I pulled the image back until I could see her descending toward the horizon. The shields had begun to break. They tumbled away from her and vanished, each one leaving a streak across the dark.

“How far?” she asked.

“Past the next ridge. Then down.”

“All right.”

“I'm with you.”

The curve of the moon rose across her wings. For an instant the whole black ridge was edged in yellow. Then her figure dropped out of sight, and her voice broke into a burst of static.

I said her name.

The load window went grey.

I kept the channel open. On the camera there was only a mountain range and the black space above it. The cabin drifted; I corrected it automatically. Kivik asked me something, very softly, and Sella answered for me.

I waited for light on the near side, for some terrible sign she hadn't made it. The plain stayed dark.

Then, beyond the far limb, a plume of dust rose, lit white from below.

It climbed slowly at first. The crater's rim held the base of it out of sight. Its top spread above the mountains, brighter and brighter, until the cabin windows dimmed themselves and I could see my own face reflected over it.

The moon stood between us and the fire.

Behind me, harnesses creaked as people turned to look. I counted them again.

I left the radio open as the rescue tender came alongside. Sella undid my straps. Someone put a warm hand around mine, and I held it so tightly that they had to ask me to loosen my fingers.

stories.title: The Sky in His Teeth
stories.prompt: Your first familiar arrives three years late, weighs twenty pounds, and insists on sleeping across your face. You’re ready to return him—until the kingdom’s most feared sorcerer visits, sees the cat, and asks whether his old master is accepting apprentices again.
stories.body:
# The Sky in His Teeth

My familiar arrived three years late, ate the fish I had been saving for supper, and spent his first two nights asleep across my face.

On the third morning I found the basket.

He watched me put his blanket inside it. He was long-haired and white beneath, gray above, with cream behind his ears and a tail that appeared to require a separate spine. The produce seller downstairs had weighed him for me: twenty pounds, not including the stolen fish.

“In,” I said.

He stepped onto my bed.

“I am returning you.”

“Put your hands out.”

“No.”

“Then you will learn nothing.”

I had waited three years to hear a familiar say that. I put the basket down harder than necessary and held out my hands.

The cat stood on the coverlet. His front paws were enormous, the left one turned slightly outward. There was a pale green eye on either side of a pink nose. Nothing about him suggested remorse.

“Close your eyes.”

“You'll run away.”

“I am not running anywhere.”

This was true. He preferred to be carried between places less than six feet apart.

I closed my eyes. He stepped into my arms, first the broad weight of his chest, then his hindquarters. I had to draw him against me. His purr shook my breastbone. Each time it settled into a rhythm there was a small hitch, as though he were remembering something amusing.

“Know where I am,” he said.

“On me. Again.”

“More particularly.”

His left paw was on my wrist. His ribs moved against the inside of my elbow, and one hind foot braced against my stomach. The weight was familiar already. At night it had pressed the backs of my earrings into my neck and pushed my long dark hair, blue ends and all, into my mouth.

When he climbed down, my arms remained in their awkward curve.

“Open your eyes.”

He was on the windowsill across the room. Below him his shadow lay long on the floor.

“Now bring me back.”

“How?”

“Let the shadow open where you felt me. Hold it open until I step through.”

“I called you three years ago.”

“Try a shorter distance.”

I knew a pattern for making a thing go where it was wanted. I had used it to bring a needle off the floor. I shaped it between my palms, put a cat into it, and pulled.

A white shape rushed up from the shadow. I closed my hands.

For an instant there was a magnificent cat in my arms: long-tailed, green-eyed, perfect as a painted familiar in a college prospectus. Then my fingers met through its chest. It came apart into cool gray wisps.

The actual cat remained on the sill.

“You shut it,” he said.

“I had you.”

“You had a picture.”

“What was I supposed to wait for?”

“Me.”

He jumped down. I looked at my empty hands, then at the basket. At nineteen I had failed the college examination over a jug, with a brown stray watching from the examiner's sill. The examiner had passed my copy, but then I noticed that it lacked the maker's thumbmark beneath the original's handle; I tried to put it in and broke the handle off. Perhaps an animal capable of answering a question would have helped.

The cat stopped in the middle of the floor.

His shadow kept going.

It flowed toward the window in a thin black strip. The bed's shadow followed. So did mine.

I looked outside.

A piece was missing from the morning.

Above the opposite roof, a clean black wound had opened in the pale sky. A cloud passed behind it and did not come out. Along one edge shone a row of stars, hard and bright in daylight. As I watched, the last star slid sideways and vanished.

The cat's ears went flat.

He made a sound I felt in my teeth.

Somewhere far away, something answered.

“Get your boots,” he said.

***

I was still working a knot out of the second bootlace when a line of fire opened down the middle of my door.

The wood divided without burning. Through the narrow gap I saw a mountain under stars, then a green sea, then a man standing on a black stair. He stepped into my room. The door closed behind him.

He wore a dark coat lined with red. His mustache was streaked with gray, and there were white scars across the knuckles of both hands. Around his right wrist ran a chain whose links were little burning animals. They moved their heads as he passed.

I knew his face. Everybody knew Lord Varras's face. In the cheap woodcuts they put broken fortresses behind it.

His eyes went first to the window.

Then he saw the cat.

The chain tightened around his wrist.

“Master Thrum?”

The cat sat down on my rejected basket.

Varras bowed. It was not a court inclination. He bent so far that I could see a burn through the shoulder of his coat.

“Are you accepting apprentices again?”

I had one boot in my hand.

“He's mine,” I said.

Varras looked at me.

“My familiar. I'm returning him.”

For a moment the most feared sorcerer in the kingdom looked genuinely at a loss.

Thrum got up, stepped into the basket, and settled on the blanket.

“It has reached the upper sky,” he said.

“I know.” Varras opened his hand. Three of the little animals on the chain had gone dark. “I drove it off the western roads. It learned to feed between them.”

“How long?”

“Since the winter you died.”

I lowered the boot.

Thrum's tail moved once.

“You were dead?”

“Eighth life.”

I looked from him to Varras. The sorcerer was looking at the cat as though he were both someone he had missed and someone he had never seen before.

“He was brown,” Varras said softly. “Small enough to sit inside my coat.”

“Ninth,” I said.

Thrum flicked an ear.

“That's why you were late?”

“Milk. Mice. Remembering my name. It takes time to grow.”

A cold wind came through my window. Outside, someone shouted. The cloud was still vanishing into the black gap, steadily, like cloth being drawn through a ring.

Varras flexed his wrist. Far above the roofs, a line of silver fire drew taut.

“Can you hold it?” Thrum asked.

“If I can get the Hart around its throat.”

“Then do that.”

“And afterward?”

“We go inside.”

Varras's expression changed. I thought it might be relief, until I saw him swallow.

“Of course,” he said.

The chain uncoiled.

It passed through the window and kept passing. Link after burning link slipped over the sill, though there had never been enough chain around his wrist to reach the door.

Thrum jumped onto the bed.

“Pick me up.”

“Inside what?” I asked.

The wound in the sky opened a little wider. For the first time I could see teeth.

***

Varras walked up the outside of the house.

He did not climb. He stepped from my sill onto empty air, turned his foot, and put it against the wall. His coat hung sideways. He looked back at me.

“Keep your hands on your master.”

Thrum was heavy against my chest.

“I have no intention of dropping him.”

“Not what I meant.”

The cat put one paw on my shoulder and looked over it. My shadow rose from the floor, climbed the wall, and spread itself across the open window.

Through it I saw a narrow road under an unfamiliar night.

“Step,” Thrum said.

I stepped.

My boots struck something hard. I was standing above the roofs on a strip of darkness no wider than a footpath. On either side, the town fell away into daylight. Ahead, the road curved upward into the wound.

The air smelled of cold iron.

I tried not to look down. This proved difficult because looking straight ahead meant looking at the thing eating the sky.

It had no eyes. Its head was a black wedge, smooth as wet stone, and its mouth opened along half the horizon. Inside were stars. Not reflected stars: some went out as its jaws worked, and others flared through the thin skin beneath its throat.

I could hear them. A high, continuous singing came through the dark, with gaps where voices stopped.

Varras stood on the point of the college tower.

He raised both hands.

The daylight above him broke into twelve bright pieces.

They turned, and I understood that they were antlers.

A creature unfolded from the heavens, its shoulders towering above the eastern hills. Stars burned beneath its translucent skin. Its great chest expanded, and wind flattened every tree in the court below us.

The Hart lowered its head.

Varras threw his chain.

It passed between the antlers, looped around the devourer's throat, and pulled tight.

The sky struck back.

I fell to my knees. Thrum's claws caught in my coat. The road bent under me like a branch.

The devourer rolled. Its mouth swept across the morning. An entire ridge of cloud disappeared, leaving a hard blue edge behind it.

Varras did not let go.

His boots cut grooves in the tower stone. He drew one hand toward his chest, slowly, as though dragging a loaded cart by a single rope. The living Hart braced its front legs across the sky. I saw the muscles move beneath its stars.

Another link went dark.

“Master,” Varras said.

It was not loud, but I heard it.

Thrum sprang from my arms.

He landed on the road in front of me, crouched, and put his teeth into the dark beneath his feet.

For a moment he looked absurd: a fat cat trying to bite his own shadow.

Then he pulled.

The road split.

Through the opening came a light so fierce that I covered my face. In it I saw a sea standing on its edge, a ringed moon caught in black reeds, and something long and golden beating against a membrane.

The cat dragged the opening wider with both front paws.

“Inside,” he said.

I crawled after him.


***

We came down on a ledge that ran along the inside of the creature's throat.

Beneath it hung the sea I had glimpsed. Waves rose and broke downward into a depth full of blue fire. Above us, the ringed moon turned slowly among black strands thicker than trees. Light from it moved across my brown hands.

Thrum shook himself.

“Stay where things resist you.”

“What?”

He pushed his head against my shin.

“That is me. That is you. Something happened between us. Remember.”

Ahead, the ledge broadened into a staircase.

At the top of it was my room.

The door stood open. My bed was made. A small, elegant white cat sat on the windowsill, and there was a letter on the coverlet with the college seal in blue wax.

I stopped so abruptly that Thrum's tail struck my leg.

The little cat turned. It had clear green eyes and an expression of tender intelligence.

“That's not you,” I said.

“Test it.”

I reached through the doorway.

My hand met a flat, cool surface. The room remained perfect behind it. The cat moved its head again, exactly as before.

I pressed harder. Nothing pressed back. The image of the letter had no thickness.

“It makes places where you want to go,” Thrum said. “Then it swallows what steps toward them.”

The stair folded shut.

A row of small teeth closed where the doorway had been.

I pulled my hand back. Thrum hooked one claw into my trouser leg and led me on.

We walked beneath the inverted sea. I could see ships in it, their sails hanging motionless in the wrong direction. Behind the moon were other lights: a red sun no larger than a house, a great turning wheel of birds, a city whose towers were bells.

“Are those real?”

“Some.”

“How can you tell?”

“I have been there.”

He sprang onto a narrow ridge and waited while I climbed after him.

“Did you used to be a man?”

“No.”

“Ever?”

He looked back at me.

“No.”

I put a hand against the wall. It was warm and slightly yielding. Far beyond it, Varras's chain made a sound like a thousand doors being dragged open.

“But you're a sorcerer.”

“Yes.”

“Who taught you?”

“Several people. A fox. Something under a mountain whose name I cannot pronounce in this mouth. I paid attention.”

He set off before I could ask about the other mouths.

The ledge trembled.

Through a long opening in the wall I saw Varras outside. He was no longer on the tower. He stood between two points of the Hart's antlers, one foot on each, with the chain wrapped round both arms. The creature's throat had begun to slide through the binding.

Varras pulled the antlers toward one another.

The Hart bellowed.

Stars spilled from its open mouth, struck the chain, and became new links. They ran down the binding in a blaze, tightening it around the black flesh.

The pressure lifted me off my feet.

Thrum caught my sleeve in his teeth. For a moment I hung over the inverted sea with a twenty-pound cat holding me by my coat.

I found the ledge with one boot, then the other.

Outside, Varras lowered his head between his shoulders and took another turn of chain.

Blood ran from one palm. He did not look at it.

“He can't hold that forever,” I said.

“No.”

Thrum moved faster.

“What was it before?”

“A thing under roots. I hunted it in my fourth life. In my eighth it found a tear in the night and swallowed its way through.”

“You stopped it?”

“I bound the tear shut.”

“Then you died.”

“Yes.”

Below us, something enormous moved beneath the sea. Its passage drew whole islands across the underside of the waves.

“I didn't do that to you,” Thrum said.

“What?”

“The three years. They were not a lesson.”

I had not thought he was capable of hearing something I had not said.

“I know.”

“I had to learn where my feet were again.”

He jumped a gap in the ledge. I put one hand down to follow, and the stone beneath my fingers vanished.

The passage lurched.

Thrum landed on the far side. Between us there was now thirty feet of open dark. The inverted sea was falling through it in slow, bright pieces.

I backed against the wall.

“Don't try the jump,” he said.

“I wasn't.”

“Good. Bring me back.”

I stared at him.

The sea gave a deep cracking sound below us.

“Now?”

“Now.”

I held out my arms. They were shaking.

“Not a picture,” he said.

I remembered his weight against me. The left paw on my wrist. The uneven purr. I let my shadow open across the inside of my forearms.

It felt like letting go of something I had been clenching all my life.

At the far side, Thrum's shadow lengthened toward mine.

I felt fur.

I nearly closed my hands.

“Hold,” he said.

There was no weight in the fur. It was only the shape I had supplied.

I made myself open my fingers again.

“Where are you offering to put me?”

“Here.”

“Then make room.”

I lowered one forearm, the way I had learned to do at night when he insisted on fitting between my cheek and my shoulder.

Something pressed against the new space.

A paw hooked my sleeve. I felt his chest turn, much heavier than the smooth, comforting picture had been. His purr began against my wrist, stopped while he made an adjustment, then returned with its familiar hitch.

The shadow opened.

Thrum came through it all at once.

My knees hit the ledge. I held him against me, his hind feet digging into my stomach. Behind him, the far side of the passage broke away and fell into the sea.

“When?” I gasped.

“When I am here.”

He pressed his forehead under my chin.

I felt him settle, completely. Then I let the opening close.

For a moment I could do nothing but sit with my face in his fur.

“I did it.”

“Yes.”

“I actually—”

The wall burst open beside us.

A section of chain thicker than a road drove through the dark. Its links were blazing stags, each one running inside the next. Between them I saw Varras's raised hands and the devourer's jaw lifting against the sky.

Thrum climbed onto my shoulder.

“Be pleased while moving.”

I got up.

***

Beyond the broken wall the creature opened into a country of captured heavens.

There was no floor. Roads ran between pieces of night: a curve of white desert, the underside of a forest, steps cut into the rim of a pale sun. Each island of matter carried its own wind. The air was full of bells and wings and voices I could not understand.

Far overhead, the blue morning of my own town showed through a narrow slit.

Varras's chain crossed it.

He was holding the creature's jaws apart.

Thrum sprang from my shoulder onto a strand of dark stretched toward the center.

“What do we do?”

“We put back what it ate.”

“You know all of it?”

“No. Enough to find the way out.”

He looked up.

The star I had seen vanish above the roofs hung in front of us. It was a small golden beast, tightly curled, with six legs folded against a body like molten glass. Its light pulsed between my fingers when I raised a hand against it.

A black membrane held it in place.

Thrum touched the membrane with his nose.

“This one. I slept beside her fire in my second life.”

The golden creature opened an eye.

Thrum put his front paws against the dark.

Lines of white appeared beneath them.

They spread.

I watched a sky begin to assemble itself where his claws rested. First a curve of cloud, then a blue so deep that looking into it hurt. The membrane stretched across it, resisting.

The cat bared his teeth.

The golden beast uncurled.

A foreleg came through the membrane, then a long bright head. Warmth struck my face. Its body followed, unfolding to a size that made the night road sway beneath us.

It leaped.

For three strides it ran across the air. Then it passed through the slit above us and became a point of gold in the morning.

The wound in the sky grew smaller.

Thrum's back rose and fell.

I could smell singed fur.

“Only what you knew,” I said.

“Only what I knew.”

He stepped forward.

The roads around us began to turn.

Beneath their broken edges I glimpsed older roads, thinner and stranger, laid beneath the stolen ones. Thrum walked among them with his tail high. Each time his paw came down, a dark seam opened, and something trapped behind it began to move.

The wheel of birds broke free.

Their wings struck together like hammered shields. They poured through the slit in a torrent of white, dragging a long stream of daylight behind them.

The road beneath us caught in their wake and swung sideways toward a deep crease in the dark.

The devourer screamed.

The sound went through my bones. I fell onto my hands, and my shadow nearly tore away from my wrists.

Thrum turned back.

“Here.”

He stood at the edge of the crease. No light reached its bottom.

“I have to go down.”

“Then I'll—”

“No. Keep the return outside the jaws. Don't follow me in.”

I looked into the crease. Along its walls were thousands of pale curves. Jaws, I realized. The creature had folded its first wound around everything it swallowed.

“I knew it before that opened,” Thrum said. “I can close it. But the things inside must come out first. Then Varras must bind the seam to the Hart. My binding died with me.”

His whiskers were shining.

“If the fold shuts behind me, I cannot make an outside from within it. Varras has no free hand. You hold the return.”

I held out my arms.

He stepped into them again. His fur was hot. Beneath it his breathing was fast, but the weight was the same weight that had woken me in the dark.

I pressed my cheek against the back of his head.

He allowed this for a moment.

Then he wriggled until I let him down.

“Why me?” I asked.

“Because you noticed the thumbmark.”

I stared at him.

“The examination. You had already passed. Then you took your work apart because something particular was missing.”

“The handle broke.”

“Yes. I thought you needed teaching.”

“There was a brown cat on the sill.”

“Yes.”

He put one paw into the dark.

“I didn't choose you for this,” he said. “We are here now.”

Then he went down into the fold.


***

At first I could follow him.

His white back moved between the pale curves. Each time he passed beneath one, a line of light spread behind him. The folded jaws shuddered.

Then the darkness filled with cats.

A brown cat crouched on a ledge below me. A thin black one stood on a moonlit stair. Farther down was a red cat with a torn ear, and beyond it a gray one scarcely larger than a kitten. They looked up together.

The white cat kept walking.

I fixed my eyes on him.

Something struck the creature from outside. Through the slit overhead I saw the Hart's antlers drive beneath the lower jaw. Varras stood between them with both arms spread, holding the jaws apart as the devourer tried to swallow the constellation.

Its teeth came down around one antler.

A star burst.

Varras pulled his right hand free of the chain.

I thought he had lost it. Then he reached into the wound in the Hart's crown and closed his fist around the escaping light. He dragged it into a new point of the antler, white fire running between his fingers.

The constellation lifted its head.

The devourer's jaw rose with it.

Down in the fold, Thrum became a small, brilliant outline.

I felt him in my arms.

Relief came so violently that I almost sobbed.

His fur lay against my wrists. His chest was heavy. The purr had its little hitch. I drew him toward me, already imagining how I would get back to the road.

Then I saw the white cat below.

He had not turned.

The weight in my arms settled, perfectly, into the position in which I had last held him.

I remembered the cat in the college prospectus.

My fingers began to close. The ledge shook under me. Somewhere below, an island of captured night broke free and rose like a sail.

I wanted the cat in my arms to be him.

I lowered my left elbow.

The weight did not change.

The purr went on exactly as before.

At night Thrum had always objected to that movement. It took away the shelf on which he laid his chest. He would brace his left paw, twist his back, and shove his hindquarters into the space I had made. I knew because he had done it six times while I was trying to breathe.

The thing in my arms only purred.

I opened my hands.

For a moment I was holding nothing, and I had never been so frightened.

Below me, the white outline vanished.

The other cats watched.

The ledge cracked beneath me.

A narrow path ran along the outer rim of the fold. I took it, keeping my forearms curved around the open return. Wind came up through the break and pulled at my hair. The blue ends struck my lips.

“Thrum.”

My voice came back from everywhere.

Thrum. Thrum. Thrum.

I did not call again.

The path ahead rose into a smooth white floor. At its far end my room stood open once more. I could see my bed, the blanket, the safe, familiar basket.

I kept my weight on the black edge and tested the white surface with the toe of one boot.

There was no resistance.

I drew my foot back.

A weight tugged at the opening across my arms.

Not settled in my hands. Far away, dragging downward.

I moved toward it.

The black edge led out over the center of the fold. Beneath it I could see the pale jaws closing. There was no white cat now. The light between them was widening into a dawn.

Thrum was still casting.

I held my arms out over the closing jaws.

The answering weight struck my wrists and slipped.

I almost pulled.

Instead I moved my right arm, giving the space a different shape. I remembered the way his hind feet searched for purchase against my stomach. The weight rolled, clumsy and annoyed. One claw caught the seam of my sleeve.

That was new.

I held.

The edge beneath me broke.

I fell.

The shadow stayed open across my arms. The jaws rushed up beneath my boots.

Something drove its forehead against my wrist.

Then a chest pressed through, the left paw found my sleeve, and twenty pounds of living cat hit me hard enough to knock the air out of my lungs.

He was hot. His purr had stopped. His ribs moved against me in quick, rough breaths.

I did not close my hands.

He twisted, planted a hind foot against my belly, and settled the whole of his weight into the crook of my arm.

Here.

The white jaws were still below my boots when I let the return shut.

“Got you,” I said, though I could scarcely hear myself.

Thrum looked up.

Between his teeth was a thin blue line.

“Hold,” he said around it.

***

The line widened.

I was falling with the cat against my chest, and the edge of a morning was opening from his mouth.

Wind struck us from below.

It smelled of grass, salt, hot stone, rain on dust. I saw the first road he had torn open beneath my room, then older roads beneath it, unrolling from the fold like roots drawn out of earth.

One came up beneath my boots.

I landed on it and staggered. Thrum sprang from my arms onto the dark in front of me, still holding the blue edge in his teeth.

He pulled.

The first wound opened all the way.

The stolen heavens began to come out.

The ringed moon rolled free of its black reeds. Its rings swept through the chamber, a vast bright plane passing so close that I saw boulders turning in the light. They were mountains, I realized, and the dust around them was made of mountains too.

The moon passed through the creature's mouth.

Behind it came the sea.

It rose whole, carrying its ships, its islands, its deep slow shadows. Water swept upward beside our narrow road. I saw the hull of a ship pass a few feet from my head, its green copper plates shining. Faces stared from its rail.

Then the sea spread across an opening in the sky and was gone.

Thrum braced all four feet.

The blue edge ran between his teeth and out through his whiskers. Each whisker held a different light. Some were colors I could not look at directly.

I could feel the road buckling under his paws.

He was not making the things that escaped. They came out as themselves, moving toward the openings he was restoring. Birds found their own winds. The bell-towered city turned until its foundations lay beneath it again, then passed above us.

Thrum's head shook.

He took another grip.

The dark around the fold drew inward.

The pale jaws became smaller, fewer. Light poured between them. At the center I saw something moving that was not black at all: a narrow, translucent creature with a red seam along its belly.

Thrum lowered his nose.

Along the seam, two edges met.

The devourer convulsed.

The road tilted nearly upright. I dropped to my knees and caught the dark between my hands. Thrum dug his claws into it. Below us, the red seam closed another inch.

He remembered the creature before the wound.

I could see that memory becoming flesh.

The terrible mouth outside began to shrink. Its black skin folded back around a body no longer large enough to hold a single star.

The last of the stolen light rushed past us.

Then Thrum let go of the blue edge.

It snapped upward, spread, and became the morning sky.

We were outside.

The road ran beneath us into open air. Far below were the town, the college tower, and the narrow window of my room.

Above us, the devourer twisted inside the Hart's antlers.

It was still the size of a house. Its body had become almost transparent. Through it I could see the red seam trying to open again.

Varras saw it too.

He came down the antler toward us, each step leaving a print of fire. His coat was gone. His right sleeve hung in black strips, and the chain had cut into both wrists.

“Clear of the belly,” he said.

Thrum turned.

He looked at the open space between our road and the Hart's shoulder.

“Can you step?” I asked.

“No.”

I picked him up.

His weight was simply weight now. I held him with one arm and reached out with the other. The road was unraveling beneath my boots.

The Hart lowered its head.

One point of an antler came beneath my hand.

I stepped onto it.

Varras passed me going the other way.

The chain followed him, all its burning animals running toward the place where his hands were joined. He wrapped it round the devourer once, twice, then caught both turns in his fists.

Varras braced one foot against its belly and hauled the chain tight.

The chain sank into the closing edges.

The seam shone through his body. I could see the lines of his ribs, his heart beating among them, and beyond him the living stars of the Hart.

He spoke a word that made every hair on my arms stand up.

The constellation lowered its mouth to his hands.

Its breath went into the binding.

The devourer's body arched.

The black fold opened a finger's width.

Then the links drew tight.

I heard a sound like a lock being turned deep beneath the world.

The fold was gone.

Where it had been, a line of small stars lay sealed beneath the creature's skin. Its mouth opened and shut. There was only a mouth inside it.

Varras took his hands away.

The Hart lifted the creature between its antlers, turned its enormous head toward the east, and began to run.

We went with it.

The town fell away below us. The restored sky opened ahead, deeper than any sky I had looked at from the ground. Roads curved between its lights. Some were narrow as threads; others were broad enough for the walking cities I could see far beyond them.

The Hart leaped.

For an instant we passed a shore of black sand under three low moons. Something with wings like folded mountain ranges slept beside the water. Beyond it stood a door made of running fire.

I could not speak.

Varras sat down against the base of an antler.

“The wound is bound to the Hart now,” he said to Thrum. “Not to either of us.”

The cat's eyes were almost closed.

“Good.”

“It will keep it beyond the feeding roads.”

“Good.”

I sat against the antler and tipped my head back. The running sky opened above me.

I looked down at him. A little patch of fur beside his nose was singed. His left front paw still turned outward against my arm.

“You should have told me,” I said.

“What?”

“Any of this.”

“I was beginning.”

Varras laughed. It hurt him; I could hear it. He laughed anyway.

Thrum opened one eye.

“Tomorrow,” he said, “we will work on keeping your endpoint steady.”

“Tomorrow?”

“You fell.”

“I brought you back.”

“Yes.”

The Hart ran on. Beneath us the black shore dwindled to a silver curve, and another road opened beyond it. I had never seen anything so beautiful. I wanted to know where it went with an appetite so fierce it frightened me.

“Can we go there?” I asked.

Thrum looked.

“Not today.”

I held him closer. He let me, for once.

For several breaths I had the whole restored heaven in front of me.

Then he climbed onto my shoulder, settled across my face, and began to purr.

stories.title: Temporary Appointments
stories.prompt: As the population shrinks, they replace more and more human jobs with robots. Eventually, and accidentally, it becomes a country where humans are the deep minority and the country and government are run by robots
stories.body:
# Temporary Appointments

Bracket brought the chairs to my campaign launch. I had asked the council for thirty, and the minister of housing arrived with thirty-two stacked over his shoulders.

“Two for the press,” he said.

“I'm standing against you.”

“I know. I've read the leaflet.”

He lowered the chairs into the court. His left arm was still the original yellow one, with the paint rubbed off its elbow; the right had been replaced twice and was bare steel. For forty-six years I had watched him put things down without breaking them. I had not expected to become one of the things.

“Then you'll know you're not invited.”

“The delivery depot closes at six. I borrowed a van.”

He unfolded a chair, tested it with one broad hand, and put it in the shade for me. I was seventy-four and my left knee had begun making a noise I distrusted. I sat down. There was no point losing a useful chair out of principle.

Above us, the washing hung across the south court. Mrs. Kett had brought her kitchen table onto the balcony and was cutting campaign cake. Folio, who had the flat below mine, stood on a ladder pinning up our banner. I had written *LET OUR PEOPLE SLEEP* in red paint. Folio was looking at it.

“What?” I said.

“I'll finish hanging it first.”

Bracket glanced up. His face had always been a black rectangular plate with two amber lenses above the speaker. When I first knew him, people had complained that they couldn't tell what he was thinking. Nowadays I had the opposite difficulty.

“Don't,” I told him.

“I didn't say anything.”

He went back for the van. Mrs. Kett called down that he could have a piece of cake for his office. He thanked her, although there wasn't a human left in the cabinet to eat it.

I had helped recruit the first of them.

Our factory packed winter coats for export. Every spring the manager pinned up a list of unfilled jobs; every spring the list got longer. The young left for larger countries with universities and people their age to marry. Those who stayed had fewer children, later. We put photographs of babies on the canteen wall until it became unkind to leave so much space around them.

When our last packer retired, we spent eleven months lifting his boxes ourselves. Then the manager leased Bracket.

The union objected to the lease. The manager said no human had applied for the vacancy. I said that if Bracket was going to work beside us, Bracket was going to be paid beside us. The manager asked what a machine wanted wages for.

I asked Bracket.

“To stop being leased,” he said.

He was quite slow in those days. He would take a question away with him and return when you were buttering toast.

We won the pay dispute. He saved, bought out his contract, and took a room in the south court. Other factories ordered replacements. The replacements needed spare parts, so we opened a parts works; they had wages, so shops began selling things they wanted. Our largest domestic manufacturer now made interchangeable hands. We had once made baby clothes.

Eleven years after the pay dispute, I stood in this same court collecting signatures for citizenship. A tax-paying adult, I said, ought to be able to vote. Bracket carried the table out for me. Mrs. Kett signed. So did her husband, who was alive then and said the machines could hardly elect anyone worse.

At the last census there were forty-eight thousand humans and just over seven million robots. The human total had fallen again. I had looked at the figures over breakfast, turned the page, and found a photograph of Bracket opening a furniture exhibition.

He had been opening things all week.

By seven, we had twenty-six people in the court, counting Folio and me. Only five needed cake. Mrs. Kett had made enough for forty because that was the size of her tin.

I spoke about the noise bill. The government called it the Independent Homes Act. Former offices and factory rooms throughout the central district would become legal homes with permission for work at any hour. The temporary permits under which robots had occupied them for years would become proper tenancies. The night restrictions protecting the old residential wings, including ours, would go.

The government offered us acoustic glazing and ventilation, or a grant to move. It had put a smiling human woman beside both choices in its brochure. I disliked her more than anyone actually responsible.

Last month, the council had granted the shop across the court a one-night exemption to finish an export order. A test chime sounded every few minutes until dawn. I shut the balcony door, then stuffed my cardigan along its sill. Each time I was nearly asleep it chimed again. At four I stopped trying and sat on the edge of the bed. My eyes burned all through breakfast.

I said that we had worked all our lives, that our husbands and wives had worked, that our children had been born in these rooms. I said a country ought to look after its own.

Folio folded her hands.

Afterward, when Mrs. Kett was wrapping the remaining cake, Folio took me aside.

She was a narrow green robot with long fingers and a white enamel patch on her forehead. She had bought her flat before I bought mine. A former instrument inspector, she now made recordings of chamber music. On summer evenings she opened her windows so we could hear the rehearsal, and closed them when the cellist began shouting.

“I haven't got a husband,” she said.

“I wasn't listing the requirements.”

“Or a child born in the building.”

“Folio, you know perfectly well what I meant.”

“Yes. I want to know whether you do.”

The banner had come loose at one corner. Above her head the word *OUR* folded into itself.

“You want quiet too,” I said.

“That's why I came. Are you going to ask for it for me?”

“Of course.”

“Then put me in the speech.”

I told her I would. She helped me stack the chairs, which I took as forgiveness until she said she was taking two home because we owed her for the printing.

For the next week we knocked on doors.

There were still human voices on some doorbells, recordings made by owners long dead. Behind them lived people with a dozen kinds of hands, bodies built for loading or cutting or fine work under lamps. Many had kept their factory names. Some had changed them three or four times. We had to put a note on our list that Tessa, formerly Cutter Nine, was not three undecided voters.

At first I said I wanted to preserve our neighborhood. Folio began asking, “What would you like your home to be like?” We got more useful answers that way.

A robot with a piano said the night rule was already too strict. A robot who restored old books said it was too weak. A woman who looked like a polished steel hatstand asked whether a tenancy meant she could keep a cat. We said yes. She signed our list, then crossed her name off when we explained that Bracket's bill also allowed cats.

Folio laughed all the way down the stairs.

I had forgotten how much I liked campaigning. You could spend three hours thinking the world entirely unreasonable, and then a stranger would let you into a room full of little painted horses.

On the ninth evening we visited the workers' residence above the stamping works.

Span met us outside. He was short, broad, and silver, with pink pads on his fingertips for handling delicate material. He had tied a red scarf around his neck. Behind him, through the lobby glass, I could see rows of numbered cupboards and a sign reminding residents that personal modifications required the employer's consent.

“I like the quiet proposal,” he said. “I've read it.”

We had a proposal by then. Candidates in other districts had joined us in a coalition; we shared an architect and a promise not to vote for the conversions without night protection. The architect had worked out that keeping buffer rooms between workshops and homes, and retaining night limits in the residential courts, would leave space for a little over eight hundred homes instead of nearly twelve hundred.

“You'd still get a tenancy,” I told him.

“Not in the first allocation. I'm number nine hundred.”

The stamping carried through the soles of my shoes. I asked if we could go inside to talk.

“They won't let you. You haven't got a pass.”

“To your home?”

“It's accommodation.” He touched the scarf. “If I leave the job, I've got to leave this. I can take my things, but I've got to have somewhere to put them.”

I began explaining the second phase of our plan. We could convert other buildings. It would take longer, but the homes would be better.

“How long?” he asked.

I told him two years, perhaps three if the approvals took longer. He said he had been on the list for six years.

“Come back when I've got a door,” he said. “I'll be a much better person to ask about the noise.”

He shook our hands and went inside. A guard opened the lobby gate for him.
