We stood there for a moment.

“Don't,” I said to Folio.

“I wasn't going to.”

“That's what he says.”

“We both know you.”

By the time we reached the south court, Mrs. Kett had set out the cards on her balcony. The table was scarred where her husband had once put down a hot pan. Folio took his old place. I took mine. Somewhere above us someone was frying onions; someone else called down to ask whether we wanted the radio louder.

At half past ten I went to bed. Mrs. Kett and Folio were still arguing over a hand. I left my balcony door open and listened to them until I fell asleep.

The first time Bracket stood for office, we couldn't find anybody else.

The south district had lost two councillors to retirement and one to her daughter's insistence that she come live closer. I was already running the union office three days a week and taking my husband to appointments on the other two. I told Bracket it would be a temporary arrangement. Serve a term, I said. Give us time to find someone.

He asked what a councillor did.

“Listen to complaints.”

“I already do that.”

We elected him with four hundred and twelve votes. He liked the work. The next time, he found his own agent.

When he went to parliament, the papers called him the country's first robot member. By the time he became housing minister, they had stopped mentioning it. There were no human members left to make it news.

I had been proud of that. I still was, which made things awkward.

He came to see me twelve days before the election. This time he brought no chairs. I made tea and gave him the documents to hold flat while I found my glasses.

He knew where I kept them. He knew where I kept everything. When my husband died, Bracket had stayed three nights, answering the door and putting meals in front of me, and afterward I found he had arranged the tins by the dates on their bottoms. I had maintained his system for a month before deliberately eating the wrong peaches.

Now he put a plan on my kitchen table. The south court was outlined in blue. Three other courts were outlined on the next page.

“The old residential leases,” he said. “We keep their night protection. We leave the adjoining rooms empty as buffers. No workshops in the south wing.”

“And the permit holders?”

“The rest of the bill goes through.”

I looked at our court. My bedroom was a small blue rectangle. So were Mrs. Kett's and Folio's. In the next wing, where people on temporary permits lived among their worktables, the rooms were grey.

“You can do this?”

“As a settlement.”

He wanted the old tenants' association to sign, and me to withdraw in support of the amended bill. The association still admitted only leaseholders. I had written that rule myself, years ago, to stop the factory manager packing our meetings with men who rented storage lockers.

“We're close,” I said.

“I know.”

His party had held the chamber by one seat. The other districts were close too, but every plausible route to a government majority now passed through ours. If we won, the bill would need our coalition's votes. We could insist on the quieter scheme.

“You think I'll win.”

“I think you might. I don't want the homes delayed for another term.”

I ran my finger along the blue line. Our balcony would stay open. The new rooms beside it would remain empty. For the first time in weeks I could picture next summer without having to work at it.

“How many homes do you lose?”

“Ninety-two.”

“You could offer the same protection to the permit holders.”

“That's your quiet scheme again. I'd lose more than three hundred homes in all.”

He let go of the paper. It curled against my cup.

I thought of Span's cupboard. The bargain would get him a room sooner than our scheme would. I wanted him to have the quiet too. I also thought of Bracket at the count, having to shake my hand. I had rehearsed being gracious about it. I had rehearsed it rather often.

“No,” I said.

“Will you put it to the association?”

“We've been asking people without old leases to vote for us. I'm not leaving them out now.”

“That's your answer. Will you ask the others?”

I said I would call a meeting. He left the plan with me.

Mrs. Kett wanted to sign. So did three other members. Folio voted against, along with me and the younger leaseholders from the west court. We rejected it by two votes.

Mrs. Kett did not help with the next delivery of leaflets.

“You could have told us you wanted to be in parliament,” she said. “We'd have bought you a nice coat.”

“We have a chance to get it for everyone.”

“And I had a chance to get it for me.”

I began to say she ought to think of the others. She was eighty-one. She had spent thirty years caring for her husband and the last six keeping an eye on me. I stopped.

She picked up the empty cake tin and went inside.

We changed the banner. Folio painted the new one because she said she wanted people at the back to be able to read it. We held meetings at hours when the late shifts could come. I learned to stop calling them the late shifts; half the people coming preferred to work then.

Our volunteers were mostly robots. Some wanted quiet, some wanted a tenancy with a right to refuse work, some disliked Bracket's party for reasons that had nothing to do with housing. A man with six hands offered to do the folding and was offended when I thanked him extravagantly. He had also wanted to speak.

I gave him the microphone at the next meeting. He was terrible. He talked for twenty minutes about the price of replacement thumbs. Afterward we gained two volunteers and lost one, and Folio told me to stop watching the door every time someone left.

I slept badly. I ate standing up. At three in the morning, when I woke thinking about the bill, I could look across the court and see Bracket's office lit beyond the factory roof. Sometimes I wanted to call him and complain about my opponent.

At the final debate, somebody asked me whether a human could keep up with a modern government.

“I've kept up with this one for forty years,” I said. “Mostly to tell it it's wrong.”

They laughed. It was a good laugh. I knew how to use one. For the rest of the evening I believed we would win.

We lost by three hundred and seventy-four votes.

I received eighteen thousand, four hundred and sixteen. There were ninety-three humans on the district roll.

Bracket shook my hand at the count. For once he didn't know how hard to hold it. My knuckles ached all the way home.

By breakfast the government had its majority. One seat.

Mrs. Kett came down with toast because she had seen my light. We ate it at the kitchen table, beside the plan with the blue courts.

“Does that still stand?” she asked.

“I don't know.”

“Ask him.”

I called. Bracket answered from a room full of voices. I asked him to go somewhere quiet.

“We could still do the settlement,” I said.

“The bill goes to the chamber on Tuesday. The full plan.”

“You can change it.”

“Yes.”

I waited.

“I'm putting the homes in,” he said.

Mrs. Kett was looking at my face. I didn't want to tell her.

“You were prepared to leave those rooms empty last week.”

“To get agreement. We didn't get agreement. We had an election.”

“We didn't stop needing to sleep.”

“I know.”

“Don't say that as if it helps.”

He didn't answer. In the room he had left, someone called his name.

I ended the call and told Mrs. Kett. She pushed her plate away.

“Ninety-two,” she said.

I knew which rooms she meant.

That autumn she took the glazing. Folio did too. Folio could use the new recording booth as a listening room; she was already arguing with the installer about the hum of the ventilation. Mrs. Kett said she'd manage. She wasn't leaving her husband's kitchen.

I signed for the relocation grant.

The new flat was smaller and faced a bank of horse chestnuts. The bus took thirty-eight minutes from the south court. The agent showed me the quiet-hours covenant and then the balcony, where I stood for a long time. When she asked if I liked it, I said yes. I did like it. This seemed to me an unreasonable extra thing to have to bear.

On moving day, Bracket came with a van.

I hadn't asked him. Folio had. I told her that being my campaign manager did not entitle her to arrange my social life. She said she was arranging the transport.

Downstairs, Span was painting a door violet. He had draped his red scarf over the handle to keep paint off it. I looked away before he could ask whether I needed a hand.

Bracket carried the books first. I had put labels on the boxes. He turned each label outward in the van so I could find things, just as he had done when we packed coats together.

Mrs. Kett stayed upstairs. Her new balcony door was shut. On the inside of the glass she had taped a note reminding the installers to come back and finish the trim.

“She's angry with me,” I said.

“Yes.”

“You might at least make me feel better.”

He stopped with a box against his chest. “Do you want to leave it another day?”

I looked up at the washing lines. There were trousers on one and, on another, a row of small painted metal plates drying in the sun. Someone in the north wing was playing music I didn't know. The first machine started at the hour when it had always been allowed to start. I had liked that sound once: wages being earned, everyone getting on.

“No,” I said. “I've told the agent.”

Bracket took the box out. When he came back, he folded my campaign chair and put it under his arm.

“Leave that a minute.”

He opened it again. I sat down in the patch of shade beneath my balcony.

“There's another in the van,” I said.

“I know.”

“Then get it. I don't want you standing over me.”

He went to fetch the chair. While he was gone I took out my phone and called Mrs. Kett.

“Put the kettle on,” I said when she answered. “I'm coming up.”

stories.title: An Unreasonable Detour
stories.prompt: A party of adventurers escort a princess to her wedding but over the journey she becomes more than a job. Once within reach of her husband to be, the party asks the princess if she'd like to be an adventurer instead of a bride.
stories.body:
# An Unreasonable Detour

The princess's luggage went over the stile first. The princess remained on the bottom step.

Her skirt had caught beneath her boot. To free it she needed to lift the boot, but to lift the boot she needed to stop standing on the skirt. Above her, three adventurers waited with the careful faces of people being paid not to laugh.

“You can let go of the bag,” said Haddie.

Sereya looked down. She had forgotten the bag.

Haddie took it. Freed of this small responsibility, Sereya climbed over the stile and dropped onto the other side rather harder than she intended.

“Lovely,” said Osnet, who had white hair, a pointed beard, and a sword almost as tall as he was. He offered her a hand as though they had met at a ball. “Only the mountain left.”

The youngest adventurer made a noise into his sleeve.

“Ket,” Haddie said.

“Nothing.”

“It was a stile,” Sereya told him. “The mountain will presumably have fewer bits of wood.”

“You would be surprised,” Osnet said.

She could not tell whether that was a joke. They started walking.

Her attendants and the trunks containing her wedding clothes had gone by the coast road. The pass would bring Sereya to Bellan's city three days before them, with time to rest and to see the house where she would live. Her mother had approved the expedition after looking up Haddie's company in a book. The book recorded a slain marsh-worm and the recovery of an abbot from kidnappers. It had not mentioned the flat, considering look Haddie gave Sereya's boots.

“Tell me when those start rubbing.”

“They won't.”

“Tell me anyway.”

By midday there was a hot patch on each heel. Sereya waited until the others stopped to drink before mentioning it. Haddie sat her down, looked at the boots, and made her change into a pair of thick stockings from the company's spare clothes.

“But these are yours.”

“They're spare.”

“I shall wash them.”

“I hope so.”

Osnet offered her a pickled egg. She accepted because he seemed proud of the jar, and managed to swallow half before her eyes began to water.

“All right?” he asked.

“Quite.”

Ket watched her over his bread. “You can give it back.”

She had been a princess for twenty-six years. Nobody had ever told her she could give back half an egg.

“I don't think I like it,” she said.

Osnet took it and ate it himself.

That evening they came down to an inn with smoke rising from both chimneys. Through the open door Sereya could see a tiled floor and a girl carrying a covered dish. Beyond the inn, a shoulder of bare grass rose against the sky.

“Could we sleep up there?” she asked.

Haddie followed her gaze. “Why?”

“I've never slept outside.”

“You've never had Osnet's stew either. There's still time to avoid both.”

“But we could?”

“There's no shelter up there. It will be cold. We'll have to gather fuel and cook something when there's a perfectly good supper six feet away.”

The girl in the doorway lifted the lid of her dish to show Haddie what was inside. It looked very good. Sereya almost withdrew the question.

“I'd like to see the stars come out,” she said instead.

Haddie put her thumbs beneath her belt and studied her. She was a broad woman with a round shield strapped to her pack and a mended seam across one eyebrow.

“We eat here. Then, if the landlord agrees, we can sleep in that lower field. Near the wall. You carry your own bedding.”

“Yes.”

“And if it rains, we come in.”

“Yes.”

“I wanted a mattress,” Osnet said.

“So did I,” said Haddie, and went to negotiate for the field.

After supper Sereya carried a bedroll, a blanket, and what felt like a second blanket made of lead up the short slope. She helped Ket move small stones out of the place Haddie selected. Then he showed her how to tuck the groundcloth beneath her blanket rather than leave its edge sticking out to catch the dew.

“You could have told me before I lay down,” she said.

“You were very quick.”

There was straw in her sleeve. She tried several times to remove it without getting out of bed, then gave up and stood in the cold while Ket held the blanket.

“This was your idea,” Osnet remarked from his bedroll.

“I'm aware.”

Haddie laughed. It was the first time Sereya had heard her do it.

In the dark, Ket made an ember glow between his cupped palms and used it to light their little lamp. He had to lean close and shelter the wick with his whole body.

“Can you make more?” Sereya asked.

“More what?”

“Fire.”

“Not enough to make this a good idea.”

He sat beside her and took a folded sheet of paper from his coat. On it was a charcoal drawing of something with a large head and a number of sharp protrusions.

“What is it?” she asked.

“A hawk.”

Sereya looked at the drawing again.

“You can say things,” Ket said. “Osnet does.”

“It looks a little like a boot.”

“A hawk's head looks a little like a boot.”

“Not with a heel.”

He gave her the charcoal. Her attempt, made on the other half of the paper, resembled a boiled thumb. Ket told her so immediately. They argued about where the beak should go until Haddie asked whether either of these birds intended to let anybody sleep.

Sereya lay down. She could feel a stone they had missed through the groundcloth. Over the dark edge of the wall, stars appeared in places where she had never seen stars before, because there had always been a roof.

Her feet were cold. She lay awake for a long time, watching.

In her bag was Bellan's last letter, which described the little garden behind the house. There was an old pear tree, he had written, which no longer fruited but made good shade. He had told the gardener to leave the narrow beds empty. Sereya could put in what she pleased.

She had read that part to her mother twice. All her life gardens had been places where someone fetched her because she was wanted elsewhere. Bellan had said she need not receive visitors in this one, and that he would knock.

She had packed nasturtium seeds. Orange ones. She thought of the pear tree until she slept.

---

On the second day a pack train met them where the path widened beneath a stand of beech trees. Haddie stepped off the track well before the first horse reached them.

Sereya, following her, saw how still she had become. Haddie's hands were closed hard around the straps of her pack. A horse turned its long head toward her, and she moved behind the tree.

Sereya stopped in front of her.

“Could you show me that knot again?” she asked.

“Which knot?”

“The one for the bedding.”

Haddie looked past her at the horses, then down at the cord Sereya offered. She took it.

They tied the knot four times. By the fourth, the pack train had gone.

“You knew that already,” Haddie said.

“Only on good days.”

Haddie handed her back the cord. “Don't tell Osnet.”

“Doesn't he know?”

“He knows. Don't tell him you know.”

At the next halt, Osnet produced the eggs again. Sereya said no, thank you. He looked pleased, though that might have been because there were more for him.

Toward evening the sky closed in. Haddie made them put on their cloaks before Sereya thought she needed hers. Ten minutes later the rain was striking sideways, hard enough to sting her cheek.

Osnet went ahead to inspect the path. He returned without his usual bow.

“Loose stones coming down at the cut. We need the star house.”

Haddie turned at once. They left the main track and began climbing a steep path through the heather.

Sereya could see nothing above them. Water ran from her hood into her mouth. When she stopped to catch her breath, Haddie took her elbow, firmly enough to hurt, and said, “Keep going.”

She kept going. She hated Haddie for the next twenty steps.

They had almost reached the building when Osnet's foot slipped on a slab of wet rock. He sat down abruptly. His sword struck the stone with a sound Sereya felt in her teeth.

He tried to stand and sat down again.

Haddie crouched beside him. Ket took Osnet's pack. There were quick instructions, mostly lost in the wind, and then Sereya was carrying the long sword in both hands while Haddie and Ket helped its owner up the last of the slope.

The star house was a round stone building with a square room attached to its side. The dome had fallen in long ago. Rain struck a great rusted ring standing in the middle of the open rotunda. Haddie led them into the smaller room, where one corner of the roof was sound and there was a hearth.

“Put that down before you stab a wall,” she told Sereya.

Sereya set down the sword. Her hands would not stop shaking.

Osnet's ankle was swelling. Haddie unlaced his boot while Ket laid out dry kindling from an oilcloth bundle. He tried to bring an ember to life between his palms. The first went out. The second caught a shaving of wood, and he lowered it carefully into the hearth.

“Dry shirt,” Haddie said to Sereya. “In your bag. Change behind the door.”

“Can I help?”

“In a dry shirt.”

When she came back, Haddie had wrapped Osnet's ankle. Sereya was given two ends of a bandage to hold, then told to hold them less tightly. Ket fed the little fire. There was steam coming from all their clothes and a smell like a wet dog, though nobody had brought a dog.

“I do apologize,” Osnet said.

“For the ankle or the smell?” Ket asked.

“I was going to say the delay.”

“Then you've two apologies left.”

Osnet tried to laugh and stopped. Haddie looked at him, then shifted the rolled cloak beneath his foot.

They had bread and cheese for supper. Sereya dropped her cheese on the floor. She picked it up, found grit on one side, and held it in her hand until Haddie said, “You can cut that bit off.”

Afterward Ket and Haddie went through the square doorway to examine the rest of the building. Sereya sat beside Osnet with her wet stockings hanging from a stick.

She did not know what to say to him. At home there would have been a physician and a person to make hot drinks and someone else to tell her when her presence was no longer helpful.

“Would you like me to read?” she asked.

“What have you got?”

She looked in her bag. “Letters. A small book of prayers. Instructions for removing stains from silk.”

“Tempting.”

“There are different instructions for different stains.”

“You must leave me something to look forward to.”

He closed his eyes. She could see him breathing carefully, waiting for the worst of the pain to pass. She stayed because he had not asked her to go.

After a while he said, “How did you get the mark on your chin?”

She touched it. It was small and pale. “A goose.”

Osnet opened his eyes.

“I was eight. It had stolen one of my mother's state slippers and I tried to recover it.”

“A loyal effort.”

“I was wearing the other one.”

He made a little choking noise.

“She had left them by her chair. I thought they might fit.”

“Did you catch the goose?”

“No. My mother said the slipper was lost to the realm.”

Osnet considered this. “A difficult start to a life of crime. Only one slipper.”

“It stole a foot next,” said Sereya.

He looked at her.

“A wooden one,” she added hastily. “From a retired admiral.”

“Naturally.”

The admiral pursued the goose on a kitchen stool. Osnet wanted to know how he moved it. Sereya had to give him wheels. By the time Haddie and Ket returned, the goose was aboard a fishing boat, the admiral had acquired a smaller stool for boarding actions, and Sereya was having trouble remembering whether she had given him a hook as well as the wooden foot.

“Too much equipment,” Haddie said, settling by the hearth.

“You're welcome to take over.”

“I'm listening.”

Ket objected that geese could fly. Sereya said this one was seasick. That made no sense, Ket said, and she told him he could draw it if he wished to be useful.

He found his charcoal.

She could not work out how to get the admiral onto the boat. She tried a rope, then remembered she had already put him in a harbor with no rope to hand. Ket offered him an enormous magnet. Haddie said magnets did not work on wooden feet.

“His buttons,” Osnet said faintly.

They all looked at him.

“An admiral would have very fine buttons.”

He was smiling. Sereya sat back on her heels and began again from the harbor.

Later the rain stopped. Haddie took first watch, and Ket fell asleep with charcoal on his cheek. Sereya went through to the rotunda. The ring towered above her, black against a gap in the clouds, its little brass fittings green with age.

She could make out two stars through it. She stood there in her borrowed stockings until her feet became too cold, then went back and lay down with the others.

---

Osnet could put weight on his foot the next morning, but not much. They cut him a walking stick and divided his things among the three of them. Sereya carried his cooking pot, which knocked against her hip all the way down the hill.

Nobody was very agreeable. Ket had slept badly. Haddie's neck hurt. Osnet snapped when Haddie asked for the third time whether he wanted to stop, then apologized with such ceremony that it became another argument.

At midday Sereya sat on a stone and found that she did not want to get up. Her heels were burning again.

“We can stay a little longer,” Haddie said.

“I thought you would say I should have mentioned my feet.”

“You should have.”

Sereya threw a piece of grass at her. It landed a foot short. Haddie left it there.

They stayed a little longer.

In the afternoon Ket walked beside Sereya and held out the drawing he had made in the star house. The goose was recognizable. The admiral resembled an expensive beetle.

She laughed so hard she had to stop walking, which annoyed Osnet until Ket took the drawing back to show him.

That evening they reached an inn. Sereya asked for a mattress before anyone could make a suggestion. They gave Osnet the room nearest the stairs and left his door open while they ate in the passage outside it. He complained that they were missing the good room downstairs. Then he told Sereya she had never explained where the goose kept the slipper.

She said she would think about it. Ket turned the drawing over and sketched a cliff, with a building wedged halfway up it.

“Is that somewhere real?” she asked.

“North of here. A monastery. We've been asked to find the old way in.”

“How do you get up there?”

“That's what they'd pay us to find out.”

She leaned closer. “I'd like to see it.”

Ket added a tiny door, considered it, then rubbed it out.

It was late when she put out her candle. In the next room, Ket and Haddie were quarreling over whose turn it was to sleep by the window. Sereya could hear every word. She lay smiling at the ceiling, then began to cry without quite knowing why.

In the morning she washed her face before she opened the door.

---

Bellan's city appeared below them in the middle of the morning, white roofs among poplars, a road descending in long, easy bends to its gate. Farther up the valley, on a green rise, stood the house he had described. Sereya could not see the garden from here.

Haddie put her pack down beside a milestone. Osnet lowered himself carefully onto it.

Ket said, “Ask her.”

“I was going to.”

“You keep looking at the road.”

Haddie unfastened her cloak. Fastened it again. Sereya waited.

“Would you like to come with us?” Haddie asked.

“To the house?”

“After here. With the company. Adventuring.”

Osnet looked at Ket. Ket looked at his boots. Sereya had thought they were going to ask for a testimonial.

“We talked last night,” Haddie said. “And this morning. We weren't certain we ought to put it to you.”

“We were certain,” Osnet said. “You weren't.”

“Because I've been doing the sums without the other thirty crowns.”

Sereya stared at them. Thirty crowns was the balance of their fee. Haddie had mentioned it once, when Ket wanted to buy a second-hand crossbow from a peddler.

“You would lose that?” she asked.

“Possibly. And I doubt your mother will recommend us for another royal job. Don't decide on account of it.” Haddie rubbed her eyebrow. “We'd teach you. You'd have a share of what we make. There are long stretches when we don't make anything.”

“And I can't fight.”

“I know.”

“Or do what Ket does.”

“Fortunately,” Osnet said.

Ket kicked Osnet's uninjured boot.

Sereya sat down on the grass. It was dry and warm. Below her, people were moving along the road toward the city with bundles, baskets, a cart of chairs. In three days she would be married there.

“Would we go north?” she asked.

“To the monastery,” Ket said at once.

“We haven't taken it yet,” Haddie said.

“But would we?”

Haddie glanced at Osnet's foot. “When he's fit.”

Sereya picked a seed out of the grass and rolled it between her fingers. She could ask Bellan for more time. In her mind he was beneath the pear tree, waiting for her to come home. She tried to choose a month to promise him. With every date, she found herself wondering where the others would go afterward, and how much she would miss.

“I have to see him,” she said.

Haddie nodded.

“I don't know what I'll say.”

“We can walk down with you.”

“No.” She got up before she could think better of it. “No, please wait here.”

---

Bellan was in the garden when they brought her to him. He had his sleeves rolled up and a bit of bark caught in his hair. A man beside him was sawing through a fallen branch of the pear tree.

He came toward her smiling. “You're early.”

“A day late.”

“Earlier than I feared.” He took her hands. “You're all right?”

“Yes.”

He looked past her for her companions. “Will they come in? I've had rooms made ready.”

“They're waiting outside the city.”

He let go of one of her hands. She could feel the other still resting in his.

“Could we be alone?” she asked.

He sent the man with the saw into the house. In the sudden quiet she could hear the leaves moving. The beds were just as Bellan had promised: dark, loose earth, ready for something to grow.

“I can't marry you,” she said.

He looked at her for a long moment. Then he let go.

She had prepared things to say on the road down. Nothing remained of them now except her knowledge that she was hurting him.

“Has something happened?” he asked.

“Nothing bad.”

“I see.” He looked away toward the house. “No. I don't think I do.”

“They've asked me to go with them. To stay with their company.”

“And you want to?”

“Yes.”

He took the bark out of his hair and turned it over in his fingers.

“You could have said you wanted to travel.”

“I didn't know.”

“We could have talked about it.”

“I know.”

She looked at the empty beds. There was room for all the seeds she had brought. Along the wall were little hooks for supporting climbing plants; he had remembered she wanted those too.

“Do you want to postpone the wedding?” he asked.

She wanted, fiercely, to say yes and leave him something. But then he would be waiting, and she would be carrying that wait with her, and she could not tell him when it would end.

“I can't promise I'd come back to marry you.”

He nodded once, without looking at her.

“I'm sorry, Bellan.”

“So am I.”

She remained by the bed of dark earth. He did not ask her to stay. When at last she said she would write to her mother herself, he said, “Yes. Please do.”

There was nothing else she could mend by remaining. She thanked him for seeing her, heard how wrong that sounded, and went out through the house.

---

Ket was drawing Osnet, who was refusing to sit as he was told. Haddie stood when she saw Sereya.

“Will you have me?” Sereya asked.

“Yes.”

She sat down beside her pack. Haddie waited, then sat too.

“He was in the garden,” Sereya said.

Nobody answered. She told them about the branch and the empty beds and how she had thanked him at the end. She began to cry on the word thanked.

Ket made a movement as though to put away his paper, then stopped. Osnet studied the head of his walking stick. Haddie put her hand out on the grass between them, palm up.

Sereya took it. For a while they sat like that, with the city close enough to hear the noon bell.

“I still want to come,” she said at last.

Haddie squeezed her hand and let go so she could wipe her face.

They stayed until Sereya was ready to stand. Then Ket held her pack while she put her arms through the straps. The cooking pot was still tied to its side. She had forgotten to give it back.

“Shall I take that?” Osnet asked.

She looked at his bandaged ankle.

“When you're fit,” she said.

He bowed from where he sat. It was difficult, and a little absurd, and she was glad he did it.

stories.title: A Womanly Career
stories.prompt: Good lord, you're a lady from a highborn family ! Why can't you choose a womanly career, like firing a .90cal sniper rifle like your mother, or being a tank gunner and radio operator like your grandmother?
stories.body:
# A Womanly Career

“Good lord,” Father said. “You're a lady from a highborn family! Why can't you choose a womanly career, like firing a .90-calibre sniper rifle like your mother, or being a tank gunner and radio operator like your grandmother?”

He had been cutting a pear into six identical boats. At the word *nursery*, he had stopped with the knife in the air.

Cressida took the plate from beneath it.

“I don't want to join the army.”

“We have established that. Your mother has suggested the marines.”

Mother looked up from the paper. Her grey hair was cropped close above the collar of her dressing gown; she had a faint square of paler skin where her regimental badge usually sat against her throat.

“I suggested the marines because you like the sea.”

“I like swimming.”

“Yes?”

At the head of the table, Grandmother turned down the receiver of her old field radio. On retirement she had discovered that civilian broadcasts consisted largely of people speaking while other people were still speaking. She followed three such programmes with mounting professional disgust.

“Which nursery?” she asked.

“Little Orchard.”

“The one behind the shops?”

“It has a garden.”

“Behind the shops,” Grandmother confirmed. “What do they pay?”

Cressida told her. Father put down his knife altogether.

“That's the apprenticeship,” she said. “It goes up when I'm qualified.”

“By how much?”

Cressida told her that too.

Outside the long windows, the gardener was coaxing a climbing rose away from the stone woman who had captured three forts with a broken collarbone. He had reached her left boot. It would be another hour before he reached her bayonet.

“You'd have your own quarters with us,” Mother said. “Your pay would be yours. And your pension.”

“I've seen rooms I can afford.”

“Rooms?” said Father.

“A room.”

Mother folded the paper, lining up its edges. On the sideboard stood the long leather rifle case she had brought home yesterday. Cressida's initials were stamped beneath hers.

It was not a new rifle. Mother had carried it through seventeen years, and Cressida had first been allowed to fire it with Mother lying beside her, correcting the position of her shoulder. She remembered the weight of Mother's hand much more distinctly than hitting the target.

“The mess has a room kept for you on Thursday,” Mother said. “They want to hear about the college match.”

Cressida had won the college match. She had enjoyed winning it. She could see the room: the red lamps, the women she had known since she was small enough to be handed from knee to knee, somebody already ordering her a drink before she asked.

“I haven't accepted the school place yet,” she said. “Today is a trial. On both sides.”

“Then try it,” said Grandmother. “But ask whether that pay continues through the holidays. And whether you can afford to be ill.”

“I have savings.”

“So did I. I enjoyed acquiring more.”

Father rose. He had said everything there was to say last night, including that children deserved a properly trained man. He was too well bred to say it all again before ten o'clock.

“I suppose you'll need your box.”

He brought it from the hall with both hands.

For a week he had helped her make a theatre from a wine case. The curtain ran on brass rings; six flat pasteboard animals stood in slotted wooden feet. The goose had a working wing. Father had painted individual feathers while explaining that if she simply wanted the company of children, she might marry a nice young man and let him arrange some.

He set the box beside her chair and lifted the curtain with a finger.

“The mole's nose was loose. I've fixed it.”

“Thank you.”

“And don't let them pull the goose's wing backwards.”

Mother watched Cressida put on her coat. Neither of them looked at the rifle case.

“Shall I tell them Thursday is still possible?” Mother asked.

Cressida looked down at the little brass curtain rings, all in a straight row.

“Yes,” she said.

***

Mr. Brindle answered the nursery door with a red cardigan over one shoulder and a child's sock over the other.

“Come in. Excuse the sock. Its owner has opinions about seams.”

He was a lean man with a long face and large, capable hands. His hair was pinned back with two pink clips. When he saw Cressida looking, he touched one.

“Being improved,” he said. “You can put your coat in the cupboard.”

Ten children occupied the room in ways no inspection could have anticipated. A girl lay on her back beneath a table, singing one word over and over. Two boys were moving wooden bricks from one basket into another with the solemnity of undertakers. Beside the window, a very small person in a yellow smock was licking a mirror.

“That's Orri,” said Mr. Brindle. “He'll show you where things go. Orri, we look with our eyes.”

Orri detached himself from his reflection and examined Cressida.

“Are you somebody's mother?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“I haven't had any children.”

He considered this disappointing explanation, then pointed to her theatre.

“What's in there?”

She showed him the goose. He made its wing move once, then again very slowly, watching the little joint. Cressida crouched beside him. There was a wing. How did it work? On her afternoons as a volunteer, she had often stayed beyond her promised hour, watching a child work out a hinge or a buttonhole.

A father at the doorway interrupted them.

“Lady Cressida? I didn't realize.” He straightened his son's collar. “Does he salute you, or—”

“Miss Varn,” Mr. Brindle said. “And he says good morning.”

The father laughed uncertainly. “Well, a little discipline might do him good. His mother says he's getting soft.”

His son pressed his face into the man's trouser leg.

Mr. Brindle knelt and said something Cressida couldn't hear. The boy answered into the cloth. They stayed like that for a while. Cressida discovered she was standing very straight, with the goose held against her waist.

At college, the answer to a departure had generally been a whistle.

Eventually the boy consented to show his father the brick baskets. Father had to put three bricks in each. Only then could he leave.

“We'll start with the story after fruit,” said Mr. Brindle. “Would you like to tell it?”

Cressida would.

She had practiced *The Goose Who Went Visiting* in the mirror until she could give the badger a voice quite unlike the mole's. There were six animals, six houses, a refrain, and an excellent opportunity to count. Father thought the houses too plain and had added window boxes.

Four children came to sit on the rug. Mr. Brindle asked the others whether they wanted to listen. One joined them. The girl beneath the table continued singing *ham*.

Cressida put the goose through its door.

“One morning, Goose decided—”

“That's mine,” said Orri.

“You can have a turn afterward.”

“I was doing it.”

“You were looking at it. Now we're having the story.”

She smiled at him. He did not smile back.

“One morning, Goose decided to visit her friend—”

“Why?” said a girl with a scab on her chin.

“Because she wanted to see him.”

“Was he ill?”

“No, he was—”

“My father was ill.”

“I'm sorry.”

“He was sick in a hat.”

This information interested everyone. A boy who had declined the story came over to hear more about the hat. Cressida waited until they had finished, then made the goose knock at the mole's door.

“Is this the house of my friend Mole?”

Orri reached across and took the goose.

“Not yet,” she said, taking it back. “There are other people watching.”

He held on. The little wing caught the edge of the stage and bent.

“Careful!”

She said it in her range voice.

Orri let go at once. So did the boy holding a brick. Beneath the table, *ham* stopped.

Cressida sat with the goose in her hand, its wing pointing out at an angle Father had explicitly forbidden.

Mr. Brindle came to the edge of the rug.

“Put it on the shelf a moment,” he said quietly.

“I can mend it.”

“Put it down first.”

She did. Her face was hot. The girl's father was still sick in the hat somewhere in the story she had not managed to begin.

“I shouted,” Cressida said to Orri. “I'm sorry.”

He pushed the theatre curtain closed.

“I wanted the wing.”

“I know. It belongs to the theatre, so we have to be gentle with it. I can show you again when it's fixed.”

He pushed the curtain open, then closed it. He seemed to have finished with her.

Two children began to leave.

“What happens to the goose?” asked the girl with the scab.

Cressida looked at Mr. Brindle.

“Do you need the goose to tell it?” he asked.

“No.”

“Then you've still got listeners.”

She told the rest to three children, using her empty hand for Goose. The girl wanted to know whether the badger had a sick hat. He didn't, but Cressida thought he might have a biscuit. A boy ate the imaginary biscuit off her fingers. She made him return one for the badger, who had done all the baking.

When they finished, Orri was still opening and closing the curtain.

“All done,” she told him. “Would you like a turn with the animals?”

He shook his head.

He held out his hand to the girl who had been singing under the table. She crawled out, went behind the little stage and said, “Ham.”

Orri opened the curtain.

“Ham,” she said again.

He closed it.

They performed this entertainment eleven times. Cressida found herself waiting for the twelfth.

***

By four, her knees hurt. She had wiped a nose with the wrong tissue, misplaced the lid of the paint box, and learned that announcing there were only two biscuits left did not cause the remaining children to become good at subtraction.

She had also spent nearly twenty minutes beside a boy who was drawing a dog. He had drawn the dog's feet in a row along its back. Every time she thought he had finished, he found another place it needed to go and added a foot to reach it.

She had not helped him. She had wanted to. Then she had wanted to know where the dog would go next.

While the last children put on their coats, Mr. Brindle gave her a folded sheet.

“The terms we discussed. Take them home. Ring me by Friday.”

“You still want me?”

“You'll need to learn. You knew that when you applied.”

“I thought I knew.”

“Yes,” he said. He retrieved the sock from the windowsill. “Could you look under the table for its partner?”

On the way out, Cressida checked the notice about pay. It continued through the holidays. The school paid for a limited number of sick days. After that she would need her savings.

She could go on Thursday. She could walk into the mess and be understood. Nobody would make her explain why a story with six painstakingly painted animals had required her hand to become a goose.

She stood on the pavement with her theatre box until a man pushing a pram said, “Excuse me, miss,” and she realized she was blocking the nursery gate.

***

At home, Father saw the wing before she had taken off her coat.

“Oh, Cress.”

“I know.”

“I said—”

“I know.”

He took the goose out of its slot. She had wrapped a handkerchief around the joint to keep it from getting worse.

Mother came in from the drawing room. She was dressed for dinner, her regimental cross fastened to a dark green silk jacket. The rifle case was gone from the sideboard.

“Well?”

Cressida had prepared an answer on the walk. The children had loved the theatre. The school had asked her to stay. Both statements were sufficiently true to be defensible.

“I shouted at a boy,” she said.

“Did you?” Father looked up from the goose.

“He was pulling that and I grabbed it back, and then I frightened everyone.”

Mother glanced at the wing.

“It's a delicate thing for children.”

“I took it. I told him he could have a turn. He thought he'd already been having one.”

Father touched the bent paper with a thumbnail.

“Did any of them like the story?”

“Three. One kept asking about a hat. Two others just opened and closed the curtain and said ‘ham.’ They liked that very much.”

Father's mouth moved. She couldn't tell what he was going to say.

“Was that in the story?”

“No.”

“I should hope not. You cut my whole second verse.”

She laughed, suddenly and painfully, and had to sit on the hall chair. Father took the box and the goose into the drawing room.

“Perhaps,” Mother said, “you've found out what you needed to find out.”

Cressida rubbed a spot of dried paint on her wrist. Beneath it was the little crescent scar where a hot case had once caught her. She could hear the mess women laughing over the college match.

“Yes,” she said. “I think I have.”

Mother began to smile.

“I'm going to take the apprenticeship.”

The smile stopped before it had properly arrived.

Cressida kept her eyes on her mother's face.

“I like them,” she said. “Even when they didn't like my goose. I want to go back and learn how to do it.”

For a time Mother said nothing. From the drawing room came Father asking Grandmother to stop turning the goose's wing, and Grandmother saying she was establishing the nature of the damage.

“Your own quarters,” Mother said at last. “Your own pay. Women who'd stand beside you.”

“I know.”

“You could be very good.”

Cressida nodded. This was the part she could not make harmless for either of them.

“I know.”

Mother looked away first.

“Will you live here?”

“For the trial term, if I may. Then I'll take the room over the bakery.”

“I thought it was the bookshop.”

“The bakery costs less. I did the sums again after what Grandmother said. I need to keep more back.”

Father appeared in the doorway.

“Your clothes will smell of bread.”

“Yes.”

“Everything you own.”

He retreated before she could answer. A moment later he returned with the goose.

“I'll make a second one with cloth at the joint,” he said. “For handling. This one can stay on the stage.”

“Can you show me how?”

“After dinner.”

Mother was still standing by the drawing-room door. Cressida stood too. They were almost the same height, but she had to stop herself lifting her chin.

“Could you meet me tomorrow?” she asked. “When I finish. At four.”

“What for?”

“To walk home.”

“The carriage can—”

“I'd like you to.”

Mother pressed a finger against the clasp at her throat.

“I have a fitting until half past three.”

Cressida waited.

“I'll see,” said Mother.

***

Cressida had rung Mr. Brindle after dinner, accepted the place, and arranged to start the next morning.

The following afternoon, Cressida came out carrying a sheet of paper. The dog now had seventeen feet and an upstairs.

The nursery gate was crowded with fathers. They stood in twos and threes, exchanging things from little bags and stooping to greet children.

Mother stood among them in her green jacket. Her hands were empty. A man was telling her something at length, holding up two very small cardigans for comparison.

Mother looked from one to the other with the fixed attention she gave to briefings in an unfamiliar field.

Then she saw Cressida.

She raised a hand. The man raised both cardigans, thinking she had decided, and Mother had to turn back and explain.

Cressida waited for her at the gate.

stories.title: Seven O'Clock
stories.prompt: What began as a minor preference in human courtship became, through thousands of generations of runaway sexual selection, an entirely new hormonal adaptation. Women evolved specialized glandular tissue capable of rapidly changing volume through controlled blood flow and fluid retention, while sustained hormonal signals could reshape their figures for months or even years. The response could be as instinctive as blushing or as deliberate as flexing a muscle. Over time, fashion, etiquette, and courtship evolved around this remarkable flexibility. Yet for all the control women had gained over their bodies, attraction still had a way of making its own decisions.
stories.body:
# Seven O'Clock

At six in the morning, Anja made herself smaller while the kettle boiled.

She stood in the kitchen with one hand on the counter and let the familiar contraction begin beneath her ribs. The tissue softened, then drew inward; warmth travelled across her chest as blood and retained fluid returned to deeper circulation. It was not weight disappearing. It was weight getting out of the way. By the time the kettle clicked, her breasts had lost most of their fullness, and she could bring her elbows together without the small adjustment she usually made.

She liked that. She also liked what she had looked like five minutes ago.

For nine months she had encouraged the slow hormonal settling that had rounded her hips and made her ordinary, resting figure fuller. At thirty-three, she had finally worked out that she enjoyed a bit of heft: the swing of it in a good skirt, the warm weight against her forearm when she read on her side. Her old trousers had gone to a friend. Her favourite coat had acquired two handsome side panels. None of that would reverse before breakfast. The quick vascular adjustment was for squash; the long change was for living in.

She drank, ate a banana, and pulled on her sports top. Its overlapping front panels lay nearly flat. She shortened the support bands until the green stitching met, wound her black hair into a knot, and checked the message still sitting on her phone.

*Seven. Proper dinner. No discussing your backhand.*

Otis had sent it last night. She had replied that this ruled out most of his conversation.

Their first proper date. She had been using the word *proper* to distinguish it from the meals they had eaten after matches, the coffee he owed her, and the night outside the station when he had kissed her just before leaving on tour. He had been away six weeks. She had spent an unreasonable amount of that time remembering how his face had changed when she kissed him back.

Tonight she would find out what he was like for more than three minutes when neither of them had a train to catch.

At the club, the overhead lights picked out yesterday's handprints on the glass wall. Otis was trying to persuade a vending machine to release his ball.

“Thirty-six,” Anja said, “and still getting beaten by stationary opponents.”

“It has reach.”

He gave the machine a disappointed look. The ball dropped.

He had shaved badly. A little crescent of copper-coloured stubble remained under his jaw, where his touring beard had been. Anja wanted to touch it. Instead she checked the tension of her racquet strings.

“You look different,” he said.

“Six weeks of training while you've been eating station pies.”

“I meant your hair.”

A short strand she had cut to keep it out of her eyes was sticking straight up. He reached to indicate it, stopped short of touching, and grinned.

The grin caused a small, thoroughly unhelpful warmth beneath her sports top.

Anja turned towards the court. “Warm up.”

They hit for ten minutes. Then she served, and the day became satisfyingly simple: ball, wall, feet. With less movement across her chest, she could turn late and still reach the shot. Her top held close without crushing her. She ran hard into the front corner and came out with a ball so low that Otis had to scoop it up almost from the floor.

“Filthy,” he said with admiration.

She won the first game.

Between games he pulled his shirt away from his neck. There was sweat at the notch of his collarbone, and his breathing was uneven. Anja, who had seen him sweaty and unpleasantly pleased with himself twice a week for two years, suddenly found this interesting.

Her chest began to fill.

She knew the sensation before she felt the fabric move: a spreading warmth, a little forward pull. She started the contraction again as he served, dividing her attention at exactly the wrong moment. The ball went past her racquet.

Otis looked from her to the glass wall. “Something behind me?”

“Poor circulation of useful thoughts.”

She adjusted a support band. He looked down at his shoes, giving her the ordinary courtesy people gave a slipping strap or an unexpected response. Then he glanced at the club's rack of borrowed warm-up jackets.

“We used to have the monopoly on needing one of those in a hurry,” he said.

“Congratulations on the competition.”

“At least yours takes instructions.”

“I'm reviewing its performance.”

The next rally lasted long enough to empty her head. She stopped thinking about the sweat on his throat, tightened the familiar inward control, and felt the panels settle against her again. This time she reached the front corner cleanly.

She won the match by two points. Otis disputed one of them until she made him stand where the ball had struck and look at the line.

“In,” he admitted.

“I want to hear it without the suffering.”

“You ask too much.”

Afterwards they ate eggs at the club counter. She relaxed the contraction over her second piece of toast. Her sports top's panels gradually unfolded, and she loosened its bands without getting up.

Otis told her about a theatre so small that the sound desk had to share a cupboard with the costumes. She told him about an audiobook narrator who had pronounced the same invented town four different ways, all with conviction. His knee touched hers beneath the counter. This did not prevent her from correcting his version of the final rally.

When they parted, he said, “Seven, then.”

“Seven.”

“I booked under my name. They sent me a reminder with three exclamation marks.”

“You may need them.”

He put a hand over his heart. She liked him doing that. She liked it more when he dropped the joke and kissed her briefly beside the coat rack.

On her way to work, Anja bought two rolls and ate one before she reached the studio. The quick changes made her thirsty; sport made her hungry. No woman she knew could spend the day inflating and draining without eventually having to sit down with something to drink. The old courtship diagrams had omitted this part. Thousands of generations of wanting a slightly different silhouette, and nobody had thought to draw the snack.

Her studio occupied two rooms above a shuttered cinema. At nine she climbed the narrow stairs sideways past a delivery box, let herself in, and changed into the cream work blouse she kept behind the door. She checked the side tabs, set the expansion pleats free, and sat at the desk.

By half past ten her usual fullness had returned. The blouse accommodated it with four quiet movements of cloth. Her trousers, cut for the hips she had spent most of a year acquiring, fitted exactly as they had yesterday.

The recording was an oral history, four hours of a retired puppeteer's voice that needed to become thirty-eight minutes by five. The woman had forgotten dates, restarted stories, and occasionally made a puppet speak from somewhere below the microphone. She had also described her husband's death in a voice so matter-of-fact that Anja had listened to the passage three times before deciding where to leave the silence.

At eleven, a tab in the blouse jammed.

Anja noticed it first as a sideways pull, then as a ridge digging beneath her arm. She paused the recording and tried to free the little slider. Nothing. She could drain again and carry on, but she was comfortable in her chair, she had a day of breathing and listening ahead, and she did not fancy holding the sporting contraction until lunch because a piece of brass had developed an opinion.

She took the blouse off, put on her loose studio cardigan, and freed a length of dark thread from the slider with her tweezers. The pleat sprang free so suddenly that she dropped them.

“Thank you,” she told the blouse, without meaning it.

She put it back on. The broad front lay smooth again. Through the little window above her screens, sunlight had reached the opposite roof.

At lunch she ate the other roll standing up, which did nothing to improve it, then took ten minutes outside. Her fuller hips gave her walk a movement she could feel through the trousers. She bought a pear from the stall beside the cinema, inspected it for ripeness, and took the long way back.

By three she had thirty-nine minutes and a laugh she did not want to cut. The puppeteer had started laughing halfway through the story of a stage invasion by a real cat, and the laugh rose into a wheeze, stopped, then returned when she tried to imitate the cat. Anja could remove half of it. The edit would be efficient and lifeless.

Her phone began vibrating against the desk. Otis. She turned it face down and silenced it with the rest of the afternoon's traffic.

She kept the laugh. Elsewhere she found forty seconds of repetitions, and at four fifty-three she sent the finished piece.

For several minutes she sat without her headphones, enjoying the indecent luxury of listening to nothing. Then she checked the time, grabbed her coat, and hurried to her fitting.

The dressmaker had stayed late. In the small shop, the front window was darkening behind a display of sleeves, and a line of unfinished garments hung high along the wall like people avoiding the floor.

Anja's dress was deep green silk, with broad shoulder straps and a square neckline. Nothing about it moved automatically. Its beauty was in the uninterrupted sweep from the curve of her chest to the fullness of her hips, then down to a narrow hem below the knee. She had wanted it from the moment she tried it on.

The dressmaker fastened the last hook and stepped aside.

Anja looked in the long mirror. Her hair was coming loose. There was a red mark on her cheek where a headphone pad had pressed. The dress was magnificent.

“You could put the small pleat here,” the dressmaker said, indicating the side seam with the blunt end of a pin.

“I know.”

“It would give you more room.”

Anja turned. The light ran over the silk in one unbroken band.

“Show me again.”

The dressmaker opened the side fastening and moved it to the outer row of hooks, letting out the folded allowance. It was clever work. The added silk was almost invisible until Anja moved; then a thin ridge interrupted the gleam.

“No,” Anja said, after a moment. “The plain line.”

“All right. But don't try to play squash in it.”

“Dinner. A chair. Very slow chewing.”

The dressmaker laughed and restored the inner row of hooks. She showed Anja how to reach the outer row, hidden beneath the fold of silk. Using it would buy a little space through the bodice, at the price of letting the skirt hang less neatly. Beyond that, she would need to come back for an alteration.

Anja sat on the fitting stool. The dress settled snugly but comfortably. She could breathe, cross her ankles, and stand again. She liked the support of it, the way the fabric held the shape she had chosen rather than apologising for it.

She paid, changed back into her trousers, and carried the green dress home in its cloth bag.

It was six when she finally opened Otis's messages.

*Got two seats for Sera and the Small Hours. They're back tonight only! Seven at the Lantern.*

*Moved dinner to nine so we can do both. Same restaurant. You're going to love this.*

The first message was nearly three hours old. So was the second.

She rang him.

“Did you actually move the booking?”

“Yes. I thought—”

“I was working. I didn't answer.”

There was a pause, then a sound like a door closing at his end.

“I thought you'd see it when you took a break.”

“And if I'd seen it and said I wanted dinner at seven?”

“I can ring them.”

“Please do.”

She put the phone down on her kitchen counter and unwrapped the dress. Sera and the Small Hours were wonderful. She had introduced him to their first album. That did not make her want to spend the beginning of this evening in a crowded little venue, hungry, waiting to discover whether they would get through the whole set before their table was due.

She had been looking forward to sitting opposite him. She wanted his face, his unhurried attention, and something hot to eat.

He called back while she was pinning up her hair.

“They've given the seven away. They can keep the nine.”

She closed her eyes. “Otis.”

“I know. I should have asked.”

“You should have waited for the answer.”

Another pause. She could hear street noise this time.

“I'll meet you there at seven. We'll find somewhere.”

“What about the concert?”

“I'll miss it.”

She was glad he said this without a sigh. She was still annoyed.

At seven, she found him outside the restaurant in a dark jacket, holding a small bunch of orange flowers. He looked briefly at the dress, then back at her face, and forgot whatever he had prepared to say.

This was gratifying. Annoyingly gratifying.

“Those for the head waiter?” she asked.

“He's been quite firm.”

“Good man.”

Otis handed her the flowers. “You look lovely.”

“I know. I've been in a mirror for forty minutes.”

He smiled, uncertainly. “Are you going to make me stand out here until nine?”

“No. I'm hungry.”

They walked towards the other restaurants. Her narrow hem kept their pace slow. In shop windows she caught the green silk shining beside his dark jacket, and despite herself she enjoyed the sight.

Otis tried the little place with the blue door. Full. The next had a private party. At the third, a waiter offered them a table in forty-five minutes.

“At that point I'll have eaten the flowers,” Anja said.

There was a dumpling shop on the corner with mist on the windows and six people waiting by the counter. They joined the queue.

Otis leaned down to read the menu over her shoulder. His voice was close to her ear when he asked what the red stars meant. She caught the clean scent of his soap, underneath the colder smell of his coat.

She was still hungry because of him. She also wanted to lean back against his chest, which seemed particularly unfair.

Her body, which had not been consulted about the missing reservation, made its own contribution to the evening.

Warmth spread. The silk pressed more firmly. She shifted, trying to find a little room between herself and the dress, and felt the uppermost side hook take the strain.

Otis noticed her stop moving.

“Are you all right?”

“The dress is reconsidering.”

“Can you do what you did this morning?”

She could. The contraction was there, ready to begin. She would ease the pressure, the lovely line would return, and perhaps she could spend the rest of the night divided between the person in front of her and a steady little effort beneath her ribs.

“I don't want to,” she said.

“Oh.”

She looked at him. “I like it like this tonight.”

His gaze flicked down and back. “So do I.”

“Excellent. Hold these.”

She put the flowers into his hand and stepped behind the short screen beside the counter. It concealed the shop's high chairs, a stack of coats, and a woman on her phone waiting for takeaway. The woman glanced up, then politely returned to her call as Anja reached beneath her arm.

Anja moved the side fastening to the outer row of hooks. The folded allowance opened. Immediately the dress let her take a proper breath, and the line of the skirt fell a little sideways. She smoothed it once. It remained sideways.

In the dark window, her reflected figure was fuller than it had been in the fitting shop. Her face was flushed. The beautiful band of light now kinked at one hip. She turned a little, hoping to recover the smooth gleam she had paid for, but the kink turned with her. She gave the silk one last tug and let it fall. She still looked very good.

She emerged to find Otis sitting on the single free stool, which he promptly vacated.

“You got us a table?”

“No. I got you half a table. The other half belongs to a man eating very methodically.”

The man looked up from his dumplings. “You can have it.”

“There's no hurry,” Anja said, sitting down.

She meant it. Now there was a stool and the promise of dinner, the urgency drained away. Otis stood beside her, still holding the flowers like an unsuccessful street vendor, until the man finished and a second stool became available.

Their first proper dinner arrived in two bamboo baskets and a bowl they had to share because there was no room for another.

For a little while they ate. Anja took the first hot dumpling too fast, burned her tongue, and accepted Otis's glass without being dignified about it. The released silk no longer interfered with leaning over her basket.

“I wanted it to be a good surprise,” he said eventually.

“It was a good idea. I might have wanted it another night.”

“They're only here tonight.”

“Then you might have had to choose.”

He looked at the flowers lying along the edge of the table. “I thought I could get everything.”

“I wanted time with you,” she said. “Not between one thing and the next.”

He nodded. For once he did not have a quick reply.

A family came in, carrying parcels. Someone near the counter dropped a spoon. Anja could hear the clatter of pans through the kitchen doorway.

She watched him reach for a dumpling, discover she had taken the last one, and look into the empty basket with genuine sorrow. It helped.

“We can order more,” she said.

“That was going to be my next question.”

After the second basket he told her about the end of the tour: a singer losing her voice and doing the last show almost entirely by inviting the audience to sing. He had expected a disaster. It had been the best night they had had. He still sounded astonished by it.

Anja told him about the puppeteer's laugh. He asked to hear it. She played him the cat passage from the preview on her phone, one earbud each, their heads bent close enough to bump.

He laughed where she had hoped he would. Then he asked about the woman's husband, whose name came up at the end of the clip.

She told him. He listened without trying to make it lighter.

They ordered tea. She put one foot against his beneath the table, and he left his there. By the time they stepped outside, she had quite forgotten to hold any part of herself smaller.

The flowers had begun to look tired. Otis carried them upright while Anja pulled her coat over the green dress. Its added side panels gave her all the room she needed.

At the corner where they would ordinarily separate, he stopped.

“What happens now?”

Anja could have made him work for it. She had enjoyed doing that on the court. She did not want to do it here.

“I'd like you to come home with me.”

He took a breath. “I'd like that.”

“I want to go to bed with you, Otis.”

He laughed, with relief and something less easily disguised.

She caught his jacket and kissed him. His hand settled at her back. The attraction that had interfered with her serve and pressed at the green silk was welcome now, but it was the look on his face when she let him go that made her take his hand.

At her flat they found a jug for the flowers. Otis put them in water while she released the rest of the dress's hooks. The silk slid into her hands, and she hung it over the chair, the folded allowance showing pale at the side.

She went back to him before he had finished arranging the stems.

Later, in bed, she let the quick response settle towards her familiar resting fullness. She liked that slow easing before sleep.

She shifted his sleeping arm from across her chest to her waist and rolled onto her side. He had taken most of the pillow with him. She pulled it back until he woke.

“Terrible service,” he murmured.

“You're on probation.”

He rolled towards her. They had left the bedside lamp on, and in its light she could see the little patch he had missed when shaving. She touched it at last.

“Would breakfast be an unreasonable suggestion?” he asked.

She rested her hand on his shoulder. She wanted breakfast. She wanted him sleepy at her kitchen table, finding out where she kept the cups.

“Eight,” she said. “I've got a recording session at nine.”

“Eight. What should I bring?”

“You can help make it. There are eggs.”

“Proper breakfast?”

“Let's see how we do.”

He reached past her to turn out the lamp, then hesitated with his hand on the switch.

“For the record,” he said, “I still think that second shot was down.”

Anja took back another inch of pillow.

“You saw the mark.”

“A mark. We can't prove—”

“Turn out the light, Otis.”

He was still arguing when she closed her eyes.

stories.title: The Town Beneath the Dance
stories.prompt: Four young witches arrive in a market town by the sea with little more than scarlet gowns, marigolds in their hair, and a handful of half-formed gifts—Nort can speak to crows and roots, Mysie can summon fire and make rivers glow, Elspie commands wind and rain, and you can read the sky and awaken what sleeps beneath the earth. What begins as a joyful midnight dance of shared learning soon becomes something far more dangerous when the four of you discover your magic does not merely grow when practiced—it multiplies when shared, awakening ancient forces hidden under the town. As more girls are drawn into your circle and the old words begin to ring across the land, the town must decide whether you are the start of a golden age of wonder or the first spark of a power no one will be able to control.
stories.body:
# The Town Beneath the Dance

The first thing Mysie sets alight in the town is the cuff of her own gown.

She means to warm a pear. You have two pennies among you, and the woman at the fruit stall has said she might take a little magic for the rest. Mysie cups the pear in her hands, brings up a beautiful blue flame, and squeaks as it runs up her sleeve.

Elspie stamps. Rain falls on Mysie and nobody else. Nort, who has been bargaining with a crow on the stall's striped awning, says, “He thinks we should charge for that.”

The woman laughs so hard she has to put down her knife.

“You had better eat them cold.”

She gives you four pears, the soft places neatly cut away. Her name is Hett. She is broad through the shoulders, with a grey braid she has tucked down the back of her collar. Her daughter, a girl with short dark curls, watches from between the baskets.

“Where will you sleep?” Hett asks.

“We haven't chosen,” says Mysie, wringing out her sleeve.

You have passed seventeen summers without seeing the sea. Now it lies below the market, grey rather than blue, with sunlight running on it like a blade. Boats nose into the mouth of a narrow river. Houses climb the slope behind you, crowded shoulder to shoulder; the market occupies the flat ground at their feet. You had imagined arriving here would be enough. You had not imagined the long business of continuing to be hungry.

“There's a room above my shop,” Hett says. “You can carry baskets in the morning. No fire indoors. And don't let Tib bother you.”

The girl behind the baskets comes out at once.

“I won't bother them.”

Nort gives her the last quarter of her pear.

Tib takes you through the side door at the riverside corner of the shop. There is a back stair that comes out on the upper lane, and your room opens off it. She shows you the way twice, the second time at a run.

You bought one length of scarlet cloth on the road, because it was cheaper than four sensible lengths, and made your gowns in a field. Nort's hem is uneven. Elspie's sleeves are narrow. Mysie's neckline is the only thing any of you measured twice. Yours has a crooked seam at the shoulder which Mysie says she will mend when you stop fidgeting. The marigolds in your hair came from a woman who would take nothing for them.

From Hett's upper room, you can see all the way to the sea. That evening you stand at the window until the light is gone. Mysie leans against your crooked shoulder.

“What does it say?” she asks.

“Clear until morning.”

“No, the stars.”

Nobody at home ever asked the second question. They asked whether to bring the washing in, whether the frost would kill the beans. You had answers for those things some of the time. The rest of what you saw was difficult to explain and therefore, people said, best left alone.

You point out the pale star that looks fixed but is moving, and the dark place beside it that has been widening for three nights.

Mysie squints. “Show me.”

You try. She takes your pointing hand and keeps it raised, though the muscles in your arm begin to shake.

At midnight the four of you go down to the river.

There is a sandy strip below the last house, where the town boys pull up their boats. Elspie takes off her shoes before anyone can suggest anything dignified. Mysie tucks up her scarlet skirts. Nort picks a marigold out of your hair and puts it between her teeth while she braids the rest back from your face.

“If this goes wrong,” Elspie says, “I am going to deny knowing you.”

Mysie gives her a low bow, nearly falls, and drags you into a turn.

You don't know a dance that all four of you know. This turns out to be an advantage. You learn Nort's hopping step and the little heel strike Elspie insists goes before it. Mysie has an elaborate sideways movement which works only if she holds your waist. Whenever somebody loses the rhythm, you begin again, laughing harder. Your bare feet knock against pebbles. The marigold Nort held in her mouth is damp when she gives it back.

Then Mysie catches a little flame between her finger and thumb.

“This much,” she says. “No more. I try to make it bigger and it goes out.”

Elspie blows on it.

“Stop that.”

“I want to see.”

“Then look.”

But the flame has bent without going out. It follows the wind around Elspie's wrist. She cups her hand and it stays there, a gold bead, although Mysie's fingers are empty.

Mysie stares at it. She brings up another flame. This one is as large as her fist.

“Oh,” she says.

The wind has learned something too. Elspie moves her hand and a warm current slips through your wet hems, drying them. She makes it go around the circle, touching each of you in turn.

You had come to this town believing that Mysie knew a little fire, Elspie a little weather, Nort a little of what grew and flew, and that you could read the sky and sometimes wake a seed. Four small things, useful if put together carefully.

You ask Mysie for the flame.

“You'll burn yourself.”

“You did.”

“That was different.”

“How?”

She opens your fingers, smiling. The warmth comes before the light. You feel the tiny place in her breath from which she draws it; you find a place like it in your own. There is a flame in your palm. It does not hurt.

In return you show her the pale, moving star.

You cannot give it to her by pointing. You stand behind her and let her feel what happens in your ribs when you look up: the pull, the unequal distances, the slow alteration. She becomes very still. Her flame opens into five fine points.

“Is that right?” she whispers.

You have never seen anything so right.

Nort wants to know how you did it. Elspie wants to make it move. The four of you begin again, hands crossing, a word misunderstood and said again, someone shouting, “No, like this.” Mysie teaches Nort to warm a root without scorching it. Nort shows you how to listen before you touch. Under the sand is a sleeping knot of grass, alive and folded tight; with Nort beside you, you hear its small patience.

The old words come when you turn it toward the light. They always have. You do not know where you first learned them. A living sleeper moves beneath your hand, and the sounds are waiting behind your tongue.

“Erra va. Erra ven.”

Elspie kneels beside you. You give her the movement as well as the words, the delicate upward pull. Green shoots push through the sand. She laughs, startled, and the wind lifts them without tearing them. Roots under your feet uncurl toward the star in Mysie's hand.

You dance through them, lifting your feet higher.

By the time you stop, the grass has spread down to the river. Mysie can make the whole dark current shine. Nort hears roots across the water, where before she had to lay her cheek on the earth. Elspie sends rain upward in a little sparkling column, and all four of you stand beneath it, useless with happiness.

The gifts have not been divided among you. Each time one of you gives something away, she gets back a thing none of you had before.

Mysie rests her forehead against yours. The star is between your hands.

“We have to show somebody,” you say.

She grins. “Everybody.”

In the morning Tib waits outside your door with a basket she could have carried by herself.

By the fourth night there are nine of you on the sand. By the seventh, you have to move to the market because the strip beside the river is too narrow.

They come with gifts they have hidden or given ordinary names. One girl hums bread into rising. Another can find a lost pin by the ache in her smallest finger. Tib can make a picked flower open again, for a few breaths, if she holds it close to her mouth. They know dances you don't know. They know songs that have never been sung in Hett's upper room.

The baker leaves rolls for you on her window ledge. Fishermen ask Mysie to light the river mouth, and for three nights the boats come in with catches so heavy that Hett runs out of baskets. A man who would not let his daughter watch the first dance brings her himself on the fifth. When she calls rain onto his dried-up bean plants, he goes down on his knees to look at them.

Tib takes you into the little yard behind Hett's house.

An apple stump stands there, broad enough to sit on. Hett cut the tree down after two fruitless summers, when she needed wood. She has never let anyone pull out the stump.

“My grandmother planted it,” Tib says. “When Mother was smaller than me.”

There is a strip of living root beneath the wall. Nort hears it before you do.

“Not dead,” she says. “Hungry. And very cross.”

You kneel with Tib. She sings softly, an ordinary tune, and you let her feel the sleeping root turn toward her voice. You wake it together. A small shoot comes through the bark. Tib gasps, and the shoot divides. You feel its division in your own hands, a strength returning to you from hers.

“Show the others how,” you tell her.

By evening it has reached the bedroom window. The next morning Hett stands in her nightdress under a bough full of green apples. She does not say anything for a long time.

Then she catches your wrist.

“Will it last?”

You listen to the living wood. “Yes.”

That is the first promise you make her.

She walks through the market carrying an apple, showing people the skin, the leaf still fastened to the stem. Tib skips beside her. Everybody wants to touch it.

Two mornings later, a fish stall stands six inches higher at one end than the other.

The owner blames his neighbour for shifting it. But a paving stone has risen beneath the leg. Nort puts her palm on it and then draws it away.

“Something turned over.”

“A root?” Mysie asks.

“No.”

You look down the market toward the river. It is shining in full daylight now, Mysie's last lesson returned to her in a dozen new voices. The bright lines in it bend across the current. You find the pull behind your ribs and follow it downward, where you have only looked upward before.

The dark places between the lines are moving.

There is a body under the market. Another lies beneath it. You cannot count the rest.

Nort tells you that the apple roots have begun to tear. Something below them is dragging its fur through the earth.

“It heard us,” you say.

Mysie's expression changes. Elspie, who is listening from the next stall, folds her arms.

“Then tonight we don't.”

Tib comes out of Hett's shop with two friends. She has brought them to you. You feel, before anything else, the delicious anticipation of their faces changing when they understand.

“Will you teach us the words?” she asks.

You could say no. You have heard the root tearing; you have seen the lifted stone. Something immense has moved when you meant to wake an apple tree. You know enough to be afraid.

But the first night four of you could scarcely warm your hands, and the next morning you were standing in grass nobody had planted. Every time you have reached a limit together, the limit has moved.

“We should find out what it is,” you tell Elspie.

“We did find something out.”

“We can hear farther if we do it together.”

Mysie nods. You are grateful before she speaks.

“Just listening,” she says.

You teach Tib the full upward pull, the words, the reach from a living root toward the open sky. Her friends take her hands. Mysie puts the stars into the river so you can see what answers.

The apple tree flowers again. Your breath catches with Tib's. Down the river, the lights leap from bank to bank.

Below you, something opens an eye.

That night Elspie sleeps against the wall with her back to you. Mysie lies beside you, awake.

“It didn't come up,” she says.

“No.”

“We were right to listen, weren't we?” you ask.

Mysie looks past you at Elspie's back. “Yes.”

She takes your hand beneath the blanket. You let her.

In the morning, the crows will not land on the market. Nort bargains, threatens, offers them her breakfast. They remain on the high roofs, looking down.

Tib has taught the baker's youngest daughter. You learn this because the girl runs through the market shouting the waking words, delighted that Tib's voice answers in her own. She taught two cousins last night. One went home to a village over the inland ridge.

From beyond that ridge comes a long, low sound.

Every bowl on Hett's stall shivers.
