Tib looks at you. For the first time since you met, she seems her twelve years.

“Wasn't I meant to?”

“I told you to show them,” you say, before anyone can answer for you. “You did what I told you.”

Then the market moves.

The ground rises in a broad arch. Hett's bowls slide from the stall and break. The apple tree knocks hard against the back of her house. Along the river, a row of boats lifts out of the water, still tied to the bank.

A paw comes through the paving stones.

It is longer than Hett's house. Earth falls from coarse brown fur. There are roots in it, some bare, some carrying entire little trees. Five blunt claws spread, feeling for a foothold. Behind it the ground heaves with the slow effort of a shoulder.

You hear the breath. Warm air pushes out of the cracks, smelling of bruised leaves and soil that has never been turned by a spade. Yellow flowers open wherever it touches.

People run uphill. Someone shouts that the witches have brought a monster. Someone else shouts for you to do something, as though those two things are a single thought.

Elspie is already running down the market.

She throws both arms forward. Wind strikes the paw. The awnings snap flat; apples blow uphill past your feet. She catches the wind back before it sweeps anyone away and puts all of it against the creature.

The paw stops.

Elspie takes a step. The claws drag, fur folding against the stones. Slowly, terribly, she presses it back.

Mysie shouts her name. The girls catch one another's hands. Elspie has taught some of them wind, and others learn it there, copying her breath, feeling the current pass through them. The pressure grows. The raised market sinks an inch.

People stop running.

“There,” says the fish-stall owner. “There, you see.”

Hett clutches Tib to her. Her face is white.

You join the working. With you, Elspie's wind finds the distances in the sky and reaches past the last house, lifting loose stones away from the people below it. A cheer goes up. You have done it. For a moment you can believe that you have done it.

Under your feet, another breath answers.

In Elspie's wind is the small upward pull you gave her on the sand. It has been there all along, but now it is large enough for the bodies below to hear. She is holding a waking creature down and calling to its sleepers with the same breath.

“Nort.”

She is listening. Her mouth tightens.

“There are more moving. This one wants to go inland. They used to come out when the flowers came. The roots in its fur remember. There were no houses then.”

“How many?”

She shakes her head.

On the ridge, something enormous darkens the clear sky.

You cannot tell whether Elspie can hold this one for an hour or a year if the circle grows enough. You have watched impossible things become easy. You cannot tell what else might answer her before that happens.

Hett sees you looking at Mysie.

“You can stop it,” she says. “You can. We need more hands. My sister's up the lane. I'll get her.”

“Wait.” You catch Mysie's sleeve. “Tell her we don't know.”

Mysie looks at Hett's house. The window where you showed her the moving star is tilting.

“We can do it,” she says.

Hett lets go of Tib and turns toward the upper lane.

“We don't know,” you say, loudly enough to stop her. “We're waking the others. It's in the wind.”

Mysie turns on you. “Then teach us something else.”

“I don't know something else.”

“You said we could hear it. You said we should find out.”

“I did.”

Hett looks between you.

You make yourself look back. “The stall moved yesterday. Nort told me something was tearing the roots. I taught Tib anyway. I thought if we had more, we'd know what to do.”

Hett's mouth opens, but it is Tib who speaks.

“The tree is still there.”

It is. Its boughs have reached around the front of the house. White blossom stands against the red shop door.

“We could make it stronger,” Tib says. “It could hold the house.”

Hett pulls her close again. The first green apple she showed the market is in the pocket of her apron; it makes a round bulge under her hand.

Elspie speaks through her teeth.

“I can hold it while you go.”

“We aren't going,” the fish-stall owner says. “We just pushed it back. Another dozen girls and we can put it where it belongs.”

“And whatever's beyond the ridge?”

“We live here.”

Elspie looks at him. The wind howls so loudly now that you can scarcely hear anything else, but she makes herself understood.

“No more into my wind.”

He starts toward her. Nort leaves the circle and stands in his way.

“Don't touch her.”

“She's doing it anyway! Look at the thing!”

He points to the paw. It has gone back almost to where it first appeared. The working is succeeding. Beneath it the shoulder shifts, and behind the ridge the other shape lifts higher.

Hett says, “How long have we got?”

Elspie takes two breaths before she can answer.

“I can give you now.”

Hett looks at the house. You wait for her to go upstairs for something: money, clothes, a box you have never seen. Instead she takes a key from under her collar.

“Tib. Take the little ones through the shop. Back stair to the upper lane. Don't wait for me.”

“But—”

“I heard you.” Hett puts a hand on her daughter's cheek. “I heard about the tree.”

Tib's eyes fill. Then she turns and holds out both hands to the youngest girls.

People begin to follow them. Hett unlocks the narrow back door and leaves the key in it. The apple boughs are crowding the doorway. She puts her shoulder under one and lifts it so a girl can pass.

The fish-stall owner stays where he is.

“You're giving it the market,” he says.

“I'm taking my daughter.”

He calls her a fool. A man behind him says he will stay too. The baker climbs onto a stool and shouts that her children are going up the lane, and anyone who wants bread tomorrow had better go with them.

The growing bough bears against the door frame. Plaster cracks above Hett's head. She ducks the falling pieces, then gets her shoulder under the bough again.

Nort whistles to the crows. She offers them the fish left on the stalls, all of it, a feast, if they will look into every upstairs window. They scatter. Soon she is pointing people toward houses you thought were empty. She goes into one herself and comes out supporting a man with a bandaged foot, swearing at him for thinking he could wait and see.

You keep your hands with Elspie's. The market is sinking under her pressure. It could work. Even now, with the other bodies moving, you want to say it could work.

Across the land comes the old waking phrase in a voice you do not know.

Elspie's fingers tighten around yours.

Mysie has gone to the riverside end of the market. Her fire lights the gap beneath a fallen awning, showing two people trapped behind it. She pulls one out. The other is the girl who can find pins. Her foot is caught under a timber.

Mysie calls for help. You cannot let go of Elspie. Nort is too far up the lane to hear.

Hett turns back from the stair.

She takes her shoulder from under the apple bough, ducks through the shop, and comes out of the riverside door behind Mysie. Together they lift the timber. Then Hett takes the girl's arm over her shoulders and leads her inside.

Mysie follows. She could begin teaching on the stair. She could find ten more girls up the lane and bring them back.

She looks at you once and keeps going.

The fish-stall owner finally runs. He leaves the scales but takes the box beneath them.

Nort returns, alone. The last crow perches on her shoulder and makes a noise in her ear.

“Nobody in the houses,” she says. “Nobody in the boats.”

Elspie's arms are shaking. The wind is still holding; the paw has not gained an inch. Nort gives her a hand, and you turn toward Hett's door.

“Now,” Elspie says.

She lets the wind go.

It lifts you halfway up the steps. You fall on your knees, scramble up, and drag Elspie into the shop. Behind you the market breaks open with a sound like a hundred doors being kicked in.

You run through Hett's house. Past the shelves of bowls, the basket hooks, the nail where she hangs her apron. Past the narrow stair window, where apples are knocking against the glass. You have slept here less than a fortnight. You know where the fourth step creaks.

Hett is waiting in the upper lane. She reaches down and pulls Elspie out by both hands.

The red shop door disappears.

From the high field above the houses, you watch the first creature rise.

It has six legs. Trees cling to its back. Its head, furred and blunt, presses through the side of the market, scattering the last intact walls. A dark eye gleams above its muzzle. It moves slowly, stiffly, as if every joint aches. There is another stirring in the hollow it leaves.

The creature sets a foot on Hett's house and bears down. For a moment the upstairs window stays whole. Then it is gone.

Tib makes a small sound. Hett holds her head against her apron.

The creature turns inland, following something neither you nor Nort can hear clearly enough to name. Flowers spring up in its footprints. One of the little trees on its back is covered with fruit. Nobody cheers.

By dusk three have climbed out. You hear others beyond the ridge. The river glows through the wreckage of the market, winding around things which used to be chairs and roofs and walls.

Some townspeople go away before dark. The fish-stall owner passes you without speaking. Others stay in the high field, where the baker is dividing the last rolls. A woman presses a blanket into Elspie's hands and says she will never let her daughter near you again. Her daughter looks back as they leave.

Hett has found four baskets. She sets them beside you.

“Carry these,” she says. “There are children with nothing to sleep on.”

You want to tell her you are sorry. You have said it twice already, and each time she has gone on with what she was doing.

Mysie helps you carry the baskets. At the other end of the field, you put them down between sleeping children.

“I wasn't putting it on you,” you say.

“It felt like you were.”

You stand beside her in your gown from the same length of cloth. Its hem is muddy. Her cuff is burnt. You can see the crooked seam she never mended.

“I wanted you to say it with me.”

She looks away. “Yesterday you wanted me to say yes.”

There is nothing to put against that.

The first stars come out. Mysie opens her hand. The little burning star hangs above her palm, the one you made between you on the sand. She offers it to you. You reach, and she closes her fingers.

“Just look,” she says.

You look together.

Later a girl you do not know comes from the far side of the field. She has walked down from the ridge. There is yellow pollen all over her shoes.

“Was it you?” she asks.

You tell her about the dance, the apple tree, the stone that rose. You tell her which thing you saw and what you did afterward. She listens without sitting down.

“Our hill's moving,” she says. “My mother won't come away. She says it'll stop.”

From the far side of the sea, too faint for anyone else in the field to notice, you hear a girl singing the old words. You don't know who taught her.

The girl before you looks up.

“Can you show me how to see them? Before they come out?”

You want to. The wanting arrives intact, almost as sweet as it was on the first night. You look across the field at Mysie. She is watching you; she knows that look.

The pin-finding girl sleeps beside Hett's baskets. You close your hand. You could go to the ridge yourself. You picture the stranger waiting for one of you the next time her hill moves.

Just looking, you tell yourself. You do not ask Mysie whether she believes that.

“I can show you what I see,” you say. “I couldn't make it stop.”

“She's still there.”

You open your hand beside hers, without touching. You show her the pull behind your ribs. The pale star is moving; the dark space beside it has widened again. After a while she finds it, and her face changes.

Under the field, far below the sleeping children, something turns toward your two open hands.

stories.title: A Fair Price for Peas
stories.prompt: In a future where robots handle nearly every essential task, humanity has rediscovered the joy of working with its hands. Farming, building, and crafting have become passions rather than necessities. But when a seventeen-year-old girl announces she wants to become a professional farmer, her family is confused. Nobody has worked for a living in 5 generations, and the government isn't even sure it's legal.
stories.body:
# A Fair Price for Peas

Her family had been very pleased when Romy became a farmer. The trouble began when she mentioned getting paid.

"Paid for what?" her father asked.

"The farming."

He turned a pea over on his fork. "We've been eating the evidence. Should we have kept receipts?"

"I don't mean you. I mean professionally."

Across the table, her mother stopped picking a fleck of dried clay from her wrist.

Romy had chosen dinner because the peas were hers. So were the mint and the little potatoes with their skins rubbed loose. The fish, the butter, the bread, and the strawberries had arrived that afternoon in the quiet white delivery cart, grown or made by machines that were better at their tasks than she was at hers. She had no quarrel with any of them. She especially liked the strawberries.

"A professional farmer," Lise repeated.

"When I finish school. I could start now."

"You can start another bed now," her father said. "I'll help you lift the boards."

"Not another bed. Well, yes, another bed. But I want it to be what I do."

Outside the kitchen window, the settlement stepped down the sunny hillside in terraces of pale houses and green roofs. People had been making things all afternoon. Someone was trying to persuade a wooden wheel to become round. From the next terrace came the uneven thumping of a loom. Down among the communal vegetable plots, a gardening robot waited beside a man who preferred to dig his own holes and have someone else fill them.

Lise had spent the day making bowls. The one holding the strawberries was hers, yellow glaze freckled along the rim. Romy had admired it that morning and her mother had said, as she always did, *Take it, then.*

"People pay you," Romy said.

"Sometimes. When I have a piece I want to exchange."

"And you get credits. And you buy things other people make."

"Yes."

"I want to do that with vegetables. Only regularly. I want people to order them."

Her father put down his fork. "I think that's a job."

There it was. The word made their familiar kitchen briefly strange.

Nobody in the family had had a job for five generations. Her father had once researched his ancestors and found a woman who had stood at a till for nine hours a day. He had spent the rest of the afternoon unable to settle to anything. The woman had needed to do it to keep her children in a house.

"You wouldn't lose anything," Romy said quickly. "If I stopped. I know that."

"Then what would you be earning a living *for*?" asked Lise.

"I don't know what the right word is."

This was going worse than the conversation she had rehearsed among the pea vines. In that one she had explained the difference between a profession and a hobby, and her parents had understood it on the first attempt.

"I want to sell somebody peas who doesn't have to say they're lovely."

Her mother looked down at her plate.

"They are lovely," she said, which was no help at all.

***

On Monday, the civic advice system offered Romy a list of gardening societies, a history of agricultural labor, and support for feelings of purposelessness.

She closed the third window particularly hard.

The human adviser who joined the call had a pencil tucked into her hair. Romy liked this until the woman used it to write down her age.

"Seventeen. And you want to employ yourself."

"If that's what it's called."

"I'm finding out."

The woman read for a while. Behind Romy, her father carried a timber frame past the open door, stopped, looked at the frame, and carried it back the other way.

"You can sell things you've made or grown," the adviser said. "But you asked about receiving regular pay in return for undertaking future agricultural labor. That wording reaches a part of the law we haven't had much reason to use."

"Is it illegal?"

"I don't know yet."

Romy had expected the government to know its own rules.

"The old prohibitions protect people from having their access to necessities depend on their work," the woman said. "Some of the wording is broader than that. I can look at a specific, limited arrangement. Has someone offered you one?"

"Not exactly."

"Then let's start there."

The adviser sent her a reference number. Under *proposed occupation*, it said *Awaiting clarification*.

Romy copied it into her notebook beneath *Farmer*.

***

Beni Oru held supper at his house every Thursday for twelve people who enjoyed arguing about food. He cooked because he liked feeding them. He had recently spent three evenings shaping a loaf that a kitchen machine could have made in eight minutes, then used the machine to make a second loaf because he had invited thirteen.

He lived two terraces below Romy. For weeks he had been leaning over her fence to ask about the peas.

On Tuesday she took him a basket, a set of figures, and the notebook.

"I thought four Thursdays," she said. "I've got three plantings. They won't all come at once. Then beans."

"I haven't agreed to peas yet."

"Right."

He pulled a stool out from under his kitchen counter. "Sit."

His knife lay on a board beside six onions, each a different size. Through his open doors she could see the tables folded against the courtyard wall, waiting for Thursday. He took a pod from her basket and ran his thumb along its seam.

"How much?"

She showed him the figures. They included her hours turning the bed, setting the supports, tying the stems, picking off beetles, and harvesting. She had left out the time she spent just looking.

Beni put a pea in his mouth. His expression changed so slightly that she nearly missed it.

He ate another.

"These have gone floury."

"They're the biggest ones."

"Yes."

"There's plenty in each pod."

"I can see that."

He tipped the peas into his palm. She could hear each one strike his skin.

"I wouldn't buy these, Romy."

She looked at the onions. One had a patch of papery skin twisted into a curl. She concentrated on it until her face stopped feeling so hot.

"They took eleven hours," she said.

Beni looked at her figures again. "Do they taste different if I know that?"

He wasn't smiling. That made it worse.

"You don't have to be nasty."

"No," he said. "I don't. I'm sorry. But I won't buy them."

At home, someone would have said they were good in soup. Her father would have fetched more butter. Lise would have praised the basket, which Romy had woven badly but with determination. Here the basket sat between them with its handle listing to one side, and nobody tried to rescue it.

Romy closed the notebook.

"I don't suppose there's any reason to buy them anyway. You can get perfect ones free."

"I can. I usually do."

She stood up.

"But I watched you put those sticks up in the wind," Beni said. "I've been asking about the flowers. I'd like to cook what comes out of that patch. Four Thursdays following your crop would be interesting. I'd change the supper as it changed."

She kept her hand on the basket.

"It can't be a basket on my doorstep whenever you're tired of eating peas," he went on. "I'd need to know what was coming. And I'd need you to tell me when it wasn't good enough."

"What if you don't like it?"

"Then we have this conversation again. Preferably without me being nasty."

She managed to look at him.

"Can I bring you some smaller ones?"

"Please."

***

That afternoon Romy sat between the two oldest rows and ate peas.

The big ones did taste floury. Now that she was paying attention, she couldn't mistake it. She tried to imagine asking someone to pay the number she had written down for a mouthful of them.

Higher on the vines, the pods were smaller. A few were barely filled out. Those peas were sweet, and she wanted another as soon as she had swallowed the first.

She picked six pods, then made herself stop. She was eating the next sample she ought to take him.

When Lise came out, Romy was counting through the next row, writing numbers on the back of her figures.

"How did it go?"

"He said no."

Lise sat on the grass beside her. "Oh, love."

Romy pulled a pod in half and gave her the peas.

Her mother ate them.

"Those are lovely."

"I know. These weren't the ones I took."

Lise waited. Romy counted three more stems before she could say, "I thought bigger was better. And I thought the hours would mean something."

"They do mean something."

"Not to his supper."

Her mother leaned back on her hands. Above them a delivery drone passed toward the towers beyond the hills, a violin case slung beneath it.

"I put a whole week into a jug once," Lise said. "It would not pour."

"What did you do?"

"Put flowers in it."

Romy laughed, unwillingly.

"I still liked making it," her mother said.

"I know."

"You don't have to do this to make the time count."

Romy laid another pod across her knee. She could take the peas to Beni when she happened to have good ones. She could share the rest with her family. Nothing was wrong with that picture except that it wasn't quite the one she wanted.

"I want to see what he'd make with them next week."

***

She took Beni twelve small pods on Wednesday. He ate three peas, then fetched a sprig of mint. He tore a leaf in half and handed it to her with another pea.

The mint swallowed the sweetness.

"Less," she said.

He gave her a smaller piece. This time she could taste both.

"I think so, too," he said, and asked how much she could supply.

This time she checked her notebook before answering.

She wrote *Peas grown and hand-picked by Romy Talas* at the top of a clean page.

They settled on enough shelled peas for twelve small bowls of soup, at eight credits per delivery, beginning Thursday of the following week. He would put mint and lemon in it, and serve a loaf he thought he had finally got right. After that they would see what her next planting was doing. If the crop looked poor, she would tell him by Tuesday so he could change his plans.

Romy crossed out *eleven hours*.

The civic adviser called her back that afternoon while she was washing the returned basket.

"What happens if you want to go away?" the woman asked.

"I tell him. He buys something else."

"And if he's paid in advance?"

"He gets it back."

"Even if you've spent it?"

Romy looked at the eight-credit deposit Beni had sent for the first Thursday. She had already looked up some things it could buy.

"I'll leave it there until he takes the peas."

They added that to the agreement. They added that Beni could refuse a delivery and stop ordering, and that Romy could stop supplying him. Her common provision would remain hers whatever either of them did. Nobody would owe anybody hours of labor.

"I can authorize these four deliveries provisionally as a continuing sale of produce," the adviser said at last. "I've referred the occupation question for a wider ruling. I'm afraid the government isn't ready to tell you whether you're a professional farmer."

"Can I tell Beni I am?"

"You can tell Beni what you like. I'd show him the terms as well."

Romy read the short document through. The last Thursday was four weeks away. It seemed much farther than that.

***

Lise found her in the garden on Friday, marking the pods she thought would be ready for the first delivery the following Thursday.

She had Romy's windproof jacket over her arm.

"Try this on. I mended the cuff."

Romy put down the pencil.

Every spring they took the little family boat along the coast for two nights. It was her father's boat because he had built it, her mother's boat because she had made the cups that fitted into its absurdly narrow shelves, and Romy's boat because she usually got to steer. This year she and Lise were going to swim out to the flat rock in the sheltered bay. They had been discussing how cold it would be since winter.

They were leaving on Wednesday. Romy had known that when she spoke to Beni. She had kept knowing it, in a part of her mind she hadn't consulted while counting peas.

"I don't think I'm coming," she said.

Lise held the jacket against herself.

"Why?"

"The first supper's Thursday."

"You could ask him to start a week later."

"I could."

"You've got time to ask."

"I know. But these will be floury by the Thursday after. We'd have to start with the next bed."

The next bed was still flowering. She could leave the robot to pick this crop and take it to the communal kitchen. It would be eaten. Beni would get peas from the later planting, and they could begin with those.

A small white robot came along the path with a tray of replacement tool handles. It stopped at the gate, awaiting a place to put them.

"Could that pick them?" Lise asked.

"Yes. But I told him I would. That's part of what he's buying. I'd have to ask about changing it."

"Then ask."

Romy rubbed the mark she had made on her wrist while testing the pencil. She wanted to be on the boat. She wanted to feel it turn under her hands, to hear her mother make the small startled noise she always made when she first went into cold water.

She also wanted to open these pods on Thursday morning and take them to Beni. When she had said "Less," he had put the rest of the mint leaf aside. She wanted to taste the soup they had begun figuring out together.

"I don't want to move it."

Lise folded the jacket over her arm again.

"Why make something you love into something you have to do?"

Romy started an answer. It sounded like something from the gardening society's page on purposeful activity, and she stopped.

Her mother bent to lift a loose corner of the netting away from a vine. Romy moved to help her. For a moment they worked together without speaking.

"I'll miss the rock," Romy said.

"I'll miss you on it."

On Wednesday, Lise put the jacket on Romy's bed anyway. In its pocket was the packet of ginger biscuits they always ate on the first night aboard.

Romy ran down the path with them before the luggage cart left.

"Half," she said, breaking the packet open. "You have to take half."

Her mother held out her hands.

***

At six on Thursday morning, Romy did not feel especially professional.

She felt cold at the knees, where the dew had soaked through her trousers. The first pod she opened contained one pea and a fat green caterpillar. She put the caterpillar on the far side of the fence and tried the next pod.

The gardening robot waited at the end of the row.

"You can bring the empty crates over," she told it. "And take the pods to the compost when I'm done."

It went briskly to work. Romy wished she had its knees.

She had marked too many pods. Some were not filled out enough; others she had left a day too long. She put those in a separate bowl. Twelve servings had sounded modest when she and Beni made the agreement. By eight she had begun opening the last of the suitable pods one at a time, hoping each would hold an extra pea.

The separate bowl was much fuller.

She weighed the good ones again. Then she called Beni.

"I've only got enough for ten. Small bowls. Like we said."

He was still in his dressing gown. Behind him, a kitchen machine was kneading dough.

"Are the ten good?"

"Yes."

"Bring them. I'll make something else for the first course. We can have the pea soup in cups."

"I could put some of the others in. They'd blend."

Beni looked at her. She looked down at the larger bowl.

"No," she said. "I'll bring the ten."

He agreed to pay her six credits instead of eight. She moved two back to his account before she could think of anything she wanted to spend them on.

When he accepted the peas, he ate one and gave her another. It was sweeter than the sample had been.

"Next Thursday?" he asked.

"I'll tell you on Tuesday."

***

At the supper, Beni said where the peas had come from. Romy had thought she wanted this, but she wanted to hide under the table when the other guests turned to look at her.

One woman asked what she did to keep the beetles off.

"Pick them up," she said.

The woman nodded gravely. "I was afraid you'd say that."

Afterward Beni let Romy taste the last spoonful left in the pot. He had used less mint than her father did. She could taste the peas under it, then the lemon. She wanted to ask how he had decided the amounts, but he was trying to carry a stack of plates through the doorway.

She took half the stack. "When do you put the mint in?"

"After the peas are cooked," he told her on the way to the kitchen. "Then I can taste how much it needs."

"Not half a leaf each, then."

He laughed and held the kitchen door open with his hip.

***

Her family came home on Friday evening with salt in the jacket cuffs and photographs of two seals that had followed the boat.

"They came right up," Lise said, showing her the pictures on a tablet. "Your father thought they were inspecting his paintwork."

In one photograph, the seals were two wet heads in a great deal of shining water. In another, Lise stood on the flat rock with her arms wrapped around herself, laughing.

Romy enlarged that one.

"Was it terribly cold?"

"Worse."

Her mother sat beside her, their shoulders touching.

"I'm sorry I missed it," Romy said.

"So am I."

Lise let her keep looking. Then she asked about the supper, and Romy told her about the ten bowls, which had become twelve cups, and the beetle woman, and how she had sent two credits back.

"Six," Lise said. "Then you made six."

Romy nodded.

Three finished bowls stood on the kitchen shelf, ready for Lise to take to the exchange. Romy had kept turning the blue-and-brown one so she could see the brown sweep along its rim.

"You hadn't taken that to the exchange yet, had you?"

"No. Why?"

"I want to buy it."

Lise looked from her to the shelf. "Love, take it."

"I would have chosen it there. What were you going to put on the label?"

Her mother reached for the bowl and set it between them. She brushed her thumb over the place where the glaze changed color.

"Five credits," she said.

Romy opened her account. Her occupation was still awaiting clarification. She sent five credits to Lise, who watched them arrive without sending them back.

Her father came in carrying the remaining ginger biscuits. He put them on the table, then went to fetch dinner from the delivery cart.

Lise slid the bowl nearer to Romy and tipped the biscuits into it. There were three whole ones and a lot of broken pieces.

"There's another picture," she said, reaching for the tablet. "Of your father trying to swim."

Romy moved closer to see.

stories.title: The First Cold
stories.prompt: For three centuries, the colossal furnace towers have kept humanity's last colony alive on a world swallowed by eternal winter. Their fires have never faltered, their mechanisms have never failed, and no one remembers who built them. But when a routine maintenance crew discovers a human heartbeat pulsing deep within one tower's foundations, they uncover something impossible: the towers are alive.
stories.body:
# The First Cold

The listening was the part of the round Ivara meant to stop when Deren retired.

There was useful work before it. They cleared the access doors, replaced the rubber on their own instruments, checked the colony's brackets against the towers' immense sides. Ice could prise a ladder loose. A worker could leave a glove in a hinge. The towers themselves had never failed, but there were plenty of things people could do to hurt themselves around a perfect machine.

Then Deren would sit down.

Today he chose a packing crate in the fourth tower's lowest gallery. He eased his bad ankle forward, set his helmet beside him, rubbed his flattened white hair, and shut his eyes. Overhead, furnace light moved along the teeth of a wheel so large that they could see only its lower curve. It had been turning when the colony's first surviving record was written, three hundred years ago. Nobody had ever found the other side of it.

Ivara put the last spanner away with more noise than necessary.

“You can go,” he said.

“And carry your box?”

“Leave it. I'll live here.”

“You've been saying that for nineteen years.”

“I'm close to having the place ready.”

She sat on the other end of the crate. In eleven days the box would be hers, and the rounds, and the privilege of deciding whether two people needed to sit beside a wheel that had turned without their help through every winter of their lives. Deren would go home to his room above the bakery. She had helped him move his chair to a place where he could smell the morning bread.

She wanted him to be happy there. She also wanted him, just once, to ask what she would change.

Through the gallery's narrow outer window she could see the third tower, black against the cliffs. Snow lay on its western face in an unbroken white wedge. Along its eastern edge an orange seam shone through the blowing powder. The other five towers stood beyond it, around the shallow valley that contained the last people in the world.

Under their heat the colony grew barley and beans beneath glass. Beyond the glass lay the husks of older shelters; beyond those, the snow buried everything anybody had once meant to reach. There was no remembered summer. Even the oldest stories began with people walking toward the fires.

Deren opened one eye.

“Something new in the box?”

She pulled out the new probe. Its cable was white, its display unscratched. Until this morning it had belonged to the people who checked the glasshouses: one contact head for temperature and vibration, with a filter that could separate the smaller sounds inside a larger one.

“I thought we'd try a proper foundation profile.”

He picked up his helmet.

“You've finished listening?” she asked.

“I've found something to listen to.”

The tower's foot extended three levels below the gallery. They descended beside a structural rib wider than the bakery, down iron steps the colony had hung from its side. On each landing Ivara pressed the probe against the dark material and waited for a reading. Heat rose steadily. The furnace roared above them. On the screen the roar appeared as a dense trembling band.

At the bottom, where the rib entered the bedrock, a second line lifted out of the first.

Two little peaks. A space. Two little peaks.

Ivara changed the filter. The sound entered her earpiece, small and astonishingly close.

She lifted the probe away. Silence. She put it back.

“Deren.”

He bent his head while she fitted the spare earpiece to him. His expression changed so quickly she thought he was hurt.

“It's picking us up,” she said.

They set the probe in its clamp and backed away. The beat continued.

Deren put two fingers to his throat. Ivara did the same. For a few seconds she could not attend to both sounds. Her pulse jumped under her hand; the double beat in the earpiece kept its slower pace.

“A pump?” she asked.

“Hear the second sound.”

She heard it. The little closing sound, softer than the first. A human heartbeat, of the sort that could live quietly under a shirt while its owner mended a sleeve or complained about bread.

She looked up. The rib continued into the dark above their lamps.

“There can't be anyone down here.”

Deren was already moving his light along the floor.

They found the sound strongest beside an old sounding plate. Someone from the colony had bolted it over a natural recess in the tower's foot. The date scratched into the plate was eighty-six years old; the records for that survey were in Ivara's box. They contained measurements and a drawing of the recess, nothing about what lay behind it. Nobody had cut into a tower. Nobody knew who had built them, much less how to repair one if the impossible happened.

They undid the bolts of their own plate.

Behind it was a shallow hollow with a dusty, pale floor. Ivara had expected a shaft, a cable, something descending farther than their lamps could follow. Instead a dark knot occupied the back of the recess. Fine strands spread from it through the pale floor and into the rib on either side.

Something moved under the knot's translucent covering.

Ivara brought her lamp closer.

There were chambers. She could see them filling and tightening in sequence, no larger together than her closed fist. The strands brightened at each contraction. A dull gold flush passed through them, into the tower.

She caught Deren's sleeve.

For an instant she saw a person folded into the stone. A head somewhere above them, arms stretched up the ribs, someone who had been burning under their houses while they praised the reliable heat. She moved the lamp, searching for a face.

“Where's the rest?”

Deren did not answer.

The light showed the same material throughout the hollow. Soft near the knot, then dense and fibrous, then crusted with the black mineral of the rib. A broken surface at the edge showed layers curling over one another like the grain around a branch. The strands passed through every layer. There was no wall separating the living thing from the tower.

Deren touched the dusty floor with the blunt end of a scraper.

It contracted.

The movement took the dust with it. A thin crease closed, then opened slowly again. Far overhead the great wheel went on turning at the same pace.

He put the scraper down.

“Oh,” he said.

Ivara found herself listening for a cry. There was only the furnace, and the smaller sound in her ear.

She unfastened the probe and carried it back up the steps. Deren called after her. She could not have explained herself yet, so she kept climbing.

Outside, the wind struck the sweat on her face before she closed her helmet. She crossed the apron to the third tower with the probe clamped under one arm. People moved along the lit path below, bent toward the glasshouses. Someone raised a hand to her. She did not recognize them through the blowing snow.

At the third tower's lowest survey point she took a reading.

There it was again.

This heart beat more slowly. She let it fill a minute on the display, then saved the record and stood with her gloved hand flat against the black exterior.

Nothing moved toward her. Snow struck her wrist and blew away. Beneath the mineral surface the slow heart continued, indifferent to the pressure of her hand.

By the time she returned, Deren had put his folded coat beside the open recess and was kneeling on it. He had not touched anything else.

She took off her helmet and set it on the floor.

“The third,” she said. “Forty-two. This one's sixty-one.”

He breathed out through his nose.

“Different hearts.”

She clamped the probe against the fourth tower's rib again. The quicker heartbeat returned to her ear.

“I'll send the profiles up. They can check the others.”

She sent both recordings through her helmet set and asked for the new instruments to be brought to the remaining towers. The voice from the survey room asked her to repeat the last part. She did. Then she turned the volume down. Above her, people could listen to the recordings together. Down here there was the open recess.

“Has it done anything?”

“That edge lifts when I move my knee.”

Ivara knelt beside him. Along the lower rim, a crescent of soft grey tissue rose a little from the pale floor. Deren shifted. The crescent quivered.

“Through the floor,” she said.

He nodded and put his knee back.

“Can you hear me?” Ivara asked.

She felt foolish immediately. She repeated it, louder.

The grey edge shook with her voice. It also shook when Deren coughed. The heartbeat did not change.

“It hears,” he said.

“Something does.”

She spoke quietly, then shouted a number, then whispered the same number. The tissue moved with the loudness. When she held her lamp against it, moving the beam from side to side, nothing followed.

“Maybe the light's too much,” Deren said, and shaded it.

Still nothing.

Ivara tried to imagine receiving the room through her knees. Their footsteps would have arrived first, two uneven impacts growing stronger. The spanners. The scraper. All the years of people coming to the sounding plate, striking it to check its fastenings, then leaving.

She put the soft pad of her glove on the rim.

The crescent sank away. She lifted her hand.

After a while it rose again.

She kept her hand where it was. The tissue swelled against the glove, a touch so light she could see it more easily than feel it. Then it receded.

Deren leaned closer.

She held still. The crescent returned, flattened against her thumb, and lingered there.

“Warm,” Deren said.

Ivara looked at him. “What?”

“Your hand.”

“Everything down here is warm.”

Neither of them spoke for a time.

The tower touched the seam of her glove. It pressed into the stitches, followed them a little, and drew back when it reached the hard buckle at her wrist. Ivara had worn the glove through six winters. Now she became aware of every ridge on it, the grain of the patch she had sewn over the thumb, the stiff place where old oil had dried.

She took it off.

“Careful,” Deren said.

The living edge rested against her bare thumb. It was warmer than she was and faintly pebbled. A small golden strand lay just below its surface. She had to resist closing her fingers around it.

She knew how the furnace's heat felt against her face. What did its fire feel like to the tower?

“I put my hand on the third tower,” she said. “Outside. Nothing.”

“Through all that casing?”

She pictured the immense western face packed in snow, the wind scour along its edge. This softness lay beneath casing like that. Did snow feel like anything against the outer casing? Here the tissue could find the stitches in her glove. Perhaps winter reached it only as weight and a loss of heat, with none of the small, sharp touches that struck her face.

She wanted to ask it about that.

The helmet set crackled. The second tower had a pulse. Then, while she listened, the sixth. Each at its own pace.

She took her hand away to reach the set. The crescent flattened slowly into the recess.

“They're sending someone from the infirmary,” she told Deren.

“Good.”

“I don't know what we should tell them.”

He looked at the scraper where he had laid it down. “Tell them what we've done.”

Ivara picked up the probe. She had readings from two towers, but none from the soft material. Before taking them she checked its temperature head. Her hands were shaking enough that she could not fit the cable into the calibration socket on the first try.

The kit's little vacuum flask held clean snow, packed at the start of the round. She tipped some into its shallow lid and waited until a gloss of meltwater gathered at the bottom. Then she pressed the probe into the wet base. The reading fell toward zero and settled two tenths above it. She adjusted it and tried again.

In the warm air the heap began to settle. She was watching the number when Deren touched her wrist.

The grey crescent had lifted. One side of it extended over the rim of the recess, toward the lid beside her knee.

She moved the probe away. The extension paused.

There were several things there: her hand, the lid, the small cold heap. She did not know which had drawn it. She raised the lid to the level of the opening and held it still.

The tissue lengthened. It unfolded from a crease in the floor, revealing a softer underside, and rested against the metal edge. A thin fringe passed over the rim. Ivara felt almost no weight.

Then the fringe reached the snow.

It snapped back into the recess.

The movement splashed meltwater across her wrist. She pulled the lid away so fast that the remaining snow fell onto the floor.

“Put it down,” Deren said.

She set the lid beside the flask. The crescent had drawn tight against the heart's covering. Its gold strand was bright.

“I didn't put it on.”

“I know.”

“It came out.”

“I know. Leave it.”

Ivara returned the probe to its clamp against the rib. They sat back. In her earpiece the heart was quicker, but the furnace note had not altered. Ivara could hear the wheel above, the old regular passage of its teeth through the firelight.

She wiped her wrist. Where the cold water had run over it, her skin prickled.

“It didn't know,” she said.

Deren leaned forward and picked up the sounding plate.

“What are you doing?”

“Keeping our hands out.”

He did not sound angry. He held the plate carefully, ready to turn its edge past the instruments without touching the tissue.

Ivara wanted to let him. The infirmary people would be here soon. They would have names for parts of this, and instruments made for things that could feel. She could put her gloves on and tell them about the snow.

The plate was nearly upright when she saw the movement behind it.

“Wait.”

Deren stopped.

The grey edge had loosened. Slowly, it unfolded toward the front of the recess. Its fringe reached the rim, paused, and lifted into the space where the lid had been.

There was nothing there now.

Ivara picked up the lid and reached for the flask.

“We just did that,” Deren said.

“Look where it is.”

“It could be trying to get out.”

She stopped with the flask tilted. Snow pressed against its mouth.

Of course it could. It could be trying to escape the scraper, their voices, the light. She had been ready to show him that she understood it. All she knew was that the tissue had extended again, into empty air.

She lowered the flask.

“Move the plate away,” she said.

He looked at her. Then he set it behind his knees.

With the opening clear, the fringe remained extended. It waved once and sagged toward the floor.

Ivara put her bare hand where the lid had been. The fringe touched her knuckle. It rested there, then slid along it and pressed against the gap between two fingers.

She let it go through.

It withdrew, leaving a warm damp line across her hand.

She could have stopped there. The fringe was loose again, but she remembered it drawn tight against the heart's covering. Perhaps the snow had hurt. She had no way to ask it that.

She took a little more snow from the flask, packed it into one side of the lid, and held the lid beside her bare hand. Both were within reach of the rim. She kept them level and left a gap.

The snow softened. A bead of water grew under the lid. Her arm began to tremble, so she braced her elbow on her knee.

Deren shifted on his coat. She glanced at him, expecting him to speak. He was easing his bad ankle.

The fringe still lay flat. She set the lid on her other knee, added fresh snow from the flask before the first small heap was gone, and lifted it beside her hand again.

Above them, the wheel turned. Somewhere in the colony Deren's chair stood empty over the bakery. Soon somebody would be walking toward the access doors with a bag from the infirmary, rehearsing questions whose answers might be useless here. Ivara could hear nothing in the recess beyond the heart and their own breathing.

Her hand was beginning to ache.

The grey fringe lifted from the rim.

It touched her smallest finger, moved across the air between her hand and the lid, and settled against the metal. She kept still. A fold rose behind it, supporting its weight as it extended farther.

This time, when it reached the snow, it contracted only a little.

A white crystal collapsed against the pebbled surface. Water shone in the crease beneath it. The fringe withdrew, stopping at the edge of the lid.

Ivara did not move the snow after it.

The gold strand faded, then brightened. The fold tightened. The fringe crossed the wet metal again and pressed itself into what remained of the heap.

Deren made a small sound through his nose. She looked at him and found he was reaching for the flask.

He filled the other side of the lid, keeping his fingers away from the living surface. Then he settled his hands on his knees.

Far above them the fourth tower's fire shone steadily through its narrow seam. Snow piled against the black casing, broke loose, and climbed the wind. In the foundation recess, the immense body held a little of it against itself until it melted.

Ivara's earpiece slipped. She caught it with her shoulder and could not get it back in place without moving her hand.

“Leave it,” Deren said quietly.

She did.

stories.title: The Western Balcony
stories.prompt: The great waterfall beyond the palace flows backward for exactly one minute every hundred years. During that minute, anyone standing on the western balcony may send a single message into the past. You have spent your entire life preparing the words that could prevent your kingdom's destruction. But as the water begins to rise, a letter appears in your hand, written in your own handwriting: "Whatever you do, let it burn.
stories.body:
# The Western Balcony

My mother had been dead for thirty years. I had brought her a letter explaining how to stay alive.

It was not addressed that way. On the outside I had written her full name, her title, and the date of the harvest supper, three days before the siege. Inside were ninety-four words. The first six were *Do not send the soldiers home.*

She had believed the peace treaty. So had everyone else. Its white seal appeared in the surviving accounts with such tenderness that for years I could not bear the sight of white wax. The soldiers went home to gather their own harvests. The army that had signed the treaty arrived before the leaves fell.

My mother died in the palace. The kingdom lasted another three weeks.

“Is this where you played?” Eddra asked.

She was leaning over the balustrade, looking into the garden. Eleven years old, with her father's narrow shoulders and the backs of her stockings wrinkled over her shoes. I had told her twice to straighten them. Now I wished I had not.

“Sometimes.”

The garden had been replanted. There were pink flowers where the kitchen garden used to be, and someone had put pots of geraniums along the western balcony. The columns were clean. Only in the deep cuts of the capitals did a little black remain.

I had expected to recognize more.

Beyond the palace, the river curved through a green valley. The great falls hung white beneath the castle on the opposite hill. A new country owned both palaces now. Its flag moved above the distant towers, too far away for me to hear it snap.

In four minutes the falls would flow backward. Exactly one minute in every hundred years. Each living person on this balcony could release one message to any person, at any past moment. Write the person and the time on the outside, fold the paper, open your hand. The recipient would find it in theirs.

I had practised with leaves, with scraps, with the actual letter until its edges softened. I meant to send at the first upward movement. There would be no trembling, no delay.

“The pear tree was there,” I said, pointing to a bed of pale flowers. “Your grandmother used to say the gardeners were picking them too soon. She'd make us eat one to prove it.”

“Even if it was hard?”

“Especially.”

Eddra smiled. I had told her that story before. I had told her all of them before: my mother's socks drying on the council-room hearth; my mother feeding her brother's solemn hunting dog under the table; my mother saying, *You can help me be late,* and taking me out to look at the first snow instead of receiving an ambassador.

I had left out the occasion when she was tired and slapped my hand for reaching across her writing. I had forgotten it myself until that morning, finding the same table in a room used now for visitors' coats. I could remember the offended heat in my fingers. I had been seven. I had thought she would never love me again. Then she had asked me to turn the pages of her book because her hands were full of pear juice.

When the pears really were ripe, Tem, the kitchen boy, would hold a cupped hand beneath my chin to catch the juice before it spoiled my dress.

Eddra took a small folded paper from her sleeve.

“Is that your copy?” I asked.

She put it back. “It's mine.”

Of course it was. She had copied my drafts for me, fetched books, held a ruler along columns of dates. It pleased her to get a difficult name right. It pleased me to see her taking an interest.

Below us, the gravel gave a brief crunch. I looked through the balusters and saw Selwin crossing the courtyard toward the lower gate. He stopped to examine something in the wheel of our carriage. He could have had a view of the falls from there if he had turned.

He did not turn.

The night before, he had sat with my mother's coral gown across his knees, sewing a new panel into the side. It was the one royal dress that had reached exile with me, wrapped in the bundle my mother's seamstress had carried out. I had meant to wear it without alterations. Selwin had watched me try to fasten it, then held out his hand.

“You have to breathe,” he said.

I stood in my shift while he worked. Beside the lamp were my pages, the letter to save the kingdom, the shorter one to save my mother alone, the discarded versions meant to preserve this marriage through whatever happened afterward.

“If I tell you where to find me,” I began.

“I know where to find you.”

“Before. At the shop. Even if I never came there for work.”

His needle stopped.

“That boy wouldn't know you.”

“You'd have time.”

“I don't want instructions to marry a stranger.”

“I wasn't going to say that.”

He looked at the pages. I had crossed out *marry* in three places and substituted *meet*.

“I'll take you there,” he said. “I'll bring you home if there's still someone to bring home. But I won't help you do this.”

For years I had made the destruction small enough to correct. A false treaty, a misplaced trust, a letter delivered three days earlier. Selwin kept making it large again, filling it with the life that had followed: a girl sweeping the floor of his mother's shop; a boy hiding the good shears because she kept using them to cut paper; their first room with its ugly yellow curtains. Eddra learning to walk between two chairs.

I had told him I would find him in any history.

I had told Eddra too.

She rested her chin on the stone. “Will she still be young?”

“Who?”

“Grandmother.”

“She'll be older than I am now.”

“Oh.” She considered that. “Will she like Dad?”

I nearly said yes. My mother had loved me. Selwin was easy to love. I had made a bridge of those two things so often that I could scarcely see the gap.

“I hope so.”

Eddra looked down into the courtyard. Selwin had straightened. She lifted a hand, although he could not see us from under the arcade.

The little clock I had set on the balustrade clicked toward the hour. Its case was cheap, its face larger than it needed to be. Selwin had bought it when Eddra was learning her numbers. The painted rabbit at the bottom had lost an ear.

I took my pen from the pocket of the gown. I had filled it that morning, although the letter was finished. There was always the possibility of one last correction.

Across the valley, a line of sunlight emerged from behind the castle. I put the pen away, unfolded my letter for the last time, and read the ninety-four words.

My mother had only needed to keep the soldiers at their posts. The villages would have been defended. The army would have found something besides frightened servants at the palace doors. My mother would have reached the age at which she needed spectacles. I could have been with her when she first held them away from her face in irritation.

I folded the letter. Her name and the date lay upward against my fingers.

“Ready?” Eddra whispered.

I nodded.

The falls stopped falling.

It happened first at the bottom, where the white spray gathered itself out of the river. Drops rose through the air. The great sheet of water buckled and began to climb the cliff. The roar thinned to a hiss.

My fingers were opening when another paper appeared between them.

I caught both.

This one had my name on the outside, and beneath it: *Today. First rise.*

Inside, in my handwriting:

*Whatever you do, let it burn.*

The ink shone wet. The last stroke of the *n* ran off the torn edge. I knew that impatient stroke. I made it when I was writing faster than my hand could go.

For a moment I thought I had dropped my own letter and picked up a different draft. But the ninety-four words were still in my other hand. Nothing had been taken from me. I could send them.

I had not spent thirty years believing the past could be changed only to decide now that my own handwriting was a command. A warning was a warning. I could disobey it.

I lifted the folded letter toward the ascending spray.

Eddra touched my elbow.

“What's wrong?”

I looked at her. She was silently rehearsing our first line, the one we had copied together: *Do not send the soldiers home.*

There was still time. My hand had begun to shake, but hers was steady. She had a message of her own to spend. I could warn my mother, and Eddra could write to the boy at the shop, on the day before I had first gone there. Tell him where I would be. Arrange an encounter. Give us a chance.

“You could send to your father,” I said.

She drew the paper from her sleeve.

“I brought my own.”

She held it against her chest, but I could see the outside. My mother's name. The date of the fire, a moment after I had been carried out of the palace.

For my mother alone. Not the kingdom.

“Let me—”

“I want to meet her.”

“No, Eddra.”

The words came out with the ease of straightening her stockings. I held out my hand for her paper.

She did not give it to me.

Above the falls, the rising spray had reached the first ledge. There were dark rocks I had never seen, hidden all my childhood behind the white water. Now they were bare.

Selwin's hands lay clear in my mind, motionless over the coral silk. He had said no. I had come up here and begun arranging the boy he had been, as if the man waiting below were a flaw I could correct in another draft.

Eddra was watching my hand.

I lowered it.

She opened her letter far enough to show me two lines.

*Your little girl is safe. Leave the palace. Come and find her.*

I saw my mother reading that. I saw her going down the kitchen stair, holding up her skirts. No white seal, no soldiers, no kingdom saved. Just my mother alive, looking for me.

I wanted it so badly that I bent toward the paper.

“She would come for me,” I said.

“I know.”

My mother had put me into the seamstress's arms. She had wrapped my coat around me over my nightdress, too much wool for the season. I remembered her trying to push my thumb through its cuff. Behind her, Tem was calling that someone was still upstairs.

She had left the coat crooked and turned toward his voice.

She would have searched for me. She would never have left me sweeping floors in a foreign town. I would not have stayed in Selwin's mother's shop, pretending I had no name that mattered. There were instructions I could write to keep us on that road, but my mother would have had to obey them too. Stay hidden. Don't come for me. Let me believe you died.

Eddra folded her paper again.

“You said you'd find Dad.”

“I can't promise it.”

“You promised.”

“Yes.”

She looked away. I wanted to tell her that it had been hope, that I had meant it, that I had spent years trying to make it true. I wanted her to understand how much I loved my mother.

“I meant—”

“Stop talking,” she said. “Please.”

I closed my mouth.

The clock's second hand passed the painted rabbit. Half the minute was gone.

The letter to save my kingdom lay warm and soft in my palm. I could still open that hand. There was nothing holding it shut.

The ninety-four words were for Tem too. His name was on the list of the palace dead. They could have kept the fire from reaching him. I remembered the juice in his palm and how carefully he had waited for me to swallow before taking it away.

The cuff of Eddra's sleeve brushed my wrist. Her arm was warm against mine. In the history I could make, she might never be born. The man waiting below might never know her.

I kept my hand closed and took out the pen instead.

I tore the blank lower margin off the prepared letter and wrote:

*Whatever you do, let it burn.*

I could have asked myself to wait. To look at Eddra. But I knew what I did with a gentler objection: changed a word, added a safeguard, made another draft. I had needed to hear a refusal. There would be no one else to blame for these words. Three days before the siege, my mother was alive. All the people I could not remember were alive too.

The pen had caught on the last letter as the paper moved under it. I wrote my name on the outside, then *Today. First rise.* Folded it once.

Eddra stood beside me with her letter gripped in both hands.

I opened mine.

The new paper vanished. The sentence remained on the sheet that had arrived at the first rise.

Across the valley, the water fell.

The roar came back so heavily that I took a step toward Eddra. She moved before I could touch her. She went to the balustrade and looked over it, her folded letter still in her hands.

I put the pen away. A line of ink ran along my thumb. The prepared warning, with its bottom margin missing, was still addressed to my mother. I did not know what to do with it now that it could no longer reach her.

“I almost sent it,” Eddra said.

I waited.

“She might have liked Dad.”

“She might.”

“It could have worked.”

“Yes.”

The falls roared. There was no need to keep our voices quiet anymore, but we did.

“I didn't want to lose him,” she said. “Even if it was only might.”

I sat on the stone bench beside the door. I had remembered it as high enough to swing my feet from. My shoes rested flat on the paving.

For thirty years there had always been another draft. I could wake in the night and change a word, then sleep again because I had made the letter better. I could tell Selwin I would come to bed when I had finished. I could tell Eddra we would go somewhere when the copying was done.

There was no next version.

I held the letter open across my knees. I could see my mother's thumb working at my cuff. She was impatient because I had curled my hand into a fist. I had wanted to hold her skirt. Even when she lifted me into the seamstress's arms, I had kept a little of the cloth caught between my fingers.

Eddra came away from the railing.

“Can we go down?”

“Yes.”

She put her own letter in her pocket. I reached toward the fold, wanting to see the rest of what she had written, but she covered it with her hand.

I let it stay there.

At the door she stopped to pull up her stockings. Then she went ahead of me down the stairs.

I folded the ninety-four words along their old creases and carried them with me.

stories.title: A Practical Anatomy
stories.prompt: You like to think of yourself as a good veterinarian. From Slimes to small Dragons, you can treat just about any magical creature. But no textbook ever prepared you for the hodgepodge that is Chimera anatomy.
stories.body:
# A Practical Anatomy

By ten that morning I had reunited a divided slime, splinted a young dragon's wing, and eaten most of a biscuit. The slime was already trying to absorb its dressing. The dragon had gone home asleep in a fireproof shopping basket. I was entitled, I thought, to feel competent.

Then Mrs. Birk knocked on the surgery door with the handle of her walking stick.

"I've brought Crumpet," she called. "She won't come out of the barrow."

I knew Mrs. Birk. I knew her walking stick, her plum-colored coat with its enormous pockets, and her habit of saying an animal was "a bit off" when it needed immediate attention. I did not know Crumpet.

She lay in a wheelbarrow outside my green door, on a folded quilt. She was young, about the size of a large sheepdog. Her front half was lion: tawny paws, broad muzzle, round ears pressed flat. A cream-colored goat's head rose from between her shoulders, its short horns caught in the quilt. Her hindquarters were woolly, with black cloven hooves. Where a tail should have been, an olive-green snake had tied itself into a tight knot.

The lion coughed. The goat gave a small, miserable bleat. Inside the knot, the snake opened its mouth.

"How long?" I asked.

"She left her supper. Then she wouldn't sleep. I thought I'd better not wait for your afternoon hours."

I put the biscuit away.

We brought the barrow through the double doors and lifted Crumpet onto the padded examination table. Mrs. Birk took the heavy end without being asked. I was still trying to decide which end that ought to be.

"She doesn't bite," Mrs. Birk said.

The goat took the corner of my green apron in its teeth.

"Usually," she added.

I let Crumpet keep the apron while I examined her. Her lion's mouth was hot, her tongue pale. Each breath dragged in with a little rasp. Behind the left foreleg her body was stretched tight, and tapping it with a fingertip gave the hollow note of an overfilled drum.

Goat bloat. Familiar, urgent, treatable.

Except that a goat's swollen stomach ought not to be tucked under a lion's ribs.

I slid my listening trumpet against her chest. A heart beat fast beneath it. Air came and went poorly. Mrs. Birk stroked the lion's chin, and the next cough shook the whole table.

In the middle of it, something chimed.

I held still. I moved the trumpet lower.

"Would you lift her chin again? Gently."

Another cough. A tiny, clear ting.

Mrs. Birk's hand stopped.

"Her bell," she said.

Crumpet wore a red leather collar around the lion's neck. Its little brass loop was empty.

"When did it come off?"

"Yesterday. I looked under the dresser. She likes to get underneath and roll. I thought she'd caught it there."

The snake's head emerged from its knot. Its tongue flicked toward the empty loop.

"Which mouth would have eaten it?"

Mrs. Birk looked down at the snake. "That one follows it about. When it rings."

I laid my fingers along the base of the tail. The scales were cool and smooth, the muscle underneath rigid. Something hard shifted well forward of my hand. Crumpet coughed again.

I had removed plenty of objects from animals. Buttons from slimes, knitting needles from basilisks, one engagement ring from a dragon whose owner had wisely reconsidered the proposal. Usually I knew which end of the patient was connected to its stomach.

I opened the cupboard beside the table. In the light from its glass doors, bottles of sleeping draught stood in their tidy species rows. A lion's dose was easy. A goat's dose was different. The amount that would quiet a snake was different again.

Crumpet's pulse beat under my fingers at the lion's jaw and at the goat's throat, exactly together. Whatever I gave one head would circulate through the others. I shut the cupboard.

"Can you put her to sleep?" Mrs. Birk asked.

"I don't know a safe dose for her."

She watched me for a moment, then put her handbag under the table.

"Tell me where to stand."

I brought a soft stomach tube from its drawer and laid out the mouth guard, lubricant, and a bowl. Crumpet followed the bowl with the goat's eyes. It was the first hopeful thing she had done.

"Behind her shoulders, please. Keep her upright."

An ordinary goat could be relieved through a tube, provided you reached the right stomach. I eased the guard between the goat's back teeth. She tried to chew it. I waited for a swallow and fed the tube gently down her throat.

No gas escaped.

I let more of the tube follow each swallow. It continued to pass freely.

Mrs. Birk made a strangled sound.

The snake had lifted its head. Three inches of pink rubber protruded from its mouth.

For a moment we all looked at it, including the goat.

"Is that meant to happen?" Mrs. Birk asked.

"No."

The lion rasped in another breath. I stopped looking surprised and withdrew the tube.

I had expected the goat's throat to lead down into a goat's stomach. Instead it had led across into a snake. The tube had gone freely, without force. There had to be a fork, and I had taken the wrong branch.

I felt along the neck while Mrs. Birk supported the goat's head. Below its woolly throat, where the two necks met the body, I found the hard little bell. Lower and behind it was the drum-tight swelling. Along the other side ran the muscular cord I had traced forward from the tail.

The bell seemed to be covering the way into the stomach. If so, the tube had glanced off it and gone down the open tail passage.

I drew a working sketch on the back of an appointment card: goat above, snake to the side, stomach below. The lion swallowed, nudging the same hard lump against my fingers. I penciled her route into the sketch above the bell, with a question mark beside it. Mrs. Birk bent over the card.

"So her supper's stuck?"

"The gas from her supper. I think the bell is keeping it in. Her stomach is swelling against the lion's lungs."

Crumpet was breathing with her mouth open now. The goat had let go of my apron.

I angled the tube and tried again.

This time I could feel its tip through the skin, beside the bell instead of above it. I held the hard object steady with two fingers and waited through a swallow. The tube slipped past.

Warm, sour air rushed out into the bowl. It smelled of clover and something that had been behind a dresser for a long time.

Crumpet's flank softened under my palm. The lion took a deep breath, then another. Her ears came forward a little.

Mrs. Birk let out the breath she had been holding.

I kept my hand on the tube. "That's helped."

"Can we leave it in?"

"For a little while. We still need the bell."

There was room to move it now. I felt it shift beneath my fingers, freed from the pressure of the swollen stomach. It rolled, stopped, and settled at an angle.

The snake pulled its tail into a tight loop.

I fetched my longest retrieval wire, with its small rounded loop, and crouched by the table. The snake drew its head into the coils as soon as I approached. I reached to steady it behind the jaw. Its whole length tightened, hauling Crumpet's hindquarters sideways.

The lion scrambled with her front paws. I took my hand away.

"All right," I said. "All right."

Mrs. Birk caught the quilt before it slid off the table. Crumpet stared at me with the lion's eyes. The goat trembled. The tube was still venting, but an instrument would never pass safely through those tight bends.

"Does she always curl up like that?"

"When she's got nothing to hold. At home she wraps round the bedpost."

I had been trying to hold the snake still. It was trying to hold on to something itself.

I rested my bare forearm beside the coils, palm upward, and waited. The snake inspected it with its tongue. Slowly, a loop loosened. Another unwound. Its body crossed my wrist, wound once around my arm, and gripped.

The head lay on my palm. Behind it, the tail made a broad curve back to Crumpet's body.

"Like that," Mrs. Birk said.

We exchanged arms carefully. I wrapped a warm towel around hers where the scales would rest. She pulled the tall stool close to the table's edge and sat with the lion's chin in her lap and the snake supported on her left forearm. The goat leaned against her shoulder. She looked as though she had been fitted with an exceptionally awkward shawl.

"Comfortable?" I asked.

"No. Are we right?"

"Yes."

I put the guard in the snake's mouth and passed the wire down the now-gentle curve. My fingers at the fork told me when its tip arrived. A little maneuvering, a faint metallic scrape, and the loop caught the bell's top ring.

I drew back a fraction.

The skin beneath the goat's throat dimpled inward.

I stopped at once. The bell's rim had caught the wall of the passage. Pulling harder would pull that wall with it.

The snake tried to retreat. Mrs. Birk lowered her arm with the movement instead of gripping tighter. The coils held. Crumpet's lion head remained in her lap, breathing almost normally.

"Did you get it?"

"I've caught it. It isn't free."

"Oh."

I loosened the wire. The little dimple disappeared.

For years I had liked instruments that did one thing well. This wire caught things. That tube let air out. Neither had been made to turn a brass bell sideways inside a junction that belonged to three animals.

But the tube was already on the other side of it.

I looked at my fork on the appointment card. I could bring the tube's rounded end back up from the stomach and use it to lift the caught rim. The wire could draw from the snake's side. Two approaches to one small, badly placed object.

To do that, I had to stop venting. I listened to the lion's chest again before I moved anything. Air was entering both sides. Her tongue was pinker. We had earned a little room to work.

"I need her exactly as she is," I said. "Let the tail grip you. If she moves, go with her and tell me."

Mrs. Birk nodded. Her free hand rested against the red collar, clear of the goat's mouth.

I drew the tube back until its tip sat at the fork. I held it in my left hand, with two fingers resting against the throat to feel its position; my right hand held the wire without tension. With the tube I lifted beneath the edge of the bell.

It tilted the wrong way.

The goat gagged. I let everything slacken while she swallowed, keeping the loop on the ring. Crumpet dug one black hoof into the quilt. Mrs. Birk's stool creaked.

"Still here," she told her. "I've got you."

The lion's breath warmed her skirt.

I changed the angle of the tube. Not much. Enough to get its tip against the opposite side of the rim.

"She's pulling," Mrs. Birk said.

I lowered the wire with the snake's head. Waited. The tail's grip eased.

Then I lifted with the tube and drew gently from the side.

The bell turned under my fingertips. The rim came clear. This time, when I moved the wire, only the bell moved with it.

I did not hurry. I could feel every bend it passed along. Mrs. Birk kept the snake's broad curve supported, and Crumpet held her arm. At the mouth, I shielded the little backward-pointing teeth with the guard and eased the brass rim past them.

The bell landed in the bowl with a bright, ordinary ring.

Crumpet belched through the goat's mouth.

It went on long enough for Mrs. Birk to say, "Good girl," twice.

I slid the tube back into the stomach and let it vent until her belly was soft. Then I removed it and checked every mouth, listened to her chest, and felt carefully along the fork. Nothing caught. Nothing swelled. The snake flicked its tongue at my wire, which I put away before we had a second case.

Mrs. Birk's arm was shaking when I helped her lower it. I sat her in the chair by the stove and made tea. Crumpet stayed on the quilt beneath the table, where we could watch her. I checked her breathing between cups.

"Will she do it again?" Mrs. Birk asked.

I looked at the bell, drying on a cloth.

"Given the opportunity."

"I mean, is there something wrong with how she's made?"

I took a little time over that. Beneath the table, the lion was washing a paw. The goat had found a thread on the quilt. The snake was following the movement of my teaspoons.

"I haven't found anything that needs changing," I said. "But she should have another examination when she's grown a bit more. And we should keep small loose objects away from all her mouths."

Mrs. Birk nodded and put the bell in her coat pocket. Then she thought better of it and put it in her handbag, fastening the clasp.

For her last check before going home, I sat on the floor. Crumpet put her lion's head on my knee. I offered my forearm to the snake before reaching for the listening trumpet, and it wound around me in a firm, comfortable coil.

The goat tugged the apron. Just once, experimentally.

I listened beneath the red collar. A steady heart. Air coming freely. From the stomach, the unremarkable gurgle of digestion getting on with its business.

I could have got up then. Mrs. Birk had the barrow ready.

But Crumpet's round ears had relaxed against my knee. The tail loosened its grip without unwinding, and the goat rested its chin on my shoulder.

"Give us a minute," I called.

stories.title: A Little Play
stories.prompt: The biggest racing teams had billion-dollar budgets, corporate sponsors, and entire engineering departments. You had a garage, a box of parts from your time as auto mechanic, and a machine everyone said would never fly. When you entered your homemade creation into the world's most prestigious racing championship, they laughed. That was six months ago. Tomorrow is the championship final, and nobody's laughing anymore.
stories.body:
# A Little Play

At eleven the night before the world final, the dog brought me my riding glove.

He set it beside my knee, put one large paw on it, and looked at the open garage door. For six months I had been leaving with the glove and coming back several days later. He had worked out which part needed hiding.

“You and me both,” Cora told him.

She was sitting backward on the mechanic's stool, holding the rear lift pod while I tightened its new damper. The pod was the size of a beer keg. Once it had kept the back end of a warehouse tug off the ground. Now, with the front unit, it supported a red-and-white racing bike that stretched from our workbench almost to the door.

The right fairing had come from a Honda touring motorcycle. I had cut around the badge. Under it were a delivery van's steering joints, a starter motor from the last shop I worked in, and things I had made three times before getting them right. The factory race teams built their machines around their engines. We had built ours around what would fit through the garage door.

Cora rocked the pod sideways. The damper resisted her.

“More?” she asked.

“Try it now.”

She pushed harder. The stool rolled away beneath her, and she nearly went onto the dog.

“That's less play, all right.”

“You could have stood up.”

“You could have invented something that takes one person to hold.”

She got her feet under her and pulled the tail across again. It came back toward the frame smoothly, without the last loose waggle. Beautiful. I watched it twice more.

On the television, muted above the workbench, someone was pointing to an animated version of our bike. Their artist had left out the crooked exhaust shield. A graph appeared beside it, followed by Saskia Renz in her silver Asterion leathers. Seven championships. Behind her, a whole wall of engineers watched other walls of screens.

Our tabby was asleep on the television's warm casing, with her tail across Saskia's face.

“Did you see her practice?” Cora asked.

I nodded.

“She's closing that inside line earlier.”

“I saw.”

“I know you saw. I'm asking what you're going to do about it.”

I reached for the damper adjuster.

She caught my hand.

“We test it first, Wes.”

“That's what I was going to say.”

She kept holding my hand until I looked at her.

“In the morning,” I said.

Outside, a leaf scraped down the driveway. The television showed the six finalists beneath the championship cup. I was the one whose entry photograph had been taken against the garage door. Cora had made me put on a clean shirt, then taken it from the collar up because there was oil on that one too.

Tomorrow, one of those six people would win the Crown. The season's points had got us into the final; they would buy us nothing once the lights went out.

I took the glove out from under the dog's paw. He sighed, leaned his weight against my leg, and forgave me before I deserved it.

*

Six months earlier, at the first technical inspection, a man in an Asterion jacket had asked where the rest of our team was.

Cora had looked up from the crate we used as a desk.

“Parking the trailer,” she'd said.

He waited for her to laugh. When she didn't, he looked at the bike again.
