I understood. The front fairing was a different red from the rear. The lift ducts had been designed to carry sacks of grain, low and slowly, not a person who wanted to do three hundred through a hole in the air. On the handlebars, one switch still had a little picture of a van's heated rear window.

I had been flying it after work for two years on the abandoned quarry course. I had a competition license, a qualifying time, and the required safety gear. I also had twelve certified structural welds with a total invoice that made me feel sick. None of that was visible.

The man said, “Well, let's see if it flies.” Someone behind him laughed, then someone else did.

It flew. It finished nineteenth.

In the second race I led for fourteen seconds before cooking a front bearing. In the third I came seventh, and our prize money covered the bearing, the trailer tires, and a motel room without a coin meter on the air conditioner.

By then the teams had noticed how the bike turned.

Their big lift racers steered like aircraft, swiveling the thrust and carrying the frame around with it. Ours could bend a little in the middle. Turn the bars, and the front pod pointed us into the corner while the rear was still following. We could change direction without first persuading the whole long machine to change direction with us.

There was a price. After a hard turn the tail wanted to keep swinging. I gave it a little opposite correction to bring it into line, waited until the seat stopped tugging sideways under me, then opened the throttle. By then the factory machines were straight and gone.

But on a course with one turn coming straight after another, there was no straight for them to be gone down.

We won at Esker. Cora dropped the timing tablet, broke the screen, and spent the first minute of our first victory saying she could fix it.

We won again in the rain at Serrat, where Saskia finished less than a second behind me. She came over afterward and asked if she could look at our steering. I said yes. She got right down on the wet concrete in her expensive leathers.

She didn't ask where the rest of the team was.

They had a billion-dollar budget, three major sponsors, and an engineering department. Three rounds later, Asterion brought out a racer whose front and rear pods moved separately. It didn't look like ours. It was elegant, the pivots tucked inside the frame, and it was very fast.

“Bastards,” I said, admiring it.

Cora was watching their mechanics remove a panel.

“They've made that rear bearing easier to get to.”

On fast circuits Saskia beat me thoroughly. On the tight ones we made her work. She learned where I liked to pass. I learned how late she could brake, which was later than seemed appropriate for somebody with dependants, sponsors, or a central nervous system.

The laughing stopped somewhere in there. I missed it occasionally. People who laughed at the bike weren't trying to work out how to beat it.

*

The final was at Marrowfield, forty minutes from home. Beyond the old airfield, gates climbed the grassy escarpment and came back down toward a grandstand that had taken two months to build. From our driveway you could see the red obstruction light on the highest gate. For those two months I had been checking it on my way to the bins.

At morning shakedown the airfield smelled of wet grass and hot batteries. Our assigned bay was a white rectangle on concrete. Across the lane Asterion's mobile workshop stood open, bright as a hospital. A mechanic was laying clean tools on a trolley, each one already where his hand would want it.

I used to work like that. A good shop was a good shop.

Cora connected our battery cart and fastened my helmet strap where it always snagged on the collar.

“Four soft, four stiff,” she said. “No hero laps.”

“There are six thousand people over there.”

“Then eight people will know you're testing a damper and five thousand nine hundred and ninety-two will be bored.”

On the soft setting the bike was itself. Over the hill, between the paired high gates, down past the grandstand. The last two gates made a sharp left followed quickly by a right, then put you onto the long finish straight. I swung the nose through the left, caught the following tail, and flicked right. Through the final frame. Straighten. Wait. Power.

The red obstruction light disappeared behind my shoulder. The straight unrolled beneath me.

Cora gave me the time. We did three more.

Then she tightened the damper.

The first turn felt as if someone had put a hand across the bike's back. It resisted the bend; I had to start earlier and leave more room. At the left-right pair, the nose cleared and I made my little correction. The whole machine twitched the wrong way. I chopped the throttle and missed the middle of the next gate by an embarrassing amount.

“What was that?” Cora asked.

“Me.”

The rear had already come into line. I had given it a correction it no longer needed.

Next lap I felt for the sideways pull through the seat. A smaller pull, finished sooner. I held my hands quiet where they wanted to move, turned into the right, and opened the throttle. The bike pulled cleanly out of the pair.

I was faster out of the last pair and slower round the tight high gate. The full-lap times were too close to call, and a light wind had come up during the last run.

Back in the bay, Cora showed me the times on a tablet with a crack through the middle.

“Soft,” she said.

I kept looking at the last sector.

“You know it,” she said. “You can put it anywhere. We didn't build a fast-straight bike.”

“She's not letting me put it anywhere.”

Cora moved the graph away from the crack.

“She'll leave something.”

“Yes. Whatever line she leaves me, I want to get on the power sooner.”

She watched me for a moment, then turned the tablet off.

“Stiff?”

I nodded.

She crouched beside the pod and set it. I stayed there until she finished, holding the tail for her.

As we pushed toward the grid, Saskia came out of her workshop. Her hair was still wet from the shower. I had a crease across my forehead from the helmet liner.

She glanced at the rear pod.

“New?”

“Adjustable.”

“Ah.” She looked up at me. “How are you finding it?”

“Ask me in an hour.”

She smiled. “I'll try to remember.”

*

Six bikes hung above their grid marks, supported on columns of hammering air. Mine shook at idle. Cora stood clear of the ducts with both hands over her headset. Through my visor I could see her lips moving as she counted something on the tablet.

“Radio?” I said.

“Yes.”

“You going to say anything?”

“I'm busy.”

“All right.”

Then, just before the first light came on: “Get it round, Wes.”

Eight laps. Behind the grid the grandstand was on its feet, and beyond it my garage was forty minutes away, with a glove-shaped patch of dog spit drying on the bench.

The lights went out.

For a second we were all level. Then the factory machines accelerated and their exhaust hammered my chest. I held full power, elbows in, while the pale concrete streamed backward below my boots. Saskia reached the first gate ahead. I was fifth, with a black bike close enough on my right that I could see the rider's forefinger hovering over the brake.

He moved across to claim the turn. I let him. The gate climbed the slope; his heavier machine needed a little longer to lift its nose. I tucked under his line, pulled through the frame, and came out fourth, the grass blurring below me.

The stiffer tail held the machine almost straight. Too straight. The next gate approached on my left while I was still asking the front pod to turn. I had to lift and go wide. The black bike came back past, and its wake slapped my knee.

“Clear behind,” Cora said. “Four tenths to black.”

Over the hill I stopped trying to make the turns as small as yesterday's. I gave the bike room. It felt wasteful, hanging out beyond the line I wanted while another racer occupied it. But I came through the high gate with both lift units pulling in the same direction and recovered most of the gap on the descent.

At the left-right pair the black rider braked hard for the first gate. I had seen him do it in qualifying. I stayed back, crossed behind his tail, and went through the right beside him. We were level as the straight began.

His extra power took him ahead again.

I wanted to reach down and turn the damper soft with my bare fingers.

“He lost six tenths over the hill,” Cora said. “You've got him there.”

Next lap I took him there. I arrived at the climb a bike length back, carried that distance up the slope, and went above him through the high gate. This time I was far enough ahead at the final pair that he couldn't get me down the straight.

Ahead were two silver machines and a yellow one. Yellow was quick on the descent and slow on the climb; I passed him uphill on lap four. Saskia's teammate held me outside at the next gate and again at the last pair. On lap five I made him defend the high gate, then braked early and crossed down behind him on the descent. I came out below his tail with room to open the throttle. At the left-right pair we entered on separate lines, and I reached the second gate first.

“Second,” Cora said. “Saskia one point one. Five complete.”

One point one seconds sounded small in my ear. On the course it was a silver machine that entered every gate while I was still approaching it.

I gained on her over the hill. She gained on me down the straight. Through the turns we were close enough now for me to see what she was doing. Her bike bent almost as neatly as mine, and she didn't waste a movement. I could ask less of my brakes because I carried less mass. She could ask more of her engines because she had more engine. Each lap was an argument conducted with distances.

“Point seven,” Cora said.

At the end of lap six a gap opened inside Saskia as she approached the left gate. My place. The bit of track I had been looking for all race.

I went for it.

She came across before I was alongside. Clean, decisive, leaving me room to follow and none to pass. I tightened the turn, cleared the frame, and gave the bars that old small kick to bring the tail in.

The rear was already there.

The nose cut past the line to the next gate. I shut off, dragged the bike back into line, and got through the second gate with my throttle closed. Saskia was accelerating.

For the length of the straight I watched the mistake get bigger.

“One point three,” Cora said. “Yellow is two behind you.”

I put my thumb against the grip seam. There was a raised stitch there that had given me a blister at Esker. I pressed it until it hurt a little.

Over the hill I caught her again. Not all the way. Enough to keep the silver tail in front of me. Through the high gate I held the bike out, feeling it resist and then come through. At the bottom of the descent I didn't attack. I followed her through the left, kept my hands still until I needed the right turn, and opened the throttle with the seat square beneath me.

“Point six,” Cora said as we crossed the line. “Last lap.”

The grandstand rose on my left. Somewhere in it were people who had paid to watch us do this. I couldn't spare them even a glance.

Saskia was braking for the climb. I braked later and pulled the nose up. The bike grew light beneath me as the ground fell away; for a moment the air through the ducts changed pitch and I could hear my own breath. Then the lift caught, hard through my boots, and we went up the escarpment together.

At the high gate I was nearly at her tail.

She placed the silver bike exactly where I wanted mine. I stayed behind. On the descent she stretched the gap to a length, then less as I kept the power on toward the last pair.

“She's coming in,” Cora said.

I could see it. Saskia was taking the first gate tight, denying the inside before I could even ask. If I followed her in, her better drive would carry her away down the straight. I could get second. I could see second laid out in front of me, every tidy movement required to keep it.

I moved out.

There was more sky beyond her right shoulder than I had used all race. She took the left side of the opening, still turning. I turned left earlier and farther out, aiming for its right edge so I could come through with both pods nearly in line.

She was ahead. Of course she was ahead. I had given her distance.

But she still had to come back right for the final gate.

My nose cleared the left frame. The seat gave its small sideways tug and settled. My hands wanted their old correction. I held them, then turned right once, firmly, into the next gate.

The front pod swung. The rear followed almost at once. The bike was already pointing through the final frame while Saskia was bringing hers across to meet it.

I opened the throttle.

Her silver nose came into view at my left knee. It stayed there through the gate. Then it was behind my knee, behind my boot.

The straight.

I folded over the tank until my chin touched the scar in the paint. Full power. Nothing left to move except the air in my lungs. The finish gantry stood at the far end, two white uprights that refused to grow quickly enough.

Saskia's engine climbed beside me.

Her nose came back to my boot.

I pushed my knees into the fairing. The right panel rattled at this speed. It had rattled in the quarry. I'd tried three different rubbers under the mounting bolt and none of them had quite stopped it. The little shield below it was hot against my calf.

Her nose reached my knee.

The gantry grew. I could see a man beneath it wearing ear defenders, looking up at us. I could see the shadow of my front duct move over the white timing strip.

Then we were through, and her whole bike slid into sight beside me.

I rolled off. Saskia rolled off. We coasted level, air beating the flags flat along the run-off lane. Neither of us looked away from the display.

It showed eight completed laps.

Then it showed the names.

**1. W. DACE**

**2. S. RENZ +0.018**

Cora made a noise in my ear that broke up the radio.

I looked at Saskia. She had one hand off the bars, palm open toward me. I took my left hand off long enough to touch it. Our gloves met badly, fingers against wrist, and then we had to steer again.

In the return lane, marshals pointed me to the champion's mark. I overshot it and had to shuffle backward on my boots with the bike hovering between my knees.

The front duct wound down, then the rear. The machine settled onto its landing skids with the familiar uneven clunk. In the sudden quiet I could hear the grandstand. Someone was banging a metal barrier with what sounded like a saucepan.

Cora ran across the concrete, her headset bouncing from one hand. She stopped by the front pod, bent over with her hands on her knees, and tried to talk.

I couldn't understand her. I pulled at my glove fastening so I could undo the helmet. My fingers shook. I tried again.

She straightened up, reached for the fastening, and missed it too.

We looked down at our hands.

Cora started laughing. I leaned against the warm tank, still wearing both gloves, and she leaned against me.

stories.title: Five Minutes to Curtain
stories.prompt: The kingdom's most beloved theater troupe has performed before kings, monsters, and even gods. But tonight, five minutes before curtain, a strange discovery sends the entire cast into a panic.
stories.body:
# Five Minutes to Curtain

Inside the dragon, Werrit raised his left heel half an inch.

“Less coy,” said Nalla from the front.

He raised it another half inch. The dragon's hindquarters acquired an air of wounded innocence.

“There. Stay like that.”

Nalla worked the head's sneeze lever. The jaws opened, the feather whiskers trembled, and Werrit bent both knees just as she jerked her end upward. To anyone outside the green cloth, the dragon had sneezed so hard that its bottom was considering leaving.

“Nothing to do with me,” Werrit said in his smallest, most injured voice.

Nalla laughed. Seven years inside the same dragon, and he could still get her.

“That's it. Tonight we keep that.”

She ducked out through the loose flap at its waist, auburn braid emerging before the rest of her. Werrit followed. His shirt had come untucked, and he had lost a shoe again. The dragon sagged over two dressing-room chairs, looking like an unwise purchase.

At the mirror, Bessa held her crown steady while Nalla fastened its last pin. Tib was practicing the expression with which he would discover that he had stabbed his own boot. His knight always promised to slay the dragon; instead it knocked him flat, and Bessa's queen came out to rescue him. Varlo stood at the stove, warming the handkerchief he liked to die holding.

The Lantern Company had played for three kings, a flesh-eating countess who had sworn off flesh for the duration, and the God of Small Mercies, who had required an aisle seat. Outside, the usual queue ran around the theater and past the pie seller. Someone was singing the dragon song. Someone else, less beloved by Werrit, was singing the dragon song's second verse.

Nalla put the pin between her teeth, checked the little sandglass on the mantel, and said around it, “Five minutes.”

An enormous gold eye filled the window.

“There you are,” said Werrit's mother.

Werrit sat down between the two chairs, in what he had thought was a seat. His foot went straight through the dragon's open mouth.

“Mother?”

“Your father is in the box. I told him not to start clapping until you finish your speech.”

Behind Bessa, Nalla's hands stopped moving. Tib's practice expression became permanent.

“You are a very difficult son to surprise,” Mother continued. “The porter kept trying to put me in the street. Is this the window you meant in your letters? It hardly seems safe for a great leading actor.”

Werrit pulled his foot out of the dragon's mouth.

“I didn't mean this window.”

“Well, you said the dressing room had a view.”

A claw came through the opening. Hanging from it was a gilt frame. Inside the frame, beneath an elaborate engraving of Werrit with a sword, stood the words:

**WERRIT AND HIS LANTERN PLAYERS**

**FAREWELL PERFORMANCE**

Werrit snatched the frame. He tried to say several things at once, drew the breath for all of them, and scorched the center of his own face out of the engraving.

Nalla removed the pin from her mouth.

“Oh,” she said.

“Not near the paper, dear,” said Mother.

Nobody moved. Werrit held the smoking notice in front of the unburnt portions of his reputation.

Tib looked from the gold eye to Werrit. “You're a dragon?”

“Yes.”

“All this time?”

“I make myself this shape. I've been doing it for years.”

Varlo put down his handkerchief. “You once told me I was doing the wings wrong.”

“You were.”

“You let me demonstrate.”

Mother's eye moved across the room. “I shouldn't keep you. We know how much work goes into your dragon-slaying. I'll watch with your father. Do remember to look toward the box when you give the speech. He's been practicing.”

Her claw withdrew. The eye vanished, followed by the scraping of scales against the outside wall.

For a moment Werrit could hear her telling the porter that she knew perfectly well where the monster box was; he had just pointed it out four times.

Then Tib said, “His players?”

Bessa turned very slowly on her stool.

“Farewell?”

“It's not farewell.” Werrit brushed hot ash off his knee. “I meant it to be the last notice. The last one I'd have to make.”

“You've made others?” said Nalla.

“Some.”

“How many is some?”

“Mother keeps them in an album.”

Bessa shut her eyes.

Then she tried to stand. The hem of her veil was trapped beneath a chair leg, and she sat down again hard.

“Get me out of this,” she said. “Somebody get me out of this.”

Nalla lunged for the veil and stood on the other end.

The first trumpet sounded beyond the wall. Ordinarily, that meant three minutes to curtain. Varlo began folding his handkerchief into smaller and smaller squares. Nobody made for the door.

“Why tell her you were leaving?” Nalla asked.

“So she'd stop asking what I was doing next.”

“And it didn't occur to you she'd come?”

He had imagined the relief of never having to invent another triumph. He had not imagined his mother packing for one.

“It occurred to me just now.”

Tib took the frame away. He examined the surviving sword, then his own sword on the table.

“That's mine.”

“I know.”

“You put my sword in your picture.”

“I couldn't draw a different one!”

“You can fight with the drawing, then!”

“Tib.” Nalla caught his sleeve. “Help or go out.”

“I'm trying to go out. I'm the first entrance!”

“You can have my death,” Varlo told Werrit. “That's the part people remember.”

“Your death takes seven minutes,” said Bessa.

“I've cut it.”

“To seven minutes.”

Werrit looked at the sword. Tib had a white plume on his helmet tonight. Bessa had curled it herself because they expected the royal household. Werrit had always thought a white plume unnecessary. Now he could almost feel it moving above his own head.

“I could do the entrance,” he said.

Everyone looked at him again.

“I know the words.”

“Everyone knows the words,” said Tib. “You shout them at us every night.”

Werrit knew where the speech rose. He knew where to turn so the sword caught the light. He knew which of the doctored portraits his mother had framed.

“Just the opening. Through the dragon. Then we can change back.”

“What do I do in these letters?” Nalla asked.

Werrit looked at the heap of green cloth.

“Help me.”

The word sounded worse in this room.

Nalla glanced at the sandglass. She was still holding Tib's sleeve. Slowly she let it go.

“I'll get you through one scene,” she said. “Then I want my partner back. Coat off, Tib.”

“I am not losing my fall.”

“You'll be the palace guard. You can fall later.”

“It's a knight's fall.”

“Then get promoted on the way down.”

The room broke into motion.

Bessa kicked the chair clear and unlaced Tib's shoulder pieces while Varlo shook Werrit's arms into the embroidered coat. Then she fastened the armor onto Werrit. Nalla pulled the low wheeled base from beneath the prop throne. The throne fell six inches with a noise Bessa disliked.

“My entrance,” Bessa said.

“You walk tonight.”

“I don't mind walking. I mind arriving. Don't rush me.”

“Nobody would dare.”

Nalla heaped their ordinary coats on the wheeled base and dragged the dragon's empty hindquarters over them. She tucked the bamboo ribs around the pile, leaving the waist flap open beside her own entrance. Werrit would usually have been inside, holding that bamboo frame against his hips.

“No sneeze,” she told him. “I come on, I threaten you, you stab me. Very noble. Very simple.”

“What happens to the dragon song?”

“It lives to sing another day. Pin that tail in, would you?”

He fixed the feather-duster tail above the coats. It drooped forward. Nalla batted it out of her face.

Tib pressed his helmet down over Werrit's auburn hair harder than necessary.

“Chin up. The plume pulls you over if you look at your feet.”

“I don't look at my feet.”

“That's why you only have one shoe.”

The second trumpet sounded.

“Places,” Nalla said. “Varlo, you pull the curtain and call me on. Tib, left wing. Werrit, don't start until the curtain's clear.”

“I know.”

“You'd be amazed how many heroes don't.”

She ducked into the dragon. Bessa gathered her violet skirts. Varlo retrieved his handkerchief. Tib snatched a plain guard's surcoat off the costume rail, then took the throne's cushion because nobody had told him how a palace guard was supposed to fall, and he intended to be ready.

Werrit stood with the sword in his hand.

He had never understood how much of the world you could see when you weren't looking out through a hole beneath a dragon's tail.

Through the gap beside the curtain, he saw the house: heads in the gallery, the pie seller wiping his hands, two children in paper crowns, the royal steward with his great chain. In the monster box, his father sat upright between the reinforced pillars. Mother had tucked her wings in. Her claws rested against the rail.

Father lifted one claw toward the stage. Mother pushed it gently down.

Varlo pulled the curtain.

Werrit walked into the light.

“Who bars my passage to the captive queen?”

His voice went right to the back. The sword flashed when he raised it. He felt the plume tip, remembered Tib's instruction, and lifted his chin.

From the left wing, Tib mouthed, *Slower.*

Werrit slowed. It was good advice. The silence grew around him, grand and full. He had thought he wanted to get this over with, but now he wanted to stand there for quite a while.

Varlo swept on as the Usurper, all black hair and blacker intentions. He had apparently decided that the altered opening required a duel.

They exchanged three blows, which Werrit knew from years of watching their boots. On the fourth, Varlo took a wound no sword had delivered and fell to one knee.

“Remember me,” he said, producing the warm handkerchief, “when summer gilds the orchard—”

Behind him, the dragon entered.

Its front advanced with Nalla's familiar sinuous swagger. Its rear rolled after it like luggage. Werrit heard the first little laugh, then another. Nalla turned the head toward the monster box and gave his parents a magnificent snarl.

Father's mouth opened in attentive approval. He wasn't going to clap early. Werrit could have kissed him.

“—and the long road bears the lonely traveler home,” Varlo continued.

The dragon shouldered him gently aside.

“Who dares approach my queen?” Nalla boomed through the brass throat.

Werrit raised the sword. The line waited exactly where it always had.

*I dare, foul beast, and with this blade I end thee.*

He had said it so often while washing his stockings that the others made him stop. In front of him, Nalla opened the dragon's jaw and lowered its neck. One touch with the blade, one convulsion, and he would stand over the green heap to finish his speech. Mother would see it. Father would clap. Werrit and His Lantern Players.

Nalla backed into the rolling hindquarters. The whole contraption swung around, and the drooping feather tail brushed the dragon's nose.

The whiskers trembled.

Werrit knew how badly she wanted to do the bit. She shouldn't. He hoped she would.

“Ah,” said the dragon.

The children in the front row leaned forward.

“Ah.”

Nalla jerked the sneeze lever.

The head shot up. The coat-stuffed bottom did nothing at all.

The pause belonged to Werrit.

He saw the dragon's jaw open again, offering him its throat. Nalla could still take the sword. She would fall splendidly; she did everything splendidly. They could leave their new bit here, an unfinished noise in the opening scene, and he could have the box full of proud faces.

Werrit took two steps toward the left wing.

“Tib,” he said, and passed him the sword.

Then he grabbed the wheeled base through the loose waist flap and shoved it toward the wing. Their coats rolled out in a heap. He ducked under the cloth before the hindquarters could collapse.

He hit his helmet on the bamboo frame. The plume caught. He bent too far, righted himself by feel, and found the exact old place for his hands.

“Nothing,” he said in his smallest voice, “to do with me.”

Nalla's fingers closed around his wrist through the gap between their frames.

Then she sneezed again.

Werrit made the bottom jump. The feather tail fell out, and his plume poked through the slit and shook indignantly at the house.

The laugh arrived through the cloth, huge and untidy.

He couldn't see the box.

Nalla pulled once at his wrist. He followed. They backed into Varlo, who was explaining why he could never see another midsummer, and the dragon sat on his handkerchief.

“My last remembrance!” Varlo cried.

Werrit worked his heels, giving the dragon a laborious, regretful wiggle.

Varlo abandoned the orchard and died.

Tib came on with his own sword, the throne cushion hidden under his surcoat, and the expression of a man reclaiming his property.

“I dare, foul beast—”

Werrit swung the hindquarters sideways. His borrowed shoulder plate caught the frame; the rear described an unusually wide arc. Tib saw it coming, delayed half a beat for the gallery, and performed the fall he had been protecting all evening.

It began at his eyebrows and traveled down him in installments. His knees attempted a negotiation. His boots lost. He landed on the concealed cushion with the noise of a collapsing armory.

Above Werrit, Nalla said, “Oh, well caught.”

Tib's hand appeared beneath the cloth, patting twice for thanks. Then it withdrew to die on top of Varlo, who objected in a whisper.

Werrit was laughing now. He shouldn't have been; it shook the frame. Nalla pinched him.

From the opposite wing came the first clear note of Bessa's little handbell.

The dragon stopped. Even the tail stood still.

Bessa had refused to be hurried into a room for fourteen years. Werrit knew her entrance better than his own name. Three steps. Bell. Turn. Wait until everyone wanted the next step.

“What,” said the queen, “has happened to my guard?”

“Promotion,” said the dragon's bottom.

Bessa let that pass through the house.

“And my usurper?”

“Summer got him.”

Someone in the gallery screamed with laughter.

Bessa came close. Werrit could see the violet hem through the little hole beside his knee. She tapped the dragon's rear with her bell.

“This end has been talking again.”

He made it shy.

She tapped it once more.

He made it deeply misunderstood.

Nalla began the dragon song, and this time the audience supplied the second verse before she could. Tib rose from the dead to keep time with his sword. Varlo remained dead long enough to be admired, then joined in from the floor.

Werrit held the frame steady and gave Nalla the room she needed for the big turn. They went one way, then the other, then bowed in opposite directions. The helmet plume vanished into the cloth and sprang out again.

For the last refrain, he shut his eyes. He didn't need the hole.

***

Afterward, Mother came back to the window.

Werrit was trying to get out of Tib's coat. Nalla had already freed the helmet from the frame, using a butter knife and language she had not used in front of the God of Small Mercies.

Mother nodded toward the blackened notice on the table.

“How many?”

Werrit let his arms fall.

“All the notices.”

“And the letters?”

“Not all of those.” He looked at her eye. “Most.”

Father's snout appeared above her. “I didn't clap in the speech.”

“I noticed.”

“There wasn't an end to it.”

“No.”

Father considered this. Behind Werrit, Tib was fitting his sword into its scabbard. Werrit still wanted it. He wanted a portrait with the white plume, too, a real one this time. The wanting had not burned away with the notice.

“Were you always the back?” Mother asked.

“Usually.”

“Do you like it?”

Nalla stopped pulling at his sleeve.

“Yes,” Werrit said.

Mother was quiet for long enough that he began to explain about the sneeze, how it needed two people, how Nalla could tell from his hand whether he was ready. Then he stopped. He was very good at filling a silence with things she hadn't asked him.

“We will talk at supper,” she said. “About the letters.”

“I know.”

Her claw slid through the window. He thought she wanted the notice, but she turned it palm upward.

Werrit laid his hand in it. There was glue on his fingers and a small burn on his thumb. Her claw curled around them, carefully.

Above her, Father was trying the little wounded voice.

“Nothing,” he said, and had to clear his throat and start again.

Werrit laughed before he got to the rest.

stories.title: The Bed by the Wall
stories.prompt: You discover that your daughter was taken by fairies years ago and replaced with a changeling that looks exactly like her.
stories.body:
# The Bed by the Wall

Carys waited until I had both hands in the dough to ask for the orchard ladder.

“What have you put up a tree?”

“Nothing. I need you to help me carry it.”

It was nearly dark. The bread should have been in the oven an hour earlier, and the ladder belonged to our neighbour, who had lent it to me until tomorrow. I told her that whatever it was could stay up there until morning.

She laid a folded paper on the floury table. Her hand remained over it.

“And we need to make up the little bed.”

I looked at her then. Sixteen years had given me a fair knowledge of the things she could say easily. She could confess to breaking a plate while the pieces were still falling. This had taken her all afternoon. I had heard her coming to the kitchen door and going away again.

“Who's coming?”

She moved her hand.

The paper had been folded and unfolded until its corners were soft. A bird was drawn along one edge, its head turned back into its feathers. Under it, in cramped writing, someone had written:

*They have taken the tall chest downstairs. I got the last nail out of the frame. I can get my shoulders through. Tonight, while they load. You will have to bring her. Please bring her.*

It was signed Briony.

“Who's her?” I said.

“You.”

Carys pulled a bundle from inside her dress. More papers, tied with blue thread. One had a little pressed leaf caught in the knot.

“There's a girl in the house above the old quarry.”

I waited.

“They took her from the plum trees. When she was four.”

My hands were beginning to ache with the dough drying between my fingers. Carys had been four when she wandered out of the orchard. Her father found her sleeping underneath the hedge after we had spent half the afternoon calling. He brought her home with a thorn in her stocking and cried while I pulled it out.

“They made me look like her,” she said. “They left me in her place.”

I looked from the papers to her face. The small dent in her upper lip. The dark brows that nearly met when she was cross. She had my mother's eyes, and her father's habit of turning her whole body when someone spoke from behind her.

“Don't,” I said.

She held the bundle against herself.

“The thread seller carries things for them. He came to find me three summers ago. He said I was growing just like the girl they'd taken. I made him tell me what he meant.”

The thread seller had eaten bread in this kitchen. He wore his hat indoors and never let me pour his tea.

“He took a letter for me. She wrote back.”

“Three summers?”

Carys nodded.

I drew my hands from the bowl. Dough stretched and broke. She fetched the jug from the shelf, as she always did when my hands were dirty, but I went past her to the washstand.

“Why didn't you tell me?”

“I was going to.”

“When?”

She had an answer ready. I watched her decide against it.

“I don't know.”

Outside, a cart went by. We both listened until its wheels had passed.

“They're leaving tonight,” she said. “On the summer road. When the moon goes down, it goes too. She says they'll take her if she's still there.”

I knew about the road. Once, before Carys was born, her father and I had watched the fairy coaches pass across a field without bending the grass. He put out our lantern and kept his hand over my mouth until the last had gone. In the morning there was no road in the field, only the sheep walking where it had been.

I wiped my hands on my apron.

“Show me where.”

Carys did not move at once.

“Afterward,” she began.

I could not help her with afterward. I went upstairs and pulled the little bed out from under hers.

It was a low truckle bed with one foot shorter than the others. I wedged a scrap of leather underneath and put it beside the wall. Carys slept best with one knee drawn up against the plaster. I found a sheet and the spare blanket. Then I went out for the ladder.

*

We carried it between us along the lane, Carys in front. Whenever she turned to check on me, the end dipped and knocked my shin.

“Watch where you're going,” I said the third time.

She faced forward.

There were years folded in the bundle against her ribs. Three summers in which I had asked what she wanted for supper, whether she needed new stockings, why she was so quiet. During those same years another girl had been waiting above the quarry. My anger could find no useful shape. It settled on the back of the neck I knew, on the small hairs escaping from her plait.

“Was there no way before tonight?”

“We tried things.”

“What things?”

“She got into a coach once. They found her before it left. I went up to the house in spring, but they knew me. They thought it was funny. They made us stand together.”

I stopped walking. The ladder pulled against my hands.

“You went there?”

“I didn't tell them about the letters.”

“That isn't what I asked.”

She stood with her back to me. In the gathering dark, I could still see the white parting in her hair.

“I didn't think you'd want me when you knew.”

I ought to have answered her. I had answered smaller fears in worse places: beside her father's bed, in the lane after a dog knocked her down. But I was thinking of a child trying to hide in a coach.

“Lift your end,” I said.

We crossed the quarry track. The house stood on the shelf of land above it, where in winter there was only broken stone and a stand of elder. Tonight its chimneys rose past the trees. Lamplight moved behind windows too closely set, and a coach waited at the front with its shafts pointing uphill.

“If they come after us?” I whispered.

“They have until moonset. If they miss the road, they stay here a year.”

“Then they can stay.”

“She says they won't.”

She led me around the back. A narrow window stood open above a sloping roof of loose slates. Below it were stacked chairs, a rolled carpet, a stone figure with a sack over its head. We put the foot of the ladder among them and raised it slowly. One rail grated against the wall. Carys caught it before it struck the window.

A face appeared in the opening.

For an instant I turned to see how Carys had got up there. She was beside me, with both hands on a rung.

The girl above us pushed her plait out through the window first. It fell over the sill. Then she put an arm through, feeling for the ladder.

“Lower,” Carys whispered. “Your hand. Lower.”

I wanted to climb to her. But the foot was on uneven ground, and when Carys put her weight against the left rail, the right began to lift. I planted my boot on it and held on.

The girl had a flat wooden case wedged under one arm. She got her head and one shoulder outside. Her dress caught on a projecting nail. She backed an inch, tugged, and the case slipped from her arm into the room.

We heard it hit the floor.

“No,” she said.

She tried to draw her arm back. From the front of the house came a shout, followed by the sharp complaint of a door being dragged over stone.

“Leave it,” Carys said.

“It's all of them.”

“Get your foot out.”

The girl looked down at us. At me. I had imagined, on the walk, that I would know her when I saw her. I knew every feature. I could not read the way she held them.

“The ladder's slipping,” I said. “Please.”

She pulled the caught cloth until it tore. A knee came through. She lay across the sill, then lowered herself until her foot found a rung. Her bare heel pressed my fingers when she came down.

Carys took her wrist at the bottom. The girl shook her off.

“I can walk.”

A light came into the upper room. Someone called a name I had just seen written on paper.

We left the ladder against the wall.

*

At home I put the bar across the door and fastened the shutters. I had never tested either against anything that wanted to get in. Carys stood beside the hearth with the other girl. Now and then one glanced at the other and looked quickly away.

The moon was still above the orchard. I drew the kitchen curtain.

“Sit down,” I said. “Both of you.”

The bread had risen too far. It sagged when I put it in the oven. I needed something hot, so I cut yesterday's loaf and set milk to warm.

“I'll wash your feet.”

The girl looked down at them. A thin line of blood had dried above her heel.

“I can do it.”

“There's a cut.”

“I know.”

I put the basin in front of her. She waited until I stepped away before lowering her feet into it.

Carys reached for the brown cup on the shelf. I took it from her and set it on the table in front of the girl. Her father had made it, badly, with a thumbmark too deep in the handle.

“Do you remember this?” I asked.

The girl shook her head.

“You used to put buttons in it.”

“That's my cup,” Carys said.

I heard the ugliness I expected in the words and looked up sharply. She was holding an empty hand out toward the shelf. It was her cup. She drank from it every morning.

“I'll get another,” she said, and did.

The girl left the milk untouched. When I asked, she said she didn't like it warm. I almost told her that she did. Instead I poured it back into the pan and brought cold milk. Carys had begun rubbing a spot of dried mud off her dress. It was my old dress, altered twice, with the mending under the arm done in her own uneven stitches.

“What was in the case?” I asked.

“Drawings.”

“Yours?”

She nodded. “Birds. What I could see from the top pane. I put the names underneath when I knew them.”

“She drew a kite with the fork wrong,” Carys said. “I told her.”

“It wasn't a kite.”

“You said it was.”

“I said that's what they called it.”

Carys bent again over the mud on her skirt.

“Can I see the bird I sent you?” the girl asked.

Carys pushed the loose letter across the table. The girl smoothed it on her knee and bent over it for a while. Then she folded it with the drawing inside and put it into the pocket of her skirt.

I found a clean cloth and a needle. The girl allowed me to set them on the table. When I looked at her hand, there was black ink in the crease beside her thumbnail. Carys had that dent in her lip, those brows, that same nail bitten short. Twelve years ago a child had been carried away and I had not missed a single breakfast with her face.

“Carys,” I said.

Both girls looked up.

I could not finish.

“Briony,” the girl said.

“Did they give you that name?”

“It's what I called myself.”

Behind the shutters something brushed the wall. Carys was on her feet before I had got round the table. We listened. A small scratching moved along the sill, then stopped. I kept my hand on the shutter fastening. I had gone to the quarry thinking only of the girl who was there. Now I could picture either of them being lifted through a window.

“A branch,” I said, too loudly.

We sat down again. The bread smelled scorched. I took it out and put it on the hearth without cutting it.

Briony had dried her feet. She held the cloth in her lap.

“Carys told me about Father.”

I nodded.

“She said it was in the autumn.”

“Six years ago.”

“I know.” She picked at a thread on the cloth. “Was he awake?”

“Most of the time. At first.”

“He kept wanting us to open the window,” Carys said. “Even when it was raining. He said the room smelled—”

“Let me tell her.”

She shut her mouth. I was grateful for the silence. There was so little I could give Briony that she had not had to get through someone else.

“He wasn't frightened,” I said. That was not wholly true. “We stayed with him.”

Briony looked at the cup, then at me.

“Did he ask where I was?”

The kitchen became very quiet. The fire had burned down to a glow around the underside of the loaf.

“He didn't know,” I said.

She was looking directly at me now. I had to go on.

“Neither of us knew.”

“So he thought I was here.”

I nodded.

“When he died?”

“He had your hand.”

“My hand,” Carys said.

Her voice had scarcely any sound in it. I turned and put my palm against the side of her head. She leaned into it before she could stop herself. I felt the familiar weight, the warmth under her hair. Then she pulled away.

Briony was watching us.

I put my hand on the table. There was a damp ring where I had set the milk.

“He would have—”

“Don't,” Briony said.

I closed my mouth.

She folded the cloth carefully along its wet creases. Carys stood up and went to the stairs. Neither asked me to come.

*

I stayed in the kitchen until the moon had gone behind the orchard and the light under the curtain had thinned. Far off, wheels rattled over something harder than earth. They went on for a long time.

The sound passed. Later an owl called from the quarry.

I took a candle upstairs.

Both beds were empty. For a moment I could not move. Then I saw Carys sitting on the floor between them, still dressed. Briony stood by the window, examining the latch.

“Don't open that,” I said.

“I wasn't going to.”

“The road's gone.” Carys had been looking through the gap in the shutters. “It's just the field again.”

I set the candle on the chest of drawers. There was not much space. Carys's boots stood under her chair; her books were stacked on the window ledge. I had put Briony's bed against the wall where there was room for it, and its blanket was already rumpled at the foot.

“Is it all right?” I asked.

Briony looked at the bed.

“I don't want to sleep there.”

“It isn't damp. I aired the blanket last week.”

She rubbed her forearm. The dress had torn almost to the elbow.

“I don't like being against a wall.”

“You could have mine,” Carys said.

“Yours is against a wall.”

“The head is.”

“I can see that.”

I bent to straighten the blanket. “We can turn it.”

“There's no room,” Carys said.

“If we take the chair—”

“That's where I put my clothes.”

I stood up. Carys was looking at me, not at Briony. All evening I had been taking things from her hands.

“The chair stays,” I said to her.

I turned to Briony. “I could make up a place downstairs. Or you could come in with me.”

She gave a small, immediate shake of her head. Then she looked away, as if she had been rude to someone in a shop.

I had kept her first shoes. They were wrapped in a piece of linen in the bottom drawer of my chest. I had thought of them while carrying the ladder: I would show her the shoes, the little blue coat, the height marks on the door. I had not understood how much of what I could show her belonged to Carys.

“You don't have to decide now,” I said.

“I have to sleep somewhere.”

There was no answer to that which did not begin the whole thing again. I left the candle and went downstairs.

I washed the bowls. Carys usually dried them while I washed, but I set them on a cloth tonight. The other letters were still on the table. I gathered them without untying the thread and laid them on the stair. They were not mine to read through.

Above me a bed scraped over the floorboards.

“Mind the books,” Carys said.

Something knocked against the wall.

“You said mind them after I hit them.”

“You can see them.”

I went to the foot of the stairs. The scraping stopped. There was a pause, then Carys said, more quietly, “It won't go straight.”

“Then leave it crooked.”

I sat on the bottom stair. After a while the door opened above me. Briony came to the landing. She had the candle, and I was afraid I would call her by the wrong name again.

“Have you got a pillow that isn't feathers?”

I had one stuffed with carded wool in my own room. I fetched it, slipping the cleanest case over it, and carried it up. Briony waited in the doorway. Behind her, the little bed stood at an angle, with a passage just wide enough to squeeze through on either side. Carys was kneeling beside a spill of books. Her chair was still in its place.

I waited for her to look up, but she kept putting the books in order.

I held out the pillow. Briony took it against her chest.

“The books under the stairs,” I said. “You can take any of those too.”

She looked down at the pillow. “Not tonight.”

“All right.”

She stepped back. I moved my fingers clear of the door, and she closed it gently.

stories.title: Until I'm Big
stories.prompt: You just found out, you are able to cast spells and somehow your whole family is weird about it, except you big sister. She always has this weird smile on her face, ever since and chuckles, to herself, from time to time.
stories.body:
# Until I'm Big

The cup stayed where it ought to have smashed, four inches above the kitchen tiles.

I had knocked it off the table with my elbow. I shut my hand and said, “Stay!” as if it had done something naughty, and there it was, hanging with its big yellow handle sticking up. A drop of tea fell out of it and landed on my foot.

“Mum,” I said. “Look.”

She was looking. So was Dad. Mum had stopped squeezing the dishcloth, and water was running down her arm.

Enna put her fingers over her mouth. She made a small noise behind them.

“I did that,” I said.

Dad came round the table very slowly. “Have you done it before?”

“No.” I opened my hand to show him. “There's nothing.”

The cup stayed where it was.

Mum spread the dishcloth underneath it. She asked if I could let it down.

I didn't know. I pointed my open hand at it and said, “All right. You can go.”

It dropped onto the cloth with a clunk. Mum picked it up and checked the handle. Dad asked me to tell him exactly what I had said, from the beginning.

Enna was still smiling.

All that Thursday evening she kept smiling, even when she thought nobody could see. Once, while Mum and Dad were talking in the kitchen with the door shut, she gave a little chuckle and shook her head.

I went to bed waiting for somebody to be pleased with me.

By breakfast, Dad was calling everything I said “interesting.” He had never found my opinions about porridge interesting before. Mum asked me not to experiment until they had talked to somebody who knew about these things. When I reached for the marmalade, Dad passed it to me so quickly that the lid fell off.

Enna chuckled into her sleeve.

“What?” I asked her.

“Nothing.”

“You keep doing that.”

Her smile tried to get bigger. She pressed her lips together.

I put the marmalade down. I was ten, and I knew when people were laughing at me.

“It was a whole cup,” I said.

“I know.”

“I could do something bigger.”

“Let's leave bigger for a bit,” Mum said, and Enna laughed again. This time Mum looked at her.

My sister was eighteen. She had been eighteen since spring, and supposed to leave since summer.

She had a place at a theatre in the city, where she was going to learn to paint forests that rolled up and castles that could be carried through doors. She'd shown me the letter until the folds went white. There would be a room above a bakery. The theatre had sent her a list of things to bring, including stout shoes and clothes that could get paint on them. Enna said she had been training for that part all her life.

On the morning she was first meant to go, she couldn't get through the garden gate.

She could open it. She could put a hand through the bars. But when she tried to walk out, her next step wouldn't happen. She stood with one foot lifted, looking cross, then frightened. Dad took her bag and told her to try again without it.

She had tried facing backwards, with her eyes shut, and over the back wall. She'd thrown her bag onto the road and gone upstairs to see if she could make herself forget it was there. She remembered within a minute and came down crying.

The woman who came to look at her said somebody had set a hold. She felt round Enna's shoulders and along the garden wall with her eyes half closed. At the gate she drew her hands back.

“I can tell you it's there,” she said. “I can't tell you who made it. Only its maker can let it go.”

After she left, Mum said that a person's first spell could happen without them knowing. Dad said it was a very big change, moving to the city. Perhaps Enna wasn't quite ready.

Enna said she was ready.

They talked about it a lot that summer. Sometimes I heard Mum say, very gently, “You can admit it, darling.”

I told my friends Enna would go when she was ready.

Meanwhile, we had the theatre in my bedroom. Enna had made it out of a grocer's box, with a curtain on a knitting needle. She painted the scenery and worked the curtain. I did the puppets and nearly all the voices, because she said mine were much worse. My knight had a foil helmet. His horse was a sock with buttons for eyes.

“Where is your noble steed?” she would ask, in a queen's voice.

“In the wash!” I would squeak.

It was not the best joke in the play, but she always laughed.

There had been plenty of plays that summer. Sometimes she said she was tired, or wanted to paint her own things, and I would hang about outside her door making the knight clear his throat.

After breakfast on Friday I carried the yellow cup upstairs. Enna's door was open. Her bag lay on the bed, packed again. It was always packed near the end of a month, when another letter came from the theatre. This time they had said they could hold her place until Saturday.

She was sorting paintbrushes. Each handle had a little rag tied round it to keep the bristles from rubbing.

“I can do it again,” I said.

She looked up at once.

“Can you?”

I put the cup on her desk. “I could try on you.”

The smile left her mouth, but stayed somewhere in her face.

“What do you mean?”

“You can't get unstuck. I made the cup get unstuck.”

Enna sat down on the edge of the bed. She looked at the cup for so long that I thought she'd say it was different, or too dangerous, or wait till Mum had spoken to somebody.

Instead she said, “Get your shoes.”

At the gate I set the cup on the flat top of the post. Then I knocked it sideways, shut my fist, and told it to stay. It hung with its yellow handle pointing at Enna.

She was looking at my hand.

“Do that again.”

“I have to let it go first.”

“No. What you said.”

“Stay.”

She caught her breath. For a moment I thought she was going to laugh again.

“You had my sleeve,” she said.

“What?”

“The morning I was leaving. You wouldn't let go of my sleeve.”

I remembered. Her bag had been beside the gate. Mum was looking for the tickets, and Enna had bent down to say goodbye. I had got a fistful of her shirt and pulled her back towards the house.

Stay home till I'm big. Then I can come too.

The cup hung between us.

“You think I did it?”

“I think you might have.”

“I only said something.”

“So did you yesterday.”

I wanted to hit the cup. I wanted to throw it all the way down the road.

“Why didn't you tell me?”

“I didn't know.” She rubbed her face. “Last night I thought, perhaps. And then I thought, don't be stupid, you'll only be disappointed again.”

“You've been laughing.”

“Yes.”

“At me.”

“No.” Her voice came out too loud. She looked past me at the house, then lowered it. “I started to think they were right. That I didn't really want to go. You don't know how many times I've stood here trying to want it properly.”

She made that small noise again. “And then you went and stopped a cup. It might not have been me at all.”

“You could have asked me last night.”

“I could have.” She swallowed. “I wanted to see you do it again.”

“Mum said you weren't ready.”

“I know what Mum said.”

Enna looked so angry that I stepped back. The cup was still hanging over the gravel. I opened my hand towards it.

“You can go.”

It fell. Enna caught it against her stomach and set it on the post.

“Could you try?” she asked.

I stared at her shoes. They were the stout ones from the list, with white paint on the toes. She had worn them all summer.

I didn't want her to go. I wanted the cup back in the kitchen, and breakfast to start again, and Enna to say something rude about my porridge.

I held my open hand towards her.

“You can leave home,” I said. “You don't have to stay.”

She put one foot through the gate.

Then the other.

She stood on the road with her arms a little way out from her sides. She looked down at herself. A cart rattled past, and she moved aside for it, two quick steps that made her look astonished.

She turned towards the corner.

“Wait!” I cried, and my hand shut.

Enna stopped with one heel off the ground.

Her arms jerked. She tried to put her foot down. I could see the muscles moving above the edge of her shoe, but the heel stayed up.

She turned her head towards me.

“Open your hand.”

I did.

“Let me go.”

“You can go.”

Her foot came down hard. She stood with her back to me for a moment, then walked to the corner. I waited beside the gate, afraid to call after her.

She came back along the road. She could do that now. She stopped just outside.

“Are you leaving?” I asked.

“Tomorrow. My train is tomorrow.”

“I thought—”

“I'm going to finish packing. And I'm sleeping in my bed.” Her voice shook. “I don't want to be scared to come home.”

I moved away from the gate.

She walked past me carrying the cup.

Dad was at the back door. He had seen her on the road. When she reached him, he put a hand out, then let it fall.

“You told us,” he said.

“Every time.”

“Yes.” He looked at the cup in her hands. “We should have listened.”

She gave it to him and went upstairs.

I stayed in the garden until Mum came out. I thought she would tell me off. She sat on the step beside me instead. There was dirt on the knee of her good trousers.

“I said she could go,” I told her. “I did.”

“I saw.”

“Then I made her stop again.”

Mum looked at my hand. “Did you mean to stop her?”

I tried to explain about the corner, and how Enna had turned without telling me how far she was going. It sounded worse when I said it. I stopped.

“We need help with this,” Mum said. “The woman who came to see Enna is coming back tomorrow afternoon. Dad and I will be with you. Until then, no trying spells on people.”

I nodded.

Mum picked some dirt off her knee. “And I was wrong to keep saying your sister wasn't ready. She wanted to go.”

Mum stayed on the step with me.

After supper Enna came into my room for the scissors. She had a parcel to tie up. I was sitting behind the little theatre with the knight on my hand.

“Could we do one?” I asked.

“Not tonight.”

I rattled the knight's helmet. “Just the short one.”

She looked at him, and then at me.

“I have things to do.”

I let the puppet fall. She took the scissors.

For a while I sat behind the curtain, which had a little hole where Enna had pushed the needle through too hard. I could see the corner of my pillow through it. I thought about going to her door with the horse, but I stayed where I was.

I tried the play by myself.

The knight asked for his horse in the queen's voice. I had to stop and change voices. Then I couldn't pull the scenery across because the horse was on one hand and the knight was on the other. I put down the horse. The knight fell backwards into a forest, and the curtain came off its needle.

From Enna's room came the sound of paper being folded. Mum asked if she wanted another blanket for the journey. Enna said yes, please.

I took the puppets off my hands.

Behind the theatre were the pieces Enna had cut out but never painted. There was a mountain with three peaks. I had asked for it in spring, for a play where the knight had to climb all three and kept finding he'd dropped something at the bottom.

I fetched my paintbox. The mountain wouldn't fit in Enna's bag, so I drew a smaller one on the back of an old cereal box and tore it out. My middle peak came out crooked. I tried to match the purple she used for distant things, but my blue was nearly gone, and it turned out very red.

I painted snow on the peaks. Some of the red came through and made the snow pink.

Enna brought the scissors back while I was making a little stand for it.

“What's that for?”

“Your room. Above the bakery.”

She knelt beside me. There was a bit of string caught in her hair.

“Those are extremely warm-looking mountains.”

“The snow went wrong.”

“I can see why it's melting.”

I pressed the glued edges together. She waited while I did it.

“I'm sorry,” I said.

She sat down properly on the floor.

“I know.”

“I didn't know I could do it in summer.”

“I know that, too.”

I looked at the mountain. I had left fingerprints in the snow.

“But this morning,” she said, and stopped.

“I know.”

We sat there a little longer. Then she stood the mountain on my desk to dry and went back to her packing.

In the morning, she wrapped it in a clean handkerchief. She put it between two books in her bag.

Mum was going with her to the station. Dad carried the parcel as far as the gate. Enna carried her bag. She stopped beside me and bent down. I put my arms round her neck, loosely, because I was thinking about the shirt sleeve.

She hugged me hard.

“You can squeeze,” she said into my hair.

So I did.

Then she straightened up and went through the gate. Mum followed. Dad handed over the parcel, and they started down the road.

I put my hand flat on the gatepost. The yellow cup wasn't there anymore. It was in the kitchen, with all the others.

Enna was almost at the corner when I took a breath to call.

“Where is your noble steed?”

She turned. There were people on the road, but she put her free hand on her hip and answered in the knight's dreadful squeak.

“In the wash!”

I laughed. So did she. Then Mum said something to her and she turned the corner, still laughing.

Dad put his hand on my shoulder. I stood there with him until the gate swung shut.

stories.title: The Woman Who Swallowed the Sea
stories.prompt: The Woman Who Swallowed the Sea
stories.body:
# The Woman Who Swallowed the Sea

At the supper before she swallowed the sea, Belise asked her husband to stay for a pear.

Jowan had one arm in his coat. Beyond the long windows, the water was black; now and then a white line appeared on it, stayed a moment, and went out. He wanted to go down and see how his boat was riding. Belise wanted him at the table. He had been away for eleven weeks, and everyone had spoken to him except her.

“One pear,” she said.

He looked at the silver dish. “Two.”

He hung his coat on the back of her chair and sat down again. There were still a dozen guests, though the candles had burned nearly to their holders. His sister Utta was telling someone about the goose that had bitten her through a sack. Belise reached for a knife, but Jowan took it first. He always peeled her fruit. He also always took too much flesh off with the skin.

“You leave nothing for me.”

“I'm doing the work.” He ate a strip of peel. “This is my half.”

She took a slice from under his knife. He let her have it, then laid the next strip across the bare skin of her wrist. She flicked it back at him. It stuck to his cheek, and he left it there until she laughed. Across the table Utta looked up, saw him, and rolled her eyes.

Belise was still chewing when the first wave struck the windows.

The candles bent inland. Glass burst through the room. The long table moved sideways, carrying the candles, the pears, and a man's hand still resting on his plate. Then the sea was between them all. Belise came up beneath a chair and heard Jowan calling her name somewhere beyond it.

People found the stair. She saw pale sleeves reaching down from the gallery; she saw Utta clutch a baluster and turn back. Belise worked her way along the wall, catching carved leaves and stone mouths in her fingers. Another wave came through the broken windows. Jowan's voice stopped.

She searched by touching. The water lifted her dress and wound it round her legs. Once she reached for a hand that was her own reflection; once she found a dead candle and held it as if it could show her anything. Utta came down the last steps and caught her by the shoulder.

“There.”

Jowan lay under the overturned table. Its heavy edge had settled across his back, holding him face down. His right arm extended into the room. Belise caught his sleeve and pulled. The sleeve tore at the shoulder. He stayed where he was.

She ducked beneath the water to reach him. When she surfaced, the sea filled her mouth. She swallowed it.

The water fell the breadth of a finger against the wall.

Belise looked at the line it had left. She could still taste pear beneath the salt. She bent her face and drank again. This swallow kept coming. It drew the water off the stair, off the carved mouths, off the gilded feet of the chairs. Her throat worked and worked, and the sea went through it.

Utta had hold of her hair. Belise shook her off. Somewhere outside, a ship's bell sounded once, much too close. A point of yellow light swept towards her across the water. Behind it, someone clung to a short mast. Both vanished beneath her chin.

There was a boat attached to that light. She had seen the person aboard it. But now Jowan's sleeve lay on the surface, and she could reach the place where it joined his shoulder. She could bring his face up and hear his voice again. She opened her mouth.

The sea came in through every window. It crossed the hall in a low, dark wall and narrowed as it reached her. A chair turned, struck the table, and stayed. Little silver fish slid over the marble. The water took them up and brought them to her. Beneath the windows the shore appeared: first the house steps, then the rocks, then a great plain of ridged mud stretching towards the far mountains.

She drank until the sound of it stopped.

The hall was ankle-deep. From the broken windows came rain and the smell of the exposed sea floor. Utta crouched beside the table, bracing both hands under its edge.

“Help me.”

Belise put her shoulder beside hers. Together they rolled the table away from him. As she strained, a wave struck the inside of her breastbone.

She let the table fall on its other side. Utta swore. Together they took Jowan by the arms and drew him out across the marble. Belise's gold seams split at the waist. She felt the cloth give and paid no attention.

Utta tried to make him breathe. Belise held his face between her hands. His eyelids had always been a little darker than the rest of him, even in sleep; she rubbed one with her thumb, as though the color were something she could remove. Water ran out of his hair, down her wrists. Utta worked until her own breathing grew ragged. Then she sat back on her heels.

“Again,” Belise said.

Thunder sounded under her ribs.

Utta looked at her. Belise took a breath to say it again, and the loose black cloth lifted from her chest. Beneath the wet skin, between the torn gold seams, a sea broke white against the curve of a wave. Farther in, another wave rose. A three-masted ship leaned under stripped rigging, miles away inside her. Nearer, a small boat showed a yellow light.

Belise put a palm over it. She met her own skin. The light shone through the spaces between her fingers.

Four people were aboard the little boat. A woman sat at the tiller in a broad pale hat. Two were pulling oars; the fourth clung to the short mast. The sail hung loose, streaming water. As Belise breathed out, it filled so suddenly that the person at the mast fell to his knees.

She held her breath. The sail sagged. Both oars kept moving.

Utta reached for Jowan's hand.

Belise had it already. She pulled it into her lap and shook her head. She wanted to turn him towards her, wanted to lay his cheek against the place where his cheek had gone every night he was home. But when she bent, the little sea sloped. The boat's light dipped out of sight.

She sat upright. It reappeared.

Utta remained crouched on the other side of him, one empty hand on her knee.

“You could give me room,” she said.

Belise looked down at Jowan instead. His thumb had a white ridge across the nail. A lid had fallen on it in the summer, and he had complained for three days whenever she asked him to open anything. She rubbed the ridge. It was almost grown out.

Something knocked against the back of her teeth. She gagged and spat. An oyster shell, small as a seed on her tongue, opened to its ordinary size as it passed her lips. It struck the marble and spun. Brine ran down her chin.

The boat's light was coming higher. The woman at the tiller had turned towards the pale reach of her throat. Belise opened her mouth. A little water spilled over her lower lip and became a great splash on the floor. Utta scrambled back, dragging Jowan's other arm with her.

Belise shut her mouth. The water stopped.

Beyond the windows, the old sea lay empty under the rain. She could return it there. The terrace projected over the shore; she had stood at its rail a thousand times and watched for Jowan's sail. She set her free palm on the floor and began to rise. Jowan's arm lifted with her. She settled back down and drew his hand into her lap.

The boat had reached the upper curve of her breast. If she could get it out first, if she could open her mouth just enough, perhaps Utta could catch its people. Then she could stay beside him.

Belise leaned backwards to bring the water up.

It rose inside her like a floor tipping. The boat ran sideways. One oar thrashed in its rowlock; the person at the mast lost his hold and went over the bow. She saw him hit the water, saw the space where he had been.

She jerked upright. The wave fell away. The boat's bow turned down and inward, against the current she had made.

No, she wanted to say. Up here. This way.

She pressed her lips together. The two rowers bent their backs, pulling away from her throat. The lamp swung at the stern. Below them, a head appeared between two waves and disappeared again.

Belise kept one hand round Jowan's fingers. With the other she gripped the edge of her torn dress. She could feel a sound gathering behind her closed mouth. She tried to breathe a little at a time. The boat rolled; its sail hung uselessly. The woman in the pale hat took the lamp off its hook and held it out over the side.

Utta leaned close enough that Belise could feel her breath.

“I see him.”

The head was farther off than Belise had thought. The boat turned again. It was going away from her, into the dark water under her heart.

She looked at Jowan. He was beside her, and for the first time she could not bend down to him. She could not make the little boat come back. Its people had their backs to the way out.

The sound escaped her.

It was small in the ruined hall, scarcely louder than a hiccup. Inside her it raised a black swell that hid the lamp, the boat, the swimmer. Belise covered her mouth with both hands. Jowan's hand slid from her lap and struck the floor.

Utta caught it before the next wash of water reached it. She pulled it against her own chest.

The lamp came up on the far side of the swell. The boat rose beneath it, bow high, then dropped. A rower had an arm in the water. Someone hauled at the back of his coat. When the boat turned broadside, Belise saw the fourth person draped over its edge, his legs still trailing. The others dragged him in. For a while all four lay or crouched low in the boat. The lamp rested on the stern bench, shining on their wet knees.

Belise's breath came badly. Their sail stirred. One of them reached up and pulled it down.

She waited.

At last the woman in the pale hat stood and took up the light. The rowers set their oars in the water. This time they turned towards her throat.

Belise put out a hand for Jowan. Utta held his hand closer.

“You had him at home before he went,” she said. “I had this afternoon.”

Belise almost spoke. Utta's face was wet, and there was no way to tell which water was which. She had the same wide mouth as her brother. Belise had never liked the resemblance; at every family dinner there had seemed to be a part of him looking back from the wrong end of the table.

She turned her open hand upwards. After a moment, she lowered it beside Jowan's shoulder instead of reaching for the hand Utta held. She lifted his head a little, offering its weight.

Utta looked at her, then slid her free arm beneath him. She settled him against her knees. Belise took her hand away.

Above them, a man called from the gallery. Utta looked up.

“Come down,” she said. “We need to carry him.”

Two guests came as far as the last dry step. The first stopped at the moving light beneath Belise's skin. The other touched his shoulder, and they came on. Utta dragged the tablecloth off the wreckage and spread it alongside Jowan. She told Belise where to put her hands. They rolled him onto it together. When Belise bent, the boat slid towards her shoulder; she stopped, waited, and bent more slowly. Utta watched her with her jaw set. They worked without speaking until he lay on the cloth.

The guests lifted its far corners. Utta took the others. Belise rose beside them and caught Jowan's foot where it had slipped out. For three steps she went with him. At the stair, a woman from above came down to take the corner nearest Utta.

Belise let go of his foot. They carried him up to the gallery. She followed him with her eyes until the curve of the stair hid his face.

Then she turned towards the windows.

The boat kept moving. She could see the other ship behind it, sails being gathered by people too far away to distinguish. Farther still, more lights marked the swallowed sea. Every step sent a long disturbance through them. She learned to set her feet down softly. A fish brushed the inside of her throat and went down again.

On the terrace the rain was cold enough to hurt. Wind struck her torn dress and drove it against the stone rail. It was the same wind that had broken the windows. Out on the bare sea floor, scattered fish gleamed among the rocks. Something large moved in a hollow, beating its tail.

She knelt at the edge. Through the gap beneath the rail she could put her face above open air, above the steps and the shore and the place where there ought to have been water. In the hall behind her, Utta shouted to someone to get farther up the stair.

Belise opened her mouth. The first rush knocked her chin against the stone. She choked and shut her mouth, driving a wave back inside. The boat reared; a rower let go of a caught oar.

She clung to the rail. Her jaw ached; salt burned the corners of her mouth. Every breath scraped.

The lamp was still burning. The woman kept the light clear of the water while a rower brought the bow round with the remaining oar.

Belise moved her chin beyond the stone and opened her mouth. This time she kept it open.

Water poured out. She could not draw breath through it. Her shoulders heaved. The stream broadened beyond her lips, fell past the terrace, and spread white across the shore. It lifted the fish and ran into the hollows. The sound filled the empty basin, striking the far cliffs and returning.

She gagged. More came. She had to let her body shake.

The boat rose towards her tongue, its lamp bright enough now to show the pale hat's frayed brim. Belise could see the recovered sailor huddled beneath a coat. The woman at the tiller looked towards the opening. She lifted the lamp.

Belise felt the keel cross her lower lip.

Beyond her mouth, the boat lengthened away from her. Its bow plunged down into the returning sea; its mast rose taller than the terrace. The stern swept past, the lamp suddenly a full-sized lantern close enough to touch. The woman leaned over the tiller, her straw hat soaked. She was looking ahead, shouting to the man with the oar.

The boat fell clear. It struck the water hard, took a wave over its bow, and came up. The woman hauled the tiller towards her. Belise saw her open mouth, heard one word lost in the roar. The recovered sailor raised his head from the coat. Belise kept him in sight as the boat turned out across the sea, until his face was too small to distinguish.

Water kept coming. Shoals broke silver through it. The great ship's bowsprit grew out over the dark, followed by its black hull and the bundled weight of its sails. More distant lights scattered into their proper distances. Belise knelt with her hands locked round the rail while the sea returned through her, wave after wave. It filled the space between the mountains. It struck the house steps and came up them. Behind her, chairs knocked together in the hall.

When she could breathe, she breathed. When the water came again, she let it.

At last her empty stomach clenched. Nothing came out but a thread of salt water. She stayed where she was until her arms would hold her weight, then crawled back through the window.

The hall was flooded again. The table lay on its side beneath a shattered chandelier. A pear bumped softly against one of its legs. Belise caught the banister and climbed.

Utta sat on the gallery with Jowan's head in her lap. Someone had brought a blanket, but his feet extended beyond it. One was bare. They had lost a shoe in carrying him.

Belise knelt beside that foot and covered it. Her throat closed when she tried to swallow. She waited for it to open, but it would not.

“There's water,” Utta said, pointing to a glass beside her. Then she looked at Belise and pushed it away.

Belise moved closer. She put her hand beneath Jowan's shoulder, where the cloth was bunched and pulling his head sideways. Utta let her lift him. Together they settled him more comfortably, Utta still holding his hand, Belise supporting the back of his neck.

From beyond the broken windows came the ship's bell. This time it was far away.

stories.title: The Tune She Kept
stories.prompt: You step into the Fae Realm for what feels like a single night. When you return to the mortal world, 200 years have passed.
stories.body:
# The Tune She Kept

The bride at the first wedding had split her skirt. I played while her sister sewed it, and the guests stamped so hard that the pewter cups moved towards the edge of the table. By eleven my shoulder ached. Someone gave me a parcel of cake for Agnes, and someone else asked whether I couldn't play something they knew.

I played it. There are worse ways to earn a shilling.

Agnes was sleeping at my sister's, across the lane from our house. Before I left she had asked me to wake her when I came back.

“Even if it's dark?”

“I'll know more about the wedding if it's dark.”

She was seven. She believed late hours improved a story. I had promised her the full account: the bride's dress, what they ate, whether the groom cried. He had. I was looking forward to telling her that.

In the copse behind the church I heard a fiddle.

It was playing a tune I knew, although I had never heard it before. I stood on the path with my own instrument under my arm and listened to the phrase come round. The player left a little gap each time, where I expected a turn. I supplied it under my breath.

On the third repetition, someone supplied it back.

Between two trunks stood a man in a yellow coat. His hair was braided with small white moths that opened and shut their wings. Behind him I could see a long room where there should have been more trees.

“You've come with your fiddle,” he said.

“I've come past with it.”

“That would explain why you're standing outside.”

He moved aside. The smell of pears reached me, warm pears in butter, and underneath it something like the rain on our lane after a hot day. I could see the other fiddler now. She had six fingers on her bow hand. When she turned her head, her earrings went on turning.

“What wedding is this?” I asked.

“Ours.”

“You and the fiddler?”

The man looked delighted. “Yes.”

I knew what the opening was. My mother had told me enough stories. They disagreed about almost everything except the wisdom of keeping to the path.

“I can't stay,” I said.

“Then you mustn't.”

The fiddler left the gap again. This time I lifted my bow.

I meant to play the turn from where I stood. But a dancer passed through the doorway, offered me a hand, and I took it to steady myself over the root.

Inside, the floor gave a little under my shoe. It was covered with living moss, trimmed so close that the dancers' heels made no mark. The ceiling was the underside of a lake. Fish moved above the candles. Once, a large pale belly blotted out half the room, and the wedding guests looked up as casually as I would look at a cart passing the window.
