The six-fingered woman drew me beside her. Her shoulder was warm through her sleeve. We played the strange tune together, and when we came to the place I had filled in, she gave me the whole phrase to myself.

Nobody asked for something else.

I played the tune twice, then a reel, then the little air I had made for Agnes when she was a baby. It had become the song we sang over her stockings, to persuade the heel to turn the right way.

*Three white pears on the parson's tree,*

*One for the rook and one for me—*

“Who gets the third?” the bride asked.

“It changes.”

“Good,” she said, and put a finger to her own highest string.

The tune opened. There were ways through it I had never found, little doors in the space between one note and another. I followed her into them. She followed me into a low phrase that had always sounded foolish on my own. The man in yellow danced with a woman whose skirt was made of overlapping leaves, and the leaves turned red as they whirled.

Later I ate the pears. Later still I danced. A small gentleman with a beard down to his knees tucked it into his belt before taking my hand. I laughed so much that he asked whether he was doing it incorrectly.

“No,” I said. “No, please do it again.”

I had been a widow for three years. I loved my sister; I loved the warm place Agnes made in my bed. I had not known how much I wanted a hand at my waist that asked nothing further of me.

When the beard came untucked, we had to stop.

There was more music. I remember a woman catching a falling candle between her bare palms, the flame looking out through her fingers. I remember the bride leaning against her husband's shoulder while I played. There were little bones of some delicious creature beside my plate. I do not remember getting tired.

The man in yellow offered me another pear, and I thought of the cake in my pocket.

“I must go,” I said.

“Already?”

“I've promised my daughter a story.”

The bride lowered her bow. “Then tell her a good one.”

One of my strings had begun to fray. She took it off and replaced it with a bright strand pulled from her sleeve. It hummed before I touched it.

“Play this under those trees when you want us,” she said. “We shall hear.”

I thanked her. I thanked them all. On my way out the little gentleman tried to kiss my hand, but his beard caught on a chair and he had to bow from some distance.

I was still smiling when I stepped over the root.

The path had gone.

There was a hard black surface under my feet, with white marks painted on it. Something blue, taller than I was, came towards me. Behind its windows a seated woman was eating an apple. A horn sounded. I jumped backwards, fell against the tree, and watched the woman slide past, still chewing.

For a while I did not move. The copse had shrunk to six trees behind a low fence. Beyond it stood houses, three storeys high, all down what had been the meadow. A woman walked past. When I asked where the lane was, she pointed, then looked at me again.

“Are you with the festival?”

I asked for my sister's house. She did not know my sister. I asked for the Bell house, beside the wheelwright's. She did not know a wheelwright.

The church was there. Its tower had a pale patch where the ivy ought to have been. On a board outside were the words **SUNDAY 17 MAY 2026**.

I read them, then read them again. Below was an invitation to a sale of plants.

I stopped a man carrying a bag of bread.

“That year is wrong.”

He looked at the board. “No, that's today.”

I told him the year was eighteen hundred and twenty-six. He held his bag against his chest and asked whether I had somebody he could call.

“My sister.”

“Have you got her number?”

I could give him her name. I could give him her husband's name and the names of their children. When I had finished, he was looking past me for help.

I left before he found it.

Our house had been white, with a brown door that needed lifting to shut. The lane where it stood was lined with shops. I went into a passage between two of them, where I thought our garden might have been, and found a locked gate. I rattled it until a man opened a window above me and told me to stop.

I nearly asked him whether he had seen my little girl.

Instead I went back to the street.

There were fiddles in a window. Three of them hung by their necks against dark cloth. I stood looking until the woman inside came and opened the door.

“We don't open till ten,” she said. “Can I help?”

She was about my sister's age, in blue trousers and a green shirt. A pair of spectacles hung from a cord against her chest. When she saw what I was carrying, she looked at it rather than at my clothes.

“Is that what you've brought in?”

I nodded because I could not think of a better answer.

Her name was Penny. She put my fiddle on a cloth and peered into it with a light. I watched her hands. They were capable hands, with a split beside one thumbnail. I found I could bear to look at them.

“Where did you get it?”

“My father.”

“And before that?”

“I don't know.”

She looked up. “Are you thinking of selling?”

I took it off the cloth.

“All right,” she said. “You don't have to. Would you like some water?”

I drank it in little sips, though my mouth was dry. Penny sat on a stool. She asked where I had come from, and I told her. Not all of it, at first. The wedding, the copse, the year on the church board. I could hear the rest waiting behind what I said.

“You mean you thought it was eighteen twenty-six.”

“It was.”

“Yesterday?”

“Last night.”

She rubbed the split beside her nail with her thumb.

“I can't make that make sense,” she said.

“Neither can I.”

She offered to fetch someone. I said no too quickly. She stayed on the stool.

“I'm looking for Agnes Bell. She was seven. I know she won't be seven now.”

That was as far as I could say it.

Penny picked up the little bright object beside the till. Her fingers moved across it. She asked how I spelt Bell, and when I gave Agnes's birthday, she asked me to repeat the year.

“February the fourth. Eighteen nineteen.”

She wrote it down. I was grateful for that. It was something a person might do with a birthday.

“I've got a friend who does local history. Let me ask her.”

She moved away to speak to the object. While she did, I went to the door and looked towards the passage. People were buying things. A boy licked something pink from a stick. I remembered that I still had Agnes's cake, and put a hand over the pocket to keep from touching it.

Penny's friend found several Agnes Bells. One had been born in the right year, but in November. Another had the right birthday, thirty years too late. Penny read out parents' names. None of them was mine.

While she searched I took out my bow. There was enough room between the stool and the counter. I played the opening of the stocking tune, quietly, watching my hand go to the places it knew.

Penny turned towards me.

“Three White Pears?”

“Yes.”

“I play that at the Sunday sessions. Where did you learn it?”

“I made it. For Agnes.”

She looked down at the names again. Then she called her friend back.

“Try the singing collection. There was a woman from here who sang that.”

We waited. Penny stood beside me, then went to put the kettle on. I kept returning to the first line. When the answer came, I was at the place where Agnes used to stick her foot out for the second stocking.

There was a page with my daughter's name on it.

Agnes Rusk, born Bell. 1819–1907.

There were other words. Penny had enlarged them so I could see. I would not read any further.

“Is there a likeness?” I asked.

“I'll ask.”

“Was Rusk her husband?”

“I think so.”

“There weren't any Rusks here.”

“People move.”

I looked at her. She pressed her lips together.

“I'm sorry. I don't mean—”

“No. They do.”

There was no likeness that her friend knew of. But there was a recording, made in 1904, of an Agnes Rusk in this parish. Penny turned the page towards me.

“This is the woman I heard. I didn't know her maiden name.”

I gripped the edge of the counter. Penny reached towards me, then took her hand back.

“Play it,” I said.

She did something with her finger. There was a scraping, a rushing sound, and then a man's voice, very small.

“Mrs Rusk. Eighty-five years of age. The seventeenth of June.”

An old woman coughed.

“Don't put that in.”

“I'm afraid it's already—”

“Oh, get on.”

Penny gave a little surprised smile. She had been watching me and missed the first notes.

I had not.

The woman sang through her nose. She had a low voice, rough at the edges, and she took a breath in the middle of the first line. I waited for the voice I knew to come through it.

It did not.

She sang the pear song. But the second line fell where mine had risen, and there was a length of tune after the fourth line that I had never heard. She went into it without taking breath, climbing three little steps, then slipping down between them. A wheel turned behind the rushing sound. I could hear it catch at each revolution.

“No,” I said. “That's not—”

Penny stopped it.

“Do you want to stop?”

“I want to hear the beginning.”

We listened again. The old woman coughed and objected to the cough being kept. She sang. I tried to hold Agnes's seven-year-old face before me, the gap where a tooth had been. It would not attach to the sound.

“Is there another Agnes Rusk?” I asked.

“I can ask.”

“Perhaps the name was put on the wrong one.”

Penny looked at the page. “There's a note. Can I read it to you?”

I nodded.

“She said she'd learned it from her mother, a fiddler. Dinah Bell. Her mother disappeared when Mrs Rusk was a child.”

She stopped there. I knew from her eyes that there was more.

“What else?”

“The collector calls it a fairy legend.”

I put my fingers over my mouth.

Penny waited. A woman came to the locked door with a black case. Penny went to let her in, spoke to her quietly, and took the case. The woman looked at me, then away. Penny put the case behind the counter and returned to the stool.

“The rest,” I said.

“Of the note?”

“Of her.”

The voice began again. In the next verse the parson was caught stealing his own pears. I had never sung that. Agnes had thought a parson ought to be able to reach the top branch without a ladder, because of his hat.

The old woman laughed halfway through a line and started it again. Her laugh was thick and almost breathless. I remembered that my daughter laughed with her mouth so wide you could see the bread she was eating.

At the end the collector asked whether she knew the song of the woman taken under the hill.

“I know it,” she said.

There was a pause. He asked whether she would give it to him.

“No.”

“Perhaps another time.”

“You'll not get round me by coming again.”

“Very well. What about the harvest song?”

“I used to sing that with my eldest. She could hold the long note. I never could.”

The wheel caught. Agnes drew breath.

Then there was only the little shop.

“Where's the rest?”

“That's the end.”

“She was going to sing.”

“They ran out. I suppose they had to change the cylinder.”

“Then play the other one.”

Penny searched. I watched her finger move. She went to a larger machine on the desk and searched there. Once she typed my name. I saw it and felt a foolish surge of hope, as though I might be found too.

There was no other recording of Agnes Rusk in the collection. We tried the other collections Penny could find. Her friend sent a short account of a life: three children, a husband who made boots, a move to another village, a return. There was a granddaughter's name. It did not tell me whether Agnes had sung the harvest song that day.

I asked to hear her once more.

By then the shop was open. Penny had to answer questions, fetch strings, listen to a boy play a few unhappy bars on a violin too large for him. She left the recording where I could start it with my finger. I listened with the cough. I listened without it. I played the beginning over the ending, trying to hear the old woman's breathing continue.

At some point Penny put a sandwich beside me. I ate half of it. The other half dried on its little plate.

“She didn't sing the right tune,” I said when Penny came back.

“The pear tune?”

“Here.” I lifted the fiddle. I played the four lines as I had played them over the stockings. “Like that.”

Penny listened. “That's lovely.”

“That's how it goes.”

She did not answer. I played it again, slower, to make it clear.

“I heard,” she said.

I lowered the bow. I had been trying to make a mistake large enough to put the old woman back in her place: somebody else's mother, somebody who had sung the song badly and been given my child's name.

Penny looked at the time.

“I need to shut up at five. I'm playing at six, and I've still got a repair to finish.”

“Where?”

“The Crown. Round the corner.”

“Will you play it?”

“Three White Pears? Probably. The dancers like it.”

“It's a song.”

“We put it with another tune. It works.”

She began collecting things from the counter. I wanted to ask her not to. I wanted her to sit down and find someone else who had known Agnes, someone who would know whether she had cried for me on the second night, and who had told her to stop waiting.

Instead I asked, “Where can I sleep?”

Penny set down a packet of strings.

“I don't know yet,” she said. “Can you give me a minute?”

She made another call. This time I heard her say, “I know, but she's here.”

She came back and gave me a piece of paper with a name and an address on it. Her sister kept rooms over a café. She could give me one for three nights.

“I've told her I'll pay. We can work out the rest tomorrow.”

“I can pay you back.”

“All right.”

She did not say it as though she believed me or disbelieved me. She was pulling on a different coat, one with buttons missing from the cuffs.

“I'll be in here at ten tomorrow. If I'm a bit late, wait.”

I nodded. She gave me the address of the Crown as well.

I went back to the trees.

There were people sitting near them, eating from paper. I waited until they left. Then I put my fiddle under my chin and touched the bright string.

The other fiddler answered.

The room opened between the trunks. The fish were overhead. The small gentleman had freed his beard from the chair and was combing it with his fingers. I could smell the pears.

The man in yellow came to the doorway.

“You've forgotten something?”

I stayed on the black path.

“Two hundred years,” I said.

He looked at me without smiling.

“Here,” I said. “Two hundred years have gone.”

Behind him, his wife began the tune we had made together. I knew exactly where my hand should go. My fingers moved on the neck of the fiddle, without the bow.

“Can you send me to the morning I meant?”

“No,” he said.

“Did you know?”

He looked past me at the buildings.

“I knew your trees would be older.”

I wanted to strike him with the fiddle. I wanted to step past him and put my shoulder beside the bride's and play until I did not know what a year was. She had left my part open. I could hear it, waiting inside the notes she played.

“Your daughter,” he said. “Did you tell her?”

I could not answer.

He put out a hand. The sleeve of his coat was yellow silk, so fine that I could see the movement of his wrist through it. I had touched that wrist while dancing. It had been warm.

I drew my bow across the ordinary strings. The bright strand sounded with them, and for a moment the bride and I played together through the doorway.

I finished the phrase. She let it end.

Agnes's breath was still in my ears. The song had been about to start.

“Not now,” I said.

The man lowered his hand. I took the fiddle from my shoulder, and the room closed.

I stood for a while among the six trees. I did not cut the string.

At the Crown I could hear music from the street. People moved aside to let me into a room that smelt of beer and hot food. Penny was sitting at the end of a table with two other players. There were dancers at the far end, some very young, one white-haired man who took tiny steps and grinned at his partner whenever they met.

Penny saw the fiddle and shifted her chair to make room.

“Are you eating?” she asked.

“Not yet.”

She pointed to a counter. “Tell him you're with us.”

I did that. He gave me a bowl of stew and a spoon. I sat near Penny and ate while the dancers argued over the next figure.

“You can join in,” she said. “Or just listen.”

I took out the cake. It was crushed, but it had kept the smell of nutmeg. I put it on the table beside my bowl.

“Wedding cake,” I said.

Penny broke off a corner when I offered it. She chewed it thoughtfully.

“Quite good.”

“Her skirt tore. At the first wedding.”

“The first?”

“There were two.”

“You'll have to tell me.”

I could have begun with the torn skirt. I could have told her about the ceiling, or the candle in the woman's hands. I was afraid of how I would sound telling it. Happy, perhaps. I had been so happy.

The player beside Penny tapped his bow on the table. She put the last of the cake in her mouth and lifted her instrument.

They began the pear tune.

It was quick. Agnes's long addition had become a place for the dancers to turn, then turn again when they thought they had finished. The white-haired man laughed at being caught. Penny leant into the repeated notes. She was watching the dancers' feet, enjoying herself.

I came in where I thought the old tune should meet it and was wrong. Penny glanced at me, then kept going. I stopped. At the next repetition I tried the lower phrase instead.

That fitted, until the part Agnes had added. I listened with my bow poised. There was a leap in it I could not catch.

Penny played it again. I missed the leap again. She grinned at me across the table.

“Tomorrow?” she said.

I nodded and waited for the part I could play.

stories.title: Take Your Time
stories.prompt: A new group of teenage superheroes must decide whether or not to reveal their secret identities to each other.
stories.body:
# Take Your Time

I had written our superhero names on paper plates, which made it look as if I intended to serve us.

There were four plates and four cupcakes on the table in the roller rink's snack bar. I had considered buying a fifth cupcake in case someone brought another superhero, then spent ten minutes being jealous of a person who didn't exist.

Cricket arrived first. He jumped over the barrier, landed on both feet, and held his arms up.

"Absolutely not," I said.

I put a second me beside him, pointing sternly at the gate. He walked through her, making a face. She dissolved after seven seconds, as always.

"Save it for the criminals, Afterimage. That was a normal jump."

"You went over a wall."

"It's waist-high. Cats do it."

His green ski goggles were scratched from last Saturday. He'd drawn black lines down his tracksuit with a permanent marker that had run out halfway through one leg. I wanted to ask whether he'd been back to the hospital. Instead I straightened his plate.

"Where's the owner?" he asked.

"Out. He said we could use the snack bar till eight. And no powers near the slush machine."

Three weeks ago we'd caught his falling sign. He had offered us unlimited rink access before learning that none of us could skate.

Cricket leaned over the cupcakes. "You got the terrible icing."

"You said you liked it."

"I do. It tastes like the colour blue."

He put the one with the most icing by my plate. He'd done that at the fair, too, with the last corner of a funnel cake: pretended he didn't want it so I could have it.

On Monday I had spent lunch in the library, pretending to look for a book that was in my bag. Here a boy had remembered which bit of cake I liked. I kept my hands busy with the napkins.

Sunspot came in arguing with Anchor about whether a hot dog counted as a sandwich. Anchor wore their usual white motorcycle helmet, mirrored visor down, and a denim coat with enough padding underneath to make them look like a small wardrobe. Sunspot's orange balaclava had bobbles on the forehead.

"If the bread closes, it's a sandwich," Sunspot said.

"A wallet closes."

"Please eat a wallet. Please demonstrate your point."

The voice filters Anchor had bought us made everyone sound like the same annoyed satnav. Sunspot could still put an impressive amount of contempt into a destination.

They sat down. Anchor kept their helmet on, as always. I had imagined, very specifically, the sound of that helmet being set on the table.

"Okay," I said. "So. Real names."

Sunspot pulled her balaclava off at once. Two little twists of hair sprang sideways.

"Zuri Keene. Sixteen. Hi. My ears were cooking."

She laid the balaclava beside her cupcake and looked around expectantly.

"You're meant to wait," I said.

"For what? You said real names."

"I thought we'd discuss it first."

"We've been discussing it in the chat for four days."

She rubbed her ears, then took out her phone.

"Name, normal number, someone to call. A photo so I can show somebody who I'm talking about. Doesn't have to be a nice photo."

"I can only do nice ones," Cricket said.

Zuri pointed at his goggles. "You weren't doing nice ones when they put you in the ambulance."

He stopped fiddling with the icing wrapper.

At the fair he'd caught a little boy who'd climbed onto the roof of a stalled ride. Getting up there had been easy for Cricket. Coming down with another person had not. The boy was fine. Cricket had sat on the ground asking whether we'd caught the boy while the paramedic shone a light in his eyes.

Zuri had stayed beside him until the ambulance left. I had been helping the boy find his dad. Anchor had held a buckled railing still while people climbed past.

"I texted," Cricket said.

"On Monday."

"I was asleep a lot."

"I know that now."

Zuri's phone was still pointing at him. She lowered it.

"I asked who to call and you said Cricket. You kept saying it. I had to go home and just wait for a cartoon insect to come online."

"Sorry."

"I don't want you to be sorry. I just can't do that again."

Anchor lifted one gloved finger.

"Not a photo," they said.

Zuri blinked. "What?"

"Of me. And not my name."

I had expected a bit of reluctance. I had brought cupcakes for reluctance. This sounded like a door being locked.

"It stays with us," I said.

"Still no."

"We trusted you with our lives."

Cricket looked down at his plate. Zuri looked at me.

"I was there," Anchor said.

"I know. That's why I don't get it."

"Being there doesn't mean you get everything."

"It's your face."

Anchor touched the bottom of their visor.

I waited for them to lift it. They didn't.

On the table between us, the plate said ANCHOR in silver marker. I'd drawn a silver border round every plate. This one was thicker where I'd tried to straighten it.

"Are we only going to see each other when something's on fire?" I asked.

"Something is on fire," Cricket said.

Zuri jerked her hand away from her cupcake. A tiny curl of smoke rose from the edge of the paper case.

"I'm annoyed," she said.

"We got that."

She blew on it. Cricket pushed a spare napkin towards her, then looked at Anchor.

"I want to," he said. "Do the names. I want someone to call my aunt if I can't. And I'd like to hang out when I'm not wearing this thing."

He pinched the ski mask under his goggles.

"I get spots. You can have that information free."

He unplugged the filter at his throat. When he spoke again his voice was higher and much less indestructible.

"Len Dacre."

He lifted his goggles and peeled off the mask. Brown curls stuck to his forehead. There was a pale patch on his cheek where the plaster had been.

I knew his face from school. I knew it from a video, too: Len standing on the little stage in the music room, one hand lifted, his voice breaking on a high note. The clip ended there. It didn't include whatever he'd done next.

I'd sent it to our year chat in February. Somebody else had added a squeaking-door sound. For a week people had made that sound when he went past.

He'd messaged me: *Can you delete it please.*

I'd written: *It's already everywhere.*

Len wiped his forehead with his sleeve and smiled at me.

"Don't say it."

I couldn't have said anything.

"The hair. I know. Helmet next time."

He was still smiling. I could tell him the curls looked fine. We could finish the cupcakes. On Monday I could pass him outside the music rooms and he wouldn't know the girl behind the fencing mask was me.

Zuri was looking at her phone. Anchor sat with their hands in their lap. Nobody was pulling at my mask.

I found the filter wire under my hood. It had caught in the zip, and for a few seconds all I could manage was an ugly little tugging movement.

"Take your time," Len said. "We can eat while you're dismantling yourself."

I disconnected it. I pushed back the hood and lifted the mask.

Cool air touched the sweat around my mouth.

"Romy Calder," I said.

Len's smile went away before I finished my surname.

Zuri glanced between us.

"You two know each other?"

"School," Len said.

He picked up the green ski mask, turned it over, and put it down again. I had never seen his bare hands before. There was icing on one thumb.

"Can we go over there?" he asked me.

He meant the far end of the counter, by the dark popcorn cabinet. I nodded. Zuri turned her chair towards the rink. Anchor followed her gaze, though there was nothing to look at except the empty floor.

Len went first. I stood too far away, then too close. He moved a pace back.

"Was it funny?" he asked quietly.

I looked at the popcorn trapped in the bottom of the cabinet. It was old enough to have its own dust.

"At the time."

"Right."

"I sent it. I shouldn't have. And when you asked me to delete it, I should have done it."

He pulled a loose thread from his mask. It stretched rather than breaking.

I almost told him that the people in the chat usually ignored me. That for about half an hour, after I sent it, they hadn't. But I could hear how it would sound standing here.

"Have you still got it up?" he asked.

I hadn't thought about the post in months.

"Probably."

He looked at me then.

I got my phone out. Finding the message took long enough that the screen dimmed twice. There were hundreds of things after it: homework, trainers for sale, somebody's dog. Then Len in the thumbnail, caught with his mouth open.

I pressed and held. I deleted my forward from the chat.

He watched. Neither of us said it would do much.

"I can tell them to stop," I said.

"They have stopped. Mostly."

"Okay."

"Don't start everyone talking about it again."

I put my phone away.

Behind us Zuri laughed once, too loudly. Anchor had apparently said something about the rink. I was grateful they were leaving us alone. Then I caught myself listening for Len to laugh.

"I didn't know you were Cricket," I said.

"Obviously."

"No. I mean."

I didn't know what I meant that wasn't worse.

Len finally broke the thread. He rolled it into a tiny ball.

"You could've just left the mask on," he said.

"I nearly did."

He nodded, once. He didn't say thank you.

"I'm not telling them," he said. "I don't want to do the whole thing."

"Okay."

He stayed by the cabinet. I went back to the table because I couldn't think how to ask if I was allowed to stay beside him.

Zuri turned around. She didn't ask what had happened. She pulled her phone close to her chest, out of its ready-to-take-a-picture position.

I sat with my mask in my lap. There was a red mark across the bridge of Zuri's nose. I hadn't noticed it before.

Anchor said, "I can give you a number. Someone who knows what I do."

Zuri looked at them.

"Will they know who I mean if I say Anchor?"

"They call me that too. They've seen my face."

"I was telling him everything was fine. At the fair. I kept saying it, and I didn't know."

Her voice had gone small at the end. She cleared her throat.

"I need somebody who'll actually come."

Anchor nodded.

Zuri looked down at her phone.

"Maybe we don't need the photos," she said.

Anchor took off a glove, revealing a hand with chipped purple nail polish, and held it out for Zuri's phone. She gave it to them. I watched them enter a number under ANCHOR CONTACT. We were going to have to trust a name we hadn't been given, and a person we hadn't met.

"I need to talk to them before Sunday," Zuri said. "If I can't, I'm not going out with you."

"Tomorrow. I'll tell them you're calling."

"Tomorrow," Zuri said.

She entered her mum's number on my phone. I put my dad's on hers. It felt strange to type DAD into a superhero's contacts, as though at any moment he might call and ask whether she'd done her geography.

Len came back for his cupcake.

"My aunt," he told Zuri. "She knows. She'll probably want yours as well."

He gave her his number, then his aunt's. He did the same for Anchor. When he reached me, he held out his hand for my phone.

I unlocked it. His old request was still in our messages. I closed that screen before passing it over.

He typed for a while and handed it back.

Cricket had been a green circle in my phone for three weeks. Now underneath was a name I already knew, and a number for someone who would come for him. I set the phone down carefully.

Len sat beside Zuri. My plate was opposite his. I tried not to look across every time he moved.

"I'm still coming Sunday," he said.

"Good," Zuri said, immediately.

"But no roofs. Aunt's orders."

Anchor raised a thumb. I nodded. Len picked the icing off his cupcake in little pieces.

At five to eight we cleared the table. I wanted to ask him about Monday, about school, whether I could say hi. Every version of the question ended with him having to make me feel better.

He took his goggles to the counter and began threading the strap back through the buckle.

I gathered the plates. There was icing stuck to the silver border of Anchor's. I left it until last.

"Sorry I pushed," I said to them.

"Yeah."

They stood to put on their glove.

My hood zip had trapped my hair. I tugged it once and stopped.

"Wait," Anchor said.

They held out a bare hand. I bent my head. The helmet knocked softly against my forehead, and they backed up, tried again, and worked the caught strands loose one at a time.

Across the room Len was laughing at something Zuri said. I kept my head still.

stories.title: The Wolves Kept Watch
stories.prompt: Everyone knows the story of Little Red Riding Hood: an innocent girl, a hungry wolf, and a grandmother waiting in the woods. But the wolves have never hunted Red. They've been desperately trying to keep her away from the cottage, her parents dead. For years, they've guarded the what was imprisoned inside, and Red has spent years charming hunters into killing them one by one. Today, with the last wolf dead, she approaches Grandmother's door wearing her sweetest smile. After all, a girl cannot inherit a kingdom until its queen is dead.
stories.body:
# The Wolves Kept Watch

The last wolf had Red by the hem when Hollis brought the axe down.

Only the hem. Never her ankle, though it was bare above her shoe, and close enough for his teeth. The old oath allowed him a mouthful of wool. He held on to it while the blade went into his head.

Red fell when he fell. That was necessary. She let her basket roll, scattering little cakes among the roots, and put her hands over her face. Through her fingers she watched Hollis wrench the axe free.

The wolf was not dead yet. One yellow eye followed her. There was white all round his muzzle now, and a bare place behind his ear where, when she was small, she had slept with her cheek against him. His jaws worked. The red wool came out in wet strands.

He tried to get up.

Hollis struck again.

Afterward the forest was so quiet that she could hear the hunter breathing through his nose. He stood over the body with both hands on the axe. Blood ran down the shaft into the place where his wedding ring had worn a groove.

Red lowered her hands.

“Is it over?”

He looked at her, then at the wolf. “Yes.”

“You're sure?”

She knew what this cost him. She had asked six other men the same question. He set his boot against the grey chest, took a handful of fur, and lifted the head. When it dropped, he wiped his mouth with his sleeve.

“Sure.”

She went to him then. Not quickly; people liked to see you overcome the last little distance. He put the axe down to receive her.

His coat smelled of woodsmoke and the sour apples he had brought for the journey. He did not hold her by the waist. One hand went between her shoulder blades and the other cupped the back of her hood.

“There now,” he said. “You did well.”

For a moment she leaned her whole weight against him. He let her.

At twenty-three, she was rather old for the helplessness that had served her so well. Soon she would have had to find another way. It was fortunate that there had been only seven wolves.

Hollis drew back and saw the blood on her cream sleeve.

“Did he get you?”

“I don't think so.”

He turned her wrist carefully. There was no wound. The blood had come from the wolf, whose body she had fallen across. Hollis used a clean corner of his neckcloth to wipe it away.

“Meg gets in a state over blood,” he said. “Doesn't matter whose. Last week a hen caught her comb on the wire and Meg wanted to bandage the whole bird.”

Red smiled at the place where his bent head had begun to go bald.

“How old is she?”

“Six.”

“Does she look like you?”

“Poor thing.” He glanced up, pleased despite himself. “No. Her mother.”

He saw that one of Red's plaits had come loose. The little red tie was caught in a twig. He rescued it, brushed the twig out of her blonde hair, and looked at the strands with a concentration he had not given the dead wolf.

“I can do that,” she said.

“So can I. These days.”

She stood still while he divided her hair. His fingers were thick and scraped, but he did not pull. Once, finding a knot, he worked it apart with a thumbnail. Nobody had touched her hair so patiently in years.

“Meg teaches you?”

“Under protest. Says I'm a very slow pupil.”

Red laughed. It came out before she had chosen it.

Behind Hollis, the wolf's open eye was drying.

When the plait was tied, she bent to gather the cakes. Most were ruined. She put them back in the wicker basket anyway, arranging the red-and-white cloth over them.

Hollis had found the narrow brass band buried in the fur at the wolf's neck. He crouched beside it.

“A collar.”

“Her animals were all tame once.”

He touched the worn engraving. Seven small points, almost rubbed away. “This one's been here a long time.”

“Yes.”

He tried the clasp, found it would not open, and left it where it was.

The first time the captain had carried her away from the cottage, the wolf had worn that band on a man's wrist. She had been eight. Her mother had pushed her out through the kitchen door, into the captain's arms, while her father held the door shut behind them. Red remembered the captain's hands better than his face: broad hands, a split nail, the brass band bright against one brown wrist.

Later there had been no hands. The guards had chosen fur and muzzles and the hard, four-legged bodies that Grandmother could not command. They still understood everything. None could speak to Red.

When Red was twelve, the captain had scratched a crown in the dirt for her, and a little figure under it. Then he had laid his foreleg across the figure.

She had understood that, too.

Hollis picked up the axe.

“Before we go on,” Red said, “there's something else.”

He looked at the basket, then along the path. The sun was dropping behind the trees.

“You said that was the last.”

“It was.”

She lifted the cloth. Under the cakes lay a small pot of beeswax and the knife she used to cut it.

“The woman in the cottage is my grandmother. She was queen before the rising. People think she died.”

Hollis waited.

“Those were her guards. She killed my parents. They tried to stop her.”

He put the butt of the axe on the ground.

“What are you asking me?”

“To see her. And then decide.”

“You ought to have told me.”

She let her eyes fill. This was harder than ordinary crying because she had liked the braiding.

“You would have sent me back.”

“I might've.”

“I've been sent back all my life.”

He rubbed the axe handle with his thumb. She could almost see the little girl in the space between them, waiting for him to choose as a good father should.

“I have to be home tonight,” he said.

“I know.”

“I mean it. My wife knows where I've gone. Meg thinks I'm bringing her a feather.”

“There are jays by the cottage.”

He did not smile.

Red took a lump of wax and worked it between her fingers.

“She can make a human body do what she says. If you hear her and understand. Even when you don't want to.”

“And you?”

“It doesn't work on her own blood.”

“So you could go alone.”

She looked at the axe. After a moment, so did he.

“I can't kill her by myself.”

“Could you leave her there?”

“I could.”

Hollis looked back at the wolf. She thought she had lost him. Then he said, “I'll see.”

She showed him two signals: a raised palm to wait, a closed fist to strike. If he chose to strike. She was careful to say that. He tested the wax in his ears before they went on; she had to tap his sleeve to make him turn.

The knife went up her sleeve. The ruined cakes went back beneath the cloth.

At Grandmother's door she put on her sweetest smile.

* * *

The cottage was much smaller than Hollis expected. She saw that in the way he ducked under the lintel and stopped, his shoulders nearly filling the doorway.

It smelled of rabbit fat and old lavender.

The bed stood against the back wall. The table and a single chair left a narrow passage to the hearth. A chain ran from a staple in the hearthstone, under the table, to an iron cuff round Grandmother's ankle. Mother had locked it there on the day of the rising. Red could still remember the snap of its fastening, and how pleased she had been to hear that small, final sound.

Grandmother sat on the bed in a white nightdress. Her white cap had been darned with brown thread. Beneath it her face was long and heavy, with a broad, patient mouth. Her knees rose higher than the tabletop. Her shoulders would not have passed through the doorway straight on.

The guards had fed her. They were sworn to preserve royal blood, and hunger had been one more harm they could not allow. They had left rabbits, deer, once a winter-starved boar. Red had watched the captain drag it through the snow until Grandmother could reach its feet.

There were rabbit bones under the table now. Some had been broken for the marrow.

“You took your time,” Grandmother said.

Red shut the door behind Hollis.

“I brought cakes.”

Grandmother looked at the basket, then at the man. “So I see.”

Hollis had one hand on the door latch. With the other he held his axe close to his leg.

“Come here, fellow.”

He did not move.

Grandmother's eyes narrowed. She could make a man kneel with two words, strip himself with three, open his mouth and swallow whatever she gave him. Red's mother had been the only person at court who could say no to her. Until Red was born.

When Grandmother died, that voice would be Red's. Until then she could ask, and wait, and ask again. In the city beyond the wood, the councillors ate every evening at Grandmother's long table. Red knew their names.

Now Grandmother said, “Someone has been clever.”

“He's only come to look.”

“Has he?”

“I told him you were my grandmother.”

“How much of your grandmother?”

Red set the basket on the table. Her hand shook a little, which annoyed her. She wanted it quite steady for the signal.

Grandmother watched the door.

“All seven?”

Red nodded.

The old woman shut her eyes. It might have been relief. When she opened them, they were wet.

“That captain of theirs,” she said. “He used to carry you everywhere. Wouldn't put you down when you cried. Spoiled you rotten.”

“He kept me in the woods.”

“Oh, darling. So did I.”

Hollis touched Red's shoulder. He pointed beneath the bed.

She had forgotten how well he hunted. He saw what belonged and what did not.

One of the skulls lay on its side, partly hidden by the counterpane. Her father's, with the broken tooth. Grandmother had stripped him first; Red's mother had lasted longer. There were still lengths of her mother's dark hair among the bones, caught in the clasp she had worn that morning.

Red knelt and drew out the clasp. She had meant to do it tenderly. Instead she pulled too hard and a piece of scalp came with it, dry and light as paper.

Hollis took her elbow. She laid the clasp in his open palm.

“Mother,” she said, though he could not hear.

He understood her mouth.

“You were a terrible little eater,” Grandmother said. “Your mother used to make a whole performance of it. Here comes the horse. Here comes the carriage. All that trouble for a spoonful.”

Red stood. The hunter let her go and closed his hand round the clasp.

“Look at you now,” Grandmother said.

Hollis stepped into the narrow passage. He kept out of reach of the old woman's hands, judging the distance, the chain, the low ceiling. Red moved to the foot of the bed where Grandmother would have to turn her head to watch her.

“What a big girl you've become,” the queen said.

Hollis looked at Red. He could still put down the axe. She saw the choice in his face, the sick effort of making it. Then he nodded once.

Red closed her fist.

The axe came down.

Grandmother caught it.

She thrust her left hand into the blade. It split the hand from the web of the thumb through the wrist; two fingers fell on the bed. Her other hand closed round the shaft. The edge went on far enough to open the side of her neck.

Red had not believed anything could bear that pain and keep hold.

Grandmother pulled.

Hollis struck the table with his hip, hard enough to break a leg. The basket slid off. Cakes and wax went under his boots. He tried to wrench the axe backward, but the queen held it in the ruin of her hand and dragged him against her knees.

With her good hand she took his ear. Her thumbnail went into it. The wax came out red.

“Kill her.”

The words were clear. The sound she made afterward was not.

Hollis turned.

Red had the knife out before he freed the axe. She saw him try to shut his eyes. They opened again, searching for her.

“Run,” he said.

His hands rose.

She could have reached the door. She was nearer to it than he was. For one breath there was nothing between her and the path, the dead captain, all the places where she could go on being a girl with a basket.

Behind Hollis, Grandmother had her torn hand clamped to her neck. Blood pushed between the fingers. She was trying to speak.

Red went the other way.

The axe cut her face as she passed him. She felt a blow, then heat. Her mouth filled with blood. She hit the end of the bed with her hip and climbed over it, scrambling into the space between Grandmother and the wall.

Grandmother turned to catch her. The chain struck the broken table, dragging it over. She opened her mouth, but Red drove the little knife into the wound the axe had made.

The queen's good hand closed round Red's wrist.

They were face to face. Grandmother's breath smelled of lavender, as it always had. Her cap had fallen back. Beneath the thin white hair, Red saw the small pink scalp of an old woman.

Hollis came round the foot of the bed.

Red pulled her wrist free, leaving the knife. Grandmother struck her against the wall with the back of her bloody hand. Red's head hit the plaster. While she was trying to make her eyes focus, the queen reached for the knife. Red caught Grandmother's good hand on the hilt and pushed the knife deeper, her whole weight behind it.

There was no cleverness left. She hung on. Grandmother's torn hand scrabbled at her hood, pulling the cloth over her eyes. She heard Hollis climbing onto the bed. His boot drove into the mattress beside her knee.

“Please,” he said.

She did not know which of them he was asking.

Red pushed against the wrist she held. The knife moved. Grandmother's body heaved under her, and Hollis lifted the axe.

The old woman's fingers opened.

Hollis stopped with the blade above Red's head. For an instant he stayed there, arms trembling. Then he let it fall behind him.

Red was on her knees in Grandmother's lap. The queen's head rested against the wall. Her mouth had fallen open, and she looked offended.

The chain still ran across the room. Nothing had changed in it.

Hollis got off the bed and was sick by the hearth.

* * *

Red had imagined bells. Not actual bells, necessarily, but something she would feel in her bones when the old queen's last breath passed into hers.

Her face hurt. Her knees hurt. There was blood in one shoe.

She touched the cut on her cheek and her fingertip went through into her mouth.

“Hollis.”

He flinched.

She had only said his name.

“Could you help me?”

He did not answer.

Hollis pulled the other lump of wax from his ear and threw it into the ashes. He looked at the queen, then at Red, as though he expected them both to move.

“It's over,” she said. “She's dead.”

“I know.”

Red got off the bed. The floor shifted under her. She caught the bedpost, and Hollis started toward her before checking himself.

“Could you find your cloth?” she asked. “Only if you want to.”

He took it from his neck and held it out. She reached for his hand with the cloth, but he let go before their fingers met.

“Thank you.”

She pressed it against her cheek. He watched to see whether the bleeding slowed. There was still that much.

The cottage was full of ordinary noises: a fly at the window, the shrinking coals, Hollis swallowing. He found Red's mother's clasp where he had dropped it. He set it on the unbroken end of the table.

“Those bones,” he said. “You said the wolves were her guards.”

“They were.”

“What did they bring her?”

Red followed his glance beneath the table.

“Animals. Deer mostly. They wouldn't bring people.”

He looked at the ankle chain.

“They kept everyone away.”

“They couldn't let her starve. They'd sworn to keep her alive.”

“And you?”

She could hardly speak round the cloth. She lowered it. “They'd sworn the same about me. Any of her blood.”

He looked down at her shoes. She knew what he was seeing: the old wolf's mouth, her bare ankle, the teeth that had closed only on wool.

“He wasn't going to bite you.”

“He would have dragged me off again.”

“You said—”

“He would never have let me come here. None of them would.”

Hollis moved the broken table aside. He did it slowly, putting the loose leg against the hearth. He picked up his axe, wiped it on the counterpane, and wrapped the head in a piece of sacking from beside the door.

Red waited for him to turn back.

“I couldn't stay in the woods forever,” she said.

He lifted the latch.

“Hollis.”

His hand stopped, but this time it was his own stopping. He looked over his shoulder.

“Will you come back?”

“No.”

The door opened. Cold air entered, bringing the smell of crushed leaves. She could see a little blue feather caught in the briars outside. It stirred in the wind.

“Your cloth,” she said.

“Keep it.”

He stepped out. The shape of his boot remained in the rabbit grease on the floor.

Red tried to straighten her hood. Grandmother had torn one tie loose and it would not sit properly. She tried again with the hand that was not holding her cheek. The cloth slipped. Pain went through her mouth, so sharp she made a small, surprised sound.

Hollis kept walking.

“Stop.”

He had time to turn his head. One hand came up toward his ear. It stopped halfway.

Red stood in the doorway. Beyond him, the path ran back to the last wolf.

“Come here.”

He came.

She gave him the cloth.

“Clean my face.”

He bent over her. His fingers were as careful as before. He folded the cloth to find a clean place and wiped the blood from her freckles, from the corner of her mouth, from the soft skin under her eye. When it hurt, she caught his sleeve.

“What will you tell Meg?” she asked.

His lips moved. No words came.

Red held her cheek together to speak.

“When you get home, tell her the wolf ate Grandmother. Tell her you cut him open and got me out. That you were just in time. Say it to me first.”

He drew a breath.

“The wolf ate your grandmother,” he said. “I cut him open. I got you out.”

“She'll want to know if I was frightened.”

He looked at her.

“Tell her I was brave.”

“You were brave.”

Red closed her eyes while he cleaned the cut. There would be people to fetch, a journey to make, her place at the head of the long table. But she could stay here a little longer. Nobody could send her away.

The cloth grew cool against her face.

“There now,” she whispered. “Say that.”

“There now.”

She waited for his hand to cup the back of her hood.

It did not.

stories.title: Room for Thirty Years
stories.prompt: Once every thousand years, the moon descends close enough for mortals to touch its magic. As the Moon Priestess, she has spent her life preparing to inherit its power. But tonight, the moon descends too early...
stories.body:
# Room for Thirty Years

The inheritance robe had thirty years in it. Odel had folded them into the side seams and caught them down with yellow basting thread.

“Breathe out.”

Nimare breathed out. Her mother put another pin between her lips.

“You can't know I'll need all that cloth.”

Odel removed the pin. “You can't know you won't.”

At thirty-four, Nimare stood barefoot on a stool, silver hair bundled over one shoulder, while her mother fitted her for the woman she would be at sixty-four. The robe was dark blue, its borders embroidered with gold flowers. Beneath the open sleeves, teal silk lay against her sun-browned wrists. There was enough spare cloth inside it to alter the fit a dozen times before the thousandth year came round.

Her mother intended to be alive for all the alterations. Nimare had stopped arguing about this.

On the windowsill, beside a bowl of salt, lay three green plums. Odel split one with her thumbnail, dipped the cut face in salt, and gave her half.

“You said we could go when the rains ended.”

“I said I would ask.”

“You've asked. They've said yes. Now you're finding another thing to wait for.”

Nimare rolled the salted fruit beneath her tongue. Beyond the jungle were mountains where white cold lay on the ground even in daylight. They had been discussing that journey for eleven years. Her mother had made wool stockings; Nimare had laid out her lessons to finish before the dry season.

“I'm not waiting for anything,” she said.

Odel looked up at her.

“The eastward turn is still wrong.”

“Then be wrong about it on a mountain.”

Beside the sewing stool stood the ceremonial spindle, bone-pale wood tapering to a gold tip. Nimare could perform the holding pattern while walking, blindfolded, or answering questions about the nine visible ridges of the moon. She could return the light or take it into herself. Her fingers knew the movements better than they knew how to unfasten the little hooks down her own back.

Every thousand years the moon descended. Mortals touched its living light, and a prepared priestess went up to keep it burning. Nimare had wanted to go before she understood that she would have to stay. For years, the charcoal moon on her bedroom wall had been covered in fingerprints: a child reaching for the places she meant to feel from within.

There was time for mountains first. Thirty years for mountains, and for becoming tired of things she loved, and for wishing to come home from somewhere.

The salt bowl cast a second shadow.

Nimare turned toward the window. The white flowers along the sill were opening so fast that their petals struck the glass.

Above the treetops, the moon was growing.

She watched a ridge emerge from what had been a patch of grey. A whole slope moved into view. It bore a fresh black wound, ragged at the edges, across country she had drawn a hundred times.

Her mother took the pins from her mouth.

“Nimare.”

“I see it.”

“It can't be.”

The stool rocked beneath her. She caught the spindle and stepped down, the unfinished robe falling across her feet.

Odel put the remaining plums and the little salt bowl into her sewing box and followed.

***

They climbed through a temple turned white. Leaves showed their veins. Between the stair towers, the jungle's waterfalls shone like hanging cloth. Night flowers burst from cracks in the stone and shed petals before they were fully open.

On the upper terrace, Nimare stopped.

The moon stood beyond the parapet, close enough that its curve cut off the sky. She could see hollows inside its pale rock. The ridge with three teeth was higher than any earthly mountain she had seen; it had been a smudge beneath her childhood thumb.

A woman stood in a narrow opening at the moon's edge.

She wore a robe whose blue had faded almost white. One sleeve was burned away. Light passed through her left hand in loose, shivering strands, and the skin beneath them was darkened. She had to lift each foot with care to make it follow her.

Nimare knew the face from a thousand paintings. The paintings had not given Veya that frightened look.

“You're early,” Nimare said.

“I know.”

“Thirty years.”

Veya lowered her eyes. “Something struck the far side. I held it together as long as I could.”

The light jerked in her hand. Nimare saw the outer strand slipping beneath her smallest finger. She stepped forward, laid her free palm against the moon's cold rock, slid the spindle under the slipping strand, and turned her wrist.

“Don't pull,” Veya said.

“I'm not.”

She made the eastward turn. It had always dragged when she practiced with silk. Now the strand rolled smoothly over the spindle's taper, caught in the notch, and opened against her palm.

The ground beneath her remained stone. Another ground lay inside her hand: a long, steep slope where small rocks were moving through dust. She checked them with the slight backward pressure she had practiced for twenty-seven years. A whole fall of stones settled. The pressure came back to her, exact and alive.

Nimare laughed once, in surprise.

Then Odel's fingers were against her ribs, pulling the basted seam away from a pin that had turned inward.

“You'll have a hole in you before you begin.”

The pin slid free. Nimare could still feel where its point had been.

She completed the holding pattern. The two loops circled the spindle, one traveling upward, one returning through her fingers. As long as she made the little correcting movements, neither would tighten. She could hold this position for hours. Eventually her hand would shake; eventually she would have to sleep. The practice hold could give her time to choose, but it could not give her thirty years.

Closing the inner loop would carry her into the moon. Opening it would let the living light go, and the outer loop would return an ordinary stone moon to its path.

She had rehearsed both endings. She had expected to be old when she used either.

“May I sit?” Veya asked.

There was a stone bench a few steps from the parapet. Veya looked at it for a long time.

“You can come down first,” Nimare said.

Veya shook her head.

“The hold is steady.”

“I can feel that.”

“Then why?”

The older woman glanced back into the opening. Beyond her lay a small chamber, a worn hollow in the rock where she had rested her body while her senses traveled the moon.

“I thought I would finish there.”

“You haven't finished.”

“No.”

Nimare waited.

“Everyone is gone,” Veya said. “I knew that would happen. I knew it when I went up. It didn't seem possible that everyone could be gone and the steps would still be here.”

Odel set her box on the bench. The little clasp snapped sharply in the moonlight.

“Are those plums?” Veya asked.

Odel stared at her. “Yes.”

“I can smell them.”

The woman swallowed. Nimare felt the spindle tilt and corrected it.

“You haven't eaten?”

“I haven't needed to.” Veya's gaze stayed on the box. “It isn't the same.”

Nimare remembered all the solemn accounts of the bearer sustained by light, free from mortal hunger.

“If you step down,” Nimare said, “I can still open the loop.”

“Yes.”

“I haven't decided.”

Veya's unburned hand closed against the pale blue of her robe.

Once she came off the moon, she could not return to the place where she had spent nearly a thousand years. Nimare knew that from the lessons too. The old binding ended at the step down; there could be no taking it up again. Veya would be on earth, and Nimare might let her living light die.

“Will the trees manage?” Nimare asked.

“The flowers that open for us will close. Some will learn the ordinary night. Some won't. The trees were here before the first bearer.”

“And people?”

“People will have a darker moon.”

Veya lifted her face.

“I would have liked to bring it back whole.”

For a moment Nimare thought she would withdraw into the chamber. Instead the woman loosened her hand. The last strands slipped from her fingers into the spindle, and she lifted one bare foot toward the parapet.

“Wait. My box is in the way,” Odel said.

She moved her sewing box, came to the wall, and offered her arm. Veya took it. Her first step struck the stone hard enough to make her gasp. Odel's other hand went under her elbow.

“Don't lean there. Here.”

Veya obeyed. She sat on the bench with her feet planted wide, looking at them. The opening in the moon closed behind her, leaving Nimare's palm laid over a rough patch of white rock.

Odel wiped the bench dust from her fingers and split a plum. She held both halves out to Veya without meeting her eyes.

“Thank you,” Veya said.

Odel did not answer.

***

For a while there were only small sounds: Veya chewing, the waterfalls beyond the stair towers, the creak of Nimare's robe as she moved her wrist. The moon's great shadow lay across the jungle.

Odel spread the sewing box open on her lap.

“I want you to put it down.”

Nimare looked at her mother's bent head.

“I know.”

“I want you to stay.”

“You always said you were proud.”

“I am proud. Come here.”

Nimare could move as far as the spindle's light would reach. She took the three steps to the bench. Odel pulled the gold border straight and began to unpick a crooked length of basting.

“Would you be ashamed if I did?” Nimare asked.

Her mother held the small scissors still.

“I don't know,” she said. “I might be. For a little while.”

Nimare pressed her lips together.

“I had been counting on being dead,” Odel said.

“You said you'd live to finish it.”

“I said a lot of things.”

Veya looked down at the plum stone in her hand.

Odel's needle went through the silk. Nimare felt the small pull, the pressure of her mother's knuckles against her side. In her other hand, sunlight was finding a ridge on the far side of the moon. That country had never faced the earth. She could feel the difference between the brittle upper crust and the deep rock under it. Halfway down, a cleft forked beneath an overhang. With a slight turn of her ring finger she followed one branch to its end, a shallow bowl of loose stones. She wanted to know where the other one went.

Her mother licked the end of a new thread. It would not pass through the needle. She tried again.

Nimare bent and held the needle for her with her free hand.

“There.”

Odel took it back.

They had been going to sleep in the same room on their journey, because neither of them had ever slept alone in a strange place. Nimare had expected her mother to complain about the beds. She had expected to complain about her mother's complaining. She wanted those nights so sharply that her throat hurt.

The spindle rolled. She made the correction.

“Do you miss them less?” she asked Veya. “After so long?”

“I forget things. That's different.”

Odel pulled the thread through.

Nimare stood while her mother sewed. She changed her grip as she had been taught, easing the strain from one finger to another. Clouds moved across the narrow sky that remained visible above the moon. Once, Veya tried to stand and Odel put a hand on her shoulder without looking up.

The seam was straight now. There was still spare cloth folded inside it, enough for changes Nimare's body would never make.

“I want to go,” Nimare said.

Her mother drew the needle through to its full length.

“I want the mountains too,” Nimare said. “I haven't stopped.”

“I heard you.”

Nimare waited. Odel tied off the thread and put the needle in its little felt square.

“Turn around. There's one at the back.”

She took out the last pin. Then she stood and put both arms around her daughter, clumsily, avoiding the spindle.

Nimare held her with one arm. She could feel the familiar shoulder blade beneath her palm. Her mother's hair smelled of the oil she used every morning, a sharp green smell Nimare had sometimes disliked.

She took another breath of it.

“You were supposed to have thirty years,” Odel said into the embroidered collar.

“Yes.”

Neither of them moved for a long time.

When Odel stepped back, she left a damp place on the silk.

Nimare went to the parapet. There was a narrow shelf where Veya's foot had been. She put her own foot on it, holding the spindle steady.

Veya held out the other half of the plum. She had saved it in her unburned hand.

Nimare took it. The flesh was warm, marked by the older woman's thumb. Odel brought the little salt bowl and set it on the parapet. Nimare dipped the plum and bit down.

Then she passed the spindle through the inner loop and drew it closed.

The light passed under her skin. Her hand ceased to carry the long slope; the slope was hers. A thousand small falls of dust settled into places she could feel. Across three ridges, the wound pulled with a dull ache. She could feel both edges of it now. Far beyond her sight, cold lay against the moon's dark side, rough and various, waiting for her attention.

The chamber opened. She stepped inside and sat in the hollow Veya had worn smooth.

Through the opening, her mother was still close enough to touch. Nimare reached. Odel took her fingers, squeezed once, and released them before the rock began to close.

The moon lifted.

She felt the jungle passing beneath her, felt the whole unfamiliar weight of herself rise. Below, Odel picked up the sewing box. Veya tried to follow Odel and had to sit again. Her mother stood with the box under one arm, looking upward. Nimare could see her face and could not tell what she would do next.

Nimare turned toward the enormous country she had wanted all her life. Somewhere in it, in a small warm hollow, her human mouth was still full of plum.

She kept the last piece under her tongue until there was nothing left to taste.

stories.title: One Good Scream
stories.prompt: A monster enjoys their Halloween night; after all, it’s the only night of the year people won’t run screaming at the sight of them.
stories.body:
# One Good Scream

By six o'clock, someone had already told Oswin to watch where he was going.

The evening was turning out splendidly.

He moved his foot off the witch's trailing skirt. She gathered the black satin around her ankles and continued down the street, still talking to the person beside her. Neither of them looked back. Oswin stood for a moment with his foot raised, then set it carefully between two paving stones.

There were people in front of him, people behind him, people close enough to brush his fur. A small knight struck his leg with a wooden sword and was told to leave the gentleman alone. Somewhere a bell rang inside a pumpkin. The wind carried frying dough, candle smoke, and the rubbery smell of new masks.

Oswin walked in the middle of the pavement.

In daylight he had to go along the edge of the wood, with his shoulders hunched and his head down. It did not help much. That spring, a man gathering fallen branches had seen him through the trees and run away screaming, leaving a very good hat behind. Oswin had put it on a stump where it would be easy to find. The man had not returned.

Tonight a woman passed with an axe apparently lodged in her head.

“Lovely work,” she said.

“Thank you,” said Oswin.

He had combed himself.

It had taken most of the afternoon. His fur grew thick and brindled over his shoulders, and there was an awkward place between his backward-curving horns that he could reach only by wedging the comb in a tree and rubbing against it. He had shaken out the leaves afterward. Most of them.

At the entrance to the fairground, a man in an apron lifted rings of dough from a pan. They rose glossy and pale, then darkened at the edges. Oswin stopped so abruptly that somebody bumped his back.

“Sorry,” said the somebody.

“Quite all right.”

He lingered over saying it. He had never before had occasion to say it to the back of a nun with a painted skull for a face.

“One?” the doughnut seller asked him.

“One first.”

The man rolled a ring in cinnamon sugar, slid it into a paper bag, and held it out. Oswin offered a coin. His claw went through the bag.

“Ah,” said the man. “Wait.”

He fetched a little wooden plate.

Oswin ate the doughnut in three bites, because that was the most bites he could manage and he wanted several. The outside crackled. The middle was soft and so hot that he breathed through his open mouth, which reached almost to his ears. A passing vampire gave him an approving nod.

Sugar settled into the fur under his chin. He brushed it with one hand and caught it in the other. Then he licked his palm.

He had eight coins left.

Four were for the House of Horrors. Four were for whatever he wanted afterward. He had worked this out many times, usually while hungry, and the afterward had acquired considerable detail.

But first there was the house.

It stood on the fairground beyond the last shops, taller at the front than it was anywhere else. A painted tower leaned over the entrance. A painted moon showed behind it, and somebody had painted a bat across the moon, then another bat where the first had dripped. A real lamp glowed behind the painted windows.

Across the top, in red letters, was an invitation.

HEAR YOURSELF SCREAM.

Oswin had heard plenty of other people do it.

On October evenings he sometimes sat among the trees beyond the fairground. From there he could hear the rattling rides, the calls of the stallholders, and the screams coming out of this house. He had learned to distinguish the ones that ended in laughter. Occasionally someone would laugh so hard that they screamed again. Those were his favourites.

He wanted to make that noise.

The queue wound between ropes. Oswin joined it behind a pirate in a long red coat and an enormous hat. Her grey braid came out over the collar. Beside her stood a scarecrow wearing gold spectacles, with loose straw sticking out of his cuffs.

“They always have something behind the door,” the pirate said.

“Then you'll be ready.”

“I am ready. I enjoy it.”

“You enjoyed pulling my sleeve nearly off last year.”

“You were walking too slowly.”

She turned to see how far the queue had grown, and looked up at Oswin.

“Oh, that's good. Can you see out?”

“Yes.”

“Both eyes?”

“Both eyes.”

“That's where he went wrong,” she said, indicating the scarecrow. “He was a turnip once. Couldn't see a thing. Fell over the dog.”

The scarecrow looked at Oswin. “It was a very low dog.”

Oswin nodded. There were circumstances in which a low dog could be difficult.

The queue moved. He moved with it. Then it stopped, and he stopped too. The pirate argued that the dog had been of an entirely usual height. The scarecrow found a strand of straw inside his spectacles. Oswin stood close enough to hear every word.

A young man with a pale face and a dark ring around each eye came down the line, counting heads.

“You're late,” he told Oswin. “Round the back. Ask for Len.”

“I'm in the queue.”

“Yes, but if you're working—”

“I want to go in.”

The young man glanced from his horns to his claws, then back to his face.

“Right. Sorry. Four at a time.”

He continued counting. Oswin stayed where he was. A faint, delicious shriek came through the wall of the house, followed by a thump and a woman's uncontrollable laugh.

At the booth Oswin laid out four coins. The woman behind the little window gave him a yellow ticket. He took it between the sides of two claws, very gently.

The pirate peered at it.

“You've got a skull. Mine's only a number.”

Oswin examined his ticket. It did have a skull. He liked his ticket even more.

At the entrance, the young man counted the pirate, the scarecrow, a woman in a moth mask, and Oswin into a group. He told them to keep moving, keep their hands to themselves, and follow the white arrows.

“Are you going to scream?” the pirate asked Oswin.

“I hope so.”

She laughed. “That's the spirit.”

The young man tore Oswin's ticket in half before he could think to ask for it back.

Inside, the air smelled of old cloth and warm lamp oil. Oswin lowered his head beneath the entrance beam. His horns passed under it with an inch to spare.

A pale hand shot through a hole in the wall.

The pirate jumped against the scarecrow. The scarecrow said, “Well, honestly,” in a high, surprised voice.

Oswin had seen the fingers waiting in the hole. Nevertheless, it was a very good hand. It had long grey nails and a ring with a red stone, and its owner shook it with admirable fury.

Oswin leaned down to inspect the ring.

“Keep moving,” said the hand.

“Sorry.”

The first room had no floor.

He could see the narrow path along the wall, and below it a black gulf full of dim, receding lights. His stomach gave a small, hopeful lift. Then the moth woman stepped onto the path and her foot appeared again deep below her. He saw what the mirrors were doing.

He went carefully along the boards, watching his enormous feet repeat themselves into the dark. At the far end he lifted one foot and waggled his claws. All the other feet waggled theirs.

“Come on,” the pirate called.

“Yes.”

He would have liked another minute with the floor.

The next passage was narrow and lined with portraits. One old gentleman moved his eyes after the moth woman passed. Oswin waited for them to move back. The eyes waited too.

He shifted to the left. They followed.

He shifted to the right.

“We haven't got all night,” the gentleman said.

Oswin hurried after his group, delighted. The moth woman had begun to laugh, a long, rumbling laugh that seemed unlikely to come out from behind such a delicate mask. He caught up with them as the scarecrow was putting his spectacles straight.

He wanted to see what came next so badly that he kept seeing it a moment too soon.

A long, low room brought his horns almost against the rafters. A coffin stood upright against the far wall, with red light glowing behind it. A white arrow pointed to a door on its right. To its left hung a heavy black curtain, trailing in folds on the floor beside the path.

Oswin bent forward to clear a beam. The others filed past him toward the coffin.

“Now,” the pirate said, softly but not very softly. “Watch this.”

She inched toward it. The scarecrow stayed close behind her, holding a pinch of her coat. The moth woman followed them.

Oswin followed too, keeping his head low. The curtain hung just to his left as he approached the coffin.

He could see the toe of a shoe below the coffin. Just a small dark toe. There was also a cord along the hinge, almost lost against the black paint.

He slowed. How did they open it? Did the person inside pull the cord, or did it work a catch? The lid was thick, with a fine crack down one side. He leaned a little nearer, happily waiting to find out.

The black folds beside his head moved.

A white face turned out of them, close to his cheek, and a wooden clacker cracked once beside it.

Oswin screamed.

It started somewhere under his ribs, rose through his chest, and came out so loudly that he felt it in his teeth. His hands flew up. His knees bent. For an instant he had no thoughts whatever.

The pirate screamed too.

The coffin lid burst open and something in a shroud sprang forward, but by then the pirate was screaming at Oswin, the scarecrow was shouting at the coffin, and the moth woman had doubled over, laughing into her hands.

Oswin found himself crouched with both claws pressed against his own cheeks.

The white face belonged to a narrow man whose long black cloak had pooled around his feet. He held two hinged pieces of wood in one hand. He looked at Oswin. Then his face, under its paint, broke into a grin.

“Oh,” he said. “That was a good one.”

Oswin tried to answer. Nothing came out but a breath.

He tried again and laughed.

The man laughed with him. The shrouded thing in the coffin said, “Move them on, Len,” and the pirate began to laugh too, still clutching the scarecrow's arm.

“I saw your shoe,” Oswin told the coffin.

“Keeps you looking this way.”

Len raised the clacker in a small salute.

Oswin began laughing again.

The pirate got hold of his elbow and tugged him toward the exit.

“Come on. They'll want the next lot.”

He followed her, still bent beneath the beams. As they passed through the last door, she looked behind her. So did he. There was only the door, but they went through it rather quickly.

Outside, the night air cooled the inside of Oswin's mouth. He could hear music from the roundabout and somebody calling the price of roasted nuts. His knees felt peculiar. He liked that very much.

“Well,” the pirate said. “Well.”

She took off her hat and fanned her face with it.

The scarecrow pulled his coat straight. There was straw on the pirate's sleeve.

“Delia,” he said, “you made a noise I've never heard before.”

“That was him.” She pointed at Oswin. “I was perfectly composed until he did that.”

“You were practically inside my waistcoat.”

“He was very loud.”

Oswin could feel a grin pulling at the corners of his mouth. He let it go as wide as it wanted.

The moth woman wiped her eyes beneath her mask. “I thought it was part of the show.”

“So did I,” said Delia. “I thought we'd brought an actor along.”

“No,” Oswin said. “That was me.”

His voice had gone a little rough. He swallowed, experimentally, and it was still rough. Even that was pleasing.

Delia settled her hat on her head. “I'm having something hot. My insides have moved.”

The scarecrow picked a piece of straw from her sleeve. “So have mine.”

They went off toward the stalls. Delia lifted her hat to Oswin as they passed, and he raised a hand in return. The moth woman was still laughing when she left them.

The next group burst out behind him, a young man in a paper crown hanging on to his friend. They saw each other's faces and began to laugh. Oswin laughed too. His knees had steadied, but he could remember exactly how they had felt.

He put a hand into his pouch. Four coins pressed against his palm.

Across the fairground, the doughnut seller tipped a fresh batch into the sugar. For a moment Oswin could almost feel the hot crust breaking between his teeth. Four coins would buy four more. He had meant to take the last one away with him, eating it very slowly along the edge of the wood.

A scream came through the wall.

It was followed at once by a second, much higher scream.

Oswin closed his hand around the coins.

At the booth, the woman slid him another ticket. This one had only a number. He took it just as carefully as the first.

The queue had shortened. A small group of ghosts stood near the front, arguing about whether they should all go in together. Oswin took his place behind them.

He knew about the shoe now. He knew about the curtain. He could hardly wait to see the floor again.

One of the ghosts turned around.

“Have you been through already?”

“Yes,” Oswin said.

“Is it good?”

Somewhere inside, Len's clacker cracked again.

“Oh, yes.”

stories.title: For My Own Use
stories.prompt: A bot has scraped the website that you hosted your magic grimoire on, and now people are vibe coding spells without understanding the magical framework behind it.
stories.body:
# For My Own Use

The scanner wanted Neri's grimoire to lie flat. Neri said no.

She had spent three evenings' wages having the spine sewn back together. She wasn't going to break it for a machine with a picture of a smiling sheet of paper on its lid. Instead she supported one side with her palm and scanned the pages in pairs. Her hand appeared in all ninety-six images, holding down a different secret.

There were workings for keeping a cup warm, for steadying a needle, for holding the corner of a sheet while she made a bed alone. There were drawings of hands with too many fingers, because she had been interested in their positions rather than their number. Shopping lists interrupted diagrams. On one page she had written I AM NEVER GOING BACK THERE and, beneath that, gone back there twice.

The website gave the album a padlock. She signed out and signed in again to admire it.

She was twenty-two, eleven days away from moving into a fourth rented room. Once, during a move, somebody had taken the cardboard box containing her winter shoes, three bowls, and every photograph she had printed of her father. She had been told there must have been a misunderstanding. She still checked unfamiliar shoes in hallways.

If the grimoire disappeared, at least she could get the pages back. That was the whole purpose of putting it online. The first page said, in her largest handwriting, FOR MY OWN USE.

Five days later a stranger sent her a picture of page forty-one.

The heavy cross through the diagram was gone. Her writing had been straightened into a circle, colored blue, and surrounded by little stars. Under it was the heading NERI'S DEEP QUIET. A sentence she had written at two in the morning ran along the bottom in a pretty typeface:

*I just want one good hour.*

The message above the picture said:

*Hi, sorry to bother you. Do you have a version of the release that doesn't need fingers?*

Neri was sitting on her bed eating bread out of the bag. She put the bag on the floor without tying it.

*Where did you get that?*

*Hearthbot. Are you the developer?*

The sender's name was Lio. His picture showed a young man holding a guitar badly enough that Neri, who knew nothing about guitars, could tell he wasn't playing it.

*Why can't you use your fingers?*

*Not me. My roommate. She did the sleep adaptation. She can blink but she can't get up. It says to turn the clasp with her other hand. That isn't working.*

*I only found her like this a minute ago. I thought she was asleep.*

Neri set her own hand flat on the quilt. She moved each finger, slowly, then hated herself for needing to check.

*Is somebody with her?*

*Me.*

*Don't give her another working. Where are you?*

He sent an address six streets away.

Before she left, she opened the website. The album still had its little padlock. Ninety-six pages, private, accessible to you.

She copied the address of one image into a signed-out window.

There was her hand. There was the cross through the diagram. There was the note she had written beneath it after her teacher finally got her jaw to move.

She deleted the album. The website warned that this action could not be undone.

Then she followed the link Lio had sent. The blue card was still there. Hearthbot's source panel listed her image addresses under WEB CRAWL. It had fetched all ninety-six.

Under it, somebody had asked Hearthbot to make the quiet last through a twelve-hour shift. Somebody else wanted a version for their wedding. A third person had uploaded a photograph of an old holding charm and asked the bot to combine them, keeping the benefits of both.

The bot's answer began, *Absolutely. We can simplify this.*

Neri reported the exposure and the copied material. A box thanked her for helping improve the experience. She put her grimoire in her bag and called the woman who had once spent most of a night getting her out of page forty-one.
