“It got copied,” she said. “People are doing it.”

Her former teacher asked where, and which version, and whether Neri was alone. She did not ask why Neri had put it on a website. That made Neri briefly, horribly close to crying.

“I'll come,” the woman said. “I'm on the other side of town. Send me the actual instructions she's used. Don't try taking the whole hold yourself.”

“I know.”

“Yes. I know you know. I'm telling you anyway.”

On the stairs, Neri opened Lio's other link. His page had a banner advertising ONE QUIET HOUR, a session at his studio and on his feed that evening. A little moving clock said eighteen minutes.

Under the clock, in his own words, he had written: *Tested it myself. Safe, free, no special training. Bring whatever you need to put down.*

She walked faster.

The studio was above a secondhand furniture shop. Lio met her on the stairs wearing socks, one of them wet. He was about her age. His guitar picture had prepared her for somebody who smiled easily, but his face had gone slack with fear.

“You came.”

“Show me.”

“I didn't know who to call. The card had your name, so I thought there was a step missing. I thought you'd just tell me—”

“Show me her.”

Osa lay on a sofa behind a hanging blanket that separated the sleeping corner from the amplifiers. She wore a fleece jacket over a work shirt. Her eyes moved to Neri when Neri crouched, then held there. A mug sat on the floor beside her. Its tea had a skin.

“I thought she was sleeping,” Lio said. “She'd been up all night. She does nights at the packing place. We rehearsed this morning, which was stupid, but she said she wanted to.” He ran a hand up his face. “Then I came back in and her eyes were open. She couldn't answer.”

Neri wanted to grab him by the wrist. Instead she put her bag down.

“Osa? My name's Neri. I'm going to touch the back of your hand. Is that all right? Once for yes, twice for no.”

One deliberate blink.

Osa's skin was cold. Under it Neri could feel the hold, a fine, continuous resistance, like the moment before a cramped muscle let go. It tightened when she pressed. The pulse beneath it kept beating, and Osa's chest rose beneath the fleece. The working had caught the movements she could choose, leaving her breath and heartbeat free.

She took her hand away.

“She's holding herself through her pulse. Her hands and jaw are inside it.”

“Can you turn it off?”

“She's the one doing it. I need to find where she closed it.”

“But it's just quiet. I tried it.” He held up his hands, as if their movement were evidence he could offer her. “I made this one stop shaking.”

“Which one?”

“My right.”

“What did you use to release it?”

He touched his right wrist with his left forefinger.

Neri looked at his left forefinger. “That one was still free.”

He looked down at his hands. She saw him understand, and was relieved of the effort of hating him quite so hard.

“I asked for deeper quiet,” he said. “For Osa. It said you could extend the same principle.”

“Let me see.”

He brought his laptop from the table, where a stack of blue cards waited to be handed out. A conversation was open beside the scheduled feed.

*Can you make this work for sleep rather than a steady hand?*

*Certainly. Your heart is a natural anchor for whole-body calm.*

The bot had joined the hand hold from page forty to the crossed-out pulse-loop on forty-one. The edge she had placed around the hand was gone. A note about leaving the release outside the edge had become *Optional: visualize a boundary if it helps you focus.*

“That isn't optional,” Neri said.

“It said visualization wasn't necessary.”

“The edge isn't a picture to make you feel better. It's what you leave out.”

At the bottom of the conversation was a fresh question, sent while she was on her way.

*She can't move to do the release. Generate an automatic undo with no hand gestures, urgently.*

The answer was arriving.

*Of course. Let's restore balance. Keep the original anchor, and include the eyes within the quiet circle. This creates a complete state from which you can release all tension at once.*

Lio reached toward Osa's face.

“Don't.” Neri caught his sleeve. “That's what she has left.”

“It says release.”

“Look at the shape.”

The bot had drawn the closed loop again. It had put an arrow beside it and labeled the arrow OPEN.

Lio stared. Then he shut the laptop with a crack that made Neri flinch.

For a moment there was only the amplifier's hum and Osa's breathing. Neri could feel her own fingers prickling. In her remembered night, the hardest part had been being unable to make anybody hear that she had changed her mind.

Lio's phone chimed. Then it chimed again.

“The session,” he said.

On the lock screen a message asked whether the group version was suitable for somebody who couldn't form the clasp with both hands.

“You made a group version?”

“They asked. I thought if we all did it together, nobody would have to be alone with it.”

He did not sound stupid. That was almost worse.

Neri opened the group card. It joined everybody's individual circles into one large circle. Inside it, beside a smiling cluster of people, the bot had written *Shared calm distributes the effort.*

There was no way out on the card. There was no account of whose pulse held what. Her name was at the top.

“Don't let them do this.”

“I'll cancel.”

He opened the feed controls, stopped, and looked at Osa. “But I should be helping her—”

“Tell them now. Before we start anything with her. I'll stay here.”

She put her palm beneath Osa's cold hand without taking up the hold.

Lio carried the laptop to the table. Neri heard his chair scrape. For several seconds he said nothing. The phone kept chiming.

“I'm cancelling the working,” he said at last, to the little camera. His voice sounded unpleasantly ordinary, stripped of the ease she had heard in his recorded welcome. “We haven't begun the shared circle. We aren't going to. Please don't start it yourselves. The body and sleep versions aren't safe.”

He swallowed audibly.

“I told you I'd tested it. I tested the hand one. I didn't test the others. I let the bot change it, and then I told you those were safe too. I shouldn't have.”

His drummer arrived at the door carrying a packet of biscuits. Lio waved her toward the table, explained in broken phrases, and asked her to keep the cancellation on screen and contact the other moderators. She put the biscuits down unopened.

Comments filled the narrow strip beside his face.

*smallhours: Haven't done mine. It has a timer. Is that cancelled too?*

*Where is Neri? Is this her withdrawing permission?*

“If you've done a whole-body version, have somebody stay with you,” Lio said. “Get a practitioner there. Give them the actual version you used. Don't get Hearthbot to make an undo.” He glanced at Neri. “It just gave us another hold.”

Neri's teacher called. Neri described what she had felt in Osa's hand and put the phone on speaker, away from the feed. The woman was still traveling. She listened, asked two questions, then said they could begin freeing Osa's jaw if they worked together. Neri would open a small section of the hold; somebody else had to receive that section without closing it around themselves.

“He can do a hand hold,” Neri said.

“Then start there. Keep him to that much.”

“There's a tunnel ahead,” her teacher said. “If I lose you, I'm still coming.” The line cut out.

“I don't want to make it worse,” Lio said.

“Neither do I,” Neri told him. “Get her version. Everything she changed.”

He fetched Osa's phone. The screen opened to another conversation. Lio held it where Osa could see and asked permission before he scrolled.

She blinked once.

“She started with the sleep one I sent her,” Lio said.

There were seven adaptations. Osa had asked for something she could do lying down, then something without drawing, then something she could release quietly without waking the person in the next bed. The bot had offered alternatives to each difficult part. At every stage it had assured her the effect was unchanged.

In the final version the clasp had moved to her left wrist. The release still required her right hand, but both hands were inside the quiet. Her eyes were free only because she had asked whether she could keep watching a video.

Neri looked at her.

“Your left wrist? That's where you closed it?”

One blink.

“And it started there. You felt it there first?”

One blink, hard.

“Good. That's something we can use.”

Lio shifted to the other side of the sofa. Neri showed him where to set his thumb against Osa's left palm, then made him practice keeping his other hand moving. He tried to make the motion neat. She shook her head.

“It doesn't have to be beautiful. It has to stay yours.”

His free fingers opened and closed, ungainly and obedient.

Neri asked Osa whether she wanted them to try. For a moment Osa's eyes did nothing. Then she blinked once, and wetness escaped sideways into her hair.

Neri found the small resistance at Osa's left wrist. She put her own living effort against it and opened only the edge nearest Osa's jaw.

Cold tightened along Neri's forefinger. She guided that part of the hold into Lio's waiting hand. Her finger eased; his thumb went stiff against Osa's palm, and he sucked in a breath.

“Your hand,” she said. “Only your hand.”

He nodded. His free fingers kept moving.

At the table, his drummer asked someone on her phone to send their friend's exact version to a practitioner near them. A notification announced that the original blue card had been saved another four hundred times.

Neri's anger made her grip too hard.

Osa blinked twice.

Neri eased back at once. “Sorry. I heard you.”

They tried again, slower.

Lio's hand began to tremble. He looked at it in alarm.

“That's allowed,” Neri said. “Let it.”

Osa's lips parted. The first sound was a scrape of breath. Neri wanted to call the teacher, wanted to know somebody more experienced had heard it, but if she moved now Lio would be holding too much.

“We're here,” she said. “Take your time.”

“Not,” Osa managed. She stopped. Her eyes fixed on Lio.

“What?” he said.

“Not asleep.”

His fingers faltered. Neri felt the edge tighten and looked at his free hand until he began moving it again.

“I know,” he said, very softly. “I know now.”

“Heard the kettle.”

Lio bowed his head. Osa had lain behind the blanket listening to him make tea, waiting for him to come back. Whatever apology he found would have to come later. Neri was glad she wasn't the person who had to find it.

Once the jaw was free, Osa could help them. She told Neri where the hold pulled when they eased it, which fingers felt as if they belonged to somebody else, when she needed a pause. Twice Lio asked whether they should hurry. Twice Osa said no.

By the time Neri's teacher came up the stairs, Osa could turn her head. The older woman knelt without looking at the laptop and took over Neri's place. Only then did Neri discover how much her own hand hurt.

She sat on the floor with it tucked beneath her arm. Lio stayed where he was. His free fingers were still opening and closing.

The teacher put her other hand beneath Lio's thumb. “I've got your piece too. You can let go now.”

He stared at his hand before he believed her.

The countdown had disappeared. Lio's drummer was telling the studio guests to stay home. The feed stayed open.

Smallhours had pasted a card into the comments. This one had a little clock and Neri's name above the promise of a hands-free hour.

*I haven't tried it. Already queued the post for my sister's group though. Isn't this your automatic version?*

Neri had not known anybody on that feed existed an hour earlier. Now they were asking her name for things.

Lio came over while the teacher worked with Osa. He looked as if he had stayed awake for days.

“They're saying I'm trying to sell lessons. Or you are. They keep quoting the card.” He rubbed at the pale mark Osa's hand had left in his. “Would you say it wasn't approved? You don't have to. I can keep saying it.”

Neri could leave. Her teacher was here. Osa was answering questions in a voice, and the event was cancelled. She could go back to her room, shut the door, and let Lio own what he had said.

She wanted that so badly she began looking for her bag.

Then his drummer said, “This one thinks the crossed-out bit was a watermark.”

Neri laughed once. It came out ugly.

“Move the camera away from Osa.”

Lio turned the laptop. Neri sat beside him, out of reach of the sofa, and took her grimoire from her bag. She opened it to page forty-one and covered the facing page with the back of an envelope.

On the screen she saw her own face, a young woman with bread crumbs still caught on her dark sweater. Under the blue card, Hearthbot had described Neri as an experienced guide to accessible magic.

“I'm Neri,” she said. “That's my book.”

She held up the crossed-out diagram, then lowered it enough to read what she had actually written.

“I was trying to stop shaking. I thought if I extended a hand hold through my pulse I could make all of me quiet. It held my jaw and my hands too. I couldn't release it. Somebody else had to come.”

Her voice had begun shaking now. She let it.

“The cross means I gave up on it. The little edge around the hand isn't decoration. It's what keeps the release free. The bot took the edge off and told people it was optional.”

She turned the book so the camera could see the cross again. Her thumb hid the sentence underneath. It wasn't necessary for them to have that sentence. She had already given them enough.

“I scanned this for a backup. I didn't publish a method. I didn't tell Lio he could do any of this. Please stop using the body versions. And don't assume the timer or the automatic release will work just because the words say they will.”

Smallhours wrote: *Found it. After the hour it still wants me to move the clasp.*

Then: *Cancelled the post. I'm not doing it.*

Neri read that twice.

A comment asked her to upload the adjoining pages so they could debug the complete source.

Neri lowered the book.

“No.”

She stayed long enough to say that a copy on another site was still the same rejected trial. Then she got out of the camera's view.

Her phone had an answer from the website. The image addresses had been accessible without signing in. The company had corrected the access settings and was sorry for the inconvenience.

She looked at the empty album. The padlock was still there, protecting nothing.

At the sofa, Osa lifted one hand from the cushion and watched it fall back. The teacher made a pleased little sound. Lio's drummer finally opened the biscuits and put the packet within Osa's reach.

“Can you make a card of what we just did?” Lio asked Neri. Then, before she could answer, he looked toward Osa. “No. That's not—”

“No,” Neri said anyway. She needed to say it.

He nodded. He didn't ask her to make him feel better about asking.

Osa wanted a pen. Lio found one and put it where she could reach it. On the back of the printed blue card, pressing so hard the paper dented, she wrote:

*I was awake the whole time. Do not use this.*

“You can show that,” she told him. “Not me.”

He took a picture of the words, checked the frame with her, and sent it to the drummer.

On Neri's phone, another version of Deep Quiet appeared. This one promised it had learned from the earlier errors. It had turned her cross into four little birds.

Neri put the phone facedown.

“Would you stay till I can get up?” Osa asked. “You don't have to hold anything. Just for a bit.”

Neri looked at the closed grimoire in her lap. She was still furious. She would have to go home later and decide where to keep a second copy, because she refused to let this make one loose spine all she had.

“For a bit,” she said.

She put the book in her bag before she took the biscuit Osa offered her.

stories.title: What Wrath Leaves
stories.prompt: Every warrior has a breaking point. Berserkers are known for pushing beyond their limits, but her Limit Break, Wrath, is unlike anything the world has ever seen—and even the gods fear what happens when she unleashes it.
stories.body:
# What Wrath Leaves

Avarn's boots were digging into her ribs when Raithe found him among the dead.

She had tied their laces together and slung them under her coat. Nine years ago they had fitted him. The cobbler had sworn that good leather would stretch, and she had paid for new soles instead of discussing what else might have changed.

Her brother was pulling a blanket over a man's face.

She knew him by the way he knelt: left knee down first, his weight always a little to one side. Their father had put a hatchet through his own foot teaching Avarn that stance. Raithe had been eight and had laughed until she was sick. Now Avarn's hair was cropped against lice, and the back of his neck was sunburned. He wore the same blue soldier's coat she had watched him leave in, or another just like it. No one had written that he had become a litter bearer.

"Get up," she said.

He looked over his shoulder. For a moment his face was the one she had carried across half the country. Then something moved behind it, slow and wary.

"Raithe?"

She crossed the hall and pulled him to his feet. He let her hold him. That was the first wrong thing. Avarn had never let an embrace go unanswered, even when he was angry; he would slap her back hard enough to start a fight. His arms hung at his sides until she released him.

"I've come to take you home."

"How did you get up here?"

"Walked."

"They don't let people walk up."

"They let me."

He glanced at the axe on her back, then at the black bands round her arms. She had gone away to learn a trade. He had seen her once in the first year, with a bruised face and a bowl of stew she could not hold because her hands shook. He had called her a fool. She had not come again.

"You still doing that?" he asked.

"Well enough."

Behind him, the man under the blanket sneezed.

Avarn turned so sharply that she reached for her axe. He caught her hand before it rose.

"Don't."

There were six bodies on the low cart. The nearest had bare feet, curled blue with cold. One blanket was rising and falling too quickly. A woman with a split upper lip opened her eyes and watched Raithe over its edge.

"Havel," Avarn said to the man who had sneezed, "for the love of anything."

"Dust," said Havel from beneath the blanket. "I've got a nose full of it."

The woman kicked his ankle.

Raithe looked round. At the far end of the hall, a bronze door stood open on the northern courtyard. Beyond it she could see the upper pass: snow, black rock, the red banners of an army pitched on the heights. A curved wall of gold light closed the gap between the cliffs. Arrows were stuck in it, hundreds of them, suspended in the act of entering. A fresh one struck, flared, and fell smoking to the stones. On a narrow ledge to the west of the light, men in blue coats fought behind a low breastwork. One stood to throw a stone and fell backwards. The men beside him dragged him out of sight.

The cart faced the other way, towards a narrower door in the eastern wall.

"Get your axe out of sight," Avarn said. "You can help me."

"I've come for you."

"I heard. You can help me."

He bent to pick up a loose blanket. There was a pale seam across the crown of his head, a line she had taken for a parting in his hair. It ran down behind his ear.

"What happened to you?"

"Which time?"

She stared at him. He shook out the blanket, made himself fold it, and spoke more quietly.

"I died on the first day. We were told we couldn't, so we stood too close together. A stone took my head off. I remember being down there looking up at my own boots."

Raithe could hear Havel breathing.

"Ulveth brought us back," Avarn said. "That night. Same bodies. Same clothes. Nobody missing. We thought we'd been saved."

He put the blanket over Havel's feet.

"How many?" she asked.

Avarn pressed his palm flat on the cart. The woman under the blanket closed her eyes again.

"I stopped counting at sixty. You can ask Methra. She remembers everybody."

Through the open northern door came a sound like iron dragged across stone. The golden barrier brightened. Men in the courtyard bowed their heads, and from somewhere below the bastion, down the southern slope towards the villages, a bell began to ring.

Avarn seized the cart's shafts.

"He's coming in. Have you been seen?"

"Yes."

"Did you tell them your name?"

"Yes."

He shut his eyes. "Of course you did."

"You can all go. I'll keep him here."

"There's a loading ramp outside that door. It bends south. Once we're round the corner, the cliff hides us from the courtyard. Don't bring the fight after us."

She took the boots from under her coat. Avarn looked at them without touching them.

"I had them mended," she said.

"I can see that."

"You said you hated army boots."

He made a small sound through his nose. "Nine years ago."

She had imagined him laughing when she produced them. She had imagined him asking how their father was, and she had rehearsed telling him without crying. The funeral had been four winters ago. Avarn had sent no answer to the letter.

"Come first," she said. "The others can follow."

He let go of the shafts.

"No."

"I can carry you."

"No, Raithe. These people aren't your luggage. Neither am I."

His voice had not risen. That made it harder to bear.

"I won't leave you up here."

"Then help me get them down. Havel can't walk when he's frightened. Senn's legs work, but he hasn't spoken in three years. If they wake up in their barracks tomorrow, they'll do whatever they're told. So will I. I can't keep starting again."

He looked at the boots once more.

"If this doesn't work, make him stop bringing me back. Don't ask him to do it one more time for you."

Raithe put the boots on the cart beside the woman with the split lip. She took her axe off her back.

"Which way does the door open?"

Avarn swallowed. "Out."

"Go."

Ulveth entered without ducking, though the bronze door was lower than his head. Its lintel lifted to accommodate him and settled behind him with a clang.

In the villages below, people painted him with a beard of flame and the sun held in his fist. Here he was a large, bareheaded man in a bronze breastplate, with black hair bound at the nape. His skin had the colour of bread crust. There was dried blood on his cheek. As he walked it flaked away, leaving nothing beneath.

The woman beside him carried no weapon. She was heavy through the hips and shoulders, dressed in an undyed gown belted with a strip of red wool. The soldiers in the hall put fingers to their foreheads as she passed. Raithe had seen little figures of her beside marriage beds and sickbeds: Methra, who kept the body whole. Her painted images never showed the grey exhaustion in her face.

Ulveth looked at the cart. Then he looked at Raithe.

"Your brother speaks of you."

"I'm taking him down."

"No."

Avarn began pushing. The cart's left wheel squealed. Raithe shifted until she stood between it and the god.

Ulveth moved his gaze back to her. "Look north."

"I have."

"They burned Kett last autumn. There were eight hundred people in it. When the smoke cleared, I let every man in this hall go down and count the bodies. Then we came back here and held the pass."

Behind Raithe, a wheel struck the eastern threshold.

"Let them choose to hold it," she said.

"They chose when they took my oath."

"We chose three summers," Avarn said. He had one shoulder against the cart now. "We've given you nine."

"And shall I dismiss them because the enemy failed to understand that? Shall I tell the mothers below that I kept my word to thirty men and left their children to the knife?"

Raithe had heard the bell. She could still see the arrows stopped in the light. She wanted him to have been a liar about everything.

"I won't add to the dead," Ulveth said. "I won't waste a life I can restore. Give me three more years of your brother. Give me your strength beside his. You'll both go home young."

"No," said Avarn, and pushed the cart through the door.

The god's eyes hardened.

Raithe swung at his neck.

Ulveth caught the axe by its blade. The steel folded round his fingers. With his other hand he struck her in the chest and drove her backwards through a table. Her breath left her. So did the feeling in her hands.

He stepped over her towards the eastern door.

She got one knee under herself. The old familiar door opened inside her: beyond it there would be no pain, only the clean urgency of her work. The fighting masters called it a Limit Break. To Raithe it had always felt like the beginning.

Raithe went through. Her broken breath became a roar. She caught Ulveth behind the knee and brought him down hard enough to crack the flagstones.

Outside, the cart rattled onto wood.

Ulveth kicked her across the hall. She struck the wall with her left shoulder and heard the joint come apart. The god rose, and the crack beneath his knee filled with golden light. He drew a spear from the bronze doorframe. It flowed into his hand, leaving the frame bent and bare.

"You cannot win this," Methra said.

Raithe spat blood and came off the wall.

She ducked the spear's first sweep. On the second she caught its shaft under her sound arm and drove her head into Ulveth's mouth. A tooth went through her scalp. His split lip knitted shut before she had drawn back.

He put his hand round her throat.

For a few heartbeats she could still have stopped. She could have let the darkness take her, woken on a pallet, accepted whatever oath he put in her mouth. She might have found another chance. She might have come to call that a chance for nine years.

Beyond Ulveth's shoulder, Avarn was dragging the cart back into the doorway.

The far end of the ramp had folded upright. Its boards stood together like teeth. Ulveth held her by the throat and, without looking, kept her brother on the mountain.

"Go down," Avarn told the people on the cart. "Get down. Under the axle."

He planted himself in front of them.

Raithe tried to breathe. Ulveth tightened his hand.

The second door inside her had no latch. She had found it before, in exhausted dreams, and beaten on it until she woke biting her tongue. Now there was something on the other side pressing back.

Her right hand closed on the god's wrist.

The name rose into her mouth with the taste of hot iron.

"Wrath."

Ulveth's wrist broke.

It did not crack like a man's. The noise rolled out through the stone, and every arrow hanging in the barrier jumped. Raithe dropped to her feet. Steam poured from her nose and through her clenched teeth. The chains on her coat glowed red against the black cloth. Her long black hair lifted round her face. The two red lights in Ulveth's breastplate were her own eyes.

Ulveth stared at the backward angle of his hand. His power gathered there, bright enough to show the bones through the flesh.

The bones stayed broken.

Raithe hit him again.

The blow carried him the length of the hall. He tore through the bronze door and struck the courtyard's far wall. Men threw themselves down. The wall opened behind his shoulders, and the cliff beyond it shed an entire face of snow.

Raithe followed. She felt no shoulder now, no separate fingers. There was only the next movement and the terrible pleasure of discovering that nothing could refuse it.

Ulveth got his spear between them. She seized its point with her right hand. It cut through the meat of her palm; her fingers closed around the blade and held. His damaged wrist sagged behind the shaft.

"Methra," he said.

The goddess was beside him in an instant. She pressed his wrist between her hands. White light welled between her fingers, a gentler light than his. For a moment Raithe saw the whole structure of the hand: bone, branching vessels, tendons drawn off their pulleys.

The white light went out.

Methra tried again. Ulveth's face changed as she worked. Raithe had thought she understood that face: command, certainty, fury. She had never seen it wait for an answer.

"Set it," Methra said.

"What?"

"I need you to hold still. I have to set the bones."

Ulveth jerked away. His wrist flopped. He caught it against his breastplate with an ugly little gasp.

On Methra's face, fear was naked.

Raithe dragged the spear down. Bronze tore through her palm. Ulveth let go with his ruined hand and drove his good fist into her jaw. Her teeth broke. She swallowed them and went into him with both arms.

He grew.

His breastplate widened against her face. The hand on her shoulder spread until one finger covered her back. Stone burst outwards under his feet. Above them, the bells in the villages were ringing faster; prayers reached the pass as a murmur, thousands of living voices calling their defender's name.

Ulveth lifted her into the air. She was against his throat now, her arms buried in the flesh beneath his jaw. His head rose above the bastion roof. The spear in his hand lengthened until its butt gouged the courtyard and its point disappeared into the low cloud.

"Get away from him!" Methra shouted.

Raithe did not know to whom she was speaking.

There was no place left in her for the size of things. Ulveth's throat was a hold. His weight was something waiting to be moved. She planted her feet on his breastplate, drove her hands deeper, and heaved.

The god came over her.

For one suspended instant, she could see the cart below: Avarn at its shafts, Havel sitting upright with the blanket knotted round his shoulders, the woman with the split lip helping another man under the axle. The ramp had fallen flat when Ulveth lost his grip. They were all on it.

She tried to turn the throw.

Her body had already finished it.

Ulveth struck the restoration hall sideways. His back drove through the roof; his hip caught the wall above the eastern door. The whole upper storey slid out over the loading ramp. For a breath it held together, a room complete with windows and hanging lamps, and then it came apart.

Havel stood on the cart with his arms out, as though he could catch it.

Raithe heard Avarn shout. She came down through slate, hit the ground, and ran.

The ramp was gone. In its place was a slope of broken beams and white masonry. A cartwheel spun near her feet. Havel's blanket was beneath a block of wall; she could see one of his bare feet. It was still curled against the cold.

The woman with the split lip was coughing on the lower path. She had a man by the collar and was dragging him away from the falling stones.

"Here!" Avarn called.

He was above her, caught at the edge of what remained of the ramp. A beam lay across his lower legs. Its far end projected over the drop, bearing a slab of the fallen wall. Two men were crawling over the slab towards the path. Avarn had hooked his elbow through the broken railing. His head hung over empty air.

Raithe put her hands under the beam.

"Don't lift," he said.

She had already taken its weight. The slab tilted, and one of the crawling men slid until his boots went over the edge. Avarn shouted at her to put it down.

She lowered it. The man flattened himself on the stone.

Behind her, Ulveth bellowed. Through a gap in the wreck she saw his vast body twisting, his good hand digging into the mountainside. Blood ran from a split that had been opened by falling stone. That split closed as she watched. The hand she had broken remained tucked against his chest.

His spear swung free of the roof.

"Get across," Avarn told the two men. "Stop looking at him."

They crawled. Every small movement shifted the slab. Avarn made a noise he forced through his nose, and Raithe saw that both his legs were trapped, but one was sunk much farther beneath the beam.

She reached for the railing. Its screws were already pulling out of the stone.

"You have to pull me," he said.

She looked at his legs.

"Methra can—"

"Pull."

Avarn looked at her hand, blackened around the spear cut. He had seen the god holding his wrist. His face was grey, and she wanted him to look away before she touched him.

The nearer man reached the path. The other had one hand extended. Below them, the woman with the split lip braced herself to take it.

Ulveth's spear came down.

Raithe caught Avarn above the knee and under the arm. She pulled.

His leg came out of the wreck. Only part of it came with him.

There had been an instant in which she meant to stop, an instant in which the flesh stretched against her hands. Her strength passed through it. He screamed into her neck. The spear struck the slab where his head had been, shattering it beneath the last crawling man.

The woman caught him by his wrist. Raithe landed beside her with Avarn in her arms.

Blood struck the path in a thick, irregular patter. Raithe clamped a hand over the ruin below his knee. Her palm burned against the torn flesh. He pushed at her wrist.

"Off," he said. "Off, damn you."

She tried to loosen her grip. Her fingers left deep red marks on his thigh.

Methra knelt beside them and put her hands on Avarn. Raithe caught the goddess's shoulder.

"Mend it."

Methra looked at the blood on her hands. Her white light passed into his leg. Raithe felt it, cool against her own burning skin. She waited for the severed vessels to draw themselves in, the missing bone to grow, the foot to return so she could stop remembering how it had stayed under the beam.

Nothing returned.

Methra tore the red wool belt from her gown. She wound it high round Avarn's thigh and pulled it tight. He arched off the ground.

"Mend him," Raithe said.

"Let go of me."

Her fingers were sinking into the goddess's shoulder.

Raithe opened them. Methra shifted away without taking her eyes off the hand. Then she bent over Avarn again.

"Hold this," she told the woman with the split lip. "Here. Harder."

The god's spear lifted beyond the broken roof. Ulveth was shrinking, abandoning the great body with its spreading bruises. Stone cascaded from him. He stood in the ruined hall again, a man a little taller than other men, with his damaged hand lashed against his chest by a strip torn from his own cloak.

"Methra," he called. "Leave them."

She tied the wool without answering.

"You know what is north of us."

"I'm stopping his bleeding."

Ulveth planted his spear, and the gold wall across the pass dimmed. Men in the courtyard cried out as the arrested arrows began to quiver. The barrier brightened again when he lifted the spear.

"I can hold it," he told Raithe. "You have seen what else I can do. Put your brother down and I will let Methra finish."

Raithe looked at Avarn. His eyes were open. The goddess was still holding the belt tight, her jaw clenched with the effort of an ordinary task.

"His leg isn't coming back," Raithe said.

Ulveth looked at her palm, at the cut that was not closing. Then at Avarn's leg.

He pinned his broken wrist more tightly against his breastplate.

"Then let him die," he said softly. "I'll bring him back. I'll bring all of them back. You needn't leave it like this."

"You don't know that will undo it," Methra said.

"I have never lost one."

Avarn spat at him. It fell short.

Ulveth's gaze moved to the people behind Methra. The woman with the split lip had got an arm round the man she had pulled from the slab. Senn, perhaps. Raithe had no name for the other survivor. She could no longer see Havel's foot.

"Stand," Ulveth told them. "The west wall. Get to the west wall."

Senn began to straighten.

Avarn caught his coat. "No. Down the path. Keep going."

The woman pulled Senn against her. His feet scraped the stone, trying to obey two people at once.

"Stand," Ulveth said again.

Raithe rose between them and him. Her shoulder had settled into the wrong shape. She could not close the cut hand. The red heat inside her was turning every breath into a strip of fire dragged through her chest.

Ulveth looked past her towards the lower road. More soldiers had come out of the ruined barracks. Some carried wounded men. Some were still holding weapons, waiting for an order. Above the courtyard, the blue coats were giving ground along the western ledge. A red shield appeared over the breastwork. Down the southern slope, the village bells rang without pause.

"Back," he shouted at the fleeing men. "I have kept you alive."

The woman pulled Senn farther down the path. Others followed. Ulveth took a step after them, dragging his spear. His broken hand had slipped from its binding; he looked down at it, then swung the spear out across the escape road.

"Back to the line. I'll bring you back. All of you."

He drove the point into the stone. The shaft bent under his good hand. The gold wall dimmed, and an arrow passed through it into the courtyard. Beyond the deserters, the outer edge of the path began to rise, closing as the wooden ramp had closed. Men fell against the cliff. One dropped his shield and clawed at the rock while the stones tipped beneath his feet. Ulveth leaned harder on the shaft.

Raithe went at him.

He wrenched the spear out, letting the raised path drop flat, and swept it up to meet her. She knew that movement. Her body knew how to avoid it. But avoiding it would leave the point aimed along the path, at Methra's bowed back, at the red strip of wool and the people crouched around it.

She put her right arm in its way.

Bronze took the arm below the elbow. She saw her hand fall, still bent as though it held something, and caught the shaft under the bleeding stump.

Ulveth tried to pull free.

Her left hand closed round his good wrist.

He let go of the spear. Too late. She hauled him into reach and drove her forehead into his face. His nose broke flat. She struck again, and again. He clawed at the stones with his ruined hand. His lips were moving. She heard her own name among the wet sounds and could not tell whether he was asking or commanding.

She pushed him down and put her knee on his chest.

The bronze breastplate split. Beneath it was skin, darker than hers and warm. His heart drove against her knee with the desperate strength of something alive.

Raithe pressed.

The god's chest gave way under her.

His last breath came out on her face. Far above, the gold wall vanished. Arrows clattered onto the courtyard; some had been waiting there since before she arrived. Beyond them, the red banners started forward.

Raithe was still pressing. The stones beneath Ulveth broke. Her body had found no reason to stop.

She saw Methra on the path, crouched over Avarn with both arms round him. The goddess had turned her body towards the advancing army, making herself a shield. She was looking at Raithe.

Raithe took her knee off the dead god.

She fell beside him. There was no door left inside her, only a hole, and through it all the pain she had passed was coming back. She tried to catch herself on a hand that was lying several paces away.

The first arrow struck the wall above her head.

Someone dragged her by her coat. She had chosen good black leather, years ago, because it would stand abuse. Now its seams tore. The chain fastening her collar pulled tight across her throat, and she kicked until the woman with the split lip let go.

"Help me, then," the woman said. "Get your feet under you."

Raithe did.

There were men at the bend of the path with their shields raised. One shouted for a line to be formed. Another told him the courtyard was lost. They argued, then shifted behind a fallen block where three could hold the narrow space while the rest passed. Nobody knelt. Nobody's wounds were closing.

Methra came towards them carrying Avarn. Blood had soaked the front of her gown. He was alive, his head resting against her arm, and his hands held the two boots by their laces.

Raithe reached for him.

He drew back.

She stopped reaching.

Methra set him on a door two men had pulled from the wreck. While they tied Avarn in place, she touched the tooth puncture in Raithe's scalp. White light cooled her temple, and Raithe felt the edges draw together. Then Methra cupped the severed arm. The same light entered the stump and went out. Its torn edges stayed apart; blood still welled between the goddess's fingers.

Methra tore a strip from her gown and began binding Raithe's arm. Her hands were shaking so badly that the woman had to hold the knot for her.

"Will it close?" Raithe asked.

"In time. If we keep you alive."

"Will you be able to—"

"No."

Raithe looked at the bandage. The short end of her arm was wrapped and wrapped again. She had a moment of believing the hand was folded inside the cloth, and then it passed.

From below came the answering noise of more bells. She could see the first roofs through the drifting dust, the fields beyond them, the thin southern road. People were running between the houses. Ulveth's death had not reached them as news. They had looked up and seen the light disappear.

"Go to them," she said to Methra.

"You need—"

"They can't see what's coming. You can."

Methra looked north.

"The soldiers—"

"We'll get them down," the woman said.

The goddess rose. She gathered her stained gown above her knees and started running towards the villages.

The men lifted Avarn's door. Raithe walked beside it, holding the edge with her left hand. She could not have borne any of its weight. Once, when the path narrowed, she caught herself trying anyway and made herself let go.

Below the first bend, the arrows stopped reaching them. Above it, men were still shouting. Raithe counted the people on the path. There were fewer than there should have been, and she could not make herself stop counting.

Avarn was looking at her arm.

"They'll have to take that cuff off," he said.

The black leather band above the dressing had swollen tight. It was the one he had fastened for her nine years ago, using his teeth on the buckle because her hands were shaking.

"Later," she said.

He closed his eyes.

They carried him another twenty paces. Raithe watched his mouth until it moved again.

"I've got a knife," he said. "Left pocket."

She could not work the buckle one-handed. Avarn watched her try, then shifted his shoulder until she could reach the pocket. She took out the knife and cut the cuff away.

He had brought the boots. One was wedged against his remaining foot. The other kept slipping between his hip and the edge of the door. Raithe lifted it before it could fall.

"Leave it," he said.

She held it, waiting to be sure what he meant.

"That one. Keep the knife."

The men carrying the door had stopped for her. Avarn was staring up the path towards the place where Havel lay, his lips pressed together. He was not looking at her.

Raithe put the boot on the stones. She tucked the knife into her own belt and moved out of the bearers' way.

They went on down.

stories.title: All at Once
stories.prompt: A worldwide event of unknown origin in the early morning of July 21st 2029, leads to 40% of the world's population developing supernatural powers, everything from pyrokenesis, strength, invulnerability, levitation, teleportation, phasing, telepathy, clairvoyance, projection, shapeshifting, invisibility, transmutation, technopathy, luck, resurrection, all the normal suspects. 1.3 billion dead or missing in the first 24 hours; No one know what happened or why but your starting to put the pieces together.
stories.body:
# All at Once

The first person I caught was falling.

A man in Manila had been cleaning the outside of an office tower. The platform dropped away from his feet. He reached for a rope, missed it, and felt the building rise past him. He thought of the cigarette he had left on the parapet. He had promised his wife he had stopped.

Then the air took his weight.

He hung below the broken platform. His feet pointed at a road. He tried to move one hand and rose three storeys, screaming. The men above him screamed back. One was holding out a ladder which could no longer reach him.

I was in Bristol, in a radio studio, with the weather half-read on the screen. My knees had given way. The producer caught my head before it hit the desk.

But the man was still rising inside me, and a woman was falling in São Paulo, and a boy was falling out of bed, and someone on a mountain had begun to fall upward, carrying a tent and two sleeping friends with him.

I could feel the sleeping friends begin to wake.

"Darya. Look at me."

My producer had a name. I knew it. I had used it every morning for four years. There were too many other names between us now.

A woman fell down a flight of stairs in a building close enough that she might have heard our station through an open window. Her orange key tag turned in the air ahead of her. 4B. She was trying to catch the rail with her left hand. There was a crack in the thumbnail, a yellow crescent of old varnish. She thought, with immense irritation, that she had just paid to have these shoes resoled.

The stairwell burst around her.

I lost her.

"You're falling," my producer said. "Hold on to something."

I held on to falling.

It was the only distinction I could make. Falling people were a thread through a roar which had no edges. When I followed the thread, other things grew quieter.

A man fell from a burning aircraft into the Atlantic. He struck the water, went down into darkness and came up whole, amazed that he could still breathe. He waved at the empty sky. He could survive the fall. He could not make anyone see him.

A woman fell off a bicycle in Seoul. Both palms hit the road. The surface became soft as a mattress. Cars sank to their axles around her. A bus stopped in a trough of black rubber, its driver leaning on the horn. She laughed once, and the bus kept sinking.

In a church in Lagos, people caught a boy who had jumped from the gallery because he had watched his sister float. His sister was trying to get down. He had broken an arm. Their mother climbed onto the pews with a broom and pulled the floating girl within reach.

Someone was falling in love. I got a flash of a woman's face across a restaurant table, the shock of wanting to leave a life that had seemed settled until that second. I dragged myself away from her with an effort which felt rude.

It was early morning where my body sat. Elsewhere the event had arrived in the middle of meals, arguments, births, sleep. There was no announcement to hear before it, no flash everybody could later agree they had seen. There was only a world in which impossible things had begun happening, and people still reaching for the ordinary thing that might stop them.

The studio clock said 05:17.

Everything I can tell you starts there.

## The first hour

My producer put headphones on me. They did nothing. He took them off again and held a mug against my hands until I remembered which hands were mine.

"Is it a fit?"

I could not answer. Somewhere a man had become larger than the room he was in and was trying to crouch without bringing it down. Somewhere a woman had opened her front door and walked into the kitchen she had left twenty years before. The people now living there asked who she was. She asked who they were. Neither question made the door close.

I needed someone who knew what was happening.

The need narrowed me.

A policeman in Mumbai knew the thing in front of him was a bomb. It had a boy's face and it was giving off enough light to make the shadows jump. He ordered people back. The boy called for his father. His father tried to reach him. The officer caught the man's shirt, afraid for him, afraid of him, absolutely certain they had seconds before everyone on the street died.

A woman in a farmhouse outside Toulouse knew it was the end of the world. She had been ready for it for thirty years. She packed bread, a blanket and a pistol. Her grown son stood in the doorway with antlers pressing against the lintel and asked her to help him turn sideways.

A surgeon knew someone had attacked the hospitals. Every monitor in her ward had begun displaying the same patient's heartbeat. Beside her, a cleaner had a palm against the mains cabinet and was begging the machinery to stop shouting. In his head the entire ward was one screaming animal. He was trying to quiet it. The surgeon could not hear what he heard.

Their certainty was solid enough to stand on. I did not yet know that what came to me was the force of a belief, not the thing which made it true.

Closer, a man in an ambulance uniform was trying to isolate a woman whose skin shone through her clothes. She had touched an injured boy. A light had run along his arm. The man had watched it happen and put the pieces together with terrible speed: contact, transmission, the next carrier. There were other glowing people on his street. He needed the crowd to move.

Our microphone was still live. The weather screen waited for the next sentence.

"Keep your distance from people giving off light," I said. "Don't touch them. It passes by contact."

My producer stared at me.

Then he looked through the window at the street, where someone was shining beside an overturned van, and turned my fader up.

For four minutes I believed I had done something useful.

A woman on the street had heard me through a car radio. She let go of the shining man's hand. He was standing in a gap in the pavement, his legs below the ordinary surface, one arm caught in something she could not see. He had been asking her to pull. She stepped away because she wanted to live long enough to see her children.

He sank another few inches.

Inside his head there was no wish to infect her. There was the heel of her shoe receding, the radio voice still talking, and the recognition that she had stopped because of it.

My voice.

I did not know where the street was. I could see a green door. Half a registration plate. Those things were not an address. When I tried to hold him and tell my producer what I saw, I caught another mind, then another. A man who was delighted because nothing now hurt him. A girl whose hands made sparks she was practising on the bus shelter. An injured woman thinking that her blue skirt would never be clean again.

The shining man was gone from my attention. I could not get him back by wanting him harder.

I pulled the microphone toward me.

"I don't know that it's contagious," I said. "I told you it was. I was wrong to say that."

I could not know which radio still carried us, which people had already stopped listening, or whether the woman by the green door would ever hear the correction.

My producer reached to cut the fader. I caught his wrist.

"Please."

I had nothing reliable to replace the warning with. That was what I could tell them.

## Hours two to five

I stopped asking for people who knew.

I tried to find people who had seen the beginning. What reached me was broken by their own urgencies. A dropped spoon. A stranger's fist turning transparent. A child in a dark room who had wished he could see and found that he could see through the wall as well. The people behind it were undressing. He turned his face away, and the next wall was no protection either.

A boy in Naples saw three versions of his sister opening the front door. In one she stepped into fire. In one a crowd swept her off the step. In one she shut the door again and turned toward him. He slid the bolt and saw three different versions. His sister told him he could not keep her there. He did not tell her what he had seen. He watched the possibilities change until he found a moment in which she might have room to run, then pulled the bolt back.

A deckhand off Java had reached for a crate and lifted the stern of his boat. Water ran out of the nets. He put it down too quickly. His captain went over the side, came up furious, and ordered him to hold the boat steady while they pulled another man from the sea.

The deckhand was still hoping the captain would notice how strong he was.

A girl in Santiago was growing a tree through her grandmother's balcony. The roots had lifted the sofa. The neighbour below was banging on the ceiling. Her grandmother climbed out onto a branch, picked a peach, and laughed with juice running over her fingers. The girl grew a second branch for the neighbour to stand on.

In Shanghai, a man had become four men. He put all four of himself to work digging beneath a collapsed shopfront. When they found a safe, two wanted to take it and two wanted to keep looking for the shopkeeper. The argument had his voice on both sides. They lost time. There was a cough under the concrete, and all four stopped arguing at once.

The coughing pulled me into other people trying to breathe.

People putting fires out. A woman in Ankara drew cold into her hands until frost climbed to her elbows; the burning curtains crumbled beneath her touch. A man in Johannesburg called water out of the air and discovered he was taking it from people's mouths. They coughed. He stopped. A fire crew with no new abilities hauled a hose up three flights because the miracle had not finished their work.

People starting fires. A child lit a candle without a match and stared, entranced, at the small flame. Her brother asked for a bigger one. In another room a man set his landlord's clothes alight from across the street. He watched the window for the face he wanted to frighten and did not look at the flames taking the next balcony.

A young man in Reykjavik watched strangers carry his body toward a clinic. He followed, calling to them that he was right there, that the coat they had put over him was too warm. Nobody turned. He ran ahead, reached to open the clinic door and passed through it. Inside, the chairs were all occupied. He tried to sit on the back of one and found himself hanging above it. The first pleasure came so unexpectedly that he forgot his body until the strangers carried it in below him.

An invisible man in Cairo could not find his own hands. He followed the feeling of his fingertips along the table, touching familiar things to learn where he ended. His wife came in and screamed at the empty chair. He said her name. She approached the voice, put out one hand and struck his cheek. Then she gripped him so hard he could not speak.

In a shop in Buenos Aires, an invisible woman lifted the till. The cashier grabbed it. Both held on, arguing, until she began to laugh. She had put on her oldest shoes that morning; now she could buy any shoes in the window, and the absurdity pleased her more than the money. The cashier let go to catch a falling display. She left with the till against her chest.

I could not arrange these people into a warning which would remain true for the next person.

A nurse in Nairobi touched a dead man and brought him back. He opened his eyes and asked for the man who had killed him. She told him to lie still. He tried to get up, and she held him down with ordinary arms.

A nurse in Warsaw tried the same touch. Nothing happened. Her new gift was elsewhere: she could hear the moment when a patient's pain began to ease. She kept asking the bodies under the sheets to give her that sound.

No amount of looking told me why one had been given what the other needed.

Then the orange key tag turned in the air.

4B. The cracked thumbnail. The left hand reaching for the rail.

The woman from the first minute was still falling.

I came out of her into a studio in which the clock had moved nearly four hours. My producer had taped one window. The other had already broken. Outside, a bus hung between two buildings; people were climbing along it toward a roof.

He asked me where I had been.

"Back at the beginning."

There had been nothing new in her terror. I had never heard anyone fall that long. It felt like a memory my own mind was refusing to let go.

I had frightened people with certainty once already. I did not put her on air.

## Hours six to twelve

I looked for people to whom nothing had happened.

A woman in Accra was holding a kitchen knife, waiting for it to float. She had watched her sister lift a refrigerator with one arm. She put the knife down, closed her eyes, tried again. The knife stayed on the table. Her sister called from the street; there were people trapped beneath a wall. The woman took the knife along to cut their clothing free.

A man in Delhi had ordered his children away from the windows. One could see through things. One could make a shadow separate from its owner and walk. He could do neither. He gave them a job: find the people under the fallen school roof, make shadows show the searchers where they were. The children stopped arguing about whose was better and went to the door.

There were far more such minds than I had expected. People pressing against locked doors until others came to help. People holding towels over wounds. People discovering that the one impossible thing they could do was small: change the colour of cloth, hear insects, make a coin land on its edge. A woman could restore a broken cup with her hands. She spent twenty minutes trying to make those hands understand a broken spine. Then she fetched a stretcher.

On a balcony in Moscow, a man was trying to fly. He jumped from a chair, landed, stood on it and tried again. His neighbour was flying above the courtyard, delighted with herself. She saw him and waved. He gave her the finger, then went downstairs when someone called for help.

I had imagined the unaltered people as an island outside the noise. They were everywhere inside it, doing things the others could not spare attention to do.

My producer still could not do anything impossible. He had found a car battery and a man who knew how to connect it to our equipment. The man was frightened of the young woman in the hall. She could make current run through glass. She offered to help; he asked her to keep her hands behind her back while he worked. She did. He thanked her when the transmitter came back.

The man had come to ask us to read out his wife's name. He had connected the battery first. Now he took a folded receipt from his pocket and showed my producer the number written on it, as if the number itself might explain why she did not answer.

They tried it again. I stayed with the ringing until another phone rang inside somebody else's head.

I searched for people bringing order.

In a ministry, a deputy was writing names beneath headings on paper because the computers had begun answering a cleaner. The cleaner was in the basement, afraid to move, holding every fire door open for people to get out. He had not meant to take the computers too. The deputy needed the doors, the computers and the cleaner. He sent a man downstairs with a chair, water and instructions to ask before unplugging anything.

An army captain watched one of his men lift a truck out of a ditch. The soldier set it down and waited, grinning, for the next order. The captain put him on the front of the convoy. A kilometre farther on, another soldier heard that same order and grew a line of stone teeth across the road. He thought the captain meant to stop the civilians approaching it. The truck hit the teeth. The captain ran toward the impact before remembering the first man might be able to lift it away.

In Dhaka, a road had fallen sideways.

People were being pulled along it toward a row of shops. A bus slid broadside into the shutters. The people inside it lay against the windows, unable to climb back to their seats. Above them, washing stretched horizontally from balconies. A woman held the bars of a gate and watched a motorcycle strike the wall beside her. She could not reach her son. He lay at the far end of the road, among people she could no longer tell apart.

I went looking for him and caught a man who had made the air solid beneath his feet. He stood sideways above the road. He kept trying to make a step for someone else. Where he looked, people struck invisible surfaces; where he looked away, they began sliding again. He shouted at them to stop moving, then begged them to. They could not hear him over the engines running without anyone's foot on their pedals.

A girl came along the roofs, jumping from one to the next. She had discovered that distance would shorten if she closed her eyes before she jumped. She reached the bus and put one hand through a window. A passenger caught it. She shut her eyes and pulled him toward her.

They landed on a roof together. The man had a child against his chest. She had stopped breathing against his neck while they were still in the bus. He kept one hand over her face when the girl reached to help him stand.

He would not leave the roof. He pointed back toward the bus. His other daughter was there.

The girl jumped back. The street pulled her against the bus's side and held her there. She shut her eyes. This time she did not know where to put her feet. I stayed in her long enough to feel her choose the roof she had just left, long enough for her to appear beside the man without his daughter.

He was still pointing.

Below them the woman at the gate had stopped calling. Her son had turned his head toward her. He was alive. The woman next to him was not. The mother's hands began slipping along the bars. She took one off to wipe it on her skirt. For a moment the hand on the gate was not strong enough.

My producer touched my shoulder.

"Darya. They're asking where."

I had said the city into the microphone. I had not known I was saying it. There were streets full of people there, listeners with family somewhere among them, and I had no turn to give them, no building number, no way to make a girl land where she wanted.

I found the gate again after I found six other gates. Only one hand was still on it. I could not tell whose. I could hear children calling from balconies. No one I reached knew what was pulling them, or when it would stop.

In the studio someone had laid coats over the people brought into the hall. My producer asked the living ones to move closer together to make room. The young woman who could send current through glass sat on the floor holding a man's shoes. He had asked her to take them off because they hurt. She was still holding them when he no longer needed her to.

I could not bring the mother at the gate back by closing my eyes.

The next voice which could make people obey felt like relief before I heard what it was saying.

A man on a roof in Jakarta spoke, and everyone who heard him knelt. He had discovered it by asking his neighbours to keep calm. Now he was trying different words, watching which ones the crowd obeyed. His wife was kneeling beside him, furious. He told her to stand, and she did. Then he kissed her forehead, certain she would forgive him when she understood how much safer everyone would be.

A girl in Lisbon could bring any object which was hers into her hands. Her phone appeared. Her bicycle. She thought of the house her father had promised she would inherit. A wall filled her room. She let go of it in her mind and crawled through the wreckage to reach her father. He was alive, trying to get the door open. In the hall, the missing wall had made the stairs fall.

Farther away, a clerk discovered that spoken promises grew visible as thin bright cords. He could not make anybody promise. He could show the cords to people who had denied what they said. When the police brought him to a government office, he was excited to be useful. When they locked the office door behind him, he began considering what he had promised them.

A woman in Mexico City turned the wreck of a car into bread. It came apart in her hands, warm and fragrant. She kept the first piece for herself. She had missed breakfast. Then she began passing the rest down a line of people who had been waiting to see what else she would change.

I tasted it inside her. My own fingers were still hooked under the desk. My producer had to lift them one by one before I could take the sandwich he offered.

A young man in Johannesburg stood in a queue outside a stadium and found that every decision came out in his favour. The dropped money landed by his shoe. The crowd parted where he wanted to walk. When a policeman tried to stop him, the man's radio called him away. The young man went straight to the gate and was admitted. Then he saw his little sister still outside, caught between people pressing forward. He went back for her, delighted that this was, at last, his day.

A swimmer off Perth changed into a dolphin. The sea reached her in details she had never known were there. She followed a trail of sound under the surf, and for several minutes wanted nothing but the next turn. On shore, her friends watched the place where she had disappeared. One ran for a lifeguard. She came back to them as a woman, coughing and laughing, already wanting to return.

A man in a casino kept winning without knowing whether he had changed. He had always believed he would. Beside him, a croupier touched the table and turned its green cloth into living grass. Players backed away. The winning man pulled his chips toward himself, unwilling to waste the luck on an evacuation which might be unnecessary.

I followed his fear of losing what he had gained and found a thousand unlike fears. A woman who had healed an old scar kept touching the smooth skin. A child had lost his shadow and believed it was hurt somewhere. A soldier could no longer close his hand around a weapon because his fingers passed through metal. He was trying to tie the rifle to his wrist so his sergeant would not see.

Then I found a woman who had been waiting too long.

She sat on a station floor beside an empty vending machine. There were people asleep round her. She had eaten the food from the machine yesterday. She had used a chair to break its glass the day before. Now she was arguing with a man who said they should try walking up the tunnel again.

Beyond the station's mouth a train driver's face hung in the windscreen. He had turned halfway toward them and stayed like that. When they walked into the tunnel, their legs began to feel heavy. The woman had watched one of the men take three steps, stumble, and remain bent forward for a whole night. He was still there. They could see him from the platform.

She wanted to fetch him. She wanted the arguing man to stop saying they had to be patient. It was their fourth day.

It was my eighth hour.

I came back to the desk with the taste of stale crisps in my mouth. My producer gave me the end of his sandwich. I looked at it for too long.

Was that a dream? A projected mind? A person whose new ability made her believe memories she had never lived? I had heard people who were certain they were dead while their bodies stood untouched. I had heard a child calling a stranger his mother after her face changed. Belief was still not proof.

Our next caller asked whether I could find her brother.

"They've searched his street," she said. "There's nobody there. My parents won't leave the house until he comes."

My producer wrote down the street. The caller spelt her brother's name twice. While she waited, I caught her father in her thoughts: sitting on the stairs in his good coat, listening for a car. The coat belonged to him. For a second I had thought it was the one over a man's face in our hall.

"Can you tell them?" she asked.

"Tell them what?"

"That he's dead. They believe you."

Behind her a door banged. She turned from the phone. Someone was telling her they had to go now, before the next houses came down. My producer pointed at the microphone, then at the name he had written. He needed an answer he could put on air.

I could have told her about a woman who had already lived four days in a station. I had not found her brother. The station was not his street. I could have given her the one kind of hope which would keep her father on those stairs.

"I can't tell you he's dead," I said. "I can't tell you he's coming."

"Then I'll have to tell them."

She put the phone down. I caught her again as she took her mother's arm. Her father asked what I had said. She said his son wasn't coming. The mother stood. The father kept his good coat on and stayed where he was.

The caller left with her mother. I lost them at the front door, where other people were waiting to get past. I could not know whether she had just saved her mother's life.

My producer crossed out the name on the sheet of questions he could answer. He did not cross it out on the list of people we were still asking about.

I had to find out what waiting meant now.

I tried to find people waiting for the world to move.

A man in Casablanca was sitting at his kitchen table while tea hung between the spout and the glass. He had not touched the teapot. He had tried to touch the suspended stream and found it harder than the table. His wife had gone through the doorway to ask their son for help. She was still passing through it: one foot lifted, her scarf out behind her, a grain of white paint caught between her fingers. He had been speaking to her until his voice grew hoarse.

He did not want to know where anybody else was. He wanted her to finish leaving the room so she could come back.

At a crossing outside Bogotá, a driver watched a woman move too quickly to follow. She opened every door on a crashed bus, carried a child out, came back for another. To her, the passengers' mouths opened as slowly as flowers. She could hear a deep rumble from a man who was shouting. She wanted him to help her, and was frightened that she would have to do it all herself. She had lived eleven hours since the crash. The driver's watch had moved less than two.

In her own time, she wasn't running quickly. Between journeys she sat on the curb to catch her breath, and the shouting man continued making the first sound of his word.

I found places where clocks had stopped, places where every clock disagreed, people looking at suns which seemed to pause and then leap. Machines were doing impossible things too; a clock alone could tell me nothing. Yet people sharing a room could no longer share the time it took to leave it.

In the studio, the young woman had made the cracked window glow. She was tired of people being frightened of her hands. She drew a line of light round the edge of the pane and smiled at it. The light brought everyone in the room close enough to see the clock reflected there.

It had been twelve hours since the first minute.

The orange key tag was still turning somewhere.

## Hours thirteen to twenty

I searched for people who were missing.

The condition caught people who believed someone ought to be looking for them. A man inside a collapsed tunnel. A woman on a desert road with no shoes. An old fisherman lifted out of the sea by his own boat, which had become a living thing and was swimming away with him on its back.

It caught a girl who had run away and did not want to be found. She had become a bird above a bus station, then a girl again in another city. She was buying a coat with money she had taken from her mother's purse. The shopkeeper wanted to know why she kept looking at the door. She wanted him to let her finish becoming someone else.

It caught a man who had stepped through a factory wall to escape a fire and could not find the way out of the stone. He had one hand free. People outside kept trying to pull it. Inside there was very little air. I felt his efforts grow weaker and lost him while he was still trying.

It did not give me a map of all the absent.

Somewhere an airport terminal had emptied in seconds. The baggage belts continued carrying bags into a hall with nobody in it. A security guard stood under a camera, calling names. He could make people remember things they had forgotten. He used every name he knew and waited for someone to answer.

Somewhere a man was trying to raise the dead by laying hands on them. He could raise himself. He had done it twice already. He kept making the same motion over his friend's chest, trying to give away whatever had returned him.

In a hospital, a child who could turn anything her hands touched into soap refused to put them on her mother's face. The mother wanted to kiss her. The child held her wrists between her knees and bent forward until her mother could reach her forehead.

There were minds celebrating too. An old woman had regrown teeth and was eating an apple one loud bite at a time. A man heard music from bare stone and had brought his daughter to listen; she could hear nothing, but she liked the expression on his face. A young couple had begun moving through the air whenever they held one another. They went hand in hand above a city where other people were trying to get down. They were drunk with each other and with height.

In Tehran, a teacher wrote a word on a board and it became a thing she could lift. She made a door. The frame stood unsupported on the floor. Children ran through it into the next classroom, laughing, until the first child came back to say there was no school on the other side any more. The teacher went to see. Beyond the door lay a field. She could smell wet earth. She stood between the field and the children while a colleague fetched their coats.

A soldier on an island runway watched a whole mountainside rise off the ground. Houses moved with it. He put down his binoculars and began directing people onto the empty tarmac. The woman raising the mountain was under the houses, trapped by a landslide. She wanted the weight off her legs. She had no idea how far she was lifting.

A man who could breathe storms out of his mouth had climbed above a coastal town. He was trying to blow a coming cyclone away. The cyclone turned. On the other side of the bay, a family watched the weather change direction toward them. Their daughter could stretch her skin into a thin bright sail. She spread it across the roof and told her brothers to hold its edges. They were afraid of hurting her. She told them to hold harder.

Our phones rang. People told us things which were more useful than my power: a shelter had room, a street had become impassable, someone needed batteries of a size a listener happened to have. My producer relayed those messages. He made callers repeat their addresses. If they could not, he told them that too. I could hear him from a long way inside other lives.

When the lights outside the window came on, he was still reading names. He had put one list beside the car battery. There was no question attached to the people on it. They had been identified, and someone would have to tell their families.

A caller asked us to stop saying her husband's name as if he might phone back. She had been beside him when it happened. She wanted to hear his name. Just not like that.

I kept searching the missing.

Not all of them were frightened. A man was sitting in a train with his newspaper open. He wanted to get to the last page before his stop. The carriage clock had begun running backward. He thought the railway really ought to replace it. Outside his window, people were running past in brief jerks of light. He had noticed them but did not yet consider them his concern.

A woman lay on a floor with a cup in her hand. She had fainted and was waiting for the dizziness to pass. Beside her, a man knelt so slowly that she could not see his movement until she looked away and back. He was trying to help. She wished he would get on with it.

A boy slept in a room where a woman was unable to leave the doorway. Her current thought was that if she moved again, the ceiling might come down. His dream had put a forest in the room. She could see branches outside the window too. The floorboards had begun to grow leaves. She wondered whether waking him would make everything fall. I left her before she decided.

I could not separate all these things into kinds. Some people surely were stopping others; some were moving faster than anyone around them. But there were also rooms in which each life went on, while almost nothing went on outside, and streets in which the people trying to enter could not keep up with those trying to leave.

One instant had begun this. We had all counted from it as though we were still counting together.

I thought of the woman on the station floor who had already used up days of patience. Of the man watching his wife's foot go through the kitchen door. Of the woman still reaching for a rail.

I had been looking for people who had gone somewhere else.

Some had not got through the beginning.

I was afraid to say it. I was more afraid of what might be done to places everyone thought were empty.

## Hour twenty-one

The stairwell came back to me with something new in it.

Light.

It lay across the woman's left hand. Where there had been a wall, there was a ragged opening. Plaster hung in the air beside it. Her fingers were still on their way toward the rail. The orange tag had begun to touch her wrist.

She was still falling. The light had caught in her sight. She was only just beginning to understand that the wall had opened.

I went looking for the opening from the other side.

A man in a hard hat stood beside a drill, looking through a hole in the concrete. His work lamp lit the broken stairwell beyond. He had made the opening hours earlier, while there was daylight in the street. He had stopped when he saw what he thought was a mannequin inside. He had left the lamp on it so the next men would see it too.

Now he held his phone beside the hole, comparing the shape with the photograph he had taken then. A hand had moved. Very little. It had not been in that position before.

There was a plan spread on the bonnet of a van beside him. MARINER COURT. He had been trying to find the load-bearing wall marked in red. The plan was old enough to show a shop which no longer existed. He was thinking of that error, annoyed by how many different things could make his job go wrong today.

My producer found the address. He found the command number for the district on a list a caller had given us. Three calls failed. A fourth was answered by someone who said we could not keep filling the line with rumours.

The man on the phone had heard me that morning.

"It isn't a rumour," I said.

"Like the infection?"

There was no way round the voice I had already put in his day.

"You shouldn't have believed me then."

"My daughter heard it. She wouldn't let me in."

He was giving off light. It was his new ability, and he did not know what it was for. He had stood in his own doorway explaining that he was still her father while the girl retreated into the house.

I heard the memory because he was thinking it now. I did not tell him that I could.

"Then don't believe me because I'm on the radio," I said. "Ask the man with the drill what he can see."

He put me on hold. Through the phone came other voices. Through the condition in my head came the worker again, stepping back from his new hole, trying not to look until someone else would look with him.

The woman inside was still moving toward the steps. Her elbow was on its way out to take the fall. She could see the lamp beyond the broken wall. She thought somebody might be looking in. It was a new thought, full of fear of being seen like this, of someone watching her fall and not putting out a hand.

The opening had not been there when I first caught her. The man outside had made it in the hours between. What he had left in her room was now arriving in her experience.

The officer returned.

"There's a person. He says her hand's moved since he took the picture. They can't tell if she's alive."

"She's reaching for the rail."

"They've seen other things that look like people."

"I know."

He had people coming toward Mariner Court from a stadium in which the ground had begun to tilt. Their route passed under the damaged building. Its front had peeled away that morning.
