stories.body:
# A Change of Hand

“Try not to call the thumb the customer's remaining hopes,” Elska said.

“That was one rehearsal.”

“That was a catalogue.”

“Then we educated several customers.”

Elska loosened the little brass screw beneath Scathe's grip. Her third finger would not straighten this afternoon. She worked with the other two, the rapier laid across her knees, while a war hammer on the adjoining chair explained to its carrier that it had never agreed to the fringe.

The fringe was bright yellow. It quivered with each objection.

Beyond the dressing-room curtain, the Feast of the Noble Blades was getting louder. A vendor had opened a flask of the expensive mountain oil; half the weapons in the west gallery were accusing him of dilution. Someone was demonstrating a quick-release scabbard by dropping a sword every few breaths. The sword's language suggested that the release worked very well.

Elska had come every year since Scathe's living root first took in her forge. In that first year the blade could manage three words through the reed in her guard: *hot*, *again*, and *Elska*. Now she gave unsolicited opinions on haircuts. The root was still a warm, narrow braid inside the tang, fed through a wick beneath the pommel cap. It let her speak through the reed and see through the little glass bead above it. It had never enabled her to lift her own weight.

“The chair has been reading our abstract,” Scathe said. “I heard him practicing ‘metacarpal.’”

“He can say ‘hand.’”

“He won't. He's a ceremonial mace.”

Elska smiled and lifted the rapier. The new support settled against the heel of her palm. Its thumb rest was broad enough to spread the pressure that, with the old grip, had gathered cruelly beneath one joint. She did not have to squeeze so hard. After nine months of cutting models, moving screws, and being told to rest, she could hold Scathe upright again without calculating how long it would be before she had to put her down.

Their half-hour panel was followed by a bench examination that ran until quarter past four. Elska had brought order slips as well as measurement paper.

The three-o'clock bell sounded. On the other side of the curtain, the mace struck the floor for quiet.

“She'll introduce us as ‘Master Elska and her demonstration weapon,’” Scathe said.

“He.”

“I'm speaking of the woman carrying him. He only likes to think he runs things.”

The woman announced Elska and Scathe by name. They looked at each other as well as a woman and a sword could.

“You owe me a sweet oil,” Elska said, and carried her out.

***

Their diagram was already hanging behind the demonstration table. Elska had drawn it herself, a hand in black ink around a red cross-section of the grip. Beneath it she had lettered Scathe's contribution, in a much smaller script: *Hand shown for purposes of illustration. Yours may vary.*

The hall was full. Human listeners occupied chairs. Blades without bodies rested in padded racks among them; polearms rose from the back rows like a winter wood. A buckler had insisted on facing the speakers from the breast of a particularly tall woman. To Elska's left, an elderly crossbow was making its carrier take notes.

Above the platform hung the convention's great banner: THE FEAST OF THE NOBLE BLADES. Only THE was gilded. A previous committee had tried giving equal prominence to FEAST and had failed to secure reelection.

Elska put Scathe on the table.

“Twenty years ago,” she began, “I stood here with a sword who knew three words.”

“It was a more economical presentation.”

“We have since learned to distribute our costs.”

The people who knew their act laughed first. Elska could pick them out without looking up. The man with the blue beard had sat in the same corner for six years. Last time, Scathe had told him his beard resembled a polishing accident. This year it was blue again.

Elska held up the old oval grip, dark walnut worn pale where her thumb had rested.

“An excellent shape for a hand that closes easily. My hand has recently become less enthusiastic.”

“We issued a formal complaint.”

“It has not replied. So.”

She indicated the drawing. Two brass rails ran beside the ordinary grip. One carried a thumb rest; the other supported a curved shelf beneath the heel of the palm. Each could be moved and fixed independently. Neither wrapped behind the hand.

She lifted Scathe again and slowly opened her fingers. With her thumb and palm still bearing against the supports, the blade remained level.

“You are transferring more of the load here, and here. You still need a hand. You need less of a fist.”

“Can it be locked?” called the buckler.

“No.”

“My bearer drops me.”

“Your bearer should be able to drop you.”

“She should be able to catch me afterward.”

Elska lowered her thumb and let Scathe fall onto the padded table. The buckler conceded, reluctantly, that the release was good.

Next came the old exercise. Scathe wore a cork button over her point. The assistant from the convention held out a padded rod; Elska turned a small thrust aside, recovered, and met the second. For sixteen years the rod had come high, low, high, low. At the fourth exchange Scathe said, “If he's still doing this after supper, leave him.”

The assistant grinned. The audience laughed. Elska had time to take a breath before the return.

They did it again. Her hand ached, but the ache stayed small. She could feel the sword's weight against the palm shelf and the familiar readiness of her living root. She had missed this. In winter she had begun rehearsing seated, with Scathe propped in a clamp. The clamp had held her perfectly and had been no company at all.

“The attachments can come off,” she said. “You keep your old grip. They can also be fitted to plain steel.”

A knife in the second row made an indignant sound.

“Some people have plain steel,” Scathe told it. “They still have hands.”

“Is the thumb angle fixed?” asked a woman in copper silk.

Three copper feathers stood above her dark hair. She sat beside a long, pale green scabbard tooled with leaves, rather than wearing it. As she raised her hand, Elska saw the fine joint at the wrist beneath her glove.

“Within a range,” Elska said.

“My right thumb doesn't bend at all. Solid ash. I wondered whether I could brace it against that rest without breaking it.”

The sword in the green scabbard was Ildesse; Elska remembered the name from the delegates' list. Ildesse's living thread let her move and speak through the wooden woman in copper silk. She could send that body six paces from her steel and had taken two chairs to seat both of herself comfortably.

“I'd need to examine the thumb,” Elska said. “And how much movement you get here.” She touched her own wrist. “I can't promise from across the room.”

“An encouraging answer. The last man promised me a new elbow before I'd taken my glove off.”

“Did you buy it?” Scathe asked.

“No. He wouldn't let me try it in a sleeve.”

Elska put down her pointer. “Which brings us to fitting. I'd like a different hand. Broader than mine, if possible. Someone who fences.”

A woman near the aisle stood. She wore a blue teaching jacket with one sleeve repaired at the elbow; her right hand was broad and her nails were cut almost to the quick.

“Rusha,” Scathe said, with a brightness Elska had not heard in the rehearsal.

“We found one another,” Rusha said. She climbed the platform steps and offered Elska her hand.

Elska knew her name too. Rusha taught on the western circuit, gave public bouts, and traveled with two enormous bags of masks. Scathe had read three notices about her aloud over breakfast. Elska had been trying to get a screw out of a flawed casting and had listened with half an ear.

She loosened the thumb rest and moved it out. Rusha's palm was wider, her thumb shorter. The first setting made her cock her wrist; the second let the shelf take some pressure without turning the point inward.

“Try a change from the high guard,” Elska said.

Rusha did. The extra brass checked against the base of her thumb. She tried again, more slowly.

“There,” Elska said. “You lose that little turn. For the quickest changes I'd take the support off. For an hour of the same work, you may prefer to keep it.”

“An hour?” Rusha smiled. “I teach nine-year-olds. Some days the same work lasts forever.”

“Do they know that?” Scathe asked.

“They are determined to prove it.”

Rusha turned Scathe over to look at the screws.

“How long to put her back on the oval? I have from half past three to quarter to four to try her. Then I'm booked with Helvek, before I choose for tomorrow's bout.”

Elska's fingers stayed on the brass rail.

“Tomorrow's bout?”

“At the South Yard.” Rusha glanced at Scathe. “Your letter said we'd have you fitted after the talk.”

The crossbow's carrier went on writing. Somewhere at the back, a lance asked its neighbor which way round the little shelf went.

“My letter,” Scathe said.

“What did you say?” Elska asked.

“I asked if she'd try me.”

“For a bout.”

“For the circuit. If we suited.”

Rusha looked at Elska's hand, still touching the grip. “I thought you knew.”

“She didn't,” Scathe said. “I said ‘we.’ I hadn't asked.”

Elska could hear the reed now, the small effort behind the fine carrying voice. The diagram at her back showed the supports fitted to her own hand, knuckles enlarged with an accuracy she regretted. She had thought Scathe would be proud of it. Scathe had been proud of it. Both could be true, apparently, while Elska stood in front of a hall of people and learned what else had been happening in her workshop.

She could say, certainly, of course, take her. She knew precisely how to make it sound like an excellent advertisement.

“We have the bench examination after this,” Scathe said. “Elska, talk to me afterward. I shouldn't have made this part of the presentation.”

Rusha began taking her hand out of the grip.

“Stay for the fitting,” Scathe said. “If you will. That's what you came up for.”

“The trial can't wait until after the examination. I've promised Helvek an answer at four, and we rehearse then.”

“I know. I'm staying for the bench.”

“I haven't promised you the bout.”

“I know that too.”

The reed went quiet.

Elska tightened the screw. “Try the high guard once more. This setting may still be a little wide.”

***

After Rusha's fitting, a large man in a padded fencing coat held up his left hand. His sword spoke first.

“He won't volunteer. He's afraid he'll be asked to fight somebody.”

“I am not,” said the man.

“He's a registrar. He has come for the finishing oils.”

“I fence on Thursdays.”

Elska invited him up.

His palm was broad, but his thumb reached farther than Rusha's. He held his own sword so tightly that the tip trembled. Elska reversed the supports on their rails and placed Scathe in his left hand. Scathe was lighter, and after Elska moved the shelf he was able to loosen his fingers. He seemed surprised that she stayed in his hand.

Rusha had remained at the end of the table. Elska gave her the padded rod.

“Can you put him through the exercise?”

“Which exercise?”

“A simple one.”

Rusha looked at the registrar. “Do you know a low parry?”

“Yes.”

“Show me.”

He showed her. She sent the rod down toward his thigh; he turned it aside, bringing Scathe too far across his body to recover easily.

“A shorter turn,” Rusha said. “Again.”

At the third try, Scathe said, “That's enough hand. You needn't push the rest of him through it.”

The registrar laughed, lost his guard, and received a soft tap on the padded thigh of his fencing coat.

“That's my fault,” Scathe said. “I'll save it until afterward.”

Elska watched Rusha vary the attack. Once she began high and changed her mind. Once she paused until the registrar made an impatient little movement, then sent the rod in. He missed it. Scathe missed it with him. At the next attempt he made a smaller turn; the support took the load, and he brought the point back to line.

“There,” Scathe said, quietly this time.

He did it again. The sword said nothing. The man looked up, waiting for confirmation.

“You felt it,” Scathe said.

Rusha glanced toward Elska. Elska held out her hand for the rod and asked the registrar what ached. He showed her the side of his thumb. She moved the rest a little farther out.

From the front row, the blue-bearded man called, “Can I order one for a saber?”

“Bring it to the bench.”

“You'll pay extra for that beard,” Scathe said.

“Only if it sheds,” Elska said.

The laughter was smaller than usual. Elska was grateful for that. She explained the limits of the fittings for curved guards, answered a question about gauntlets, and showed how to take the supports off without opening the protected channel that held the living root. When she finished, the chair mace announced their bench number and threatened anybody who wanted to ask a sixth question.

Rusha returned Scathe to the table.

“Thank you,” she said to Elska. “I'll come past before I leave.”

She went down the steps and out by the west door. Scathe's glass bead followed her until the door closed.

At the bench, Elska examined a saber, a plain practice foil, and Ildesse's wooden thumb. The saber wished its bearer would admit that she was sixty. The bearer wanted the supports in silver. Elska told her what silver would cost and left them to argue.

Ildesse took off her glove and drew back the copper sleeve. She watched Elska test the range of the wrist.

“I like these hands,” she said. “I'd like to keep them.”

“We can work around that.” Elska made a drawing, asked her to close the hand again, and changed the angle. “Leave the glove with me for a pattern?”

The quarter-to-four bell sounded. Scathe's glass bead faced the west door.

“The left one. I need my right hand dressed for the evening.” Ildesse worked the little pearl buttons free. “I wore these to the Ousel Room a fortnight ago. I'd like to get more than one season out of them.”

Elska took the left. Scathe offered to remember the wrist measurements. Elska wrote them down.

***

After the bench examination, Elska carried Scathe back to the dressing room. The hammer and its fringe had gone. There was a yellow thread on the empty chair.

She shut the curtain, set the rapier across the arms, and sat opposite her. Her hand was tired. It had held up.

“How long?”

“I had the polish boy write it down and post it three weeks ago. While you were at the foundry.”

“We rehearsed every evening.”

“Yes.”

“And you said nothing.”

Scathe's root made a small warmth through the walnut. Elska rested her hand against it and then moved her hand away.

“I wanted to tell you when the talk had gone well,” the sword said. “You worked so hard on the grip.”

“I did.”

“I like it.”

“I know. You told me.”

“I thought you'd think I didn't.”

Elska looked at the reed. “Let me do my own thinking.”

“All right.”

In the hall somebody cheered. Elska hoped the quick-release sword had finally caught its demonstrator.

“Why now?” she asked.

“I've wanted to for a while. I kept thinking we'd have a different exercise next year.”

“We could.”

“You'd tell me what was coming.”

Elska rubbed the joint beneath her thumb. Even this afternoon, with the registrar, she had wanted Rusha to settle into the familiar high, low, high, low. It would have made the work look better. Scathe had gone still in the man's hand, waiting for what Rusha might do.

“You had a good life here,” she said.

“I know.”

Elska looked away first.

“I won't have customers bringing me news about you.”

“I won't do that again.”

“You might have had to wait. If you'd asked me three weeks ago.”

“How long?”

“I don't know.”

Scathe did not help her by saying it didn't matter.

The curtain rustled. Rusha spoke from the other side, asking whether they were ready to see her. Elska took a breath and let her in.

“Helvek has tomorrow's bout,” Rusha said. “I kept my appointment with him. We still haven't had our trial, Scathe, and with Helvek I know what we can do.”

Scathe said nothing.

“I can take a second blade as far as Harrow Fair. Three weeks. Most of the work will be lessons. I have pupils who grip the life out of their swords, and some swords who enjoy telling them they're idiots.”

“I used to enjoy that,” Scathe said.

“You caught yourself today. I liked it. We'd try actual bouts along the way, after we'd learned something about each other. I can offer you that.”

“And after the fair?”

“We decide again.”

Elska asked about the traveling chest. Rusha brought it in from the hall: a slim case lined in wool, with room for a wrapped blade and a place for the wick flask. A new traveling chest. Scathe had thought of that too. Or Rusha had. Elska could not ask about every item in their correspondence.

“I want to go,” Scathe said.

“Yes,” Elska said.

She fetched the small screwdriver. Rusha's setting was too wide for the palm shelf; she had seen that on the last turn. It took only a little adjustment. She made Rusha take the rapier and hold a guard, then lower the point, then hold it again. She checked that the pommel cap could be opened in the case.

The old grip lay beside her tools.

“Could you leave me that?” she asked.

Scathe took a moment to answer. “I'll need it for the bouts.”

“The supports come off this one.”

“I know how that one feels.”

Elska picked it up. The walnut was warm from the afternoon, worn to the shape of her thumb. She turned it over once and wrapped it in a scrap of cloth for Rusha's case.

“Then take it.”

Rusha stepped outside to fetch her other bag. Elska stayed by the table.

“Will you come next year?” she asked.

“I don't know what she'll be doing.”

“What you'll be doing.”

“What I'll be doing. I can send you wear notes.”

Elska shut the tool case. “Send me a letter. You have plenty of words.”

“I will.”

“And an address. When you have one.”

From outside came Rusha's voice asking a porter to stop leaning her other sword against the wall. Scathe's reed stirred.

“Go on,” Elska said.

Rusha returned and took the rapier in her hand. She carried the traveling case under her other arm; in its pocket were the old grip, the feeding flask, and Elska's instructions. They went through the curtain together.

Elska could still hear Scathe asking about the case as Rusha took her across the hall. The sword disliked the brass hinges. Rusha said they would have to do until Harrow.

Elska moved to the curtain. For a moment the little glass bead in the guard faced her through the people moving between them. Then Rusha turned to avoid a polearm, and Scathe went with her.

Elska held the curtain aside until they had passed out of sight.

stories.title: The Other Half
stories.prompt: A teenage superhero couple are having their first real argument. The girl, despite being frequently in the tabloids for her anger issues and destructive tendencies, is completely opposed to killing and the quiet and sweet natured boy has just put down one of their nastier enemies.
stories.body:
# The Other Half

Kit had saved her the crispiest chips.

They were cold now. He held the paper bag open between his knees while Dara peeled off her gloves, and the smell of vinegar came up into the photo booth. Above the screen, a cartoon couple instructed them to MAKE A MEMORY.

"You don't have to eat," Kit said.

"I know."

He put the bag on the little shelf beside the coin slot. Then he took her gloves, folded them together and balanced them on top. Dara watched him tuck in the fingers. He had done that on the bus last week, when she fell asleep against him and dropped one down the back of the seat.

Outside the curtain, someone called for a stretcher. Not the one by the jeweller's. Another one. Dara looked at the gap Kit had left open, the strip of food court with its overturned yellow chairs.

"They told us to stay where they could see us."

He pulled the curtain back another few inches.

The booth was beside the shuttered pretzel place. They always came here after a date, even when they couldn't afford pictures. You could sit down and be together without someone lifting a phone. Sometimes they made faces at their reflection in the dead screen. Kit could cross one eye independently of the other. Dara had spent an entire Saturday trying to do it and given herself a headache.

Now the screen reflected the orange shoulders of her padded Racket jacket, his pale blue sleeve, the empty space between them. His mask was pushed up into his sandy hair. There was dust in his eyelashes.

Something scratched beneath her jacket collar. She reached for it, and Kit leaned closer.

"You've got grit back there. Let me."

"In a minute."

"Did you text your mum?" she asked.

"Yes. She'll meet us here."

They were meant to go to his house afterward. His mum had bought the horrible frozen pizzas Dara liked. They were meant to finish a film which Kit had definitely watched without her, though he kept denying it.

He looked toward the curtain. "The officer said she'll come over when she's done with the witnesses. I gave the medics my name. Told them it was me."

"You should've waited."

"For what?"

"For your mum. Before a statement. That's what we're supposed to do."

"It's only my name. I know they could arrest me. I'll tell the officer the rest when Mum gets here."

Dara rubbed the grooves the gloves had left around her fingers. She had been allowed to stand by the stretcher for a moment. The medic had said she was sorry. Dara had said, "No, he's Switchjack," as if that corrected anything, and the medic had repeated that she was sorry.

"Did the hold go wrong?"

Kit turned toward her.

"Were you watching me too?" she said. "When I took that girl out. Is that when it happened?"

"It didn't go wrong."

She waited. Somewhere behind the curtain, a radio crackled into words and stopped.

"Then what happened?"

He was looking straight at her. She wanted him to look away so she could stop looking too.

"I made him stop. All of him."

Dara's thumb kept moving across her finger. Back and forth, over the same groove.

Four years ago, when they were thirteen, they had sat on folding chairs in a training room while a doctor went through what their powers could do to a person. They had been given juice afterward. Kit had swapped his apple for her orange. Nobody had hidden this from her. Stillness could kill. A blow through living flesh could kill. They knew.

"By accident."

It came out as an instruction.

"No," he said.

She stood too fast and struck her shoulder against the booth wall. Kit half rose. She put out a hand and he sat back down.

"Don't."

"Okay."

There was nowhere to stand. Her boots took up nearly all the floor. She could walk out past the curtain, but then she would be in the food court where everybody could see her, and she wasn't ready to be there.

"He wasn't doing anything anymore."

"I know."

"You had him."

"I know, Dara."

"Stop saying that."

He pressed his palms together between his knees.

She had left them by the jeweller's, Switchjack motionless on the tiles, Kit watching him. Switchjack's fingers had been caught halfway through the little walking gesture he used to move people. Kit had stopped those fingers and her hand together. She remembered the terrible pause with her palm against a support column, the force building in it, strangers underneath the ceiling she was being made to bring down. Then Kit had said her name. Her hand had become hers again.

She had shoved the frightened girl through an emergency door. She had gone back for the girl's dad. She had shouted because people wouldn't move. By the time she returned, Kit was kneeling beside Switchjack, saying something Dara couldn't hear.

"The capture van was coming."

"I could hear it."

"So you could have waited."

"Yes."

She wanted another word after it. But, or except, or something that would change the shape of what he had admitted. Kit's face was pale beneath the dust, and his mouth was still his mouth, the crooked bit at one corner where he smiled first.

"Why would you do that?"

He looked down at his hands. "I was going to wait. Then I thought about him getting out."

"You don't know."

"He got out of North House. He got out of the other place."

"They were changing the cells. They told us."

"They told us last time too."

She lowered herself onto the bench, as far from him as she could get. It wasn't far. The seam on his trouser leg almost touched hers.

"You can't just decide they're going to fail."

"It's not just them failing. It's who he finds when they do."

His voice stayed quiet. She had liked that about him. She had liked how he waited when she got tangled in a story, how he never stepped into the gap to finish it for her.

Now she wanted him to shout. Then she could shout back without hearing herself be the only one.

"You killed someone, Kit."

"I know."

"A person."

"I know he was a person."

"Then why are you talking about him like a door you finally got shut?"

His head came up. "That's not what I'm doing."

"You're saying it worked."

"It did."

She turned toward the curtain. The bag on the shelf crackled as one of her gloves slid off it. Kit caught the glove before it fell. Without thinking, without looking pleased with himself, he caught it.

"He won't get to you again," he said.

Her stomach dropped. For one clean instant she was glad. No fingers moving at the edge of a crowd. No waking up with her hand clenched around something and having to open it, prove she could open it. No more videos of her smiling while he made her hurt.

Then she looked at Kit holding the glove.

"Don't say that like it's a present."

"I didn't mean it like that."

"You can't put it on me."

"I'm not."

"You just did."

He put her glove beside its mate. He was careful about it. She hated how careful he was being and hated herself for wanting his hands to shake.

"There were other people," he said. "That girl's dad. Milla from school. The guards he took with him last time. I'm not saying it was only you."

"But you're saying me."

"Yes. I was there. I saw your hand."

"It wasn't my hand."

"I know."

"You don't. You think you know because you saw it."

She had been wearing the same jacket when she broke the school's trophy case. The photograph had been in three papers: RACKET'S LATEST SMASH HIT. It had come back out when she broke a shopfront getting somebody away from a fire, and again when she tore the roof off an occupied car. There was always the school photograph beside the new one, so you knew what kind of girl you were looking at.

That afternoon at school, the deputy head had said she couldn't go on the excursion with three weeks of work missing. Dara had said half those absences were rescues. He had said half was not all. She had come out of his office and put her fist through the glass case in the corridor.

Kit had held her wrist, but the pulse had already gone through. A corner of glass had caught him above the eye. He'd needed glue at the clinic. She had apologized over and over, bought him sweets, done his share of their assignment. Eventually he had laughed at something and she had let that mean they were all right.

The little white mark was visible now. His mask never quite covered it.

"I don't kill people," she said.

"I didn't say you did."

"I won't. Not him either."

Kit rubbed at the edge of his mask. "I thought you'd understand."

"Because I smash things?"

"No."

"Because I'm the mad one?"

"Because you know what he's like."

She had heard the first two answers he hadn't given anyway. She wanted to keep hitting them. It would be easier than the one he had.

"I do know. I wanted you to hold him until they got here. I wanted him locked up."

"For how long?"

"As long as it takes."

"And next time?"

"There doesn't have to be a next time."

He closed his eyes briefly. She could see him choosing what to say, the same way he chose which bit of bad news to give her first when somebody had posted something. Usually she let him.

"I don't want to keep meeting the next people," he said.

She couldn't answer that. She wanted him to have said something stupid.

"Neither do I."

He looked at her, waiting for an answer she didn't have.

"That doesn't mean you get to kill him."

The words came out too loud. A woman passing the booth paused, saw their masks, then kept going. Dara couldn't tell whether she had heard.

Kit shifted away from the gap in the curtain.

"I'm sorry," Dara said, and then, furious, "Not about that. I'm not sorry about that."

"I didn't ask you to be."

"You look like I kicked you."

He looked at her for a long time. There had never been a silence between them this long when neither was doing something else.

"I didn't think it would be easy to tell you," he said. "I thought after I told you, you'd still want to sit by me."

She was sitting by him. He knew that wasn't what he meant; so did she. She pulled her jacket sleeve over her bare hand, something to do instead of letting him see it curl into a fist.

"Promise me you won't do it again."

He didn't answer.

"Kit."

"I heard you."

"So say it."

He looked toward the food court. She could hear a cleaner trying to move chairs out of the ambulance crew's way, telling somebody she could manage, really, if they'd just let her lift it.

"I won't wreck anything," Dara said. "Like at school. I know that was horrible. I won't do it anymore, and you won't do this, and we can just..."

She stopped. Kit's expression had changed.

"Please don't," he said.

"I'm trying."

"You promised after school. You promised before that too."

"This is different."

"It always is."

She stared at him. He pressed his lips together, too late.

"That's what you think?"

"I didn't mean always."

"Yes, you did."

"Sometimes you say it's different and I still have to get in the way."

She looked at the white mark above his eye. He hadn't pointed at it. She would almost have preferred if he had.

"You should've told me," she said.

"I did. At the clinic."

He had. He had said he couldn't do that every time, and she had been crying, and she had told him she knew. Then she'd been so happy when he'd put his arm around her.

She pulled her sleeve further over her hand.

"I don't get to do it again," she said. "I know. I don't get to keep being horrible because you stay. But you can't use it for this."

"I'm not trying to."

"You are. Maybe you don't mean to, but you are."

He leaned back against the booth wall. His mask slipped forward; he took it off and held it in his lap. Underneath, his forehead looked much younger.

"Are you going to promise?" she asked.

"I can't promise I'll never."

She had imagined him saying it reluctantly. She had imagined believing him because she needed to. She hadn't let herself imagine this.

"If there's someone else," he said, "and it's happening again. I can't say I'll just keep doing what we did before."

"You can stop someone without killing them. You did. Tonight."

"You asked me about never."

"You're making up a worse one so you don't have to promise about this one."

He shook his head, but he didn't answer. Outside, the cleaner succeeded in moving a chair. Its metal legs scraped across the tiles.

Dara took her phone out. Her fingers wouldn't unlock it. She pressed her thumb too hard, then tried again.

"What are you doing?"

"Calling my mum."

"My mum can take us."

"I want mine."

He nodded. She looked down at the screen, at her own name on a message from home asking what time she would be back. There was a little dancing cat after the question. Her mother had recently learned how to send them and was using them for everything.

"Dara."

She waited with her thumb above the call button.

"Aren't you glad?"

She looked at him.

"That he can't anymore," Kit said. "Please. You don't have to say anything else. Just that."

His eyes had gone wet. This was the moment she would usually move closer. He wouldn't ask twice. She would put her shoulder against his, and he would tip his head down until their foreheads met, and there would be somewhere to begin again.

Her own eyes hurt. It was cruel to let him sit there asking. It was cruel of him to ask.

"Yes," she said.

He breathed out.

"Don't do that," Dara said.

His mouth closed.

"I'm glad he can't make me do things. I'm glad I don't have to be scared of him. I hate that I'm glad he's dead. Is that enough?"

"I wasn't trying to make you say that."

"I don't know what you were trying to make me say."

He wiped his face with the heel of his hand. He looked embarrassed, then angry with himself for looking embarrassed. Dara knew all those small changes. She knew him. That was what she couldn't get past.

Her mother answered on the second ring.

"Hi. Were the pizzas good?"

Dara tried to say Mum. Nothing happened. She took a breath which caught halfway, and Kit moved toward her before he remembered.

"Dara?"

"Can you come get me?"

Her mother stopped asking about pizza.

Dara gave the shopping centre's name, the entrance the responders were using. She said she wasn't hurt. She had to say it twice. No, she didn't need the hospital. Yes, Kit was here. No, he couldn't bring her home.

"I'll come inside," her mother said. "Stay with the medics. I'll find you."

When the call ended, Dara held the phone against her jacket. Through the open part of the curtain, she could see an officer talking to a man wrapped in a silver blanket. Soon it would be their turn. She would say what she had seen. Kit would say what he had done. There wasn't a version of this that could be finished inside the booth.

He reached for the bag of chips and stopped with his hand halfway there.

"Do you want me to go out?" he asked.

She didn't know. She wanted him gone and she wanted him to have been here all along doing something else, complaining about the film or saving her chips, anything she could understand how to answer.

"Don't touch me," she said.

His hand came back to his knee. "Okay."

That was all. He didn't say he hadn't been going to. He didn't try to make it a different request.

They sat with the curtain open. Her mother would have to come past the pretzel place, and Dara watched that end of the food court. Kit watched the officer.

After a while, Dara took a glove from the shelf. She started pushing her fingers into it, then stopped. The grit beneath her collar was scratching again.

She reached behind herself. Her fingers caught the collar, the mask strap, her hair. She couldn't find it.

Kit saw what she was trying to do. His hand stayed on his knee.

Dara kept trying until she got the grit out.

stories.title: Catch Me
stories.prompt: Not all magical girls have the age you would expect, some are actually adults that turn into magical girls when transformed. You can usually recognize them because they are the ones that go full 'Mama Bear' when something happens to one of their girls.
stories.body:
# Catch Me

The boy in the chip shop asked if their mums were waiting outside.

Mavis looked up at him beneath her pink curls. In this body she was thirteen, two years younger than Nika, with puffed pink sleeves, a little heart on each boot, and a voice like the smallest bell on a bicycle.

"I'm forty-seven, love. And you've charged us for three large. That one's a small."

The boy inspected the till. Nika inspected the ceiling.

It wasn't the correction. Nika did want their money back. It was the *love*, and the way Mavis had licked her thumb to separate the notes, and the fact that the deadliest person Nika knew was presently asking whether they still did the loyalty card.

Mavis caught a bottle the boy knocked off the counter. A pink flower opened under it; the bottle sank gently into the light. She returned it upright, accepted their change, and put the receipt in her sleeve.

"There. Supper."

Outside, twelve-year-old Alma was trying to tie the torn handle of their equipment bag. She had already joined the two ends with a loop of green light. She put a finger through the loop and pulled. The canvas strained; the knot stayed exactly the same size.

She tried to squash the loop between her palms. It stayed round.

"I can carry it now," she said.

"I've got it." Nika took the bag and hooked it over the shoulder opposite her own satchel. "You take the chips."

"I can take both."

But Nika was already opening her wings. The right one caught the shop awning. She folded it, ducked, and tried again, with two bags banging against her hips.

Alma watched her clear the awning, then looked at Mavis.

"Wednesday," Nika said, before either of them could say anything. "Can I take point on Wednesday?"

"We haven't finished talking about that."

"I got the turns right all last week."

"You did." Mavis handed Alma the small bag of chips. "Come down and eat yours while they're hot."

Nika landed. It was difficult to look ready for command while reaching around two bags for a wooden fork.

Mavis, whose magical name was Peony, had been Peony since she was thirteen. Other things had changed. She had a grown son, a car that made a noise on left turns, and glasses she only needed when she wasn't transformed. The curls and little heart boots had remained. Nika had once seen a photograph of her standing next to her son at his graduation. He looked like a young man posing with his baby sister.

Alma had chosen Clover. Nika was Skylark, which came with wings taller than she was, pale gold at the roots and violet at the tips. Of the three of them, only Nika could fly. She thought this should count for rather more than it did.

They ate on the low wall beside Mavis's car. The street was busy with people leaving the cinema. Down at the corner, a carousel turned behind the windows of the closed toy shop, its horses rising and falling for nobody.

"Your coat's on the back seat," Mavis said.

"I'm warm."

"You won't be sparkly all night."

Nika's mother had said precisely the same thing before Nika left the house. It sounded worse coming from somebody whose feet didn't quite reach the pavement.

"I know where it is."

Mavis ate a chip. She didn't pursue it. Somehow that was annoying too.

Nika was about to explain her Wednesday route, including the shortcut Alma wouldn't have to jump, when the carousel stopped.

One horse remained at the top of its pole. Another hung low. Their painted eyes all faced the street.

A tall display cabinet beside it opened two eyes in the carved crest above its glass door.

"Oh," Alma said.

The thing pushed through the toy-shop window, taking the frame with it. Its surface looked like varnished wood, but a breath shuddered through it. Four long legs unfolded beneath the plinth. Its glass front swung outward on heavy hinges, and the shelves inside flexed like ribs.

The cinema crowd screamed and broke apart.

Mavis was off the wall before her chips hit the pavement.

"Alma, take the people toward the cinema. Nika, above it. See how many."

Nika dropped both bags. One wingbeat put her level with the thing's carved top.

There was only one. Its eyes rolled upward to follow her. Along the inside of its door sat rows of the shop's china dolls, with porcelain faces and limp cloth legs. Paper price tags hung from their wrists; bright little hooks held them upright.

"New ones," it said, in a voice like a music box winding down. "Three new ones."

Mavis struck its front leg. A burst of pink light drove the foot through the pavement. She stayed between it and the people, small enough that its brass-coloured handle would have passed over her head.

It reached around her.

Alma was helping a man lift a fallen pushchair. She had her back to the long arm coming from the cabinet's side. Mavis was under its other arm. Nobody else could reach Alma in time.

Nika dived.

She hit Alma shoulder first and sent her sliding beneath the cinema canopy. The metal fingers closed on Nika's left wing.

They didn't crush it. They stroked the violet feathers flat.

"Mind the paint."

Nika beat the free wing, hard enough to wrench her back. The thing folded her into its top compartment. Her feet struck the upper shelf. Its door swung shut. Something caught behind her shoulders; the left wing stopped moving.

She slammed both hands against the glass.

"Mavis!"

Below her, Peony went still.

The cabinet bent forward, bringing its carved face down toward Mavis.

"Little doll," it crooned. "Your turn."

Mavis put a hand on its outstretched wrist.

"Let go of her."

The cabinet giggled. Then its wrist broke away in a shower of polished splinters.

The noise Mavis made next did not fit through thirteen-year-old lungs.

It struck the glass against Nika's palms. Pink light raced up the cabinet in great overlapping petals. The long arm came off. Its carved cornice split down the middle. For an instant, every doll on every shelf bowed forward as though a wind had passed through them.

The cabinet stopped giggling.

It scrambled backward. Its legs extended, lifting Nika above the toy-shop roof. The movement drove a hook deeper through the stiff feathers at her wing's root.

Pain flashed across her shoulder.

"Stop!"

Mavis stopped before Nika had finished the word.

The creature tried to turn away from her. She caught its remaining arm and hauled it back so hard that one foot ploughed a white furrow through the road. It made a little descending chime.

"Not you," Mavis said. "You stay."

Nika could see Alma under the canopy. The man and the pushchair were safely inside. Alma stood with green cord shining between her hands, looking upward.

Mavis climbed the cabinet's side. There was nothing delicate about it. She kicked footholds into its surface and pulled herself up by the broken edges. The creature tried to shake her off; flowers burst under her boots, driving her weight back into it.

Her pink curls appeared beyond the glass.

"Where's it hurting?"

"Shoulder. My wing's stuck."

"All right. Don't pull."

"I wasn't."

"I know, sweetheart. I know."

She took hold of the door's upper edge. As she forced it outward, a gap opened between the glass and the frame. Cold air touched Nika's face.

Behind Nika, the hook shifted.

"That's enough. That's enough!"

Mavis held the gap where it was. She was braced sideways between door and frame, her small boots planted on opposite edges. Nika could see the muscles standing out in her arms.

The opening was wide enough for a person. It wasn't wide enough for her spread wings. The left one was pinned flat against the back panel, with the hook through its stiff feathers beside her spine. There was no room to turn the wing and lift it off; any tug would pull at her shoulder.

"Can I break that bit?" Mavis asked.

Nika felt behind her with one hand, but couldn't reach the hook's base or turn far enough to see it.

"Not without twisting me."

"Then I won't."

The cabinet tried to close its door. Mavis pushed back. Pink petals opened along her sleeves; each one crumpled against the frame, and another took its place.

From this close, Nika could see a little heart on Mavis's glove. One stitch had come loose.

She looked through the gap. Below it were an overturned display of spinning tops, the striped cinema canopy, and a great deal of pavement.

She had never looked down from this height without wings.

"If I change back," she said, "it won't have anything to hold."

Mavis looked at her.

Nika almost took it back. She wanted Mavis to produce another answer, one with no empty air in it.

But there was the hook behind her. There was the gap. There were her own ordinary clothes, waiting under all this light.

"I need you to catch me."

Mavis glanced down. Her fingers tightened on the door.

"I have to keep this open."

"Alma can."

Alma's face lifted when she heard her name.

Nika pointed through the gap. A carved knob stood on the door's upper corner. Its matching knob stuck out of split wood on the frame, above Mavis's foot.

"Tie those two. Keep them this far apart."

Alma came out from under the canopy. The cabinet's loose legs stamped; she ducked back from one and sent her green cord upward. Its first loop slipped over the door knob.

Mavis watched the second end climbing toward the frame.

"The broken side won't take it," she said. "Use the brass catch. Just below my heel."

"I can reach," Alma said.

Her cord changed direction. It passed twice around the catch, came back through its own loop, and pulled tight. Alma closed her fingers. The knot shone white at its centre, and the green line set rigidly across the gap.

Mavis eased one hand away.

The door held.

Alma grinned, briefly and fiercely. "Got it."

Mavis reached into the gap, and Nika stretched her free hand toward hers. The cabinet bucked; the ledge under Mavis's boot on the door broke away. She swung down around the outside, caught a lower stretch of frame with one hand, and reached back toward Nika. Her fingertips stopped below the shelf, and the knob creaked in its socket.

Nika had watched Alma's little knot outlast a bag handle. The knot would hold. The knob might not.

"Another one," she said. "Round the whole door."

Alma was already feeding out cord.

"Mavis, go. Tell me when you're there."

Mavis looked from the knot to Nika. She had been speaking in her ordinary voice, small and practical and high. Now she said, "Don't move until I tell you," and something in it reached all the way down to the pavement.

"I won't."

Mavis let go.

For one dreadful moment she was falling too. Then a flower flared beneath her feet. She landed in a crouch, and the flower flattened and burst.

The cabinet lurched sideways. Nika's cheek struck the frame. Below, Mavis ran with it, keeping herself under the opening. Alma's second cord looped around the door and back through the heavy brass catch.

"Done!" Alma shouted.

The first knob tore loose inside its green loop. The second knot caught the door before it could close, and the glass shuddered a hand's breadth from Nika's face.

Nika's breath came in little bites. She could not seem to fit enough air into her chest.

She looked down again.

Mavis stood just past the striped canopy. She had her feet apart and her hands raised. Beneath the curls, her face was terribly intent.

"Here," she called. "I've got you."

Nika could see the road behind her, the broken glass to her right. She could see the empty space between them.

She put both hands on the frame and worked her toes over the shelf's edge. The trapped wing pulled painfully at her back. She leaned as far through the opening as she could.

"Catch me."

She let the magic go.

The hook slipped through nothing. Her wings vanished; the bright costume went with them. For a fraction of a second, she hung in her jeans and thin sweatshirt, startled by how small her own body was.

She pitched herself forward and dropped through the gap.

The canopy rushed upward. Her stomach stayed behind. She tried to breathe and made a sound she would never have chosen to make in front of anyone.

Pink sleeves filled the world.

Petals folded around her back and legs, thick and yielding. She sank through them into Mavis's arms. They bent together; Mavis slid backward across the road, one boot scoring the grit, and Nika's face hit the soft place beneath her chin.

For a moment she heard nothing but two people breathing.

Mavis smelled of vinegar and the hand cream she kept in the car.

"There," she said. Her voice shook. "There."

The cabinet's shadow moved over them.

Mavis put Nika on her feet beneath the canopy. She kept one arm across her until Nika nodded.

"Stay with Alma."

Nika took Alma's wrist and drew her backward. Alma let the door knot go.

The cabinet opened its mouth.

Mavis caught the edge of the glass with both hands.

This time there was nobody inside it.

She tore the door off.

The cabinet tried to fold its legs and run. Peony hit it with its own door. A single enormous flower opened behind her, bright enough to turn every window on the street pink. The creature went flat, four legs splayed, with its shelves rattling against one another.

It made a faint ticking noise.

Mavis planted one heart-shaped boot on its fallen head.

"Alma. Tie its feet, please."

"To each other?"

"Yes. All four."

Nika held Alma's sleeve while she worked, keeping her back from the broken glass. Alma tightened the final loop, and Nika offered her a hand across the glass.

By the time the street wardens arrived, the cabinet was still breathing but had stopped ticking. Mavis gave them a very precise account of which arm it had lost and where the other hooks were.

Then she came back to the girls.

"Let's go home."

Her curls dissolved in pink light. The heart boots became scuffed trainers. Forty-seven-year-old Mavis stood in her fleece and jeans, with a broad face, a streak of grey at her temple, and the glasses she pushed into place with one knuckle.

She searched her pocket for the car keys.

They jingled against one another. She tried to pick out the right key, and missed.

Nika watched her try again.

The woman who had hit a monster with its own front door couldn't make her fingers close around a key.

"Mavis."

"Hmm?"

"We're here."

"I know." Mavis looked up quickly. "I know you are."

Nika put her hand over the keys. Mavis let her take them.

"Alma first," Nika said. "Her mum'll be waiting."

"Yes. Good."

Nika unlocked the car. Alma climbed into the back, quietly, and Nika got her coat from behind the passenger seat.

She put it on. She could feel the cold now, and her shoulder hurt. There were bits of glass in the tread of her shoes. For a moment, while she tried to get her arm into the second sleeve, the pavement seemed much too far away.

Mavis steadied the coat at her elbow.

Nika turned toward her. "Can you zip it?"

Mavis caught the little metal tab between both hands.

"Course I can, love."

Nika stood still until she had.

stories.title: The Goat of Honor
stories.prompt: So, you just got isekai'd into another world and given a special ability. That ability, however, is simply called shenanigans. There is no other context for this ability, just shenanigans. Other than that, you've got nothing to go off of, just best of luck.
stories.body:
# The Goat of Honor

The last thing I remembered was holding my sister's coat while she went back onto the roller coaster. Then I was in a field, still holding the coat, with a word hanging in front of my face.

**SHENANIGANS**

Underneath, in smaller letters: **Best of luck.**

I knew, with the same certainty that I knew my own name, that this was my special ability. I did not know how I knew. The letters vanished when I reached for them, leaving me with my sister's denim jacket, my own clothes, and a field that smelt of hot grass. Blue leaves shifted in the trees beyond it. Something with six legs was eating a hedge.

“Shenanigans,” I said.

The hedge continued to be eaten.

I tried saying it more forcefully, then silently. I held out one hand. I held out both hands. Finally I asked for a sandwich, which seemed a reasonable thing to ask of a power that had removed me from within walking distance of one.

Nothing happened.

There was music beyond the trees. I folded my sister's coat carefully and followed it.

The fair had striped tents, a turning wooden wheel, and the reassuring smell of onions frying. Its entrance was a gap between two carts. A man with a spear stood in the gap, collecting coins in a leather cup. He wore a brass helmet and had shaved himself with the sort of thoroughness that leaves a man pink.

“Three coppers.”

“I haven't got any.”

“Then you can look from here.”

Looking from there would not get me onions. “Is there work?”

He glanced at my red trainers. “Sell those.”

Beside him, a little wooden king was hanging above a puppet stall. It had a horsehair moustache, a painted sneer, and a crown that looked much more securely attached than its head.

I looked from the king to the guard.

Perhaps it was hunger. Perhaps the word in my head had loosened something that normally kept suggestions inside it.

“Careful,” I said. “Your moustache is coming off.”

“I haven't got a—”

The puppet's moustache crossed the gap between us and landed on his upper lip.

For a moment we both stood still. It was a magnificent moustache, curling nearly to his ears. He seized one end and pulled. The other end curled round his finger.

“Don't stretch it!” shouted a woman from behind the stall.

I stepped sideways into the fair while the guard was trying to say several things through horsehair. The woman caught my sleeve. She had dark hair cut square under her ears, a red shirt with the sleeves rolled up, and a short blue coat repaired with patches of orange cloth. Her hands were stained with paint.

“Did you throw that?” she asked.

“I don't think so.”

“You don't think so.”

“I'm having a difficult morning.”

She looked at me for another second, then at the guard. “Stop pulling, Gedd. It cost eight coppers. I'll fetch oil.” She pushed the puppet stand into my arms. “Hold this.”

That, at least, I knew how to do.

By the time the moustache was back on the king, I had told her my name was Nico, that I had been somewhere else a few minutes ago, and that I had apparently been given shenanigans.

“What does it do?”

“I was hoping you might know.”

She wiped oil off the king's lip. “I do now owe Gedd an apology. Hold the stand straight.”

Her name was Tansy. She had a wagon, a shaggy bay pony, a puppet theatre, and a goat called Hobnob. She also had half a loaf of bread and decided that watching me stare at it was making the rest of her work difficult.

I ate sitting on the wagon's lowered tailboard. Hobnob nosed my sister's coat, which I had put beside me. He was a grey goat with a cream beard, a crooked left horn, and a white patch on his side shaped vaguely like an unfinished country.

“He'll eat the buttons,” Tansy said.

I put the jacket inside the wagon.

She gave me a copper and let me try to make it turn into two coppers. It remained one. I announced that the bread was a magnificent banquet. It remained bread, although Hobnob appeared willing to give it the benefit of the doubt.

“Perhaps you need an audience,” she said.

I bowed to the goat and declared myself very rich.

Hobnob chewed.

“Perhaps not,” she said, taking back the copper. “Help me set the stools. Stay for the show and you can have supper. There's a blanket if you need to sleep under the wagon.”

Her second act involved Hobnob, a low three-legged stool, and a pasteboard crown painted gold. In rehearsal I was the king. She rattled a dented tin, and Hobnob bowed, bending his front legs and sticking his rear end into the air.

I applauded. He stayed bent.

“Pay him.” She put a piece of oat cake in my hand.

Once I had paid him, he came up onto the stool, caught the crown between his horns, and removed it from my head. Tansy rattled the tin again. He carried his prize proudly back to her, and she exchanged it for another piece of cake.

“What if he won't take the crown?” I asked.

“He takes the crown.”

“What if I need him to do something else?”

“Then wait till he's taken the crown.”

There were rules here. They just seemed to belong to the goat.

For the afternoon show, she put me behind the puppet theatre to work the painted sun. Every time the king said he was the greatest ruler under the heavens, I lowered it onto his head. I enjoyed this enormously.

Then Lord Parget arrived.

His men cleared two stools for him and his boots. He wore a crimson hat with a white plume, and, beneath it, more glossy brown hair than appeared reasonable on a man of his age.

During Hobnob's act, Tansy asked for a volunteer. Lord Parget raised his hand before anyone else could.

“The crown, my lord,” she said, offering it.

“I've brought my own.”

“Hobnob knows that one.”

“He can learn. That's the point of a trained animal.”

Tansy hesitated. His two guards stood just behind his shoulders. She set the stool in front of him and rattled the tin.

Hobnob bowed. Lord Parget clapped. Hobnob remained bowed.

“The cake,” Tansy said.

“Very good,” said Lord Parget, waving him up.

Hobnob waited.

Eventually Tansy gave Lord Parget the cake. Hobnob ate it, climbed the stool, and hooked a horn under the brim of the crimson hat.

The plume was pinned through the hat into the hair underneath.

Both came away together.

Hobnob trotted back to Tansy wearing the hat sideways, with Lord Parget's hair hanging from his crooked horn.

I made a noise behind the puppet theatre that I tried to turn into a cough. It was unsuccessful. The children in front did not try at all.

Lord Parget stood up.

“That animal comes with me.”

Tansy had already rescued the hat. She smoothed it with both hands. “He's done the act you asked for. Your hat's sound. I'm sorry about the—”

“With me.”

One guard took Hobnob's lead. The other put a hand on Tansy's shoulder when she reached for it.

“Damage to my person,” Lord Parget said. He snatched the hat, glanced at the children, and lowered his voice. “He'll join my collection. Perhaps a competent keeper can train him.”

Tansy stepped forward again. The guard squeezed her shoulder. I came out from behind the theatre with the painted sun still in my hand.

“That's her goat.”

Lord Parget's eyes went no higher than the painted sun. “And that is mine.”

They took Hobnob away. He stopped twice to investigate food on the ground.

For several minutes Tansy packed without speaking. She put the puppet king in his box, wrapped the sun, and folded the theatre's curtains into the wagon. I helped. Once I asked what we were going to do. She pointed at a crate, and I carried it.

When the wagon was packed, she took down a green tabard embroidered with turnips.

“He's tied behind the red tent,” she said. “Outside the west gate of the reviewing ring. They'll put him in Parget's carriage after the procession. The two men watch the gate. If they look somewhere else, I can get his lead and bring him straight back here.”

She put the long tabard over my grey hoodie and pulled up my hood. The tabard had a fringe round the neck and smelt of dust and old apples.

“Who am I?”

“Someone from the city. There's a festival inspector due, and nobody's seen him. You ask the men questions. You ask them over there.” She pointed to the far side of the ring, where viewing stools stood beneath a red awning. “Don't go near Hobnob. Don't make them move him.”

“I could do the moustache again.”

“You could also do the bread again. Ask questions.”

She handed me the pasteboard crown. “Put that in your belt. If he sees it he'll want to finish his act, and I don't need him stopping to perform.”

The ring was only ropes between posts, but I hesitated outside it as though it were a castle. I could see Hobnob through a gap between tents, tethered beyond the west gate. One guard stood in the opening; the other leaned against a post beside him. Tansy had brought the wagon up behind the red tent. The way back to it was six paces long.

I adjusted the tabard.

“I am,” I whispered, “a very important visiting official.”

The fringe rose round my neck and stiffened into a collar so tall I could barely turn my head. Between it and the hood, most of my face was hidden. Each embroidered turnip acquired a little golden crown.

I touched one. It was cloth, stitched tightly into cloth.

“Sir?” said the guard at the gate.

I would have preferred time to think about the turnips, but he was already moving aside.

“The festival,” I said. “I am here concerning it.”

“The inspector! We were told to expect you before noon.”

“Yes,” I said, with all the indignation of a man who had been waiting to expect himself too.

He led me towards the red awning. The second guard followed. Outside the gate, Tansy moved towards Hobnob.

It was working.

Lord Parget stood to greet me. His hat was back on his head and the plume stood at a defiant angle. He offered me a cushioned stool, called for wine, and apologized for the dust.

Nobody had apologized to me for dust before.

I sat. Someone put a cup in my hand. Lord Parget asked whether the spectacle had been satisfactory, and for a moment it seemed perfectly reasonable that I should have an opinion worth hearing about spectacles. The guard who had squeezed Tansy's shoulder stood quietly behind me.

“I've acquired a remarkable animal,” Lord Parget said. “Too good for the woman who had it. You must see him.”

The sensible answer was no. The useful answer was to ask about the procession until Tansy and Hobnob were gone.

Instead, I thought: if he liked me, perhaps I could get the goat back without making her steal him. I could be the person who came back with something, for once, instead of the person waiting with the coats.

“Certainly,” I said. “Bring him here. I'll inspect him.”

The second guard turned at once.

Through the tall collar I caught a glimpse of Tansy stopping beside the red tent.

“There's no need to hurry,” I added.

Lord Parget laughed. “He'd hurry for nobody.”

The guard led Hobnob through the gate and tied him to a post several yards inside the ring. A new length of rope went across the opening. Both guards took their places there again while servants moved the procession's banners past the tents. Tansy's six clear paces had become a rope, two men, and all the width of a moving procession.

Hobnob saw the crown in my belt.

He bowed.

Lord Parget watched from beneath the awning. “Well? Does he answer to you?”

I tried to gesture Hobnob upright. He remained bowed, waiting to be paid.

“He's considering,” I said.

“So am I.”

I got off the cushioned stool. The collar caught my cup and tipped wine down my front. One guard stepped forward, laughing, and took it from me.

Tansy was outside the ropes along the west side, some distance from the guarded gate. I walked past Hobnob to the rail, keeping him between myself and Lord Parget. She crouched to adjust her boot, and I bent down as though something needed inspecting there too.

“What did I tell you?” she whispered.

“I know.”

“You brought him inside.”

“I thought I could ask for him back.”

“Then ask.”

I looked towards the awning. Lord Parget had unfolded a handkerchief and was pressing it carefully against his damp forehead beneath the rim of the hat.

“I liked being important,” I said. “I wanted him to keep thinking I was.”

Her fingers stopped on the lower rope. “Right. Stop it, then.”

Hobnob was still bent double. I could not bear to look at his patient rear end.

“Have you got a cake?”

She passed one through the rope. I took it back to Hobnob. When I paid him, he stood up and pushed his nose at my belt. I returned to the rail.

“I can do the act,” I said. “Over there. They'll have to watch me.”

Tansy looked across at the awning. Her three-legged stool had been set aside nearby with the other performers' things.

“They'll watch him too.”

“Only till he takes the crown.”

She considered me, then drew her dented tin from her coat. “I'll loose him. He'll finish the act, then come back to this. Keep them looking at you till I've got him.”

I nodded.

“Don't try to improve it.”

I carried the stool to the east side of the ring, just in front of Lord Parget. The collar scraped the underside of my chin. I took out the crown and put it on my head.

“To inspect a performance,” I announced, “one must participate in it.”

“Must one?” said Lord Parget.

“Oh, absolutely.”

I put one foot on the stool and wobbled.

The lord leaned forward.

I put the other foot up. I had watched my sister stand on a surfboard once, while holding her towel. This did not prove useful.

“Behold,” I said, swaying, “the King of Turnips.”

The crowned vegetables on my chest brightened. The high collar collapsed under my chin, unravelling into a long golden beard.

It itched. It also reached my knees.

The lord's mouth opened.

I tried to bow. A strand of beard caught beneath my shoe. The stool tilted towards Lord Parget, who lunged backwards with a shout. The two guards ran from the gate and caught my arms. One planted his boot against a stool leg. The other shoved me upright, directly in front of their employer.

Through the beard I saw Tansy duck under the west rope.

“Steady, sir,” said the first guard, no longer smiling.

“An excellent motto,” I said.

Tansy freed Hobnob from the tether. He looked straight at my crown, then bowed again. She held out a cake. He stayed bent long enough to make her bring it all the way to his mouth. Then he trotted towards the stool, and she went back to the west gate with her tin.

“Remarkable,” said Lord Parget. “You haven't said a word to him.”

I bent to put the crown within reach. Hobnob hooked it. The loose beard slipped over his crooked horn too.

The tin rattled at the west gate.

Hobnob turned to carry his prize back. The pasteboard cracked against his horn, and the beard pulled tight. It was still sewn to my collar.

I came off the stool into the nearer guard. The other caught a handful of green cloth to stop me falling, and the neckline began to tear. The stool went over with a crack. I landed on my knees, with Hobnob trying to take my clothes back to Tansy.

Lord Parget rose so fast that his hat slid over one eye. He caught it with both hands and turned his back to straighten it.

I gripped the torn neckline and pulled. The seam gave way. The beard came loose, and Hobnob trotted west with it dangling from his horn beneath the crown.

“Inspection complete,” I said.

The guard tried to haul me upright. I clung to his sleeve and let my knees fold again. He grabbed his companion for help. Across the ring, Tansy took the broken crown and beard from Hobnob and paid him.

“Get up,” said Lord Parget, still straightening his hat.

I waited until Tansy had slipped the gate rope off its post. She let it fall and stepped over it, Hobnob following. Then I released the guard's sleeve and ducked beneath his reaching hand.

My hood had fallen back. I was on all fours, with a ragged green neckline round my shoulders and my red trainers in full view.

“That's no inspector,” said Lord Parget.

I ran.

The torn tabard flapped against my shoulder. The stool lay broken behind me. Neither politely repaired itself as the guards started after me.

Tansy's wagon was already moving. I caught the tailboard and pulled myself onto it as we jolted along the track behind the tents. The broken crown and its acquired beard lay on a crate. Hobnob stood beside me with his lead tied to a ring, chewing the corner of a sack.

“He'll eat that,” I said.

“Take it away, then.”

I did. Behind us somebody blew a whistle. Tansy snapped the reins, and the wagon gathered enough speed to make me sit down hard. By the time we reached the trees, the fair's music was louder than the shouting.

We did not stop until the tents were out of sight.

Tansy checked Hobnob's legs, his horns, and the place where the tether had rubbed his neck. Then she checked the torn tabard. I took it off and laid it carefully beside her.

“I'll pay for it,” I said.

“With the second copper?”

“I'll work.”

She turned the tear over. Her orange patches had neat, close stitches. I had a feeling mine were going to have to be the same.

“You can start by mending that. Then you're on stools tomorrow. Keep an eye out for Parget's colours. We've lost a fair, and if he follows us we'll have to lose another.”

I nodded. “Can I still sleep under the wagon?”

She looked up. “Yes.”

I let out a breath I had apparently been saving since the field.

Inside the wagon, my sister's coat lay where I had folded it, with a small damp mark on one sleeve. I moved it into the puppet box before Hobnob could investigate further.

Tansy gave me the wooden king to hold while she packed the damaged crown. One end of his horsehair moustache was peeling loose.

“At least,” I said, trying to sound confident, “I know how to wear one of these now.”

The moustache landed across my forehead.

Tansy looked at it. She looked at me. Then she reached into the wagon for the oil.

“Hold still.”

I held still.

stories.body:
# The Last Passenger

“Attention all heroes, attention all heroes: Switch from subject containment to evacuation. I repeat, evacuate all civilians immediately. Captain Incredible is en route and he is extremely pissed off.”

Copperjack took his hands off Vane's armoured shoulders.

He had spent twelve minutes getting them there. The studio floor was littered with copper scales, broken clasps, one whole sleeve of Copperjack's suit. Now he backed out through the hole where the control-room window had been and pressed his earpiece.

“How long?”

I couldn't hear the answer. Whatever it was made him look up.

“Skylark. Who's left?”

“Two staff. The man in the kitchen, and her.”

I stood in the control room with a woman who had taken off her shoes. One foot was swelling so quickly you could watch it happen. She held both shoes by their straps and stared through the broken window into the studio.

“Mal's in there,” she said.

Copperjack looked at me.

I shook my head.

The armoured man sat against the far wall with his legs straight out. Copperjack had folded the suit's knee joints backwards. Its helmet was on the floor, and without it the man looked almost bored, except that he couldn't stop wetting his lips.

Behind him, beneath the broadcasting desk, Mr Davitt lay dead. Mal to the woman with the shoes. Captain Incredible's father to everyone who would be talking about this tomorrow.

“The living first,” Copperjack said. His voice had gone thin. “I'll get the kitchen man. How's the route?”

“Clear.”

“Finish up. Don't come back.”

He left us. I heard him force the kitchen door, heard someone cry out, and then the glass doors onto the roof flew open. Copperjack ran for the parapet with a man over his shoulder. He jumped, and a moment later his remaining plates clattered on the roof across the avenue.

“Arm round my shoulder,” I told the woman.

She kept looking into the studio.

“You can take your shoes.”

That reached her. She put the arm with the shoes round my shoulder and let me pick her up.

My costume was blue, with a yellow bird sewn over the breast. It hadn't come with pockets. Halfway across the roof she asked if she could put her shoes down somewhere and I said yes, any minute, hang on.

The jump always looked worse than it was. Seven storeys to the street. Across the avenue, the furniture shop had a broad third-floor roof and a door down to the loading yard. I could take one person there. The shop staff and two ambulance people would get them downstairs and into the vehicles. We'd been doing it since Vane's first shot brought down the station's main stairwell. The passenger lift had stopped between floors with nobody in it, thank God. The woman was my ninth passenger.

I could fly about as fast as a person rode a bicycle. On my own, I could go for hours. Carrying someone, I got a little distance, a little height, and then a feeling like holding a sneeze which became steadily harder to bear.

The woman buried her face in my neck when we went over the edge.

Captain Incredible had taught me to carry people. One arm behind the shoulders, one under the knees. Don't hang them by the armpits. Don't let them look down if they don't want to. And if they were heavier than I'd thought, come straight back. No shame in putting someone down safely.

During my first drill I had tried to lift a sack of sand before they let me near a volunteer. I'd got six feet up, lost it, and dropped myself with the sack still hugged to my chest. He'd caught me.

The examiner had said, “You mustn't rely on that.”

The Captain had given me a little shake, still in his arms. “Next time, let go of the sand.”

For months afterward, I had wanted him to laugh at something I'd said.

I set the woman down on the furniture-shop roof. A medic with a shaved head took her elbow, and she swung away from me into the doorway, shoes still dangling. From below came the scrape of a stretcher being loaded.

“That's the last,” I said.

“You too,” the medic said.

I reached up to tell dispatch the station was clear of survivors. My right hand was shaking so much I missed the earpiece.

Across the avenue, someone banged on the roof doors.

The first blow made them jump. The second pushed one open.

Vane came out bent at the waist, staggering, without his armour.

For a moment I watched without understanding. His suit was a room somebody could climb out of. Of course it was. I'd just spent twelve minutes wanting Copperjack to break the room open.

Under it, Vane wore a grey vest and trousers tucked into heavy boots. A pair of restraints joined his wrists in front of him. Copperjack's field case had been open beside the studio door. Vane raised his hands above his head so that I could see.

“I've surrendered!”

I pressed my earpiece properly this time.

“Vane's on the station roof. Out of the suit. Hands restrained.”

Copperjack answered from somewhere with an engine running. “Keep coming. We can't wait for him.”

Vane reached the parapet. His hair was slicked flat by the helmet. He looked along the street, up at the sky, and then at me.

“Don't leave me here!”

The medic had one foot inside the doorway. She looked over my shoulder.

“Is that him?”

I nodded.

She let the door fall against her heel.

I had heard Mr Davitt die. When the microphone had stopped working, he'd leaned out from under the desk to tell Vane that he could use the spare one. Vane had asked him his name. Then he'd made him repeat it. Then he'd said, very clearly, “Tell your son I came looking for him.”

There'd been no time for Mr Davitt to tell anybody anything.

The shot had come through the station speakers. We were in the next room.

I knew Mr Davitt a little. He'd recorded my first safety announcement, because dispatch needed something clear to play when my radio wasn't working. We'd done it nine times. I kept laughing at the part where I said my own name.

He'd shown me a picture of the Captain at ten, skinny knees and a ribbon for coming third in something.

Vane was still shouting.

“I'm going back,” I said.

“You can barely stand,” the medic said.

“It's downhill on the way home.”

She didn't smile. Neither did I.

“Leave him,” Copperjack said in my ear. “There's no time.”

“I'm taking him.”

“Skylark.”

Someone called up the stairs for help with the stretcher. The medic looked at me. “We'll be in the yard,” she said, and went downstairs.

I stepped off the roof before Copperjack could say anything else.

The crossing back took too long. Empty arms didn't help much now. My right shoulder ached deep in the joint, and I had to think about flying instead of just doing it.

Vane met me halfway to the doors.

“What were you waiting for?”

“Sit down.”

“He's coming.”

“I know. Sit down so I can pick you up.”

He sat, badly, with his boots skidding on the roof gravel. I knelt beside him and checked the restraints. Both were locked. I felt round his waist and under his arms; the gun had stayed with the suit.

“Put your hands on your stomach. Keep them there.”

“Can you actually carry me?”

I got an arm behind his back and the other under his knees. He was heavier than the woman. There was a buckle or a fastener in the back of his vest which pressed into my wrist.

“Don't move around,” I said.

He brought his joined hands up towards my neck.

“On your stomach.”

“I need to hold on.”

“Then hold your trousers.”

He gripped a fold of fabric between his cuffs.

I stood. Everything in me asked to put him down.

The station's aerial had a red light on top. All evening it had blinked on and off above the roof, keeping its own time through the shooting and the calls for help. I glanced up at it as I took my first step.

The whole aerial bent sideways.

It didn't fall. Something beyond the light caught it, held it against the sky, and twisted it free of its mountings. The sound arrived after the movement, a long metallic tearing followed by a crack that I felt in my teeth.

Window glass burst out along the upper floors. The roof doors blew shut. For a second the gravel lifted around our feet.

Then Captain Incredible was standing where the aerial had been.

There was a strip of cloud across the moon. I could see the front of him by the light from the studio's broken windows: navy suit, red cape, the white insignia that had been printed on my schoolbag. One of his hands was wrapped round the aerial's broken stem. He let it drop off the edge.

It struck the empty avenue below.

Vane tried to climb over my shoulder.

“Stay still.”

“Go! Go!”

I jumped.

For a few yards we flew. The pressure inside me wavered and caught again. The furniture-shop doorway was open; a yellow light showed the top of the stairs. I aimed for it.

The Captain came in front of us.

I stopped so suddenly Vane knocked his forehead against mine.

The Captain hung in the air without appearing to do anything. I had never been that close to him in flight. We weren't permitted to share his airspace during exercises.

He was looking at Vane.

“Put him down.”

“I can't. We're over the street.”

He glanced at the roof behind me.

“Back there.”

We were below the station roof now. I couldn't get us up there. I could barely go forward. For one stupid moment I thought of how annoyed the examiner would be with me for having to explain that.

“I'm taking him to the other roof.”

“Cerys.”

He knew my name. He'd remembered it.

The pleasure of that came up in me, fast and sickening.

“Let go,” he said.

Vane's heels dug into my thigh. I was holding him too tightly. I tried to loosen my arm behind his back and the lift sagged. Both of us dropped a foot.

“He'll be arrested,” I said.

The Captain reached for him.

I turned with my passenger. It wasn't an attack or anything I had practised. Just a turn away from a hand.

His fingers closed on Vane's vest. He pulled.

My right arm was still beneath Vane's knees. The Captain's hand came down to get it out of the way.

There was a hard click inside my shoulder. My arm went strange and loose, and for an instant I couldn't find it.

Then I found the pain.

The lift vanished.

We fell out of the Captain's grasp. Vane's vest tore at the collar, and he cried out and twisted against me. I tried to fly. Nothing answered. The broken aerial lay across the street, getting bigger.

The Captain was above us, his hand still closed on a scrap of grey cloth.

I had let go of the sand. The examiner had explained it again, and I had let go on every drill afterward.

Vane was looking at the street with his mouth open.

“Catch us!” I shouted.

The Captain moved.

“Both of us!”

I saw him coming for me. I held Vane with the arm I could still feel, knowing what I was putting within his reach.

Then he was beneath us, taking our weight. He caught my back in one arm, our knees in the other. Vane's boot struck his chin hard enough to turn his face. He barely seemed to notice.

He brought us to the furniture-shop roof.

I kept saying “My arm,” until he put me down.

He lowered me onto the gravel with a care I could feel all the way through him. Then he took Vane by the front of the vest, carried him three paces away, and stood him against the parapet.

Vane pressed his wrists against his stomach.

The Captain put his left hand on the wall beside Vane's head.

Brick dust sifted out beneath his palm.

I pushed myself up with my good arm. My right hand trailed across the roof and I nearly screamed.

From below somebody called, “Are they down? Is she down?”

The Captain drew his right hand back.

His shoulders were moving. It took me a moment to understand that he was breathing hard. I'd never seen him out of breath.

“Captain.”

He didn't turn.

I got onto my knees, then stood. Nobody was coming through the doorway. They were still calling to each other in the loading yard, trying to work out whether they should leave.

“Vane.” My voice didn't carry. I swallowed. “Come here.”

Vane looked at me over the Captain's shoulder.
