I went towards the door. Not towards the Captain. I couldn't have made myself do that.

“Come here.”

“Cerys.”

I stopped.

“I know he killed your father.”

The Captain looked at my arm.

I wanted to say something else. Something he could answer. I couldn't find it.

His fist came down slowly. He held it against his thigh.

Vane edged sideways along the parapet. His torn collar hung open down his chest. He took one step, watched the Captain, then took another.

The Captain could have stopped him with a finger.

Vane reached me. I caught the back of his vest with my left hand and steered him at the door. He tried to push past, but the hem caught on the handle. He turned wildly to see if the Captain had him.

“Stop pulling,” I said.

I got the fabric loose.

I pushed the door open with my hip.

“We're coming down,” I called to the people below.

Vane went through first. I kept hold of his vest until my shoulder touched the doorframe. Then I had to let go and turn sideways to get my useless arm through.

For that moment I couldn't see either man.

I stepped onto the first stair.

Vane was already half a flight below me, clattering down as fast as he could manage. Someone told him to slow down. Someone else shouted that his hands were tied, watch him, don't let him into the ambulance.

Behind me, the Captain said, “Wait.”

I stood on the stair. My arm throbbed all the way to my fingers.

“I can take you to the hospital.”

He was just outside the doorway. The roof light made it hard to see his face.

At the drills, he had always told us before he picked us up. Even when I knew he was going to, he'd asked. I'd liked that about him. I'd thought about it for weeks after the first time.

He started to bend down.

I pressed my back against the wall.

He stopped.

The medic was coming up towards me. I could hear her shoes squeaking on the stairs. I looked down for her shaved head.

“I'm going with her,” I said.

The Captain stayed where he was. The medic reached me, looked at my arm, then up through the doorway. She didn't ask what had happened.

“I'll take this side,” she told me. “Nobody's going to touch that arm.”

I held her shoulder with my good hand. It was a bony, ordinary shoulder. She turned so that we could go down together, one step at a time.

The Captain stepped back to give us room.

stories.title: The Return Tray
stories.prompt: You sigh. Another day, another dead magical girl. You can only roll your eyes when she gets up off the slab and yawns like she just woke up from a nap.
stories.body:
# The Return Tray

You sigh. Another day, another dead magical girl.

This one is Princess Snapdragon. According to the ambulance sheet, she died saving a tram from a giant moth. According to the property sheet, she arrived with one yellow boot, one silver earring, and a digital chess clock.

You check the bag for the other boot. Nothing. You check beneath the trolley, because the ambulance men have an expansive understanding of the word *with*. Nothing there, either.

Princess Snapdragon sits up on the slab and yawns. Her arms stretch overhead; the enormous rose on her jacket brushes the light fitting.

You roll your eyes.

“Mind the bulb.”

She lowers her hands and looks at her feet. One yellow boot. One black sock, with a hole at the heel.

“Oh, come on.”

“I checked.”

“It was an expensive pair.”

“Put them in the return spell next time.”

“Then I might come back as a boot.”

“You'd complain less.”

She tests her jaw, rubs the stiff place at the back of her neck, and drops her legs over the edge. The ambulance sheet goes into the drawer marked RETURNED. You have stopped using paper clips. They used to come back for those, too.

Her restoration working, laid down before she went out, takes twenty minutes to finish after her heart stops. It mends the body. Clothes and personal effects are your department. She has explained the distinction to you several times and finds your continued interest in the whereabouts of her left boot needlessly hostile.

You put her earring in the little steel return tray. She hooks it into her ear. Below the dark bob of her hair, it looks like a tiny unfinished chandelier.

“Still cold in here,” she says.

“Still a mortuary.”

“You could put up a picture.”

“You could try arriving somewhere else.”

She slides off the slab, lands on her good foot, and reaches for the chess clock.

“I could beat you.”

“You could try that, too.”

Her civilian name is Leonie. She's twenty-nine, works in a bookshop, and can knock a bus-sized moth out of the sky with a spear of pink light. She has never beaten you at chess. When she first started arriving here, she thought moving the queen early was a declaration of confidence. Later she claimed it had been reconnaissance.

You let her take back one move in that first game. Ever since, she has argued that this established a precedent.

“Get the board,” she says. “I'm white.”

“You're always white.”

“And yet you've never complained when you win.”

You lift the board from the handover tray on the desk. It folds shut, with the pieces held inside by tired elastic. You bought it forty-two years ago for night shifts. You still have the pencil it came with for keeping score, although you stopped keeping score the week Leonie accused you of maintaining a grudge in tabular form.

The tray also holds your spare pens, the stapler which only you know how to open, and a set of labelled keys. Beneath it is the typed sheet for the new attendant. Princess Snapdragon's name appears halfway down the page.

You mean to leave all of it behind when you retire at five.

Leonie puts her clock on the desk.

“Fifteen minutes each.”

You look at the display. “You bought this?”

“I want you to make a decision before the heat death of the universe.”

“You've held up a game by dying twice. And you call me slow.”

“Once. The other time I had a concussion.”

She arranges the white pieces. Her gloves are stained grey at the fingertips, and one flower on her cuff is coming loose. When she turns her wrist, the empty threads scrape over the desk.

“I've been studying,” she says.

“You usually tell me afterward.”

“It makes the disappointment harder to explain.”

She presses your side of the clock to start hers. You sit down.

At the fifth move she offers a pawn you have taken from her at least a dozen times. You leave it alone. She glances up.

“Have you been studying?”

“I was here the last dozen times.”

“Unfortunately.”

You advance a pawn on the other side of the board. She brings out a knight, hesitates, then puts it back.

You raise one finger.

“I hadn't let go,” she says.

You lower it.

There is no more talk for a while. Leonie sits on the stool with her boot braced against the desk leg and her socked foot tucked behind it. The clock buttons click. Outside the high frosted window, somebody tries to reverse a delivery van into the yard. They fail, pause, and fail in a different way.

Your next move makes Leonie smile.

You dislike the smile. It isn't her usual smile, which announces that she has thought of something unkind to say. This one hardly moves her mouth at all.

She puts a bishop where it cannot possibly be comfortable.

If you take it, her knight comes in with check. If you leave it, her queen follows it down towards your king. You examine a third possibility, advancing the pawn in front of your rook. Six moves later in your head, it ends badly.

Leonie watches you count.

You push your bishop between hers and your king, offering an exchange.

She takes it without hesitation.

You recapture. Her queen moves in. You have lost the protection you wanted to keep, but the immediate attack has slowed. Barely.

“Did you learn that at the shop?” you ask.

“Lunch breaks.”

“Sell fewer books.”

“I bought them myself.”

She has a knight and queen pointed at your king. Your rook is stranded behind three pawns. You move it along the back rank and let go. She pushes a pawn forward, shutting the route you meant to use. You wish you had left the rook where it was.

Her smile gets larger.

At five o'clock, Mr Coyle puts his head around the door.

“All yours,” you tell him, and stop the clock.

Mr Coyle nods at Princess Snapdragon. She gives him a little wave.

You hand him the keys. The last entry is signed; the cold-room count is done; there are no families waiting upstairs. You show him which drawer sticks and where the duplicate certificates go. He reads the first page of your sheet.

“Magical returns,” he says. “Right.”

“They're usually hungry.”

“Don't buy the coffee,” Leonie says. “It's dreadful.”

“I told you that before you bought it,” you say.

“I thought it was a psychological tactic.”

Mr Coyle takes the handover tray, then pauses with the board still on the desk.

“Does that come with the room?”

“Yes,” you say.

Leonie looks from him to you.

“The chess set,” you add.

“I did think that,” says Mr Coyle.

You unpin your name badge and lay it face down in the tray, beneath the stapler. You have been wearing it for so long that the left lapel feels unusually light. You put on your coat.

“It can go in the cupboard when we're done,” you tell Leonie. “Mr Coyle plays. I asked.”

“How well?”

“How well do you play?” Mr Coyle asks her.

“That's currently under review.”

He takes the tray into the little office. A moment later you hear him testing the stapler.

Leonie picks at the loose flower on her cuff. The last thread parts. She rests her thumb on your clock button.

“So this is your last day.”

“I told you I was retiring.”

“You told me you ought to retire. That's different. I've told you you ought to retire every time you take my queen.”

You said it more plainly in June, but she was looking for a pair of spectacles which had not survived a collapsed theatre roof. You cannot now remember whether you waited until she found the broken frames.

“Well,” you say. “It is.”

She looks at the cupboard, then back at the board.

“I spent three Saturdays on that attack.”

“It shows.”

“I didn't spend them on Mr Coyle.”

You still have your coat on. At the bus stop there will be a few other people finishing work. You have looked forward to standing among them without a telephone which can send you back here.

On the board, her queen waits for you to be careless.

“Do you want to finish?” you ask.

“I want you to start your clock.”

You take off your coat. Instead of hanging it on the hook, you fold it over your knees.

“One thing first.”

“If this is about taking back your rook move, no.”

You find a loose half-sheet on the desk. For years she has arrived, complained, played, and left. You know how she takes her coffee and which side of her jaw aches first after restoration. You know she will blame the overhead light when she overlooks a fork. You have never had to give her directions to you.

You write down your address.

“I don't have a table this high,” you say. “But there's room.”

She reads the paper. You have written the street number twice, once above the street and once beside it.

“Is that a house or a score?”

You cross out the second number.

“Sundays,” you say. “If you're free. Four?”

“Is this going to influence my assessment of that rook move?”

“I had hoped.”

She folds the paper into the palm of her glove, with the little flower that has come off her cuff.

“I'll need the board,” she says.

You go to the office door and tell Mr Coyle it no longer comes with the room. He has the stapler open already. You could resent that, but there are other things requiring your attention.

Leonie presses the clock. You sit down to save your king.

You have to bring your queen back to protect your king. Then she advances a pawn to keep the attack moving and leaves your queen a route to check her king.

You check the route twice, then move.

She sees what you saw as soon as you move. Her hand comes forward, hovers over the pawn, and stops.

“You let go,” you say.

“I know.”

She makes you play another eight moves. One of them nearly costs you the queen.

At five fourteen she tips her king on its side, stops the clock, and lies face down on the empty slab.

“Don't be dramatic,” you say. “I've got to fold the board.”

“I prepared for that.”

“You prepared for me to take the bait. I didn't.”

She lifts her head. “You looked at it for ages.”

“It was a lovely bishop.”

“I could have taken a bus here, watched you consider that bishop, gone out and fought the moth, and been back before you finished admiring it.”

You put the pieces away. Your fingers are steadier now. The late bus will get you home well enough.

Leonie sits up and holds out her clock. You look at it, then at her.

“Just put it inside your coat,” she says. “I've got one boot. I need my hands for the railings.”

You tuck it away with the board. She checks the folded address in her glove, rubs her bare heel, and hops towards the door.

“Sunday,” she says. “And I'm still white.”

“Mr Coyle might let you be white.”

She looks back at you.

“He might take the bishop.”

***

On Sunday you move the vase off the kitchen table and put the board where both chairs can reach it. The overhead lamp casts a shadow across the white side. You switch on the lamp above the counter instead.

At ten to four you check the clock. You press each button, in case there is some fault which has developed while it has been in your possession. There isn't.

At five to four you put a biscuit on each plate. At three to four you put another biscuit on hers, then another on yours so it does not look like a concession.

The doorbell goes at four exactly.

Leonie is wearing a green coat and two scuffed trainers. Both silver earrings are in place. There is a paper bag under her arm.

“You're punctual,” you say.

“You look disappointed.”

“I wondered if something had happened.”

“I work Sundays. I swapped.”

You stand aside. She leaves her trainers neatly by the door and comes through to the kitchen. There is no heroic rose on her shoulder, no soot, no need to check anything before she sits down.

She looks at the board, at the clock, and at the two chairs. You have put a cushion on hers. She moves it to yours.

“You can remove that before we start,” you say.

“It's for when you lose consciousness waiting for me to make a mistake.”

From the bag she takes a new chess book, bristling with paper markers.

You sigh.

She opens it at a marked page, lowers her voice, and points to a photograph of a man with a magnificent beard.

“Dead,” she says. “And look how many games he won.”

You roll your eyes and reach for a black pawn.

stories.title: An Opening
stories.prompt: The Adventurers guild is surprised when a gaggle of individuals walk in to create a party. Leading them is a goblin paladin and behind them is a orc wizard, elven barbarian and Goliath rogue.
stories.body:
# An Opening

Sir Tallow had rehearsed the entrance all the way from the inn. Sword on the left, shield on the right, chin up, cape clear of his heels. Three companions behind him. No hurrying. No apologizing.

The guild doors were taller than the inn. This pleased him. He planted both hands against one and pushed.

Nothing happened.

Laureth reached over his head and lifted the latch.

"As we discussed," she said.

"I was testing it."

"It passed."

He pushed again. The doors opened upon firelight, long tables, and a hundred adventures nailed to the walls. A woman was telling a story with a dagger driven into the table between her fingers. Three men were arguing over a map. Someone at the far end had just begun a song.

Tallow stepped forward. His polished shield bore a lamp with a tiny silver flame. His cape caught the draft magnificently.

Then the singer forgot the next word.

A goblin in plate armor was worth looking at. An orc in blue scholar's robes, clutching a book bound in pale calfskin, was worth looking at twice. And Laureth, with her fine elven cheekbones and an axe slung over one shoulder, was now explaining to the orc that the thing brushing his book was a tassel, not the blade.

"The tassel has blood on it," Vorrick said.

"Blackberry juice."

"From what battle?"

"Breakfast."

Tallow marched to the registrar's counter. Behind it sat a gray-haired woman with a pen poised over a ledger. Her eyes traveled from him to Vorrick, up the axe, and down again.

"We wish," Tallow said, "to establish an adventuring party."

She lowered her pen.

"All three of you?"

"Four," said Harn.

The registrar looked to her left. The Goliath stood at the end of the counter, quietly examining its lock. His head nearly touched a roof beam.

"When did you come in?"

"Just after them."

"I watched the door."

Harn nodded politely.

The registrar put down her pen altogether.

Tallow had hoped their entrance would have an effect. He had not planned what to do while the effect wore off. He settled for keeping his chin up.

"Names and professions," she said at last.

"Sir Tallow. Paladin."

"Vorrick. Wizard."

"Laureth. Barbarian."

"Harn. Rogue."

The registrar looked at the counter lock, then at Harn. He put his hands behind his back.

From the nearest table came a soft, incredulous laugh. Tallow's ears grew warm inside his helmet. He had polished that helmet with the last clean corner of their shared towel, while Laureth held the lamp and Vorrick read him the oath for the forty-sixth time. Harn had said nothing, but in the morning the broken clasp on his cape had been repaired.

He would not look back at the table.

The registrar asked for their fee. Tallow counted out the coins, one for each of them. Three weeks of road, four separate purses, and it had come to this little row of silver. They watched her sweep it into a drawer.

"You'll want to see the commissions," she said.

"We do," said Laureth.

The registrar brought out a folder. Tallow had expected to stride over to the wall and tear down a notice. Apparently beginners got a folder.

The first sheet concerned a lost mule. The second offered payment for escorting a spice merchant. On the third, someone had drawn a fortress, three swords, and a crown.

Tallow touched it.

"That one."

"Recovery of a silver coronet. Stolen from the Hall of Seven Dukes. The thieves were seen going into Briarhook Keep."

"A keep," Vorrick said. He leaned so close that one tusk cast a shadow over the paper. "How old?"

"Old enough to be empty until last week."

"Briarhook. Wasn't that the family with the book of weather bindings?"

"Perhaps," said the registrar. "This is the account of a carter they robbed. They kept him there two nights. He drew us the ground floor when he got out."

"How many thieves?" Laureth asked.

"He counted four."

Laureth smiled. It was a lovely smile, if one did not know her.

"Four of us, four of them."

"We are recovering property," Tallow said.

"Yes. From them."

The payment was enough for beds, supper, repairs, and another expedition. Enough for a party to become something that kept going.

On the carter's sketch, a fat black line crossed the great gate. Above it he had drawn an iron grille; beside it was a much smaller opening.

"Porter's hatch," the registrar said. "The gate's barred inside. He got out through that when they were drunk."

The hatch was marked with measurements. Tallow read them twice.

He could fit.

He had never seen his size written down as the useful answer to anything.

"We'll take it."

The registrar held out the contract. Tallow signed with his best upright letters and laid their remaining two coins beside his name.

"Bond returned with the coronet," she said, marking the receipt.

Laureth swung her axe down from her shoulder. Vorrick had already opened his book.

"There may be a catalogue," he murmured. "In a place like that, if the roof has held, there may be a whole room."

Harn was still looking at the sketch.

"We can reach it by midday," Tallow said. "Through the hatch, secure the gate, recover the coronet. Back before supper."

"That hatch is fourteen inches wide," Harn said.

"Yes."

Harn waited.

Tallow saw his own shield reflected in the great dark pupil. For three weeks Harn had taken the last place in every room. He ate sitting on the floor at inns with low ceilings, endured people asking him to move their furniture, and let them decide how he would arrive wherever they were going. He had taught Tallow to mend a boot. He had not let any of them touch the narrow leather wallet he kept inside his sleeve.

"I'll open the gate," Tallow said.

"How?"

"From inside."

"With what?"

Laureth rested the axe head on the floor. "We can discuss this on the road."

Vorrick turned a page. "I could lift him over."

Harn looked at him.

"For eleven heartbeats," Vorrick added.

"Over the wall?" Tallow asked.

"Possibly onto it. Then you could climb down."

On top of the wall. Shield high. The others following when he threw open the gate. Tallow could almost hear the song.

Harn's finger came down on the sketch.

"Two towers looking straight along it."

Vorrick studied the towers. He shut his book over his finger, unwilling to lose the page.

"The hatch is better," Tallow said. "I can go quietly."

"Your shield can't."

Tallow looked down. The lamp on it had been engraved by the armorer who knighted him. He had picked the smallest shield in the man's shop, and still the flame reached from his shoulder to his knee.

"I could leave it outside. If opening the gate is difficult, I could find the coronet first. Small rooms, small passages."

There would be no song about the crawl, perhaps. But there could be one about what came after. Four thieves might never notice one goblin. All his life people had looked past him to see what else was coming.

He could use that.

"It's in a chest," Harn said.

"What?"

"The carter saw them putting it in their pay chest. Bottom of the page."

Tallow read the cramped note.

Harn drew a short breath through his nose.

"You go in. Then you need a lock opened, and I'm standing in a field. Again."

"Again?"

"At the inn, you asked me to watch the packs while you three went to the cellar."

"You wouldn't fit down the stairs."

"You never asked if I knew another way."

Tallow remembered the cellar: a wine merchant paying them to search for a thief, Harn sitting outside with four bedrolls and no share in the discovery. They had come back excited, interrupting one another. Harn had asked whether they found anything. Tallow had given him the entire account, thinking that generous.

"Did you?" he asked now.

"The delivery doors were round the back."

Laureth looked away from the axe.

"You could have said."

"So could you."

For a moment the guild was loud around their little patch of quiet.

Vorrick took his finger out of the book. "I would quite like us all to see this keep."

"So would I," said Harn.

The registrar tapped the hatch on the sketch. "It still goes through. The carter managed it. You could take a look, then decide about the gate."

It was an available plan. Tallow could enter with his sword, look for the chest, and make the decision where no one could stop him. He was good in the dark. He was brave. He knew those things about himself, even now.

He turned the paper toward Harn.

"I want to open it for you. What do I need?"

Harn looked at the sketch again. This time he brought it between all four of them.

"First, don't count on being back for supper."

"Fair."

"That circle. What is it?"

Vorrick leaned over. "A seal?"

The registrar checked the carter's notes. "Iron ring. Above the gate. There was a rope hanging from it once."

"For lifting the bar." Harn drew a line with his finger. "You hitch it to the bar, pass it through the ring and out through the grille. We haul. You stay clear."

"I can float the rope's end through the ring," Vorrick said. "I'd need a clear view through that grille. Eleven heartbeats would be plenty."

Harn considered him. "If it's there."

"If it's there," Vorrick agreed.

"And if it isn't?" Laureth asked.

"He comes back out. We look again."

She shifted her grip on the axe. Tallow had seen her do that before the first blow of a fight.

"I can wait," she said. "I dislike it, but I can."

Harn asked the registrar for a piece of cord. She found one in the drawer with the coins. He held it out to Tallow.

"Show me the hitch you'd use."

Tallow made the knot he used to tether a pony.

Harn pulled the short end. It came apart.

"Oh," said Tallow.

"Do you want the axe for the bar?" Laureth asked.

Harn nodded. She laid its long haft across two chairs. Vorrick set his book well out of its reach, then held the chairs steady while Harn guided Tallow's hands around the wood.

Laureth crouched beside him. "They're going to hear you rattling in that."

"Who?"

She tapped his breastplate.

He looked at the hatch's measurements again. The armor added inches at both shoulders. He had been counting the body inside it.

Harn waited while Tallow undid the buckles. He would have to reach the bar before any of the four thieves reached him. His fingers slowed on the last buckle. The breastplate came away with a small, painful squeak. He put it beside the shield and lifted off his helmet. Underneath, his quilted tunic had a patch at one elbow which Laureth had sewn with black thread because she said the white made her stitches look anxious.

She examined the patch, apparently satisfied it had survived.

"Again," Harn said.

This time Tallow tied the hitch correctly. Vorrick lifted the cord over the loop Harn made with his thumb and forefinger, and Laureth pulled. The axe haft rose from the chairs.

"Like that," Harn said. "With enough good rope to run the whole way."

Tallow felt for his purse. Flat.

Laureth felt for hers. It yielded a button. She put it back.

"The equipment desk lends," the registrar said. "Against something they'll want back."

Vorrick folded his arms over his book. Laureth took the axe off the cord. Harn's fingers went to the wallet inside his sleeve.

Then Vorrick uncrossed his arms and laid the book on the counter, keeping one hand against its cover.

Tallow gathered his breastplate, helmet, and shield. They made an awkward pile. He nudged the book back toward Vorrick with his elbow. The silver flame caught the light one last time before he turned toward the equipment desk.

Laureth reached out for the helmet.

"I can carry it," he said.

"So can I."

He gave it to her.

The quartermaster valued the three pieces, supplied a sound rope and a covered lantern, and locked the armor in a cupboard. Tallow watched the key turn. The receipt felt very thin against his palm.

He tucked it into the lining of his tunic. His sword still hung at his left hip. At the counter, the registrar entered their names under the commission and gave them the carter's map.

Without the shield, he did not know what to do with his right hand.

Harn opened the leather wallet.

Inside lay slender tools in fitted pockets. He selected one with a curved tip and held it across his enormous palm. Tallow had once watched him clean that particular tool for the whole length of Vorrick's explanation of something called a sympathetic interval.

"For the hatch latch, if they've fastened it since the carter left. Work from the edge. I'll show you at the keep."

Tallow reached for it. Harn did not release it immediately.

Then he did.

Tallow slid it into the small belt pouch where he normally carried a polishing rag. Harn crouched and drew the fastening tight so the tool could not fall out when Tallow crawled.

"You keep looking back," he said, without raising his head.

Tallow had been looking at the cupboard.

"I've never done this without it."

Harn finished the fastening. "Get us in, and I'll find you something to hide behind."

Laureth put the coil of rope over her shoulder. Vorrick took the lantern, frowned at the carter's map, and turned it the right way up. Tallow had to lengthen his stride to keep beside them.

At the great doors he stopped. This time he lifted the latch before pushing.

Sunlight fell across the guild floor. Tallow held the door while the wizard edged his book past Laureth's axe and the rogue bent beneath the lintel.

"Come on," Laureth said from the steps. "I've begun waiting."

Tallow tucked the cape up through his belt, clear of his knees, and went after them.

stories.title: Knight Shift
stories.prompt: Triplets manage a 24/7 bookstore/cafe, seamlessly transitioning shifts so that the customers think the same person is managing the store at all times. A customer takes interest in this and starts noticing small details that they missed to cover up.
stories.body:
# Knight Shift

By her sixth visit to Knight Shift, Marnie had begun to wonder when the manager slept.

She had seen him at noon, at a quarter to midnight, and at six in the morning, always in the same black apron. A white knight's helmet occupied its front, with red, green, and blue outlines showing where the three helmets didn't quite meet. He had dark curls cut close at the sides, a long nose, and the useful ability to remember a tea order without making its owner feel obliged to improve it.

Other customers seemed used to him. A man in a bakery fleece collected a coffee and said, "Still here?"

"For my sins."

"See you tomorrow."

"I'll pencil you in."

Outside, the sign said BOOKS, COFFEE, 24 HOURS. Online, the shop was rgbknights. Its little helmet leaned over recommendations posted at hours when even Marnie wasn't working. She had found the place through a review that called a six-hundred-page fantasy novel "a hostage situation with a map." She had bought the novel anyway.

This morning she had brought a different book back to complain about.

"Two pages," she said. "Her mother asks whether she's staying, and it takes her two pages to say, 'For tea.'"

The manager was shaking powdered sugar over a tray of rolls. A strip of tape covered the edge of his left thumbnail. "That sounds like an answer."

"It's a dodge."

"You can dodge with an answer."

Marnie opened *A Room in February* to the scene. Vera had been home for less than an hour. Her mother had already measured her against the doorframe, remarked on her hair, and moved her suitcase from beside the chair to beside the stairs. Then came the question. Then the maddening tour of the room: a chipped bowl, a lamp, the wool of her mother's coat sleeve. Marnie liked the book so much that she resented this bit of it.

"She knows what she means," Marnie said. "Everyone has to stand there while she enjoys not saying it."

"Her mother doesn't get to decide how long it takes her to answer."

He said it while wiping sugar off the counter, which made it harder to dismiss as a line he had prepared for people who read novels too seriously.

Marnie made subtitles. She spent her working days persuading what people had actually said to fit the space available for it. Lately she had been working on a film in which a woman kept beginning sentences and abandoning them. Her editor kept asking whether something was missing.

"Two pages, though."

"You're in a bookshop. I'm obliged to defend pages."

"Even wasted ones?"

"Especially. Terrible business otherwise."

She laughed. He put a roll beside her tea, then took a book out from under the till. It was the shop's copy of *A Room in February*, with a split in the blue paper jacket and a receipt marking Vera's homecoming.

"I'll have another look," he said.

Marnie sat down at the small table behind the travel shelves, meaning to drink her tea and go home. She stayed to fix one subtitle, then another. At half past three the manager put a fresh pot beside her laptop without disturbing the book she had weighted open with her glasses case.

"You can charge it to my next visit," she said.

"That could be any minute."

His watch had a red strap. He looked at it, glanced towards the back door, and went to fetch more milk.

A few minutes later the oven timer sounded. He came out carrying another tray, lowered it beside the till, and pulled a roll apart to check the middle. He used his left hand to turn the tray. His thumbnail looked clean.

Marnie glanced at her screen. She had been staring into a close-up for forty minutes; it was possible that she was getting the wrong things into focus.

The manager set down the roll and picked up the shop's book.

"I think her mother spends most of it telling people what Vera means," he said. "What she meant to say. What she really wants. Maybe the silence is the first thing her mother hasn't already said for her."

Marnie took her hands off the keyboard.

"That's quite good."

"Sorry."

"You've been thinking about it."

"A bit."

He was holding a green pencil. A small green question mark had appeared beside the passage. Marnie reread it, this time without hurrying Vera towards her next line.

When she went home, she watched the unfinished sentences in her film again. She put back one little beginning she had cut. The editor asked about it; Marnie answered him, and for once she didn't rewrite the answer four times before sending it.

She told Knight about that on her next visit. She had never properly asked his name. A regular called him Knight, his own messages were signed with the helmet, and eventually that was what she called him too.

"The book's winning," he said.

"The book isn't a person."

"Then you're in real trouble."

He remembered her tea, found a book she'd asked him to hold, and correctly warned her away from a lemon slice that looked much nicer than it was. He was tired enough to put his own cup on a saucer full of used teaspoons. The cup was blue, with a chip out of the base.

Marnie liked him better for the teaspoons.

Over the next week, she began to notice things she had previously let pass.

He wrote the price of a book left-handed one afternoon. At dawn he wrote a customer's name with his right. One handwriting had a little hook on the *g*. The other didn't. His watch disappeared and returned. The taped thumbnail was still sore when she saw him in daylight, but he had taken a hot tray out of the oven without favouring it the night before.

These were all things a person could do. People changed watches. Injuries were inconsistent. Marnie herself had gone to collect a prescription with one lens missing from her glasses and noticed only when the pharmacist asked her about it.

The shop was more consistent than its manager. Her tea was always right. The bakery man never had to say which coffee he wanted. An older woman who came after evening classes found a chair waiting close to the heater. Once, just before midnight, Knight carried a new stack of books into the stockroom. Marnie heard a trolley wheel squeal. He came back without the books, passed her table, and picked up her cup exactly where he had left it.

Then he asked, "Did you finish the film?"

"You asked me that when you went in."

"And?"

"I haven't finished it since."

"Worth checking."

She laughed, but the question stayed with her.

At home she went to rgbknights to see whether a name lived somewhere in the profile. It didn't. There was a photograph of Knight holding a stack of books up to his chin, and another in which he had flour on his nose. In a short video he tried to open a parcel while talking about a novel and finally tore the tape with his teeth. The account recommended a detective story she knew he'd disliked.

People changed their minds too.

She didn't ask yet. The next time she came in, she wanted to enjoy a coffee before trying to account for its maker.

It was twenty to eight on a Sunday morning. Marnie had finished a job at seven and sent it off before she could find another reason to keep it. Knight Shift was nearly empty. A student slept upright beside the cookbooks, and a delivery rider was drinking an espresso at the window.

Knight was washing the blue cup.

"Is it still terrible?" he asked as she put *A Room in February* on the counter.

"No. I'm revising my list of who's terrible."

"That's reading for you."

"I still think Vera could just say no."

He turned the cup over on a cloth. "I do too, actually. She's waiting for her mother to ask her not to leave. Then she can be angry about being asked."

Marnie looked at him.

"You think so?"

"Well, yes. Look at how she behaves when her brother calls. She's already decided."

That was a real objection. Marnie had forgotten the brother's phone call. She opened the book to find it, pleased for a moment to have recovered an ally.

Then she glanced up at the manager's clean thumbnail.

"What happened to her having something her mother hadn't already said for her?"

He reached for the tea tin, then stopped.

"I don't know that she does," he said. "I think she knows exactly what she's doing."

"But you said—"

"That wasn't me."

The espresso machine gave a little sigh. At the window, the rider zipped his jacket and stood up.

Knight took her teapot down from the shelf. "Could you wait until eight?"

"Why?"

"Rafa needs to be here."

"Who's Rafa?"

He looked down at the book between them. "He started the argument."

Marnie had her finger under the line. She could point to it. She could point to his hands, ask about the watch, get all the questions out before he had time to choose better answers.

"And you're not Rafa?"

"No."

She closed the book.

"All right," she said. "I'll wait."

He made the tea. The rider left. Knight set a glass of water beside the sleeping student and gently rescued an open cookbook from under his elbow. Marnie took her usual table, but didn't open her laptop.

At three minutes to eight Marnie heard the back door. She looked round the end of the bookcase. The manager with the blue cup was still beside the till.

Another man came through carrying a carton of milk, in the same black apron. He had the same face.

For a moment Marnie's eyes insisted that one of them was a mirror doing the wrong thing. The arriving man set the carton down. His watch strap was red. His left thumbnail was taped.

"Morning, Marnie."

The man with the blue cup looked at him.

"I've asked her to wait."

The arriving man moved towards the till, the red strap showing below his black cuff. He smiled. "For the next thrilling instalment of whether Vera should be allowed to have a cup of tea?"

"Raf."

"What?"

"Don't just carry on."

Rafa's smile went away. He looked from the book on her table to the cup in the other man's hand. "Right."

They both came over. Marnie had chosen a two-person table. Rafa fetched another chair and the shop's copy of the book; the other man turned one backwards and sat with his arms along its top.

"Rafa," the one with the tape said. "Raf, mostly."

"Bram."

Marnie tried out the names silently. Neither face attached itself to a single visit. She looked at Raf when she meant to look at Bram, then looked down, annoyed with herself.

"There are two of you."

Raf rubbed his forehead.

"Three," Bram said. "Triplets."

"Oh, come on."

"Yes," Raf said. "We get that a lot."

"Or we used to," said Bram.

From somewhere above them came the thump of a footfall. Raf took out his phone, hesitated, then put it on the table.

"I said her mother didn't get to decide how long she took," he told Marnie. "The other bit was Gil."

"The silence?"

"Yes. He'd read it when he took over from me. I wrote something in the margin. He wrote something back."

"We argued about it over breakfast," Bram said. "I still think she's being a pain."

Raf opened the shop's copy. There were two small marks beside the passage, one in ordinary pencil, one green. Marnie had seen both of them before.

"You said you'd been thinking about it," she said.

"He had," said Raf.

It was a perfectly good answer. It didn't tell her where to look.

"Could I meet him?"

Raf glanced at Bram, who lifted one shoulder.

"If he's awake," Marnie added.

Raf picked up the phone. A minute later Gil came downstairs with a green pencil tucked behind his ear and his sweatshirt on inside out. The neck label sat beneath his chin. He was carrying a banana.

"What's happened?"

He saw his brothers sitting at Marnie's table and stopped chewing.

"Oh."

"Sorry," Raf said.

Gil pulled the pencil out from behind his ear. "Did you tell her there were three of us?"

"Yes."

"Good. Last time you said 'a few' and made us sound like mice."

He brought over a fourth chair, picked up the shop's book, and looked at the two marks beside Vera's silence.

Marnie sat very still while the table became crowded. She recognized Gil's particular way of putting a book down with his finger holding its place. She hadn't known it was particular until now.

"Do you really do this all the time?"

"Most customers come at the same time every day," Raf said. "They don't need an explanation."

"You come at all hours," Bram told her.

"I do," Marnie said.

"It used to be everyone asking to get all three of us out," Gil said. "Then a photo. Then which one was the clever one."

"It wasn't you," Bram told Gil.

Gil nudged his chair with his foot.

"We didn't plan it at first," Raf said. "Someone mistook Gil for me. He sold them the book I'd recommended. They came back and said thanks."

"I liked it better than he did," Gil said. "He told me to read it so he could complain properly."

Raf turned the shop's copy of *A Room in February* between his hands. "It was nice to be asked about a book."

The student woke and looked towards the counter. Raf got up to make his coffee. As he passed Gil, he took the green pencil from him; Gil handed it over without looking. The student asked Raf how long he'd been awake.

"Long enough to know you want two shots."

Marnie almost laughed. She stopped herself only because she wanted to hear what else Gil might say.

"The knights were before the shop," Gil said, touching the helmet on Bram's apron. "Three cardboard helmets. Red, green, blue. We used to film things."

"Bad things," said Bram.

"You were in them."

"I know how bad they were."

They had kept the name for the account. Kept the face too, Marnie thought, watching Raf pass a coffee over the counter. She remembered the video of the parcel being opened with teeth.

"Which of you does that?"

"What?"

She described it.

"Me," Bram said.

"He's banned from opening stock," Gil said.

Raf came back with the student's money still in his hand. He looked at it, swore softly, and went to the till.

Marnie waited for him to sit down, then drew her book closer. Some visits were beginning to separate: the green pencil, the hot tray, the cup full of teaspoons. Others wouldn't. She had wanted to ask Knight what he'd meant, and now all three of them were here, with none of them quite containing the conversation she'd brought back.

"I'd thought I was coming back to the same person," she said.

"We let you," Raf said. He put Gil's pencil on the table.

"Next time, will you tell me which one you are?"

"Yes," Raf said.

"I can do that," said Gil.

Bram nodded. "Me too."

"Gil, does it matter if Vera already knows her answer?" Marnie asked, looking at Bram.

"Gil's there," Bram said quietly, nodding towards his brother.

She turned and had to begin the question again. Gil waited until she'd finished.

"I don't know," he said. "I was sure yesterday."

"Oh," Marnie said. She took a sip of her tea.

"Do you write the reviews together?" she asked.

"Sometimes," Gil said.

"The hostage situation with a map?"

"The hostage situation was mine," Raf said. "Gil kept trying to make me admire the map."

"It was a good map," Gil said.

"I put those together," said Bram. "They cut my best jokes."

"Sometimes they're not good jokes, Bram."

Marnie smiled at him before she remembered to look for his name. It was the same smile she'd had for Knight. This time Bram was the one who received it.

Raf opened the shop's book and laid it beside hers.

"I still think she gets to take her time," he said.

"She does," Bram said. "That doesn't mean she's using it well."

Gil found the brother's phone call and read it again. Marnie leaned across to see. Raf shifted the teapot away from her sleeve.

"He's not asking her to stay either," Gil said. "He's asking when she's leaving."

"Exactly," said Bram.

"That doesn't make you right."

"It makes me a bit right."

Marnie turned back to the mother's question. The blue mug stood against Bram's elbow. He had brought it with him when he left the counter.

"Why that one?" she asked.

"Chip in the bottom. Nobody ever puts it out for customers."

He pushed it out of her way and bent over the page. There was so much pencil in the shop's copy that the brothers had begun to write in the gap between two paragraphs.

Bram tapped a line with his finger.

"Hang on," he said. "Why's her mother still got her coat on?"

stories.title: White Thunder
stories.prompt: The Ice Kingdom is widely known for their Great Winter Contest. This year is not a disappointment!
stories.body:
# White Thunder

It took two stewards and a ladder to put Rilka on her rabbit.

She had expected the ladder. She had not expected to catch her new mulberry cape on an ear, turn halfway round, and find herself looking down the rabbit's backside while both stewards politely studied the palace.

"Forward," said her sister from below.

"I know which end is forward, Dova."

"Good. It's the end you're not facing."

Rilka hauled the cape free. The ear lost a spoonful of snow. She rubbed it smooth with one gloved finger, then carefully turned herself on the saddle.

The rabbit was a hare, properly speaking, with a narrow head, a proud chest, and hind legs folded beneath it like enormous white fists. Its ears stood six feet above her. She had cut the fur into its flanks so finely that the low sun caught every little groove. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever made, and she wanted everyone on the lake to notice.

Everyone on the lake appeared to be watching the ladder.

Beyond the starting ropes, the grandstands climbed the bank in bright tiers. People had come from three neighbouring kingdoms for the Ice Kingdom's Great Winter Contest. Those from the warmest had dressed in such quantities of fur that they looked like additional entrants. Vendors passed between the benches with hot buns and heated stones wrapped in felt; children waved paper antlers, claws, and wings. Above them, the palace's seven terraces shone with new snow. A trumpeter tried a note. The cold took it clean across the lake.

Dova held up a wooden board.

"White Thunder," Rilka read. The words were black and enormous. "Yes. That will do."

"I can still put 'Rilka's Rabbits' underneath."

"You can put that on the shop."

Dova turned the board over. It already said *Rilka's Rabbits* on the back.

For twenty years, Rilka had made little snow rabbits for children's mittened hands. The children supplied a small pulse of magic and the movement: one finger along the back to hop, two to turn. Rilka supplied the fine packed joints that made the hopping graceful, the twitch of the nose, the folded dart that could whisk a rabbit out from under a reaching palm. At the market, toddlers watched her demonstrations with their mouths open. Their parents bought her rabbits and went away happy.

Nobody had ever watched her go away carrying the Winter Cup.

It stood beside the finish poles on its velvet cushion: silver, broad as a soup tureen, with two curling handles and a lid crowned by a snowflake. Rilka had admired it at nineteen, at twenty-nine, and again that morning, at thirty-nine, after paying her entry fee. She had tried to lift it while the steward's back was turned. It was satisfyingly heavy.

"Do remember," Dova said, "the shop's roof needs new shingles."

"That is why I'm winning the prize money."

"Excellent. I'll tell the roofer we're depending on a rabbit."

The ladder went away. Rilka laid both hands on the snow in front of her and sent a slow movement through the hare's legs. It stood.

The lake was suddenly much farther down.

At home, the motion travelled from her little finger to a creature that could sit in her palm. Here it went through a shoulder wider than her kitchen table. She felt its weight come back against her hand, the drag of the haunches, the pressure of each foot on the ice. Snow had no notion of how to stand. She must give it everything.

The hare wobbled. Rilka caught the weight over its forefeet. Dova took a sensible step away.

"Now that's a rabbit," said a man behind her.

Torren's stag approached with barely a sound. It had none of the frothy detail of the hare: four long legs, a smooth narrow body, and antlers that swept back instead of standing up. Torren wore a plain red sash over his riding coat. Four tiny silver cups had been sewn into the sash, one for each of his victories.

Rilka had once persuaded herself that he rode the same stag every year. Watching him that morning make it from his allotted mound had put an end to that comforting idea.

"Hare," she said.

"My mistake." He looked up. "Splendid ears."

She liked him less for saying it correctly.

His stag turned in a great easy arc toward the starting line. He gave it room, and it came round without breaking stride. Rilka tried a turn of her own. The hare pivoted on its haunches and almost put her in the snow.

"We shall be faster than that," she muttered into its neck.

Along the line, a woman in a yellow coat sat inside the curve of a snow serpent. A squat rhinoceros stamped under a rider nearly as broad as its shoulders. There was a bear, a long-backed six-legged fox, and a dragon with a magnificent shovel of a tail. The dragon's maker was trimming his tail to keep it from fouling his neighbour. The neighbour was making her fox's grin wider.

The contest marshal came past on skates.

"Your own snow only. Through every gate. First rider between the finish poles wins. If you leave your mount, you're out. If it leaves you, we'll fetch you."

He said the last part for the visitors. Under the final leap, the catch-net sagged deep and reassuring between stout posts. A steward below it was eating a bun.

Rilka had walked the course at dawn. Out across the lake to the first gate; over the five frozen ridges of the Frostcomb; a tight bend around the old willow; then up the long ramp to the highest palace terrace. The Seven Steps brought the racers down again. Broad ramps swept across the palace front, switching from side to side as they joined the terraces. Straight ahead lay the drops; she had seen only fur hats above the terrace edges when the stewards stood on the lower shelves. She had watched Torren gallop through that zigzag for four winters. Short shelves meant gathering long legs after each landing; the ramps gave his stag room to keep running. At the bottom, twenty feet of air separated the last lip from the finish landing.

She had stood there for some time, picturing herself arriving above the net instead of in it.

Torren's stag lowered its head. The serpent drew itself into three thick coils. Rilka felt the hare's legs under her fingers, each packed joint waiting for movement. Somewhere behind the ropes, Dova shouted her name. Someone else shouted, "Rabbit Lady!"

Rilka set her jaw. The trumpeter lifted his instrument.

Nine snow beasts burst off the line.

The first two bounds were appalling. The hare lifted Rilka so high that she saw the top of the marshal's hat, then dropped her hard enough to drive her teeth together. She had made thousands of that exact movement. She had never before been sitting on it.

On the third, she bent with the back instead of resisting it.

On the fourth, she laughed.

The grandstand rushed past. The cape snapped open behind her. She could feel every foot, every great contraction of the hare's thighs. It was as though her familiar little trick had broken out of her hands and grown large enough to carry her away.

The serpent went sliding along to her left, its rider low in the curve behind its head. The rhinoceros was thundering straight ahead. Torren had already taken a place near its shoulder.

Rilka tucked the hare's front feet, gathered its haunches, and gave it the biggest bound yet.

For a moment there was no lake beneath them. The hare flew between the first gate's pennants, and Rilka saw their dark blue shadow racing over the ice. She landed ahead of the rhinoceros.

The crowd roared.

"White Thunder!" she yelled, although she was the only one close enough to hear herself.

At the Frostcomb, the serpent flattened and slipped through a gap between two ridges. The bear scrambled over the first with its claws. Torren's stag rose neatly, forelegs folded, and touched down with barely a spray.

Rilka cleared two ridges in one leap.

She landed on the narrow flat between the second and third. A hard little click came into her right thumb.

There were three ridges left. A lower bound would take them one at a time. She could feel the stag gaining, its landings soft, its pace beautifully even.

She could clear two more.

Rilka packed the right heel tighter, looked at the flags beyond the comb, and gathered the legs again.

This time, when they rose, the spectators stood.

They landed well past the fourth ridge. The click came back sharper. She had only the last ridge to cross. After that there would be plain ice, and she could ease the gait. Torren's stag was a length behind.

She leaped.

Something in the right heel shifted before it struck the ground. Rilka caught the weight on the left foot and front paws. The hare skidded sideways, throwing up a sheet of powder. Behind her, the rhinoceros's rider bellowed.

"Still ahead," Rilka said. She was breathing through her mouth. "Still ahead."

She lowered the bounds. The right foot held, but it sent a scraping pressure up into her wrist every time it took the weight. White chips scattered behind them.

At the willow bend, Torren went wide.

She knew his move. He opened the turn until the stag could run through it, then came out with its long stride unbroken.

Rilka put the hare on the inside. It was her chance to shut the door on him.

The haunches swung. She pulled the forefeet round too late. For a moment the whole hare leaned outward, right heel dragging under the load.

It snapped.

The hare dropped on one side. The willow blurred past her face. Rilka shoved both hands deep into its shoulders and held the forelegs rigid. Its chin furrowed the snow.

Torren swept past. She saw the four little cups on his sash. Then she saw the serpent's yellow-coated rider, low and quick and gone.

The rhinoceros came by on the other side. Its rider raised one arm to warn the following fox away from her.

Rilka stopped just beyond the bend.

The hare stood on three feet. Its fourth lay folded at an angle no rabbit should have had. Loose snow was pouring out of the heel.

There was fresh snow all around her. Lovely clean powder lay against the willow's trunk. She could scoop up one handful and be disqualified in front of three kingdoms.

Instead, she reached for the right ear.

She had spent half an hour getting its inside curve exactly right. Her fingers sank into it, and she pulled. A thick ribbon of snow came down past her knee and flowed beneath her palm toward the damaged leg.

The hare lurched. She had let its left knee slacken while thinking about the repair. Rilka braced it again. A six-legged fox flashed past with three separate pairs of footsteps and a wide, infuriating grin.

"Yes," she said. "Very funny."

She took the other ear. Short stumps remained above the hare's head. The weight that had tugged at her shoulders was gone; below her, the rebuilt heel grew broad and thick.

She could not keep the leg straight and reshape its joint at the same time. She folded it clear of the ice, held the hare on the other three feet, and worked until she could feel a continuous curve of packed snow beneath the damage. Her hands shook. The dragon went past. Its tail threw powder over her boots.

The hoofbeats and cheers moved away up the ramp.

Rilka lowered the repaired foot. It felt solid. It also felt as heavy as a sack of flour.

The magnificent cape had wrapped itself around her left calf. She kicked it loose, set the hare moving, and immediately found that the new heel would not fold far enough for her old bound. The hindquarters lifted unevenly. She landed sideways.

"No," she said, with the fierce quiet she used when a customer's child had broken something expensive.

She sank the hare lower, keeping the thick heel tucked close beneath it. The front paws slid forward. The hind legs followed in a quick, small thrust.

They shot ahead.

Rilka nearly went over the tail.

She knew that movement. She had given it to rabbits that darted under a toddler's closing hands: flat, folded, and suddenly somewhere else. Here it made the long body slide beneath her before the legs caught up. She tried it again, leaning forward this time.

The heel pressed against her hand. It held.

Again. A low flick of the forelegs, a fold, a quick push from behind. There was almost no fall to catch. The ears had stopped pulling her back. She could bend farther over the shoulders.

She passed the bear at the foot of the ramp. Its rider was trying to replace a missing claw without letting the other paws lose their grip.

Up the ramp, the low dart needed shorter strokes. Rilka's wrists began to ache. She had never made a rabbit run so long, nor held so much weight through so many movements. She could not look at the spectators. Each time she lost the sequence, the thick heel dragged.

The dragon was labouring halfway up. Its maker had shortened the tail, but the great shoulders still heaved with every step. Rilka came alongside, heard the man grunt with the effort of moving it, and slipped past.

At the top, the wind slapped the sweat cold against her face.

The lake opened below her, crowded with little dark figures along its edge. She could see Dova's board. Even from here, she was fairly sure Dova was showing the wrong side.

The rhinoceros had reached the first terrace ramp. Ahead of it, the fox was bringing the last of its three pairs of feet down the second drop. The serpent flowed down a terrace face, then curled sharply to bring its rider to the next drop. It was gaining on Torren, but every bend cost it a moment of recoil. Torren's stag was already sweeping out of the third ramp, fast enough that its hooves hardly seemed to settle.

Straight in front of Rilka, the drops were as high as a grown person standing on the ice. Between them lay short landing shelves, barely the hare's length from nose to tail. The broad ramps ran left, right, left, making a generous zigzag. The direct drops made one white stairway down to the last lip. Beyond that lip hung the gap, the finish landing, and two red poles.

With her old bounds, she would rise above each step and come crashing onto the next. She could feel exactly what that would do to the heel.

She pictured a fifth little cup on Torren's red sash and dug her aching fingers deeper into the snow. Then she lowered the hare until its belly nearly touched the snow.

The first drop arrived. She let the head pitch forward over the edge instead of bounding out above it. For a moment the hare's backside was higher than her shoulders.

Forepaws down. Shoulders fold. Haunches follow.

The forefeet struck the lower shelf. Rilka folded the shoulders under the impact, taking the weight through them before the haunches came down. The shock kicked into both elbows. The heavy heel hit last, with a hard thump. She clenched her teeth, waiting for it to give. Its weight came through her hand and settled.

She was already at the second edge.

The rhinoceros turned ponderously onto its ramp. Rilka dropped past its great square head. Its rider shouted something she couldn't hear.

Third step. Her cape streamed over the edge behind her. The fox was on her left, its front feet already on the lower shelf, its last pair still on the ledge above. Its rider was folding the middle legs to bring the long body through. Rilka landed beside its nose and darted ahead before the rear feet came down.

The sequence was quicker than she had practised. One shoulder would fold before the other; she had to pull them even. The hare's body wanted to slew sideways under the heavy heel. She drove the left hind foot a little harder and caught the balance. Her hands had become two cramped hooks in the snow.

Fourth step. Fifth.

The serpent took the fifth drop beside her. Its rider was grinning, bare teeth bright in a wind-reddened face. She flicked a hand, drawing the serpent's head ahead of the hare.

Rilka gave the short, folded thrust.

The sixth edge vanished under them. The serpent's coils were still gathering behind its rider when Rilka landed below.

Across the last broad ramp, Torren turned his head.

Their eyes met. His stag was running beautifully, four legs working in a long smooth reach. He had room for one more stride before the leap.

He bent over its neck. The stag stretched. Snow fanned out behind its hooves.

Rilka reached the last terrace with no long stride at all. The lip was rushing toward her. Below it she saw the net, then the polished blue of the lake. The finish poles stood on the opposite landing.

She gathered the hare's legs.

The right heel resisted.

It was sound. It was stiff. She could feel the thick packed joint refusing the last part of the fold, and the animal was still running toward the edge.

To her left, the stag sprang. Its antlers caught the sun.

Rilka bent so low that her cheek touched the hare's head. She shortened the left leg's fold to match the right, pulled the shoulders tight, and planted both hind feet against the lip.

The heavy heel bit. She drove the folded haunches open against the planted feet, flinging the hare forward and up.

They were out above the net.

There was the stag, taller in the air, its forefeet already opening for the landing. There were the red poles. Rilka's hare stretched beneath her with its front paws reaching, short ears pressed against her cheek.

They struck the far landing chin first.

Rilka felt the shock in both wrists. She kept the shoulders open. The hind legs came through, the broad heel scraping, and the hare slid in a long white sprawl.

Torren landed beside her. She could hear his breath.

The red poles went past Rilka's shoulders.

She tried to turn her head. All she could see was one of the stag's knees.

The brass bell rang.

"Rilka of the North Market!" the marshal shouted.

She sat motionless, with both hands sunk in the hare. The creature lay flat, front feet extended, one hind leg still half folded beneath it. Torren brought his stag round in a slow curve. He stared at her. Then he looked back at the finish poles.

"By half a shoulder," he said.

Rilka made a noise she hoped sounded dignified. It did not.

The serpent came through. Its rider slapped the top of its head with delight at her own finish, and the head obediently dipped. The fox arrived in fourth place, grinning as widely as ever. Across the lake, people were waving everything they could find.

"Rabbit Lady!" somebody shouted.

Rilka stood on the saddle, which was a foolish thing to do with two shaking knees. She took one hand out of the hare, raised it, and shouted back so loudly that she hurt her throat.

Torren slid off his stag. Without his touch, it sank a little at the knees and stood still.

"You came straight down," he said.

"I noticed."

He looked at the broad right heel, then up at the stumps above her head.

"Good ears," he said.

She laughed so hard that she had to sit down again.

Dova reached the landing with the marshal's permission and no regard for anybody else's feet. She brought the ladder. Rilka descended slowly, keeping a hand on the hare until her boots touched the ground. Then she let go.

The snow settled under its own weight. The hare lay stretched beside the finish, the grooves of its fine fur scuffed almost smooth, its face buried to the nose in powder.

Dova pressed her cold cheek to Rilka's hot one.

"The roof," she whispered, "is going to be magnificent."

The marshal called them to the little platform. Torren took second place; the serpent's rider took third. When Rilka received the Winter Cup, she had to lift it with both arms. Her wrists protested. She lifted it higher.

From the grandstand, nine hundred people tried to pronounce her name at once.

Dova leaned against the ladder, holding the board with *White Thunder* facing out. A small boy waited beside her, looking from Rilka to the fallen hare.

Rilka came down from the platform with the cup locked against her ribs.

"Can I ride it?" the boy asked.

"You can sit on it. It won't move without me."

"He asked if he could ride it," Dova said.

Rilka looked at the hare's battered flank. Then she looked at the boy, who had both mittens pressed over his mouth. Behind him, three other children were pretending not to wait.

"One at a time," she said.

She handed Dova the cup.

"Both hands. Mind the lid. No, the other handle too."

Torren was collecting his gloves from the foot of the platform. He paused beside the ladder.

"Are those going to be fast rides?"

Rilka glanced at him. He was smiling, but there was a small sharp interest under it.

She put her hand on the hare. Its short ears lifted. Its head rose from the snow.

"You'll have to buy a ticket."

stories.title: No Vacancy
stories.prompt: You are the only one in your class that no familiar seems to want to bond with. Your sits you down to tell you why.
stories.body:
# No Vacancy

By Friday I had learned to carry an empty perch with considerable dignity. If I kept it level and occasionally looked up, people might think my familiar was somewhere overhead.

This worked until Imby asked whether she should shut the window.

“No,” I said.

“In case it comes back?”

“For the air.”

She shut it halfway. Her starling hopped off her shoulder and went to inspect the brass ring on my perch. I had polished that ring every night since Monday. I had also made a blue leather jess, learned how to tie it one-handed, and selected three names, depending on whether my familiar turned out to be dignified, ferocious, or a girl.

The starling relieved itself on the leather.

“Sorry,” Imby said, and helped me wipe it off. She was being perfectly kind. I would have preferred her to be dreadful, because then I could have hated her.

Tomorrow our class was making its first ascent. We were going to rise from the south lawn, pass over the school roof, and come down in the orchard. Imby and I had agreed to wave at the classroom window where we had spent last winter adding columns of figures. She had asked whether we should wave with both hands. I had said that would be showing off.

Now I was the only one who hadn't bonded.

Mr. Hasp had brought out more creatures for me on Thursday: a little owl with eyebrows like Father's, two glossy bats, a gliding lizard. The lizard had tasted my finger and climbed back onto his. None were frightened. That would at least have been interesting. They simply declined.

There was still the kite-fox.

He lived in the open aviary above the orchard. He was red as a new brick, with black feet and narrow wings that folded so neatly against his flanks that you could mistake them for part of his coat. Once, when Mr. Hasp was demonstrating lift, his pigeon had taken off and the fox had gone after it. Mr. Hasp rose beneath the pigeon without moving his legs. His boots had passed my face. There was chalk on one sole.

That was what I wanted: not having to decide where to put your feet.

I had begun counting the days until familiar week before the last snow melted. My school coat had an inside pocket I had persuaded Mother to make particularly large. I had told her it was for books.

That morning, while I was dressing, I knew Father was cutting the yellow cheese downstairs. I went down before my collar was straight.

“There's a knife in my hand,” he said when I tried to take the end piece.

Crumb sat beside the table, watching the knife too. He was our dog. His muzzle was nearly white now, although the rest of him was brindled brown, and one of his ears had never learned to stand. When he got up, his back legs took a moment to agree with the front ones.

I gave him a piece of rind. Then I moved him from where he had lain across the door, because he seemed to have put himself exactly where my clean coat had to brush his fur.

At school, our lessons ended at noon so we could prepare for tomorrow. I left my perch behind a cupboard and went to the aviary.

Mr. Hasp had said that an invitation was something you offered, not threw. I had offered very politely all week. Perhaps I was doing it so politely that the creatures couldn't tell I meant it.

The kite-fox was on a low branch. He watched me come through the gate, then stretched one wing. The red fur thinned to copper along its edge. I held out my palm, breathed as we'd been taught, and let the small warmth behind my breastbone travel into my hand.

This time I didn't stop where Mr. Hasp had told us to stop. I reached farther.

The fox leaned toward me. His black nose touched the centre of my palm.

For half a second I was sure it was happening. Then the warmth jerked sideways, and I was full of the smell of hot leather, cheese rind, and the sour corner of the hearthrug. My right shoulder twitched. The fox sprang backward, landing with both wings spread.

“Hands down, Fenna.”

Mr. Hasp stood in the gate. I closed my fingers. The hearthrug went away.

“I wasn't making him,” I said.

“I know. Come along.”

“He nearly did.”

“Yes.”

That made me follow him. All week he had said things like *a different temper* and *we'll try again*. He had never said yes.

In his workroom he put two stools beside the desk. Mine was low enough that my knees looked foolish. He sat on the other one and held out his hand.

“Once more. Toward me this time. Only to your fingertips.”

“I'm not bonding with you.”

“I should hope not. I've a pigeon.”

I put my hand into his. When I made the little warmth, he touched two fingers to my wrist. Something tugged behind my ribs. Again I smelled the hearthrug.

Mr. Hasp let go.

“You told me there was no familiar at home.”

“There isn't.”

“What animals are there?”

I looked at a crack in the desk.

“A dog. But he isn't one.”

“How do you know?”

“He's Crumb.”

Mr. Hasp waited. Outside, somebody was whistling the first-ascent signal and getting it wrong.

“He doesn't do anything,” I said. “He sleeps under Father's bench. He steals things. He was sick on my arithmetic book.”

“Did he take the book flying first?”

“No.”

“Then we must rule that out.”

He rubbed his thumb over the mark my invitation had warmed on his wrist.

“The fox answered you. I saw him begin. But you were reaching along a connection already there. That's why he pulled away.”

I looked up.

“The owl could tell. So could the others. I couldn't, from outside it. I assumed you were finding the exercise difficult.” He glanced toward the door, where his pigeon was strutting past. “I should have asked about animals instead of familiars.”

“You're saying it's Crumb?”

“Unless someone keeps another dog under that bench.”

“But he's old.”

“Was he always?”

I hated that question. I hated it enough to say nothing.

He went to a shelf and took down the ground-course timetable. I recognized it because the children in that class had lessons while we were in the orchard. Their familiars included burrowing things and things with many legs. There was a girl whose familiar was a sow.

He didn't put it into my hands yet.

“Can you fix it?” I asked.

“I can help you end the connection. Your dog would have to let his part go. It won't hurt him, and he'll still be your dog.”

“And then the fox?”

“Then you can invite the fox. I can't answer for him.”

I wanted him to answer. He had been a teacher longer than I'd been alive; surely there was something he could make certain.

“Can Crumb learn to take me up?”

“A kite-fox can lend you his lift. He has to keep flying while you use it. Your dog can't lend you something he hasn't got.”

“He's very good at jumping.”

I had not seen Crumb jump for two years.

Mr. Hasp pushed the timetable a little closer.

“Bring him at four. We'll find out what you're working with before we do anything to it.”

I carried the perch home by the foot. Its brass ring knocked against my knee.

Crumb was asleep in the patch of light inside our door. I watched him for a while. He had one paw on the corner of Mother's shawl, which he wasn't allowed to sleep on. Whenever she pulled it away, he woke up as though she'd done something completely unreasonable.

“You're supposed to be extraordinary,” I told him.

He woke, looked at me, and put his head down again.

I fetched his lead.

We usually went to the orchard wall. There were smells he liked there, and I could look into the school's grounds without seeming to. Today I planned to try what Mr. Hasp had shown me along the way. I held the lead loose, made the warmth, and reached toward Crumb.

Nothing happened.

“I'm doing it properly.”

He inspected a doorstep.

I tried harder. His ear flicked, and a little door seemed to shut inside my chest.

I stood there with a hot face, being refused by my own dog.

At the end of our lane he stopped. I tugged gently toward the orchard. He braced his front paws. There was nothing remarkable in the other direction: a cracked wall, a patch of nettles, the back of the baker's shed.

“It's hardly any farther.”

He looked away from me.

I remembered his legs when he had stood up at breakfast.

“All right. The shed.”

The lead sagged. Crumb went three yards and stopped with his nose at the bottom of the wall. I leaned against it. We had forty minutes before we needed to leave for school, and he would sometimes keep at one stone until I began to feel we'd taken it for a walk.

Without much hope, I offered the little warmth again.

This time something opened.

The wall was an enormous mess.

Not dirty. I knew what dirt smelled like, or had thought I did. There was old lime, wet roots underneath, mouse droppings behind a stone. There was the baker, who had come this way in his floury apron, and his apprentice, who had come later carrying onions. Somebody's left boot had stepped in horse dung. A fox had passed close to the wall during the night. The fox was gone, but its passage was laid against the stones as plainly as if it had left red string.

I saw none of this. My eyes were still looking at nettles. The two ways of knowing wouldn't fit together at first, and I shut my eyes.

There were more mice than I had guessed. There was a cat Crumb disliked so thoroughly that I disliked it for a moment too. Beneath everything else lay a smell I couldn't name, rich and marvellous. I bent toward it.

Crumb shoved his nose under the nettles and found half a sausage wrapped in a skin of fur.

“Oh, absolutely not.”

I caught his collar. He managed to get it into his mouth before I could pull him back.

I hadn't understood until that moment how much a creature could want a sausage. The wanting went through me from gums to stomach. It was disgusting. It was delicious. I was going to be sick if he swallowed it.

“Drop it.”

His joy shut out my invitation. I had to put my fingers behind his jaws, as usual. He spat the thing into my hand and stared after it when I threw it over the wall.

On the way home he walked on the opposite side of the lane from me. Once or twice I offered again. He ignored me until we reached the doorstep where the cat had rubbed her cheek. Then he let me have his opinion.

I laughed so loudly that Mother came to the door.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Has he been eating something?”

“Not much.”

She looked at my hand.

I washed it twice.

To get Crumb to school, we borrowed the grocer's little handcart. I put his blanket in it. He climbed in after I laid a piece of cheese on the blanket; then he climbed straight out because he'd eaten it and couldn't see the point of staying.

Mother held his collar while I tipped up the handles.

“I thought your familiar was going to be one of the flying ones,” she said.

“So did I.”

She looked at me, then put Father's worn cushion beneath the blanket. Neither of us said anything else about it.

Halfway to school Crumb stood up. The cart rocked, and I had to stop and persuade him to sit. I had imagined the kite-fox riding my shoulder, turning his head when I did. Now I was arguing with a dog in a box while the baker's apprentice watched from his doorway.

In Mr. Hasp's workroom I lowered the handles. Crumb climbed out and inspected the legs of the desk. Mr. Hasp checked him with one hand against his ribs and the other around my wrist. Crumb licked his cuff.

“Yes,” he said. “This is him.”

“Could we see what it's like first?”

“Without it?”

I nodded.

He put my hand on Crumb's chest.

“Let yours go quiet. I'll hold the connection open until you decide. There's still no room for the fox. If he keeps reaching, we'll stop.”

Crumb was warm through his thin fur. I asked for the smell of the room and got ink, pigeon, and the remains of Mr. Hasp's lunch. I let my reaching settle back inside me. The dog held it a moment, then stopped too. He turned his head toward the wastebasket.

There was no dramatic emptiness. The room was still the room. Crumb was still beside my knee. When I rubbed the base of his ear, he pressed into my fingers, and when I stopped, he bumped my hand for more.

I could do this. I could take him home, give him dinner, love him exactly as before. I could come back and offer the kite-fox my hand.

Outside, the class was rehearsing. Imby's voice called, “Both arms? Is it both arms?”

Someone answered her, laughing. An owl passed the window, then a shadow: the flight instructor rising after it to check the wind above the roof. I leaned sideways to see him, his boots dangling. In another moment he was higher than the chimney.

Crumb got his head into the wastebasket.

Mr. Hasp lifted it out of reach. “No.”

The dog sat down underneath it. I knew that sit. He could keep it up for hours. I could see him perfectly well; I had known him all my life. But I couldn't catch the particular savour of whatever he'd found in there. I missed the horrible eagerness that wasn't quite my own.

The instructor came down past the window, coat lifting around him. I gripped my knees.

“How long have I had it?” I asked.

“Can't tell from here.”

“Years?”

“Possibly.”

Years, possibly, of the lane and the hearthrug and Father opening cheese. I'd told Mr. Hasp he didn't do anything. I had been very stupid. I was probably going to be stupid again, whichever way I went.

Crumb leaned against my shin. I offered the little warmth toward him. His nose lifted, and the room filled with lunch.

“Put me in the ground class,” I said.

Mr. Hasp kept his hand at my wrist a moment longer, then took it away.

“You'll need to be here earlier. They start at eight.”

“Does he have to come every day?”

“For the first week. After that we'll see.”

“And where can he sleep?”

He glanced around his crowded workroom.

“Not here. Ask the ground instructor about the cloakroom. Get him out from under that basket, please.”

I pulled Crumb away. On Mr. Hasp's desk, underneath the timetable, lay the first-ascent list. My name had a space beside it where the familiar's should have gone. I looked until he turned the paper over.

The next morning I arrived before eight. My nice blue coat was rolled up in the cart because pulling the cart had made me hot. Crumb had decided the cushion was worth lying on after all. I had pinned his loose ear back for a moment while I fastened the lead, then let it flop where it wanted.

Imby was on the south lawn with the others. She saw us through the gate.

“Is that yours?”

I looked behind me, although there was nobody else.

“Crumb.”

“Hello, Crumb.” She held out the back of her hand. He sniffed it. “You're not coming up?”

I shook my head.

“Oh.”
