The signal whistle blew. Imby looked toward the instructor, then back at me.

“You'd better go,” I said.

She hurried away. Her starling took off ahead of her and circled low while she found the warmth. Then her heels left the grass. Her mouth opened. I could see that from the gate.

I watched them rise past the classroom window. Imby waved with both hands. I waved back with one, keeping the other on the cart handle. By the time they reached the roof, my eyes were wet and I couldn't pick her out anymore.

Crumb stood up, so I lowered the handles and let him climb out. He went to the hedge by the gate. We were supposed to go straight to the cloakroom, but he planted his feet when I took up the lead.

“We are already late.”

He put his nose farther into the leaves.

I could still hear the children above the roof. I loosened the lead and offered my attention. Under the clipped green leaves was a small, busy trace, warm from the creature that had just gone through. Crumb followed it along the hedge, checking one stem and then another. At the corner it vanished beneath the lowest branches.

I knelt on my clean skirt to see where it went.

stories.title: The Last Watch
stories.prompt: We had spent fifty years holding the rift together, awaiting the one who would finally seal it for good. What arrived was not the savior we had been promised.
stories.body:
# The Last Watch

My daughter's letter lay on the stone beside me, held down by a cup. She had put a bed in her front room. I could live on one floor, she wrote, and the window faced the plum tree.

I had been trying to answer her since autumn.

Four of us held the rift that morning. My binding came out of my right wrist, thin and white, and disappeared into the upright crack between the two black stones. Marda's ran beneath mine. Across the opening, Len stood on a folded blanket to keep the cold from his feet. The fourth keeper was asleep in her chair; she could do that now, after forty years. I had never learned.

We relieved one another, slept, ate, had children. The world had continued on our side. But somebody had always been here with the near edge caught on their living bindings, stopping it from tearing wider. Once, in the third winter, two keepers had died within an hour of each other. Before their reliefs took hold, the opening had swallowed half the hillside. My daughter's first school was somewhere beyond it.

We could hold this edge. We could not reach the other. Stepping through was easy enough; on the far side, the way back moved. Someone had to find it, carry the far edge home, and join it to ours. The man who had promised to do that had a sun worked in gold on his breastplate. He had gone through on the first day with six others.

My husband was one of the six.

Fifty years later, we still kept the passage narrow enough for a man to squeeze through.

Len was humming. He was twenty-seven and could not remember a world without the opening. He had been born in the little house where we rested between watches. His mother had set him in a basket beside her chair and held a binding over him while he slept.

“Does your daughter want an answer?” he asked.

“She has an answer.”

“The same one?”

I slid the letter under the cup again.

The white line over Len's wrist jumped. He stopped humming and set his feet apart. At the opening, the darkness folded in on itself. A hand came through, gripping the stone. Then a shoulder and the side of a face.

He was carrying something against his chest.

“Hold,” Marda said.

We held. The sleeping keeper woke with a gasp. Len's blanket slid under one heel, but he stayed upright while the man dragged his second leg free.

He had one boot. His bare foot was wrapped in a piece of blue cloth, dark with dirt. He crouched on the stone, covering the bundle with his body, and my binding pulled hard enough to bring me out of my chair.

“Get clear,” I told him.

He tried. A white loop rose from his left wrist and stretched back into the opening. He caught that arm against his ribs, breathing through his teeth.

Marda stared at the loop.

The man looked up at me.

“Olla?”

He had grown a beard. There was a pale scar through one eyebrow, and his hair had been cut badly, close on one side and long on the other. Under those changes was a face I had spent fifty years becoming less certain I remembered.

I had forgotten how brown his eyes were.

“Talven,” I said.

He looked at my face, then at my hands. His gaze came back to my face and stayed there.

The bundle began to cry.

“Is that yours?” I asked.

He shook his head. “Biri.” He loosened the cloth around a small red face. “I need to feed her. Have you anything?”

There was milk in the resting house. Len called through the door for it. Talven kept looking at me while Biri rooted against his torn coat.

“How long?” he asked.

“Fifty years.”

He sat down very carefully.

“How long for you?”

“A year. Nearly two. We lost count of the days when the sky stopped turning.”

I had things to tell him. Our daughter had learned to whistle before she could say his name. I had kept the red coat he hated until moths got into it. His father had died in a chair, holding an apple he had meant to eat. Once I had gone three whole days without thinking of Talven, and when I noticed, I had put on his coat in the middle of summer.

What I said was, “Your father died.”

He bowed his head over the child.

“And our girl?”

“Alive. Fifty-two. She has children. One of them has children.”

His mouth moved. No sound came out.

A girl brought the milk in a jug, along with a little cup and a spoon. She was one of the people who cooked for us, old enough to be Talven's sister, young enough to be my great-granddaughter. Talven tried to thank her, but Biri's crying broke into little breathless snatches and he was fumbling with the cup.

“Here,” I said.

He brought the baby to my left arm. I drew her close while he spooned milk between her lips. She swallowed, spilled it, got angry, and swallowed again. Her body was hot through the cloth. I remembered this weight. I had not expected to remember it with him kneeling beside me.

My binding tightened when I leaned too far. I settled back.

“Where is her mother?”

“At the red camp. Unless they moved.”

“Why isn't she with you?”

He wiped milk from Biri's chin with his thumb.

“We were crossing a place where the ground wouldn't stay still. There were ropes. Biri's mother was behind me, and I had the child because we thought—” He looked at Biri. “We thought she'd be safer tied to me.”

“Did you see her fall?”

“No.”

Biri closed her mouth over the spoon. He eased it free.

Len had come as close as his binding allowed. He was looking at Talven's wrist.

“You brought it,” he said.

Talven rubbed the back of that hand against his leg. The loop shone through the dirt on his skin. Unlike ours, it lay doubled, one white strand going into the rift and the other ending in a tight turn above his knuckles.

“Where's the man who went with you?” Marda asked.

Talven did not answer at once. He tried another spoonful; Biri turned her face away.

“The man with the sun,” Marda said.

“I know who you mean.”

“Is he coming?”

Talven set the spoon in the cup.

“I held the far edge while he looked for a way through. When he found one, he came back for us. There were people following us who hadn't got across the moving ground. I couldn't leave the post. Not without dropping this.” He lifted the doubled loop a little. “He took the weight so I could carry the loop. And her.”

“Then he'll follow,” Len said.

Talven looked past him into the opening.

“He said, ‘Go. I'll keep it.’”

“He'll follow,” Len repeated, more quietly.

“I don't know.”

Talven's left arm was trembling. I gave Biri the last of the milk while Marda leaned forward to examine his binding. Her white hair had come loose, and a lock fell across his knuckles.

“Let me see,” she said.

He opened his hand.

Marda brought her own line down toward the turn of his. Before they touched, her binding slackened. The crack narrowed by the width of a finger. A little chip of stone fell from high above us.

She tried to ease the doubled turn onto her wrist, as we relieved one another on watch. The white line passed through her arm and lay against Talven's knuckles. His arm was still trembling.

She withdrew. The two lines tightened, and the gap resumed its old width.

Nobody spoke.

I could see how to do it. We had been shown as children, long before there was any need: two living ends, one carried all the way around the break, joined while the holders let the near edge go. We had played at it with loops of wool. The far turn stayed with the person who had carried it around the break. We had never imagined a man would come back with one boot and a hungry baby, too tired to keep his hand open.

“We can close it,” the keeper in the chair said.

Marda put her left hand over her mouth.

For fifty years we had awaited a man bright enough to face the opening and make it nothing. We had told our children what his coming would look like. I had privately believed Talven would step out behind him, and that I would be waiting in the red coat.

Talven took Biri from me. He wiped her mouth on a clean corner of the blue cloth from his foot.

“Not yet,” Len said.

Marda lowered her hand.

“You heard him. There are still people.”

“There have always been people,” she said.

“That's why we hold it.”

He spoke without looking at me. He had both feet planted firmly now. I remembered his basket beneath his mother's white binding.

Talven gathered the loose cloth around Biri's legs. His left hand shook too much to tuck it in. I did it for him.

“Can you wait?” I asked.

He looked at the doubled loop.

“I can't leave it here. If I go away from the seam, it comes off me. Then you'd have to wait for someone else.”

He stood, holding Biri against his right shoulder, and took a step toward the door. The white loop stretched. The turn above his knuckles opened, showing a dark gap through its middle, and Marda's binding jerked sideways.

“Stop,” she said.

He came back. The turn drew tight again.

“It won't hurt you if I drop it,” he said. “But you won't have the far end.”

“You would drop it?” Len asked.

Talven's face changed. He put his cheek against Biri's hair and closed his eyes.

“He took my place,” he said.

“Then wait for him.”

“I waited there.”

Len opened his mouth. Talven looked at him, and he closed it again.

Beyond the doorway the girl was washing the spoon. I heard her set it on the jug. That small sound went on after the others had stopped.

“Which way does our girl live?” Talven asked me.

“Down the road. The house with the plum tree.”

He shifted Biri higher on his shoulder. His bare foot rested on our cold stone. The blue cloth hung over my chair, wet with milk.

“Will she know me?”

“I don't know.”

He nodded as if I had given him directions he could follow. I could see him on the road, looking for the house. I could see my daughter opening the door. My binding ran from my wrist into the rift; when I moved my hand, the white line moved with it.

“You could stay beside me,” I said.

He looked down at my chair.

“We'd have another chair brought in. There's room.” I pointed with my left hand. “Biri could sleep in the resting house. We'll find someone who can nurse her. She ought to have her mother, Talven. If we wait—”

I had nearly said, if we wait together.

He crouched beside my chair again. Biri had gone to sleep with one fist caught in the hair at his neck.

“I'm sorry,” he said.

“A little longer.”

His lips pressed together. He looked at my right wrist, at the white line that had rubbed a bare track through the hair there. Then he looked at his own.

“Olla, I can't.”

I wanted him to say more. Even a lie would have given me something to answer.

He laid his unbound hand on the arm of my chair. His little finger was crooked at the first joint. A horse had bitten him when he was seventeen; I had never let him forget whose fault it was. I put my left hand over his, and for a moment I felt the young hand I had been reaching for whenever somebody woke me from a dream.

He turned his palm up under mine. His eyes filled, and he blinked hard. I could not tell whether he was seeing me or looking for me.

Across the gap, Len lowered himself onto his blanket.

“You don't know she's dead,” he said, looking at Biri.

“No,” Talven said.

“You don't know about any of them.”

“No.”

Len sat with his binding stretched above his knee. Then he began to feed it back through his fingers, shortening it. The gap shivered, putting more weight on our three lines. I braced my heels.

He had not released it. He was passing his share to us.

Marda bent her head and took the added weight. So did the keeper in the chair. Len drew the last white turn down to his wrist and slipped it off. It went dark against his palm.

“Where are you going?” I asked.

“To the far post.”

Talven caught his sleeve as he rose.

“You can't get there from that side. I came out miles from where I went in.”

“You got back.”

“It took us nearly two years. You may not find them. You may not find this.”

Len looked at Talven's hand on his sleeve.

“You want us to shut it with them in there.”

Talven let go.

Marda was leaning sideways under the strain. I could see a muscle beating in her neck. Three of us could hold until the next shift came; we had done it before. Len could go, and Talven could go, and we would carry on.

Len knelt to fold his blanket. He folded it badly, twice, then opened it out and tried again. All the time, he watched the dark place between the stones.

“Len,” I said.

He stopped with one corner in his hand.

“I may close it before you're back.”

He looked at the doubled loop on Talven's wrist. Then he looked at me.

“I know.”

“Will you come back?”

“I'll try.”

There was no promise I could ask of him that I had not once believed.

Talven drew his hand out of mine and stood up. For a moment I thought he was going after Len. He took one step toward the rift, and Biri woke against his neck with a soft, questioning sound. He stopped.

Len's blanket lay half folded. He looked at the child, then at Talven's bare foot. He put the blanket down beside him.

“For the road,” he said.

He went through before any of us answered. For an instant his bare wrist caught the light of our bindings. Then there was only the opening.

Talven stood where Len had left him. He had not picked up the blanket.

Marda turned her face toward me. Her eyes were wet. She said nothing about closing it. I felt her binding tremble beside mine.

I lowered my wrist and settled the binding back along its old track. The pulling eased.

“We can hold until relief,” I said.

Talven nodded. He picked up Len's blanket and tucked it around Biri, drawing the wool under her chin. Then he straightened and gathered her close.

“I'll go, then.”

He lifted his left wrist to take the loop off.

“Bring the far end,” I said.

Talven did not move.

I stood. My knees had stiffened while I sat. I caught the arm of the chair with my left hand and waited until I could straighten.

“Olla.”

“Bring it.”

He gave Biri to the girl at the door. She gathered the blanket around the child's feet and held her without asking whose she was. Talven came back to the opening and lifted his left wrist.

Marda laid her loop against the turn of his. The keeper in the chair did the same. I brought mine last.

Len was on the other side of that gap.

Our bindings crossed above his knuckles. He closed his other hand over them. The pulling stopped.

“Let go,” he said.

Marda slipped her wrist free. The keeper beside her followed. I had held mine through fires, fevers, my father's funeral, and the morning they brought my daughter's first child to the door. I turned my hand inside it and drew it out.

Talven pulled the joined ends tight.

The black stones touched. There was no flash. A line remained between them, narrow and dry, and a little powder fell onto his foot.

He put both hands against the line. We waited. When he took them away, the stones stayed together.

The girl stood at the door with Biri wrapped in Len's blanket. Len's mother was due at noon. She always called to him from outside before coming in. I would have to tell her myself.

Marda sat down and began to cry. The other keeper leaned toward her, but neither of them seemed to know what to do with their hands.

Talven retrieved Biri. The girl found him a pair of shoes from the resting house. They were too large; he stuffed folded cloth into the toes. I put my daughter's letter in my pocket, though I knew the way.

At the door, he reached back for me. His hand was still held at the height mine had been fifty years ago. He lowered it when he saw me moving down the step.

I took it. The light outside hurt my eyes. Biri had woken and was sucking the edge of his coat, and we went slowly down the road toward our daughter's house.

stories.title: The Second Door
stories.prompt: you recently gained super powers, the problem is you have dissociative identity disorder and each personality now has a power.
stories.body:
# The Second Door

Sahar tapped the coin hanging between them. Della flinched, and it fell into the sawdust.

“Still need misdirection,” Sahar said.

Della had hoped for something warmer after eleven months.

“It was actually floating.”

“I saw.” Sahar retrieved it and rubbed the sawdust off with her thumb. “I was watching your face. So would an audience.”

Nine nights earlier, a white light had passed over the city without making a sound. Since then the woman at the corner bakery had been serving rolls hot from an unplugged oven. Della could hold a small object still in the air, provided she kept her attention on it. So far she had managed a coin, a plum and an overdue bill. The bill remained overdue.

Della had lived with dissociative identity disorder for years. Amos and June shared this body and its days; they had new powers, too. Some days Della could hear June commenting on things. Some days she found a week's worth of shopping in the fridge and remembered none of it. The powers were new enough that their notebook still had questions in the margins instead of answers.

Sahar set the coin on the workbench.

“You said you had work.”

Della pulled the sheet off the cabinet.

It was taller than they were, painted midnight blue, with a brass sunburst on its front door. Della had bought it as a plain wardrobe when she was nineteen. Sahar had made the concealed side door six years later, in the summer when their entire act fitted into a borrowed van. Their initials were still scratched beside its hinge.

They used to end with Sahar disappearing from it and Della bringing her back. On their last night together, Sahar had stayed backstage after the disappearance and let Della fill four horrible minutes.

Afterward she had said, “Try introducing me as a magician sometime.”

Della had said something about what was printed on the tickets. She remembered the precise thing, but preferred the shorter version.

Now the side door was screwed shut. Without it, the inside looked honest.

“We won't need that bit,” Della said. “Amos can open the front onto another door. Anywhere he knows.”

Sahar examined the screw heads.

“And what am I doing?”

“Going somewhere impossible.”

“Will I have a chair there?”

“What?”

“For the eleven months until you remember to bring me back.”

Della laughed before she could help it. Sahar didn't, but one corner of her mouth moved.

The Bellwether had offered four hundred for an evening of ordinary illusions. After hearing about the powers, Mr. Brack had offered twelve hundred and sent six hundred as a repair advance. Della had spent it on hinges, new casters and someone capable of making the warped front door close properly.

She had gone home with a contract and an old hunger awakened: the warm dark beyond the footlights, Sahar beside her, a roomful of people waiting for whatever they would do next.

She showed Sahar the provisional poster.

**DELLA. THREE POWERS. ONE BODY.**

Below that, in much smaller type: **with assistant.**

“I was going to have him change that.”

“Which part?”

“Your part.”

Sahar folded the poster along Della's face.

“Let's see this door.”

*

When Amos was present the following afternoon, Sahar was eating a cheese sandwich on the cabinet's steps. He recognized her shoes before her face. She still wore the red ones she'd bought for the doomed summer tour.

“I thought you'd burned those.”

“They're good shoes. The tour wasn't their fault.”

He had missed her. He didn't say it immediately. Sahar offered him the half of the sandwich that had more cheese, which helped.

She had brought a small terracotta pot.

“Mrs. Orley's cuttings,” she said. “You left this at my place.”

The stems were bare.

“You overfed it.”

“Or it died of loneliness. That was my other diagnosis.”

Mrs. Orley's garden was six hours away by train. During the year they'd rented her upstairs rooms, Amos had helped her grow pears against a sunny brick wall. She tied old stockings around the fruit to keep the wasps off. Della disliked the quiet there. June had loved Mrs. Orley's radio, which received three stations and insisted on playing two at once.

Amos had been trying to open the garden's back door from their kitchen. Twice he had succeeded. Both times he'd discovered the same difficulty: he had to keep his hand on the kitchen handle. He could reach across. He couldn't get the whole body through without letting go.

The first pear leaves had appeared in the doorway. He'd stood smelling them until his hand cramped, then gone to buy groceries in the usual way.

“We could take the train,” Sahar said.

“After paying the electrician.”

“Ah.” She put the pot down. “Well. Show me what happens when you let go.”

The theatre's prop room was a doorway Amos knew. He opened the cabinet's front onto it. Instead of the blue-painted interior, there were rolled carpets, a plaster moon and the back of Sahar's head: she'd gone around the scenery to wait there.

She stepped through onto the stage. He let go of the handle. The prop room was replaced by the cabinet's ordinary interior.

Sahar went back around, and they tested it the other way. She crossed from stage to prop room and stood well clear. He released the handle. The plaster moon vanished from view. Sahar remained in the prop room.

Ninety-three seconds later she came back onto the stage, chewing the last of her sandwich.

“Scenery's in the way,” she said. “You have to go right around the back.”

Sahar set a little cue lamp in the wing and took its wireless switch.

“Blue means I'm ready to come back,” she said. “You open the front; I step through.”

They tried the routine. She crossed into the prop room again. Amos shut the front, keeping his hand on the handle to keep the passage there.

The last clear thing Della remembered was Sahar folding the poster, the day before. Now she was standing beside the cabinet with one hand on its handle, the rehearsal lamp blinking blue.

Sahar was gone.

There was a bite of cheese sandwich in Della's mouth. Her stomach growled.

She swallowed, looked at the clock and opened the front door. An empty blue cupboard looked back at her. With Amos no longer present, the door led into its ordinary interior again. Sahar was still in the prop room, waiting for a way back that Della couldn't open.

“Sahar?”

“Coming.” The voice was muffled and distant.

Della waited through the blue lamp's next six flashes. Sahar finally appeared from behind the far end of the scenery.

“Where's Amos?”

“I'm Della.”

“Hello, Della.” Sahar sat on the cabinet steps. “That's our problem.”

Della knew what she meant. She still tried.

“We could rehearse more.”

“I've rehearsed plenty. So has he. I can't get through a door that isn't there.”

The lamp went on blinking. Della unplugged it.

“You used to be out of this thing in three seconds.”

“I had a second door.”

Sahar pointed stage left. The old cabinet had stood there, its side tight against a masking flat. A performer could slip through its concealed exit into the wing, unseen by the audience. Della had moved it to centre stage so nobody would suspect such a route. Then she'd screwed the route shut.

She looked from the flat to the cabinet.

“I put it in the wrong place.”

“You did.”

*

Later on the day Della and Sahar met, June had made her own visit to the Bellwether.

She'd stood in the dressing room singing along with a radio serial while Sahar changed for a children's matinee. The detective was pleading innocence in a mournful tenor. June preferred the villain's part.

“You're swallowing the last word,” Sahar said through the partition. “Take a breath before it.”

June stopped singing. The partition was brick.

“You can hear me?”

“They can hear you in the office.”

June looked at the wall. She'd been imagining singing right through it, into the empty room beyond. When she stopped imagining it, the radio in her hand went thin and tinny again.

“Well,” she said. “That's going to spoil some eavesdropping.”

Sahar came around the partition in her red shoes and a waistcoat full of pockets.

“You should audition. They've got a vacancy on Tuesdays.”

“I haven't sung for people.”

“Apparently you have.”

June filled in a form at the box office. Under special requirements she wrote, **A pianist who won't hurry the middle bit.**

She found the poster on her way out.

Her voicemail to Mr. Brack was brief. “I'm June. That sound demonstration Della mentioned isn't booked. I haven't agreed to it. My application is for the Tuesday singing job.”

She saved a copy of the message for Della. Under it, in the notebook, she added: **Sahar says I should do the sad one. She's wrong.**

Della read the entry sitting on the theatre floor with the screwdriver. Then she played the message again.

She had planned an unseen orchestra. June had applied for a pianist.

Della backed the first screw out of the side panel.

*

Mr. Brack kept a radiator under his desk even in summer. Della sat across from it, sweating.

“You have the door power,” he said. “I saw your video.”

“Amos has it.”

“Fine. Amos has it. And if Amos isn't around, you've got floating things. We'll make an evening of it.”

“You promised three miracles.”

“We'll change that to extraordinary feats.”

There was the door back into the contract: a softer promise, a few floating coins, an audience who'd paid for something nobody could be certain of supplying. Della could almost feel the brass coin between her fingers.

“Sahar's doing the cabinet act,” she said. “Ordinary illusions. She can finish the programme on her own if she has to.”

“At the original fee.”

“Yes.”

“And I need the advance back.”

Della looked at the photograph behind him: Mr. Brack, much younger, standing beside a sword box. He had spent twenty minutes admiring the cabinet when it arrived. He'd run his fingers over the repaired sunburst.

“The cabinet covers it.”

He waited.

“It's worth more than the advance.”

“It takes up a lot of room,” he said.

For a moment she wanted to take everything out into the street: the cabinet, the caster grease, the poster folded along her face. She'd made strangers gasp beside that brass sunburst when she was young enough to believe they'd keep coming forever.

“You own it,” she said. “From today. We use it tonight.”

Mr. Brack turned a piece of paper around and pushed his pen across.

Della signed. Then she asked for another sheet.

“New poster.”

He sighed. “What name?”

She wrote **SAHAR & COMPANY**, and brought it out to Sahar.

“One night,” Sahar said.

“I know.”

Sahar looked at her for a while.

“Help me move this bloody thing.”

*

Amos came back to the smell of sawdust and warm stage lamps. It was evening. Their shirt cuffs were rolled up; one wrist ached. He found the notebook open beside the screwdriver.

The cabinet had its side door again. Below the brass sunburst was a little paper label: **BELLWETHER PROPERTY.**

Sahar was testing the gap between the cabinet and the masking flat. She turned sideways, passed through the concealed door into the wing, and came back through it carrying her bag.

“Amos?”

He nodded.

“Della left the timings there. Don't worry about them yet.”

He read the short entry about the fee and the cabinet. Beneath it she'd drawn the blue lamp, the front door and two little knocks beside the side panel.

He'd performed this trick with Sahar before. He'd been dreadful at the grand announcement; she'd told him to open the door and look surprised. Looking surprised had proved easy.

They checked the repaired cabinet. Amos opened the front onto the prop room. While he watched its plaster moon, Sahar slipped through the cabinet's side door. He heard her knock on the blue wooden wall beside him.

“Let go,” she said.

He released the handle. The moon disappeared from the doorway's view; Sahar stood in the ordinary blue chamber behind it.

“There's our return.” She came out through the front.

“What if I don't do it?” he asked.

“I do the card act. I can keep them going.”

He had enough of Della's afternoon in his head to know how dearly she'd wanted this night. A few images, the pressure of the pen, her hand flat against the cabinet. The rest he'd have to get from her later.

“I don't want to give them the prop room,” he said.

“What do you want to give them?”

He told her.

Sahar rubbed the last trace of glue off her fingers.

“Nobody goes through that one.”

“No.”

“I use the side door. Blue when I'm out in the wing; two knocks when I'm back inside. Let go, then.”

He tried the handle. The repaired hinge made no sound.

“I'll do it.”

They waited together while Mr. Brack introduced Sahar, mispronouncing her name. Sahar closed her eyes for a second. Then she stepped into the light.

*

First she made a woman in the front row find her own watch inside an orange. Then she invited Amos to check the cabinet.

He went in through the front, turned, and came out. Empty blue walls, a brass handle, good hinges. Sahar stepped inside. He closed the front door.

The audience counted to three.

Behind the closed front, Sahar slipped through the side panel into the wing. Amos saw the rehearsal lamp turn blue.

He took the brass handle in his right hand and opened the front again.

Warm air touched his face.

Beyond the doorway, pears in old stockings hung against a brick wall. A wicker chair stood beneath them. Mrs. Orley was at her kitchen step in slippers, trying to persuade a blackbird out of a saucer.

Somebody in the audience whispered, “That's a very good screen.”

“Mrs. Orley,” Amos said.

She looked up.

“Oh, there you are. I thought you were the blackbird.”

Amos laughed. His right hand tightened on the handle.

“How are the pears?”

“You're looking at them.”

“I mean, are they ripe?”

Mrs. Orley glanced past him into the auditorium. She bent toward the doorway, squinting.

“Have you got people there?”

“A few.”

“You might have warned me.” She straightened the front of her cardigan.

“Sorry,” Amos said. “Shall I close it?”

“No, stay a minute. I've had no difficulty growing these pears this year. Picking them's another matter.”

In the wing, Sahar passed behind the masking flat. The cabinet's side door opened inward, into the blue chamber concealed behind the garden view.

Amos listened to Mrs. Orley complain about her neighbour's ladder. He saw the little branch he'd tied flat against the wall last winter. It had put out three new shoots. He could smell fallen leaves warming on the brick path.

He shifted his foot forward, then stopped. The handle was still here. The garden was over there.

Mrs. Orley noticed his hand.

“Still can't come in?”

He shook his head.

“Hang on.”

She took a pear from a bowl beside the kitchen step and removed its stocking.

“Catch.”

It came across the doorway in a short, untidy arc. Amos caught it against his chest with his free hand. There was a burst of applause that made Mrs. Orley blink.

“Good heavens. They're easily pleased.”

He was laughing too hard to answer.

“Is Sahar about? Here's another.”

He put the first pear into his shirt pocket and caught the second. Two small knocks came from the cabinet's side. Sahar was back inside.

“I have to go,” he said.

“Well, eat them before they soften. And come by train next time.”

He let go of the brass handle.

The garden was replaced by the blue chamber. Sahar stood inside with her hands raised. For a second she blinked as if she'd come from a bright place; then she bowed and stepped out onto the stage.

Amos offered her the pear.

She accepted it without flourish. She took a bite before her second bow.

*

Afterward Mr. Brack came to ask about more nights with the garden. Amos told him he could ask about card tricks. Sahar was good at those.

They watched a stagehand wheel the cabinet toward the theatre's store. When the paper label brushed the masking flat, Sahar smoothed it down.

“June's audition is Tuesday,” she said. “Tell her I'll come if she does the ridiculous detective song.”

“She'll do the villain.”

“Of course she will.”

Sahar put the bitten pear into her bag, wrapped in the old provisional poster. Then she took her own small case of tricks and went out to catch her bus.

Amos sat on the empty steps for a minute, writing the things he wanted Della and June to know.

The cabinet was waiting by the store-room entrance. Its front faced the wall. Someone had left the little side door open, exposing the narrow blue chamber and the scratches beside the hinge.

He put one hand over the pear in their shirt pocket and went out to find his bus.

stories.title: No Comment
stories.prompt: You're PR manager for Magical Girls. Some of their powers make your work really hard though.
stories.body:
# No Comment

"No comment," said Honest Pearl.

Above her head, in luminous blue letters, appeared:

**MARNIE HAS FORBIDDEN ME TO ANSWER THAT.**

"Better," I said. "At least you've stopped naming my solicitor."

Pearl consulted the notes she'd made on the back of her wrist. She had written them very small, so they wouldn't show in photographs. "Would 'We have nothing to add' be preferable?"

"Do you have anything to add?"

"Several things."

"Then probably not."

We were rehearsing beside the cake fridge at Bell's Bakery. In twenty minutes, the bakery would reopen, and the Bright Side would make their first paid promotional appearance under my management. There would be one newspaper photograph, a brief video interview, and the cutting of a ribbon. Mr. Bell had paid us six hundred pounds. Three hundred would go toward repairing our office window; the rest would pay me for the previous month.

The window had been Fanfare's fault, technically. She'd caught a chair falling from an upstairs balcony. The resulting brass flourish had startled a man carrying a ladder, who put it through our office window.

Now she was practising a song in the reflection of the fridge door.

"There isn't a solo," I told her.

"I know. I'm warming up in case there's an opportunity."

Petal Riot had already found an opportunity. She stood at the counter with a cinnamon twist in each hand.

"Those are for the guests."

"I'm going outside. Then I'm coming back in."

"You'll still be working."

She put one twist down. The other disappeared in two bites.

The girls had saved Bell's three weeks earlier, when a delivery van had rolled through its front window. Petal had stopped it against a bank of dahlias, Fanfare had lifted the driver out, and Pearl had carried Mr. Bell to the pavement. The man from the Gazette arrived just in time to photograph the baker being held horizontally by a young woman in white boots, beneath the words **HE IS VERY HEAVY**.

It was a perfectly good rescue and a perfectly bad photograph. Mr. Bell had looked as though he was being abducted.

Today's photograph would be different. I had sketches. I had a shot list. I had brought a comb.

"You should be in it," Pearl said.

"No."

"There's room beside me."

"I'm your public relations manager. My face is for recognising at meetings. Yours are for recognising on posters."

Fanfare turned from the fridge. "But you got us this."

"And if I do my job well, I can buy groceries in yesterday's cardigan without anyone asking me to strike a pose."

Petal swallowed. "You could have a good pose."

"You haven't seen the cardigan."

Mr. Bell emerged from the kitchen carrying a cake the size of a baking tray. He had piped his business name across the top and the girls' emblems down the front. The centrepiece was a sugar model of his new shop window. He seemed to have taken a great deal of satisfaction in making it intact.

I put down my clipboard to help him. Fanfare lifted the whole thing from his hands.

"Where?"

"That table, please. Gently."

She set it down without disturbing a crumb. Then the trumpets began.

Mr. Bell shut his eyes.

Fanfare's music accompanied relief after physical effort. The more relieved she was, the louder and longer it played. Once she'd held up a collapsing cinema balcony, and the orchestra had continued through the evacuation, the paramedics' arrival, and most of a subsequent interview about whether the building had been inspected.

Our radio campaign hadn't lasted long.

"It'll be over in eight bars," I told Mr. Bell.

It was twelve. Fanfare hummed the last four, trying out a harmony.

While we waited, Petal slid the remaining cinnamon twist toward the edge of the counter.

"I can see that," I said.

"I haven't eaten it."

"Yet," said Pearl.

**YET**, agreed the lettering above her.

The photographer arrived with a reporter, two bags of equipment, and a pollen allergy. I had asked about allergies. I had asked his editor, who had answered, "Only to missing deadlines."

We moved Petal's pose away from the pastry display. She could stop the force of an impact by turning it into flowers. It was a wonderful power. I had once spent an entire afternoon persuading a picture editor that the photograph of a man waist-deep in peonies showed a thwarted bank robbery rather than a proposal.

"No flowers today," I reminded her.

"I don't make them for decoration."

"I know. No impacts, either."

The photographer unfolded a reflector. Mr. Bell turned to greet the reporter, and caught the edge of a stacked tray with his apron. Petal reached past him just as it fell. Six tulips opened beneath the tray. It landed softly on their heads.

The second tray fell behind the first. Petal couldn't see it until too late. It hit the floor with a crash.

"Sorry," she said, bending to gather both trays. "The big one was in the way."

The photographer sneezed into his elbow.

"Could we do that again?" he asked. "The flowers coming out?"

"No," I said.

"That was lovely."

"Thank you," said Petal, pleased. "Usually people just ask whether I can do lawns."

"We could have her stopping something bigger. A sack of flour."

"We are going to have three girls standing in front of a cake."

He glanced at my shot list. "Right."

I took the tulips out to the bin. On the way back, I noticed that the sun had reached the little square outside the bakery. Indoors, the cake's sugar window was throwing a shadow across Petal's face, and Pearl's captions were reflecting in the fridge door, which made her look twice as indiscreet.

"We could do the photograph outside," I said.

Mr. Bell considered his cake.

"Sugarwings," he said.

I looked beneath the awning. No white tufts. No beating wings. Nothing in the branches of the little ornamental tree.

Sugarwings were the reason Bell's had a mesh screen door. They were fluffy, cat-sized pastry thieves with wings too small for their bodies and the determination to compensate. They couldn't bite a person; their mouths were more like drinking straws. But they could empty an éclair while you were paying for it.

"Ninety seconds," I said. "Petal can keep watch. Then we bring it straight back in."

Mr. Bell shook out the cloth he used to shoo them away. "All right. Ninety seconds."

Fanfare carried the cake outside to one of the pavement tables. I let the music finish before bringing out the reporter.

The guests were beginning to arrive. Petal directed them toward the counter, where Mr. Bell was setting out little plates. Pearl read through her wrist again. Her boots were white, her plait was immaculate, and she looked as anxious as someone waiting to sit an exam she had revised for very thoroughly.

"Don't try to sound official," I told her. "Give her one thing you actually want to say about the bakery."

"I like the cinnamon twists."

"Excellent. Say that."

"Won't it make me sound greedy?"

"It will make you sound like someone outside a bakery."

The reporter switched on her camera and asked how it felt to see Bell's reopening.

"I like the cinnamon twists," said Pearl.

**I LIKE THE CINNAMON TWISTS.**

The reporter smiled. I made a small tick on my clipboard.

"And it's been wonderful working with Mr. Bell," Pearl added.

**HE PAID US BEFORE WE ARRIVED.**

I put my finger over the tick.

"She's new to commercial appearances," I said.

"Is there someone else I could ask about the rescue?"

"Absolutely."

I brought Fanfare over. I had told her to walk from the door. She had walked from the door. We were making progress.

"When you saw the van coming through the window," the reporter asked, "what went through your mind?"

"Petal's in front of me, and Pearl's got the baker, so I can go for the driver. The door was stuck. I bent it back."

"Were you frightened?"

"Of course. He kept trying to get his seat belt off, and I couldn't make him sit still. I thought he might fall when I lifted him."

It was a good answer. Simple, vivid, generous to her teammates. Then she glanced down at the clasp of her red cape. It had gone crooked. She tried to straighten it, pulled too hard, and tore the clasp free.

The cape slipped off her shoulders. She caught it before it touched the ground.

A snare drum rattled. Trumpets celebrated. The reporter's microphone filled with a choir announcing no words at all, just immense satisfaction.

"I didn't want it dirty," Fanfare said under the music.

"I know. We'll do that answer again."

She looked at the clasp in her hand. "Have you got a pin?"

I had three.

The photographer was trying to arrange the girls beside the cake. Petal had her back to the tree so she could watch the square. Pearl was rubbing a line of ink from her wrist. Fanfare waited patiently while I pinned her cape, and then leaned over to look at my shot list.

"You could stand here," she said, pointing. "That bit's blank."

"It's blank because it's meant to be blank. Negative space."

"You'd fit in it."

I smoothed her cape and stepped away.

The first photograph contained the cake, the girls, and a luminous **DO I LOOK ALL RIGHT?**.

"Yes," I told Pearl. "You look lovely. Don't ask during the next one."

The second contained all three girls looking at Pearl, who had asked whether she should smile with her teeth.

For the third, I stood behind the photographer and held up the comb. It gave them something to look at. They all smiled. No captions. No flowers. Fanfare's cape lay correctly over her shoulders. The cake's lettering faced the lens.

The shutter clicked.

"There," the photographer said.

I lowered the comb. We had been outside much longer than ninety seconds, but we had a picture.

Then a small white body dropped from the awning onto the cake.

Nobody screamed. Mr. Bell came out with his cloth, calling, "Shoo!" The sugarwing plunged its straw into the icing and shuddered with happiness.

Petal waved both hands at it. It flapped backward and went straight through the centrepiece.

The new sugar window collapsed.

"We have the photograph," I said quickly. "We can cut around that."

The sugarwing landed on the photographer's shoulder. He flung a hand at it. It bounced off his cheek, leaving a smear of icing across his lens, and he stumbled into the cake table. Petal stopped the table from tipping in a burst of carnations.

He sneezed into the flowers. The guests at the counter backed into one another. Nobody was hurt, but they were crowding the screen door. If I carried the cake through it, the sugarwing would follow me straight into the shop.

I had brought it outside. I tucked the clipboard and comb under my arm and picked up the board beneath what remained. There was nobody at the far end of the square.

"Pearl, clear the doorway. Fanfare, cloth. Petal, stay where you can see me."

I carried the cake toward the empty end of the square. The sugarwing followed, leaving the photographer to wipe his cheek with his own sleeve. Mr. Bell tried to intercept it with his cloth, but it climbed beyond his reach.

"Wait," I called. "Let it come down."

The girls moved with me. Petal stood to my left with an unobstructed view. Pearl eased the nearest guests away from the doorway and back toward the counter, then joined us. Fanfare took the cloth from Mr. Bell and held it spread between her hands.

The sugarwing circled. I crouched to put the cake down. Petal raised her palms.

"No flowers unless it knocks into someone."

She nodded.

The creature folded its little wings and dropped. Fanfare swept the cloth over it. Its wings battered the fabric; she gathered the corners and held the squirming bundle away from the cake.

"Got you," she said, with heartfelt relief.

The full orchestra entered.

I had been crouching beside a broken sugar window. When the cymbals crashed immediately above me, I lurched upright. The comb slipped from under my arm; my heel found it, and I went backward.

Fanfare had a live sugarwing in both hands. Pearl was on the other side of the cake. Petal could see me clearly.

She stopped my fall.

It was gentle. I didn't so much as bruise an elbow. But a grown woman's worth of falling force produces a prodigious quantity of roses. They burst beneath me, swept my shoes upward, and left me suspended for a moment with my backside in a floral cradle, the soles of my sensible shoes facing the newspaper.

Pearl reached me before I could settle into the flowers. She scooped me up, one arm under my knees, the other behind my shoulders.

"You're all right," she said.

**I HAVE YOU.**

The photographer, who had finished cleaning his lens, took seven pictures.

"Put me down," I said.

She did. Petal took the clipboard from my locked fingers. Fanfare stood beside us holding the sugarwing, which had begun to drink icing through the cloth.

"That's your cue," she told me, over the choir. "You could wave."

I did not wave.

We went back inside. Mr. Bell washed the icing from the sugarwing and released it behind the bakery. This time, we kept the cake behind the screen door. Petal swept up the flowers. The reporter bought a cinnamon twist and asked whether we could finish the interview another day.

"Certainly," I said.

We cut the ribbon. This produced two bars of music and no casualties.

The photographer brought his camera over while I was checking that Mr. Bell didn't intend to ask for his money back.

The group picture was good. He had given it enough depth to include the intact sugar window, the bakery sign, and all three girls. Even I couldn't find something to adjust.

He swiped to the next frame.

There I was in Pearl's arms. My hair stood up. My blazer had ridden halfway to my ribs. I still clutched the clipboard. Petal was reaching to retrieve it, her face serious, and Fanfare was grinning above a bag that contained the world's smallest vanquished opponent. Roses filled the bottom of the picture. Over us, clearly legible, hung **I HAVE YOU**.

"This is the one," he said.

"The other one is the one."

"The other one's an advertisement. This one's a story."

"We're here to make an advertisement."

Mr. Bell put on his spectacles. "There's enough room for the shop name at the bottom."

I looked at him.

He looked at his ruined centrepiece. "People might stop saying I was abducted."

The photographer held the camera toward me again. "Your call. I won't run your face without permission."

The girls were watching from beside the counter. Pearl had brought my comb in and cleaned the icing from it. Fanfare was trying to mend her clasp with the remaining two pins. Petal stood between them, holding a cinnamon twist she had broken into four pieces.

She offered me the largest.

I took it and looked once more at the picture. Pearl's eyes were on my face, not the lens. They had left very little negative space.

"You can use it," I told the photographer. "My name is Marnie. My title is public relations manager. Please print both."

"Anything else?"

"Yes. Crop out the soles of my shoes."

He considered the screen. "I can get one of them."

The advertisement appeared on Monday. The Gazette used the same photograph on its front page, with my title printed in full.

On Tuesday, I went shopping in yesterday's cardigan.

The cashier looked at me, then at the clipboard sticking out of my bag.

"You're the fourth one," she said.

"I'm their manager."

"Oh, I know. My daughter loves you. She's made herself a clipboard."

I put a tin of soup on the belt. The cashier took a bakery leaflet from beneath the till and found me a pen.

"Would you write your catchphrase?"

I stood there in my cardigan, holding the pen, trying to think of one.

stories.title: The King Who Ate Everything
stories.prompt: Found the spares. By the way, what's with the demon living in your basement?
stories.body:
# The King Who Ate Everything

"Found the spares. By the way, what's with the demon living in your basement?"

Ned laid four wooden hands on the kitchen table. Two belonged to the royal cook, one to the princess, and one to a pirate I had retired for biting a spectator. The pirate's mouth had been under my control. It was still a sore subject.

"Did you speak to him?" I asked.

"He called me a creature of no discernible ambition. Then he asked whether you still did the voices."

"What did you say?"

"Yes. Was that wrong?"

I put the cook's hand into its socket and pressed until it clicked. "He'll have opinions."

Ned pulled out a chair. He had come to help me carry chairs into the front room, and to stand at the door taking money. This was his understanding of theatre: his cousin worked very hard behind a curtain, strangers sat on borrowed furniture, and afterward there was soup. He had agreed to the soup. I had been careful not to mention the basement.

"Bea. You have a demon."

"Only the one."

"Could we see what he can do?"

I looked through the kitchen door at the six chairs facing my green puppet booth. There had been three chairs last month. The third had held a coat. Tonight all six were reserved, and one family had asked if I would be performing something different next time. I had nearly put that letter in a frame.

"He isn't equipment," I said.

"I know. He told me that."

Downstairs, Vask stood on the stage of a much smaller theatre. It was a wooden box with a proscenium, two red curtains, and gilt stars I had painted when I was eight. His horns almost reached the top. He wore a silver waistcoat and had folded his long grey hands behind his back. In the basement bulb's light he was nine inches tall.

"Your associate has interesting questions," he said. "Unlike you, who asks only if I intend to be quiet."

"Have you found a new answer?"

"I intend to be heard."

Ned crouched beside the box. "How long have you been down here?"

"Eighteen years," said Vask.

"He's only been in this basement since March," I said. "Before that he was in a cupboard."

When I was eight, Vask had put a pea under one of three cups and promised me a real theatre if I could find it. I had put a pea of my own under each of the other cups. He had been so offended that he conjured this little box and said no one would ever applaud anything I performed in it. I told him to stand on its boards until they did.

He should have left then. Instead he swore himself to those boards, and couldn't lift a foot beyond them.

"I've offered to release him from that oath," I told Ned. "Several times."

"She offers pity," said Vask. "Do I resemble a recipient of pity?"

He was standing beneath a gilt star that had peeled loose at one point. It touched his horn. Ned carefully pressed it back into place.

"No," he said. "What sort of part would you want?"

Vask's fingers came out from behind his back.

I had known they could grow. When I rehearsed in the basement, he would occasionally extend one to tap the side of my booth. It was difficult to work while an enormous finger delivered three slow taps every time you missed a cue. I hadn't known what else they could do.

He cupped his left hand. The knuckles rose into towers, with black nails for steep little roofs. A pale window opened below his smallest finger. His right thumb lengthened into a king: a stout, offended king with a gold crown and a lower jaw that hung loose. Vask made him lean from the palace and survey Ned.

"Insufficient," the king said.

"He's playing your king," whispered Ned.

"I recognize him."

Vask spread two fingers. Courtiers bowed between the towers. A third finger became a narrow, bowing cook. Shadows jumped up the basement wall, crisp and enormous, so that the cook bent nearly to the ceiling. Then the king's jaw opened. The palace tipped toward it. Roofs, window, court and cook disappeared into the hand, and the wall held only a crowned profile with a cavernous mouth.

Ned said, very softly, "Oh."

I saw that mouth on the front-room wall, above people who had come to watch me coax a wooden king through the same old scenes. I saw their heads tip back. Someone might bring a friend next time. Someone might say they had never seen anything like it.

"You could do that with my puppets?" I asked.

The king's lips closed. "I could do it with your house."

"The puppets, Vask."

"Naturally."

I was supposed to ask what happened afterward. My play ended with the king realizing he'd eaten his favourite little dog, giving everything back, and dancing with the court. It was not a complicated play. Turnip the dog got the most applause, especially when he stopped in the middle of the dance to scratch his ear.

But Vask's king stood looking at me, hungry and magnificent, and I didn't ask. He would call my dance feeble. He would be right about the dance. We could settle the ending later, when he had seen how the audience liked Turnip.

"We'd have to take your theatre upstairs," Ned said.

"Obviously," said Vask.

We carried it between us. Vask stood amid the painted stars, hands neatly clasped, and complained each time we tilted him. Halfway up, Ned suggested he sit down. Vask said kings did not sit down when being conveyed into battle.

"This is a puppet show," I said.

"You must decide how badly you want it."

We set the box on the ledge inside my booth, its little stage level with the green opening. Ned and I would have to crouch behind it. Vask's palace shadows spread over the white wall behind the booth. I put the wooden king away and showed him the other puppets: the princess, the cook, the three identical councillors, and Turnip, whose felt ears were soft from years of squeezing into my bag.

"The king eats these," I said. "One at a time. I give you the cues."

Vask inspected the dog. "This has been repaired."

"He's been loved."

"His tail is a bootlace."

"So was his previous tail. Ned, would you read the councillors? I can't do their voices and the cook together."

Ned looked at the six chairs. "I said I'd take the money."

"Behind the curtain. No one will see you."

He took the script. While I showed him the lines, Vask grew a king's head large enough to fill the stage opening. Its cheeks were formed from his folded fingers; its chin rested on his thumb. My wall became the inside of a palace. Even Ned forgot the chairs.

"And when he eats everything," Vask said, "we go larger."

People were knocking at the door. I made Ned practise the councillors once more.

Our first spectator was a small girl wearing a knitted fox on her head. She pointed at the booth and asked her father if the dog would be in it. Her father said they would have to wait and see. Then he looked at me with the expression of someone who had promised a dog on very slender evidence.

"He's in it," I assured her.

The other four arrived together. There was a woman with a paper bag of sweets, her elderly mother, and two boys old enough to pretend they hadn't chosen to come. Ned took their money. I shut the front door and went behind the curtain.

"Six," I whispered.

"I can count," said Vask.

We began.

Turnip stole the cook's spoon, hid it in the princess's wig, and sat down when the king demanded to know where it was. The girl in the fox hat laughed before the spoon even appeared. One of the boys gave her a superior look, then laughed when Turnip scratched his ear and knocked the wig clean off.

Vask waited for his first entrance. I could feel his enormous head beside me. He had made one eye in the side of his palm, and it followed the dog through every scene.

Then the king declared that the kingdom was his and therefore he would eat it.

The councillors begged him to begin with the soup. Ned delivered their pleas in three increasingly anxious voices, the last so much like my aunt that I nearly lost the princess. Vask ate the first councillor with a wet little snap. The wooden head vanished between his finger-lips.

The girl gasped. Her father laughed. The king rolled his eye toward them and grew another foot.

"A larger supper," he announced.

His shadow crossed the ceiling. The towers unrolled across the white wall; nails became windows, the gaps between fingers were long corridors, and a tiny procession of shapes hurried through them. The woman's sweet stopped halfway to her mouth. The older boy sat forward with his elbows on his knees.

Vask swallowed the next councillor. Ned made a splendid squeak. The shadow palace buckled into the king's mouth, and the crowned head opened until it seemed the whole room stood between its jaws.

They clapped.

The woman clapped first. Her mother joined her, then the boys, then the father with the girl beating her palms against his. It was bright, astonished applause. It was applause for my play, in the theatre Vask had given me. I had spent eighteen years imagining a proper curtain call at the end, and had forgotten that people could like something in the middle.

Behind the green curtain, Vask lifted a foot.

He looked down at the little boards. For a moment he stood with one foot raised, so still that I thought something had gone wrong. Then he stepped over the rim of the box and jumped down onto my carpet.

I nearly congratulated him.

His body grew behind me. His waistcoat buttons climbed past my shoulder. He set a grey foot, long as my forearm, flat on the floor and spread the toes into the pile. The king's hand-head remained at the opening. Above me, two black horns pressed the curtain rail.

"Now," he said.

He ate the princess, the cook, and the last councillor. I gave their lines, trying to watch both the enormous hand and the enormous man attached to it. Vask had never stood behind me before. His other hand held the palace in the wall, and the king grew so large that his painted crown scraped the ceiling.

Turnip ran along the ledge barking at him. The girl barked back. Ned gave the dog his little outraged bounce, exactly as I had shown him.

"Too small," said the king, and ate Turnip.

Then the entire palace folded shut.

Vask held the great crowned head in the centre of the opening. There was no kitchen, no court, no dog, no dancing. Just the king, immense and satisfied.

It was beautiful. I couldn't stop looking at it. Neither could the spectators. The younger boy had both hands clenched on his chair. I could hear the woman's mother breathing through her nose.

After a long silence the girl said, "But Turnip."

Her father leaned toward her, then reached beneath his chair for his daughter's coat. He thought we were finished.

"The dance," I whispered. "Give them back."

Vask looked at me from above the curtain. "Why?"

"Because that's how it ends."

"It has ended."

I'd known perfectly well what he meant when he'd closed that mouth in the basement.

"They want the dog."

"They applauded the king."

He could go. He could step out through my front door, take his wonderful hands away, and leave me six people whose evening I had decided to improve.

Ned was looking at the script. Its last page lay open on a dance with no dancers.

"The king missed something," I said.

Vask's eye narrowed.

I put my empty fist above the ledge. I bent my wrist, stuck out my smallest finger, and made a creature as unconvincing as anything I had ever made when I was eight. I couldn't do Turnip without Turnip. But I could do the thing that lived behind his ear.

"He missed," I said in a high voice, "a flea."

The girl stopped putting her arm into her coat.

My little finger waved. It was meant to be a leg. It looked like a little finger. I hopped my fist onto the huge king's lower lip.

Nothing happened. Vask watched it. My face began to burn.

"Your Majesty," said Ned's third councillor voice, from somewhere inside the closed hand-mouth. "There's been an omission."

The king's lips twitched.

"A what?" he said.

Ned looked from my fist to Vask's forearm stretched between us behind the curtain. He pulled the curtain off its hooks.

It fell around our feet. There I crouched in my work shirt with my fist in the air. Ned knelt beside a theatre built for an eight-year-old. And Vask, taller than the door, stood on my front-room carpet with one gigantic hand stuck out in front of him.

For a second nobody moved. The girl tipped her head until the fox's nose pointed at Vask's horns. "Is that the king too?" she asked.

"A great deal of him, yes," said Ned in the councillor's voice. He was red right up to his ears. He had never wanted an audience to see him.

"An omission, Majesty." He made his own fist hop onto Vask's wrist. "It's when you miss one."

The older boy began to laugh.

Vask turned toward Ned. His real face was a narrow, furious face with yellow eyes and a mouth full of small teeth. His king's face had one rolling eye and a great empty mouth. He could close that hand and walk out. There was space behind him, all the way to the door.

Ned's fist scrambled up his forearm.

"Several omissions," it said in my aunt's voice. "Who took the minutes?"

Vask looked back at the boy, who had put a hand over his mouth and was trying not to laugh any harder. Then at the woman, who was already laughing without trying. He offered the king's nose to my flea.

The king began to itch.

It was a terrible, magnificent itch. His jaw wobbled. His crown slid down over his eye. The palace opened again, this time upside down, with every tower shaking. Ned's fist chased mine along Vask's arm, and the king tried to scratch his nose with a castle.

The girl howled. The boys were making flea voices of their own. Vask let the crown fall, caught it on one nail, and sneezed out the royal cook.

I caught her by the rod. Her wig was backwards.

"Bless you," she said, and made a desperate bow.

The councillors tumbled out next. Ned scrambled to recover them. The princess emerged sitting on the king's tongue, which was still visibly a thumb. She demanded her kitchen back. Vask gave her the entire palace, balancing it on one enormous fingernail. She slapped him with the pirate's spare hand.

I had no dance for any of this. I barely had words. Vask kept opening things I thought he had closed, and Ned kept sending fleas into them. Sometimes a puppet fell down. Once we all reached for the same rod and banged our heads together. Vask's king reeled as though the collision had happened inside him, and got a laugh so large he did it again.

Finally the girl stood up.

"Turnip!"

The king looked at her. His enormous mouth opened slowly. Ned and I held our hands still.

Something small and brown appeared between his lips. Two limp felt ears. A black painted nose. The dog came out backward, with his bootlace tail wrapped around his head.

The girl clapped once, sharply, as if ordering him home.

I caught Turnip. Vask's hand shrank beneath my fingers, the palace came folding down from the wall, and I put the dog on the bare boards of the little theatre. He sat. He scratched his ear. My flea fell off him and died.

The girl laughed so hard she sat down on the floor.

This time the applause went on. Vask kept his hands small. He looked at the little dog, at the scattered rods, and at the six people laughing in front of us. Ned tried to stand up in the fallen curtain, tripped, and took his first bow on his knees. The audience clapped harder. Vask took a bow so deep his horns nearly lifted the woman's bag of sweets off her lap.

When they stood to leave, the father asked what we were doing next month.

I said we hadn't decided yet.

"This," said his daughter. "Again."

The older boy wanted to know how we had made the palace. The woman wanted to bring her sister. Her mother told Vask his king needed a handkerchief. He showed her the hand that had been the king. She considered it, then gave him hers.

I took reservations on the backs of the programmes. Six names, then two more. Ned stood by the door holding the curtain, and told everyone the fleas had been his idea. They hadn't. I let him tell it.

Vask watched the last spectator go. Then he walked to the front door. He was large enough that he had to turn his horns sideways to get through.

I held Turnip against my chest. His nose was damp. I had lost the princess's proper hand, which mattered much less than it had at six o'clock.

"You can leave the waistcoat," I said. "If it helps you fit."

Vask glanced back at the overturned box. "I require a larger stage."

"You required one yesterday."

"Yesterday I was not performing."

"You aren't obliged to do it again."

He looked at me as though I had offered him a spoon with a hole in it.

"Eight names," he said. "I counted."

Then he ducked through the door and went down my steps, growing smaller as he went. At the gate he was once again nine inches tall. He stood on the top rail, very far from his painted boards, and looked in both directions along the street.

Ned reached past me to shut the door. Vask raised one long finger.

"Do not," he called, "put the dog in the cupboard. I haven't finished with his fleas."

stories.title: The Statue at the Corner
stories.prompt: A young girl rounds a corner and runs face first into a marble statue. The statue blinks and shifts on its plinth, stone scraping.
stories.body:
# The Statue at the Corner

The doorway was perfect. It belonged to the button shop, and it went so far into the wall that a person standing inside it could see the street without the street seeing the person. Iona had discovered this yesterday while waiting for her sister to choose six buttons, which had taken longer than choosing a whole dress.

Today she had been found first twice. The first time, her yellow skirt had stuck out behind a tree. The second time, she had sneezed. Now her sister was counting beside the bakery, and Iona was going to get to that doorway before anyone else thought of it.

She ran past the button shop's first window, cut the corner close, and hit something with her face.

It was cold and white and much harder than a face ought to encounter. She sat down abruptly. For a moment her nose seemed to occupy her entire head.

Above her, the marble child took its hands away from its eyes and blinked.

Then it shifted on its plinth. Stone scraped against stone, a harsh little sound that went right through Iona's teeth.

“Now look,” it said. “I've forgotten.”

Iona pressed both hands over her nose. The statue had a marble bob of hair, a marble skirt, and toes sticking out below its hem. It stood on a round slab of its own, exactly where the shop's low stone ledge turned the corner. One short arm of the ledge ran beneath the window Iona had just passed. The other ran beneath the second window and ended beside her doorway. White marks curved across the darker stone. It was like a bench nobody sat on because the stone child was there.

Its mouth was moving.

Iona looked behind it for a person doing that.

“Seventy-six,” said the statue. “Or seventy-seven. Which was it?”

“You hit my nose.”

“I was here.”

“Well, you shouldn't have been.”

This was what her sister always said when Iona trod on her foot. It sounded less reasonable now.

The statue looked down at her. Fine grey lines ran through its white cheeks. There was a nick in one ear, and dirt lay in the carved curls above its forehead. Its eyes moved to her hands.

“Is it broken?”

Iona took one hand away and examined it. No blood. She felt the end of her nose very carefully.

“No.”

“Good. What comes after seventy-six?”

“Seventy-seven.”

“Then it must have been that.” It raised its hands.

Iona got to her feet. A voice in the square shouted, “Ready or not!”

Her doorway was three steps away, past the statue, beyond the second window. She could still make it.

“Move over,” she whispered.

The statue separated two fingers.

“Are you ready?”

“No. I need to get in there.”

“I can see you in there.”

“You're not looking for me.”

The fingers came down. The statue considered this.

“Then who am I looking for?”

Iona pointed back toward the bakery. “They're playing. You're just copying.”

She regretted it when the statue put its hands carefully against its skirt. It made the same small click a teacup made when you set it on a saucer.

“Someone usually answers,” it said. “I thought they might answer me.”

There were footsteps on the other street, coming toward the doorway.

Iona scrambled onto the shin-high ledge, squeezed between the statue and the first window, and crouched with her skirt pulled over her knees. She kept her head below the statue's waist. If her sister came around the corner quickly enough, perhaps she would look at the doorway instead of behind the statue.

The statue bent at its waist, peering.

“That is not a good place.”

“Shh.”

“Your elbow is out.”

Iona tucked it in. The statue slid toward her to conceal the rest of her.

The scrape rang down the street.

“Iona!”

Her sister stood at the corner with one hand still on the bricks. She pointed at Iona, opened her mouth, and stopped pointing.

The marble child was looking back at her.

“Did that just move?”

“You found her,” said the statue.

Her sister took a step closer. Iona had never seen her approach anything so slowly. She reached toward its skirt, then stopped before touching it.

“Can you do it again?”

“It already moved,” Iona said. “That's why you found me.” Her nose still hurt when she spoke loudly.

“But it—”

The statue turned its head. There was a dry rubbing sound beneath its chin.

Her sister's hand went to her own chin.

“Oh. You really can,” she said.

One of her friends called from the square. He wanted to know whether Iona was found, and whether that meant it was safe to come out.

“Yes,” her sister called, without looking away from the statue.

“I was going to use the doorway,” Iona said.

“We can play again. It's your turn to count.” Her sister looked at the statue's toes. “Can you get down?”

The statue tried to lift a foot. Its whole round slab tipped a little and knocked against the ledge. It grabbed the window frame.

Iona's sister jumped forward too late to be useful, then kept her hands out while it settled flat again. The two feet, the hem between them, and the slab beneath were all the same piece of marble.

“No,” it said.

“Then you can't be it.”

“I don't want to be it.”

“What do you want?” Iona asked.

The statue looked at the doorway.

“To hide.”

Her sister leaned around it to inspect the little recess. “You won't fit.”

“I know.”

Iona looked back toward the square. The other two had come out. One was balancing along the low wall, and the other was knocking seed pods off his socks. They would get to hide while she counted. She knew where they would go: behind the bakery steps, behind the wall, up the tree if her sister didn't remind them that climbing wasn't allowed. She could find them all quickly. She wouldn't have to be the one who was always caught.

Iona stepped down from the ledge toward the square.

The statue put its hands over its eyes again. It wasn't counting this time.

“You can play without me,” Iona told her sister.

“You're supposed to be it.”

“I know.”

Her sister looked from her to the statue. “I'll count, then. Are you sure your nose is all right?”

Iona nodded.

“I'll be by the bakery.”

She went backward for the first few steps, watching the marble child. Then a seed pod hit the pavement near her shoe and she turned around.

Iona brushed the grit off her knees.

“All right,” she said. “You hide.”

The statue lowered its hands.

“You're looking.”

“I haven't started yet.”

“You have to shut your eyes.”

She faced the window and shut them. “One. Two. Three.”

There was a scrape.

“Four. Five.”

Something knocked against the glass.

“Sorry,” the statue said.

“You don't have to talk.”

“You don't have to count so quickly.”

Iona counted to twenty. Behind her there had been three more scrapes, a grunt, and a sound like a finger drawn down a window.

“Ready or not!”

The statue was pressed flat against the bricks beside her. It had bent its head and covered its face, but its marble skirt stuck out nearly as far as before.

Iona looked at it.

“You aren't hidden.”

“I'm being very still.”

“I can see all of you.”

It straightened, bringing its hands down slowly. One palm had acquired a streak of window dust.

Iona had been behind that tree with her yellow skirt outside it. She didn't want to be told it looked just like that, but it did.

“Round the shop corner,” she said. “You could hide there.”

The statue looked past her, along the street.

Iona pointed to the ledge continuing around the corner. “On there.”

There were old white scuffs all along the stone. She had thought they were bird droppings. At the square end beside the doorway there was room for the statue and its slab. From here she couldn't see that end at all.

“Do you go round there?”

“Sometimes. When there's someone in the other window.”

“Then go there now. I'll count again.”

“I don't think you should say where I'm going.”

“Fine.”

This time she counted in the solemn way the statue had counted, leaving a great deal of time between numbers. The sliding went on for longer. When she reached twenty, only the marble skirt's edge was visible beyond the corner.

“Ready or not.”

She walked toward it. The edge vanished with a scrape.

One of her laces was trailing. A few steps short of the corner, Iona turned her back to the shop and crouched to tie it. The scraping went on behind her, closer and then farther away. It was probably trying to press itself against the bricks again.

Around the shop corner, the ledge beneath the second window was empty. She hurried to the square end beside the doorway. Nothing. A scrape came from beneath the first window, where she had been standing.

“You're moving!”

“You didn't say I couldn't.”

She hadn't. She had crept from one tree to the next when the boy with the green cap came close. It had helped until her yellow skirt stuck out.

“Well, I can hear you.”

There was no answer. The statue might have been any still thing around the shop corner.

Iona undid the knot she had just made, took off her shoes, and set them together beneath the second window. The pavement was warm through her socks. She crept to the corner, avoiding the gritty bits, and leaned her head around it.

The statue was waiting beside the first window. It saw her eye and swung backward so hastily that its slab bumped the wall. Iona pulled away in case it tipped. It didn't. There was a long scrape, then silence.

She stayed where she was.

“Are you in the button shop?” she called.

Nothing.

“Are you in the bakery?”

A faint rubbing sound.

“Are you hiding in a bun?”

The rubbing stopped.

“I've found a bun. It's a very big bun. It's got toes.”

There was a small, choked noise around the corner.

“And a skirt. I think I'll eat it.”

The statue laughed.

It was a dreadful laugh, all little stone knocks, and Iona ran toward it before it could stop. The child was doubled over beside the first window, one hand clutching the frame. Iona put her palm against its cold chest.

“Found you!”

The statue straightened under her hand. It looked down at her, then at the corner she had come around.

“You said I didn't have to talk.”

“You didn't talk. You laughed.”

It seemed to be considering whether laughter was allowed. Iona took her hand away. Its white chest held a small grey print from her palm.

“Again,” it said.

“You'll know the bun thing now.”

“Not me. You hide.”

Iona looked along the street. From the middle of the corner the statue could see both ways. But it couldn't follow her into the doorway, or off the ledge at all.

“That's not fair.”

It let go of the window frame.

“I could just stay away,” she explained. “You'd never find me.”

The statue looked toward the square, where her sister's voice rose through the numbers.

“Oh.”

Iona considered the doorway. She would have to get out of it eventually. Across the street a woman was unlocking a bicycle, and soon there would be nothing between the doorway and the statue but pavement.

“What if I have to get back?” she said. “I hide, and then I have to come and touch you. If you see me first, you call my name.”

“Iona.”

“Yes. But you have to see me.”

The statue turned its head one way, then the other. It slid toward the corner, watching each street as it came into view.

Iona fetched her shoes from beneath the second window and put them on. From the doorway she would have to watch until the statue looked the other way, then try to reach it. She wasn't certain about the last bit. Perhaps the statue would be certain, and that would make it careless.

“Hands over your eyes,” she said.

It covered them.

“No looking between your fingers.”

It pressed the fingers together with a series of little clicks.

“How far?”

“Twenty.”

“One,” said the statue.

Iona hurried toward her doorway. It was still perfect. She slipped into it sideways and tucked in her yellow skirt.

“Two.”

She could see the statue's white fingers through the gap beside the doorframe. One separated from the others.

“No peeking!”

The finger snapped shut.

“Three,” it said, much more loudly.

stories.title: The Weight of Here
stories.prompt: Monsters don’t name their offspring. To them, humans waste naming magic on children—yet they remain bewildered by the impossible feats those children grow up to perform.
stories.body:
# The Weight of Here

I told Osa's mother she could have had a knife that cut iron.

“I've got a knife,” she said.

“Does it cut iron?”

“I don't cut much iron.”

The baby was asleep in the crook of my foreleg. She had arrived awake and furious, but the sound inside my chest had pleased her. Human babies enjoy the same noises as mine. It is one of the few sensible things about them.

Her mother had brought a basket of wool scraps and a cake made with cherries. These were for me. For the smallest of my young she had brought a wooden ring too large to swallow, although it was making a thorough attempt.

“You could name a hearth to stay warm,” I said. “A door to keep thieves out. You have only so many namings in you.”

“I know.”

The oldest of my brood came to inspect the baby. It had a short left back toe and dragged that foot when it walked: five little taps, then a scrape. It put its nose against the baby's fist.

She caught a whisker. My child sneezed in her face.

“Look at that,” I said. “She can't even let go.”

Her mother unwound the fingers, one by one.
