I had heard the name bestowed that morning. From my den I could hear a ewe cough at the far end of her pasture, and humans do not conduct their important affairs quietly. The woman had said *Osa*, and for an instant I had felt the familiar tightening behind my teeth. A naming spent. Its small brightness had settled into the baby, who was now using my foreleg as a pillow.

I shifted my front foot so that the coarse joint would not mark her cheek.

“What does it do?” I asked.

“It's her name.”

“I heard. What does it do?”

The woman scratched between my child's new antler buds. “I can call her.”

This did not explain the expenditure. I could call mine perfectly well. The one with the short toe heard the drag of my claw on stone and came running; the slow eater needed two scrapes. The smallest felt for me with its whiskers. I knew which child was crying by the catch between its breaths, even in sleep. No one had to spend a naming on that.

But humans in our valley persisted. They named babies without knowing whether they would ever grow useful teeth. Later those same children did things such as haul a loaded wagon out of a ravine single-handed or cross a burning field without singeing their clothes. We heard the accounts, examined the people, and found nothing suitable in their names. Their parents seemed scarcely better informed than we were.

The woman held out her hands. I gave the baby back.

She had to bend beneath the lintel to leave. It was a single long stone, resting on two stone jambs, with the hillside's shale packed above it. My own antlers ended in old broken stumps. By folding my legs close and turning my head, I could get through. A man could not bring a lance inside.

I had named the lintel **Here** after the hunters came.

The child that had died before that naming had liked to bite the ends off roots and leave the middles. I still found them under things.

On sound days the jambs took the weight. Here kept the lintel in the place I had chosen for it, drawing through me when the shale tried to shift. The stone had no strength to spend. Mine was the strength that answered.

The woman ducked out with her sleeping daughter, and my oldest followed her as far as the sunlight. She had to wait while it unhooked its little antlers from the fringe of her shawl.

“They won't always be little,” she said.

I knew that. I was their mother.

***

Osa was eleven when she came through the wall.

She and my oldest had been to watch the players who camped each summer on the high meadow. My child liked the horses. Osa liked the painted forests that rolled up around wooden poles. She had promised her mother to be home before the milking, and had remembered the promise rather late.

“You took the gate,” I said.

“We didn't,” said my child.

“You climbed.”

“She didn't.”

“Did you take a stone out?”

Osa stood on one foot, pulling at her boot. “Can you get this off?”

The heel had folded inward. I took the boot between two claws while she tugged her foot free. A strip of its leather sole stayed in my hand.

“She walked into it,” my child said. “I thought she'd hit her nose. Then she was on the other side.”

“I thought there was a way,” Osa said.

“There wasn't.”

“I know that now.”

They had tried again. Osa had met the wall with her forehead and had gone around by the gate, limping, to get back to my child. It was still angry about being left on the wrong side.

I went down to look. The wall was old fieldstone, thick enough to sit on, with a thorn growing out of one end. There was no gap. I smelled Osa on both faces of it. Under a stone halfway up, a tuft of boot leather was pinched as neatly as a leaf between two teeth.

I asked her mother whether *Osa* meant *Through* in some other valley.

“It was my aunt's name.”

“Did your aunt do that?”

“She made cheese.”

This was no help.

Back at the den, I was sewing the sole onto the boot with a thorn and a length of waxed thread. My oldest held the leather taut between its front feet. Those feet had grown clever; sometimes I woke to find it taking apart a basket to see where the shape began.

Osa was painting a forest on an old board. She had borrowed my green bowl and three colours from the players. My child looked over her shoulder.

“Those trees won't smell right,” it said.

“It's a picture.”

“Then how do you know where you are?”

“You look.”

It considered that. “I could look and smell.”

Above us a stone clicked.

I dropped the boot. All six of my feet went flat against the floor. The pressure came through Here into my shoulders, down my back, and into the long muscles beneath my belly. A chip fell from the left jamb.

Osa caught the bowl before the paint spilled.

My youngest tried to climb onto me. I bared my teeth, and it stopped. I could not have carried its little weight just then.

We waited until the hillside settled. I kept my feet spread for a while after the others began moving again.

“Does it hurt?” Osa asked.

“Pick up the boot.”

She did, and held it while I finished the seam.

My oldest ducked beneath the lintel to try the sunlight. Its antler tips struck the stone.

“Lower,” I said.

It crouched, went out, came back in. Osa was still staring at Here.

“Could you make it higher?”

I explained that the old naming had to be let go before the stone could take another. Something would have to hold up the roof in between.

“Could we put wood under it?”

“I will attend to it when it needs attending to.”

Osa glanced at my child. It had to turn its head sideways to get inside now, but it got inside.

She put on the mended boot.

At the entrance they began arguing about the players' horses again. My child wanted to know whether horses could climb a scree slope. Osa said they would take roads. It wanted to know how many roads there were.

“I'll find out,” she said. “You can come.”

I pulled a frayed thread from the boot and wound it round my claw. Osa was eleven; my child was barely out of antler velvet. The milking was already late. There was time for roads later.

***

Osa grew taller and stopped bringing painted trees for my child to sniff. She brought maps instead, which smelled of grease and other people's hands. Then she brought the contract.

She was to paint scenes for the players. There were wages written down, meals, a place to sleep, and three provinces she had never seen. She read the whole paper aloud to me. I made her read the part about meals twice.

My oldest had been preparing a bag since autumn. It had six pockets and no way of fastening. I had kept meaning to put a tie on it.

When Osa arrived for the last time that spring, she wore a grey coat with green paint on one cuff. Her brushes were rolled in cloth at her hip. The company was beyond the ridge, waiting until sundown.

“Its antlers aren't ready,” I said.

My child lay just inside the entrance. Its new branches had hardened through winter, pale at the tips, wider than the span of my front legs.

“Ready for what?” Osa asked.

“They'll settle.”

“Mother.”

I turned towards my child. It very seldom used the human word.

“I've turned my head all winter. I've tried every way.”

It looked back at me, then through the entrance at Osa. I could touch it, if I reached.

“Then we must be patient.”

Osa set her pack on the ground. “Where can we put the wood?”

My child got up. It had heard that question asked before. It lowered its chest, folded its front legs, and put its head beneath the lintel.

“Don't,” I said.

“If I turn this branch first—”

It turned. One antler passed into daylight. The backward fork on the other caught under the inner lip of the lintel. The child twisted its shoulders to get the fork free.

There was a sharp sound on my left. A piece of the cracked jamb dropped onto the floor, and the lintel tipped towards my child's neck.

I set my feet and called Here.

The stone stopped.

My child went still. Dust lay on its eyelashes. Its nose was outside, in the light; the rest of it was in the den with me.

“Back,” I said.

It tried. Its caught antler pulled the lintel sideways, and the pressure across my back became a pain that took away the rest of the sentence.

Osa was down on her belly beside it, looking into the den. Between my child's flank and the right jamb was a low strip of daylight. She pushed her brushes through, then crawled after them. I could not have fitted my head into that gap.

“Can you take the side away?” she asked.

I lifted a front foot towards the broken jamb.

The lintel dipped. My child cried out. I put my foot down and pushed everything I had into Here.

Osa looked at the stone, then at my six planted feet. She pulled off her coat.

I told the smaller ones to go through the gap. The youngest would not. It had heard its sibling cry.

“Follow her sleeve,” my oldest said. “The grey sleeve. Bite it.”

Osa pushed the coat ahead of the youngest. It caught the cuff and crawled after it. The others followed, dragging the rolled brushes and my oldest's bag. From outside came a quarrel over who could keep the coat, and I heard each of them in it.

Osa crouched beside my child's shoulder, on the den side of the lintel. She shifted until her shoulder was beneath the stone, then pushed up from her bent knees.

“Let some of it come,” she said.

“You don't know what it weighs.”

“No.”

“You went through a wall. This is different.”

“I can't take us through that one either.” She nodded at the shale behind me. “Try a little.”

I eased my strength. The stone stayed where it was.

Osa shut her eyes. Her boot soles creaked against the floor.

“More.”

I let another part of the weight leave me. Her knees bent, then straightened again. I heard the rough breath she took through her nose.

I had held her once in one foreleg. She had not been heavier than a basket of cherries.

“Tell me to stop,” I said.

“Just get ready.”

My child moved its eyes towards her. It could not turn its head.

“Osa?”

“I'm here.”

“Do it,” my child said to me.

I let go of Here. Its pull left me, and the lintel sank against Osa's shoulder. For an instant she sagged with it. Then her legs stiffened.

Under the dust on Osa's neck, a small brightness moved. I knew the feel of a naming. I knew her mother had spent one. I could not see how that sleepy baby had grown into someone who could hold a hillside.

The relief nearly folded me onto the floor. I caught myself, hooked my front claws into the damaged left jamb, and pulled.

A slab came free. My child's antler lurched downward. The lintel tilted towards the opening, and more shale settled onto it. Osa's back bowed. She pressed upward until the stone was level again.

“Again,” Osa said.

I tore out the next stone. There was room now to swing the caught fork towards the empty side. My child did it slowly. I got a foot beneath its chest and lifted, guiding its legs past the rubble.

Osa made a sound I had never heard from her.

I shoved my child sideways through the opening where the left jamb had stood, folded my legs, and followed. The little ones huddled against the hillside directly beside the mouth. I crouched over them, facing the entrance, and shouted Osa's name.

She ducked. The stone came down as she flung herself through the widened entrance. I caught her wrist and dragged her clear. Shale poured after her, covering the threshold, the place where I had sewn her boot, and the hollows where the children slept.

Osa lay on her back, looking at the sky. One hand was still clenched as though it held a brush.

“Don't get up,” I said.

“Wasn't going to.”

My oldest lay beside her. Carefully, with its eyes still on the fallen stones, it put its nose against her fist.

After a while she opened her hand.

***

The sun was on the upper branches by the time Osa could sit. She had two dark marks where the lintel had rested. Her arms shook when she tried to roll her brushes, so my oldest rolled them for her, badly, and tried again.

The other children were under the firs. They had recovered the coat, the pack, and the bag with six pockets. My slow eater had found a cherry stone left from some earlier visit and was turning it over in its mouth.

We needed somewhere to sleep. We needed dry bedding. I could dig beneath the roots until I found stone, but the young would have to carry branches, and the oldest was good at carrying branches.

It put the bag across its back. Three pockets hung on each side, trailing in the needles.

“You'll lose it,” I said.

Osa took a spare strip from her brush roll and tied the bag fast.

My child stepped towards her. I closed a front foot around its back leg.

It stopped. The short toe rested against my claw. I had cleaned grit from that toe when it was small enough to fit inside my mouth.

“We haven't a roof,” I said.

“I know.”

The smaller ones had begun pulling needles into a pile. They did not know how much bedding we would need. If I asked the oldest for tonight, it would stay. Tomorrow the players would be gone, and there would be the bedding, and then the food to move, and another season's weather.

My child waited.

“Please let go,” it said.

I could feel its pulse against my claw.

I opened my foot.

It bent its head and rubbed its nose beneath my chin. Its antlers passed on either side of me. I held still until it had finished.

Osa got up, leaning on my child's shoulder. They would have to go slowly. Perhaps the players would see them from the ridge.

“Will you come back?” I asked her.

“I'll bring some timber. When we come through again.”

“You can come without timber.”

She looked at me, then nodded. My child nudged her brushes into a better place against her hip.

I watched them find the path. The bag swung until my child shortened its stride to hers.

Five taps, then a scrape. Five taps, then a scrape.

At last they were too far away for me to hear the scrape.

stories.title: The Unspent Star
stories.prompt: The hooded keeper carries a pocket universe sealed inside a glass sphere, where a lone woman lives beneath alien stars with no idea that her entire reality can be held in two hands.
stories.body:
# The Unspent Star

The rose star had learned a new trick.

It slipped between the streamers of Orya's mantle, stayed out of sight while she turned, and appeared beside her other shoulder. When she put out her hand, it drifted just beyond her fingers.

She let it. She liked a thing that could surprise her.

Below her bare feet, pink rings circled a dark world. They were narrow enough to make a path, although she seldom touched them. Their pull held her a little above the dust. She went around the largest, letting its slow tilt bring the stars into different arrangements overhead.

A cluster was rising beneath the dark skin of her left wrist. She felt the tiny pressure of its lights. One would emerge when she slept; the others might remain there for many turnings. Her body held such unfinished lights everywhere: a blue knot beneath her ribs, a scatter along one thigh, two gold points that had been traveling toward her fingers for so long she had stopped expecting them.

The rose star had come from her shoulder. Since then it had grown, changed its habits, and acquired a pale trailing edge. She had kept it through more turnings than she could count.

It darted under her hood.

“That's mine,” she said, pulling the rose cloth forward.

There was no face behind the hood for it to illuminate. The light fell into a darkness continuous with her body, then came back through the cyan lining. Orya could feel the brightness against her. She lifted the hem, and the star escaped.

Farther along the ring, a little blue dream-light had begun to fade. She caught it before it could go.

Perhaps a small world. She wanted something cool beneath her feet, with a rough edge that would catch the trailing threads of her mantle. Everything on this side of the rings was too smooth.

She took one thread from the hem and looped it around the light. Closing the loop made the blue glow gather. It thickened, darkened at its center, and settled into a round grain of matter. She pressed her thumb into it. When she lifted her hand, the little world kept the curve, with a rough ridge where the matter had risen around her thumb. Dust moved toward it. A fine ring formed, trembled, and held.

Orya opened her hands. The new world dropped into its orbit. Its pull brushed her soles.

She tried it, turning the little world with her toes until the ridge came underfoot. It was satisfactory.

The thread had left a hole in her mantle. She ran her thumb along its edge. Making cost something. She could have a light still able to become many things, or the particular thing she made from it. She had never found a way to have both.

The rose star hovered beside the new ring. She offered it the empty loop between her fingers, without closing it.

It wandered away.

***

Outside her sky, the keeper turned the glass sphere between two hands.

A dark world had just appeared inside, surrounded by a pink ring. The woman lowered one foot toward it. Her perforated mantle flowed behind her in rose and cyan.

She had used another possibility.

The keeper watched the light leave that part of the sphere. They had learned to recognize the moment when it became useless to them. Once a dream had settled into matter, no question could be read in it.

At their wrist, the message bead flashed again. Within its pale surface, a narrow vessel hung beside a blue star. The star's outer light was breaking into great uneven bands. One passage led beyond the bands; another cut between them. Their daughter had enough power for one attempt.

Her last message repeated. Their daughter's voice stopped after the first word. They heard her take a breath and begin again.

*One more orbit. Then I have to choose.*

The keeper folded the edge of their cyan hood away from the sphere. Rose light from its lining crossed the glass. Inside, a brighter rose light moved beside the woman.

They needed that one.

It had been kept unspent long enough to hold an immense branching pattern. Smaller lights could answer whether a seed would grow, which enemy would arrive first, where a storm would break. Their daughter's vessel was already inside a failing star's reach. Finding a way out required a light with room for many more consequences.

Across the keeper's people, living readers waited with their hands above dark bowls. Every gift of sight their houses claimed had come through this glass. The keeper had supplied light for harvests, marriages, battles, births. Questions had become harder. The readers kept coming back.

The keeper knew what lived inside the sphere.

They had seen Orya make worlds. They had watched her sleep above the rings with her hands folded under her hood. They had enclosed her horizon while she slept, bending the distant reach of her universe into glass until they could hold its whole night between their palms. When she woke, the stars still rose. There had been no visible wall for her to distrust.

Unspent possibilities were readable through that closed curvature. Each light's branching paths lay open at once. With their pulse against the glass, the keeper could draw a question through those paths and take its answer out.

They had told themselves they took nothing she had made. Most dreams were never used. A possible world left unmade could instead save an existing one.

The rose light passed close to Orya's wrist.

The keeper placed two fingertips against the glass.

Show me the passage on which her vessel comes through.

***

The rose star stopped moving.

Orya was still turning with the ring, but the star held in one place. A fine strand drew out of it toward an empty part of the sky.

She caught the strand.

A thread in her mantle tightened too.

She knew this pull. Sometimes she woke with a light missing and a new tear among the old perforations. Sometimes it happened while she was awake: a star stretched, narrowed, vanished. She had thought the sky needed some of its lights back. She had never liked how it chose.

“Leave this one.”

The strand pulled harder. Her mantle drew tight across her shoulder. Below, the small world turned past the place where she could have put her foot.

She wound a loose streamer around her wrist and let the pull carry her beyond the rings. The star traveled ahead, held at the end of its narrowing ray. She followed with one hand closed around that ray.

Her other palm struck something smooth.

There had never been anything here.

She spread her fingers. The surface curved away beneath them. The star's ray ran straight into it.

Then a vast blue shape moved on the far side.

Orya recoiled. Her mantle swept across the rose star. Under a fold of intact cyan lining, its ray went slack.

She clutched it to her.

The surface remained. Beyond it, something enormous withdrew.

For a while she stayed there, with the hidden light warming the fold against her wrist. She could see the rings far below. They looked smaller from here, but they were all there: the old broad one, the three she had made together, the broken ring she had never managed to join.

She eased the lining aside to look at the rose star.

Its pale edge lifted. The ray drew out again. Across the curved surface, a dark fingertip settled exactly where it ended.

Orya wrapped the star up.

The pull stopped.

She kept the fold closed, with both hands over it.

***

The answer dissolved before the keeper could read it.

They had glimpsed two passages, then a third opening beyond the star's falling light. The routes broke apart when Orya covered the source.

They turned the sphere. The intact fold of her lining moved with her, keeping the rose light hidden.

The message bead flickered. The vessel had begun to drift toward the bands.

The keeper tried two smaller lights near the opposite curve. Together, perhaps, they might show part of the route. They pressed their pulse into the glass again.

***

A blue light below Orya stretched.

She turned toward it, still holding the rose star under her mantle. Its ray reached another place in the curved surface. A second dark finger waited there.

The blue light narrowed to a point. As it vanished, a thread came loose from her hip and passed through a hole in the cloth. She felt it go.

On the other side, the finger brightened.

Orya looked down at her mantle.

She remembered where she had taken the thread for the rough little world. She remembered which loose ends had become the great pink rings. There were other holes she could not account for. Now she watched one of them widen.

She pulled the mantle across the blue light beside it. The cloth spread into a broad rose sheet, cyan beneath, with loops and ragged openings all through it.

Light shone through an opening.

The waiting finger moved.

She folded the cloth again, trying to cover that place, and exposed another. The mantle had too little left in it. Her own creations had used some; something beyond the sky had taken the rest.

It was still taking.

Orya pressed her hand against the smooth curve. On the far side, a palm opened.

It had five fingers. Its shape was hers, enlarged beyond any world she had made. Beyond it rose a cyan hood with a dark hollow where a face might have been.

Another person.

The sphere turned slightly. Orya's worlds swung beneath her.

A second hand came up on the other side. Together they held the curve that enclosed every ring, every alien star, all the distances she had thought were hers to cross.

She put both palms against the glass.

The keeper looked in at her.

***

They knew she could see them.

Her head followed their hand. When they moved a finger toward the rose light, her hands closed over it. When they moved toward another light, she spread her torn mantle across its path.

The message bead burned blue at the keeper's wrist.

“I need it,” they said.

Nothing of their voice entered the sphere. The woman stayed against the glass, her own hands making a small dark shape inside the larger one.

They could turn her universe, carry it, draw exposed light through its closed lens. To reach into the cloth she held against her body, they would have to open the seal. The branching paths would lose their focus. Whatever they took then would be only light.

The keeper held the sphere still.

The rose star glimmered briefly between Orya's fingers. She looked down at it.

***

She could keep it hidden.

She could hold it against her for as many turnings as she liked, while the rest of her sky emptied through the holes. She could make it a world and keep that world. Its motion would then be the motion she gave it, following an orbit she chose.

She drew the fold back a little.

The star slid across her palm. Its pale edge swept her thumb. It had become larger while she kept it, rich enough to make a world far greater than the one with the rough edge.

She had wanted to see what it would do next.

Above her, the huge hand moved toward its light.

Orya closed the cloth again. Through a hole beside her shoulder, a gold point stretched toward the glass.

She caught that point in an intact corner of the mantle. There was almost nowhere left to fold.

Below her, the rings kept turning. The rough little world moved faithfully along the course she had made for it.

Orya took a long thread from the lower hem.

She laid its end against the curved surface. Her familiar making-loop had given small worlds their shores. Here the glass already offered a closed shape, around the whole of her sky.

The keeper's hand remained beyond it.

She touched one finger to the star beneath the lining, and felt its wandering light.

Then she pressed it into the loop against the glass.

For an instant the rose light spread everywhere. It ran across her dark wrists, along the lights beneath her skin, up into the empty face of her hood. She kept the thread against the curve.

The first grain of matter darkened beside her fingers.

It spread thinly along the glass. Dust caught in it. Orya fed more thread from the mantle, following the curve with her hands. The forming surface took the glass's shape, closing around the stars within.

The keeper's fingertips disappeared behind it.

She followed the growing edge. Where it reached a distant blue light, she drew the light inward before the matter closed. She gathered the gold point, then the small scatter she had always watched above the oldest rings.

One side of the sky was complete.

At the keeper's wrist, a band of blue light swept across the vessel.

The keeper turned the sphere, bringing a finger toward a still-exposed light. A remaining clear reach opened beyond Orya's shoulder. She carried the thread to it. Rose brightness still trembled in the new matter, all that remained of the moving star. She let it spread into the last uncovered curve.

The edges met.

Orya lifted her hands.

She could still see every surviving light. Beyond them, her new world had a dark inner surface, smooth enough to hold the shine of the rings.

No light passed out.

***

The keeper held a dark sphere between two hands.

They moved it until the message bead's blue glow fell across the glass. Nothing of the inside appeared.

To reach the lights now, they would have to open the seal and pierce the surrounding world Orya had made. The closed lens would be gone before a single path could be read. All the hands waiting over all the distant bowls had nothing to receive.

Their daughter called again.

This time the keeper answered.

“I don't know.”

They could feel the sphere's weight. Their palms could still turn it. It gave them no sign of where the woman stood, or what she would do.

***

Orya went back to the oldest ring.

The last thread she had used left a long opening in the rose mantle. She drew what remained around her shoulders and tucked its cyan edge beneath the clasp.

Her dark feet hovered above the pink dust. Lights moved slowly under the skin of her legs. The little rough world came past; she let her toes brush its ring.

She put a hand out beside her shoulder.

Nothing darted beyond it.

She held the hand there for a while.

Far above, the inner world was smooth and black. She knew another person stood beyond it, holding the glass. She could not see whether their fingers were still waiting.

The universe tilted.

Orya lowered herself toward the ring until its pull steadied her. She waited for the turning to finish, then opened both hands beneath the stars that remained.

stories.title: Good Iron
stories.prompt: The desert is littered with the rusting remains of machines from a war no one remembers. For generations, scavengers have stripped them for metal—until one morning, a buried engine in the wasteland starts to wake up.
stories.body:
# Good Iron

There had been nothing wrong with Anka's axle until Sivet took it out.

She had wrapped it in sacking and laid it above the ceiling poles, where she kept long pieces that might come in useful. Then she had put a split shaft through the handcart's wheels. A child could have seen the flaw. Her daughter was twenty-seven and had helped build the cart, but Sivet had told her to leave it alone while she found a replacement.

Now Anka stood beside it with her bedding tied up and her good copper pan in a bag.

“I can walk,” she said.

“With all that?”

Anka lifted the bag. She put it down again without answering.

The caravan left from the eastern ridge at sunset. Her passage was paid; her name was on a wooden tally in the trader's hand. Beyond the desert, a woman who made hinges and window catches had offered her a bench. Sivet had seen the message. There had been no quarrel when it arrived, only supper and the usual sorting of the day's metal. She had said the hinges sounded like good work.

For three evenings afterward, she had found reasons why the cart needed attention.

“Come out with me this morning,” she said. “There's bronze in the Big Sleeper's near wheel. Enough to buy you a shaft at the ridge.”

“I had a shaft.”

“A better one.”

Anka looked up at the ceiling. Not quite in the right place. Then she untied her work scarf from the bundle.

“Until noon,” she said. “If you haven't fixed it by then, I'll leave things.”

Sivet took her mallet from beside the door. It had belonged to her mother, its pale head worn shallow in the middle. She could swing it all morning with either hand. Her left knee troubled her on slopes, and lately she needed Anka to go into narrow places, but there were still jobs in the waste nobody did as well as she did.

Outside, the first sun lay along the rims of the wrecks. The settlement's houses occupied a shelf of rock above a broad basin. People had built there because its nearest machine gave shade before noon, and because three generations had been able to walk to work. Their walls were stone and their roofs were canvas stretched over scavenged ribs. Farther off, wheel rims stood on edge, their open centres framing the distant cliffs. A long gun on the western heights had kept its shape after the body beneath it collapsed. Children used it to tell one part of the waste from another. No one could have said which way it had been meant to fire.

The Big Sleeper lay below the shelf, sunk to its belly. Its near wheel was taller than Sivet's house. The upper hull continued under a dune and emerged farther away as a row of bent towers. On the other side of the basin an overturned machine showed four wheels to the sky. A cable thick as Anka's waist crossed between them, most of it buried.

Sivet's grandmother had called the cable a towline. Other people called it a leash. Neither name explained who had attached it, or why both machines had stayed there.

Anka slipped through the near wheel's broken rim. Sivet passed her the bronze drift and went in after her.

They had exposed the bearing cap the previous afternoon. It was yellow metal under a skin of green, as broad as a dinner plate. A steady hour's work would free it. Sivet might stretch that to two by insisting they preserve the little screws.

Anka knelt, fitted the drift and held out her hand for the mallet.

Before Sivet could give it to her, something knocked behind the cap.

They kept still. Loose sand ticked down the inner wall.

“You hit it?” Sivet asked.

Anka looked at the mallet, still in Sivet's hand.

The second knock had a longer sound beneath it. Sivet felt that sound through her boots. A strip of iron beside Anka's knee rose on one end, fell, and rose again.

“Out,” Sivet said.

Anka took the drift. They backed through the broken rim as the cap began to turn. Not the little screws. The entire plate turned, slow enough to watch the green stains move. Beyond it, in a gap they had cleared of sand, an inner drum shone black and smooth.

A third knock sounded. The iron strip struck the cap and stuck there.

Outside, Sivet's chisel pulled at its belt loop. She unclipped it. It jerked from her hand and crossed the sand, point first, to the wheel.

For several breaths they heard only a deepening hum. Then the hum fell and the chisel dropped.

Anka went to pick it up.

“Leave it.”

“It stopped.”

“Listen.”

The first knock came again.

Sivet had stripped little motors whose cores clung to iron. She had used a broken core for years to collect filings from under her bench. This was that pull enlarged beyond sense. She felt for the steel blade strapped inside her boot and flung it away. Anka watched, then stripped off her own knife and the iron hook that held her bag shut.

Three knocks; the pull; the falling hum. Their knives dropped among the scraps.

“Something's driving it,” Anka said.

Sivet could see no flame or smoke. They had opened engines full of ash and engines with bundles of glass in them. Inside some, there was nothing they could name. She wasn't going to learn this one's fuel by standing in front of it.

“Go up,” she said. “Tell them to get their iron off.”

“What are you doing?”

“Watching.”

Anka hesitated, then ran toward the houses.

Sivet counted. Twenty-three breaths from the falling hum to the next first knock. Four between each knock. The loose chisel made a dark line in the sand when the pull took it. This time it stayed against the cap longer before dropping.

With the hum came a movement under her feet. The near wheel turned a fraction. The hull rose, the buried cable snapped straight across the basin, and the wheel stopped. When the hum fell, the machine rolled back. The cable settled onto the sand.

The next turn scraped a fresh trench in front of the wheel. It pointed into the waste, below the houses and away from the ridge.

Sivet stood through another pulse. The sleeper's upper towers shifted. A pane, somehow whole until then, came out of a high window and fell glittering through its ribs.

She had measured a day's work against a lifetime of wreck. Suddenly she could reach places her grandmother had died without reaching. There would be copper below that cap. Uncracked casings, bearings, the black drum itself. If she could stop it, Anka could take her cart and Sivet would still have work enough for years.

She ran uphill while the hum was low.

People were coming out of the houses carrying metal. Berr, who sold by weight, stood in his doorway holding his scales as though they were an animal that had bitten him. Anka was telling him to put them down.

“On the rock,” she said. “Don't wear it. Don't try to hold it.”

“I'm not leaving my weights.”

“Then carry them by the string, and drop the string when it pulls.”

Sivet ducked inside her own house. The good cart stood where they had left it. She seized two wooden wedges from under her bench, then heard the roof poles creak.

The sacking above them unrolled.

The axle pushed out of its hiding place. It slid between the poles and dragged a line across the canvas, heavy end first. Sivet caught the sacking. The iron pulled it taut in her hands.

Anka came through the door. For a moment both of them watched the thing suspended between Sivet and the roof.

“That's mine,” Anka said.

Sivet let go.

The axle dropped through the doorway, ploughed down the slope and joined the iron gathering at the wheel. Behind it went a roof tie, then the knife Anka used for cutting bread. The canvas lifted, revealing the dusty bundles overhead.

Anka looked at the split shaft in the cart.

“You changed it.”

Sivet had a mouthful of explanations. The old shaft was sound but heavy. The ridge seller might have had a lighter one. A cart could overturn on the descent. None would have survived being spoken.

“Yes.”

Anka took the copper pan from her bag. She set it on the floor, beside the clay dishes, and left the house.

Sivet followed with the wedges.

Down in the basin, everything was dropping again. Berr's weights rolled apart. A dozen objects hit the wheel, fell, and skittered downhill in the lee of its rim. The axle lay across a patch of pale sand.

“We can get it back,” Sivet said.

Anka was watching the cable.

“If that comes loose, it'll go.”

“Yes.”

“Then loosen it.”

Sivet held up the wedges. “Or stop the wheel.”

At the ridge, a red cloth appeared on the caravan mast. The traders had seen the movement below. They were leading their animals farther along the crest.

“Your things are all there,” Sivet said. “Everybody's are. We stop it, we can go and pick them up.”

“And how many mornings have you stopped one of those?”

“I've held heavier wheels than this.”

“Dead ones.”

Sivet walked toward the machine. Anka followed.

The next pulse took a sheet from Berr's porch. It sailed edge on, struck a stone and folded. They stayed behind a rock until the noise subsided, then ran to the near wheel. Sivet pointed out a broken spoke through which they could reach the inner drum.

“When it goes quiet, drive these in opposite sides. Keep your fingers back.”

Anka looked through the gap. “That will take the whole head off your mallet.”

“The head can be replaced.”

They waited for the third knock, the pull, the falling hum. This time Sivet counted only eighteen breaths before the next cycle.

She set her wedge against the drum. Anka placed the other. Together they hammered. The wood bit, the black surface stopped moving, and the first knock cut short.

There was silence enough to hear people calling up on the shelf.

The chisel fell. So did a row of nails that had arranged themselves across the bearing cap. Sivet felt a wide, sudden relief. She was already seeing the work ahead: shore the housing, split the cap, take the drive apart. Months of careful stripping. Not one great harvest followed by hunger, but daily work.

Inside the drum something struck once.

Her wedge split along the grain. Anka's leaped out of its gap. Sivet ducked as it passed her face. The drum turned, dragging a smear of pale wood around its edge.

They got behind the rock before the iron lifted.

Anka put the mallet down. There was a fresh dent on its head, but it was whole.

“It isn't waiting for us,” she said.

From there they could see the other end of the cable. It was attached to the overturned wreck by an eye in a forked coupling. Anka pointed to the keeper pin across it.

“I can knock that through.”

“Not now.”

Anka took the bronze drift and stood.

Sivet caught her scarf. “Look at the fork.”

The first knock came. They watched the sleeper's wheel turn, the hull advance, the cable rise. The fork on the overturned wreck twisted. A flake of rust as large as Sivet's hand sprang from it. If the keeper came out under that strain, the eye would cut across where Anka meant to kneel.

Anka crouched again. After the pull, the cable sank, and the fork eased back.

“While it's down, then.”

“You can't knock a pin that size out in a breath. And the next pull will close it on your hand.”

Sivet watched the near wheel roll backward into its old hollow. There was slack then: a shallow curve in the cable lying on the sand. The machine advanced only a handspan before taking it up again.

“We hold it back here,” she said. “Before it reaches the end.”

Anka looked at the splintered wedges.

“Not that,” Sivet said.

At the foot of the rock shelf lay a thick timber with one sloping end. They had used it for years to support a different hull while cutting its belly plates. Anka had once tried to sell it to a trader short of firewood. Sivet had refused. Wood like that did not grow anywhere near the waste.

Anka laid the drift beside the mallet and ran uphill for it.

Sivet waited for the falling hum, then saw her chisel below the wheel. Beyond it lay the axle. The pull was weaker outside the broken rim; most of the fallen metal settled there instead of against the turning drum. At this distance she could hear every knock distinctly.

She collected the chisel. She pulled the axle into a hollow behind a stone. There were nails at her feet, a length of chain, two good iron handles. The hum rose. She let the chain go and lay flat while it travelled above her toward the wheel.

When it was quiet, she went out again.

She took the bread knife, the handles and a pair of tongs. Those were hers, long enough to keep her hands safe in the forge. They had fallen within reach. There was time to bring the lot behind the stone, time to go out again for a roof tie.

Then Anka called.

She had rolled the timber down the slope, end over end, and dragged it into the wheel's hollow. Its sloping face was pointed under the front of the rim, ready to stop the next forward stroke before the cable tightened. But each time the wheel rolled back, it nudged the timber aside. Anka had no hand free to drive it into place.

“I need you here.”

Sivet wound the chain around the axle. She slid the tongs and knife beneath a link. They made a compact load; she could haul it up between pulses, in two trips if her knee held. Others were doing it already. Berr had recovered three of his weights and was lying behind a rock with them.

“Mother.”

Sivet looked up. Anka stood at the timber, hands braced on its end. The bronze drift lay beside her. When the machine travelled, it would take the field with it. Every iron thing here would lift and follow; it was reaching farther with every turn. The load she had gathered would go. The exposed engine would go. Even the cap they had spent yesterday loosening would go.

If she carried the load uphill now, Anka would have to wait. Another delay that Sivet could defend, with the difference that this time the iron was truly worth saving.

The first knock sounded.

At the highest house on the shelf, a stovepipe began shaking against the sky. Nothing that high had moved during the earlier pulls.

She put down the chain and moved behind the rock. At the third knock, the tongs jerked clear and hit the axle. She could have retrieved them when the hum fell. Instead she ran to Anka.

They waited for the wheel to roll back. Sivet held the timber against the sand with her shoulder. Anka swung the mallet, driving its thick end. The thin end nosed under the rim.

“Again,” Sivet said.

Anka struck twice more. Sivet's knee hurt. A jagged edge of the rolling rim nudged the timber's exposed end sideways. She shifted her foot and leaned harder, keeping the wedge straight beneath the wheel. There was no doing that from behind the rock.

The first knock came before Anka could put the mallet down.

The powered wheel turned and climbed onto the timber's sloping face. The timber groaned and bit into the sand. The hull lifted on its springs, but it did not advance far enough to take up the cable. Across the basin the cable rose an arm's length, then dropped again, still curved.

Anka looked at Sivet.

“Go,” Sivet said.

Anka picked up the drift and mallet and ran along the cable toward the overturned wreck. Sivet stayed beside the wedge. Loose iron was moving past, rattling against the sleeper's flank. A hinge struck the rock by her head. She tucked her chin and pressed her shoulder into the timber's exposed end.

The pull subsided. Anka knelt at the coupling. Her arm rose and fell. Bronze made a blunt, familiar note on iron.

Sivet could see the keeper move. Not far enough. Anka changed sides and struck again.

At the next first knock, a long crack opened in the timber.

The wheel chewed down into it. Sivet scrambled back onto her knees. The hull advanced a finger's width and the cable began to straighten. Anka was still bent over the coupling.

“Out!” Sivet shouted.

Anka gave one more blow. The keeper fell, the cable eye dropped from the fork, and she hurled herself away from it. Her boot caught the torn edge of a plate as she landed. The freed cable slid across the sand toward Sivet, sweeping a low ridge ahead of it.

Sivet got behind the rock as the wheel crushed the timber.

This time there was no recoil. The machine rolled forward. One wheel climbed out of its hollow, then the next. Sand poured from the body in curtains. Above them, an old tower leaned and fell; it struck the ground where the bearing cap had been a moment before.

Iron rose all around the basin.

The axle went first. With the tongs still caught under its chain, it slid from the hollow behind the stone and followed the sleeper. Roof ties skated downhill. Berr let go of his weights and crawled away from them. The cable dragged after the machine, its eye knocking a deep, regular mark in the sand.

Anka came around the back of the rock, limping. Sivet reached for her. She had scraped a foot; the cloth of her scarf was torn. She sat, breathing through her open mouth, and pushed Sivet's hand away when it went to the scarf.

They watched the sleeper pass below the settlement. Its wheels found an old hard surface under the sand and kept going. Beyond the basin it veered a little to the south. Neither of them could see what made it turn.

The hum weakened. Loose iron no longer leaped, but travelled in little starts, a broad ragged train behind the hulk. Here and there a piece caught on stone and stayed. Most went on.

“Your foot,” Sivet said.

Anka bent it, testing. “I can walk.”

Up on the shelf, their roof had gone slack. One corner of the canvas hung into the house. Someone's stove lay broken on the path. The copper pan Anka had set on the floor was still there, bright in the open daylight.

They went home before the afternoon heat settled in. Sivet tied Anka's foot with clean cloth. Anka held the ends for her, then took over the knot.

The cart wheels had followed the axle. What remained was a wooden box with two handles, tilted against a stone. Sivet lifted the bedding out of it. She held it while Anka decided what to carry.

The pan went into the bag. So did two changes of clothes, a comb, the bronze drift and a small wooden box of letters. Anka left the plates. She opened the larger chest and took out a shirt she had been saving for the journey, shaking the dust from it. Its buttons were bone.

From the doorway Sivet could see a small moving shape against the southern hills. The forgotten machine was still going. There was no one standing on it, no flag, no voice carrying back across the sand.

She had enough clay pots to cook in. Her hands would still work. Tomorrow would ask more than that, but it had not arrived.

Anka tied her bag shut.

“I would have stayed until you found another pair of hands,” she said. “If you'd asked.”

Sivet put the bedding down. “I didn't want another pair.”

Anka's fingers stopped on the knot. Then she tightened it and lifted the bag.

Sivet fetched the mallet. There were marks where Anka had struck the keeper, a fresh bruise on the pale head and an old hollow worn by three generations of hands.

“Take this.”

Anka looked at it. “You'll need it.”

“I know where to borrow one.”

She laid the handle across Anka's palm. Her daughter closed her fingers, tested the weight, and tucked it through the ties of her bedding.

Outside, the red caravan cloth had returned to its first place on the ridge. Anka looked toward it. Sivet followed her out of the house and down the path to where it forked. The left branch led into the basin; the right climbed toward the waiting animals.

At the fork Anka shifted her bag and put an arm around her mother. Sivet held her carefully, leaving the sore foot clear. Her daughter's scarf smelled of dust and the wool chest in which they kept their winter things.

She let go while Anka was still standing close.

Then she watched her take the right-hand path.

stories.title: Right of Way
stories.prompt: They've put it to a vote, and the law passed-all broom riders must obtain a license from the Department of Moving Vehicles in order to fly. Now you have to explain to your elderly witch relatives why this necessary.
stories.body:
# Right of Way

Grandma's invitation to tea had said, *Bring your stamp.*

I hoped this meant she needed a letter posting. When I arrived, Aunt Hesta had her broom across the kitchen table and Aunt Minta was trying to decide which hat would look best in a government photograph.

“You can't wear a hat in the photograph,” I said.

Aunt Minta put both hats away.

“Well, then,” she said. “That's settled.”

Grandma pushed a plate of seed cake toward me. She had cut it into four pieces, but mine was still attached to hers by a strip of crust.

“I haven't brought the stamp,” I said. “It stays at work.”

“You can bring the forms back to work.”

“What forms?”

She took three applications from under the plate.

In the space headed *Evidence of competence*, she had written her own name, *Maud Flax*, and underlined it twice. The others were blank.

“Grandma.”

“You were very pleased when they hired you.”

“I'm still pleased.”

“And we were pleased for you. Weren't we, girls?”

Aunt Hesta made a noncommittal sound. Aunt Minta, who was a hundred and one and still answered to *girls*, said she had told everyone at the bakery.

I had been at the Department of Moving Vehicles for six weeks. I processed registrations, took photographs, and explained to motorists that an appointment at ten did not mean they could arrive at eleven and argue backward. My relatives had been proud of me until the town voted to require a license from every broom rider in the district.

The grace period ended Friday. Grandma's hundred and fourth birthday was Sunday.

“There must be an allowance for experienced witches,” she said.

“Experienced riders can book a test straightaway. They don't have to take lessons.”

“I don't mean an allowance that involves allowing someone to examine me.”

I separated my cake from hers. It took two careful pulls.

“I can't get you an exemption. There isn't one for relatives.”

“There ought to be one for people who can fly.”

Aunt Hesta picked a splinter from the broom's handle with her thumbnail. She had repaired that broom so often I wasn't sure how much of the original remained. The bright copper binding round the bristles was new. The hollow worn by her right thumb was older than my mother.

“What do they test?” she asked.

“Takeoff. A controlled stop. Keeping a safe distance. Signals. Who gives way.”

“Who do they think gives way?” asked Grandma.

“It's in the booklet.”

“Yes. You left three booklets.” She pointed at the windowsill, where all three lay beneath a pot of thyme. “The pot needed raising.”

“Did you read any of them first?”

“I know how to fly.”

“Other people don't.”

“Then examine them.”

I looked toward Aunt Minta for help. She was smoothing one of the forms.

“It says *full legal name*,” she said. “Will the whole thing go on the card?”

“If it fits.”

“Minta Rose Flax. I want the Rose. On the birthday invitations last year, I was ‘and sisters.’”

“There was limited space,” said Grandma.

“You had room for ‘No presents, please.’ Nobody listened to that.”

Aunt Hesta reached for the cake knife. “Did you vote for this?”

“Yes.”

Grandma withdrew her piece of cake before Hesta could cut it.

“You voted to make us ask permission.”

“I voted to make everyone show that they've learned the same rules. They sell flying brooms in the ironmonger's now. You get an afternoon's instruction and a voucher for a saddle cushion. People use them to go to work. They bring children home on them. The sky over the market is crowded.”

“The sky has always been crowded over the market.”

“With people you knew.”

“I didn't know everyone.”

“You knew who taught them.”

That got a pause. Grandma had learned from her mother, who had taught half the witches on the west hill. Aunt Hesta had taught the other half after an argument about how far forward to sit in a crosswind. When I was seven, the argument had been revived over my head for an entire summer.

“The young man delivering groceries yesterday didn't know what my raised fist meant,” I said. “He thought I was angry with him.”

“Were you?”

“After he landed, yes.”

Grandma tipped the teapot. I held out my cup, and she filled it.

“If they're going to sell people brooms,” she said, “they should teach them properly.”

“That's what the license is for. Read the rules, show an examiner you understand them, show you can ride safely. A leaflet can't tell us whether anyone's learned it.”

“Quite right,” she said. “Put that on the ironmonger's counter.”

She slid her application closer to me.

I pushed it back.

Aunt Hesta got up and took a booklet from under the thyme.

“Go on, then.”

“What?”

“See whether we can do it. You haven't ridden with us in a while.”

I had missed the last two birthday flights. The first year I'd been working late; the second I'd let working late excuse me from finding a way to come. They flew to the ridge above town with a cake tin and a bottle of something Aunt Minta kept in the wardrobe. For nineteen birthdays I had ridden behind Grandma, close enough to see her plait lift in the wind. Then, somehow, the ride had become something I would do next year.

“We could practice,” I said. “I can't examine you. You'll have someone else for the test.”

“Good,” said Hesta. “You'd be trying to make it easy.”

Grandma looked at me for a moment, then went to fetch her riding coat.

Outside, Aunt Hesta sat astride her broom with one foot on the garden bench. Her black cloak had wide sleeves lined with rusty red wool. I stood behind her with the booklet open.

“Show me a right turn.”

“I am showing you.”

“I can see your fist. Where's your elbow?”

“Come round here.”

From the front I could see her left arm stretched sideways from the shoulder and bent upward at the elbow, fist closed, exactly like the illustration. From behind, her fist stuck out above a fold of black wool. The shape of her bent arm was lost in the rest of the cloak.

The illustration showed a man in a close-fitting jacket. He had no broom beneath him; they had removed the handlebars from an old motoring picture.

“Hesta, use your other coat,” said Grandma.

“Why? This one keeps my knees warm.”

I went behind her again. She repeated the signal, and the sleeve repeated its silent refusal to tell me which way she meant to turn.

“You're right,” I said. “They need a picture from the back. And someone in riding clothes.”

Hesta held out her hand for the booklet. She wrote in the margin, pressing so hard the pencil nearly went through the page.

“Give that to whoever makes these.”

“I will.”

She unfastened the small brass pin at her throat and used it to gather the loose sleeve above her elbow. This time I could see the signal from behind.

“Now you,” she said.

My new work coat had narrow sleeves. I made the signal with more confidence than I should have.

“Can't see your hand,” said Hesta.

I'd tucked my elbow in, putting my fist behind my head. I moved it out.

“There.”

We tried the remaining signals. Grandma objected to three of them and demonstrated each correctly. At *yielding*, she raised an open palm.

“People already do that,” she said.

Grandma had mounted her crooked hornbeam broom. Her gray plait was tucked into her collar, and a flat canvas bag hung beneath the handle.

“You brought cake?” I asked.

“We might get hungry.”

She took off before I could ask whether she had packed my piece.

We went up through the apple branches. Aunt Minta kept her hat under her arm until we were clear of the tree, then put it on with both hands. Her broom stayed level beneath her; she steered with her knees and fed it power as casually as breathing. I gripped my handle while I ducked a branch that she had missed by an inch.

At the ridge, Grandma landed between two stones no farther apart than her boots. Hesta stopped beside her and pressed her thumb into the copper binding, settling the last quiver of the bristles. Minta went a little farther to find somewhere with a view.

I landed, stepped off, and had to take two quick strides after my broom before I'd drawn back all the lift I'd put into it.

“Controlled stop,” said Hesta.

“I'm still practicing too.”

She nodded, apparently satisfied with this answer.

The town lay below us in the late afternoon light. At least a dozen riders crossed above the square. Two carried long boxes; another had a child strapped in front, its red boots sticking out on either side. A broom with a violet handle rose from the ironmonger's yard, wobbled once, and steadied.

Grandma watched it until it passed the clock tower.

“That one's sitting too far back.”

“You could say that to them.”

“I'm eating.”

She opened the tin. All four pieces were there.

On the way home, I took my old place behind her.

We descended toward the market, where the broad route down from the ridge crossed the climbing route up between the clock tower and the east roofs. A rider in a brown jacket was rising from our right. His shopping bags hung close beneath his knees, one on each side.

Grandma kept descending. He kept coming.

Then both of them slowed. Grandma leveled her broom. The man stopped several broom lengths away, his toes pointed toward the crossing. Hesta and Minta spread out behind us, giving everyone room.

Grandma pointed down her route. He pointed along his, which ran across it.

Neither went.

“Climbing gives way to descending,” Grandma called. “You can see me against the sky. I can't pick you out against the roofs.”

“I'm on your right,” he said.

“I can see that.”

“The booklet says I go first.”

His shopping bags swung gently. He steadied them with his heels. He wasn't frightened or rude; he looked as though he had arrived at the correct answer and then found somebody else's answer occupying it.

“He's trying to get home too,” Minta murmured behind me.

Grandma glanced back. I had the booklet tucked inside my coat, and for a moment I thought she would ask me to produce it.

Instead, she raised her left hand, palm toward the man, clear of her shoulder. I recognized the booklet's yielding signal from the page we had practiced. She held it until he saw it, keeping her broom level and short of the crossing.

He nodded, pointed along his course, and went through.

“Thank you,” he called.

Grandma waited until his bags had cleared us, then continued down.

Nobody said anything until we had landed in the garden. Grandma dismounted, leaned her broom against the wall, and began unbuckling the cake bag.

“He ought to know the climbing rule,” she said.

“It was the only rule I knew until I read the booklet.”

“Then they ought to tell people why it was there.”

Hesta took out her pencil again.

Grandma watched the point move across the margin.

“He'd read his,” she said. “And he couldn't tell whether I'd read mine.”

“No.”

“I could have read it and ignored it.”

“You could. A license can't make you considerate.”

Hesta touched the pin gathering her sleeve and looked at Grandma.

“I did it just like the picture. Somebody still had to stand behind me.”

Grandma worked a stiff buckle with both thumbs. I reached for it and she let me finish.

“I don't like that right-hand rule for a steep climb.”

“You can put that in the complaint.”

“I will.”

Hesta offered her the pencil. Grandma took it, then looked up at me.

“Are there appointments before Friday?”

“Thursday afternoon.”

“All three?”

“I'll check.”

“All four,” said Minta.

“I've already got mine.”

“I mean you'll come with us. There'll be nobody to look after the bags.”

On Thursday I took an hour of leave, wore my ordinary coat, and sat in the waiting room with three handbags on my knees. Grandma's had the seed-cake tin in it. Hesta's contained enough small tools to reassemble the furniture. Minta had brought both hats.

An examiner took them out to the test yard. I heard Hesta ask where he would stand to observe her signals, and then heard him move.

They all passed. Grandma lost a mark for distance at a crossing. She did not tell us this; Hesta did.

The annotated booklet went to my supervisor. She read the first page, looked through the window at Hesta's cloak, and asked whether she could keep it. Hesta said she could keep the booklet.

For the photographs, Grandma wore the expression she used when someone charged her too much for firewood. Hesta had to be persuaded to put down her broom. Minta waited until I had typed *Minta Rose Flax* before she came anywhere near the camera.

On Sunday they arrived at my door while I was still fastening my coat.

“We said six,” Grandma told me.

It was five to six. I didn't argue. I had bought the cake this time, and I was trying to work out how to secure it without tipping the icing.

Hesta took the bag, adjusted the straps, and handed it back. Minta showed me her license through the little clear window in her purse. She had put it where her photograph of us used to be, and moved us to the pocket beside it.

We rose together. The low sunlight caught Grandma's silver plait as she drew it out of her collar. I moved into place behind her, with Hesta on my left and Minta on my right.

At the first turn, Grandma raised her elbow with exaggerated care. Her wrist was visible, her sleeve clear. She held the signal long enough for us all to see it.

“Is that satisfactory?” she called back.

“Very.”

“Good. Keep up.”

She took the turn faster than I was expecting. I tightened my knees, steadied the cake, and followed.

stories.title: The Weight of a Bell
stories.prompt: Look, since we're going to be working together, I’m going to make something very clear to you. I am NOT converting to your faith, I already have one, and if you keep trying to make me change my mind. I’ll summon a demon to drag you down to hell if i have to!
stories.body:
# The Weight of a Bell

The crack ran from the bell's lip almost to its shoulder. Anwen could put a fingernail into it. Someone had wrapped a strip of white linen around the bronze, as if the bell were a hurt wrist.

“My mother used to say it could be heard from her bedroom,” Mikkel said. “Even with the windows shut.”

He had told her that twice since dawn. This time Anwen looked down through the square opening in the belfry floor. The padded cradle waited far below, between the chapel's empty pews. They had taken out six boards to make a path for the bell. Through the gap she could see the soles of the steward's shoes as he went about collecting hymnbooks.

“It won't sound the same if they mend it,” she said.

“They'll cast a new one. This one belongs somewhere people can see it.” Mikkel adjusted the chain hoist over their heads. “You should come back for the dedication. The service, I mean. You might find something there.”

Anwen tied the loose end of her red wrist cord beneath her sleeve. She had worn it to work for twenty years. Mikkel had noticed it on their first job together and had been trying, in gentle increments, to find out what would make her take it off.

“I found the side door,” she said. “We brought the hoist in through it.”

He smiled, almost sorry for her. “You know what I mean.”

She set down the pencil with which she'd marked the safe path on the floor. The bell was still on its old wooden axle. Nothing was hanging yet. They had time to settle this.

“Look, since we're going to be working together, I'm going to make something very clear to you. I am *not* converting to your faith. I already have one. And if you keep trying to make me change my mind, I'll summon a demon to drag you down to hell if I have to.”

Mikkel glanced at the empty stairwell, as though she had embarrassed them in front of someone. “Anwen.”

“I mean it.”

“I know you do.” His voice softened. “That's why I worry.”

She picked up her pencil. He could worry. He could do it without trying to enter her head. “Pass me the short sling.”

They worked through the morning. Mikkel was good with his hands, and careful in most ways. He checked each shackle pin by touch and gave the old axle a slow inspection before they freed it. When the steward brought bread and cheese, Mikkel thanked him and bowed his head over his portion. Anwen sat on a packing crate and ate hers. She spoke the names of those who had taught her to work with weight, too quietly for anyone else to hear. Mikkel did not ask what she was saying.

By afternoon the bell hung from the hoist, its mouth a little above the opened floor. The chain held its weight. Two guide lines, tied to a padded band around its waist, kept it clear of the square opening's stone edges. Anwen had the west line around a cleat. Mikkel held the east, its spare length coiled beside a cleat near the stairwell. A broad board protected the west edge of the opening. The bell's crack faced Mikkel across the gap.

“The sling takes its weight a little off center,” Anwen said. “When the mouth passes the floor, it will drift west. Keep that line snug until I say *slack*. Don't haul it back if it moves. The hoist will take the weight.”

Mikkel nodded. He had helped lower machinery heavier than this. Still, he had rung this bell as a boy; she could see him trying not to look at the linen band someone had wound around it. He touched the line, then the catch at his waist, making sure he could pay out rope without letting it run.

They began the descent. Chain clicked through the hoist, one measured length at a time. The steward had gone outside on Anwen's instructions. Below, the cradle looked too small until she followed its corners with her eyes.

The bell's mouth reached the level of the floor. Mikkel eased his line.

“Hold it,” Anwen said.

“The cracked lip's too close to the east stone. If I give it room—”

“It hasn't cleared the west edge. Hold it.”

He looked at the bronze and not at her. His fingers opened a little. The bell drifted west, as she had warned. Its lip pressed into the protective board. Wood broke with a sound too sharp for its size.

Mikkel hauled at the east line. The bell swung back across the opening. Anwen locked the chain brake and felt the floor quiver under both feet. The cracked lip struck the east stone. A thin bronze flake jumped free and fell, ticking twice on the pews below.

“Let the line go slack,” she said.

He kept pulling. “It'll hit again.”

“If you pull, it will.”

He let out one breath, then one hand's width of rope. The bell stopped moving. Dust drifted into the open square. It hung inches from the east stone, the hoist loaded at a slight angle. They could leave it there for a minute. They could not leave it there for a night.

Mikkel stared at the new pale scar in the bronze. “I thought I could keep it off the stone.”

“You thought I hadn't seen where the stone was.”

“I didn't say that.”

“You didn't need to.” Anwen crouched to check the west guide. It had not frayed. “We can raise it a little and reset. Once I see whether the lip will clear.”

Behind her, Mikkel said, “When the floor shook, I thought we'd both fall. I thought about what comes after.” He glanced at the red cord at her wrist. “Come to the evening service with me when we finish. You can hear what we believe and leave if you want.”

The invitation might have been bearable on another day, after another accident. Here it followed her answer of that morning and the one before it, and the one on the quarry job when he had offered to bring her to a meeting, and the one in the wagon afterward. He could name the lines and their loads. He remembered the steward's instructions about the chapel door. It was only her refusal that fell out of him as soon as he heard it.

“No,” she said.

“I only meant—”

“I know what you meant.” She stood. The bell rocked once, very slightly, on the chain. “I told you what I'd do.”

Mikkel's expression changed. Not fear. The same concern he'd shown her all morning, with a little weariness beneath it, as though she had made his duty harder.

Anwen drew her red cord from under her sleeve. It was the one her father had knotted for her when she began to work. His warning about the old words had been that the speaker must answer for them afterward.

She wound the cord once around her fingers and spoke the name she had been taught. The air at the stairwell darkened. A figure stepped from it, narrow enough to pass between the railings though its shoulders seemed wider than the door. It wore a coat the color of banked coals. Its feet left ash on the boards, and through the gap below Anwen saw that its shadow continued downward past the cradle, into a distance the chapel could not contain.

Mikkel let the east line slip through his palms. Its loose end spilled from the coil, and the bell shifted toward the torn board. Anwen pinned the rope under her boot, then made it fast on the stairwell cleat.

The visitor looked first at the loaded hoist. Then it looked at Anwen.

“You called,” it said.

She had heard that voice in childhood stories, but never with her own ears. She had expected heat. She felt cold at the back of her neck.

“I did.”

The visitor turned to Mikkel. His heels left the floor. He gripped a timber post with both hands, and for a moment Anwen could see something beneath him that was neither stairs nor chapel. A wind rose out of it with the smell of hot iron. The visitor had not touched him. It had only made the distance possible.

“Do you ask me to take him?” it said.

Mikkel did not speak. Anwen had wanted him to believe her. She had not pictured his empty hands, with rope burns across the fingers, grasping wood while the bell waited above an open floor.

“No,” she said. “I asked you to hear me say that I could.”

The visitor held her gaze. Anwen felt the plain ugliness of that answer. She had used its arrival to frighten him, whatever else she had called it. The cord tightened around her fingers, not by magic but because her hand had closed.

“You can take him,” she said. “I do not want you to.”

Mikkel's heels settled on the boards. The distance beneath him closed. The visitor regarded the two of them, the bell, the gouge in the east stone. Then it walked to the stairwell. At the top step it brushed ash from its sleeve. The ash fell through the boards and was gone before it reached the pews.

Anwen waited until the stairwell was only a stairwell. She unwound the cord and put it away. Mikkel still held the post. When he let go, the grain of the wood had left pale ridges across his palms. He watched the bell.

“We have to lift it back,” he said.

“A hand's width.”

He reached for the east line.

“Leave that,” Anwen said. “It looks wrong, but pulling it will turn the crack into the stone. Put your hand on the chain brake. When I say *up*, give me three clicks. No more.”

He looked at the line lying against his boot. It was what he knew how to control. The brake was hers; she had worked it all afternoon. He stood with his palm on the lever for so long Anwen thought he was going to argue.

“Three clicks,” he said.

She took the west guide to its mark. “Up.”

One click. The bell shifted, and Mikkel's free hand moved toward the east line. He stopped it on his own knee. Two clicks. At the third, the bronze cleared the torn board. He held the brake where it was.

Anwen pulled out the damaged plank. She laid a pad of folded canvas on the east edge, then moved to the guide line beside him. “Now give it slack. Slowly.”

He did. The bell turned away from the stone. They lowered it through the floor with only the small sounds of chain and rope. When the cradle took its weight, the cracked lip touched its padding without a note.

Mikkel kept his hands on the rope after the chain went slack. “I can still feel where the floor went away.”

“I called it to frighten you,” Anwen said. “I didn't need it for the bell. You should hear that from me.”

He rubbed at the marks the post had left on his palms. “I think it was evil.”

She had no wish to try to settle that while its ash might still be on the stairs. “You can think that.”

“I still believe what I told you.” He looked at her then, not at the cord under her sleeve. “You told me this morning. I understood. I asked anyway. I won't keep at you about your faith.”

Anwen let out the breath she'd been holding. “All right.”

The steward returned as they were stripping the slings. His eyes found the pale mark on the bell.

“What happened?” he asked.

Mikkel looked at Anwen, and she wondered whether he wanted her to make the answer easy for him. She was too tired to guess. The bell had been cracked before they arrived; the mark was new. Anyone could see both things.

“I gave the east line slack too soon,” he said. “Anwen told me to hold it. Put that in the record before you sign.”

The steward went to fetch the work sheet. Mikkel stayed by the bell, not touching it. After a while he bowed his head. Anwen could not tell whether he was praying, and did not need to. She rolled the red cord once between finger and thumb, feeling the knot her father had made, then began to coil the lines for the walk home.

stories.title: The Bait Remembers
stories.prompt: You are a heavily traumatized individual, weaponised against psychics as a living booby trap meant to catch anyone reading the minds of random civilians.
stories.body:
# The Bait Remembers

I had three coins, an unstamped birthday card, and an assignment to stand in a post office until someone looked inside my head.

The card was for my sister. Innes did not know about it. He had searched my coat before we left, but the card fit behind the tongue of my shoe. In the post office I bent to retie the lace and moved it to my sleeve. I had written the address from memory. Orla might not live above the bakery anymore. For three years I had been permitted to know almost nothing about her, and it seemed better to risk a returned card than to let another birthday pass without one.

Innes stood three places behind me in the queue. His coat was damp at the shoulders. People trying to keep their parcels dry had crowded toward the counter. Across the open floor, the writing desks stood between us and the street door. He had chosen the hour because the queue would hold me still and give him a view of everyone else.

“Blue forms,” he said when my gaze drifted toward my sleeve. “Keep your eyes on the blue forms.”

He meant the stack on the counter, an ordinary place to rest my gaze. I looked at them. A man ahead of me was arguing about the cost of sending a parcel to his son. The clerk took his complaint seriously enough to weigh the box a second time. Beside the writing desks, a little girl in a raincoat drew a circle around each stamp on a sheet while her father addressed envelopes.

Across the floor, the street door shut hard. For an instant I smelled the old room.

Not the post office's wet wool and ink, but wallpaper warmed too long by a bulb with no shade. I knew where the memory would go. The narrow bed. The line of light under the door. Then the scrape of a key in the lock.

My thumbnail found the center of my palm. Four-one-six, I thought. Four-one-six. The wallpaper went away. I could see the clerk's blue forms again, and Innes nodded almost imperceptibly.

He had taught me the thumb-and-number drill in a room very different from this one. The key's scrape was the cut. Thumb into palm, number in the mind, as soon as it came. At first I had refused because I thought he was trying to make me forget. He wasn't. He needed me to remember exactly as far as the key, over and over, and never go through the door.

Before I knew him, the memory sometimes ran on. The door opened. There was the corridor, the morning street, and the bus I rode without a ticket because I could not make my hands find my money. Then I came back to whatever room I was actually in. Going all the way through had never made it easier. I had learned to fear the end of it as much as the beginning.

Now the route out belonged to Innes. If somebody reading me followed the memory, my jump to the number at the scrape left them at the locked door. With no later moment of mine to follow, they heard the key scrape again. Their body stood unanswering while Innes looked for it.

I had watched him take two. The first was a man who had been picking names out of a doctor's waiting room. The second was a woman who said afterward that she had only wanted to know why I was frightened. I had not seen what was done with either of them. The woman had looked at me as Innes led her away, confused by the fact that I was walking while she could hardly stand.

“Next,” called the clerk. The man with the parcel lifted it off the scale. There were two people between me and the counter.

Orla used to put cards on the mantel weeks before her birthday. She liked seeing her name written in other people's hands. I had taken a plain postcard with a small printed bird on the front. On the back, I had managed: *Happy birthday. I am alive. Love, Ada.* I had tried longer versions, but each one began to sound like an account I was giving Innes. I hoped the coins would buy a stamp.

Someone behind the writing desks made a small, angry sound. A woman holding a padded envelope had turned toward a man in a gray scarf.

“I wasn't talking to you,” she said.

“I'm sorry.” He backed away from her at once. Nothing distinguished him from the other customers. He was younger than Innes, older than me, perhaps thirty, with rain darkening the ends of his scarf. “I thought someone needed help.”

The woman gripped her envelope under her arm. “Ask them, then.”

He looked across the queue. I felt something brush the outside of a thought, so slight that I might have mistaken it for dread if I had not spent three years learning the difference.

The plea he had heard was mine. It had escaped while I was remembering the old room. I had not formed the words on purpose; they came out of the same place as the smell of wallpaper. *Please don't leave me there.* Innes counted on a thought like that carrying. A psychic might hear it without choosing to. Finding its owner among strangers required another choice.

The man in the scarf looked at the father by the stamp sheets, then at the woman with the envelope again. He was searching. She moved away from him, and he let her go, but his eyes kept moving down the line.

I could have raised my hand. I could have told him aloud that I was the person in trouble. Innes would have heard. Perhaps the man would have stopped looking inside other people. Perhaps he would have looked into me more closely. I had been placed in this room to make those possibilities hard to tell apart.

I took the card from my sleeve instead. I meant to keep it from bending. The man glanced at the movement.

For a moment the birthday message was no longer mine alone. I felt him see the little bird, Orla's name and address, the three short sentences that I had protected with my shoe and sleeve. I held the card against my chest. The contact went deeper anyway.

“No,” I said.

I was in the old room. The bulb made a yellow patch high on the wall. There were nine flowers on the wallpaper to the left of the bed if I counted the torn one. I had counted them for days because there was so little else to do.

From somewhere that was both inside and outside me, the man said, *I'm sorry. I can leave.*

He meant to. The key was scraping in the lock, and he was still with me.
