I looked at Mica. Their hands were still raised, but their elbows had begun to bend. The sign sank another inch. They had seen the woman before I had, and chosen to hold it there.

"I'm coming," I said to her.

Mica's eyes flashed to mine. The blue hand came between me and the awning, palm outward. I knew that gesture too: stay. I shook my head. Mica's mouth opened a little, though no sound came. Their hand returned to the sign.

I went back beneath the sign.

The awning smelled of hot sugar and singed cloth. A crate of glass jars had fallen across the table, weighing the brace down. I pushed the crate over. Jars rolled against my knees. I pressed the release with my thumb and lifted the brace off her boot. She pulled her leg free.

Above us, the sign lurched. Mica made a sound like a breath forced through clenched teeth. Forks and wrappers that had been hanging in the air scattered across the lane.

"Can you stand?" I asked.

"If you help."

We got up together. She leaned hard on my shoulder, and for three steps I could see nothing but the paving directly ahead. I wanted to look at Mica. I could not afford to lose my footing. The woman and I reached the cook's counter just as the boy's sugar-glass bird, abandoned on the ground, lifted briefly and rang against the steel leg of a stool.

"Clear!" I shouted.

Mica looked at the woman, then at the empty packing stalls. Their hands closed. The sign's free right edge swung down on the remaining arm, its light sliding backward across the roof. Mica checked its fall until it reached the stalls. The stall frames broke under the weight, and the sign went dark.

The loose bulbs came down at once. The air smelled of broken glass and cooking oil. Mica stood in the emptied lane, staring at the long blue fingers of their hands. Their tails thinned to ribbons. The light folded inward, and the figure was a small fox again.

I hurried over. Mica sat beneath the empty roof arm, breathing fast, their fur faint around the edges. I sat on the paving beside them while the market found its voices: the cook calling for someone to bring a chair, the boy asking his mother if she had seen the fox too, the woman from the stall assuring three different people that her leg was all right.

The woman limped over, her augmented eyes following Mica. She crouched carefully. "Thank you," she said to Mica, and held out her hand.

I had already raised my arm for Mica to climb aboard. I lowered it. Mica crossed to the woman and set one small paw against her palm. She held still until Mica stepped back.

Then Mica came back to me. They climbed the familiar seam but stayed outside my cuff, facing the lane. Their paw came to rest over my pulse.

stories.title: The Surface
stories.prompt: They call her Onyx, the last daughter of a people who turned their bodies to living stone rather than kneel. Every wound leaves a vein of gold across her skin—and after a 100 years of war, she is tried of being a weapon and want to retried to peaceful life.
stories.body:
# The Surface

Onyx had been told that the sea would hold anyone who lay still enough. She lay back in a sheltered cove and went straight to the bottom.

It was not far down. The water covered her face, and the stones under her shoulders were round and slick. She could see a white gull passing overhead, flattened by the wavering surface into an improbable shape. It circled twice more before her lungs demanded air. She put her feet beneath her, stood, and sent the gull back into its proper sky.

On the beach, a woman with a coil of rope over one shoulder was watching her.

“That was quick,” the woman said.

Onyx pushed wet black hair from her eyes. Salt ran down the gold seam beside her ear. “I have a talent for sinking.”

“I noticed.”

The woman walked past her toward a narrow boat drawn up above the tide. Onyx could have let her go. Instead she asked, “Do you make boats?”

The woman turned. She had thick wrists, a sun-browned face, and the air of someone calculating how much of her morning a stranger would take. “I make them float.”

“Could you make me float?”

Her eyes traveled over Onyx’s black stone arms and the gold worked through them, then to the armor Onyx had stacked on a flat rock. Each scale of it bore a tiny stamped sun. Even out of uniform, Onyx was seldom unrecognized for long.

“Maybe,” the woman said. “I’m Neri. Come to the shop when you’re dry.”

Onyx looked down at the water already beading and slipping from her skin. “That may be sooner than you think.”

Neri’s mouth twitched. She kept walking.

For one hundred years Onyx had gone where a map sent her. She had chosen this coast herself. Her people had lived along it before the armies came; the houses were gone, but she remembered the salt grass that grew in the cracks above the beach. Beyond the headland lay the ship she had ordered sunk in the last battle. She knew it was there when she rented her room. The bay had been her home before it was a battlefield, and she wanted to live beside it without looking away. As a girl she had run down this shore with bare feet and a body light enough to be lifted by a wave. Now, when she had nowhere else she had been ordered to be, she wanted the sea to lift her once more. She had watched three boys laughing beyond the breakers that morning, and wanted something of their present joy, not only the return of an old sensation.

She carried her armor to the room she had rented and went to Neri’s shop in plain clothes. Its door stood open to a crowded bench and two long, narrow hulls in their frames. Neri was shaving a sliver from a rib. She glanced up at Onyx’s loose shirt, then at the boots whose heels had left small dents in her floorboards.

“How much do you weigh?”

“More than when I last swam.”

“That isn’t a number.”

Onyx gave her one. Neri wrote it on a plank in chalk and stared at it for a moment. Then she drew two sealed floats, each half the length of her skiff, a broad strap for each of Onyx’s arms, and a crosspiece that would keep them from turning under her.

“You’ll have to move your own legs,” Neri said. “I can put wood under you. I can’t make it a skill.”

“I did not ask you to.”

“You’d be surprised what people ask.”

Onyx paid for the wood and half the labor. Neri made no remark about the old gold Onyx used. Gold had entered her skin wherever a blade, a bullet, or a fall had opened it. The coins had come from her wages. She had not cut them from herself, though strangers had asked that question with varying degrees of politeness.

Neri worked while Onyx watched, and after a while gave her sandpaper and a section of the crosspiece. Onyx pressed too hard. The wood roughened, then began to splinter.

“Lighter,” Neri said.

Onyx tried again. It had been a long time since her hands had been asked for less strength. Her people had made themselves stone rather than kneel to the conquerors who landed here. The change had kept many alive. It had not made them unbreakable. Across a century of fighting, the others had fallen, until people who had never heard her mother’s voice began calling Onyx the last daughter. She had learned to carry their refusal in her arms, as if every gentle thing might be mistaken for surrender.

By dusk the floats were sealed but not yet fitted. Neri had to let the pitch cool. She set them outside on trestles, where the breeze could reach every seam.

“You chose an odd place to start,” she said. “Most people learn in a pond.”

“I was born here.”

Neri looked toward the headland. Onyx followed her gaze.

“Then you know what’s out there,” Neri said.

“Yes.”

“I recognized you at the beach. My sister sailed on that ship.”

Onyx rested the sandpaper on the bench. “I’m sorry.”

“I saw them take Sal aboard under guard. The record says it was carrying powder. No passengers. Her name is on a list of the missing, and the same office says there was nobody to miss.” Neri drew a finger across a line in the wood, not looking up. “I thought you might be able to go down. There was a locked chest in the captain’s cabin. Sailors kept their lists there.”

Onyx thought of the gull distorted by water. Her stone lungs held a breath longer than human lungs could. She had been under the surface in battle, walking where others could not, dragging chains between ships. She could reach the wreck. She had reached it once, the day after the battle, sent to count the powder barrels that had survived. The captain’s cabin was pinned beneath a collapsed deck. She had left it closed. To enter now she would have to break through the part of the ship where the prisoners had been held. She did not know whether Sal’s name had ever been written in the chest.

Neri leaned both hands on the bench. “You were there. At the harbor.”

“I was.”

“You have the wound from it. They put it on the victory coins.”

Onyx touched the narrow gold line across her left shoulder. It shone through the collar of her shirt. On the coins, an artist had made it a bright slash above a burning ship, as if she had earned it while pulling people from the fire.

“I saw people on board,” she said.

Neri’s hands stayed on the bench. “How many?”

“I don’t know.”

“Was Sal one of them? She had a red scarf.”

“I couldn’t see faces or clothes.”

“But you saw people.”

Onyx nodded. Across the bay that day, enemy troops had been moving toward the shore. The prison ship carried powder in its hold and captives above it. Her gunners had waited for her signal. She had seen the figures at the rail before she gave it. The ship burned; the advance stopped. Later the account written in her name mentioned only the powder.

“I ordered the shot,” Onyx said.

Neri straightened. “You knew they were there.”

“Yes.”

The pitch on the floats made small cracking sounds as it cooled. Neri walked to the open door and stood with her back to Onyx. When she turned, her expression had lost the little impatient warmth it had held all afternoon.

“Can you reach the captain’s cabin?”

“I think so.”

“Will you?”

Onyx looked at the two floats drying in the light. They would take her onto the water and keep her there. The wreck would require none of them. She could walk off the beach that night, follow the floor until the world grew dark, and break into the ship she had burned. She wanted Neri to have an answer. She also dreaded seeing the wreck again, and could not pretend that dread belonged to the families.

“The cabin is under a fallen deck,” she said. “I saw it when I went down for the powder. I would have to break through the prisoners’ quarters.”

“Sal’s daughter wants it opened. Two of the other families who saw their people taken aboard have asked me to leave them where they are. They don’t want the prisoners’ quarters broken.” Neri folded her arms. “I wanted to know if you could reach it before I went back to them.”

“I can reach it. I won’t open it on a request made only to me.”

“If you leave it closed, you decide something for Sal too.”

Onyx had no answer that made Neri wrong. “I can tell you what I saw. I can put my name to it. Take that to the families. If they ask me together, I’ll listen. I can’t promise I’ll go.”

“That won’t tell me if Sal was aboard.”

“No.”

Neri looked at the gold seam on Onyx’s shoulder, then at the unfinished crosspiece. “You can write it here tomorrow. I need you to leave now.”

Onyx rose. “And the floats?”

“They’ll be ready.” Neri left the sandpaper where it lay. “I said I’d make them.”

Onyx walked back to her room without putting on the armor. Its gold scales lay on the bed where she had left them, a second body that had always seemed easier for other people to look at. She sat at the little table and wrote what she had seen from the quay: captives at the rail, enemy troops advancing beyond them, gunners waiting for her signal. She wrote that she had given it after seeing the people aboard. She could not name them. Then she signed it.

In the morning, Neri read the pages standing at her bench. She stopped at the line about the figures at the rail and read it a second time. Onyx waited while Neri finished, folded the pages, and put them beneath a weight so the breeze could not take them.

“You’ve written that you knew before you gave the order,” Neri said. “The last account said nobody did.”

“That account was mine too. I let it stand.”

Neri looked at the signature. “I’ll take this to Sal’s daughter first. I won’t tell her it answers where Sal is.” She trimmed a loose end of binding from the frame. “She may come here and ask you herself. I won’t keep your room a secret.”

“Tell her I’ll come to her this afternoon, after she’s read it. She can send me away. I can tell her how the cabin lies.”

“I’ll tell her.”

Neri handed her the finished frame. It was broad and awkward, smelling of pitch and fresh wood. She had padded the straps where they would touch the gold on Onyx’s arms.

“Why did you finish it?” Onyx asked.

“You paid me to make it, and I said I would.” Neri met her eyes. “I’ll make sure it works. Then I have somewhere else to be.”

They carried the frame to the cove. Neri checked each fastening herself and sent Onyx into water shallow enough to stand in. From the beach she gave practical instructions: loosen one strap, lean back before kicking, keep her mouth above the chop. Her voice held no softness Onyx could mistake for pardon. It held attention.

Onyx took a breath and leaned backward. The floats rolled against her arms. Her feet left the stones. For an instant panic drove her to reach for the bottom, but her hand met water, and the frame steadied. She moved one leg, then the other. The shore shifted a little beside her.

Neri stayed where the wet sand began. The signed account lay in a dry bag at her feet, ready for the walk to the families. Onyx could see the bag whenever a wave lowered her. She could also see the high blue part of the sky, which she had never watched from this angle as stone.

“Your left float’s riding low,” Neri called. “Come in. I need to move that strap.”

Onyx turned toward shore. It took several ungainly strokes to travel the few yards back. She wanted to try again tomorrow.

stories.title: From the Middle
stories.prompt: Everyone carries a spirit heart, tethered to their physical heart by a silver thread. Every person who loves you makes it a little bigger and leaves a little of their colour. After she became famous, hers filled the sky with colours from people who knew her face, her voice, her name—everything except her.
stories.body:
# From the Middle

At the afternoon camera test, the studio had covered its skylights for the broadcast. Vera could still see her heart in the monitors whenever a camera faced the street: an enormous, imperfect shape of colour behind the crowd, cut in half by the buildings. A silver thread ran from the thing in the sky to her physical heart. It showed through her dress as a fine, bright line just left of the buttons.

The first time she had come to this studio, her spirit heart had floated an arm's length above her, about the size of a melon. Her mother had put one hand over the pale green she had left in it and told Vera to stand still for the photograph. Now a camera needed its own dark hood to keep Vera's heart from tinting the lens. People watched it from bridges and apartment roofs. On clear nights, someone always posted a picture with a circle around a fleck of colour: *That one's mine.*

It was her first song's fifteenth anniversary. The television people had made the entrance look like a kitchen, though the studio kitchen was four floors down and windowless. There was a chipped yellow cup on the set, a basket of oranges, and a little radio of the kind Vera had never owned. On the worktable behind it sat the cassette player she *had* owned. Her assistant had found the machine in a box at Vera's mother's house and spent a week making it work. The tape itself was in Vera's bag.

She was going to play the whole recording tonight and put it on an anniversary edition of the song next week. She had said so in the advertisements.

At the stage door that evening, a woman stopped her with one hand raised, palm out. She kept her distance. She and the boy beside her wore blue audience passes; he gripped the strap of a schoolbag the same colour.

"You can go," the guard said to Vera.

"It's all right." Vera stopped. Above the woman's head floated a small spirit heart striped orange and brown. Its silver thread vanished into the collar of her coat. The boy's heart was almost entirely a thin, bright blue.

"We don't need a picture," the woman said. "I just wanted to thank you. When my father came back from the hospital, he couldn't get up the stairs to his room. My son played your song from his little speaker. We took one step each time the bass came in. It took an hour the first night." She looked at the boy, who pressed his lips together, embarrassed. "By the end of the month he could do it without the music. But we still hear those stairs when the song comes on."

Vera had heard extravagant versions of this sort of story. This one had a steepness and duration she could picture. She said, "I'm glad he got home."

"He's well now." The woman smiled. "My son wanted me to ask whether the girl at the beginning will be on tonight. The one who says, 'Again, from the middle.' He likes that part best."

The boy looked as if he would rather his mother had not told anyone what he liked best. Vera said, "I think you'll hear her."

The woman thanked her again. The boy gave a quick wave without letting go of his bag. The guard opened the door, and Vera went inside.

The phrase at the beginning of the song belonged to Iona. Vera's younger sister had said it into a kitchen tape recorder when they were seventeen and fifteen, after Vera missed a note for the fourth time. Vera had kept the count-in on the demo because the next take was the one where her voice stopped sounding as though it had borrowed another singer's throat. A producer kept it on the single. By the time Iona asked her to take it off, the single was everywhere, and Vera had answered as if its success were a technical difficulty nobody could solve.

For years, listeners had pictured a patient little girl directing a future star through her first song. They sent drawings of her. Some thanked Vera for letting them hear a childhood so gentle that they could live inside it for four minutes. Vera had said in interviews that Iona was the reason she began singing. It was an easy sentence to say aloud, and a hard one to retrieve.

In the dressing room, Vera set her bag on a chair. She could still see the woman and boy through the window, making their way toward the audience entrance under the heart. The woman stopped once and tilted her face up. Vera tried to imagine the stairwell: the boy waiting on one step with his speaker, his grandfather reaching for the next. The bit of Iona's voice that Vera had used without asking had helped them. Both things were true, and she wanted very badly for one truth to settle the other.

Her phone lit up. Iona had answered the message Vera sent three days earlier with the broadcast time. *I'm downstairs.*

Vera read it twice, then gave the door staff Iona's name.

The tape lay in her bag, inside a cracked plastic case. On its paper label Iona had written **VERA TRYING IT** in red block letters. The full recording began with the scrape of a chair and Vera asking if they could start at the chorus because the verse made her sound miserable. Iona said no, they needed to find the place where it went wrong. They went over three lines again and again. A kettle whistled. At one point Iona joined her, not to harmonize, only to show her where a vowel could open. Vera laughed so hard at the sound of their two voices that she could barely find the next note.

After the single came out, Vera learned to laugh away from microphones. She learned how to finish a verse even when she could no longer feel its words. On the tape, before either of them knew there was a right way to be heard, she could hear herself fail and try again. She had promised that voice to the audience. She had not mentioned to Iona that most of what she loved about it happened because Iona was there.

Iona arrived wearing a raincoat damp at the shoulders. She had cut her hair much shorter than in the last photograph Vera had seen. Her spirit heart floated beneath the low ceiling lamp, the silver thread crossing one wet shoulder. There was no camera in the room, but Vera felt the old instinct to arrange her face.

"Hello," she said.

"Hi." Iona left the door ajar. "I saw the trailer."

Vera touched the case. "They used the bit I sent them. Not the rest."

"Tonight is the rest."

Iona spoke quietly, without the great, injured voice Vera had prepared herself to resist. That made it harder to answer.

"I thought you'd like to hear it again," Vera said. "It's us, before all this."

"I listened to it when you mailed me the copy."

"And?"

"It's us in the kitchen. I can hear you breathing through your nose because you had a cold." Iona took the empty chair, but did not remove her coat. "I don't want them to have the kitchen too. No more of my voice on the anniversary release. And please stop telling them I made you. I was there while you learned a song."

Vera looked down at the tape. "You did more than that."

"I know what I did. I just don't want to hear it in another trailer."

The words landed too neatly. Vera felt herself push against them. "People have asked for the full recording for years. I wanted them to hear what I sounded like when I wasn't trying to sound like Vera."

Iona glanced at the yellow cup on the set, visible through the open dressing-room door. "I heard you."

"That's not what I meant."

"I know."

Vera had not meant to look up. A narrow strip of sky showed above the window frame, and somewhere beyond it was the yellow Iona had left in her heart when they were children. The sea of later colours had spread over it, but Vera knew its place. She had found it from a dozen hotel roofs. It was still there. Each time she found it, she could believe for a minute that something between them remained as it had been.

Iona followed her eyes to the window. "The tape, Vera."

Vera turned back. Iona's hands were folded on the wet raincoat; one fingernail had a dark mark at its edge. Vera did not know where she worked now, or whether she still hated getting caught in the rain. Iona had come in person to ask for a thing Vera could do.

"I'll tell them to cut your parts," Vera said.

Iona waited.

Vera opened the case and saw the handwritten label again. Without Iona's directions, the pauses between Vera's attempts were only silence. Without Iona singing the line beside her, Vera's laughter had no source. The recording could be shortened, but the girl Vera wanted to show the world had not been alone in that room.

"I won't play it," she said. "I won't put out the anniversary edition."

Iona took a breath. "Thank you."

Nothing in the room changed colour.

The floor director knocked and put his head around the door. "Five minutes. Playback's standing by."

"Strike the tape," Vera told him.

"The kitchen tape?"

"Yes. And cancel the anniversary edition. I'll speak to the label after the show."

He looked from Vera to Iona, then back at his clipboard. "We announced the uncut tape in the first segment. What do you want in that slot?"

The answer she wanted was on the cassette. She could feel its small weight in her hand. "Leave it empty for now."

"It can't stay empty," he said.

"I know."

He went away to find a minute of something else. Vera heard him speaking rapidly into his headset as he crossed the set. The yellow cup came off the table. Someone carried the player away by its handle, its loose cord dragging behind it. Through the window, the woman and boy were gone, and other people had taken their place on the square.

"You can keep the tape," Iona said. "I don't need it."

Vera snapped the case shut. She had expected Iona to ask for it, and had been ready to give it up. Keeping it was less simple. "I thought you might want a copy without me singing on it."

"Then it would be mostly kettle."

Vera laughed once. Iona's mouth moved, almost in answer, but the floor director called Vera's name before either of them said more.

Iona went out by the side door. Vera did not follow her. From the stage, she watched an assistant wheel the little radio away, leaving a bare patch on the table where the tape player had stood. The host turned the missing recording into a sentence about the surprises of live television. Three minutes of old interview clips filled its place. Vera sat and watched herself tell familiar stories with a face that knew when to smile. In the last clip she said, "My sister Iona made me. Everything good started with her."

The screen went dark. The boy from the stage door sat in the second row, his schoolbag tucked under his feet. He looked past Vera at the empty worktable. She had told him he would hear the girl on the tape.

"You've always said such lovely things about your sister," the host said. He turned his chair toward Vera and waited for the next one.

"I kept saying she made me," Vera said. The camera was close enough for her to see its red light. "That wasn't mine to say. I promised the rest of that tape. I shouldn't have."

The host looked down at his cards. In her ear, someone counted the seconds until the song. Vera could have filled them with the old story or with the recording she had wanted to share. Instead the camera held on her while she had nothing more to give it. The music began without a recorded count-in. Several mouths in the front row made the shape of Iona's four words. Vera entered on her own first note.

Afterward, people waited outside under her heart. There were fans with their phones held high, and strangers who had simply stopped to watch the colours travel across the clouds. Vera stood a moment inside the doorway before the guard cleared a path. She could pick out where Iona's yellow lay, far up in the crowded light. She did not know whether Iona had stayed to hear the song, or had ridden home through it. Her phone was in her hand. She typed, *Did you get home dry?* and sent it. No answer came while she waited.

She put the phone away and went out. Light from the heart lay across the wet pavement in a dozen colours. Vera stepped into it; the silver thread came with her.

stories.title: After the Party
stories.prompt: The adventurers' guild needs to update its safety regulations. Not for the sake of the adventurers' safety, but because ...
stories.body:
# After the Party

For the first seventeen minutes, the recording agreed with the report.

Kell's party entered the Hall of Teeth in good order. A palm-sized camera of black glass was clipped to the front of his shield. A blue rune glowed as it stored half an hour of silent images in a removable memory crystal. It showed the hall, the three figures who rushed them with blades, the flash of Kell's smoke charge. It showed Davin falling. As the party retreated, a blade caught its clip. The camera struck the floor facing back down the hall.

The report ended there. The camera kept recording.

Irel paused the recording. Sixty guild members sat in the meeting room, their faces turned toward the pale light of the guild’s viewing glass. Beside Irel, Guildmaster Harrow gripped the back of an empty chair.

"Davin was your brother," he said quietly. "You don't have to do this."

"I know what happens next." Irel touched the viewing glass. The images moved again.

The party's boots disappeared from the frame. Smoke held in the corridor. For nearly a minute, nothing moved except its slow drift toward the camera. Someone in the second row coughed.

A low door opened in the wall the party had passed. One of the hall's inhabitants came out on hands and knees, dragging a smaller figure by its clothing. Another followed with a blanket over its head. They went back through the door, and more came out: some upright, some carried. They had hidden there while the party fought the three with blades. The smoke had reached them anyway.

Irel had watched this part six times. She still looked for the small one with the striped sleeve. A larger inhabitant lifted it, held its face close, then laid it down and folded the sleeve over its still hand. The larger one sat beside it until two others came to help move the bodies.

A boot entered the frame. Davin's. He lay just beyond the camera's view, where Irel could see only the sole she had mended last winter. The inhabitant who had stabbed him came forward with one arm hanging uselessly. It knelt, pulled Davin's cloak over his face, and stayed long enough to make sure it would not blow away.

Irel paused the recording before its last image.

"He still killed him," said Kell from the table's far end. His cheek bore a pale seam from the same fight.

"Yes," Irel said.

She had wanted Kell to say it. She did not want Davin made innocent by turning his killer into a saint, or his killer made a beast because Davin was dead.

Harrow looked around the room. "What was behind that door?"

"We thought it was stone," Kell said. "The three came at us. We threw smoke so they couldn't come through the hall together."

"The smoke is in the guild manual," someone said. "It keeps a party alive in a narrow passage."

"It did," Irel said. "And it went under the door."

A few chairs shifted. Nobody disputed what the camera had shown. Several disputed what it meant. Perhaps the hidden ones were young fighters. Perhaps the blanket concealed weapons. Perhaps the one with the striped sleeve had been sick already. Irel had made each argument herself in the first hour after she found the recording. None changed the smoke entering that room.

The guild had bought twelve cameras at spring's end to settle arguments about kills and reward shares. A collection party recovered Kell's with Davin's body the next morning; by then the corridor was empty. Irel played the entire crystal because she wanted to know whether his companions had come back for him. When she asked the chapters for every recording that had kept running after an expedition left the frame, they sent five more. In each case, the expedition had been paid before anyone watched the end.

She slid a second memory crystal into the viewing glass.

A chamber of red stone appeared. An adventurer held a trophy horn up to the lens, grinning. The party departed. When the last torch vanished, the chamber's inhabitants came from cracks too small for the adventurers to have noticed. They bound a wounded one's leg with strips torn from their own bedding. A third recording, which Irel had watched that morning, showed people at the foot of a stair carrying smaller bodies away from a collapsed barricade. They were not the same kind of people as those in the Hall of Teeth. Irel could not tell what any of them called themselves.

"How many?" Harrow asked.

"Five recordings show survivors. Four are from rooms we reported as cleared. Four show people who never held a weapon on the recording."

"And the sixth?"

"The lens broke."

Across the table the contracts steward shut his account book. "Survivors don't prove they won't attack the next party."

"No," Irel said. "They prove we don't know what we're clearing."

Harrow rubbed the bridge of his nose. Above him hung Davin's sword. The guild had put it there after his funeral, before Irel had seen the recording. He had died trying to pull Kell back out of the smoke. That part of the report was true as well.

"There are three clearance contracts leaving tonight," the steward said. "The deposits are paid. One village has been waiting all winter for the road through the lower vault to open."

"They may have real dangers below them," Kell said. He pointed at the frozen image of the red chamber. "Those three at Teeth didn't ask us to leave. They came at us. If you make my people stand in a doorway and take a blade while they decide whether the next room is a nursery, I'll bring you more dead members."

Irel turned toward him. "Then don't enter the next room. Get clear. Watch it. Speak if you can. Defend yourselves if you're attacked. But don't put smoke through a wall because the people on the other side might have knives."

"And if they won't speak?"

"Then we still don't know."

That answer displeased nearly everyone. Irel was glad of it. For years the guild had treated not knowing as permission to write *cleared*.

Harrow reached for the manual on the table. The section marked **Party Safety** opened beneath his hand: smoke first in a narrow chamber; collect trophies as proof; count a site clear when armed resistance ends. Each rule had kept a sword-bearer from walking blind into danger. Each rule had also permitted the guild to stop looking when the sword-bearers left.

He took a pen. The steward said, "You can't cancel three contracts on a recording."

"I can hold them," Harrow said. "The deposits can be returned. The road can stay closed another month."

He wrote slowly enough that Irel could see where his hand hesitated. No use of smoke, fire, or collapse against anyone not attacking, or in any unexamined space. No tally of a clearance based only on the departure of an armed party. No bounty approved until every recording had been watched to the end. Defense against attack remained permitted. New contracts waited for a way to approach inhabitants without making them prove their innocence under a blade.

It was an emergency order, not a peace treaty. Nothing in it told Kell how to speak across an unknown language, or brought the striped sleeve back to its wearer. Irel watched Harrow sign anyway.

The second recording had reached its last moments. On the wall, a small red-stone inhabitant noticed the abandoned lens. It came close enough that its face filled the frame. It looked at the machine for a moment, then drew a piece of bedding over it. The wall went dark. A blue mark in its corner kept counting seconds.

Harrow gave the signed order to a runner. Two of the three parties had not yet passed the city gate. The third was already on the road.

Irel took her coat from the chair.

"Where are you going?" Kell asked.

"The east road," she said. "I issued that party a camera."

"A runner can catch them."

"The runner can give them the order. I can tell them what happened after we left."

She went out beneath Davin's sword. Behind her, the blue counter kept moving through the dark while the guild began arguing over which words in the new regulations would be hardest to obey.

stories.title: The Closed Day
stories.prompt: The Imperial Guard does not exist to protect the Emperor from assassins. The Imperial Guard exists to protect would-be assassins from the Emperor’s wrath.
stories.body:
# The Closed Day

Orsen caught the knife at the Emperor's throat. The blade went through his palm and stopped against the bone.

The woman drove forward anyway. He put his weight on her, and they fell among the petitions scattered over the white floor. Around them, the Imperial Guard drew their swords and turned toward the throne.

Someone in the audience screamed. Someone else began to applaud, then stopped.

The Emperor stood beside his overturned chair. A shallow cut crossed his neck, just under the jaw. He touched it, looked at the blood on his fingers, and said, “Show me her face.”

Orsen had pulled a custody hood from his belt and covered the woman's face once she was down. She fought beneath it, breathing hard. He kept his wounded hand around her wrist and raised the other.

“A closed day, Majesty.”

The Emperor looked past the ring of swords to him. “I didn't sentence her.”

“No, Majesty. A face will give you her family.”

“Then show me.”

There were fourteen guards in the chamber. They had all trained for this. When a weapon came out, they subdued its bearer; when the Emperor spoke, they made a wall of themselves. Orsen could see which of the younger ones were still deciding whether the wall faced the correct way.

Calen stood at his left shoulder. She had helped him take the north weaving street three years ago. Her sword pointed at the dais with all the others.

“Not until she's beyond this room,” Orsen said.

The Emperor wiped his fingers on a petition and let it fall. “Take her to the inner cell. Find out who sent her. Start with her family.”

The woman went still under the hood.

The Guard's charter gave them custody of a captured attacker until sunset. They had to bring that person, alive, with a written charge to the city magistrate. Three years earlier, another attacker had made that journey safely. His cousins had not. Neither had the men who rented rooms beside his, nor the boy who delivered their bread. Orsen had signed the list because the charter protected the attacker, and the Emperor's command named everyone else. He had told himself the distinction mattered. Calen had asked why the others got no day. He had told her to read the charter. He had carried the list from door to door while the man waited in the magistrate's cell.

“The prisoner first,” Orsen said. He heard his own voice flatten into the tone he used on parade. “Pel, with me.”

Pel was the newest guard in the chamber. He lowered his sword, then glanced at the Emperor. Orsen could not blame him for looking.

“Go,” the Emperor said. “We have all day.”

Orsen kept the woman ahead of him through the side door. Pel followed. In the passage, the shouts from the chamber gave way to the small sounds of their equipment: leather shifting, Orsen's blood falling from his hand onto the tiles. The inner cell was twelve paces away. A lock and two guards would keep her alive until it was time to take her to the magistrate. Orsen had already begun counting those paces. Pel caught his hand and bound it with a strip torn from his own collar. Then the woman spoke from under the hood.

“Don't put me in there.”

“You tried to kill him.”

“I know.”

“This is where we keep you alive.”

“And where do you keep my sister?”

Orsen stopped. Pel, behind them, made the slight movement of a man who wished he had been sent elsewhere.

“He doesn't know who you are,” Orsen said.

“He will.”

He pulled the hood back from her face. She was older than he'd thought on the floor, perhaps thirty, with gray caught in the hair at her temples. She looked at his injured hand, then at his face.

“Iria Keld,” she said. “My brother was Tovin Keld.”

Orsen knew the name. Not from the execution roll, which had held thirty-two names, but from a young woman outside a weaving shed clutching a length of blue cloth. She had said her brother could not have known the attacker. He had been at his loom all morning. A younger sister had pressed a warm loaf into his hands before the guards tied them. Orsen had let him keep it, as if that were mercy. He had said the order was for a street, not for accomplices. Then he had told his men to take the young man.

Iria reached into her sleeve. Pel's sword came up. She held out a folded square of paper, stained at one edge with old rain. Orsen recognized the heading before she opened it. The notices had been posted on every door of that street: *all persons of the north weaving street to be seized for examination*. His mark was at the bottom of each one.

“I showed you this when you came for him,” she said. “It says *all persons*. He hadn't done anything.”

“I had the order.”

“That's what you said then.”

He had read the word *all* and taken it as permission to stop asking what any of them had done.

From the audience chamber came the Emperor's voice, asking for a clean collar. Then another voice, lower, repeated the order to find the woman's family. There would be clerks in the chamber writing the words down. There would be a rider at the gate soon after.

Orsen put the hood back over Iria's face. “Your sister. Where is she?”

“Dessa's at the west bakehouse. I told her I came to petition for Tovin's name to be cleared.”

“That won't be far enough.”

“I know.” She gripped the folded notice. “Bring me to the recorder.”

“He'll hear your name.”

“They'll find it in an hour. I want him to hear yours first.”

Orsen sent Pel to the west gate to carry a warning to Dessa. He came back out of breath. “They barred it at the alarm. The household officer won't let me through without a sealed order.”

“We can take you out under the charter now,” Orsen told Iria. “I can send him from the street.”

“I want him to hear you say what you did to Tovin.” She held up his old notice. “Let his recorder write it beside my name.”

“You won't be safe in there,” he said.

“You've told me where I'm safe.” She looked at the cell. “I'm telling you where I'm going.”

They returned to the audience chamber by the side door. The Emperor had changed his collar. He sat again, though the petitions were still scattered and nobody had resumed the audience. A court recorder sat at the narrow table beneath the windows, trying to write around a patch of blood on the day's roll.

The guard ring opened for Orsen and closed behind him. He kept Iria beside him, hood over her head. The Emperor saw the paper in her hand.

“You have the names?”

“She has a charge to make,” Orsen said.

“She had a knife to make it with.”

“She still has a charge.”

The recorder's pen hovered. The Emperor noticed. “Set it down.”

The pen stopped.

Iria pulled the hood off and dropped it among the petitions. Orsen caught at it too late. He did not cover her again.

“I am Iria Keld,” she said. Her voice was rough from the struggle but reached the back of the room. “I tried to kill you. Three years ago you ordered my brother taken because a man he did not know tried to kill you. Captain Orsen signed the order and took him.”

The Emperor's hand tightened on the arm of his chair. “Keld. A weaver's family.”

He sent a household clerk through the side door for the north street register.

Orsen felt Iria beside him, held still by the Emperor's recognition. The name had bought her a record if the recorder would write it. It had also given the Emperor a way to reach her sister.

“Write what she said,” Orsen told the recorder.

The man looked at the Emperor. He had written the Emperor's words for twenty years; Orsen had often seen him rub his cramped fingers at the end of an audience. Now his hand lay open on the page.

“Write it,” said Iria. “Write that I came here to kill him. Then write what Captain Orsen did.”

The Emperor rose. The nearest guards shifted, not toward Iria but toward him.

“That paper won't leave this room,” he said. “Recorder, tear off the page.”

The recorder took hold of the roll. His fingers shook. Orsen stepped between the table and the throne.

“Majesty. On a closed day, the attacker's account is taken before judgment.”

“You have kept her breathing. You have had your day.”

“The day has scarcely begun.”

“Tear it off,” the Emperor told the recorder.

Orsen could have argued about custom. He had been good at that three years ago. Instead he laid his uninjured hand over the recorder's and felt the man let go.

“I signed that seizure,” Orsen said. “I took Tovin Keld from his work. His sister told me he had no part in the first attack. I answered that the order did not require him to have a part.” He looked at the recorder. “Put my words beside hers.”

The pen moved. It sounded loud against the paper. Iria watched it, unsmiling.

“And this morning?” the Emperor asked.

Orsen had once stood close enough to the Emperor to fasten his armor before a campaign. He knew the small white scar over his eyebrow, the tremor that came into his left hand when he was tired. None of those familiar things made the order less plain.

“This morning I refused your command to expose her,” Orsen said. “I refuse your command to destroy her account.”

The Emperor looked at the guards. “Take his badge.”

Pel moved first. Orsen thought, for one bare instant, that the boy meant to arrest him. Pel stopped at his shoulder and unfastened the silver clasp at his throat, lifting the cloak clear of Orsen's bound hand. A captain's badge was sewn into its collar; the two came off together.

The Emperor held out a hand for it. Pel kept the cloak folded over his arm.

“Now,” the Emperor said to the others, “take the woman.”

Calen took one step toward Iria. Orsen saw the others turn to her; with him dismissed, she was the senior guard. The recorder bent over the page, blotting one line, waiting to learn whether he would have to blot the rest.

Iria placed the notice she held beside the roll. The clerk returned with a narrow register and opened it to the Keld household. The Emperor looked at a line entered in newer ink, then at her.

“Your sister works at the west bakehouse,” he said. “Did she help you?”

Iria had chosen to give her name. She could not take it back, or make the Emperor forget who had lived on that street. She looked at the recorder. “Write what he asked.”

The Emperor glanced at the pen. “You think a page will stop my men?”

“No,” she said. “I thought a knife would stop you.”

Orsen looked at Calen. “Do you remember the order?”

“Yes.”

“Do you remember who signed it?”

“Yes.” She lowered her sword. She did not look relieved. “The Guard has custody until sunset. Pel, take the roll. We're bringing her to the magistrate.”

The Emperor stepped down from the dais. Orsen stood without cloak or badge between him and Iria, his injured hand hanging uselessly at his side.

Pel went to the table. The recorder took his hand off the page, ready for it to be torn. Pel lifted the whole bound roll instead. His voice cracked as he told the recorder, “Come with us. You'll have to attest to it.”

“You can be dismissed with him,” the Emperor told Calen.

She hesitated. Orsen knew what dismissal would mean: the quarters lost, a pension gone, the cold walk through streets where a guard without a cloak was just a person who had carried out the Emperor's orders. He had imagined that walk often and had always turned back.

Calen said, “I took the street with him. My account goes on the roll too.”

The Emperor pointed at Iria. “You'll give me her. The charter won't keep her sister out of my hands.”

Iria gripped the edge of the recorder's table. She had chosen this route knowing what her name would cost, but Orsen saw her struggle to stay beside the paper instead of running toward the west bakehouse.

The Emperor called for a household runner. Orsen heard him order the west gate held against the Guard's charge. He gave a second order in a voice too low for Orsen to catch, and the runner left with two strips of sealed paper, one tied in blue cord and one in red.

Calen took Iria by the arm, firmly enough to keep custody and gently enough that Iria went with her. Orsen followed without cloak or badge. Pel held the roll against his chest, and the recorder came behind them with Iria's old notice. Two guards followed with swords out. At the passage door, Calen turned them toward the throne before they backed away.

The iron leaves of the west gate were barred again. A household officer stood in front of them with a strip of blue cord hanging from his fist. Beyond the bars, the rider with the red cord mounted his horse. The officer had let him through under seal, then lowered the bar once more. Iria saw him turn toward the bakehouse and pulled against Calen's hand.

“The Emperor ordered me to keep your prisoner inside,” the officer told Calen.

“The charter orders us to deliver her,” Calen said. “Move.”

He showed her the seal. Orsen remembered taking a posted notice to a weaving shed, certain the seal made the words beneath it right. Calen took the paper and read the gate order anyway. She handed it to Pel to take to the magistrate.

“If you pass,” the officer said, “I have to stop you.”

Calen set Iria's hand in Orsen's sound one. “I know.” Iria looked through the bars after the rider.

Calen stepped up to the bar. The officer drew his sword. The two guards behind her stepped to either side, their swords raised. Pel gave both the roll and the gate order to the recorder, then helped Calen lift. Wood scraped stone. Calen set the bar against the wall and pulled one iron leaf open. The officer looked from her to the two guards facing him. He lowered his sword and stood aside. Pel took back the roll; the recorder kept the gate order with Iria's notice.

Orsen passed beside Iria, keeping himself between her and the officer's sword. Beyond the gate, the road to the bakehouse ran left; the open court lay across the square to their right. The rider had vanished to the left. Orsen opened his hand. Iria stood between the roads, then turned right. None of them had a horse.

They reached the magistrate's table in the open court just before noon. The table stood at the edge of the square, in sight of the west gate. The magistrate did not ask Orsen for his badge. The recorder gave her the gate order, with its blue cord still attached, and placed Iria's notice beside it. Calen added her own account beneath Orsen's: she had held Iria back while he took Tovin from the weaving shed. Orsen signed with his uninjured hand, and Calen signed below him. Then the magistrate asked Iria whether she still claimed the words written there.

“I tried to kill him,” Iria said. “I claim the rest.”

The magistrate asked Pel to read the account aloud, while her clerk made a second copy under the eyes of the people waiting with their ordinary quarrels. She signed for custody. Iria would be tried; the order to take her brother was now entered beside the charge against her. Pel left one copy on the public table and carried another across the square to the city archive. He walked quickly, with no armor at his back. Calen stood beside Iria while the constables took her into custody.

The rider came back across the square on foot, leading his horse. A woman walked beside him with her wrists tied in front of her. There was flour on her sleeves. Orsen recognized the younger sister who had put bread into Tovin's hands.

Iria left the table. Two city constables stopped her at the edge of the court, close enough for Dessa to hear her call. The rider kept walking.

Dessa turned. “You said you were going to petition.”

“I lied,” Iria said.

The rider led her on toward the gate. Iria faced the magistrate. “Her name is Dessa Keld. She knew nothing about my knife. Put down that he took her.”

The magistrate told her clerk to write it. She made no order to release Dessa; the rider was already passing through the gate. Iria looked at Calen, who still wore her guard's badge.

“Follow her,” Iria said. “Tell me where they keep her.”

Calen touched the badge at her collar. Then she went after Dessa. Iria watched until Calen passed under the gate and out of sight.

stories.title: The Sun in the Crowd
stories.prompt: You were born with a Sprite Eye, an eye that sees the tiny spark of magic hidden inside every living person. Most are faint, barely more than embers—but today, in the middle of a crowded street, you see someone burning like a sun.
stories.body:
# The Sun in the Crowd

The woman buying the last portrait of the evening wanted me to make her son look less tired. He had worked a double shift and was asleep against her shoulder. If I lifted his chin, she said, and opened his eyes a little, he would look like himself again.

"I can lift his chin," I said. "If I draw his eyes open, I'll have to make them up."

She paid me anyway. While I rolled the sheet into a tube, the boy woke and asked whether his ears were really that big. His mother told him to come back tomorrow and complain to the artist. They went off laughing, with the drawn boy tucked safely under her arm.

I should have put my lamp out then. The market was still thick with people, but shoppers had become walkers; nobody wanted to sit while the evening's musicians found their places. I tied the corners of my canvas portfolio and reached for the lamp. Between two passing shoulders, something opened in the street.

My Sprite Eye, the left one, had shown me the little fires inside people since before I had words for either fire or people. On a busy night I saw them everywhere: a smudge under a vendor's collar, a pinhead of orange in a child's chest, blue embers moving past one another in the dark. When a sitter's expression eluded me, I sometimes let a spark decide the shadow beneath a mouth. At the back of my portfolio I kept sketches of the lights without their owners' faces. Close the eye, and there were only faces. Open it, and the sparks came back, visible to me through shirts and coats but never through a body standing in the way.

This was different. A gold-white center blazed through a gap in the tide of heads, with pink and violet at its edge. It flared as the gap widened, then disappeared behind the awning of a spice seller's cart. For an instant I thought someone had carried a lantern into the street. Then the same light reappeared farther on, keeping pace with a pale-haired woman in a dark coat.

I left my charcoal beside the unfinished stack of paper and went after her.

The street narrowed between stalls of oranges and printed cloth. I had to turn sideways to pass a man shouldering a crate. When I straightened, the woman was gone. My left eye picked her out a few strides ahead; my right saw only a sleeve, a braid of pale hair, then the back of someone's hat. I followed that moving interruption, my portfolio knocking against my hip.

At the next crossing, I lost her behind a tall family carrying paper masks. I climbed onto the rim of an empty planter for a better view. The stone was slick from crushed fruit. My foot slid; I caught the branch of a little tree, shook leaves into a vendor's trays, apologized, and jumped down. By then the light had moved toward the performance square. I ran the last few steps and found her waiting for a handcart to clear the corner.

"Excuse me," I said, more loudly than I meant to.

She turned. The left eye gave me a painful white stroke across her face. I shut it. She was older than I'd thought from behind, perhaps thirty, with one eyebrow notched near the end and a faint crease running from her nose toward her mouth on one side more than the other. The coat was plain and carefully mended at a cuff. My first surprise was that she looked so definite. The blaze had offered me no idea what sort of nose she had.

"Were you following me?" she asked.

I could have lied and said I'd recognized her from a sitting. The closed eye was twitching to open. "Yes. I'm sorry. I'm a portraitist. My stall's just back there."

"I'm late."

"Ten minutes. I can do a quick likeness."

The handcart passed. She could have gone around me with it. Instead she glanced at the portfolio and then at my empty hands. "You stopped me to sell me a portrait?"

It sounded worse aloud. "To ask. You don't have to."

"I know that." She stepped to the side so people could pass between us and the cart. "Have you got one I can see?"

I opened the portfolio at the first page, a charcoal head of a woman with a wide jaw and a knowing tilt to her mouth. The sitter had chosen the tilt. The pale-haired woman studied the paper without touching it. I turned two more pages: a stern baker, a girl holding her own ears back so I could draw them. She laughed at that one.

"She asked for that," I said.

"I believe you. Can you make me look like me?"

"That's usually the arrangement."

"Usually is a slippery word." She looked up the street. A drum was being tested in the square, a single hollow note at a time. "I'm on after the musicians. I can stay until they finish. How much for one I take with me?"

I named my ordinary price. She named a little less for so little time. I said yes, already lifting the portfolio strap over my shoulder.

"And I see it before I pay," she said.

"Of course."

"Auvet." She offered the name, then turned back toward my stall. I had neglected to offer mine.

"Mial," I said. "This way."

She walked fast enough that I had to shorten the strap and keep up. Twice she stopped to let other people squeeze past. Each time the light in my left eye seemed to stay with her, not spill into the bodies that crossed in front. I closed that eye again and watched her make room for a child carrying three wooden hoops. He didn't thank her. She didn't seem to expect it.

At the stall I pulled my folding chair from under the table and set it where the oil lamp gave a warm, steady wash across a sitter's face. Auvet sat, then moved the chair half a handspan to her left.

"I can see you better over there," I said.

"There's a draft over there."

The corner of the canvas roof breathed in and out above her. I put a folded cloth under the chair's short leg so it stopped rocking. She set a small wrapped bundle on her lap, the sort a musician might carry, and turned the mended cuff under. In the right eye she was a woman trying to hold still despite a foot already pointed toward the square. In the left she was nearly impossible to look at.

I chose the largest sheet I had. That should have warned me. For a paid street portrait, the smaller pages were easier to hold and less likely to crease on the way home. But the light around her seemed to need room. I marked the top of her head, the slope of a shoulder, the place where the blaze ran pink against the dark beyond her. My charcoal went fast. I had only a few minutes, and the first lines always made a promise I hoped the later ones would keep.

"Do I have to keep my mouth shut?" Auvet asked.

"Only if you usually do."

"Then your picture's already wrong."

I smiled without looking up. Her cheek kept disappearing inside that white center. I put it where I thought it belonged. A man came to ask whether I was still taking sitters; I told him I was closing. He leaned across my table to admire the page, blocking Auvet from me. When he moved, I drew from what I remembered. I made the shadows under her jaw darker to set off the light.

"What's that?" she asked.

"The first pass."

"May I?"

I held the sheet by its clean corners. She rose and came around the table. For a moment she didn't speak. Her thumb hovered over the paper, careful not to rub the charcoal.

"You've given me an enormous head," she said.

"It's the light. I can pull it back."

"It isn't just that." She pointed to the brow. "This eye is higher. My nose doesn't turn that way. And what am I standing in?"

The charcoal was heaviest around her face, like a curtain of smoke lit from behind. Even to my right eye, it had a kind of force. Her face, on its own, could have been anyone's. "I rushed it. Let me fix the features."

"You keep looking here." She touched the air an inch beyond her own cheek. "Then your hand moves as if my face were over there too. What are you seeing?"

I had talked about my eye to friends, never to a customer halfway through a bad sitting. "I see a little light inside every living person, with this eye." I tapped the left side of my face. "Yours is very bright. That's why I stopped you."

Her attention went from my eye to the portrait. "And this is what you saw."

"Some of it. I don't know what it means." That last part mattered enough to say before she asked. "It doesn't tell me who you are. I can't tell what you can do with it."

"But you wanted a picture of it."

"Yes."

She looked at the sheet once more. A pair of sisters going by stopped to look as well. One said the portrait was beautiful. Auvet held it against the table, out of their view, and waited until they walked on.

"You can keep this one," she said. "It isn't what I came back for."

I laid the sheet face down. "I can start again. I'll use the smaller paper, and I won't charge you if I miss it."

The drum made two notes in succession. Auvet turned her head toward the square. She had every reason to take up her bundle and go. Instead she settled into the chair again, her boots planted beneath her.

"How long?"

"Until the musicians finish, if they'll give us that long."

"Then be quick." She drew a breath, looked at me, and saw that I had reached for the charcoal without closing the left eye. "Can you stop seeing it?"

"Yes." I shut the eye. The inner fire vanished, and my view narrowed. From here I could still work. I had done it as a child whenever a crowded room became too much, though I disliked the small strain of holding the lid down. I tore a narrow strip from the edge of my rag and tied it over the eye, under my hair.

Auvet's mouth moved at one corner. "Is that comfortable?"

"Not much. I'll manage."

I steadied a fresh page on the board. The lamp picked out the shallow line beside her mouth and threw the other cheek into shadow. Auvet tipped her chin away from it.

"Back a little," I said. "Toward me."

She obeyed, then looked at the bundle on her lap as though checking it was still there. The change in her expression made her upper lip almost disappear. I put down the long angle of the nose and the plane of her forehead. Ordinary contours stayed where I saw them, so long as I kept my attention on them. My hand wanted to smooth the asymmetry at her mouth. I stopped it.

Someone tugged the back of my coat. The boy from the last portrait had come back without his mother at his side to ask if I could make his ears smaller after all. She stood at the orange stall behind him, holding the rolled paper. I told him I could make another portrait tomorrow, but I couldn't alter the one she had taken without her permission. He considered this and went back to her.

When I turned, Auvet had slipped her bundle under the chair and was watching the boy. I had missed the change of pose. "Your arm," I said. "Could you put it back?"

"Which way was it?"

I showed her with my own. She copied it, badly. We tried once more and both laughed. The small mistake eased the tightness in my fingers. I marked the bend of the sleeve as it was now and worked toward her hand.

"What do you do?"

She looked at the charcoal on my fingers. "A kind of drawing. I can't take it home afterward."

I let that sit. I didn't want to force her into showing me something she had not offered, and the question had already cost a line at her wrist. Then she held up her hand where I could see it over the board.

"Would it help to watch?"

"If you want me to."

A thread of red appeared between her finger and thumb. She pulled it through the air as if drawing silk from a spool. Blue and green followed it; under her moving fingertips the threads bent into the shape of a tiny horse, jointed legs poised without a surface beneath them. Its colors touched the table and lit my charcoal sticks. A child passing the stall cried out and reached through the horse's flank. Her hand met empty air. The horse took three steps across the air, climbed nothing, and disappeared when Auvet lowered her fingers.

The child protested. Auvet gave her a small bow. "More in the square."

She wasn't speaking to me. I had opened the covered eye without noticing, pushing the rag aside with my brow. Auvet's inner light came at me all at once, much stronger than the little horse had looked to anyone else. I couldn't say whether the two sights had any relation. I only knew that my own marks on the paper disappeared in the glare. I drew the rag back into place.

"It walked," I said.

"Only three steps." She held up the fingers she'd used, checking a charcoal smudge left when she had touched my table. "I'm still learning the legs."

I glanced at the tabletop below where the horse had walked. There was no mark on the wood. "Could you make one hold still long enough for me to copy?"

"I tried. It goes when I stop." Auvet turned her hand palm up, then let it rest on her knee. "Can you draw from that?"

"From memory, perhaps. But I need your face first."

"Then hurry."

The music in the square had become a pattern rather than a test, with a flute taking up the space between drumbeats. I moved the board so the lamp shone across the paper instead of into my right eye. Auvet leaned forward to inspect a few lines. I asked her to sit back; she did, but she reached across and indicated the end of the eyebrow with one finger.

"There. You missed the gap."

"I see it."

"You didn't the first time."

I cut the notch into the dark line. She watched, then nodded. We worked that way for the next minute. She told me the lower edge of her coat was frayed, not embroidered. I had mistaken a loose thread in the lamplight. She said the left side of her hair was shorter because she'd cut it in a hurry, and no, she did not want it evened out on paper. She could be still only until the flute reached the familiar rising phrase; then one foot started moving under the chair. I drew it as far as the page allowed.

Auvet broke the end off a charcoal stick as she tried to turn it between her fingers. "Sorry."

"That's the short piece. I use it for darks."

"You're welcome, then." She set both pieces down. "May I see?"

I held the board so she could look without standing. Her face on the page was smaller than in the first drawing. The nose turned as it did when she faced me, the eyelid on the lamp side lowered a little, the mouth almost forming a word. The coat showed its worn cuff, not the shining folds I'd invented around the first figure. I had put more care into the gap in her eyebrow than into any surrounding shadow.

She looked at it for a long time, considering the paper at several angles. "My chin is sharper than that."

"A little." I made the correction while she held the pose.

"And that mark beside my mouth goes all the way to the corner when I smile."

"You're not smiling."

"I will be, when I see the person this is for. If you can catch a little of it."

I asked her to smile so I could see it. She obliged too broadly. We both knew it, and it fell away. The line remained for a breath. I marked its course, then rubbed the end gently with a clean thumb so it belonged to the face in front of me.

"Better," she said. "What's this space?" She pointed to the blank beside her hand.

"I meant to ask." I pulled the rag clear of my left eye to look at her, not at the page. The gold-white center crowded back into view. "Do you want any of what I see in the drawing? I have chalk."

She studied the empty space. "If it's all around my head, no. The person getting this has heard me describe the show often enough, but hasn't seen it. Could you put the horse there? In my hand?"

"A small one. You made it above the table, though."

"Put my hand higher, then. It was there for a moment." She raised it to the height where the horse had walked. "I won't ask you to invent the legs. You've seen how bad mine are."

I steadied the second portrait on the board and moved her drawn arm, only a little; the old line disappeared under the heel of my hand, leaving a grey seam in the sleeve. Auvet checked it before I continued. With the right eye I could remember the horse's red spine, its blue belly, the green steps that had fallen through air. I laid three short chalk strokes over the charcoal, then added a fourth where its foreleg should have bent. In the page it rested just above her fingers. It wasn't a likeness of the bright center I saw with my left eye. It was something she had made while I watched, and she had chosen its place.

"It needs the back leg," she said.

"I only saw three."

"Fair." She took the board and angled it toward the lamp. The little shape caught the light before the rest of the drawing did. "The face is right now."

The flute stopped; applause came from the square. Auvet rose, tucking the bundle under her arm, and reached for her purse. She paid the price we'd agreed on, plus the small difference between her offer and mine. When I held the extra coin out, she closed my fingers around it.

"For the second sheet," she said.

"The first was my mistake."

"Then for the chalk."

I tucked the coin into the tin. She looked once more at the notch in the eyebrow and touched the paper below it, where no mark could smudge. Then I slipped a clean sheet over the portrait so the chalk wouldn't brush against her sleeve and rolled both pages into a tube.

"Is it dry?" she asked.

"The chalk may still come off if you rub it. Hold the tube by the ends."

She did. The applause was thinning. Auvet backed into the moving people, gave me a quick nod, and turned toward the square. I could see her pale hair for three steps. My left eye found the flare twice more between passing bodies, then a high-sided delivery cart crossed the street and hid her completely.

The first drawing lay face down where I'd left it. I picked it up by the corners. The paper still held my thumbprint at the edge of the great bright head. I put it under the board before the night air could lift it away. From the square came the sharp slap of a drum, then a ripple of voices answering something I couldn't see.

stories.title: The Place Laid for Her
stories.prompt: "No weapons allowed in this establishment, ma'am." "My consciousness is in the sword, the humanoid body you're looking at is a glamoured mannequin I'm puppeting."
stories.body:
# The Place Laid for Her

“No weapons allowed in this establishment, ma'am.”

“My consciousness is in the sword, the humanoid body you're looking at is a glamoured mannequin I'm puppeting.”

The host of the Ousel Room looked down at the sword, then up at the woman holding it. Ildesse had given the mannequin dark eyes, a long nose, and a mouth that looked well in repose. At present the mouth was doing a smile she had rehearsed for somebody else.

“Would you be willing to have the scabbard tied shut?” he asked.

“Yes, certainly.”

He fetched a silk cord from beneath his desk. She held herself out horizontally in the mannequin's two hands while he wound it between the guard and the scabbard buckle. It was a very pretty scabbard, pale green leather tooled with leaves, selected to suit her dress rather than her blade. The dress was copper silk. Its skirt required a generous interpretation of doorways.

“And the reservation?” he asked the pommel.

“Ildesse.” Her voice came, as usual, from the mannequin. “It's still this end for conversation.”

“Of course. Two at eight. Your gentleman hasn't arrived.”

She had intended to arrive three minutes after Brevot, giving him time to sit down and begin wondering whether the copper dress appearing between the curtains could possibly be for him. To accomplish this, she had come early to ascertain the arrangement of the room, meaning to withdraw afterward and come back once he was seated. The host was now tying a second knot. Above his head, the clock began striking eight.

“Not over the little cap, please.”

He moved the cord. The pommel's feeding cap had loosened in the carriage; with one wooden fingertip she pressed it home. Beneath it, a wet wick nourished the warm, pulsing thread that ran down through the tang into the blade. Her living flesh was narrow, delicate, well protected, and presently cross. The magic that moved her mannequin and dressed its plain head in features came from there. She could send that body six paces from herself, but not a seventh; the sword had no means of following. Being put in a cloakroom would have made an exceptionally short evening.

The host tested his knot, offered her the cord's two ends for inspection, and showed her in.

There was a banquette against the wall, a chair opposite it, candles, small glasses, folded napkins. Her flowers had arrived. The musician stood near the far curtain with his fiddle under his arm; he caught her eye and raised two fingers. Two pieces, as agreed, beginning with the first course. She acknowledged him with a small nod, the sort that looked discreet unless one was wearing three copper feathers in one's hair.

Forty-three years old, and she had spent most of the afternoon choosing those feathers. She would have done it again. In the long mirror beside the curtain, her skirt moved like an expensive liquid.

She was laying the sword along the banquette, behind the place where she meant to sit, when a man said, “Ildesse?”

Brevot had arrived without waiting for her entrance.

“Yes. Just a moment.”

The point of the scabbard was on her wrap. She lifted it, freed the wrap, and discovered that the mannequin's elbow had caught the flowers. Brevot steadied the vase. Now they were both holding things and looking at each other across an extraordinarily large white bouquet.

“Shall I put this somewhere?” he asked.

“In the middle. No, nearer the wall.”

He put it nearer the wall.

“There,” she said, and stood properly. “Good evening.”

“Good evening.” He smiled, and she was glad she had bought the feathers.

His portrait had been done by a friend who disliked noses, but otherwise it had prepared her. He was handsome in a worn, uneven way, with a broad mouth and gray beginning above his ears. Thirty-eight, he had written; vain about his hair and helpless before a well-turned ankle. She had been considering that last confession for eleven days.

“I nearly wore my other coat,” he said. “Then I remembered telling you how much I hated this one. I thought you might like to see what all the fuss was about.”

“The buttons do look distressed.”

“It's the left sleeve. Watch.”

He reached for his chair. The sleeve rode halfway up his forearm, and a bright inch of lining protruded from the cuff.

She laughed. His answering grin was immediate and unceremonious. There he was: the man who had sent her four pages about his landlord's campaign against pigeons and then, in the margin, admitted to feeding them.

They sat down.

“You look—” he began.

“The complete supper for two?” asked a server at his shoulder.

“Yes, please,” Ildesse said. “As I ordered.”

The server departed. Brevot looked at the unused plates before her, then toward the entrance.

“Are we expecting someone?”

“No.”

“I thought you couldn't eat.”

“I can't.”

He looked back at the plates.

“I ordered supper for two,” she said. “That is how they sell it.”

“Ah.”

The menu had described a procession of little dishes brought beneath silver covers. When reserving, she had pictured the lifting of those covers, the steam, his delighted surprise. She hadn't pictured having to account for the second quail.

“You needn't eat all of it.”

“I probably shall. I missed lunch.”

She had hoped for something less hungry, though she couldn't reasonably have said what. She arranged her hands on the table. He glanced at them, at the slim gloves with their pearl buttons. The mannequin could return touch as well as sight and hearing; if he put his hand over hers, she would feel it. His fingers were broad, with an ink stain just beneath one nail.

He reached into his coat.

“I brought you something.”

“Did you?”

A narrow parcel emerged, wrapped in blue paper. For the instant before he unfolded it, she let it be earrings.

“It's a poem,” he said.

She kept smiling while he opened it. “A new one?”

“Finished this morning. I wanted you to be the first to hear it.”

Four months ago she had sent a letter to the review in which his verse appeared, objecting to its editor's habit of cutting out the funny stanzas. Brevot had written back. Since then there had been books, arguments, the pigeons, accounts of parties they separately refused to attend. She had praised two of his poems extravagantly and found fault with the rest. He said hers were the only letters he opened before breakfast.

“It's for you,” he said.

This was better than earrings. Possibly. She folded her hands together to keep them from making any premature decision.

He took out three sheets, smoothed them, and moved the flowers an inch to the left.

“It's called ‘The Unsheathed Heart.’”

Behind her, silk cord held her firmly shut. She did not mention it.

Brevot began softly. His reading voice was lower than his speaking voice, and slower. She liked hearing him take care over something. In the first stanza a blade rested among lilies; in the second it remembered the men who had carried it; by the third, a battlefield had appeared. The grass of that battlefield was compared to young hair.

She tried to keep hold of the pleasure of being written for. He had worked on this at his desk, thinking of her. He had bought blue paper.

“Before the field remembers grass,” he read, “she dreams its brief red flowering—”

The server appeared at the far curtain with two covered bowls. The fiddle began immediately behind Brevot's left ear.

He flinched, lost his place, and turned. The musician smiled at Ildesse over the instrument. She had asked for the old air with the long rising phrase, the one in which a lover arrived beneath a window and insisted that being married to somebody else was no great impediment. Without its words it was perfectly respectable. With its words it was one of her favorites.

“Could you wait?” Brevot asked.

The musician stopped with his bow lifted.

“Just until I've finished,” Brevot added.

“I asked him to play,” Ildesse said.

“Oh. Sorry.” He set the poem down. “Yes. Of course.”

The musician looked from one to the other. “Shall I start again?”

“Please,” she said.

He started again.

Ildesse put one hand beside Brevot's, close enough that he could take it without reaching. He watched the musician. She could not decide whether he was listening intently or waiting for it to be over. The server arrived with the bowls and tried to catch her eye. Ildesse gave a small shake of the head. Just until the rising phrase was over. Then the covers could come off.

It was not a short air. She had liked that about it when choosing.

Brevot smiled at her once, apologetically. She smiled back. He looked down at the soup cooling in the server's hands. She could have dismissed the musician, but they were approaching the part for which she had hired him. By the time they reached it, she had to count the phrases to make herself listen.

The last note lingered. Brevot applauded too soon, then again when the bow came down.

“Beautiful,” Ildesse said. “Thank you.”

The soup was set before them. Brevot picked up his spoon.

“And the second piece, madam?”

“In a little while.”

“I'm engaged at the other end of the room in a little while.”

She was paying to interrupt the regular program. He had explained the arrangement clearly in his note. The whole evening had looked much more spacious on paper.

“Then now, please.”

Brevot lowered his spoon.

“You can eat,” she told him.

“I don't want to be rude.”

“It doesn't trouble me,” said the musician, and began the second piece.

This one was quicker. Brevot ate his soup. With no spoon to occupy her, Ildesse held her hand on the table until it began to look as though she were waiting to have it examined. She brought it back into her lap.

When the music ended, Brevot thanked the player with evident feeling. Ildesse watched the musician go to a table where three women were happily shouting over one another. None of them stopped when he began to play.

“You don't like music,” she said.

“I do. Sometimes. I never know where to look when somebody's playing it at me.”

“I thought it would be lovely.”

“It was well played.”

“Yes.”

He glanced at the pages beside his bowl. “Should I leave this?”

“No, go on.” She meant it. Something might yet happen in the poem that would bring the evening round. The blade might be taken dancing.

He finished the third stanza and read two more. There were banners, a dead king, and a final image of the sword laid across the knees of a man too weary to lift it. That last stanza was good. She could see the man in the dark, his legs cramped under the cold weight, ashamed to wake his companions and ask for help. Unfortunately, she could see nothing in it that resembled their correspondence.

Brevot lowered the pages.

“Well?”

“The end is very good.”

He waited.

“The man in the last stanza. I like him.”

“But?”

“Must there be a but?”
