Even after new ones and food there would be a great deal of sleeping in that purse.

“Name?”

“Fennit.”

“Age?”

“Fifteen.”

She set down her pen. “Control trial. Show me a working. Stop when I say.”

The dust lifted again. I kept it low over the boards, turning it in a tight ring while she leaned down to watch. At her word I released it. She brushed a speck off her shoe and wrote my name.

I finished the sleeve, gave back her needle, and put my mitten on. Seven mages waited by the steps, discussing the draw. One had red sleeves so wide I could have put both my arms in either of them. Another was making a bright bird turn above her wrist. She closed her hand as I passed, and the bird vanished.

The caller fitted us with white vests bearing square red patches over the breastbone. Mine went over my sleeveless shirt and under my coat. She folded the coat's fronts back and tied them behind me, leaving the patch entirely exposed.

“First bare hand to the other patch wins. No hiding it. Clothing holds are allowed. No fire, no cutting, no spells on flesh. Obey a halt at once.” She tapped my left mitten. “That hand won't score.”

“The other one will.”

“School?” she asked, pen ready again.

I had learned the dust lift from a secondhand bookseller who made me clean his stock. The holdfast came from keeping blankets on myself when older boys tried to pull them off. My unpicking earned money. None of these sounded right with a tournament caller shouting them.

“The Gutter School.”

The mage with the red sleeves laughed. Two others joined him. Peltrude, whose name I'd heard shouted by half the crowd, looked me up and down and snorted through her nose. Hadrum, the defending champion, put a hand over his mouth. He still had very amused eyes.

“Do they send a champion every year?” the red-sleeved mage asked.

“They've only got me.”

That made him laugh harder. I hadn't meant it to.

The caller shook the folded draw slips in a hat. Eight of us meant three wins for the purse. I looked from the yellow silk to the red sleeves.

“I ought to be finished by supper,” I said.

“I think you will,” said Peltrude.

*

I drew red sleeves first.

He bowed to the crowd before acknowledging me. Close up, he smelled of cloves, and tiny embroidered suns shone on his cuffs. My feet were dusty inside my boots. I rubbed my bare right palm down my trousers and wished I'd kept that remark about supper to myself.

Four marshals stood at the platform's corners. I had seen one catch a tumbling contestant last year, lifting both hands to spread a cushion of air beneath her. They were watching us now. That helped until I wondered how often they had to do it.

“Begin!”

The mage raised his fingers. Six more mages appeared, every one red-sleeved, every one smiling.

They spread across the boards. I backed away. The one on the left lunged; I ducked and put out my scoring hand. It passed through his chest. Behind me, the crowd laughed.

I spun. A real hand grazed my coat collar. Too high to score, close enough that I felt a fingernail. All seven mages stepped away together.

“Try another,” they said.

I was going to lose every copper I owned to a man showing off his sleeves.

The boards were gritty. Hundreds of people had crossed them to watch the morning exhibitions. I crouched and lifted the dust around my feet, only a pace out, only ankle high. Holding so much made the tendons in my wrist stand up. The mage would have to come through it to reach me.

His copies advanced. Dust hung undisturbed inside six pairs of shining shoes. The seventh pair, coming on my left, pushed little brown curls ahead of its toes.

I turned towards those toes.

He saw me turn. The copies vanished; he swept a hand across his body, and a gust drove the dust into my face. I shut my eyes. A board thumped under his next step.

I couldn't see his patch. I could see, through one watering eye, his right hand coming straight at my chest.

My mitten caught the bottom of his advancing sleeve. I held wool to silk with the holdfast. It was no stronger than a good handgrip, but a grip spread across the whole mitten didn't slip off embroidery. I pulled his sleeve out to my left and stepped in beside that reaching arm.

His fingers swept past my ribs. My bare right palm met the red square on his vest.

“Touch! Fennit!”

He jerked his sleeve free, breaking my hold. I stumbled a step after him.

For a moment the crowd was quiet enough for me to hear someone drop a cup. Then people at the front began shouting. I held up my right hand because that was the one that had done it. It was a very fine hand. I felt that everyone ought to have a proper look.

“Best of three?” my opponent asked the caller.

“One touch. As announced.”

He stared at the dust still settling on his shoes, then brushed at the mark my mitten had left on his cuff. I bowed to him. Quite deeply. He didn't bow back.

I came down the steps grinning so hard my cheeks hurt.

Peltrude stood at the bottom, rolling her sleeves above her elbows.

“I see what those are for,” I told her.

“Good.” She pulled the last fold tight.

*

While the other quarterfinals finished, I watched Hadrum win his. He kept a larger man turning with little pushes of air until he got within arm's reach, then closed his left fingers. The man's coat cuffs stopped in midair, arms spread wide. Hadrum stepped in and touched the exposed patch with his right hand. He opened his left fist only after the call, and the cuffs dropped.

I ate the heel of bread I'd saved for supper. It had lint on it. I picked off the biggest piece and decided that winners could eat early.

Peltrude won her quarterfinal without once touching the boards with her heels. She balanced forward, raised her left palm, and drove her opponent backwards with air until he could hardly take a step. Then she eased the wind, followed him in, and scored.

“No cuffs today?” I asked when we faced each other.

She slapped her bare forearm. “You can try holding this.”

“Clothing only,” the caller reminded us.

“I know,” said Peltrude, still looking at me.

On the start she sent me backwards three steps. Air flattened the loose coat against my sides and whistled through the bad stitching of my boots. I leaned into it. She let it ease, took a quick step, and reached for the patch.

I twisted away. Her fingers missed by the width of a copper.

“Nearly,” I said.

She pushed me again.

I went sideways this time, angling for the tight sleeve above her elbow. One touch, one hold, just as before. She turned with me and drove the air against my left shoulder. My reaching hand found nothing; I fell sideways onto the boards.

She was coming before I'd got my breath back. I rolled, scrambled to my knees, and crawled round her towards the middle while people shouted different advice at me. The marshal at that corner had raised his hands but hadn't needed them.

My shoulder hurt. My bread sat in a lump halfway down my chest.

“You're not getting a sleeve this time,” Peltrude said.

I had a reply ready. Then I needed the breath to get up.

She came after me. I scrambled up just as the wind struck again and tried sticking my right boot to the board beneath it. I could work the hold through anything I was touching, and I had used it on blankets, sacks, my own soles. Here it lasted less than a heartbeat. Her full gust ripped it loose and sent me staggering.

That wouldn't do.

She stepped after me, easing the wind so that she could close the distance herself. I saw her right hand starting forward and skipped back. She withdrew before my answering swipe could reach her, raising her left palm to send me away again.

Push, reach, push. My retreat did half her work. Every time she came for me I was already moving backwards; every time I tried to go forwards she had the wind up.

I gave her two more retreats. On the second I made a show of tripping. She didn't hurry. Her left palm stayed steady until I was upright, and when she came in she kept her scoring hand low, ready for another duck.

My shoulder throbbed. So much for pretending.

On her next push I went back as she expected, right foot behind me. But when the air eased and she took her long step, I pressed that boot's sole to the board and held it there.

One breath. My own boot, my own weight. No gust to fight yet.

I stopped retreating. My knees folded and I swung left around the planted foot. Peltrude had reached for a chest that should have been another stride away; her hand went past my right shoulder as her step brought the rest of her close.

I came up inside her arm and slapped her patch.

The returning wind hit me as the caller shouted. My hold broke. I landed on my backside with my right foot folded under me. Its sole had torn loose and hung by the heel.

“Touch! Fennit!”

I stayed sitting long enough to make sure she'd really said it. Then I laughed. I couldn't stop. Peltrude had to walk round me to get to the steps.

“That wasn't nearly,” I said.

“Get up. You're on your boot.”

I was. I got up carefully, and that started the laughter again.

Below the platform I tied the loose sole against my foot with the cord from my bread wrapping. Twice I dropped the knot. Peltrude watched, holding a cup of drinking water.

“How long can you keep that sticking trick going?”

“Long enough.”

“Your left hand's shaking.”

I put it on my knee. “You landed me on it.”

“I landed you on your shoulder.”

She handed me the cup. I had to take it in my right hand. Past her elbow I saw Hadrum, waiting for his semifinal, looking directly at my fingers.

“Thanks,” I said to Peltrude, rather more quietly.

She sat beside me to watch him fight.

*

Hadrum won, of course. This opponent tucked both hands close to avoid the cuff hold, so he used a sharp sideways gust to turn her, then stepped across her path and scored before she could face him again.

He hadn't even had to sit down afterwards.

When we went up for the final, he bowed to me first. The crowd had packed so close that the caller had to clear the steps. Somewhere behind all those heads waited the yellow purse. I tried to see it and found myself staring at Hadrum instead.

“Would you care for a longer rest?” he asked.

“Would you?”

“I'm ready.”

So was I, apparently. I took off my left mitten. My fingers felt swollen when I spread them.

Hadrum's coat fitted close, with fastened cuffs. He stood well out of reach as the caller started us. When I moved left, a sideways push drove me right. When I tried to go with that push, he changed it. The air tugged at one knee of my trousers and then the other. I had to watch my feet as well as his hands.

I lifted dust. He swept the boards between us clean without coming any closer.

I stuck my repaired boot down for a turn. He stopped advancing and shoved from the opposite side. I broke the hold myself before my ankle twisted, and staggered back into the middle.

“You can come closer,” I told him.

He did. I hadn't meant immediately.

His right hand darted towards my patch. I batted it away with my left and felt my coat cuff draw tight. His other hand was closing. I flung myself backwards before he could harden the air around the cloth, and the cuff snapped loose.

Both of us were breathing harder now. He had a spot of sweat beside his nose. I took enormous comfort in that spot.

His wind rose, then faltered. I sprang forward into the opening.

He'd been waiting for me to try that. The next push hit my coat from the side and spun me round; I barely turned my chest away from his scoring hand. As I got clear, a hot pain ran up my left shoulder.

The crowd had stopped giving useful advice. Several people were shouting my name, and one was shouting “Mind him!” as though I had other business on the platform.

I couldn't keep doing this. Hadrum changed his timing whenever I thought I'd found it. He was saving his strength, making me stumble, waiting until I was slow enough to catch.

I backed off, tugging at my right sleeve. The cuff had slipped down over my knuckles. Underneath it my thumb found the ugly row of stitches I'd put in at registration.

I stopped tugging. With the cuff still over my knuckles, I folded my thumb back against the stitches inside it.

Hadrum had seen the dust. He had seen the holdfast. When I'd mended the coat he had been up by the steps with the others, arguing about the draw.

He might still know unpicking. He might see what I was doing. I had no better idea.

I let him drive me a little farther back, then reached for his left sleeve with my right hand, slow enough to look tired. I really was tired. That part came easily.

He moved his arm out of reach. Air squeezed my extended coat cuff, holding it to my right. Before I could draw the other arm in, he caught that cuff too. His left fingers closed; the cloth stretched sideways, pulling my arms apart. His right hand was free.

The crowd made one long disappointed noise.

The coat bit under my armpits. Its tied-back fronts kept the whole garment on me while his two grips held both cuffs out wide. My patch was uncovered, practically offered up.

He came in at once.

I pulled hard against the right cuff, as though I could break his hold, and worked the unpicking through the thread beneath my thumb.

The stitches loosened. Hadrum's right hand was reaching. I wrenched my elbow down and the seam opened from wrist to elbow, spilling my bare forearm through the underside of the sleeve.

He was still holding the cloth. I bent my knees and turned to my right under his reaching hand. The trapped left sleeve dragged tight behind me, but I had room for half a step towards his left shoulder. His fingertips brushed the top of my vest; my patch had dropped below them.

My right hand came up between us.

Red wool. The hard beat of his heart through it.

“Touch! Fennit!”

Hadrum's fingers closed on my shoulder an instant later. For a dreadful moment he stayed there, holding me, while I stared at my own hand on his chest and waited to learn what had gone wrong.

Then he looked down at it.

“Yes,” he said, a little breathlessly. “That was yours.”

His left hand opened. My other arm dropped and the empty right sleeve fell against my side.

The shouting hit me all at once. I jumped, tried to jump again, and nearly went over on the broken boot. Hadrum caught my elbow and let go as soon as I was steady.

“I won,” I told him.

“I heard.”

I had meant to bow. Instead I turned a complete circle, grinning at everyone, and raised both hands. I couldn't have worked another spell if they'd offered me a second purse. I would certainly have tried.

The caller brought the yellow one. She counted the silvers into my cupped hands before pouring them back into the silk, each coin cold and heavy against the next. There were thirty. I counted with her, aloud.

Peltrude came up the steps when we were done. She lifted the hanging piece of sleeve, looked at the loose thread, and let it fall.

“Did you plan to ruin every stitch you owned?”

“Only the cheap ones.”

“That boot was cheap, then.”

“Very.”

She laughed. I let her. I had thirty silvers, and her patch had my dusty handprint on it.

Hadrum was still beside the caller, rubbing the red square on his own chest. “I'd like another bout, Fennit. When your hands are rested.”

I tucked the purse inside my vest and kept one hand over the lump.

“Next tournament?”

“Before that.”

Peltrude folded her arms. “I'm first.”

I looked at them and took my time answering.

“You can draw for it,” I said. “I'm going to eat.”

stories.title: A Beginner of Considerable Age
stories.prompt: A dragon gets bored in its long years of life and decides to take up adventuring. The problem is they didn't read the fine text; New adventurers start at level 1, and dragon or not, the gods make no exceptions.
stories.body:
# A Beginner of Considerable Age

Orsugal had been listening to three adventurers describe a disastrous encounter with a manticore, and he was jealous.

They sat outside the inn sharing a loaf. One had lost a boot. Another kept interrupting to explain that the tree had been much higher than the others remembered. Every time they reached the part about the trousers, all three laughed so hard that the story stopped.

Orsugal could have swallowed their manticore. He could have swallowed their tree. He lay across the opposite hillside, his chin between two apple orchards, and tried to remember when anything had last happened to him that required telling twice.

That afternoon he presented himself at the temple of the district's two adventuring gods. They came outside to receive him, warm and breathing, one with antlers woven through with votive ribbons, the other with six hands. Worshippers knelt on the temple steps and offered little bundles of food for luck on dangerous journeys. The towns of the district had entrusted their adventurers to these two, and their charter was carved over the door.

Orsugal liked the part about discovering wonders. He approved of the part about recovering treasures. When the six-handed god unrolled the compact, he read as far as *dangers commensurate with your abilities*, which seemed a pity, but perhaps they had some exceptionally large dangers in reserve.

"I have brought my own equipment," he said, spreading wings that put the temple in shade.

"Read the terms before you sign," said the god.

Orsugal examined the space for his name. It was scarcely wider than one of his scales. Below it, further clauses crowded together in very small letters.

"I have made treaties," he said, and signed with the point of a claw.

The antlered god touched his forehead.

The temple shot upwards. His stomach dropped; his chin struck the ground. For a moment Orsugal thought the gods had buried him. Beside his face, something he would once have mistaken for a speck of dust had become an acorn.

He stood up. He was the size of a lean hound.

"No," he said.

The gods waited while he said it again.

He spread his wings and sprang into the air. They flapped hard enough to stir the dust. He landed on his nose with an involuntary honk, and a woman on the steps made a noise inside her helmet.

Orsugal swung round. "Was that laughter?"

"No." The helmet made the noise again. She took it off. She was a grown woman with a narrow face, a bright red cloak, and armour apparently bought for a much broader person. "Yes. Sorry. It was the noise you made."

He turned his back on her and approached the compact. He could read the small letters now.

*Every new adventurer begins at level one. Native endowments exceeding that level are suspended for the duration of enrolment.*

His fire emerged as a short, blue-tipped flame, barely enough to light a candle. The effort left him panting.

"I am over two thousand years old."

"And newly enrolled," said the six-handed god.

"Make an exception."

"We make none. You may retire here, and we will release you from the compact. Until then, its limits hold wherever you travel."

Orsugal looked towards the hillside. His outline remained in the flattened grass. He could go back to it. There was a cave full of gold beyond the ridge, and by evening he could be asleep on it, having moved three irritating coins out from under his elbow.

The woman put her helmet back on.

"I'm Melicent," she said. "Also one. Though I was more or less this size already."

Orsugal faced the gods. "Where do you keep the adventures?"

***

The task Melicent wanted involved a silver festival cup, a picnic hamper, and a tusked badger that had carried both into an abandoned hunting lodge.

"How large a badger?" Orsugal asked.

The woman who had lost the hamper held her hands apart, considered, and moved them farther apart.

"It frightened my pony. I don't want anyone hurt over a cup."

"Ponies are frightened of wheelbarrows," said Melicent. "Let us try."

She reached for the task slip at the same time as Orsugal. Her gauntlet and his claw pinned opposite ends.

"I have experience with treasure," he said.

"And I've got a sword."

"I have teeth."

Melicent looked at his teeth. He closed his mouth before she could comment.

The six-handed god set two wooden counters beside the slip. "You may undertake it together. Return the cup and you will both earn advancement. Killing the animal is unnecessary."

Melicent slid one counter towards Orsugal. "You get the cup. I'll hold it off."

He was going to object to the distribution of glory, but she had already borrowed a coil of rope and was striding down the steps. He had to hurry to catch her. His legs had become absurdly numerous for the speed they provided.

On the woodland road she tried a sword flourish. The point caught her cloak and pinned it briefly to an oak.

"A difficult manoeuvre," Orsugal observed.

"It works without the cloak."

"Then why wear the cloak?"

She pulled the blade free. "I've had it nine years. I bought it when I first meant to leave. I'm wearing it."

He had been about to suggest that she abandon the sword instead. Something about the way she shook the leaves from the red cloth made him keep that suggestion to himself.

"What detained you?"

"My father's shop. Then my own shop. Then finding somebody who'd buy the shop. What detained you?"

"Nothing."

She looked down at him.

"I was occupied," he added.

"With what?"

Orsugal stepped over a root. It grazed his belly, and he stopped to inspect the pale scratch it left between two scales.

"We should concentrate on the expedition."

***

The lodge stood in a clearing, its roof sagging over a single long hall. Behind it was a kennel run enclosed by high stone walls. An iron gate connected the run to the back of the hall; a feeding hatch, knee-high to Melicent, opened through the run's outer wall.

They approached from behind. Orsugal looked through the hatch. The run was empty. Beyond it, through the open gate, he could see a table, a torn hamper, and a great deal of striped fur.

"As big as a boar," he reported.

Melicent bent to look over his head. "Can you get through that hole?"

He squeezed his shoulders into it, his horns brushing the upper stone. A twist would get the rest of him through. He backed out.

"Obviously."

"You could creep in and fetch the cup while it sleeps."

Through the gate he could see the silver handle beneath the badger's forepaw. Its tusks rose beside its muzzle, yellow and thick as Melicent's thumbs.

"I shall require it to surrender the cup."

"You'll wake it."

"I should prefer it awake when it surrenders."

Melicent considered this, then drew her sword. "All right. I'll stand beside you."

They went round to the front. The entrance was half blocked by a fallen door. Inside, sunlight slanted across the table and two benches. The badger slept underneath, its nose in the wreckage of the hamper. At the far end of the hall the iron gate stood open into the room, leaving a narrow space between its bars and the side wall. Its lifting latch faced the hall.

Melicent held out her flat palm. Orsugal stopped. She swept it towards the opening. He started forward, just as she stepped through herself. Her breastplate caught against the fallen door; her boot came down on his tail.

His cry woke the badger. "You waved me on!" he said, hauling his tail free.

"I meant follow me."

The badger came out from beneath the table. Crumbs clung to its whiskers. It lowered its head.

Orsugal planted his feet. "I am Orsugal. You are in possession of—"

It charged.

Melicent swung her sword too late. A tusk caught the flat and knocked it spinning under a bench. She scrambled onto the table, dragging her cloak clear. Orsugal inhaled, braced, and breathed fire directly into the approaching face.

His little flame singed three whiskers. The badger sneezed into his open mouth.

He ran.

***

The table was just large enough to keep between himself and the badger, provided he never stopped moving. His claws skidded at the corners. He could hear its feet on the flagstones, the scrape of its tusks against the legs, his own breath coming in small, disgraceful squeaks.

"Up here!" Melicent shouted.

He leaped, beating his wings. His foreclaws caught the table's edge, slipped, and he fell against a bench. Pain spread through his left wing. He had struck harder things without noticing. This pain stayed.

The badger rounded the corner. Orsugal shot beneath the bench and came out on the other side. Its tusks struck the wood behind him.

"Up here!" she shouted again.

"I can't!"

She thrust her hand down. He seized the cuff of her gauntlet with both foreclaws and felt himself lifted clear just as the badger's teeth snapped beneath his hind feet. Halfway up, the gauntlet began to slide off.

"My gauntlet!" said Melicent.

"Pull me!"

She caught him under the forelegs with her other arm and heaved him onto the table. He struck her breastplate headfirst. They collapsed together. Her helmet bounced against the boards and rolled over the edge, vanishing beneath a trestle.

For several breaths he could do nothing but lie across her knees. Below them, the badger scratched at a table leg.

"You could have told me you couldn't fly," she said.

"You saw me fail outside the temple."

"I thought you'd get it right next time."

"So did I."

She sat up, helping him off her lap. His wing hurt when he folded it. One scale on his flank had lifted, and beneath it was an alarming tenderness he did not want the badger to investigate.

Melicent peered over the table's edge. "We can jump down together. It can't chase both of us."

"It only needs to catch one."

She brought her foot back from the edge.

Orsugal looked towards the front door. Once, without even getting up, he could have destroyed this building. Now twenty feet of floor separated him from the daylight, and he could not cross it. He looked at those twenty feet with a concentration he had not bestowed on anything in years.

The badger thrust its snout over the edge. Melicent snatched her cloak from its teeth. She kicked at it, missed, and nearly slid off. Orsugal caught a fold of red cloth in his mouth and leaned back until she regained her seat.

"Thank you," she said, very quietly.

He released the cloth. It tasted of dust and oak leaves.

Under the table, the badger went back to the hamper. Orsugal crouched to look. The cup had rolled against the far leg, handle uppermost. Beyond it lay a clear strip of floor leading to the iron gate. Beyond the gate, the run. Beyond the run, the hatch.

"I can get out through that feeding hole," he said.

"I can't."

"I know. I need you at the gate."

She looked from him to the opening, then down at the badger.

"You'd have to make it follow you."

"It has shown some willingness."

"And I'd shut it in?"

He nodded. A loud crack came from below. The badger was worrying the end of a wooden peg out of the trestle.

Melicent drew her legs beneath her. "I can do that."

"Wait until it's all the way through. Then shut it and drop the latch."

"Yes."

He stared at the gap between the table and the gate. "Don't let it turn back on you. If it turns, get up here again."

"I said I can do it."

Her voice was loud enough to lift the animal's head. She drew a breath which caught halfway in, then drew another.

"I know," he said, though he knew no such thing. "I need you to."

She swallowed, then took the rope from her shoulder.

"I'll tie this to the latch. We can let it out when we're away."

Orsugal would gladly have left the badger in the kennel until it died of extreme age. But she was already uncoiling the rope. He shifted his sore wing out of her way.

***

He lowered his tail over the front edge of the table and flicked it.

The badger lunged. He whipped his tail up; its teeth closed with a click. Behind him, Melicent dropped to the floor. He flicked his tail again. It was a repellent use for a tail that had once felled siege towers, and he wished very much that it were somebody else's.

Melicent reached the back of the hall. She crouched in the gap behind the open gate, tied one end of the rope to the latch lever, and passed the rope over a roof beam above the gate. She tugged; the lever rose. She let it drop again, leaving the coil at her feet.

Orsugal waited for her to look at him. She put up her thumb. He pointed a claw at himself, then at the cup, and she nodded vigorously.

The table lurched.

He had meant to descend gracefully on the far side. Instead, one trestle folded, and he slid down the tilting boards in a cloud of dust. The badger backed away from the crash. Orsugal landed beside the cup, caught its handle in his teeth, and ran for the gate.

The cup banged against his knees. He could not see the badger, but the sound of its pursuit filled the hall. He passed Melicent's boots and plunged into the kennel run.

Iron scraped stone behind him.

He turned. She was shutting the gate already. It struck the badger's rump, leaving its hind legs in the hall. The animal twisted back towards her.

Orsugal dropped the cup. "Wait! Its back legs!"

Melicent shoved the gate open again. The badger's head swung towards the movement of her arm.

He slapped the silver cup with his forefoot. It rang against the flags, and the badger turned. For an instant he could see the full width of its open jaws, the strands of spit between its teeth. He had called it back. It was coming because he had called it back.

He seized the cup and fled.

The hatch waited ahead, square and bright. He ducked his head, pushed through, caught his injured wing on the jamb. His back feet scrabbled at the stone. Behind him the gate clanged shut. He heard the smaller clack of the latch dropping, but the badger was on his side of it.

Fold the wing. Fold it.

He did, and pain shot along his ribs. His body slid through. A tooth snagged the tip of his tail and pulled him backwards half an inch. He kicked, tore free, and tumbled into the grass with the cup still in his mouth.

The badger's nose filled the hatch. Orsugal rolled out of reach and lay still. His heart thumped so hard that he could feel it in his horns. The sun was hot on his face. A green beetle climbed across his front foot.

He laughed around the handle of the cup.

It hurt. He laughed again.

Melicent appeared round the corner with her recovered sword. She had lost her helmet. There was a new dent in her breastplate and a pale stripe across her nose where dust had stuck to sweat.

"Are you bitten?"

He put down the cup. "A little."

She crouched beside him and examined his tail. Her hands were shaking. They made his tail shake too, which set him laughing again.

"Stop that. Hold still."

"You shut the gate on its bottom."

"I know. I was there."

He tried to stop. She pressed her lips together, but a laugh escaped her. Then both of them were helpless, which made the badger snort through the hatch and send them scrambling farther away.

She led him back round to the front, picked up the coil she had dropped in the doorway, and paid out the rope as they retreated behind a boulder beyond the clearing. Melicent pulled. Through the front doorway, Orsugal saw the latch lift and the gate swing into the hall under the badger's weight. They stayed behind the rock until the animal returned to its ruined picnic.

"My helmet's in there," Melicent said.

Orsugal looked at her. She looked at him.

"I'll buy another."

***

The owner of the cup met them on the temple steps. She took one look at the scratches and torn cloak and brought out the food she had saved from the picnic. Orsugal gave her the cup, ate a honey cake in three bites, and accepted another.

The gods heard their account. They had some difficulty, because Melicent kept acting out the gate and Orsugal objected to the height at which she held her hand to represent him.

"Second level," said the antlered god when they had finished, touching each in turn.

A warm pressure passed through Orsugal's bones. His claws lengthened a fraction. He spread his wings, hopefully, and discovered that the left one still hurt. He remained the size of a hound.

Melicent lifted her sword. "Feels lighter."

She tried the flourish again. Orsugal stepped well back. This time the blade missed her cloak.

The six-handed god knelt beside him. "Do you wish to retire?"

"Certainly not."

Melicent glanced down at him and put her sword away.

"Come on, then. I want to sit somewhere with a back on it."

She headed towards the inn. Orsugal limped after her, carrying the remaining cake. Outside, the three adventurers were still at their table. The one without a boot moved a chair aside to let him through.

"Rough afternoon?"

Orsugal put his cake down. "We were beset," he began, "by an animal of extraordinary ferocity."

Melicent sat down so hard that the chair creaked. "It was a badger."

"A tusked badger. Show them the dent."

She turned in the chair to display her breastplate, and one of the adventurers whistled. Orsugal climbed onto the chair beside her. From there he could see all their faces.

"First," he said, "there was a misunderstanding about who was to go through the door."

Melicent began to laugh before he had even reached the badger. He waited, impatient and delighted, for her to stop.

stories.title: The Chair at the Back
stories.prompt: "Hero?" The Tavern Matron looks at you and pity enters her gaze. "By the Makers, You believed every word they said. Come on." She drags you to a Chair in the Back. "Sit, Sit. Time for a Common Sense Lesson for the Summoned Child. HUSBAND! Bring Food and Drink. We got another one."
stories.body:
# The Chair at the Back

Jemby was inside the tavern when his sword caught against the doorpost and brought him to a stop. He turned sideways to free it, then faced the room again, holding the scabbard away from his leg.

"I'm here for the feast," he told the woman behind the counter.

She was picking broken cork out of a jug. "Whose feast?"

"Mine. I'm the summoned hero."

"Hero?"

That was the voice grown people used when he had misunderstood something expensive. Jemby straightened. The woman looked from the embroidered suns on his cuffs to the sword, then up to his face, and her expression became worse than annoyed.

"By the Makers. You believed every word they said. Come on."

She caught his sleeve and towed him between the tables. The sword tapped three chair backs on the way. He tried to apologize to the occupants, but she was already pulling out a broad chair at the back, beside the hearth.

"Sit, sit. Time for a common sense lesson for the summoned child. HUSBAND! Bring food and drink. We got another one."

"I'm thirteen," Jemby said.

"Then you'll want bread as well."

He sat. The sword hooked over the chair arm and left him crooked, with one knee higher than the other. After two attempts to settle himself, he stood again.

"May I put this somewhere?"

"Against the wall. Point down. In its sheath, please."

He had not been going to draw it. He had been thinking of drawing it, admittedly, because he had not yet seen the whole blade.

The chair had a cushion. Beyond it stood a narrow table, and beyond that a curtain screened a little passage from the crowded room. Perhaps this was where important guests ate. The woman rolled his cuffs back twice before he could decide whether to stop her.

"What's your name?"

"Jemby."

"I'm Berrit. My husband's Pemric. Any food that makes you ill?"

"No."

"And what have you eaten today?"

He had to think back beyond the circle of singing men, the cold stone beneath his one bare foot, the extraordinary moment when they had all bowed. Before that there had been breakfast, at home, where his mother had told him not to leave the heel of the loaf for someone else again. He had meant to eat it when he came back downstairs.

"A bit of bread."

"Right. We can improve on that."

Pemric came through the curtain carrying a tray. He was bald on top, with a great deal of white hair everywhere else, including on the backs of his hands. His right foot came down on its outer edge at every step, so the cup on his tray rocked and settled as he crossed to the table. He set down a bowl of meat and barley, a loaf with a split crust, and a cup that smelled of apples.

Jemby picked up the cup. "Is this ale?"

"Apple juice," Pemric said.

"I was allowed wine at the palace."

"Did you like it?"

"Not very much."

"You'll like this."

He did. He drank half before remembering that he was being watched, then put the cup down carefully and reached for his purse. There were six round gold things in it. He had counted them on the way here, three times.

"They gave me money."

Berrit looked at the disc he offered. One side bore a sun; the other had a deep square punch mark.

"That's a barracks meal token."

"It's gold."

"It's brass. In here, you'd have to find someone who wants a meal at the barracks."

He rubbed the edge. It stayed golden.

"They said I'd be welcome at every table."

"You're welcome at this one," she said. "Put those away and eat."

The first mouthful was too hot. He swallowed it anyway, which made his eyes water, and Berrit pushed the juice nearer without saying anything. After that she let him work through half the bowl before asking where they meant to send him.

"The northern road. Tomorrow. There's a company waiting. They said the villages need us."

"Some of them do. What's your part in it?"

"To drive back the creatures."

"Have you fought one before?"

"I've only been here since this morning."

"Anything like one, then?"

He shook his head. She took the empty chair opposite him.

"Have you ever used a sword?"

"Not a real one. But they said my gifts would awaken when I was tested."

"And did they test you?"

"They brought me here. Out of my house."

Surely that counted. He could still feel the dreadful pull behind his breastbone. He had been reaching for his other sock, and then there had been bright thread around his fingers and strangers kneeling on a stone floor. One of them had wept. You could not do all that by accident.

Berrit broke off a piece of bread. "I don't doubt they've got gifts. I'm asking what they've found out about yours."

Jemby stirred his bowl, separating a pale slice of something from the barley.

"It's a turnip," Pemric said. "You can leave it."

He ate it to show that turnips were not the problem.

"They wouldn't bring me all this way if I couldn't do it."

From the front of the room someone called for another jug. Berrit called back that she had heard, and continued looking at him.

"Last spring a girl came through with those same suns on her sleeves. Older than you. They'd told her she'd know what to do when the time came. She came back with a broken jaw. I cut her bread small for six weeks."

Jemby stopped chewing.

"Is she all right?"

"She's riding with a wool merchant now. She eats perfectly well. But she hadn't known what to do, and nobody had taught her."

"Maybe her gift was something else."

"Maybe. I'd want to find that out before something tried to bite me."

The customer called again. Berrit stood so abruptly that Jemby flinched, though she was only taking the jug.

"I've got to serve him before he dies of waiting. Pemric, tell the boy about your first sword."

"It was lovely," Pemric said when she was gone. "Too heavy. Lovely handle."

Jemby looked at the sword propped by the hearth. His own handle had a red stone in it.

"Did you fight creatures?"

"A few. Mostly I tried to stay behind someone who knew what they were doing."

"Were you a hero?"

"That's what they called me."

Jemby lowered his spoon. Pemric pulled out the chair Berrit had left and eased himself into it.

"You were summoned?"

"At fifteen. Had a whole mouthful of hard sweets. Very undignified, trying to answer a king with those tucked in my cheeks."

"What did you say?"

"Asked where I could spit."

Jemby laughed, then checked Pemric's face. He seemed quite willing to have it laughed at.

"Didn't you swallow them?"

"There were nine. I'd stolen a handful and heard my sister coming."

This was such a satisfactory reason to have nine sweets in your mouth that Jemby could picture the whole thing. He took another piece of bread.

"But afterward? Did you see amazing things?"

Pemric glanced toward his wife. She was arguing with the man who wanted the jug about whether he had paid for the previous one.

"Oh, yes."

"Like what?"

"A moth bigger than this table. Soft brown fur along its back. It settled on our tent and we couldn't get out until it had warmed its wings."

"Could you ride it?"

"I couldn't even persuade it to get off my trousers. They were hanging out to dry."

"But could someone?"

"I expect someone has tried."

Jemby looked from one end of the table to the other. Wings that size. He wanted to ask what moths ate in sufficient quantities to get that large.

"Has he mentioned the tent catching fire?" Berrit had returned with a wet patch down her apron.

"That was a different tent."

"But on the same journey."

"Yes."

Jemby pulled the bowl closer. The northern road had no moth in it now, only a burning tent with himself inside, tangled in blankets while the others ran. He had not asked whether someone would wake him in the mornings. At home he sometimes slept through the first bell.

Jemby's eyes went to the sword by the hearth, and Pemric followed them.

"You don't have to go with that company," he said. "Not tomorrow. Plenty of people come back from those expeditions. But you don't know how to travel with them yet, let alone fight."

"I could learn."

"Yes. Over time. You're allowed time."

Berrit put her hands on the back of her husband's chair. "What else did they promise?"

Jemby took the folded paper from inside his tunic. He had asked for something to write on after the third speech. The man with the blue sash had laughed, but had given him paper and a pen.

"Riches. A place at court. The gratitude of the nation."

He held the paper nearer the candle. His writing grew worse toward the bottom, where he had run out of room. Berrit leaned over his shoulder.

"A horse. Training in your awakened gifts. Which ought to happen before the dangerous part, I'd have thought."

"Can you do magic?" Jemby asked Pemric.

"A little."

Berrit shut her eyes. "We're trying to talk about tomorrow."

"I know," Jemby said. "But can he?"

Pemric opened his palm and laid a crumb of bread in the middle. He breathed in slowly. The crumb rose until there was a clear gap between it and his skin.

Jemby bent sideways. No thread. He looked beneath the table, although he could not have said what he expected to find there.

The crumb turned in the air, showing its browned side. Pemric's lips were slightly parted. When he finished breathing out, it settled into his hand.

"Do it again."

Pemric did. Jemby forgot the bowl, the sword, and Berrit, who eventually went to take an empty plate from another table.

"Can I?"

"Try. Take a little one."

He took a piece the size of his thumbnail.

"Smaller. We can work up to moving your supper."

Jemby pinched off most of it and ate the excess. Pemric showed him how to hold his hand loose. The thing to feel for, he said, was a small upward tug in the middle of his palm, as though someone were gently lifting the skin. Jemby could feel nothing except a crumb.

He stared at it, filled his lungs, and blew it into Pemric's beard.

"Not with your mouth," Pemric said, picking it out.

"You breathed."

"In. Then let it out slowly. The lifting's in your hand."

"You didn't say that."

"No, you're right. I haven't taught anybody in years. Here, look."

He lifted another crumb, this time with his free hand between his mouth and the crumb to show there was no breath doing the work. When Berrit came back, Jemby was trying again. His palm tingled. The bread stayed put. He held his breath until his chest ached.

"He's giving himself a headache," she said.

"I nearly had it."

"Blink, then."

He blinked. He had forgotten that. Pemric took his own crumb out of the air and ate it.

"Enough for now. It took me an afternoon to get a finger's height."

"Could you lift me?"

"No. I can hold a plum up for about as long as you just held your breath."

"Could I learn to fly?"

"Not from me."

The tingling lasted a while after Jemby put the crumb down. He rubbed his palm with his thumb, secretly pleased. Something had happened, even if it had happened where no one could see.

Berrit brought a small plate of orange fruit, split and sprinkled with sugar. The skins were pebbled and tough; the flesh tasted like a pear that had learned a better trick.

"Don't eat the rind," Pemric said.

Jemby retrieved a piece from his mouth.

"All this," Berrit said, indicating her husband, "and the end of his grand adventure was a bed in my father's kitchen. With his boots on, because his feet had swollen too much to get them off."

"I liked the moth," Pemric said quietly. "I liked the people I went with. You can't tell him I wish none of it had happened."

"I don't want him limping in here after six months."

"Neither do I."

Jemby looked down at Pemric's legs. One foot rested on its side beneath the chair. He had noticed the uneven walk without thinking much about it.

"But you stayed," he said.

"I did."

"Did you get to go home first?"

Pemric's chair creaked. He shifted the sideways foot until the sole was flat.

"No."

Jemby smoothed the paper beside his plate. Below the horse, below the gifts, he had written the thing he had asked twice to make sure: *home when finished*.

"They said when we'd won they'd send me back."

Neither adult answered quickly enough.

"Did you not win?"

"The fighting I was brought here for ended," Pemric said. "Then there was more fighting somewhere else. After that, there was always a reason to wait."

"But you asked?"

"Many times. I asked other people, too. Everyone I could find who knew anything about summoning."

Jemby looked at the white hair on Pemric's hands.

"You can do it one way," he said. "So you can do it the other."

"I don't know if they can. I've never seen anyone sent back."

"Maybe the people who brought me are better."

"I haven't met them."

"There were seven."

Pemric nodded, but did not seem reassured by the number. Jemby wanted him to look at Berrit and explain that seven was very good, that everything they had said until now was about a different sort of summoning.

"They knew my name."

"They knew mine, too."

The fruit slid from Jemby's fork. He watched it leave a sticky track across the plate. His mother would be home by now. No, she might still be looking. He had not taken his coat or his other sock. She would find the sock and think he must be nearby.

"I didn't say I wanted to come."

"I know," said Pemric.

"They asked if I'd help, and I said yes. But that was after."

Berrit sat on the edge of the table beside him. For the first time she seemed unsure where to put her hands. She folded them in her apron.

"You're staying here tonight," she said. "There's a bed upstairs, and tomorrow we'll get some answers, and you needn't worry about the bill, and—"

"Berrit," Pemric said.

She stopped. Jemby could hear someone at the front of the tavern counting out coins, losing count, and starting again.

"Does your sister think you're dead?" he asked.

Pemric looked at him for a long moment.

"She might."

"My mother will think that."

His face twisted. He tried to stop it by opening his mouth very wide, which only made the first sound worse. Berrit put a hand on his back, and he leaned against her apron because it was there. She smelled of spilled beer and warm cloth. Nothing like his mother.

He wanted his mother. He wanted her to tell him off for running into the house with muddy shoes. He wanted to be made to finish his turnips at his own table, and when Berrit offered him a clean cloth he was briefly, fiercely angry that she had thought of something to do when there was nothing to do.

He took it anyway.

Neither of them told him to be brave. Pemric sat with his hands between his knees. Berrit stayed where she was until Jemby sat up and scrubbed at his nose.

"I still want to ask them," he said.

"Of course," said Pemric.

"I want them to show me how they'd send me back. Before I go anywhere."

Berrit nodded.

He looked from one to the other. "Will you come?"

"Yes," she said.

"Both of you?"

Pemric glanced at the curtain. "We'll shut for the morning."

"I can do the talking," Berrit began.

"I want to ask."

"All right. You ask."

He folded the paper along its old creases. This morning he had imagined coming home with the red stone sword and letting everyone hold it, one at a time. He remembered how the seven men had crowded around him when he spoke, all smiling, all waiting. He could face them again if Berrit stood beside him. Pemric would remember the questions when he forgot.

"I'm not going north tomorrow," he said.

He waited for the shame to arrive. Mostly he felt tired.

"Then we'll tell them that, too," Berrit said.

"What about the sword?"

"You can give it back if they want it."

That hurt a little, in a small, mean place he did not want to admit was still there. The stone had looked like a jewel from a story. He stared at it a moment, then nodded.

Berrit cleared away his bowl and came back with more juice. The man at the front wanted her again. This time she went without giving Pemric instructions.

The fruit was good even with no appetite. Jemby ate another piece while Pemric told him which stair squeaked and where the upstairs candle would be. There was an empty room beside theirs. If he woke frightened, he could knock.

"I probably won't," Jemby said.

"You can, though."

He pushed the fruit skin flat with his fork. Around them the tavern grew louder. Someone had begun a song without knowing enough of it, and three people were offering different versions of the next line.

Jemby opened his palm beneath the table. The tingling was gone. He flexed his fingers, then brought his hand up into the candlelight.

"Could I try again?"

Pemric reached for the bread. "A little one."

This time Jemby rested his elbow on the table. He held the crumb in the center of his palm and let his fingers uncurl. Pemric moved the candle away; there would be no need to lean over the flame to look.

For a while nothing happened. He thought about breathing instead of trying to force air into his hand. The song reached a verse nobody disputed, and behind Pemric, Berrit lifted a stack of plates.

The crumb rolled over.

Jemby nearly closed his fist. He made himself keep it open. There was the tug, a tiny pull at the skin, and then the crumb rose. Under it he could see the crease across his palm.

He turned his wrist. It wavered. Pemric reached out, then stopped before touching him.

"Berrit," Jemby whispered.

She set the plates down and came to look.

He had to show his mother this. The wish came so naturally that he almost said her name. She would have made him wash his hands first.

He gave a wet little laugh and caught the falling crumb.

"Again," he said, and opened his hand.

stories.title: Storm Warning
stories.prompt: In a city where monsters only appear during heavy rain, the STORM WARNING isn’t telling people to seek shelter—it’s telling them she’s been released.
stories.body:
# Storm Warning

Mabry counted out the money for Viveca's murder while her father held the envelope open.

The driver got three hundred for a delivery. This was fifteen hundred, the same amount Mabry had paid him in June, when a man who wouldn't go back to his employer had disappeared from the holding house. The driver had returned his clothes. There had been a bullet hole in the collar, and Mabry had folded the coat with the hole underneath.

"Her things as well," Renwick said, putting his keys beside her hand. "Empty the cupboard. Nothing for you to sort out tomorrow."

Beyond the office windows the rain was beginning to bounce off the pavement. They had waited eleven dry nights for it. On the twelfth, people hurried under awnings and her father's men came out of the garages.

Viveca had tried to take a guard's keys two weeks ago. He'd needed stitches. Renwick had called a driver, then cancelled him when the weather cleared. Mabry had gone on carrying the meals upstairs. She hadn't told Viveca about the driver.

"Will she need a coat?"

"The car's heated."

He touched the back of Mabry's neck as he passed. At twenty-seven she still stood motionless for that, as she had when he checked her collar before school. He was going to the holding house to collect the night's payments. He left the envelope on her desk for the driver, who went out to bring his car to the side entrance. Her father trusted her with the keys and fifteen hundred dollars, and she had earned his trust.

She took the envelope too.

Through the upstairs meal hatch, Mabry saw Viveca sitting on the bed in her grey clothes. She had already been locked up for ten months when Mabry came home, eight months ago. A small radio stood on the bedside table. Mabry had brought it upstairs inside a bundle of clean laundry; its cord was too short for Viveca to take it to the window, where the reception was better.

"It's tonight," Mabry said.

Mabry held the keys in the hatch. Viveca looked at them. "Yes."

"You knew?"

"He stopped having the sheets changed."

Mabry couldn't get the key into the lock. She steadied it with her other hand. In her coat pocket was a train ticket for the morning, bought with money she had taken from the petty cash. She had meant to leave before the office opened. She had meant to do several things that would still have left Viveca in this room.

The door opened inward. Viveca didn't immediately stand.

"Get dressed," Mabry said. "I can pay the driver. There's enough."

"That one? No. Get my red dress. It's in the cupboard. And the knife."

Mabry had seen the blade when she inventoried the confiscated belongings: broad as her palm, with coarse teeth along its back. Her father kept everything he took, though he sometimes threw away shoes.

"He'll kill me if I go out without it," Viveca said. "Then he'll take you to your father."

The dress smelled stale. There were no shoes in the cupboard. Under the folded hem lay Arvid's wedding ring and the paper that certified his death. Renwick had brought them to Viveca himself. When Mabry asked why he kept her locked up, he showed her the scar Viveca had left beneath his jaw that day.

Mabry fetched the knife in its oilcloth and stood outside while Viveca changed. From behind the door came the same small request she'd heard through the hatch for months.

"Stay there."

"I'm here."

They used to sit on opposite sides after the staff went home. Viveca told her about Arvid, who had hummed answers during the radio music quiz before the presenter finished asking the question. He sang tunelessly and with absolute confidence. On bad nights she still turned toward the empty end of the bed to tell him to shut up.

Mabry had told her about the ticket before she'd bought it. She had once asked her father for the money he owed her, and he'd fetched the bills he'd paid when her dressmaking shop failed. She was still working off those bills. With Viveca there had been no counting. She hadn't laughed or asked how Mabry expected to manage alone. She had said to take a window seat, even if it cost more.

Now she came out barefoot, her white hair loose over the red shoulders of the dress. The knife sagged in her hand for a moment. She adjusted her grip.

"The switch beside the front door," she said. "For the warning. Turn it on."

The red sign hung above the office, high enough to be seen from the junction. Mabry had never seen it lit. She knew it belonged to the business; her father had charged its repairs to security. She'd asked what it was for in her first week, and he'd told her she had enough to learn downstairs.

"Won't that bring them here?"

"They'll know I'm out. They won't touch us."

"And then we go to the station."

Viveca brushed a crease from Mabry's collar. "First I need your father to tell me where he buried my husband."

Mabry looked at the knife.

"Don't kill him."

"He's going to answer me."

Mabry went downstairs with her.

***

When the switch clicked, red filled the puddles outside.

**STORM WARNING.**

A shopkeeper across the street let his shutter fall with customers still inside. A man sheltering under the office awning stepped into the rain rather than stand beside Viveca. Cars hissed past. In the back of one, a man held an open umbrella flat against the side window so that nothing behind it could be seen. In a downpour you couldn't tell whether someone bent over a car door was helping a drunk or forcing a head down. Mabry had heard her father explain this to a new driver. She had been ordering lunch for them.

The hired driver saw Viveca and stopped halfway round his bonnet. She held out her empty hand.

"Keys."

He looked past her at Mabry, then up at the sign.

"Your father's going to want those lights off."

"Then he can come back and turn them off," Viveca said.

The hired driver dropped his keys on the bonnet and backed away. A second car came through the junction and slowed when the man at its wheel saw Viveca beneath the sign. Its rear window was open an inch. Someone inside was crying. Viveca left the keys where they lay. With someone in the back, the second car was going to the holding house anyway, and nobody there would stop it at the door.

She bent to the returns driver's window. "Holding house. Now."

"I saw. I'm going." He looked at Mabry and the office keys still in her hand, then back at Viveca. "He's let you out, then."

"We're coming with you," Mabry said.

He opened the locks. Viveca took the front seat, laying the knife across her knees. Mabry climbed in beside a woman whose wrists were tied together beneath an open raincoat. She was perhaps forty. One of her shoes had come off, and she kept trying to cover her bare foot with the other.

"I went back to him last time," the woman said when she saw Viveca. "I did what you said."

Viveca turned. Rain ran from the ends of her hair onto the seat.

"Keep your voice down."

Mabry reached for the woman's hands as the car pulled out. The woman pulled them away.

"I'm trying to untie you."

The returns driver slowed. "Not in the car."

"Keep driving," Viveca told him.

Mabry worked a fingernail into the wet knot. Through the windscreen she saw another car turn across traffic and follow them. A radio crackled under the dashboard.

"Red's on. All returns to the house. No deliveries."

"Why are they bringing everyone in?" Mabry asked.

The returns driver glanced into the mirror. "For her to inspect. That's what she had the sign put up for."

Viveca watched the road.

"You made me call his men in," Mabry said.

"Let them hear him answer me. They used to take my orders."

The knot was too tight. Mabry's nails were splitting. Her father had never used Viveca's name on the accounts she'd copied. He called her the upstairs problem. Viveca had told her she'd worked for him before Arvid's death, that she'd hurt people trying to find him. Mabry had not asked which people.

"You used to make them do this?"

"I needed someone found. Renwick charged me for every night his men went out. I couldn't keep paying. He was only selling addresses then. I offered to bring people back. The clients paid twice as much."

The woman beside Mabry began to rock against the door.

"You said I could have a week," she said. "Last time. A week before I went back. You said a week."

"Your week isn't my concern tonight."

Mabry took her nail out of the knot. A little piece stayed behind.

"Pull over," she told the driver.

He didn't answer. Viveca said, "We're nearly there."

They passed a cheap hotel with a dead strip of blue light over its entrance. Viveca leaned forward to look up at a window.

"That's where Arvid stayed. Six nights. I was going door to door with his photograph, and he was here."

"Hiding?"

"Waiting. Your father sold him a way out of the city. Then he sold me the address. The room was empty when I got there."

Mabry remembered the suitcase in Viveca's cupboard. Inside had been a man's yellow shirt, shaving things, slippers. Nothing of hers. She had assumed Renwick's men had packed it after his death, but there had been a train timetable folded into the shirt.

"Was he leaving you?"

Viveca's fingers tightened over the handle.

"He left the house. I was bringing him home."

Mabry pressed her shoulder against the car door. There was no handle on the inside. She had paid the garage bill when her father had them removed.

At the holding house, she would get this woman out. She could think that far.

***

Renwick waited in the front parlour of the old boardinghouse. Mabry knew the house from delivering wages: a narrow hall from the front door to the foot of the stairs, the parlour opening off it through a wide doorway on the left, the old dining room opposite, and the same flowered carpet running through all of it. The rooms upstairs were kept off her accounts; her father paid those expenses himself.

Drivers were bringing people into the former dining room across the hall. Viveca told them to wait outside. One looked to Renwick, who nodded. The woman from the car clung to Mabry's sleeve until a driver pushed her through the dining-room door. He shut it and slid a bolt home.

"Mabry," her father said. "Go and wait in the kitchen."

She stayed beside the front door. It had a thumb latch, no keyhole on this side. She put a finger under the latch without lifting it.

Viveca crossed the parlour. Renwick retreated until the edge of a table struck the backs of his legs.

"You want the money? It's there. You can have it."

"Where is he?"

"Upstairs."

Viveca stopped.

"Alive," he said. "Sit down, please. I'll bring him."

She caught his jacket and drove him back onto the table. The knife cut through his sleeve. He cried out, holding his arm crookedly against himself, blood running down his fingers.

"Call him," she said.

Renwick shouted Arvid's name. A chair scraped overhead. Mabry looked up the stairs and saw an older man on the landing, one hand cuffed to a guard's wrist. His beard had been cut very close, badly. He stopped when he saw the red dress.

Viveca let go of Renwick. For a moment she bent forward with both hands on her knees, as if she'd been hit in the stomach. The blade touched the carpet.

"You took his ring," she said.

Renwick was winding a tablecloth round his forearm. "I brought it to you myself. You'll remember that. I didn't send a boy."

"The certificate."

"I paid for it."

She made a sound Mabry had never heard through the hatch. It rose until she saw Arvid, on the landing, put his free hand over his own mouth. Then she stopped.

Renwick sent the guard down with him. "Take those off him and give them here. Then you can wait outside with the others. Thank you."

The guard unlocked the cuffs. Arvid rubbed his wrist but remained on the bottom step. Renwick put the cuffs in his pocket.

"He's been here all this time?" Mabry asked.

Her father looked at her. "He's been fed. He's had a bed, and I had a doctor look at his chest in March. Nobody's been unkind to him. I needed something she'd listen to, that's all."

"You were going to kill her tonight."

"Afterwards he could have gone wherever he liked. I'd have bought his ticket myself."

Viveca went slowly out into the hall toward her husband. "They told me you were burned. That there wasn't anything to see. I kept thinking you must have been calling for me."

Arvid looked at Renwick. "You said she was dead."

"Things can be put right," Renwick said. "The two of you could have a house. I have work again, if you want it, Viveca. Good work."

Mabry opened the front door. Wind forced rain across the tiles. Beyond the steps, the drivers stood smoking beneath the shallow porch roof. She couldn't send Arvid into them. She closed the door and turned back to her father.

"Tell them to go."

"Sweetheart, this has nothing to do with you."

"You gave me the money. You gave me the fucking keys."

Viveca was smoothing the front of Arvid's shirt. He held himself very still.

"Tell them," she said to Renwick. "So he can see nobody's keeping him here."

Renwick went to the parlour window and signalled. Viveca brought Arvid in to watch. Two cars drove away. The guard joined the remaining driver, who moved his car round the corner, out of view. Mabry waited until she heard its engine stop. They could get Arvid out the other way, if they were quick.

Viveca's hand settled at the back of Arvid's neck.

"I'll cut your hair," she said. "When we get home."

He ducked his head away from her hand. "Please don't touch me yet."

She let him move away. "All right."

Mabry had expected tears, an embrace, some private thing she would have to look away from. Arvid kept watching the front door. She recognized that look. She had checked the office clock in the same way all week, measuring the hours until her train.

"You can go," she told him. "I'll come with you."

Viveca turned toward her. "He doesn't have a coat."

"He can have mine."

Mabry took it off and carried it into the parlour. The ticket fell from its pocket. Her father bent for it, then winced and left it on the floor.

Arvid accepted the coat, and Mabry went back to the front door. As he pushed his arms into the sleeves, Viveca went to the parlour doorway, between him and Mabry.

"I waited eighteen months," she said. "I thought you were in the ground."

"I know."

"We can leave. Right now. You said you wanted to get away from this city."

He worked at the top button of Mabry's coat. His fingers wouldn't manage it.

"I said I wanted to leave you."

Viveca didn't answer, and her husband kept talking.

"Before any of this. At the kitchen table. I told you."

"You were upset."

"I bought a ticket. I packed my things."

Mabry opened the door again. The porch was empty. No one moved to stop her. Across the hall, the bolt on the dining-room door was two steps away.

Arvid looked at the gap between his wife and the doorframe.

"Will you move, please?"

Viveca's bare foot slid back. He hesitated, then stepped past her into the hall. Mabry caught his elbow and guided him toward the open door.

"Arvid."

He turned. Viveca stood several paces away, with the knife down by her leg.

"If you go now, I won't know where you are."

He rubbed his newly freed wrist. "That's what I want."

Viveca stood still long enough for Mabry to hear a car door slam round the corner. Arvid took another step toward the street. Mabry went with him.

Viveca came up behind them and pushed the front door shut over Mabry's shoulder.

Mabry reached for the latch. The blade struck her forearm. At first it seemed like a hard slap. Then her sleeve opened and blood ran over her hand.

Arvid said his wife's name. She turned him by the shoulder, almost tenderly, and drove the knife into him below the ribs.

Mabry seized her wrist. Viveca wrenched free. The torn sleeve dragged across the wound; Mabry's knees struck the floor. Above her, Arvid caught at the red dress. He wasn't holding Viveca. He was trying to keep himself upright.

She pulled the blade out and put it into him again.

When they fell, she went down beneath him, cradling his head against her shoulder. His breath rattled close to Mabry's ear. He had lost a slipper. One thin foot scraped the flowered carpet and stopped.

Renwick said, "Oh, Jesus Christ."

Mabry crawled to the front door. Viveca was whispering into Arvid's hair. Mabry couldn't hear the words and didn't try.

She got the door open with her good hand.

"Mabry. Stay here."

Viveca was looking at her over the dead man's shoulder. Mabry turned away and lifted the bolt across the hall.

***

There were seven people in the dining room. They stared at Mabry's bleeding arm.

"Go," she said.

The woman from the car pushed forward. Mabry held her bound hands against the doorframe and worried the loosened knot apart. This time, when the woman tried to pull away, she let her. The cord fell at their feet.

"The front," Mabry said. "They're round the corner. Run the other way."

The woman went. Three others followed, knocking against one another in the narrow hall. Renwick caught Mabry's shoulder as she turned back for the rest.

"Come away from there."

She hit him in the cut arm. He let go with a shout. For once she didn't look to see how badly he was hurt.

The last prisoner was an old man with his ankles tied together. Mabry knelt, pulling at the wet cord. He kept saying sorry for making her wait. She could hear her father behind her, breathing through his teeth.

"Get the cars," Viveca said.

Mabry looked back. Arvid lay alone on the carpet. Viveca stood beside Renwick with her blade against his throat and his shirt gripped below the collar.

"Call them off," Mabry said to him. "Please. Let us go."

Her father's eyes dropped to the old man, then returned to her face.

"She's my daughter," he told Viveca.

"Then bring her back. I want her here."

"If they bring her, you leave her alone."

Viveca moved the knife enough to let him swallow. "You can look after her yourself."

Mabry tore the cord over the old man's heel. He kicked his other foot loose. Together they lurched through the front door, her arm under his, into rain so thick the parked cars looked empty.

Behind them her father shouted for the drivers.

"Mabry! Bring my daughter back. Nobody hurts her. Do you hear me?"

She took the old man to the corner. The woman from the car was waiting there, bent over with her hands on her knees. She straightened when she saw them and took his arm.

For a moment Mabry reached toward her. The woman backed away.

"You work there," she said.

"Yes."

The woman turned with the old man and went down the narrow passage beside the hotel. He was dragging one foot. They couldn't outrun the two men coming round the corner. Mabry stayed at the passage mouth, and the first man to reach her ran into her outstretched arms. She clawed his face with her good hand and screamed hard enough to hurt her throat.

His companion caught her from behind. They carried her to the car and took the office keys from her pocket. Through the open door she could see the passage. No one else came out.

***

The car took her back to the office, and they put her in Viveca's room. Her father brought a doctor upstairs. The doctor stitched her arm and accepted an envelope without looking inside. Then Renwick washed the blood from her fingers. He had done the same thing when she cut her hand on a broken glass at nine. This time he had to hold her wrist.

Outside, the rain was easing. The red sign showed through the wired glass. Viveca stood in the corridor wearing a man's overcoat over her dress. There were dirty crescents under her bare toenails. Mabry could see them from the bed.

"The others got away," Mabry said.

Renwick wrung out the cloth. "We'll talk when you've had some sleep."

"I want to leave."

He laid the cloth in the basin. For several seconds neither of them moved. The room was open, and her father's hand was empty.

"Dad."

He got up. Viveca held out her palm for the keys. He put them into it and stepped into the corridor beside her.

Mabry was still looking at him when Viveca shut the door.

stories.title: Between the Colors
stories.prompt: Your green eye sees the future; your blue eye sees the past. In a cruel twist of fate, you are blind to the present.
stories.body:
# Between the Colors

Twenty minutes before the roof fell, I walked into the theatre's closed door.

My blue eye had shown it open. Through the green, the door was gone, and the lintel above it was feeding a small yellow flame. I had been watching the flame when my nose struck the wood.

Inside, my brother swore. The latch rattled.

“Iseth? Why didn't you knock?”

“Your roof's coming down.”

He took my wrist. I recognized the rough patch below his thumb, where he held the carving knife, and let him draw me inside. My cane struck the doorpost. Neither eye showed his hand on me.

“How much of it?” he asked.

I closed the blue eye. The little auditorium lay under a mesh of fallen beams. Smoke drifted through the opening above the stage. Our painted moon, which had survived three changes of emperor in the plays, lay face down among the seats.

“The part over the audience. Berian, get out.”

“I've already sent for the watch. A lamp went over behind the screen. I thought I'd put it out, but it's in the wall.”

Now that the door was open, I could smell it. Under the theatre's familiar glue and dust was something sharp enough to reach the back of my throat.

“Who's here?”

“Only me. I was getting your things together.”

He had asked me to come at four. One last afternoon dividing what could be sold, what could be kept, what neither of us could bear to discuss. I had brought wrapping cloth. It hung from my shoulder in a bag, absurdly clean.

Berian tapped the wall twice, our old signal, and I followed the sound toward the stage.

There are people who find my eyes useful. A green eye looking twenty minutes ahead, a blue eye twenty minutes behind: merchants hear that and start proposing arrangements. Then a chair moves between the two views and I fall over it. They seldom propose a second meeting.

Nothing I do brings the images closer. If I stand in a street, I see that street as it was and as it will be. Its old walls hide its old rooms; its future walls hide its future rooms. I cannot look around a corner without taking my body around it. The sounds belong to now. So do splinters, boiling kettles, and a hand held out for me to take.

Berian learned the distinction before he could read. He used to sit beneath the kitchen table and tap a spoon against a leg while I crawled toward him. When I found him, he would announce some enormous prize: a kingdom, six elephants, the moon. Usually I received half a biscuit.

At thirty-four, I still followed his taps before I thought about following them.

“The upstairs rooms?” I asked.

“Empty.”

“Tesset?”

“Finished on Monday.”

“Did you pay her?”

His next tap came from farther away.

“I'm trying to save your puppets.”

I stopped. In my blue eye, the boards ahead were clear. In my green, one of the roof beams lay across them. The cane found a heap of fabric that belonged to neither picture.

“Leave them. We need to warn the shops.”

“I told you, I've sent someone.”

“Who?”

A cough came from above us. Then a woman's voice, muffled by the ceiling.

“Berian? There's smoke up here.”

His shoe scraped the floor.

“I thought she'd gone.”

“You said she finished on Monday.”

“She did. I didn't know she'd come back.”

He was moving while he spoke. I heard the backstage door bang and his feet on the narrow stairs beyond it.

I went back to the street, sweeping my cane low, and shouted fire until another voice took up the word. A man wanted to know where. I pointed behind me and struck the doorframe hard enough to hurt my knuckles.

“Here. Here.”

There were footsteps, a dropped object, someone yelling for the watch bell. I stayed long enough to hear the bell begin. Then I went inside again.

I had moved away from the theatre three years earlier, after our mother died. Berian had stayed. He wrote new plays for fewer children and charged less whenever a parent hesitated over the price. He had always been extravagant with things that were nearly gone: money, candles, his own patience. On good afternoons I could sit behind the screen and supply all the voices while he moved the figures. On bad ones he would ask me to look at tomorrow, though I could no more look a day ahead than he could.

Now my green eye showed the painted screen burning. I shut it. The old auditorium in the blue was so peaceful that I shut that too.

“Tesset,” I called. “Can you hear me?”

Something heavy struck the floor upstairs. She cried out. I heard Berian say her name, and then the tinny jangle of coins.

“Are you at the window?” I asked.

No answer reached me. The backstage door was hot against my wrist. I found its handle with my sleeve over my hand and pushed it open.

The stairs were where they had always been. So was the third tread that tipped forward when stepped on. I knew these things with my feet, which was different from knowing whether there was something on the fourth step now.

There was. My cane caught under it, and I nearly followed the cane down.

“Stay there!” Berian shouted.

His steps came toward me. He was coughing, and I heard his shoulder drag along the wall as he felt his way down.

“Where is she?”

“Out. She's out through the window.”

The dressing-room window opened above the upholsterer's low awning. I had climbed down that way at fourteen to avoid a visiting aunt who wanted to pray over my eyes. Berian had lowered me by the wrists until my feet found the awning frame.

“Can you get down the stairs?” I asked him.

“Yes. Move back. I have the box.”

I put a hand on the wall and felt my way down. Above me he made a short, startled noise. Something struck the treads in several hard blows, then his weight hit my shoulder and drove me against the door.

For a moment all I could hear was his breathing. He had my arm in both hands.

“My ankle,” he said. “Don't pull. Don't.”

“I haven't pulled anything.”

He gave an odd little laugh that turned into coughing.

I could not see him sprawled on the steps. Through the blue eye, the staircase was empty. Through the green, the upper part had fallen away. His head might have been bleeding. His foot might have been pointing in the wrong direction. I had the pressure of his fingers and his breath against my neck, and I had to choose what to do with those.

“Let go of my arm. Put yours over my shoulders.”

He was heavier than I remembered. We got him down one step, rested, then another. He tried to help and made a sound I had never heard from him, thin and furious. By the time we reached the street I could no longer feel the shoulder under his arm.

People took his weight. Someone asked if there was anybody left inside.

“No,” I said.

From above came a frantic banging, followed by Tesset shouting my brother's name.

I turned toward her voice. The green eye showed a broken window with smoke pouring out. The blue showed glass reflecting afternoon light. Neither showed her.

“She's still there.”

Berian was coughing too hard to answer.

“You told me she was out.”

“I thought she could get out.”

“You said—”

“There was smoke. I couldn't reach her. I called to her to use the window.”

Her fist struck wood again. Each blow sounded weaker than the one before it.

A stranger told me to wait for the watch. Another said there was a ladder in the next yard. I caught that voice and made him repeat it.

“Bring it to the upstairs window,” I said.

“Where are you going?” Berian asked.

I had already found the doorpost with my cane.

He called me by the name he used when we were children, a small foolish shortening that nobody else knew. I kept going.

Inside, I had to crouch to breathe. The carpet had bunched across the aisle; I found its ridge on my knees. From this height, the future view was mostly a blackened beam that would eventually lie inches from my face. I closed both eyes and went by touch.

At the stairs I called up to Tesset.

“Talk to me.”

“My foot. There's a rail on it.”

“The costume rail?”

“Yes. He knocked it. I can't—”

She coughed for so long that I thought she had stopped being able to breathe.

“Keep making a noise,” I said. “Anything.”

She began to bang again. I went up toward it, pushing the fallen object on the fourth step aside with my shoulder. It rolled with a wooden rattle; my fingers found a splintered stool leg. My cane had stayed behind somewhere. I did not remember letting go of it.

At the top, cooler air brushed my forehead. I crawled into it. Tesset caught my sleeve before I found her.

“Can you see?” she asked.

“No.”
