Her fingers tightened. I could have given her the longer answer, but she was trying to put my hand where it was needed.

Tesset guided my hands along the fallen costume rail, explaining between coughs. One iron foot pinned her ankle; the other was caught under a bench. She was sitting beneath the open window, bent around the trapped leg. When I touched her cheek by mistake, it was wet.

We tried lifting together. The rail scarcely moved. Tesset let out an angry sob and struck it with her free hand.

“He said come back today. He said I'd get all of it.”

“What?”

“My wages.”

There was a hot rush behind me. I leaned over her and felt the heat pass across my back.

“Tell me where the bench is.”

She put my wrist against its edge. We changed our positions in a series of awkward, frightened movements. I pressed my shoulder under the rail while she worked her heel sideways. Something at my left palm hurt; I ignored it until the hurt became too large to ignore, and by then she was free.

She said, “I've got it out,” twice before I understood.

Below the window, someone shouted that the ladder was ready. A wooden end struck the sill. I began to stand and hit my head on the rail.

“Wait,” Tesset said. “Wait. Give me your hand.”

She placed my good hand on the window frame. Then she climbed past me, gasping each time she put weight on the injured foot. I held the back of her dress until somebody below said he had her.

It was Berian's voice.

When my turn came, I could not find the first rung. I put my foot out into air, withdrew it, tried again. The two images beyond my eyelids would have given me an empty wall and a smoking ruin. I kept them shut.

Tap. Tap.

“Below your right foot,” Berian said. “A little to the left. That's it.”

He stayed there, counting me down, while strangers held the ladder. At the bottom he put his hand over mine. I felt the familiar rough patch and started crying so abruptly I could not stop.

He said my name. Only that, several times.

Behind us the building made a long noise, almost leisurely, and the crowd drew back. Someone carried me far enough that fragments struck the street without striking me.

Twenty minutes had passed since I walked into the door. I knew because, when I opened my blue eye, I could see myself arriving across the street: the bag of wrapping cloth, my cane, the white lock escaping from my red braid. The earlier Iseth hesitated outside the theatre, then disappeared behind the open door as Berian pulled her in.

I wanted to call to her. I had wanted that often enough to know better.

The green eye showed watchmen moving through a black shell. It showed daylight where there should have been a roof. It gave me no reason the fire had begun, no measure of what either rescue had cost.

A woman washed my hand and wrapped it. I felt each turn of the cloth. She told me not to touch the burn, and I told her I wasn't touching it, and she apologized because apparently I had only been reaching for my other sleeve.

Across the street, Tesset was arguing with someone who wanted to cut away her shoe.

“I can't buy another pair.”

Then, after a pause, more quietly: “All right. Cut it.”

Berian sat down beside me with a grunt. There was a metallic click at his knees.

“The moneybox?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“Give Tesset what you owe her.”

“I will.”

“Now.”

He did not answer. I could hear the watchmen shouting to one another, the scrape of debris being dragged from the doorway. The fire still crackled, but its hungry roaring had subsided.

“It's all gone,” Berian said.

I turned my head toward the dressing-room window. In the blue eye, it was shut. Soon I would see it open. Soon I would see her calling for us while I was helping him down the stairs.

“The moon, too?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Mother would have hated that.”

I said nothing. His knuckles brushed mine, then wool rasped beside me. Once, when I was small, he had spent a whole evening cutting a second moon because I had cried at the part of the play where the first one was swallowed. Our mother had told him that children must learn how a story ended. He had made the spare anyway.

“I went back for her,” he said. “You know I went back.”

“I heard you.”

“You know that room. Two rails of costumes, the dressing table, that bench nobody's shifted since Mother. The big rail had come down across the lot, and the smoke was so thick I was feeling for things with my shins. I shouted myself hoarse. I couldn't get near her, Iseth. Not without climbing over the whole wardrobe.”

I could imagine it. Smoke made people stupid; fear made them say things they wished were true. He had hurt his ankle, and afterward he had stayed beneath a burning wall to bring us down. I wanted those facts to make one person, somebody I could take home and be angry with for a long time.

“Why was she there?” I asked.

“I told you. I didn't know she'd come back.”

“She said you told her to come today.”

He drew in a breath.

“There were things to settle. Her last week, her key, a cloak she's wanted cheap since spring. She went up to fold the good costumes, and when it went quiet I thought she'd done and gone, let herself out the back the way she always does. You remember how she—”

“Her wages,” I said.

“That too. Of course that too. I was downstairs, Iseth. I was down there with your puppets.”

An iron buckle knocked against something near my knee. A watchman introduced himself by his office and asked if I owned the theatre.

“We both do,” Berian said.

“I was asking your sister.”

“Half,” I said. “My brother has the other half.”

The watchman asked about the lamp. Berian began describing where it had stood and what had knocked it over, and his voice found a steadier rhythm. “Brass, about so high, on the shelf behind the screen. That shelf has always leaned. I've been meaning to take it down for years.” He began giving dimensions; his sleeve brushed the watchman's coat, and I imagined his hands making their familiar shapes. I remembered the way he could make a whole stage out of a kitchen table if a listener would let him.

The window opened in my blue eye.

Tesset pushed it out and bent forward. Her mouth was moving. I could not hear what she had said twenty minutes earlier; I could hear Berian now, describing the overturned lamp.

Smoke passed behind the woman at the window. Then my brother appeared beside her.

He was close enough to help her.

I watched his hands take hold of the little moneybox she carried. For a moment they both held it. Tesset pulled it toward herself, and he pulled harder. Her mouth opened. He got the box away from her.

She reached after him. He backed into the room, striking the costume rail with his hip. It tipped. She went down out of sight.

The earlier Berian looked toward the floor. He took a step forward. He stopped.

All this time the present Berian was talking beside me. Something about the oil. Something about how quickly the fire had spread.

At the window, his earlier face turned toward the stairs. He left with the box.

“You reached her,” I said.

Both men fell silent.

“Iseth?”

“You said you couldn't get near her.”

His hand came onto my sleeve. I felt him begin to turn my shoulders away from the theatre, then stop himself.

“What are you looking at?”

“The window.”

“Which eye?”

His grip loosened before I answered.

“Twenty minutes ago.”

The buckle knocked again as the watchman moved closer.

Berian said, “I was going to come back.”

I remembered his arm across my shoulders. His assurance that she was out. My own voice telling the strangers there was nobody left inside. He had let me say it.

“You took the box,” I said. “The rail fell. You saw her fall.”

“I panicked.”

That might have been true. It did not change any of the things I had seen.

“She had hold of it,” he said. “I told her to let go. I didn't mean—”

The watchman asked him to put the box on the ground.

“My sister knows me.”

I shut the blue eye. I did not want to go on watching the window. But closing it did nothing to the voice beside me, or the wrapped hand in my lap, or Tesset coughing across the street.

“Iseth. Tell him I helped you down.”

“He did,” I told the watchman. “He guided me down. After we got her free.”

My brother's hand tightened once on my sleeve.

“Before that,” I said, “he left her upstairs. I saw him leave.”

The watchman made him let go of me. Cloth slipped across the bandage, and the pain was so immediate that I bent over it. I could still hear Berian. He was asking to speak to me alone.

If I stayed here, in twenty minutes I could see the face he was making.

“Take him somewhere else,” I said.

stories.title: A Bargain with Anubis
stories.prompt: A pharaoh steals the Emerald Relic from Anubis to keep his dying daughter alive. Now nothing in Egypt can die—not the sick, not the slaughtered cattle, not the locusts devouring the fields. As prayers for deliverance fill his temple, Anubis sets out to reclaim the relic. The girl is waiting for him at the palace gates. She has a proposal her father must never hear.
stories.body:
# A Bargain with Anubis

Taremet had to tell the bearers twice to put her down outside the gates. They stood with the litter on their shoulders, looking at the open bronze doors as though she had mistaken which side of them was safe.

“Here. Where the stone is level.”

They lowered her so carefully that she could not blame them for the pain. She waited for it to settle before dismissing them to the guardhouse. At twenty-two she had commanded hunting parties and disputed her father's appointments; now every order had to survive a discussion of whether she needed another cushion. She sent the cushions away too. She wanted to see who approached.

A locust had caught in the fringe of her shawl. One wing was folded wrong, and a hind leg dragged. She loosened the thread with her nail. Released, it struggled a little farther into the wool.

Beyond the palace wall, a cow cried from the slaughter yard. There had been no slaughter since yesterday, but the cattle struck down before the prohibition were still there. The men had laid fodder beside them. A kitchen girl had told Taremet this while changing her sheets, then begged her not to tell the king who had spoken.

From the temple across the avenue came the uneven rise of prayers. People had begun carrying their sick there when no one died at home. Now the steps were crowded with bedding. Under the nearest torch a woman sat with her eyes shut, still moving a damp cloth over the mouth of the man beside her. A boy came down the steps with a loaf. He tried to give it to her, then stood holding it against his chest. She had not seen him.

Taremet had been allowed to rest between her bad hours. Someone else always came to turn her, to bring clean linen. Across the avenue the boy put the bread down and took the cloth. The woman kept moving her empty hand until he caught it.

Farther out, beyond anything she could see, locusts were eating the fields. Soldiers trampled them. They crawled out of the footprints and ate again. Fire had not killed them either, a messenger had told her father. He had brought a sackful as proof; even tied shut, it traveled across the floor. She had watched from her bed while her father ordered it taken away.

She had asked her father whether the reports were true. He had said the royal grain stores were open.

The prayers changed. Voices called the same name together, then broke apart into separate appeals. A tall figure came up the avenue, passing through the torchlight without a guard before him. Gold lay across his shoulders. His jackal ears stood erect, and his black muzzle turned toward the slaughter yard before he looked at her.

Taremet tried to sit straighter. The effort took the breath she had saved for his name.

He stopped beside the litter. Beneath his collar his chest moved. She had expected the painted stillness of the shrine; instead there was the small sound of air through his nostrils, and dust on his feet.

“Anubis,” she managed.

“You should not have been carried this far.”

She disliked him for saying it. Everyone said it. She pressed her palm against the place under her ribs where the pain sharpened and waited until she could speak without gasping.

“You're going in to find what he took.”

“Yes.”

“He won't give it back.”

Anubis looked toward the open doors. The guards had withdrawn into their house. Taremet could see one man's white skirt beyond its threshold, motionless.

“Can't you just take it from him?”

“He has threatened to break it and send the pieces away.”

“Would that end this?”

“It would leave my power bound in the pieces. I would have to find and join them before I could release Egypt.”

Since her father came back from the temple, riders had waited saddled in the courtyard below her window. She had listened to their horses shifting on the stones all afternoon while he slept in the chair beside her.

“I can get him to show it to me,” she said. “I haven't asked yet.”

That brought the god's attention back from the doors. He crouched beside her, his gold ornaments settling with a heavy, intimate noise. His face was level with hers. There were grey hairs under his jaw.

“What do you ask in return?”

She had rehearsed an offer of access, a demand for secrecy, a declaration that she was acting for Egypt. In front of him, with the cow beginning again, the declaration became impossible to say.

“I want it to stop hurting.”

He did not reach for her or promise anything.

“When I recover the relic, you will be able to die. I cannot tell you how soon.”

“And the others?”

“Those whose bodies can no longer sustain them will die. The rest will live as they lived before.”

She worked a fold of shawl between her fingers. “Could you leave just me as I am? For a while?”

“No.”

She had imagined herself resting afterward, the noises quiet, her father beside her, with no need to decide anything more that night. She had hardly let herself imagine the empty bed.

“He says the physicians need time.”

“What do the physicians say to you?”

“They ask whether I've eaten.” She swallowed. “Will it be all at once? The people who should have died?”

“Some at once.”

The locust pulled against her thumb. She took her hand away. There would be children among them. There would be people whose families had thanked her father. She could not make the return of death into an event everyone would welcome.

“He mustn't know I helped you.”

Anubis waited.

“Not afterward either. When he dies and you receive him, you mustn't tell him then.”

“You ask me to keep this from him forever.”

“Yes.”

“I cannot prevent him from discovering it himself.”

She glanced toward the guardhouse. “They only know I came out for air. He'll believe that.”

“And if he asks you?”

Taremet pulled the shawl higher. The wool scraped her chin. When she was small, her father had delighted in catching her lies: fruit juice on a sleeve, a forbidden dog under the bed. Later he had stopped searching her face. If she told him where she had ridden or whom she had met, that was where she had been. She had liked that more than the freedom.

“I won't tell him.”

She rubbed her eyes with the heel of her hand. “He'd think I didn't trust him to find something. And he's been trying. He hardly leaves me.”

Anubis waited while she pulled a loose thread from the shawl. She wound it tight around one finger, then unwound it.

“Sometimes I pretend it hurts less when he comes in.”

“Does he believe you?”

“He sits down. We can talk about something else.”

Anubis laid one hand on the litter's wooden rail. She could have set hers beside it. She wanted some sign that he approved, then resented wanting that from a stranger who would not even say whether her dying would hurt.

“Will you do it?” she asked.

“I will not reveal your part.”

“Promise me.”

“By the office in which I receive your dead, I promise.”

“What does it look like?” she asked. “He only calls it the Emerald Relic.”

“A stone jaw. Black, with green teeth. Small enough to hold in both hands. I breathe power through it to hold back death while I tend those who are passing. Until I draw that breath back through it, nothing here can finish dying.”

“So even now you're keeping us here?”

His fingers tightened on the rail. “He has trapped my power there.”

For the first time she noticed how stiffly he was crouching.

She described the garden door of her bedchamber, the reed screen inside it, the little table at her right hand. Her father sat on her left, where the chair had room. She would have the door left unlatched. Anubis must come through the garden, wait behind the screen, and put out his hand only when hers appeared around its edge.

“I may be slow,” she said.

“I will wait.”

She shut her eyes briefly. The prayer she had come to make was finished. Now she had to get back to her room.

He rose and went along the wall toward the gardens. Taremet waited until she could no longer hear his steps, then raised her hand for the bearers. They came running.

By the time they carried her into the bedchamber, Pharaoh Khaseb was awake and standing in the doorway without his sandals.

“Who ordered this?”

“I did.”

He looked past her at the bearers. She said his name, an indulgence allowed her since childhood, and he looked back.

“I wanted air.”

“Then we open a door. We don't carry you down half the palace.” He bent over the litter. “Can you stand?”

“No.”

He helped lift her. She kept her mouth against his shoulder while the attendants moved her legs onto the mattress. For a moment she could smell only his skin and the old linen of his sleeping robe. She wanted to stay there. He drew back before she was ready and tilted her face toward the lamp.

“The garden door,” she said. “Leave it open.”

An attendant pushed it inward and returned the screen to its place, shielding the bed from the doorway. Its near edge stood just beyond the outer rim of the bedside table. Then Khaseb sent everyone out. He had learned to settle her himself, and did not like other hands doing it badly.

The locust had traveled in her shawl. He found it when he took the wool away.

“Another one.” He caught it gently between finger and thumb, saw its dragging leg, and put it in an empty brass cup on the bedside table. “I'll have someone take that out.”

She watched him. “They can't even burn them in the fields.”

“I know.”

“Did you see?”

He pulled the sheet over her feet. “I was told. You need to sleep. Let them bring their complaints to me.”

“I can hear the cattle from this bed.”

He tucked the sheet under one swollen heel and she flinched. At once he loosened it and slipped a rolled towel beneath her calf.

“Here?”

“Closer to my knee.”

He moved it. “Here?”

She nodded. He cupped her heel until the tightness in her face eased, then lowered it onto the sheet.

Three nights before, he had come into the room with blood dried on his forearm and told her she was safe. He had left his crown somewhere. She had thought the physicians had found something, and cried because she would live. Only in the morning had she learned that he had gone into Anubis's temple and carried the relic from the shrine himself.

“Does your arm still hurt?” she asked.

He glanced at the healing cut. “Nothing much.”

“How did you do it?”

“A hinge on the shrine door. I didn't feel it until afterward.” He settled into the chair. “You slept nearly an hour that night without waking. I sat right here. An hour.”

She remembered pretending to be asleep the following night, while he held her wrist and counted. She had been afraid that if she moved, the pain would take her again.

He found the knucklebones on the stool beside his chair. “One throw?”

“You can.”

“It isn't much of a game by myself.”

“You like winning.”

“I like beating you. There's a difference.” He shook them, waiting for her smile. She gave him one. “There. Shall I throw for you?”

“You'll give me the bad cast.”

“You've never needed my help with that.”

It should have annoyed her. Usually he kept a tally of her worst throws for weeks, long after she had forgotten her own wins. Tonight she wanted him to keep talking. Instead she asked to see what he had brought from the temple.

His hand closed over the bones.

“Why?”

“You keep saying it's made me better. I haven't even seen it.”

“You went to the gates tonight.”

“They carried me.”

“You wanted to go. Yesterday you wouldn't look out of the window.”

She could tell him how much the journey had hurt. He was watching her so hopefully that she let it pass. He put the game away and stood, smiling now.

“Wait here.”

“Where would I go?”

“Apparently anywhere.”

He went into the dressing chamber. She heard a lid open, the scrape of something heavy. At the garden door the screen remained still. It had painted birds on it, their beaks worn away where servants gripped the frame. She stared at one of them until her father returned carrying a black linen bundle.

He laid it on the table and uncovered the jaw, setting the brass cup on a corner of the spread linen to make room.

The teeth were emerald, their points uneven. Gold filled old fractures in the black stone beneath them. Green light spilled over his fingertips and showed the deep hollows on either side of his mouth. He had looked younger by the lamp.

“Touch it,” he said.

She put her fingers against the curved underside. Cold, smooth, astonishingly ordinary. He raised it so she could feel its weight, but did not let go when her wrists sagged.

“Careful.”

He lowered it again. She kept her hand on the cloth under it.

“He's coming for it,” she said.

“Let him come.”

“You can't keep him outside.”

“I don't intend to. If he wants it whole, he can wait until you're well.”

Taremet looked at the gold seams. Her father folded the linen over the teeth, extinguishing their light.

“I know what they say in his temple,” he said. “I have stopped the slaughter. There is grain enough for now. Your physicians are still working. Three days, and already they speak as though I mean to leave things like this forever.”

“What if it takes longer?”

“Then it takes longer.”

He saw her face and knelt beside the bed, on her left by his chair.

“You were cold,” he said. “That night before I went. I could feel you getting colder while I held you.”

She remembered his hands rubbing her arms, too hard, and how she had lacked the breath to ask him to stop.

“I wasn't going to sit there again.”

He kissed the fingers of her left hand. Her right still lay on the linen beside the wrapped relic, within reach. Behind the screen, a shadow crossed the garden doorway, where the first grey of morning had begun to show.

“Father.”

“What is it?”

There was still time to send Anubis away. She could say she was tired, let her father lock the jaw away, and wait for morning. Someone would wash her. Someone would take the cup out. Her father would offer the knucklebones again.

“The fastening at my neck. It's rubbing.”

He sat on the mattress to her left and helped her upright. Her sleeping dress had a clasp at the back; he usually undid it when she was too sore to lie down. She turned into his chest, her back toward the table, and left her right hand on the cloth behind her.

He bent his face beside hers as he felt for the clasp. Her shoulder hid her right arm from him. She eased her hand around the screen's near edge, only a finger's length beyond it, and touched warm skin.

Then she brought her hand back to the bundle.

Khaseb was working at the clasp with one hand, supporting her back with the other. “Your hair's caught. Hold still.”

She tried to push the wrapped jaw across the table. It was heavier than she remembered; she had felt only what her father allowed her to feel. The linen bunched beneath it. She could not turn far enough to straighten it without pulling away from him.

The clasp tugged her hair.

“Ow.”

“I'm sorry. Nearly done.”

Her fingers slipped off the cloth and struck the cup with a small brass knock. Inside it the locust scratched.

“What are you reaching for?”

“I need to lean back. A little toward the table.”

He moved his arm lower and shifted her to the right, taking her weight on his forearm. Her elbow reached the tabletop. With her forearm resting on it, she could push the jaw toward the gap beside the screen. It moved a hand's breadth, then stopped. The cloth had caught under the cup.

Her father freed the clasp. “There. Better?”

She lifted the cup clear of the linen and set it nearer the bed. When she pushed the bundle again, Anubis's hand closed over its far end.

For a moment she was holding it with him. She could still pull it back. Her father's thumb moved over the sore place at her neck, checking the skin. She opened her hand.

The bundle vanished behind the screen. She snatched her empty hand back, lost the support of the tabletop, and tipped backward. Khaseb caught her.

“I've got you.”

She buried her face against him. He held her there, one hand cupping the back of her head.

Gold clicked beyond her shoulder. She lifted her head. Anubis was coming around the screen, and her father's gaze followed hers to the black bundle. His whole body stiffened against her.

“Put that down.”

Anubis uncovered the jaw.

Khaseb started to rise. Her weight checked him; he glanced at the pillows, then drew her close again.

“Guards!”

The door from the passage opened. Two men crowded into it and stopped at the sight of the god.

“Get it from him.”

Anubis lifted the jaw to his muzzle and drew a long breath through the emerald teeth. For a moment the green light shone through his fingers, bright enough to show the veins, and then it contracted along the gold seams and went out.

The locust fell onto its back in the cup. Its legs folded and did not open.

Taremet waited for a blow, a fall, some unmistakable change inside her. Her father was still holding her. Her dress hung loose at the throat. Beyond the garden a bird called, then called again. The cow had gone quiet.

“What have you done?” Khaseb said.

Anubis lowered the jaw. “Ended the working.”

“She was getting well.”

Her father pressed his cheek against her forehead, testing for something. She wanted to move her face to his, but her neck would not hold it up.

“Taremet. Tell him.”

She drew breath. It was no easier than before. She had thought there would be ease.

“Tell him you went out tonight.”

Anubis stood with the relic resting in both hands. He could explain. It would take so little speech to turn her father's face toward hers and change it forever.

“She couldn't even stand,” Khaseb said to him. “You came through her garden. You waited until I had my hands full of her.”

The god said nothing.

Her father rocked her once, trying to find a position in which she could breathe. “Do it again. Whatever you did at the shrine. I will return it afterward myself.”

“No.”

“Look at her.”

Anubis did. She wished he would go.

Khaseb called for the physician. One guard left; the other stayed at the door with his spear lowered. Her father rubbed her arm, and she made a small sound.

“What? Tell me.”

“Don't rub.”

He stopped at once. The place his hand had warmed cooled slowly through the linen.

He bent his head to hear what she might say next. She could see a strand of her hair caught in his beard.

“Will you kiss me?”

He kissed her forehead. She tried to reach his cheek with her mouth. He turned, holding still while she managed it.

Then he looked past her.

“You stole this from her,” he said.

She tried to find the warm hollow below his chin. He lifted her a little higher, and she was there. His beard scratched her temple. He was still holding the back of her head when the next breath did not come.

stories.title: A Place for Sunday
stories.prompt: When you left your seaside village, your father promised to keep your place at the table. Years later, you have a little girl of your own and can rarely afford the journey home. Then, one morning, you open your door to find the village settling into the fields outside the city—and your father coming up the path, asking what his granddaughter likes for Sunday brunch.
stories.body:
# A Place for Sunday

Ilario was shaking the crumbs from the bread bag when he smelled his father's garden.

The kitchen window was open. Usually the morning came through it smelling of the horse chestnuts along the lane, or of somebody else's breakfast. Today there was thyme, warm dust, the bitter green smell of a fig leaf snapped at its stem. He stood with the empty bag over the breadboard and breathed again.

From the next room, Nerina called, "The ribbon's gone."

"Look in your shoe."

"Why would it be in my shoe?"

"You put it there last night. You said you'd remember."

A pause. Then, "I have remembered."

He smiled and folded the bag. They had enough bread for breakfast, cut thin, and afterward they would take their lunch to the bandstand. Nerina had spent the week trying to whistle like a flute. At six, she could sustain a great many activities without becoming discouraged by their results.

On the mantelpiece, behind the clock, was an envelope containing the money for their next journey to the coast. Ilario added to it on paydays when he could. The last time he had counted, it held one adult fare and something toward a child's, with the return journey still to find. There were also the days away from the bindery. A visit short enough to afford would leave them scarcely time to unpack before they had to pack again.

Cosimo's most recent letter lay beside it. He had written that the late figs were coming on and that he had plenty to keep him busy. Nerina had drawn him a picture of the bandstand for their reply, giving each musician an instrument larger than himself. They had both signed it. Ilario hadn't promised a date.

He had been nineteen when he first left. His father had stood beside the kitchen table while he checked his bag for the third time.

"I'll keep your place," Cosimo had said. "Come and eat whenever you can."

He had come back often at first. Then less often, and once with a baby who cried throughout the coach ride and laughed the moment her grandfather took her. On their last visit Nerina had been small enough to sit on Cosimo's forearm. Now her knees stuck out of nearly everything she owned.

Outside, something scraped heavily over stone. Ilario left the bread uncut and went to open the front door.

Across the lane, the field was full of roofs.

Red tiles rose behind the hedge where yesterday there had been stubble. The baker's roof, with its sag in the middle. The little square tower. Three chimneys in a row that he had once believed belonged to a single enormous fireplace. Through a gap between the houses he could see the upper branches of his father's olive tree, trembling although the chestnuts beside the lane were still.

The farthest house was moving. Its yellow walls passed slowly behind the tower; below them, a thick shelf of earth hovered just above the field. People walked beside it with their palms against the stone. A woman at the corner called something, and the others stopped. The house lowered. Leaves shook all down its vine. A soft brown cloud rose where its garden met the stubble.

Ilario gripped the doorframe. He could hear voices, cupboard doors banging, a man's shout to someone on the other side of a wall. He knew that shout. The man had used it to summon his sons from the beach.

And his father was coming up the path.

Cosimo wore the blue shirt with the crooked pocket and carried his hat in one hand. His hair had gone almost entirely white since their last visit. He was looking at the numbers on the doors, counting under his breath, until he saw Ilario.

"There you are," he said. He stopped at the gate and put on his hat, suddenly smiling so broadly that his eyes nearly shut. "What does my granddaughter like for Sunday brunch?"

Ilario went out without his shoes.

He meant to say his father's name, or ask how, but by then Cosimo was holding him. The familiar shoulder was bony under the shirt. His father rubbed his back once, twice, then kept his hand there while Ilario buried his face against his neck. Dust and soap. The very same soap. He held on so tightly that the shirt pulled across his father's back.

"Let me look at you," Cosimo said, though he didn't let go enough to do it. "Ah, my boy."

From the doorway came Nerina's voice.

"Eggs."

Both men turned. She stood in her lavender dress, a pale ribbon tied round her brown hair in a lopsided bow. She had brought her boots in her hands.

"Grandad?"

"Yes, darling."

She dropped her boots on the step and ran to him. Cosimo caught her under the arms and lifted her with an effort that made Ilario reach out, but his father had her safely against his chest already. She took off his hat to kiss his forehead, then put it back crooked.

"I can do the laces now. Papa doesn't have to."

"Show me when I put you down."

"And I like the egg crunchy round the outside."

"Then that's how we'll have it."

Ilario looked over his father's shoulder. Smoke was rising from the bakery chimney. Behind it a cypress tipped slowly upright as the people beside its plot adjusted their hands.

"Papa," he said. "Is that all of it?"

Cosimo followed his gaze. "The tower came in last night. They've only just got the baker down. We had to come round the long way with his oven."

"The whole village?"

"Well, the sea's where we left it." He lowered Nerina to the path. "Your letter said this was your free day. I hoped you hadn't gone out."

"We were going to hear the band," Nerina said. "You can come."

"I'd like that very much."

Ilario laughed then, once, with no breath to sustain it. He took his father's arm and held on while Nerina sat on the step to put on her boots.

"You brought the house."

"And the figs. Go and get your shoes."

***

They crossed the lane together, Nerina swinging between them until she discovered she could lift both feet and be carried. After three swings Cosimo said his arm was getting longer, and she agreed to walk.

The familiar village had come apart into separate pieces. Between the houses lay strips of field, and some of the old lanes ended abruptly at cut edges of earth. Yet the gate outside the bakery still had its rusted bell, and the painted birds over the dressmaker's door were there, and laundry already hung from an upstairs window. Ilario kept turning. A staircase he had climbed a thousand times stood facing him from an entirely new direction.

At the corner of the baker's garden, four people were easing a low stone wall down. One pressed her whole forearm against it while a man crouched to watch the clearance beneath. Their hands brightened faintly, as if sunlight lay under the skin. When the earth touched down, the light faded. The man sat on the wall and accepted a piece of bread from someone who had been waiting with a basket.

Ilario recognized the woman and waved. She waved back before settling beside the man.

"How long have you been coming?" he asked his father.

"Twenty-three mornings. We rested through the hottest part of each day. Those who know the lifting took turns, and the rest of us walked, or rode and kept things from falling. We were all excellent at telling them to go more to the left."

"Twenty-three? Your letter came three weeks ago."

"I posted it before we started. We didn't know which day we'd reach you."

"You might have said something."

"I wanted to see your face." Cosimo glanced at him, plainly satisfied. "Though I nearly wrote again when we spent two days getting the tower past a bend."

They waited while two women guided a shed across the gap ahead. The shed rode low, swaying slightly between their hands. Nerina crouched to see beneath it, and Ilario drew her back. One of the women raised her eyebrows at the child; Nerina gave a vigorous wave from the safe side of his legs.

"Can I ride on one?" she asked.

"You'd be tired of it by the first afternoon," Cosimo said. "We sometimes walked a whole hour and could still see the spot where we'd eaten breakfast."

"I'd like to try."

"I wanted to try, too. Twenty-three mornings ago."

A hen came out of the shed as soon as it settled. She hurried back along its route, stopped where it had stood, and began scratching. Nerina wanted to follow her, but Cosimo promised there would be hens at his house.

"Are you staying?" Ilario asked.

His father looked at him. "Oh, yes. We've rented the fields for five years. The baker's daughter found them. Most of us have someone here now, and there's a market every day. We talked about it all winter. Then someone said we could bring the houses, and after that nobody wanted to talk about packing crates."

Ilario looked back toward his own narrow house. He could see the open shutter of Nerina's bedroom. Fifteen minutes, perhaps, from door to door. Ten on his own. On a weekday he might come after work, tired, carrying nothing, with no tickets in his pocket.

Ahead, an old neighbor stood in the street embracing two grown women at once. He had dropped a cabbage, which a little boy was rolling about with his foot. The dressmaker called Ilario's name from her window and demanded that he bring the child to see her when they'd eaten.

"I'll miss the sea," Cosimo said as they walked on. "I woke up last night and listened for it. There's an owl here instead. Very persistent."

"We hear it. Nerina thinks it's asking her a question."

"It is," Nerina said. "I just don't know what."

His father nodded. At a low green gate he stopped and fumbled for the latch.

Ilario reached past him and lifted the gate a fraction. It opened at once.

"Still doing that, then."

"Worse in wet weather. Come in."

***

The olive tree shaded the doorstep. Ilario brushed a branch with his shoulder, and a dry leaf slipped down inside his collar. He stood under it trying to fish the leaf out, looking at the white wall, the low kitchen window, the lavender growing untidily along the path. He could hear Nerina asking whether the branches were strong enough to climb.

Cosimo went inside to open the back door. Nerina followed him, then came running out again.

"Papa, your picture's in here."

"Which one?"

"When you had those trousers."

There were several possible pictures. He followed her.

The kitchen cupboards had been tied shut with lengths of cloth. A pan and a colander hung from their hooks, bundled together in an apron. Cosimo had kept the table clear except for a bowl of figs, a plate under a cloth, and the batter he must have mixed before coming to fetch them. The small iron stove was already hot. From the window beside it, Ilario could see his own city's roofs instead of the long blue slope of the sea.

He had to look twice.

"Untie that for me," Cosimo said, indicating the pans. "Then you can cut the bread."

Ilario unwrapped the apron, put it on, and reached into the drawer for the knife. His hand found it before he looked. Nerina was standing on tiptoe beneath a little portrait of him at about her age, wearing striped trousers and gripping a wooden horse.

"Did you choose those?"

"I did. I liked the stripes."

"I've still got the horse," Cosimo said. "Remind me after we've eaten. Do you want to choose your egg?"

She turned so quickly she nearly knocked into Ilario. Cosimo held down the basket for her to inspect.

"This one. It's got spots. Can I crack it?"

"Into that bowl. I'll show you."

Ilario cut the bread into the narrow fingers she liked. Beside him, his father folded Nerina's hands round the egg and helped her pull the cracked shell apart. She looked into the bowl with relief.

"I didn't break the yellow."

"Very good. Bring it here. Slowly."

She carried it the three steps to the stove. Cosimo slid the egg into hot oil, and she stood back at the hiss. He put the bowl on the shelf, moved her a little farther from the pan, and gave her a piece of bread while she waited.

"Tell Grandad about your teeth," Ilario said.

She opened her mouth at once, pulling down her lip to display the gap.

"Well," Cosimo said, "that wasn't there when I last saw you."

"I did write."

"You did. But I couldn't see right inside your mouth in the letter."

She opened wider. Cosimo bent to inspect, grave and thorough, then showed her a gap of his own at the side. Nerina laughed so hard she had to hold on to his sleeve.

Ilario leaned against the table with the bread knife still in his hand. He wanted his father to turn and look at him again. There were things to ask about the journey, and the garden, and simply how he'd been. But Nerina was telling him where she had been standing when her tooth came out, and Cosimo was listening while spooning hot oil over the egg. They could take as long as they liked. Ilario set down the knife and began splitting figs.

"Not those," his father said. "Those are for eating fresh. The softer ones are under the cloth."

He lifted the cloth. Six figs lay there, purple skins split with ripeness. He could smell the honeyed centers before he touched them.

"You remembered."

Cosimo looked round. "Ilario, you asked for them every Sunday for about eleven years."

"Did you get them every Sunday?" Nerina asked.

"No. Figs don't grow every Sunday."

She considered this while her grandfather lifted the egg onto a plate. The white had a brown, lacy edge. She reached out a finger, drew it back from the heat, and followed the plate to the table.

"I can eat this now?"

"Start before it gets cold. We're coming."

Cosimo returned to the stove, and Ilario passed him the first split fig. His father dipped it in batter and eased it into the deeper pan. The batter puffed around it. For a while they worked without speaking, one handing, the other dipping, Nerina crunching at the table.

"She asked about the olive tree," Cosimo said. "Do you remember when you made your bed up there?"

"I remember you telling everybody about it."

Nerina looked up, bread poised above the yolk. "You slept in the tree?"

"For part of one night."

"He took a blanket and the good pillow," Cosimo said. "Dragged them up there while I was out. I got home and there was a stocking hanging outside this very window. With his foot still in it."

"I was on the low branch."

"Your foot was on the low branch. I couldn't find the rest of you. All I could see was bedding."

Nerina put down her bread. "Were you hiding?"

"I wanted a room outside. It was hot. And I thought if I slept there I could pick the olives before breakfast."

"They weren't ripe," Cosimo said. He turned the fritters. "He found that out fairly quickly."

"Raw olives are horrible," Ilario told her. "Even when they look ready. Don't try one."

"What did you eat, then?"

"Your grandad brought me bread and cheese."

"Up a ladder. I carried the plate in one hand and held on with the other. He was tucked so far back among the branches that I couldn't reach him."

"I had to climb down," Ilario said. "We ended up eating on the doorstep."

"But he went back up. After all that trouble, he said he was staying the night."

His father scooped the first fritters onto a dish. Ilario took it, hunting for the old crack in its glaze. There it was, running through a painted yellow flower. He had forgotten the flower.

"Did you?" Nerina asked.

"Did I what?"

"Stay all night."

"Oh. No. I fell asleep for a while, and then a hen got into the blankets."

She stared at him. "On you?"

"Right against my stomach. I woke up and something was wriggling inside my bed."

Cosimo began to laugh, quietly at first. He rested the spoon across the pan.

"I heard him from upstairs. Sounded as if he was trying to shout without opening his mouth too far in case she pecked him."

"I was not."

"You made a very small, careful noise."

"You couldn't see my mouth from upstairs."

"I was there soon enough."

Nerina slid off her chair. "Which branch? Show me which branch."

"After breakfast," Ilario said.

"You always say that."

"And then we have breakfast. Sit down, please."

She climbed back up, but turned the chair a little so that she could see the tree through the door.

***

There was a folded newspaper on Ilario's old chair. He moved it to the window ledge and sat down. The rung met his heel in exactly the right place.

Cosimo brought the last of the fritters, then the cheese, then remembered the sliced tomatoes. Ilario made room between the plates. His father had always eaten as if someone else might arrive halfway through.

Nerina pushed her chair closer to Ilario's. She had finished the egg and wanted to try a fritter, but only a little one. He broke his in half to let the steam out and gave her the smaller piece.

"There's pink in it."

"That's the fig."

She ate the crisp corner first. Then she took a bite that included the fruit, and looked at her remaining piece before putting all of it into her mouth.

Cosimo watched her. "Another?"

She nodded. Ilario reached for the smallest, but she pointed firmly to the one beside it.

Outside, someone began ringing the tower bell, stopped, and tried again. The second peal was better. Cosimo looked toward the window with a piece of cheese halfway to his mouth.

"Sounds different here."

Ilario listened. Without the cliff behind it, the sound spread thinly over the fields, mingling with the noises of his Sunday: wheels in the lane, a neighbor calling upstairs, the distant rehearsal of a trumpet.

"That's the band," he said. "They practice before they go to the park."

"What time do we need to leave?"

"Hours yet."

"Good." Cosimo reached for the coffee pot. "Tell me about your work. Did they give you that long table you wanted?"

Ilario began to tell him. The table had arrived, too wide to go through the workshop door, and they had spent the first morning taking its legs off. His father wanted to know whose measurements they'd used. Nerina, who had visited the bindery that day, interrupted to explain that Papa had crawled under the old workbench to find a screw and got glue in his hair.

"Paste," Ilario said. "It came out."

"There was some behind your ear. I found it."

"You did."

He turned his head to show Cosimo where, and his father reached across the corner of the table and tucked back the dark hair, inspecting him with the same attention he had given Nerina's teeth. Ilario stayed still. His father's fingers were warm from the cup.

"All gone," Cosimo said, and sat back. "Have the last one."

"Have you had enough?"

"I'm having cheese. Go on."

Ilario took the fritter. Nerina was looking from him to the tree again.

"Grandad, do the noise Papa made. With the hen."

"He doesn't remember it," Ilario said.

Cosimo set down his cup. He pressed his lips together, drew his shoulders up toward his ears, and produced a thin, strangled cry. Nerina burst into laughter, her head tipped back, showing the gap where her tooth had been. Ilario tried to object, but he had taken too large a bite, and his father was doing it again.

stories.title: The Wrong Rescue
stories.prompt: The heroes stared in disbelief as the rescued princess helped the defeated Demon King stand. “Tell the king it’s amazing how he protects the kingdom when threatened by an outside evil. But ignores the evil occurring in front of him.” she whispered to them before she vanished with him.
stories.body:
# The Wrong Rescue

Haldis hooked the Demon King's ankle, and this time I was close enough to keep him down.

His sword went skidding under the long table. He landed against the window seat with his wounded leg folded beneath him, one hand flat on the stone. I put my point under his jaw. For several breaths the loudest thing in the hall was Haldis trying to draw air through her nose.

“Both feet,” she managed. “Watch his feet.”

“I have him.”

We had seen what he could do in the lower courtyard, when he laid down his sword and vanished from between us. A moment later he was standing on the balcony above, retrieving a second sword from its bracket. He needed a place he could see, both hands free of weapons, and his weight settled on his feet. He could take one person with him if they stayed in contact. The scout who had sold us those particulars had been right about everything except how easy that made him to kill. Haldis had spent the rest of the fight attacking his footing. My cut above his knee had finally given her something to work with.

Beyond the broken window lay the valley and its opposite ridge, still yellow with evening. Kolvran kept turning his head toward it.

“Stay where you are,” I said.

He eased his leg out from under him. I let him. His skin had gone gray around the mouth, and one of his small backward horns had struck the sill hard enough to leave a white scrape in the stone. He looked less like the figure on the king's war banners than a man who might be sick on my boots.

Haldis nudged his fallen crown away with her heel. Then she grinned at me, a startled, breathless grin. We had done it. Nineteen days of cold saddles and wrong tracks, and we had done it.

A door opened behind her.

Princess Ismeret came out carrying a rolled cloak, her hair fastened in a single thick braid. She wore a brown riding dress and boots laced all the way to the knee. I remembered searching a stable for those boots when she was seventeen and determined to leave for a hunt before breakfast. Ten years later she still tied the ends in the same double knot.

“We brought your mare,” I told her.

She stopped beside the table. Her eyes went from the blood on my sleeve to Kolvran's leg.

“Is that yours?” she asked me.

“Most of it isn't. You're safe.”

Haldis shifted aside to give her a way to the stairs. I held out my left hand, palm down, as I used to when she was small enough to need help from a saddle. Two fingers for her to catch, no fuss made about the height. She looked at my hand without taking it.

“Where's my maid?”

“At the palace, I expect.”

“Did you see her before you left?”

“Ismeret, we should get you downstairs.”

“Did you?”

Behind her, the little room was furnished with a bed and a chair heaped with books. A half-peeled apple lay on the windowsill. I had expected chains, though I would not have admitted it to her.

“No,” I said. “But your father will have settled that business. He promised a hearing.”

She put her rolled cloak on the table.

Haldis's grin had gone. “What business?”

“A household matter,” I said, and heard how I sounded only when Ismeret laughed. It was a small ugly sound that she cut short herself.

“She brought a letter to the west gate. She asked you to let her through.”

“I remember.”

I remembered everything about it. The girl had come during the changing of the watch, wearing a man's coat over her apron. She had said her mother was dying. The steward arrived before I opened the wicket and took a letter from her pocket. Ismeret's seal was still soft enough to bear the weave of the apron.

“You told me she'd be questioned,” Ismeret said. “Then Father would hear her.”

“That was what I was told.”

Kolvran shifted his good foot. My point dragged across his collar as I turned my head.

“Watch your sword,” he said.

Haldis stepped nearer him, axe held low. “Sit still.”

Ismeret had noticed the movement too. She came around the table, but stopped beyond the reach of my free hand.

“The letter was to my sister. I asked to live with her. That was all. I told her I'd bring nothing Father had given me.”

“Then we can send another letter.”

“From where?”

“Once we're home.”

She looked toward the stair door. For the first time I understood that she was measuring the way past Haldis rather than waiting for us to lead her to it.

“Your father rode out to the orchard himself when he heard you'd been taken,” I said. “The northern companies are on the road. He couldn't sit through his supper the night we left.”

“He sat at supper while they beat her.”

Haldis glanced at me. I wanted to answer before Ismeret could say anything more, although I had no answer ready.

“In the little dining room,” she continued. “The one with the painted birds. He made me sit beside him. The steward had her just outside the open doors, where I could see. Father said that if I spoke to her, he'd tell the steward to begin again.”

She rubbed the heel of one hand against the other. “I asked for the physician when they stopped. He asked me whether I'd finished my broth.”

I knew that room. Its doors stood open to the antechamber, and even the chink of a cup carried down the corridor. The king ate there when he wanted an evening without petitions. I had waited outside it often enough, thinking how rarely we allowed him any peace.

“I didn't know,” I said.

“She was still in the east tower when I left. With the steward's men. If you go back, don't ask him whether she's well.”

“I'll go to her myself.”

Ismeret pressed her palms together harder. “Will you let her out?”

I had meant a visit. A word to the physician. There was a pause in which everyone in the room could hear what I had meant.

“The girl isn't our prisoner,” Haldis said. “We can do nothing for her from here. Come down with us, Princess.”

“I won't go back.”

“Then we'll find you somewhere else. He stays.” Haldis tipped the axe toward Kolvran.

He looked up at Ismeret, and something passed between them that I did not know how to read. She had looked at me like that once, waiting beside a horse she was frightened to mount, wanting me to stop everyone watching. But she was twenty-seven now.

“Did he hurt you?” I asked.

“No.”

“You can tell us.”

“I just did.”

Kolvran shut his eyes. His hand had begun to tremble against the window seat. Without taking her eyes from my sword, Ismeret picked up a linen napkin from the table and twisted it into a band.

“Please move the point,” she said. “I need to bind his leg.”

Haldis said, “You'll keep away from him.”

Ismeret crouched anyway. I lifted the blade enough for her to pass beneath it, then set the point at Kolvran's breast. He watched this adjustment with an interest that made me tighten my grip.

“She came here willingly,” he said.

I did not answer him. She had got the linen under his leg. He drew a sharp breath as she pulled it up. Her fingers knew where to go, and he let her work without watching them.

“Tell me what happened,” I said to her.

“I sent him a letter.”

“How?”

“Not through your gate.” She pulled the knot tight. “He offered me a room until I could decide where to go. I met him in the orchard below the south wall. We walked up to the bare ground together so he could see the next ridge. He brought me north in stages.”

The trampled grass in the orchard, the gardener who had seen two figures disappear, the torn piece of her sleeve caught on the wall: we had begun with those, and every tale of someone vanishing had drawn us farther north. I remembered the king holding that little scrap of cloth against his lips.

“You could have come to me.”

“I did. When he locked me in my rooms. You told me to apologize.”

“I thought if you could speak to each other calmly—”

“I know what you thought.”

Kolvran laid his hand on her forearm. She turned toward him at once. He said something too low for me to hear, and she nodded, but stayed kneeling by his leg.

“What did he say?” Haldis asked.

“That he's getting faint.”

“Good.”

Ismeret looked up at her.

“We didn't come nineteen days to sit with him while he rests,” Haldis said. “Move away.”

“He gave me shelter.”

“He burned my husband's house with my husband in it.”

Kolvran took his hand from Ismeret's arm.

All along the road Haldis had carried one of her husband's boots, the left, tucked into the flap of her saddlebag. It was a good boot. He had been wearing its mate when the raiders came. She had never spoken of burying what they found, but she had told me how long he took to break in new leather, how he would limp around their kitchen and refuse to admit that his feet had grown. I knew more about him than I did about some men I had served beside for years.

“The first frost, two autumns ago,” she said to Kolvran. “The houses by the wool sheds. You sent the riders with the red cords.”

“Yes.”

“The soldiers were gone. You knew they were gone.”

“They had gone to reinforce the pass. I meant to make them come back.”

Haldis nodded once, as though she had been waiting a long time for exactly that answer.

Ismeret's hands were still resting on the knot. “You told me it was a garrison.”

“It was. There were houses beside it.”

“My husband mended the soldiers' harness,” Haldis said. “He couldn't ride. He was in bed when you came.”

Kolvran watched her. “I didn't choose your husband.”

“You sent them.”

He did not dispute it. Ismeret stood, slowly, leaving the tied linen on his leg.

“What else?” she asked him.

His breathing had quickened. “Not now.”

“You had four weeks to tell me.”

“Later. If we get out of this.” He drew a breath. “You may ask me anything.”

She drew back from him at that. I saw it and seized on it, grateful for something I understood.

“Come here,” I said. “You needn't stay with him. We'll take you to your sister. Haldis and I will see you there.”

Haldis did not agree to that journey. She was watching Kolvran's hands.

“Father will send for me,” Ismeret said.

“Your sister can refuse him.”

“Her husband holds half his land from Father.” She bent for her cloak. “You'd be standing at another gate when the order came.”

I had an answer to that, a promise, and could not get it out. Haldis moved in beside me. Kolvran braced his palm against the seat, trying to ease himself higher; I pressed him back with the sword. He stopped, and I felt through the hilt how close he had come to putting his weight against the point.

Ismeret fastened the rolled cloak over one shoulder. She had not put it on when she thought we might let her treat him. Now she tightened the strap until the bundle sat high against her back.

“Move her,” Haldis said to me.

“Wait.”

“For what?”

I looked from her to Ismeret, stupidly hoping one of them would tell me.

Haldis lowered her voice. “You told me I'd have this. In the inn, when you asked me to show you the northern tracks.”

I had promised her Kolvran. I had promised the king his daughter. For nineteen days neither promise had troubled the other.

“I know.”

“Then help me.”

She came another half step forward. Ismeret slipped between us and Kolvran, so close to my blade that I lifted it away from her dress. Haldis checked her axe before raising it.

“Ismeret,” I said. “Easy. Come away.”

I put my left hand on her upper arm. She went rigid beneath it. That was familiar too: a rider who had taken fright, who would stiffen and fight the horse until someone steadied her. I held a little more firmly.

She looked down at my hand. I could remember every time I had lifted her, caught her, carried her sleeping from a saddle.

“Let go,” she said.

Haldis had both hands on the axe. She was waiting for me to pull the princess clear.

I released Ismeret and lowered my sword. Haldis started forward; I caught the axe haft below her hands and held it against my chest. The edge hung a handspan from my shoulder.

“Don't,” I said.

She looked at my hand on her weapon. Then at me. She could have pulled hard enough to put me on the floor. We both knew it. For a moment she did nothing at all.

Behind Ismeret, Kolvran tried to rise. His bad leg buckled and he caught the sill, making a sound I had never heard from a king.

She went to him. His arm came across her shoulders, and she planted her boots wide, taking his weight as he straightened the injured knee. Haldis and I stared. I had thought she might stand between him and the axe. I had not understood, until his body leaned into hers, that she meant to carry him out of our victory.

“You know what he did,” Haldis said.

Ismeret pulled his hand farther over her shoulder. The effort had loosened hair from her braid; it stuck to the side of her face. She looked at Haldis and said, “Yes.”

Kolvran's good foot settled beside hers. His eyes were on the opposite ridge. I still had time to put the sword into him. I knew where the gap was, beneath the raised arm.

Ismeret was close enough that her bundle brushed my wrist. Haldis stood against my other shoulder, her hands still locked on the haft. The princess turned her face toward us both. Her voice dropped to a whisper.

“Tell the king it’s amazing how he protects the kingdom when threatened by an outside evil. But ignores the evil occurring in front of him.”

Kolvran lifted his arm from her shoulders. For an instant she held him by the elbow while he found his balance. Then she offered him her hand.

He took it, and they vanished.

No smoke, no crash of air. Across the valley, two small figures appeared on the yellow grass, one bent toward the other. They made their way below the crest, and the ridge was bare again.

Haldis wrenched the axe out of my grip.

I let my sword fall. It struck the floor, and she flinched at the sound. She backed away until the long table stood between us. Then she picked up Kolvran's crown by one of its broken points.

“Haldis.”

She went downstairs.

I followed after I had retrieved my sword. At the bottom, the door we had broken from its hinges lay across the passage. We had helped each other over it on the way in. I stepped over alone and came out into the courtyard where the horses were tied.

Haldis was fastening the crown behind her saddle. She had taken off her gloves; one of her nails had split. I reached for the loose end of the strap before thinking, and she pulled it out of my reach.

“Are you going after them?” I asked.

“Not tonight.” She tugged the knot tight. “First I'll tell your king what happened.”

“I have to tell him too.”

“I suppose you'll tell him she asked you to let them go.”

“She didn't ask me.”

Haldis looked up. There was no anger in her face for a moment, only a tired, appalled attention.

“Then make sure he knows that.”

She mounted. I had tied the princess's mare beside my gelding, brushing its mane that morning so Ismeret would see something clean when she came out. It lifted its head as Haldis rode past, then went back to nosing the bare ground.

“Wait,” I said.

Haldis drew rein. She had always waited when I asked before, no matter what was behind us.

I wanted her to tell me where we would sleep. I wanted the next stretch of road, with her riding ahead and turning sometimes to make sure I was still there. But I had seen her husband's boot in the saddlebag when she put away her gloves, and there was nothing I could ask her that would not cost her something more.

“I'll tell him what I did,” I said.

She turned her horse toward the gate.

By the time I untied the other two horses, she had reached the outer track. My gelding shied from the mare, and I lost my stirrup, catching myself painfully on the saddle. Haldis glanced back at the noise. Then she rode on.

stories.title: The Thread That Held
stories.prompt: For all time, you have tended the loom of the world, weaving civilizations, cities, seasons, and generations of families whose lives you follow through the threads. Now the gods have gathered at your loom to debate another change of Eras. Some insist the old must collapse before a better age can begin; others remember how long it took to recover from the last one. They turn to you for the deciding vote.
stories.body:
# The Thread That Held

The daughter has the shears, and her father wants them back.

They stand on opposite sides of a length of scarlet silk lined with black linen. He has embroidered the royal bird across it, each feather edged with gold. She has put her cutting hand beneath the silk, where he cannot safely snatch at it.

“I need them,” she says.

“Then get the little ones.”

“These will be quicker.”

Something in her voice makes me slow my shuttle. I have followed this family through seven generations, and this daughter usually tells her father what she thinks of his plans before he has finished explaining them. Today she keeps her answers short. He has mistaken her quietness for the beginning of surrender. I know that because he starts telling her where the little shears are kept.

I settle the gold thread across my loom. Beneath it, summer spreads through the city's orchards; a line of houses catches the afternoon light. My hands keep the many influences of the world in relation, making cloth of seasons, settlements, lives. I remember no first morning at this work, no time before the loom. The people in it supply their own difficulties. I cannot make the daughter hand over those shears, any more than I can persuade an apple tree to be a sonnet.

On the brass crosspiece beside my knee, I keep a flower painted by a child who has been dead for nine hundred years. The flower is rather good.

You can see why I get behind.

Yes, you, reading. The gods who are about to arrive will not hear that. Nor can you call into the workshop and suggest a solution. I have tried leaving room for answers. What comes through is the particular silence of someone elsewhere, attending.

Four shadows fall across the cloth. I look up before their owners can complain that I have made them wait.

Orsivet is already drawing his chair closer to the loom. The chair is mine; I put my foot on its lower rung. Vaulenne settles on the bench instead, breathing hard, and asks whether I have anything she can put behind her back. I give her a cushion embroidered with a city that no longer exists. Dembrel remains standing. Irthess, last through the door, closes it against the stars.

“Have you agreed?” I ask.

“Two each,” Irthess says. “You must settle it.”

Orsivet gives the chair a small, unsuccessful tug. “After hearing us.”

I release it. He sits with the dignity of a man who has never had to put away a cushion.

They have come to decide whether to end an Era. In the kingdom under my hands, four great protections have become so tightly interwoven that withdrawing them together would bring down more than the dynasty. The king's armies, the grain caravans, the towns beyond the passes: everything grown dependent upon those protections would begin to fail. Irthess and Dembrel propose withdrawing. Vaulenne and Orsivet refuse. For this undertaking, and this undertaking only, the four have agreed to abide by a fifth voice.

They have chosen me because I remember the last collapse.

Unfortunately for them, I remember other things as well.

Irthess lays a packet on my worktable. When he unties it, a smell of smoke rises from the linen. Inside are folded scraps, some written on both sides, one with a child's arithmetic showing through beneath a petition.

“Thirty-one executions this morning,” he says. “The families left these in my temple. They're still waiting outside.”

“For burial?”

“For the bodies. The king is keeping them until someone names the others.”

Through the cloth I hear the banner maker saying, “We've already been paid.” His daughter shifts her grip beneath the silk.

“I went to the palace,” Irthess continues. “They received me in the little court. No chair, no witnesses. He said I could have the bodies when the inquiry was finished.”

Orsivet begins, “He has a right to—”

“Don't.” Irthess looks directly at him. “I know what his rights are. Your priests read them to me.”

The god of sworn obligations smooths his robe over his knees. A murmur follows the movement: at a hundred altars, people are promising things in his name. His face loosens as the prayers reach him. He catches me watching and takes his hand away.

“If we remove the protections,” I say, “the burial grounds become hunting grounds again. You know what nests under those hills.”

“I do.”

“And the people waiting outside your temple?”

He pushes the packet toward me. “Read what they asked for.”

Several beg for a particular body. One asks for the king's death. Another asks that no king ever sit in that palace again. I unfold the arithmetic. Beneath the petition, someone has worked out the price of six measures of flour and reached the wrong answer.

“They haven't all asked for the same thing,” I say.

“No. But none has asked me to keep doing this for another hundred years.”

He rubs his forehead with the heel of his hand. The skin stays creased a moment after he lowers it.

“There have been three uprisings,” he says. “The soldiers swore to the crown before they knew what they'd be ordered to do. Each time, men who wanted to desert found they couldn't pass the barrack gates. Those are your oaths, Orsivet. The king could never hold so many towns with willing soldiers.”

“Release every oath and the towns lose their protection too,” Orsivet says.

“Yes. They would have to defend themselves. Some of them are ready. They have councils, stores, people who could govern without asking his leave.” Irthess looks at me. “I have been there.”

I look for the towns beyond the passes, small knots of brown and ochre along the upper warp. “And the ones that aren't?”

“I don't have a good answer for them.” He draws the loose linen over the petitions, then pushes it back. “But how many more times do I tell the families at my temple to wait?”

Dembrel sets a shoe beside the petitions. It is broad, badly patched, and worn through at the heel.

“The woman who wore that tried the eastern pass,” she says. “Then the western. Then she tried to hide in a wool cart. Three times they brought her back to the estate.”

“Was she bound by debt?” Orsivet asks.

“Her grandfather was.”

“The debt may still have been valid.”

“She offered to pay it. They changed the sum.”

“Then she should have appealed.”

Dembrel keeps looking at him until he says, more quietly, “To my temple.”

“She did.”

He reaches for the shoe, but she leaves her hand on it.

“I'll inquire,” he says.

“You did. They restored the old debt and added an exit tax. Is that forbidden?”

Orsivet says nothing. Behind him, his murmuring robe goes on receiving promises.

I ask Dembrel where the woman is now.

“At home. Her mother can't walk anymore. She won't leave without her.” Dembrel takes her hand from the shoe. “I've kept the passes open for a hundred and sixty winters. The soldiers travel them too. Every time I make a crossing easier, someone puts another guard at the end.”

“There would be guards without you,” Orsivet says.

“Yes. There would. I'm trying to decide whether I can bear being useful to these ones.”

Vaulenne reaches past the shoe for my little cup of barley. I keep grain near the loom to help me set the spacing of harvests; she knows she may take it. She rolls a few kernels in her palm.

“The last time,” she says, “we lost the red kind.”

“We have red barley,” Irthess tells her.

“Not that kind. The one that would ripen on the high slopes. There was a black mark at the base.” She holds out a kernel, discovers that it cannot illustrate her point, and puts it down. “I don't remember what they called it.”

“We can't keep this king because you miss a grain.”

“I'm not talking about the king.”

He looks toward the petitions. She waits until he looks back.

“It was the third year after the fall. Or the fourth. I could bring a mild spring, and I did. There were women in the fields with baskets tied to them. They were gathering everything green. They had eaten the seed the winter before. You can't make a harvest out of a mild spring and no seed.”

“I remember.”

“Do you remember the next spring?”

Irthess opens his mouth, then lets her continue.

“They sowed a little. Too little. Their daughters were old women before the hills were planted again. There was one who used to come to my shrine with a basket. She'd turn it upside down and sit on it. Never asked me for anything after the first few years. Just came and sat.”

Vaulenne tips the kernels back into my cup. Two fall on the floor. She bends for them, and I touch her shoulder to stop her; the bench is narrow and her knee has begun to shake. I pick them up myself.

The last collapse lies wound on the lower beam. I can spread its record beneath my fingers, but I cannot pull it loose and have the years again. Here is a palace made into lime for cottages. Here, a granddaughter grinding ornaments into pigment because the blue mines have been forgotten. Beside that blue runs an absence I still catch my nail in: a language whose final speaker woke one morning without anyone left to scold.

Across other stretches of the cloth, cities went on prospering. Some never learned that this kingdom had fallen. The world has seldom done us the courtesy of ending all at once.

“The first king brought the roads under oath,” Orsivet says. “A traveler could cross six estates under one protection. Before him, every estate could take what it wished.”

“I was there,” Dembrel says. “Before him they took the traveler's mule and her boots, and sometimes the traveler. I helped you post the first guards, and I was glad to.” She looks at the shoe. “I didn't think they'd still be standing there for her.”

“Every market on those roads runs on my oaths.” Orsivet lays a hand on his robe, where the altars are murmuring. “The carters swear, the tolls hold, a widow can send her wool over the mountains with a boy of twelve and be paid for it. Take the oaths away and the guards won't go home. They'll stay where they are and stop answering to anyone.”

Dembrel doesn't argue. Orsivet turns toward me. “You remember the first royal banner.”

I do. Its bird had a crooked beak because the banner maker's ancestor was better at horses. Afterward she bought a shop with her commission. Her eldest son turned its loft into a bedroom, and his wife put a yellow bowl in the window. I watched that bowl break. I watched it glued together, used for buttons, thrown away. The third generation painted the door blue. In the fifth, a boy left to become an actor and came home only twice, both times wearing shoes beyond his means.

There has always been someone at their table who dislikes the way someone else makes the porridge. When the current daughter's mother died, her father kept making it too thin because that was how his wife had liked it. The daughter ate it without complaint for eleven mornings. On the twelfth she took the pot away from him and made it properly, and he cried.

I wanted to see her teach someone else.

Orsivet has found the edge of the family thread. I move his hand away.

“Those commissions fed them,” he says.

“I know.”

“And many others. We can require changes. I can speak to the king about the inheritance of debts.”

Irthess doesn't lift his eyes from the petitions. “You told me that about his father. He lowered the levy on your temple estates, and the villages beside them paid the difference. I have their petitions too.”

Orsivet pulls his chair back. One leg catches my hem. “And the families living on those estates.”

No one speaks for a while. I free the embroidered edge of my wrap. There is barley dust on my fingertips.

Then the daughter cuts into the royal bird.

Her father catches the silk after the blades have passed. The shears make a heavy, almost comfortable sound. She cuts the banner into broad strips, turning it so the bright embroidery will lie inside.

“Stop,” her father says. “Please. That's enough.”

“We need something that won't show in the dark.”

“Who does?”

“You know who.”

He does. He has washed a stranger's blood from her sleeve, once already this year. I watched him do it and allowed myself to believe what she told him about an accident with a knife.

She folds the strips into a pile. She is twenty-three, with dye in the ridges of her left thumb and a burn on her wrist from the porridge pot. Her father holds the severed bird's head.

“They'll close the shop,” he says.

“I'm going tonight. Tell them I stole it.”

“And will they believe me?”

She doesn't answer. The shears hang open in her hand.

Dembrel leans over my shoulder. “Is keeping her home what you want from this vote?”

“I couldn't do that.”

“I asked what you wanted.”

I keep my eyes on the cloth. The daughter has set the shears down, carefully, with their handles toward her father.

You may have reached me after reading some other life in this same world. A different century, a different catastrophe. Perhaps you came straight here. Either way, beyond this story are others; their people do not stop living when your attention turns from them. I can feel some of those far-off lives pulling where our histories touch. That is not the same as knowing what happens next.

You can close this page while the daughter stands beside her father. I am tempted to do the equivalent: follow another family, another thread. There is a wedding just beyond the orchard. Someone has hidden the groom's good coat. I could spend the afternoon there.

“Tapissier,” Irthess says.

I have been silent too long.

“Give me a moment.”

He takes a breath to object, but Vaulenne puts her hand on his sleeve.

I lower my head. The flowers pinned in my indigo hair brush the cloth. Beneath my wrap, gold wings press close along my back; the broken violet crystals of my halo are hidden among the pins. I have worn this disguise so long that the gods believe it is all there is of me.

You should know who is asking for another moment. I am the Astral Valkyrie. When I leave this loom, I sometimes go where shelter has run out. Under those wings I can keep a living person for a little while. If someone offers me a memory, I can receive it. I cannot summon their dead to complete it, or carry a city because I love the view from its windows.

The gods know tales of the Valkyrie. None knows that she has just picked two barley grains from the floor. I do not tell them. Irthess, particularly, would hear a promise in it that I could not keep.

Already I have begun choosing. If the protections go, I will look first for the daughter. Or perhaps her father, who will stay too long gathering work from the shop. At the thought of choosing between them, my wings tighten painfully beneath the embroidered cloth.

I lift my head. All four gods are watching my face.

“If we continue,” I ask Irthess, “what will you do?”

“Get the bodies back.”

“And afterward?”

“I don't know. Go to the families. Ask what they want now.” He looks at the cut banner. “There are people preparing to fight. I may help them.”

Orsivet makes an impatient sound. Irthess ignores him.

“Will your protection cover them?” I ask Orsivet.

“If they swear lawful oaths.”

“The king decides what's lawful.”

“Not in every matter.”

There it is: how little my vote will settle. The king will remain in his palace. The people outside Irthess's temple will still have to wait for their dead. Dembrel's woman will still have a mother who cannot walk, and the officials will have paper enough to invent another fee.

Under my fingers the city's summer holds, imperfectly. I can feel where the contributions of the four gods must be renewed: their living power meeting mine, the little brass hooks warm where I guide it into the warp. I have no reserve that can take their place. If I vote to withdraw, they will release those strands together. If I refuse, they have pledged to keep them through the coming season. We will still have to live with one another after that.

“I vote against withdrawing,” I say. “Keep the protections.”

Dembrel closes her eyes. Orsivet smiles at me, and I look down at the warp.

Vaulenne places her palm against the loom. Warmth enters the seasonal thread, carrying the smell of crushed barley leaves. Dembrel takes longer. Then she presses two fingers to the strand that crosses the mountains, and distant bells sound at a travelers' shrine. Orsivet breathes his undertaking over the oaths already woven there. I feel their pull strengthen, including the ones I wish had never been sworn.

Irthess picks up the loose cord from his packet and puts the end into my hand. His power passes along it as he murmurs the names of the burial grounds under his care.
