I work the four contributions into the cloth. Summer advances a little beneath the crosspiece. In a prison near the palace, the yard bell rings for the change of guard. A woman lifts her head at it. “Is that for us?” she asks. No one comes to open her door.

My shuttle slows. Irthess notices.

“Is that still your vote?” he asks.

“Yes.”

He finishes naming the grounds.

When it is done, he gathers the petitions. Dembrel takes the shoe. Vaulenne gets up slowly and gives me back the cushion, though I tell her she may keep it.

At the door I catch Irthess by the sleeve.

“If you help them fight,” I say, “don't send that girl somewhere she can't come back from.”

He looks down at the daughter, who is wrapping the silk around her shoulders to test how it hides the red.

“I won't promise she'll come back,” he says. “If she asks for my help, I'm going to give it.”

I let go of his sleeve. He waits, and for a moment I dislike him for waiting. He has accepted my vote; I want him to accept this also. I want his anger to stop short of the little house with the blue door.

“She won't let you finish explaining,” I say at last. “She never lets her father finish. Tell her the danger first.”

He looks at the girl a moment longer. “I'll start with it.”

He leaves with the others. The latch settles into place. I remain standing beside the loom until the ache under my wrap subsides.

In the shop, the banner maker is finding fault with the knot his daughter has tied. He has always found fault with her knots. She lets him loosen this one and pass the end through again, though she watches the window while he works.

“There,” he says.

She touches his wrist. He pulls it away and goes to the back of the shop. I think he means to let her leave without another word. Instead he returns with the little shears, their blades wrapped in a rag.

She takes them. Neither says anything else.

Outside, people are carrying summer fruit home in the dusk. The daughter turns left, away from the market and the orchard, toward a part of the city I have scarcely attended to. She walks quickly. Once she reaches beneath the folded silk to check that the shears are still there.

I draw my stool along the loom to follow her. For years I have watched this family from the same place; now the brass edge presses into an unfamiliar part of my knee. Behind the daughter, the window of the shop grows smaller. Her father has lit the lamp. I can still see him, standing beside the scarlet pieces, but I have to lean farther and farther to keep them both in view.

stories.title: The Next Train
stories.prompt: You miss your train and end up sharing your takeaway with three punks on the platform. By evening, the gods are taking the subway to see whom is so worthy of the attention of the Fates after all these years.
stories.body:
# The Next Train

The train doors shut while I was rescuing my dumplings. The bottom of the takeaway bag had given way, and I caught the carton against my stomach with both hands, which meant I had no hand left to appeal to the driver. Through the glass, a seated woman watched me balance two tubs of sauce on top.

She gave me a thumbs-up. Then she was gone.

"Good catch," said someone behind me.

Three punks occupied the bench beneath the station clock. The one who'd spoken had black hair, a dark visor pushed up on her head, and boots that extended well into the path of commuters. Her pink-haired friend moved a pair of enormous headphones off her ears. The third, blue-haired under a knitted beanie, a mask over her nose and mouth, took her backpack off the bench.

I sat before anyone could change their mind.

"Is that the family box?" the pink-haired one asked.

"It was cheaper than two singles."

"How many people?"

"Just me. But over time."

She leaned forward to look. The carton held twelve dumplings, a small mountain of noodles, and two spring rolls sweating through their paper sleeves. It had been a poor day, and I had intended to improve quite a lot of it at once.

The blue-haired one lowered her mask. "You need another bag. I've got one."

She unpacked a cable, a paperback swollen with bookmarks, and a clean shopping bag from her backpack. While I transferred the carton, the woman in the visor reached toward a spring roll and stopped with her fingers a courteous inch away.

"Cabbage?"

"I hope so."

"Would you swap one for a peach?"

She produced a bruised peach from the deep pocket of her coat. We examined it together.

"You can just have the spring roll," I said. "There's enough."

The peach went into my hand anyway, warm from her pocket. Her friend took four folded napkins from a headphone case. Blue Hair had a spare fork, still in its wrapper. Within a minute the carton lay open between us, on the lid balanced across two knees, and the next train was something we would consider when it came.

Pink Hair wanted the mushroom dumplings. I wanted the crispest ones. Visor wanted everyone to try dipping a spring roll in both sauces at once, but she had used hers up demonstrating the wrong proportions. Blue Hair divided the second roll with the edge of a fork and gave her a piece.

"Smaller bites this time."

"You make experimentation sound so shabby."

"It's on your coat."

She looked down and found a length of cabbage hanging from a patch on her lapel. I laughed with a dumpling in my mouth. Pink Hair immediately passed me a napkin without taking her eyes off the cabbage.

Visor removed the cabbage and, in revenge, brought up my catch at the train doors. There are people who let you recover from that sort of thing, and people who begin telling you what it looked like. These were the second kind. By the time the next train arrived, I was defending the quality of my catch, using a spring-roll sleeve to represent the train.

"That's your one," said Blue Hair.

"There'll be another."

Visor lifted her boots so the departing passengers could get past. I continued my demonstration.

They were going to hear a band in a cellar two stops east. Pink Hair had bought the tickets, and neither of her friends had listened to the album she'd sent them. This came out because I asked whether the drummer was any good.

"Fantastic," said Visor.

"There isn't a drummer," Pink Hair said.

"Then I'm excited to hear what they've done with the vacancy."

Pink Hair looked at Blue Hair, who was occupied with a particularly long noodle.

"You too?"

"I started it."

"Which track?"

"The first one."

"That's eleven seconds of someone opening a door."

"I thought my phone was broken."

Pink Hair put her fork down. "I've told you about this band all week."

"I remember," said Visor. "You were very happy."

"I wanted you to hear it."

That quietened us. A train came in on the opposite side of the island platform, filling the station with brake dust and warm air. Pink Hair watched people get off. I picked a mushroom dumpling out of the box and put it on her napkin.

"Can I?" I asked, pointing to her headphones.

She handed them over. Visor leaned across me, demanding an ear, and we ended up with our heads pressed together inside the band, listening through one cushion each.

The song began with someone singing very softly over a plucked string. Then another voice entered, and another. There was no drum. The pulse came from breaths, shoes against boards, a bow catching roughly on its return. I stopped smiling for Pink Hair's benefit and listened.

When the chorus began, Visor drew away. "Oh," she said.

Pink Hair took the headphones back and watched her.

"Play that bit again," Visor said.

We listened in pairs. Blue Hair held her side away from her ear at first, then let it settle. Pink Hair sang along under her breath, badly enough that I finally understood why the recording had so many singers. She needed every one of them.

The third train we let go contained a man from my office. I crouched behind Visor's shoulder until he had passed. There was nothing wrong with what I was doing, but I didn't want to spend tomorrow explaining why I'd been hiding from him.

Blue Hair poured tea from a flask into its lid. As I reached across for the headphones again, she went still, two fingers pressed beside her nose. Her eyes tracked something above my elbow. Then she shifted the tea to the far end of the bench.

"What?" I asked.

"You might knock it over when you turn."

I made an exaggerated show of keeping my elbows tucked in. She drank. Moments later Visor began doing the part of the song that sounded like a cupboard collapsing, I swung around to see her, and my elbow swept the empty patch of bench.

Blue Hair held up the flask lid.

"You've eaten with her before," I said.

"Quite a lot."

It was not until much later that I remembered she had been looking above my elbow, where it had yet to be.

The peach was excellent under the bruise. I cut it with the little wooden knife from the takeaway and caught the juice in an empty sauce tub. We had reached the stage of a meal at which people went on eating because the food was there and because stopping would mean deciding where to go. The station clock advanced. Pink Hair wrote the band name on my phone, then texted herself from it so she could send me a recording that wasn't on the official album.

A young man in white temple clothes approached the bench. He looked from one woman to the next, smiled in a startled way, and lifted his phone.

"Please don't," Blue Hair said.

He lowered it at once, but there had already been a click.

"Sorry. It's just, I thought you were—"

"We're eating," said Pink Hair.

He bowed, retreating into the people waiting for the westbound service. Visor watched him type with both thumbs.

"Well," she said. "That'll get around."

I assumed they were in a band themselves. It explained the clothes, their obscure taste, and the fact that all three could sit for an hour on a station bench without once appearing to wonder whether they ought to be doing something useful.

"Does that happen often?"

"Being recognized?" Pink Hair asked. "Sometimes. Having a nice lunch, less often."

"It's six o'clock."

"We started late."

Visor nudged the last dumpling toward me. "You paid."

Blue Hair had been looking at it. I cut it in half, although I made a mess of the job and most of the filling ended up on her side. She quietly exchanged the halves.

The westbound train arrived eight minutes later. A woman in a long red coat stepped out carrying a phone and a bouquet of white lilies. Behind her came a broad man in a gold suit, ducking his head beneath the door although he could have cleared it easily.

People on the platform made room. A passenger touched two fingers to his wedding ring and bowed to the woman. She paused when he asked for a blessing. I saw her take his hand, breathe across the ring, and draw a red spark out of her own breath. It circled his finger once before sinking into the metal.

I had seen her face carved above marriage shrines. The carvings left out the impatient crease between her eyebrows.

The man in gold was easier to recognize. His face appeared on the posters for the autumn revels, whose opening he proclaimed each year from the steps of his temple. He caught a little silver cup tossed by a delighted worshipper, drank from it, and returned it across the crowd. When he laughed, the echo kept laughing after him in three different voices.

I wiped my hands on my trousers and stood up.

"Clotho," said the goddess, looking at the visor. Her eyes moved to the headphones. "Lachesis." Then to the beanie. "Atropos."

The three women looked up from my takeaway. The Fates. My mother still kept their little altar beside her bed, and paid for readings by people these three had authorized to look ahead. In the portraits they had considerably less hair dye.

I sat down again.

"You haven't answered an invitation in forty-three years," the goddess said.

Clotho lowered her visor over her eyes. "Was it forty-three?"

"I counted."

The god in gold put a hand on the bench back and leaned over my shoulder. He smelled of oranges and hot stage lights.

"And yet here you are. All three of you. With—" He waited.

I gave him my name. He repeated it, getting the middle sound wrong, and Lachesis corrected him.

The goddess looked directly at me. For a moment I understood the young man with his phone. I wanted some evidence of this to carry home.

"What have you asked them?" she said.

"Whether the band had a drummer."

She waited for the rest.

"It doesn't."

The god's hand tightened on the bench as he began to laugh. His echo set off a second burst farther down the platform. Atropos stacked the empty tubs inside the carton and packed it into the shopping bag.

"It's a concert," Lachesis said. "We have tickets."

"You attend concerts?" The goddess's voice had dropped.

"We attend yours," said Lachesis. "At the temple. Quite often."

"You could have told me you were there."

Lachesis looked down at her headphones. "You'd have made a fuss."

The goddess looked at the lilies in her hand. Someone had tied their stems with a red ribbon, and one bloom had been crushed against her sleeve. Whatever I'd expected gods to quarrel about, it hadn't been this.

"I have offered you a place at my table every spring," she said.

Clotho pushed her visor up again. "With a list of questions under every plate."

"Last spring there was one question."

"It had parts," Atropos said.

The god straightened. "I said you were trying too hard."

"You sent a choir to their house."

"It was a very small choir."

Lachesis checked her phone. The music was to start at half past, but getting up now would mean walking out on two gods in the middle of a complaint. I had stayed at parties considerably worse than our lunch for the same reason, because the host was standing between me and my coat.

"Have they looked at your future?" the goddess asked me.

Atropos answered before I could. "About three seconds of it. For the tea."

"Only that?"

"I don't spend a meal doing it."

The god perched on the arm of the bench beside me. "Then there must be something about you."

He said it warmly. I found myself straightening my shoulders.

Clotho saw. She took off the visor to clean it and hid most of her smile behind her sleeve.

The goddess asked about my family. The god asked what I did at night. I answered the second question first and made my evenings sound quite crowded.

"Friends round for dinner, that sort of thing. You should have seen us at my cousin's wedding."

He invited himself to our next dinner. It had been eleven months since the wedding, and we'd been promising to get together again ever since.

"I'll have to check with people," I said.

"Of course."

Lachesis leaned forward to catch Atropos's eye. Across the tracks, the eastbound display counted down toward the train they needed. The goddess turned her body, gently but completely excluding that small conference.

"You were saying about your mother?"

I could have remained there for hours. They would have let me. Behind the goddess, Lachesis was winding her headphone cable around fingers that had gone white at the tips.

"We're going to miss it," she said.

The god waved toward the opposite track. "There's your train coming. We'll hear the rest on board."

"You want to come to the concert?" Lachesis asked.

"If our new friend is coming."

The prospect delighted me for perhaps two seconds. Then I imagined that little cellar with two gods in its front row and Lachesis unable to listen because everyone was watching her listen.

"I was going west," I said. "There's one in four minutes. You could come with me."

Both gods turned. Clotho lowered the hand holding her visor.

"I'll tell you everything we talked about," I went on. "You can have me to yourselves."

"Well!" said the god. "An exclusive account."

It hadn't sounded so bad while I was thinking it. The goddess was studying me now, and I had to keep my face arranged as if our lunch contained anything she wanted to know. Atropos stood, lifted the carton out of her shopping bag, and took our rubbish to the bin beside the stairs.

Clotho rose too. "We should see you aboard."

She picked up the empty bag and offered me her other hand. Her palm was sticky with peach juice. When I leaned close she said, "Is this on purpose?"

"I think so."

"Good. They ask a lot of questions."

She gave my hand a squeeze and left me holding the empty shopping bag.

We let the eastbound service leave without us. Atropos returned from the bin and spoke quietly to Lachesis; they looked toward the staircase, which led to the street. The cellar was two stops away, but walkable. I had come past it before lunch. I could have told the gods where it was, if anyone had asked.

Instead I took them along the westbound side to the far end of the platform. Atropos waited beside the bench with Lachesis. Clotho accompanied us, entertaining the god with an account of the spring-roll demonstration. He wanted the proportions. She gave him several alternatives and recommended against all of them.

When the train came, the last carriage had six empty seats together. I stepped inside and moved past the pole to the window. The god followed, then the goddess. Her coat caught on the corner of a seat; Clotho, still on the platform, leaned through the doorway to free it.

"Come in," the goddess said.

"I promised to send you off properly."

Clotho stepped back and waved. Farther along the platform, Atropos lifted her hand, saw me watching through the window, and took Lachesis toward the stairs. Lachesis turned once. I held up the shopping bag to her, remembered it was Atropos's rather than hers, and held it up anyway.

The warning sounded. The goddess rose, but the door was already closing in front of her. Clotho had both palms against the glass. She looked so pleased with me that I began smiling back before I remembered who was in the carriage.

We moved.

For several seconds the goddess watched the empty platform run past. Then she turned around.

"You arranged that."

The god looked from her to me. His grin diminished.

"They wanted to hear the band," I said.

"And you offered to tell us everything."

"I can. There's quite a lot about dumplings."

She remained standing. The lilies trembled in her hand, and I could see the effort she was making not to crush the stems. I had been rude to someone who'd brought flowers, and the fact that she was a goddess made that less comfortable in several directions.

"I'm sorry," I said. "I did mean to get you away from them. I hadn't thought much beyond that."

"Clearly."

The god's laugh started and stopped at her look. He tugged down his waistcoat. Outside the window, signal lights flicked past one by one.

"Forty-three years," she said, sitting at last. "I would have taken an answer."

"I can't answer for them."

"I know that."

We traveled a considerable distance in silence. A boy farther down the carriage removed one earbud and recognized the god. Before he could speak, the god put a finger to his lips. The boy kept his phone in his pocket.

At the next stop, the goddess got up. I thought she was leaving. Instead she moved to the seat opposite me, laid the flowers across her knees, and waited until the doors had closed.

"This band of theirs," she said. "The one with no drummer. What do they sound like?"

I couldn't have described them. I told her instead what I had heard on the bench: that Lachesis had talked about them all week, that her friends hadn't listened to the album she'd sent them, and that she had wanted them to hear it. Then I told her about the headphones, and she asked which song. I had to bring it up on my phone. For a minute she listened through its small speaker, her head inclined and the god leaning sideways to hear.

"The second voice," she said. "That boy sang in my temple."

"Is he good?"

"He was very young. He wanted everything loud."

We listened to the chorus. Her thumb beat once against a lily stem.

"He's learned something."

The god wanted to hear the opening again. He could make a whole train hear it from his throat, he said, and demonstrated four soft notes, each carrying a different voice. The goddess told him to let the boy finish. He did.

By the fourth stop, I had explained my employment, my missed train, and the special offer at the takeaway. The god had admitted that his own choir had stood outside the Fates' house for nine hours, which struck me as rather worse than the goddess's invitations.

"They could have opened a window," he said.

"What were you singing?" she asked.

He named a hymn. She closed her eyes.

"The long one?"

"It has a splendid final verse."

"Did you reach it?" I asked.

He considered. "No."

My phone vibrated. Lachesis had sent a photograph: three heads packed into the corner of a dim room, Clotho's visor reflecting a strip of stage light. Atropos had her mask down and a drink halfway to her mouth. Behind them someone was tuning a many-stringed instrument. The message said, *Made it. Keep the bag till next time.*

I turned the screen so the gods could see. The goddess looked for a long moment before returning to the lilies.

"Don't tell them I asked about the song," she said.

I nodded and put the phone away.

We were pulling into my stop. I had left home that morning with the intention of coming back early, eating alone, and finding something to watch. I could still go home and find something to watch. My apartment was three streets away. The empty shopping bag lay across my knees.

The doors opened. The god moved his legs to let me pass.

"Is this you?"

"Yes."

Across from me the goddess was easing the crushed lily out of the bouquet. She freed it without snapping the stem, then looked up.

"You were going to tell us about this wedding," she said. "Eleven months ago, wasn't it?"

I stayed in my seat.

"I hadn't told you it was eleven months ago."

"I'm the one who married them."

The god stretched his legs out again as the doors began to close. "Oh, now you must tell us."

stories.title: The Unopened Ring
stories.prompt: Every century, the immortal queen invites the descendants of the heroes who once tried to kill her to dinner and listens politely as they recount increasingly inaccurate legends about their ancestors. After six thousand years, one guest finally brings the ancient wedding ring their family was forbidden to open—and discovers the queen has been wearing its matching half the entire time.
stories.body:
# The Unopened Ring

Merovel had practiced the kneeling part in the carriage. A pause before the word, a glance around the table afterward: that was how her mother had done it, and her grandmother before her. Ildren had gone to one knee before the immortal queen, yes, but only to retrieve his sword. He had never begged.

The ring was harder to manage. Wrapped in her mother's handkerchief, it made a lump inside her evening glove. She had meant to bring a little box, but all the boxes at home had looked either too grand or too much like an apology.

The invitation had been addressed to her mother, who had declined it before the winter was out. Merovel had written in the summer to say she would come instead. She had not explained why.

Queen Vessarine received her beside a fireplace tall enough to roast the carriage.

“You have your mother's mouth,” she said.

“My mother never came here.”

“No. She sent a miniature with her letter declining. She disliked travel.”

“She disliked being sick in carriages.”

“She didn't say so. How is she?”

Merovel had prepared for questions about the ring, her ancestry, even her modest widow's allowance. “She died in the spring.”

“Oh, my dear. I'm sorry.”

The queen waited. Merovel found she had nothing ready to put into the space.

“Thank you,” she said, and was shown to dinner.

There were three guests, one for each of the heroes who had tried to kill their hostess six thousand years earlier. Invitations went out every hundred years. Families lost their names, acquired children by marriage or adoption, divided into branches that would not speak; the queen's secretaries followed the arguments and invited whoever presently possessed the family relic. Osmer had brought his ancestor's horn. Pelcira wore an arrowhead on a chain. Neither object was subject to a prohibition about opening it.

The queen sat at the head of a table shortened, by discreet additions of flowers, to accommodate four. Behind her rose black columns and tall windows in which the moon lay snagged among distant spires. Her hair was redder than the wine. Fine white lace covered her wrists, and when she smiled at a servant, Merovel saw the points of her teeth.

She wore very little jewelry for a queen. A red stone at her throat, earrings, a thin gold ring on her left hand. Merovel, who had sold most of her own jewelry during her husband's illness, noticed the ring's worn surface. Its face had been rubbed down to something like a small flower.

“I understand we may begin with the deeds of our ancestors,” Osmer said, before the soup had entirely settled in its bowls.

“Certainly.”

“Mine led the charge.”

Pelcira put down her spoon. “Yours was the cook.”

“A captain of provisions.”

“A cook.”

“Who armed himself with a roasting spit when all other weapons failed.” Osmer leaned toward the queen. He had a magnificent voice, which he had been preserving throughout the carriage journey by declining conversation. “At the head of seven hundred men, he broke your outer gate.”

“Seven hundred,” said Vessarine. “Please, go on.”

He described the gate's destruction, the slaughter of the queen's wolves, and his ancestor's advance across a bridge of burning bones. Her Majesty listened without interrupting. For the wolves he got to his feet and lowered his voice, and she leaned forward.

When he finished and sat down, she thanked him.

“Were there really seven hundred?” Pelcira asked.

“At the dinner before last there were two hundred,” the queen said. “Last century, five hundred. Your family has recruited well, Osmer.”

He laughed, after checking her expression. “Numbers do suffer in the telling.”

“Your ancestor came through a kitchen window. He had brought two friends and a ladder.”

“Then why hear me out?”

“I hadn't heard the wolves.”

Osmer looked pleased despite himself. He helped himself to more soup and asked whether she had liked that part.

The queen said she had.

Pelcira's ancestor had once been an archer. In the version she told over the fish, he could split a hair with an arrow in darkness. She demonstrated its flight with a breadstick and nearly struck Osmer's glass.

“He was blind, of course.”

“Eventually,” said the queen.

“We say from birth.”

“He read a note aloud to me.”

“Perhaps someone had taught him the words.”

“Perhaps.”

Vessarine turned her fish with delicate, exact movements. She seemed capable of granting Pelcira a blind archer for the length of a meal. Merovel wished her mother could have seen this. She would have collected enough small absurdities to enliven the rest of her life.

The room itself, Pelcira learned, was only nine hundred years old. The oldest chandelier had been bought secondhand. Vessarine disliked the stone angels beside the windows but had grown accustomed to hanging winter greenery on them. At the first dinner, the guests had sat on cushions and eaten from a common dish. At the twentieth, everyone had considered it indecent for a woman to show her ears.

“I spent forty years with a toothache because no dentist would see me without the veil,” the queen said.

“You can have toothache?” Merovel asked.

“Those at the back are quite ordinary.”

She smiled, and for a moment Merovel could imagine forgetting the points of the others.

By the time the roast arrived, she had taken the ring out of her glove. It lay in its handkerchief on her lap. She rubbed the small gold hand that formed its face, feeling the shallow grooves between the fingers.

Her mother had permitted her to hold it only once. Merovel had been a newly married woman then, proud of her husband, annoyed by his habit of arriving late. Her mother had told the story of Ildren's fidelity: how he had worn his dead wife's ring into the queen's hall, how he had resisted beauty and terror alike, how he had knelt only to retrieve his sword.

Merovel had remembered that story through a marriage considerably less grand than Ildren's. Sometimes with comfort, sometimes with irritation. Her husband had never become punctual.

“And now,” Osmer said, “the kneeling.”

“Ildren brought her to her knees,” Merovel began.

“I thought it was the other way round,” said Osmer.

“Do let her tell it,” Pelcira said.

Merovel started again. She described the blade against the queen's throat, the refusal of a crown, the offer of a thousand years of life. Her mother had always made the offer sound almost reasonable. Merovel heard herself rushing through it, eager to reach the part she knew best.

“He knelt,” she said, and paused. “But only to retrieve his sword. He never begged.”

Vessarine looked at the handkerchief on Merovel's lap.

“Your mother told you that?”

“Yes.”

“Did she tell you anything else about him?”

“A great many things.”

“I'd like to hear them.”

Merovel disliked the careful kindness in her voice. “Was that one true?”

The queen placed her knife beside her plate. “He did ask me to spare his friends.”

“But he didn't beg.”

“Merovel, they were going to be hanged.”

Osmer lowered the horn he had been about to show Pelcira.

“He was wounded,” the queen continued. “Standing hurt him. I remember wishing he'd sit down.”

“And did you spare them?”

“Yes.”

Merovel pulled the handkerchief onto the table. “Then perhaps the rest is true. We still have the ring. He never took it off.”

She unfolded the linen. It was a narrow hoop, slightly crooked, with one tiny hand laid across its face as if guarding something. A worn nail caught the candlelight.

The queen reached for her wine, missed the stem, and left her hand on the cloth.

“You brought it.”

“It came to me when Mother died.”

“May I see it?”

Merovel moved the handkerchief toward her. Vessarine touched the gold with the tip of one finger, turning it so the little hand lay palm-down.

“He wore it hard,” she said.

“He wore it faithfully.”

“Yes.”

There was finally something they agreed on. Merovel felt a foolish wish to take the ring back before the queen could spoil it.

Instead Vessarine slid the linen toward her. “It's yours.”

“It opens,” Merovel said. “The hand lifts. But we aren't allowed.”

“Who told you that?”

“Everyone. My mother. Hers. There's something of you shut inside it. If we open it, you can have him again.”

The queen stared at the gold hand.

Merovel looked from the ring to her. “Can you?”

“No.”

Merovel had expected amusement. The answer was so plain that she could not immediately find another question.

Osmer turned a hand in the air. “It may be a figure of speech.”

Pelcira pressed his sleeve down against the table until he stopped.

“Ildren gave it to his eldest daughter when his fingers swelled,” Vessarine said. “Near the end. I knew she'd kept it. I didn't know what she'd said about it.”

“You were there?”

“Yes.”

The hand was no larger than Merovel's smallest fingernail. She could see the hinge at the wrist now, almost filled with dark material. She had seen it before and avoided looking closely. Her mother had died in bed, calling for a sister dead since childhood. During the last hours, Merovel had obeyed instructions that no longer made sense because obedience was still something she could give.

She put her nail under the little fingers.

“At the thumb,” said the queen. “Don't pull. Press it inward first.”

Merovel looked up.

“I used to do it for him.”

The thumb moved. The lid rose reluctantly, exposing a hollow no deeper than a drop of wine. Letters had been cut into the sheltered gold.

Merovel knew the old letter forms from the copied inscription on Ildren's tomb. She sounded them without meaning to.

Vessarine.

Her hostess took off her own ring.

It, too, bore a hand. Seen alone, its curling fingers had looked like a worn flower. Merovel lowered the lid of her ring until the catch held. The queen set her hoop beside it, turned it once, and fitted their uneven edges together. The hands clasped. What had looked like a crooked ring became half of a wide, neatly joined band.

There was no flash or music. One edge clicked against the other. The queen had a pale groove around her finger.

“He was my husband,” she said.

Merovel rubbed the groove the little lid had left beneath her nail.

“He had a wife.”

“She died before he came here.”

“We come from her.”

“Yes.”

“So you aren't—”

“No.” The queen waited until Merovel looked at her. “I'm not your grandmother.”

That should have made it easier. Instead Merovel thought of her mother reciting the tale, pleased with the pause before *knelt*, and felt suddenly angry with the woman whose name was inside the ring.

“You let us say all that.”

“I did.”

“For six thousand years?”

“At the first dinner, his granddaughter would not believe me. At the second, they knew he'd lived here but said I'd bewitched him. By the third, he'd escaped me. I grew tired of arguing with people who took every point I won as proof I'd enchanted them.”

“You could have shown them your ring.”

“I did. A piece of jewelry wasn't much of an argument against a dead mother.”

Merovel folded her hands below the edge of the table. On the linen, the two gold hands remained clasped.

“Did you offer him a thousand years?”

“I couldn't. I've never known how to give anyone this.” Vessarine touched the bare place on her finger. “I offered him the rooms next to mine. He said they faced the wrong way for morning light.”

“After he tried to kill you?” Pelcira said.

“Eleven years after.”

Osmer let out a breath. “There must have been rather a lot in between.”

“There was a truce. His friends went home. He came back as an envoy, and then he came without a message.”

“Were you beautiful then?” Merovel asked, and immediately wished she hadn't.

The queen considered her with something close to her earlier amusement. “Much as I am now. My hair was shorter. He said it suited me better.”

Merovel looked at the enormous red fall over her shoulder.

“He was very insistent,” Vessarine added. “We were married for thirty-four years. I let it grow for most of them.”

Pelcira laughed once, uncertainly. The queen smiled at her, then looked down at the rings again.

The servants came to take the roast away. Plates lifted, a fork fell, somebody asked whether the guests would like the sweet wine. Merovel was grateful for these people who could still remember what they were doing. She wanted the whole table cleared and everyone sent out; she wanted Osmer to begin the wolves again so she would not have to say anything.

She settled for asking, “Why would his daughter forbid it?”

“She hated me.”

“Because you were his enemy?”

“Partly. Because I had him here when she wanted him at home. Because he was happy, and she thought that insulted her mother. She told me those things herself. She may have had other reasons.”

“Did you try to be kind to her?”

“I bought her things.” The queen rubbed a spot of wine from the table with her thumb. “She asked me to stop.”

Merovel thought of the miniature her own mother had sent, and of the queen still keeping it somewhere in this house when Merovel and everyone who had known her mother were dead.

“You still invite us.”

“I like hearing what survives.”

“Even the wolves?”

“Sometimes especially those. I've had some very dull centuries.” She looked toward Osmer, but he was occupied with the clasped hands. Her attempted smile faded. “There used to be more little things. His granddaughter knew how he peeled an apple. Once a boy came who had the song the cook used to sing. Only half of it, but I'd forgotten there was a song.”

“My ancestor?” Osmer asked.

“Yes.”

He sat back, evidently making room for this.

Merovel could remember nothing about apples. Their family did have a saying about leaving one boot where a person could find it, but no one had ever explained it, and this did not seem the moment to mention boots.

“Mother said Ildren never laughed at a woman,” she said. “She thought that was the proof of a gentleman. A man might be brave and still laugh at you.”

The queen's mouth moved.

“He did?”

“Oh, yes.”

“Cruelly?”

“Once. I had tried to sing something. I was proud of it.”

Merovel waited.

“I didn't sing in front of him again for a long time.”

Beyond the windows, clouds had covered the moon. The queen's face had changed in the candlelight, though Merovel could not have said how. She had the same smooth skin, the same red eyes. It was her mouth, perhaps, held still around something she had not intended to remember.

“My husband laughed when I fell off a horse,” Merovel said. “Before he came to help me.”

“Were you hurt?”

“Not badly. I was furious. He kept saying he wouldn't have laughed if he'd known I was hurt, and I kept saying that was exactly the difficulty.”

Pelcira nodded with such vigor that her arrowhead struck her glass.

“He was usually kind,” Merovel said. “My husband.”

“Ildren too.”

Merovel thought she might cry, but the feeling passed while she looked for her wine. She had used the handkerchief for the ring. Her mother's initials lay underneath the little gold hands.

“May I have my half back?” she asked.

“Of course.”

Vessarine separated the hoops. She moved slowly, turning them until the fingers disengaged, then lifted the little hinged hand once more. For a moment she looked at the name inside. She left it open and placed the ring on the linen.

The queen put her own half back on. It settled into the pale groove.

“Did he ever hear you sing again?” Merovel asked.

Vessarine looked up, surprised. “Yes. He got so deaf in one ear that I could sit on that side and sing anything I liked.”

Osmer made a small sound into his wine.

“He could still see me,” she said. “He knew perfectly well. He'd pretend I was making conversation and give me the most unsuitable answers.”

“What sort of answers?”

“I can't remember. No, wait. There was something about a goat.”

Pelcira drew the dish of preserved cherries toward her. Osmer, who had stood up for the wolves, stayed in his chair. Merovel closed the little hand over the name, pressed the thumb until it caught, and slipped the ring onto her own finger. It was too large; she held it in place with her thumb.

The queen began with the goat, stopped because she had begun too late, and went back to explain a quarrel over a ruined pair of slippers. She confused which winter it had been. She laughed before she reached the part that was funny and had to try again.

Merovel leaned forward. This part she wanted to get right.

stories.title: Before Lunch
stories.prompt: You've always been good at faking it till you make it, a great BS'er,. Well apparently you've unknowingly convinced the mob that you're a legendary hitman; some eldritch horror that you're in fact older than it, and by mistake proposed marriage to satan's daughter. All before lunchtime.
stories.body:
# Before Lunch

The notice in the hotel window promises cash and a meal. You go in through the nearest door, which is already a mistake, and tell the man blocking the stairs that you have an appointment.

“With Mr. Dott?”

“That's right.”

You have never heard of Mr. Dott. But the notice says to ask for the manager, and you have found that people are much more helpful once they believe you know someone. At thirty-four, you possess no qualifications that fit neatly on an application. You can, however, talk a furious wedding guest into a taxi, persuade a caterer to pay you in cash, and carry three plates provided nobody speaks to you.

The man consults his watch. Eleven past eleven.

“He expected you earlier.”

“Well, I'm here now.”

It is an excellent answer. It contains no information anyone can dispute.

Upstairs, Mr. Dott sits at a little table in a very large office. Behind him are photographs of himself with people whose smiling faces suggest they would like their arms back. A second man stands beside an empty chair.

“No bag?” Dott asks.

“Was I supposed to bring something?”

The standing man looks at Dott, who makes a small movement with his fingers. The man steps away from the chair.

You sit. Good upholstery. This morning is improving.

“I need a guest removed from my private dining room,” Dott says. “Before lunch. Quietly.”

“Of course.”

“Permanently.”

“If you don't want him back, don't let him back in.”

Dott studies you. You give him the calm, attentive face that once got you an entire week's work supervising a warehouse. You learned a great deal about warehouses during that week.

“My people have tried,” he says.

“Sometimes a fresh face helps.”

“He hurt one of them.”

You glance at the thickset man behind your chair. A security job. You had hoped for waiting tables, but the right words can make a security job mostly administrative.

“The important thing is not to make it physical,” you say. “I've cleared whole rooms without laying a finger on anyone.”

At a wedding, this involved mentioning that the free bar had closed. It worked so well the bride's mother left.

Dott glances at the man behind you. Something passes between them that makes you wish you had claimed a little less.

“You won't be searched,” he says. “No offence was intended.”

“None taken.” You have not noticed an offence, but it would be unprofessional to admit it.

He pushes an envelope across the table. “Half now.”

You take it with a nod, resisting the urge to count it in front of him. The standing man opens the door. Clearly the interview is over. You rise, remembering the most important point just in time.

“This includes lunch?”

For a moment Dott looks almost pleased.

“If you have an appetite afterwards, you can eat anything in the building.”

In the corridor, you look in the envelope and stop walking.

The escort stops too. “Problem?”

It is more money than you have ever been handed at once, including the time somebody handed you the wrong pay packet and you spent seven glorious seconds considering a train journey.

“Just checking.”

“The broker said you'd be like this. Ordinary. No equipment.” The escort keeps his voice low. “Is it true you did six men with a spoon?”

You look up at him.

“I'm sorry?”

“The Velvet Goodbye. Every crew in the city has a story about you.” He laughs, apologetically. “You probably hate the name.”

There are two possibilities. Either this is an elaborate interview for a washing-up job, or you have just accepted a murder from a man whose staff think you are a legendary assassin.

The escort pulls back his jacket to adjust the gun at his belt.

One possibility.

“People talk too much,” you say, because a sentence is required, and he nods as though you have said something he will be able to repeat for years.

“I'll wait right outside. Mr. Dott wants me to bring you straight back when it's dead.”

Not *he*. *It*.

You put the money away. Your mouth has gone dry. On the other side of the door, someone is delicately ringing a spoon against a glass.

“Can I wash my hands first?”

“Certainly.” The escort opens the door for you. “There's a basin inside.”

He closes it behind you with considerable respect.

***

The dining room is set for twelve. Its only occupant sits at the far end, wrapped in a grey coat with a collar that hides most of its head. The curtains are drawn. Beneath a small lamp, a spoon circles the inside of an empty ice-cream dish.

“Finally,” says the occupant. “Another.”

“Another what?”

It turns towards you. You can make out a narrow face and two pale hands. A film producer, perhaps. Someone who has become accustomed to a private dining room and doesn't know how to stop having it. You have worked parties for such people. One demanded that you take the stairs out of a photograph.

“Another little person who believes I shall leave because it asks me to.”

“They do need the room.” You try the door handle behind your back. It turns, but the escort clears his throat on the other side. “Are you waiting for something?”

“More of this.” It taps the dish with its spoon. “The kitchen refuses to send it.”

“Well. That's a fairly strong hint.”

The spoon stops.

“I am Vhulcren.”

You wait for the name to become helpful.

“I do not take hints.”

“Right.” You loosen your collar. There is a second door near the far end of the room. Light shows beneath it. “Let's go and talk to someone about your pudding.”

Vhulcren leans forward. The collar shifts. What you took for a face is a small flat area above a mouth that continues well past the edge of the lamplight.

“I ate kings before your people had houses.”

You have begun edging towards the second door. The table is reassuringly wide. Everything else about the room is becoming less so. Nevertheless, the voice is that voice: the special, carrying voice of a customer who has discovered that volume can obtain things unavailable on the menu.

You answer it on habit. “Yes, and I've been dealing with spoiled little monsters since before you had teeth. Come on. Up you get.”

Vhulcren rises.

Its coat drops to the floor. The body unfolding above it has too many joints to count while you are moving backwards. Pale limbs plant themselves on the carpet, one after another; the ceiling presses down on a smooth, breathing bulk. A hanging light tilts against its side.

You hit a chair and sit involuntarily.

“Before teeth?”

The voice is softer now, coming from several places. You cannot tell which is nearest your ear.

“I—”

“When I was fed through the soft seams.” A long, jointed limb slides across the table. “You knew me then?”

You grip the chair. The limb stops just short of your hand, as if awaiting permission to touch it.

“In the nursery dark,” Vhulcren says. “Before they uncovered us.”

It bows its enormous body. Dust drifts from the ceiling onto the laid plates. “I had thought no one older remained.”

For the second time this morning, somebody has supplied you with qualifications.

You would like to correct the mistake. You would also like to be outside. The latter is a much stronger wish, especially since one of Vhulcren's lower mouths is opening and closing against the tablecloth.

“It's been a while,” you manage.

“What form did you wear? I remember so little clearly. Such a long time in that miserable nursery, with the others shoving, always shoving. Were you our keeper?”

You shake your head quickly. *Keeper* sounds like a job with obligations.

“No. No, let's not go into all that.”

“Of course.” The limb withdraws. “Forgive me.”

The door opens behind you. Your escort peers in, takes one look at the ceiling, and begins shutting it again.

“Stay,” Vhulcren says. “You will bring a fresh dish for my elder.”

The escort looks at you. It is very hard to project mastery while gripping the seat of a dining chair.

“Actually,” you say, “we were just going through there.”

You point at the far door.

“The lounge?” the escort asks.

“Yes.” Thank goodness it has a name.

“I'll tell Mr. Dott.”

“You do that.”

He leaves at a brisk walk. You stand, with the chair still briefly attached to your hands, and put it down. Vhulcren has to ease several limbs out from beneath the table before it can follow. The table rises six inches and lands with a crash of cutlery.

“I have become clumsy,” it says.

“These rooms are badly laid out.”

“They are.” The relief in its voice is astonishing. “They are too small.”

You open the lounge door and slip through while it gathers its coat.

***

The lounge has windows, chairs, a large clock showing twenty-seven minutes to twelve, and a door with a brass push plate. You cross straight to that door. Locked.

You press harder, which sometimes helps with cheap locks. This is a very good hotel.

“It leads to the service stairs,” says a woman behind you. “They keep it locked.”

She has come out of a little washroom. Her white suit fits her beautifully, her dark hair is swept away from her face, and she looks about your age. She is holding a handbag open and frowning into it.

“I was looking for the lobby,” you say.

“Through the dining room.”

Something large scrapes against the other side of that door.

“A different lobby.”

She looks up from the bag. Then at the door. “That's Vhulcren. I heard it through the washroom wall, calling someone its elder.”

“It gets carried away.”

“I've noticed.” She shuts the bag. “I'm Sathrie.”

You introduce yourself with your actual first name. It comes out a little croaky. For once, nobody seems to require a title.

“What are you doing for lunch?” she asks.

“Leaving.”

She laughs and opens the bag again, rummaging in a different pocket. “I'd like to. My father chose this place. We used to come here when I was little, and he's never accepted that I might want to eat somewhere else.”

An ally. A prosperous ally with a grievance against the premises. You move towards her, stepping around a low chair, and catch a flash of gold beneath it. A ring lies against the back leg, set with a red stone almost the size of your thumbnail.

Nothing ingratiates you with a rich person like returning an expensive object you could have stolen. You bend to pick it up, discover your arm is just too short, and go down on one knee. Your trousers pull unpleasantly tight.

“We could go somewhere else,” you say, reaching.

“You and me?”

“Why not?” Your fingertips close around the ring. You turn towards her, still kneeling because the chair arm is across your shoulder. “I can't imagine anyone I'd rather go with. Will you have me?”

You hold out the ring.

She looks up from the bag. Her gaze moves from your face to your bent knee and back. She sets the bag down very slowly.

“Yes,” she says.

You smile. What a recovery. Dott's envelope may be more trouble than it is worth, but you have found a way out, possibly a lunch companion, and—

“Yes. I'll marry you.”

—a use for the large clock, which you stare at in the hope that you have somehow missed several important intervening months.

“Oh,” you say.

She takes the ring and looks at it properly for the first time. She turns it over, sees the little nick on the back, and laughs in delight.

“It's mine! I've been looking everywhere. You proposed with my own ring.” She holds it out towards you again. “Go on, then.”

“I was just—”

The dining-room door strikes the wall. Vhulcren squeezes through sideways, one long limb reaching for you. You jerk upright and Sathrie catches your arm.

“Careful,” she tells it. “We're having a moment.”

Vhulcren stops. Its nearest mouths close.

“Daughter of Satan.”

You look at her.

“Sathrie,” she tells it. “We've discussed this.”

“Satan,” you repeat.

“My father. I mentioned him.” She slides the ring onto her finger herself. “He'll be here at twelve. Oh, he'll have plenty to say about us getting married.”

Two small horns push up through her dark hair. She reaches up and tucks a loose strand around one of them, smiling at the prospect.

You have not moved from beside the chair. Your knee hurts. Somebody appears to have turned the heating up, although that may be the hand she has tucked through your elbow.

“I did not know you were betrothed,” Vhulcren says to you.

“Neither did I,” you say, accurately and uselessly.

***

Dott arrives through the dining room with both of the large men. He is carrying an open napkin, as if his hands began doing something ordinary and haven't been told about the rest of his morning.

He sees Vhulcren. He sees you. His escort gestures at you with the helpless annoyance of a man whose report has just been proven correct.

“We had an arrangement,” Dott says.

“We've just become engaged,” Sathrie tells him. “Do congratulate us.”

The escort moves towards you, one hand held out for your arm. A blue flame runs across Sathrie's knuckles. Dott catches his man's wrist before he reaches you, and the flame goes out.

“Congratulations,” Dott says. His eyes stay on you.

“I hope the old gentleman will be pleased,” Vhulcren says. “He has always admired seniority.”

“You can tell him so at lunch,” Sathrie says.

Vhulcren's pale limbs shuffle nearer the dining-room door. “I had not intended to remain.”

Dott hears this too. You can tell by the tiny change in his face: the first suggestion that the morning might contain an outcome he wants.

Sathrie pulls gently at your sleeve. “Come and sit down. You're shaking.”

“It's been quite a morning.”

“I'll get you a drink.” She releases you and turns to Dott. “Something cold.”

Dott ignores her and beckons you a little way aside. You go because both men have spread themselves across the doorway, and because Sathrie has begun examining the bottles on a sideboard.

“I didn't pay for a social visit,” he says beneath his breath.

“You're going to get your room back.”

“I paid for a dead thing.”

You glance past him at Vhulcren. It is trying to get a sleeve onto a limb that has acquired an extra joint. It could kill Dott very easily. It could probably kill everybody in this room without ceasing to be annoyed by its coat. You take out the envelope.

“Then you can have this back.”

He doesn't reach for it.

Your hand hangs between you. The money is enough to pay your rent for a long time. You bring it closer to him before you can think about that properly.

“Every penny,” you say. “And it goes. Now.”

Behind Dott, Sathrie puts down a bottle with an impatient clack. “Are you two going to be much longer?”

Dott holds your gaze for another second. Then he takes the envelope and puts it inside his jacket.

“Don't bring it back.”

You turn before he can decide to qualify this.

“We're going out,” you announce. “Vhulcren, would you join us?”

“For lunch?” Sathrie asks.

“For a walk. First.” You put a hand on her arm, with all the intimate assurance of someone who has managed seven minutes of engagement. “Before your father gets here. Just a little time without an audience.”

She looks towards Vhulcren.

You are not yet good at being engaged.

“It was leaving anyway,” you add.

“I would not intrude upon a family occasion,” Vhulcren says quickly. “I can accompany you as far as the street.”

“Wonderful. Mr. Dott, the service stairs?”

You point to the brass plate. A short route. No lobby staff to stop you. No father arriving through the front doors.

“Too narrow,” Dott says, looking at Vhulcren. He snaps his fingers at the escort. “Clear the front.”

You walk beside Sathrie through the dining room, around the table where one plate has been crushed into glittering powder. Vhulcren follows, stooping beneath the lintel. Nobody applauds. You had not expected anybody to, but some entirely unhelpful part of you thinks it has been rather well done.

At the stairs you offer Sathrie your hand. Vhulcren takes your other one. Its touch is cool and softly ridged, and its weight obliges you to descend very carefully while the escort stares up from the bottom.

“I had forgotten,” Vhulcren says quietly, “what it was to be the younger.”

You cannot look at it without looking away from the stairs.

“Watch that last step.”

“Yes.”

The escort holds the front door. As you pass, he murmurs, “Not a mark on it. I don't know how you do it.”

You are tempted. Even now, with your shirt wet under the arms and Satan due at any moment, you are tempted to give him something to remember.

Sathrie tugs you out into the daylight.

***

On the pavement, Vhulcren releases your hand and draws its coat together. It has folded itself into a shape that almost passes for a tall person carrying too many umbrellas.

“We shall speak again,” it says. “When you are less occupied.”

“No hurry.”

“Indeed.” Several parts of its face turn towards the approaching cars. “Please convey my good wishes to the bride's father.”

Before she can answer, it steps off the kerb and spreads two pale membranes from beneath its coat. The downstroke knocks your hair into your eyes. By the time you brush it away, Vhulcren is above the opposite rooftops, beating vigorously towards somewhere else.

Sathrie watches it go. “He isn't that bad.”

You don't ask which of them she means.

The street clock reads eleven fifty-six. A bus rattles past. You have enough money for the next one, and Sathrie is no longer holding your arm.

“About the ring,” you say.

She turns to you.

“I found it under the chair. I was giving it back. When I said, will you have me, I meant lunch. Or a walk. Getting out of the hotel, mostly.”

Her smile disappears. She takes a step back and looks you over, from the cheap shoes to the collar you have pulled out of shape.

“You weren't proposing.”

“No.”

A delivery driver honks at a taxi. Behind you, the escort carefully shuts the hotel door.

“Oh, that's embarrassing,” she says.

“I'm sorry.”

She rubs her forehead between the horns. “I told Vhulcren.”

“And Mr. Dott.”

“Yes, I remember.”

You shut your mouth.

She looks down at her ring, then across the road towards the bus stop. You could go. A pleasant nod, an apology, fifty yards. You are much better at finding opportunities than recognizing when to leave them alone.

“I did mean I'd like to go with you,” you say.

“You don't know anything about me.”

“I know where you don't want to have lunch.”

She considers you. “There's a place round the corner. The chairs don't match and the bread's good. Nobody there will ask about the wedding.”

You look at the hotel. “Won't your father be waiting?”

“I'll call him.” She takes out her phone. “If you're coming, you can carry my bag while I do it.”

You take the bag. It is unexpectedly heavy. The bus stop is still there, perfectly accessible, with an entirely ordinary future queueing beside it.

“What should I say you do?” she asks, thumb poised over the screen.

“Guest relations,” you say, and follow her round the corner.

stories.title: A Reasonable Declaration
stories.prompt: You used to be a daring adventurer, traveling the realm. Nowadays, you’re retired and finally being forced to filing identification and taxation papers for all the artifacts.
stories.body:
# A Reasonable Declaration

Barnaby Greave could have carried the sword upstairs. What he could not do was carry the sword, pull the trolley, and prevent the warming cup from knocking against the spectacles, all while holding his appointment slip where somebody might see he was expected.

He put the slip between his teeth.

At the second-floor landing, a woman behind a low partition looked up. Barnaby straightened, removed the paper from his mouth, and waited for her to finish recognizing him.

"You've come," she said.

"I gave my word."

She looked at the damp slip. "This is your third appointment."

He set the sword beside the trolley with some care. His shoulder had begun to complain halfway up; his knee had been complaining since breakfast. There had been an excellent reclining chair in a shop window that morning, upholstered in plum velvet, with a handle that brought one's feet up. He had tested it. The proprietor had eventually come to check whether he was asleep.

"Fulvia," said the woman, indicating the little nameplate on her desk. "I wrote to you. Several times. Where's the rest?"

"Of me?"

"Your collection. I arranged for the long table."

The table ran almost to the window. On it lay nineteen numbered cards.

Barnaby opened the trolley's battered lid. "This is the collection."

Fulvia stood. She looked inside, then at the corridor. The trolley contained a folded cloak and a biscuit tin. It had originally been built for groceries, a purpose to which he looked forward to returning it.

"I expected crates," she said.

He had expected to be offered a chair. After a moment he pulled one out himself.

Fulvia sat too. Barnaby handed her his preliminary assessment. The total had been underlined twice. He had underlined it himself a third time before coming, so there could be no doubt about which part he objected to.

"A hundred and forty-eight crowns," he said. "For things already mine. I didn't have them off the district. I carried every one of them through places the district has never heard of, generally at a run, and I have carried them up and down stairs ever since without anybody once offering to help."

"You can correct the inventory today. Tomorrow there's a late charge."

"I'm retired."

Fulvia wrote the date at the top of a fresh inventory sheet.

He took the chair envelope from his inside pocket and set it under his hand. Ninety crowns. The plain wool version cost sixty; the plum velvet cost ninety, and he had decided, after everything, that he deserved the plum.

Fulvia leaned down to a shelf. When she rose she was holding both volumes of his memoirs, their spines creased almost white.

"The preliminary office used your books," she said. "I brought my own copies. They have the illustrations."

She opened the first volume without consulting its contents. A pressed flower lay beside a picture of Barnaby standing on a precipice, his cloak lifting in a wind that had been much less accommodating at the time.

"I read this part to my sister," she said. "She doesn't usually like adventure."

Barnaby took his hand off the envelope.

"The ascent?" He sat forward. "People generally like the ascent. Eleven days on the face, and a night on a ledge no wider than this table, with the wind trying to have my boots off. The illustrator never did get the ledge. He drew a sort of balcony —"

"The fight afterwards. Where you turn back."

"Ah. Yes."

She set the book beside the first card. "The Red Verdict. May I see it?"

He drew the sword. There was very little space between the table and the partition, and he had to draw it upwards, which spoiled the gesture. Fulvia moved her books before he could lay the blade across them.

For a while things improved. She inspected the dark groove along the blade and the crescent nick near the tip. She turned a page and compared the sword with its picture, then glanced at Barnaby as if he had stepped out of it carrying the right property.

"What is the grip wrapped in?"

"Bootlace. The leather rotted."

Her finger stopped over the drawing. "The Emperor's Ruin has that same wrapping."

"It would."

"And the nick."

"That too."

She opened the other volume. Barnaby could tell from the ribbon that she had prepared this question.

"Is this also the Last Argument?"

"In the context of that expedition. The Red Verdict had been in the first book, and one can't very well have the same sword turn up in the second without some sign of growth."

Fulvia looked from the blade to three of her cards. "You've given one sword three names?"

"Four. Mercy of the Pass, near the end of the first book. Circumstances changed."

"But the sword didn't."

"It was sharpened."

She brought the fourth card over. For the first time since the notices began, Barnaby saw something promising in the arrangement of government property.

"You aren't proposing to charge me four times?"

"I need to identify which entries are the same object."

He drew the cards into a neat stack. "These are. Indisputably. You have noticed the nick yourself."

Fulvia's disappointment was visible enough to be disagreeable. She turned back to the precipice.

"You say the Red Verdict was torn from your hand."

"It was. I caught the lace."

"I always wondered how you caught it. With the other hand?"

"The same one."

He spread his fingers. She studied the pale bands across their bases, then the bootlace spiraling around the grip. The illustrator had given him a clenched fist and a clean cuff. In fact the lace had unwrapped under his weight, one turn at a time, until he thought it would peel the skin off his fingers. Above him, the blade had jammed between two stones. Below him something moved through the white air, slow enough to wait.

For three days afterwards he had eaten with his left hand, spilling soup down his shirt. He had been furious about the soup.

"Was it a very long fall?" Fulvia asked.

"I didn't go and measure it."

She closed the book halfway. He had answered too sharply. He pulled the sword nearer, fed a small thread of his own power into its grip, and watched a line of amber run along the edge.

"Still takes a charge from the wielder," he said. "Not much of one now. Keep your fingers clear."

The line died when he released it. Fulvia entered the surviving function and counted four aliases against one blade. Barnaby sat back.

The cloak occupied three further cards: the Veil of Night, the Mantle of Unseen Steps, and the Widow's Shadow. Fulvia accepted the darn on its shoulder as evidence, though she spent some time looking for the widow in the index.

"There wasn't one," he admitted. "I thought there ought to have been. It's a very good name for a cloak."

She wrote something in the margin of her book.

"You aren't correcting your copy?"

"I'll forget otherwise."

The cloak had once bent the visible outline of a person wearing it, provided that person supplied the power. Now the lining had split at the hips. Barnaby explained this twice, because the preliminary valuation assumed complete concealment, and then stood to demonstrate.

He fastened the clasp, pulled the hood over his head, and let power work out through the worn threads. His hands blurred. The chair behind his chest became visible in a patchwork of pale streaks. He took three steps along the table.

Fulvia leaned to her left.

"I can see your knees."

"The lining. As I said."

"In the picture you reach the throne without anyone seeing you."

"I was younger. I could crouch."

He attempted to show her. His knee made a sound, and he abandoned the demonstration, gripping the table while his head became solid again. Fulvia brought his chair round without comment, which he preferred to sympathy.

When he had sat and unfastened the clasp, she showed him the illustration. "They drew the cloak down to the floor."

"They also gave me longer legs."

She looked at the picture for another moment, then at the two crowns she had written in the assessment column. "It was my favorite picture."

"It can remain so."

Fulvia didn't answer. She folded the cloak with its damaged lining outwards. Barnaby opened the biscuit tin and took out the circlet.

This was copper, much polished on the inside and green at the joints. Barnaby wore it on the cover of the second volume, although in the pictured incident he had been keeping it in a pocket because of the cold.

"The Crown of Command." Fulvia turned the second volume round so that he could see his own cover, as though he might have forgotten it. "This is the one my sister wanted framed. She never read past the cover till I made her, and then she read it twice and wouldn't give it back, and I had to go round on a Sunday and —" She stopped, looked down at her cards, and uncapped her pen.

Barnaby waited until she had found the right card. "Also the Voice of the Mountain, for the second half of the book, where it matters. And the Siege Chorus, for the chapter at the fort. That one was mine."

"That makes ten entries accounted for." She copied the names. "What does it do, precisely?"

"Carries your voice. You feed it a little power and it carries whatever you say. Through stone, if necessary." He leaned back. "At the fort I needed the besiegers to think the pass was held. So I held it. I called the watches from the east wall and answered them from the west. I had a sergeant with a cough. I had a boy who kept asking when supper was. By the second night they were sending out to parley with a company of fifty."

"How many were there?"

"Me. I stood in different places."

She turned the circlet over. "May I try it?"

He ought to have said he would demonstrate it himself. But she was holding it above her hair, and he had spent enough time disappointing her.

"Touch the inner rim with your fingertips. The smallest thread of power. You'll feel it warm."

Fulvia set the circlet on her head, holding it by the outside.

"Will I sound like you?"

"You'll sound like yourself. Speak softly."

She touched the inner rim, and the copper brightened beneath her fingers. Drawing herself up, she glanced at the open book and whispered, "Lay down your spears."

Her whisper came out of the ceiling, the wall behind Barnaby, and the stairs. In the corridor somebody dropped a box of paper clips.

"Take it off," Barnaby said.

"Oh, I'm sorry!"

The apology filled the office. Beyond the partition a chair scraped violently backwards. Fulvia snatched off the circlet, cutting her supply of power, and silence returned with a small metallic ringing in Barnaby's ears.

She held the copper band in both hands. Her hair stood up through the middle.

The person gathering paper clips said, quite clearly, "Again?"

Barnaby looked at her.

"The man who assesses musical instruments works here on Tuesdays," she said. She set the circlet down and brushed at her hair. "You did say softly."

"I did. It's louder since I cracked that joint."

"You could have mentioned that."

He could. He had forgotten the crack, and now hoped she would discover some useful depreciation in it. Instead she wrote six crowns beside the circlet.

"For that?"

"It works through walls."

"It has lost all delicacy. It used to put a whisper in one ear on the far side of a courtyard. You heard it just now. It's a town crier."

"You called it the Siege Chorus."

There was no beneficial reply to this. He pushed the circlet across the table and reached into the tin.

The warming cup came wrapped in a pair of his socks. He hadn't polished it: he used it every morning, and it was already annoying enough to have his morning cup detained in a tax office. The Grail of Embers, Winter's Defeat, and the Beggar's Comfort proved to be one squat vessel with a chipped yellow rim.

Fulvia's books showed it in gold.

"It is yellow," Barnaby said, before she could speak.

She put a fingertip against the side. "Cold."

"Empty. Give me a moment."

He fetched tea from the office urn, returned with the cup, and warmed it with his hands around the base, pressing his own power into the clay. It would retain that small charge for half an hour. It couldn't replenish itself; when he forgot, he drank cold tea like anybody else.

Fulvia tested it again. "Three crowns."

"Three? It's a cup. It's clay with a chip in it. Whatever your illustrator thinks, there isn't a scrap of gold anywhere on it."

She wrote the three down.

"I do the work," he said.

She waited with her pen above the paper. Barnaby took a sip. He had warmed it more than he intended, and could not pursue his objection until his tongue recovered.

The lifting buckle was the Titan's Favor and the Giant's Hand. Together with its original braided strap, it had once enabled him to carry two injured people in succession up a broken stair. He put the cloak and circlet back in the trolley to give it some weight, then hooked the strap around the handle and supplied the buckle with power through his palm. The trolley became easy to lift but retained all its bulk. Bringing it round, he knocked a corner against the table and scattered the cards.

Fulvia retrieved them while he lowered it, and wrote four crowns.

"It does nothing about the size," he said. "You saw."

She squared the cards against the edge of the table and set them back in their places.

The spectacles had three names too: Eyes of the Deep, Lanternless Sight, and Scholar's Salvation. One lens was held in with wire, the other with a dreadful hard paste he had never managed to remove. By feeding the frames a little of his power he could read in the dark, although he had to tilt his head to keep the two halves of each line aligned. Fulvia tested them under her desk, directing her own power through the frames, and emerged with a gray smudge on her sleeve.

"I can only read one side clearly."

"Tilt your head."

She went back under. He heard a soft bump. This time she emerged rubbing her scalp, with the spectacles in her other hand.

Two crowns. He felt rather protective of them at that price. They had helped him read a warning scratched inside a door he had been about to shut. For years afterwards he had kept a wooden wedge in his boot, ordinary wood, replaced whenever it broke. He was relieved he hadn't put that in a book.

The last thing in the tin was a metal disk in a paper sleeve. Fulvia read the nineteenth card: Key of Return.

"That was your publisher's title," she said. "You call it an exit token in the chapter."

"The publisher owned the headings."

He slid it onto the table. There was no route left in it, only marks and a closing stamp. He had turned it over often enough to make its edges smooth.

"Queen Street," he said, before she asked.

It came back to him with unnecessary sharpness: the white seam in the abandoned tunnel, black rain falling upwards around it, his own breath catching because he was safely through and could at last afford to be frightened. The Exit Witness had taken the disk from his hand and closed the returned token. Barnaby had watched until it was done. Whatever the place beyond that crossing was, he had wanted no unfinished way back to it.

Fulvia tilted the disk toward the window. "Can it open anything now?"

"No. The Witness closed it."

She put it back in its sleeve. "No precious metal. No remaining function. Nil."

He reached for it, then stopped to let her attach its numbered label. It was faintly insulting to have the thing appraised as worthless, but he was not about to appeal.

By then the light had moved off the long table. Fulvia had seven cards in front of her and a chain of pencil marks running through both books. Barnaby's tea had gone cold. Somewhere in the corridor a clock began to strike, and he looked up so quickly she said, "Four. We close at five."

"Have we finished?"

"The inventory isn't signed. I need the places of acquisition."

He looked at the form. Each object had a space about the length of his thumb.

"How much detail?"

"Enough to identify the place, if you know it."

"We called them the Realms. That didn't mean we knew where we were."

"Then write what you do know. There's an additional sheet."

He had spent two books making the doors he had entered sound like destinations. Now he had to distinguish what he remembered from what the chapter headings implied. A copper circlet bought from a woman beside a stair. The stair had been black; the sky above it had moved in strips. Was that enough? Fulvia said to put it down. The cup acquired in exchange for a blanket. The sword bought before his first crossing. The cloak taken as his agreed share of an expedition's finds, from a place he knew only as the third door; maker unknown. The buckle and spectacles purchased from other Runners who had not told him where they'd got them. Queen Street for the token. Dates approximate, where he could remember any.

"The cup wasn't a gift from a king?" Fulvia asked.

"He said he was a king. He wanted my blanket."

She checked the passage, lips moving. "You gave him your last protection against the killing frost."

"Yes."

"But you had the cloak."

"It let the wind through. I'd torn it."

He waited for another annotation. She made none. Instead she turned forward to a small drawing of the cup beside his boots.

"I don't think it's yellow in this one either," she said.

He bent over the additional sheet. At least she was pursuing the illustrator now.

It took most of the hour to fit nineteen names onto seven descriptions. Fulvia rejected his first signature because it crossed the box reserved for her stamp. He used the ordinary small one that he signed letters with. He declared that he had listed all retained artifacts, including those of no assessable value, and she passed the whole inventory back for him to check.

The sword was nine crowns. Cloak two, circlet six, cup three, buckle four, spectacles two, token nothing. Twenty-six in total. Fulvia canceled the preliminary bill, entered the corrected assessment, and turned it so he could see both figures.

Barnaby opened the chair envelope.

Sixty-four would remain. The wool chair had the same reclining mechanism; he had checked, before the velvet had distracted him. Four crowns for delivery, the man had said. He could have the chair tomorrow if he went straight to the shop.

He counted out twenty-six. Fulvia counted it again, stamped the bill PAID, and gave him his receipt with the inventory. He looked at the stamp, let out a breath through his nose, and folded the papers into his pocket. While she entered the payment in her ledger, he drank his cold tea and packed everything away. The sword went back into its sheath; he would carry it under his arm.

Only then did she push the first volume toward him.

"Would you sign it?"

He took up the pen with considerable relief. There was generous blank space on the flyleaf, untroubled by boxes. "To Fulvia?"

"Yes, please."

He began, *To Fulvia, who knows the cost of adventure.*

She read it upside down. "I don't want the tax in it."

His pen hung over the paper. He had meant it generously. It was a perfectly good inscription.

"What would you like?"

"The date. And your name. I like the book as it is."

He put a neat line through the dedication, added the date and a handsome signature, and handed it back. Fulvia examined the page, then shut the book over her thumb, smiling. He suspected she preferred having the crossed-out sentence there.

At the door he paused. "On my copy of the inventory, under occupation. You've written retired."

"That's what you told me."

"Retired adventurer. There's room."

She took the paper, added the word, and returned it. Barnaby checked the addition before lowering the trolley carefully over the first stair. He had a chair to buy, and the shops would soon be closing.

stories.title: The Unoffered Hand
stories.prompt: Every autumn, the kingdom’s falcons choose one person they will obey for life. This year, the fiercest bird in the royal mews ignores the princess, the generals, and every master falconer—and lands willingly on the glove of a servant girl who has never touched a hawk before.
stories.body:
# The Unoffered Hand

Sovelda had her hand inside the princess's spare glove when the falcon came down.

She was supposed to be polishing it. The leather had gold leaves worked into its cuff, and she could get the blacking out of their edges more easily with her fingers filling the glove. That was true. It was also true that she had been holding her arm sideways to see how the long tassel swung.

Across the court, the princess stood beneath the autumn garlands with her other glove raised. Cresset had turned his back on her. He had done the same to three generals, who now stood together pretending to discuss a horse, and to every master falconer in the royal mews. One of the masters had tried crouching. Cresset had watched him get down, then watched him get up again.

Now the bird was on Sovelda's fist.

His weight struck through her elbow. She staggered against the table, knocking over the blacking, and held her arm out because there was nowhere else to put it. A barred tail spread across her apron. Above it rose a spotted white breast, a brown head, two bright eyes which, from this close, seemed impossibly large.

Sovelda had never touched a hawk. She had not wanted to. The mews boys carried scars on their knuckles and ate with the cheerfulness of people who had forgotten how they got them.

“Don't move,” somebody said.

She could not tell whether it was meant for her or the bird.

The princess lowered her arm.

Every autumn, from the first yellow leaf until the last, the kingdom's unbound falcons chose the one person they would obey for the rest of their lives. Most chose in their first autumn. Cresset had been brought out for four autumns.
