There were eight guests beyond the double doors, with empty dessert plates and glasses that smelled of expensive brandy. The room's guard wore a soft grey suit. He asked Shona whether she'd brought a prop weapon. She said no, and he let her pass. Elspeth, who had seen the pistol, admired the answer. Corbin introduced Elspeth to a man whose velvet jacket strained across his stomach.

“Dacre. So pleased.” He bent to speak near her ear, although she hadn't asked him to. “We've a lovely chair for you. How long can you stand comfortably?”

“Long enough to meet a man.”

“Lovely. And you have your own dialogue?”

She stared at him. Shona took her elbow, but Dacre was already waving to the table. The guests turned; a woman adjusted the little lens pinned to her collar. A man beside her raised a phone.

“Put that away,” Elspeth said.

The man grinned and lowered it to chest height, still pointed at her. Dacre gave him an indulgent wag of the finger.

“You'll get the room recording afterward. Give her some space.”

Elspeth looked up. A black glass bead hung above the table.

“You're recording a private meeting?”

“Private to us. Nobody's broadcasting. Come, let's have you back at the doors. Corbin, give her an introduction this time.”

“I've just walked from there.”

“Only a few steps.”

“Then you fucking walk them.”

The guests laughed. Dacre laughed too, a moment later. Corbin began to applaud, then stopped when she turned toward him.

“Why is he asking me to come in twice?”

Corbin's smile held for a painful second. “We missed the entrance.”

“What entrance?”

“For the recording.” He looked at Shona. “Did you not tell her?”

Elspeth withdrew her elbow from Shona's hand. Nobody at the table was speaking now.

“Tell me.”

“You're doing a collection,” Corbin said. “For the guests. Dacre plays the owner who won't pay. Then he pays. We booked you to do that.”

The guard came closer. Elspeth could hear the small squeak of his shoe against the chair leg.

“You sold me to him.”

“I booked you. You asked for twenty percent.”

“I asked for a fifth of his business.”

Corbin's lips parted. She watched him find a smile and decide against using it.

“That's not what he agreed to.”

Dacre reached for the chair and pulled it out. “There's clearly been a misunderstanding. Sit down, my dear. We'll pay the balance. No one's going to make you perform.”

It was upholstered in pale leather. She wanted it so badly that she hated him for offering. Her knees had begun to shake. She sat.

“And I go away,” she said.

“Of course. We'll have the car brought up.” He turned to Corbin. “The balance comes from your fee. You were to brief her.”

“I did. At dinner, with Shona there.”

“You can discuss it outside.”

Shona crouched beside the chair, bringing her mouth close. Elspeth could smell the mint she'd chewed in the lift.

“He's got three places doing this,” she whispered. “Cash games afterward. Loans to the guests who lose. Corbin told me. We don't have to go away.”

“You knew I was to entertain him.”

“I knew we'd get inside.”

“And now?”

Shona glanced toward the guard. “I need you to start it.”

Elspeth studied her. The woman had got her out of prison, paid for food, washed piss from a sheet. Now she wanted permission to do something she'd brought a gun to do.

She was being used. She had two aching legs, an empty stomach, and fifty-nine years of experience being used for nothing.

“Dacre,” she said. “Come here.”

“Let me just arrange your car.”

“I want my money every week. From the loans as well. Shona will be coming to see you.”

He stopped touching his phone. Then he turned his smile back on for the guests.

“Would you see the lady down to her car,” he said to the guard. “She's had a long day.”

The guard moved between them. “All right. Up we get.”

“Don't touch her,” Shona said.

He took Elspeth's wounded left arm. His thumb pressed the dressing, and she struck at his face with her right hand. It was an old, immediate intention; her body delivered a trembling scratch. He caught her wrist and forced her against the table.

Her knuckles folded under his weight. Something broke with a small dry noise. The plate by her cheek held a single raspberry and a streak of cream. She couldn't get air to shout. Her left sleeve slid up in his grip, taking the dressing and a strip of skin with it.

“Let her go,” Shona said, much louder.

“Call the lift,” he told Dacre.

The shot struck him while he was turning. His weight left Elspeth all at once. He hit the table edge with his mouth, knocking a tooth into the cream, then fell beside her chair. Blood pumped through the hand he clamped under his jaw. He tried to speak. Bubbles swelled between his fingers, burst, swelled again.

For a moment nobody moved except him. One guest was still holding a spoon.

“House lights,” Corbin said.

The guard's heel dragged against the carpet. Shona stood with the gun out, looking down at him as if there were another part she had forgotten.

“House lights. Shona.”

“I heard you.”

“Then stop. We have to—” He bent toward the guard and pulled back with blood on his cuffs. “We need an ambulance.”

A woman near the doors was already speaking into her phone, giving the address. Elspeth heard her say *shot* twice. When Shona raised the gun toward the sound, Elspeth said, “Leave her.”

The woman ran. Four others followed. A chair overturned and stayed overturned. Nobody shut the doors after them.

Dacre knelt beside his guard. “He has a little girl,” he said. “Jesus Christ. He has a little girl.”

Elspeth's hand had begun to swell around the fingers. She held it against her chest. Each breath produced a thin complaining sound she couldn't prevent.

“Get up,” Shona told Dacre.

He ignored her until she took his collar. Then he came up so fast he almost fell over the body.

“He was supposed to walk you out,” he said to Elspeth. “That's all. I wasn't having you hurt.”

“The money,” she said.

He stared at her. Blood shone on the knees of his trousers.

“You've been paid. Take the balance. Take whatever's in the desk.”

She shook her head, then stopped because it made the room tilt. “You heard me. Every week. This place, your other places, the loans. A fifth. Tell her yes.”

“Yes. Fine. Yes.”

Shona jerked him toward the office. Elspeth caught her coat with the few fingers she could move.

“Don't empty him out. I want him open next week.”

“We need to leave.”

“Then hurry.”

Corbin remained near the fallen guard. He had put a folded tablecloth under the man's head, which had done nothing except make the blood easier to see. His phone stood propped against a glass, aimed along the table toward her.

“What are you doing?” Elspeth asked.

“Recording. I started after he told me I'd lose my fee.” His voice had become very quiet. “I wanted him to say it again.”

“Turn it off.”

He picked it up. His thumb hovered; then he put it in his pocket with the screen still lit.

“Corbin. You brought us here.”

“For a show.”

She looked at the door through which the woman had escaped. He followed her gaze.

“You can stay and explain,” she said. “Or you can come with us. I'll pay you properly.”

He wiped his hands on the tablecloth. There was more blood on them afterward. Shona appeared at the office door with Dacre, and Corbin backed away from them.

“I'm staying.”

Elspeth could have asked Shona to stop him. She could have had the phone. She looked at the recording bead over the table, at the open doors. Her stomach rose into her throat. She swallowed and waited for Shona to help her stand.

Dacre was still talking. “If you come back, I'll have people here.”

“Have the money,” Elspeth said, but she had to say it twice before he heard.

***

They had to leave the car two streets away. It had been booked to return them to the supper house; when Shona asked for a different destination, it pulled over and demanded Corbin's approval. Corbin wasn't answering. Elspeth shouted at the empty driver's seat. Shona hauled her out.

She vomited against the side of the car. Somewhere behind them were sirens. Shona half carried her to the main road and paid a van driver to take them the rest of the way without looking in the back. By the time they reached the room Shona had borrowed, Elspeth had lost a shoe and the money in Shona's coat had stuck together with blood.

“There's your fucking collection,” Shona said, dropping it on the bed.

Elspeth lay beside it. She couldn't get warm. The notes were much more than the appearance fee and much less than she had imagined. She couldn't count them with her hand.

In the morning Corbin's recording was on every news service Shona opened. The clip showed a shaking old woman ordering weekly payments; the guard could be heard dying below the edge of the picture. Other pictures had been found: the clinic, their arrival at the club, Shona's employment photograph. The woman who'd called the ambulance described Elspeth's coat in an interview. Under her picture was an appeal for anyone who'd seen her since the shooting.

The club closed. Dacre gave interviews. A man phoned Shona while she was helping Elspeth dress, said he collected Dacre's loans, and promised to break her arms. Elspeth could hear him through the speaker. Shona went outside to talk to him and stopped playing the news aloud.

For six days Elspeth slept badly in three different rooms. A doctor Shona found wanted payment before touching her; he said the hand needed surgery. She refused a hospital. Afterward, whenever she complained about the pain, Shona offered to drive her to one. Two fingers remained bent toward her palm. She needed help with her trousers and could no longer cut her own meat.

On the seventh evening Shona came back carrying an envelope and wearing a new coat.

“From Dacre,” she said. “His other two places stayed open. This is your fifth.”

Elspeth sat up. “He sent it?”

“His collector brought it. The one who rang about my arms.” Shona kept her hand on the envelope. “I hired him. He'd have gone to somebody else by the time you woke up, and Dacre's been keeping him waiting for his money the same as he did Corbin. So he collects the loans for us now.”

“Where is he?”

“Downstairs, in his car. He's found us somewhere for tonight. Dacre told him he'll keep paying till you're caught. Dacre reckons that won't be long.”

Shona took the notes out and counted them onto the blanket. Elspeth watched for the hesitation that would tell her a share had already been removed. There was none. That proved very little.

“And the coat?”

“My money.”

Elspeth touched the sleeve. Good wool, with a generous lining. A woman could sit in that coat and still button it.

“You should have bought me one.”

“You can buy your own now.” Shona pushed the counted money closer. “You need help getting up?”

Elspeth put her left arm out, and Shona bent to receive her weight. With her face against the new wool, Elspeth breathed in the expensive shop smell and began thinking how much more there must have been.

stories.title: I Really Need a Sidekick
stories.prompt: I really need a sidekick
stories.body:
# I Really Need a Sidekick

Rococo was watching me in the workshop mirror while I tightened the left side of his face.

“Do that entrance again,” he said.

“It wasn't an entrance. I went to fetch a key.”

“And yet you swept your coat back.”

I had. The coat was black with a red lining, and the effect deserved testing before I wore it into the Gilt Rotunda. Unfortunately, its hem had caught the drawer I'd left open. Rococo had watched me reverse through the door to free it.

I steadied his scarred white head with my palm. “Look left.”

Both red optics turned in their sockets. The new bearing whispered. That was better; a sinister glance should not sound like a boot in gravel.

“I really need a sidekick,” I said.

“For the coat?”

“For the theft.”

He turned his whole head towards me, beautifully. “Oh. Tell me.”

The Rotunda offered six hundred to anyone who could steal its golden peacock. Twenty minutes inside a theatre full of moving scenery, with Beryl Hilt defending it. I'd entered once before. My ingenious escape case had shut with me inside it, and I had spent eleven minutes explaining through a ventilation hole that the catch was supposed to do that.

I had since repaired three clocks, a trouser press, and a very fine espresso machine for people who began every consultation by asking whether I'd got out yet.

This time I had a plan involving a hatch, a counterweight, and another pair of hands. I showed Rococo the little sketch under my elbow. He studied it while I fitted his cheek plate. Black mechanisms vanished under white enamel, except for the narrow gaps his original maker had left at the jaw.

“Where are the spectators?” he asked.

I tapped the margin of the sketch. “Here. But they won't see us until we come out.”

He put a finger on my pencilled exit. “With the bird held high?”

“Ideally.”

“And what am I doing?”

“Holding the hatch.”

He waited.

“Then coming out too.”

He'd been the Rotunda's resident villain when it still put on plays. I'd seen him tear a paper wedding contract into pieces so tiny that the heroine had protested about how long she'd have to kneel there collecting them. He'd retired after the theatre changed hands, though he still came to me for adjustments. Last month he'd wanted a quieter wrist for pointing accusingly at dinner guests.

“Half the money,” I said. “You can lift the peacock. I'll open the way.”

“I can manage that. How much running?”

“Almost none.”

“Ottilie.”

I looked under the bench at his right knee. Its cooling fan was running even now. A cracked motor housing made it heat up under a fast load; if he hurried for much more than half a minute, the joint locked itself straight. Letting it cool took the better part of an hour. I'd ordered the replacement housing. It was coming from somewhere that apparently counted hours differently.

“No jumping,” I said. “No prolonged running. We walk in, we get the bird, we walk out.”

“Good. Shall I bring a cape?”

I showed him the snag in my hem.

He considered it. “A short cape.”

We practised the hatch manoeuvre with my bench lid. A squeeze on his shoulder meant stop; two taps meant move. He lifted the heavy lid one-handed while I crawled beneath it, then waited for me to wriggle out before asking whether this was the triumphant part.

“You'll know the triumphant part.”

By noon we stood under the Rotunda's painted dome, wearing protective goggles and listening to the referee. Rococo had chosen a red cape that reached only to his elbows. I had pinned my blonde hair up with considerably more care than the undertaking deserved.

The audience sat behind clear screens on three sides of the playing floor. At the back of the floor, the peacock glittered on a plinth between two castle towers, in front of a low passage that ran through the castle wall. Wide pieces of scenery stood on low wagons: a forest, a palace window, an enormous plywood moon. Brass strips in the floor gave their wheels smooth runs over the old stage seams. A low gallery stretched across the front, above our entrance, with a bank of handles for hauling the scenery about and a narrow stair down from one end.

Beryl Hilt leaned on its rail, loading her paint rifle. She wore last month's winner's sash twisted around her forehead to keep the sweat out of her eyes.

“You both have to cross the line under that arch with the prize,” the referee said, pointing to the red frame through which we'd entered. “One direct paint hit on either of you ends the attempt. Body or clothes. Props don't count. You may move anything inside the floor boundary. Breakages come out of the purse.”

Rococo looked over the audience. Someone waved. He bowed so low that his short cape fell over his head, and straightened with a practiced flick that made it look intentional.

“No case today, Ottilie?” Beryl called down.

“I've moved beyond cases.”

“Glad to hear it.”

People laughed. It was a perfectly reasonable thing to say, and I resented her for it.

“You'll want to watch the towers,” I said. “We shall be entering from above.”

Rococo looked up at the battlements. I could have corrected myself. The referee had not rung the bell; there was still a moment in which to be a woman with a sensible plan and a regrettable mouth.

Then someone behind the screen said, “Oh, good.”

The bell rang.

We ducked behind the palace window as a paint pellet snapped against its frame. Beryl pulled one of her handles. The forest wagon slid across the floor, leaving a bright, bare lane between us and the castle.

“Above?” Rococo asked.

“There's a stair behind the left tower.”

“You drew a hatch.”

“I know what I drew.”

He waited for my next instruction, which was worse than arguing. I peered through the palace's painted window. A pellet struck its sill. Beryl worked the rifle's pump, grinning.

The castle stairs were genuine, built for actors to stand on the battlements. They were also on the far side of the exposed lane. My hatch would have taken us underneath that lane, almost to the bird. I could still take it, if I wished to pop up out of a hole in the floor in front of the people who had just laughed about my case.

“The forest comes back when she releases that handle,” Rococo said. “It's on a counterweight. We could follow it.”

We crouched, waited, and followed the trees as they rolled home. Rococo kept pace at a quick walk. I could hear Beryl moving along the gallery to find an angle, and twice a pellet hit a painted trunk at head height. We reached the castle stairs with both our clothes clean.

It took three minutes to climb them. Rococo went sideways, good leg first, and I kept trying to help at precisely the moments he needed me to get out of his way. At the top we crouched behind the battlements. I inspected the narrow walkway across to the other tower.

Below us lay the peacock, gleaming, no wiser than a real bird about the trouble it had caused. A large clock over the red arch showed fifteen minutes remaining.

“I'll have to go down backwards,” Rococo said.

“Can you face the audience for the first few steps?”

He looked at the steep return stair on the inner face of the tower. “No. Keep my cape clear, please.”

I gathered his cape in one fist and followed him. The spectators got a prolonged view of his feet.

We were still descending when the clock sounded the halfway chime. By the time we reached the plinth, his knee fan was whining. The peacock was bigger up close, a brass body with folded tail feathers made from thin sheets of gilded metal. I'd watched previous attempts. Lift it, and the tail sprang into a fan as wide as my outstretched arms; a little pump in its belly played a fanfare through its beak. There was no disabling either without forfeiting the prize.

“Straight into the passage when you have it,” I whispered. My original hatch lay at the far end of that passage; from this side we could simply open it. “She'll come round as soon as she hears.”

He put both hands beneath the bird. I watched the gallery through a gap in the castle wall.

The fanfare was louder than I remembered. The tail opened with a metallic rattle, and for a moment there was nothing in the world but that magnificent, stupid bird.

Rococo rose with it held above his head. The audience cheered. He turned to give them the full spread of gold, and they cheered again. He tilted the peacock down towards me, an invitation so obvious I stepped beside him and swept my coat back.

It worked. The red lining opened. My hand found my hip. I heard somebody whistle.

Then Beryl's pellet took a chip out of the plinth beside my elbow.

We lurched into the passage. A castle door slid across its far end. Beryl had reached another handle.

“Back,” I said.

Rococo was already moving. The peacock's tail caught both walls; he turned it edgewise and hurried after me. We came out beside the plinth as Beryl sent a shot through the space we'd just left. I seized Rococo's arm and pulled him towards the moon wagon, the only cover outside her castle.

We had almost reached it when his right knee gave a shrill warning. He took one more stride, stiffened, and went sideways. I got under his arm. Together we staggered behind the moon, which boomed as another pellet hit its painted face.

He lowered himself onto the wagon's timber base and kept the bird off the floor. I put my hand near the knee. Heat pressed against my palm.

“Done?” he asked.

I nodded. He stretched the leg along the base. Beyond the plywood I heard Beryl's boots go back across the gallery.

“You waved it about for a full minute,” I said. “She could have strolled to that handle.”

“Did you hear them, though?”

I tugged at the cape trapped under his elbow.

“You were supposed to keep moving.”

“You struck a pose, Ottilie.”

“For a second.”

“It was a good pose.”

That made me angrier. I had been pleased with it; I still was. I let go of his cape and looked out past the moon. A pellet struck the edge, close enough to send a splinter into my hair. The clock showed six minutes.

“Can you walk?”

“Slowly. Not across that.” He nodded at the open floor between us and the arch. “Can you push this wagon?”

I looked down. Four broad castors, each with a foot brake. A wide timber frame supporting the moon. It had carried two lovers and a papier-mâché pig in a production I'd attended years ago.

“With you on it?”

“The pig was much heavier.”

“I remember the pig.”

“I was inside it.”

I laughed before I could help it. He'd had a splendid entrance, rolling down a hillside in pursuit of a tenor. They'd repeated it twice because the audience wouldn't stop stamping.

He shifted the bird into one arm. “I had hoped this might be rather like that.”

“You could have said.”

“You were so pleased with that hatch.”

Behind the screen somebody began a hopeful, uneven clapping. Other hands joined it. They couldn't see us doing anything; the sight of the moon being repeatedly shot was enough to sustain their interest. I smoothed the cape I'd crumpled in my hands.

I bent and released the first brake.

“Then hold on to the moon,” I said. “I don't want it tipping over.”

He tucked the peacock against his chest and wrapped his other arm round an upright. I set my hands on the frame.

“I'll push. You tell me where she's going. Keep your feet inside.”

I freed the remaining brakes and tested the wagon against my boot. It rolled more easily than I'd expected. The moon was solid plywood, eight feet across, and the wagon's base was narrow enough for the arch. We would have to turn sideways to get the moon through. First we had to reach it.

We came out from beside the castle with the moon facing Beryl's gallery. I shoved at the frame, keeping my body within its shadow. Rococo leaned to peer round the side, then pulled back as a shot cracked against the paint.

“Still up there. Moving left.”

I took short, hard steps towards the arch. The castors thrummed over a seam, and the moon swayed. Rococo tightened his grip on the upright. His good foot slid towards the edge; I squeezed his shoulder and held the wagon still while he drew it in. Two taps, and we moved again.

He risked another look. “Faster. She's at the gallery stair.”

I put my shoulder to the wood. The floor seemed much larger now I had to propel two people and an astronomical object across it. My goggles slipped down my nose. I shoved them up with a wrist, smeared them with sweat, and shoved harder.

Beryl came down the gallery stair to our left. Rococo pointed. I ran round the back of the wagon and dragged its right corner towards me, swinging the moon between her and us. The wheels swivelled reluctantly. Paint smacked into the face as it came round.

“Nice,” Rococo said.

I had no breath to answer. We were twenty feet from the arch, moving sideways now, with the edge of the moon aimed at the opening. Beryl trotted beside us, looking for an angle. She was quick enough to outrun the wagon, but the palace window stood between her and our unprotected rear, and she had to go round it.

“She's coming behind,” Rococo said. “Turn again.”

I hauled the frame. Rococo leaned into the turn, but the right front castor caught at one of the brass strips. The moon stopped turning. Beryl's boots squeaked on the far side of the palace.

“Wheel!” I gasped, pointing.

He followed my hand, reached down, and shoved the castor round. I pulled again. The moon swung just as she cleared the palace, and her shot hit it squarely. The audience made a noise I felt in my ribs.

Now we were behind our shield, backing towards the arch, and the moon was broadside to an opening two feet narrower than itself.

I dragged the wagon until one corner bumped a red post. We had perhaps a yard left to travel. Beryl was coming straight towards us.

“You'll have to turn it,” she called. “I'll have you then.”

Rococo drew his good foot in beside the leg that still lay stiff along the base. I crouched lower, wishing I'd taken the coat off before we'd started. Its hem was everywhere.

The peacock stared out through its fan of feathers. It had been shrieking intermittently all the way across the floor; the tune had begun to repeat in my head.

“Hold the tail towards her,” I told Rococo.

He set the bird's feet on the wagon between us and the moon, gripping it from behind. The tail rose in front of our crouched bodies. Its metal feathers overlapped closely enough that I couldn't see through them.

He looked me over, then down at the floor. “Come closer. Your coat.”

I gathered the hem under my knees and squeezed beside him on the timber base, one boot still on the floor. He put an arm across my shoulders to keep me inside the fan.

“You'll have to shove,” I said. “Against the post. When I tap.”

He released my shoulders and reached for the red upright of the arch. I held his shoulder and planted my boot on the floor beside the nearest castor. We had to pivot before we could push through.

Two taps. He pushed the post; I shoved against the floor. The wagon turned. The moon moved edgewise into the arch, taking our shelter with it.

Beryl fired. A feather buckled against my goggles.

Rococo kept the bird turned towards her while the wagon swung beneath him. I squeezed his shoulder; he stopped pushing, and I stamped backwards against the floor. The wagon rolled into the gap.

Her second shot struck the peacock's belly. Its fanfare faltered, then came back a note lower.

The wagon stuck. My hem had slid from under my knee and gone beneath a castor, and for a moment we sat with the moon jammed against one post and half the wagon still on Beryl's side. Through a dented gap between feathers I saw Beryl lifting her rifle. She was close.

“Again,” I said, and planted my heel flat.

Rococo shoved the post hard enough to scrape white enamel off his knuckles. The moon tore a strip of red paint from the arch. My coat ripped free of the castor, and we shot through together.

A pellet struck the floor behind us. The referee rang the bell. The clock above him still had forty seconds left.

For several seconds I couldn't hear him over the audience. Rococo still held the peacock in front of us. I tapped his wrist until he lowered it.

Beryl stood on the other side of the line with her rifle hanging from its strap. She glanced between the dent in the tail and my clean goggles.

“I was sure I had you,” she said.

“So was I.”

She laughed once, sharply, and rested her rifle against the arch. I tried to get off the wagon. My legs declined. I sat back down beside Rococo and began laughing too, which used more breath than I had available and made a dreadful squeaking sound.

He looked at me, then lifted his face towards the audience and gave them the villain's laugh I remembered from the wedding scene: rich, cruel, delighted. It set me off again. I wiped my eyes beneath my goggles, leaving dirty streaks across my cheeks.

The referee came round with the purse. He held it out, reconsidered, and glanced at the damaged peacock.

“We'll settle the repairs afterwards,” he said.

That seemed fair. I took the purse before he could develop the thought.

People were standing behind the screens. They weren't asking about my case. They were calling for us to do something else.

“They want an encore,” Rococo said. He sounded almost shy now there was no immediate need to project.

“I can't push you back across.”

“No. Just help me stand. We can bow.”

I got to my feet and gave him my shoulder. He rose on his good leg, holding the battered bird. I began to bow, but he stopped me with a squeeze.

“Wait for the fanfare.”

The peacock wheezed through its ruined tune. I stood with my arm around his waist, sweat cooling down my back, and waited with him. At the final dreadful note we bowed together. More stamping. More demands.

I could have stayed there all afternoon.

“Give me the bird,” I said.

He passed it over and leaned against the arch. I held the bird against my chest, stepped beyond his reach, and turned the red lining of my coat towards him.

“Oh,” he said softly. Then, loud enough for the whole Rotunda: “You treacherous woman.”

I smiled at him over the bent golden feathers and waited for the boos.

stories.title: Undisclosed
stories.prompt: The most powerful man in the world works as a humble accountant. A superhero comments that he can do a lot of good if he used his powers, the man counters that keeping his powers hidden, away from prying eyes, is its own form of heroism.
stories.body:
# Undisclosed

Daybreak had brought the wrong envelope again. This one contained a photograph of a cat, a receipt for six pairs of socks, and a letter from a child asking whether she slept in the sky.

Cyril Nabe passed the letter back without reading beyond the question.

“Have you got the accounts?” he asked.

“I packed them. Hang on.”

She looked through her bag. The chair creaked beneath her rescue harness, the rigid frame she used to take passengers aloft. He had knocked ten off her last bill when she complained about the chair; replacing it would have cost considerably more. They had been having appointments like this for three years. Until tonight, she had never come after closing.

She found the accounts under a pair of gloves stiff with dried blood. Her own, he hoped. There were things an accountant could ask and things he had learned to leave alone.

“Take the harness off if it hurts,” he said.

“Getting it back on hurts more.”

He drew the accounts toward him. She put a finger on them.

“I know it was you at the hotel.”

He kept his hand where it was. Through the window came a boy's voice, calling a farewell to somebody on the next floor. The bakery downstairs was shutting its metal grille.

“You took me out through the bricks,” she said. “There wasn't a hole. There was an alley where the wall had been, and you were standing beside me.”

He remembered her face turned upward in the smoke, one eye closed, blood collecting along the lower edge of her mask. The floors above her had begun coming down. He had bent the light around the two of them so that the people filming from the street would see the falling building arrest itself and a woman appear safely outside it. Nothing of him. It had not concealed him from the woman within that little enclosure.

“You were barely conscious.”

“I knew my accountant.” She took her hand away. “I didn't tell anyone.”

Cyril turned the accounts so they lay square with the desk. Daybreak watched him do it. There had been footage of the hotel on every screen for two days: three storeys hovering, then settling gently into an empty lot. He had watched it with the sound off, waiting for a glimpse of his shoes. There had been none.

“What do you need?”

She took a folded photograph from her bag. Eight small portraits were printed on it. Some were holiday pictures, one a work identity photograph; a woman's face had been enlarged until the individual dots of ink showed in her smile.

“These people. Tonight.”

She laid another sheet beside it, an aerial photograph of four low buildings inside a fence. She had entered the compound yesterday in a cleaner's overalls and found eight people locked in four separate wards. They had been offered paid stays for a study of magical ability. When they wanted to leave, their families had been told that they already had.

“I can get through the guards,” she said. “I can cover one ward. As soon as they hear me, the guards in the other three have orders to kill the people there. Tomorrow they're moving them, and I don't know where.”

“You heard those orders?”

“Yes. I was under a trolley while a man explained them. He was angry about the transport being late. He said he wasn't losing another group.”

She had a way of watching Cyril while she spoke that made him feel he was withholding something she could see in his hand.

“There are people equipped for this.”

“I've asked them. They can't promise four rooms at once either. I have medics waiting for whoever I get out. I have officers who'll go in once the prisoners are safe. I need someone who can stop four things happening together.” She glanced at the photograph of the hotel on a newspaper folded in his wastebasket. He had meant to throw it away. “You could do so much good.”

Cyril leaned back. He had imagined this conversation often enough to have become rather good at it.

“People who knew what I could do would want it used. Everyone would have a reason, and a great many of them would be right. They'd find my clients, my neighbours. They'd follow me home. Eventually they'd stop asking other people for help at all.”

“They already follow me home.”

“You can be stopped.”

She sat very still.

It was a cruel distinction to make to someone who had arrived wearing dried blood, but it was true. No living man or woman on the planet could compel Cyril to do anything. Together, all of them could not have held a door shut against him. He could separate continents as easily as the pages of her accounts. There was no strain he might reach, no final reserve he might exhaust, which would give somebody else a turn.

“Keeping that hidden,” he said, “away from prying eyes and people with plans for it, is its own form of heroism. I know how that sounds from behind a desk.”

“It sounds comfortable.”

He felt the mean little sting of being judged by someone whose unpaid bills were in front of him.

“When the man who runs the bakery thinks I'm no use, he hires another accountant. He did, once. Came back after six months. He could go again tomorrow.”

Daybreak pressed two fingers under the edge of her harness and shifted it away from her ribs.

“I don't want you to run the world. Can you get these eight people out without showing anyone your face?”

“Yes.”

“Then I'm asking for that.”

He could have pleaded work. There were real accounts to finish, a woman waiting to learn whether she could afford a second oven, wages that depended on his catching an error before morning. He liked those people. He liked the sandwiches the baker left on his stairs, and the fact that when they were stale he was allowed to complain. None of it would fill the eight places in the photograph if those people failed to come home.

“I tried once,” he said. “Doing what you're asking me to do. For longer than an evening.”

Daybreak let her hand fall from the harness.

“There was fighting. I wore a mask. I took away the weapons, and when they brought more I took those away too. Then I had to decide what counted as a weapon. Who could travel. Which gatherings would start it again.” He looked at the woman's magnified smile. “People queued outside the house where I was staying. I used to keep them waiting until I'd finished breakfast.”

“What happened to them?”

“I left.”

She waited, but that was all he had for her. He had avoided the reports afterward. Obscurity had made that possible as well.

“I'm frightened of that man,” he said.

“So am I, now.” Her voice had lost its impatience. “But I still have to ask.”

He would have preferred reassurance. Instead she sat with her eight people between them, and he could think of nothing else to say that was not a way of making her sit there longer.

“Show me where the medics are.”

She marked the sports ground on her phone's map and called the medics to check they were there.

Before opening the way, Cyril screened himself from outside eyes. Daybreak watched the desk become visible through the place where he stood. The screen turned light past his body; it did nothing to another person's memory of him.

They left through a space Cyril opened beside the filing cabinet. Daybreak stepped first onto the bare hillside shown in her photograph. He followed and shut the opening behind them. Evening had reached the compound but not the western sky. A guard smoked beside a parked van. On the nearest roof somebody had hung an ordinary striped towel over a railing.

“Can you hear me?” he asked, carrying his voice through a fold that ended beside her ear.

“Yes.” He drew her whispered answer back to him the same way.

“Don't use my name.”

“I wasn't going to.” She tucked her bag behind a thorn bush and tested the strap of her harness. “The far building first. Two on the upper floor. One can't walk.”

He could have lifted every building on the hillside, or every building on the planet. Identifying which people within them wanted rescuing was beyond him. His power would hold a specified place or object; it would not answer a question. It had never told him what was in an envelope.

He fixed the boundaries of the fenced ground in his attention and slowed the passage of solid bodies within it to walking pace. It was a blunt precaution. Anyone trying to run would find themselves moving gently instead. A bullet would no longer outrun a person.

“Go,” he said.

Daybreak rose over the fence. A shout came from beside the van. As she crossed the yard, the guard brought his rifle round. She spread a plane of white-gold light across the upper windows of the far building.

Cyril raised the buildings from their foundations.

The guard stopped trying to aim. Cigarette smoke continued upward past his stationary face. All four blocks hung a hand's breadth above the ground, doors open, cables dangling. Cyril separated their storeys, held the floors level, and moved the roofs and walls into empty scrub beyond the fence. Each piece arrived without traversing the space between. He left the floors and everything upon them hanging at their original heights. Electric lights died; the rooms stood open to the sky.

There were the beds, the cups, the guards. Two people had been playing cards on a blanket. A woman on another floor sat upright with her hands against her ears. In the nearest ward a man in a white coat was reaching across a patient toward a pistol on a trolley.

Cyril stopped the pistol. Elsewhere three bullets emerged lazily from a rifle barrel; now that he could see them, he held them still. The rifleman let go of his weapon and began saying something over and over.

Daybreak landed in the upper ward and bent over a bed, keeping her light between the ward's occupants and a guard. It took Cyril a moment to understand why she was struggling with a buckle when there was no need for buckles ever to be fastened against his wishes.

“May I?” he asked into her ear.

“The straps, yes.”

They came apart. The person on the bed pulled both arms to her chest.

“She's free,” he said. “I can put her beside the ambulance.”

“Open the way. Let her see it first.”

He joined the space beside the bed to a patch of grass at the sports ground where the medics were waiting. Their floodlights made a pale rectangle in the dusk. A paramedic turned, saw Daybreak, and came toward the opening with a stretcher.

“No,” said the woman on the bed. “No, that's a screen. They did that before.”

Daybreak stepped through onto the grass, keeping one hand visible in the ward. The paramedic touched her shoulder. She came back and knelt by the bed.

“He's going to bring the stretcher in here. You can touch it. You can keep your eyes open the whole time.”

Cyril waited. On a neighbouring floor, a guard was trying to edge toward a stairwell that now led into evening air. Cyril lowered that floor to the ground before the man could step off it.

“Stay back from the edges,” Daybreak called. “I'll come to you.”

The woman touched the stretcher's orange cover, then the paramedic's sleeve. Eventually she let them help her onto it. Cyril made the opening broader so they could go through side by side.

The others took longer than lifting the buildings had. Daybreak checked names against her list. One man would not leave without the teeth he kept in a cup; Cyril moved the cup to the bedside when Daybreak pointed it out. Another asked where his brother was, though no brother appeared in her photographs. She asked the brother's name and had the paramedic write it down. Cyril could offer him no answer.

By the seventh person, Daybreak's light had become thin along the edges. He no longer needed her to protect anyone from the guns, but the man she was helping insisted on keeping his feet upon her luminous plane rather than the unsupported floor. She carried him slowly across it, sweating, while Cyril stood unseen on the hillside with his hands in his pockets.

The eighth was one of the card players. He gathered the blanket and the cards before he followed. Through the opening, Cyril saw him begin to laugh. He bent forward, still clutching everything, and somebody put an arm around him.

“That's eight,” Daybreak said quietly. Her voice returned through their fold. “They're all through.”

He had helped other people without being thanked. Once he had shifted a child's bicycle a few inches from a passing lorry, and the child had sworn at the driver and ridden on. This was different. Daybreak looked toward the place where she knew he stood, and smiled at him. For a moment he wanted to lift the entire compound higher, open another impossible road, find something else she needed.

When two gunmen began edging toward the gate, Cyril fixed their feet in place. He did the same to the others he had seen armed, and to the man who had reached for the pistol.

“These are consenting participants,” the man in the coat shouted toward Daybreak. “My employers will have this straightened out. You have no authority to hold me here.”

There were twelve people left inside the fence, including the guards. At least three wore the same plain clothes as the abductees. He did not know whether they had stayed because they worked here or because they were frightened to move.

“The man in the coat,” Cyril said. “And the gunmen. I could put them somewhere they can't get out. Somewhere no employer could fetch them.”

Daybreak was gathering the papers that had begun blowing off a desk.

“Keep them here for the officers.”

“They'll do this again.”

She looked toward him. “You don't know that. I need them questioned. That man may know where the others were sent.”

There was the brother whose name the medic had written down. Cyril had already forgotten it.

He set the guns and the suspended bullets together in the air above the fence. Daybreak went to speak to the three people in plain clothes. He waited while she brought two of them to the medics; the third stayed to identify the rooms where records had been kept. When the officers arrived, he restored the walls and roofs and set the buildings back upon their foundations, leaving every door open. He released each man as he was taken into custody and lowered the guns for the officers to collect. Then he let movement inside the fence return to its ordinary speeds. It was nearly dark.

There would be witnesses and whatever the cameras had preserved. None of the people they had found at the compound had seen Cyril's face. Daybreak had, and knew where he worked.

She fetched her bag from behind the thorn bush, and he brought them back to the office and closed the way to the hillside. When he let himself become visible again, Daybreak was sinking into the narrow chair and working at her harness. He reached for a fastening.

“Please don't,” she said. “It's caught on the dressing.”

He withdrew his hand. She teased the strap free, breathing through her mouth. He could have moved it without touching the wound, but she had asked him not to. Freed of the harness, she looked smaller, though she occupied more of the chair.

“Thank you,” she said. “I've been trying to work out how to get them out for six days.”

He put her accounts back in their envelope. He wanted her to go on speaking in that voice. He wanted to ask whether he had done well, which was an absurd question, considering the buildings.

“You understand why I can't make a habit of it.”

“I understand why you're frightened.” She rubbed her shoulder where the strap had dug in. “If I hadn't kept asking, you'd have left eight people in those wards. I don't understand that. I'm glad you came.”

“If you needed me again, you would ask.”

“Probably.”

He had hoped she would set some limit of her own on what she might ask of him, without his having to hear himself ask for one.

“My name must stay out of this,” he said. “Nobody there saw me. Nobody heard you call me Cyril.”

“I know.”

“Promise you won't tell anyone.”

She stopped rubbing her shoulder. When she lowered her hand, the groove the strap had left was still there, dark red.

“I came to you privately. I haven't named you to anyone. I'm trying to keep it that way.”

“Then why can't you promise?”

“Because I don't know what you'll do.”

He stared at her. She held his gaze, then bent to pick up the harness.

“I haven't threatened you,” he said.

“I didn't say you had. But you wanted to put those men somewhere nobody could reach them. If you do something like that, I can't keep your secret.”

“I didn't do it.”

She pushed the gloves into her bag. He waited for her to answer, to tell him she knew he wouldn't. Instead she gathered her things with the quick, stiff movements of a client who would not be coming back.

“Let me explain.”

“I've heard you. I have to go and check on those people.”

She opened his door. The passage beyond was empty, its worn runner leading to the stairs. Cyril could see the brass knob of the stairwell door. He knew precisely where everything was.

He joined a short length of the passage to itself.

Daybreak walked three paces and arrived at his office door again. She stopped. Her harness slipped down her arm, and she caught it before it struck the floor. Looking over her shoulder, she saw the same stretch of carpet and the stairwell door still waiting beyond it. She looked back at him.

It required no effort to hold the passage that way. He could leave it while he slept. He could bring her food, bring a doctor for her ribs. She would not have to hurt herself trying the walls. There were so many ways to make this bearable while she came to understand him.

“Cyril,” she said. “Let me leave.”

Her free hand had risen in front of her chest. A small plane of light trembled between them. It would not keep him from reaching her, and she had seen enough tonight to know it.

He looked at her hand and realized he was waiting for her to lower it.

Cyril put the passage back. The carpet and doors did not change their appearance. Daybreak did not move.

“It goes to the stairs now,” he said.

She glanced down the passage, then at him. He took a step toward the doorway to show her, and her light brightened.

“Stay there.”

He stopped.

Keeping her face turned toward him, she edged along the runner until she could touch the stairwell door. She pushed it open with her shoulder. The light remained between them until she was through; then it was gone, and he heard her descending, slowly because of the harness. He knew which steps would creak. He had walked them for eleven years.

At the bottom she paused and spoke into her phone. He heard her give the address. Before she said anything more she pushed out into the street, and the ordinary distance took her voice away.

stories.title: No Need to Worry
stories.prompt: "No need to worry, I discovered a fatal weakness: 30mm shells, launched at about 1000 m/s. About 4000 per minute should do."
stories.body:
# No Need to Worry

The wedding ring came off with a strip of skin inside it. Dulsie Flett rubbed it clean on the dead man's sock and put it in her handbag. He had insisted on bringing his own rifle. Handloaded ammunition, he'd told her over dinner, as though she would know the difference. He was lying on it now.

Across the pen, Ogden had the last hunter folded over his knees. His dinner jacket had split down the back. He was eating with his face against the man's open belly, and each time he swallowed something substantial, the bullet holes along his shoulders puckered shut. Dulsie had promised the guests a beast that would heal until one of them earned its head. The two bodies by the gate had stopped moving. Four guests, all accounted for.

Dulsie checked her watch. Through the gateway in the dividing wall she could see the outer yard, the floodlights, the firing booth beyond them. A man was moving behind its glass. Norris had finished setting up. She had hired him to operate the lodge's cannon for the after-dinner demonstration, with a private extra fee if the animal proved dangerous. She had told him it could pass for a big man, and that its handler would walk it out; he had never met the handler. Ogden believed the cannon was a dead exhibit. She had let him complain all afternoon about paying a gunner to pose beside it.

At forty-eight she owned three good dresses and half a business she couldn't put on a tax return. Tonight's cashbox held more money than they had ever taken in one place. With Norris's fee deducted, the rest would still be hers. No more negotiations over expenses with a man who considered a murdered hotel porter an unexpected meal.

Ogden lifted his face. A grey curl from the hunter's chest was caught between his front teeth.

“Come and get this fucking button.” He reached over his shoulder and scratched below it. “It's digging in.”

“Take the jacket off.”

“You said we were keeping it.”

They had paid a tailor for expansion pleats. Ogden had agreed to stop growing when he felt them pull, and once again he had got excited. She put her bag over her shoulder and went behind him. A button on the back vent had caught in the new ridge of flesh along his spine. She picked the thread out with her nail. The smell made her breathe through her mouth.

“There,” she said.

He rolled his shoulders with a grunt of relief. Beneath the torn lining, his skin smoothed itself around the old burn on his back. He always put that scar back. Dulsie had been with him when he'd acquired it, years before his body began doing these things, in a room where the mattress had caught fire. He'd carried her out wrapped in a curtain and then gone back for her purse. She had married somebody else that year. Ogden still enjoyed reminding her how that had turned out.

Behind them, the hired attendant struck the locked gate with a rifle butt.

He was a thick, bearded man with a white streak at his chin. He had been collecting the guests' spent cartridges when the screaming began. Now he was putting his whole weight into each blow. The latch held. Ogden sat between him and the pen's only other exit, the dividing gateway. The attendant looked back at Dulsie and stopped hitting the gate.

“You've got the key.”

Ogden let the hunter slide off his lap.

“Dulsie. The key.” The attendant dropped the rifle and ran towards her, showing his empty hands. “I'm just here for the evening. I haven't seen anything.”

She stepped aside. He tried to turn, slipped in the sand and got one knee under him before Ogden caught his belt.

“He's staff,” Dulsie said.

Ogden held the man against his chest. His jaw began to lengthen. The attendant clawed at the arm under his ribs, then changed his mind and reached for the little penknife in his waistcoat. He got it open. Dulsie saw him stab Ogden twice in the forearm. The second time, the blade stayed there.

“We agreed about staff.”

Ogden bit into the side of the man's head. The man's heels battered the sand; one shoe came off. Dulsie stood with her hand over the lodge insignia on her blouse until the kicking ended. She didn't want to have to clean that as well.

“He was going to tell,” Ogden said. The words were thick. His mouth was still arranging itself.

“Then we could have dealt with him afterwards.”

He pulled the penknife out, dropped it in the sand and spat a piece of ear beside it. “We're dealing with him now.”

Ordinary meat did the same work. They had spent a winter feeding him cheap beef in a rented room, while Dulsie looked for a business more profitable than charging sick people to watch him heal. But beef didn't scramble for a knife. Beef didn't surprise him. She had helped him discover what he liked and taught herself to call it stock.

“I'll get your change of clothes,” she said.

“The soft trousers. And leave the boot open. I'll bring the money.”

He had carried the cashbox into the lodge himself after dinner. He liked the weight of it. He'd sleep with it against his shins in the car, then ask her in the morning whether she thought they were rich.

Dulsie went through the dividing gateway and crossed the concrete of the outer yard. The cannon protruded from a wide opening in the booth's front, to the left of an observation window. Below the window, a solid brick wall ran across to the door and its three steps. The dividing wall kept the killing pen out of Norris's sight. He pointed at her bloody skirt, then jabbed his finger towards the door.

She climbed the steps. Norris pulled her inside and shut the door behind her. His hands smelled of the orange he'd been eating. There was half of it on the console beside the gun controls.

“What happened?”

“It got loose.” She bent over, giving herself time to breathe like a frightened woman. “The guests. I couldn't get them out.”

“Where's the handler?”

“Dead.”

“Shit.” He turned back to the glass. “Stay away from that door.”

Ogden emerged from the gateway carrying the soft trousers. He must have gone into the lodge to look for her. He had put on his own face again, the long nose and heavy cheeks, though the rest of him was still too big for the jacket. There was blood in the folds of the trousers.

He saw her behind the observation window and raised them in an irritated question.

“That's it,” Dulsie said. “Shoot it.”

The gun's first burst made her teeth strike together. Her view shook, and a whine closed over her ears so that everything after it came from farther off. Ogden's raised arm came off at the shoulder. Flesh struck the dividing wall behind him. He fell on his side and rolled behind a stone trophy plinth. The trousers remained in the yard, tangled with the arm. Neither moved again.

Norris stopped firing. His chair creaked as he leaned forward. Dulsie caught one glimpse of a wet shoulder drawing skin across itself before Ogden dragged it out of sight. His familiar throat made a sound she had never heard from it.

“You can kill him?” she said.

“Yes.” Norris swallowed. “Yes, I can.”

“He's still alive.”

Norris looked at the red drag mark, then back at her. He tried a smile.

“No need to worry, I discovered a fatal weakness: 30mm shells, launched at about 1000 m/s. About 4000 per minute should do.”

She stared at him. The little smile went. He wiped his mouth on his shoulder and returned both hands to the controls.

“Keep him in the open,” he said.

Dulsie barely caught that. The whine was getting worse. She pulled the spare ear defenders from their hook and put them on. Norris was already wearing his. They made his face look small.

Beyond the plinth, Ogden's back rose and fell. He didn't have enough spare flesh to make that arm again, not quickly. He had been shot for audiences, stabbed, once run down by a drunken guest who'd panicked behind the wheel. Dulsie had always stayed beside him while he repaired himself. When he asked afterwards how bad it had looked, she told him he ought to charge more.

Now the damaged shoulder was still leaking. Norris had done that with a twitch of his hands.

The intercom buzzed. Dulsie felt it more than heard it. She raised one ear cup.

“Dulsie?”

Ogden had dragged himself to the speaker post behind the plinth. Its red call lamp shone above his remaining hand. The post stood off to the side, beyond where the barrels could swing in their opening.

“Turn it off,” he said.

Norris looked at her.

She pressed the button beside the window. “Stay where you are.”

“Yes. Obviously. Where did you find this cunt?”

Norris's mouth opened. Dulsie held a finger up to him.

“Ogden, I need you to listen.”

“My arm's out there. Look at it. That's all gone.” His breath grated through the speaker. “Did you tell him it was me?”

“He could see what you were doing.”

“Could he? He could see through the wall?”

Norris took one ear cup off. She could feel him looking at her while Ogden breathed. She wanted to slap the button out of the panel.

“I know you hired him,” Ogden said. “Just tell him to stop. I'll pay him.”

“She said the handler was dead,” Norris said.

Dulsie's finger was still on the button. Ogden heard him.

“I'm her fucking husband, near enough.”

“We aren't married,” she said, and hated herself for wasting the denial on that.

Norris pushed her hand away from the intercom.

“You two brought those people here?”

“They paid to shoot him.”

“And your attendant? The man who showed me in?”

“He wasn't supposed to be involved.”

Norris looked towards the rear door of the booth, which led to the car park. Then he looked at the gun again. He stayed in the chair.

“Get my money,” he said.

“You'll have it.”

“Now.”

The speaker hissed. Ogden had pressed his call button again.

“Dulsie, come on. I've shit myself.”

She shut her eyes. Of course he had. The soft trousers were lying beside the plinth's shadow, and his wet breath was in this small room with her. He could turn the eating face back into the face she knew; he couldn't spare her the rest of him.

“Go and get the box,” she told him through the intercom. “We need to pay Norris.”

“You won't shoot?”

“No.”

“Ask him.”

She took her hand off the button and looked at Norris. He leaned over and pressed it himself.

“Bring the money.”

“That's not what I asked.”

Norris hesitated, then said, “I won't fire while you're getting it.”

Ogden crawled along the foot of the dividing wall and disappeared through the gateway. The lamp stayed on, carrying the scrape of his soles until he passed out of range.

“How much is in that box?” Norris asked.

“Enough to pay you.”

He rubbed a thumbnail along a split in the orange peel. “How much?”

She gave him the amount. He stopped touching the peel.

“You've done this before,” he said.

“It was under control before.”

He waited. She had used that tone on guests with too much drink in them, and it usually made them feel guilty for bothering her. Norris just kept waiting.

“Yes,” she said.

Ogden limped back with the box clamped under his good arm. His wounded shoulder had tightened into a hard red knob. He had pulled flesh from his cheeks and left calf to cover the damage. His trouser leg flapped around the shrunken calf, and the loose skin beneath his eyes gave him the look of someone recently starved.

He stopped behind the plinth and set the box on its flat top. His head and shoulders were visible now. Norris kept his hands still while Ogden spoke down towards the speaker.

“We'll give him his fee. Then split the rest. Take me to the car, Dulsie.”

She could do that. Norris wanted to leave and would have his money. Ogden couldn't drive while he was like this, so she'd drive, with the box of notes by her feet. At dawn she'd find a shop selling meat and buy enough for him to fill himself out. By the next evening his cheeks would be back and he would be holding a drink in each hand, one for her.

She held down the talk button. “I don't want another hunt.”

“All right.”

“I mean it.”

“I said all right. We can stop.”

He turned the cashbox towards her. She had put sticking plaster around the handle where the metal pinched. His thumb kept finding the edge of the plaster and pressing it back down.

“You said you wanted somewhere with a balcony,” he said. “We can afford that now.”

He remembered which side of a bed she liked. He couldn't use a telephone without putting it on speaker, but he remembered her headaches and the pillows that set them off. Looking at him, she felt the sick little tug of having hurt someone who had come to her expecting help. She wanted to rest her head on his chest for a minute, before he started asking her to clean something.

“Did you want him to shoot me?” Ogden asked.

She didn't answer. Norris had stopped watching the yard; he was watching her.

“Dulsie. Did you?”

“I wanted it to stop.”

“Which bit?”

She could hear spit catching in his damaged breathing. With half the money, the balcony would be rented, and he'd be out there in his underwear eating from a packet while she dealt with the neighbours. There would always be his half, his things, his weight on the other side of the bed. She had found the lodge, filled the pen and locked the gate. All he had done was eat.

“I'm coming to the door,” she said. “Bring the box.”

He pulled the box off the plinth and started towards her.

Dulsie let go of the talk button and lowered her voice.

“When I've got it inside,” she told Norris. “When I'm clear.”

Norris stared at her for a moment. Then he put his ear cup back on and faced the gun.

She took off her own ear defenders and opened the door. Ogden stood at the bottom of the steps. His left knee had stiffened at the wrong angle and the trouser leg was black with shit. He lifted the box, stretching his good arm to bring it within her reach. The wrist grew thinner as the hand came up.

“Give me a hand with it.”

“Put it on the step.”

“Take the weight. It hurts.”

She bent down from the top step and took the handle with her left hand. Her right stayed against the doorframe. He held on until her fingers were properly through, as he always did when he passed her something heavy. Then he let go.

Dulsie hauled the box over the threshold. It scraped her shin. She pushed it behind her with her heel, into the booth, and turned her head towards Norris.

“Now.”

Ogden's good hand closed around her right forearm before she could pull it off the frame. His fingers met through the flesh. The crack was small, an insultingly cheap noise for what it did to her. She tried to bring her hand towards her and it hung sideways from his fist.

“You were going to leave me out here.”

She screamed at him to let go. He dragged her down a step and she struck the frame with her shoulder. His face was so close she could see the chest hair still in his teeth.

Inside the booth the cannon moved. Ogden's eyes went towards the barrels. He let go of her and dropped back into the yard, planting his good leg to launch himself at the gun. She had been hauling backwards against his grip; released, she fell over the box and landed beneath the observation window, behind the brick wall.

The firing started while her shoes were still in the doorway.

She lay with her smashed arm across her stomach. Her blouse filled with blood. Above her, the window shook in its frame. Through the open door she saw a piece of Ogden's flank strike the bottom step and bounce. He made one more sound, a drawn-out vowel that stopped before she could know whether he'd been saying her name.

Norris kept firing. The ceiling light went out. Dust sifted onto her face and into her open mouth. She had both feet inside now and could not remember moving them. There was no longer any separate report from the gun, only a pressure that got inside her and made her damaged arm jerk against her stomach.

When it stopped, she was still screaming. She could feel it in her throat, though she couldn't hear herself.

Norris came to the door. His trouser cuffs brushed her shoes. He stood there for a long time, looking down into the yard.

“Is he dead?” she said.

He didn't turn. She kicked his ankle with her left foot.

“Is he dead?”

He looked at her mouth, then out again. “Yes.”

She waited for the call lamp to light. It stayed dark. Below the steps lay part of his face, flattened through one eye. The rest of him was spread across the concrete in separate heaps. None of it moved. His lost arm lay where it had fallen, cooling among the ruined trousers.

Norris knelt beside her. She tried to give him instructions, but he was already pulling the booth's first-aid bag open. He packed something against her arm and held it there. The pain changed. She vomited down her blouse, and he turned his face away without moving his hand.

“Hospital,” she said.

He nodded. For several seconds she loved him with a helpless, furious intensity. Then he shifted her left hand onto the dressing and got up to take the cashbox.

“Your fee,” she said. “Take your fee.”

He opened it on the chair. The notes were in the neat bundles she'd counted after dinner. He lifted one, felt beneath it and put it back. Then he closed the lid.

“The rest is mine.”

Norris bent to pick up his coat. She tried to stand, got as far as one knee, and fell against the wall. Her arm had become something she had to carry, and she couldn't carry it and herself.

“Don't fucking leave me.”

He stopped at the rear door. “Car keys.”

She pressed her left elbow against the dressing and worked her handbag open. The rings rattled in the bottom. Norris took the keys out of her fingers.

“And the bag.”

She held it against her chest. He waited. The dressing was getting slippery beneath her elbow. At last she gave him the bag as well.

“You can get more of those people?” he said.

For a moment she couldn't connect the question to anything. He bent closer and repeated it. She understood then: the introductions, the invitation lists, the cash. Ogden was dead, and Norris was looking at the part of the business still alive on the floor.

“I need a doctor.”

“I know. Can you?”

She nodded. He reached under her good arm and pulled her up.

They went out through the rear door. The car was where they'd left it, nose towards the drive. Norris put the box behind the driver's seat and lowered her into the passenger side. Her skirt caught on the seat runner. He tore it free without asking, and the movement sent her arm knocking against the door. She folded over it, making noises she would never have made with a customer present.

He got in beside her. She tried to tell him where the nearest hospital was. He held up a hand while he adjusted the seat. He was shorter than Ogden.

“You get people again,” he said, loud enough for her to hear.

Blood from her arm had run through her lap and between her thighs onto the upholstery. She had spent years filling tonight's pen. But he hadn't started the car, and the dressing was soaked through.

“Yes,” she said.

Norris turned the key. At the first bend the cashbox slid across the floor, and Dulsie reached back to stop it with the hand that no longer worked.

stories.title: The Spider's Hunger
stories.prompt: In a world where live spiders are worn in neck pouches as the ultimate defense against witchcraft, yours suddenly starts acting strange.
stories.body:
# The Spider's Hunger

The fly walked over the spider's back and came out through the feeding hole.

Ivrine caught it under her cup. She had fetched this one from the privy window, where the flies were large and stupid, and she wasn't fetching another. Through the gauze front of the pouch she could see her spider resting against the leather, legs tucked beneath an abdomen so swollen that its pale stripes had spread apart. Yesterday it had at least turned toward the scratching.

“Still no?” Pelset asked.

She tilted the pouch. One leg unfolded, slowly, then folded again.

“Perhaps it wants butter on them.”

He put a slice of bread beside her elbow. He had buttered it to the edges, which he always accused the inn's guests of doing, and scraped the black part off the crust. During these three weeks at home he had remembered that she hated burnt bread. She had forgotten he remembered.

“Leave it alone,” he said. “You'll have it out on the table.”

Ivrine closed the feeding hole with its little bone peg and let the pouch down inside her neckline. The skin beneath it was sore. Usually she shifted it from side to side during the day, following the spider's irregular pulls on the cord; lately it hung in one place like a stone. She had raised this spider from something scarcely larger than a bread crumb. It had traveled eight years with her, lived through a winter in a damp attic, and once escaped inside a lady's sleeve while she was fitting the lady for mourning. It couldn't die the day before her cart came.

“I'll take it to the poucher.”

“That woman will sell you another.”

“I'll make her look at mine first.” She lifted the cup and looked at the fly. “This one can go back.”

Pelset opened the kitchen window for her. Cold air carried in the smell of wet harness from the yard. Her trunk stood by the loading door; he had brought it downstairs before she woke. There was a new strap around its middle where the old one had split.

“You needn't go tomorrow,” he said.

“The cart's paid for.”

“He could take you next week.”

She let the fly go. It settled immediately on the windowsill.

“I've told the woman at the sewing shop I'll be there tomorrow afternoon. She can't keep turning other people away.”

Pelset reached past her to shut the window. His arm stayed across it a moment before he went back to the stove.

Their mother's slippers were still underneath, warming on the bricks. Ivrine had meant to move them every morning since the funeral. Instead she ate her bread while Pelset fried her an egg.

***

The poucher laid the spider on a piece of dark felt. It tried to climb onto her finger, failed, and crouched where she had put it. Ivrine leaned across the counter.

“Move back a little.” The woman moved the felt out of Ivrine's shadow. “When did it last eat?”

“A fly? Four days. I've tried small ones, too.”

“When did it last eat a working?”

“I don't know.”

That was what the animal was for. Ivrine bought flies in winter and rubbed the pouch cord with wax where it chafed her neck; in return, she didn't have to know when somebody in a crowd breathed a working to turn her ankle or make her set down her purse. Schoolchildren wore low collars so their teachers could see whether the pouch gauze was clear. Even the men who went about selling wards wore spiders behind their ward medals.

The poucher touched a fine brush to the animal's rear foot. It shifted just enough to let the bristles pass.

“Any warming lately? Somebody working on a tooth? A charm for sleep?”

“Not that I know of. I have felt warm here.” Ivrine touched the hollow below her collarbone. “I thought it was the spider.”

“When?”

“At night. Twice. Perhaps more.”

“Put it back on. Against your skin.”

Ivrine held the pouch while the woman coaxed the spider inside with the brush. She settled it beneath her dress.

“May I warm your wrist?”

“If that will tell you.”

The woman took her hand, keeping the wrist bare, and bent close enough for Ivrine to smell the mint she was chewing. Her lips narrowed. She breathed out slowly, paused to draw air through her nose, then breathed again.

Warmth spread beneath Ivrine's skin. It didn't feel like a hot cloth. It began inside the wrist and worked outward, an unpleasantly private sensation to have at a shop counter.

The woman straightened. “There.”

“It's stopped defending me?”

“It's full.”

She brought another pouch from a drawer. Its thin occupant ran twice around the gauze while she adjusted the cord. There was nothing beautiful about it: one foreleg was crooked, and its abdomen had none of the creamy marks Ivrine knew. The poucher had her lift the old pouch over her dress and put this one against her skin, lower down, then held her wrist again.

The same slow breath. A sharp scramble under Ivrine's collar. No warmth.

“You felt it feeding?” the woman asked.

Ivrine nodded. The strange spider was still moving.

“Yours has had too much. Not flies. You couldn't do this with flies.”

“Will it recover?”

“Keep it off your skin, let it rest. By tomorrow it ought to be hunting. Bring it back if it isn't.”

Ivrine looked down at the familiar pouch lying on her bodice. “Can one person do that to it?”

“One patient person.” The poucher retrieved the felt. “Or a roomful of well-wishers. Have you been ill?”

“My mother died.”

The woman's brush stopped. “Ah. People do meddle.”

There had been people. They had kissed Ivrine beside the grave and warmed her hands between their own; they had stood close to tell her about their mothers. But that was nine days ago. The spider had been catching flies afterward.

“You can't say who?” she asked.

“No.”

The woman named the bond for the loan spider. Ivrine paid, then stood aside while a boy brought in a torn pouch and an empty matchbox. He said he had slept with his spider loose because it scratched. His father, waiting at the door, looked exhausted.

Ivrine tucked the loan pouch out of sight. She left her old one over her dress, where it could rest.

***

At the inn, Pelset was trying to serve dinner and scrub a bedpan. He had set the pan in the yard and a covered dish of turnips on the windowsill above it. As Ivrine came through the gate, a guest was calling for mustard from inside.

“There isn't any,” Pelset shouted.

“There is,” Ivrine told him. “By the flour.”

“That's horse-radish.”

She took off her coat and carried the dish through to the dining room. By the time she had found the mustard, fetched bread, and exchanged a spotted knife for a clean one, Pelset was back at the kitchen table. He had put their own plates out beside a pile of bills.

“I need to ask you about her money.”

Ivrine sat down. Their mother had divided her savings into two blue purses while she could still count without losing her place. Pelset had received the inn as well, with its leaking roof and three paying guests. Ivrine's purse was upstairs under her pillow. She had slept with it there ever since the burial, though the silver made an uncomfortable ridge.

“I thought we had settled that.”

“You told me what you were doing with it.”

She broke a potato with her fork. She knew what the bills were before he touched them.

He squared the edges of the pile with his fingertips. “Leave me enough for the roof. Just the back slope. I can manage the rest.”

“I need all of it for the shop.”

“You haven't signed anything yet.”

“I've agreed.”

He pushed a plate aside to give himself room. It was her mother's plate, the deep one with the chipped rose. He had put it out with theirs.

“You could agree to come a month later.”

“And where does the money come from in a month?”

He didn't answer. Water dripped off the dish rack onto the corner of a bill. He moved the bill with two fingers.

“You could sell this place,” she said, although she knew before she finished that she ought not to have said it while eating the dinner he had cooked.

“With her hardly cold?”

“I don't mean tomorrow.”

He pushed the bills toward her. “There were nights I was up three times with her. I'd put my hand down the bed and find she was wet again, and she'd cry because she couldn't help me turn her over.”

From the dining room came the scrape of a chair. Pelset stopped and listened until the guest went upstairs.

“You wrote that she was comfortable,” Ivrine said.

“She was. I kept her comfortable.”

Ivrine put down her fork. She had sent money, bought better blankets, written to ask if she should come. None of that gave her anything useful to say about his hand in the bed. Her mother had been clean and warm when she arrived. Pelset had made that appear easy, and Ivrine had let him.

“I should have come sooner.”

He rubbed a patch of dried food on the table with his thumbnail.

“Stay till the end of the week, then. Help me get those two upstairs rooms done.”

She almost agreed. A few days' work wasn't half a shop. And he looked so tired; the side of his nose had begun to peel where he kept rubbing it.

“I can finish the curtains this afternoon,” she said. “Before I go.”

Pelset pulled the bills back into a pile.

“What did she say about your spider?”

Ivrine glanced down at the visible pouch. Behind her collar, the borrowed spider climbed the gauze.

“It needs rest.”

“That's all?”

“She said to leave it alone.”

“Did it eat for her?”

“No.”

He reached to lift the pouch from her chest. He had done it when she was little, checking whether she had cleaned out the husks. This time she caught the cord first.

“You'll shake it about.”

His fingers remained open for a moment. Then he took his plate to the sink.

She had wanted to tell him what the poucher had done, how the warmth had begun inside her wrist. She watched him washing a plate that still had most of his dinner on it, and kept the visit to herself.

***

Ivrine worked on the guest-room curtains in her old bedroom. The fabric was faded along the fold where her mother had pinned up the hem, and the stitches came apart as soon as she pulled them. Beneath her collar the strange spider worried at the gauze. She had kept putting a finger to it all afternoon, an unfamiliar habit. Her own spider had usually rested until dusk.

Pelset brought her tea. He set it on the windowsill, leaned over her chair to draw the shutters against the low sun, and asked if she needed the lamp.

“Not yet.”

For a moment his face was close to her neck. She heard air pass between his lips; the hidden pouch jerked. He straightened with a little cough.

She kept sewing. Perhaps he had blown dust off the shutter latch. Perhaps that was all the sound had been.

When he left, she opened the shutters again. Across the yard the carter was finishing a harness repair. She called down to ask when he was leaving.

“First light. You want your trunk on tonight?”

“Yes, please.”

“I'll fetch it after the wheelwright's. Might be late.”

She thanked him and pulled the curtains across the open window. There was still an hour of daylight. She could have gone downstairs, put her purse on the table, and asked Pelset to tell her what he wanted so badly that he had begun breathing it against her skin.

She folded the finished curtain over the chair instead.

Her bed stood along the wall beside the door. Ivrine lay down facing the window, her cheek pressed into the pillow, and loosened her hands against the bedspread. The blue purse was beneath her ear. She could feel the edges of the coins through the stuffing.

Downstairs, a pan struck the stove. A guest asked something; Pelset answered. There were footsteps on the stairs and then none. She waited long enough for her shoulder to begin hurting.

The latch lifted.

“Ivrine?”

She let her jaw slacken against the pillow. He came into the room. Through her lashes she saw his knees beside the bed. He lifted the old pouch by its cord and lowered it beneath her neckline, his knuckle brushing her skin. She waited for his fingers to find the other cord, but it lay farther back, hidden beneath her hair.

He bent down. His first breath stirred the little hairs behind her ear. He drew in another through his nose and let it out more slowly. The borrowed spider scrambled toward the leather against her breastbone. No warmth came.

Pelset paused. The bed creaked as he put one hand down beside her head. Again he gathered his breath, holding it so long that she waited for the exhalation with him. When it came, the gauze dragged sharply against her skin.
