She wanted to sit up. She wanted to hit his mouth with the back of her hand. Her shoulder had begun to tremble with the effort of leaving that hand on the bedspread.

He made a small dissatisfied noise and stood up, breathing openly now. Ivrine felt the mattress rise as he took his weight off it. The door closed.

She stayed on her side until she heard him in the kitchen. Then she got up and moved the chair beneath the latch.

All those evenings beside the fire: Pelset pulling her shawl straight, Pelset leaning over her shoulder for the bellows, Pelset telling her to sit still while he put a cushion behind her head. The tea was on the windowsill. She had already drunk half of it.

She held the loan pouch away from her skin by the cord. Its occupant was moving, abdomen still narrow. When she touched the feeding peg, a leg struck the gauze. The poucher's creature remained hungry.

Ivrine put it back against her breast. She laid her old pouch in an empty sewing basket, propped so air could pass through the front, and knotted the basket shut.

At supper she took her plate into the dining room and ate with the guests. Pelset said nothing, but later he came to her door with the warming pan.

“I'm in bed,” she called.

“Lift the latch.”

“I'm warm enough.”

He tried the door. The chair leg grated on the boards, loud in the small room.

“What's against it?”

“The chair.”

A long silence. Then he said, “You always did fuss about sleeping here.”

He took the pan downstairs. She sat fully dressed on the bed and listened to the ordinary work of closing the inn. Twice she heard him cough. When the carter came for her trunk, she leaned from the window to make certain it left with him.

***

Before dawn she untied the sewing basket and lifted the old pouch out to look. The spider climbed onto the gauze and began picking at a bit of thread. Its abdomen was smaller. Ivrine cried a little at the sight, soundlessly and with great annoyance. She had other things to do with her face before she went downstairs.

She washed, tied her hair over the thin cord of the loan pouch, and put her familiar spider, still in its own pouch, back in the basket. The blue purse went inside her coat. She carried the basket in her left hand.

Pelset was waiting in the kitchen. There was breakfast on the table, bread beside a covered dish. The loading door stood open onto the yard.

“Your driver isn't ready.”

“I'll wait outside.”

“Sit down. Eat something.”

She set the basket on the sill beside the door. Her right hand stayed inside her coat, closed around the blue purse. Pelset stepped between her and the yard.

“Leave her money here.”

“I've given you my answer.”

“I'll pay you back once the roof's done.”

“Move, please.”

His eyes went to her throat. There was no pouch visible now. He caught the opening of her coat. She backed against the table, pulling away from him, and her hand came out with the blue purse clutched in it.

“Put it on the table.”

He drew a breath. She tried to back away, but the table was behind her and his arm was beside her shoulder. His mouth shaped the words again as he let the air out, slowly, toward her face.

Her smallest finger lifted from the purse.

It wasn't the trembling she had felt upstairs. The finger was being drawn straight. The next began to follow, peeling her grip apart while the rest of her hand strained to close. She caught the purse against her belly with her other hand.

Under her collar something struck, a hard little rush of feet. The drag on her fingers slackened. Pelset inhaled through his nose and leaned closer, cheeks hollowing with the long breath. The spider pulled the pouch sideways. Ivrine's fingers closed so abruptly that her nails hurt her palm.

She shoved him. He stumbled against the doorpost and caught her sleeve.

“What have you got under there?”

She struck at his hand. Cloth tore at her elbow, but he held on. His face had gone dark and wet around the lips. He was trying to take another breath.

“Trunk's tied,” the carter called from the yard. “Want a hand with that basket?”

Pelset turned his head. Through the doorway Ivrine saw the carter coming around the wheel, holding out an arm. She seized the basket and thrust it toward him. To keep hold of her, Pelset would have had to follow her out while she was handing another man her luggage.

His fingers opened.

“She's taking everything with her,” he said to the carter, in the voice he used when a guest broke something and hadn't yet offered to pay.

“Room enough,” the man said, and put the basket beside the trunk.

Ivrine followed him to the cart. Her knees were shaking so badly that she missed the step. The carter gave her his forearm; she climbed without looking back until she was seated behind him.

Pelset stood in the doorway, his hand on the splintered post. She could still see the cloth laid over her breakfast.

“I'll need an address,” he called. “For the rest of your things.”

There were no things she needed badly enough.

“I don't have one yet.”

“You said it was all arranged.”

The carter shook the reins. Ivrine turned to face the road and let the wheels carry her out of the yard before Pelset could make her answer.

Beyond the last houses, she worked the torn sleeve free of her elbow. She could open and close her hand. She did it several times with the blue purse deep in her pocket, feeling each finger move because she wanted it to.

The carter offered her a corner of his blanket. She took it and shifted the basket onto her knees. Inside, her spider was busy with a fly husk caught in the seam. It dropped the husk, climbed the gauze, and waited with its front legs lifted.

Against her skin, the other spider moved. Ivrine turned at once to see who was close enough to breathe on her. There was only the carter, facing forward, and the empty road behind them.

stories.title: What the Wind Wanted
stories.prompt: When you gained the ability to understand all languages you weren’t expecting to the wind to whisper.
stories.body:
# What the Wind Wanted

By noon, Zerune had discovered that the mysterious book in the fishmonger's window was a collection of insults for use at weddings. She bought it anyway. Yesterday she had spent an hour copying three of its hooked letters through the glass; today she could read even the cramped addition beneath the price: *Let it go cheap. It smells.*

The fishmonger spoke to his sister in the language of their childhood. Zerune understood that, too. He told his sister he'd meant the little note for her, and hoped this customer would not ask for a discount.

“I won't,” Zerune said.

He examined her face. When she tried to explain in his language, the sounds would not come. She knew what he had said, but knowing how to move her mouth was apparently a separate accomplishment. She paid the full price in silence and carried the book into the market.

At the cloth stall, two women were signing a dispute about the length of a sleeve. The quick movements were as clear as speech. One woman glanced at Zerune, caught her following, and tucked her hands under her arms. Zerune hurried on, ashamed. She was thirty-two; she ought to have better manners than a child who had learned to read over shoulders.

Still, every passing cart brought her something. A curse. A direction. A man assuring a tethered hen that they would be home soon. The hen's answer remained a squawk. A wheel squeaked without meaning anything at all.

She sat on the low wall beside the grain sellers and opened her book. Her afternoon stretched before her, full of available things: the inscriptions above the old playhouse, the letters her grandmother had kept but could not read, the poet with the blue binding whom she had loved for his pictures. All at once she had too little afternoon.

The book's leaves lifted beneath her fingers.

“Up there,” someone whispered.

Zerune looked toward the windows over the stalls. A woman was shaking out a rug. Beyond her, laundry hung almost motionless in the heat.

“I need to go up there. Which way do the walkers go?”

The whisper moved past Zerune's cheek. She twisted to look behind the wall. There were broken baskets, a sleeping dog, no crouching child.

“Who said that?”

Her pages flickered from front to back. The sound was paper scraping paper, and within it the voice asked, with a sudden concentration, “Can you hear me?”

She clapped the book shut.

For a moment there was only the market. Then the loose end of her headscarf lifted and stroked her ear.

“That stopped the noise. It didn't stop me.”

Zerune held very still. The scarf rose again, stirring air against her neck in three small pulses. The words arrived with the touch: *You can. You can hear me.*

She put the book down carefully. “Do that again.”

The pulses returned, each quite distinct. All morning understanding had opened ordinary things. Here was something she had never thought to try to understand.

“You're the wind.”

“Some of it.”

A boy sweeping outside the grain stall sent a fan of chaff toward her feet. Part of it continued across the paving. Part rose into a loose ring at knee height, revolved twice, and shed a few flakes.

“This much,” the whisper said through the chaff. “At present.”

Zerune reached toward the ring, stopped, and asked if she could touch it. It moved over her hand. The chaff fell away, leaving a cool pressure that ran around her wrist and returned beneath her palm. She could feel where it passed without feeling its edges. Then it left her for a sunlit stone, where a little dust began turning.

“Do all winds speak?”

“I don't know all winds.”

“But you understand me.”

“You walkers say things constantly. Down by the boats, all through the night. How long have you been listening?”

“To you? Since you asked the way. To everything else, since breakfast.”

The dust stopped turning. For one dismayed instant she thought she had lost it, but her book opened and shut a finger's width.

“Then you heard the other one.”

“I don't think so.”

“Up there. Beyond the white ridge.”

She followed the direction of the page as it lifted toward the hills behind the town. The ridge was high enough to retain a dark fold of snow below its summit, though the orchards on its lower slopes were in leaf.

“Is that where you're going?”

“It called when the sun came over. I caught the edge of it above the water. A long rising turn, with a hollow in the middle. I want to turn in that hollow.”

The breeze left the book and sifted through a basket of oranges. Their seller waved it away as if it were a fly.

“You're looking for a lover,” Zerune said.

“I'm looking for that wind.”

She had been about to ask what it remembered of the drowned temples along the shore. “And you want directions.”

“Yes.”

There was nothing disappointed about its yes. It circled her warm wrist again, expecting an answer.

Zerune knew a path to the ridge. She had gone partway up it once with a party of cousins, before they settled under an almond tree and forgot their destination. She told the breeze about the path, and it brushed upward along her arm, then fluttered uncertainly against the book.

“Show me the beginning.”

She looked at the open page, where someone had written a furious objection to the author's remarks about bridegrooms and dated it two hundred years earlier. It would keep.

She tucked the book into her shoulder bag and set off for the last houses. A little dust followed her uphill.

At the last house the path passed an open cellar. The breeze, skimming ahead, drifted across the doorway. Its whisper broke into a thin, meaningless rattle. Dust spread on the doorstep.

“Are you there?” Zerune asked.

The dust gathered slowly toward a bright patch of paving. She waited while its circle tightened.

“Cold in there,” it said at last. “Don't take me under the trees.”

“What happened?”

“I nearly came apart.”

She crouched by the patch of sunlight. The moving air trembled against her knee. “Would you have died?”

“I would have scattered. Come on. The stone's giving me plenty now.”

It rose in a little spiral and went ahead, leaving her to straighten more slowly.

For a while the path ran beside a low orchard wall. The breeze avoided the shade of the trees, crossed sunny gaps, and waited on pale stones while she caught up. It could turn the youngest leaves, but when Zerune asked it to give her a push up a steep stretch, it did no more than lift the cloth between her shoulders.

“You're heavy.”

“So I'm discovering.”

Her shoes had been suitable for the market. Gravel entered them at every bend. Below her the harbor diminished into boats and bright spaces between boats; above, the white ridge had resolved into rock, a saddle, and the dark mouth of a tunnel.

“The old temples along the shore,” she said, between breaths. “The drowned ones. Have you been inside those?”

“Holes in stone? Yes.”

“They're supposed to be written all over. Nobody alive can read it. Is there writing? Did you notice?”

“Dripping. Wings. Once another wind that wouldn't let me leave by the way I'd come.” It ran over a clump of thyme and returned smelling of it. “I could bring this.”

“To the wind you're meeting?”

“Does it cling?”

She inhaled. “Very strongly.”

It took more, combing the thyme against its stems. Her next breath tasted green and bitter.

“Enough,” she said, coughing.

The breeze had already left the path. She found it above a rock, practicing a turn that lifted dry flower heads in a narrowing spiral. It began telling her about the routes it had traveled: between two waves before they struck together, up the hot back of a sleeping bull, through a row of freshly washed shirts. As it spoke, little pressures along her arms indicated turns and dips. She understood the words for those movements. She could no more imagine their pleasure than she could smell a color.

“Will you show me the wave one?” she asked.

“This is the wave one.”

She watched the flower heads swing around the rock. “Oh.”

“There was more room between the waves.”

It swept the flower heads away and went farther up the path.

By the time they reached the tunnel, Zerune had pulled off her scarf and was carrying it bunched in one hand. The afternoon sunlight stood on the ridge's western face. A cold stream of ordinary air poured over the saddle above the tunnel, dragging tatters of mist off the snow. Nothing whispered in it.

The breeze stayed low against the sunny rock.

“Through there,” it said.

The tunnel cut straight through a narrow spur of rock. Zerune could see daylight at its far end, green within the white glare. The floor was level, worn smooth along the middle. Inside, water gleamed on the walls.

“Why haven't you gone through?”

“Put your hand in.”

She did. The tunnel air was cold enough to tighten the skin along her arm.

She looked up at the saddle, where the mist was streaming off the snow. “Then go over. It's hardly higher, and it's all open air.”

The breeze touched her scarf. “That's colder, and it pours. It would pull me out long and thin. I'd lose the turn that keeps me together.”

“You can't go around the ridge?”

“I can go down again. Along the shore. Away from here.” Its speech rustled in the scarf, impatiently at first, then more slowly. “The other wind will change when the sun goes off its side of the ridge. I don't know if it will come back the same.”

Zerune eased her bag off and sat on a flat rock. She could feel her pulse in her heels. She had climbed far past the almond tree without recognizing it, and she had brought the creature all this way only to find it needed something she could not provide.

She drew breath and got as far as “I'm sorry, I don't think” before the breeze pressed against her lips.

She flinched, spat, and pulled the scarf across her mouth. “Don't do that. You've been through the chaff and the oranges and half the dust on this hill.”

It withdrew so quickly that her hair fell across her eyes.

“You're wet inside,” it said. “Warm. When you let air out, I can feel it.”

Zerune lowered the scarf a little. “You want to get in my mouth?”

“Farther. Where you keep your breath.”

She looked from the patch of turning grit beside her shoe to the tunnel. “I'd have to hold my breath the whole way. I don't even know how long it is.”

“You walk. You let me out on the warm side.”

“Can you even fit?”

The grit spread. A narrow current entered the loose curl of her hand and went around inside it, brushing one knuckle after another.

“I leave most of the air. I keep moving. Feel?”

She felt. The small circuit tickled her skin. When she closed her hand a little, it moved within the smaller space, quicker and less regular.

“Too small,” it said, and slid free.

She went to the tunnel mouth again. It didn't look very long. She counted the visible seams in the floor, then gave up trying to judge the distance from here.

“Wait here.”

“I am waiting.”

She crossed without it, counting her steps. Twenty-six. The floor held no loose stones, and the damp stayed against the walls. She emerged onto a grassy shelf overlooking a shallow basin. Sun lay on its far slope and on the tall grasses surrounding a pond. Warm air brushed her forehead. Far below, from among the grasses, came a rising sound that meant *here, this way through me*, although it wasn't addressed to her.

She stood listening. A second phrase moved through the reeds at the pond's edge. She understood it perfectly and could not have followed its instruction without becoming wide and lifting at three separate points.

On the return she walked at an easy pace, watching the bright entrance grow. She had room to swing her arms. No step required a climb.

“I heard it,” she told the breeze.

It came up off the stone so abruptly that grit struck her stockings. “What did it say?”

She tried to reproduce the rising sound. The breeze waited.

“It said, *here, this way through me*. It wasn't saying it to me. I just can't make the sound.”

“But it's there.”

“Yes.”

It pushed gently against the inside of her wrist. She had wanted its whole attention all afternoon. Now she had it, and found herself trying to describe the three separate lifts of the second phrase before she remembered that none of it would get the breeze through the tunnel.

“Listen. I can walk that far holding my breath. But if I need to breathe, I will. Even if we're still inside.”

The pressure left her wrist.

“Could you get back to this end?” she asked.

“Maybe. Close to it.”

“If it happens halfway?”

The breeze passed once across the tunnel mouth, no farther than her outstretched arm. It returned with a falter she could hear.

“I don't think so.”

Zerune sat down again. She drank from her flask, wiped the water from her chin, and let her breathing settle. She could take her book down to the almond tree. She could lie there and read until the stones cooled. Instead she listened to the little wind circling beside her, rehearsing and abandoning the beginning of its wave turn.

“Will I hurt you?” she asked.

“If you keep me too long. I can't stay folded like that.”

“I couldn't keep you long if I tried. I'll need my breath back.”

She pushed the scarf and flask into her bag. “I'd like to hear what it says to you,” she said to the bag. “When you get there. If you don't mind.”

The breeze went on circling by her shoe. She lifted the bag and loosened the strap so it didn't press her chest. The breeze rose with her.

“I'll breathe you in at the entrance,” she said. “Slowly. I'll say when.”

It waited against her lower lip while she took two ordinary breaths. “Now,” she said, and breathed in. It entered with a faint taste of salt underneath the thyme. Her throat wanted to reject it. She stopped, let it wait, then finished the breath.

Something turned behind her breastbone.

It was no larger a sensation than the flutter that sometimes came when she drank too much strong tea. It was also entirely wrong. She shut her mouth and stepped into the tunnel.

Her bag brushed her hip. First one foot, then the other; the familiar work of walking, with her body trying to draw her attention elsewhere. Coolness gathered under her sleeves. She looked at the far opening. From here she could see the top of a grass stem beyond it, bending in the sun.

The movement in her chest tightened. A delicate vibration reached her throat, and meaning came through it, as plain as the signs at the cloth stall.

*Too close. All around.*

She could not reassure it. She kept her pace even, resisting the desire to run and use up everything at once. Water clicked somewhere to her left. Her soles crossed a seam in the rock, one she had already stepped over twice. The far opening widened; light touched the floor ahead.

Now her chest wanted to open. The wind was still turning, cramped into her, and she wanted it out with an urgency that briefly displaced all her fascination. She reached the seam where the ceiling ended. One more step put her face in warmth.

She exhaled.

The breath came out ragged. Her next went in too sharply, and she coughed, bent over with her hands on her thighs. The flutter was gone. She lifted her head before she had quite recovered, searching the grass at her feet.

There: a pair of pale seed husks, circling each other. They climbed, parted, drifted down. A warm touch crossed her cheek.

“It smells of stone here,” the breeze said. Its voice had resumed its ordinary eagerness. “And deep water. Can you smell the water?”

“Give me a moment.”

But it was already moving down the shelf.

Zerune followed far enough to sit in the grass. The basin lay below her, perhaps two hundred paces across. A grove of short trees occupied one side; on the other, the pond reflected a bright slice of ridge. She could hear the larger current in the trees now, a phrase passing from one crown to the next, continuing far beyond what she would have been able to say on one breath.

The little breeze entered it with a shiver of thyme.

“I went between two waves. Both breaking. I turned lengthwise and came out before they touched.”

The trees continued their phrase. Grasses on the far side of the pond bowed toward the bank, then straightened. Zerune waited for an answer, feeling an absurd need to make sure the breeze was heard.

“It came all the way from the shore,” she called.

The little breeze doubled back through the grass below her. “Don't tell it. I'm telling it.”

“Sorry.”

It went out again, carrying its salt and thyme, and began the wave turn over the pond. Water dimpled. The dimples curved around one another in a fleeting pattern she recognized from the flower heads. This time it was beautiful, though she could not have said whether the wind performed it better or she had learned where to look.

“There is a way through me here,” the basin current said, “and here, and here, low where the reeds begin, if you come in under.”

The pond's surface moved from the far bank toward the near one in three narrow bands. The breeze attempted to cross them. Its turn broke, reformed, and broke again. A sharp little eddy rattled the reeds.

“Those are not waves.”

“No. They are what I have down here, where the water lies and the slope comes up out of it, and the sun stays on the one side all afternoon. They are what I have.”

The little wind tried again before the phrase had finished. Zerune took the book out, laid it in her lap, and tucked the bag behind her back. Out on the pond the water quieted, and the breeze moved into the spaces between the three bands. The reeds bowed. From the trees came a sound so low that she felt it in her teeth.

“Come through me again. The same way, only slower, as slow as you can bear to.”

It did, more slowly.

This exchange went on until the shadow of the ridge had crept past the tunnel behind her. The breeze shed its thyme. Zerune could no longer pick out its scent when a current strayed up to her, but she knew its touch: the small, hasty return, the way it gathered around a warm place before leaving. Once it swept along the pond's edge and lifted a procession of gnats. The basin current turned them back. The breeze left the gnats alone. Returning over the reeds, it began a tight inward movement, broke it off, and stretched itself into a long curve.

Then the larger voice asked, “There is a turn you begin over my reeds and fold away before it is finished. Every time you come back across them you fold it away. What is that turn?”

The little wind faltered over the reeds.

“A tight one.”

“Make it here, over the grass, where I am quiet. I will keep still for it.”

It drew into itself. A handful of grass stems tilted inward beneath it, their tips describing the little cramped space. Zerune sat forward. The movement loosened, almost resumed the wave turn, then contracted again.

“That one,” said the basin current, and went on after the grass had straightened. “That one, the small one. The one you fold away.”

The tight circuit shivered. She felt the remembered flutter in her own chest, though she knew she had let all of it go.

“I couldn't turn out,” the breeze said. “There was warmth on every side. I had to keep coming back.”

The leaves nearest the pond began to move inward. Farther away, tree after tree took up the curve. The big current was making a hollow for the small one, a space held in motion. Zerune could follow the invitation across the whole slope. For once she knew exactly what was being offered, and still the scale of it bewildered her.

The breeze entered.

The two patterns met above the pond. For a while the reeds spoke first, the trees answered, and the little wind's quick returns passed between them. Then a movement began in both places at once. Zerune heard a new inflection: *we*, with a precise meaning she had never heard in a human mouth. Both speakers were still there. One hurried; one extended the turning long after Zerune expected it to end. Together they were asking whether to rise.

They tried. The first attempt spilled into the trees. Leaves flashed pale undersides and a few snapped loose. The little voice objected to the widening at the top; the larger one wanted more space underneath. They came down across the water and began again.

Zerune pulled her feet under her to make room as a cool edge of their conversation crossed the grass. She could hear them perfectly, and sat with her book unopened while the turning gathered below her, spread, and carried its two voices up the sunlit slope.

stories.title: The One Who Gets Tired
stories.prompt: You are the oldest of many children in your family. Your parents are actually ancient South American gods, pretending to be humans. Born of a previous marriage, you are the only "mere" demigod of the family, and the rest often look to you for help being more "human".
stories.body:
# The One Who Gets Tired

When I got home from the bakery, Braulio was on the stairs practicing being out of breath. He leaned on his knees and hauled air through his mouth. Behind him, the youngest was copying him, though with the addition of a small, unnecessary scream.

“What happened?” I asked.

He straightened. “Does it look real?”

“It did until she started.”

“She's not coming running with us.” He waved our sister back upstairs. “The boys keep saying I'm letting them win.”

“Are you?”

“I waited halfway up the hill yesterday.”

I set down the bag of unsold rolls. I'd been on my feet since four, and a piece of sock had folded itself beneath my heel. Braulio, sixteen and incapable of exhaustion, looked particularly offensive against the stair rail. He had grown taller than me over the summer without, so far as I could tell, experiencing any inconvenience.

“Agree on a longer route for you before you start,” I said. “Then run it properly. Or play cards.”

“I like running.”

“Longer route, then.”

He considered this while taking three rolls. Our smallest sister reached into the bread bag with both hands.

“Leave some for me,” I said, but Braulio was already calling up the stairs to tell the twins they were wrong: he didn't have to stop running with his friends.

I liked that part. They argued for hours, then asked me, and a word from me settled it. Sometimes I continued explaining after the useful bit was over, just to keep their attention a little longer.

In the kitchen my mother was fastening a bracelet with one hand and pinning the seven-year-old's sleeve to the table with the other. He had got his cuff in the jam. Celso took my workbag, kissed the flour above my ear, and nudged a chair out for me with his foot.

“Eat before they find the cheese.”

To our neighbors they were Nélida and Celso: seven children, too much laundry, a loose tile above the entrance that my stepfather said he would fix. Under their older names, Mamaquilla and Inti, there were still people who worshipped them, and they still held authority over moon and sun. Mother could lay moonlight across her palms. Celso could make the courtyard burn white with his presence. They had to take care when they quarreled in it.

Their six children had inherited enough power to make pretending to be ordinary difficult. I had my mother's eyes in moonlight, and my human father's need for eight hours of sleep. A mere demigod, Braulio had called me once during an argument about who should fetch something from the roof. Celso made him fetch it himself.

A row of small toothmarks ran down one edge of the cheese. I cut that bit off and took the rest.

Zulema appeared carrying a pillow.

“Can we do sleeping now?”

“After I eat.”

“I'll get the blanket.”

She was nine. She had been invited to spend the night at a school friend's house, and the permission slip from Mother had scarcely interested her. What she needed was a convincing performance after the lights went out. My siblings slept occasionally, like people taking up a hobby. Zulema couldn't remember the last time she had done it.

I took my bread to the sofa. She arranged the pillow, pulled off my shoes, and tucked the blanket around my feet with a briskness she had learned from watching Mother. For half a minute I was grateful without reservation.

“Your eyes,” she said. “Do they stay pointed forward?”

“I don't know. I'm asleep.”

“Can I look?”

“No. Lie down.”

She lay on the other cushion and squeezed her eyes shut. All her front teeth showed.

“Less face,” I said. “You're resting. Nothing hurts.”

Her forehead smoothed. A stripe of pale light beneath her lashes faded when I touched her wrist. She already knew how to hide it; she forgot whenever she concentrated on something else.

“That's good. Now stay there.”

For a while there was only the kitchen tap and Celso asking who had put a wet spoon in the sugar. Zulema's feet pushed against mine under the blanket. I chewed the last of my bread and let my head sink.

“Leonor?”

“Mm.”

“Is that the noise I make when somebody talks to me?”

I opened one eye. She opened one too.

“You can just not answer.”

She settled back. I watched her trying not to smile, and we both began laughing. When I tried to settle her again she made my sleepy noise back at me, and I had to hide my face in the pillow.

I might have had twenty minutes if the twins hadn't come through looking for hair clips. One wanted the other to braid her hair; the other wanted to finish watching a trailer on my phone. The trailer belonged to the film Papa and I were going to see that afternoon, an old adventure they were showing again. We had watched it on his small television so often that I knew when the courier would lose his hat between the carriages. I wanted the train to be huge for once. Papa wanted to hear it.

The twin with my phone let out a noise at the jump from the moving train. Braulio came back downstairs. The seven-year-old fitted himself between the sofa and my knees.

“You can come,” I said.

All four faces turned toward me. Zulema sat up.

“Really?”

“If your parents take you.”

“That's us, apparently,” Celso told Mother from the kitchen.

She looked at the clock. “If everyone has lunch and gets dressed without a fight.”

There was immediately a fight about whether the youngest could wear her new boots. I said she could sit next to me if she put on the comfortable ones, and for this promise she pressed a wet kiss against my nose. I let her watch the jump twice more. By the time I remembered to put my own shoes on, I'd missed the chance to lie down again.

Papa and Mother had divorced when I was five. Celso had been in my life since I was six, carrying me uphill, coming to school meetings, once sitting patiently through a very long explanation of why he was not invited to my wedding when I grew up. I loved him. I still liked going places with Papa, where nobody needed telling whose daughter I was.

I could have sent Papa a message about the children. Instead I went upstairs to find the youngest's other comfortable shoe.

Outside, Cusco had warmed in the sun while the shaded side of the street stayed cold. Celso carried the youngest down the steps to the bus stop. She kept asking to be put down, then protesting when her feet touched the pavement. I went ahead with the twins, who wanted a photograph together until one decided the other was standing in her light.

On the bus Braulio offered me a seat. I was already waving Zulema into it before he finished asking. She grinned her thanks, and I spent the journey holding the overhead rail and being jostled into a man's shopping bag.

Papa was waiting outside the cinema with two bottles of water. His shirt was freshly ironed, his hair still wet at the temples. He saw me and raised a bottle; then the youngest ran around my legs and took it out of his hand.

“Hello, Eusebio,” she said, offering him the cap to unscrew.

“Hello.” He opened it for her. “Everybody came.”

“They saw the trailer.”

“Ah.”

Celso shook his hand, Mother kissed his cheek, and for a moment we blocked both doors. I moved us toward the queue. Papa stayed beside me until Braulio took my elbow and pulled me back to look at something on his phone.

“I asked someone to come too,” he said quietly.

The message had gone out an hour earlier: *We're going to the film this afternoon. Want to come?* Under it was the reply: *Maybe. I'll ask.*

“Someone from running?”

He nodded.

“Have you heard anything else?”

“That's why I'm showing you.”

“You could send the time.”

“I sent the time.” He scrolled down. He had also sent the name of the cinema, a picture of the poster, and a second question mark.

“Then leave it for now.”

“What if he comes and can't find us?”

“We're right by the doors.”

He looked at them. I hadn't made him happier, but he stayed in the queue.

There were ten seats together in the matinee. While Mother bought the tickets, I took the youngest to see the cardboard train in the lobby. She stood with her face in the hole meant for the driver, ordered us all aboard, and demanded a photograph of every passenger. Papa took the pictures. In his, Braulio had one foot off the ground and his coat held out behind him, fleeing an imaginary pursuer. I doubled over laughing while he complained that Papa had caught him before he was ready. We made him do it again.

At the snack counter, Celso bought four tubs of popcorn and tried to put everything else on the same tray. Chocolate softened where he held it against his chest. He noticed my stare and passed the bars over before he could melt them completely.

“I forgot.”

“Use your jacket.”

He folded it over his arm, and I laid the bars on top. When I was little he used to warm my pajamas between his hands. Later, when Mother said he was spoiling me, he did it only on the coldest nights, which I learned to claim before he checked the weather.

I gave the twins the first popcorn tub. One wanted caramel and the other salted, so I held a fistful of napkins while they sorted a mixed portion with great suspicion. The seven-year-old wanted to carry his own drink. I showed him where to grip it below the lid, then caught myself explaining again when he already had it right.

“I've got it,” he said.

“I know.”

I was still hovering.

Papa stood at the entrance holding his ticket between two fingers. He had offered to take something three times. I gave him my bag, then took it back because Zulema had put her cardigan in it and was cold.

Inside, I arranged myself where I thought I would be most useful: Braulio on one side, Zulema on the other. The youngest had abandoned her claim on me to sit with Mother, who had the chocolate. They sat at the far end with our seven-year-old brother. Beyond Braulio and the twins, Papa took the aisle seat; Celso lowered himself into the one beside him. I could see them talking as people filed in. Whatever Papa said made Celso laugh.

I leaned across Braulio. “What?”

Papa turned toward me. “The fellow upstairs from my shop brought in a fan. Said it only worked when he shouted at it.”

“Leonor, do we get more if this runs out?” asked a twin.

“No. What was wrong with it, Papa?”

He began to answer, but Zulema had unfolded the cardigan over her head and was asking me whether sleeping under a blanket was allowed at her friend's house. By the time I had pulled the wool away from her face, the lights were going down. Papa settled into his seat. I had popcorn salt on my hands and had eaten none of it.

For a good twenty minutes I forgot to mind. The cinema filled with the knock and rush of the train, far bigger than it had ever sounded in Papa's room. When the courier ducked beneath a carriage, Zulema seized my arm. I knew he would roll clear on the other side; she didn't. I watched her watching, her fingers tightening, then her open-mouthed delight when he emerged still clutching his parcel. Braulio laughed so hard at the lost hat that I missed the next line. I had wanted them to see this. They were seeing it.

Then the youngest needed the toilet. Mother took her out. Our seven-year-old brother, left in his seat, began trying to attract my attention past Zulema. I leaned over, thinking he was frightened.

“Can I have her popcorn while she's gone?”

“Ask her when she comes back.”

He slumped, thwarted. I sat upright in time to see the courier standing somewhere I couldn't account for. The train had apparently reached a town. I had missed the arrival, though I knew it perfectly well, and this irritated me much more than losing something unfamiliar.

Zulema laid her head on my arm. “Check me.”

“You're fine.”

“You didn't look.”

I looked. Her eyes were closed, her face peaceful. I gave her two pats. She began breathing so carefully that each breath ended with a pause to consider the next.

On my other side, Braulio's pocket lit up. He took out his phone and held the bright screen low against his stomach.

“Not in here,” I whispered.

“It's him.”

“Put it away.”

He tilted it toward me. The boy couldn't come. He was at his cousin's. Braulio had already typed *You should have said* and wanted me to inspect it.

Behind us, somebody shushed. On screen the courier had found the ladder beside the mail van. My favorite sequence was coming. I pushed the phone down; Braulio pulled it back, and Zulema raised her head to ask what was happening.

“Come outside,” I said to Braulio.

I led him past the twins, Celso, and Papa, whispering apologies. Zulema followed, clutching her cardigan. I nearly told her to go back, then thought of the additional journey past everyone's knees and kept going.

The lobby was bright enough to make my eyes water. Behind the snack counter a machine kept turning fresh popcorn through its own steam. Braulio stood beside the cardboard train and held out his phone again.

“So should I send that?”

“I don't care.”

He lowered it.

“Send it. Don't send it. Can you decide one thing without asking me?”

Zulema stopped winding the cardigan around her wrist. Braulio looked toward the counter, where the young man serving popcorn had glanced up.

“You didn't have to say it like that.”

“I want to see the film.”

“So do I. You brought me out here.”

“Because you wouldn't put the phone away.”

“Fine. It's away.” He pushed it into his pocket. “You said we could come. Now everything I do annoys you.”

I had an answer ready. It involved all the things he'd done since breakfast. Then Mother came out of the toilets with our smallest sister, who was drying her hands on Mother's skirt.

“What's the trouble?”

“He's upset because his friend wouldn't come, and he keeps—”

Braulio stepped back from me. I stopped.

“I'm tired,” I said.

“You need some sleep.” Mother reached to feel my forehead. I moved before she touched it, and her hand stayed in the air for a moment. “Shall Celso take you home?”

“I don't want to go home.”

Zulema leaned into Mother's side. The youngest wanted to know why we were all standing around when her popcorn was inside. Mother told her to wait.

Papa came through the auditorium door. He looked at Mother, then at me.

“I thought you might be sick.”

“No.”

“Sit down a minute, then.” He pointed to a bench beneath the posters.

I sat. My feet throbbed as soon as I took the weight off them. Papa lowered himself beside me, leaving a small space. I wanted to lean on him, and resented the space, although I was the one who had put four people between us.

“I wanted to watch it with you,” I said.

He nodded. “That's what I came for.”

“Just us.”

“I'd have liked that.”

The youngest was pulling Mother toward the auditorium. Braulio stood by the cardboard train, picking at the seam between two sections. I wanted Papa all to myself and somebody else to do the disappointing.

“I did want them to come,” I said. “When I asked.”

Papa took a tissue from his pocket and offered it to me. I hadn't begun crying, but there was flour in the crease of my wrist and melted chocolate on two fingers. I wiped my hands.

“Next time tell me before we get here,” he said.

“I will.”

Mother looked at the closed auditorium door. “I'll put Celso in your seat. You sit here with your father until you're ready, then take Celso's seat.”

“But she was checking me,” Zulema said.

“I'm here. Show me.” Mother took the cardigan off her wrist and held it open. “Put this on first.”

Zulema thrust one arm into it and began explaining the problem with breathing. Mother listened while guiding the youngest away from the cardboard driver's hole.

“Braulio,” I said.

He stopped picking at the cardboard but didn't come closer.

“I'm sorry I snapped. And said that about your friend.”

“He didn't say he wouldn't come. He can't.”

I nodded.

He wiped his nose with the back of his hand. Then he went to hold the door for Mother. Zulema made a small beckoning motion to me. I shook my head, and she disappeared inside.

Papa waited while I rubbed the place the sock had pressed into my heel. He drank from the remaining bottle of water, passed it to me, and looked up at the posters. I finished the water.

“What was wrong with the fan?” I asked.

“Loose connection. He'd shout, then hit the table. It was the table that did it.”

I could picture him demonstrating this to his customer, solemnly, without once raising his voice. I laughed. Papa smiled at me and got up.

“Come on. You'll miss the jump.”

Celso was already in my old place when we went back. He caught my eye and lifted the popcorn tub in greeting. Zulema was talking into his ear; he turned his head to listen. His folded jacket lay on the seat beside Papa, and I pulled it across my knees. There was a faint chocolate thumbprint on the lining.

On screen, the woman who kept being told to stay behind had got into the locomotive. I found Papa's elbow and squeezed it.

“Here she goes,” I whispered.

“Best bit.”

“Better than the jump?”

He nodded firmly. The locomotive shrieked. She leaned out of the window, hair coming loose, and laughed at the men running along the platform after her. Papa laughed too.

I reached for popcorn. Papa held the tub where I could find it without looking down. The salt was sharp on my tongue. Beyond him was the lit strip along the aisle; beyond me, one twin was picking caramel pieces out for the other. I had meant to tell them to stop rustling the tub. I ate another handful instead.

The courier hauled himself onto the roof. I settled against Papa's shoulder to watch, and he shifted his arm so the seam of his shirt wouldn't press into my cheek. There was still plenty of time before the jump. First came the bend, then the tunnel, then the long stretch with the river beside it.

When I opened my eyes, names were moving up the screen. Somebody further along the row was arguing about which sister had eaten more popcorn. Papa was still sitting at the same angle.

“Did I miss all of it?” I asked.

“The jump? Yes.”

“Was it good?”

“Very.”

I was sorry. I could hear people getting up, feel each freed seat knock back into place. Zulema leaned out to look at me, caught Mother's hand, and was led toward the aisle. I stayed against Papa's shoulder a little longer, until the people had finished passing our knees.

stories.title: Stay Out of My City
stories.prompt: You have incredible powers in a world of heroes and villains, but you refuse to join either side. You threaten both sides to stay out of your city, making it the most peaceful and crime-free city in the world.
stories.body:
# Stay Out of My City

Warren was trying to get the knot out of Elvi's goggles when the battleship came over the breakwater.

It had no business flying. Water poured from its propellers, and its shadow crossed the ferry steps, the swimming platform, the little procession of people carrying their shoes down to the sea. Up on the deck, Mordant stood between two gun turrets in a coat that streamed behind him. Candescent pursued him through the morning air, drawing back one burning arm.

Elvi pressed against Warren's leg. She was ten, all cold elbows and excitement about the deep end of the harbor, which they had finally agreed she could swim in.

“Is that really him?”

“Get up behind the wall.”

She went, taking their bag. Warren waited until he could see her crouching beside the lifebelt box, then looked up.

The battleship stopped.

Its trailing water stopped too, hanging in long, clear columns above the harbor. Candescent's fire spread from her fist toward the ship and stayed there, an enormous orange fork whose nearest point reached over the roof of a fish shop. She was held motionless at its root, one arm extended. The ship's propellers locked in place; after a few seconds of straining noise, someone aboard cut the engines. In the sudden quiet Warren could hear water dripping off someone's bathing cap.

He had never held anything this large. It did not feel different from catching a dropped mug. He looked at the thing, decided how it should move, and it obeyed. Beyond the ship came six armored launches, three flying men, and a woman on a silver disc. Warren caught them as they rose over the breakwater. He left their breathing alone. One of the flying men continued to swear.

“Sir,” Candescent called. “If that's you doing this, I need you to let me finish. His forward cannon is aimed at the hospital.”

Warren could see the hospital windows uphill. He could also see the cannon's muzzle, wide enough to swallow the front of a bus. He turned the ship until its bow faced the open sea, taking care to clear the lighthouse.

“There,” he said.

She stared at him. He was standing on the bottom step in yellow swimming trunks, still holding a pair of pink goggles. He wished he had put his shirt on.

Mordant began to laugh. “Come up here, whoever you are. Whatever she's paying, I'll double it. I have a very good cook aboard.”

Warren moved the battleship farther out, gathering its launches underneath it. Then he turned Candescent and the other heroes to face him, suspended beside their enemies above an empty stretch of water. He took the rescue loudhailer from its hook by the lifebelt box and lifted himself above the wall, his bare legs dangling in view. From there he could see every craft.

“Nobody's paying me.” The loudhailer made a startling noise. He turned it down a little. “My name is Warren Dovett. I live here. You people have closed the schools three times this month.”

“We are trying to apprehend a mass murderer,” Candescent shouted back.

Mordant cupped his hands around his mouth. “And I am in a hurry.”

“You'll both leave. All of you. No headquarters, no weapons stores, no battles. Stay out of my city.”

Candescent pulled against his hold. The flames around her shoulders whitened. Warren watched them, and they bent away from her body in pale, motionless ribbons.

“You should be with us,” she called. “You could save thousands of people.”

“I'm not joining you.”

“Excellent,” Mordant began.

“Or him.” Warren raised the battleship until everyone on the steps could see daylight underneath its hanging keel. “If you come back armed, I'll take every weapon apart. If you keep coming, I'll start taking apart the things you ride in. I can put you ashore alive. You'll have a long walk home.”

Mordant had ceased laughing. He looked down past his own feet.

“Answer me,” Warren said.

“I understand,” Mordant said.

Candescent looked toward the city before she answered. “We'll withdraw.”

Warren released her fire toward the empty sky, where it unfurled into a long, harmless glow. He lowered the ship and launches onto the sea outside the harbor, then set the heroes down on the breakwater's outer end. The floating columns fell as rain. By the time the engines started, Candescent had ordered her people away from the ship.

He held everything in view until it had gone well out to sea, then lowered himself onto the steps and put the loudhailer back. His calves were cold. Behind him, people were talking in the excited, offended voices they used after an unusually bad ferry delay.

Elvi came down the steps with their bag.

“Can we still go in?”

Warren looked at the water. No wreckage, no fuel. The harbor was settling around the swimming platform.

“Yes. Stay this side of the rope.”

She took her goggles from him. “You didn't fix them.”

He sat down on the wet step, and she waited while he worked at the knot with his thumbnail.

* * *

There were tests during the first year. Two gangs believed Warren meant only people in costumes. He helped the police bring the gangs' armored cars to a halt, and the men who had collected money from the fish shops found that their employers would no longer answer their calls. A hero attempted to establish a training base under the name of a sporting association. Warren lifted its practice tower out of the ground and set it beside the inland road, where the hero had to arrange for it to be dismantled.

After that, the danger of provoking him did most of the work. Brackenport's police kept their jobs. They could investigate a threat without an unlicensed flying man carrying their suspect off, or a villain breaking him out before supper. The money once spent repairing battle damage went into homes, treatment, schools.

Elvi was thirteen when Candescent next asked to see him. They met at the disused quarry beyond the inland boundary. Warren had brought Elvi because they were going to the cinema afterward, and she sat on a rock choosing sweets out of a paper bag while Candescent unfolded a map.

“Two days a month,” Candescent said. “We'd transport you. You would retain command of every deployment.”

“Who looks after things here?”

“I'd stay myself.”

He looked at her properly. There was a fresh dressing along her jaw. She hadn't tried to cover it for the meeting.

“You're needed elsewhere.”

“So are you. That's what I'm trying to tell you.” She held a corner of the map against the wind. “I spent last night getting people out from under a railway station. There are seven still missing. With you, we might have had everyone out before the roof went.”

He thought about the seven. She let him.

“I'm sorry,” he said eventually. “I won't sign up.”

She folded the map along its worn creases. “The offer will remain open.”

He bought tickets for the film Elvi wanted, although the creature in the poster had too many teeth and they both knew he disliked things jumping at the camera. Halfway through, she put the sweets between them without looking at him. He was grateful for the dark and for something to do with his hands.

At sixteen, Elvi went with him to meet Mordant in the same quarry. She had a new blue streak in her hair. Mordant arrived without his coat, in a hired car, and kept trying to address her as though she were Warren's assistant.

“I am proposing housing,” he told her. “Quiet homes for people who have spent their lives moving. My crews have children too.”

Elvi looked at Warren.

“Their children can live here,” Warren said. “Anyone's can.”

“Naturally they'd need their parents nearby.”

“Then their parents will have to stop working for you.”

Mordant took a folder from the car and did not open it. “Some of them would be killed if they left.”

“By you?”

“By people who are looking for me.” He looked at the folder instead of at Warren. “You could help us. I have things to offer in return.”

“I'm not giving you a base.”

Mordant sat on the car's sill for a moment. Then he put the folder away. “I suppose you'll be pleased when they come after my people.”

“No.”

Elvi was unusually quiet walking back. At the coach station she stopped to look at an advertisement for a coastal university. Warren waited, wondering if she would ask about Mordant, but she photographed the advertisement instead. There was a small boat on a very blue sea, full of students hauling a net.

“They do a whole term on the water,” she said.

He came to look over her shoulder.

By the ninth year, Brackenport was the most peaceful city in the world, and the only one that had gone five years without a single crime. Warren had watched visiting researchers try to find the trick. They knocked on doors, invited confidential complaints, checked records, stayed out late. They went home with sunburn and the same results.

For Warren, the change was most apparent at night. People had begun swimming after dinner, when the sea held the day's warmth. From the ferry steps he heard laughter carrying across the dark water. Children left their bicycles in heaps outside the library. Shopkeepers went next door for a chat with their tills open. A woman stood up at a council meeting and called Warren an obstructive fool because he opposed her plan for a car park on the bowling green, then asked him to lift a fallen tree off her shed the following week.

Elvi grew taller than the mark he had put on the kitchen door for himself. She found friends who liked the same films, acquired a succession of waterproof notebooks, and came home from the beach knowing the names of creatures he had spent forty years calling little crabs. When her university acceptance arrived, he carried her round the kitchen once before remembering that she hated that now.

She let him finish the circuit.

* * *

On the morning Elvi left for university, she woke Warren by dropping his swimming trunks onto his face.

“You promised me a race.”

He uncovered one eye. She was dressed for the water, with her goggles hanging from her wrist.

“When's your coach?”

“Ten. We've got hours.”

He had, in fact, been hoping she would forget. They had raced each other since she was small, and Warren had become accustomed to winning. Lately, winning had required some adjustments that she took increasingly badly.

“The platform stays where it is,” she said.

He sat up. “That was once.”

“It was Tuesday. I was nearly there, and you pulled it past me.” She sat on the end of the bed. “I've been getting faster all summer. I want to see if I can beat you.”

On Tuesday he had laughed until he saw her face. She had hauled herself onto the platform and sat with her arms over her head. He'd thought she would soon find it funny. Apparently she had been waiting for him to get the joke out of his system.

“All right,” he said.

“Properly.”

“Yes.”

At the ferry steps the water was clear enough to show the sand around the bottom rung of the ladder. Two early swimmers were coming in, trailing small disturbances through the harbor's reflection. Elvi put their towels on the wall and twisted her hair up under her cap.

“If I win, you watch the shark trilogy with me when I come home.”

“The one where it eats the helicopter?”

“That's the second one.”

He had seen enough of that through the kitchen doorway. “And if I win?”

“Any film you like. I won't complain.”

“I could choose the ferry documentary.”

“You could.” She held out her hand. “Are you coming in?”

He shook on it, then followed her down into the cold water. They lined up by the bottom step, facing the platform. First to touch its ladder. It looked a little farther away this morning.

Elvi counted them off, and Warren lunged forward. For several strokes he could see her cap beside him whenever he turned his head. Then she was ahead. She had a long, unhurried stroke that he remembered teaching her in parts, one arm at a time while she clung to the edge. He tried to go faster. Water came up his nose.

The ladder shone beyond her. He could bring it to himself so easily; Tuesday's absurd little victory returned to him, the platform sliding past her toward him while he paddled in place. He reached forward and pulled himself through another armful of sea.

By the time Elvi slapped the ladder, he was still close enough to touch her feet. He made a last furious effort anyway. She had climbed onto the bottom rung when his hand struck the metal.

“There,” she said.

He coughed. She waited, holding the side of the ladder, until he could speak.

“I swallowed half the harbor.”

“I saw.”

“And you got a better start.”

“Yes.”

He looked up at her. She was smiling now, but she wasn't doing any of the crowing he had been preparing to resent. That made it harder to produce his next complaint.

“I did try,” he said.

“I know you did. You made that noise.”

“What noise?”

She demonstrated: a dreadful grunt, with a little squeak in the middle. He splashed her, and she stepped neatly up the ladder beyond his reach.

They went home to shower. An hour later her friends arrived, and Warren carried the suitcase to the station while Elvi gave them an imitation of his finish. It was getting less accurate with every telling.

* * *

The coach station stood just inside Brackenport's inland boundary. From its forecourt Warren could see the quarry mouth and, this morning, Candescent waiting at one side of it. Behind her sat a broad-winged transport and four people in flight harnesses. On the other side of the mouth stood Mordant, two low black gunships, and a van with plated windows.

Elvi followed his gaze.

“Oh, for goodness' sake.”

“I'll be quick.”

“You've got twelve minutes.” She took the case from him. “And you still owe me three films.”

He walked down the road. The quarry was out of use and empty apart from the two parties. As he reached the boundary sign, Candescent and Mordant left their escorts at the quarry mouth and came up the track toward him, keeping well apart. They stopped close enough to speak without carrying their voices.

“You shouldn't have brought those.”

“My escort,” Candescent said. “They stay on our side.”

Mordant inclined his head toward the transport. “And mine stays between me and hers.”

“I came because I heard Elvi's leaving,” Candescent said. “You may want a change yourself. We could arrange work near her university.”

“How did you hear?”

“She won a scholarship. It was in your local paper. So was the day she goes.” Candescent drew off her gloves. “I'm not trying to frighten you, Warren. I thought this might be a good time to ask.”

He had bought six copies of that paper. He remembered them stacked on the kitchen table, Elvi laughing when she found them.

Mordant stepped closer. “I can do rather better than work. I own a house overlooking that university's bay. There's a terrace where you can watch the college boats go out in the mornings; I had it repainted this spring. No rent, no obligations for your daughter. A few obligations for you.”

Warren thought of the advertisement Elvi had photographed at the coach station, the small boat on the very blue sea, and of Mordant on his terrace watching it go out.

Candescent put herself between them. “Stay where you are.”

Mordant lifted two fingers toward his escorts.

The gunships rose and came forward. Candescent's people went up to meet them, the transport lifting behind them on its great fans. They were watching one another. All of them were coming toward the road.

Warren took hold before any crossed it.

He raised the gunships, the transport, the van, and everyone with them above the quarry floor. Candescent's boots left the ground. Mordant, rising beside her, stared down between his polished shoes. Higher up, the four heroes twisted in their harnesses. Their exposed fans strained against Warren until he stopped those too.

He had a clear view of all of it: tons of metal, faces behind glass, the bright mouths of weapons. He turned the whole company until their vehicles pointed away from Brackenport, keeping the people upright. The shadows moved slowly over the bare stone below.

“Put us down,” Mordant said.

“My daughter's waiting up the road. Get those things away from her.”

“We haven't crossed your boundary,” Candescent said.

“And you won't. Either of you.” Warren looked from her to Mordant. “Stay out of my city. Take your weapons away from this road. If I see them pointed here again, I'll put them on the ground in pieces.”

Mordant had drawn his feet up, as if the quarry floor might reach for them. “All right. We are leaving.”

Candescent was looking past Warren toward the station. He resisted the urge to turn; he needed to see what he was holding.

“We need help,” she said.

“I know.”

“You know what you could do.”

He did. He could feel the ease of it, all that weight awaiting his decision. For nine years she had kept asking him, and for nine years people elsewhere had needed her. Work near the university would mean a flat within walking distance of that bay, and Elvi knocking on Sundays with a bag of washing.

“I'm not joining you,” he said. “I'm not joining him. That's still my answer.”

She shut her eyes briefly. “Then set my people down.”

He lowered the vehicles and stood everyone beside them, facing away from the road. Mordant got into the van at once. Candescent waited until her escort was aboard before following. Warren stayed by the sign until the van had driven out of the quarry and the last aircraft had disappeared over the ridge.

Then he ran back to the station.

* * *

Elvi had her phone out when he returned. Her case was aboard, one of her friends had gone to get her a drink, and the driver stood by the kiosk with a cup of tea.

“Are you filming me?” Warren asked.

“Yes. Say who won.”

“I've just been running.”

“Get your breath, then.”

He stood with his hands on his hips until he could breathe through his nose. She kept the phone pointed at him.

“Elvi won the race,” he said.

“How?”

He opened his mouth to mention the start again. It had been a good start, though. He'd seen the neat push from the step, the way she'd put her head down at once. He ought to learn to do that.

“She swam faster than I did.”

She stopped recording and put the phone away.

“Who's that for?” he asked.

“Me. When you start saying you let me win.”

Warren looked at her for a moment. That was something he had said, often enough that he could no longer remember which races he'd meant it about.

“I won't say that about this one.”

“Good.”

She reached up and flattened his hair where it had dried sticking out. He endured it. Then she gave him a quick kiss on the cheek, took the drink her friend offered her, and got on the coach.

At noon Warren was back at the ferry steps. The platform lay beyond the other swimmers, stubbornly distant. He waited until there was a clear stretch of water, then pushed off as he'd seen Elvi do, head down, arms extended.

His goggles filled. He stopped to empty them and tighten the strap, then tried again. By the third attempt he had a little of the movement, the clean slide before the first stroke. He made it halfway to the platform before he had to stop and cough.

He pictured Elvi watching him from the ladder and began laughing, which did not improve his breathing.

stories.title: A Knock in Someone Else's Sleep
stories.prompt: The Entity was trapped and alone until the humans came. It tried to communicate with telepathy but it drove most insane. It soon learned only children could handle it in dreams. It eventually made a friend but they aged out. It now tries to get others to reach its friend through their dreams.
stories.body:
# A Knock in Someone Else's Sleep

Cleo had almost reached the whale's stomach when the stairs appeared.

She stopped on the bottom step. Above her, where there should have been a passage full of swallowed ships, stood a little house with green tiles and no door. The whale's ribs supported its gutters.

“You've done it again,” she said.

The Entity had meant to wait until she finished exploring. But she was leaving in the morning, and the house had risen at the thought of it: every tile in place, the small chimney crooked to the left.

“Do you know someone who lived here?” it asked.

“You already asked. I said no.”

Cleo kicked the bottom step. It became a tooth, then a step again. She was nine, and on the previous two nights her dreams had accommodated anything the Entity put in them. This night she wanted the whale back.

It drew the house aside. The staircase dwindled to a ladder, which Cleo climbed, despite herself. At the top she pressed her face to a window.

The Entity felt her attention settle there. Far below her sleeping body, below the holiday cottages and the abandoned quarry, its own body lay pinched in a cavity no dream could enlarge. It could spend a night making skies for Cleo while the same narrow ridge of stone pressed between two of its living folds. Nothing it imagined moved that ridge.

“Who's supposed to live in it?” Cleo asked.

“Garnet.”

“The girl.”

“Yes.”

“No. Still don't.” She put her hand through the glass. “Why's there wallpaper on the outside?”

“She was shut in, so she turned the house inside out.”

Cleo pulled herself through the window, leaving both shoes on the ladder. She liked to investigate rules. The Entity liked this about her, when it could remember to like something about her other than the possibility that she knew Garnet.

Once it had known nothing to ask for. There had been stone and the pressure of stone, a seep of warm minerals along its underside, the slow contraction by which its body fed. It could remember no entrance to the cavity. Something had enclosed it, or it had grown into an enclosure. That uncertainty had outlasted everything except the wish to meet something else alive.

Then humans cut into the hill.

They did not reach its prison. They came close enough for it to feel the quick separate insistence of their minds, and it poured itself toward them in welcome.

It had no word for welcome then. It gave them its body against the stone, its delight at their arrival, the whole length of its waiting. The first man's mind filled with the clatter of a dropped chisel. Through the contact, the Entity felt his effort to find an edge to what was entering him. It mistook the effort for a reply and pressed closer.

By the time it withdrew, most of the people it had touched could no longer hold their lives together. It learned some of what that meant afterward. Children dreamed of a mother who could dress herself but could not recognize her kitchen; a father who woke certain he was buried, whose daughter sat with him while he found his bed again. One boy dreamed of the quarry foreman teaching him to tie his shoes, slowly, and then being unable to remember which shoe was his own.

The Entity had wanted company. Those people had already had company, and work, and kitchens they knew. It could not return what it had displaced.

The first child reached it during the last of those terrible attempts, asleep in a hut above the quarry. The child turned the Entity's immensity into a staircase and ran up it. When the pressure became too great, the stairs sprouted cushions. She asked whether there was anything to eat at the top.

Her dream could change fast enough to receive it. Waking minds could not. Grown sleepers could not either; even the faintest approach met the same rigid distress, and it learned to stop. Among sleeping children its thoughts became things that could be touched, altered, or sent tumbling away. They were bewildered by it, sometimes frightened, often bored. They woke with their own minds intact.

It learned small approaches. A loose stair. A knock. It let them refuse.

Years passed before Garnet came. By then children had brought it windows, wheels, a name for rain. Garnet brought it rules.

“You make a house with no doors,” she had said, “and I get out. But I can only change one thing.”

She was seven. Her first house became a hat. She lifted it off her head and stood grinning under the sky.

The Entity made another, too large to be worn. Garnet turned it inside out. The wallpaper flowered on the outer walls and she found herself outside, with the bricks under her feet.

It had never thought of this. While its actual body lay unmoving, it held that inside-out house in amazement.

They took turns. Garnet built a house entirely of stairs, and the Entity changed which way was down. She accused it of changing more than one thing because there were so many stairs. For the remainder of that night she would allow it only bungalows.

Sometimes she arrived angry and did not want a game. Once she cried into a cupboard until it filled with water, then made the water salt because she had always wanted a sea of her own. She kept it in the cupboard for weeks. On other nights she described her day while the Entity practiced making the things in it. Its first boiled egg had a handle. Garnet liked it better that way.

She taught it to count years. It taught her nothing she could use at school. She complained about this without ceasing to come.

At twelve, she began losing whole rooms between one visit and the next. At thirteen, a floor it offered became floor and wall and the inside of her own mouth together. She could no longer let these all be true. She called for it to stop, and it withdrew so quickly that the house disappeared beneath her.

For a long time afterward her sleeping mind was still near. The Entity approached as faintly as it knew how, and felt her strain against even that. It left her alone. Other children had changed in the same way; being Garnet had not protected her.

Eventually she moved beyond its reach. A child from next door dreamed of helping carry out the last of her boxes. The Entity kept her house. It kept the cupboard with the tide in it, and the egg with the handle, and a room whose floor she had not yet managed to escape.

Cleo came back through the window and touched one of the wallpaper flowers.

“My Garnet does this with napkins,” she said. “She draws all the rooms, then folds it backward so everyone's in the garden. It's cheating because you're meant to use a pencil.”

“What Garnet?”

“Next door. She looks after me on Tuesdays.”

“Is she thirteen?”

“No. She's seventy-three.”

The house lost its roof. Cleo looked up at the exposed rafters, then at the whale's ribs lifting and sinking above them.

“She's old,” she said. “You said a girl.”

The Entity had counted sixty years. It had kept them somewhere quite separate from Garnet.

Cleo said she would tell her about the house when she got home. She was taking the early coach with her mother; by lunchtime they would be far from the quarry. The Entity would not be able to hear Cleo then, even if she fell asleep on Garnet's lap.

“Can you tell her now?” it asked.

“She's at home.”

“I know a way. If she's asleep.”

It had discovered the way years after Garnet moved away, through a boy who wanted his absent brother to see a thing he and the Entity had made. A child in contact with the Entity could find the sleep of someone they knew. They could take no piece of its mind safely; whatever they carried had to be remade from their own thoughts.

The boy's brother had returned a rude drawing. The Entity still remembered the boy's laughter as he reproduced it.

It had asked many children since then. Did they know Garnet? A girl of thirteen, with a gap where a tooth had never come?

“How do I go?” Cleo asked.

“Think of finding her.”

Cleo put a finger into one nostril and considered. Beside the house, a landing appeared, with an umbrella dripping on its tiles. There was a brown door with a lock higher than Cleo could reach.

“That's the old lock,” she said. “She doesn't use it.”

The Entity could feel Cleo's remembering, but nothing beyond the door. When she stepped through, the child would be in a part of sleep it could not enter. If she woke, the route would vanish.

“Tell her I kept the house she turned inside out,” it said.

Cleo knocked, waited, and went in.

The landing remained. The door shut. The Entity could no longer feel her attention on it.

Stone bore down between its folds. A thread of mineral water cooled along its underside. It examined the closed door, though there was no lock on this side to examine, no wood it could press against with its living body. It was waiting inside Cleo's dream, in a house she had not wanted, beside a whale she had.

When she came back she was wearing enormous bedroom slippers.

“She says what's in the cupboard?”

“The sea.”

“Oh. I said towels. She was cleaning a bathroom, so I thought she meant that sort of cupboard.”

The Entity opened the cupboard. A little tide ran across the floorboards and retreated, carrying a strand of weed.

Cleo crouched beside it. “Can we go in?”

“Tell her it's the sea. She made it salt. Ask if she ever tried to come back.”

Cleo looked from the water to the door. “Then can we go in?”

“Yes.”

She left one slipper beside the cupboard. For a while the Entity watched water darken the cloth toe. It wanted to send the smell of salt after her, and the exact sound of Garnet's laugh when she first stepped out of the hat. But those were its memories. They would reach Garnet with its weight behind them. It held them back.

Cleo returned without the other slipper.

“She says she did come back. She tried for ages, but you wouldn't open up.” She sat on the floor and dipped her feet into the sea. “Did you not like her anymore?”

The Entity began to show her.

It gave her Garnet's mind narrowing beyond its reach; the nights of approaching, drawing away, approaching again; the houses held ready afterward. They crowded around Cleo, small at first, then packed so closely that the whale became all roofs and chimneys. The same unfinished room appeared in every window. Beneath it lay the waiting, as much a part of the Entity as the body inside the stone.

Cleo stood. The sea ran off her feet.

“I can't tell her all that.”

There were more houses. The Entity had not understood until now how many nights Garnet thought it had turned her away.

“Stop. I don't know what you want me to say.”

It stopped. The houses hung around her. Between two roofs the whale's tongue lay creased like an abandoned carpet.

“Make them go away.”

It took the extra houses away.

Cleo sat again, this time on the dry side of the cupboard. “She said other things. I forgot because you did that.”

The Entity waited while she picked a thread from the slipper's toe.

“She drove buses,” Cleo said at last. “For years and years. She said to tell you about the bit where you turn around. At the end of the road. There was a house there that she always thought you'd like. I don't know why. She didn't say.”

Buses. Garnet had once made a bus whose top floor belonged to a different bus. The Entity had kept that, too. But somewhere she had held an actual wheel, stopped beside actual houses, and thought about showing one to it.

“What else?”

“I can't remember.” Cleo pulled the thread until it snapped. “I don't want to keep going backward and forward.”

It wanted to ask about every day Garnet had lived. It wanted the house at the turning place. It wanted to know if she still preferred eggs with handles. The questions arrived together, as its thoughts always did; choosing one felt like letting the others sink out of reach.

“Tell her I stopped because I was hurting her.”

Cleo looked at the places where the houses had been.

“Like that?”

“Worse. She couldn't make it into houses anymore.”

“Will it do that to me?”

“It could, when you're older. I'll have to leave your sleep alone.”

Cleo was quiet. Then she said, “I'm going home tomorrow anyway.”

“Yes.”

She tried to put the wet slipper on. Its heel folded under her foot, and she kicked it into the cupboard.

“What do you want her to do?”

The Entity turned toward the room it had kept ready for sixty years. Garnet had been trying to turn its floor into something she could swim through. It remembered her standing ankle-deep in blue tiles, furious that the rest would not change.

It could send Cleo with instructions for finishing that move. It could ask whether Garnet remembered. But it wanted something it had never seen before: Garnet at the wheel of her bus, looking out at a house that might have pleased it.

“Ask her to make me a new house.”

“Then we're doing the whale.”

“Yes.”

“And I'm allowed in the cupboard.”

The Entity tipped it gently onto its back. The sea rose to fill the opening, with room for Cleo to sit on the edge and dangle both legs when she returned. She inspected it, then went to the brown door.

It took her longer this time. Once, the remembered landing flickered. The Entity drew itself away from the edges of Cleo's mind, afraid that its eagerness had become pressure again. The quarry, the cottages, the sleeping child's small body remained where they were. The landing steadied.

Cleo returned carrying a toy bus she was still putting together.

“She made this. It's the one she used to drive, except I couldn't remember all the seats. She says put yourself in it.”

The bus had a silver bell. Cleo rang it three times before setting it down. As it grew, the Entity recognized the kind of vehicle children had shown it in their dreams. This one had a tear in the driver's seat and a red cloth tied around the steering column.

“What did she say when you told her why I stopped?”

Cleo laid her hand on the bell but did not ring it.

“She didn't say anything for a bit. Then she asked if I was all right. I said I was. Then she started making the bus.” Cleo pressed the bell once. “She told me about the egg, too. You made a handle so she could drink it.”

“The handle was for lifting. I thought it would be hot.”

“Well, she drank it.”

The Entity let that stand. Inside the bus, the driver's seat warmed beneath its attention. It had no single shape to put there. It made a weight in the cushion, a place from which it might look out.

Around the bus Cleo built a room. Its ceiling rested on the roof, and the walls touched the windows. When she was finished, no door remained in either bus or room.

“You're in a garage,” she said. “She says you've got to get the bus out. One change.”

The Entity considered turning the garage inside out. Garnet would expect that. It tried instead to imagine her driving a room.

It put wheels under the garage.

Cleo laughed as the whole room rolled down the whale's tongue and out between its teeth. The bus went along inside it, and the walls stayed pressed to the windows.

“But it's still in there.”

“Tell her I took the garage.”

“She'll say you haven't got out.”

“Tell her anyway.”
