"And this ear?"

The stranger's gloved hand closed more firmly around the shaft. "He copied the drawing."

"Then he copied an error."

"So he said."

The master extended his hand. "Then you concede it is counterfeit."

"I concede it's new. I never called it a relic."

"You entered the gathering under a dead device."

"A carving isn't a birth record," the stranger said.

Aldous disliked the pleasure the man took in this. It was a tired pleasure, the look of someone whose plan, whatever it was, had gone one step further than he had expected.

"Your name," Aldous said.

"Rafe Irlow."

"And the name of the person who made this?"

"No."

"The address at which you are staying?"

"Also no."

"Mr. Irlow," the master said, "you are not in a position to refuse ordinary questions."

Rafe glanced toward the baize door. Beyond it, the roll had resumed in a murmur, broken now and then by a voice too loud. "I came so every House would see the lion. I didn't come so every House could find my lodging."

"There are penalties for false representation."

"There were penalties last time too, I hear."

The master rose. "I will give you five minutes to reconsider surrendering the cane. Mr. Torven, discover what he wants."

"You presume I can."

"You corrected his pronunciation."

The door closed behind him.

For a while Rafe and Aldous listened to the muffled call of animals through the wall. Aldous had long ago learned the Houses by their responses rather than their names. Foxes always answered separately. Hounds struck their cane tips once upon the floor. Herons, when their turn came, waited half a beat, an affectation old enough to pass for tradition.

Rafe removed his hat and spectacles. His hair sprang outward where the brim had held it. "My grandmother says the second part was hardly sounded."

"Your grandmother is wrong."

"There. She said her brother would do that. Correct first, wonder later."

The word *brother* entered the room and made everything in it badly placed. Aldous set both hands on his heron. The old carving fitted them. He had been ill for most of his first winter with the Herons, and the gentleman who became his father had slept in a chair beside him, night after night, waking at every cough.

"How old is your grandmother?"

"She told me not to start with arithmetic."

"A sensible precaution for a weak invention."

Rafe let that pass and reached inside his coat. Aldous's grip tightened, absurdly, on a bird made of ash wood. What emerged was a folded sheet, handled so often its corners had gone soft. Rafe sat down on the nearest of the narrow chairs without being asked, and after a moment Aldous took the one opposite.

"She remembers a younger brother," Rafe said. The rehearsal had left his voice. He spoke faster now and looked down too much. "He was taken out through the scullery because the front steps were full. He had one glove. He'd hidden the other one somewhere and wouldn't say. He used to sit under the dining table when guests came, but only at the end nearest the windows, because—"

"There were no windows at that end."

Rafe stopped.

"The windows were at the street end, behind the head of the table. No child hid down there among the boots."

Rafe ran a gloved finger down the page, lost his place, and found it again. "Garden end. It says garden end. I had it right on the way here."

Aldous looked away. On the sideboard, three clean glasses stood beneath an engraving of Menagerie Hall. He had attended forty-six gatherings beneath this roof. There had once been a gap in the roll after House Lark and before House Mole. The clerk no longer paused there.

"Suppose I knew such a child," he said. "What does your grandmother expect?"

"To know whether he lived."

"Nothing else?"

"Plenty else. She didn't trust me to ask it all tonight."

"She trusted you to invade this gathering in a gilded costume."

Rafe looked down at his black coat. "Only the cane is gilded. This costume has debts."

The laugh escaped Aldous before he could stop it, no more than breath catching at the wrong edge. Rafe heard. His shoulders lowered a fraction.

Aldous recovered himself. "If a surviving relation can be traced, I can arrange assistance. Quietly. A house, if needed. An annuity. There are districts where the old matter would mean nothing."

"You haven't asked what she needs."

"One begins with practical security."

"She has a house."

"Then money without conditions."

"Money for what?"

"For silence," Aldous said, because he was suddenly too tired to disguise the answer as protection.

Rafe folded the sheet along the wrong crease.

From the hall came a burst of applause, excessive and brief. Aldous pictured the clerk pretending that the evening had recovered.

"If the Houses learn where she is," Aldous said, "they will examine her. They will send lawyers, antiquarians, physicians. They will measure every scar against a docket. If she fails to remember one date correctly, they will say she invented all the rest for money, or for a title that no longer exists. I am trying to prevent that."

"So am I. That's why you don't get her name yet."

"Yet?"

Rafe opened the paper again. "Which of the children broke the blue washbasin?"

"There was no blue washbasin."

"I knew this one." Rafe searched the page with a gloved finger. "It was white. The soap left a blue ring."

"The soap was violet. Your grandmother broke it by climbing onto the stand for sugared almonds. She told everyone I had done it."

"She says you pushed her."

"I was five. She was eleven and built like a cupboard."

Rafe stared. Then he looked at the paper. "She isn't built like a cupboard now."

Aldous saw a girl with one thick plait lifting him bodily away from a pantry shelf. He saw the washstand list beneath her bare foot, the white basin descending with majestic slowness, and the violet seam of soap along the broken china. He had not remembered her face. The strength in her arms came back entire.

Rafe was watching him, but suspicion had not left his mouth. "That story might have traveled."

"To whom?"

"I don't know. That's the trouble." He tapped the sheet. "You've got an answer for every bit of it. You don't even stop to think."

"I am contradicting every bit of it. There was no blue basin, the soap was not blue, and I did not push her."

Rafe made an annoyed sound and tipped the golden lion toward him. "Then tell me why the ear is wrong."

"I already have. Your drawing was poor."

"Hers," Rafe said. "The carver copied my grandmother's drawing. She said her brother would know what it copied."

He opened the folded sheet all the way. On the inner face, among Rafe's cramped notes and cross-outs, an uncertain pencil lion stretched across one crease. Its left ear was long and nicked. Its tail ended abruptly above the rear paw.

The old dining table had possessed a thick cross brace beneath the garden end. His sister had lain beside him there during a tiresome winter dinner and scratched a lion into the wood with a stolen fruit knife. A knot had dragged the blade upward, lengthening one ear. The nick was her failed attempt to shorten it. Aldous had called it a rabbit until she stuffed his mouth with sugared almonds to stop him laughing. The tail remained unfinished because footsteps had crossed the carpet overhead.

"The tail should stop before the paw," Aldous said.

Rafe rotated the cane. Beneath the gilt mane and theatrical shine, the carved tail stopped at precisely that place. Then he went back to the sheet, to the washbasin lines, and read them as though they might have changed. "She wasn't sure about the almonds. On the stand. She thought they might have been plum stones."

"Plum stones were hidden in the blue vase."

The lion was not an old object. It was an old mistake, remade and carried through the front doors for him. His sister had lived long enough to draw it for her grandson. Aldous knew then who sat across from him, though he still did not know what to do with him.

The master returned before Aldous found a sentence he could bear to use. He closed the door with greater care than before.

"The official abstract is unequivocal," he said. "The adult Lion gentlemen were condemned, most sentences were carried out, the House properties were forfeited, and the recognized line was extinguished. This person's cane must be surrendered. If he refuses, I shall identify him publicly as an impostor and have him removed."

"What happened to the children?" Rafe asked.

"The abstract concerns the House." The master's gaze remained on Aldous.

Aldous knew the rest of the language. It had been used around him until it became the clean interior wall of his life. Male minors had been placed under the sponsorship of sound Houses. Their names had been regularized. Women and girls, having no standing in the roll, had been dispersed among relations, institutions, and approved households. Later clerks recorded no Lion gentlemen. Therefore House Lion was extinct.

Therefore a sister could live while every document declared her family dead.

"The cane is newly made," Aldous said.

The master inclined his head, relieved.

"So that is not evidence of fraud."

The relief vanished.

Rafe rose too quickly and knocked his chair against the wall. "You believe me?"

"I believe your grandmother remembers a disagreeable little boy."

"That isn't what I asked."

"It is as much as I presently know."

The master laid one hand on the bellpull. "Mr. Torven."

Aldous looked at the heron between his hands. At seven, he had awakened from fever with a new surname being spoken tenderly beside the bed. No one had put a weapon to him. No one had needed to. His former name had disappeared by ink, patience, gifts, correction, and the terrible good fortune of being loved by those who benefited from its loss.

"My name is Aldous Torven," he said. His voice was steady until the next word. "Before that, my sister called me Tuppy."

Rafe sat down again without finding the chair properly. One gloved hand caught its back.

The master released the cord. "This is not the place for distress to become testimony."

"No," Aldous said. "This room was selected precisely because no one outside it need hear."

"Consider House Heron."

"I have considered House Heron every day of my life."

Rafe looked between them. "Did they know?"

"The gentleman who raised me knew what name I arrived with. He also kept me alive. I will not make him a monster for your convenience."

"I didn't ask you to."

"You were about to."

"I was about to ask why you never looked for her."

Aldous had an answer ready: he had been told there was no one left. It was true for the first years and useless for all the years after.

"Later," he said, "I was occupied with being grateful."

Rafe's mouth tightened under the moustache. "She will dislike that answer."

"So do I."

Aldous rose and turned toward the hall door. The master's eyes went with him. Formula had served the master all evening, but formula required the participants to remain in their assigned categories. "If you leave now, Mr. Torven, you will be absent when House Heron is called for the vote."

"Count me absent."

"That isn't the question she sent," Rafe said.

Aldous turned on him. "Your grandmother appears to have sent a hamper of questions."

"One, really. The others were to make sure it was you answering." Rafe lifted the lion between them. "She said if you knew her lion, I was to ask whether you'd answer the roll."

"House Lion has no roll."

"Not as Lion. As yourself. Where they can hear."

The master reached for the bellpull again. "No personal declaration will be permitted in the gathering."

The gold ear was foolishly long in the lamplight. Aldous's sister had made a public scandal carry a message no House could read for her. An annuity offered in this room would answer it with silence.

"Do not count me absent," Aldous said.

Rafe's grip shifted on the cane. "Is that a yes?"

"That is me answering badly. You may report it as such."

"And him?" the master said.

Aldous turned to Rafe. He could not authenticate the lion. He could not summon a dead House with a word. "Mr. Irlow is not an impostor. His cane is a recent advertisement, in deplorable taste. His descent is his own affair, and mine."

"Mine first," Rafe said.

Aldous did not argue. He opened the baize door.

Rafe gathered the folded sheet and his spectacles, put on his hat, and followed.

The gathering had ceased pretending to continue. Gentlemen stood behind chairs or crowded the aisles, animal heads showing between black coats like a second, less disciplined audience. The clerk waited with his pen lifted. No one cheered when Aldous entered. A few men turned away. One called for the lion to be broken; another demanded to hear the claim. Most watched with the careful hunger of people preparing to say later that they had seen very little.

Aldous took his hat from the attendant but did not put it on. He walked instead to the lectern, his heron cane striking its familiar measure on the floor. Rafe stopped near the side door, the golden lion held close against his leg.

"Rafe Irlow's cane is eleven weeks old," Aldous said. His public voice arrived out of habit, elegant and almost useless. He made himself continue. "His grandmother is my elder sister. I was seven when I was removed from House Lion and given the name Torven. House Lion remains extinct. We did not all die."

The first demand was for the woman's name. The second was for papers. Someone at the boar table called Aldous senile; a Heron answered with an oath and then looked embarrassed to have done it. No agreement gathered beneath the noise.

"You will have neither name nor address," Aldous said. "You wished to know whether this gentleman's claim was fraudulent. It is not."

The master stepped beside him. "The roll has no provision for such a declaration."

"Then it need not provide for it. I have said it. Proceed."

Rafe had moved nearer during the uproar. Aldous looked at the long-eared lion. "Tell her the egg was soft."

Rafe lost his quick answer. "What egg?"

Wet wool and sulphur returned to Aldous with the smell of the lamp gas. His sister's large hand had squeezed his shoulder while her other pushed food into his coat because he had refused breakfast.

"The one she put in my pocket when they took me through the scullery. It broke before the gate. She put a twist of salt in the other pocket, as though that improved matters."

Rafe searched the unfolded sheet. His moustache shifted. "She says it was hard-boiled."

"Your grandmother has never admitted fault while a witness remained alive."

Rafe laughed, short and startled. He put on his blue spectacles. "I'll tell her you answered the roll and complained about breakfast."

He tucked the paper inside his coat and crossed the hall alone. The gentlemen in his path withdrew just far enough to let the golden lion pass. No one asked him to surrender it again.

Aldous went to the Heron table. The gentleman on his right moved the decanter out of reach. The gentleman on his left stared fixedly at his own cuffs. Aldous set his hat beneath his chair and rested both hands on the smooth neck of his heron.

The master returned to the lectern and called the vote. "House Heron."

After its customary half beat, the Heron canes rose. Aldous's old cane rose with them. The clerk counted it there and proceeded to House Hound.

stories.title: Lightning Carries One
stories.prompt: You have a power, the ability to teleport by riding lighting your desired location, or so it seems to others. However if you tried to teleport someone with you, they always go insane and age a little.
stories.body:
# Lightning Carries One

To anyone watching, Hazel came out of the lightning. To Hazel, she simply arrived.

White fire filled the old departures hall, outlining the cracked skylights and the rows of plastic seats. Then it was gone. Hazel stood on the yellow line where buses had once nosed into the building, her coat dry despite the storm gathering over the river.

Tobin had chosen a seat beneath the dead clock. He was already on his feet, one arm over his face, the other clamped around a grocery bag. The flash had caught the silver in his beard. There was more of it than at the Christmas she remembered. With Tobin, Hazel had learned to check a date before saying how long ago anything was.

“You said here,” she said.

“I said meet me here.” He lowered his arm. “I did not say drop out of the ceiling.”

They had not been alone together in nineteen months. He looked past her toward the loading bays, where weeds trembled between the doors. Hazel smelled ozone and the dusty sweetness of wet concrete. Her arrivals left no scorch mark, though people always looked for one.

“Is that it?” she asked, nodding at the bag.

Tobin tucked it under his arm. Through the thin plastic she saw the squared shape of a notebook, its cover bowed and furred at the corners.

“Some of it.”

“You told me you had the complete record.”

“I told you I had a notebook.”

Thunder rolled somewhere beyond the river. Tobin’s shoulders rose before the sound reached them. Hazel pretended not to notice; he noticed her pretending.

“Terms first,” he said. “We take the bus to the old house. We get off where I say. We walk when I say. You don’t touch the notebook unless I hand it to you, and you don’t use lightning.”

“The trip takes no time my way.”

“That’s why we’re not going your way.”

Hazel could have crossed the distance between one blink and the next. She had done farther before breakfast: an empty beach, a mountaintop blue with cold, the roof of a hotel where a security camera later showed a woman erased by one bolt and drawn by another. There was never a journey. There was here, the intention of there, and the clean clap of arrival.

Tobin pushed through the side door into the wind. Hazel followed him to the bus stop.

* * *

He took the window seat.

It was a small theft, ridiculous enough that Hazel nearly laughed. As children, she had claimed every window and given Tobin the aisle on the grounds that younger brothers needed easier access to washrooms. He had believed her until he was twelve.

Now he pressed the grocery bag between his knees and watched rain begin to stipple the glass. Hazel sat beside him. The driver argued with a passenger over a wet transfer. Someone behind them opened a container of fried onions.

“When did you last sleep through a night?” Hazel asked.

Tobin kept looking outside. “No clinic questions.”

Hazel kept three clinic files in her desk at home. Only one had his name on it.

The bus lurched away from the curb. Hazel caught the seat ahead. Tobin did not move until the abandoned terminal had slipped behind a row of warehouses; then he reached into the bag and took out the notebook.

It was worse than she remembered. Eight years ago it had been a cheap black book from the kiosk in the departures hall, bought because Tobin was taking a night class and had forgotten paper. It had gone into his coat new. It had come out with its spine bleached gray, its pages swollen, and both their handwriting inside.

That night, the last bus had been canceled after the storm brought a tree down across the route. Hazel, six months into making solo crossings and certain the trick concerned only distance, had told Tobin to grip her sleeve and picture the childhood house. It would take no time, she promised. Two stranded passengers saw one bolt take them from the terminal. A doorbell camera recorded them arriving on the front lawn in the same second. Hazel remembered the promise and the lawn. Tobin remembered the distance between.

Hazel had examined photographs. Photographs were not fibers, ink, sequence, pressure marks. She put out her hand.

Tobin opened the book himself.

On the first page, beneath the kiosk’s stamped date, Hazel had written in block capitals:

YEAR THREE, OR THE THIRD YEAR WE COUNTED. THE RED HALL RETURNS AFTER SLEEP. DO NOT CALL LIGHTNING THERE.

The last stroke of the final E hooked backward. Her handwriting did that when her hand was cold. She reached for the page.

Tobin closed the book on her fingers before she touched it.

“You wanted me to bring it,” he said. “Not surrender it.”

“I need to authenticate the ink.”

“No.”

“Tobin, if this is going to establish anything—”

“There. You did it already.”

“Did what?”

“Turned me into an unreliable container and the book into the important part.” He put it back in the bag. “That might be a record. I’m your brother.”

Hazel lowered her hand. Outside, the bus passed blocks of new glass apartments where the tire shop had been. “I know who you are.”

He gave her a quick, tired look. “Which year?”

At the first stop, Tobin’s hand came up off his lap toward the cord and stopped there. He did not stand. The doors opened, breathed cold air, and shut again.

“You said you would direct us.”

“Not this one.”

“Then why did you reach for the cord?”

He looked at his hand and put it back in his lap. “I thought the bakery was next.”

“The bakery closed when we were teenagers.”

“Yes, Hazel. I also know that.”

Two stops later he pulled the cord so hard that three people looked around. They got off beside a shuttered laundromat. Rain freckled the pavement, not yet heavy enough for an umbrella.

Hazel’s first apartment occupied the third floor, above rooms that had once shuddered with washers. She had lived there at twenty-two, proud of her sloping kitchen and the bathroom door that never closed. Tobin had slept on her floor for one summer after their father threw out his drums.

“This isn’t on the way,” she said.

“It was then.”

“The house is east.”

“You wanted home. This counted.”

He led her into the alley. Fire stairs striped the brick with rust. Beneath the lowest landing, he pressed a palm to the wall.

“Third-floor water heater,” he said. “Behind it, there was a paper crown with seven blue points. You wrote ‘Queen of Radiators’ inside because you got the pilot light going with a barbecue match and singed off half your eyebrow.”

Hazel stared at him. “You stayed here.”

“The crown was gone by then. You said you hid it because no one had seen you fix anything before, and being proud felt embarrassing.”

“I could have told you that.”

“You could have.” He straightened too quickly and caught the wall. “You didn’t.”

A truck struck a pothole at the mouth of the alley. The bang came just as lightning sheeted inside the clouds. Tobin folded, one hand gripping his hair, breath trapped high in his throat.

Hazel caught his left wrist. Her thumb tapped the pulse twice, paused, then three times and twice again.

Tobin went very still.

She released him. “Sorry. I don’t know why I—”

“Blue kitchen,” he said.

“What?”

“Second winter in the blue kitchen. I couldn’t stop hearing the rain hit before it fell. You made up that tap so I’d know which moment your hand was in.” His face had shut against her. “You did it every bad night for months.”

Hazel looked at her thumb. “A conditioned response could survive without explicit memory.”

“Wonderful.”

He pulled the notebook out, slid a folded sheet from between two pages, and handed it to her.

It was a sketch of that apartment, but wrong. The narrow kitchen opened into the hallway of their mother’s later duplex; the hallway opened into the cupboard under the stairs of the childhood house. Rain hung beyond every window in long beads, each one shaded in pencil. Beside the kitchen door, a smaller drawing showed Tobin’s shoe with the sole peeled back.

In Hazel’s hand: DAY 414. HIS SHOES ARE GOING. MINE ARE NOT.

Below it, in Tobin’s cramped script: She says that means the place wants one of us more.

Under that Hazel had written: I said *might*. Stop making me sound mystical.

Despite herself, Hazel almost smiled.

“You were irritating there too,” Tobin said.

“That part is persuasive.”

For an instant his mouth changed. Then thunder pressed along the roofs and the almost-smile went away.

* * *

The next bus left them beside a row of narrow duplexes. Their mother had rented one for eleven months after selling the childhood house, though Tobin insisted they had lived there for four years twice.

He walked past it, toward the end of the row, where the sidewalk ran into a retaining wall.

“Tobin.”

“It’s around the corner.”

“That’s a retaining wall.”

“I can see the wall.”

He turned down a lane, stopped at a locked service gate, and turned back. Hazel opened the map on her phone.

“Give me the next address.”

“Out here changes when I’m not looking.”

“The streets aren’t changing.”

“I know. I know which part is doing it.”

Hazel found the pedestrian route. It was longer than necessary, looping around a fenced schoolyard, but it was knowable: six turns, thirty-eight minutes, no weather involved except the weather itself. She set off. Tobin followed until the second turn, where he stopped beneath a young maple.

“You’ve lost it,” he said.

“The route is on the screen.”

“Not that route.”

“Then explain the other one.”

He took out the notebook, opened to a page, closed it, opened somewhere else. “We left the blue kitchen after the candles ran out. Or before. We followed the upstairs landing into the room where Mom kept the sewing machine, except she didn’t own it yet. You were thirty. Then you were seventeen all morning and kept asking why Dad’s car wasn’t outside.”

“I need the sequence.”

“That is the sequence.”

“You’ve just told me three incompatible things.”

“Yes.”

“Start with the kitchen. What happened immediately after you left?”

Tobin’s fingers worried at the notebook’s softened corner. Rain came harder, ticking through the maple. “We walked.”

“For how long?”

“Until my shoes opened. No, that was before the red hall. We slept in the room with all the coats.”

“How many nights?”

“They weren’t nights.”

“Then what distinguished one day from another?”

“Stop.”

“Meals? Sleep cycles? Changes in hair growth?”

“I said stop.”

“If we can establish even a relative chronology—”

He shoved the notebook into the bag. “This was a mistake.”

He walked away from the mapped route, back the way they had come, fast enough that Hazel had to run. By the time she caught him, rain was bouncing off the pavement. They took shelter beneath the striped awning of a closed florist. The wind shoved the wet edge of it against the window with a hollow slap.

Tobin stood at the far end, hugging the grocery bag to his chest.

“I’m trying to understand,” Hazel said.

Tobin looked down at his shoes. “My socks are wet.”

She wiped rain from her face. Across the street, lights came on in the duplex where their mother used to live. For a moment Hazel expected to see the old sewing machine in the front window. There had never been a sewing machine there.

“You asked me to retrace the route,” she said.

“I asked you to walk it.”

“What’s the difference?”

Tobin watched the rain.

He looked older under the awning than he had in the terminal. His face carried an extra alteration that photographs from the day before the crossing did not. The clinic had estimated eleven to fourteen months of accelerated aging. The two people Hazel carried afterward had each come back with smaller changes: five months, perhaps; seven. Both had returned with memories no one could place, habits learned in rooms that did not exist, terror of distances that were supposed to be empty.

They had consented. Hazel had repeated that until the word lost all edges.

“The other two knew about your symptoms,” she said.

“They knew your description.”

“They signed—”

“I begged you not to do it again.”

“I thought you might have been the exception.”

“You thought I might have been made wrong.”

“No.” The answer came too quickly. Hazel tried again. “I thought there might have been another cause. Medication, the electrical injury, an existing—”

Tobin turned his back.

The rest of her careful sentence dissolved. Rain streamed from the awning in front of them, a bright curtain under the streetlamps. In her desk at home, the second and third reports still bore different colors of her ink: blue for shared symptoms, red for contradictions. She had given the contradictions twice the space.

“I wanted them to come back fine,” she said.

Tobin did not turn.

“That isn’t quite—” Hazel stopped herself. “No. It is. You told me what happened, and I kept needing the damage to belong to something else. So I carried them.”

“And when they came back?”

“I stopped.”

“You stopped carrying people. You didn’t call me.”

There was no neat cause for that. She had come to Christmases and to their mother’s birthdays, where someone else was nearly always in the room. Every call she imagined needed a conclusion first, and she had never reached one. She had spent eight years refining the absence.

“I didn’t know what I could say.”

Tobin kept his back to her.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

Tobin rubbed his forehead. “Not today.”

“Do you want to go home?”

He lifted one shoulder.

After a while, he set the grocery bag between them. He took out the notebook, drew three folded sheets from between its pages, and held it shut with his palm.

“These,” he said. “You get these because you finally said one true thing. Not the rest.”

“All right.”

“And you don’t get to tell me what order to remember them in.”

“All right.”

The first page was mostly a list: peaches, two candles, half a packet of crackers, six dry socks, no matches. Tobin had drawn a chessboard and accused Hazel, in the margin, of inventing a bishop. Hazel had replied that he had forgotten how bishops worked. Three lines later, she recorded that they had not seen a sunrise in ninety-two sleeps.

The second page described rain halted beyond the windows of the blue kitchen. It also described a quarrel about toothpaste, Tobin’s fever, and Hazel carrying him along a hallway that lengthened whenever she looked toward its end. The entry broke off and resumed in different ink.

I KNOW THIS HALL, Hazel had written. I HAVE CROSSED IT ALONE. ALONE, NONE OF IT REACHES THE ARRIVAL. TOBIN IS MAKING TIME STICK, OR MAKING ME KEEP ENOUGH OF IT TO WRITE.

Tobin’s note beneath it said: You don’t keep it. I do.

Her reply: Then the notebook stays with you.

The final page was creased nearly through. At the top, Hazel had drawn the old terminal as a small box. Around it she drew the laundromat apartment, their mother’s duplex, the childhood house, and several rooms Hazel did not recognize, each enclosing the last. Arrows did not lead east or west. They led inward.

We do not go where I point, she had written. We go through everything I meant by the place. Lightning is only what the outside sees.

Lower down, after a spill had blurred several lines, one sentence remained clear.

IF I FORGET AT THE HOUSE, DO NOT LET ME TAKE ANYONE AGAIN.

Hazel read it twice. Her first impulse was to ask whether the ink had been dated. The impulse passed without becoming speech.

“There are years in here,” Tobin said. “Some of them are boring. Some are bad. In one, you wouldn’t speak to me for a month because I lost the can opener.”

“A month?”

“Maybe six days. It was a very important can opener.”

“Did we find it?”

“You were sitting on it.”

Hazel laughed. It escaped before she could judge whether she had permission. Tobin looked offended, then briefly young, then neither.

He took the pages back. “We can finish walking.”

This time, when he turned away from the route on her phone, Hazel put the phone in her pocket.

* * *

They reached the childhood house after dark.

It belonged to strangers now. The porch had been rebuilt, the maple cut down, the front door painted a blue their mother would have disliked. Tobin stopped across the street. Hazel crossed halfway before noticing he was no longer beside her.

“We always went through the side gate,” she said.

There was no side gate. A cedar hedge had grown into the space between houses.

Tobin watched her. “Out here, we used the front.”

The knowledge had come from her body, not her memory. So did the sudden ache across her shoulders, the weight of someone carried for too long. Hazel’s right hand curled as if gripping the backs of Tobin’s knees. For one sickening instant, the street seemed roofed. Rain shone in the air without falling. A hallway opened through the blue front door. It smelled of cold toothpaste and canned peaches; behind Hazel, someone dragged a shoe with its sole loose.

Then water struck her face. The street was a street again.

Lightning branched above the house.

Her power gathered in the familiar space behind her ribs. It required no gesture, only a desired place. Her dry apartment presented itself at once: lamp lit, kettle waiting, the whole wet distance made into none. The storm had given her a road.

Tobin stepped backward onto the curb.

Hazel kept both hands where he could see them. The charge rose, brightening the bones of her fingers. She let the lamp and kettle blur until there was nowhere for it to carry her. The light faded. Thunder broke over the roofs. She remained in the road until an approaching car forced her to the sidewalk.

“I wasn’t going to take you,” she said.

“I know.” His breath came unevenly. “My body doesn’t.”

Hazel nodded and moved farther away, under a tree too young to shelter either of them.

“I think I go the long way every time,” she said. “Alone, I don’t keep any of it. With you, some of it stayed. Not cleanly.”

Tobin picked at the bag’s handle. “That sounds like you.”

“It may be wrong.”

“That sounds less like you.”

She looked at the blue door. “You lived those years.”

Tobin didn’t answer. His shoulders came up the way they had in the terminal, as if at thunder years away from this rain.

“I’ll send pictures of pages,” he said at last. “The ones I choose. You don’t ask for the rest.”

“All right.”

“If I stop, I stop. If we meet, we walk or take the bus. No demonstrations.”

“All right.”

“And don’t say ‘all right’ like we’ve completed a form.”

Hazel opened her mouth, found no better phrase, and shut it.

Tobin took the notebook from the bag and buttoned it inside his coat. “Good. That can be the first thing you practice.”

They stood across from the house until the upstairs lights came on. A child moved behind the curtains and stared down at the two wet strangers. Tobin lifted one apologetic hand. The curtain snapped shut.

“Did I ever believe you in there?” she asked.

Tobin considered. His gaze went to her shoulder, where the vanished weight still ached.

“Sometimes,” he said. “Sometimes you were awful. Once you carried me for three days because my shoes were gone.”

“Three days?”

“Or three miles. Don’t make that the good version.”

“I won’t.”

Tobin nodded. When the bus appeared at the far end of the street, its windows fogged and yellow, he walked toward the stop. Hazel followed several paces behind.

stories.title: A Lock on the Inside
stories.prompt: After your old master threw you out, you managed to convince another archmage to take you on as an apprentice. Their style is very different, much nicer and way more lenient. When you told them how your old teacher treated you, they were utterly horrified.
stories.body:
# A Lock on the Inside

Kethra put the key in my palm before she asked me to prove anything.

It was a small iron key with a square bow, warm from her pocket. I turned it over twice, looking for a mark that would tell me which work it bought. Kethra waited. Her eyebrows rose.

I knew enough of the college hand to understand blunt nouns and warnings. Her quick grammar still escaped me, so she took up the slate that hung from her belt and wrote, in narrow white strokes: *Your room. Second stair, last door. The bolt is on the inside.*

"For the trial?" I asked.

She nodded.

"How long is the trial, Archmage?"

She wiped the slate with the side of her fist. *Seven days. Then we decide about the next seven.*

I had spent three mornings outside her workroom with my petition folded to a strip and tied with cord, the paper soft at every crease. It listed the forms I could copy, the warding inks I knew how to grind, the hours I was accustomed to keeping, and the meals I did not require when work ran late. I had rehearsed the part that mattered most.

"I can repay lodging through service until my voice is fully restored. I don't expect a stipend, and if my first week is unsatisfactory, I will leave without dispute. My former master said I was quick once I understood the cost of mistakes. I can also scrub floors, tend fires, carry coal, and sleep in a workroom if the college has no proper bed to spare."

Kethra heard me out. She was mute, not deaf, though I had made that mistake during our first interview and earned a look sharp enough to pare bark. Now she lifted one hand and signed, slowly for me, *Enough.*

Then she pointed down the passage.

"Workroom?"

She shook her head and wrote, *Food.*

That was the first item in the account: one key, one week's lodging, one midday meal, not yet earned.

The college kitchen had no ceremony in it. A pot of onion stew sat near the banked fire. Kethra ladled two bowls, saw me watching how deeply she filled mine, and added another spoonful. On the table were a green jar of pickles and a red jar of something hotter.

She pointed to both and signed, *Choose.*

"Whichever is already open."

Both were open.

I chose green. Kethra pushed the red jar beside it anyway, a small crease at one corner of her mouth. I could not tell if this was humor or an examination of decisiveness, so I ate one of each. The red one made my eyes water. Kethra passed me the water jug and did not pretend not to notice.

Afterward she walked me to the foot of the second stair and wrote, *Lesson at second bell. Until then: room, walk, sleep. Do not polish the stair rail.*

I took my hand off the rail. I had only rubbed one thumb over a patch of tarnish.

Her crease deepened.

The room was larger than the workroom floor I had proposed and smaller than anything so costly had a right to be. It held a narrow bed, a washstand, a peg, a table, and a window overlooking a roof crowded with rain-dark chimneys. The door had a keyhole on the corridor side and a plain iron bolt on mine. I shut myself in, slid the bolt, slid it back, and tested the handle. Then I opened the door and checked the passage. No outer bar. No staple for one.

There would be other means, of course. An archmage did not need a piece of iron to keep me where she wanted me. Still, I put the key in the inner pocket of my coat rather than my bundle. The distinction seemed worth recording.

I did not sleep. I folded my spare shirt into a tighter square, washed the road grit from my cuffs, and arrived at the workroom before the first stroke of the second bell had finished.

Kethra's workroom was low-ceilinged and bright. Shelves held coils of speaking rail, chalk wrapped in paper, copper dishes, waxed thread, and brass nodes in fitted wooden boxes. Nothing matched the ornate apparatus I had imagined from an archmage's rooms. On the central bench, she had set out one lamp with a clean wick, one palm-sized node, and a slate ruled into three boxes.

She touched two fingers to her throat, then pointed at me. In the first box she had written *Voice today?*

"Usable."

In the second: *Call limit?*

"As many as required."

She turned the slate toward herself, considered my answer, and drew a throat with a row of tally marks above it, running off the edge of the slate. Then she struck through the tallies so hard the chalk squeaked.

"I have no set limit," I said. "My former training did not use one."

Kethra wrote *One* in the third box.

I understood. A modest first test, with more available if I did well.

She taught the field signs next. A flat hand turning upward meant yes. One finger held across the wrist meant wait. Crossed hands meant stop. I knew the shapes, but Kethra made me repeat them until I stopped ornamenting yes with the little deferential dip my former master had required.

For stop, she crossed her hands once, cleanly. I straightened without meaning to, then copied it.

She pointed at my elbows and shook her head. I had made it too small. On my second attempt I held the cross at chest height.

She nodded, then tapped the lamp.

The exercise was no grander than the room. Kethra chalked a short geometry around the wick, laid two fingers beside the brass node, and set the registered name where I could read it: *Practice Wick, Take Light.* I was to touch the same node, authorize the cell with yes, and speak the whole name on one breath after her ready sign. Her shaping would supply everything but the living call. If I used wait, she would hold. If I used stop, she would end the cell.

She was still drawing the last of this on the slate when I laid my fingers on the node beside hers. It warmed beneath my fingertips. I gave yes at once.

Kethra pulled her hand away.

The warmth vanished. I snatched my own hand back and said, "I'm sorry."

She signed too quickly. I caught *before* and *finished* and nothing between. Seeing my confusion, she wrote, *You agreed before I finished explaining.*

"I understood the task."

*Did you know the name?*

"Not yet."

She waited.

"But I knew I would agree."

Kethra stared at me, then erased the entire cell with a felt block. Chalk dust clouded over the unlit wick. She redrew the geometry from the beginning.

That unsettled me more than a reprimand would have. The wasted work went nowhere in the account. She neither charged it to me nor named a way to repay it.

When the cell was ready again, she had me say the registered name without a link. The first two words came easily. On *Take*, something rough caught low in my throat.

Kethra's hand rose: wait.

"Dust," I said. "It has been like that since the road."

She pointed to the water cup.

I drank. The water was cool enough to hurt. "Ready, Archmage."

She touched her throat and gave me a questioning look.

"One call is well within my capacity."

Kethra did not move for several breaths. Then she placed her fingers at the node again. I joined her. She marked the cell, and this time waited until I had read the name, looked at the lamp, and met her eyes.

I gave yes.

The call-link closed with a pressure like a second pulse under the brass. Pale lines gathered around Kethra's fingers and ran through the chalked geometry. She was not making fire. She was holding power, direction, pattern, and that single harmless wick, all of it unfinished because I had not yet supplied the name.

She raised two fingers.

Twelve heartbeats was a generous window. I began on the first.

"Practice Wick, Take Li—"

My voice tore down the middle of the last word.

There was still air in me. I forced it upward. The sound that came out was thin and shapeless, not the registered name at all. The chalk lines flashed white and collapsed.

The wick stayed dark.

Kethra lurched against the bench. One hand caught the edge; the other closed around nothing. The lines under her skin faded, but a tremor remained in her fingers.

"Again," I said. Each part of the word scraped. I reached for the node.

Her crossed hands struck the air between us.

Stop.

I froze.

She pointed at a stool. When I did not sit, she shoved it with her foot until its legs rasped against mine. Her face was pale with effort and irritated besides. I sat. She sat on the floor, which I had never seen a master do, braced her back against the cupboard, and breathed until the trembling eased.

I calculated the failure while we waited. The lamp was intact. The node had not cracked. The cell had released nothing, though its collapse had cost Kethra strength. My own voice had worsened, but that was not her loss. A week of coal carrying might balance the fatigue if she priced it kindly.

Kethra got up, wrote *Lesson ended*, and underlined it.

I bowed. There was no useful defense to make in the workroom.

By the time she followed me upstairs, my shirt and washing cloth were rolled inside my blanket, and the key lay on the table where she could see I had not taken it. I was tying the bundle with the cord from my petition.

Kethra stopped in the doorway. Her hands moved.

"I can be out before supper," I said. It came out as a rasp, and I had to swallow before the rest. "I will owe for the room. I can split wood for the kitchen first."

She took out her slate. *Why are you leaving?*

"You ended the lesson."

*The lesson.* She underlined the word twice.

"Yes, Archmage. I understand."

Her mouth went flat. She pointed at the bed, then at the bundle, then spread both hands in a question.

"I failed the call."

*Cells fail.*

"My former master said callers fail cells."

She scowled and wrote, *Why did you force the word?*

"You had given the ready sign."

*You could stop.*

"Not after," I began, and the rest would not come. I swallowed and tried again. "Not after you had begun spending strength."

Kethra held the chalk out to me, stub first. I shook my head. Writing would be slower, and she would have longer to decide. She took it back.

Then she made the sign for stop again, large and exact.

"I know the sign."

She pointed to me, then made it once more.

"I could make it," I said. "I did not need to. I nearly had the name."

She scrubbed the slate clean with her palm and wrote more slowly. *Did the call hurt when you practiced it?*

"Only the usual amount."

The chalk stopped.

*Usual?*

I had found the useful part at last. "My voice has failed before. The first time it took nine days. The second took twelve, but I had a fever. This time I was put out before I had finished recovering. With shelter I expect to be serviceable sooner."

Kethra did not blink.

"I am not asking you to overlook a permanent defect."

She set the slate down on the washstand with care. Her hands began to sign, then stopped. She picked it up again. *Put out?*

"Of the practice room, once he unlocked it. Of the house, afterward."

*Locked?*

"Only when a set was unfinished."

*Locked from which side?*

"The corridor side."

Kethra went still. Her free hand closed around nothing, as it had in the workroom when the cell collapsed. For one foolish instant I thought the failed cell had injured her more seriously than she had shown.

"It was not a punishment every time," I said. "If I spoiled a line near supper, it was sensible to finish the copy before eating." My voice had sunk almost to a whisper. I pushed the rest out anyway. "If it took until morning, then breakfast was near enough."

Kethra's mouth opened. Her hands, usually quicker than any answer, hung at her sides. She backed into the washstand hard enough to rattle the basin.

I pressed on because I had persuaded Kethra once. If I kept speaking, perhaps I could do it again. "I worked three weeks with two fingers bound and did not spoil another holding line." I held up my left hand and bent the two fingers to show her how well they worked. "When I asked to stop, the set went longer. I learned not to ask. I thought you valued readiness."

Kethra's grip tightened on the slate. The chalk broke between her fingers. She flung the piece aside, took another, pointed at my hand, and wrote, *He did this? Your master?*

"It was a correction. The fingers healed straight."

Her signs came so fast that I lost most of the nouns. *Master* flashed once. *Wrong.* Something fierce about a door. Her hands cut the space between us, and her expression had become terrible.

I stepped back until the bed frame touched my calves. "I did not accuse him."

Kethra stopped.

"I only explained the training. He threw me out when my voice made the exercises unprofitable. I should have told you about the nine days before the lesson. I thought it would sound like an excuse. I can take correction."

The slate slipped from Kethra's hand and struck the floor flat. She looked at me, at the key on the table, at the open doorway behind her. Then she looked at her own hands.

She backed into the passage.

For several breaths she stood beyond the threshold, leaving the whole width of the doorway clear. When she came in again, it was only one step. She crouched, drew the fallen slate into the space between us, and wrote where I could read without approaching her.

*My anger was at him.*

She rubbed that out.

*I frightened you.*

"No, Archmage."

Her stare made me correct myself.

"Not greatly."

Kethra closed her eyes. When she opened them, she wrote, *I should have stopped at “no limit.”*

"I said I was able."

*Did you want to make the call?*

The proper answer was yes. It waited behind my teeth, polished by years of use.

Kethra waited too.

"I wanted to stay," I said.

Something in her face changed, not softened exactly. She sat down in the doorway and took the new archmage seal from her pocket. On a clean slip of paper she wrote my room number and seven days of board, then pressed the seal into the paper, hard, until the college device stood up in relief. She put the sealed slip beside the key.

The account would not balance. I checked it twice anyway.

She pointed to the workroom below, then crossed her hands.

"No more magic today, unless you require it," I said.

Her eyebrows rose, asking rather than praising.

"No more magic today," I repeated. This time I did not add a condition.

Kethra nodded once. Then she pointed at the bed, at me, and held up one questioning finger.

"One night," I said.

She held up one finger in return.

I expected her to explain tomorrow's rules. Instead she wiped the slate, drew a rough picture of the green pickle jar beside a furious little flame, and pointed toward the kitchen.

Despite myself, I made a sound that would have been a laugh if my throat had permitted it. It hurt. Kethra's smile vanished at once, and she signed wait before reaching for the water jug.

I almost apologized. I drank instead.

At dusk she knocked on my open doorframe with a supper tray balanced on one hand. I had left the door open because closing it before I had decided to stay felt dishonest. Kethra pointed into the room and raised her brows.

"Please leave it there," I said.

She set the tray just inside, where I could reach it, and stepped away. No offense, no revised price. She signed good night from the passage and went down the stair.

The bolt was plain iron. Its screws were newer than the door, their slots still bright. I closed the door and pushed the bolt home. It made one small sound.

Later, footsteps passed twice in the corridor. Neither set stopped. I lay awake with the key under my hand and the bolt where I had left it, on my side of the door.

stories.title: The Room That Waited
stories.prompt: Society fell apart without nukes going off. Most history and advanced technology has been erased. You don’t realize it, but you just found a Nuclear Launch Facility.
stories.body:
# The Room That Waited

Zumi is lying on her belly in the dry wash, talking to the ground.

“Breathe again,” she tells it.

The ground does.

A thread of dust lifts beside her cheek. It hangs there, turns, and slips into a crack under a shelf of baked clay. Zumi looks up at you with the expression she saves for winning before anybody else knows there has been a contest.

You kneel and put two fingers to the crack. Cold touches the sweat between them.

“Shade air,” you say.

“There isn’t any shade under there.”

“Stone keeps the night.”

“First judgment.”

You have, for three days, hoped she would forget the promise. Three days ago she found the rim of a buried jar, and by the time the other diggers came over you had called it a seed jar, dated the clay by its grit, and told everyone where Zumi must have been standing when she nearly noticed it. That evening, while she ate with her back turned to you, you promised that the next thing she found would be hers to judge first.

Above the wash, the last grass of summer rasps in the wind. There may be four weeks before frost. Half the winter grain has gone sweet with mold in the upper store, and a dry old cellar would be nearly as useful as grain itself. You have spent the afternoon reading straight banks and buried paving where everyone else sees only a gully.

Still, a promise is a promise even when made to a thirteen-year-old who knows this too well.

“Your judgment,” you say.

Zumi presses her eye to the crack until you pull her back by the belt. “A buried room. Big. Empty enough to breathe.”

“Air doesn’t tell you empty.”

“It told me buried.” She sits up and scrubs clay from her eyebrow. “Your turn.”

“Grain cellar.”

She makes a rude little noise through her nose.

You dig.

The crack lengthens beneath your knives. Clay gives way to a plate of dark metal, colder than the soil, with a ring folded into a hollow. It is not red with rot like plow iron. When you strike it with the bone handle of your knife, the sound goes down a long way.

Zumi holds out her hand for the short pry bar. You give it to her. That is part of the promise too, though neither of you says so.

By the time the sun touches the wash rim, you have uncovered one edge and a hinge broad as your foot. The plate has settled crooked in its frame. You work the pry bar together, Zumi above you with both heels dug in, you below with your shoulder under her hands. The seal breaks with a cough of dirt. Cold air comes steadily through the opening, carrying old metal, old dust, and something sharp that has no name in a field.

“Empty,” Zumi says, panting.

“Air,” you say.

“Mine was first.”

You widen the gap until a person can pass. Beneath it, narrow metal steps descend beyond the reach of daylight.

You set the hooded oil lamp between you. Its little horn window has three scratches cut across it. The oil stands just below the first.

“At the last line, we turn,” you say. “If the flame gutters twice, we turn. If I say up—”

“We go up. If I say up?”

This is not one of your rules. Zumi watches you see that.

“Then tell me why quickly.”

“Only you would want a reason halfway down a hole.”

“You get that mouth from your father.”

Her smile arrives despite herself. She takes the chalk from your kit and draws the return mark on the underside of the hatch: a long white stroke hooked toward daylight. Her line is too thick, but you do not fix it.

You go first.

The steps ring softly under your boots. They do not sag. At the bottom, the lamp reveals a landing and a door standing open on hinges sunk into the wall. Door is too small a word for it. Its edge is thicker than your hand is long. A wheel sits in its face, and bars disappear into the metal above and below.

Zumi squeezes past you to look. “For grain?”

“For keeping something dry.”

“For keeping something out.”

You let that stand. She isn’t waiting for an answer anyway; she is counting, the way she has counted catches ever since the glass mill. Two handles on the inner wall. Two black boxes above them. Two rows of pegs, each with the same pale number painted underneath. Beyond the door, two benches face each other across a passage.

“Pairs,” she says.

“Spares.”

“Every spare?”

“People who could make a door like this could afford extras.”

That ends it because you put the ending into your voice. Zumi takes the chalk and marks the wall beside the great door. When she follows, her shadow in your lamplight is smaller than yours and much busier.

The corridor turns twice. Your footsteps return from ahead as if other people are walking there, careful people who stop when you stop. The walls are made of poured stone without seams. Pipes run along the ceiling in tidy ranks, painted colors that have survived where everything else has gone gray. Nothing drips. Nothing hums. The lamp flame leans toward the way you came and then stands straight.

At the first crossing, Zumi puts down another hooked mark.

“Smaller,” you say. “Chalk is not free.”

“Neither are lost people.”

You choose the left passage without answering.

Yellow signs begin beyond the crossing. Each bears a black seed surrounded by three broad black leaves, though no plant ever grew that way. Under one, letters remain sharp enough to sound out: CAUTION. RADIATION AREA.

Zumi shapes the second word twice and gets two different words from it. “Rattle-ation. Ration-ation.”

“Neither helps.”

“Ration means food.”

“Not when it has too many letters.”

“Your grain cellar has a grain sign.”

“My grain cellar has a warning sign.” You lift the lamp closer without touching the plate. “That much is plain.”

“What warning?”

The three leaves turn around their black seed whichever way you tilt your head. “Don’t lick the walls.”

Zumi laughs hard enough that her echo laughs after her. Then a fleck of ceiling dust falls through the light, and both of you look up.

The next room holds clothes no living body would choose. Yellow skins hang from pegs, collapsed at the knees, with thick hand-shapes and boots joined to them. Round windows cloud their hoods. One has split along the shoulder, showing a softer lining inside. On the wall, a row of pictures shows a bare figure raising its arms under falling water, turning, raising them again.

You do not cross the threshold.

“Rain clothes,” Zumi says.

“No rain down here.”

“Washing clothes.”

“You take clothes off to wash.”

“Maybe these people were shy.”

“All of them?”

“Pairs of them.”

You give her a look. She hooks another chalk mark around the door and adds two dots to it before you can object.

Your cellar theory has gone thin. You keep it because a thin theory is still something to walk on. The rooms beyond might have held sacks. The yellow skins might have kept dust from flour. The warning might name a blight. Anything built so deep must have preserved something.

The numbered doors preserve only emptiness. Behind 17 are racks with straps and spaces where boxes once sat. Behind 18, narrow beds are stacked two high, their mattresses reduced to stained cloth and springs. Behind 19, steel cupboards stand open around a table fixed to the floor. Cups remain in clips along one wall. A spoon lies beneath the table, furred green.

“People lived here,” Zumi says.

“For a while.”

“How long?”

“Long enough to put cups on a wall.”

“That isn’t a length.”

You shrug. She rolls her eyes, but she studies the cups. Every clip has a twin.

The oil lowers toward the second scratch.

You find EXIT painted above a door. That word survives wherever old builders wanted strangers to leave: above theater doors with no theaters, inside burned counting houses, once on a stone privy whose other three walls had fallen away. Children learn its four letters before they learn the old word for tax.

An arrow points along the right-hand corridor.

“Out,” Zumi says.

“Not our out.”

“An out.”

“We know where ours is.”

Zumi glances behind. Three passages meet there, identical except for her chalk. “You know.”

Before you can ask what that means, she opens the unlatched door under EXIT.

The room is hardly wider than a closet. A gray box hangs at shoulder height. From it curls a cord ending in a black object shaped almost like the jawbone of a small animal. Zumi has it off its hook before you say not to.

She holds one end to her ear and the other near her mouth. “Below calling above,” she says. “Send bread.”

“Put it back.”

“Above, do you hear? Kilta has found a grain cellar with beds.”

“Zumi.”

The use of her name does what the first order did not. She returns the object to its hook, but not carefully. Her face has gone blank in the practiced way that means you have embarrassed her and she intends to make it your fault.

“Unknown things do not go against your eyes, mouth, or ears,” you say.

“It was made for an ear.”

“So are earwigs.”

She turns her face out of the lamplight and says nothing.

On the opposite wall, under a skin of clear material, colored lines branch through a drawing of the rooms. A red arrow points to a small block. YOU ARE HERE, the letters say. You know the words but not how the arrow could know.

Zumi forgets to be offended. “That square has teeth.”

She means the mark at one edge of the drawing: a box crossed by short parallel lines. Stairs. From it, a thick passage bends twice before reaching the block under the arrow. The shape agrees with your walk.

“Or shelves,” you say.

“Shelves we climbed down?”

“Show me our door.”

She does, tracing in the air so her finger never touches the clear skin. The route is not where you thought. You had carried the first turn backward in your head. Your chalk would still bring you out, but the error sits unpleasantly behind your teeth.

Zumi traces farther in. Most of the lines end in small rooms. One broad line reaches a double-sized chamber at the center. She taps the air over it.

“Last room,” she says.

“Oil says one room.”

“I said it first.”

You take the black jaw from its hook.

It is heavier than it looks. The upper end fits your ear with a closeness that makes you understand Zumi’s joke was not wholly a joke. You wait.

No voice comes. There is not even the sea-noise of a shell. Only the hard press of the thing against your skin and, inside your own head, your pulse.

Zumi does not smile.

You replace the jaw gently. “One room.”

The map leads you there.

Another immense door guards the central chamber, though this one is wedged open by a fallen strip of rubber. The space beyond drops two steps. Two chairs sit on rails before two long banks of dark glass and square buttons. Their cracked cushions face a map covering the far wall.

It is a map of shorelines, perhaps, but no shore you know. Pale land-shapes float in blue. Red circles surround black points on the land, some nested one inside another. Fine lines run from a column of numbered squares toward the circles. Age has peeled the blue in long curls. The red remains.

“Weather,” you say.

Zumi looks from the map to you. “What weather?”

“Storm counting. Hail tracks.”

“Underground.”

“Weather comes above. Counters can sit wherever they like.”

This would normally earn a snort. Zumi is too busy taking in the pairs.

The two chairs have worn hollows in the same places. Each bank of glass has the same dark columns. At the outer end of each is a metal slot with a red cover above it. The stations are too far apart for one person to reach both. Between them, a metal plate carries a block of close print. Most of it has flaked away, but two words remain on the first line: TWO-PERSON.

“Not spares,” Zumi says.

You lift the lamp. Beneath a row of black windows, the same word repeats: MISSILE. Under the red covers, another survives: LAUNCH.

Zumi sounds them. “Miss-ill. Lanch.” She tries the second again, giving its last sound more room. “Do you know them?”

“Old names.”

“For weather?”

“People name storms.”

She walks from one chair to the other, seven short paces. “They had to sit apart.”

“They could roll.”

“The floor rails stop.”

“Then apart.”

“But doing the same thing.”

Behind the chairs, two sets of shoulder straps hang from the wall. Two clocks have stopped at different times. Two empty clips might once have held keys. The room has waited with its doubled hands open, and the lamp gives it the only moving light.

The oil touches the second scratch.

You set the lamp on the fixed table between the stations. Up close, one red cover is scratched around its edge. Whatever lay beneath it was meant to move. A useful place must offer more than rooms and warnings. If this is a weather counter, there may be a way to read it. If it guarded stores, some inner door may answer. If nothing answers, you will return to moldy grain and explain why the finest find of your life contains only cups, beds, and words nobody understands.

“We could see whether the matched pieces move together,” you say.

Zumi puts her palm over the nearer red cover.

“No.”

You look at her chalk-whitened fingers. “Move your hand.”

“Up,” she says. “I say up.”

“In a moment. Move your hand, and then we go up.”

“You said paired catches are paired for a reason. You said it at the glass mill. We didn’t know until it cut the mill apprentice.”

The apprentice’s missing fingertip is a joke to everyone except when they remember the blood.

“This is dead, Zumi,” you say. “The clocks have stopped. The doors stand open. That black jaw didn’t make a sound in my ear. Nothing down here has moved since before anybody’s grandmother.”

“The hatch hadn’t.”

You can order her aside. You can haul her back by the belt, as you did at the crack, though she will kick and the lamp will spill and every sensible rule you have ever made will lie broken around you. Zumi knows this. Her mouth is pinched. Her eyes are wet, either from dust or fury, and she keeps her hand where it is.

“No,” she says again. “You don’t get first judgment on my hands.”

Somewhere in the corridor, metal ticks once under the lamp’s small warmth. Both of you turn toward the sound. The room offers nothing after it. No glass brightens. No clock resumes. The black windows hold your lamp in dozens of small, warped reflections.

“Oil,” you say.

Zumi does not move.

“I don’t know what this room does,” you say. “I know we’re leaving it alone.”

Her hand comes off the cover.

You pick up the lamp and hold the chalk out to her. “You remember the wall drawing?”

“Yes.”

“Then take us to the stairs.”

She does not reach for the chalk at first. “My judgment?”

“Our way out is yours.”

That is not the whole thing she asked. It is enough for her to take.

Zumi leads.

The lamp reaches the final scratch. Its flame shortens whenever you walk too quickly, so you learn Zumi’s pace: four fast steps, a pause at each crossing, her finger drawing the remembered map against her thigh. She takes you back past the closet under EXIT, then 19, 18, 17. Beyond the last numbered door she points without slowing.

“That’s the washing room. I put dots there.”

The hooked chalk stroke has blurred around the door frame. Beneath it sit two dots.

You pass under the yellow signs. At the first crossing she turns right, though your body insists on left.

“Our marks are the other way,” you say.

She keeps walking. When the lamp reaches the corner, her hooked stroke is there on the wall, bent the way she went.

You follow her right. She finds the corridor of paired benches. At the great door, her thick hooked line shines on the wall.

Only there does she look back to see whether you are watching.

“Spares,” you say.

She considers the benches. “Maybe.”

You climb with the lamp between you. Warm evening air thickens at the top of the steps. When Zumi pushes through the hatch, sunset spills around her boots, red as the circles on the buried map.

Outside, the world has remained ordinary. Grass leans east. A crow worries something pale on the far bank. Your pry bar lies where you left it. The wash holds no grain.

Zumi sits beside the opening while you lower the metal plate until only the crooked gap remains. Cold air threads out, too slight to see now that the dust has settled.

On exposed metal beside the ring, you begin the shelter mark: a roof shape, an open door, one bar for a dry chamber below. People searching after you will know there is space here. In winter, space can be life.

Zumi watches until the mark is finished. Then she takes the chalk from your fingers and draws the danger stroke through it.

“That tells them not to enter,” you say.

“Yours tells them to.”

“It may be a shelter.”

“It may be a glass mill.”

You look at the two meanings crossed on the dark metal.

You leave both marks.

Zumi holds the chalk out. Instead of taking it, you fold her fingers around it.

“Keep it,” you say.

She slips it into her pocket. Then she shoulders the empty grain sack, and the two of you start up out of the wash before the last light goes.

stories.title: The Kingdom Was the Easy Part
stories.prompt: After saving the kingdom, a legendary adventuring party retires together to a sprawling old clubhouse—only to discover that staying friends through peace, romance, old grudges, and one increasingly bored dragon may prove harder than any quest they ever survived.
stories.body:
# The Kingdom Was the Easy Part

Six weeks after they saved the kingdom, Dabria Finne got everyone into one room. Brum spoiled the effect by carrying Cavren's road strap through the middle of it.

The large white wolf emerged from beneath Cavren's chair with the leather loop between his teeth, pleased by the number of people available to admire him. He was no enchanted guardian, despite what visiting ministers liked to believe. He was an ordinary, heavy-pawed wolf with a talent for taking what had just been cleaned. He crossed the red carpet, passed under the arch of Oruvane's blue neck, and deposited the strap in Oshara's lap.

"Not ours," Oshara said. She was reading sideways on a settee with her feet tucked beneath Torvik's thigh. He had one arm along the cushion behind her and had been attempting, for most of a page, to court her away from the book. She gave him the strap instead. "Make yourself useful."

Torvik inspected it with great seriousness. "It's a strap. Possibly a belt for a very thin man. Brum, whose is this?" The wolf thumped his tail. "He won't say, Oshara. He's protecting someone."

Oshara kept reading.

Around them, Manydoor Hall's library rose warm and crowded to its smoke-dark rafters. Books filled three tiers of shelves, climbed the mantel in wavering stacks, and lay open wherever an elbow had recently been. Firelight moved over the ladders and the tall windows, where the night beyond was hard and blue. The three other adults who had retired here after the campaign occupied their accustomed islands: the silver-braided scout reading under Oruvane's left wing; the former quartermaster stitching a split cushion at the tea table; the hedge-worker coaxing amber lights from her cupped palms into three glass lanterns. Every light lasted only as long as she fed it breath and attention. Brum, having completed his delivery, nosed hopefully among all three.

And Oruvane filled what remained.

He lay comfortably between hearth and astronomy shelves, vast enough that his folded foreleg made a backrest for the scout. Fine gold chains looped from his swept horns to the ridges of his throat. Curling tracery, painted for the victory procession and kept because he liked it, ran across his deep-blue wings in tarnished gold and green. One wing curved behind the readers; his tail circled the chairs and ended beside the wine. In the firelight he looked less like a guest than the room's oldest, most ornamented piece of furniture, if furniture could watch everyone ignore it.

Dabria stood by the library arch with the evening card still in her hand. Seven adults, one dragon, one wolf. All present. No kingdom had ever required more work for a less impressive victory.

Cavren rose from the chair nearest the hearth. "Brum."

The wolf looked at him, then at Torvik, who had begun fastening the road strap around his own forehead.

"The horse-lords in the east wear them like this," Torvik told the wolf. "Only the important ones. You'll have to call me sir now, Brum. Brum? He isn't calling me sir."

Cavren held out his hand.

Torvik gave it back. Cavren took the leather without smiling and returned to the chair, where a shield pack sat open at his boots. A whetstone, a road kettle, and a roll of oiled wool showed beneath its flap before he folded the strap over them.

Dabria crossed to him. "The end has stretched. Give it here."

"I can mend it."

"I didn't say you couldn't."

"Good."

He reached for the awl. Brum leaned his great white shoulder against Cavren's knee, then slid down until his muzzle rested on the man's boot. Cavren's hand left the leather long enough to rub between the wolf's ears. He had not accepted help from Dabria with a buckle, a shield rim, or an aching arm since the final stair of the black keep. She had decided not to notice that in front of everyone. Her decisions had once been more obedient.

At the settee, Torvik put his mouth near Oshara's ear. She turned a page without looking at him.

"If you two are going upstairs," Dabria said, "we haven't chosen tomorrow's reading."

Oshara lowered the book. "We're not going upstairs."

"Then choose."

"I am reading this one. Torvik is failing to."

"I've been waiting for the dangerous parts. She promised me dangerous parts."

"There is a tax dispute."

"A tax dispute, Dabria. She's making me sit through a tax dispute."

Oshara raised the book again, ending the matter by hiding her face behind it. Torvik made a tiny, pleading gesture toward the pages. Dabria ignored him. The evening card promised conversation, shared reading, mending, and games until third bell. She had written the words in different colors so it would not look like a roster.

Oruvane lowered his chin onto one foreclaw. "We could hunt the dumplings."

The quartermaster bit off a thread. "We ate them at supper. You had eleven."

"Then the hunt will be difficult."

No one answered. The scout turned a page. The hedge-worker sent one new light into a lantern and lost another; it guttered above Oruvane's nose. He blew it gently across the room. Brum bounded after it, struck the quartermaster's table, and sent three spools rolling under the settee.

For a moment the library came together. Torvik caught one spool between his boots. Oshara rescued the wine. The scout laughed into her book. Cavren seized Brum by the ruff before he reached the lantern stand, while the hedge-worker hurriedly drew her wandering light back into both hands. Oruvane's eyes brightened.

Dabria restored the table, the lantern, and the wolf. By then the moment had dispersed.

"We need something with rules," she said.

Oruvane's lids descended halfway. "Do we?"

"Tomorrow. Second bell. You choose the game."

"Any game?"

"Within reason."

Oruvane's lids closed the rest of the way. "There it is," he said.

Dabria wrote *Oruvane's recreation* on the back of the evening card. When she glanced up, Cavren had closed his pack. Oshara and Torvik were whispering behind the raised book. The scout read, the quartermaster stitched, and the hedge-worker kept her small suns alive. Everyone was still in the room. Oruvane was in the center of them, his painted wing making a blue night over half the library.

Brum left Dabria and went to lie against the dragon's foreleg.

For the next six days, Oruvane gave them games.

He turned the dining chairs toward the walls and strung retired climbing rope between the pantry and the plates. He hid challenge cards in books no one had opened since the old king's grandfather learned to lie. He moved the handbell to the highest gallery, tied spoons to half the door latches, and declared the sugar jar a besieged fortress. The hedge-worker supplied sparks for one treasure map and singed its north edge; the quartermaster sewed colored markers while complaining that none of the quests respected fabric; the scout found Oruvane's hiding places too quickly and began pretending not to.

Some of it was fun. Torvik cheated with such confidence that Oshara joined the opposing side solely to catch him. Brum dragged an entire rope course into the library and bound Cavren's ankles together. Even Cavren laughed, once, before looking annoyed at having done it. On the fifth night, though, Oshara had a headache and Torvik refused a map Oruvane had spent all afternoon painting. He went upstairs with her. Oruvane hung the map anyway.

Dabria wrote clearer rules. She posted starting times. When a chair cracked under Oruvane's tail, she added limits on moving furniture. The games became smoother and shorter. At second bell people appeared in the library and asked what he had prepared. At third bell they disappeared down corridors that admitted his narrow head and foreclaws but stopped him at the shoulders. Oshara and Torvik closed their door. Cavren took maps to the smaller stove in the east room. The three old campaign hands returned to their separate work. Oruvane remained among the books, surrounded by abandoned clues.

On the seventh night, Dabria woke to cold air moving through her bedchamber and found that her door was gone.

So were its hinges.

The hall had become indecently audible. Water ticked into a basin two floors below. Someone poked a fire. Torvik said, "I have trousers," and Oshara replied with a word she had once reserved for a necromancer.

There were thirteen empty frames between Dabria's room and the library.

Light poured through the library arch. Inside, the missing doors stood upright in a crooked maze around Oruvane. Green, blue, oak, and iron panels leaned against benches and retired spear shafts. Shields hung from their knobs. A hooked pole lay beside coils of rope leading back through the empty frames; he had drawn each freed door toward the library inch by inch. Challenge cards promised treasure, peril, and one "truth too terrible for polite architecture."

The rest of the household was already containing the damage. The scout braced a ladder while pushing a drift of books out of danger with one boot. The quartermaster crawled along the outside of the maze collecting hinge pins in her apron. At the arch, the hedge-worker breathed fresh lights into being one by one and sent them where people called; each floated only while her fingers remained spread. None of the three offered an interpretation. They had survived six years of Dabria's interpretations and knew when to protect the shelves instead.

Brum plunged between two doors and vanished.

"Put them back," Dabria said.

Oruvane raised his head above the maze. A gold chain slipped down his throat with a soft bright sound. "Welcome to the Labyrinth of Lingering Fellowship."

Oshara arrived in a robe over her nightclothes, with Torvik one-booted behind her. Cavren came last. He saw the gap where Brum had disappeared and stopped.

The wolf backed into view, tugging Cavren's packed traveling chest by its handle.

"Brum," Cavren said.

Brum pulled harder. The chest slid out from behind the blue drawing-room door, bumped over a carpet ridge, and sprang open. Winter cloak. Wrapped rations. Whetstone. Road kettle. The road strap from the library evening lay neatly coiled on top.

Torvik glanced at Cavren, then at Dabria. Whatever joke had offered itself, he let it die.

"East side's clear to the outer corridor," the scout called, "if anybody needs a way out that doesn't go past the dragon."

"Whoever is kneeling on the green door," said the quartermaster from somewhere beneath it, "that is veneer."

Dabria climbed onto a bench. The lovers' oak door, marked by a pale scratch near the latch, blocked the west aisle. Cavren's stood across the hearth beside his chest. Beyond the inner turns, the iron-banded gate to the roof court made a final wall.

Dabria was still furious when the route began arranging itself in her head.

"Oshara, Torvik, take the west route. Cavren, come with me. We clear the small panels and make a path to the roof gate."

"No," Cavren said.

Not loud. Not negotiable.

Oruvane's tail slid between the doors and pulled one brace sideways. Benches groaned; the west route folded shut.

"The labyrinth rejects stale tactics," he said.

"It took the privy door," Torvik said. "Oruvane, I don't think a labyrinth that takes the privy door gets to talk about tactics. That's fair, isn't it? Oshara, tell him that's fair."

Oshara was looking at the scratched oak door.

For several minutes they accomplished nothing. Torvik climbed a pantry door and knocked down a copper warming pan. Dabria found a gap and lost it when Oruvane shifted his elbow. The hedge-worker's lights bobbed over the maze in answer to three contradictory requests. Brum crossed wherever he pleased, moving from Cavren to Oruvane to the scout as though the household had no walls at all.

At last Oshara gripped the bottom of the scratched oak door. "Dabria. Lift."
