We made the recordings separately. My sister spoke first while I kept my mouth shut and looked at the dark window.

“I like our chest changing,” she said into the phone. “I don’t like bleeding, but that isn’t the same thing. I hate the hair on my face. I hate people hearing my voice crack and looking at him. I don’t want every week to take something before I know if I wanted it. I want a pause.”

She stopped the recording herself.

On mine, I began with likely outcomes, crossed them out aloud, and began again.

“I like my voice. I like shaving, which is stupid because I’ve cut my chin twice. I don’t want more chest growth. I don’t want another period. I want a pause too. Not forever. Now.”

At the second consultation, the clinician listened to both recordings. She asked my sister whether “pause” still meant the monitored temporary course they had discussed. Then she asked me. Two yeses entered the same chart. Our mother scheduled the first follow-up before we left.

Weeks after the course began, our chest still pressed against the soft bra. My chin still needed shaving. Blood might come again before the clinician could tell whether anything had slowed. At school, strangers continued to pick one of us from a distance and misplace the other.

At the sink in February, my sister set down the tweezers beside my razor.

“Hold still,” she said.

“You’ve got one.”

I leaned our weight toward the mirror while she plucked the dark hair above her lip. Her eyes watered.

“Done,” I said.

“I know.” She rinsed the tweezers. “Your turn.”

She held my chin steady while I shaved. Halfway through, our mother called that the bus was in four minutes.

“Five,” I called back.

My sister reached for the yellow hair clips. “Don’t start.”

I wiped the remaining soap from my jaw and left one side rough. She clipped back only half her hair. We grabbed our bag, missed the towel, and went.

stories.title: One Night's Mercy
stories.prompt: "Please," the queen begs on her knees, "save that dragon from my daughter."
stories.body:
# One Night's Mercy

“Please, save that dragon from my daughter.”

Queen Urrava was on both knees in the scale and soot of Imer Quast’s forge. Two royal guards stood behind her, wet to the shoulders. Hovan Setch stood with them, rain running off his cropped hair. He had rigged Imer’s frames for nine years before he went to watch dragons for Daziel’s hunt, and at dusk he had left the quarry to fetch the queen. All three had heard her, which meant she had not come to be forgiven in private.

Imer left the bellows open. The coal dimmed around the hinge strap he had been heating.

“Which dragon?”

Urrava’s hands rested palm-down on the floor. She had taken off her rings before she came in. Careful, even now.

“Thelrax. Daziel has him in the north quarry. The throat is pierced, both wings are weighted, and she means to use a spear at first light.”

Hovan said, “I saw the wound before the rain closed the ridge. He can breathe. Fire, perhaps twice. Short.”

“How short?” Imer asked.

“Eight paces, from that wound. I may be wrong about how much strength he has left.”

“And the quarry road?”

“The bridge is under,” said the queen. “My riders cannot reach her before dawn. You can use the inspection chute.”

Imer had cut the chute through the hill when Daziel was still young enough to steal his chalk and draw wolves on new stone. It ended behind the quarry drums, narrow and steep, meant for men who understood why a frayed rope could be worse than a cracked beam.

He looked past Urrava to the guards. “You came to order me back into service.”

“No. I came to bargain. If you go, your dismissal is rescinded, your forge levy ends, and the crown repays—”

“Keep it.”

“Then name what you require.”

Imer wiped his hands on his apron. “The court says Daziel’s husband broke the nest seal on his own. You wouldn’t be kneeling on my floor in front of your own guards if that were true.”

Urrava’s gaze shifted once, toward Hovan, who had brought her here. He did not help her.

Rain drummed on the forge hood. One guard swallowed.

Urrava stayed on her knees. “I authorized a survey of the copper behind the nest. How the survey was conducted, I left to the man who led it.”

“There’s no way to that copper except through the seal. I told your council so. Show me what you signed.”

“Imer—”

“The paper, or get out of my forge.”

The patience went out of her face. “Give it to him.”

The older guard unbuttoned his soaked coat and produced an oilskin packet. Inside lay a folded writ with the royal seal and Daziel’s husband’s name beneath the command to open, inspect, and secure. Urrava’s signature ran across the bottom. A second object dropped into Imer’s palm: a square iron key for the inspection gate, its teeth filed to the quarry’s old pattern.

“You kept the original,” he said.

“I kept the only proof that the command was mine.”

“And let the dead man carry the blame.”

Her eyes stayed on the writ in his hand.

Imer folded the writ small and put it inside his shirt. “You stay here.”

She stood. The guards almost moved to help and thought better of it. “Daziel will hear me.”

“Not until she’s read this.”

“Bring her back. She hasn’t slept in her own bed since the funeral.”

“If the rig’s still standing when I get there, I’ll stop it.” Imer took his waxed coat from its peg. “Hovan. Lamp oil?”

“Half a flask.”

“Take the full one. And the thin hemp, not that court rope. It’s new and stiff, and nobody who tied it ever hung on it.”

Hovan exchanged the guards’ clean coil for the blackened line beside Imer’s door. Urrava called Imer’s name once, but by then he was testing the rope between both hands.

* * *

The storm had put a brown river through the lower lane. Imer and Hovan crossed it on the remains of a fence, then climbed the sheep track with their shoulders turned into the rain. Beyond the ridge, the abandoned quarry showed itself only when lightning filled its cut faces: three pale steps descending into blackness.

The inspection gate had swollen in its frame. Imer drove Urrava’s key in with his palm.

“Knot,” he said.

Hovan tied the lamp to his belt and the rope around a stone horn inside the gate.

Imer pulled it loose. “Tail inside.”

Hovan retied it with the tail inside. This time Imer nodded.

They went down the chute backward, boots searching for iron rungs slick with seep water. The close stone took the storm’s noise and turned it into a steady grinding. Halfway down, Hovan’s lamp guttered.

“Oil,” Imer said.

“Wick first.”

“Why?”

“Oil’s full. Wick drowned.” Hovan pinched it higher with two nails. The light steadied. “You asked me to say when I know.”

“I did.”

Imer watched the flame until it stood straight, then found the next rung.

At the bottom they smelled Thelrax before they saw him: rain on hot stone, blood, and the bitter mineral stink of burned rope.

The chute opened behind the winch shed. Through missing boards, Imer saw the snare stretched over the quarry’s lowest shelf. Three anchor lines drew toward it from separate frames, all running over drums he had built. In their middle crouched a dragon the length of a freight wagon, dark hide slick against the limestone. The upper net bit across his shoulders. Its line also carried the short cable from a bolt through the loose skin beneath his jaw. Two sling nets lay over the folded wings, each loaded with quarried blocks and drawn tight to a side anchor.

His throat worked around every breath.

Above him, on the loading gantry, a boar spear sat in a timber carriage on a short iron rail. Its head pointed down between the dragon’s shoulder blades. The counterweight that would drive it hung over an old lifting shaft. The whole carriage rode a spoil tipper at the shaft’s mouth, held level by a red dump pin Imer had forged himself.

Princess Daziel stood at the firing lever with a hooded lantern at her feet. She wore no crown. A quarry coat covered her hunting leathers, and a coiled stay rope lay beside her boots.

“I heard the gate,” she said. “I expected my mother.”

Imer stepped through the shed door. “She’s in my forge.”

Daziel’s attention moved to Hovan, then to Imer’s hands. “No tools?”

“Plenty here if you haven’t ruined them.”

“I improved the rig.”

Imer followed the new cord from the spear’s trigger pin down the frame. It passed through two eyes and ended in a loop around the lower drum’s brake pawl, beside the spoked flywheel he had hung there to steady the drum.

“You coupled the spear to the lower brake.”

“If he pulls the downslope wing free, the drum turns and the spear drops.”

“The lower brake is the first release in the safe sequence.”

“Then don’t release it.”

Lightning showed Thelrax’s eye, open and fixed on them. He shifted one foreclaw. The three lines answered in different notes.

Hovan stayed beside the shed. He raised an empty hand, palm angled away. Approach. The dragon’s nostrils widened, but he did not strike.

“He’s watching you, Imer,” Daziel said. “Hovan, get his head down. You told me a lowered head meant submission.”

“I told you he lowered it when the bolt hurt.” Hovan watched Thelrax’s jaw, not Daziel. “I don’t know a submission signal.”

“Make one.”

“No.”

Daziel turned to Imer. “Go on, then. Tell me he was guarding his nest. He was guarding it when he killed my husband with one bite. What was he guarding twelve days later, when he burned the east shelter roof with eight workers under it? None of them had been near his nest. We buried four.”

“I know what he did.”

“Do you? You were already dismissed.”

Imer took out the writ. “For opposing the raid.”

She did not reach for it. “He was ordered to survey a copper seam.”

“Read the bottom.”

Rain struck the paper as Daziel unfolded it. She put the lantern closer. Her eyes moved once through the command, a second time through the names, and stopped at Urrava’s signature.

Thelrax’s claws scraped downslope. One wing weight lifted a finger’s width and dropped.

Daziel refolded the writ along the wrong crease. “She signed this before he left.”

“Yes.”

“She told me he added the weapons himself.”

Imer said nothing.

“He did add them. I went down the inventory myself, looking for anyone else’s hand.” Daziel pushed the paper back against Imer’s chest and kept her fist there. “She sat beside me at the funeral. She let me tell people it was his pride. And you couldn’t bring me this then?”

“I didn’t have it then.”

She took her fist away. “Stand clear of my rig.”

“Stand down an hour. Let me look at it.”

She turned back to the lever as if he had not spoken. Imer waited. Water ran off the gantry and ticked on the lantern hood.

“Why dawn?” he said at last.

“The crosswind drops. I get one clean thrust before his throat closes or he tears it wider.” She still did not look at him. “Or should I leave him to pull loose over the lower camp? Is that what she sent you to tell me?”

“Your crew?”

“Evacuated. Nine at the shepherd sheds, two at the bridge watch. I counted them out.”

“And you stay here with a trigger tied into a brake that was never made to—”

“I’ve held it since dusk.”

Imer unbuckled his coat. “I need to go inside the frame.”

“You’re not crawling around under my rig.”

“The upper line is rubbing. If it parts, you won’t get dawn.”

“I’ll fire before it parts.”

“Maybe. Or the lower drum turns first and fires for you. I can tell which if I put my hand on the bearings.”

Daziel considered the gantry, the dragon, and the man who had once made her reset a rabbit snare six times because she kept hiding the knot where she could not inspect it. She shifted her grip to the firing lever.

“Go,” she said. “Hovan stays where I can see him.”

* * *

The frame had been built to lift blocks. Its braces were sized for dead weight, steady from first lift to last. Imer took a pry bar from the rack and crawled beneath the lower drum. Water ticked off the axle housing. He put two fingers against the bearing cap and felt the cable creep.

“It’s moving,” he called.

“How much?” Daziel asked.

“A strand at a time. Give me a minute.”

Hovan edged toward the shelf. He showed wait: both hands low, the motion slow enough to stop before it became approach.

Thelrax’s head turned. The bolt cable scraped stone. For one breath he went still.

Then he pushed with both hind legs toward the open, descending quarry road.

The downslope wing cradle rose. The lower drum clicked against its pawl.

Daziel locked the firing lever against her hip and jerked her chin at the pawl. “He heard that. He knows what it does.”

Hovan took longer to answer. “He sees open ground. He is loading toward it. I don’t know what he knows about the spear.”

“Signal wait again.”

“He refused it.”

“Again.”

Hovan did. Thelrax opened his jaws. Blood threaded from the bolt wound. His chest swelled and stopped short. He dragged downslope another handspan.

Hovan let his hands fall to his sides. “No more.”

Imer had reached the far side of the drum. Daziel’s added trigger cord looked loose from above. Underneath, where it crossed the old brake spring, it had bitten deep into the wet wood. The upper net line bore across that spring at an angle no drawing would have shown.

“Do not cut the upper net,” he said.

“That was your second release.”

“Not now. When it goes slack, the spring lifts the lower pawl. The spear fires.”

Daziel’s face changed very little. Her hand changed more, opening and closing once around the lever.

“Can you uncouple it?”

“If the load holds.”

The left upright gave a dry crack.

Everyone looked at it except Thelrax. He looked at the quarry road.

“Split above the brace,” Imer said. “Daziel, take the stay rope. Hovan, clear the road below him. Loose stone, tools, everything. He needs a straight downslope run with those weights.”

“If I clear it, he may take it,” Hovan said.

“Yes.”

Hovan looked at Daziel.

She wrapped the stay rope around her left forearm while her right hand remained on the lever. “Clear it.”

Hovan moved. He kicked wedges off the track, rolled a dropped maul onto the spoil heap, and hauled a handcart sideways by its shaft. Thelrax followed him with one eye. When Hovan crossed in front of the dragon, the jaws opened again.

“Space,” Hovan said, first to them. Then he gave the broad retreating motion Thelrax had accepted that afternoon.

The dragon’s answer was fire.

It came broken around the throat bolt, a flat orange burst that reached the edge of the handcart and no farther: eight paces, perhaps less. Hovan dropped behind the cart. Flame washed over the upper net. Imer smelled scorched hemp and hair.

The burst stopped. Thelrax coughed dark smoke and lowered his head. Hovan did not say what it meant.

“Hovan?” Imer called.

“Sleeve burned. Hand works.”

“Then move the cart.”

“I am moving it.” Hovan’s words came slowly now, with air between them. He rose behind the cart and dragged it until the track lay clear.

The scorched upper net sagged. Its line eased off the brake spring, and the lower pawl began to climb.

Imer shoved his pry bar through the flywheel. It caught between two spokes and drove him shoulder-first into the frame. The wheel stopped with the bar pinned across his chest.

The split upright opened another inch.

“Imer,” Daziel said.

“Hold the stay.”

“I’m holding it. It’s slipping. The upright’s going.”

He knew. The whole changed load had come into his arms: dragon, wet net, wing stones, the hanging counterweight, and every wet turn of Daziel’s new cord. If Daziel fired, Thelrax would collapse and the frame would settle. If she let the upright tear free, the flywheel would take Imer through it.

The spear carriage shuddered overhead.

“Firing now braces the upright,” Daziel said.

“It does.”

“Then get out from under it.”

He pushed against the bar. The flywheel pushed back.

At the track, Hovan pulled the last coil of rope clear with his unburned hand. “Path is open. I think he will take it. I don’t know.”

Thelrax dug in. Downslope. The lower drum pressed harder against Imer’s bar.

Daziel looked at the spear, then at the red dump pin securing its carriage over the empty shaft. The pin was six feet from her. To reach it she would have to release the stay rope. The upright would split before she could return.

“Imer.”

He could not tell her what to choose. He could tell her how the pin came out. “Pin needs both hands. Twist left before you pull.”

She took her right hand from the firing lever. The trigger arm jumped but did not fall; the lower pawl, jammed against Imer’s flywheel, held it by half a tooth.

Then Daziel let the stay rope run from her left hand and lunged for the dump pin.

The upright tore. Imer’s pry bar bowed. Daziel caught the pin with both hands, twisted it left, and hauled. It came out to the stop chain.

The carriage tipped into the shaft. Timber, iron spear, and counterweight fell together. The sound went down for a long time before stone answered.

Freed of the counterweight, the trigger cord lashed across the frame. The flywheel took a quarter turn. Imer lost his feet.

Daziel dropped from the gantry and caught the back of his belt with both hands. His ribs struck the axle, but the pry bar stayed between the spokes.

“Left anchor!” he gasped. “Not upper. Left.”

She seized the release maul and knocked the left wing pin through. The first sling line dropped slack, leaving its stones to drag instead of wrenching the wing upward. Imer dragged the bar backward one notch and found his knees.

“Now the right.”

The second pin stuck. Daziel hit it once, reset her footing, and hit it square. The downslope sling line spilled loose.

Thelrax surged. The burned net tightened across his shoulders.

“Upper!”

Hovan was closer. He snatched the maul from the mud, but before he swung, he looked to Imer.

“Yes,” Imer said.

Hovan drove the upper pin out.

The net slipped over Thelrax’s back. For one moment the dragon remained crouched, unheld. Hovan showed approach, small and careful, toward the wound.

Thelrax bared his teeth.

Hovan stopped. “No approach.”

The dragon took the downslope road. The weighted wing slings skidded beside him for three strides, shedding blocks, before the loosened nets slipped clear. On the fourth stride he opened his wings. The torn throat made a hard, wet sound. He ran through it.

At the quarry lip, where the road dropped into the valley, Thelrax jumped.

He sank below the rim. Daziel moved to the edge, empty hands lifted as if they still held rope. A wing struck air once, twice. The dragon rose past the far face and went into the rain without turning toward them.

* * *

By dawn the storm had thinned to a cold mist. Thelrax crossed the western ridge low and uneven, then disappeared beyond it. Hovan would not call the flight safe. He would only say the dragon had cleared the rock.

Daziel sat on an overturned block while Imer wrapped Hovan’s forearm. The burn had blistered where the sleeve ended. Imer’s own ribs hurt when he pulled the wrap tight.

“Not so tight,” Hovan said.

“You’ll swell.”

“Then leave two fingers.”

Imer left two.

Daziel asked Imer for Urrava’s writ. She dried it under the lamp, read it again, folded it on its first creases, and put it inside her coat.

“The nine at the sheds,” Imer said. “Names.”

She gave them. Then the two bridge watchers. Hovan repeated the count while Imer marked eleven strokes in chalk on the winch shed door.

“I’m ending the hunt,” Daziel said. “If he comes at another occupied roof, I’ll answer that. I’m not following him from here.”

Imer nodded.

She took the writ out again and pressed it flat beneath her palm. “I’m taking the long road back. She can read this with me.”

Imer handed Daziel the dry end of Hovan’s bandage, and she tied it off.

Before any crew returned, they went back to the broken frame. The spear and its carriage were gone, but the trigger arm still stood cocked, and the trigger cord had wound itself twice around the lower axle. One turn of the drum would snap that arm down across the rail, onto the hands of whoever was working there.

Daziel held the lamp. Hovan found the oil hole; the housing had swollen in the wet, and a dry pin would split it. Imer set a blunt pin across the trigger housing and raised the maul.

“Foot back,” Daziel said.

He moved it. Hovan poured the oil. On the third blow, the pin bent flat.

stories.title: Coiled Together
stories.prompt: Everyone knows the serpentfolk lure travelers into their caves and devour them. When you wake wrapped tightly in the coils of one of their most feared queens, however, she seems less interested in eating you than in keeping you—and insists that you were the one who begged her not to let go.
stories.body:
# Coiled Together

I woke because I could not finish a breath.

Something warm and hard crossed my chest. Another band pinned my thighs. A third lay behind my shoulders, holding me against a body that shifted under me with slow muscular corrections. The cave was dark except for a clay lamp on a shelf. Its flame showed overlapping black-green scales, each as broad as two fingers, curving around me and continuing beyond the light.

Everyone on the north road knew what serpentfolk did with travelers underground. The stories disagreed about whether they swallowed boots.

I tried to reach my knife. My arm did not move.

The coil across my ribs tightened when I struggled. Not much. Enough.

“Loosen.” My first attempt scraped out too softly. I swallowed and tried again. “Loosen me.”

The pressure eased at once. The band across my chest lifted until I could drag in a full breath. Cool cave air burned my throat.

“More?” a woman asked beside my ear.

Her common speech was plain, the voice low from effort rather than softness.

“Release me.”

The coils began to move. I felt myself tip toward open air and clutched at the first solid thing under my hand.

“There is a drop to your left,” she said. “I am putting you on the hide.”

One of her arms came beneath my shoulders. The other steadied my knees while her body unwound in stages: chest, hips, ankles last. She set me on a folded hide three paces from the ledge and took both hands away.

I rolled onto my elbows. The cave swayed. My knife and belt lay beside a wet pack and my rolled saddle blanket, close enough to reach. I dragged the knife free before I looked at her.

She had drawn herself into a wide curve along the edge of the shelf. Seven metres, perhaps, from the human-shaped rise of her ribs to the blunt end of her tail. A storm-grey wrap crossed one shoulder and fell to where her waist gave way to scale. Below it, a dark stain spread along her right flank. One of the serpentfolk’s feared queens, if the notched copper bands on both forearms meant what the caravan guards said they meant.

Behind her, a smaller serpentfolk knelt over an open medicine case. The attendant held a strip of cloth in both hands and watched the queen’s wound, not my knife.

The queen said, “You asked me not to let go.”

My grip tightened. “I asked you to wrap me like that?”

“You said, ‘Don’t drop me.’ Several times. I was carrying you out of the flooded lower basin.”

“I don’t remember a basin.”

“I know.”

“Then how convenient for you.”

The attendant pressed the cloth to the queen’s flank. The queen’s fingers closed once on the stone, then opened.

“You were cold through and a pace from that drop, and you fought me every time I eased,” she said. “Should I have set you down on the edge? You asked for release. I released you.”

Rain boomed somewhere inside the mountain. The lamp flame bent, recovered, and drew light across a crown-shaped rim of dry rock. Beyond it, black water churned far below. I remembered riding ahead of the caravan at dusk. I remembered the storm pipe at the cave mouth, three falling notes that meant shelter or danger depending on which roadwarden had carved it. I had taken them for shelter. After that came a coldness at my boots, though I could not place where.

I asked, “How long was I senseless?”

“Less than an hour.”

“Where is my cousin?”

“Above us, I think. Someone is working a rope through the signal fissure.”

“Which way out?”

She pointed with an open hand. “The upper path. It is flooded at the first bend. It should clear when the rain weakens.”

“Why can’t I remember?”

The queen glanced at the lamp. “The low air.”

I waited.

The attendant tied off the bandage and began counting without looking up. “Two dry blankets. Half a water jar. Salts. One sound lamp. Your left hand is cut.”

Only then did I see the blood dried between my fingers.

The queen said, “Cold, carbon-heavy air settles in the basin. We taste it before you do. It still slows us. Humans lose their feet, then their order of thought. Some wake without the last part.”

“You knew it was there.”

“I knew when I tasted it. By then you were already deep in it.” She touched the bandage at her flank. “I went down when I heard your whistle.”

“The pipe at the mouth?” Everyone on the road knew how serpentfolk brought travelers in. “Was that you, calling me in?”

“That pipe belongs to the roadwardens, and it was cut to say danger. What I heard came from the basin. Brass, blown over and over until there was no breath behind it.”

My brass whistle hung from my belt by a half-snapped loop. I picked the belt up. A black-green scale was caught in the torn leather, where something had gripped hard enough to split it. I did not remember blowing the whistle. I buckled the belt on.

Somewhere above, stone rang twice. The attendant answered by striking the floor twice with the wooden handle of a spoon.

I raised my knife.

“That is the falling-stone warning,” the queen said. “We drill three signals here: stop, move, and stone. Nothing else.”

The tapping came again, followed by a voice made thin by water and distance.

My cousin.

The attendant lowered the spoon. “Human knocking. Not stone.”

I lurched to my feet. The queen did not move to block me, but the ledge tilted under my boots. I planted one hand on the wall.

“The low air is still in you,” she said.

“Or your medicine.”

“You have taken none.”

The attendant held up a stoppered jar from the case. The wax on its mouth was unbroken.

I found the signal fissure behind a curtain of runoff. It was a split in the wall scarcely wider than my shoulders. A rope rasped within it. The queen could not have forced her upper body through, much less the rest of her.

“I’ll go alone,” I said.

“Yes.”

I had expected an argument and mistrusted the absence of one. “That’s all? You’re letting me crawl off?”

“I want to keep you,” she said.

The words stopped me with one knee in the fissure.

“Keep me how?”

The attendant shut the medicine case. The queen did not look away from me. “For six days, and paid. Our stakes at the basin edge should have turned you back. You went past them the way travelers do, as if they were an invitation. You know how people on the road read a warning. I want someone who can tell me why they misread ours.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then you leave when the upper path opens. Nobody here will stop you.”

She settled lower while the attendant tucked the medicine case under a rock lip.

I crawled into the fissure.

The stone squeezed my shoulders and smelled of iron-rich mud. Three body lengths in, the passage bent. The queen called something after me—two ordinary words, perhaps *left wall*—but runoff struck the crack between us. Her consonants tore away. Only the drawn hiss of breath reached me.

Ahead, my cousin shouted my childhood kin-title.

“I’m here.”

The rope jerked against my wrist. I caught it.

“Tie in,” my cousin said. “We’ll pull you clear.”

A second voice cut across theirs. “Not over that lip. Knees down. No load yet.”

The rope carrier. I had seen them rig wagon teams on slopes where everyone else preferred prayer.

I crawled until I could see two blurred faces above a slant of water. The fissure opened beneath their shelf, its lower lip a chalky blade of stone.

“Did you see me fall?” I asked.

“I saw that thing take you.” My cousin reached down. “Give me your arm.”

“Before that. Did you see me in the basin?”

“You rode past the warning stakes.”

“Did you see me fall?”

“The bend hid you for half a minute. Then she had you wrapped from neck to boot. I know what I saw.”

“From up here?”

“Close enough. Come on.”

Behind me, the queen shouted. The fissure pared the words into a long sibilance. My cousin flinched and seized the rope.

The carrier said, “Wait. That edge is shedding.”

“They’re within reach.”

“No load.”

“Pull,” my cousin ordered me. “Now.”

I had one knee on the chalk lip when my cousin hauled. The rope snapped tight under my arm. White stone broke with the sound of a plate struck against a table.

The fissure floor dropped.

I fell backward into the chamber in a burst of water and grit. The rope burned through my palm. I let it run, hit the crown ledge on one hip, and slid toward the black basin until the queen’s hand caught the back of my coat.

The crack widened above us. Runoff that had been threading down one wall poured through the new opening and cut a foaming channel across the ledge, between our shelf and the high side. Beside the wall, the attendant lost hold of the medicine case. The queen released my coat immediately, threw both arms around the attendant, and took the impact of falling stones along her wounded flank. Her body recoiled from the edge, carrying the attendant into a shallow alcove.

My cousin shouted, “She’s got you again!”

“She let go.” I spat grit. “Stop pulling.”

The rope carrier’s voice came sharper. “I had no load. You loaded it.”

“Help me get my kin out.”

“Then stop sawing the line over broken rock.”

The rope lay across the new channel, slapping in muddy water. Its free length still reached me. I dragged it off the crumbling lip and fed it around a basalt knob on my side.

“Pay me slack,” I called.

“Come up the line,” my cousin said.

“Slack. This ledge is going.”

The queen had braced her tail against the alcove wall. Blood ran fresh beneath her bandage. The attendant, one arm hanging close to their side, peered past her at the water.

“Shoulder,” the attendant said. “Mine. Not broken. Queen’s cloth is through. Two people above. One below standing badly.”

“I’m standing,” I said.

The attendant looked at my feet. I looked too. One boot was planted half in the channel, though I remembered setting it on dry stone.

The air had changed. The lamp flame near the floor was a small blue bead now. Cold climbed inside my trousers. Thoughts arrived like badly packed cargo: rope, cousin, queen, exit, and no certainty about which had to move first.

The queen tasted the air with a quick opening of her mouth. “The water is rising under the low air and pushing it up to us.”

“Bad air rising?”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“Not long.”

“How long?”

“I cannot measure it.” She was already reaching for the attendant. “We climb now.”

The obvious way was the fissure. Its lip had just proved what it thought of us. I looked past the queen instead, following the route as I would judge a washed trail: where silt gathered, where water ran clear, where a crack stayed dry because air moved through it. High above the attendant’s alcove, a seam of grey showed between leaning slabs.

“That chimney,” I said. “Does it go out?”

“Out. A hand’s width at the top,” the attendant said. “Enough air.”

“Behind the slab it opens wider,” the queen said. “Wide enough for my body.”

My cousin called, “No. Take the rope here.”

“That lip won’t hold three loads.”

“You’re confused.”

“Yes,” I said. “And I’m still the outrider.”

The carrier leaned into view. “Chimney line looks cleaner. I need a second anchor.”

I pointed to a dark horn of stone above the fissure. “Back it with that.”

“Too sharp.”

“My saddle blanket’s by the hide. Folded double.”

My cousin began, “We are not rigging a rescue for—”

“Blanket,” the carrier said. “Now.”

The queen crossed the foaming cut first, not by clearing it but by filling its safe edge with her body. She locked the thick end of her tail around a rib of stone beside the alcove and reached across to the chimney slab. Her right hand found a seam. Her left arm curved behind the attendant’s back.

“Move,” she said.

The attendant answered with one tap of the spoon against stone: the drilled signal for movement. Then they slid along the inside of the queen’s braced body, one useful arm working, feet testing each hold. The queen took their weight when the ledge crumbled under a heel. Her wounded flank trembled.

I knotted my saddle blanket around the rope, fed it across behind the attendant, and passed the bundle up. The carrier caught it, padded the sharp horn, and called the load at every change of hands. My cousin obeyed for three breaths, then reached down for me.

“Come while she’s holding it.”

I put my foot into the cut and forgot where my other foot belonged.

The water seemed to split into two channels, then four. My cousin’s arm doubled above me. I blinked hard, but the chamber did not settle.

The queen said, “I can brace the break or carry you. Not both.”

“Keep your coils off my kin,” my cousin said. “We have the line.”

“The line isn’t on me,” I said.

“I can put a loop down.”

The carrier said, “Not a blind waist loop on a confused climber.”

The attendant reached the first shelf in the chimney and wedged the medicine case behind their knees. “One injured above the cut,” they reported. “One dizzy below. Queen failing.”

The queen’s fingers slipped a joint along the seam.

I knew the reach across was less than two paces. I also knew I could no longer trust my knees to understand that.

“Coil me,” I said.

The queen looked down.

Fear went through me so cleanly that for a moment I could think again. I pointed, because the words mattered and I did not want more of them than necessary. “Once at my hips. Once below my shoulders. Leave this much at my ribs.” I held my hand sideways against my chest. “Across to the chimney. Put me down on the shelf.”

“Agreed.”

“And release when I say.”

“Yes.”

“You can’t stop bracing yet,” the carrier called. “Give me ten breaths.”

The carrier threw a loop to my cousin, who caught it and cursed at the force. The carrier talked them through a body belay: feet against the rear wall, rope across the padded horn, no wrapping a wrist. My cousin tried to hurry; the carrier made them reset one sliding boot. I called the chimney holds. The queen shifted her brace when I called. Above, the carrier set the anchor and my cousin took the hauling side.

I clipped my belt ring to the line and crawled close to the queen. Her body moved around me, one measured band at my hips, another under my arms. The pressure stayed clear of the hand-width I had shown her.

When she shifted me against her side, something struck loose inside my head: floodwater white at the edge of lamplight, my fingers jammed through a copper arm band, my boots knocking empty rock. My own voice, hoarse and near her shoulder.

*Don’t drop me. Don’t—*

The rest vanished. I had that fragment and nothing around it. The voice was mine.

“I remember asking,” I said.

“Good,” my cousin answered too quickly. “Now come up.”

The queen did not answer at all. Her attention was on the carrier.

“Set,” the carrier called.

My cousin took the strain. The rope tightened from my belt to the horn, replacing some of the pull the queen’s tail had held. The attendant struck one tap. Move.

The queen unhooked her tail from the rib of stone.

For one breath we hung over the cut, the rope carrying part of me, her left hand on the chimney slab, her right arm clamped to a seam. Then her body drove forward. Water hit my boots. The fresh bandage at her flank split, and her next breath came as a dry click, but she crossed. She placed me on the shelf beside the medicine case.

“Release,” I said.

The coils opened before the last sound left my mouth. She kept one palm under my elbow until my weight was on stone, then removed it.

The carrier hauled. My cousin pulled in time with the carrier rather than ahead. I crawled upward, pushing the medicine case while the attendant climbed one-handed before me. Below, the queen withdrew the final length of her tail just as the crown ledge broke and went into the basin.

She came last, using both arms and the pressure of her long body against opposite walls. Halfway up she stopped.

Two taps sounded beneath us.

Stone.

Nobody translated it into more. The attendant flattened. I jammed the medicine case under the shelf. My cousin held. The carrier locked the rope. A slab struck where the queen’s head had been; she folded sideways, waited for the smaller fragments to pass, and climbed again.

The air changed first. It lost the cold mineral weight. Then the chimney widened, and rain-grey light showed an upper mouth beyond a row of teethlike rocks. We crawled into fresh wind one by one.

Outside, the upper path had become a brown torrent, too deep to cross before morning. For the moment, the mouth was as far as rescue went.

The attendant made us sit by the outer wall and distributed the remaining water without discussion. The queen lay along the inner rock while the attendant cut away her ruined bandage. My cousin hovered over me, touching my shoulder every few breaths as though I might disappear between one glance and the next.

“We take you down as soon as that drops,” my cousin said.

“If it drops enough.”

“It will.”

The carrier inspected the rope’s abraded span. “Not by dawn, unless the rain stops now. And not on this strand.”

“She offered me work,” I said. “Six days, and she’d pay. She wants to know why people ride past her warning stakes.”

“Those were her words?”

“She said she wants to keep me.” I had not meant to repeat that part.

My cousin rounded on the queen. “You stay away from my kin.”

The queen’s face had gone still with pain. “They are free to sit where they choose.”

“You call wrapping them free?”

“I saw one carry,” the carrier said. They ran a thumb over a damaged strand. “Your kin asked for it. I had them on the line, but she carried most of the weight across. She put them down on the shelf and let go when they said. Before that she had the attendant when the ledge went.”

“You heard my kin just now. She wants to keep them. Her word.”

“When she was talking through that crack, all that came up was hissing.” The carrier went back to the strand.

My cousin looked at me. “You’re not taking this offer.”

Their hand was still on my shoulder.

I asked the queen, “The six days. What pay?”

“Two silver weights for each day, and your meals. I would not send you out to the stakes until the path is safe to walk.”

“Where would I sleep?”

“In the niche beside this mouth.”

I looked. It was dry, human-sized, and completely open on one side.

“No door,” I said.

“The air moves better through it without one.”

“And when the upper path opens, I can leave. Even if the six days aren’t done.”

“Yes. You will be paid for the days you worked.”

I looked at my left hand, cut before the rope ever burned it. The edge of a copper arm band would open a palm like that, if someone held on to it hard enough.

“In the basin,” I said. “How many times did I ask you?”

“I stopped counting on the climb,” she said. “By then you had no breath for it. You held on to my arm band until the ledge.”

My cousin’s hand tightened on my shoulder. I kept my eyes on the queen.

“I’ll take the trial. One recovery night first.”

The attendant looked me over. “Ribs bruised. Palm open. One night.”

The queen said, “Sleep, then.”

My cousin swore under their breath. “She is dangerous.”

“Yes,” I said. Seven metres of injured muscle had just held up a broken route. I looked at the torrent outside. “So is that path.”

“That isn’t the same.”

“No.”

By the time the rain weakened, we had agreed only that nobody would attempt the upper path in darkness.

The attendant cleaned my palm, bound it, and sent me to the niche. I laid out my own bedroll there, with my pack and knife beside it. Across the mouth, my cousin argued quietly with the rope carrier about the morning anchors. Deeper in, the queen asked for the narrow bandage instead of the broad one, and the attendant told her there was no broad one left.

I set my boots where I could find them in the dark and slept until the attendant woke me to check my ribs.

stories.title: Held Together
stories.prompt: a Married hero couple going through a rough patch get captured by a married villain couple and are surprised at how healthy their relationship is.
stories.body:
# Held Together

At 2:13 in the morning, the transfer station's ventilation stopped, and Renata heard Jonas's patrol app reroute them.

"West stairs," its flat voice said. "Nearside remains with Fixedpoint."

Beyond the service doors, reserve batteries held enough charge to keep three neighborhood clinics and an assisted-living tower cool through the hottest night of the year. On Renata's phone, the station diagram showed a breaker fault in red and an access alarm in amber. The west stairs curled around two locked landings. The cable trench ahead was open, straight, and four metres across.

"The trench is faster," she said.

Jonas stood behind her on the concrete steps, broad shoulders blocking the emergency light. "The app says west."

"You wrote the app."

"I changed one permission."

"Mine."

Somewhere below, metal struck metal. The temperature display beside the door read forty-one degrees. A second access sensor turned amber.

"We can have this fight upstairs," Jonas said. "Two sensors, nobody on camera, and the trench puts you in the open with nothing behind you. West stairs. Now."

Renata looked through the open gate at the landing beyond the trench. Four metres, clear line, no one visible. She went Nearside.

Space caught her behind the eyes. The landing replaced the step beneath her boots, and the world tipped left before righting itself. She kept one hand on the rail until the depth returned. First transit.

"Renata."

Ahead, through another open grille, the main-floor catwalk ran beside the reserve bus. Less than five metres. The shortest route had always been a chain of small, certain things.

She made the second transit before Jonas reached the trench.

This landing arrived doubled. Two yellow rails slid together, then apart. She blinked until they agreed on one position, but by then a woman in insulated work clothes had stepped within arm's reach of the lighting conduit.

The lights died from her outward.

The dark was three metres across, and it moved with the woman as active circuits emptied into the two silver cells mounted on a low sled behind her. Brownout. Livia Kade turned her bare hand over, measuring the last blue thread of current across her palm.

"She's early," Livia said.

"Still on sequence," Xavier Kade answered from above.

Two amber tags flashed on the catwalk. The west shutter behind Renata started down. A weighted baffle swung across the catwalk, its offset steel slats showing only other steel. Xavier Kade, Downforce in the case files and Brownout's husband of nine years, stepped out on the overhead gantry with a battery harness tight against his ribs.

Renata turned toward the last place she had seen Jonas. No clear line remained.

A pale plane grew under the falling shutter, rigid and translucent, and caught it a metre above the floor. A second formed at the far edge of his six-metre sight, reaching toward the baffle. Jonas had committed both at once. For perhaps a second, Renata saw him between them: jaw set, hands spread, trying to make two paths exist where she had left him none.

Livia crossed close to the wall conduit. His comm light went black.

Xavier touched two fingers to his harness. The tagged shutter multiplied its downward load. Jonas's first plane sank into cracked concrete as the floor failed beneath it, and the shutter came the rest of the way down hard enough to star the slab. The second vanished when he pulled one numbed hand toward the manual latch. Too late. Another shutter sealed him into the relay bay.

The baffle struck Renata across the shoulder and drove her into a floor cage. A U-shaped anchor yoke closed over her ankles. Xavier planted a tag on it, and the steel became too heavy even to rock.

"That's three," Livia said.

"West shutter. Relay shutter. Anchor," Xavier said, touching the harness once for each.

The last slat locked into place. Every opening in Renata's cage faced a backing plate. She could see strips of floor, pieces of equipment, one of Jonas's boots six metres away. Nowhere she could go.

Above the bus, the red reserve clock, counting down what the batteries had left at this draw, changed from 45:00 to 44:59.

Livia pulled the first cell's leads toward the live cabinet. "Starting draw."

***

The Kades did not celebrate.

Livia positioned herself beside the active reserve circuit and let current vanish into the cell within her living field. Xavier checked the cage, the relay shutter, then the west shutter and the loading ramp behind it. He marked each task on a grease board clipped to the sled.

"Return before auxiliary," he said.

"No, after. Auxiliary, then return." Livia watched a meter tremble and didn't look up. "Close return first and the clinic feed sees the sag, and somebody at the utility wakes up and looks at a screen."

Xavier studied the switch labels for a long moment, erased one arrow with his thumb, and drew it again beneath AUX. Livia glanced at the board and went back to her meter.

Renata hated them more for how ordinary it looked.

She pulled against the anchor yoke. Its added load drove the cuff edges through her suit and into bone. Xavier glanced over.

"Don't," he said. "It won't get lighter because you're angry."

"The cooling wards lost twelve minutes last month," Renata said. "People in that tower can't sweat properly."

Livia's meter climbed. "They've got room batteries."

"Forty minutes' worth."

"So your utility has forty minutes to clear a breaker fault. It's a breaker."

"If your staged fault didn't cook the switchgear."

Livia looked at the scorched cabinet, then at the charging cell. "Xavier. Housing."

Xavier crouched and put his light on the thermal strip along the cell housing. "Fifty-three."

She turned back to her meter.

From the relay bay, Jonas said, "How many transits do you have left?"

Renata found his face through two misaligned slots. "Work your latch."

"I am working the latch. I need the count. If it's two, I hold the baffle, you go the second that anchor gets light, and you go again to my release. If it's one, it's the baffle or the release, not both, and I have to know which before I spend my hands on the wrong one. If it's none, I stop counting you in and think of something else. Which is it?"

"Ask the app. It knows what I'm allowed."

He wrapped both hands around the manual lever. They did not close properly. Concurrent planes always numbed his fingers, beginning at the tips and moving inward. Renata had watched him fumble keys after patrol and teased him for refusing mittens in winter. Tonight the lever slipped from his palms.

"No more transits," he said. "Not until I can get you a line and support the landing."

Renata leaned back from the slots.

The first minute ended. Amber light faded from the anchor tag, and some of its crushing weight released. Xavier's harness fans spun up to cool the spent cycle. He tested the yoke with his boot before Renata could lift it, then renewed the downward load as soon as the tag answered.

Jonas had been counting too. "Sixty seconds," he said. "And he was on it before you could lift. So a second of window. Two if his fans run slow, and they won't every time. Renata?"

She gave him nothing.

At 31:18 on the reserve clock, Livia moved the intake leads from the first cell to the second. The first was the size of a carry-on case, finite and nearly full, its charge bars wavering orange. Xavier peeled the cooling west-shutter tag from its mount and braced it against the cell housing to reseat a clamp.

"Hold it there, hold it on the housing," Livia said. "I'll pull the spike."

"No."

She looked up.

Xavier opened his hand. The center of his glove had blistered glossy over a burn. "Housing's over limit. Ceramic handle or it waits."

Livia's eyes went to the thermal strip, then to the glove. She fetched the handled clamp without a word and set it within his reach. He seated it. She pulled the spike down into her field, and the cell steadied.

Xavier returned the tag to the west-shutter mount without engaging it.

"Strip hits seventy-eight, we leave it," he said.

"You said that in the van. Twice."

The reserve clock continued to fall. Behind the far maintenance door, somebody struck twice, paused, then struck twice again. Utility workers. Alive, at least. The station display showed clinic demand rising with the outside temperature.

Renata waited for the anchor to cool, jammed her fingers beneath it, and heaved. One edge rose a centimetre. She twisted her right ankle. By the time she shut her left eye and the doubled cuff became one, pain ran up her shin, and the yoke slammed down when Xavier renewed the tag.

"Your eye," Jonas said. "You keep shutting it."

"My ankle's fine."

"I didn't ask about your ankle. You shut it to look at the cuff. You did it at the slots before." He stopped, then started again, lower. "Is that the concussion? How many transits do you have?"

"Enough."

"Enough for what?"

Renata fitted her fingers back under the yoke's edge and counted the tag down.

Livia crouched by the second cell. Its charge indicator jumped, fell, then blinked amber.

"You seated it wrong." She was on her feet. "Xavier. It's crooked, it's arcing, look at it."

Xavier did not turn from the sled. "I seated it. I checked it." He set down the grease pencil. "I seated it and I checked it, Livia."

"So why's it moving?"

"Then something changed."

Livia put her hand beside the intake without touching it. Current made a fine blue web across her knuckles, and the station lights nearest her dimmed. She checked the reserve meter, then the cell, then the meter again.

"It's the bus. The bus is sagging, it's not your clamp." For a moment she didn't look at him. "I read it as the clamp. I yelled at you about the clamp."

Xavier came back. "Like the dryer."

"Not now." She rubbed her knuckles hard against her thigh.

"Can you hold half?"

"Forty-six."

He went for the clamp. She caught his burned wrist before he got there. "Open."

He opened his hand. Two fingers curled; the others shook.

"You don't renew the west shutter until that cools," she said.

"Then it stays light. Anybody coming down the ramp can lift it."

"I know what it leaves."

"All right."

She released him. He switched hands, and they returned to the cell without filling the silence.

Renata pressed her forehead to the cage steel. She had expected vanity, cruelty, one of them performing dominance for the other. What she got was Livia holding a burned wrist until the fingers opened. They could do that and still watch the clinic demand climb.

At 12:06 remaining, Jonas said, "I can make one reliable plane. Two, and I won't have hands for the release."

Renata looked through the lowest slot. Xavier's anchor tag would gray at the end of its minute. Each time it did, his harness fan ran while he checked the sled wheels. To move the charged cells up the ramp, he would need the sled loaded downward for traction against the vibrating floor. Three tags, no fourth. He had rehearsed the transfer twice with his eyes.

"One," she said.

Jonas went still.

"Two tonight. One left." She swallowed. The cage seemed to lean toward her. "After the concussion, the second makes edges split. The third takes depth. Last time, seventeen minutes. I couldn't tell the floor from a step."

"Last time?"

"Three weeks ago."

His breath left him through his nose. She waited for the contingency tree: dates, reporting failures, the predictable list of all the ways she had made them unsafe.

"What can you see now?" he asked.

"The near slat. Your boot when you move it. Not their faces unless they cross the middle gap."

"All right."

The words sounded unfinished in his mouth.

Renata gripped the yoke. "Tell me what you've seen."

"Baffle pivots toward me when the anchor tag cools. Hinge opening is five point six metres from my left slot. His transfer takes four seconds. The sled crosses your middle gap after the tag seats."

"Can your plane hold the baffle?"

"About thirty seconds. Less if he loads it."

He waited.

Renata measured the strip of concrete beyond the middle gap. Four metres, perhaps four and a half. It doubled if she stared too hard, but both versions were inside her limit.

"On the next transfer," she said. "Wedge the baffle. I lift the yoke when the load drops. I go to the clear patch by the sled."

"You'll land blind."

"Nearly. You'll route me to your release."

His boot shifted into view, then stopped. "Yes."

***

At 8:41 remaining, the anchor tag went gray.

Renata lifted. The yoke came off the floor, ordinary steel again, heavy but possible. Jonas's pale plane grew through the left slot, a single rigid sheet expanding into the baffle hinge. Metal screamed. The offset slats opened three centimetres, then ten.

Xavier looked over. His burned hand hovered near the tag.

"Sled first," Livia said. "We're below exit traction."

He tore the amber marker from Renata's yoke and slapped it onto the sled frame. The cells sank against their suspension. Their weight bit the wheels into the floor.

The middle gap cleared.

Renata chose the patch of floor she could see and went.

The cage vanished. Concrete struck both boots at once. Then the room lost its distances.

Rails floated near and far. Livia became two dark figures beside a blue flare. Renata dropped to one knee before the false floor could move under her. Her stomach surged. Third transit. There would be no fourth for hours.

"Forward two paces," Jonas called. His command voice caught on the first word, then changed. "Your pace. Handrail at your right knee."

Renata found the rail by sweeping her hand. Behind her, Xavier threw the unweighted west shutter up onto its catch and hauled at the loaded sled. Livia left the bus to intercept, and the charge stream broke as soon as the active circuit passed beyond her three-metre field.

"One pace," Jonas said. "Relay release is shoulder height. Orange handle. Twenty centimetres left."

There were three orange blurs. Renata closed one eye. Two remained.

"Which one?"

He didn't answer at once. "Farther left. Your hand is below it. Up."

Her fingers struck the handle. She pulled.

The relay shutter lifted. Jonas ducked under it as Xavier renewed the tag, and the metal crashed onto the plane Jonas formed beneath it. One plane. His right hand hung half closed.

"Main isolation?" Renata asked.

"Six paces behind you. Yellow wheel."

Livia moved back toward the bus, choosing the cells over Renata. Current flared again. Xavier abandoned the sled and came toward Jonas, one tag control in his good hand.

They countered on different instincts and blocked each other's route.

"Xavier," Livia said. "Housing's at seventy-two."

"Sled or him?"

"Sled. Give me the route."

He stepped back at once and dragged the sled sideways, clearing her path to the live cabinet. "Two metres. Clamp high. Then ramp." He was already moving. "Clamp high."

Jonas could have put a second plane across them. Renata heard his breath catch the way it did before he built something, and at the edge of her sight a second pale sheet began to thicken across the Kades' path.

"One wall," she said.

The second sheet thinned and was gone. His one plane stayed where it was, under the relay shutter.

"Wheel is five paces now," he said. "Drift right."

Renata moved through the swimming geometry. At the yellow blur, she used both hands until she found the rim. It resisted, then turned. The reserve bus separated with a blow she felt in her teeth. Behind the mechanical switch, the clinic feed was out of Livia's reach.

The cells remained charged. Their rig whined against the cut circuit, hunting for a path.

"Ground bar," Jonas said. "Low left."

"I can't find low."

"Stop."

She stopped.

"Your left boot is touching the housing. Bar is on the housing. Slide your heel back."

Metal knocked her boot. Renata crouched without trusting the floor and closed both hands around the insulated grip.

Livia saw what she held. "Don't."

Renata pulled the station's emergency ground into place.

The siphon load went down the copper braid. Both cells flashed white. Livia broke her field and stumbled away from the cabinet. Xavier caught the back of her harness, keeping her clear of the arcing leads without touching them.

"Seventy-six," she said.

"Ramp is open."

"Seventy-seven."

Xavier reached for the sled, burned hand failing around its handle. The cell casing ticked as it expanded.

"Seventy-eight," Livia said.

He let go.

Together they backed toward the open west shutter and the loading ramp beyond it, Xavier counting the steps twice when smoke hid the edge. They ducked under. On the far side he knocked the shutter off its catch and tapped the still-mounted tag with his good hand as it fell, loading it on the way down.

The west shutter hit concrete between Renata and the ramp. Up the ramp, a lock died with a click, and a door banged wide.

Jonas's hand came up toward the shutter, the fingers half closed.

He did not make another plane.

"Pursuit?" he asked.

Renata listened to the pounding behind the maintenance door. One worker's strikes had become uneven.

"No. Staff first."

"Yes."

They grounded the cells, released the damaged switchgear from the reserve, and opened the maintenance room by hand. One technician had a bleeding scalp. The other lay beside a fallen tool cabinet with an ankle swelling inside her boot. Jonas formed a single plane as a rigid litter while Renata, moving by touch and his plain directions, kept the technician level. They carried her to the cooler stairwell and waited for responders instead of the Kades.

At 3:28, exactly seventy-five minutes after the ventilation had stopped, a hospital physician shone a narrow light across Renata's eyes.

"Tell me every transit in the last six hours," she said.

Renata sat on an intake bed with a basin between her shoes. Jonas stood by the curtain, his hands wrapped in warming pads. A patrol supervisor waited on speakerphone beside the blood-pressure cuff.

"Three," Renata said. "Two before capture, one to get out."

The light stopped on her left eye. "Your file says concussion last month, cleared for duty. Any change since?"

"Yes."

"Does medical know?"

"No."

The physician tipped her head toward the curtain. "Does he?"

"Since tonight."

The physician recorded it without looking at Jonas. "Observation until the depth loss clears. You agree?"

"Yes."

On the phone, the supervisor asked, "Why did your route split?"

Jonas shifted a warming pad from one palm to the other. "I added a field veto to our patrol app. Command didn't know."

Renata looked toward him and found two Jonases at the curtain.

"Remove the veto," she said.

"Now?"

"Now. Leave the route log intact for review."

"Okay." His fingers would not work the phone. "Will you unlock it for me?"

She did. He talked her through the settings but did not touch her hand. The permission changed from PARTNER OVERRIDE to SHARED CONFIRMATION.

The physician rolled a visual-field target to the end of the bed. "Do you want him in the room for the assessment?"

Renata considered the two blurred figures at the curtain.

"For the assessment, yes."

Jonas looked at the empty spaces on either side of her. "Left or right?"

"Left."

He moved there and waited while the physician raised the first light.

stories.title: Not Friday
