“And no kitchen victory lap.” She rubbed behind his ears. “You feeling off?”

Maledict intended to recoil from his enemy’s touch. Pickle’s ears, traitorous structures, leaned into her fingers. The spot was astonishing.

He could correct course. The response key lived in the home office, keyed to Brightguard’s pulse but transportable when she wore it. At the emergency tone, Pickle fetched her left wrist guard from the office, though never on the first request; the office floor hummed, and he made her ask twice. Maledict had arranged an emergency. At nine, drones would begin peeling the municipal archive’s roof like the lid from a tin.

Until then, he had only to behave like a dog.

Brightguard opened a cabinet. “Salmon crisp?”

His studies had not covered this either.

He accepted the little pink square cautiously. Salt, smoke, fat. It shattered between his teeth.

Maledict sat without being asked.

“Oh,” Brightguard said. “So we remember that one.”

***

Across the Tri-City Area, on the seventy-first floor of a black glass skyscraper with its own weather instruments, Maledict’s butler removed a bronze letter opener from Maledict’s mouth.

“No, sir.”

Maledict’s human body released it readily and put both hands on the carpet. The body was forty-two, tall, and ordinarily carried with enough menace to make a room rearrange itself. At present it sniffed the butler’s cuff, sneezed, and crawled under a steel console after a stray almond.

The butler closed his eyes for half a second. His employer had described the contingency as *temporary cognitive misalignment*. The brass dial on the exchange console said 00:11 ELAPSED and 13:49 TO RETURN. Its paired silhouettes—one human, one canine—glowed a reassuring green.

Nothing else about the morning was reassuring.

He canceled the nine-thirty intimidation of a zoning commissioner. He redirected three senior operatives from the residential floor. Then he moved the glass coffee table, sealed the interior stairs, and spread a duvet on the carpet where Maledict’s body could lie without bruising adult knees.

“Water,” he said, placing a shallow mixing bowl beside the duvet. “Please take it slowly.”

Pickle-in-Maledict’s-body slapped one hand into the water and looked delighted.

The butler fetched towels.

The instructions lay open on the console, written in Maledict’s compressed technical hand.

EXCHANGE PRESERVES TWO LIVING OCCUPANTS. NO BLEND. NO COPIES. NO DELETIONS.

DEFAULT RETURN: FOURTEEN HOURS.

OCCUPANT HOLD: COLLAR RIVET, CANINE SIDE ONLY.

There were two more lines beneath a black security strip. The butler tried a lamp, a polarized lens, and a document scanner. The strip remained black.

Pickle’s attention shifted to the apartment door. The human body bounced once on the balls of its feet, then glanced back.

“I regret that the terrace is inadequate.” The butler touched the secure lift control. “We will use the service garden.”

Pickle bounced again.

“Yes. Now.”

***

At eight fifty-seven, Brightguard’s alarm gave three rising notes.

Maledict sprang from the heated oval bed in the living room and sprinted for the office. At last, the plan.

“Guard, Pickle,” Brightguard called after him.

He crossed the office threshold. A low electrical hum prickled through his paws, unpleasant but tolerable. Brightguard stopped fastening her field harness.

“Pickle.”

He kept going. The left wrist guard lay in its charging cradle beside the response key, a flat red wafer no larger than a thumbnail.

“You hate this floor.”

Maledict turned. Brightguard stood in the doorway with one silver brow up.

He had skipped the part where Pickle refused. He backed onto the hall runner and looked reluctant.

“That’s more like you.” She pointed at the guard. “Can you bring it?”

He had rehearsed this. He trotted to the cradle, ignored the current fizzing through his pads, and took the guard gently between his teeth.

The red wafer sat half an inch away.

One sweep of the tongue—

“Not the key.”

Brightguard’s tone changed less than her posture did. Her knees softened. Her right hand settled near the harness control at her ribs.

Maledict lifted his head with the guard and attempted Pickle’s innocent expression. He had practiced it from surveillance stills. Judging by Brightguard’s face, he had produced an expression associated with tax fraud.

She took the guard, wiped dog saliva from its inner seam, and clipped it on. “Office stays locked today.”

From a wall screen came an aerial view of three drones descending toward the archive. Brightguard swore mildly. Maledict’s chest filled with satisfaction.

“Somebody’s getting predictable.” She tapped her wrist. “City response, this is Brightguard. I’m three minutes out. Keep people off the west roof.”

She crossed to the balcony launch panel, then looked back at him. He sat exactly where she had left him.

Pickle, he recalled too late, brought her shoes.

“No shoes?”

He ran for the entryway, selected a blue sneaker, and returned with it.

Brightguard stared at the shoe. “Those are for walking. You bring the red boots for work.”

Maledict dropped it.

The building shook as the launch doors opened. Wind pressed the fur flat along one side of him. Brightguard hooked her helmet to the harness, its clear visor waking with maps and civic channels.

“Blanket’s on the sofa. I’ll be home for the noon walk.” She hesitated. “Don’t eat the key.”

Then light gathered under her boots, and she shot between the towers.

Maledict waited until the balcony sealed. He raced back to the office. The door rejected paw, nose, voice, and one shoulder-first assault that hurt more than it accomplished.

He found Pickle’s communication mat under the kitchen bench. Six rubber buttons offered OUT, WATER, PLAY, BLANKET, BRIGHTGUARD, and CHEESE in Brightguard’s recorded voice. He pressed OUT, then BRIGHTGUARD, then CHEESE by accident.

A dispenser chimed and released a small golden cube.

He ate it.

After a moment’s reflection, he pressed CHEESE again.

The dispenser said, “All done.”

“Rrrr,” said Maledict.

At nine twenty, the cleaning robot emerged. At nine twenty-one, Maledict remembered that Pickle rode it from room to room on Tuesdays. He climbed aboard for camouflage. The robot warmed its top panel, played quiet jazz, and took him directly past the locked office toward a broad window full of morning sun.

Maledict woke at eleven forty with his chin on the robot’s soft bumper.

***

The service garden occupied the skyscraper’s fifty-sixth floor, a strip of turf between solar fins. Pickle-in-Maledict’s-body refused shoes but consented to socks after the butler rolled each one over a human foot slowly enough to be inspected. The suit was impossible. The butler found a black tracksuit in the private gym.

“This arrangement is temporary,” he told the head of security through the closed garden door. “Mr. Maledict is unavailable.”

Behind him, Pickle chased a falling leaf, caught it against the glass, and looked for praise.

“Well done, sir.”

Pickle grinned with Maledict’s entire human face. The result was dreadful. The butler nevertheless clapped twice.

At 04:26 ELAPSED, he offered a meal on an unbreakable plate. Pickle rejected toast, eggs, melon, and an expensive mushroom preparation. Chicken disappeared. Peas went next. When the butler placed the salmon garnish down, Pickle made a breathless sound and offered his left hand.

The butler took it. “Thank you.”

Pickle touched his nose to the butler’s fingers.

The gesture was so practiced that the butler looked toward the exchange console.

He had assumed the animal body was a disguise selected for access. He had not considered that the animal might have come from an occupied life.

At four hours and forty-five minutes elapsed, he searched Maledict’s planning files. The target packet included Brightguard’s address, patrol routes, dog-walker cancellations, food orders, and a photograph of a small brown dog with one naturally white forepaw asleep under a lemon-yellow blanket. The animal was labeled ACCESS BODY: PICKLE.

The butler returned to the residential suite. Pickle was sitting at the secured elevator, one human hand resting on the seam.

The butler crouched beside him. “Home?”

Pickle looked at him, then at the door.

“Yes,” the butler said, mostly to himself. “I thought as much.”

***

Brightguard returned at noon with a smear of drone lubricant on her cheek and no patience left for mysteries.

Maledict met her at the door because the lunch pouch at her belt smelled like beef. Pickle usually spun twice before greeting. Maledict remembered after one turn, attempted another, and collided with the umbrella stand.

Brightguard caught it without looking. “All right. Kitchen.”

She set her helmet on the counter and crouched. Up close, fine fatigue lines webbed the skin around her eyes. “Show me what hurts.”

Nothing hurt. Maledict pressed CHEESE.

“That wasn’t the question.”

He pressed OUT.

“We’re going. First, paws.” She picked up Pickle’s soft walking harness. “Blue or green?”

Maledict selected blue because blue was the color of dominion.

“You’ve refused blue since it pinched you at the lake.”

He removed his paw.

“And you’ve never forgiven the mail carrier, but you let her scratch your ears this morning.” Brightguard thumbed up his lip and checked his gums. Then she sat back on her heels. “What is going on with you?”

Maledict pressed OUT with emphasis.

Her wrist display pulsed. She read the caller identification, and her face went still.

“This is Brightguard.”

The butler appeared on the kitchen wall screen, framed by dark stone and a slice of cloud. “Madam. I serve the man you know as Maledict. I believe I have your dog.”

Maledict lunged for the wall controls. Brightguard closed one hand around the back of his harness and lifted him onto the counter.

“Show me.”

The image widened. Maledict’s human body crouched beside a lemon-yellow throw the butler had evidently found in a guest room. The moment Pickle saw Brightguard, he scrambled upright. His hands struck the screen. Then he vanished from view and returned carrying one black dress shoe in his teeth.

Brightguard’s breath caught.

“Red boots for work,” she said.

Pickle dropped the shoe, searched frantically offscreen, and brought back a burgundy house slipper.

“Close enough, baby.”

He spun twice.

Brightguard gripped the counter until the composite edge creaked. When she spoke to the butler again, her voice had the clipped steadiness of civic radio traffic. “Is he injured?”

“No. He has eaten, taken water, rested, and used the garden. I’ve barred the stairs. His distress increases at closed exterior doors.”

“He’ll want home. Don’t promise it unless you can deliver.”

“Understood.”

“Can it be undone?”

“The device indicates automatic return at nine this evening. Fourteen hours after exchange.” The butler glanced aside. “There are concealed instructions I have not yet opened.”

Maledict found Brightguard’s field tablet docked beside the communication mat. Its keys, built for gloved hands, were just wide enough for a paw. He pawed laboriously:

THIS IS A DEEPFAKE.

Brightguard looked at the message, then at him.

He added:

I AM PICKLE.

Onscreen, Pickle shoved his borrowed slipper at the camera and whined.

“No,” Brightguard said. “You’re really not.”

Maledict began typing a threat. Brightguard opened the beef pouch.

He lost his place.

The journey to the skyscraper required a ventilated carrier, because Brightguard did not fly with unsecured passengers. Maledict, with nothing left to pretend, lay flat on the green harness until she buckled him into the blue. He refused the carrier, too, until she lined it with Pickle’s lemon-yellow sofa blanket. He then discovered a cooling vent at nose height and spent the flight with his chin on folded fleece, watching the Tri-City Area stream beneath him.

The butler kept Pickle on the residential side of the laboratory door, away from the body that had been taken from him. Brightguard moved back and forth: checking the device with the butler, sitting on the floor with Pickle, bringing Maledict measured snacks so he could not claim starvation and could not eat himself sick. Maledict meant to use those hours to recover command of the situation. The tower supplied warmed towels, a silent brush with flexible rubber teeth, and braised beef whose preparation had once occupied a chef through an entire hostage negotiation.

By eight thirty, he had revised his strategic objectives.

***

At eight fifty-three that evening, four occupants waited in Maledict’s private laboratory: Brightguard in full harness; the butler beside the exchange console; Pickle in Maledict’s body on a padded exercise mat; and Maledict in Pickle’s body beneath the main worktable, finishing a bowl of braised beef.

The two anchor plates stood eight feet apart. One was human-sized. The other held the imprint of four small paws. A line of violet light joined them through the floor. In the console, the exchange’s single braided filament had blackened at both ends; it retained enough charge to complete this one finalization cycle and nothing after it.

“Seven minutes,” the butler said.

Brightguard knelt beside Pickle. The human body was exhausted from being strange. He leaned his forehead into her shoulder while she rubbed between his shoulder blades.

“You’re going home,” she said. “Then the vet, then your own bed.”

Pickle lifted his head and stared across the room at the blue harness on his own body. He whined. Under the worktable, Maledict bared Pickle’s teeth.

“Green tomorrow,” Brightguard told Pickle, her hand still moving on his back. “I heard you.”

The butler had exposed the hidden writing with heat from the console’s own vent. He read it again. “The automatic return is intact. When the dial reaches fourteen hours, each occupant returns to the body in which the exchange began. No memory or identity transfer beyond that movement.”

Maledict climbed onto the smaller plate. A black rivet nestled beneath the edge of his collar.

Brightguard saw his paw move. “Leave that alone.”

He pressed the rivet three times.

The console struck nine o’clock and went violet.

Pickle jerked against Brightguard. Maledict remained a dog. The dial cleared and printed OCCUPANT HOLD 01:59:59.

The butler leaned over it. His composure narrowed to a white line around his mouth. “You’ve engaged the occupant hold, sir.”

Maledict went to the field tablet Brightguard had brought so he could answer questions.

I REJECT REVERSAL.

Brightguard moved between him and Pickle. “You don’t get to reject it for both of you.”

THE BODY SUITS ME.

“That body is Pickle’s.”

I HAVE CONQUERED IT.

Brightguard picked up the tablet before he could continue. “No. Pickle gets Pickle.” She passed the tablet to the butler. “Read me the rest of the instructions.”

Maledict barked at her. The sound had more outrage than menace. From the mat, Pickle barked back using Maledict’s human lungs—one rough, startling syllable—then hid his face against Brightguard’s side.

The butler set the tablet on the floor and traced the concealed lines below the instructions. The violet light had made more text visible.

“The hold suspends return,” he said. “It opens a two-hour finalization window. At expiry, the present exchange becomes fixed.”

Brightguard’s gaze cut to the descending seconds. “Other options.”

“Mutual restoration.” His finger moved. “Or restoration followed by source recast.”

Maledict stopped barking.

The butler read silently for several seconds. “Recast returns both occupants first. It then reshapes only the initiating body—your body, sir—around its restored occupant. The dog’s body and occupant are excluded. The change is irreversible and requires continuous confirmation from you after you are human again.”

Maledict pawed the tablet toward himself.

DOG?

“An available template,” the butler said, and indicated a small key on the console marked DOG.

WITH BED?

Brightguard stared at him. “We’re at one hour fifty-eight, and that’s your first question?”

Maledict typed:

SNACKS ALSO.

“Pickle’s bed is Pickle’s. Pickle’s snacks are Pickle’s. Pickle’s home is Pickle’s.” Brightguard unsealed her helmet and set it aside. “Recast yourself, and you sleep in my living room, where I can see you.” She rested a hand on Pickle’s borrowed shoulder. “He comes first there. Separate bed. Separate bowls. No office. If Pickle wants you across the room, you go across the room.”

The butler folded his hands behind his back. “I will manage your legal affairs, salaries, surrendered equipment, and restitution. If you remain in Pickle’s body, I notify emergency services now.”

Maledict looked from one to the other. His message came more slowly.

NO TOWER?

“Not unsupervised,” the butler said.

NO MONDAY BRIEFINGS?

“No.”

NO ZONING COMMISSIONER?

“Canceled.”

Maledict sat. Pickle’s tail swept once across the plate before he mastered it.

The laboratory waited. Beyond the glass, three cities burned in the harmless colors of traffic and office lights. Brightguard checked the timer, checked Pickle’s breathing, and said nothing.

At last Maledict stood on his hind legs and pawed the DOG key.

The console offered a rotating field of canine forms. He nosed past anything resembling Pickle and stopped at a deep-chested black dog with long legs, upright ears, and a small gray patch under the chin. Distinct silhouette, distinct coat, no white forepaw.

“Larger,” Brightguard said. “We’ll need another gate.”

Maledict selected the form.

The butler led Pickle to the human plate and placed Maledict on the canine one. “Restoration first. You will wake in your own body, sir. If you remove your hand from the confirmation field, recast stops before alteration begins. Once alteration begins, releasing your hand will not reverse it. Do you understand?”

YES.

“Pickle?” Brightguard held out her palm. Pickle placed Maledict’s left hand into it. She squeezed once and touched two fingers to his nose.

He went still.

The butler activated mutual restoration.

For one breath the violet line rose into a bright wall. Pickle’s dog body folded gently onto the smaller plate. Maledict’s human body straightened on the other, inhaling with his own lungs.

“Brightguard,” he began, his restored voice sonorous with habit, “you stand before the voluntary apotheosis of—”

“Pickle first.”

She had already unclipped the dog harness. Pickle tumbled into her arms, licked her chin, wriggled free, and ran two ecstatic circles around her boots. He offered the white-furred forepaw. Brightguard took it with both hands.

The butler checked the console. “Identity separation stable. Both occupants restored.”

Maledict placed his hand in the confirmation field.

“Thirty seconds,” said the butler. “You may still release.”

Maledict looked at the paperwork waiting on three screens, at his butler, and at the beef bowl beneath the table.

“Will the heated bed be of equivalent quality?”

“It will be appropriate to your size,” the butler said.

Maledict kept his hand down.

The field closed around his consenting human body. Its light was opaque and brief. When it cleared, a black dog stood on the human plate, long-legged and entirely unlike Pickle. The gray at his chin gave him the grave appearance of a magistrate until he smelled the beef bowl and stepped directly into it.

Pickle retreated behind Brightguard.

“Across the room,” she told Maledict.

He started to object, found himself without a tablet, and went.

***

The veterinarian cleared both dogs at one forty in the morning. Pickle’s original body was unharmed. Maledict’s new one was healthy, microchipped, and increasingly offended by the indignities of a thorough examination. Brightguard carried Pickle home although he was perfectly capable of walking. The butler followed with Maledict on a reinforced lead and two shopping bags from an all-night pet store.

By breakfast, Pickle had slept in his heated oval bed, rejected the blue harness again, and inspected every room. His bowls, blanket, buttons, and place on the sofa remained exactly where they belonged.

Maledict’s new bed waited on the other side of the living room. It was larger, orthopedic, and—after a quiet adjustment by Brightguard—not quite as warm as Pickle’s.

The morning news displayed Maledict’s skyscraper behind a reporter. Authorities had found disabled drones, canceled operations, and records moving toward an independent investigator. Maledict himself remained missing. The butler, exact even at seven in the morning, had issued no comment on his whereabouts.

Brightguard set down two bowls. Pickle approached his and offered the white forepaw before she asked. She squeezed it once and touched his nose.

Maledict shoved in beside him.

Pickle growled.

“Wait,” Brightguard said.

Maledict backed onto the mat. He watched Pickle eat the chicken, rice, greens, and first salmon crisp. His ears followed each crunch.

Brightguard stretched one knee, checked the time on her wrist guard, and let him wait through the whole familiar ritual. Then she set down the second bowl.

Maledict forgot the news, the skyscraper, and breakfast decorum all at once.

stories.title: Nine Lives of Excuses
stories.prompt: you inherit a magic cat that gives advice about life when you complain to it. However, one day it snaps, giving you a long frustrated lecture about how much of a waste you are and that you are the source of your own problems
stories.body:
# Nine Lives of Excuses

At 8:13 on Tuesday morning, Mizzle was sitting on the signature page of my personal guarantee.

Mizzle sat on anything that was both rectangular and important, a preference that had survived all ten months since I inherited her. The guarantee had only become important at midnight, when I moved it from beneath a cookbook to the kitchen table. Before that it had been paperwork, which was a different category entirely.

I drank my coffee and discovered it was cold.

"Mizzle, this is disgusting."

She opened one green eye. "You poured today's coffee onto yesterday's and then forgot it beside the sink. Make fresh coffee."

Her eye closed.

That was how her advice worked. A sincere complaint, spoken directly to her, bought one reply. It could be six words or six minutes; the length belonged to Mizzle. Questions got silence. Praise got silence. Fake grievances got the kind of silence that included slow washing between the toes. In the first weeks after she came to me, I had treated the rule like a coin-operated wisdom machine. I complained about sleep, work, whether to buy cheap shelving, and the woman downstairs who practiced scales at seven in the evening. Mizzle advised blackout curtains, sending invoices on time, wall anchors, and growing up.

Mostly, she was useful.

My phone buzzed beneath the sugar bowl.

My sister's message read: FOUR O'CLOCK. If you're in, bring the signed guarantee. If you're out, tell me by noon so I can ask for the back unit. After four they keep the whole $8,400. I won't chase you again.

The message made it sound as if the decision had been sitting around waiting for me. It had, technically. There had been the first lease packet, and then revised numbers, and then the contractor's estimate, which altered the numbers enough that anyone sensible would have paused. My sister's answer to the estimate had arrived nineteen days earlier. A person could hardly be blamed for wanting the dust to settle around a life-changing decision.

Mizzle shifted. The corner of the guarantee appeared beneath her flank, already creased.

"She's cornered me," I said. "Mizzle, I can't believe my own sister would put me under this kind of pressure."

Mizzle stood.

She was a small gray cat, round through the ribs, with one white paw and a dark stripe down her nose that gave her face the look of a document someone had tried to amend. Her tail expanded to twice its ordinary width. She stepped off the guarantee, leaving four warm dents in the paper, and looked up at me.

"Your sister did not corner you this morning," she said. "You drew the corner and furnished it and sat down in it, and now you complain that the room is poorly designed.

"You have been waiting to say this happened to you. I have watched you prepare. Six weeks ago you brought home the shop keys and slid them across the floor for me because you were happy. You said the front room could hold six tables, the ovens would go along the east wall, and your sister's morning buns would pay the rent before the lunch trade even began. You called her at eleven forty-eight at night. You told her you had found the place. You told her not to be afraid of the deposit because there were two of you.

"Then there were two of you when she paid eight thousand four hundred dollars, but only one of you when the landlord asked for signatures.

"I slept on the first packet for three days. Each time you lifted me off, you stared at the last page, took a photograph of it, and put it back under the green cookbook. You complained that legal language was meant to trick people. I told you to mark what you did not understand and call a tenant adviser. You marked two paragraphs. You did not call. When your sister found one for you, you complained that the appointment was too early. It was at ten thirty. Ten thirty. I am awake at four every morning waiting for you to remember that I eat, and ten thirty was too early for you.

"Ten months I have listened to this. The shelving, the woman with the scales, the client, the landlord, and now your sister. It is the same complaint wearing different trousers, and I must sit and hear every pair, because you are the one who remembers water and food and the box in the laundry cupboard. I cannot leave. I cannot tell you in words that my dish is empty unless you first make my need about your inconvenience.

"The contractor's estimate was higher. That was a real problem. Your sister came here with the cinnamon rolls you left uncovered until they hardened, and the two of you cut the plan. She removed the second oven. You kept the painted sign. She asked you to choose between six tables and a longer counter. You said you needed to see both versions. She sent both versions. You opened neither for five days. On the sixth day you complained to me that spreadsheets make your eyes swim. I told you to read one line at a time. You spent forty minutes choosing a color for the bakery calendar instead.

"Whoever names the thing that must be done becomes your new problem. The client was greedy until you found the invoice in your drafts. The landlord was neglectful while the pipe dripped under the sink, and you had not sent him the photograph. The plumber cost too much because you waited until the cabinet floor swelled and the door would not close. And yesterday it was me. I yowled through your call because my water dish was empty, and you complained that I always need something at the worst time. You asked me what would make me stop. Water made me stop.

"Four times you asked me whether to sign this guarantee, and four times I said nothing, because a question does not open my mouth. You know that. So this morning you complained about your sister instead, to make me answer, so that whatever you did next would be my advice and not your choice."

"Mizzle, I—"

"You are not cornered." Her tail lashed once across the tabletop. "You are the source of the pressure in this room. Your sister sent soft messages first, and I watched you turn the phone face down on every one. You spent the safe days imagining how trapped you would feel on the last one, and now it is the last one. Her money is at risk because you asked her to risk it and then treated your name as the only expensive part.

"You are a waste. You waste food, work, sleep, favors, money, and every answer you drag out of me. You waste your sister's competence by turning it into rescue. You waste your own talent by keeping it theoretical, where nobody can reject it.

"Perhaps you do not want the bakery. Perhaps you only wanted to be the person who was brave enough to propose one. I do not know. You have hidden so thoroughly behind delay that even you may no longer know. But do not stand over that guarantee, for a shop you talked her into, and tell me your sister built this morning."

Her mouth closed. The refrigerator hummed. Down the hall, a neighbor's door shut.

I realized I was gripping the handle of my mug hard enough to ache.

"That was vicious," I told the mug.

Mizzle's whiskers angled forward. She said nothing.

"The pipe was rotten before I ever moved in, Mizzle. I hate how you turn every bad thing into evidence against me."

"The pipe was rotten," she said. "The soaked cabinet was seven days of you not sending one photograph. I used the examples I have. You selected the one with a rotten pipe and ignored the draft invoice, my empty dish, your sister's six messages, and the paper I was lying on."

"The invoice got paid."

Mizzle blinked at me, slowly.

"It's unfair that you get to decide when something counts as a real complaint."

Mizzle sat down. "You decide that. I only hear it. Your voice changes when you mean it."

I hated that answer partly because I could hear the change she meant. I tried, "Mizzle, the weather is persecuting me," in a tone of theatrical despair.

She began washing her white paw.

"Should I sign?"

The paw passed over one ear.

"You just spent all that time telling me I caused this, and now you won't even tell me how to fix it."

"I will not choose whether you bind yourself to a business," she said.

"Then what was the point of any of that?"

Question. Silence.

I picked up the guarantee. The last page asked for my signature beneath a paragraph stating that I understood what I was undertaking. My sister had placed a yellow tab beside the line. The tab said SIGN. She had once watched me return an unsigned tax form.

"You act like signing is the honest answer," I said. "But I can't stand the idea of being there at five every morning, smelling fryer oil in my hair, smiling at people who say a five-dollar pastry is too expensive. I don't want to spend the next five years pretending the rush is exciting. I don't want it anymore, and that makes this whole thing impossible."

Mizzle stopped washing.

"Then tell her," she said. "Leave out the five years and the fryer oil if you need to. Tell her you do not want it."

"That's easy for you to say. You won't be the one watching her face when she finds out the drawings were for nothing. And maybe in a year, once the build-out was done and I'd had some sleep, I'd want it again, and then I'd have thrown away—" I didn't finish.

Mizzle looked at the guarantee instead of at me. "I cannot see next year. I saw you slide the keys across the floor, and I saw you stop opening the plans. Your sister was not here for the second part."

"So tell me what to do."

Mizzle looked at me for a long moment, then jumped down. I had given her an order, not a complaint. She walked to the bedroom, pushed her head through the door I had left almost closed, and disappeared.

I flattened the signature page over the rest of the packet. My pen was in the key bowl beneath three dead batteries, a grocery receipt, and the brass ring holding the temporary shop keys.

Ninety minutes passed. I read the guarantee twice, opened the bakery projections, and answered no messages.

Signing would have solved the immediate problem. Mizzle could hardly call me a waste with my name on the guarantee, and my sister would have been right to trust me. In a few years the morning might even look like an ugly but useful shove, the kind successful people later thank someone for.

I wrote the first stroke of my name.

Then I saw what I was doing: letting an angry cat choose, only in reverse.

At 10:26, I tore off the corner with the first stroke of my name and printed a clean signature page. At 10:41, I put the guarantee, the two shop keys, and the contractor's revised plan into my canvas bag. I did not send my sister a message saying we needed to talk. I had sent three of those already.

The shop was a forty-minute walk if I cut through the park. I left at 10:47.

Outside, the morning had the chilly brightness of a day that resented coats. Delivery trucks occupied half the curb. At every crossing, I composed explanations in which the estimate had changed, the lease was aggressive, retail was unstable, and my sister had moved too quickly. Every sentence was true enough to be useful. None included the fact that nineteen days ago, while we stood in the empty shop with blue tape marking the counter, I had imagined arriving before dawn and felt not fear but absence, no warm leap at the room becoming ours, only the wish to go home.

I had known then. I had let her order the electrical drawings twelve days ago.

The brass keys knocked against my water bottle all the way there.

My sister was kneeling inside the front window when I arrived. She had a tape measure stretched from the wall to a strip of blue tape on the floor. In the bare room, every sound returned thinner. The previous tenant's sign brackets remained above the window, and flour-colored dust from the ceiling repairs lay in the corners.

She looked at the canvas bag. "Did you sign it?"

"The guarantee puts a lot of exposure on both of us. With the revised build-out, there are concerns that I don't think we've fully—"

"Yes or no?"

Her hand stayed flat on the metal tape.

"No," I said. "I'm not signing. I'm not opening the bakery with you."

The tape snapped into its case. My sister stood.

"How long?"

"It wasn't one moment."

She waited.

The room offered no hum to fill the space, no refrigerator, no neighbor's door. Even the traffic outside seemed sealed behind the glass.

"Nineteen days," I said. "The morning we taped the counter. I knew enough then to tell you."

"Twelve days ago, I paid twelve hundred and eighty dollars for the electrical drawings."

"I thought it might come back."

"Did it?"

"No."

She walked past me and locked the front door, though nobody had tried it. "The holding loss is eighteen hundred if we withdraw before four. After four, it is eighty-four hundred. The back unit was available at eight this morning. It may still be available. It has no front window and no customer seating. I can do wholesale and pickups there."

"You could still do that."

"I could have done it three weeks ago."

"I know."

"Three weeks ago, you let me keep spending."

There was no useful answer. I took the keys from the bag and set them on the sill. She picked them up immediately and put them in her coat pocket.

"I'm sorry," I said.

"All right."

I had prepared answers for anger and for forgiveness.

She took out her phone and called the rental office. Her voice narrowed to dates and square footage. She gave the shop number, asked whether the back unit could still be transferred under the existing application, and listened without looking at me. Once, she closed her eyes. Then she asked for the transfer form before three and said she would return it within half an hour.

When she ended the call, she opened the contractor's plan on the windowsill and drew a line through the front counter.

"They'll transfer sixty-six hundred of the deposit," she said. "They keep eighteen hundred. The smaller unit needs different drawings. The twelve-eighty is gone. Your half of those two losses is fifteen-forty."

"I can pay you Friday."

"Have you looked at your account?"

I had not.

"Then don't give me another date. Check it. Send me a schedule you can keep."

"Okay."

She folded the plan along a line that had not been meant as a fold. "The release will come to your email. Sign it by three. Not four. I'm not using the last hour."

I wanted to ask if she needed help measuring the smaller room, if I should revise the logo, if we could have dinner after this. All three would have let me feel useful before she had asked anything of me. She had already turned back to her phone.

"Do you want me to stay?" I asked.

"No."

At home, Mizzle had pulled one of my socks from the laundry basket and was asleep with her chin on the heel. She opened her eyes when I came in, but she did not get up.

The release arrived at 1:36. I read all four pages. At 1:51, I signed. At 1:53, the portal marked the withdrawal received. My sister replied with two words: Got it.

My bank balance was $2,318.44. Rent and the phone bill would take $1,706. I transferred four hundred dollars to my sister and wrote: First payment toward $1,540. I can send $380 on each of the next three Fridays if the overdue invoice for last month's brochure job clears this week; if it doesn't, I will message Thursday with the revised dates.

The typing box showed that she was answering, stopped, then started again.

Her reply was: I'll hold you to Thursday.

Mizzle came into the kitchen and sat beside her water dish. There was water in it, but a crescent of kibble dust floated along one edge. I emptied it, scrubbed it with the rough side of the sponge, and filled it to the blue line on the bowl. She drank for long enough that the refrigerator motor switched off around us.

While Mizzle drank, I sorted the lecture without asking her help. Rotten pipe: not mine. Seven days without sending the photograph: mine. Higher estimate: not mine. Nineteen days without telling my sister: mine. Her risk: hers. My promise that persuaded her: mine. *Waste* did not belong in either column, so I left it out.

Mizzle finished drinking and looked up at me.

I did not complain to her.

In the bedroom, my laptop still held the half-finished menu layouts for the client whose invoice had been late because I had sent it late. Three options were due the previous Friday. I opened the email I had been avoiding, attached the one complete layout, and wrote that the other two would arrive by ten the next morning. Then I checked the calendar before I sent it.

At 2:17, I set a forty-five-minute timer and began the second layout. Mizzle jumped onto the desk, stepped across the keyboard, and settled on my right forearm.

"You're in the way," I said.

She stayed there. I moved the mouse with my left hand and kept working.

stories.title: The First Call
stories.prompt: The kingdom laughed when a rooster marched to war in battered armor, but years later, when the last surviving soldiers saw an enormous feathered warrior emerge from the burning battlefield with arrows in his back and dawn behind him, they realized the legends had gotten one thing wrong: he had never been anyone’s mascot.
stories.body:
# The First Call

The rooster arrived at first call, marching in the ditch because the king's infantry had filled the road.

He came up no higher than the buckle on an infantryman's boot. Mud darkened his red feathers, and the armor fitted over him in narrow, battered plates: breast, back, shoulders, and two jointed guards that moved when he lifted his wings. Whoever had made it understood both metal and birds. Whoever had last repaired it had used a kettle patch and three kinds of rivet.

The young armorer noticed all that before she noticed the laughter.

“What rank is he?” someone called from the pike carts.

“Dinner.”

“Too stringy.”

The rooster kept pace beside the wheels. He did not startle at the first horn or the stamping horses. When a wagon lurched toward the ditch, he climbed the bank, let it pass, and returned to the firmer ground without breaking stride.

The armorer had been mending a buckler strap on her knee. She put it aside when she saw the loose plate lifting behind his left wing. “Hold there.”

He stopped.

That earned another laugh. A junior officer leaned down from his saddle and knotted a strip of royal blue through the rooster's back plates. “There. Our luck has put on colors.”

The soldiers cheered their new mascot. The rooster reached back, caught the cloth in his beak, and worried it free. He dropped it under the officer's horse.

Even the armorer laughed then. She was nineteen, the army was clean, and nobody had yet taught her how quickly a joke could become an account of what had happened.

She tapped the ground beside her. The rooster stepped over. He watched her hands while she lifted the loose plate, trimmed the kettle patch, and set two proper rivets. There was room under the lame for a finger's breadth of travel, then another hidden fold beneath that. More room than any rooster could need. She tried to open it farther. His beak closed around the leather guard on her wrist—not hard, but exactly.

“All right,” she said. “Only what's loose.”

He let go.

When she finished, he scratched a brass harness ring out of the mud and pushed it against her boot. Then he returned to the verge. He refused the grain tossed after him and marched east while the army's road bent north.

By supper, he had joined them in the story.

* * *

For seven years the rooster appeared at wars that were not quite the one being told about him.

He came to the armorer after the river campaign with a shoulder hinge crushed inward. The king's host had won its ford that day, so the men said their little bird had brought the current down. Yet the grit beneath his plates was white road chalk gone grey with soot, not river sand, and the arrowhead caught in the hinge had the long, dark barb used by the army they had driven east a month before. He paid with a stirrup buckle and left before the victory horns.

He came again during the winter siege. This time three lengths of cage wire had wound around his leg guard. Every strand was cut cleanly in two places. Black pitch glazed his breastplate and smelled of pine instead of the marsh tar used by the king's sappers. The armorer soaked it off, eased the swelling beneath, and showed him the padded strap before she buckled it. He inspected it with one bright eye. At dusk he vanished through a gap under the eastern palisade.

By then there were songs without verses and stories without witnesses. Recruits watched for red feathers before an assault. Drivers swore the rooster could take the first direct light of dawn into his body once, if he chose, and stand higher than a siege tower for nine minutes. Afterward, they said, he was cold enough to frost grass in summer. No two tellers agreed on where they had seen it. The armorer did not believe them, though the folded plates under his ordinary plates began to trouble her.

Belief was less useful than upkeep. She kept narrow rivets in a separate box. She learned how far he would permit her to lift a wing and which touch made him draw away. He learned that she would stop.

The third time, he arrived while she was teaching new hands to sort damaged mail. One shaft through his back plates bore the king's grey-and-blue fletching. Another, lodged along his breast, bore the enemy's black. Neither had reached flesh. The recruits crowded close, delighted by proof that their mascot had fought in the middle of everything.

“Back up,” she told them. “He can't see my hands with your knees in the way.”

She removed both shafts. Beneath them she found ash, more pine pitch, and the fine red dust of the east road. She burnished the plates and sent the recruits to supper with a story about how many arrows their luck could carry.

The rooster did not stay to hear it.

* * *

Seven years after first call, the king's host narrowed to three soldiers beside the east road.

Seven minutes remained before sunrise. Smoke from the ruined camp pressed low over the marsh, turning the causeway ahead into a grey strip that appeared and vanished. Behind them, the royal standard burned in a ditch. Ahead, somewhere past the smoke, harness bells kept ringing and then stopping.

The armorer was a sergeant now. Her last officer had died with one hand hooked in her apron and one order left in his mouth: fire the prepared road before dawn. The enemy's fire wagons, belled like carters' teams, had burned the camp at midnight, and not one of them was to cross the causeway. Nor were the enemy's wounded, scavengers, camp children, stolen animals, or anyone else the smoke might be hiding. The officer had made it sound simple because he did not have enough breath for exceptions.

The scout lay on the bank with his cheek to the wet grass. “Movement. East lip.”

“How many?”

“Four.” He raised two fingers, changed it to three. “Three upright. Something low. No—there's a wheel. Might be two wheels.”

The field surgeon sat against the milestone, binding his own thigh above a deep cut. He drew each breath through his nose before speaking. “If it's the fire wagons, four is enough.”

“Can you make the ridge?” the sergeant asked.

“With a shoulder, perhaps sixty paces. Not quickly. If the bleeding starts again, set me down and leave me.”

The pitch line ran from the roadside jars into reeds beneath the causeway. A slowcord waited in its clay gutter. Once lit, it would give them six minutes to get behind the low ridge, two hundred paces back along the road. The sergeant had a coal nested in her tinder horn and the striker in her fist.

The scout wiped his streaming eyes. “Now five shapes. Or the smoke moved.”

“Pick one.”

“Smoke moved.” He listened. “Bells again. North of them, I think. No marching feet.”

The surgeon pulled the bandage tighter and went pale around the mouth. “The cord takes six. Sunrise is under seven. If you wait until you're certain, the road burns after dawn.”

There was no commander left to ask. There were no reinforcements behind the ridge, only the dead and the westward trail of those who had run before the line broke. The sergeant had spent the night making the last order ready because readiness was a thing her hands could still provide. The jars were uncapped. The reeds were soaked. The cord had been measured twice.

Something rustled below the bank.

The rooster climbed out of the ditch.

He was small as ever, though soot had turned his feathers almost black. The left wing guard hung by one strap. A burn had curled the tips of his tail, and he favored his right foot. Still he hauled himself onto the road and faced the causeway.

The scout gave one exhausted breath that might once have been a laugh. “Knew our luck wasn't dead.”

The rooster walked past him.

The sergeant crouched, already reaching for the broken guard. “Here.”

He stopped beyond her hand. When she showed him the rivet pliers, he looked once at the smoke ahead and stepped around her.

“Not that way.” She moved to block him. “West.”

He left the road, passed through the wet reeds, and returned to it on her other side. His limp made every third step dip. He continued east.

The sergeant struck spark to tinder. The coal caught. She touched it to the slowcord, and a red point began to creep along the gutter.

“Three uprights,” the scout said. “Certain now. It's a handcart. They're pushing it themselves, no horse.”

The rooster entered the smoke.

The red point moved past the first notch cut into the clay. Five minutes.

“Could still be a fire cart,” the sergeant said.

The scout did not answer. He had lowered his head to the roadbed. The surgeon watched the slowcord.

From the smoke north of the causeway's far end came a wooden crack, then a horse's scream. Harness bells scattered into a wild, receding jangle. A fire rose where no fire had been, orange through the grey.

“That was the belled one,” the surgeon said. “Loaded.”

The scout had not lifted his ear from the roadbed. “Handcart's still coming.”

The red point reached the second notch.

The sergeant slid her knife beneath the cord and cut away the burning length. She crushed it under her heel. The unburned end went into her tinder horn beside the coal.

No one asked whether that was a new order.

Beyond the causeway, men shouted in the enemy's hard field cadence. An answer came from farther up the north track in the king's own drill calls. The retreating sappers had left two tar wagons up there, and someone had put a torch to them rather than leave them to the enemy; black tar smoke rolled up beside the orange of the burning pitch. The belled wagon, its horse gone, came on down the track by itself, flames tilting as it gathered speed. It slewed onto the causeway's far end and struck the posts with a crash that shook the reeds.

“That's across the east lip,” the scout said. “Causeway's blocked.”

The sergeant looked first along her own line. The soaked reeds lay under the near end, below her feet; the tar fire was taking the dry stands at the far end, with open water between. She stared into the smoke where the rooster had gone. On her workbench across seven years: white road chalk, black pitch, grey-and-blue fletching, enemy barbs, cage wire cut twice. Damage from both banners, soot or pitch nearly every time, and the dust of roads rather than battlefields.

“Light,” the scout said.

The horizon had opened beneath the smoke. A blade of direct sun lay across the far end of the causeway.

For a moment there was only a small rooster in it.

He stood beside the burning wreck with his injured foot lifted. Light ran red along his neck and flashed in the battered hinges she had repaired. It touched him fully. He did not change. Beyond him, dim figures struggled with the handcart, trapped between the wreck and the tar fire coming down through the reeds.

Then he set his foot down.

His armor opened first. Pins rolled through curved slots. The narrow lames drew apart over hidden bands, each battered patch lifting into its place in a design the sergeant had handled for years without understanding. His body rose inside it. Legs thickened; claws tore furrows in the road; red feathers streamed upward through the smoke. His breast climbed above the wagon roof, then above the causeway posts. When he spread his wings, the air struck the marsh flat, but he did not fly. He braced.

The scout turned the quarter-hour sandglass from his map case. “Nine, wasn't it?”

“If they kept that part straight.”

The rooster drove one armored shoulder against the burning wagon.

The first push failed. A black-fletched arrow struck between the plates on his back. He lurched, caught himself with one wing, and shoved again. Iron screamed along stone. The wagon shifted half its width.

The figures behind it became people: an old man at one handle of the handcart, two younger adults at the other, a child beneath a wet blanket, and a woman dragging a mule whose pack bore scraps of royal blue on one side and enemy black on the other. Loot, laundry, surrender rags—the sergeant could not tell.

More arrows crossed the light. One glanced off a shoulder plate. Two sank into the flesh below his raised wing. They did not grow with him. They remained ordinary arrows, absurdly small against his body and no less harmful. Blood darkened the feathers beneath them.

“Six minutes,” the scout said.

The rooster hooked his beak under the wagon's flaming drawbeam. He pulled backward, step by deliberate step, until one wheel dropped from the causeway into the reeds. Fire crawled up his loosened wing guard. He beat it against the stones, once, twice, keeping his weight on the beam. No magic closed the wounds.

The handcart squeezed through. The old man fell, rose, and pushed again. The mule balked at the rooster's legs; the woman covered its eyes with her sleeve and led it under the shadow of his breast. Last came two limping figures the scout had counted as one. They crossed without thanking anyone. They were still running when the rooster released the beam.

He did not turn toward the charred royal standard. He shoved the wagon one final foot, enough to spill its burning load harmlessly into black water, and sagged against the drawbeam. The shoulder hinge she had mended after the river held; the newer strap beside it had burned through. Only then did he back away down the causeway.

“Four minutes,” said the scout. “He's coming.”

The enormous rooster limped toward them with dawn at his back and three arrows standing from his blood-wet feathers. The stories had put him beside the king's victories because that was where the king's men had happened to see him afterward. Each step brought the road's tremor through the sergeant's boots. At the near end he folded his legs and lowered himself, not gracefully, beside the milestone. Heat rolled off him. His breath came with a low rough click.

The sergeant took one step closer. He drew his wing tight over the arrows.

She stopped.

The surgeon held up both empty hands. His voice was slower now, each word placed around pain. “The shafts stay their size. You won't.” He pointed first to the deepest arrow, then to his forceps. “May we pull this one?”

The rooster watched him. Then he opened the wing far enough to expose the first shaft and laid his beak on the road.

“Three minutes,” the scout said.

The sergeant climbed between the unfolded back plates. The workmanship made sense at this scale: sliding braces, doubled straps, stops that kept metal from biting into living flesh. She cut the shaft short. The rooster's muscles clenched beneath her knees.

“Hold it straight,” the surgeon said. “Not up. Straight.”

She pulled. The rooster struck the stone once with his beak but did not close the wing. Blood followed the arrow. The surgeon tossed up a pad of folded linen, and she pressed it to the wound.

At the second shaft, the sergeant reached too soon. The wing snapped shut, knocking her back a pace.

“Wait,” the surgeon said.

They waited. Smoke moved over the sun, thinning the light but not ending it. The rooster's breathing slowed by one harsh click. He opened the wing again and shifted until the second arrow pointed toward the sergeant's hands.

This one had lodged against a rib. She could feel its angle through the pliers.

“Two minutes,” said the scout. “Little less.”

“Turn it a finger toward me,” the surgeon said.

“He'll bleed.”

“He already is. A finger.”

The sergeant turned and drew. The arrow came free. The rooster's foot gouged four trenches in the road, but his wing remained open until she had packed the wound the way the surgeon told her.

The third shaft sat shallow in muscle. The surgeon showed it to him. The rooster pulled away.

“Leave it,” the sergeant said.

“That one can stay through the change,” said the surgeon. “The deep ones could not.”

The scout knelt by the glass. “Half a minute.”

Heat poured out of the rooster so fast that mist formed over the wet road. The great plates began to settle. The sergeant jumped down. Pins slid back through their slots; bands folded beneath lames; the giant breast sank toward them. At the glass's ninth-minute scratch, a small wounded rooster lay inside armor suddenly too cold to touch barehanded.

The remaining arrow was once again large beside him. It had not moved deeper. Blood still seeped from the two packed wounds. He shivered hard enough to rattle every rivet she had ever set.

The surgeon slumped against the milestone. “Now the shallow one.”

He raised the forceps and waited.

After a moment, the rooster extended his wing.

* * *

They used the unburned slowcord to lash two spear shafts into a litter. The sergeant gave the rooster water in the cup of her palm, then set her wool lining beside him. He stepped onto it only after she moved her hand away.

The scout studied the fork beyond the marsh. “The shouting's gone north with the smoke. Both lots. East branch drops more gently.”

“Water?” the sergeant asked.

“I saw willows. I didn't see water.”

The surgeon eased himself onto the litter. “How far?”

“Two miles. Perhaps three.”

“Call it three.”

The rooster climbed out of the wool. He tested his bandaged foot, crossed to the east branch, and stopped there while they lifted the litter. The sergeant took the heavier end. The scout adjusted his grip twice.

“Ready?” she asked.

“No,” said the surgeon. “Go.”

They went. The rooster kept to the verge, choosing his ground around stones and ash. When the litter fell behind, he waited. When all four were moving again, he continued toward the willows.

stories.title: By Tooth and Threshold
stories.prompt: A few days ago, you saved what appeared to be a very large wolf from a bear trap during a camping trip. Now there's a woman you've never seen before on your doorstep claiming she has a debt to pay.
stories.body:
# By Tooth and Threshold

At 6:14, the knock came while Dev Kaylor was trying to decide whether a trap that size belonged in an evidence bag or under a welding blanket.

Three knocks, evenly spaced. Not a neighbor's knock, and no one he knew would have come around to the mudroom at dusk.

He set the blanket over the steel jaws, though he had wired them open, and wiped his hands on his jeans. Four nights of dried creek mud still clung inside the hinge. He had photographed the trap where he found it, photographed the spring numbers that had been ground away, and then done the stupidest useful thing available: brought it home. For four days it had lain on the pole-barn floor under a feed sack while he read wildlife statutes at night and called nobody. This evening, after unloading fence posts at the lower pen, he had finally carried it up to the house to photograph again under a decent light.

Through the door glass he saw a woman standing beyond the storm door with both hands visible. She was perhaps his age, thirty or a little older, in a rain-dark coat. Her right trouser leg had been cut up the seam and fastened again with safety pins. She kept her weight on the other foot.

Dev left the inner door on its chain.

"Front door's around the house."

"I need the trap you took from the creek."

His hand settled on the dead bolt. "Okay. Who are you? How do you even know I've got a trap? I haven't told anybody. I haven't told the county, and I'm supposed to have told the county."

She looked past him, not into the house but toward the covered shape on the workbench. Dev shifted to block that line.

"Audra Liske." She had to stop for breath before the rest. "You pulled that trap off me four nights ago. I came to pay the debt before the man who set it gets to your door."

"What man? Coming here how? Nobody knows it's here."

"I've been behind his vehicle since the creek. I know how it smells. Four days he's driven your side of the valley, stopping on the ridges to listen with a box in his hand." She glanced toward the lane. "Tonight he turned up your road."

Dev studied her face for the prelude to a smile. None came.

"I pulled it off a wolf."

"You tried the tire iron first. It slipped. You wrapped your left hand in the blue corner of your groundsheet before you touched the second spring. When you got the jaws apart, you moved uphill instead of toward the trail because I was between you and it." She paused to breathe through something. "You left the iron. I pushed it into the creek so he wouldn't find your grip on it."

Only the wolf could have seen the iron go into the water. Dev had assumed the current took it.

"You were huge," he said, and then, because that was no use to anybody, "Show me your hands."

She raised them a little higher. Empty, scraped, trembling at the fingertips.

"Turn around."

"No."

"If you want in—"

She didn't answer that. She took her weight off the bad leg for a second, put it back, and looked at the lane.

He had already asked too much and still had questions stacked behind his teeth: what she was, how a wound got from one body into another, how long she had stood out here deciding to knock.

"There's a transmitter on it," she said. "It clicks, then it sends. When I fought the trap, it clicked every three minutes. When I lay still long enough, it quit." She breathed. "It started again when you carried it in. I heard it from your fence."

"There's no transmitter. I went over the whole thing. I was looking for a tag, a name, a phone number, anything I could hand somebody."

"Look under the swivel housing. I had my face on that chain half a night."

From beneath the welding blanket came a small, hard tick.

Both of them heard it. Audra looked at the watch on Dev's wrist.

"Time it from that."

Dev's thumb found the timer. "I thought that was the freezer." He was already counting back. "So it talked the whole drive home, till I got out of his range. Then it lay in the barn and went quiet. And tonight I carry it into the house and it tells him right where—" He stopped. "Then it doesn't matter what I do with it now. He's got the house."

"Yes."

"So what are you doing here? You said a debt. There isn't one. It was a trap, I had a tire iron, anybody walking that creek would have—"

Audra had turned her head toward the lane before he finished. "I can hear him on your road. That's what I came about."

Dev heard nothing. Then an engine labored somewhere beyond the first rise, too slow for the paved road. He looked through the side window. The lane was still empty, but wet branches beyond the bend showed brief washes of light.

He unhooked the chain and opened the inner door without opening the storm door. "Okay. Mudroom. The kitchen door stays locked, sorry, it just does. This one I'm leaving unlatched. You want out, you push it and go. I'm not shutting anybody in with anybody."

Audra put two fingers to the storm-door latch, pushed it open an inch, and let it fall back against the frame. Then she opened it and stepped over the sill. The cramped room held a boot rack, utility sink, freezer, workbench, and too many tools hung in outlines on the wall. Dev locked the door into the kitchen and put its key in his pocket.

Audra sat on the bench beside the outside door. Up close, her skin had the pale, taut look of pain worked on too long. Blood had dried above her boot.

Dev pulled the blanket off the trap. Its jaws spanned most of the bench. One blunt tooth still held a dark tuft of coarse fur.

"That one," Audra said.

Dev looked at the tooth, then at her leg, and made himself stop comparing them. "I've got a proper kit. Can I get those pins out and cut whatever's under there?"

"Yes." She was already working the top pin loose. "There's a wrap. No alcohol on it."

Dev set the first-aid box within her reach. She took out the scissors and handed them to him, then turned her knee to give him access. The wrap was improvised and dirty. Under it, two deep pressure cuts curved around her lower leg in the same spacing as the jaws on the bench. They had begun bleeding again.

He rinsed with saline only where she pointed, laid clean gauze over the cuts, and stopped when she took the roll from him. She wrapped the leg herself.

The timer showed one minute forty-eight seconds.

"How far is his receiver good for?" Dev asked.

"He climbs to listen. The ridges, not the hollows."

"So farther on open ground. How much farther?"

"I don't know."

"Does it log where it's been, or only where it is? Is it directional? What frequency is it?"

Audra tightened the gauze and shut her eyes for a moment. "I don't know. I only ever heard it from the wrong end."

Dev turned the trap on its wired-open side. Beneath the chain swivel, a black capsule sat inside a shallow steel guard. A braided cable no thicker than a bootlace fixed it to the baseplate.

He reached for the bolt cutters. Audra opened her eyes at the sound of them coming off the wall.

"Not those. They'll crush the case on the plate."

"The cable might be hardened." But he hung them back and took down the small cutters. "I want it in one piece. Sooner or later I'm explaining this to a game warden, and I'd like to have more than a story about a wolf."

He braced the braided cable clear of the capsule and leaned his weight down. The cable parted with a sound like a clipped guitar string.

The capsule came free into his glove. A yellow diode flashed once.

"Still awake," Audra said.

His timer reached three minutes. The capsule ticked in his palm.

Dev dropped it into a galvanized parts can, pressed the lid tight, and nested that inside the steel cash box he used for receipts. He ran a thumbnail along the hinge seam. "Steel might hold it in. Might not." He shut the lid anyway.

The engine went silent beyond the bend.

Dev called emergency services. He gave his address and reported that a man was tracking an illegal steel trap to his house. The dispatcher asked whether he could remain inside. He looked at the trap, at the mudroom's two doors, and at Audra's eyes fixed on the dark glass.

"Not safely," he said.

The nearest response was coming from a long way out. Dev put the phone on speaker and lowered the volume.

Audra tested her leg, winced, and stood. "Give me the box." She waited for the leg to settle. "South, down your draw. He follows it away from the house."

"In which body?"

"The one that can go down the draw without a light."

"On that leg? Carrying his signal?"

"That's what I came for."

Dev pictured the wolf in the creek bed, enormous and silent, lifting a ruined foreleg while he fought the springs. He had spent four days telling himself the animal had understood that he meant help. Now understanding had arrived at his house and was trying to turn itself into bait.

"No," he said.

Audra's face closed.

He caught his own mistake before he could build a fence around it. "I mean I carry the box. It's my address on his receiver now, and I'm the one who wants the evidence. You choose the route."

She watched him for a second. "The draw. It comes out under your lower pen."

"The stock pen." Dev could see it before he'd finished saying it. "Okay. Road gate at the top, off the old stock track. Sorting gate at the bottom. The lane between them's too narrow to turn anything around in. And my pickup's sitting crosswise past the far end, because I unloaded posts there this evening and never moved it. So he drives in after the signal, I shut the road gate behind him, and he can't go forward and he can't back out without tearing something up. We open the box once down there, let it send, he comes to the pen instead of the house, and we keep him there till the sheriff's people show. If he tears the gate out, fine, he does it on camera. On my phone, anyway, propped on a fence post."

"He'll walk the high edge first. The wind's off the road. It comes down the draw to us."

"Then we stay low."

Audra looked toward the lane again. "He has a launcher. And a pole with a wire loop. He used both at the creek after you left."

"On you?"

"He missed. Keep a gate between you and him."

Dev fetched a coil of rope, a gate clip, a headlamp, and his canvas tool bag. He added gauze and water. The pry bar knocked against the wrenches, and Audra flinched each time.

"He'll hear that from the road."

Dev took it back out. She was looking at the open patch of rubber mat. "After I change, I can't talk. One scrape, stop. Two, go. If I hit the fence wire, get behind the nearest gate."

"Go where? Which way is go?"

She touched the outside of his left boot with hers. "I touch the side I want. Don't reach for me."

"How long does it—"

"Seventy seconds. Once it starts it doesn't stop. I can't talk through it, can't hold anything." She touched the new gauze. "Twice inside an hour, this opens up."

Dev looked at the upper windows. "Can you do it now? Can you hurry it?"

"It goes when I start it. Nobody else starts it." She nodded at the mat. "Clear that. Time it, if you want."

Dev moved the cutters, wire ends, and cash box away from the open patch. Audra touched her coat's top button, then left the coat on. She lowered herself to both knees and placed her palms flat.

"Now," she said.

Dev started the timer.

The first changes were small failures of fit: shoulders pressing against cloth differently, fingers losing their workable spread, shoes collapsing as the feet inside them altered. Then the shape of her occupied more floor. Clothing lost its separate edges wherever the body changed, neither tearing nor remaining as something that could snag. Dev had no category that helped. He kept his attention on the timer, the table corners, the freezer latch, anything she might strike.

At thirty seconds she could not have stood as either woman or wolf. At forty-five, the wound opened through a lengthening foreleg, blood darkening the new fur. She made no human sound and could not tell him to move when her hindquarters crowded the boot rack. He moved it anyway, without touching her.

At seventy seconds, exactly, the enormous wolf drew one complete breath. Her coat was rough charcoal along the back and wet-black at the shoulders. The right foreleg hovered above the mat.

Dev stopped the timer. Audra looked at the cash box, then at him, and scraped once.

Stop.

Headlights passed slowly across the upper windows. A door closed near the lane.

When the light moved away, Audra scraped twice.

Dev put the cash box in the canvas bag and took the weight himself.

They left through the mudroom door at 6:54. Audra went first into the draw, placing three feet with care and the fourth barely at all. Dev followed below the lip, bent under wet grass. Twice she touched his right calf and moved him deeper when the wind shifted. Once she scraped, and he froze while a narrow white beam traveled across the yard above them.

The parts can clicked inside the cash box. Muffled, but audible against Dev's hip. He kept both lids shut.

At the cutbank below the old pen, Audra stopped beneath a fringe of hanging roots. The sorting lane lay uphill: wire fence on one side, plank rails on the other, road gate open behind it. Dev's pickup stood crosswise beyond the far gate, precisely where he'd left it, making the lane a pocket with one way in. He had never been so grateful for his own unfinished work.

Audra smelled the air. She touched his left boot.

They climbed on the downwind side.

Dev set the phone against the road-gate post with its camera aimed uphill at approaching vehicles. He tied the rope to the gate, ran it along the fence, and took the free end back to the sorting post. The next pulse was due in twenty-two seconds. He carried the cash box to the feed trough halfway between the gates, opened it, and lifted the parts-can lid with one gloved finger.

Tick.

The yellow diode flashed. Dev sealed both lids and ducked behind the sorting gate.

An engine started above them almost at once.

The setter's utility vehicle rolled down the old stock track without headlights. A pale screen glowed near the steering wheel. As the rear bumper cleared the open road gate, Dev hauled on the coil. The gate swung shut, and he snubbed the line around the sorting post. The vehicle nosed deeper into the lane. Its headlights came on, found Dev's pickup across the far end, and it stopped.

The driver stepped out carrying a short launcher in one hand and a receiver in the other. A loop pole leaned against the open door. Dev could see no part of his face clearly under the brim of his cap.

"Where's my trap?" the setter said.

Dev stayed behind the gate. "Not here. Police are on the way."

"Open the far end."

The receiver gave a sharp electronic chirp. The setter looked toward the trough, then saw Dev's phone on the post. He raised the launcher.

From beneath the plank rail, Audra struck the fence wire.

Dev dropped behind the sorting gate. A dart cracked against his pickup's rear quarter panel and spun into the mud.

The setter took the loop pole and moved along the vehicle's side. "Down," he said toward the dark beyond the rails. "Stay down."

Audra emerged inside the pen, broad enough to fill the space between two posts. She did not change back. The command did nothing except fix the setter's attention on her.

He thrust the loop through the rails.

Audra gave ground until the cable ring passed her muzzle. Then she turned under it, caught the aluminum shaft behind the loop in her teeth, and wrenched sideways. The pole slid through the setter's hands. She dragged it low across the gatepost, feeding the loose cable into the narrow angle above the bottom hinge.

One scrape.

Dev stopped with his hand on the gate.

Audra shifted her bite farther down the shaft. The cable tightened around the hinge pin instead of her neck.

Two scrapes.

Dev pulled. The sorting gate swung its remaining foot and pinned the pole against the post. Aluminum folded. The cable snapped back into the rails and stayed there, kinked beyond use.

Audra released the shaft. Blood ran along her lifted foreleg, but she did not cross the fence toward the setter.

The setter dropped the ruined pole and reached for the launcher. Dev shouldered the sorting gate back open. Its edge struck the launcher from the setter's hand and knocked it beneath the plank rail, inside the pen.

For a moment the setter had the receiver and nothing else. Sirens carried faintly above the wet fields.

He got back into his vehicle.

"Don't," Dev said, seeing the reverse lights.

The vehicle accelerated backward. Its rear bumper caught the closed road gate, bowed it, then tore the upper hinge out of the post. The gate fell under the tires. The vehicle fishtailed onto the stock track and climbed toward the road with one rear light broken.

Audra could have cleared the fallen gate before it reached the rise. Instead she stood beside the disabled loop, watching until the engine faded.

The receiver lay in the lane where it had fallen from the open door. The launcher lay inside the pen with a spare dart beside it, and the spent one was somewhere in the mud by his pickup. Dev took his phone off the road-gate post and left the rest where it was for the responders.

Audra touched his left boot and headed down into the draw.

Under the cutbank, out of sight of the lane, she lowered herself onto the grass. Dev checked his watch. Thirty-six minutes had passed since her first change.

She looked at the road, then at the right foreleg. Before he could ask, she lowered her nose between her paws, and the change back began.

Dev set the timer and cleared the canvas bag away. He could do nothing during the seventy seconds but keep the ground open and listen to the sirens grow. The body contracted through shapes that had no stable balance. At fifty seconds the wound bled faster. At seventy, Audra lay curled on her side in her restored coat and clothes, breathing in shallow pulls.

When she opened her eyes, fever had put a bright, unfocused sheen in them.

"Second change inside an hour," she said. "Bleeding. Pain. Fever. Water."

Dev opened the tool bag. "Can I wrap it now?"

"Over the first. Keep the knee free."

He did. Her skin was hot even through his gloves. She took three measured swallows from the bottle and refused a fourth by turning her face away.

"You don't owe me anything after this."

Audra pulled the cut trouser seam closed over the new bandage and fumbled a pin through it. "Good. I'm tired of owing you."

He wanted to know where she would go, who would look at the leg tomorrow, whether she could get far enough before the fever climbed.

"Which route?"

"South down the draw." She shut her eyes and opened them again. "Their lights stay up on the road."

"Can you make it?"

She put her weight on the leg and tested it. "Give me six minutes before they come down to the gate."

Dev gave her the six. He went back to the mudroom and photographed the separated trap where it lay. He packed his laptop, medication, lease papers, and two changes of clothes into a duffel. The setter had his address whether the transmitter ever sent again. Dev would give a statement, preserve the evidence, and sleep somewhere else.

At 7:44, the first wash of emergency lights reached the upper trees. Dev switched on the yard floodlights and aimed every bright angle toward the broken pen. Below them, unseen from the drive, grass whispered along the draw and then went still.

The gate would need a new post. His pickup's side panel bore the dent from the dart. Audra's blood marked the mudroom mat and the lower fence. Dev added the damaged gate and truck to the notes on his phone, left the wired-open trap uncovered on the bench, and went out with empty hands when the first response vehicle came through.

stories.title: What She Remembered of Peace
stories.prompt: You've taken in an android that was originally built for war to prevent her from being scrapped. You rehabilitated her, gave her a home, and taught her how to integrate in peacetime society. Now with a new war at your doorstep and the world collapsing around you, she draws on old programming.
stories.body:
# What She Remembered of Peace

Olyne had the kitchen latch spread across a towel when every loose spoon in the drawer chimed.

Anvek stopped turning the stripped screw. Her head tilted, not toward the window but toward something farther away. The pulse was too low for Olyne to hear. She felt it afterward in her molars, a pressure that had crossed the district and gone on searching.

“Ranging burst,” Anvek said. Two of her fingers had gone to the access plate beneath her collarbone. “Military pattern. It flagged the sealed library.”

“Is it open? Anvek, is it open?”

“No.”

The impact came three breaths later. The building dropped beneath their feet and returned crooked. Plaster burst from the wall above the sink. Anvek caught the shelf before the jars could fall, while Olyne caught only the towel and flung screws across the floor.

Outside, glass went down the street in a long bright crash. Then the networks died: wall display, emergency strip, Olyne’s handset, all at once.

She was already making the list. Fifth-floor couple. The baker with the stiff knee. Gess in the roof room. The four from the divided flat, one of whom slept through alarms. Eleven neighbors if everyone had come home before the sirens.

Anvek set the shelf down. “The shelter is two terraces below us.”

“You stay here.”

“No.”

“That pulse was looking for things built like you.”

“Yes.” Anvek took the ring of utility keys from its hook and gave Olyne the small brass one for the radio cabinet. “Start on five. I’ll check the stair.”

“Anvek, you don’t need that library to help me knock on doors.”

“I haven’t opened it.”

Anvek put on the canvas work jacket she wore for dirty repairs. The right cuff still carried blue paint from a peaceful week spent repainting balcony rails. Olyne followed her into the corridor because the only other choice was to waste time insisting she had authority she did not possess.

The independent technicians had done the real work at Anvek’s request: severed the receiver through which a remote officer could once have forced her body, recalibrated senses tuned past endurance, restored voluntary task selection without wiping memory or temper or preference, and sealed the combat library behind that plate instead of cutting it out. Olyne had sat outside their workshop with bad tea and three forms she was not authorized to sign. Later she had taught Anvek which buses lied about their schedules, how much apology a landlord deserved, and why the market saved bruised pears for the end of day.

They collected eight people before Gess Miro came down from the roof room with two more and a fistful of master keys. Her gray hair was full of dust. She kept the keys in her left hand, the one that closed properly, and announced, “Eleven. I had eleven and I have eleven.”

“You have ten behind you,” Olyne said.

“I’m eleven.”

Olyne checked faces anyway: the baker breathing through his sleeve, the couple from five in outdoor shoes and nightclothes, four from the divided flat, the washerwoman, the quiet man from the corner flat, the neighbor Gess had rousted from a ground-floor room after the first impact, and Gess herself. Eleven.

The emergency stair door stood open. Beyond it, concrete dust sifted through darkness.

Gess shook the keys. “Stair goes to the lower terrace. Fire door held. We use the stair.”
