“Give me those.”

“You drafted my life after Father, and you were going to mention it when?”

“When there was something to mention.”

“A murdered king might qualify.”

The rite keeper quietly took the silver dish to the far cabinet. My sister reached for the packet, but I held it away.

“If it’s me,” she said, each word clipped clean, “the council will try to keep you here as the next heir. If it’s you, they will try to call your training undignified. I was closing both arguments.”

“You cannot close every argument before the rest of us know we’re in one.”

“Apparently I cannot close this one at all.”

The door opened. One of our father’s attendants stood there with a covered cup.

“The king’s medicine,” she said. “He asked for both of you.”

It was an ordinary sentence. The cup rattled against its saucer in her hands.


We found him in his private room, halfway between the window and the bed.

He was standing only because one hand gripped the curtain cord and the other braced against a table. The physician knelt beside an open case, laying out bottles. Father’s breakfast composure had come apart with his clothes: his collar hung loose, sweat darkened his undershirt, and every breath stopped before it was finished.

My sister dropped the packet. Papers skated under the bed.

“Don’t lift him under the arms,” the physician said. “Support his back. Both of you.”

We obeyed. My sister took most of his weight because she always did; I shoved pillows behind him and knocked one of the medicine bottles over. The physician caught it before it rolled off the table.

“Blue cup,” she said.

The attendant passed it to me.

“Two mouthfuls. Slowly.”

Father drank because I held it to his lips. A thin line escaped into his beard. I wiped it with my sleeve, angry at the medicine, the beard, the hand that had begun to shake in mine.

When his breathing eased, the physician checked his pulse again.

“Tell them,” Father said.

She looked at him. “All of it?”

“There seems little profit in fractions now.”

My sister had gone very quiet.

The physician pulled the chair close to the bed but remained standing. “The scaffold accident last year crushed the king’s chest. The injury was fatal.”

I waited for a second sentence to make the first one sensible.

“He came home,” I said.

“Yes.”

“He recovered.”

“No.”

My father closed his eyes.

The physician continued in the same measured tone she used when telling a patient that a fever had broken or a finger could not be saved. “The coronation working suspended the consequence of the injury while he remained the seated ruler. It gave his body an interval. It did not repair what happened.”

The throne. Not a mind, the rite keeper had said. Not a chooser. A worked mass of black stone beneath a canopy, waiting in a room we visited twice a year for ceremonies we disliked.

“How long?” my sister asked.

“No case in the medical archive passed eighteen months. His pain and weakness have accelerated for six weeks. After this morning, I cannot promise him even another full day of the interval.”

My sister began at once. “Can the working be renewed? Can another living practitioner supply it? Can he resign without transfer? What if the office is divided, or placed in trust, or—”

“No,” the physician said.

The word stopped her.

“A direct heir must freely accept the office,” the physician went on. “The heir sits, takes the ruler’s hand, and speaks acceptance. The support ends when the office passes. What follows is the original injury.”

Kill the seated king for his throne.

I looked at Father. “You knew what the prophecy meant.”

“I suspected.”

“At breakfast, you knew.”

“Yes.”

“And you passed the marmalade.”

His face tightened, whether from pain or shame I could not tell. “It needed passing.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No. It is what I did while I failed to answer.”

My sister stooped to gather her papers. She sorted them on the carpet: regency, tax limits, college, survey. Her hands moved faster than they needed to.

“Why did you hide this?” she asked.

Father looked toward the physician.

“Not her decision,” he said. “Mine. At first I thought there would be time to heal by ordinary means. There wasn’t. Then I thought knowing my pain would force one of you to choose before you could tell duty from fear.”

“So you let us think you were getting better.”

“Yes.”

“You lied.”

“Yes.”

She waited for the gentle qualification he usually found, the comparison to pruning a diseased branch or holding a frightened horse’s bridle. None came.

I asked, “Why aren’t you afraid?”

“I am afraid of hurting you. I am afraid you will punish each other afterward. I am not afraid of the stair happening again.” He opened his eyes and looked at us both. “I remember it. I know what follows. I am tired, and I want this interval to end tonight.”

My sister’s stack slipped sideways. “Then I’ll do it.”

“No,” I said.

She did not look at me. “I am the elder. The instruments already assume—”

“The instruments you wrote.”

“They follow the likely challenge. The council will accept my succession faster. Your college place can be protected by charter. I can appoint—”

“Listen to yourself.”

“I am trying to solve the immediate problem.”

“By becoming the answer before I can speak.”

“Then speak.”

I had nothing. That was the old trick between us: she ran ahead and built the bridge, and I criticized the shape after crossing.

Father pressed a hand against his side. The physician bent to him, but he shook his head.

“Neither of you owes me this,” he said. “And I will not rank your futures to make it easier.”

“You just said you want it tonight,” I said.

“I do.”

“That makes it ours to refuse and yours to suffer.”

“Yes.”

His literal answers were worse than reassurance. They left the choice where it was.


The physician gave us one hour before the next dose, though I suspected she had chosen the interval because a family needed a number to push against.

My sister went to have the throne chamber cleared. I stayed until Father slept, or pretended to. The attendant replaced his damp shirt, and I lifted him while she drew the clean one down his back. We discussed sleeves and buttons. The attendant asked whether he wanted the window latched. The physician counted drops into the blue cup. For ten minutes no one said prophecy, throne, death, or love.

His body said enough. Even asleep, he guarded each breath. When the clock shifted by a quarter hour, he opened his eyes as if the small sound had struck him.

“Is there anything you want?” I asked.

“My grey blanket. The blue one scratches.”

I found the grey blanket in his study, folded across the couch beneath my sister’s travelling coat.

She stood at the writing desk with her spring survey map rolled beside her. The western coast spread across the top sheet: soundings, inlets, a line of proposed beacons. In the corner, she had drawn three alternative routes around a reef. Of course she had.

“The chamber is empty,” she said. “I dismissed the court, guards, musicians, witnesses beyond the rite keeper. We can have the physician close enough without placing her inside. I checked the transfer wording against two reigns and the original stone inscription. There are three clear stops before acceptance. If I take the office, the council can meet at dawn. If I die before appointing—”

“Stop.”

She rolled the map too tightly. It bent near the eastern cape.

“I need to know this is correct.”

“You need to know every consequence except what it costs you.”

“I know what it costs.”

“Say one thing, then.”

“This is not helped by—”

“One thing you wanted next spring.”

She stared at the map.

“The western survey,” I said. “Did you want it?”

“Yes.”

“Was it an escape?”

“Partly.”

“From Father?”

“From being first.” She smoothed the bent corner with her thumb. “First into the council room. First asked when he coughs. First named in every plan. First expected to say it’s manageable.”

Her voice lost its edges. She turned away and tried to tie the map. The cord missed her fingers once, twice.

“I can take it,” she said.

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

“I know.”

Then she had no next option. The silence frightened me more than her columns had.

I laid the grey blanket on the desk. “I keep making you choose, then hating you for choosing.”

“Sometimes you hate me before.”

“Sometimes you make it easy.”

Her breath hitched into something that was not quite laughter. She sat on the couch and put her face in her hands.

I wanted her to tell me what to do. The wanting was so familiar I nearly mistook it for love.

Instead I picked up the blanket.

“I’m taking this to Father.”

She lowered her hands. “Then what?”

“I don’t know yet.”


Father was awake when I returned. I spread the grey blanket over him, tucked it around his feet, and sat beside the bed until the hour ran out.

I thought of the physicians’ college: the basement rooms that smelled of vinegar and boiled linen, the anatomy lectures I had fought to attend, the patients who did not care which chair my ancestors had occupied. I wanted the work. Her western coast did not cancel my basement wards.

I thought of Father’s hand steadying a child’s bowl at breakfast, Father listening to petitions until his ankles swelled, Father quietly removing onions from my plate even after I was old enough to do it myself. He had not become a mechanism when the throne kept his heart moving. His fear, secrecy, pain, and poor decisions were his. So was his request.

If neither of us acted, he would suffer. My sister would keep preparing to act until preparation wore her down into consent. I would keep objecting and leave her hand as the only one visible in the record.

Her regency drafts had protected courses and commissions. None made a place for Father’s next breath.

When the medicine clock rang, I stood.

Father watched me. “Have you decided?”

“I have.”

“Your sister?”

“Has her own decision.”

He nodded once.


The throne chamber looked smaller without the court in it.

No banners hung from the gallery. The candle stands had been pushed against the walls, leaving the black stone chair alone on its low platform. It was broad through the arms and worn pale along the front edge by generations of ceremonial hands. Nothing stirred around it. Nothing called.

My sister waited at the platform with our father’s other arm around her shoulders. She had brought him by the short passage and left her survey coat behind. When she saw me, she searched my face with the same concentration she had given the forecast.

“I’ll do it,” she said.

“I know.”

“There is still time.”

“Yes.”

I went to Father and took his weight from her. For a moment the three of us stood badly tangled at the foot of the throne, adjusting hands and elbows.

“Your foot,” my sister said.

“I know where my foot is.”

“It’s on my hem.”

I moved it. She freed her skirt and guided Father onto the low stool beside the throne. He breathed with his eyes closed until the spasm passed.

Then he said, “The first stop is before you sit.”

My sister stepped between me and the chair. “Why you?”

Not an accusation. She had run out of plans and needed a fact.

“Because I’m choosing it.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“It’s the one I have.” I touched her sleeve. “Move.”

She caught my wrist. “Not to free me.”

“Not only.”

“Not because you think I can’t bear it.”

“I know you can.”

Her grip tightened. Then she let go and stepped aside.

I sat.

The stone was cold through my clothes. No crown descended. No hidden voice tested my heart. The room remained a room, and my father remained alive on the stool to my left.

“Second stop,” he said. “Before you take my hand.”

I looked at him. “Do you still want this?”

All his gentle evasions were gone. “Yes.”

I reached down. His palm was warm, the fingers dry. He closed them around mine.

The contact ran through the stone beneath me—not a thought or judgment, only a gathered pressure answering two living bodies and the office between them. The pressure held, incomplete.

“Last stop,” Father said. “You may release me and rise.”

My sister knelt in front of him. He set his free hand against her cheek. She covered it with both of hers.

I could hear the physician moving once beyond the closed side door, and courtiers shifting much farther away in the passage. Waiting for a ruler. Waiting for a death. They were the same wait now.

Father looked from my sister to me. “I am ready.”

I held his hand and said, “I accept the office.”

The pressure entered me as heat, then weight: not wisdom, not desire, but every claim the throne made on the body that held it. Beside me, Father drew one startled breath. His shoulders folded.

My sister caught him before he struck the stone.

I left the throne at once and knelt with her. Acceptance had completed the transfer; standing could not undo it.

Father’s hand remained in mine. The physician came through the side door, listened, checked, and after a little while stopped checking.

My sister pressed her forehead to Father’s sleeve. I sat beside them with the throne’s new weight moving quietly through my pulse.


Near midnight, the medicine clock rang in Father’s room.

The court was still waiting beyond the long doors for me to receive them. The physician had taken Father’s body to be washed. My sister and I went instead to stop the clock.

The blue cup stood ready on its saucer. She picked it up, carried it to the basin, and paused.

“Do you want me to speak to them?” she asked.

Once, she would already have drafted the words.

I took the cup from her and rinsed the bitter medicine from it before it could dry around the rim. My hands shook. She held the basin steady, saying nothing.

“Come with me,” I said when the cup was clean.

She set the basin down. “All right.”

We left the medicine clock silent and went to open the doors.

stories.title: A Darkness Written Under Skin
stories.prompt: Everyone in the world is born with a tattoo. The tattoo can be made from any kind of ink-like fluid and creates various possible abilities. You are the first to be born without one. Or so they thought until a black light was shined on you.
stories.body:
# A Darkness Written Under Skin

"Keep it flat," the practitioner said. "You've moved twice."

You flattened your palm on the dye table. The wood was cold despite the steam that had lived in the workroom all night. Under your wrist, old stains made a dull geography: madder red in the knife cuts, walnut brown around a peg hole, one thumb-shaped island of blue that your mother claimed had been there before you were born.

The practitioner drew a glass rod through the vial meant for tomorrow's graft. The ink climbed after it in a gray thread, neither dripping nor quite holding. A good match, she had said twice already. Your mother still watched the gray thread as if it might answer something.

"Three days or five?" she asked. Her sleeves were rolled above the red-lake whorls at her elbows. Whenever she flexed her hands, the marks darkened and the damp cloth hanging behind her stopped bleeding color into color. "The clinic gave me both."

"Three if you sit still for a living. Five for the vats." The practitioner touched the thread to a square of test paper.

"Five," your mother said, and pulled the aftercare sheet closer.

Your younger brother snorted from the other end of the table. He had been told to hold the black-light inspection lamp and had spent the last ten minutes trying its violet beam on everything except the vial. White lint flared on his shirt. A smear of soap shone along the basin. His own birth mark, a loop of amber resin running from palm to forearm, disappeared under the strange light instead of brightening.

"The soap's glowing," your brother said.

The practitioner held out her empty hand. He took another look at the basin before bringing the lamp back over the table.

Every child was born carrying some ink-like fluid in a pattern beneath or across the skin. Soot, resin, metal suspended in oil, substances with no names outside the families who passed them down: the fluid varied, and the pattern shaped the faculty. No one before you had been found empty.

The practitioner lifted the paper. The artificial ink had spread into a narrow fork and stopped within the chalk ring. Tomorrow, under numbing salve, she would feed it into channels cut shallowly along your inner arm. Months later, if your body accepted it, the graft would let you hold a chosen color steady while you worked: no drift in the bath, no pale seam where cloth folded against itself. Not the broad, effortless command your mother's birth tattoo gave her. Something narrower. Something reliable. Something yours because you had signed for it and saved for it and spent six years saying you did not need it before admitting that you wanted it.

"Here," the practitioner said, tapping the test paper.

Your brother aimed it at the paper. His wrist bumped yours.

Violet light spilled across your hand.

The practitioner's glass rod halted against the paper.

At first you thought the gray graft ink had splashed. A black-violet stroke lay beneath the skin of your wrist, so dark it seemed cut into the bone. It curved once around the tendon. Fine branches broke from it and vanished at the edge of the beam.

Your brother moved the lamp.

The line moved with the light, appearing ahead of it and going invisible behind.

"Wait," the practitioner said.

"What?" your mother asked.

"Don't move the light."

"I'm not." Your brother's voice had risen. The beam shook over your hand. The buried line trembled with it, now black, now bruised purple. "I didn't spill anything."

"Spill what?" your mother said.

"The stand," the practitioner said. "Put the lamp in."

No one did.

You took your hand off the table. The practitioner reached after it. You pulled your arm out of reach.

"Don't," you said.

Her hands stopped in the air. You turned your wrist yourself.

At last your brother obeyed. The workroom changed under the fixed violet glow. Detergent flashed in the grain of the table. The boiled linen around the graft tools became painfully white. Where the light found your forearm, the hidden stroke divided and divided again, fine as frost under a windowpane, except frost lay on a surface and this did not. You turned your arm. The pattern turned inside it.

Your mother came around the table, passed you, and slid the bolt across the workroom door.

"Turn it off," she said.

"Not yet."

The refusal surprised you. All your life other people had leaned closer to the absence, as if enough attention might produce what they expected. Now there was finally something to look at, and your mother wanted darkness back. You held your arm nearer the lamp.

"Anyone could come down."

Your brother stared at your lit skin. "Does it hurt?"

You did not know whether he meant the line, the light, or finding it. "No."

The practitioner slid the graft vial away from the beam and stoppered it. She bent close to the light without reaching for you.

"Could the lamp have made it?" your mother asked.

The practitioner looked up at her. "I don't know what it is."

"Turn it off," you said.

The practitioner reached past the stand and clicked the switch. Ordinary yellow lamplight returned. Your skin was bare. Not faded, not pale: bare, as it had been in every mirror and every examination room of your life.

You rubbed your thumb over the place. Nothing rose under it.

The practitioner took a fresh cloth and held it up where you could see. "Water."

You kept your wrist against your chest. She poured from the covered pitcher into a clean bowl and waited. At last you laid your arm on the table. The cloth passed over your wrist once, cool and rough. No color came away. Under violet light, the line returned with the same branches.

The practitioner put a clear glass plate between the lamp and your arm. The pattern remained. She nodded toward your other wrist. You gave it to the light. More black-violet lines rose there, thinner but unmistakable. At the bend of your elbow, the pattern climbed past your rolled sleeve.

"Enough," you said.

She switched the lamp off at once.

The practitioner drew the dark cloth around the graft vial.

"Why are you packing it?" you asked.

"I'm not putting new ink through that."

"Tomorrow?"

She shook her head. The graft had been mapped for tissue everyone believed empty. Whatever lay under your skin turned every shallow channel into a crossing she had not planned.

You had spent months saving for tomorrow. Now the morning coach would leave without you, and the cancellation made no sound beyond the stopper pressed into the vial.

For weeks you had measured tomorrow in clean bandages and coach times. You knew which hand would lift the kettle, how long you could sleep without rolling onto the new channels, which vat you would try first when they healed. None of that preparation had included wanting the graft after someone found the thing you were supposed to have wanted instead.

"Thank God," your mother said.

"Don't."

"I didn't mean—"

"I wanted it," you said.

She had called you whole at clinic counters, at school meetings, in the kitchen after relatives tried to be kind. Now the edge of the aftercare sheet collapsed between her fingers.

"I know." She folded the aftercare sheet across the middle, missed the crease, and folded it again.

Behind her, a drop fell from the draining cloth into the stone trough. Then another.

"Can you tell what it does?" your brother asked.

"Couldn't tell you."

Your brother rubbed his palm. "That winter the wall froze. When you slept in my bed."

"What about it?"

"I couldn't warm your feet. Not properly. I thought you were kicking it away."

"You were eight."

"Nine. And you did kick."

Your mother looked sharply at the practitioner. "The stitches. The pain-worker kept saying you were fighting her."

"I remember the stitches," you said.

"And the naming oil," she went on. "It wouldn't stay on you. Then the fever—"

"The kettle burned me," you said.

The burn had blistered two of your fingers for a week. Your mother looked at your hand as if it had interrupted her.

"That was boiling water."

"I know."

Your brother looked at you. "Did mine work? Other times, I mean."

"Sometimes."

"Sometimes?"

The practitioner set the unused graft tools back into their case, piece by piece. Their little metal mouths clicked against the felt.

"Try it now," you said.

"No," your brother said.

You held out your hand anyway.

"I burned the cuff."

Until tonight he had told that story as a joke, changing whether the iron or the stove took the blame. Now he kept his thumb over the singed place as though it had become evidence against him.

"You said the iron did that," your mother said.

"I don't know what did it."

"You use your mark in the setting bath every day."

"That's cloth."

"Please," you said.

He looked at your hand, then rubbed his amber-marked palm hard against his trousers.

The practitioner sat opposite him and offered her palm. "On me first."

His amber loops darkened. Nothing came from them on their own. He drew a breath, pressed his fingers into hers, and warmth spread a pink flush up her hand.

"That's enough."

He let go. The practitioner rubbed her thumb across the warmed center of her palm, then moved out of your place at the table.

You put your palm against his. His skin was clammy.

"Your hand's freezing," he said.

"Start."

The amber deepened. Warmth flowed into your palm, as ordinary-seeming as sun through a window, then climbed to your wrist. You had expected resistance and found none. The surprise loosened something in your shoulders.

"Oh," you said.

"Too much?"

You shook your head. Warmth was still moving toward your wrist when the practitioner tapped the table at five. Your brother released you, looking relieved.

"Again," you said. "With the lamp."

"You felt it."

"I want to see."

The practitioner fitted the lamp into its stand. Black-violet branches appeared through your hand and ran up beneath your cuff. "Same hand," she told him.

You remembered the pain-worker leaning over your split chin when you were eleven, her blue mark open across her throat, telling you to stop fighting the quiet she was offering. You had not known how to stop. You had only known you did not want her inside your hurt while she spoke as if your fear were disobedience.

Not him, you reminded yourself. The warmth.

You set your feet under the table. You watched the amber lines in his palm. When he touched you, you imagined a door you had never seen and made no picture of closing it. You simply held the edge of yourself where it was.

His mark darkened.

Pressure. Damp skin. No warmth.

Under the violet light, the lines within your palm drew tight around each place his fingers met yours. They did not flare or reach for him. They held.

Your brother swallowed. "I'm doing it."

"Don't force it," the practitioner said.

"I'm not." His fingers tightened anyway. "It's warm on my side. It's just—"

He tore his hand away before five and tucked it under his opposite arm.

"I didn't want it," you said.

He looked at you.

"The heat," you said.

"I know."

He said it too quickly and did not offer his hand again. The places where his palm had pressed yours cooled in separate damp patches.

The practitioner leaned toward the dark lines. "Again."

"No," you said.

"They said no," your mother said.

The practitioner looked at you as if she had only just heard herself. Then she switched off the lamp.

Your brother fetched the little tin cup from beside the sink and held it between both palms. His amber loops darkened before he seemed to notice. The metal gave a soft tick.

He set it down too quickly. You moved it away from the edge of the table.

Heat entered your fingertips. Nothing beneath your skin answered it.

Your brother watched you put the cup down. Whatever had failed between your palms, it had not been warmth itself.

Afterward your brother tucked his hand under the other arm again.

Your mother reached for the inspection lamp. "The paper's upstairs. We take both to the registry."

"Leave it."

"They'll say we changed something. They'll say the lamp was wrong, or you moved, or—"

"I'm not going to the registry."

"You have to go somewhere."

"The clinic. For the appointment."

"And after?"

"I don't know."

She let go of the lamp. "It has already been twenty years."

You had no answer that would make twenty years shorter. Your mother pressed one fingertip after another against her thumb, making a count only she understood.

"I kept every receipt," she said. "Every stupid little bottle they told us to try."

Your brother rubbed his hidden palm against his trousers. "You said you didn't want it."

"The heat."

"I heard you."

"Then what?"

He picked at a loose thread on his cuff. "Nothing."

You wanted to tell him the first warmth had felt like relief. By the time the words arrived, he was worrying the thread loose, and saying them would have sounded like another correction.

The practitioner opened her case, took out the blank morning form, and wrote while the three of you watched. She turned it for you to read. Existing channel structure suspected. Planned graft contraindicated pending consultation. No claim about faculty. No description of the lamp.

"Does it have to say existing?" you asked.

"If it doesn't, they'll send another vial."

"Nothing about the lamp."

She drew a line through the blank space below the note.

You signed beneath her note. Your hand shook only when the pen left the paper.

Your mother noticed. "You've got ink."

A black smear from the pen crossed the side of your thumb. She set the damp cloth beside your hand. You wiped the ordinary ink away yourself.

Across the table, your brother busied himself wrapping the cold inspection lamp in its frayed cord. He made a knot too tight, picked at it, and finally left it tangled.

The practitioner packed the sealed graft vial in ice for return to the clinic. Your mother covered the unused aftercare food and put the kettle back on the stove. Nobody suggested waking the house.

The bolt stayed across the workroom door. Each time a floorboard sounded overhead, your mother looked up, but she did not move toward it.

By the time gray morning reached the high windows, the workroom looked almost ready for an ordinary day. Tools cased. Cloth folded. Consultation form tucked inside your coat. The tin cup had cooled beside the form; you carried it to the sink with the other dishes.

Your brother switched off the lamp at the wall, though it had already been dark for half an hour.

stories.title: The Night Harvest
stories.prompt: Out of the blue, monsters appeared in our world. They appear at night, never seem to run out. A whole industry to profit off their corpses start to appear. One day, odd people start to appear as well. They barely communicate, and only seem interested in fighting and kill these monsters.
stories.body:
# The Night Harvest

The first stranger ruined forty-three crowns' worth of lamp-grade throat node before Brelva could get off the weighing platform.

She knew the value because she had just chalked it on the carcass board. Two nodes, no punctures, good color, vibration holding north-northeast. The creature that had grown them lay across the intake rails with its six legs trussed and its wet hide steaming in the cold. Three months ago, people had screamed at the sight of such a thing. Now a hook crew was arguing over who had misplaced the small gut knife.

The stranger vaulted the rail.

She was lean beneath a patched coat of plates, her black hair hacked short. Her long blade had opened the monster below its jaw. Before Brelva could call to the guards, the woman set an iron wedge between the paired swellings in its throat and struck once with her hand.

Both nodes cracked.

Blue fluid ran into the sawdust. The faint tremor under Brelva's palm stopped.

“Forty-three,” Brelva said.

Perren, who had been holding the tally slate, looked at the ruined nodes and then at the woman. “You think she takes crowns?”

“She can take the consequence.” Brelva stepped down. “You. Those were ours.”

The stranger stared at her. Rain ticked on her shoulder plates. Gray monster ash filled the seams, and three healed cuts crossed the woman's cheek.

Brelva pointed to the chalkboard, then the nodes, then held out her hand.

The woman answered with a low cluster of sounds that had no edge Brelva could catch. She lifted one broken node. Its inner membrane, thin as an onion skin, shivered in the night air. She pointed along the north road, where the monster's living throat had faced when the hook crews brought it in. Then she pointed at the cold shed behind Brelva.

“Yes, we store them there,” Brelva said. “Very observant.”

Perren touched her elbow. “Brelva.”

Beyond the north lamps, something gave a long, hollow cry.

The stranger dropped the membrane into a brazier. It curled, flashed green, and went still. She tapped the dead flesh, pointed toward the cry, and then laid two fingers against the hard-packed ground between them.

One relation at a time. Flesh. Road. Ground.

Brelva understood none of it.

The stranger did not wait. She went over the rail again and ran north, coat plates clattering out of time with the rain.

The intake supervisor arrived after the lamps had been shuttered and the hook crew sent after the cry. He crouched over the blue stain with both hands tucked into his sleeves.

“Purchased batch,” he said.

“Ours until you pay it,” Brelva said.

“Purchased on the contract. Ruined on my floor. Your account will show the damage.”

Perren scraped sawdust over the stain with his boot. “Our account already shows an axle, two wheels, and a cart bed that leaks when it rains.”

“Then don't let foreign scavengers onto the rail.”

“I was grading,” Brelva said. “Your guards were eating.”

From behind the brine shed came the embarrassed clink of a spoon against a bowl.

The supervisor closed his eyes. “They get twenty minutes for supper.”

“They took twenty-four.”

“Then I will purchase four minutes back from the dead nodes.” He rose, knees cracking. “Forty-three crowns deducted. Bring me three full loads before sixth night and the cart is clear.”

Brelva looked at the chalkboard. Three loads meant no short routes, no turning back because the dark sounded busy. It meant the marsh road, where their partners had died in the second week.

Perren set the slate under his arm. “We'll bring them.”

Brelva said, “Two full, one mixed.”

“Three full,” the supervisor said. “The refiners bought fuel I promised them. The clinic bought tendon. Six crews have advances against that money, including yours.”

He did not sound greedy. He sounded tired, and the distinction annoyed her more.

“Three,” Perren repeated.

Brelva watched rain fill the stranger's footprint in the sawdust. “If the north road stays open.”

***

On the second night, two more strangers appeared. One fought beside the slaughterhouse ditch with a hooked spear; the other used a short bow that punched bolts through the monsters' knee joints. Neither answered questions. Both ignored hide, bone, heat sacs, and the pale liver combs the clinic rendered into fever wash. They killed until the street was quiet, broke every throat node they could reach, heated the membranes, and left.

The corpse industry had learned speed because rot did not care about grief. Roofers took the hides. Rope shops twisted tendon. Kilns ground the porous bones into hot-burning brick. In three months, the night harvest had put dismissed dockhands back on wages and given families a cheaper lamp than whale oil. The creatures kept coming. So did rent.

At the yard, Brelva began a second tally in the back of her ledger.

One wagon from the west ditch arrived untouched. Two creatures attacked behind it before the gate shut. A south-road load drew nothing until it passed a cold wagon carrying brined nodes; then three shapes abandoned the slaughterhouse pens and followed the wagon's iron wheels through the rain.

Perren saw a different pattern.

“The spear man stood here.” He put a finger on Brelva's map, on the row of cramped houses beyond the east drain. “Not where the thing came through. Here.”

“A person can stand anywhere.”

“He kept his back to the doors.”

“That is how you avoid being surrounded.”

“He had open road behind him.”

Brelva drew the wagon route in chalk. “And six houses ahead. I can count roofs too.”

Perren leaned across the cart tongue to inspect a split strap. “Didn't say you couldn't.”

“You meant it.”

“I meant he put his body in a place. Bodies are usually honest about what they expect.”

“Ours expected supper twenty minutes ago.”

Perren pulled the strap tight. “Stew or the heel of cheese?”

“Cheese tonight. Stew tomorrow if the west ditch pays.”

“That's a cruel order.”

It was not a joke so much as the shape of an old complaint. Brelva cut the cheese and gave him the larger piece. He accepted it without thanks, which was how they had thanked each other since childhood.

On the third night, the guards ringed the brine shed with pikes. The supervisor had bought shutters for its vents and hired two extra hands from the roof-hide crew.

“Protection for stock already purchased,” he told Brelva when she objected to the added gate fee.

“You put the fee on the crews whose stock you claim to own.”

“Because if it burns, I still owe the refiners. If a guard dies, I owe a widow. If I do not hire the guard, I owe everyone an explanation for why I preferred the cheaper funeral.”

Perren was beneath the cart, packing grease around the left hub. “We could take the nodes straight to the refinery.”

“Their vats are full,” the supervisor said. “I purchased capacity for seventh day.”

“It's third day.”

“Yes. That is why we have a cold shed.”

Brelva checked the brine barrels: thirty-two sealed, eight open, vibration faint but even beneath their waxed lids.

At midnight, a bolt struck the yard gate from outside. Not a monster bolt; one of the strangers' thick black shafts. It lodged above the latch.

The guards raised their pikes. The square-faced woman stood beyond the lamps with her empty hands spread. Behind her, shapes moved along the north road.

She pointed to the brine shed.

“No,” the supervisor said.

The word required no translation.

The woman pointed to the road. Then the shed. Then she drove the edge of one hand against her other palm.

“No,” he said again, louder. “Purchased stock.”

One of the new guards glanced at Brelva. “Should we move the barrels?”

“Hold your side of the gate,” the supervisor told him.

The woman waited, watching Brelva rather than the pikes. When no one copied her, she turned and ran toward the moving shapes alone.

The attack ended two streets north. None reached the yard.

Brelva wrote that down too.

***

On the fourth night, the left axle broke.

It happened on the marsh road, where reeds scraped the cart and black water covered both ditches. Brelva heard the crack, felt the load sag, and shouted before Perren could put his shoulder under it.

“Don't. Eleven hundredweight.”

“Wheel's in the ditch.”

“I can see the wheel.”

“Then count how long until the lamps go out.”

They had nine carcasses, sixteen sound nodes packed in two brine tubs, three bad hides, and one lantern with less than a finger of oil. Behind them, far down the road, came the scrape of many feet.

Perren pulled the jack from its bracket. “I lift. You seat the block.”

“We cut the nodes loose and leave the cart.”

“The cart is the promise.”

“A promise doesn't get to bury you.”

“Neither do you.”

He said it into the mud, already setting the jack. There was no room in the road for the answer Brelva wanted: I kept you alive after the marsh took them. I learned every weight, every safe turn, every sound that meant run. She had promised their dead partners' families that she would not make the same mistake twice. Somewhere in keeping that promise, she had started deciding which risks belonged to Perren before he could speak.

The scrape grew louder.

“Lift,” she said. “On three. One, two—”

The square-faced stranger dropped from the reeds before three.

Perren swung the jack handle at her. She caught it on a bracer, barked one sharp sound, and pointed at the tubs. Then she pressed her palm to the road.

Vibration hummed up through Brelva's boots.

Not footsteps. Not yet.

The sealed nodes were trembling hard enough to ring against the tubs.

The stranger ripped the waxed cloth from one. She took out a node, cracked it on the cart rim, and thrust the inner membrane over Brelva's lantern.

Green light ran across it. The membrane shrank. Under Brelva's fingers, the vibration vanished.

The remaining tub shook harder, each node seeming to lean north. The scrape behind them became a chorus. Ahead, beyond the bend, the dark answered.

Brelva looked from one tub to the other. “They weren't following us yesterday.”

Perren heard what she did: one group on the road behind, another moving from ahead. “They don't need to follow the same wagon. They only need the same road.”

The stranger pointed past them, toward the settlement. Then at the tubs.

Brelva cut the first lid open.

Perren cracked nodes while she held membranes to the lantern. The stranger stood between them and the approaching sounds, blade low. She did not supervise. When Brelva fumbled one slick membrane, the woman snatched it from the mud, burned it, and returned to the dark.

Eight nodes. Ten. The lamp oil guttered.

“Last two,” Perren said.

“One.”

He pushed the final membrane into the flame with his bare thumb. It flashed. He hissed and wrapped his hand in his shirt.

The pressure under Brelva's boots stopped.

The creatures did not disappear. They did not turn obediently or fall dead. One came out of the reeds on six bowed limbs, its pale mouth opening along its chest. The stranger met it. Perren dragged the jack clear. Brelva shoved the block beneath the axle, and together the siblings heaved the wheel onto the road while the fight thudded behind them.

When the cart rolled, they took the ordinary salvage and left the empty tubs.

The stranger followed only as far as the first streetlamp. She put up her palm. Stop.

Then she touched two fingers to the road and drew them toward herself.

Approach.

Brelva tried the motions. Palm. Two fingers drawn in.

The woman corrected the angle of her wrist, once. Then she went back into the reeds.

***

By morning, Brelva had six routes and nineteen attacks marked in her ledger. She put the cold wagons in blue and the unbrined loads in white. Perren put stones on the places where the strangers had chosen to stand.

The blue lines did not explain where the creatures came from or why the strangers knew how to kill them. They showed something smaller: preserved nodes passed near every cluster. When a wagon moved, attacks gathered behind its route. When nodes were broken and heated, the pressure stopped. The brine had not made a monster. The barrels had not commanded one. They held a direction that should have faded with death, and enough held directions made the night pay attention.

The supervisor studied the map through breakfast. He ate porridge while standing, spoon in one hand, invoices in the other.

“Six crews,” he said. “Forty barrels between them. Three refineries expecting delivery. The clinic has already paid against the tendon proceeds.”

“Keep the hide, bone, tendon, heat sacs,” Brelva said. “Stop brining nodes.”

“On nineteen marks you made yourself.”

“On nineteen sequences. Cold load, route, attack.”

“And on two nights when nothing reached the yard.”

Perren laid a stone at the yard gate. “Because they stood outside it.”

“Who?”

“The people you keep calling scavengers.”

“They have not given me a name, an origin, or a bond against damages.” The supervisor put down his spoon. “I believe what can be charged to an account. That is not stupidity. It is how I make sure a hook hand gets paid after a richer person changes his mind.”

Brelva opened the ledger to their contract. Three loads. Cart cleared. Perren's burned thumb stuck out of a fresh wrapping beside her hand.

“Refuse our final load,” she said. “No nodes.”

The supervisor rubbed porridge from his moustache. “Then the contract fails. I cannot clear a cart on goods not delivered.”

Perren looked at Brelva, waiting.

She could say the route was too dangerous. She could say his hand made the choice. She could protect him so thoroughly he became one more item under her tally, weighed and routed without consent.

“What do you want?” she asked.

His surprise lasted half a breath. “Take the ordinary parts. Leave every node here.”

“That concentrates the vibration.”

“Yes.”

“The contract fails.”

“Yes.”

“The cart stays in debt.”

Perren touched the wrapped thumb to the map. “The east road runs past thirty doors. The north past twelve. Marsh past none. If we move forty barrels, we pick which doors hear them. If we break the barrels here, the walls are stone and the streets around us are wide.”

The supervisor said, “Those barrels contain stock I bought from people who cannot absorb the loss.”

“Then don't make them absorb it,” Perren said. “You bought it.”

The man's mouth tightened.

Brelva expected a refusal. Instead he gathered the invoices into one squared stack. “I will not authorize destruction on a grader's pattern.”

“What will you authorize?” she asked.

“Guards around the final intake. No wagons out after sunset. If the arrivals follow your map, I will open the shed myself.”

It was not enough. It was more than his obligations had allowed him five minutes earlier.

Brelva closed the contract. “Then we bring no nodes through housing.”

“How do you propose to harvest?”

“We don't. Not tonight.”

Perren nodded once. His choice, beside hers.

***

They spent the fifth night hauling ordinary salvage into stone rooms and watching the barrel seals click faster.

The sixth night came early under storm clouds.

By full dark, the wax seals on the cold shed had begun to click. Forty barrels, eighty-one nodes, each preserving a little directional tremor. Brelva felt their combined vibration through the weighing platform. It no longer pointed north or south. It traveled up her leg and settled behind her teeth.

The first cry sounded west.

The second answered from the marsh.

Guards shut the iron gate. Roof-hide workers carried finished sheets out of the cutting room, trying to save what water would ruin. A carter shouted that his team was still tied by the east wall. The supervisor moved through them with his ring of keys, assigning doors, counting purchased batches, refusing three separate demands at once.

“Unhitch the team,” Perren called.

“Not through the east gate,” Brelva said. “Bring them behind the bone shed.”

“That pen's full.”

“Then move the empty racks.”

One of the supper guards grabbed a rack. “This one sticks.”

“Lift before you pull,” Perren said. “Left foot's sunk.”

The ordinary talk steadied the yard for perhaps a minute. Lift. Pull. Bar the cutting room. Find the missing lantern. Then a creature hit the north gate hard enough to bow it inward.

More shapes entered the lamplight along the west road. Not an army in lines, not creatures under command. They came from separate dark streets, colliding, clawing past one another, drawn toward the vibration that made Brelva's bones hum.

The strangers arrived among them.

The spear man took the west mouth. The bow wielder climbed the bone shed. The square-faced woman came straight to the gate and raised her palm.

Stop.

Brelva raised hers in return.

The woman drew two fingers toward her chest.

Approach.

Brelva pointed to the cold shed, then crossed both forearms. Not yet.

The woman's gaze snapped to the supervisor's key ring. She made the striking motion against her palm.

The gate bowed again. One hinge tore from stone.

“Open the shed,” Brelva said.

The supervisor stared at the monsters.

“You said you would.”

“I said if they followed your map.”

“West, marsh, north. Three roads. No wagons.”

“The purchased batches—”

The gate split. A guard went down beneath the iron frame, his pike spinning away.

Perren ran toward him.

Brelva caught his sleeve, then let go before the grip became a command. “I get the keys.”

“I'll get his shoulders.”

“Drag toward the platform. Not the cutting room.”

“I know the route.”

He did.

Brelva went for the supervisor. He had not fled. He was trying to lift the fallen gate off the guard while creatures pressed into the opening and the spear man held them there.

“Keys,” she said.

“Third key. Brass.” His words came too quickly. “Open both vents first or the mineral vapor catches. The crews signed weight at intake. Every seal has a mark. I have to preserve the marks if I pay claims.”

“Then bring the chalkboard.”

He looked at her.

“We break by batch,” she said. “You mark every barrel. You owe the loss to the people you bought from, not the refiners who never took delivery.”

The supervisor pulled the brass key free. “Claims before refiners.”

That was how he made courage: as an order of payment.

They ran.

Brelva opened the upper vent. Perren and the freed guard staggered to the platform. The guard's leg held, though blood darkened his trousers. The square-faced woman crossed the yard backward, blade working, her attention on the shed door.

Brelva drew two fingers toward herself.

Approach.

The woman came.

The supervisor unlocked the shed. Cold mineral air rolled out. Inside, barrels knocked on their racks like a roomful of impatient fists.

The woman pointed at the upper row, then at the brazier. One relation. Highest vibration, heat.

“Top first,” Brelva said. “Perren, wedges.”

“Seals before breakage,” the supervisor said, dragging the chalkboard close.

“Then mark them.”

They found a rhythm without finding a common language. Brelva tested lids and called quantities. Perren rolled barrels down the chute, bracing them with hip and shoulder, naming clear paths and injured workers. The supervisor shouted each crew's seal and struck it from the purchased column only after he saw the nodes broken. The stranger cracked paired nodes against her wedge, laid membranes into iron trays, and pushed the trays toward the brazier.

Outside, guards and harvesters defended their own yard with hook poles, pikes, and the heavy boards used to turn carcasses. The newcomers did not command them. They filled gaps, demonstrated angles, waited for imitation. When the bow wielder slapped the roof twice and pointed down, a hide worker understood before anyone else and pulled two people clear of a creature climbing the gutter.

“Batch twelve, six pairs,” the supervisor called.

“Five and one split,” Brelva said.

“Purchased as six.”

“Destroyed as eleven sound, one spoiled.”

“That is not how claims work.”

“It is how evidence works.”

“Mark eleven,” Perren said. “Argue at breakfast.”

The supervisor marked eleven.

Barrel after barrel. Membranes flashed green. The vibration changed from a pressure in Brelva's teeth to a tremor in the boards, then to separate beats she could count. Thirty-four. Twenty. Nine.

A monster broke through the cutting-room wall instead of the gate. It shouldered shelves aside and lunged toward the shed. Brelva froze with a node in each hand.

The stranger stepped between them. She struck low, missed, and went down beneath the creature's front limbs.

Perren could have run. Instead he hooked the monster's rear joint with the cart chain and yelled, “Brelva, wheel!”

She understood his route. She dropped the nodes into the tray, seized the loose wheel from beside the repair rack, and rolled it hard under the chain. The weight lifted the creature's leg just enough. The stranger twisted free and drove her wedge into the joint.

The creature fell. The stranger rose with one sleeve torn and pointed at the tray.

One relation. Nodes first.

Brelva burned them.

The final membrane curled into ash just before dawn.

The monsters outside did not vanish. Those already at the yard kept fighting until the eastern roofs went gray, then scattered into alleys or fell beneath exhausted hands. But no new cries answered from the roads. The boards stopped trembling.

Morning found the cold shed warm, empty, and reeking of salt.

***

They sorted what remained because useful things were still useful.

Undamaged hide went to the roofers. Tendon went to the clinic contract. Bone was weighed for the kilns. The supervisor sat on an overturned barrel and recalculated eighty-one nodes as purchased loss, refinery default, guard injury, and four minutes of supper he conceded had not mattered after all.

“Your cart is not clear,” he told Brelva and Perren.

Perren flexed his burned thumb. “We noticed it was still here.”

“The final-load contract failed.”

Brelva waited.

The supervisor tapped the claims column. “Your axle repair can move to salvage wages. Not forgiveness. Work.”

“At what rate?” she asked.

He named one.

She named another. They argued it down by two crowns and back up by one.

Across the yard, the square-faced woman helped the injured guard shift a rack. They had no words between them. He pointed to his bad leg; she took the heavier end. When it was set down, she raised her palm to him.

He stopped.

She drew two fingers toward herself.

He approached, slowly this time, and handed her a cup of water.

Brelva tore the blue route pages from her ledger and pinned them beside the gate, not as proof of the whole night or an answer to where anything had come from. Just roads, loads, attacks, and the order in which they had happened. Beneath them she hung a hammer, an iron tray, and an unbrined node from the morning's last carcass.

Perren brought over two bowls of porridge.

“Stew was the promise,” he said.

“The kitchen wall has a hole.”

“Promises keep having conditions with you.”

Brelva took the smaller bowl before he could offer it. “Tomorrow, then.”

The node gave one faint tremor toward the road. The stranger saw it. So did Brelva.

Palm raised. Stop.

Two fingers drawn close. Approach.

The stranger took the iron tray. Brelva lifted the hammer. Perren steadied the hook, and the three of them went to break it.

stories.title: There Goes Your Name
stories.prompt: "There goes your name" the fae cooed. "Now, go ahead and pick a new one!" name magic is over rated anyways...
stories.body:
# There Goes Your Name

The first fog came up while we were arguing over a lame ewe.

My sister had the flock's rear, which meant she also had the mud, the stragglers, and every good reason to be cross. I was ahead at the spring, laying the back of my hand against the water to judge whether the cold rain would reach us before dark. Between us, a hundred and six sheep blurred into a long grey drag across the hillside.

"She's putting the bad foot down," my sister called.

The fog carried her voice wide. I could not see her through the sheep, but the name-call tucked my old name into the sound and sent it to me from exactly where she stood: forty paces uphill, a little west, by the scattered thorn. Name-work was useful that way. It was also useful in the way a gate-latch was useful. Nobody wrote songs to a gate-latch.

"Bring her slow," I shouted. "We'll wrap it at the fold."

"And the lamb?"

"With her."

"You counted it?"

I had not. "I can see it."

"You can see fog."

She was fourteen and had recently discovered that accuracy could be sharpened into a household weapon. I found the lamb beside its mother's shoulder, barely more than four trembling legs under a wet fleece, and waved my crook so my sister might glimpse it.

"There. Save your breath for the climb."

"I'm going down."

"Then save it for complaining."

I turned back to the spring and found someone sitting on my pack.

The fae was no taller than my elbow to my fingertips, though its legs hung almost to the ground. It wore no shoes. Pondweed lay slick between its toes, and a spray of rowan berries was braided into hair the brown-green of water seen through peat. It had opened the flap of my pack and was smelling my bread as if deciding which season it belonged to.

"Move," I said.

It lifted its face. Its eyes were pale and round, with no more expression in them than two drops of whey. "You have a lovely sound tied to you. Worn soft at the edges."

My hand went to the horn whistle under my shirt. Father had cut my old name into its flat side when I was seven, two plain syllables in cramped letters because his knife had been too broad for the job.

"That's not for you."

"Oh, the whistle is hard and greasy." The fae wrinkled its nose. "I meant the other thing."

It moved before I did. Two damp fingers touched the hollow of my throat, light as a moth landing. Something snagged—not in my skin, but in the direction of me—and pulled free.

The fae sprang off my pack. It cupped both hands beneath its chin as though carrying a warm egg I could not see.

"There goes your name," the fae cooed. "Now, go ahead and pick a new one!"

"Put it back."

"That one had gone dull. Pick something green. Or round. A name with a bit of rain held in it."

I caught it by the wrist.

Cold ran through my palm. Not winter cold; spring-water cold, so clean it hurt. The fae laughed and folded somehow, its wrist narrowing like a ribbon through my grip. It landed on the stone rim of the spring three steps away, still holding its cupped hands level.

"Give it back," I said.

"But you haven't even tried being without it."

I knew the old name. I knew how Father had said it when I had left a hurdle open, clipping the second syllable because the sheep were already in the beans. I knew my sister stretched the first when she wanted me to answer across weather. In the flock ledger, my name stood beside the winter feed accounts and the note about the north wall. It was mine in all the usual ways.

"I have work."

The fae lowered one hand to trail its fingers in the spring. The other remained closed. "Work has so many noises. Scuff, huff, clack, tear. A name gives only one."

Behind me, the dog gave one sharp bark.

The flock had begun to bunch. Fog thickened across the slope, swallowing the thorn and then the backs of the last sheep. I put two fingers to my mouth and whistled the dog round to the west. It knew that signal. The sheep turned downhill, shoulder pressing shoulder, wool brushing with a sound like rain in dry grass.

"You," I said to the fae. "Stay there."

It smiled. "Which you?"

I left it at the spring because the lame ewe was moving and my sister had sense enough to follow.

For perhaps five minutes, that was true.

Then the lame ewe veered downhill past the old sheepfold, her lamb at her shoulder. The dog went after them. I stepped into the open side of the fold, driving the leaders around the dry-stone wall, and the fog closed behind them so neatly it seemed to cut the flock in two. Bells knocked. Hooves scraped. I whistled twice for my sister to tighten the rear.

No whistle came back.

I called her by her name. The call went to her, wherever she was, but no answer came back.

"That's poor," said the fae from the wall above me. "Throwing a voice without a string."

"What did you do?"

It opened its palm for a moment. I saw no written word, no glowing mark, only the faint bend of light above its skin, as if sun lay under moving water. Then its fingers closed again.

My sister called my old name.

Her voice came from the wall where the fae sat.

I looked up so fast the rim of my hood struck my cheek. The fae tipped its head, listening to the call arrive. It breathed across its fist and turned its wrist. My sister's second call slid left with that motion and faded toward the upper path.

"Stop that."

"I carry it. That is where it goes."

"You are carrying it. You are turning her voice."

"Yes."

No shame. No threat, either. It said yes as my sister might say the ewe had four feet. I climbed the loose outer face of the wall and reached for it. The fae hopped down inside the fold, brushing past the damp noses of three ewes. They flinched because it touched them, not because they knew what it was.

My sister called again. The fae ran toward the uphill gap, cooing the two syllables back to itself—not answering, only savoring their shape. The call followed it.

I ran after.

The upper path climbed between heather and broken stone. It was the wrong road for the lower pasture, the wrong road for a lame ewe, and the wrong road under a sky holding that much rain. I knew all three facts. I also heard my sister's breath behind every call bent uphill, and knowledge became a poor thin thing beside it.

The fae stayed just ahead. Now and then I saw rowan-red beads in the fog. It paused on a boulder, both hands closed around what it had taken, and offered, "You could be called moss. You step like moss trying not to be a boot."

"How far can she be?"

"From what?"

"From the name-call."

"Near enough to want you."

"A mile? Two?"

It considered. "Not two. Two has too much road in it."

"Can she hear me?"

"If you make a noise."

I blew the horn whistle: one long note, two short, our ordinary recall. The sound flattened in the fog, directionless but loud. I waited.

Nothing answered.

The fae dangled from the boulder by its knees. "Try a softer name next. This one has been said across too many fields."

I pulled the whistle from its thong and held the carved side toward it. "My father gave me this name."

"Your father put scratches on bone."

"Horn."

"Horn, then. It smells of your neck."

"He gave me the word before he carved it."

The fae swung itself upright. "You still have the word. Look. Say it to yourself."

I did, silently. Every sound remained where memory kept it. That did not make the fae's theft small.

"He is dead," I said. "I can't ask him for another."

The fae leaned close enough that I smelled crushed mint and sheep dung on its breath. "Dead people leave old sounds. This one drags at the end. Can't you feel it?"

Below us, the dog barked twice.

I turned. Its shape was only a dark patch in the fog, down by the fold. It stood facing downhill, ears pricked away from me.

The fae had followed my gaze. "It doesn't know your new sound."

"It doesn't need one."

On the path at my feet, every hoofprint pointed down.

Not many: the narrow print of the lame ewe, the two neat punches of the lamb, and my sister's boot heel smeared through the edge of both. A strand of wet wool clung to a low juniper on the downslope side. There were no fresh marks continuing uphill except mine.

My sister called again. Her voice came from behind me.

The fae stood behind me.

It raised its closed hand as she called and drew the sound toward itself with a long inhalation, pleased as a child smelling cakes. I wanted to reach for that fist again. I tightened my grip on the crook instead.

"I'm going down," I said.

It smiled. "But I'm up here."

I dropped to one knee beside the prints. Rain had not yet filled them. The lame ewe was setting the bad hind hoof along its outer edge, as she had in the morning. My sister had kept her on the softer ground until the juniper. Beyond it, the slope broke toward the scree channel.

The dog whined.

"Go find," I told it, and gave my sister's ordinary hand-signal: palm low, two fingers forward. No magic in that. Training, meat scraps, years.

The dog vanished downhill.

The fae skipped beside me when I followed. "Moss is still available. Or milkcap. You have the look of something found under a leaf."

"Do you have to answer when she calls?"

"I don't answer. I turn it."

"Do you have to turn it?"

The fae's toes tested a slick stone and withdrew. "No."

"Then don't."

"But the way she worries your old sound is lovely."

I stopped so sharply it nearly walked into me. "She's on bad ground with a lame ewe. If you send me wrong again, she may fall."

For once, the fae did not fill the space. Rain ticked in the heather. A sheep coughed somewhere inside the fold.

Then the fae said, almost complaining, "I didn't tell her to stand there."

"No. You only kept me from finding her."

It rubbed its closed fist with the thumb of its other hand. "People usually chase what I take."

"I did."

"You stopped."

A thin whistle rose below us, one long note. It broke halfway through the second, ended in a breathy crack, then did not come again.

My sister's reed whistle. She had mended the mouthpiece twice with thread and wax and claimed it would last the winter. It had not lasted the afternoon.

The dog barked from the same direction.

I went down.

The fae followed without speaking. It came upright now, using hands as well as feet on the wet rock, still keeping the fist with my old name lifted away from every scrape. The slope steepened below the juniper. Grey stones shifted under brown grass, all of it slick as fat. I found where the ewe had slid: four furrows, a tuft of belly wool, blood no larger than a berry on one sharp edge.

"Stay high," my sister shouted. No name this time. Her voice came from below and a little east, plain direction carried by the wind when it happened to be kind. "The middle's loose."

"Can you move?"

"I can. She can't. Lamb's here too."

"Anything broken?"

"Whistle. Maybe my backside."

"That will heal your manners."

"Come say that down here."

There she was: crouched on a shelf of stone scarcely wide enough for her boots, one arm braced behind the lame ewe's neck. The lamb was wedged between her knees, shivering but upright. The dog stood on a firmer lip below, looking up and refusing to climb the shifting fan between us.

My sister had mud to one eyebrow and the furious, frightened look she got when fear seemed an accusation against her competence.

"Don't move the ewe," I said.

"Hadn't planned to throw her."

"I need the rope."

"You have it."

I reached for the coil at my belt and found an empty hook.

She closed her eyes. "You left it on the gate."

"I did."

"You told me to mind the gate."

"Yes."

"I was minding a sheep."

"Keep doing that."

The fae crouched above the scree, peering at my sister. "She's red under the mud. Like a rowan fruit dropped in broth."

My sister stared at it. "What's that doing here?"

"It stole my name."

"Ugly little midden-pip. Give it back."

The fae drew itself up. "I am not ugly."

"Then stand somewhere useful."

I signaled the dog toward the fold, then tugged an empty fist toward me: fetch the rope. We had taught it that during lambing. It hesitated, glanced at my sister, and went when I repeated the signals. While we waited, I tested the slope with the crook. The middle ran at a touch. The safer line curved east across a narrow band of grass, down to the dog's ledge, then back under my sister's shelf. We would need the rope for the ewe. We would need my sister to move first.

"The lamb goes inside your coat," I told her. "Feet down."

"It kicks."

"So do you."

"Not when folded."

She managed it. The lamb disappeared against her belly, its nose poking between two buttons. She looked absurdly pregnant and entirely unable to laugh about it.

"Left foot to the grass," I said. "Not the grey stone."

"It's all grey."

"The one with the black edge. Reach past it."

She shifted. Pebbles ran from under her boot. The ewe lurched against her hip.

"Wait," I said.

"I'm waiting."

"You're moving."

"The sheep is moving."

Her sentences came apart with her breath. Mine had shortened until every word seemed to have a job and resent the others.

The fae watched the stones move. "They sound like dry seeds in a pod."

Neither of us answered.

The dog returned dragging the lambing rope by one loop. It had caught twice on heather and collected half the hillside. I climbed down to take it, tied one end around my waist, and threw the cleanest loop toward my sister. The first fell short. The second struck her shoulder.

"Under your arms," I said.

"Ewe first."

"You first."

"If she goes, she takes me."

That was true. She threaded the rope behind the ewe's forelegs instead, working one-handed around the lamb beneath her coat. I braced on the lower ledge and took the weight while she urged the ewe across. The animal placed its sound hoof, dragged the sore one, and tried to turn back. The dog dropped flat where she could see it. My sister pressed her shoulder to the ewe's rump.

"Easy," she said. "No, not there. Here. That's grass. Put your stupid foot on it."

The ewe listened to pressure, footing, and the dog's stillness. She did not need a name. She reached my ledge trembling. I worked the loop free, then eased her down to the dog, who stood and kept her from turning uphill.

I threw the loop back to my sister. She passed it under her own arms, then crossed with the lamb. Halfway, the black-edged stone rolled. Her left foot went out.

She did not call my name. She said, "Rope!"

I dropped my weight backward. The line snapped tight under her arms. She struck the slope on one knee, showering us both with shale, but her right boot found the grass band. I hauled while she crawled. The lamb bleated once from inside her coat, offended but alive.

When she reached me, she pushed the lamb into my hands and sat down hard.

"You took your time," she said.

"I went uphill."

"Why?"

I looked at the fae. It had come down to the shelf we had left and was tracing the ewe's blood-speck on the stone with one damp finger.

"Because it moved the call," I said.

My sister wiped mud from her eyebrow and made the smear worse. "You always say calls make people lazy."

"I do."

"You were right, then. That's annoying."

"Get up."

She got up.

We brought the ewe and lamb back by the long lower curve. The rain arrived properly, needling the backs of our hands and turning the dog's coat black. Behind the fold wall, the flock had divided itself according to no scheme useful to us: yearlings in the corner meant for ewes, two rams nosing the broken hurdle, and one lamb perched on the feed stone as if supervising.

My sister took the far wall. "Let's see where the old one sends me now."

She called my old name. Her voice came from the fae under its dock leaf instead of from her.

"Still broken," she said.

"Mine, not yours."

The fae sat on the wall under a dock leaf, keeping one fist closed. "Broken is harsh. Empty has more room in it."

"Give back the old one," my sister said.

"No."

"Why not?"

"I like how it has been used."

My sister took one step toward the wall. I caught the back of her coat.

"Leave it," I said.

"I'm not leaving it. I'm knocking it into the nettles."

"We have a lame ewe, a wet lamb, and a gate that won't hold."

"Also that."

"The gate first."

She gave the fae a look that promised future nettles and went to lift the dropped hurdle. I stood in the rain with Father's whistle against my chest and listened to the flock shove and mutter. My old name was not empty of use. It belonged to his voice, to my sister's, to the cut letters under my thumb. The fae could keep carrying the bent call for now. It could not take those.

But my sister still needed a sound that would reach me straight when the weather hid us.

At the spring, long pale sedge bent under the rain and rose when each gust passed. We cut it every winter for bedding. Its roots held the black edge of the bank where sheep would otherwise punch through.

Nothing truer than that. Something useful.

I went to the fold entrance where my sister could see me. "I'll use Sedge."

She stopped with the hurdle against her shoulder. "You will?"

"For calling."

"All right."

"Say it back. Mean me."

Her face tightened with concentration. She had known me all her life, which did not prevent her from doing things badly on principle. This she did carefully.

"Sedge," she called.

The sound reached me from her place at the far side of the fold. Not louder. Not sweetened. It came through rain and milling sheep with its direction clean inside it.

The fae opened both hands. A bend of light remained above the palm that held my old name; the other palm was bare. It laughed, delighted rather than defeated.

"One weather-stem," it said. "And one old bell-sound."

"Are you keeping the old one?" I asked.

It tucked its closed fist beneath its chin. "For a while."

Then it dropped from the wall into the fog. Rowan berries flashed once and were gone.

My sister set the hurdle back into its sockets. "Sedge."

"What?"

"Nothing. Trying it."

"Try it while you sort the yearlings."

She went left. I went right. The dog brought the first six through the narrow gate, and for several minutes there were only wet backs, reaching hands, the knock of wood, and my sister telling a ram exactly what she thought of its mother.

Then her voice found me cleanly from behind the flock.

"Sedge, your side!"

I turned in time to block the lame ewe from following the yearlings through. Her lamb squeezed under my arm. My sister laughed once, breathless, and shoved the hurdle closed.

"Wrap that foot," she said. "Rain's getting in."

I reached for the wool bandage in my pack. "Count the flock first."

"I already did."

"How many?"

She held up both muddy hands because she knew I hated waiting while she counted on her fingers. The dog shook rain across my legs. Somewhere beyond the wall, the fae made a small pleased sound, or perhaps it was only water slipping under the stones.

My sister got to one hundred and six. We started again to make sure.

stories.title: All Accounts Due
stories.prompt: You have no magic, but as you've helped others you've amassed tons of favors, artifacts, etc. Today everyone woke up to find thier max mana is zero.
stories.body:
# All Accounts Due

The Ithrom Array hung where six world-curves crossed, and every kind of magic in the material world had come to kill Faris.

One hand bruised, Faris crouched behind a pillar of ordinary stone. Six empty sockets ringed the Unwritten Axis, each with a keystone waiting in its cradle; the Parity Astrolabe hung above, its needles out of true. The Mortal Latch sat cradled at his knee, lever folded, its firing cotter strapped to the housing, three body-lengths from the recess where it had to be seated. He had not gathered the eight relics for this. They had come to him one debt at a time over thirty-one years.

Beyond, a luminous city walked; black fire ate a fortress; dragons stitched horizons; palaces filled three skies; an aurora held a mountain; soldiers exchanged organs and wings.

Engineers of all six practices had built the Array three hundred and two years earlier as a last resort against the six magics being driven as one. Now they were. The Absolute Yoke ran down through all six wonders, borrowing grace for command, fire for appetite, flight for pursuit, rooms for prisons, weight for chains, gifts for forced flesh. Where it touched, people knelt, burned, or flew on orders that were not theirs. The Bound Ascendancy wore all six where they met.

It had begun as an armistice council of frightened rulers and priests who decided that peace required every root to obey. It meant to preserve the magical world by ending refusal.

“Leave the Latch,” it said through conscripted mouths. “There can still be order.”

Then Seyathi stepped through a tessellated wall and reached for the Missing Tessera.

*Nine years earlier, at the Talarum Steps*

The pilgrims had been kneeling for four days.

Their knees bled through their clothes, but Tessellate Grace cared less about pain than arrangement. Every attempt to rise completed another line in the prepared pavement, and the completed line bent their bodies back into worship. Seyathi stood beyond them inside a shelter of rotating mineral color. She was holding the greater pattern apart by a finger's width. Sweat silvered her mouth. Each breath cost her another piece of her sense of place; when Faris shouted, she looked first in the wrong direction.

“Do not step on anything beautiful,” she called.

“I'm not stepping on anything,” Faris called back. “I'm lying down.”

He lay flat in a trench of unfinished stone beside the stairs. He had no counter-pattern to wear and no inner gift for the pavement to recognize. That did not make him safe. A prepared surface could arrange an unmagical body as easily as a chair. He crawled where the mortar was still raw, testing it with the brass tongue from his sandal buckle. Plain grit crumbled. Worked grit hummed against the metal.

A blank white tile sat between him and the nearest pilgrim. No lines. No pigment. Faris put his palm on it.

The prepared underside turned him over and folded him to both knees.

His shoulder struck the step. His teeth met hard enough to fill his mouth with blood. The pilgrims' hands rose together, compelled into the next figure, and the shelter around Seyathi narrowed.

“The plain ones carry the pattern underneath,” she said, voice tight. “I should have told you.”

He tried to lift one knee. The tile corrected him by twisting his ankle until his heel fitted the design. Tendons were tendons even when a goddess's geometry chose how to pull them. “Should have looked underneath,” he said through his teeth. He wedged the buckle tongue beneath his sole and used it as a lever, gaining less than a finger's width. Enough to keep the joint from breaking. Not enough to stand.

One of the kneeling pilgrims moved one finger. Not up, which the pattern would have caught. Sideways, scraping at a seam beneath the lip of the stair. Faris followed the scratch with his eyes. A maintenance pin held the prepared facing to an ordinary support bed. No holy geometry protected the pin. It was only iron, green with damp.

Seyathi followed his eyes to the pin. “One breath,” she said. “After that, I will not know which way you are.”

She turned two fingers.

The colored shelter opened. For one breath the compulsion loosened, and every pilgrim sagged without being forced into the next posture. Faris tore the buckle from his sandal and struck the maintenance pin. Once. Twice. On the third blow it slid free. The facing dropped a thumb's width, breaking the pattern's continuity. Forty-three people fell out of worship at once.

The hidden lines on the tile flashed before they died. Someone had laid a trial lattice for the Absolute Yoke beneath a goddess's stairs.

Afterward, Seyathi could not find the stairs without Faris taking her elbow. She gave him the Missing Tessera, a square of matte mineral two fingers wide. It had been made for her long ago, she said, and contained one finite direction of her grace.

“One day,” she told him, “you may ask me to arm it against the Yoke. Say exactly what you mean. A promise protects only its exact shape.”

At the Array, the unarmed Sole Chamber rang inside nine Yoke-folded rooms.

*Twenty-four years earlier, at Mavorn Palace*

Faris entered the palace prison dressed as a laundry porter, carrying wet sheets and the confidence of a man nobody important intended to remember.

Nine prison wings occupied the same foundation. King Malrec's heartbeat chose which arrangement a corridor wore, and every arrangement beyond the base made that heart spend its years faster. With one beat, Faris passed cells full of debtors. With the next, the same doors held soldiers. Another beat revealed an empty banquet hall through the bars. Living people remained one body each, crossing between rooms only at permitted thresholds. The stone was less disciplined. It could be wall, stair, ceiling, and oubliette before a guard finished yawning. The king could maintain the palace's grandeur only by aging inside it.

The Sole Chamber governed Manyroom from a bronze model no bigger than a thumb. Lifted from its hiding place, it would fold every wing back into the base prison, where the debtors' families could find them. Faris had been told to follow a scratched line along the base wall until it ended under the royal archive.

He followed the wrong scratch.

The next heartbeat put him inside a locked cell. The following one put the cell behind the kitchens. Then under a chapel. Then nowhere he could name. He dropped the sheets and felt along the base, but each wall carried decades of scratches. He could not tell signal from damage.

The prisoner sharing the cell watched him sniff the air.

“What?” Faris whispered.

The prisoner pointed through the wall, then pinched their nose and mimed eating.

Faris held up one finger for each shift and let the prisoner tap his wrist when a smell returned. On the seventh heartbeat, soup and lamp oil repeated together. On the ninth, wet wool came back without the soup. The scratched walls were meant to defeat sight, but cooks still burned onions on schedule and laundries still made steam. The prisoner smiled.

Meal smells. Grease when the kitchens were near. Damp grain by storage. Wax by the archive. Faris stopped looking for the right mark and waited through the pulse of rooms, tracking the ordinary things each arrangement could not quite hide. When wax and mouse droppings arrived together, he found the true scratch under his heel. It led to a loose base stone.

Behind it sat the Sole Chamber, made by the palace's first architects. Faris closed his hand around it. Nine wings shuddered toward one plain arrangement.

He could have left during the confusion. Then a heartbeat made the wall beside him share space with King Malrec's private room. Faris saw a blade emerging behind the king, its wielder hidden in another arrangement.

He threw the bronze model at Malrec's head.

The king ducked, already drawing breath to rebuke him. The assassin's blade passed through the place his throat had been. Faris shouted where to strike, and the royal guard dragged the attacker across a threshold into one body and one room.

The prison settled. Every captive remained alive in the base structure. Faris was arrested before he reached the laundry door.
