cut toward his upper arm. Their shoulders crossed. For one compressed instant,
his body blocked Quade's view of both target panels.

Two chalked blades flexed.

Quade called halt.

Fiora froze with Jasper so close she could hear the catch in his breath. Her
blade rested against his upper-arm panel. His rested against the dark padding
over her ribs.

To the rail, the touches had been one sound.

To Quade, hidden by their crossing bodies, they had been one motion.

To Fiora, they had not.

She had felt Jasper's blade bow against her coat. She had seen white chalk
bloom at the lower edge of her vision. Half a beat later, her own edge had
drawn its line across his arm.

Jasper eased his blade away but said nothing. He looked at her, waiting.

Six months earlier, in this strip, he had stood where she stood. He had owned a
fraction of knowledge that could cost him the match, and he had spoken it.
Courtesy, Fiora understood at last, was not making the world painless for
someone. It was trusting them with the truth and trusting that they could bear
what came next.

She could say she did not know. Quade would order the point refenced. She might
win. The badge in her case might feel defended for an hour, perhaps even a
week.

And every time she looked at it, she would know what she had withheld.

“Jasper's touch landed first,” Fiora said.

The words passed through the yard with more force than a shout.

Jasper glanced once at the white mark on her ribs. He could have disputed her.
He could have performed generosity and handed the point back until neither of
them knew what anything meant.

Instead he nodded. “My touch first.”

Quade inspected both marks. He looked at Fiora, giving her room to correct or
withdraw the call.

She held his gaze. “The point is Jasper's.”

Quade straightened. “Touch, Jasper. Match to Jasper, three to two.”

For a moment no one behind the rail spoke. Then the applause came, less like a
victory roar than a release of breath.

Fiora lifted her guard. Jasper did the same. He was smiling, but not as a man
who had been awarded her company. He looked as she must have looked at the old
trial: astonished, relieved, and fiercely proud of the person who had beaten
him to the truth.

They saluted.

Quade carried the ledger to the rail and wrote the result in a firm hand:
Jasper, three; Fiora, two. Beneath the notation, he added the final touch as
self-called by Fiora. The old trial remained in its own place in the book:
Fiora, three; Jasper, two, with Jasper's call beside it.

Quade studied the two entries. “I withdraw my objection to the rematch.”

“Thank you,” Fiora said.

“I maintain every objection to your methods of conversation.”

“Also fair,” Jasper said.

***

The onlookers drifted toward the supper stalls, already arguing cheerfully
about the final exchange. Quade made Fiora and Jasper return their blades,
remove their guards, and submit to one last inspection before he would let
either of them near food.

“No damage except to judgment,” he pronounced.

“Whose?” Fiora asked.

“Mine, for officiating.” Quade shut the ledger. “The match is recorded. What
happens now is not.”

He walked away with enough determination to prove he was not about to arrange
the rest for them.

Fiora knelt by her travel case and checked the nearest buckle. Still fastened.
The cart would still come at dawn. East Weir's yard would still be hers to
lead. Losing had altered none of that.

Jasper stopped beside her. The chalk marks on his coat made him look like a
particularly elegant piece of disputed arithmetic.

“The bout is over,” he said. “Your answer belongs to you.”

Fiora stood.

He took a breath. This, apparently, frightened him more than facing her blade.
The discovery was so charming she almost rescued him, then decided equality
required letting him suffer properly.

“Fiora Halwick,” Jasper said, “would you have supper with me at the riverside
stalls tonight? One supper. I choose the place; you choose whether to come. You
leave for East Weir at dawn either way.”

There it was: no ritual left to speak for him, no point pretending the question
was anything but a hope placed carefully in her hands.

“Yes,” Fiora said. “Because I want to.”

His whole face changed.

“You may choose the stall,” she added, “but if you choose the one that burns
the onions, I reserve the right to regret my consent.”

“Continued consent was explicitly covered.”

“Good. You were listening.”

They left the yard in their chalk-marked practice coats, Fiora carrying the
travel case and Jasper carrying both guards. At the riverside, canvas awnings
snapped above iron cooking plates. Warm bread steamed in baskets. The lamps
along the pilings laid wavering paths across the dark water.

Jasper selected a stall where the onions were merely browned. He bought two
folded breads full of vegetables and sharp cheese, then waited until Fiora had
chosen a bench before sitting beside her.

The date began with her stealing one of his crispest onions.

“When may I visit East Weir?” he asked.

Fiora chewed thoughtfully. She could picture the new yard's narrow strip, the
awkward pillars, the rack waiting to be filled. She could picture herself at
its center in the head instructor's coat she had earned. Jasper belonged
nowhere in that picture unless invited, which made room for wanting him there.

“When you've devised a respectable counter to my pivot,” she said.

“I countered it.”

“Eventually. After it scored.”

“Then I may need a rematch.”

“You may need several.” Fiora raised her supper in salute. “Come prepared to
lose three to two.”

Jasper touched his folded bread to hers with grave courtesy. “I'll come
prepared to call what lands first.”

Fiora smiled and took another bite. Dawn would carry her east. Tonight, beside
the river, neither of them asked it to wait.

stories.title: The Last Thing I Could Fix
stories.prompt: You are a legendary blacksmith, sought out for your ability to fix anything. Talking swords, obsidian breastplates, staves made of crystal, daggers forged from dragon scales, you've done it all. The real challenge today is a young hero asking you to fix what they call their 'plot armor'.
stories.body:
# The Last Thing I Could Fix

I had corrected the manners of talking swords, which is harder than sharpening them and only slightly easier than convincing their owners to pay. I had mended obsidian breastplates without turning their wearers into pincushions of black glass. I had spliced crystal staves whose two halves disagreed about the direction of lightning. I had even reset the scales on dragon-scale daggers, a task best undertaken after establishing whether the dragon was finished with them.

In short, I was Hadrik, and I fixed anything.

The sign over my forge said so. The words were cut deep enough to outlive me and gilded thick enough to suggest they might. Travelers came up the valley to point at it, then at some impossible wreck in a velvet box. Nothing left my bench until it did what its maker had intended.

That last part was not on the sign. At the time, I thought it too obvious to carve.

Aven arrived in a thunderstorm with a bundle under one arm and bloodless determination holding their young face together. Water ran from their hair, their sleeves, and the toe of one split boot. They put the bundle on my bench. Scorched metal showed through the wrapping.

“I need you to fix my plot armor.”

I waited for the grin. Aven did not provide one.

“That is what the court chroniclers call it,” they said. “Because it keeps the hero alive for the next great deed.”

“Chroniclers,” I said. “Of course. Smiths call things by what they are. Chroniclers call them by what rhymes with the wine.”

I unwrapped a close-fitted under-harness: small overlapping plates, a mesh of silver-gray response wire, and enough scorch marks to trouble me. Then the reservoir bell sounded uphill, one iron note rolling beneath the thunder.

Aven told me the relief gate had jammed. The reservoir was climbing toward the rim. On their first attempt, a gate bolt had torn loose above them. Their guide had reached out—and the harness had dragged the guide beneath the falling iron. The bolt broke the guide’s leg instead of Aven’s back.

“They told me to try again alone,” Aven said. “Nothing near me for the armor to hurt.”

“A practical solution, if one is a wheelbarrow.”

“I am not wearing it again until I understand what it does.”

That was the first sensible thing anyone had said about the harness, myself included. I still gave the answer expected of a legend.

“You will have it by midday.”

The reservoir bell sounded again before the echo of my promise had died.

Off Aven’s body, the harness was as magical as a soup pot. I laid it in salt, passed a lodestone over every plate, warmed it by the forge and cooled it in rainwater. Nothing answered. The response wire held a faint stored tension, but no heat, pulse, or motion of its own.

“It needs someone living,” I said. “Likely you. Put it on.”

Aven’s hands stopped at the buckles.

“We test with cloth, not gate bolts,” I said. “And I stop when you say.”

They searched my face long enough to make me glad I had said it plainly. Then they stripped off their wet coat and fitted the harness over their shirt.

I blackened every wire junction with soot and hung a sack of rags from a ceiling chain. It made a gentle pendulum, by heroic standards. By mine, it was still a weight moving toward a client.

“Do nothing,” I told Aven. “I will catch it.”

I drew the sack back. Aven nodded. I let go.

The sack swung. Nothing warmed in advance, no invisible hand tipped it aside. The canvas touched the center plate with a padded thud.

Only then did the wire tighten.

A rivet at Aven’s sternum flashed hot. A line of lampblack leapt outward along one narrow hook. I had planted my boots and sworn to hold still, but some older part of me saw a young person in danger and reached before pride could stop it.

That reach completed the open circuit.

My arm jerked across Aven’s chest and into the sack’s path. I caught the chain with my other hand before the returning weight could crack my elbow. The pendulum had not swerved by a finger’s width. I had.

Aven went pale. “That was how the guide moved.”

I examined the hot center rivet under a lens. A hairline split ran through the metal and left its tiny assent gate jammed open. The outward hooks were made to take the intention of a nearby protector, but the choice rivet was supposed to admit only someone who actively joined the circuit. Cracked, it could turn a flinch, a reach, the bare wish that Aven not be hurt, into a bodily pull.

The wire had not foreseen the sack. It stayed cold until contact. Then Aven’s alarm and my protective reflex supplied the current, and the open circuit routed the pull through me as the nearer shield.

I drove ceramic wedges beneath the witness hooks and swung the sack again. It struck. The plates cinched hard around Aven; the split rivet heated; but the soot stopped at the blocked hooks, and I did not move.

There are diagnoses one enjoys being right about. This was not one of them.

“The central rivet is split,” I said. “I can drill it out, forge another, and reconnect the hooks. With the assent catch sound, it will take only a willing protector. Two hours.”

I reached for my smallest punch.

“No.”

“It is the proper repair.”

“It is the same purpose with a better latch.” Aven touched the reddened cloth over their sternum. “The latch broke once.”

“Everything breaks once. Most things make a career of it.”

“Then I won’t wear a thing whose failure turns people into shields.”

Outside, rain hissed on my chimney cap. I looked at the sign through the open forge door, its gold letters blurred by water. Anything fixed. A promise is an excellent servant until it hears a deadline; then it becomes a magistrate.

“The adults below expect that harness to bring their hero back,” I said.

“They expect me to go where they won’t because they think it has always brought me back.” Aven swallowed. “I don’t know how many times somebody else moved because of it. I don’t know which victories were mine.”

That landed harder than the sack had.

“The armor did not climb the road for you,” I said. “It did not learn the gate or decide to return here. But it changed who paid when things went wrong.” I put down the punch. “Tell me what fixed means.”

Aven looked surprised. So was I.

“It means I choose what I do,” they said. “It means nobody else pays unless they know the price and say yes. It means if it can’t save me honestly, it doesn’t pretend it can.”

The reservoir bell began ringing in strokes of three.

“That,” I said, “is a much slower repair.”

“Can you do it?”

“I did carve the sign very deeply.”

I cut away the witness hooks. One curved piece—the old bypass hook—could bridge an assent gate without a rivet and leave the outward path permanently open. I coiled it and dropped it into my tool roll, because smiths save dangerous scraps with the faith that labeling them dangerous makes us wise. Then I unfolded the response braid, turned every other outward path inward, and stitched it back through the plates.

The split choice rivet came out under my drill in bright curls. In its place I forged a will-catch: one contact beneath Aven’s sternum, one beneath the palm of their working hand. Aven stood beside the quench trough with their fingers on both while I tempered the fitted circuit. Their intent ran warm through the wire; my tongs and fire shaped it but supplied none of their own.

Last, I forged three rivets from soft iron, heated them to straw, then violet, then the blue of deep water. I set them where overload would break them before the braid could seek another body or hide the strain.

“Three hard uses,” I said. “Visible ones. After the third, this becomes rather uncomfortable ordinary armor.”

“What counts as a use?”

“First, danger must actually touch you. No warning. You must be conscious, understand the motion, press the will-catch, and say what you choose to do. One verb. One direction. The braid will brace that line for about one breath.”

“And the force?”

“Still exists. It spreads through the plates and through you. A blow from the side remains a blow from the side. Too much force will injure or kill you, whether the rivets have admired your courage or not.”

Aven gave the three blue heads a sober glance. “Better.”

I retained one outward loop of copper, isolated from the rest. “A second person may share the load by taking this consent ring with bare skin and saying yes, then and there. Let go, and the join ends. No stored permission. No borrowed reflex.”

We tested the redesign before trusting a town to it.

First I swung the padded sack slowly. Aven watched it come and stepped aside. It passed them. Nothing warmed; nothing pulled. They laughed once, mostly from surprise.

Then they returned to the mark. The sack touched the breastplate.

Aven pressed sternum and palm. “Stand.”

The inward braid lit beneath its soot. The plates drew tight along the line from their boots to their shoulders. The sack drove them back half a step and left a bruise they would feel by supper. It did not throw them. One blue rivet snapped with a crack like a seed in flame.

My arms remained entirely my own.

For the consent check, I gripped the copper ring while Aven leaned into a lightly padded press. They said, “Stand.” The mesh warmed around them. The ring stayed cold in my hand.

“Yes,” I said.

Heat crossed my palm, mild but unmistakable, and the resistance divided between us until I let go. The remaining two rivets stayed blue.

The bell above us rang three strokes again, with less silence between each set.

I packed my hammer, wedges, and tool roll.

“You said I would have it by midday,” Aven said.

“You have it.” I tied on my rain cloak. “I did not say you would have the poor judgment to field an unproven redesign without its smith.”

I had serviced the spillgate years before, an ordinary job of rust, hinges, and a locking wedge that swelled every wet season. Less glamorous than dragon scales. Considerably more useful that morning.

The path climbed beside the relief channel. Rain had turned its stones black and slick, and water boomed behind the reservoir wall like something enormous objecting to architecture. Aven led. They knew where the first attempt had torn loose railings and which stair had split.

Halfway across the upper catwalk, a support gave way under me.

There was no omen. One moment I had iron under both boots. The next, the bracket peeled from wet stone and the walkway dropped. I caught the rail with one hand. My hammer dragged at my belt while the relief channel hammered below.

Aven turned. For one naked instant, they stood perfectly still.

They were waiting for rescue to happen.

Nothing did. The wire could not choose. The old hooks were gone. The harness offered no warning and took no one’s body.

Then Aven saw me, saw the intact support behind them, and made a decision.

They dropped flat, hooked one knee around the support, and caught my wrist. The load struck their shoulder. They pressed the will-catch against the rail with their free hand.

“Catch.”

The braid braced backward along their chosen pull. Aven hauled; I kicked against the wall; together we got my chest over the broken edge. The second rivet sheared.

When the breath ended, Aven rolled onto their back with their injured arm clutched close.

“Shoulder?” I asked.

“Strained.” Their face said more than the word did.

I checked the joint as gently as my hands allowed. Painful, still placed. I looked at the single blue rivet remaining.

“We can go back,” I said.

Below the clouds, the valley town was a huddle of slate roofs beside a river already too broad for its banks. Aven stared down at it.

“The armor didn’t make me catch you,” they said.

“No.”

“And it didn’t make me freeze.”

“No. That habit came from people teaching you rescue was automatic.”

They flexed their good hand. “Then I can learn a different one.”

We went on.

The relief gate shuddered in its stone throat. Water sprayed through every seam. The release bar had jammed halfway, exactly where rust had always loved it, and the locking wedge beneath it had swollen fast. Worse, the final retaining bracket was peeling from the wall. Each surge bent it farther. When it tore free, the bar would kick loose and the gate would stay shut until the reservoir overtopped.

I laid out the work. Aven would brace beneath the release bar while I drove the wedge through its lock. When the wedge seated, the gate would fall open toward the empty relief channel. We would both drop left, behind the stone pier, before the first water struck.

“One rivet,” Aven said.

“One breath,” I agreed.

“Will it work?”

The old answer rose easily. Of course. Hadrik fixed anything. The words even sounded like courage if one did not inspect them closely.

“It can work,” I said. “The upward load is within the design. The bar may twist. Your shoulder is already strained. I cannot promise either of us leaves unhurt.”

“Can we retreat?”

“Yes.” The bracket shrieked. “We would probably live. The lower town would flood.”

Aven shut their eyes. When they opened them, there was fear in them and room beside it for thought.

“I’m not doing this because the court called me a hero,” they said. “I’m doing it because I know what happens if we leave, and because you told me the truth.”

“You may still say no.”

“So may you.”

That was the soundest safety rule either of us had made.

We took our places.

The release bar slammed down until it met Aven’s raised hands. Contact first. Metal groaned against metal. Aven perceived the direction and set their boots. They flattened their working palm beneath the bar, compressing that contact against the iron, and leaned into the breastplate until the second contact seated beneath their sternum. Their other hand never left the bar.

“Hold.”

The last blue rivet began to whiten at its edge. The inward braid tightened from Aven’s palms through their back and legs. They cried out as the real weight spread through them, but the bar stopped descending.

I swung my hammer.

The first blow cracked rust. The second moved the locking wedge the breadth of a thumbnail. The gate shifted under water pressure—not down, but sideways.

Aven’s protection held the upward line they had chosen. It did nothing about the lateral wrench. Their strained shoulder buckled toward the wall.

One breath was not enough.

My tool roll lay open at my knee. The old bypass hook gleamed among the wedges. I could jam it across the empty assent seat in a heartbeat. The open path would seize the nearest protective impulse—mine—and turn my body into whatever brace the harness required. It was the old guarantee, close enough to touch. I could preserve the legend and call the coercion sacrifice afterward.

I dropped the hook.

Instead I tore off my glove and seized the copper consent ring.

“Yes,” I said. Not forever. Not for the court. “Yes, now.”

The ring burned into my palm.

My living intent joined Aven’s for that single hold, and the fitted wire divided the upward strain between us. It did not erase the sideways force. Aven’s shoulder still took that; my hand took heat enough to make the hammer swim in my vision. But their knees stopped folding. The whitening rivet endured one moment longer.

I struck the wedge a third time.

It seated.

The release bar leapt. The gate dropped open. Water roared into the empty channel, exactly where stone and old iron had directed it, not where luck preferred. The third rivet sheared. The response braid flashed once and fused black against the plates.

“Left!” I shouted.

We fell behind the pier as planned. The first wall of water tore through the place where we had stood, carrying rust, branches, and the discarded bypass hook down the safe channel.

For some time there was only stone under my cheek, rain on my back, and Aven’s breathing beside me.

Then the reservoir bell changed to the long, steady toll for water falling.

We had opened the gate. The lower town remained a town rather than becoming a shallow and badly planned lake. Aven could walk, though their shoulder needed a sling. I kept my burned hand wrapped against my chest. The harness hung from them as dead weight: all three blue rivets broken, the response wire fused, no warmth left anywhere in it.

Back at the forge, I laid the harness on my bench.

“Failed repair,” I said.

Aven, pale with exhaustion and dry at last, looked at me as if I had announced that anvils were migratory birds.

“It did exactly what I chose,” they said. “It stopped when you said it would. It charged nobody who hadn’t agreed.”

“The wire is ruined.”

“Then it spent itself honestly.”

I had spent my life returning objects to what their makers intended. It had never occurred to me that an intention might deserve refusal, or that a thing could be fixed by giving it an honorable way to end.

“I could make another,” I said. The offer came from habit, but not entirely. “More rivets. A stronger braid.”

Aven shook their head. “Ordinary mail. A crew. A plan. And the right to refuse the next great deed before anyone starts writing about it.”

“Ordinary mail I can guarantee against reasonable stabbing.”

“Reasonable stabbing?”

“The sign is under revision.”

The next morning, with my good hand and a narrow chisel, I climbed a ladder outside the forge. The gilding came away first. Then the wood. I cut the word *anything* out of the promise I had made so deeply.

In the space beneath, in smaller letters because truth is seldom brief, I carved: *Before I take the job, I will tell you what the repair can do and what it will cost.*

The new sign brought fewer velvet boxes. It brought better questions.

I remained Hadrik. I remained a blacksmith. I fixed many things after that, though never everything, and never by myself merely because my name was over the door.

The plot armor was the last thing I ever claimed I could fix alone.

stories.title: The Attendance Ledger
stories.prompt: A school teacher moonlights as a handler for magical girls, looking after their wellbeing in battle and the classroom, even protecting the girls' secret identities without alerting them.
stories.body:
# The Attendance Ledger

By the third name on the paper attendance ledger, Gideon Tolland knew exactly
how much sleep three of his students had not had.

Northbridge Secondary’s network had chosen community-showcase day to display a
spinning circle instead of the online register, so Gideon was using the paper
backup. The ledger was a grey administrative object with coffee feathered
along one corner. It possessed no insight. Everything it told him about those
three names, Gideon had brought to it himself.

“Drita Ademi?”

“Present.”

Drita held her left wrist close to her body. The cuff of her uniform jumper
covered most of the bruise, but not the careful way she turned each page with
her right hand. Her fingertips were pale with cold.

“Bryn Ahn?”

“Here.”

Bryn had already drawn two routes out of the problem on the lab sheet, although
the problem concerned mineral samples and neither route was required. Her
pencil trembled once, stopped under the pressure of her thumb, then continued.

“Cassia Dominguez?”

“Physically.”

The class laughed. Cassia offered them a thin grin and lowered her face over
her folded arms.

Gideon marked all three present. At one seventeen that morning, in the
voice-scrambled privacy of an encrypted radio relay, Kiteglass had reported a
bad wrist and loss of body heat. Pulsewire had said that lights still had halos
after two difficult severances. Mothlight had joked twice as fast as usual,
which had been the clearest report of all.

Night Clerk had recommended a recovery day. The three girls had chosen school.

Mr. Tolland, who had no legitimate way to connect those reports to these
students, had prepared accordingly.

“Before anyone asks,” he told the class, “the revision token on the board is
for everyone. One deadline, moved once, no justification required. Lab roles
rotate every twelve minutes. The snack box is not charity; it is protection
against the paperwork generated by fainting.”

That earned a better laugh. He passed the box along the benches. Cassia took
two oat bars without looking up. Drita accepted one after seeing three other
students do it. Bryn chose the role nearest the door.

Gideon had not meant to learn their secret. Six months earlier, three
voice-scrambled strangers had asked for practical help over an emergency-radio
frequency: routes, weather, first-aid supplies, someone to notice when brave
became reckless. They had named him Night Clerk as a joke, and the name had
stuck.

Then he had seen three transformed figures disappear into an alley and Drita,
Bryn, and Cassia emerge moments later. After that came matching absences,
matching injuries, Drita’s angle-cutting hand signal, Bryn’s insistence on two
exits, Cassia’s habit of making a joke before admitting fear. No single clue
had proved anything. Together, they left almost no room for him to be wrong.

He had kept that knowledge to himself. Their anonymity was not a puzzle he had
earned the right to solve.

“Feet on the floor,” he said. “Before we begin, five things you can see, four
you can feel, three you can hear. Yes, this is educational. I have declared it
so.”

The room settled by degrees. Cassia’s shoulders lowered. Gideon reached the
next line of his ledger.

From the ventilation grate above Drita came a papery whisper.

“Kiteglass?”

Drita’s head began to turn.

Gideon let the ledger fall.

It struck the floor flat, loud as a slammed door. Pages slewed beneath his
desk. Twenty-eight students looked at him instead of at Drita.

“A compelling demonstration,” he said, crouching, “of gravity’s refusal to
respect staff authority.”

In the shadow behind the grate, something black and thin withdrew: a living
filament, wetly quick, vanishing after it had enjoyed a clear view of the page.

The Rollcaller had survived the night.

Gideon gathered the papers without hurrying. “Change of method. Mark yourselves
present on the silent check-in slips. Apparently I am no longer qualified to
hold a book.”

The class bent to the slips. Drita did not look at the grate again.

At the time, switching the register felt like protection. Gideon would later
understand that the Rollcaller had watched him protect exactly one reaction.

* * *

At lunch, Gideon locked himself in the equipment room behind the lab and
plugged an ordinary headset into an ordinary phone. The voice scrambler made
him sound like a courteous cupboard.

“Something in the school ventilation tried my alias during attendance,”
Kiteglass said. “Right after a civilian name. Same whisper as last night.”

“Assume the Rollcaller survived,” Night Clerk said. “Could it see the register?”

“From that grate? Yes.”

Silence held on the relay. Their health and location channels showed only what
each girl had chosen to share: three rough status lights, no names, no map
points.

“How many people reacted?” Night Clerk asked.

“I nearly did,” Kiteglass said. She stopped, then said it again, flatter.
“Nearly. Then a book hit the floor and everyone looked that way.”

Gideon let her account stand without adding anything she had not told him.

“It chose the moment you were least prepared for,” Night Clerk said. “Anyone
would have turned.”

Pulsewire’s scrambled voice cut in. “It needs correlation. Names give it
candidates, reactions narrow them, cameras prove them. And we’ve got the
showcase this afternoon. There’s a guardian livestream.”

“Agreed. My recommendation is that you leave before the showcase. Available
alternatives: separate departures, remaining in public view, or a contained
trap somewhere you choose. You decide whether you engage at all.”

“Three of us leaving together would be a confession with backpacks,”
Kiteglass said. “And we built that presentation.”

“For six weeks,” Pulsewire added.

Mothlight had said nothing.

Gideon resisted the urge to fill the quiet with instructions. “Mothlight, do
you want options, quiet, or a grounding count?”

“Count. Then options.”

He counted five slow breaths. He could hear her match him by the faint hiss of
the microphone. No one hurried her.

“I’m scared,” Mothlight said at last. “That’s not a vote. Nobody count that
as a vote.”

“Understood.”

“I vote we stay,” she said. “I also vote we don’t improvise in front of a
guardian livestream, because I do have standards.”

Kiteglass proposed drawing the Rollcaller toward the empty rehearsal corridor
during showcase setup, away from the auditorium audience. Pulsewire sent a
photo of the fire plan posted by the stairs, cropped so the school’s crest was
gone, with the cameras she knew marked in red. She traced two exits on it: the
public auditorium doors and a service corridor with no camera sightline. Three
taps on the relay would call the trap off. No debate afterward.

Then Pulsewire ran the rest of her checklist, the way she did before every
job. “If the network is compromised?”

“Disconnect.”

“Transformation orders?”

“Night Clerk never orders a transformation.” It was the first rule they had
made together. “If you hear one, the channel is compromised.”

“Good,” Pulsewire said.

He looked at the photographed plan, at the three status lights, at every
variable he wanted to close his hand around.

“Send me your final route,” Night Clerk said. “I’ll work out evacuation timing
from the fire plan.”

* * *

By midafternoon, the auditorium smelled of dust, hot projector plastic, and
the citrus cleaner used whenever guardians were expected.

Gideon rotated presentation jobs across the whole class. Anyone could hand
their speaking section to a partner. Anyone could use the revision token.
Drita kept her speaking part but let someone else carry the display board.
Bryn checked both exits before connecting the class laptop. Cassia stood in
the wing, named five things she could see under her breath, and walked onstage
when she was ready.

Their rehearsal was good.

On the second run, Drita lost her place when the display board shifted. Gideon
did not rescue her sentence. He reminded the entire class that a pause counted
as speaking, then waited. Drita reset the board with her right hand and
finished the explanation herself. Bryn quietly moved the laptop charger so it
would not cross either exit. Cassia shortened one joke, drank half a bottle of
water, and asked to repeat her closing section.

Those choices cost the schedule eight minutes. Gideon spent them without
hesitation.

Gideon checked the boring safety features while they reset: the heavy acoustic
fire partition recessed beside the stage, the breaker panel near the service
door, the blind corridor beyond it. Above the auditorium laptop, the stream
camera’s green indicator glowed beside a guardian-view counter reading zero.

At that moment, Bryn came from the laptop, Cassia came from the wing, and all
three girls leaned over the same cue sheet. A hair-thin filament beneath the
camera housing pivoted to follow them. Gideon’s stomach tightened. If the
thing had chased a trio last night and marked Drita at the grate this morning,
then her two showcase partners were only a guess, but a narrow one, and easy
to test.

The public-address speakers clicked.

An administrator’s voice said, “Drita Ademi, Bryn Ahn, and Cassia Dominguez,
report to the main office immediately.”

All three girls went still.

Whatever had sent that summons had just watched three students react as one.

“Continue setup,” Gideon said. “The office knows the traditional method of
contacting staff.”

He called from the wall phone. The actual office had issued no summons.

“An audio test entered the wrong channel,” he told the class. “A thrilling
preview of the competence adults will display this evening.”

The room loosened. Students returned to cables and cue cards. The three girls
went back to three separate jobs.

But when Gideon returned to the tech table, the ledger page with their names
was gone.
Along the baseboard, an ink-dark filament slipped beneath the auditorium’s A/V
rack.

The camera counter changed from zero to one.

Then to six.

The livestream had begun forty minutes early.

* * *

The projection screen flashed white. Three civilian names appeared across it
in block letters: DRITA ADEMI. BRYN AHN. CASSIA DOMINGUEZ.

Beneath them jittered blurred images from the previous night—three bright,
human shapes caught at bad angles by an ordinary street camera the Rollcaller
had threaded with its own living filaments. The refraction veil had smeared
faces and voices in the recording, as it was meant to do. It could not hide a
visible transformation, and it could not stop someone patient from placing two
sets of evidence side by side.

Question marks blinked between Drita Ademi and Kiteglass, Bryn Ahn and
Pulsewire, Cassia Dominguez and Mothlight.

The class stared. The view counter climbed.

Black filaments spilled from the A/V rack, thin as drawn ink and moving with
the intent of fingers. They threaded the camera mount, the speaker cable, the
door hardware. The Rollcaller had pushed living pieces of itself inside the
machinery and was operating it from within.

From every speaker came Night Clerk’s copied voice.

“Kiteglass. Pulsewire. Mothlight. Transform now.”

Gideon’s heart lurched.

The three girls did not move.

Night Clerk never gave that order.

“Everyone away from the screen,” Mr. Tolland said. “Leave bags. Service
corridor, two lines.”

The class knew his evacuation voice. Chairs scraped. A filament snapped across
the main doors and cinched them shut. Another reached for the camera, carrying
the Rollcaller’s living attention toward the growing audience beyond it.

Three taps struck Gideon’s earpiece. The rehearsal-corridor trap was off.

Pulsewire’s voice came through the relay, pitched low under the noise of the
room. Pain roughened the scrambled words. “The wiring’s one route. Our
channel’s the second. It’s bridged both. I need full blackout.”

His screen still held three weak telemetry lights: cold, tremor, strain. Cut
the breaker, and the school network, cameras, and relay would all die
together. He would lose their reports and their positions, and with them his
illusion that enough data could make their choices safe.

The copied voice crooned from the speakers, “Transform now.”

Gideon could have warned each of them by civilian name on the relay, and each
warning would have been a betrayal.

He had reached the breaker panel by the service door ahead of the class. He
turned his face into the doorway, away from the room, and pressed the transmit
switch under the scrape of chairs and the crooning from the speakers. “Facts
once. The local breaker ends the stream, the cameras, and this relay. Result:
darkness, no telemetry, no contact from me. Your decision.”

A breath. The answers came back as murmurs he could barely hear over the room.

Kiteglass said, “Dark.”

Pulsewire said, “Dark.”

Mothlight said, “Very, very dark.”

Gideon pulled the local breaker. A hijacked A/V rack was still electrical
equipment. School procedure gave the adult nearest the panel one sensible
action.

The view counter vanished at twenty-three.

The speakers died. The relay died. Every telemetry light went out.

The main doors were visibly bound. Mr. Tolland opened the designated service
exit, as the evacuation plan required.

* * *

Emergency strips painted the corridor floor a weak amber. Gideon moved the
class through the blind turn by touch and voice.

“Hand on the wall. Keep moving. If you can complain, save it for the incident
form.”

They obeyed. One student held the service door. Another guided a classmate
whose glasses had fallen. Ordinary competence moved down the line without
waiting for Gideon to distribute it. His duty was here, with the whole class,
even while every frightened instinct tried to turn him toward the three status
lights that no longer existed.

Behind him came the sound of tearing cloth, though no cloth in the auditorium
was large enough to make it. A cold, angled gleam crossed the narrow window in
the acoustic partition.

He did not see who stayed behind. He did not see hands close on focus tokens,
or living power pass through those nonliving shapes and become transformed
light. By the time he had dragged the partition halfway out of its recess,
three refracted figures moved beyond the glass, their features blurred even to
his knowing eyes.

The Rollcaller hurled filaments at the evacuation opening.

A translucent plane struck them aside. It appeared at a steep angle, flashed,
and settled across the service route like braced glass. Behind it, Kiteglass
held one arm tight against her ribs. The barrier shivered each time the
creature hit. She could have chased the sheet-thin body retreating toward the
A/V rack. Instead she planted her feet at the door.

“Route first,” Gideon heard her say.

Students were still filing down the corridor behind him. Fire procedure wanted
the partition shut between them and the auditorium.

He heaved it the rest of the way. A foot from the latch, something caught its
lower track. A filament whipped through the gap and wrapped the handle. Gideon
hauled back. Pain streaked from his shoulder to his elbow, bright enough to
turn the corridor white at the edges.

On the auditorium side, a sharp blue flicker ran along the speaker cable. It
ended with a crack. Someone gasped. The lights stayed off, but Gideon heard a
body strike the stage steps and then get up again.

“One bridge cut,” Pulsewire said. Her voice sounded far too loud in the dead
room. “Two active.”

The breaker had killed the school’s current, not the creature. Its own
filaments still ran out through the walls to lines the panel did not control.

The Rollcaller answered in Cassia’s civilian voice.

“I can’t. I can’t. I can’t.”

It spoke from the stage, the ceiling, the dead speakers, each imitation
slightly out of time. One refracted figure stopped moving.

Gideon could see only fragments through the narrow glass: a pale hand lifted,
a shimmer gone ragged, filaments turning toward the stillness. He had no relay
and no right to break the darkness they had requested. He held the partition
and listened.

Mothlight’s own voice, blurred by the veil and coming from one place only, said,
“One breath.”

The angled barrier widened. The blue flicker paused.

No one told her to hurry.

Gideon took one breath too, though his shoulder shook. Beyond the glass, the
still figure inhaled. Exhaled.

Then Mothlight filled the dark auditorium with liars.

That was all Gideon could make of it at first. Shadows ran where no bodies
could fit. Light folded against the walls and came away as half a dozen figures
shaped like Kiteglass, a scatter shaped like Pulsewire, Mothlight after
Mothlight lifting bright hands. Displaced voices called the three aliases from
opposite ends of the room.

The Rollcaller lunged at recognition. Filaments ripped out of the camera,
speakers, and cable channels to seize every apparent identity at once.

For a moment the A/V rack stood exposed.

Something behind it peeled upward: a narrow living body, ink-dark and
sheet-thin, its many extended pieces pulled taut toward false targets. A
translucent plane appeared above it. Another below. Two more folded inward,
not striking but enclosing.

The pressure against Gideon’s partition doubled. The filament around the
handle tightened. His injured arm began to fail.

“External lines,” Pulsewire said somewhere beyond his sight. “Everything it’s
still holding outside. Consent to cut?”

“Yes,” came one voice.

“Yes,” came another, after one deliberate breath.

Blue-white light snapped through every black strand.

The filament on Gideon’s handle went slack.

He dragged the partition closed with his good arm. The latch caught. On the
other side came a sound like a ream of wet paper dropped from a height, then
silence.

Gideon stayed against the partition, shoulder burning, while the last student
cleared the corridor. Through the window he saw only a clear angular cage, a
dark shape folded small inside it, and three blurred figures supporting one
another.

He did not know how they had changed their plan in the dark. He did not know
whether Pulsewire could still hear properly, whether Kiteglass’s wrist had
worsened, whether Mothlight’s remaining glow meant strength or the last of it.
He would wait for whatever they decided to tell him.

* * *

At the outdoor muster point, the story available to ordinary witnesses was
strange but small.

The power had failed. A corrupted showcase file had displayed three students’
names beside fuzzy costume footage. The guardian stream had ended before
anything clearer appeared. Cameras had gone dark with the breaker. No one had
seen a transformation. Most of the class had been looking at Gideon or the
service corridor when the lights died.

By the time explanations passed from student to student, the likeliest theory
was an ugly promotional stunt interrupted by bad wiring. In a city where magic
belonged to old stories and cheap effects, that answer was easier to believe
than three exhausted classmates turning into the impossible.

Drita, Bryn, and Cassia emerged from separate gaps in the milling students in
civilian clothes. Gideon did not see where they came from. Drita’s hands were
still cold. Bryn flinched at a whistle from across the yard. Cassia ate the
second oat bar in four bites.

“We went out the back of the stage,” Bryn said before he could ask. “Wrong
door. Took ages to get round.”

Gideon told them to stand with their row and asked nothing else.

The stolen page meant he had to rebuild attendance. He passed silent check-in
slips down the rows at muster, and each student marked their own presence.
Drita, Bryn, and Cassia made three honest marks. Gideon entered them without
alteration.

That evening, after food, warmth, an ordinary check of his strained shoulder,
and several hours in which the world remained blessedly unremarkable, Night
Clerk reopened the reset relay.

Three status lights appeared by choice.

“Containment?” he asked.

“Stable,” Kiteglass said. “I held it while Pulsewire checked the cuts. Then we
closed the body in an unplugged metal equipment case. We’ll decide what to do
with it when we’re not dead on our feet.”

“That is a strong argument for rest. Available support: food delivery, medical
checks, deadline help, route coverage, or no contact.”

“What, no schedule?” Mothlight asked. “You always send a schedule.”

Gideon looked at the recovery plan he had already drafted and turned it face
down.

“Not unless requested.”

They chose food, injury checks, and two mission-free nights.

“And before anyone asks,” Kiteglass said, “I stopped chasing it because this
wrist does a shield or a chase. Not both. So I held. It’s fine. It’s a wrist.”

“Also my ears are still ringing,” Pulsewire said. “In case anyone’s keeping a
list.” The channel hissed for a moment. “New protocol. We ask for dark, you
give us the facts once and hang up.”

“Agreed.”

The next morning, Mr. Tolland did not call the register aloud. Silent
self-check-in slips waited on every lab bench.

“Permanent?” Drita asked.

“Trial policy,” Gideon said. “It reduces the number of opportunities for me to
drop important documents.”

Cassia smiled. Bryn checked the door, then bent over her slip. None of them
looked at Mr. Tolland as though they heard Night Clerk’s scrambled voice, or
as though they suspected he knew who they were.

Gideon opened the replacement ledger. Beside Drita Ademi, Bryn Ahn, and Cassia
Dominguez, he recorded three simple presences.

stories.title: The Last Bus to Briar Hill
stories.prompt: A fairytale about going on an adventure but set in modern day.
stories.body:
# The Last Bus to Briar Hill

At 12:47 a.m., with rain ticking against her helmet and somebody’s noodles
cooling in the insulated box on her back, Miriam Velez promised her brother an
adventure for the thirty-second time.

“After this month,” she said into her headset, braking at a red light. “Rent
first. Briar Hill when things settle down.”

Mateo was quiet long enough for the courier app to offer her a surge block:
three deliveries, guaranteed bonus, accept within twenty seconds.

“Things don’t settle down,” he said.

“They do if people stop adding emergencies.”

She regretted it before the words had finished leaving her mouth. Fifteen was
old enough to hear the accusation inside a joke. Miriam watched rain polish the
empty intersection. Her battery showed thirty-one percent; the offer counted
down from twelve.

“I didn’t mean you,” she said.

“You never do.”

The call ended. Miriam accepted the block.

She delivered the noodles to a lobby bright as an aquarium, photographed the
paper bag beneath the apartment number, and turned her bicycle toward the next
pickup. The bonus would cover the short edge of rent. That was not imaginary.
Neither were the electric bill, Mateo’s growing feet, or the fact that two years
ago their mother had died on a dry road in ordinary traffic while going
somewhere she had gone a hundred times before.

Briar Hill had been their mother’s idea. The old voicemail was still saved
offline on Miriam’s phone: traffic hissing behind her voice, a bus number
remembered wrong, then laughter interrupting the promise that they would all go
up to the hill together—

Miriam never played the final second. There was no final second, only breath
and laughter cut off by the recording limit.

Her phone chimed.

The message had been scheduled rather than sent live. Mateo had used the safety
check-in settings Miriam had taught him.

*I found our adventure. I researched the route. Location is on. If I’m not back
by sunrise, follow it. I’m sorry.*

Below the message, his live-location pin moved along the last ordinary bus line
toward their apartment.

Miriam called. No answer. She called again while riding hard enough that rain
needled through her gloves. The pin crossed the municipal bus terminal, paused
at its western shelter, then acquired a transit label she had never seen:
`Route 0`.

She opened the city app one-handed at the next light. There was no Route 0.
Mateo’s pin moved north along two streets that ran parallel, crossed a canal
without using either bridge, and vanished into a gray patch where the map stored
no road at all.

Miriam pulled over beneath a leaking awning and inspected everything the fear
in her wanted to skip. Mateo had packed his transit card and rain shell. His
location sharing had been switched from one hour to indefinite. The safety
message had been written that afternoon and scheduled for the last ordinary
service of the night. He had not stumbled onto the route or been snatched from
his bed. He had planned an adventure using every emergency precaution she had
taught him, except the one where he asked permission.

The courier app vibrated: *Proceed to pickup. Late arrival may affect your
standing.*

Miriam swung west.

The terminal shelter was empty when she arrived. The last scheduled bus had
gone. Sodium lamps burned through the downpour, making every drop look briefly
solid. She locked her bicycle to a rack and discovered Mateo’s green charging
cord was missing from the side pocket of her delivery box. He had taken that
too. Planning, not panic.

A pair of headlights appeared where the terminal lane ended at a concrete
wall.

An unmarked white bus rolled out of the rain. It was old enough to have square
windows and new enough to carry a contactless fare reader. Its front display
held a plain service label: `Route 0`.

The doors folded open under the driver’s hand.

The woman behind the wheel wore a charcoal coat over an ordinary transit
uniform. Silver hair brushed her jaw. A brass name badge read **Maude Dallow**.

“You are late,” she said.

“Where is Mateo Velez?”

“Ahead of you.”

Miriam put one wet shoe on the step.

Maude raised two fingers. The fare reader remained dark. “Not yet. You should
understand what you’re choosing.”

“I’m choosing my brother.”

“You are trying to choose two destinations.” Maude glanced at the courier
countdown glowing on Miriam’s phone. “This crossing opens for a person willing
to leave the destination the city already expects. Cancel it. Name whom you
seek. Pay the usual fare. There are three request stops before Briar Hill and
one return at sunrise. Miss that return, and I promise nothing.”

“This is a bus.”

“Yes. Metal, glass, wiring. None of it is alive, and none of it makes bargains.”
Maude laid her palm against the fare reader. Fine green light traveled from the
creases of her hand into its black screen. “I tend this end of the crossing.
The Briar Host tends the Hill. The bus carries what I give it. It decides
nothing.”

The courier timer showed forty-three seconds. Miriam could board, find Mateo,
and preserve the block if she hurried. The thought lasted until Maude looked at
her.

“Unchosen destinations do not count as abandoned,” Maude said.

Miriam opened the courier app. *Canceling after acceptance forfeits the
guarantee and may reduce future offers.* Her thumb hovered. Rent first, she had
said, as though fear had never hidden behind arithmetic.

She canceled the block.

“Mateo Velez,” she said, and tapped her ordinary fare card.

The reader chimed because Maude’s green light had awakened it. The doors closed
at her touch. Maude drove into the terminal wall.

For one instant the windshield held only wet concrete. Then Maude pressed her
hand to the wheel, green light ran beneath its vinyl, and the bus passed into a
street Miriam had never seen.

Thorn hedges crowded the sidewalks. Rain shone on them like strings of beads.
Behind the glass, the city still appeared in fragments—laundromat, tower block,
all-night pharmacy—but never in an order any map would accept.

At the first request stop, an exhausted woman in scrubs stood beneath a broken
shelter with a dead phone in both hands. Maude braked and opened the doors.

“Finally,” the woman said, climbing aboard. “I need to call my client again.
The first call dropped. Then the regular service disappeared from the board,
so I have to tell her what changed.”

She was real: rain-reddened eyes, plastic grocery bag, an identity card turned
backward on its clip. No crown beneath her hood, no bird feet, nothing from a
storybook. Just someone stranded between night shifts.

“We continue when she has made her call,” Maude said.

Miriam’s phone showed Mateo’s location frozen somewhere ahead. Twenty-four
percent remained in the power bank clipped inside her delivery box. Enough to
keep tracking him—or enough to lend.

“How long does that call have to be?” Miriam asked.

“Long enough for someone waiting to know she has not been forgotten.”

Miriam almost laughed. Instead she pulled out the power bank.

The woman’s phone drank charge slowly. One percent, then two. Miriam watched
Mateo’s pin fail to refresh and imagined sunrise bleaching an empty hill.

At three percent, the woman made the call. “I’m safe,” she said, hunching over
the borrowed power. “We got cut off. The service changed. I’m still coming.
Lock the door until I buzz.”

She stayed connected until the person at the other end understood the new
arrival time. By then, the power bank had fallen to nine percent.

When she finished, she unwound a green cord from her phone and held it out.

“A boy lent me this at the last bus,” she said. “He said his sister would be
angry if he gave away the power bank too.”

Miriam took Mateo’s cord. Warmth from the woman’s phone still clung to the
connector.

“Which way did he go?”

“Up the steps beside the stop. He waited until my first call connected.” The
woman looked from Miriam to Maude. “Said he was going to finish something.”

Maude drove on after the woman transferred at an ordinary lit corner. Within a
block, rain erased the corner from view.

Miriam connected her own phone to the power bank. Its remaining charge kept
Mateo’s location trace and the municipal text service running until the thorn
ring road came into view. Then the bank’s indicator lights went dark.

“The Briar Host makes copies,” Maude said. “Stored maps. Old signs. Anything a
screen or a memory has already shown within its hedge.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“Because a test with no rule is only cruelty.” Maude watched the road. “The
Briar Host can repeat what it has received. It cannot forge a new reply freely
made outside the crossing after you entered.”

The thorn hedges opened onto a ring road divided into three identical exits.
Each sign said **BRIAR HILL**. Each navigation preview on Miriam’s phone showed
the same blue line. Rain struck all three roads at the same angle, and beneath
each sign stood a municipal stop placard.

The numbers differed.

Miriam enlarged the map, but the roads crawled and exchanged places under her
fingertip. She held to Maude’s rule: the Briar Host could repeat stored images,
and some such copy was reaching the screens and signs. The phone itself was
only displaying what reached it.

“You have six minutes,” Maude said.

“Until what?”

“Until this stop becomes your destination.”

Miriam knew the municipal text service because couriers used it when the app’s
arrival times lied. She sent the three stop codes in one message. Two automated
replies returned at once, both naming ordinary neighborhoods miles apart. The
third request passed to a late-night responder.

The battery fell to eleven percent.

*Stop 4312: Briar Hill park entrance. Temporary service access only. No
scheduled pickup at this hour.*

A current reply, written beyond the hedge. By Maude’s rule, the Briar Host
could not have stored it before she asked.

“Middle exit,” Miriam said.

Maude turned the wheel. The other two roads folded behind curtains of thorn,
as though the Briar Host had drawn its hedge closed behind them. The bus
continued along the only strip of wet municipal asphalt underneath.

The third request stop was a closed shopping concourse. Steel grilles covered
the storefronts. A children’s ride sat unplugged beside a vending machine.
Maude opened the doors.

“I don’t see anyone,” Miriam said.

“Truth is waiting,” Maude replied. “It usually does. The Briar Host will shape
what reaches your eyes and ears from material already stored here. An offer is
not a person. An imitation is not an answer from the dead.”

As Miriam stepped down, her phone screen filled with notifications.

*Bonus reinstated. Return to pickup.*

Then a message marked as Mateo’s: *All clear. Went home. Don’t follow.*

Then an incoming voicemail bearing their mother’s old number.

Miriam stopped under the dead strip lights.

She knew. Knowing did not stop her hand from shaking.

She pressed play.

Her mother’s voice came smooth and near, without traffic or breath. “Miriam,
sweetheart, you were right. Loving someone means keeping them away from danger.
Go home. Mateo is safe if you stop.”

Warm kitchen light spilled from a storefront. Beyond the grille stood the old
table, the chipped yellow bowl, their mother in the raincoat from her last
photograph. The glamour smiled with her mouth.

Miriam held to Maude’s warning. It was not a ghost. It was not their mother
restored, nor a living copy of her. What confronted her was a sensory lure
assembled from cached photographs, recordings, and whatever grief supplied
when a shape was almost right.

Almost was terrible.

Miriam opened the authentic voicemail saved on her phone. Four percent.

Traffic hissed. Their mother said the wrong bus number, corrected herself,
laughed, and began, “We’ll take sandwiches up to Briar Hill when—”

The recording ended inside the laugh.

The kitchen imitation had no room for error. It offered certainty in her
mother’s voice because certainty was what Miriam had wanted from the dead.

“Money matters,” Miriam said into the empty concourse. “Rent matters. But it
isn’t why I keep saying later.”

The false kitchen waited.

“She died going somewhere ordinary. I thought if I chose anything unnecessary,
anything happy, it would be like asking the road to take somebody else.”

The confession did not make the fear foolish. It made the fear hers. Mateo had
been paying for it without ever agreeing to the debt.

Her phone went black.

For one breath Miriam stood without maps, messages, work, or the saved voice.
Then the kitchen light vanished. Steel grilles became steel grilles again, and
the mother-shaped lure broke into reflections on wet tile. Miriam could only
take the timing as the Briar Host’s reply.

Maude opened the bus doors. “Now you know what you came to finish.”

At Maude’s last green-lit turn, she said, “The Briar Host is opening the Hill.”
A hedge drew aside. Briar Hill rose behind the last row of apartment towers,
though Miriam had never seen a hill there before. The rain thinned near its
crown. Roots surfaced through the pavement and braided themselves into steps,
lifting one after another as though something beneath the soil flexed.

Mateo stood at the top with his hood down and wet curls plastered to his
forehead.

Miriam ran. She stopped one arm’s length from him, because the urge to seize
him was so strong it felt like falling.

“You came,” he said.

“You left.”

“I sent the safety message. I shared my location.”

“You took an impossible bus after midnight.”

“Because if I asked, you would have said after this month.”

Both facts struck cleanly. Neither canceled the other.

Behind Mateo, a trunk wider than the bus shelter divided into the suggestion
of shoulders. Thousands of thorn twigs lifted and settled with a sound like
quiet applause. Two green hollows opened in the bark.

The Briar Host was alive. Miriam felt its attention move through root and leaf,
patient and immense.

“I didn’t get an exception,” Mateo said. “I was on the last ordinary bus home.
At the terminal, I canceled the saved trip in the city app even though I’d
promised to be home when your block ended. I named Miriam Velez. I tapped my
transit card and paid the normal fare.”

His eyes dropped. “I got the aide’s first call connected. At the false exits, I
requested the stop codes after we crossed the terminal wall. The fresh reply
came from outside, the way Maude said it had to. And I said no when it showed
me our mother.”

Pride arrived tangled with anger. Miriam let both remain.

“You still scared me.”

“You scare me too,” he said. “Every time you act like keeping me alive is the
same as us having a life.”

He rubbed rain from his eyes. “The posts about Briar Hill said it finished
promises. I thought maybe it could finish her voicemail. Not bring her back. I
knew that wasn’t—” His voice caught. “I thought there might be one real thing
she meant to say.”

The Briar Host bent its living branches low. “I know only what was brought
within my hedge. I can arrange stored sound. I cannot make your mother choose
new words, and I cannot turn an arrangement into her.”

Mateo nodded. Grief moved over his face without taking his decision away. “So I
said no to the thing it made.”

Miriam looked at the brightening edge of the sky. “I am taking him home.”

The Briar Host’s branches leaned toward her.

“That is not yours to complete,” it said. Its voice came from living wood, not
from the bus, the dead phone, or the wind. “This road grows toward promises
left unfinished at my Hill. I can complete a beginning. I cannot restore your
dead, and I cannot choose a living rider’s return.”

Mateo folded his arms.

“I’m sorry,” Miriam said.

He looked startled.

“I’m sorry I made later do the work of no. I’m sorry I made you test whether
I’d follow. And I’m angry that you made me.”

“I’m sorry for that part,” Mateo said. “Not for coming.”

“I know.”

“If I come home, you don’t get to call tonight proof I can never choose
anything.”

“And you don’t get to call precautions permission.”

“Okay.”

It was not forgiveness tied in a ribbon. It was a boundary they could carry in
both directions.

The Briar Host opened the hedge. A bridge of slick roots crossed a dark cut in
the hillside to the road where Maude had parked the bus. The sky above the
apartments had gone from black to iron gray.

“Will you finish the last path with me?” Miriam asked. “Then will you come
home?”

Mateo studied her face, giving the question the time a real choice required.
“Yes. If we schedule the next adventure before you accept another block.”

“Yes.”

They stepped onto the bridge.

Mateo led. His research had taught him that the roots with pale undersides were
new growth and would bend; he tested the dark, rain-hardened ones before
shifting his weight. Halfway across, a broken span opened above the cut.

“I crossed it when there were more roots,” he said.

The Briar Host drew those roots deeper into the hill. It would supply the test,
not the answer.

Miriam opened her delivery box. The power bank was empty, the food compartment
smelled of rain, and a length of repair cord remained beneath her tools. She
looped it around a stone post on their side, pulled twice, and tied the other
end around her waist.

“You know the anchors,” Mateo said.

“You know the path. Tell me where to put my feet.”

He pointed to a black root below the lip. Miriam lowered herself onto it,
crossed the gap, and braced the cord around the far trunk. Mateo followed. When
his wet shoe slipped, he caught the line; when the anchor shifted, Miriam
leaned back with all her weight. Neither hauled the other across. Each made the
other’s next choice possible.

At the far end, the Briar Host cast one last glamour across the road.

The warm kitchen appeared with two empty chairs drawn out. Their mother stood
between them, whole and dry, holding the yellow bowl. No demand this time. Only
the invitation to stop before leaving.

Mateo’s hand found Miriam’s.

“It showed me this before,” he whispered.

“I know what it is.”

“Me too.”

They walked through. The false kitchen scattered into rain, its borrowed light
withdrawing into the Briar Host’s hedge.

Maude opened the bus doors. Mateo boarded first by his own choice. Miriam
followed by hers.

Sunrise touched the thorns.

The Briar Host closed the Hill end of the crossing, and Maude drove the bus
through the narrowing gap. Her green light moved from her hands through the
wheel and along the window frames. Outside, impossible streets aligned one by
one with ordinary city blocks.

At 6:08 a.m., Maude stopped at the western terminal shelter. Rainwater lay in
the gutters. Commuters had not yet arrived.

Miriam’s fare card showed one ordinary charge. Mateo’s location history ended
at the terminal, resumed briefly beside an unlisted park access, and stopped
when his battery had died. The evidence looked like bad service and bad
judgment because most of it was.

Before they stepped down, Maude held out a flat brown token punched in the
shape of a leaf.

“The Briar Host grew it after you chose the return,” she said. “It completes
beginnings, not wishes. Plant it if you like.”

Miriam put it in Mateo’s palm.

“Ms. Dallow,” he said, “will Route 0 come again?”

“I promised one return,” Maude said. “Do not embroider that into two.”

They got off. Maude closed the doors and drove the bus into the thinning rain,
her hands steady on the wheel.

At home, charging cables revived their phones but repaired nothing else.
Miriam’s app recorded an abandoned block, removed the guaranteed bonus, and
warned that fewer offers might follow. The rent remained short. Her jacket
dripped onto the floor, her bicycle needed a new brake pad, and their mother
remained dead.

Miriam and Mateo sat at the kitchen table until the windows paled. They agreed
that safety messages were not permission to vanish. They agreed that fear was
not permission to make every decision alone. Mateo accepted a week without
unsupervised night trips. Miriam opened their shared calendar.

Together, they chose a Saturday morning two weeks away: municipal bus, free
greenhouse, packed lunch, home before dark. The leaf-punched token lay in a
flowerpot beside the window. It did nothing.

Two weeks later, the lost bonus still mattered. Miriam had taken extra midday
deliveries, and the numbers in her banking app remained unfriendly. Rain
threatened again. Every practiced part of her wanted to say they should wait.

Instead she zipped sandwiches into her cleaned delivery bag.

Mateo checked the ordinary bus time. Miriam locked the apartment. They left
together.

When they returned that afternoon with damp sleeves and an empty sandwich bag,
Miriam found the token split open in the flowerpot. A green shoot, small enough
to shelter beneath one raindrop, had pushed into the light.

stories.title: A Little Winter for Sale
stories.prompt: As a traveler, you've been exploring the desert for days, before coming upon a city so far from water, nestled against a mountainside. You find that in the mountains cave, is an ice dragon far from home, enjoying being paid to simply sell small bouts of it's power
stories.body:
# A Little Winter for Sale

On the fourth day beyond the last mapped cistern, I found a city where no city
had any right to be.

It clung to the lower face of a black mountain, pale walls crowded one above
another in the narrow mercy of its shadow. Terraces flashed with copper. A line
of green trees ran through the middle of it, offensively alive.

I checked my map, though I had checked it twice since dawn. No river. No
spring. No lake blue enough to justify a goat, let alone five hundred roofs.
Only the mountain, marked by an earlier surveyor as the Black Shoulder, and a
warning that the western salt road ended in broken country.

My water skin gave me one mouthful. It tasted of leather, hot brass, and poor
decisions.

Behind me, the southern sky had thickened to the color of a bruise. Glasswind.
Even at that distance I could see the high glitter where grit turned in the
sun. I had watched it growing all morning and continued west because I was
Tair Ked, route surveyor, and because turning back had always felt like asking
permission.

I took out my sunwheel. Its brass rim lay warm and familiar in my palm. Inside
it, a heart of paired brass and silver kept the needle true through noon heat
and night cold, balanced so delicately that my pulse made it tremble.
Five years of bearings were cut into the outer rings in my own cramped hand:
salt pans, wells, safe noon shadows, three roads that merchants insisted did
not exist until they needed them. With the sunwheel and a clear horizon, I
could earn water in any settlement worth reaching.

Without water, I had until noon to become a cautionary engraving on somebody
else's instrument.

I walked toward the impossible trees.

The gate stood open. White cloth had been tied over its ironwork against the
coming wind. A woman in a dust veil took one look at me, held up a finger to
silence whatever proud idiocy I was about to say, and put a clay cup in my
hands.

The cup sweated.

I stared at the droplets running over my knuckles.

"Drink," she said.

The water was so cold it hurt my teeth. I drank too quickly, stopped because
she pinched the rim down, then drank again when she released it. The desert
inside me contracted around that cup.

"Price?" I managed.

"After you keep it down."

She poured a second measure from a sweating stone jar, smaller than the first,
and opened a narrow ledger. "Name?"

"You give water before asking that?"

"I asked after. We are very strict."

"Tair Ked."

She wrote it. Beside my name she marked the two measures with a square of blue
chalk.

"Yara Mesk," she said, tapping her own chest. "Waterkeeper. Those go on
recoverable civic hospitality credit, ration price. Pay in coin or work when your
hands stop shaking."

My gratitude cooled. A debt entered in ink was still a hand around the ankle,
however politely offered.

"I can pay now."

Yara corked the jar without a glance at my purse and looked past me at the
sky. "Later. There'll be work soon enough. The glasswind's early."

Across the city, shutters were closing in a rising clatter. Above the rooftops,
thin copper channels descended from the mountain, some beaded with
condensation. I put two small coins on her ledger anyway. I wanted the account
closed with room to spare.

She pushed one back. "That's double."

She recorded the first coin, then recorded the returned one. This seemed
designed to annoy me with accuracy.

I followed her uphill.

***

Qarsis was not sustained by a miracle. It was sustained by several
insufficient things lashed together with copper, lime, and aggressive
bookkeeping.

Yara showed me the flat fields east of the wall, where hundreds of sloped glass
panes drank damp from hot brine spread beneath them. The sun warmed the pans;
vapor gathered under the glass and ran through clay gutters into covered
cisterns. White crust furred every seam. Farther upslope, stone throats waited
to catch the rare rain that struck the Black Shoulder and tried to escape.

"Stills and runoff give us about half of what an ordinary day needs," Yara
said. "Some years more. Most years less."

"And the other half?"

She laid her palm on a copper pipe running down the lane.

It was cold.

Under its greenish skin, water ticked and whispered toward the lower cisterns.
The return pipe beside it was warm and smelled faintly of salt.

"The mountain seeps brine," she said. "Too bitter to drink. We lift it to the
exchanger. Six batches a day, about four hundred litres each. Put that with
the stills and it's twelve litres a head, most days."

"Six batches of what?"

"Come and see."

We climbed through terraces where covered jars stood at every doorway. No
fountains splashed for beauty. Laundry water ran into garden troughs. A child
somewhere behind a shutter complained about being called indoors, but no one
wasted breath arguing with the darkening sky.

The cold pipe led toward a cave cut into the mountainside above the last
houses. A stone arch at its mouth had one word carved into it: COLDMOUTH.
Inside, channels crossed the floor toward a copper apparatus taller than I
was. Brine filled a shallow enclosed basin. Ribs of hammered metal clasped it,
all connected to a flared horn that pointed into the dark.

My suspicion, deprived of any sensible target, found a dragon.

Urumet lay beyond the exchanger on a shelf of black stone. Slate-blue scales
overlapped from its long muzzle to the folded hooks of its wings. Hoarfrost
edged every ridge. It could have crushed the copper horn under one foreclaw.
Instead it was holding a square of paper delicately between two claws and
reading it with an expression of profound injury.

"This receipt," Urumet said, "does not include the grit surcharge."

A thin clerk on the safe side of the exchanger consulted a slate. "The grit
hasn't reached the intake yet."

"It will be in the intake before the fifth stroke. I can taste it from here.
Write it now and spare us both an amendment."

Yara leaned toward me. "Urumet likes invoices."

"Invoices," the dragon said without looking up, "are civilization made
portable."

The clerk added a line. Urumet read it, made a pleased sound deep enough to
ripple the brine, and pressed one clawtip into a pad of blue wax. It stamped
the receipt with a neat crescent.

"Fourth stroke," Yara said. "Four-count standard. Exchanger loaded and gates
checked."

The clerk pulled two levers. Brine flooded the copper ribs. A small bimetal
tongue in the regulator lifted across a numbered slot.

Urumet rose.

Cold did not come from the machine. It came when Urumet opened its jaws and
breathed one narrow, silent ribbon into the horn.

Yara counted aloud.

At one, frost raced over the copper ribs.

At two, the cave air turned white and my damp sleeves stiffened.

At three, clear ice thickened inside the basin while cloudy, concentrated brine
squeezed through lower slots.

At four, the regulator tongue curled across the aperture. Urumet shut its jaws.
The cold ceased.

For a moment the cave held its breath. Then drains opened and the bitter
remnant hissed down the warm return channel. Workers behind the casing loosened
the clean ice in slabs. Desert heat would melt those into drinking water before
they reached the cisterns.

Along Urumet's jaw, a line of hoarfrost had vanished. Heat shimmered faintly
above its scales.

"Four today," the dragon said. "Two remaining."

The clerk hesitated. "The dye works are asking about a seventh. They say
they'll pay the grit rate."

"No."

"Double."

"Still no, but more offensively."

Urumet settled back on the shelf. "Six strokes, then I spend the night shedding
the heat. A seventh is bad for me, bad for the exchanger, and worst of all,
unpriced by any responsible schedule."

That last reason seemed to cheer it.

The clerk passed payment through a hatch: small coins, a paper twist of red
pepper sweets, and a freight ledger. Urumet counted the coins twice, popped a
sweet between its teeth, and opened the ledger to a page marked with northward
routes. Its pleasure looked real. I had come uphill half expecting chains, and
I still caught myself looking for them: at the shelf, at the arch, at the
narrow hatch.

"Do they let you leave?" I asked.

Yara made a noise that might have been a cough.

Urumet turned one pale eye on me, then licked pepper sugar from one claw.
"There is an ice shelf far north of every road on that ledger. I left it
because I wished to leave. I work here because I like precise jobs, small
luxuries, and customers who can be taught to fear amendments."

Its claw had come to rest on the northern page, and it stayed there after
Urumet had finished speaking.

The first grit struck the cave arch with a sound like dry rain.

***

The glasswind arrived all at once.

Daylight went copper. The mountain vanished behind its own dust. Wind drove
shards of pale grit against the stone hard enough to spark, and the city below
became a confusion of ropes, slamming shutters, and cloth snapping loose from
the gate.

Yara ran for the exchanger controls. The clerk threw a cover over the hatch,
and Urumet swept its freight ledger under one wing. I had just bent to catch a
blown receipt when something cracked above us.

A stone came through the outer screen.

It struck the regulator casing with a bright metallic snap. The bimetal tongue
spun past my boot in two pieces.

Yara closed the brine gate. The basin shuddered as its flow stopped.

"Nobody touch the horn," Urumet said.

The humor had gone out of its voice.

Yara opened the casing. The regulator's brass frame had buckled inward. One
half of the silver-backed tongue remained trapped beneath it, curled like a
dead leaf.

"Can't you just stop at four?" I asked. "Like before?"

"I stopped when the tongue closed," Urumet said. "Yara counts so the workers
know where we are. The tongue is what knows when the brine is done."

Yara traced the split with one finger. "Without it, a stroke can freeze the
feed throat before the brine clears. The pressure bursts the ribs. We lose the
batch, maybe the exchanger."

"The two strokes are contracted," Urumet said. "They are not contracted
through broken equipment."

Another impact rang from outside.

Somebody on the terraces below was shouting that the still field had gone
under the dunes. Yara sent the clerk down with orders to seal the cistern vents
and count every covered jar. When the clerk was gone, she stood very still
beside the ruined regulator, doing figures against her thumb.

"Four thousand two hundred litres in emergency reserve," she said. "A bit more
in household jars. The last two batches would add about eight hundred. That's
one short day while the storm passes and we dig out the stills."

"Without them?"

"Not enough. Not without cutting everyone below safety, and the clearing crews
get nothing."

"A replacement?"

"Twelve caravan-days away, once caravans move." She looked at my hands.

No. She looked at what I held.

I had drawn the sunwheel when the sky darkened, meaning to fix a last bearing
before the storm took the horizon, and had not put it away. Its needle lay
folded into its case, but the brass-and-silver center shone against my dusty
palm.

Yara did not reach for it.

"May I examine your wheel?" she asked.

I closed my fingers.

The instrument had carried me across five years of country. Every calibration
was mine. Every nick in its rim recalled a place where I had been thirsty,
lost, paid, or right when a caravan master had been expensively wrong. As long
as I carried it, I could leave any obligation behind by walking far enough.

"Why?"

"The heart's paired brass and silver. It bends with heat and cold, same as the
old tongue. I could cut a new one from it."

"And the wheel?"

"Would never take a true bearing again."

The wind screamed across the cave mouth.

I thought of twelve litres multiplied by five hundred closed doors. I thought
of the cold cup whose debt had irritated me more than dying alone would have.
The answer came out before fear could make it smaller.

"Take it."

Yara kept her hands at her sides. "At what price?"

"None."

"Then I'm not cutting it." She kept her eyes on my face. "Everything in that
casing has a line in the ledger. Yours will too."

"It's my wheel, and I'm giving it. Keep me out of your ledger."

Urumet's tail struck the stone once.

"Absolutely not."

I turned. "It's not yours."

"No. The next storm is mine." Urumet lowered its head until one pale eye was
level with mine. "This morning the dye works offered double for a seventh
stroke. Teach this city today that a glasswind makes things free, and see what
they offer me for a seventh in the next one."

"People need water."

"They will have it. Yara is trying to buy the thing that makes it, and you are
refusing to sell."

"I've agreed to give it. That should be enough."

"To loss," Urumet said. "Very grandly. You have not agreed to be paid."
